paragraphs.text: On the divine revelations given to Abraham

First discourse, for the first Sunday of the Annunciation: On the divine revelations given to Abraham. Response: The angel appeared to Mary and brought her good news: “From you the light of the world has dawned, my brothers.”

Remorse of mind stirred me to turn toward instruction and walk along the path of studying the Scriptures, from which I had strayed. My mind had been occupied with studying the divine Scriptures, and I loved the pure expression of their meanings. I contemplated their meanings, how delightful they were, and never ceased searching out the mysteries within them. My mind labored night and day over the mystery of their words, and I longed to understand the force of their precepts. My mind was occupied with this study, feeding on words, but the evil one captured me and hindered me from it without my noticing. My thoughts sank into weariness as though into sleep, and distractions came in like raiders and plundered my study. The passions in my limbs set snares of silence for me, and my impulses fell silent, abandoning the study with which they had been occupied.

Remorse over these things troubled me exceedingly, beyond measure, and as though startled out of sleep, I rose at the voice of instruction. Instruction itself called me and roused me from my weariness; as though enticing a child, it drew me toward its study. “How long will you sleep, you sluggard, you lover of sleep? Get up and listen to the voices of the books of the Spirit, which are full of wonder. “The revelations in the books of the Spirit are full of great wonder, and Moses bears witness, he who was the firstborn at the beginning of revelations. “He related how creation was established in the beginning, and he made known to us the origin and lineage of our race. “In his book we saw the road filled with humanity’s journey, and various accounts were arranged along it like milestones. “Like a foundation, he set down Adam, the beginning of humanity, and proceeded from one to another until he reached Abraham. “He counted twenty generations from Adam to Abram, and at Abraham he changed the pattern of his narrative’s progress. “At Abram he brought the course of his words to an end, yet without ending it, and began describing the various revelations given to him. “The Spirit of revelations revealed to him in the spirit, in a spiritual way; he revealed and made known the Creator [?] and his ministers. “Through Abraham, the lover of humanity fulfilled his will and promised him that through him the nations of the earth would be blessed. “The Creator called his beloved friend the father of nations and set the confession of his faith before those who beheld it. “To his faith he gave the treasure of the promise contained in his words, so that he might open a path toward his being for everyone who believes. “By his faith he declared that he knew the God of all, and righteousness arising from his free choice was credited to him. “His own free will was the guide along the course of his labors.

And he stirred himself and reached toward promises that were beyond him. Through promises, the Lover of the righteous bound his friend to himself, and his friend asked him how and when they would be fulfilled for him. “How shall I know that your loving words will be fulfilled for me, and that you will establish me in possession of the land, as you promised?” Through a sacrifice, the Lord showed his servant the purpose of his love, and through animals he revealed and explained to him what was to come. “Take three animals, Abram, to confirm my words: a three-year-old calf, a three-year-old ram, and a three-year-old goat. Take two birds in accordance with the promise, and set your mind at rest with a turtledove and a young pigeon. Divide the bodies and place the pieces opposite one another, and through their division portray an illustration of what is to come. Lay out the birds without dividing them into pieces, and through their wholeness direct your thoughts toward the fulfillment.” Through these things the good Lord taught him the ways of his will, so that he would direct his mind’s [?] toward things to come. The righteous man [?] his Lord’s [?] and prepared the sacrificial animals, dividing them into twelve portions. He laid out the turtledove and the young pigeon without dividing them, and waited for fire to descend and consume his sacrifices. He carefully guarded the sacrifice for his Lord and would not let birds eat any of his offerings. All day he guarded his sacrifice from harm, and at sunset he was found worthy of a divine revelation. He saw a furnace from which a flame rose, and a fiery torch at work consuming the divided portions of his sacrifices. Great wonder suddenly flooded his mind, and he marveled at how orderly the presentation of his sacrifice was. The Creator’s power gave him wisdom to understand the mystery of the revelations, so that he would know that the time of the things he had seen was far off. Now that the sequence of the written words is complete, let us turn back and recount the force of the meaning hidden in the words.

I heard the words that Moses recorded in the book he wrote, and words were covered with words as with a garment. A garment of words was spread over the words of the Spirit, and I wanted to know why they were concealed. Their lack of clarity made me investigate them, so that I might understand and make known to my friends the lessons of spiritual things. Come, listener, hear the meaning of Abram’s sacrifice. Look and consider how delightful the kinds of sacrifices are. Through the three animals he taught him to understand the enslavement of his descendants, and through their subjection he showed him the arrangement of the number of the tribes. The righteous man’s descendants were to be divided into twelve tribes, and he cut them up and divided them through the division of the three animals. For three generations his descendants were to be enslaved by foreigners, and through the mute animals he portrayed the toil of their oppression. In their youth they were to be harnessed under the yoke of slaves, and for this reason he commanded him to sacrifice a three-year-old animal. He was to honor the Creator’s name with sacrifices, and he made his sacrifice like a [?] before his descendants. Through the names of the animals, he outlined for him different forms of protection, and drew him a pattern so that he could clearly see his Lord’s purpose. He depicted for him the whole order of the Law through his sacrifices: the sheep, the bull, the turtledove, and the young pigeon. From the animals he taught him three [?], and from the birds two, specifying their names in full. Through the creatures that move on the earth, he showed him his suffering among foreigners; through the flying creatures, he revealed to him that he would depart from bondage. Through the turtledove he depicted for him life in the wilderness, and through the young pigeon, rest in the land of the Canaanites. Through the bird that loves deserted places, he instructed him about the wilderness outside; through the bird of settled places, about life among nations and cities. On this condition he did not divide them when they were sacrificed: the people were not to mingle with the nations, whether in the wilderness or in settled places. As Abram guarded the carcasses from harm, he contemplated his Lord’s help for his descendants. Through the bird he represented the harm inflicted by the Egyptians:

And he showed that the strength of his help was mightier than the Egyptians. He depicted and showed him that slavery among the Egyptians, and for this reason he placed each limb opposite its counterpart. They were unable to help one another. The Knower of all was considering this bondage. Through the three animals he represented three generations for him beforehand. At the close of the day he showed him the time when they would be delivered: after they had been worn down, they would then be freed from slavery. The deliverance of his offspring was being revealed through the acceptance of his sacrifice, as the fire consumed his sacrifices with pleasure. Through the fire he showed him how radiant the deliverance of his offspring would be: they would be freed from slavery in everyone’s sight. He depicted two events for him in the vision of the flame: the liberation of his people and the harsh punishments of the Egyptians. In the brightness of the fire he contemplated the acceptance of his sacrifices, and in the smoke, the severity of the punishment of those being scourged. With discernment he contemplated what had no discernment, as it brought joy to one side and distress to the other. It consumed Abram’s sacrifice with pleasure. It [?] passed from one to another as though it could discern. The righteous man himself was astonished and amazed at this discrimination: how discerning it was, and how carefully it kept to the order of its consuming! Moses said that astonishment fell upon Abraham because his mind was being led to gaze upon things far away. The things he saw through revelation were far away, and for this reason he was astonished and amazed. The voice of revelation instructed him in the hints of hidden things, so that he would know that the vision was certain, but its time was far away. “Know for certain,” the Lord was saying to his servant, “that your offspring will live as foreigners among strangers.”

“For four hundred years,” he said, “he will be a slave to slaves, and through subjection to his fellow servants he will learn my lordship. I myself established the designation of slavery among earthly people, and I placed the yoke of Shem, the freeborn, upon Ham the slave. With that slavery with which the righteous man yoked the contemptible Ham, I am yoking your own descendants, since they do not serve me. On this condition I established the designation of slavery on earth: to make my lordship known, that I am Lord of slaves and free people. Upon Shem I bestowed an honored name through the mouth of the righteous man, and in Ham I yoked everything created under the yoke of my lordship. Look, Abram my friend, I have marked out a clear road for you. Walk rightly through visible things toward hidden things. Look, I have shown you the slavery of your descendants and the freedom of your descendants, so that through both they may learn the proper order of slaves and free people. Through experience I teach them the different kinds of my commandments, so that they may know how to preserve the proper order between me and humanity. In the furnace of slavery I test the inclination of their soul, so that amid hardships they may seek ways to find relief. For three generations they will be slaves to the slave of slaves, and the fourth generation will cast off the yoke of their toil.” With these words the Lord reassured Abram his servant, and [?] showed him forms of revelation greater than this. Great is the [?] of the eyes, far beyond words, just as the light of the sun is brighter than darkness. For words were what was spoken at the time of the sacrifices, and they were a great distance from the events themselves. In this revelation a clear vision was being disclosed, bearing fresh good news of conception and birth. This revelation was disclosed at noon, at the time when the sunlight is very strong. The righteous man saw the vision with his bodily eyes, gazing through the light upon the Lord of light. The righteous man saw three forms of three men, and they walked in keeping with the forms in which they were clothed.

Abraham too looked at them as men, and did not know that this was a vision without bodily composition. The nature of spiritual beings is without bodily composition and without a body, and when they are sent to earthly people, they display a body. They did not truly acquire a body through a transformation; rather, they display in the air a form that has no bodily composition. At their creation they received great power from the hidden Power, and through that power they display the power of his divinity. His power accompanies his creatures as he wills, and he does this above all through the heavenly powers. He gave the spirit a form without making it composite, in a spirit of revelation, and came to Abram in three bodily forms. Suddenly he saw three men coming to meet him, and he rejoiced greatly and welcomed them as men. With great love he went out to meet them, as befitted their greatness, in the manner in which he used to welcome people into his dwelling. Righteous Abram received them as human beings, and afterward he realized that they were not human beings but spirits. Spiritual beings put on bodily form and came to the servant to announce new tidings to him. The Lord and his servants came to the servant who loved his Lord, clothed in the likeness of servants and of the Creator. The God of all was going to take on the likeness of a servant, and through Abraham he depicted beforehand what was to come. The liberator of humanity was to come from Abraham, and by what he did he prepared the way for what was to come. The Word, the Father's offspring, was going to take on humanity, and they would call [?] by his name: God, King, and Lord. He was going to make a visible body a temple for his love, and he came to Abram in that bodily likeness. He knew that Abram's descendants would find fault, so by his coming he cut off beforehand the pretext for their scheming. He knew that they would say, “How can God become a human being?”

And he demonstrated this in the form of a body, a body that brought joy to Abram. Abraham saw God in a human body. It was not a body, however, but something resembling a body. What the righteous man saw was not a body as it appeared to him, but a body resembling a body, though no body was there. Abraham too was uncertain about this: whether what appeared to him was indeed a body or was not a body. His faith made the righteous man righteous. He saw the hidden one in a visible body and believed that he existed. He saw the three clothed in one form, but left the two and spoke with the one as to the Lord. Righteous Abram called the righteous Lord “Lord” and asked him to come into his home, as his servant. The Creator also heard his plea, just as he entreated him, and entered with his servants to depict a bodily figure. Through a human body he was reconciling everyone with his majesty. He took two spiritual beings with him and came to his servant. He now put an end to that conflict in Paradise and reconciled the heavenly beings with those on earth. He brought everyone together with him to Abraham's house and seated them at supper with his majesty. He invited heaven and earth and called them to Abraham's house to show them the greatness of his love for humanity. He revealed the greatness of his love to spiritual and bodily beings by entering with his servants to visit a member of his household. In a human home he dismantled the barrier of wrath between himself and humanity, and he called the heavenly beings as witnesses to humanity's reconciliation. Through humanity's reconciliation, they too became friends of humanity, and they rejoiced that they and humanity had come to share one equality. The Creator [?] one equality for everyone together.

And he gave them rest at the evening meal that Abram [?]. He entered with his own companions to visit his own, hidden from everyone; and heaven and earth were astonished at the wonder surrounding him. Those who could speak and those who were silent marveled, aloud and in silence, when they saw that the one reclining on earth had no limit. Oh, that spiritual and bodily reclining at table, where the Lord and his servants reclined together on equal terms! Oh, the meal prepared in Abraham’s house! It was eaten, yet was not consumed by those who ate it. Oh, how great was the feast that the righteous man prepared! His food was sufficient for heavenly and earthly beings. Heaven and earth reclined together in the righteous man’s house: the God of all, who is without limit, and his own creatures, who have limits. He revealed to Abram the banquet that takes place on high, through that meal at which he reclined with spiritual beings. In Abram’s son he was to give definite expression to his loving purpose; and he revealed this through the great love he showed Abram. He showed the righteous man his great love when he came to visit him, and through things close at hand he drew for him a pattern of distant things. At the end of time, everyone will be with everyone in love; and he showed this through his love for Abram, the friend of love. The house of the father of nations became a second heaven, and earthly and heavenly beings dwelt in it. Something new, which had never happened before, suddenly happened in Abraham’s house; and the spiritual beings marveled at its immense wonder.

The heavenly powers marveled at its immense wonder: “What is this that the Hidden One has done among earthly beings? “Since the day we came into being, we have never seen anything like what has happened, nor have we heard that the Eternal One showed himself to his servants. “Look, up to now it has been a little less than [?] thousand years, and he has not disclosed to us the hidden greatness of his love.” For humanity’s sake, the lover of humanity revealed his love to us; and he showed this toward Abraham more than toward anyone else. From among them all he chose two spiritual beings for his visit, and they came to Abram in the visible likeness of men. Abraham, too, received them as men, and paid honor to their visible appearance. He prepared and set out fine flour, a calf, milk, and butter, for he thought these fitting expressions of love. The Creator, too, lovingly accepted his loving intention, knowing that this would benefit earthly beings. Oh, that Power whom heaven and earth cannot contain! For humanity’s sake he limited himself while remaining unlimited. For humanity’s sake he came to a man whose name was Abram [?]; and he who is foreign to food and drink ate and drank. The Word was destined to take from him one of humankind, and through his hands to accomplish what was to happen at the end of time. He was making that human being one with his love, and imprinted human things in his divinity. That man made use of food and drink, and he first ate so that by eating he might confirm that he had a body. The son of Abraham was formed with a body and soul, and [?] beside his father, clothed in the various bodily members. Abraham, too, was examining his bodily nature, wondering whether what he saw really was a body or not. Perhaps, in keeping with the immaturity of that time, he thought that spiritual beings too ordinarily lived on human food. Perhaps he also thought this as a human being; and for love of him, he did this, although he did not do it. For he did not do it, nor is it done—not in any way whatsoever,

because the self-existent Being is exalted above bodily forms. The Judge has none of the natural properties of earthly beings. He was not, and is not, confined within the work of his hands. He has no boundary that confines him within its limits, for he is outside everything and beyond everything, and everything is on this side of him. In love he reveals the hiddenness of his love to the one who loves his love, so that he may stir up zeal in those who love his love to gaze upon him. In Abram he set up the sign of his love before those who see, so that they might see the hidden through the visible, although they do not see. Abraham too saw him in love, although he did not see him; and his own voice testifies that no human being can see him and live. Abram did not see the one hidden from everyone, children of Abraham! Take care not to go astray and lead others astray on account of Abram. Abram was righteous, and his love was truly genuine. Yes, he truly saw forms that were not made up of parts. Without composition, he saw the sight that cannot be grasped; and without limit, he gazed upon the likeness that cannot be likened to anything. It is the custom of the God of all to act in this way, because passing creatures cannot bear to see his divinity. In this form he revealed himself for twenty generations, and in the tenth he decreed a threat and destroyed everything. With Noah he began to deal peaceably with humanity, and once again he counted ten generations, up to Abram [?]. With Abram he completed twenty generations of humankind and began to reveal forms of gentleness and kindness. In a gentle appearance he revealed his will to the lover of his love, and kindly spoke with him according to his understanding. In his conversation with him, the threats of the sentence of judgment ceased: the transgression of the commandment, the destruction by water, and the division of speech. To him alone he made a promise that would not prove false: that through his offspring the nations would return to the true worship of God. With this thought you brought him down to enter his presence. He entered, although he did not enter, because his nature does not enter into anything. The nature of his being is not confined within anything that exists, since there is no limit to his continuance, which has no beginning. Without beginning and [?] end, he exists and exists. However much anyone may say, his words fall short.

By his word, I too said what I have said, yet my mind was not able to grasp the full extent of what I said. I said that it is written that the Creator entered Abraham’s house—not as one confined within limits, but in an appearance. Abram, a man, saw God in the appearance of a man, and welcomed him into his house as a man who could be seen. I said that he welcomed him as a man, not as a man by nature. [?] The divine nature cannot be seen by the eye. It was not his nature that Abraham saw in the appearance he beheld, but a mystery being expressed through the body that would come from him. Through the body that would come from him, he was turning everyone toward knowledge of himself, and he announced to him beforehand the good news filled with life for humanity. Humanity’s life was hidden from everyone in the God of all, and through Abraham he revealed it before the eyes of all creatures. All creation was gazing at the vision of Abraham [?], and could not get enough of seeing the sight that cannot be seen. Speaking and speechless creatures alike marveled, aloud and in silence: “What is this—that the world is gathered into Abram’s house?” Rational beings marveled still more at this wonder, because they possess minds capable of carefully examining things that are not revealed. It was them that the Maker of all allowed to share in the mystery of his revelation, because they could be trusted to keep the secret between him and them. For it was a mystery concealed from all creatures, and he revealed it to the two rational orders of beings: angels and human beings. He revealed his will to two angels and one human being, and showed them, through a mystery, the secret of his hiddenness. The mystery of his love was to be revealed through a human being, and for this reason he took spiritual beings with him and entered Abram’s presence. For that entrance was a wonder, and a very astonishing one. Although it was visible, it was not clear to those who saw it. Neither did the spiritual beings understand the force of its meaning, nor did Abraham know what it was or whom it concerned. They were gazing only at its appearance, in a human way, and were unable to approach its meaning. The hidden will was teaching them, the servants of the Hidden One, not to exhaust themselves searching into the hidden reality that cannot be grasped.

By the power of his will they gazed without ever having enough, and they did not cease pursuing their inquiry about him. The birth pangs of love pressed upon the mind within them: when would the hidden sign bring forth the power of its hidden meaning? The angels and Abram longed to understand the words, and waited to see something that would answer their desire. Both sides were wearied by this longing: “What is this—that he has limited himself without being limited, and has entered his house in an appearance that cannot be seen?” Why did he agree to have every kind of hospitality prepared for him, when the nature of his being does not admit bodily things? Look: by his power he gives life even to our nature without food. How he did this thing that he did is altogether a wonder. The statement Moses made is full of great wonder: that the Lord of creation was being fed by his creatures. An ineffable saying, a saying spoken by Bar Hebraeus: the Being who is above all reclined on earth with his creation. Abraham set visible kinds of food before the Invisible One. And who would not marvel that food enters one who has no bodily composition? The onlookers, too, observed with their senses and perceptions; yet although they saw, they did not truly see. What happened in Abram’s house did not happen in actual reality, but in a mystery that speakers cannot express. The nature of the divine Being cannot be expressed by our words. Therefore, what was described did not happen just as it was described. For the words Moses wrote concerned things without bodily composition. They were composed, yet they were not composed bodily. It was not a body that Abram refreshed with food and drink, but an appearance that took shape without a body. It was not a body that bodily hands grasped, but a spirit whose power is subtler than that of spirits. The kinds of food were not being swallowed through the senses.

Rather, the material food was disappearing into the air. For it was divine power that accomplished these things—the power for which it is easy to fashion everything out of nothing. He comforted Abram through what he did in Abram’s house, so that through deeds he might fulfill for him the promise of his words. He promised him the return of the nations through his offspring [?], and showed himself to him as fully—as fully as a human being can bear to see. The creature could not bear to see his Maker, and for this reason he fashioned likenesses before his eyes. What Abram saw with bodily eyes were likenesses—not exact likenesses, but a resemblance. For everything that happened in that revelation was a resemblance: a human appearance, human speech, and human food. It was the God of all who wisely did this, as his power is accustomed to act in every generation. He came through Abraham to visit the creation he had made, and showed him his love in the same form in which he had shown it to Adam. He showed Adam great love within Paradise. But when Adam forgot his love, he died through sin, and he and his children came under condemnation. He came to Abraham’s house to pay Adam’s debt, and clothed himself in the likeness of that form from the land of Eden. The transgression of the commandment was being annulled through that meal, and the undoing of death was being revealed in Isaac’s conception. Two died in Eden by eating the fruit, Eve and Adam; and on the day of the revelation he revived [?] two, Sarah and Abram. For Sarah and Abram were dead through the barrenness of their bodies, like that death of Eve and Adam through eating the fruit. Abraham heard the good news of the resurrection of all in that utterance: “Sarah your wife will have a child.” The same voice that cried out to Adam, “You will become dust,” called to Abram, “Look, I am bringing your dead body back to life.” The whole human race came to life in Abraham,

because through his offspring the nations return to the Creator. The return of the nations was being revealed in Abram’s vision, along with the great peace between the Creator and his creatures. Great peace filled the house of the father of all, and heaven and earth were feasting on the day of his banquet. The Lord of creation reclined at the head of his armies, and the assemblies on high were at peace with those on earth. Everyone together was enjoying the wedding feast of love, and created beings were praising the Maker’s name. “Glorious is the Creator!” the spiritual beings cried out in Abraham’s house, “for he has shown his love and reconciled us with himself, and us with everyone.” “Worthy of praise is he within whose bounds the worlds are contained, for he humbled himself and reclined with us at the table. Heaven and earth owe him a single thanksgiving, for he spoke words of peace with us, though we had not sought him. Oh, how great a new thing the Lord of creation has done! Though he is in everything, he confined himself to one place. Oh, that mighty one who holds everything by his powerful command, who showed himself like a poor man before what he had fashioned! Oh, that treasury whose gifts sustain the worlds, who asked a member of his household for alms like a beggar!” Abram offered alms of love to the Maker of all, and he repaid him with the reward of a child who gives life to humanity. Humanity’s life was hidden in Isaac, Abram’s child, and was passed from one to another like a pledge. Generation after generation handed on Abram’s pledge, until it reached the generation of the source of our life. The source of life was to appear from our humanity, and he announced him beforehand through the revelation he showed Abram. This is the reason for the whole account we have related, and in it the earlier and later things are bound together. This is the limit within which worlds and generations are bounded, and within him the whole structure of the heights and depths is contained.

Paul testifies that everything is contained in the Law, and the Law itself has its fulfillment in Christ, who brings everything to fulfillment. It was Christ who was being spoken of in Abraham’s house, and in a symbol of his peace the Lord mingled with his creatures. This very peace, which came about at the end through one human being, he depicted beforehand in that supper at Abraham’s house. That undying delight which takes place on high is what the Lord and his servants celebrated among those on earth. In a harbor of peace the Hidden One gives everyone a place to rest together, and through what happened he gave a pledge of what is to come. Look, all these things came from the Lord of all through Abraham. Come, let us carefully examine the purpose within them. Look, the hidden Being has opened a road for us to travel to meet him. Come, let us learn wisely to observe the order of hidden things. See, he has revealed and shown us the greatness of his love through a human being. Come, let us strive to bind our love to his will. See, he has chosen to call us to delight in his glorious gifts, and he gave us an example in the food he ate in Abraham’s house. Abram prepared bodily food for the bodiless one, and he said that he ate, although he did not eat, because of his love. That he did not eat is surely attested for us by speaking and speechless beings, since they acknowledge that the hidden nature is without composition. He did not reveal his nature in his appearance to his servant. He instructed his servant to direct himself toward the purpose of his love. He called Abraham a good friend because of his love, and taught him to observe the proper order of love toward his Creator. He tested the upright man in many ways, although he knew him, so that coming generations would know the various ways he tested him. He promised him a child, gave him a child, and confirmed his words. Then he turned and asked for him as a sacrifice, a fragrance pleasing to his will. “I desire you to offer me a sacrifice, Abram my friend. Satisfy my will by sacrificing your son, because you love me. “Through testing I have learned your love: you are a good friend, and the comfort of your friends pleases you far more than your own. “The food of your love has pleased me greatly, more than anyone else’s, as I experienced at that feast in your house.

“At that feast I openly revealed my kindness before the spiritual beings. Now, between you and me, I want you to satisfy my will. “A great mystery has been hidden within me from eternity, together with my divinity, and I am ready now to reveal it privately to you in your love. “Something has been determined by me from the beginning that has no beginning, and I am eager to show it to you as to a friend. “My mind is ready to bring forth a new creation a second time, and I am calling you to share in its formation. “Through a human being I will carry out my hidden will, and I will make him the one mediator between myself and humanity. “Through his mediation I will show my love before all creatures, just as I showed it in that original formation and [?]. “In the human image I disclosed my hidden being at the beginning, when I created: that I exist, and that I am three persons in one nature. “After this nature, which was not brought into being by a craftsman, I named the human image when I formed it. “For his sake I created everything hidden and visible, and I appointed him steward over the things I formed. “Through him, now too, I will bring my love to fulfillment in deeds, and renew the creation that has grown old through mortality. “Death ruined the beauty of what I formed because of humanity, and through a human being I will renew everything together with humanity. “To [?] the [?], I will carry out what I have said, so that they may not boast that they have indeed defeated me through Adam’s errors. “Through Adam himself, that is, I will show them the authority of my lordship, and through the condemned man I will humble them, showing how low they are. “They condemned Adam to death, the image that portrayed my hidden being, and through death I will undo the yoke of death.” Sin made death a death for mortals, and through a mortal I am wiping it away from mortals. Through the evil one's counsel, sin and death gained authority, and I do not want my servants to be someone else's slaves. All beings belong to me, those who can speak and those who cannot.

I do not neglect the creation my hands have made. From nothing I created everything as I pleased, and now through something I am renewing it so that it will never perish again. With a human being I completed the creation that came into being in the beginning, and through a human being I am renewing everything together with humanity. From you, Abram, I am choosing this human being, because of the love you have shown me beyond all who have lived. I call you the father of people who have lived and who are yet to live, because you loved me and hated the errors of Chaldean religion. I am making your son lord and king over my creatures, so that everyone may know that the name I gave you is true and distinguished. I called you the father of nations, Abram, among those on earth, and through the offspring who comes from you I am confirming your name in deeds. In the offspring who comes from you I am bringing my whole purpose to completion, and in him, as in a temple, I am making those who can speak and those who cannot dwell. I am making your offspring a temple for my kingship, Abram, and in him I receive loving worship—love—from every creature. In him the creation that I created from nothing worships me, and I give him the honored name of my divinity. The one who possesses the voice spoke these things with Abraham, not openly but in an inexpressible mystery. The hidden mystery cannot be expressed by the mouths of speakers, yet, difficult though these things are, he spoke them with Abraham. The Hidden One, who cannot be expressed, spoke with Abraham and taught him the manner in which he should offer him his son as a sacrifice. I ask you for a sacrifice of love, my friend. Offer it to me as the order of love requires. I am going to take a pledge of peace from his offspring. Prepare the way for the true sacrifice through the symbolic sacrifice. I know that the offspring who comes from you is fault-finding, and they will find fault with me when I fulfill my purpose in your son. Through a bloodless sacrifice I am rebuking their contentiousness,

so that they will not find fault when the true sacrifice is performed. Take, then, your son Isaac, your offspring whom you love, and make him a burnt offering to me on the mountain that I will tell you. Oh, that voice! How dear it was, and how difficult! It was spoken, yet could not be expressed as it truly was. It was dear in love, in keeping with the divine command, yet very difficult for the weakness of human nature. The Lord of nature strengthened the one who was weak by nature, to show that he could constrain his nature through love [?] for his Lord. Abraham’s Lord made Abram a furnace of testing, and in him human weakness was tested and gained strength. The mortal man’s mind gained great strength, and although he was [?], in his mind he was immortal. O mortal man who forgot his mortal nature, whose will trampled down the harsh stings of mortality! O man subject to suffering, whose passions were harnessed beneath his mind! He made them run in the arena of his capacity to suffer. O steadfast man who mounted like a charioteer and subdued the passions of his body and the impulses of his soul! O mind entirely harnessed to hardships, which cast off the weight of its passions as though it were not harnessed! O how he restrained his inclination with a bridle of silence! It grew still and quiet, ceasing its headlong, troubled course. Did his mind not ponder, as it was accustomed to do: “What is this new thing that the God of all has asked of me?” Did the impulses of his soul not give rise to various thoughts: “When has anyone offered another human being as a sacrifice to the Hidden One?” A hidden power strengthened the understanding of this man of understanding, and he did not weaken in the struggle with the passions of body and soul. The sweetness of his loving devotion to his Lord compelled the righteous man and took the bitterness from the gall—the gall with which natural affections are mingled. O Abram, you good friend of faith!

You forgot the cherished attachments that nature possesses. Rightly, then, did he who chose you from all the nations choose you and make you the head of everyone who imitates your loving devotion. In love for his Lord, the fervent man fulfilled his Lord’s will and took his son to go to the place that had been shown to him. The voice commanded him to offer [?] his sacrifice in a distant place, so that he might be tested in the sight of those on earth and those in heaven. Before the eyes of all creatures, he was displaying his soul’s endurance: how steadfast he was, never weakening under the hardship of his journey. For three days he traveled, keeping silent and free from doubt, and he did not reveal the secret of his Lord’s will to his household. He concealed from everyone the secret between himself and his Lord. Not even to Sarah did he reveal the preparation in his mind. He kept his Lord’s secrets concealed between himself and his Lord, so that the truth of his love for the Lord who chose him might be firmly, firmly established. His Lord’s command was more precious to him than anything, and he prepared his own will in accordance with his Lord’s will. The impulses of his soul were bound to this will, and he waited to see what would happen at the end of his journey. The three days of his journey were completed. He raised his eyes, saw the place, and rejoiced at the sight of it. To his bodily eyes, God showed the place where his son was to be sacrificed, and to his mind he revealed the foreshadowing of what was to come. The true sacrifice was destined to take place where the symbolic sacrifice occurred. He showed him the place so that the symbol would correspond to the reality. In this place Christ was destined to become a sacrifice, and he revealed him beforehand through a symbolic sacrifice, before the events took place. For Isaac’s sacrifice was a symbol of Christ’s, and it was entirely fitting that sacrifice should resemble sacrifice. The Creator’s power fashioned its likeness according to his loving will, so that those who heard these words would not doubt the events. With this purpose the three-day journey took place, so that sacrifice might bear witness to sacrifice, and the pattern to the reality.

Abraham too directed his mind toward this purpose, and his soul settled upon the place of sacrifice that his Lord had shown him. At the place of sacrifice he fulfilled his own will and his Lord’s will. He built an altar, arranged the wood, and bound his son. He drew the knife, and with the knife he drew forth his resolve. But a voice stopped him, telling him to hold back his hand from his beloved. “Abram, Abram!” the spiritual being called to the bodily man. “Hold back your hand, and refrain from killing your son as a [?]. “Refrain from the sacrifice of human blood that I asked of you. Take and offer me instead the blood of a speechless creature in place of one who speaks. “I do not seek human blood at this time, because it cannot blot out the debtors’ bond with its blood. “Humanity’s debt is not paid with human blood until a perfect man comes forth from humanity. “I know the time suited to perfection, and I am not mistaken about when a human being will redeem humanity. “I have revealed humanity’s redemption to you, Abram, through the occasion of the sacrifice, so that everyone may know to await the time of humanity’s redemption. “Through this event involving you, I have opened a road toward that which is [?], so that people may travel toward the promised hope of death’s abolition. “For this reason I arranged these circumstances and asked for a sacrifice: to reveal to humanity my hidden will toward humanity. “Through you, Abraham, I have revealed to created beings my will concerning all. Listen, become wise, and make others wise through your wisdom. “But do not think that I rejected your sacrifice as imperfect. See, I have granted you the means to carry out my will through the sacrifice of a lamb. “I give you a mute lamb in place of one who speaks, and through the speechless creature I teach you the kinds of sacrifices. “I ask you to offer me three sacrifices: two that speak and one [?], the pattern and the reality. “I have accepted Isaac’s death symbolically in place of the reality, and in place of Isaac, the speechless blood of the quiet lamb. “See, I have restrained you so that the appointed order of the end of the ages may be preserved. Fulfill your desire with the sacrifice appropriate to this time, and await the time.” Through a revelation of the Spirit, he signaled to him to look at the top of the tree.

And suddenly he saw a lamb hanging there, symbolically crucified. In the wonder that was taking place for Abram, the forms of its likenesses were unlike all other likenesses. All sheep graze on the earth, being earthly creatures, but Abram’s sheep was feeding at the top of a tree. At the top of the tree hung the lamb that had appeared to him, and instead of nails, the branches of the tree were fixed in its body. The foreshadowing of the Truth had mounted the cross in the likeness of the Truth, and its whole body was held fast, as though for death. Death on the wood was destined to [?] undo death, and he hung the lamb at the top of the tree to proclaim his death. Otherwise, let us ask why the lamb was in the tree, and who hung it there, contrary to the usual order of dumb animals. Dumb creatures without a soul are accustomed to move about on the ground. What, then, was this—that it alone was hanging in the tree? It is clear that it did not bind itself to the tree, and it is not true that someone else bound it and hung it there. Truth bears witness, and its testimony cannot be false: a hidden command hung it in the tree as a symbol of the Truth. He who loves our race showed us beforehand—showed us—the mystery of our Savior, so that when he saves us, we may not wonder how he saved us. The descendants of Adam were to be saved through the death of a human being, and he depicted beforehand the mystery of our salvation in the death of the lamb. John too called the Savior of our race a lamb, because he was destined to save our lives through the sacrifice of his death. The sheep that saved Isaac’s life was one of the sheep, and the man who saved humanity through his death was one of humanity. The silent creature that rescued Isaac traced out the path of his death. This is what he meant when he said, “Abraham saw me and rejoiced in the day of my death.” Abraham saw the day of his death—not that he actually saw it, but that through revelation he saw the day of his death. His death was hidden in the death of the lamb that Abraham sacrificed, and the life of every human being was hidden in the deliverance brought by its sacrifice. If someone says that the discourse I have delivered is merely a string of words, let him then offer his own account, and I will accept it. Let him show me from the Scriptures the force of the meaning of his words.

Then I will concede to him that he was right to rebuke me as a fool. No, my fellow human being, the Scriptures were not written foolishly, nor did I invent out of my own mind the meaning and power within them. My thoughts have inclined toward the very purpose of the Scriptures, and from reading them I learned to speak about their meaning. I did not establish my words through a pattern of things that are untrue, but through mysteries that closely correspond to the revealed Truth. The Truth bears witness that my discourse has not strayed from the Truth, and that I have not exchanged the truth of his words for words of falsehood. From the Truth himself I learned to deliver a discourse about him, and I submitted my mind to his instruction as to a teacher. I am a disciple of the books of the Spirit, which the Spirit wrote, and I am certain that my mind has not strayed from the Scriptures. Trusting in the power within them, I followed them, and through their help I obtained the help I needed to speak. The words within them have been my study throughout my life, and I have no desire to stop and neglect attending to them. Through experience I learned what studying them is like, and how beneficial it is to engage with the words of their interpretations. I received good material from them with which to trade, and I do not cease trying to repay their kindness, even if only with words. I am eager to repay with words the kindness of those who have taught me wisdom, lest I be guilty like a debtor who borrows and cheats his lender. I am a debtor, and I do not deny the obligation of my debts. I struggle to repay with words in place of deeds. I saw how laborious the words of the books are to read, and I wanted to know the reason for this labor.

A desire stirred me to labor over them with the effort they require, and to learn thoroughly the force of the meaning within them. The force of their meaning attracted me to become their companion and to occupy my life with the good study that gives life. The power of the Spirit expressed them through a mouth of flesh, so that people of flesh might meditate on spiritual things. This study attracted even me, weak in thought, and I occupied my mind with words filled with the study of words. In the book of Moses I saw this subject treated abundantly, urging anyone who studied it to study it again. The account of the righteous was stored within it as in a treasury, and more abundant than all the others was the account of Abram. The account of Abram awakened in me a desire for this subject, and from his story I called upon understanding to seek out hidden things. I began to reflect on hidden things and investigate why these words are hidden from those who speak. Why are they not clear, as the power within them is manifest? Then perhaps the mind would run to uncover what is not revealed. If the force of their meaning were as easy as reading them, it would be easy for everyone to love the study of excellent things. The one who knows everything did what he did for our benefit: he concealed the power of the Spirit’s words in obscurity. He honored and exalted the teaching itself before its students, so that fleshly eyes would not despise it because it was readily apparent. Everything openly displayed is held cheap by bodily sight, while everything hidden from those who look is precious and beloved. This is the reason spiritual words are hidden, and through their hiddenness the power that expressed them is to be exalted. The power of the Spirit expressed them through the mouths of bodily beings, and for this reason their meanings are not easy to hear. It is very difficult for a tongue of flesh to [?] in the Spirit, just as the nature of mortals is foreign to immortals. The nature of mortals was destined to become immortal, and he chose [?] Abram and made him the beginning of a new life. Through Abraham’s son, all your people, all of them, were to be renewed, and in Abraham himself he depicted a pattern of what would happen through his son. With this expectation Abraham too was longing:

To see in his son a vision of humanity’s renewal. Abraham saw the renewal of humanity in the sacrifice of his son, who died without dying and portrayed death and life. He was counted as dead from the moment his father bound him, and he came to life symbolically by the will of the God of all. It pleased the God of all, and he wanted him to be a sacrifice; therefore he accepted his sacrifice as though it had taken place. The one who knows everything did not do this out of a change of mind, asking for a sacrifice and then turning back and saying, “I do not want it.” It was not through a test that he learned of Abram’s love, as it is written; nor did he wish to carry it through to completion when he asked him for a sacrifice. He knew Abraham and everyone before anything existed, and among created things there is nothing that has existed or will exist that he does not know. The things he made were [?] within his bounds, while he is within everything and outside everything, without limit. Let no brother think ignorantly that he asked Abraham for the sacrifice of his son because he did not know. He did not himself learn of the righteous man’s love, as people suppose; he taught people to acquire love like Abraham’s. Everything he did concerning Abraham served humanity, and for humanity’s sake he chose him from among people and called him his friend. He showed humanity the mystery of the renewal that will take place at the end, so that they would ponder what is to come and when it would happen. He showed what was to come through the death of Abraham’s son: that through the death of one human being, humanity would live. People die two deaths and come to life twice: once in symbolic baptism and once in reality. Isaac died symbolically and came to life symbolically, portraying for us the death of baptism and the life that comes from it. Our Savior died a real death on the summit of Golgotha, and he truly came to life with real life and gave life to all. We have therefore died both symbolically and in reality, and we are destined to live a real life without decay. “Christ,” it says, “rose from the dead and dies no more.”

Therefore the whole of human nature rose with the one who shares its nature. The nature inherited from Adam is one in all who belong to Adam, and if a part of it has risen, the whole of it has risen. “He raised us up with him to the place where he ascended,” Paul said. And if this is true, our whole nature ascends there. “Our old self,” it says, “was crucified with him.” See, we died with him, came to life with him, and he made us reign with him. With him in death, with him in life, and with him in glory—who, then, can separate us from fellowship with him? If God is for us, as it is written, who can hinder the salvation of our lives? The Creator himself [?] by his own self to his friend Abram: “Through you all nations will be blessed, through my name that is upon them.” See, he fulfilled his words to Abram through the deeds themselves, and people became children of Abraham, as he had promised. All the nations were bound to this hope, waiting for the time when they would become Abraham’s children. The children took pride in Abraham’s lineage and did not want the nations to become relatives of his descendants. The One who sees everything saw the envy in this thinking and rebuked them by changing Abram’s name. Abram was called the father of one people only. After a time, he called him Abraham, the father of nations. His father’s original name was lowly and insignificant to him, and for this reason he changed the name of his friend. The Creator called the son of the Chaldeans by the Creator’s name, because he was going to raise his offspring to the height of his name. He was going to give an honored name to Abraham’s son, and he honored Abraham’s name beforehand with the name of the one who was to come. For the sake of his offspring, Abram’s Lord honored Abram, so that he would know that the blessing was not his own. The nations of the earth were not blessed through him and his children until one of his descendants [?] and blessed humanity.

One of his descendants became the firstfruits whom he chose from among all, and offered himself as a pure sacrifice and reconciled all. Through his death, Abraham’s son reconciled all with all, and gained a [?] that cannot be compared with those of the past. Through his death he made up for the deficiency of his fellow human beings. For this reason he became greater than all, and everyone worshiped him. Together with the Creator, he receives the worship of all from everyone. This is the wonder: everyone worships him together with the divine Being. The new thing that happened among earthly beings is full of wonder: their nature became an object of worship together with the divine Being. Look, our nature has gained an exalted rank beside the one who gave it existence. Come, let us strive to give thanks to the one who raised us up. Look, one of us has become a victor who conquered and gave victory. Let us ask him to help us in the struggle against the passions. Look, we have been redeemed through the true death of one of our race. Let us not turn back and die in sin after he has shown us mercy. Look, we have been purchased with pure blood from our own humanity. Let us not be sold into the evil slavery from which he rescued us. Look, the God of all has [?] and accepted one from among us all. Let us no longer be distracted by bodily desires. Look, we have received the new good news that the dead will live. Let us turn our minds toward that order of things that cannot perish. Look, a smooth road has been opened to the heights above. Through our conduct, let us grow wings with which to fly. Look, we are invited to the divine King’s wedding feast. Let us prepare clothes worthy of the name of that banquet. Look, we are called children of the inheritance, heirs of everything. Let us bind our love to the love of the name of the head of our inheritance. Look, he has ascended and reigns above rulers and authorities. Let us rejoice and be glad that our race has been raised above everything. Look, our lowly nature is glorified together with the one who chose it. Let us ourselves join in thanksgiving, if it is glorified. See, the words spoken at our formation have been fulfilled: we have become an image worshiped together with our Creator. See, heaven and earth bow down to us in that man. Let us give thanks to him who raised us above everything. Let our hearts believe and our mouths confess without doubt that the hidden Will clothed himself in our nature and renewed us in ourselves.

With soul and body, with our whole being, let us sing praise to him who made us worthy to praise his majestic name. Let us occupy our souls with these things without growing weary, and give our inclinations no room to wander in delusion. The distraction of earthly desires is delusion. Let us not indulge our desires, lest we be condemned with the guilty. The night of bodily desires has passed, and the light of a way of life that does not die has dawned. Let us show ourselves to the eyes of those watching as people in the light, so that they may join us in thanking him in whose light we have seen light. The manifestation of our Lord, who shone forth on earth, is a great light. It drove the error of idolatry away from earth’s inhabitants. Come, inhabitants of earth, look and contemplate true worship, whose light is brighter than the luminary that shines on earth. Our Lord also called his proclamation light and fire, and through it earthly and heavenly beings were enlightened. See, the world has been illuminated by the great light of the Creator’s name. Let us remain in his light, so that we may not be tormented in the outer darkness.
On the divine revelations given to the fathers and prophets.

Second discourse. For the second Sunday of the Annunciation. On the divine revelations given to the fathers and prophets. Response: Blessed is he who teaches us, disciplines us, and makes us his own, my brothers.

The Creator drew the image of his revelations in the human mind, and people began to draw spiritual images. He placed the medicine of life in a nature full of mortality, and they acquired immortal life in their minds. In their minds he spoke with these bodily beings and taught them to meditate on his hidden things. Spiritually he showed them the ways of his will, so that through visible things they might see [?]. From the beginning he revealed hidden things to their nature and gave them wisdom to understand the power of his greatness. He revealed the power of his greatness in the formation of Adam’s dust and taught him to describe how he had been formed and put together. The child of dust was put together from dust, and after he had been put together, he breathed a spiritual soul into him. He spoke within his soul about the formation of the rib taken from him, and he began to say that the portion belonging to Eve came from him. Through the spirit of revelation he learned this lesson. It was not within his own power to explain a cause hidden from him. The mystery of the deliverance of his body and soul was hidden from him, and after he had been formed, he acquired the understanding to perceive his own being. With the eye of the spirit he looked at his nature and how it was constituted, and he praised and magnified the one who formed him and everything. Here is the beginning of the work of the spirit of revelation, when the Lord began to reveal his love to earthly beings.

To teach them how dearly he loves the human race. He showed humanity his loving affection through his revelations; and although he is hidden, he spoke with humanity about the ways of his hiddenness. A power from him spoke with the hidden mind within them, and they began to speak spiritually, in his likeness. He spoke with them in two ways, bodily and spiritually, since their nature is both bodily and spiritual. He appeared in bodily form to Abram’s household, and in his choice of words they regarded him as they would a human being. In bodily fashion he rebuked Adam for his wrongdoing, and Adam heard his footsteps within Paradise like the sound of a human being. In their own language he engaged them in conversation with him, and taught them to offer sacrifices of love. He taught them to offer him sacrifices of love, so that through the sacrifices he might teach them that he knows everything. Through sacrifices he examined the hidden inclination of their minds, and rebuked Cain because his soul was not pure within. With an audible voice he spoke to him whose soul was foul: “I do not accept a sacrifice that is not clean of stains.” Wicked Cain turned the rebuke into an occasion for evil, and instead of sorrow and repentance of soul, he brought forth murder. The murderer killed and concealed the blood of his brother, whom he envied; and a voice called to him in bodily fashion: “Where is Abel?” In bodily fashion he demanded an accounting for the bodily blood, and showed that it has a time to return to life. Two recompenses could be heard in the blood that spoke: the shame of the demons and the joy of the heavenly hosts. In this [?], he gave a voice to what had no voice, to make known that human nature belongs to him and that he created it. The Good One taught human nature wisdom throughout all generations, and fashioned revelations in every form for their instruction. For their sake he removed Enoch and kept him alive, to lessen for them that threat pronounced in Paradise. Here he stirred their minds concerning the resurrection, and portrayed in one human being a demonstration that they would not perish. The hope of humanity’s renewal also filled Lamech with wonder, and he revealed and displayed it in the peace that would come through the child born to him.

Through Noah the harsh frost of the floodwaters was brought to an end, and the curses pronounced in Paradise were also being undone. With an audible voice he made them hear the announcement of their destruction, but they scorned and made light of that voice which warned them. Noah alone listened to the voice and understood its meaning; he believed and affirmed that its threats would be fulfilled in every way. The righteous man, son of a righteous man, feared his threats, and built a house that sheltered the remnant of the world. A small remnant remained of the speechless creatures and of those endowed with speech, and he brought them over to a beautiful and peaceful land. With a bodily voice he instructed Noah about these things: how they were to enter the ark and how they were to leave it. After some time, he spoke with him through this same voice and taught him the rules for eating the flesh of animals. He too blessed his own offspring with a tangible voice and yoked the two in subjection to the noble Seth. He showed that hope would dawn for human nature from Seth, and for this reason he directed his sons to live with him. From him Abram, the son of the promise, was destined to come, and in him the turbulent course of twenty generations would find rest. On this condition, the command drew him out of Babylon, to become the beginning of the chosen people and the promise to the nations. Through the Spirit he declared to him, “Leave the land of your birth,” and he accepted and took to heart the voice that spoke with him. Through speech and silence he trained the good servant, so that, as he gained wisdom, he would yoke his sons under his Lord’s yoke. He strengthened him through that promise concerning his descendants, and he longed to learn precisely when it would happen. Abram asked when it would happen and how it would happen, and the Lord answered him with a clear voice and spoke with him. “Take animals and offer sacrifices to my honored name, and I will teach you how my promise to you will come about. “With three animals, depict the enslavement of three generations, during which your descendants will live among foreigners and afterward be set free.

“Take three that are young and fine according to the Law, for this is how it requires lawful sacrifices to be. “Divide them and place each piece opposite its counterpart, and depict their enslavement as they are crushed, one against [?]. “Through the turtledove and the young pigeon, which are not divided, represent their dwelling amid devastation and amid peace. “Through the birds that descend on the pieces you divide, depict the injuries that tyrannical nations inflict on our children. “In your concern and your guarding of your sacrifices from the birds, remember my care and how deeply it is concerned for your offspring. “Since the sun set and only then were your various sacrifices accepted, understand that the time of my promise to you is far off. “Since the fire devoured and completely consumed your sacrifices with delight, see that your loving willingness pleases me much more than sacrifices.” Abram, the chosen one, learned these things through a clear voice. He believed and affirmed that a time lay ahead in which wonders would take place. Here, the communication of the things I have recounted took place at night, not in a dream or in a spiritual vision. He disclosed a sign that distinguishes a tangible voice, just as one human body differs from another. He showed him the various forms of his revelations in bodily fashion, through the understanding that bodily nature is accustomed to use in examining things. In this form he and those with him came to him. Although there was no body, he showed him there the appearance of a body. The righteous man saw three men at the entrance to his house and received them as men, in keeping with their appearance. Through what he did, he revealed to the righteous man what was to come: that his child was destined to dwell lovingly in his son. Abraham’s son was destined to become a temple for his love, and he prepared the way for his appearing before he appeared.

He foreshadowed his appearing by entering his servant’s house, so that, when he appeared, the reality would not seem foreign to the symbol. He was appointing a body of his own for his embodiment, and he showed it symbolically before it came about bodily. He was calling him by the name of his greatness in sacrificial worship, but his love stooped down, and he called himself by the name of a man. Abraham, too, looked upon him as a man and thought that he was honoring the righteous and giving them rest. The Lord and his servants clothed themselves in the appearance of modest men, and they were both awe-inspiring and beloved in the righteous man’s eyes. He welcomed them with great love as righteous men and refreshed them with bodily food and drink. They showed the bodily man the appearance of eating, and although they were eating, they were not truly eating. Their love gratified Abram’s love through the eating they displayed. It was not that they were eating; rather, they taught him the affection of their love. The Good One showed the affection of his love through what he did: he entered his servant’s home bodily, although he had no body. At that visit he gave bodily form to two spirits along with himself. It was not that he became embodied, but that he maintained the form of the appearance. For what was seen bodily was an appearance, and this is the wonder: although there was no body, it portrayed a body. The Creator worked a great wonder for Abraham: he showed himself bodily, although he did not reveal himself. He displayed a body, although his divinity has no body, and he ate and drank, although his nature does not receive food. His nature does not have the natural properties that other natures have, for even the designation “nature” is foreign to his nature. For lack of names, we give him the designation “nature,” because a created being habitually uses whatever is available. According to this usage, the Lord of natures was called a nature. He came among human beings in human form, under a borrowed designation.

What happened in Abraham’s house took place under a borrowed designation. Let no one suppose that it truly happened just as it is written. Moses recorded that visit as he was commanded, and placed it in his book as a foundation for the building of truth. The Lord did everything he did among his servants to build up truth, and above all, what he did for Abraham. He was destined to accomplish humanity’s salvation through Abraham’s offspring, and he honored the righteous man with a symbol of the salvation that would dawn from him. Let us not, then, entertain foolish thoughts about the Creator, as the feeble-hearted heretics do. I have heard the foolish thoughts they entertain about such matters, and for this reason I have mentioned them in the midst of my discourse. Because of them I have followed the path of repeating these words, for I know the ugly stain of their thoughts. I am not unaware of how confused the course of their words is, and how easy it is for them to twist what is straightforward. Because of the distress they cause, my thoughts have struggled at times, and they have not ceased, nor do they cease, from battling their wickedness. I have mentioned their wickedness many times, not to boast, but to rebuke their lack of discipline. Without understanding, they continually travel the path of the Scriptures, and with their disputes they confuse people’s progress. With their disputes they have continually provoked me too, and they do not let me travel quietly along the path of my discourse. I long to travel along the path of divine visions, to know and make known the reason for their differences. I have seen that their varied forms abound in every beauty, and that they declare the word of truth in body and spirit. In body and spirit Isaac too heard the Spirit’s speech, which reminded him of that promise made to his father. The wise son pondered his father’s promise and strove to pass on to his sons the promise of life. Like an athlete, he prepared himself for the blessings, and he wished to give them, but the divine command restrained him. He wished to bless Esau the firstborn with abundant blessings, but the command that rules over everything did not permit him.

The righteous man was caught as though in a contest, amid the surge of his words. He wanted to give, but held back and stood divided. Oh, the wonder that was taking place with the righteous man! He longed to give but could not do so at all, because he was being constrained. Though he did not wish it, the Creator acted through his servant’s will and gave the promise belonging to Abraham’s household to the one worthy of it. Here, in love, he compelled the upright man to do these things, and what happened with the two brothers was entirely just. That will which sees everything had seen Jacob and had chosen him beforehand, before he came out of the womb. Just, then, was the choice made by the God of all, and it was worthy to guard the treasure of the promise of life. Jacob carried the promise of life in the movements of his soul. He traveled along the road and saw a vision at the beginning of his journey. He saw a ladder standing on the earth, its top in the heights, and the God of all above the height of its full length. He saw angels ascending and descending swiftly, carrying out the will of the Lord who had sent them. This was the dream Jacob saw, not delusions. While asleep, he saw a vision that cannot be seen. It was not with his eyes that he saw the ladder or the spiritual beings, nor could he, as a human being, see the Lord. For it was a vision displaying the forms of events and making known his descent and his ascent. The ascent and descent of the spiritual beings encouraged him and taught him not to grow weary from the toil of his journey. If spiritual beings labor so greatly in their tasks, how much more ought he not to become fainthearted in the face of hardships! The vision he saw taught him patience, and that whoever endures is destined to receive a reward for his [?]. He strengthened him in faith, hope, and love, and for this reason he called the place the House of God.

He named the place where he saw the vision the House of God, and made a vow to pay the various tithes there. At the end of his labors he saw another vision like this one, which taught him what he had been taught at the beginning of his journey. He fled in haste when he left Laban’s house, and his flight closely resembled his earlier descent to Mesopotamia. During his flight he saw a camp of heavenly beings, who reminded him of the vision he had seen at Bethel. He saw the awe-inspiring appearance of the ministering ranks, and approached and grasped their chief as though he were a man. He engaged the spiritual being in a fierce struggle, wrestling to receive from him the power of blessings. “Bless me [?],” Jacob said to the spiritual being. He asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Jacob.” “From now on you will no longer be called by this name. Instead, your name will be Israel—one who has seen God.” Isaac’s son did not see God bodily, but rather a vision that spoke in God’s name. Righteous Jacob perceived this vision with his senses, and with his hands he grasped the spiritual being as though he were a man. The spiritual being himself was teaching him to wrestle, so that when he overcame him, he would know that he could overcome his brother. This was the reason for the struggle that took place here: it reminded him of that vision of the ladder. That revelation and this one here had the same purpose. There it was a dream, and here a vision while awake. While awake he saw that camp of heavenly beings, and named the place after the event shown in the vision. He named the place where the vision appeared to him Penuel, because he had seen the spiritual being face to face. It was the spiritual being whom he saw and grasped bodily, not the Nature that created creation out of nothing [?]. That Being cannot be seen by seers, nor can seers gaze into his hiddenness. Through the form of a vision, he taught the righteous the name of his Being, to stir up zeal in the unrighteous so that they might become righteous. Jacob was righteous, and the ways of his life were beloved.

And rightly he gave him the name “seer of the Godhead.” Through the eye of the spirit, he showed him an incorporeal sight, and taught him how to portray its likeness before seers. The vision that appeared to him possessed great power, and he passed it on to his sons as an inheritance from God. Through the Spirit, the righteous man blessed his sons as he had been commanded, and revealed and declared the final outcome of their deeds. Joseph too gazed spiritually at distant things, and the vision of the sheaves and the heavenly lights interpreted [?] them. In his dreams he depicted the greatness of his rank and the humiliation of his brothers: he was being exalted, while his brothers were descending to the rank of slaves. In every way the Lord instructed his servants, so that they might become witnesses to his care for humanity. He appointed Job as one of the witnesses to his care, and the title of witness suited him better than anyone else. The descendant of Esau, who sold his rank, became a chosen witness and showed that the children of evildoers can become righteous. Job was righteous, and his faith was steadfast. The prophet rightly placed his name in the book of the righteous. The hidden Will honored the righteous in every generation and portrayed their righteousness like an image before those who beheld it. The righteous Will portrayed the image of his righteousness in Moses and appointed him to be a skilled scribe of his hidden things. More than to anyone else, he revealed to him the mysteries of his hidden things and raised his rank above the ranks of his companions. He made him chief of those who beheld his hidden things on earth and taught him to portray things unseen as though they were visible. On the mountain he portrayed a vision of fire before his eyes, and from it [?] he conveyed to him the sound of his name. He saw the vision that appeared to him in a lowly kind of plant: in an ugly thornbush that bore no pleasant fruit. The Creator customarily shows his power through something despised, to teach humanity that he created the creation out of nothing. Something, however lowly it may be, is better than nothing, just as a substance that exists is more real than a shadow. In a lowly thornbush he showed Moses a wondrous vision:

Fire and a thornbush, and the thornbush in the fire without being destroyed. A vision and a voice were being revealed from within the fire, and he perceived the sight and the sound with his bodily senses. The voice called the Israelite “Moses” and showed him that it knew who he was and whose son he was, and made his ancestry known to him. “[?], the Lord of your ancestors’ household,” he said to him, “and I have come down to deliver Abraham’s offspring from slavery.” These things were heard distinctly by the one endowed with senses, and were seen in body and spirit by the one endowed with sight. Through a tangible sign he taught him the power of his lordly name: he transformed the staff and made it truly become a snake. With this very staff he chastised the Egyptians with ten plagues, and with it he divided the sea, and the people crossed as on dry land. It was not the staff that possessed the power of his lordly name; rather, divine power accomplished these things through it. By this same power he sweetened the waters that had been bitter, and at his command he brought up quail and sent down manna. By it he split the rock and made water flow from the flint, satisfying the people’s need for drink and bringing his love to fulfillment. He showed everyone the power of his greatness through these deeds and made them known through a man who stammered and had difficulty speaking. He chose a stammering man from the whole mortal race, and through him revealed the power of his being and the ordering of everything. He made him, a mortal by nature, a second lord on earth, and gave him power to recount in order the formation of the worlds. On the mountain he showed him spiritually the formation of the worlds: how creation was formed in the beginning out of nothing. Love of these things stirred the Israelite’s mind, and he began to plead, “Show me the glory of your divinity.” Moses thought he was seeing him as one sees a human being, and did not know that this hidden being cannot be seen. As to a friend, he showed him something in place of his hidden being:

He portrayed a likeness of the greatness of the glory of his face. The vision of his glory made the stammerer more glorious than anyone, and fleshly eyes could not bear to look at him. The mortal did not see God with bodily sight, for this is difficult and beyond the grasp of rational beings. The Power hidden from all creatures showed him his glory, so that he would know that his divinity is beyond comprehension. It was an angel who served in the Lord’s place, and he displayed a wondrous vision before the eyes of those who revered him. Everything that happened on Mount Sinai was his doing, and there was no sound Moses heard that he had not uttered. Paul testifies that it was an angel who gave the law—not that he himself gave it, but that it was spoken through him. The divine command moved the angel, and he interpreted the provisions of the law in Moses’ hearing. Moses was appointed as a mediator between him and the people, and he explained and spoke spiritually. The Spirit played upon his mouth as upon an instrument, and made glorious sounds speak in the people’s hearing. Oh, that Power, possessing no audible voice, who expressed the various purposes of his will through the work of his hands! He carried out his activity in three stages: toward the spiritual beings, toward the son of Amram, and toward the members of his people. He passed the utterance he held from one to another, like a king who commands one person, and that person another. He was honored like a king by the spiritual beings, and the spiritual beings conveyed his words to earthly beings. On the mountain he showed the place of his feet as though he had a body; although there was no body, he portrayed bodily likenesses. He gave a new decree to the instrument who appeared in his name; it was written on two tablets, on this side and that. The firstborn letters of the alphabet were written on them, and they preceded all the letters in all books. He made Moses the master of teachers among earthly beings:

He was the first to read the written text of his words. The command that formed created things out of nothing itself wrote them, not with hands but by a gesture.
