The Creator does not have bodily hands, although it is written that the Lord’s hand wrote them. He commonly uses the image of hands in all sorts of descriptions, since people too perform their deeds with their hands [?]. In this manner he acted toward Moses and Joshua son of Nun, and in turn toward the righteous in every generation. He made one angel the messenger of his activity, the one who was called Michael and Azazel. It was about him that he spoke to Moses on the mountain, when he reassured him: “Look, my angel will go before you and guide you.” He gave the minister of his divinity his own name, and commanded Moses to fear him as he would the Lord. It was he who appeared to Joshua son of Nun in the form of a man, visibly equipped with weapons. He was not a visible man, as the account says, but the likeness of a man, though no man was there. “I am the commander of the armies,” he told him, “and I have now come to teach you the order of my leadership. “I am the one who performed everything that happened through Moses, and I am performing the things that happen through your own hands.” This same man, who called himself by the name of a man, was the one who brought about all the disasters of the Canaanites. He took the land of Palestine and gave it to Israel, fulfilling and completing the promise made to Abram. He showed Gideon a sign through the fleece and the dew, showing that he could destroy the Midianites without weapons. He taught Gideon to fight without weapons, so that when he was victorious he would not boast of his weapons. He also told Deborah to summon Barak, so that he would go out and put to shame the pride of Sisera, the mighty warrior.

It was he who also taught Jael [?] various tricks, so that under the guise of affection she might trap the crafty man who oppressed the people. Through women’s hands he humbled the pride of the kings of Hazor, to proclaim the power of the one who sent him, whose might can accomplish anything. It was he who revealed to Manoah’s wife what Samson was to do: how he would overcome the Philistines through the sign of his hair. On his head, the foremost of his limbs, he displayed the sign of his strength, so that he would know that the power of his greatness was not human. Again, he condensed the diffuse air and made it a solid mass, and brought down rain as Samuel the priest had asked. With the sound of thunder he rebuked the people who had asked for a king [?], to teach them that they had not acted rightly in fulfilling their desire. The Creator himself did everything he did through the spiritual being; the spiritual being could not perform things beyond his own power. Through spiritual beings he exercised his power toward created things, not because he needed them, but to make known that he is Lord over all. His power does not need help from the work of his hands, and creation bears witness that he alone called it into being and established it. The Maker of all did not do everything he did through their hands, for the things he did without them are beyond counting. Revelations came to the righteous throughout the generations, but it was not they who ministered their revelations to them. Look, righteous David sang his prophecy in the Spirit, and not one of the ministering orders came near it. The power of the Spirit spoke with the soul of the man whose soul was pure, and composed the sounds of spiritual songs. He did not hear the speech addressed to him through his senses, but through the mind that knows how to listen to the Spirit's speech. The skilled singer sang everything he sang spiritually. Nothing in his singing was without the Spirit [?]. Nor did an angel interpret for him so that he could then sing. The power of the Spirit played upon the harp of his soul, and his bodily senses gave voice like strings. The Spirit held the tongue of his mouth like a pen, and with it wrote various spiritual melodies. In this respect his words differ from those of the prophets, and they are not given the designation of prophecy. His book bears the title “Psalms of Songs.”

The expressions “the utterance of the Lord” and “the word of the Lord” were not there. It is the one Lord who expressed his word through the mouths of his faithful ones, sometimes through a sign and sometimes through plain, open speech. In truthful speech Ahijah heard his Lord's command, and he tore the cloak he was wearing into twelve pieces. The Shilonite received this through a revelation of the Spirit, and gave the son of Nebat [?] ten pieces of his covering. Here the action took place openly, not symbolically, for Jeroboam visibly received ten pieces. Openly Elijah also restrained heaven and earth, and through his actions checked the air in its course. Openly he received plainly visible food from the [?] of ravens, and with his bodily limbs he traveled and reached the woman of Zarephath. [?] he multiplied flour and oil in the widow's house, and he lived and gave life according to the will of the one who delighted in him. Openly he snatched a plainly visible dead man from the mouth of death, and before everyone's eyes he offered sacrifices [?] and brought down fire. With his body he heard a voice and saw a vision. With bodily eyes he saw an earthquake, fire, and wind. In the same way [?] he heard the sound of gentle speech. The son of sojourners received these things openly, and turned to proceed toward the goal shown to him. Let no one devise absurd allegories here, but let everyone accept these things in their plain meaning, as they were spoken. This is plain, pure speech without concealment, and there is nothing in it resembling those who dream dreams spiritually. Elisha followed this path of openly revealed speech, received the Spirit, and performed mighty deeds before the eyes of those who watched. Before the eyes of those watching, he healed the water with salt and an earthenware bowl. He threw a piece of wood after the iron and raised it to the surface.

With an explicit word he cursed the boys who had insulted him without cause. Bears came out and tore them apart without mercy. Without concealment, he gave the Shunammite woman a child; and when the child suddenly died, he returned and raised him from the dead. In this same manner, he made water abundant in a deserted place and provided sustenance for three kings who were in need. In the same way, he neutralized the bitterness in the pot. He multiplied bread and produced abundance beyond the ordinary. With his bodily eye he saw the spiritual beings surrounding him. He struck the Edomites with bewilderment and blinded them. Through a revelation of the Spirit, he saw the messenger who was coming to put him to death. He announced beforehand that the famine would end and there would be abundance. A bodily man, he placed a bow in the king’s hand and showed him that he would defeat the Edomites three times. The bodiless Spirit put spirit within him after his death, and he raised a dead man who suddenly came into contact with his remains. That command which gave him a double share of prophecy itself performed through his hands kinds of signs that were beyond him. Very exalted were the kinds of revelations the righteous man received, and human weakness falls far below such things. Isaiah saw this glory within the sanctuary. He was distressed and lamented the wretchedness of human nature. “Woe to me, wretched as I am!” the righteous man said before the revelation, “for my lips are unclean, and the people of my ancestral house are unclean.” Spiritually he saw the vision shown to him. He marveled and was astonished at the greatness of the vision and the lowliness of humanity. Isaiah saw an awe-inspiring vision full of wonder: the King over all, and the heavenly armies attending him in splendor. It was not with his eyes that he saw the throne of the Godhead, nor was it through hearing that he received the seraphim’s cries of “Holy.” For what he saw in his mind was an incorporeal vision. The name of God was depicted within it, not God himself. God was not sitting like a human being within the sanctuary, nor did the spiritual beings have wings like a bird. Nor was the coal that was brought near him really a coal,

but a representation of the mystery of our salvation, which would take place at the end. As a symbol of salvation, the seraph brought it near [?] to his lips and opened the way for that forgiveness granted to all nations. The incorporeal being held the corporeal thing with tongs. This is the wonder: he shrank back from something inferior to himself. The coal is immeasurably inferior to the angel. Why, then, did the angel tremble before a silent thing? It was not the unthinking coal that the watcher honored, but the mystery that was being disclosed through its silence. Here let us learn how great is the power of the mystery of our salvation, since the spiritual seraph did not approach its representation. Here let the foolish pride of Judaism be put to shame: they read the Scriptures but do not understand the meaning of the Scriptures. Let the factions of heretics also stand ashamed, who will not allow our Lord’s body to be a body. Let the righteous sweat condemn the arrogant, who cast the storm of bodily sufferings upon the Godhead. Let everyone who hinders me from traveling along the path of my discourse stand condemned, without acquittal. I long to travel along the path of divine visions, and now I wait to enliven my mind with their revelations. My discourse journeyed from the son of Amoz to the son of Beeri, and marveled greatly at the spirit of revelation that came to him. “Go,” he said, “take for yourself two disreputable women, and through their promiscuity portray the evils of two tribes. Without refusing, accept living with promiscuous women, and show the people how detestable their deeds are. Through these disreputable women, portray images of their depravity, and through the women’s conduct pronounce a threat against their sins. Let your children’s names be scourges against the offenders, so that, when they are scourged, they may desist a little from their evil deeds. Through your wives and your children, scourge those who are full of wrongdoing,

and make them know that there is justice and there is forgiveness.” This is the purpose of the prophecy of pure Hosea, and the revelation in Joel’s message resembles his. He proclaimed a fearful report to the members of his people and astonished them with the kinds of scourges spoken of by his mouth. “Listen, elders, and tremble, inhabitants of the whole land, for the time has drawn near when you will be destroyed in the face of afflictions.” He called the captors locusts, crawling locusts, and crickets, and set out the scourges they would inflict, one after another. The seer of hidden things did not see locusts, but the devastation wrought by the Assyrians and Babylonians. He named the Assyrians locusts and crawling locusts that creep along, and he called the Babylonians crickets that strike and wither. This is the force of his message, the message of Joel, the herald of the Spirit; and with his threats is mingled lamentation for the day of return. Amos, the shepherd of sheep, also directed himself toward the same purpose. He raised his voice and scourged the people and the nations alike. The seer enclosed the people and the nations within a single threat, and taught them that his word would be fulfilled through events. Obadiah also confirmed his words with a threatening voice, and humbled the pride of the Edomites by his sentence of judgment. Jonah served two purposes at once in his prophecy: the overthrow of Nineveh and the repentance of all the nations. The son of Amittai saw the return of the nations in the scourges of Nineveh,

and he trembled and was alarmed that the nations were coming in and the people were going out. The Hebrew cast himself into headlong flight, so that he would not be called a prophet who proclaimed estrangement. The Spirit sent a wind through the air against the fugitive, caught him in the surge, and brought him in and imprisoned him in the belly of a fish. His Lord bound the headstrong servant with bars of flesh, so that he would not learn to hate the peace of humankind. The divine revelation called him to bring peace to humankind. Because he would not go, it buried him in a fish and raised him again as a symbol. For that descent into the sea was a symbol of the salvation that would come at the end for all nations. The son of Amittai died as a symbol of the salvation brought by our Lord's death, and the conversion of the Assyrians symbolized life for everyone. Through the Ninevites, Jonah brought all humanity back and opened a road for preaching among the nations. Thus the pattern of his message differed from that of the other prophets, because he did not include his own people in his prophecy. Micah's [?] course followed the path of his companions, and he too delivered the message that Amos delivered. He too made his people hear terrifying words and instructed them with news of captivity and return. Spiritual was the manner of revelation given to that temple of the Spirit, and through the Spirit he announced that Christ would come and save the nations. Nahum announced the downfall of the Assyrians: when they were humbled, the people would find relief from subjection. Righteous zeal against evildoers set Habakkuk ablaze, and he believed and affirmed that vengeance would come in answer to his zeal.

Zephaniah brought down the blows foretold by his companions through his people's captivity, then turned and announced that the yoke of Babylon's kingdom would cease. Haggai urged the building of the holy temple and told the people about the coming of the Scythians. Zechariah's forms of prophetic revelation were exalted, and glorious was the imagery of the awesome visions he saw in his mind. The Spirit who chose him showed him spiritual things in his mind and drew in his understanding images without material composition. Spiritually he saw chariots and their riders being sent to destroy the nations that had humbled the people. Through the Spirit he also contemplated the lampstand of the Spirit of grace, and without using his senses he gazed at the lamps above it. Through the forms of his visions, he announced the people's prosperity: the leadership of kings and priests would be restored to them. With two olive trees he represented both priesthood and kingship, and he saw them standing on the right and on the left. He gave them names according to their functions: one, “Gracious,” and the other [?], “Cord of Destruction.” With a scroll he depicted the sentence of judgment against all nations, and with horns, the ways in which dominion would be abolished. The prophet of the Spirit depicted everything spiritually, and he too announced beforehand the onslaught of the Greeks. This is the aim of the Spirit of prophetic revelations, and toward this same aim Malachi, who seals the mysteries, directed himself. The words of the Spirit’s messenger were like a seal, and he sealed the words of prophecy and apostleship.

The Spirit showed him the coming [?] of the Antichrist, and how the son of sojourners would come and silence him. The prophet quiets the fierce conflicts of embattled demons and exposes that deception before the eyes of those watching. On this condition the [?] of creation preserved him: to display through him the power of his greatness to the ages to come. The Lord of the prophets revealed the power of his greatness to his prophets and taught them that through human beings he would make them wise. Through Jeremiah he taught wisdom to the brutish world and harnessed it, as to a yoke, with the yoke of the words of his mouth. The son of Hilkiah placed a wooden yoke on his neck and began to cultivate human minds with the sound of his words. This was the aim of that diligent worker’s labor: the words of the Spirit, which he interpreted in the hearing of the people. The son of Buzi also chose this task among the Babylonians: to cultivate human beings with the voice of divine revelations. In Babylon, the exile received the spirit of revelation, where the people and the nations supposed that there was no God. The divine command showed him the forms of the chariot, to which the whole world was harnessed, speaking and speechless beings alike. He saw [?] and speechless beings harnessed beneath the Creator, while the Creator himself was borne in glory above everything. That chariot which the prophet saw was not a physical chariot, nor was the movement of the wheels beneath it bodily. They were not wheels running backward, nor were they living creatures possessing the appearance of four faces. The Spirit put together that chariot which was not a composite thing, and Ezekiel, the skilled seer, saw it spiritually. Through his vision he rebuked the Israelites and the Babylonians, who thought that the God of all was not in every place. With this vision he struck down that thought and assertion:

To make known that he is over all, in all, and beyond all. On this condition he depicted forms without forms and taught his servant to depict them by recounting them in words. The son of Buzi [?] divine artistry and began to depict the truth of his revelations before those watching. He recounted to all the people the vision that had been shown to him and solemnly warned them not to doubt what they had heard. Daniel also made them hear the report of these things; he interpreted dreams and rebuked kings to their faces. Through dreams the spiritual one taught him the forms of hidden things, and although they were dreams, they performed the work of prophecy. With the eye of the spirit of prophecy he saw everything, and nothing was disclosed to him except through the Spirit. The Spirit showed him how to interpret the dreams of the great statue, and at his interpretation the Babylonians [?] and bowed down before him. Through the Spirit he revealed to the tyrant king his coming humiliation, and answered him and taught him that, once humbled, he would be exalted again. Through that same Spirit he saw the dissolution of Babylon’s kingdom, which the incorporeal hand of the Spirit was writing for him. It was the Spirit who showed him a vision greater than other visions, encompassing the whole world within its bounds. He represented the vision shown to him by a great sea, with four heavenly winds above its surface. He saw four beasts rising from the sea, and the appearance of each differed from that of the others. He called three of them a lion, a leopard, and a hideous bear, but he would not give the fourth the name of any animal. It too was a beast, however fearsome he might say its appearance was, for at the beginning he said, “I saw four beasts.” The captive did not see bodily animals, but a representation of the dominion of the nations of the earth. By the fearsome lion he designated Babylon, the source of confusion.

And by the name of the leopard he designated Cyrus, the ruler of Persia. By the bear he represented the kingdom of Media, weak in strength, and by the fourth beast the Greeks, quick of mind. By the great sea he represented the inhabited regions of the whole earth, and by the four winds the powers of the heavenly beings. He apportioned the entire world among the spiritual beings, and they administer the affairs of its four quarters. Through this vision the Spirit gave the prophet understanding and taught him that they would come to an end, and the people would return and dwell in the land. In the dreams of the night he saw a vision full of wonder, and although it was a dream, it fulfilled the order of prophecy. He is a righteous prophet who humbles kings while in exile, and as a prophet he explained the vision of the four beasts. The Spirit showed him many visions among all his visions, and at the end depicted for him a likeness of our Lord’s death. He depicted a likeness of his death for the righteous man, a son of the Hebrews, and called him by his name: the Messiah, who comes to seal the mysteries. Through his death he made known that there would be nothing more after his death, for it brings the arduous course of prophecy to completion. The prophet of the Spirit set a seal upon the revelations and sealed them so that they would be kept safe until his appearing. Everything that happened among the Hebrews happened for the sake of his appearing, and prophets and kings announced it beforehand, before it took place. Gabriel, the spiritual being, also proclaimed his appearing, and this was the reason he was sent to Daniel. Daniel, the man of desire [?], heard the name Gabriel and was greatly astonished at the news he heard, which was unfamiliar to him. He had never heard the name Gabriel at all until he heard it from the spiritual being who called him by his name. For this designation that the righteous man heard was a new name, and it seems that the course of the Law comes to rest with his name. The name Michael was present throughout the course of the Law; even now he is called the commander of the people's army. He was the one who carried out the administration of the Law, from the beginning of the people's election to the end. His work of visitation began with Hagar,

until he heard that voice addressed to Mary. An appointed term had been set for him by the Creator, and when he saw that it was approaching, he gave his leadership to his companion. Gabriel took the leadership of the Israelites and gave it to the nations, in accordance with the expectation expressed in prophecy. The prophet revealed his name in prophecy, so that he would not be treated as a stranger when he was sent on his mission. He was destined to come and bring the good news of our Lord's appearing, and questions would have arisen about what this unfamiliar name meant. If his name had not been in the archives of prophecy, the Israelites would not have accepted his proclamation. Even the heralds of the proclamation would have doubted, asking, “Who, then, is this Gabriel, whose name is unfamiliar?” Daniel resolved this doubt through prophecy and placed the name like a guide at the end of his book. Through this designation, the name Gabriel, he marked out a path: the course of the name Michael comes to rest, and his own begins. The name Michael is the name of a spiritual angel, while the name Gabriel means a man sent from God. The name of this man points to that man who is one of us, whom the righteous man also called “man” in his proclamation. Otherwise, what is this distinction between one name and another? For they are alike, and they are spirits without composition. The nature of spiritual beings has no bodily names. Why, then, do only two have names? Their ministry reveals the names of their persons; although they are alike, one name differs from the other. The severity of scourges is mingled into the name Michael, and for this reason his designation is veiled in the book of Moses. The name Gabriel is a designation filled with the meaning “man of peace.” Mary bears witness, for he gave her good news filled with peace. Gabriel gave good news of peace to her whose soul was pure, and although it was something new, she received it in faith. What the spiritual being proclaimed was something entirely new:

that a virgin would conceive without a mate or sexual union. By the power of the Spirit he drove questioning from her mind, for even the difficulties of nature are easy for him. In many ways he confirmed his message that she would conceive, and he gave an example from Elizabeth, announcing that she was pregnant. Zechariah had seen this very spiritual man, and it was he who gave him the good news about that child who was greater than other children. In the holy temple Zechariah saw the spiritual angel, and he trembled and was terrified by the glory upon his face. “I am the man whose name is Gabriel,” he told him, “and the Lord has sent me to bring the good news of your son’s conception. Your son is the messenger who goes before the one coming to save humanity, and I have come to reveal that the day of his appearing has arrived.” He confined him to silence so that he could not speak about anything he had heard, until the appointed time for the day of his son’s birth was fulfilled. This was the beginning of the spiritual being’s mission: he announced the conception of the courier who goes before the King. From here he began to prepare the way for our Lord’s appearing, and [?] carried out the visions of the day of his revelation. He was the one who revealed the day of his birth to the shepherds, and he also made the sound of his praise heard among those on earth. Everything spoken in the proclamation belongs to him, and he was the one who ministered the various revelations to the disciples. He was the one who approached our Savior at the time of his suffering, and he encouraged him so that he would not falter at the news of death. He was the one who rolled the great stone away from the entrance of the tomb, and the women saw him standing there in the likeness of a man. Together with his companion, he suddenly stood before the disciples and amazed them with the splendid glory in which they were clothed. He carried out everything that happened and happens in the proclamation, just as Michael also acted in guiding the people. The same will that guided the people through Michael carried out its various revelations through Gabriel in the new covenant. This spiritual being’s rank is greater than that of other spiritual beings, just as his proclamation is greater than everything else.

The name of Christ our Lord is far greater than all created beings; the one who announced his conception is greater than all his companions. My speech has magnified the greatness of his rank, not out of flattery, but to make known how glorious the good news he proclaimed is. Glorious is the salvation he proclaimed on earth before its inhabitants, and heaven and earth bear witness with us that our salvation is great. The heavenly hosts marveled at the greatness of his power, and they ministered his various revelations before his heralds. The spiritual angel chose Philip, one of the seventy, to go and proclaim the good news of life to those without hope. In the one man whom he turned to faith through his word, he portrayed thousands of Midianites and Cushites. Here the saying of our Lord was fulfilled, when he said, “I have come to cast my teaching among those on earth.” The fire of his proclamation blazed more fiercely than fire, and it found fuel among all the nations, on sea and land. By his mighty power he conquered the beastlike world and humbled the pride of Judaism and paganism. The heralds of the faith triumphed in the land of Judea, and the message they proclaimed had its beginning in Jerusalem. Through the Spirit of revelation, Simon opened the way to the nations; he cast his net and caught Cornelius first. The son of Jonah saw a great vision high above: a beautiful sheet containing creatures of every kind. All the nations were hanging in that vessel he saw. And this was the wonder: in a single cloth he saw everything. For this vision was a vision in the mind. Peter saw it spiritually, not bodily. Spiritually he heard the voice saying, “Get up, slaughter and eat,” teaching him not to shrink back from sinners. He called the unclean nations by the name of creatures without speech; the hidden will receives them as members of the household. Through Cornelius he opened the way for the conversion of the nations, and he sketched it out beforehand through the instruction of the chief of the disciples. A bodily man saw a spiritual angel in bodily form. The angel commanded him to summon a bodily man who would give him life.

The words spoken by the spiritual being deserve wonder: he teaches a human being through a human being, without teaching him himself. The angel observed a great order in his mission: he did not approach the exalted rank of leadership. The Lord of the apostles gave the apostolic office the command to speak the proclamation in the hearing of the nations. “Go,” he said, “make disciples, baptize and teach among all the nations, in the name of the divine Being: three names, one will.” The spiritual being obeyed that command when he was sent. He spoke a word but did not wish to complete it through deeds. This is the purpose of [?] human beings: that through human beings they should call human beings to the proclamation. The head of humanity himself chose human beings and sent them to catch human beings for the worship of truth. With his nets he caught the untamed world, brought it in, and enclosed it within the fortresses of faith. With this net the skilled fisherman caught Paul and sent him on the road of proclamation among the nations. He called him a chosen vessel when he brought him into the apostolic office, and showed him that he could bring human beings to maturity in faith. He fulfilled the will of the one who sent him better than anyone else. For this reason he was deemed worthy of revelations higher than himself. It is a very exalted thing for a person to be raised to the virgin of heaven [?]. Though it is very high, he reached it, as it is written. It is said that he went to the land of Eden, which is very far away, and there heard speech unheard by human beings. Oh, the wonder that speakers cannot express: he heard a report and spoke speech that cannot be spoken! Indeed, man, the statement your mouth speaks is difficult, and no one knows how to recount it before listeners. But if it is permitted to speak the words you heard, how did you hear or speak words that are difficult? The statement is very profound, chosen Paul, and he himself bears witness that he could not explain the force of its meaning. “I know,” he says, “that I went to Eden.” He himself recounted this:

I do not know how I went, but only that I went. The Spirit revealed to me spiritually only that I went; my mind could not comprehend the way by which I went. Let us therefore say to anyone who says concerning Paul's statement, “If he did not know, it is presumptuous for us to dispute with him”: “It is presumptuous to seek out words that cannot be spoken, and arrogant to seek what no one is permitted to hear.” Yes, mortal nature is not permitted to hear them until it becomes immortal; then it hears them. Something new happened to that man who spoke them, and he rightly said that he spoke and heard in an extraordinary way. He heard the unutterable speech in an extraordinary way; it is therefore clear that he passed beyond the order of mortality. Paul alone wished to be like the immortals, and the Power that gave him strength to do these things bears witness. For it is the Creator's power to make something out of nothing and to raise his servants above anything that can be expressed. He is the one who taught the members of his household the various forms of his wisdom and put into words what is difficult to express as it was heard. His power strengthened the weakness of the human mind, and they instructed the world in glorious things that were not visible to it. Very glorious were the words the apostles spoke on earth, and no one knows how to recount the power of their meanings. The one who makes humanity wise acted wisely in everything he did, and bound everything in perfect love with the Lord of all. My thoughts recalled this purpose, which brought everything into harmony, and I mingled its account with the account of divine visions. The visions that the righteous saw were also for its sake, and like guides they prepared the way for the day of his revelation. The day of his revelation brought the course of all revelations to rest and bound human beings and heavenly beings together in peace with him. Through peace with him, reconciliation came about between him and everything, and nothing remained that was not reconciled with the Creator. The lover of humanity accomplished this through a human being.

Through him he tore down the barrier and abolished death and the adversary. Through him he promised immortal life to mortal nature and raised it in hope before the day of resurrection should come. He knew temporal life, whose course is wearisome, and prepared beforehand another life, restful and peaceful. He knew that mortal nature was worn down by mortality, and promised to release it from the yoke of death. What he accomplished at the end of the ages was known to him, and he disclosed it beforehand through the revelations he revealed to his servants. The holy ones were like guides going ahead of his will, and he prepared a way for human beings to advance toward his will. Look, people have seen how much he loves the human race, for in that very nature he displays the love of his kindness. He showed his love through visions in various likenesses, and brought them together in the single likeness of one human being. He chose one man from the whole mortal race, called him by his name, and gave him the [?] of his divinity. See, human being, how greatly the Maker of all has raised you up: he took what was yours and lovingly gave you what was his. Glorious is the will that called him by the name of his glories; the mouth of all creation is too small to give thanks with us. The debt for the love shown to us cannot be repaid. Can those who speak and those who are mute recount the many forms of his greatness? He alone is able to intercede for our salvation; [?] he knows that our race is incapable of repayment. He who needs nothing does not seek repayment from us, but seeks to teach us that, when we repay, we may rejoice according to our capacity. He is teaching us when he urges us to repay. This comes from love, not from a desire to satisfy any need of his own. Glorious in his being, he deserves praise from every mouth. Though his glory is within himself, he urges his servants to praise him. Response: Blessed is he who exalted his servants through his revelation and made them temples for his greatness.
On the Revelations to Abraham
Third Discourse, for the Fourth Sunday of the Annunciation: On the Revelations to Abraham

The Lord of creation chose one people to be his own, and through them taught all the nations the power of his greatness. He left all the nations to the freedom he had placed in their nature, and through his revelations drew one inheritance close to himself. He placed the seal of his name upon them and marked them, so that they would not mingle with the other peoples and forget his name. He set the law of his words before them like a wall, and bound them with observances as with a rope. He chose a dwelling for himself among the people he had chosen to be his own, to teach them how greatly he loved the members of his household. Through sacrifices of flesh and blood, he urged them to offer him sacrifices of love, as to the Hidden One. He honored them in the sight of the other peoples through his mighty acts of help, and exalted them above the nations through the victory of his power. He showed that he was just by disciplining them when they sinned, and proclaimed his power through the victory he gave in battles. He established order for all the nations and appointed rulers, but he guided the people he had chosen in his own name. It was not out of malice that he rejected the nations and chose one people. Through the people he chose, he revealed beforehand what was to come. Through one people he wished to teach all the nations that his command made everything, and that through it everything continues to exist. He laid that people like the foundation with which a house is begun.

Upon it he completed the building of the nations, as he pleased. He planted Abraham among the nations like a root and nurtured his soul through divine revelations. He cut a shoot from a bitter tree, then replanted it, and its branches bore fruits of praise. From paganism, barren of spiritual fruits, Abram’s love brought forth fruit full of delights. Of his own accord he brought forth an early harvest and gave him a voice of thanksgiving; as firstfruits he offered the fruit of his faith. The command of the Creator’s power drew him out of Babylon, to leave his country and go live in a foreign land. The One who knows everything revealed this to him in a mystery: “Leave error behind, and come be enlightened by the light of knowing me.” “Free your will from the chains of deaf, carved idols, and I will give you freedom of soul in whom you worship.” “Leave the inheritance of your ancestral household, full of thorns, and I will grant you an inheritance of love toward my lordship.” He was not saddened at leaving his country and abandoning his people, nor was he troubled about why he must go to another land. The prospect of being a stranger, full of hardships, did not distress him, nor did the lack of love among foreigners sadden him. He journeyed from his country along a road full of sufferings and pains, and along with his limbs his thoughts journeyed after his Lord. He became a stranger to kinship with his own people, and cherished and loved belonging to his Lord’s household. He left Babylon, the spring that watered Chaldean religion, and made his way to Haran, the mother that gave birth to sorcery. The serenity of his soul was not disturbed by Babylon’s divinations, nor was his faith stained by Haran’s sorceries. His loving resolve did not change with the change of country, nor did he give way to the worship of images under any pretext. The country did not weaken his righteousness; through his loving resolve he kept his faith steadfast. His body was deprived of physical offspring, yet he continually brought forth fruits of praise within his mind.

Physical barrenness accompanied him and Sarah [?], yet their thoughts continually bore the fruit of thanksgiving. His Lord tested him through barrenness as though in fire, and he displayed his beauty through thanksgiving without doubt. It was not to learn about him, for he knew him before he was formed; rather, he revealed to coming generations the endurance of their faith. He moved him to live as a foreigner among strangers, so that he might sow love and faith in barren land. He left Haran to go to the land promised to him, to cast the fire of his love there and burn up the forest. He set out, holding fast to his Lord’s promise, which does not deceive; against hope, he believed in hope that he would inherit the land. The righteous man set out under the pledge concerning the land promised to him, and believed with certainty that his offspring would comprise many nations. He became a temporary resident in the land he had received only by promise, and lived as a stranger in the country pledged to him. He increased his cultivation in the land of Canaan through revelations, and he yielded the fruits of hope, love, and faith. Every day he heard the voice saying, “Your descendants will inherit the land.” Yet there was no heir [?], and the voice continued without fulfillment. “Lift up your eyes,” he said, “and look at the blazing lights in heaven, and measure the sand on the seashore, if you can. “So numerous will the offspring of your body be,” the voice proclaimed to him, “and your descendants will be beyond counting, just as I have said. “Stretch your thoughts toward the four directions and look at the lands that your descendants are destined to conquer and bring under a single tribute. “By myself I have sworn,” he said, “and in my hidden nature I do not lie: through you the peoples of the earth will be blessed through faith. “Because you stripped off the hateful garment bearing the name of paganism, I will cover the disgrace of the nations with your faith. “Because you blazed a trail by confessing one Creator, I will draw everyone along the path of your love to faith in me.

“Because you willingly opened a door to my hidden lordship, through you I will open the door of life to those dead in wrongdoing. “Because you did not doubt my promises, though they were far off, I will make you a leader of the living in the kingdom on high. “Because my lordship shone within your mind, though I am hidden, from you will arise the one who gathers the nations together. “In return for your sojourning in lands full of troubles, I will make you a peaceful harbor for all who are distressed. “Upon you I will build a structure of love and faith, and through you I will strengthen all the nations in the hope of life.” Through promises, the One who knows everything tested the upright man. He believed—he believed in things far off as though they were near. Although he knew that the man did not doubt his promises, through testing he revealed the genuineness of his faith. Before testing him, he knew that his love was steadfast; before calling him, he had already discerned that he would not doubt. He wanted to encourage his fellow human beings through his conduct, and he recorded his deeds in the book of his words so that they would imitate him. He portrayed the beauty of his faith like an image, so that everyone might fix his steadfastness in their mind. His body had withered through barrenness as though from thirst, but he watered his soul with the irrigation of the Spirit and bore fruit. He said that he would give the land of Canaan to his descendants, yet he drove him from it like an exile to the land of Egypt. He raised the rod and struck the land with a severe famine, so that because of the famine he would flee from it to another country. He intensified his testing by making him move from country to country, so that everyone would hear that he had not grown weak in the face of troubles. He fled from the famine to save his life in the land of Egypt, but they cut him in half and snatched away from him the rib that was his companion. He did not grumble because wicked men had taken the land of his descendants, nor did he doubt because they had taken from him the vine that would bear his fruit.

He was certain that the voice that had called him would not prove false, and that no other mate would approach the soil of his wife. He grew rich in that land and [?] greatly in his abundance; the wealth of his faith surpassed earthly things. He lived in a region that demons had cultivated through sorcery, and the fruits of his faith flourished among the weeds. O tree that grew amid thorns and struck down their evil fruits with the branches of his love! O sojourner who entered as a guest [?] among foreigners, before whom kings and nobles bowed against their will! O foreigner who came to provide for his livelihood, yet raised a rod and struck the people of the land! The Lord, it is said, struck Pharaoh the king and his household because of Sarah, Abram’s wife, whom he had seized from him. While he was being afflicted along with the world through the plundering of his possessions, the wronged man’s wealth was increasing at his Lord’s command. His honor increased because of Sarah, whom the king had taken away, and he gave thanks to his Lord, who gave him wealth through these circumstances. The wise man grew rich in a land impoverished in knowledge, and he took up his wealth to go to the land that had been promised to him. He returned and settled in the land of Canaan as though it were his own, keeping his eyes on his Lord’s promise to give it to him. The years of his life reached ninety-nine, and God spoke with him through a revelation, telling him to circumcise his flesh. The servant fell on his face and worshiped before his Maker, who established a covenant with him to mark his offspring with his name. He changed his name, by which he had been named for one people, and called him by a name interpreted as “father of nations.” Along with the change by which he called him “father of nations,” the voice called to him: “Now receive the child I promised. Look, my promise to you is being fulfilled in deeds, and by grace I am giving you a son beyond the natural order. Look, I am watering your dead body and giving it seed, and bringing forth a shoot from a root that has grown old and worn out.

I am comforting barren Sarah in her barrenness, and making the pruned tree blossom with fruit of her own. I am removing the reproach from her body—the name of barrenness—and giving her a child as a reward for her endurance.” The promises were fulfilled, and the gifts to the barren began, for the Hidden One came openly to give the righteous their reward. The Lord, it is said, revealed himself to Abram in the land of Mamre, while he was sitting at the entrance of his house in the heat of the day. O fervent man, whom the fierce heat did not cool! He scorned comfort so that his hospitality would not be diminished. He raised his eyes as he watched the roads, seeking to bring his love to fulfillment by providing food for those in need. Abraham saw a new sight, full of wonder: three Watchers clothed in human form. He ran joyfully, fell down, and bowed before the spiritual beings, begging them to let him fulfill his love by attending to their comfort. Through revelations, he addressed them by the Creator’s name: “My Lord, do not pass by the house of your servant, who is waiting for you.” O Being, hidden from everyone and unseen, who revealed himself to Abraham in human form! O righteous man, who was worthy to see, in a mystery, the Father's Word, who was to clothe himself in a human body! Three [?] entered Abraham's house in bodily appearance, and Abraham spoke with only one as God. The Father's Word clothed himself in a form [?], in a mystery, and Abram rejoiced to see the Hidden One in a chosen body. He welcomed the Lord and the servants according to what he saw.

He refreshed them with bread and water, according to his understanding. The spiritual beings, too, responded to his hospitality: out of love for him, they appeared to eat, although they did not eat. It is not the nature of spiritual beings to take food, nor are heavenly beings nourished by earthly things. They responded to Abram's love through the food they appeared to eat, while they themselves remained without nourishment, as was their custom. The Lord and the servants accepted the good servant's love and rewarded him with conception and [?] beyond the course of nature. He spoke with him: “At this time [?] will return to you, and barren Sarah will bear fruit while she is alive.” He accepted his love and rewarded him with the announcement of conception. He also revealed and declared the punishment of the wicked who had trampled on his ordinances. “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come up to me. I will go down and see whether their deeds are as I have heard.” O Knower of all, whose love bears with the waywardness of our race! Though he knows the evil of our inclinations, he delays his anger. He revealed to Abram that he would rain fire on the insolent, and showed that he would relent: if there were righteous people, he would quiet his anger. Abraham saw that his Lord's will was eager to forgive, and he begged and pleaded that he might desist from his wrath. He humbled himself before the Creator in his prayer, recognizing that his nature was too lowly to plead for forgiveness. He accepted his loving petition as he pleaded: “If there are righteous people, I will not destroy the land in anger.” Abram asked, “If there are fifty, will you spare the land?” And the Gracious One went down with him as far as ten. “If there are ten righteous people in Sodom, I will spare it.” Though he knew there was only one, he said, “If there are.” The spiritual beings departed from Abram and came to Sodom, and Abram's kinsman welcomed them as Abram had. The bodily beings lusted shamelessly after the spiritual beings with fleshly desire, when they saw them wrapped in flame. The Knower of all sent them on this condition: that they should be witnesses to the wickedness of the people who had corrupted the established order. Because their base nature had strayed far and corrupted its way, the Good One did not mingle mercy with his anger when he judged them.

With fire he struck down the frenzy of the lustful people's desire, and made the land an example of the wickedness of those who had acted insolently. He rescued the righteous man from destruction with the wicked, and through the one who escaped he showed his mercy, for he loves humanity. Abraham rejoiced that he saw the Hidden One through his revelations; though he was made of dust, he was deemed worthy to speak with the divine Being. His Lord accepted his loving plea by rescuing Lot, comforted him, and rewarded him with conception and a child. The promises were fulfilled, the pledges took effect, and Sarah conceived and bore a child outside the order established in nature. The righteous ones who had waited for their reward received it, and they gave thanks to the voice that refreshed their limbs. In Isaac the barren righteous ones received what had been promised to them, and they rejoiced to see, in the one who was near, the one who was far off. Through a single miracle, the One who knows all comforted them and showed them, as in a mystery, what was to come. In return for their willingness, by which they chose to please him as Lord, he made them worthy to see the mystery of the Hope of the nations. He rewarded the desires of those cut off from offspring: from them would arise the one who gives abundant hope to the hopeless. They rejoiced and were comforted because they saw a hope that would not prove false, which the one who made the promise had sealed with oaths when he gave it. The Firstfruits of the fulfillment of the mysteries among the righteous also confirmed this and said, “Abram saw me and rejoiced in expectation of me.” Through Isaac’s birth he comforted them in their barrenness, and through the mystery of his sacrifice he brought them into what was like a furnace. The Lord called through a revelation, “Abram, [?]! Take your only son and offer him to me as a burnt offering on the mountain.” “I ask you to present a new sacrifice to me, for I know that your love for me does not prove false.” The good servant did not delay in carrying out his Lord’s command, nor did he grumble that his Lord had reversed and taken back his spoken promise. The father rose early the next day, as he had been commanded, and with a sincere heart prepared wood for burning his son. For three days the voice led him along the road, and the righteous man’s love did not waver in his readiness.

The one who had called him revealed and showed him the place of sacrifice. He left his servants behind and took his son, in accordance with his will. He took a knife, fire, and wood to prepare the sacrifice, but did not reveal to his household the secret of Isaac’s slaughter. The servants remained at the foot of the mountain on this understanding: he would go up with the boy, worship, and return. The sacrifice spoke to his sacrificer, the child to his father: “Here are the fire and the wood for the sacrifice, but where is the lamb?” The father answered his child with words of hope: “My God will see to it and provide himself a lamb for the sacrifice.” He comforted his son with hope in his Lord, so that he would not be distressed; and the son, for his part, accepted his father’s words as trustworthy. He built an altar for the burnt offering, arranged the wood, and bound the sacrifice. Willingly, he drew the knife to slaughter his son. O mind, whose love [?] along with the limbs, which loosened the affection that bound it through love for its Lord! O mortal, clothed in the sorrow of fleshly suffering! When the pangs of affection struck him, he overcame his own nature. O athlete who wrestled with himself and conquered the passions of the body through the strength of his mind! The heavenly beings marveled at the endurance of this new priest, who restrained his affection so that he might bind his love to the love of his Lord. He raised the knife to slaughter his son without hesitation, but a voice stopped him: “I do not want a human sacrifice.” The Lord called to him, “Abram, Abram!” He spoke with him: “Hold back your hand from your heir, and do not destroy him. Your sacrifice, together with your willingness, is accepted as though it had been slaughtered. For you have now made your love for me known before the spiritual beings. Because you obeyed my command and did not delay in carrying it out, your descendants will be like the sand on the seashore. Because you did not withhold your son from the knife, to be a sacrifice, I have sworn by my own nature that I will pour out my blessings upon your offspring. In return for the offering your hands presented with an undivided heart, through you I will establish the peace that the transgression of the commandment shattered. It was not a human sacrifice that I desired you to offer me.

Through what you have done, I wanted to reveal in you what is to come. Through a human sacrifice I will establish peace for all, and in the sacrifice of your son I have portrayed beforehand the death of my beloved. Even if your son dies, he cannot pay the debt of his race. My Son, who comes from your descendants, will dissolve the dominion of death through his death. At the end of the ages I will take one from among your descendants and make him a perfect sacrifice that atones for all. In Isaac’s death I portrayed the death of the one who died [?]: he too would die, but his body would not decay in Sheol. In the binding of Isaac’s hands I portrayed the nails in his hands: here in a symbol, and there in reality, in the deeds themselves. Love and affection for his Lord bound Isaac, while love and affection for his race will bind him. In Isaac you fulfilled your love and affection toward my lordship, and in him I will reveal my riches and my love toward all. In Isaac I stamped an image of his death and his resurrection to life, for I will raise him after his death, and he will not decay. A mute ram delivered Isaac at my command, but he will be delivered through the hidden power that dwells in him. I have made you a source of life, Abram, here and there. Through the symbol of the reality, I am fulfilling my promise to you. See, I have shown you the mystery of salvation in the sacrifice of your son: at the end of the ages I will sacrifice one for the salvation of all. See, I have given you a mute sacrifice. Carry out your intention! Untie the one who can speak, slaughter the silent one, and complete your sacrifice. See, Abraham, I have rewarded your love for me: the mystery I concealed from the heavenly beings I have revealed and shown to you. Abram, I am going to clothe myself in your offspring as in a garment, so that through his manifestation we may proclaim the power of my only Son.”

By choice I dwell in him, the firstfruits of your offspring; and at the doorway of his body everyone worships my nature. See, I have accepted the sacrifice of your hands together with your willingness. Go down, looking upon the fulfillment of your sacrifice, which is the salvation of the nations. Abram raised his eyes and saw a ram on the mountain, which a divine command had bound at the top of a tree to deliver his son. He carried out his intention and completed his sacrifice with a mute ram. He rejoiced to see the reality in the mystery that his hands had served. With this expectation the Good One gladdened the righteous and brought them to the foremost rank in the kingdom on high. Through them he promised all who made themselves ready by their conduct that he would give the weary rest beside them, as in a harbor. He honored them with promises of things to come and portrayed their way of life for future generations. He invited the nations from the four quarters to their bridal chambers, to come and rejoice spiritually at their banquets. Abraham was found worthy to be a leader in the kingdom on high, because through his faith he opened the way for the return of the nations. His confession was like the foundation at the beginning of a house, and in him love, hope, and faith were brought to completion. Because the righteous man endured the barrenness of his body without doubting, he made him the father of the nations that resembled him in faith. Let Abram, through his conduct, be like a mirror, and let us examine our soul to see whether it is disfigured by hidden wrongdoing. Let us sow hope and love in the soil of his faith, and reap spiritual fruits that have no end. Let the barren, deprived of the promise, contemplate him and, following his example, obtain a child beyond all expectation. Let those worn down by life travel the road in the company of his love, so that he may be with them as a peaceful harbor amid their troubles. Following the pattern of his wealth, let the rich also acquire wealth and become fellow heirs with him in the riches on high. Let those who possess earthly treasures imitate him and acquire with him heavenly treasures that do not perish. Let his beauty be like a mirror for all who look, and let them acquire love for the poor by providing food in this life.

Let wealthy women who possess much look at Sarah: though she had possessions, she served the spiritual beings with her own hands. Let her humility rebuke wealthy women, for she did not exchange her commitment to Abram for the wealth of Egypt. Let the steadfastness of her faith [?] accuse the foolish women who ask unclean demons for a child. Let the length of her years rebuke adulterous women, for at a hundred [?] years she received a child beyond all expectation. Let Sarah be a revealing mirror for the daughters of Eve, and let them look at her without doubting the Creator. Let lovers of wealth see themselves in Abram, who managed his wealth and humbled himself like a poor man. Let the righteous, through their conduct, be clearly visible images, and let everyone paint an image of their beauty within his mind. In love for our souls, let us bind our love to the Creator, so that he may reward our faith together with his faithful ones.
On the Birth of Our Lord

The third discourse on the birth of our Lord.
Response:
Blessed is Christ, who on the day of his birth made the earth [?] and gladdened heaven, my brothers!

In love and mercy, the Creator wished to give life to everyone, and he sent his Son to bring everyone back to the knowledge of him. The Father's Word set out from the Father without moving away, and came to our dwelling, though he was in our [?] and in everything. His will set out, and in his love he came to those on earth, while his nature remained unchanged in what he was. The God of all did not travel or move away in his nature, for the divine Being has no [?] in which to travel among his creations. For he does not travel by departing from what he is, since he remains eternally what he is, without change. He showed his love to the human race by coming, so that the renown of his salvation might become very great in their eyes. By his descent he honored the lowliness of Adam's clay. For if the divine Being came down to him, how much greater he is than everything! He chose to descend to his corrupted image under the [?] of a child [?], to cast it again in the furnace of the Spirit and renew it. He gave the dust of the son of ashes the title of the divine Being. When he fell and became corrupt, he descended and raised him from the ashes. He called it his image, with a borrowed name [?] befitting his greatness, for everything created is far inferior to the divine Being. His nature is immeasurably exalted above created things [?], and he has no visible form like those made of dust. He exalted his image by calling it his image, so that he might bind everyone to himself, and through the title of his image they might come to love knowing him. The Maker of all gave everyone a share in the honor of his image, and by testing it he taught them to hate wickedness.

Through the [?] he tested his image as in a furnace, and through the trial he revealed the beauty of its rational nature. The envious one saw the exalted rank of Adam's image, conceived wickedness, and gave birth to deceit against the innocent one. The mighty one drew the bow of anger with the bowstring of deceit, and struck him down with the cruel arrow of desire for the fruit. Through deceit he overthrew the image bearing the name of the divine Being, and through his tricks he undid the love of [?] of all. He disturbed the peace of kinship with the [?] of wickedness, and cut off the road by which human beings journeyed toward the Hidden One. Rational beings and speechless creatures became estranged from the human race, and abandoned hope at its fall: it would never rise again. The unclean demons shouted and laughed at his fall, and the evildoers rejoiced when they saw the abasement of the one honored above all. When the Good One saw the humiliation of his image and the arrogance of the wicked, he took pity on his image, so that the insolent would not mock it. His love drew him to have compassion on the image he had fashioned, so that the power of his wisdom would not be nullified along with its corruption. He knew before forming him that he would sin, and his love anticipated him with forgiveness, as the wise do. He foresaw what happened before the man acted foolishly; it was not out of regret that he decreed the fitting course of the road to death.

He looked upon him with the eye of the Spirit before he came into being. The transgression of the commandment through desire for the fruit was revealed to him; the cause of the man’s life was not hidden from his knowledge. No new thought drew him toward saving the man. The mystery that he revealed at the end had been hidden with his being. In the secrecy of his love he was preparing the salvation of our lives. He reserved for the end the great wealth of the power of his ministries. So that, when the heart’s childishness came to an end, it might receive his wealth, at the completion of the ages he opened the treasury of his divinity. He enriched the poor from the treasures of the revelation of [?]. The mystery of the Son [?] and the Spirit had been hidden together with our salvation. Through our [?], all creation learned of the Trinity. Through us the spiritual beings received a new confession of faith. The Godhead is three persons, one in nature. Through us he opened the treasury of his mercies before his creatures. Rational and speechless creatures entered and were placed in the bridal chamber of life. He honored us, at the beginning and at the end, above everything that came into being. He called us his image and made us the dwelling [?] of his divinity. At the beginning he honored us by forming us as the work of his hands. At the end his love dwelt in us and reconciled everything. He did not send one of the spiritual beings to visit us. He sent the Word who is from him and called us to know him. In the manner of a word, the Father’s offspring journeyed from the Father. A word is hidden in the soul, yet journeys and rests without any change of place. His will journeyed from the height and came down to the depth. He prepared a dwelling in the fortress of flesh for the will of his love. The soul and the word that comes from it are hidden from those who look. Ink and a tablet display it to the eyes of the senses. The Father’s Word had been hidden from everyone, sharing his hiddenness. He depicted his will on the tablet of our body, and we saw his glory. It is only by name that the pen depicts a word on a tablet. The word is hidden in the soul, and the mouth expresses it in words. Under a borrowed name, the Word too dwelt in a womb of flesh. On the lyre whose strings are our body, he sang his will. A word is hidden in the soul and revealed through actions. It is wholly in the soul and wholly present to everyone, yet it cannot be seen. The Son is with his Father, hidden in the Hidden One, yet revealed through his love. He is wholly in his Father and wholly in all creation, yet he is not confined. And if among created things there is something that, although it comes from another, is with him and outside him without separation, how much more fitting it is to confess of the hidden nature in the divine Being that he is still with his Begetter and with all creation. [?] of a word, the Only One journeyed from his Begetter. And the will [of his love] dwelt in the womb to save our lives. He did not confine himself in his nature within a womb of flesh. By his will he fashioned flesh and made it his dwelling. It was not his nature that was bounded by a limit; he came within limits. His will put on what is finite and enclosed everything within it. He wished to abolish the sentence of death that lay upon us. His will ascended in mortality to abolish death.

On this condition the hidden one came to us in visible form. Through one of our race he explained to us the power of his acts of service. His will set out and came to his own, to visit his own. As befits the boundless one when he visits his own, he sent his will through a spiritual messenger. He had the angels proclaim new words in fleshly ears. With a sign of peace, his will sowed seed in the soil of flesh. To uproot my errors and sow hope for the hopeless, the angel greeted Mary with peace at the beginning of his words. To undo the bonds of that utterance which pronounced judgment, he mingled peace with grace and gave it to the pure woman. To wash away the bitterness that the evil one sowed in Eve’s ears: “Peace to you, Mary, kinswoman of Eve, who was destined for death. For the fruit that comes from you will undo the bonds of mortality. Peace to you, woman, fortress of flesh, the structure of humanity! For the King wishes to erect an image within your limbs. Await the temple he wishes to fashion by the Spirit’s power, to be a dwelling in which he will live by his will. Without pigments they are painting [?] on the tablet of your body, to reveal through it the authority of his hidden begetter. He will be great, and older and more glorious than all. He will receive the rank and the great name, the name of the divine Being. To him will be given sovereignty over David’s throne, and he will reign over all without handing his crown to another.” Now let the quarrelsome come, clothed in pride, and show us to whom the angel’s words apply. Let Eutyches, the worker of falsehood, stand up with his disciples and explain to us who it is that was conceived by the Spirit’s power. Let the Egyptian, the [?] apostle, come with him too and show us who it is that received David’s throne. Let the insolent men of our own day stand with them too and show us who it is that reigns over the house of Jacob. Stand up, Egyptian, at the head of the camp of your partisans, and encourage the ranks of your armies against the truth. The aim of our discourse is directed especially toward you, because you have disrupted the established order far more than anyone else. From you sprang the hateful [?] of being subject to suffering, for you confined the boundless one [?] within bodily limbs. You, as the shield of the heretics, answer our objection: Who is the one conceived, whom the angel announced in Mary’s ears? If the Word lowered himself to become flesh, what compelled the Spirit to come and complete his conception? Why did he not fashion himself in the womb? That the Spirit and the Father's power descended, and then he was formed. When did he abandon the name of divinity that he shares with the one who begot him? That only now he gave him the exalted name of holiness? Reveal and explain to us the hidden mysteries of your secrets. How did the Spirit form the Father's Word in the womb? How did the Spirit give bodily form to the spirit that has no shape? How did a little womb contain the one who contains everything? How did he cut short the eternity of the one without beginning?

And did he begin to be a new being against his will? Whose flesh was it that the Spirit formed into limbs? Is the flesh his own, [?] is it from Mary's body? Did he change himself into flesh in his own nature or in ours? [?] and explain to us, so that we may know your intention, which inclines toward confusion. If it was his own nature—[nature]—that became flesh in the womb, then the promise he spoke to David was false. And if it was flesh that he formed by his own power, then his own nature remained in what belonged to him, without change. But if he changed himself in his own nature or in another, then he possesses divinity in name and not in reality. There is no time that can cut short the eternity of divinity. And if it can be cut short, it is not divinity but something belonging to time. Far be it from us to say this like evildoers! Instead, let us confess that all that is divine is without end. For neither height nor depth nor anything within them can shake the structure of the teaching our soul confesses. Let us have no other hope in which to boast, except this: that the Word was not diminished in our body. Let those who can speak and those who cannot cry out with us, in voice and in silence, that the Father's Word remains in his own nature without change. He did not change his nature and become lowly flesh. Instead, he took flesh from what is ours and honored it with what is his. His own nature remained in its glory without alteration, and what he took from us he made one with himself in honor. It was not to become flesh that the one hidden from all came. He formed flesh so that through it he might reveal his hiddenness. [?] of the Spirit formed a man from a daughter of humanity, so that in his majesty people might see the one hidden from all. Without the materials of human seed, he formed him in the womb, to exalt his conception above the ordinary course of those like him. Through the Spirit he fashioned him and filled him with the spirit of the power of his will, so that from his fullness he might give life and bring life to [?]. He made him complete and perfect in body and soul, so that through him he might free body and soul from slavery. As a firstfruit, the maker of all chose him from among all, so that through him he might give unending life to [?]. The spiritual beings rejoiced with new voices at the announcement of his conception, and began to incline toward the purpose of peace for humanity. Gabriel sowed [?] good news in Mary's ears: a new conception, not through the natural action of human seed. The [?] virgin bore fruit whose seed was a voice. And the Spirit sang a song of praise on the harp of her soul. She offered a song of thanksgiving as payment for the new conception. Blessed is he who chose a dwelling for himself [?] within my limbs, the maker of all, worthy of praise from every mouth. In my lowliness [?], he wished to raise up Adam's dust. In the first month, Gabriel sowed conception in her ears. And she brought forth the ear of wheat of the bread of life [?]. He grafted the power of life into the [?] of her body, and she bore the cluster that gladdens everyone in the month of Kanun.

At the season when the earth first conceived Adam, the firstborn, the second Adam was formed in the earth of her body. One heavenly being was the messenger announcing his conception. On the day of his birth, many descended and shouted praises. The angel gave Mary a sign to confirm her conception: fruit that blossomed in bodies [?] that had grown old and worn out. "Look," he said, "Elizabeth too has conceived unexpectedly. This is the sixth month in the reckoning of her pregnancy." The messenger who goes before the king has been conceived unexpectedly. And the king has been conceived outside the usual order, without sexual union. Mary carried a great treasure within her limbs. She set out to learn the angel's [?] through experience. A ship laden with riches entered the house of the poor. Suddenly the barren womb grew rich at the sound of her words. The king's citadel greeted the servant's mother. The infant began to leap in the womb before his Lord. O pregnant women who gained understanding from the children in their wombs! O mothers who were taught wisdom by their infants! The barren woman carries the fervent voice that proclaims hope. The virgin carries the fulfillment of the mystery and the hope of the nations. The herald heard the voice of the mother of the King of kings. He rejoiced at her presence and gladdened his mother through the Spirit of revelation. The barren woman cried out [?] before the child conceived in virginity, and said in response, "Your child is blessed above all children!" Who had granted the barren woman that there should come to her a woman deemed worthy [?] to become the mother of the Lord of all? Mary heard that the heavenly being's words were true. She gained hope without any doubt in her mind. She returned home with the gift she was carrying. She waited to see her hope revealed. For nine months she concealed her treasure in the ship of her body. Until she reached the harbor of birth in the manner of infants, she sailed among the waves of slander from insolent people. Until she arrived in Bethlehem as expected, a decree went out from Augustus, king of the nations, that everyone should register in his own country for the poll tax. Joseph too set out for the land of Judah, for the town of David. He took his betrothed with him, as commanded. The earthly king's command gathered people together, to [?] them again under the authority of his rule. The decree for the poll tax became an occasion for life, and had a deed of freedom drawn up for humanity. Through the king, word was heard of the king who had appeared in Judah. People began to write the deed of their lives in his name. A prompting led him [the earthly king] to issue the decree. So that through him he might reveal the sovereignty of the kingdom on high. In the city of David, the promises made to David were fulfilled. The course of prophecy also came to rest in Bethlehem. Labor pains pressed upon the ship carrying the wealth of all,

and she opened the treasury before spiritual and bodily beings. A hidden command gathered the heavenly beings, and they descended and proclaimed good news to those without hope. Their voices became like trumpets, and they proclaimed on earth: “Rise, you who are sunk in sleep, and shake off the weight of the sleep of wickedness!” The spiritual beings [?] to the bodily beings, “Good news for you! Come, receive freely the record of their debts through the king who has appeared!” To the shepherds they revealed the mystery of the one who shepherds all. He taught them the truth made plain in the infant and his mother. Bodily beings heard the promise of life from spiritual beings, and the voice of the promise gathered them to the event. To those of the household they sent [?] and awakened them. To the outsiders he sent his signal and gathered them. He strengthened the members of the household through the promise, and encouraged those far away through a shining star. With those within he spoke through beings who could speak, and made himself heard by those outside through silent things. He sent a star like a messenger after the nations, so that they might come and see the salvation of life among the nations. In a mysterious way he spoke with them through the stirrings of the soul, and through a sign of light he showed them the way of life. Through the very thing by which they had gone astray, he made them wise enough to learn the truth. He made the objects of worship into guides before their worshipers. Through astrology the erring went astray and introduced destinies, and made the heavenly lights lords of death and life. To the star they assigned supremacy and the power to subject others, and it subjected them beneath its lordship through what they practiced. He showed a vision of light to the children of error, which one of the watchers was making move before their eyes. It was not a natural body suspended in the sky that descended to them, but a command that was being manifested through a shining star. A spiritual being was carrying the sign that the command had given him, and he made it shine like a heavenly light for the children of darkness. That the event was indeed not a natural occurrence is attested by its course, which differed from that of the heavenly lights. It alone changed the order of the movement of its course, and lowered its height toward those on earth so that they could look at it. Its appearance and its movement were constantly before their eyes, until they entered the land of Judah, when it concealed its light. Among foreigners it displayed its light and the course of its journey, but among those of the household it drew in its rays and concealed its light. It was not its own decision to move and to cease its journey. The command hid it from their eyes at the appointed time. He wished to rebuke the circumcised people through the uncircumcised nations, as foreigners sought the king like members of the household. Those uncircumcised in the flesh asked those uncircumcised in mind: “Where is the king who has been born in Judah, as expected? A shining star has revealed and made known to us his birth.”

And draw us to him, so that we may offer him loving worship. Those of the household saw the children of error seeking the truth. Though unwilling, they repeated the declaration of prophecy. Through this repetition, revelation [?] to those far away. So that they might come and become chosen witnesses against the unjust. The outsiders cried out to those within and awakened them. Those sunk in slumber stirred at the sound of the reminder from the books of the Spirit. The king too heard the news of the king; he trembled and was alarmed. Perhaps the appointed time of the prophecy had been fulfilled! The news of the king had fallen upon the ears of the Edomite, and he pondered whether the decree in Jacob’s words had now been fulfilled. The foreigner heard that a king was rising from among the dead. Anguish seized him because the words matched the events. The cunning fox saw the tracks of the lion’s cub. He began slipping into the burrows of deceit to hide himself. He summoned the Magi and questioned them with a show of affection. He asked at what time they had seen the sign of the king’s star. He pretended that he was asking so that he might worship. But in his mind he sharpened a sword to shed blood. The Chaldeans heard the promises in the words of [?]. They did not perceive the deceit concealed in his mind. In their innocence, the blameless men departed from the king. The guide that had left them appeared before their eyes. Along with its light, understanding also dawned in their minds. It made them aware of the deceit that the king had secretly devised. The hidden command that drew them to worship the king also taught them the devices that deceit had contrived. They traveled wherever the light of the command moved before their eyes. Until it came and brought them to a halt at the king’s door. The messengers whom the Hidden One had sent entered the dwelling of earthly people. They saw the king in a lowly dwelling and did not doubt. O command that strengthened wavering impulses! They were not weakened by the doubts of frailty. The Chaldeans maintained great discipline in their minds. They did not ask about [?] and the king’s authority. The command placed bridles of silence upon the impulses of the soul. It disciplined them so that they would not stumble through doubt. They ran gently under the mind, their charioteer. They paid homage to the body upon the chariot in which the king rode. They honored and worshiped the Hidden One in his visible form, lowly in appearance. In the bodily form they saw spiritual realities through the impulses of the soul. They opened the treasures they were carrying with their symbolic signs. They presented them and revealed the force of their meanings.
