Through gold they declared the authority of the one who reigns over all. He requires from everyone the tribute of confession spoken by the mouth. Through myrrh they showed that he would first suffer as a human being. And then be raised above death through the power of the one who assumed him.

Through frankincense they revealed the power of his hidden nature, concealed from all. To him, speaking and speechless beings alike owe loving worship. They gave him gold as to a king who rules over all. They offered myrrh, which is very fitting for bodily sufferings. They paid him frankincense as thanksgiving from his creatures. Through a visible sign they gave him praise, more pleasing than anything else. In three gifts they summed up and included all offerings. Each of them, in his own way [?], proclaimed his authority. The three presented three sacrifices in the King's temple. They rose early and proclaimed the Trinity, hidden from all. They completed the course of their proclamation through their offerings. He taught them another route through revelations. Herod saw that the Assyrians had utterly scorned him, and he poured out his fury mercilessly on the children. In the slaughter of little children he [?] the evils he harbored. Because of the infant whom he had heard would take his crown and reign over all, he took vengeance on the children with deadly jealousy. With this intention he took vengeance on the children: that the one who had [?] him might perish with them. The Idumean became frenzied and [?] to shed blood. He raised his sword against the camp of Jacob's ranks. The weeping of infants resounded in the land of Judah. The women were being consumed by the sound of lamentation. Rachel wept and could not be comforted [?] in her sorrow. For she saw her children being slaughtered unjustly. Weeping and lamentation filled the streets of David's town. As the mothers lamented over their infants, the children became pledges of peace through their deaths. The King received them lovingly as firstfruits. Temporal death cut their lives short before their completion. He invited them into the bridal chamber of endless life. They died for the sake of the one who came to give life to the human race. They opened a path for people to travel through suffering to life. They gave their lives for the sake of the Life who gives life to all. So that new life might refresh them in the kingdom above. The bloodthirsty one poured out his fury by killing them. He thought he had gained relief from the arrival of news about the King. Yet the desire behind his deceit was not fulfilled. For a hidden command cut apart the snares of the schemer. The child on whose account the sword had been drawn escaped. He appeared openly as a demonstration of [?]. Mary, who had conceived the maker of infants [?], paid what was due. She presented a sacrifice according to the law for the one who opens the womb. She marked his body with the seal of Abraham's household. So that the great covenant concerning the expectation of the nations might be confirmed in him. Here is a demonstration through which the hidden meaning of the words is revealed. Let us ask whose flesh it was that a human hand circumcised. Come, you [?] who have confused the order of flesh and spirit. Let us see whose flesh was sealed and who presented sacrifices. If the Word changed himself and became flesh, What compelled him to mark himself with the human seal, receiving circumcision in his body in what he had become? In whom was the promise of his words to the righteous fulfilled? How did we nations become members of the household of [?] Abraham? And if It was not a body belonging to Abraham's household that received the seal,

Then the promise to Abram is also false. For Mary gave birth not to David's son, but to the Word. Oh, show us whose body it was that received the seal! Come, learn, and leave behind the pride of your thoughts. Why do you wander along a path full of falsehood? Come with us, and we will show you the way of peace. Why do you bend toward a target that has received evil? Stretch your minds and consider with us the two who became one: the Word and the body. The bridegroom’s friend set this goal before us. Come, let us learn [?] one confession of the soul. The Word had it written that he became flesh, not in his nature. Rather, the Word dwelt in flesh—the hidden in the visible. He said that he dwelt, not that he changed from what he is. For it is not possible for him to become it and dwell in it in his own nature. One can dwell in another in perfect love. How can one, all alone, dwell in his own person? The Father’s Word humbled himself willingly. He made his power dwell in the pure body that Mary bore. It was not in his essence that he humbled himself and came to birth. The will of his love was with us in [?], and he called him by his own name. Mary did not give birth to the essence that is hidden from all. She bore a human being entirely like the members of his race. Hands did not circumcise a spiritual being without bodily composition. The one whom bodily hands circumcised was bodily. Mary is human, belonging to the humanity of Adam’s lineage. The child born from her resembles her in body and soul. Mary is equal to other women in her formation. But her child is greater than all the children of Eve’s daughters. Her child resembles bodily beings in body and soul. He is [?] and more glorious than bodily beings in his formation. His nature resembles that of his mother, from whom he comes. Yet he is higher than she, because his bodily composition did not come from seed. He is wholly human, with the completeness of body and soul. He is also God, for he became a dwelling for the God of all. He is the son of a human woman; the nature of his bodily composition comes from her. He is the Son of the divine essence, worthy of this through the power of the one who assumed him. In body and soul he resembles his bodily brothers. In authority he is equal to the Word, the Father’s offspring. In birth, conception, and bodily sufferings, he is wholly human. In the glorious things that he received and inherited, he is God of all. My thoughts did not conceive a division into one son and another. Let no heretic find fault with the distinctions in my words. I spoke of two natures, distinct from one another. I do not count two persons, as the wrongdoers do. I acknowledge as one the Father’s Word and the body taken from us. When I worship the spiritual one in the bodily one, my mind offers one confession without division. I kiss the king’s garment for the king’s sake. I distinguished the natures because of the sufferings and the glorious things. One who suffers and does not suffer: the Word and the body. Disputes arose over Mary and whom she bore. For this reason I uncovered what was concealed through the distinctions in my words. The divine essence has no ordinary mother of flesh. Why do you cloud the clarity of truth with the fumes of your wickedness? The one hidden from all did not come into a new existence.

He who cannot be bounded holds everything within bounds. Mary is the mother of the second Adam, not of the divine being. Like the earth, she too conceived without sexual union. That command which gave the earth a sign, and it brought forth Adam, itself fashioned an image within her bodily members, in Adam’s likeness. He wished to cancel the sentence that had condemned Adam. He made the guilty innocent and acquitted Adam. Through desire for [?], the first man became guilty and brought condemnation upon his children. Through endurance, Adam gained victory through Adam. Through Mary he canceled that utterance spoken in Eve’s ears. There was death there, but here there is life that restores Adam to life. In Eve’s ears the rebel sowed the [?] of death. In Mary’s ears the angel proclaimed the message of reconciliation. He had imprisoned Eve in the prison of childbirth pains. Through the blessings bestowed upon Mary, he lifted the threat. Because of Adam he cursed the earth to produce thorns. Through the son of Adam he cultivated it in glory, so that it might yield glory. He wished to renew the image that had been ruined by the filth of wickedness. He cast it through the Spirit and presented it as spiritual gold. Mortals sinned in soul and body and became indebted to sin. He freed them through human beings, in body and soul. For this purpose he took a human being from a woman. He armed him with the Spirit to rescue his race from the strong one. Now it is right for us to give the pure woman a name: “Mother of the image in which [?] hiddenness is revealed.” Let us call the child Christ and Son, King and Lord, the form of a servant who became Lord through the one who assumed him. If the heretics stumble because of me, let them argue with him over my calling him Word and body. From him I learned to call him by the names Servant and Son, when he said, “Look, I am going to my Father and my God.” If he is God, how does he go to his God? If he is the Maker, how did he receive a second existence? The Godhead has no God, you heretic! The one who fashioned everything has no maker. Stop your blasphemies! Be silent; do not shout like Legion, the leader of your ranks. Go and rest a little from the battle of your blasphemies. May we never give our allegiance to you, but only to the truth. Neither death nor life separates us from our hope. Light does not mingle with darkness, which is alien to it. Nor does the confession of our soul mingle with deceivers. One confession of one God is firmly fixed in our soul: that he has existed eternally, just as he is, without change. It is written in our hearts that he has an offspring begotten from him. We are certain that no interval of time separates him from his offspring. We do not doubt that there is also the Spirit, a person who is from him, and who is equal to him in everything he possesses as God. We also confess this event that took place at the end of the ages. Who saved us through his Son and reconciled the heights and the depths with us.

By “his Son” I meant the Word who is from him and the body that is from us. One spiritual and one bodily, the hidden in the visible; two in nature, the form of the servant and of the Creator. One in being, who willed and honored his own through his own. Every acknowledgment is fitting for him, the one who orders everything, who wisely led his own to knowledge of him [?].
On Our Lady Mary

Discourse 4, on Our Lady Mary. By the same author; the fourth discourse. To be recited on the Friday of the commemoration of Our Lady Mary. Response. Blessed are you [?], Mary, virgin mother, in whom all creatures rejoiced; the angels and human beings were saved through your child. My brothers.

The Creator wished to reveal the greatness of his love among human beings, and he sent out a proclamation to the heavenly beings: “Let us make human beings.” He created everything from nothing and took no counsel. But when it came to humanity, he said, “Come, let us make human beings in our image.” He made spiritual beings but did not wish to disclose the image of his being. Yet in forming lowly dust, he revealed his hiddenness. In [?] everything, he sought neither help nor [?]; but for dust he asked everyone for help and counsel. He brought creation into existence when it did not exist, but did not call it his image. He took from it a [?] portion and called it his image. With a signet he sealed what he had wisely done, so that through it he might teach the works of his hands to know his name. He wished to reveal [?] the name of his being in the human image: although he is indeed one, there are with him persons who are equal. Through a mystery he revealed to his works the power of his hiddenness, and through a visible image he showed them what is impossible. Through the things he formed, he taught the world only that he exists. But how he exists he did not wish to reveal until now. He kept the mystery of the revelation of the persons until the completion of his work, and taught everything the power of his being and the power that is with him. Before everyone he made that proclamation heard: “Let us make humanity.” The powers above marveled at it, wondering what it meant and to whom it referred. The spiritual beings stood in great amazement as they listened and heard it [?], and they marveled insatiably at its novelty. “What is this new thing that the hidden Nature has proclaimed? Whom is he calling to help him form his image? “With whom does he take counsel, and how does he make the image of his being? How can the work of his hands resemble him? “Who is there with him who possesses creative power, whom he invites to the forming of the image of his likeness? “It seems that he has other persons with his being. Otherwise, what does that saying mean: ‘Come, let us make it together’? “If he had said ‘Come’ to a single person, it would have seemed that he was addressing one. But now that he has said ‘Come’ in the plural, it seems that there are two.” The spiritual beings did not learn openly what I have said. They pondered it deeply: what was the power hidden in the oil? They only heard it inwardly, in a mysterious way; they could not fully grasp the force of its meaning.

This alone did the Creator [?] wish to make known to them: that there was something with him, hidden along with his own hiddenness. He revealed a mystery to them, not the explanation of the mystery, so that when it was disclosed, it would not be displeasing in their eyes. For their sake he sounded a voice without an echo, and for their instruction he extended his work over six days. In six days he completed his [?] and finished his words; on the seventh he rested, although he was neither [?] nor weary. On the sixth day he uttered those words, “Come, let us make.” He made an image and bound together in it rational beings and beings without speech. He skillfully composed his handiwork of body and soul, so that it would resemble both heavenly and earthly beings. He placed him like an image in the world, the King’s city, so that rational beings and beings without speech might look on him lovingly. He fashioned the innocent man like a furnace for testing everyone, so that in its heat he might test the discernment he had placed in rational beings. He brought him into a splendid place and set him there, so that everyone might be stirred to jealousy over him, to see who rejoiced in his love and who was saddened by his rank. Through the honor given to the earthly man, he tested the heavenly hosts and exposed some of them: the gold of their thoughts was counterfeit. He set a boundary for him, knowing that he would not keep it, so that through this he might reveal the evil one’s disposition and will. He forbade him to approach one fruit of the tree. When the evil one noticed, he became envious, [?], and made a mockery of him. Envy blinded the discernment of the ruler of the air, and he refused to look upon the splendid beauty in the image of man. It was not man whom the envious one, agitated by envy, envied, but the Self-Existent One, who called man the likeness of his own image. The rebel insolently envied the hidden Self-Existent One; and when he could not harm the [?], he harmed his image. Like a spy, the deceiver came to the innocent man, plundered his wealth, stripped him, and left him naked. By dishonoring him, he imagined he was dishonoring the Creator’s name. Blinded by envy, he did not know that he was harming himself. He pelted him as though he were a [?] of the King of kings, and instead of stones he hurled insulting words at him. “It was out of envy,” he said, “that the Creator barred you from the tree, so that you would not become his fellow heir in his divinity. “The tree from which he barred you possesses divinity. If you eat, you will become a god like the gods.” The evil one hurled these words at the image of the Good One. He overturned him and threw him down, exulting and laughing at his downfall. The Good One, full of goodness, also looked upon this mockery and had compassion on his image, so that it would not be mocked by the rebel. He disciplined him for his wrongdoing, then turned back and mercifully showed him favor, so that the one who had maliciously overthrown him would not boast. He decreed a fitting [?] of death for his folly, and made his body a fountain flowing with life for his race. Drops of humanity streamed from his body to the four quarters.

And he filled the earth with rational fruits from his limbs. Living fruits sprang from him who had been killed by eating. The enemy saw this, and anguish seized him over the change in him. He thought that if he ate from the tree, he would die forever. But the Good One did not wish his desire to reach fulfillment. The body placed in him a medicine of life from its own life, so that he might continue running with his line of descendants without end. Through the seed that he brought forth from himself, he preserved the name he had given him, so that the name of his majesty would not be erased from his offspring. He inscribed the name of his majesty on the tablet of the man he had formed. When the evil one defaced it, he inscribed it again in Seth, a second time. He said of Seth that he resembled Adam in everything, because the mystery of the continuation of his race was hidden in his body. He did not call Cain and Abel the image of Adam, because one was to die, and the other was to perish under a sentence of judgment. Life dwelt in the third son whom Adam fathered, and the son of Amram rightly called him the image of Adam. Adam’s Lord was destined to take on Adam’s image. From the beginning he established it beforehand in Adam and his sons. He laid his name like a foundation in the building of humanity, so that, one upon another, they might build up the image of the one who was to come. On this condition he took counsel: “Let us [?] humanity.” And in this arrangement he called him the image of his hidden being. He was destined to make one of humanity a dwelling for his love, and he therefore called the human form the image of the hidden being beforehand. From the beginning he placed the name of his being upon humanity, so that there would be no doubt when he fulfilled it in deed. This deed of his had been reserved for the end of the ages. He performed it beforehand in mystery, until he brought it to completion. Otherwise, let anyone who argues against my words say in what respect the human image resembles the Godhead. How, then, can a created and composite nature resemble the hidden One, who has no composition? How can something made be like its Maker? And how can what is limited contain the limitless One? How can we affirm that humanity is the image of the Godhead, since the Godhead has neither limit nor composition? And granted that he is the image of the hidden being, as it is written, where is he, now that he has decayed and returned to his earth? Look: death has destroyed every generation, and they continue to decay. Where is the image, since there is no resemblance among human beings? And if someone says that it will come to be when humanity is renewed, even then humanity cannot resemble him in essence. No, human being! The divine Being has no visible image, nor [?] for those who pass away to resemble the deathless One. Only through love can human beings resemble [?]. And the Maker too, through love, likens what is his own to what is his own. In love he called the human image the image of his hidden being, and in grace he called it by names higher than itself. In grace he gave it the name of his own being at the beginning of time, to portray the mystery of what [?] at the end of time. At the end of time he would confirm for it the name of “image.”

For this reason he portrayed wonders beforehand in the things to come. From the beginning he was [?] toward this fulfillment, and on the strength of this hope he exalted the creature he had formed. For this reason he chose for himself one people from among the nations and separated it from all the others, so that the leaven of life might be preserved within it. For this reason he honored the upright, one after another, so that they might preserve the mystery hidden in their bodies. The righteous, too, agreed with one another on this condition, and passed on and handed over the leaven within them from one to another. Adam gave it to Seth, who was called by the name of “image”; and from Seth it passed to Enoch, to Lamech, and to Noah, who pleased God. Noah prophesied and gave it to his son through blessings. He said, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Shem, who brought peace [?].” From Shem it passed down through the generations to Abraham, and Abram guarded it diligently, more than [?]. The Creator, seeing that he was diligent in guarding his image, chose him and appointed him steward of the treasury of his name. Through him he wished to reveal the great treasure he had placed in his fathers [?], and through him he promised to bless everyone through the offspring that would come from him. For his offspring he established a great covenant that would not prove false, and he sealed his covenant with him through oaths that could not be annulled. This is the reason for the election of Abram and his descendants: that he should guard the treasure of life until it was revealed. Otherwise, let the son of Abraham who hates the nations say [?]: why did the Creator choose him above everyone else? Why did he give him alone the law that imparts life, and exclude the nations from the law hidden within him? If the entire race of Adam belongs to him, why does he choose one and reject another, showing favoritism? It is favoritism to make one great and another small, and not justice, when [?] they are one, yet are not one. If he is the Creator to whom both the people and the nations belong, why [?] is his work as Creator impartial, just as he himself is impartial? No equality is evident in the election of the people if the nations are not permitted to enjoy its blessing. No, son of Abram, do not divide the equality of our race, and do not stir up a dispute between us and our Maker. Your election is the means within which the treasure of life is hidden. Let our mortality be revived through the shoots that spring from you. The Creator chose you for the life of humanity and placed life within you. Why does it grieve you that people live through [?] your life? The election of Abram and his sons was for everyone's sake, so that, like guides, they might show people the way to life. Life lay hidden under that dispensation of the law and was passed mysteriously from one person to another. The promise set out from Abraham and rested in David; from David it continued onward until it reached Mary. In Mary the promise of life completed the course of its journey. It entered her bodily members, rested, and settled like [?] in a harbor. The daughter of humanity became a peaceful harbor for the human race, and the cruel waves of mortality no longer battered it. Like a ship, she carried our entire race in her bosom, brought it out, and set it on the shore of the kingdom on high. A spiritual being descended from on high, from the presence of the Hidden One, and set her on course to sail swiftly to the appointed destination on high.

He dropped good news and new tidings into the ears of the mortal woman, and she marveled greatly at the unfamiliar voice speaking with her. The angel proclaimed a new conception without sexual union, and she accepted it in faith without doubt. In faith Mary yielded to the heavenly messenger, just as the earth had yielded in the beginning to the Creator’s voice. The same command that signaled to the earth, so that it conceived Adam, fashioned the second Adam in the soil of her bodily womb. The same craftsman who took dust without hands formed within her a body resembling that first one. The same Being who breathed the breath of life into Adam created a human being akin to the one at the beginning. In a new way, alike yet unlike, he fashioned Adam, so that Adam might resemble Adam in everything belonging to Adam. His will took some of Adam’s own clay, assembled it, and skillfully made it into a body and soul. With his own hand he portrayed anew that image which death had ruined, depicting it in the same likeness on a bodily tablet. His command blended life-giving medicine into his features, so that he would be able to give life to dead bodies. He built him like a temple for his divinity to dwell in, so that in him he might receive loving worship from all created beings. He mixed something from all created beings into the clay from which he was fashioned, to bind everything together in him in the peace that transgression had undone. He enclosed rational and speechless creatures within the bounds of his body and soul, so that they might look upon him as an image possessing every likeness. He made him a dwelling of love for himself and for all, so that created beings might dwell in him through love, and he himself by his own will. Through what he had done, he revealed his divinity to his servants, so that they might direct their attention to the true purpose of revealing the persons. Through his handiwork he revealed the persons who were with him and had been hidden in him; through the way he formed him, he pointed them out as though with a finger. Through the novelty of her conception, he proclaimed his hidden Son on earth and taught that he has a Son equal to his own being. He gave the child, the second Adam, the name of his own Son, to open the way of fatherhood and sonship. The angel too called him the Son of the Most High, as he had been commanded, so that through his name he might reveal that begetting which cannot be fathomed. He was destined to ascend to the exalted rank of the Father's Word, and beforehand he depicted that rank in his name, before the deeds took place. He was destined to become one with the Son who has no beginning, and he placed upon his head the name of his being like a crown. By grace he gave a crown and rank to the mortal, and divinely exalted his conception and birth. For the sake of all, he chose him from among all as the firstfruits, so that through him he might reconcile all to himself, for he is all. He called him to be the cause of peace and set him between himself and humanity, so that he might reconcile divided humanity through the peace of his name. Gabriel too greeted his mother with peace at his conception, and summoned and called upon the power of the Most High to descend upon her.

The Spirit and the Power together overshadowed his mother, and conferred upon him in full the great name belonging to the hidden Son. It was not the hidden Son who came to bodily birth; it was the son of a human woman to whom the hidden will descended. The hidden will descended from on high, not the hidden being, and dwelt in the womb, not by nature but in love. His will descended to fashion a bodily image, not to fashion his own person, who exists eternally. He overshadowed another to sow life in mortality, not to [?] life from us through being formed. Otherwise, how can he become what he becomes without being emptied of what he is, and thus come into being? A new coming into being is the complete dissolution of the former state, since what is being formed cannot remain as it was. The Father's Son is eternally existent, not subject to time; and if he came to a second birth, he ceased to be what he is. He is without composition and without limit, like his Begetter; and if he was confined within a womb of flesh, he became like every human being. Everything the Father has, he too has without beginning; and if he was formed by the Holy Spirit, he is wholly a created thing. Say that the Spirit fashioned in the womb the one who was in the womb. If that is so, then he is fashioned, not the Maker. No, man, there is no maker who makes himself; nor can the word of his mouth [?], by way of example. The nature that exists eternally cannot turn and come into being, nor can the limitless acquire a limit to its boundlessness. Far be it from me to say that the eternally existent one underwent coming into being! Spare me from affirming that flesh confines the one whom no limit contains. I do not accept something difficult to accept, nor do I assent to the inconsistency of the hidden one being formed. I do not believe that the one without beginning had a beginning, nor that the one who forms everything formed himself bodily. His command formed flesh in a fleshly womb, so that through it he might renew the flesh worn out by mortality. He composed the flesh in a new way, without sexual union, and filled it with the Spirit so that it might give birth to humanity spiritually. Through the power of the Spirit he brought his conception and birth to completion, and made him holy, a holy temple for his loving will. From the beginning of his formation, his love dwelt in him. It did not leave him, nor will it ever leave or withdraw. That will which formed him in the womb walked with him. By the might of its power he overcame all powers and reigned over all. I call him and the power that accomplished everything in him one—one, not as those who divide do, by mixing distinct natures. I call the hidden will and the visible body one. Yet even so, I do not blend the hidden with the visible. I am not unaware that there are distinctions between the one and the other, because created nature is inferior to the Creator. I do not confuse the established order of the hidden nature, nor do I dissolve the [?] of the visible body. The hidden remains hidden, however much you mingle bodily things with it; and the body remains a body, however much you blend spiritual things with it. The hidden nature is not blended with the body except through love.

Nor is the visible mingled with the hidden except in name. In name it is possible to call them one in being, provided that the one who calls them this does not [?] their distinctions. On this condition I have called [?] two one in love: the Son of Being or the Son of Humanity, one person. The Son of God exercised his will in the Son of Man. He gave him what was his and took what was his, but not by nature. By his birth without beginning he honored his birth, and by his authority without end he exalted his rank. He called him and established him in the exalted rank of his divinity, so that he would take the place of the hidden one for the work of his hands. The visibility of the visible image took the place of his hiddenness, so that through his visibility he might proclaim the power in which everything is hidden. Like a trumpet, his visible birth proclaimed to created beings that birth which was begotten from eternity, without beginning. The conception and bodily birth belong to him, without the Father's Word sharing in his bodily experiences. His was the conception, his the birth, and his the circumcision. He was the one who offered a sacrifice to the hidden one for his formation. He suckled milk; knees carried him, and a mouth kissed him. He was the one who crawled about with children in the streets. He grew by gradual stages, little by little. He also received the power of wisdom through the power of the Spirit. He fulfilled the righteousness of [?] the Spirit for thirty years. He paid the debt to the God of all and reconciled all. He was the one who was baptized by John as someone in need, and the herald buried his limbs in a tomb of water. He was the one who received the power of the Spirit in the sign of a dove, and the Father's voice testified concerning him that his love was true. He fasted and became hungry, as his nature required of him. He was the one who seized [?] in the harsh wilderness. His were hunger, thirst, and sleep. He grew tired, sat down, and asked for water to relieve his thirst. His is the visible body that undergoes suffering, and his is the soul that bears the burden of discernment. His is the anguish, his the sweat, and his the prayer. He was strengthened by the spiritual being so that he would not grow weak. He was in the upper room, he was in the court, and he was at Golgotha. He received unclean spit from unclean mouths. His is the cross, his the nails, and his the spear. He bowed his head upon the wood and gave up his spirit. The body— —was his, the one that remained in the tomb for three days; and the soul was his, the one that departed to Eden and returned to him. He lay among the dead without suffering harm, and he was raised by the power of the Creator who was hidden in him. In him was hidden the great power of the Father's Word, and through the might of that power he was strengthened to overcome his sufferings. The Son of God dwelt in him willingly, and while hidden in him, he did not share in his weaknesses. In him [?], from the time the angel brought the good news to his mother; in him by a will whose manner and nature cannot be explained. In him before the sufferings and after the sufferings, without change; in him on earth and in him in heaven, without end. I do not say that the power of the divine Being departed from him:

neither when he died nor when he put off mortality. I count him as one with the eternal Being because of his rank, and I call him one Son of God, not a part. I do not say “two,” as the ignorant man says. I say “one,” however much he falsely accuses me. No, accuser, do not accuse me unjustly as you usually do. You have not heard from me that I [?] a son [and a son] for God. No, insolent man, do not reproach me insolently. You have not seen me [?] off the path. No, quarrelsome man, do not struggle against my words. You have never detected that I have departed from what is right. No, deceitful man, do not accuse me before deceitful people. I have not [?] you, so that [?] the testimony of your words should be accepted. What do you want with me, blinded by senseless envy, that you dispute my words without cause, as though justly? What have I to do with you, contentious man full of quarrels, that I should angrily stir up pretexts for you to fight with me? By your hidden [?], you whose love dwelt in our visible body, rebuke the insolent people who insult you by attributing susceptibility to suffering to you. By the [?] of your being, eternal One who has no beginning, silence the voices of those who confine you within a womb of flesh. Because of you, quarrelsome people shout at us, because we call you by the living name that befits your name. They constantly fight against your life to put it to death; and because that is impossible, look, they falsely put you to death. Those dead in wickedness greatly desire your death, and they do not understand that your nature is beyond all harm. Why do you rage, you who are full of anger, seeking to kill Life? For there is no way for Life to cease to live. Why do you toil to imprison the Spirit within bodily members? For heaven and earth are not sufficient to confine him. Why do you hate the one who says that the Self-existent One does not die? For whether he says it or not, the Self-existent One does not die. Why do you despise the one who exalts our lowly body? For whether he magnifies it or not, it reigns in glory. What do you gain by putting the immortal one to death? And what do you lose if our body reigns with the divine Being? To whom is it not clear that the Self-existent One is above harm? And who does not know that suffering and death belong to the mortal [?]? Perhaps, if the mute had mouths capable of speech, they would have been our companions in this: that the Self-existent One does not die. Perhaps, if those without understanding had discernment, they would despise the one who makes the hidden nature suffer. Come, you [?], judge fairly with those who speak, who conceal the manifest truth by denial. Be ashamed and hide yourselves, if only a little, you who possess speech. Stop debating the suffering of the one who cannot suffer. Be quiet! Do not cry out insolently against the divine Being, lest you become companions of the Accuser in judgment. The zeal of your thoughts resembles the Accuser,

for he too, under the guise of love, reviles the name that is worshiped. Why do you become companions of the wicked, who lack understanding, and estrange yourselves from blessings without end? Flee, you weak ones, from association with the murderer, and come, take refuge in the life hidden in faith. Let us believe that the Self-existent One willingly put on a body from among us, perfected it through sufferings, and through it decreed life for all. For the sake of life he took it from us as firstfruits, and called it by his name, so that it might give life to all in his name. Through a man from among us, the hidden Will gave us life. It is this man who died, was raised, lived, and gave life. It is he who released the departed from the bonds of Sheol and went out to proclaim the new good news of the resurrection of the dead. He died and lived by the power of the life dwelling in him. While he was in death, the living power of his life was above death. That Will which accompanied him did not abandon him, nor did it neglect to help him at the time of suffering. It was with him at the trial, with him on the cross, and with him in the tomb. Yet although it was fully with him, it did not share in his weaknesses. The nature of mortals experienced, in its own sphere, what belonged to its nature, while the hidden nature remained in its own sphere without change. It did not change, and again I say that it did not change. If anyone is angry, let him be angry again: it did not change. What changed was human nature, subject to suffering: it stripped off suffering and put on the glory of those who do not die. It was a mortal who suffered on the cross, apart from the Word; and by the power of the Word he conquered death and distributed life. He was mortal, and again I say that he was mortal. Yet even so, I call him and the [?] one. He himself, at his trial, endured the humiliation in which we were humbled; and through his own testing he learned to help those who are tested. Through his victory he gave victory to our [?], and through his endurance he wove a crown of praise for our nature. The power that dwelt in him crowned him with great glory, and summoned [?] Watchers and human beings to praise him. He showed the Watchers and human beings his glory and the greatness of his rank, and gathered them to gaze upon him on the day of his ascension. He left him on earth for forty days after he rose from the dead, so that through his bodily presence there he might reassure his doubting race. To reassure his race, he showed the nails and the spear in his body, and ate and drank after he had become immortal. The hidden power that overshadowed him perfected him in everything, and when he was made perfect, it raised him to the heights above everything. The day of his ascent was far more glorious than all other days, and splendid was the path he opened toward the heights. Company after company of spiritual beings stood gazing at him, to see how a body could fly through the air in a way contrary to what was customary. The Watchers and human beings saw something new in him, the head of humanity: he opened the gates that had been closed against human beings.

The gaze of all followed him spiritually until he reached the place where there was no possibility of seeing. A hidden command drew aside before him the veil of the heights, and he entered and beheld that imperishable dwelling. He entered the great and perfect tabernacle to minister, and he will never hand his office over to another after a time. Alongside the divine Being he took hold of authority without end, and through all generations he exercises his royal scepter over all and in all. Who would not marvel at the greatness of the divine rank, since he made us heirs with him in his glory and authority? Who would not give thanks for the unfathomable wisdom of truth, which exalted the work of his hands alongside his greatness? Who would not praise the craftsmanship of the awe-inspiring Maker, who bound the world to a single human being and [?] by his name? His will fashioned a single human being in the likeness of an image, and raised him and placed him above everything, to judge everything. He placed him like a mirror in the heights, above everything, so that through his visible appearance they might see the beauty of the Hidden One’s hiddenness. Through his bodily existence he wished to show his love to everyone, so that they would not wear themselves out investigating his hiddenness. In him he set a limit for everyone against investigating what cannot be investigated, and turned everyone’s gaze toward him so that they would no longer wander. In that dwelling he made his body a second heaven, to serve in place of both light and eyes. He is entirely light to anyone who gazes upon his brightness, and any other luminary is reckoned as nothing compared with his light. Within the sphere of his body the Will is hidden from everyone, and it makes him beautiful to behold in the eyes of those who see. The wisdom of truth comes forth from him like rays, and he makes everyone wise through that knowledge which cannot be grasped. There the Master of masters does not teach wisdom; he gives discipleship rest from the peoples, so that it will not be divided. He settles human beings and spirits in a harbor of peace, and they no longer ponder the things over which they labored during their temporal life. [?] the flow [?] of words and deeds comes to rest, and no one asks, “What is this, and why?” No one asks where the hidden, unsearchable One is, for inquiry about him is uprooted from the mind. There the creature cannot speak about the Creator, for the door of the unchanging will is shut before it. It does not question how he exists, hidden from everyone, for love quiets its thoughts so that it does not doubt. Through the visible one it sees the hidden One, though not by sight, and in him its soul’s desire is fulfilled without anything lacking. There the scripture saying that humanity is an image is fulfilled, for in humanity the image of the divine Being is revealed to the eyes of all creatures. There he became Lord [?] in them, in bonds.

He reigns over everything, and everything is subjected to his authority. There the demons who treated his lordship with contempt are put to shame. They bend their knees and proclaim him holy against their will. There the divisive schisms of the heretics cease, for they no longer persist in ignorant passions. There the war they prepared against the hidden One ceases, and there the battle formation they arrayed against the revealed one comes to rest. There they acknowledge two true forms. The form of the servant and that of the Creator are one person. There all tongues confess one person. They constantly repeat one proclamation of holiness to the Word and the body; they constantly worship the body and the Word with equal honor [?]. Understanding that they are two and are proclaimed as one, they see a great wonder there through their worship. For together with the Creator, the creature receives loving worship. This deserves wonder, and the mind is too small to comprehend its marvel. How does creation worship itself in the temple of the body? Who can examine this precisely? Who can say how great it is and what its power is? Only the power of the divine Being can declare how great it is, and he knows it—where he accomplished it with skill. This craftsmanship is his own craftsmanship, for he is the craftsman who created—who created creation out of nothing. He skillfully fashioned his servant according to his purpose; and [?] it had been determined from eternity, including how he would accomplish it. He accomplished it at the end, though he had known it from the beginning. Before it existed, it was visible to him just as it came to be. At the end of the ages [?] his will, perfect in his being, and he poured down his love abundantly upon everyone and in everything. He revealed the great wealth of his divinity to his servants and appointed a human being to be his steward over what was his. A ruler chose one from among human beings as he wished, stamped him with his name, and gave him the rank of king. He called him to judge in the place of his love and stationed him before his creation, to stand in for his own invisible self. There he takes the place of the Eternal One for angels and human beings. At the sight of his body, the gaze rests and inquiry falls silent. This is the reason for the greatness of his rank and authority: to proclaim the power of what is hidden through what is visible. Two very precious reasons are hidden in his name: one concerns his being, and the other his love toward all. Created beings [?] could not see the hidden Eternal One, so he comforted them with the sight of his body, so that they would not be overwhelmed. They were also deprived of divine fellowship. He made an indescribable sharing, entered into fellowship, and brought them into fellowship. The source of our life is exceedingly great and beyond understanding. However much we may say, we fall short of saying what it is.

Even if heaven and earth became mouths in our place, they could not adequately describe it as it truly is. Although it is very great and beyond the understanding of all creatures, contentious people did not even consider it to be anything. Shame on you, heretics! How unjust you have been! You have wronged the Good One, whose love has no equal. You quarrelsome people who never desist from disputes, why are you tearing down the lofty height of the building of truth? You deceitful people, more deceitful even than the wicked, why are you splitting apart the harmony between humanity and divinity? Divinity wished humanity to be honored through what belonged to it. What harm [?] is it to you that human beings have become children of God? The Eternal One gave the work of his hands a share in his exalted rank. What trouble is it to you that they should share in freely given grace? Stop, you contentious people, fighting against this! Look and consider how angels and human beings marvel at it. See the great heavenly beings praising it! They have never ceased to glorify it, declaring how glorious it is. It was well arranged that human beings should become divine. No one can adequately repay with thanks the one who arranged it. It was good that created nature should reign with the Creator. No creature can object, asking why it is so. Do not, then, you witless heretic, find fault with that wisdom which has done well in everything it has done. Come, if you wish, praise and exalt with all creatures that craftsman who gave his handiwork a share in his greatness.
On the Epiphany

Homily 5. On the Epiphany.
Fifth homily.
By the same author, likewise his, on the Epiphany.
Refrain: Blessed is the fountain that flowed over the Jordan! Adam drank, and his thirst passed away.

The Creator wished to fashion Adam as a rational image, and he blended spirit with the ingredients of his lowly clay. First he formed an earthen vessel from dust, anointed it with spirit, and the whole became a living soul. He shaped the limbs in the [?] of visible clay and breathed [?] an invisible spirit into what was visible. O painter, who concealed the power of his craftsmanship and placed the beauty of his splendid image within the panel! Through the craftsmanship of mortality they are beautiful on the outside, and they show those who see them the beauty of their construction. Through the craftsmanship of divinity they are beautiful within, and the outward things are like a covering for the inward things. The Maker of all made [?] a twofold vessel: a visible body and a hidden soul, one human being. The Creator made the outward part from [?], plain in appearance, and fashioned the inward part from the hidden greatness of his power. He placed a precious treasure, full of life, in what was dead and lowly [?], so that it might give life amid mortality through the power of its own life. The inward singer, endowed with understanding, sang on the strings of the body, and its dwelling became beautiful with the sound of the melodies of the living spirit.

The living one sang a song of praise in the temple of his dwelling, and rational beings and speechless creatures gathered [?] at the sound of his melodies. The mortal stood like an image within [?], and spirits [?] and bodily beings marveled at his features. For [?] time, the beauty of the temporal image endured. Wickedness rose like filth over his features. The pigments of his beauty faded [?] through eating the fruit [?]. He took on the color of mortality by eating from it [?]. Sin erased the name of life from the image [?] of the King. She inscribed [?] in her own name vanity and death upon his limbs. The passage of time corrupted and wore him away in mortality. Death trampled him and ruined the beauty of his rational nature. His adversary also mocked and laughed at his humiliation. He gave up hope of ever being renewed from his corruption. When [?] saw that the wicked were mocking the image of the Image, he had pity on his image, so that it would not be dishonored by the insolent. The image [?] the king’s authority through its visible presence. Through its features it displays the beauty of the one who [?] it. In the image of Adam, his Lord’s authority was made visible. Through his features the power of his Lord’s hidden nature was revealed. When Adam fell and death ruined the image of his features, the King sent compassion and mercy to raise him up. He sent two messengers of peace to honor his image. They proclaimed throughout the earth the message of renewal for mortal humanity. Through his creation he revealed to created beings the power of his hidden nature. Through its renewal he showed them the riches of his love. He exalted the renown of its renewal far above that of its creation, to amaze the heavenly beings at how [?] his love was. Through his creation they had been bound from the beginning. Through its renewal he gladdened those who had been sorrowful. His will descended to his creation in fitting love. On the tablet of Adam’s body he painted a second Adam. In Adam’s likeness he painted Adam with the pigment of his command. He renewed Adam and his descendants through the son of Adam. The second Adam came forth from the womb as though from the earth. He resembled in every way that first one whom the earth brought forth. In body and soul the second Adam was equal to Adam. But in authority he is Lord of Adam and his descendants. He is equal in nature, but greater in [?] than all who have come into being. The angel who announced his conception and called him Lord bears witness. In many ways the second Adam is greater than Adam. The rank he attained cannot be compared with that of created beings. His conception is exalted, since it was not mingled with human seed. And praise his birth, for heavenly beings were his heralds. He alone received and inherited the title of Lord. So that heavenly and earthly beings would obey him. His nature testifies that he is an earthly being, from among earthly beings. And the title of his authority cries out and proclaims that he is divine. He is earthly because of his human body and soul.

And he is heavenly because he became a dwelling for the God of all. Earthly beings were astonished and marveled at the greatness of his rank. And the Father and the Spirit confirmed the declarations and showed that he is the Son. He chose messengers from among spiritual beings and bodily beings. So that heaven and earth would become mouths announcing his coming. He also honored the messengers who proclaimed him. And he exalted those who announced him in the sight of those watching. From among earthly beings he chose John, the voice spoken of in Scripture. And he sent an angel, who announced his conception beyond all expectation. That messenger who proclaimed the conception in Mary's hearing, He also informed Zechariah about John. One spiritual being brought the good news of the servant and the Lord. And he proclaimed conception to virginity and to barrenness. The childless old man's turn had come to serve as priest in the Holy of Holies. And he completed his service and heard [a voice], the voice of the angel proclaiming. The spiritual being revealed himself in great glory. And the childless old man trembled and was terrified at his splendid radiance. The angel reassured the earthly man in a gentle voice. He said, “Do not be afraid, for my coming to you is a cause for peace. The Hidden One has accepted the sacrifice of your hands and your thoughts. And he has sent me to you to give you the reward for your labors. Receive fruit in return for your sacrifices and your [?]. From Elizabeth, the barren old woman whose bodily members have died.” The childless old man heard the announcement of an extraordinary conception. And he doubted greatly in his mind, wondering how it could happen. The spiritual being saw that the bodily man was looking to his own nature. And he confined him to silence so that he would not doubt what he had heard. The angel bound two of his faculties: speech and hearing. So that his silence and his deafness would be his witnesses. It was not in anger over his doubt that he prevented him from speaking. He bound him for a purpose: that everyone would believe when it was revealed. It was not fitting for him to boast of the vision he had seen. So that he would not become, as it were, a herald of his own glories. Silence taught his people about the hidden vision. And it reassured them so that they would not doubt when it was explained. For nine months the angel bound him with the restraint of silence. Until the barren womb bore fruit according to his promise. The words he had heard from the spiritual being were fulfilled in deed. And he received the fruit, spoke and heard, and offered praise in return. He gave him his name as he had learned from [from] the revelation. Grace, which proclaims the mercies that show favor to human beings. John went out as a messenger before the King. And the divine command drew him to spiritual training. For thirty years he grew up out in the wilderness. As he meditated on the hidden things of proclamation, a divine sign drew him out of his quiet study. So that he might train himself in divine contemplation throughout his life, he grew up apart from people, strengthened by wisdom. Until the spirit of revelation called him to proclaim, he suddenly shone out like the sun from its sphere. He drew the world after the light of his proclamation.

At the river Jordan he opened the treasury of the one who sent him. He cried out, “Come, sinners, receive forgiveness!” Through forgiveness of wrongdoing he awakened those asleep in wrongdoing. Those who were submerged stirred at the sound of forgiveness offered without toil. His voice became like a trumpet in the people's ears, and he gathered them to [?] the promise of forgiveness of wrongdoing. He promised to give them birth in the womb of the waters and to renew them through repentance, as in a furnace. He cast the net of his words [?] over all [?], and enclosed them within the hearing of his proclamation. Through forgiveness he attracted them like a chief collector, and then explained [?] the reason for the winning appeal of his words. [?] suddenly, and he changed his voice in the people's ears: “I am a servant and attendant of the one who chose me. “I am a messenger ahead of the king of whom it is written that he is coming. He sent me to proclaim that he has now arrived, as expected. “He commanded me to grant forgiveness of wrongdoing through water alone, until he himself comes and gives the Spirit along with forgiveness. “Through water and the Spirit he abolishes mortal birth and brings forth spiritual seed for the resurrection of the dead. “In the furnace of the Spirit he recasts the image that wrongdoing disfigured, and bestows the beauty of heavenly beings on earthly beings. “In the womb of the waters he gives people spiritual birth, and they are recognized by a new name: the firstborn of the Spirit. “He frees the body from slavery to mortality and delivers the soul from the stirrings of desires. “He forgives wrongdoing and gives the Spirit as a pledge, so that his heirs will not doubt his promises. “Look, he stands among you, hidden from your eyes. Even I, who proclaim him, do not know him. “Through a sign he revealed to me that I should proclaim his dawning among those in darkness, so that through my words they might see the light of righteousness. “I am a lamp, not the sphere of the mighty sun; nor can a ray [of the sun] be compared with its greatness. “I am smaller than he beyond measure and beyond reckoning, and I am not worthy even to untie the sandals on his feet. “From the gift of his abundant wealth he gave me a little, and my senses were enriched by the treasures of his hidden love. “My thoughts were deemed worthy of a little drop of the Spirit from him, and I gained strength to proclaim his hidden things. “Revelation compelled me beyond the prescribed order of proclamation, and from the womb I was eager to come out and learn his words.” Although he chose me for the mission of proclaiming him, he did not wish to show me the radiance of his face except through a mystery. I do not know him through the sight of the outward senses. Through the Spirit he gave me a clear sign so that I might learn who he is. The one who told me to proclaim the birth of baptism depicted the form of a dove and showed it to me through the Spirit of revelation.

He revealed this to me mysteriously, as to a member of his household. “The one whom you see receiving it is the Lord.” This is also the reason I proclaim and baptize: to prepare a road along which people may travel toward his revelation. Look, he has arrived, and the dawning of his light is now near. Let everyone cleanse the ugliness of his soul, so that he will not be put to shame. He holds the sword of the Spirit in his hand to test people, and with it he cuts off anyone who withholds the fruits of praise. His word is living and much sharper than a sword. Its searching penetrates beyond the senses into the movements of the soul. He is Lord over all and also the judge of the living and the dead. Through his examination he will separate the good from the wicked. Every authority is placed beneath the dominion of his sovereignty, and his command rules over spiritual and bodily beings. Come, let us register our souls and bodies for him as a poll tax, and offer him purity of soul instead of tribute. O herald, who both encouraged and frightened! The sounds of his proclamation were full of love and fear. Through his name and his voice he scattered mercy [?] into everyone's ears, and he placed the bridles of the sentence of judgment in the mouths of the insolent. He was raised like a rod against wickedness to scourge it, and through his name he proclaimed hope to those without hope. His name means grace, which freely shows favor to people, yet the sword of the word of his mouth was sharpened like an avenger's. Through his name he erased the debt document of humanity, which had incurred debt through sin, and he enrolled people as servants of the one who sent him. His words descended like rain upon the soil of humanity, and he watered people with the word of his mouth so that they would bear fruit. Suddenly he cried out through the Spirit of revelation who spoke with him: “Look, the Lamb who [?] blemishes and forgives debts! This is the one of whom I said, ‘He comes after me, yet he is before me.’ I do not know how to describe him, for he is both older and younger. He is younger than I am in [?] his birth in a bodily frame, yet he is older than I am in the things to come [?] his mysteries. Who is younger than John, you uncircumcised in heart? And how is he older, yet comes last? Reveal and explain it to me. Whom does he call the man who comes after him [?], and whom did he name the living Lamb who takes away wickedness? If [?] came down, took a body, and became flesh, what compelled him to cleanse our wickedness through flesh [?]? Why did he not take away the wickedness of our race through his divinity, without bringing his great glory down to lowliness? Or perhaps flesh possessed a power greater than his own? And was this why he changed himself, to conquer through what is lowly? Far be it! Let us neither say this nor [?] that the power of his being needs the power of lowly flesh. It was the flesh that grew and gained strength through the divine Being; the divine Being did not gain help from a mortal. The divine will [?] the bodily one, and he conquered and gave victory to his fellows through the strength of the one who assumed him. It was he whom the son of Zechariah called the pure Lamb,

who through his sacrifice cleanses the blemishes of his own race. Nor did he again name and call him the man who comes afterward, who at the end of the ages judges and sets everyone free. For his sake he became a harp for [?] revelation, so that in him the age-old voices of prophecy might be brought to their conclusion. The Spirit revealed him to him, and he saw him coming and longed to meet him. He rejoiced to see the hope for whom prophets and kings had longed. He saw him coming to him like everyone else to be baptized by him, and he began pleading that he himself should be baptized by him, rather than baptize him. “I need to be baptized by you, as one who is lacking—not for you to come to a poor man to be enriched by him. You are the spring that gives mortal humanity life to drink. What do you need to receive from a mortal to make you full? You are holy, and through you those whose souls are unclean are purified. How can you seek purification of soul, you who cleanse blemishes? Yours is the treasury of all wisdom and hidden things. What can the skilled master learn from his disciple? You are the radiant one who illuminates everything with the light [with the light] of his face. What use to you is a little flame, a lamp of speech? Yours is the overflowing sea of mercy that washes away wrongdoing. Why do you bathe the greatness of your glory in ordinary water?” “Allow it now,” the King replied to the herald. “This is how it is fitting for righteousness to be fulfilled in me. Allow it; do not reveal my greatness and my honor before the eyes of those watching while I carry out and fulfill everything that is written. Allow me to be baptized like someone lacking and in need of mercy, so that in my own person I may make good the deficiency of the human race [?]. I belong to the very race that became indebted to sin. Allow me to pay the debt recorded in the document Adam wrote in Eden. My frame is made from the very clay that the passions swept away. Allow me to fire its soft clay with fire and the Spirit. I come from the stock that death swallowed and whose life it smothered. Allow me to descend symbolically into the water and bring it up. I belong to the race that became captive to the evil one through its own free will. I will go out and bring back our people's captives from the rebel. My ancestors wrote a bond of death and became indebted to sin. I have made a pledge to pay it beforehand in a mystery. They corrupted and wore out the beautiful image of our bodily frame. I will descend and wash the filth of wrongdoing from its features. In the [?] of water I am casting the likeness of our image, and instead of fire I am breathing into it the Spirit of life. Unless I myself wash away its filth, it will not be purified; and unless it descends with me into baptism, it will not be forgiven. The Creator chose me from among mortals as the firstfruits and appointed me to be a ransom for their lives.” Through me, as through a sacrifice, he wished to reconcile his servants to himself. He accepted my offering and decreed peace for everyone through my hands. And because he wished to do so and set me apart from everyone for the sake of humanity,

I ought to repay the debt on behalf of everyone to the God of all. Through the second birth I prepare the path of peace, and I go [?] everyone who comes through the mystery of renewal. For the sake of my coming, the command chose you and the voice called you, so that I might call humanity to the birth that takes place through my hands. Let me be baptized in the water by your hands, as though in a tomb. I will take mortality down with me and bring it up again. I will now be baptized as someone who needs cleansing, and afterward I will show my power by cleansing the unclean. The herald yielded to the one who sent him because of what he heard, and the priest agreed to lay his hand on the high priest. O John, who ministered in the outer sanctuary, who was found worthy to enter the Holy of Holies, where he had not been permitted to enter! O member of a race that is deficient and needs forgiveness, who opened the [?] that had been hidden from past generations! John did not enter the sanctuary of the high priests; he mystically opened the entrance to the heavenly one. He brought to completion the order in which he had served as priest according to the Law, and began to serve mystically as priest in the higher rank. He left the ministry of baptisms among the Jews and began to follow the rule of atonement for the nations. He approached to baptize the great sea that washes sinners, and opened the gate that had been shut in humanity’s face. The high priest went down into the waters, was baptized, and sanctified them. He endowed them with the power of the Spirit to give life. The Holy One approached the inert and speechless element and made it a womb that gives birth to people spiritually. He went down and was immersed in the womb of the waters as though in a [?]. He rose and returned to life, and mystically brought Adam back to life. He came up from the womb of the new mother in an extraordinary way, and the Spirit descended and anointed him with divine power. He anointed him with the Spirit, not with the oil prescribed by the Law—a choice oil far superior to its companions. The Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained with him, and through a visible sign revealed his hidden nature. Through the dove he showed that he had received all the riches of the Spirit, and that the Spirit remained in him without change in the manner of his dwelling. He depicted a sign through the peace-loving bird: that the peace of all remains in him unshaken. In a sign of peace, the hidden power descended and remained in him, and the Father confirmed it through a voice: “This is my beloved.” He anointed him with the Spirit like an athlete entering the contest, and made a voice heard by those watching the contest. The spectators heard only the voice with which the Father proclaimed, but they did not perceive the anointing in the likeness of a dove. He anointed him in secret, in the sight of only one person, who was ministering. For this is what the great order of anointing commands: only priests are permitted to consecrate the oil,

since, as members of the household, they are admitted to behold the greatness of his rank. John too, as the attendant and friend of the bridegroom, was granted through revelation the privilege of beholding the Spirit who descended. He alone saw the gift in the likeness of a dove, and testified and said that the vision was true and the union great. “I saw,” he said, “the Spirit, the hidden nature, in the symbol of a bird, descending and remaining—the hidden one in the visible one—in perfect love.” The intermediary who was ministering testified that the Spirit descended, and the Father laid his hand upon him through the voice, as a sign of our renewal. Now that the rite of the water is completed and the Father has set his seal, let us inquire who it was who received the Spirit and the name of Son. Who was it who descended and dwelt in whom, in the symbol of a bird? And whom did he call the Son in whom he delighted and upon whom he bestowed his love in full? Who descended into the embrace of the water as one in need? And who was it whom the Spirit anointed in love, and who acquired power? If it was the Word who composed himself and became flesh, why did he not himself anoint his flesh? Why did he not give power to the composition of his body, so that the Spirit descended and strengthened his body through anointing? If he is equal to the one who begot him in love and power, why did he bestow on him a name by grace, as though he were in need? If he is spiritual and shares the essence of the Father and the Spirit, why does he descend, while another bears witness, and thus he is exalted? How does one descend to his companion when they have no limit? And how does one self-existent being anoint another self-existent being who lacks nothing? The purpose of the oil is the greatness of a glorious rank, for the one who is chosen receives a rank through the oil. And if the Holy Spirit anointed the Only Begotten and filled him with the Spirit, then he received anew a rank of great glory. And if he received greatness at baptism through the oil and the voice, how is he equal to the one who begot him and to the Spirit who is from him? And if these things I have said are unfitting—as indeed they are unfitting—then let us inquire who it was who was exalted through the oil. One who is not [?] is not blessed by someone lesser; and one who is [?]—why does he need the [?] of oil? The embrace of the water cannot contain the one who has no limit, and the greatness of a rank does not exalt the one who is higher than all. For he is what he is, and he remains eternally in that very being of his; the nature of his being does not change from what he is. Everyone who is perfect in the true sense of being does not change; and if he changes, he possesses being only in a borrowed sense. Everything that is made depends on the power of the Maker, and cannot endure without the command of the one who established it. Whoever grows greater through anointings is made greater by another; and if he were already great, he would not grow greater than he is.

Nothing in nature loses what is its own in exchange for what is not its own. How, then, did the one who makes all things great change himself into what is ours? God forbid that we should say or think, like wrongdoers, that the Father's Word lost what was his own through what he took from us. It was the one assumed who grew by stages, not the one who assumed him. It was the lowly one who acquired an exalted name through the power of the one who assumed him. The image corrupted by the filth of wrongdoing, through the craving for the fruit, was the very image that the Spirit recast in the furnace of baptism. The potter took a lowly vessel of weak clay and remade it into a vessel fit for glorious things. The Creator took the very nature of Adam's clay. He kneaded it with water and fired it with the Spirit, and it acquired beauty. Our nature had incurred a debt and had also been pledged to death and the Evil One. Through this very nature of ours, the Creator paid the debt of our race. Our self-will [?] spoiled the beauty of our splendid image, but he painted us anew with spiritual pigments. Wicked envy erased our outward images, but now he changed them and inscribed them beneath the surface of the tablet. Our race had been cast into exile like a criminal. But when it was humbled, the voice that released it showed it compassion. It was imprisoned in Sheol, and the cords of death were laid upon it. The mercy that had formed it took pity on its lowliness, came down, and rescued it. It was entirely rotten and ravaged by the sores of wrongdoing. Compassion bandaged it and washed away the corruption of its wickedness. He chose one member from the whole body of humanity and taught him through the Spirit to heal the pains of his fellow human beings. He formed one man anew, outside the usual order, and through him renewed the nature worn out by mortality. He fashioned him without the ingredients of human seed. With the medicine of the Spirit he purified and fashioned him in body and soul. He put him together in body and soul, making him in Adam's likeness. So that through him he might renew the bodies and souls of his fellows, he fashioned him as a pure dwelling, according to the desire of his love. So that through his composition he might bind everyone together in his love, he wished to receive humanity's worship in the temple of his body. And so that he might openly show everyone his hidden power, he raised him for thirty years in bodily life and human companionship. He grew up in the sight of those watching and before his face. After a time, when his bodily growth was complete, he wished to announce the renewal being accomplished through him. He chose a herald from his race and sent him ahead of him. The voice written about in prophecy went out and proclaimed. He gathered and brought in the descendants of Jacob who had been scattered. He told them the news of the King they were awaiting and invited them to the King's spiritual wedding feast. And amid [?] they received the King, though they were unwilling. He called him the Lamb and identified him as the sacrifice that atones for all. Through his baptism he depicted death, life, and the renewal of all. He compared him to a bridegroom because of his love for humanity. He called those of his race who had joined him the bride. He celebrated the wedding through the banquet of faith.

He joined to himself the church of the nations, the holy bride. Instead of purple garments, he clothed her in the [?] of baptism. He placed on her a crown woven entirely with the seals of the Spirit. In the splendor of the Spirit, he displayed her glory before the eyes of those watching. Although he was earthly, he gave him the crown of the kingdom on high. The Father's [?] exalted him far above everyone. Through the testimony, “This is my beloved, who fulfills my will,” the Father cries out, the Son is baptized, and the Spirit descends. Three witnesses laid their hands on him with royal authority. It was a member of our race who was baptized and acquired the name of sonship. To him were given supremacy and the crown on high. He is the one whom the Spirit anointed with power and remained beside. The Father testified about him with a voice declaring that his love was true. He is the one who was found worthy and became a dwelling for the Father's Word. He was honored with the name of the Being who is above all. He too bears witness to the things that happened to him. For among human beings, things befitting a human being were being done. In human baptism, it was a body that was baptized by embodied people. He opened a path for the members of his race toward [?]. The rank and name he inherited proclaim that he is one of the mortals. For by grace he became heir and lord of the heights and the depths. The Spirit he received in the sign of a dove revealed and made known to us that he too belongs to our race, which is deficient and needy. Through the gift, he supplied and made complete what he lacked, and he gave the members of his race a share in the riches of the Spirit. Like every embodied person, he was baptized in material water, and the womb of baptism gave birth to him spiritually. In the name of the Being, in three names, he was baptized and sanctified: the Father through the voice, the Son through love, and the Spirit through the anointing. With three [?] they perfected him in his presence, for the name he received. He grew great in name and deed and reigned over all. At the announcement of his conception, the name of sonship was promised to him. [?] in a mystery through spiritual birth. “Son of the Most High,” said the Watcher, “who is destined from him [?]” It was a human being who received the Spirit in the form of a dove. It was a human being whom the Spirit anointed with [?] power, so that by the power of [?] he might drive out demons [?] and heal diseases. He was a human being in body and soul, apart from wrongdoing. He glorified him through the Spirit, and the body became God and man. I call him by the name “Barnabas” [?] because of his body, and I give him the name “God” because of his rank. One [?] I [?] body [?] Son of God, one in being, which is not split by divisions. I distinguished the natures by the designation “two,” not two sons.

One [?], the Son of the Being and the body that is from us. I call him Christ and Son for two reasons: because he anointed him with the Spirit, and through love he became Son together with the Word. When I say “Word and body,” they are two in nature, just as a body and the soul within it are one human being. The soul in the body and the body in the soul are distinct and equal. Everyone testifies that they are two, yet they are called one. The Word is in the body, on the model of the word—[?] the word within the soul—which is in the soul and outside it without division. On this model the structure of my confession is founded, as I join two distinct things into one complete whole. If the heretics wrong me with slander, let them show who it was that was baptized and whom the Spirit anointed. Let us present the case to a judge who listens carefully, and bring witnesses from the archives of those filled with the Spirit. Let the parties stand opposite one another, as in court, and let the command serve as the legal expert who hears both sides. Let them show in court to whom these things I have said apply. If they are vindicated, then it will be clear that they were right to wrong me. Without quarrelling, let them reveal the meaning hidden in the words. If they are aiming at the mark, then they are right. If they dispute with me before a judge, I am not afraid, for the king’s order puts a bridle in the troublemaker’s mouth. The accusation against anyone who flees from the law is plain, and before the court I pronounce him guilty because of his rebelliousness [?]. I do not depart from the divine laws, nor do I exchange the Lord’s tribunal for another court. Here I stand before the judge who sees what is hidden. Let every accuser demonstrate his charge openly through deeds. Why do they cover the falsehood within them with the appearance of truth? Whom are they misleading, as though they were champions of true things? Why do they boast of the size of their party [?]? Ignorance has little strength before anathemas. Even if they win through disorder, it is no victory, but the coercion of arrogance that conquers by [?]. [?] [?] with insolence against the truth, and brought the truth low under the pressure of the moment before [?]. The shameless defeated the name of justice, though justice cannot be defeated. Justice has never been defeated, as they supposed. They subtly misled them with their words and made them think that they were acting as champions of the truth. They deceitfully wear the skins of lambs [?], but they are wolves in their deeds against the truth. Which of them [?] succeeded in his fraud without being exposed? Which one won in a just trial, rather than through arrogance? Look, the teachers who instructed them were defeated and exposed, and the pure Church drove them outside her gates. The Paulianists and Eunomians have been uprooted and cast out.

The followers of Arius and Novatus became outsiders. The words of the teachers of falsehood also lost their force. What account should be taken of their disciples, barking dogs? I am not afraid of Eutyches, for he aims at error. Nor do I bow before the Egyptian, for he won by the fist.
