Nor do I lose heart before those who inherit their ways, for they are [?], mockers and babblers when it comes to teaching. They cry out when they are thrown into confusion, like Legion, and the voice of Jesus quiets them, as it quieted Legion. At the sound of their disorderly disputes, my thoughts wandered and strayed far from the path they had been following. I set out on the king’s highway to travel in the king’s company, but the noise of bands who feared the truth [?] held me back from my journey. It was not out of fear of their words that I turned aside from my discourse. I was ashamed for them, lest they truly disrupt my journey. I was stirred with zeal against the narrowness of their minds, as unlearned people seized the rank of teachers. Through what I have related, I sought to make the simple heart wise, so that it would not be confused by reports of tumultuous voices. My thoughts painted the king’s image on a tablet of words, and through my verses I wished to display it to the eyes of those who look. I was granted leave to depict the image of the promise in his words: he gave forgiveness to the members of his household through the seal of his name. He pledged and promised the resurrection of the body and the salvation of the soul, and wrote them on the two tablets of water and Spirit. He set up the standard of life in baptism for the armies, so that they might encamp beside the ordered ranks of the kingdom on high. In the water he set up the new pattern of birth from the Spirit, so that everyone who willingly follows that pattern receives freedom. Here is the gift of the kingdom on high, which cannot prove false. Come, let us strive to receive freely [?] the riches of the Spirit. Here the pattern is set before the learners for them to imitate. Let the heart believe, the mouth confess, and the inward movements encamp. Look, the king himself has opened a new road. Come, let us travel along it toward the destination while there is light. Here is an open womb that gives birth to human beings spiritually. Bury mortality in baptism and acquire life. Let everyone hear that voice: “This is my beloved,” and let love cry out to the one who lovingly gave life to humanity. With John, let us cry out with one voice in thanksgiving: “This is the Lamb of the God of all, who cleanses blemishes.”
On Saint John the Baptist
Homily 6, on Saint John. By the same author: the sixth homily, on Saint John the Baptist. Response: Glory to him who revealed the mystery of his will to the one who loved his will. [?]

Until he prevailed, and one righteous man vindicated them. They were worn out by the [?] of their labors over hidden things, until Truth brought them into the open and gave them rest. In the exercise of hope they pondered this hope, until they touched it with their outward senses and were then comforted. In every form they longed for what came to pass, until it happened, and then the course of their struggles came to rest. From one to another they handed down the hope of their promises, until a single revelation concerning one righteous man brought it to its goal. A single revelation brought their revelations to an end, and the voice that silenced the voice of their revelations bears witness. From the heavenly voice they proclaimed this in a lofty voice: “In John the revelations of prophecy came to an end.” The Law, it is said, and the mysteries of prophetic revelations reached the completion of their disclosures through John. His birth brought the course of mysteries and wonders to rest, and revealed and made known the mystery of spiritual revelation. At the birth of the righteous man, grace revealed the power of his goodness and opened a road for people to travel toward the promise of life. Like a [?], this son of old age came to humanity’s barrenness, and people began bearing fruits of praise to [?] the Creator. The Spirit of revelation disclosed the mystery of hidden things to his father, and he gave thanks and said, “Blessed is the Creator who has visited him.” The Spirit gave wisdom to the pure priest, a son of the Hebrews, and revealed and showed that the time of humanity’s salvation had drawn near. Through the horn arising from him for humanity’s salvation, which was revealed to him, the unclean demons who had pierced our race are themselves pierced. On the occasion of his birth, he revealed to us the mystery of the [?] of our lives. [?] He revealed to us the mystery of the salvation of our lives through the Lord of all. He named his son after the compassion that has mercy on the guilty. The name John is a name of compassion that has mercy on people, and his mission as a messenger portrays the image of the King of kings. Like a messenger, the herald went out before the one who was coming, and made his dawning known to those in heaven and those on earth. Outside the usual order, he traveled the path of proclamation, and while still a child he began the labors of perfection. Oh, the perfect one! While he was not yet fully developed in his bodily senses, the Spirit perfected him for the mission of a messenger before the King. Oh, the uneducated one! Though he had not been schooled in the light of books, his mind gave wisdom to the wise and to those trained in books. Oh, the one who had the stature of uncomprehending infants, yet imparted the taste of understanding to people of every stature! Oh, John, conceived naturally beyond the course of nature! Your very conception proclaims a conception without sexual union. Without sexual union the King [?], whose messenger you are, was conceived; and outside the usual order you revealed him to the order of creation while in your mother’s womb. In your mother’s womb you saw the mother of the King of kings, and revealed her to your mother, so that she might bless his mother, the mother of lords. Your mother called Mary [?] “the mother of the Lord,” and through her offered thanks because he had revealed the mystery of hidden things to her. Oh, the wonder that took place among the daughters of Eve! They bowed down to give thanks to the infants within them.

Who had ever seen women pregnant in an extraordinary way, prophesying about the greatness [?] of the infants within them? Who has considered the novelty of the wonder of two women who conceived suddenly, outside the order that ordinarily governs women? The wonder within them was spoken of among the Hebrews, and people marveled at these new and extraordinary conceptions. Against all expectation, the mother of the servant and the mother of the Lord conceived: one in old age, and the other without sexual union. Here, among Abraham’s daughters, what is written about Abraham was fulfilled: “Without hope, he looked for hope.” Elizabeth gained good hope through an unexpected birth, and her offspring became a giver of hope to those without hope. John carried good news on the tip of his tongue and called to people: “Rise [?], take courage, and gain hope!” He proclaimed the good news of life to those without hope and explained the kinds of good things they could not see. Hail, John, beautiful in body and perfect in [?], who became a voice to [?] human beings and heavenly beings! Hail to you, a man who, before reaching maturity among men, became a messenger from God to our humanity! Oh, how wonderful is the account of the story concerning you! No one knows how to recount the various aspects of your [?]. I wanted to recount the various aspects of your conduct before the listeners, but my mind is afraid that it may not be equal to setting your story in order. It is a great [?] to recount the various aspects of your history, and it is presumptuous to climb to the height of your story. Your story is greater than all our stories, we who are flesh, and the quest for you is lofty, in keeping with your exaltation above those who are born. Among created beings, none can describe you as you are, except that one who proclaimed [?] before many. Before many you revealed the mystery of humanity’s salvation, and you portrayed the dove of his sacrifice as an image. The Spirit of revelation drew you into the wilderness for this purpose, and I wanted to know the reason you moved into the wilderness. I heard those who share your service [?] the story about you, and my mind swept me away to listen closely to those beautiful things. I saw the image of your conduct as the fishermen portrayed it, and I turned my thoughts to contemplating the beauty of your labors. Through arduous labors the Spirit taught you how to conduct yourself, and although you were mortal, you portrayed images of immortal beings. The power of the Spirit became your teacher and [?], and taught you an order greater than the order of those arranged in ranks. You became a disciple of spiritual instruction, and it gave you the lofty rank of a teacher. Come, listeners, hear the wonder concerning John, who was brought up without the training of those who rear children. People customarily teach other people habits and disciplines, but this river [?], where there were no people, became everything. The one who grew up in the wilderness had learned discipline better than anyone, and [?] even the wilderness marveled at the wonder of him. He dwelt in the wilderness in great wonder, without consolation.

And like a discerning person, it marveled at the tranquility of his peace. Hail, John, who brought peace to the unreasoning wilderness, and turned and brought peace to bewildered reason! Human habitation resembled a lifeless wilderness and was deprived of the good things that come from loving truth. People were full of the forest of injustice and the thorns of wickedness; human life was being choked, and no one noticed. Nature lay breached, and the law of the spirit was being destroyed; passions and brutish demons were wasting it away. John’s voice plowed the world with a twofold plow, and instead of seed he sowed in it the hope of forgiveness of wrongdoing. Adam’s race had died through excessive wrongdoing, but at the voice of forgiveness it stirred from its wrongdoing as though from sleep. The guilty, children of the guilty, heard the voice of forgiveness and arose to erase the record of the debts they had incurred through sin. Adam [?] a record of debts in the land of Eden, and his sons increased it with the interest of shameful deeds. The human race was occupied with [?] until they heard John’s voice and then became modest. On this condition, the one who chose him chose him as his messenger: that he should reconcile the strife of the worlds, a [?] of peace. For this purpose he raised him in the wilderness, away from people, so that he would know how to reconcile divisions among people. The one who knows everything did this [?], so that through his servant he might [?] his servants toward his lordship. The divine command set peace before him as his goal, so that he would incline toward it with the movements of his soul and the senses of his body. The Spirit clothed him completely in spiritual armor, so that not one of the Accuser’s arrows would pierce him. The Accuser was preparing to fight against his thoughts, and he armed him with the Spirit like a mighty warrior in armor. Like a mighty warrior, he committed himself to the struggle; he steeled himself even to death in the battle against his opponent. The heavenly hosts marveled at his diligence: how steadfast he was, never slackening in his arduous contest. The tyrannical demons marveled at his courage: how he overcame their power amid the stirrings of his body. Through treachery he was thrown into two fierce battles: the warfare of brutish demons and the passions of his body. The demons cunningly schemed to weaken him, and the impulses of his soul did so through the stirrings of desire. Through the Spirit’s power he was strengthened in body and soul, and through it he overcame his desires and the Evil One’s desire. Nature silently demanded its natural dues from him, while demons cunningly laid deceptive snares for him. Two adversaries were fighting against his free will, yet he, all alone, did not shrink from the struggle. He labored through hardships in body and soul, and this is the wonder: though weary and worn down, he fought and conquered.

His bodily nourishment was scant and less than customary, while his way of life was lofty and exalted above that of bodily beings. He fed on lowly locusts and wild honey, and the Spirit’s power sustained him on little food. The power that strengthened the great Moses in his twofold fast established endurance within his soul in the face of its stirrings. The command that gave Elijah strength through food also strengthened him to [?] the passions of desire. Elijah traveled for forty days on little food, but John lived for thirty years on scant food. For thirty years the righteous man traveled a wearisome road, yet as he toiled, the road seemed to him as though it were not difficult. Hail to you, man who travels a road full of danger! The many evils and dangers of the road did not shake you. Hail to the fervent man who blazed with love for his Lord and was not chilled by the struggle for his Lord! Hail to the warrior who was armed with the armor of labors and did not take off his armor, night or day, for thirty years! Hail to the athlete who entered into combat with bodiless beings, while spiritual claws did not [?] the frame of his body! Hail to the fighter who has no equal among earthly beings! Perhaps even the companies of heavenly beings are inferior to him. Hail to the mind that persevered so greatly in arduous labors and did not grow slack through the long, drawn-out, exhausting time! Hail to the limbs [?]! How much weight they bore in their afflictions [?], yet they did not weaken or give up in the struggle of extraordinary labors. John traveled the path of labors in an extraordinary way, and the ways of his life were unfamiliar to mortals. No mortal travels a road like this, and no earthly person has fought in the arena in which he fought. Without companionship, he occupied himself with good meditation. Who would not marvel that weariness did not overpower him? Without [?], he comforted himself with unseen things. Who would not say that the Spirit bound him to hidden things? Where, then, were the violent passions of human beings, that they could not stand against the power with which he fought? How did bodily desire, the fire of both [?], grow cold, so that its boiling heat did not burst out in the bodies of the righteous? Where did the love of money, the spring of evils, dry up, so that its flow did not reach the height of this resolute man's soul? Who [?] bound the love of money, that cunning hawk, so that it did not lodge its claws in that swiftly winged mind? Who stilled the agitation of turbulent pride, so that it did not disturb [?] the steady mind of the upright man? Who put the bridles of [?] on the passion of anger, so that it did not flare up in its usual way to trouble the soul [?]? Who put an end to murderous envy, so that it lay dead within John as in a tomb? The turbulent passions were buried within him as in a tomb.

Although they were alive, they were lifeless in the face of his soul's freedom. They dwelt within his mortal nature as though lifeless, and he did not allow the desire within them to rule over his limbs. They had the power to stir him as a human being, but the power of the Spirit roared at them, and they trembled before it. Trembling and [?] had fallen upon the passions within John, and they were afraid to approach him in their usual ways. He suffered through them as one subject to the passions of his own soul, but through his endurance he rose above their sufferings. Through endurance he overcame human passions. He became changed, and his conduct was like that of someone who was not human. The righteous man lived apart from people, like someone who was not human, until the time came for the appearing of the King who had chosen him. At the completion of the ages, the one who brings the ages to completion suddenly appeared, and he began to cry out that the time of mortality was over. “Its time is over!” the herald cried concerning the world's allotted time. “The time has arrived for the passing of the age whose time is fulfilled.” The son of Zechariah called to sinners, “Repent!” [?] And he taught them to wash away wrongdoing through baptism. The son of barren parents opened up baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and he began to bring forth new people from within the water. The trumpet blast of his voice proclaimed the mystery of renewal, and those dead in wrongdoing stirred out of their wrongdoing as though from sleep. The children of Abraham were sunk in the sleep of wrongdoing, and the voice of the herald, himself a son of Abraham, awakened them. The people, whose understanding was idle, boasted in Abraham's name. The righteous man rebuked them for boasting unjustly in names. “Do not boast in Abraham's name, children of Abraham, and do not rely on a name that is devoid of mercy. “You are obliged to show the fruits of your labors. With purity, repay the debts of love to the one who loved you.” John sowed these words in the ears of the people, and everyone began to blot out the record of their debts. He showed them how to wash away the record of their debts with water, until the one who washes away wrongdoing and gives the Spirit should come. With water alone he was washing away the people's wrongdoing, and he was teaching them about the one who would come after his words. After his words, the dawning that brings joy to all appeared, and he began to seek him and show him to the eyes of those watching. He openly showed the greatness of his rank—how great he was—and how insignificant he himself was when compared with his greatness. “He is greater [?],” he said, “as the heavens are high above us, and I am not worthy even to loosen the sandal on his feet. “He is King over all, and also [?] of angels and human beings. There is no created being that does not worship him as Lord. “The power of the divine Being gave him titles higher than himself. That is why I said that angels and human beings worship him. “It is not by nature that he possesses the title of one worshiped by all. The nature above all [?], so that he might be honored by all.

“I, who am his servant, am amazed at the greatness of his rank. Look, I am ready to reveal the greatness of his rank to human beings. “For humanity's sake, the Lover of humanity honored him with this name, so that he might atone for humanity's wrongdoing through the sacrifice of his body. “Humanity's wrongdoing disturbed the peace of humankind, and he willed, through one human being, to reconcile human beings with the angels.” The good servant proclaimed these things before the Lord of all, and, like a debtor, paid his thanksgiving to the Lord who had chosen him. The Hebrew sowed these words among his own people and prepared them to welcome the King who had appeared. The righteous man set these means before the wicked, so that by every means they might hate the injustice that had made them hateful. He wanted to transform human ugliness through the beauty of his words, and he sanctified the water and absolved them of their sins. The forgiver of sins taught him the rite of forgiveness, so that he might prepare a road for that perfect and good forgiveness. The forgiveness John gave was not entirely perfect, because he could not give the Spirit along with forgiveness. He promised forgiveness through water alone, and showed that there was a forgiveness greater than his own measure. “Look,” he said, “a man is coming afterward who is far greater, who forgives injustice, bestows the Spirit, and gives life. He grants people possession of immortal life, and they no longer fear the changes brought by mortality. By his death he destroys the dominion of death that ruined humanity, and overthrows the towering arrogance of the tyrannical demons. The demons cast the human race into the pit of death, but a human being arose and cast them into the pit they had dug. Satan struck the head of our humanity down into the depths of injustice, but a human being turned back and broke the sting of his bitterness. The gall of his bitterness spread throughout the whole race, but from our own race came a healer who healed our pains. The lover of our race chose a skilled physician from our race and taught him to heal the ailments of his race with the medicine of the Spirit. The divine command gave him the medicine of the Spirit, and with it he healed all kinds of evils in a divine manner. Like the sun, his revelation dawned amid the darkness and drove away the error that had spread over everyone and throughout everything. John’s voice cried out on earth about his coming, and error trembled, and the foundations of the structure of injustice shook. The son of Zechariah made his word flash like a sword, and the demons were astounded at the sharpness of the words of his mouth. As though with a sword, he laid waste the camp of error, and the ranks of truth were strengthened by his courage. The king chose a courageous soldier and sent him ahead of himself, equipping him with a power whose strength could not be overcome. The valiant [?], the son of the Hebrews, took pride in his armor and did not shrink from combat with the adversary. In every battle he defeated the enemy, and the more he conquered, the more victoriously he fought. Without ever having enough, he ran along the road of toil.

And he did not grow weary of fighting against injustice. Night and day he carried his weapons against injustice, and the chill of toil was more pleasant to him than comfort. The righteous man [?] hated the wickedness of hateful injustice, and devised ways to erase its name from humanity. He loved people because of his love for the lover of humanity, and he longed to bind people to the love of their Lord. The good servant’s love was bound to the love of his master, and he awaited that declaration: “Good servant.” John was a good servant to the good Master, and the Good One, seeing the goodness of his labor, marked him with his name. He marked with his name the son of Abraham who was marked by circumcision, and placed in his hand the sword of the Spirit to destroy wrongdoing. Human wrongdoing raised a rebellion against righteousness, and he wished through John to humble its tyranny. The righteous man, who hated wrongdoing, longed to kill it, and never rested from his struggle against evil deeds. He gave himself to the struggle even to death, and he died without dying, for his portion was the hope of the dead returning to life. Through a wicked accusation, the righteous man died unjustly, and his death became a witness [?] to his proclamation. He armed himself against the king, that wicked tyrant, and raised his voice, exposing and revealing his depravity. The depraved man behaved shamefully, and the holy man stood courageously against his wrongdoing. He was rising up against the divine law, which had decreed that the marital union should not be [?]. The wicked man [?] into union with his brother’s wife, and John burned with zeal for the law that had laid down this restriction. For the law he burned with the zeal of the law, like Phinehas, who burned with zeal and rose fiercely against those who committed sexual immorality. The law threatens the sexually immoral through the mouths of the righteous, and continually destroys the forms of sexual immorality through the hands of the upright. Zimri, who committed sexual immorality, he killed with the sword of the law; and Herod, with the rebuke of the Spirit’s word. Through Phinehas the law of the Spirit displayed great zeal, and through John the force of rebuke. There he exacted payment in blood for the wrongdoing of the wicked, and here through a word that was far sharper than a sword. The righteous man raised the sword of his word against Herod, and did not shrink from his authority or the crown he wore. John remembered that saying which David had uttered, and courageously rebuked the king who was bold in sin. Herod kindled an evil sin, worse than all others, by wronging his brother through union with his brother’s wife. The contemptible fool was behaving madly over his brother’s wife, and when the righteous man saw it, he burned with zeal and rose fiercely against his shameful conduct. [?] toward the goal of uprightness, and he exposed and rebuked the deceit before many people. He knew the deceitfulness of the Edomite,

and exposed it beforehand, until he brazenly killed him. The most wicked of all imprisoned the righteous man, and schemed about how to fulfill the desire of his inclination. He longed to kill him and awaited the day of his death, so that, when the righteous man died, he could bring his depravity into the open. Herod and Herodias made an evil agreement to extinguish the light that exposed the wrongdoing within them. The wicked devised a wicked plot between themselves, to silence the trumpet’s voice that silenced wrongdoing. The deceitful laid treacherous snares for the [?] soul, not knowing that when they caught him, they would themselves be caught in turn. The king kept the deceit [?] of his heart for his birthday, so that on the feast day he might reveal the deceit hidden within him. An abhorrent plot lay hidden in the Edomite’s heart, and he was waiting for the moment when he could reveal the wickedness of his intentions. The wicked man held a wicked banquet for his troops, and invited and summoned the leaders of the people to rejoice with him. The wicked man spread the pretense of a dance over his foulness. The foolish woman’s daughter, with whom he was infatuated, came in and danced. The filthy dance pleased the filthy man before those reclining at the table, and he boasted extravagantly in his promises. The fool pledged half his possessions to the foolish woman’s daughter, but she would accept nothing except the one she desired. The wicked woman conceived an evil desire, like someone intent on harm: she opened her mouth and asked for the head of the one who hated wickedness. Oh, you wicked man, how wicked you are, and how obvious your wickedness! You do not shrink from the ugliness of [?] wickedness. Oh, how shameful is the appearance of your insolence to those who hear you, as [?] openly the desire of your depravity. “Give me the righteous man’s head on a platter,” the foolish woman demanded. She did not hold back from speaking words full of crime. A great crime and double wickedness lay hidden in her words. Those who heard her words were stunned, amazed, and bewildered. She asked for the righteous man’s death as the payment for her depravity. And the king, it is said, was grieved when he heard this announcement of death. Oh, the grief that was no grief, belonging to that deceitful heart! It was wrapped in a show of grief while rejoicing and exulting. Oh, the pretense that was cloaked in a show of sorrow, while eagerly hastening to shed blood wickedly! The king’s grief over what distressed him was false, and Scripture did not choose to expose the schemer’s deceit. This is how falsehood knows how to mislead people: under an appearance of goodness, it conceals the fraud of its deceit. The liar spread falsehood over his wickedness and sent orders [?] for the righteous man’s head, as though unwilling. He very much wanted it, since it had turned out according to his wishes, and he covered his wickedness with a pretense as though with a garment. Because he had sworn, the twisted-minded man made deceitful excuses, claiming that it was not fitting. Oh, you wicked man, wholly wicked! That your word [?], or that you shed innocent blood? You deceitful man, in whom there is no place [?], sound and [?]:

Which is evil: falsehood or [?] murder? Tell a lie, you wretch—even though it is wicked for someone to lie—and do not presume to shed the blood of a holy man. The wicked man put on the pretense of oaths like a garment. He concealed and misled, although his wickedness was obvious. Oh, the deceitful pretense [?] of the vile man, who without shame put on grief over an offense full of filth! Oh, the [?] of the hard heart, like stone, which was not softened by a horror worse than all horrors! Oh, the woman filled with shameless insolence, who did not shrink from shedding blood before the dinner guests! Oh, the vile hands of the foul-souled woman, which carried the head of the righteous man, crowned with victory! Oh, the brazen eyes of the haughty woman, which felt no shame as they gazed at the righteous man's blood! Oh, the [?] of the king and the woman, full of insolence, who passed innocent blood around among their banquet dishes! They carried the righteous man's head along with the banquet dishes, and they did not tremble before the righteousness hidden within it. Oh, how justice too remained silent at this wickedness and did not reveal the power of its zeal as it usually does! For it could have shaken the earth and swallowed them up, as it did to that insolent company of Dathan and Korah. For they deserved that unprecedented punishment, and even then they would have been let off lightly in comparison with that unparalleled crime. There is no equal to the hateful crime those vile people committed, since there is no one greater than the man whose blood they wrongfully shed. Among those born, no one is greater or more exalted than John. Therefore, the reckoning for his blood is more severe than every other reckoning. I saw the holy man's blood flowing through unclean hands, and horror seized me: who was overcoming whom through injustice! An unclean woman was carrying the righteous man's head and mocking him: “Where is all your zeal?” On a platter of food, the one who fed the living came in with the food. This is the horror: how could they eat that meal? Oh, the feast mixed with innocent blood! They thirsted for the holy man's blood as though it were wine. Herodias did not thirst for a cup of wine as much as she longed to hold the righteous man's head in her hands. No desire suited her vileness as well as the desire to see his blood flowing on the ground. By shedding his blood she fulfilled her beastly desire, and like a wild beast she [?] his body with her hands and her movements. Oh, the wanton woman, abandoned to fleshly desire! When she had had her fill, she began to eat human flesh. Oh, the contentious woman who fought against the truth! She did not relent until she rested in the faithful man's blood.

Oh, the foolish woman, driven mad by desires, who poured out her bitterness on the one who was drawing her away from foolishness! Listen, women, to the horror that a wanton woman committed. She became a female dog and bit the righteous man's body. [Tremble, foolish women, at foolishness like hers, so that you will not be called Herodias, the murderer of the righteous man.] Be amazed and take warning, women held captive by desires, lest the captor who captured Eve in Eden capture you. Desire for the fruit captured Eve like a child, and she estranged us from the delights of paradise. There is no exile of which you women have not been the cause, nor have we been taken captive by desires without you. Who drove the ancestor of our generations out of Paradise? Was it not the senseless desire of your mother Eve? Who destroyed everyone together in the dreadful waters? Was it not the shamelessness and loose behavior of the daughters of Cain? Who shut righteous Joseph in prison? Was it not the lustfulness of one of you, a woman full of insolence? Who advised righteous Job to utter complaints? Was it not a daughter of Eve, whose advice resembled that of Eve her mother? Who made Samson, mighty in strength, a laughingstock? Was it not [?], whose story cannot be concealed? Who put a blemish on David, whose mind was pure? Was it not the sight of a frail rib from your ranks? Who made a fool of King Solomon, the wisest of all? Was it not the turmoil caused by the loose women who attached themselves to him? Who made Ahab a hater of good things? Was it not Jezebel, that hateful fountain of disgraceful deeds? Control the course of your soul’s inclination and of your eyes, so that those traveling on the road do not stumble along the path of your gaze. Look about you properly, and adorn yourself with modesty, lest you remain outside the door with the foolish women. Prepare oil and go out in the company of the wise women, lest the lamp of your love go out and you become a laughingstock. Do not adorn yourself with the outward adornment of the face, so that those who look do not go astray through it. Look carefully to the beauty of your soul. Restrain your steps [?], together with your eyes, from shameful things, so that they do not call you a filthy stone thrown into the street. Look and understand that your eye and the adornment of your face are a trap, and that senses and impulses are caught by you as in snares. You are entirely a trap buried in the ground before travelers, and no one knows that [?] falls into your traps. The snares of your desires are woven with crafty knots, and it is very difficult to escape your tricks. You resemble a partridge that calls its own kind to their death, kills its companions with its cries, and dies itself as well. Like a partridge, you display your appearance to whoever looks at you, and with your seductive movements you catch the simple like birds. A double death is confined in the cage of your evil inclination, and it calls people toward destruction as though toward peace. The speech of your mouth is like bait set before the naive.

And when they long to eat from it, they die in sin. There is no hunter who [?] more than you at catching people, and there is no bird whose call is as lovely as your seductive movements. You are cunning [?] greatly in the craft of catching people, and no one knows how to recount your tricks. Your inclination is wise in reading the books of the one who kills people, but your heart is foolish when it comes to studying true wisdom. He has been a teacher [?] to you from the beginning, and you have read and studied his writings, sinned, and caused others to sin. Leave off studying the deceitful scribe who teaches falsehood, and come and meditate on the books of the Spirit, which give life. Do not be like your mother Eve, who carried out his counsel, ate the fruit, and brought forth death for Adam’s household. See, hope has been cut off, and death has been slain by the fruit that came from you. Do not make the bitterness of death sprout again through your schemes. It is enough that you killed us by the eating of the fruit your mother [?] desired. Do not put us to death through desire for your body as you did through the fruit. Stop! Do not be a sinful trap before those who look at you, for all regions have become entangled in the snare of your face. If only your face were as ugly as your mind, so that [?] the simple-hearted would recoil from your ugliness. If only you did not have so much adornment of gold and pearls! Perhaps those who love adornment would then pay no attention to conversation with you. Who, then, would put a restraint on your eyes and your movements, and take you away and shut you up in an enclosure with wild beasts? Who, then, would put the seal of silence on your tongue? Perhaps it would stop ruining the ranks of [?]. Blessed is the one who stopped his ears so that they did not heed your words, and became deaf to your wanton conversation. Blessed is the one who [?] is with you, yet is not with you, and lived with you but protected himself from your harm. Blessed [?] is the one who did not lose sight of the purpose of his words when speaking about you, and was not bewildered by the shifts of your frivolity. Who caused this—these things I have said? Was it not the shamelessness of Herodias, which surpassed everyone else’s? Because of this I recounted the [?] of your offenses, to show people how evil the wickedness of women is. The wickedness of women raged and rose up [?] beyond proper order, and I mixed the account of your shameful deeds into the account of the righteous man. The account of the righteous man compelled me to recount the kinds of foolishness—how foolish and how cunning shameful women are. The righteous man’s death called me and awakened me as though from sleep: “Rise, mortal, and see the man who died at a banquet [?].” The banquet [?] of wickedness wronged his mighty deeds, and impiously mixed [?] the righteous man’s blood as though it were wine. He who chose him as his messenger saw his blood being mixed,

just as he had watched Abel’s blood. He said, “The voice of Abel’s blood cries out to me.” Surely John’s blood cried out even louder than his. John is greater than all the righteous who have been and who are. Therefore his sorrowful death is more precious than all other deaths. His death was sorrowful: he died at a banquet full of filth, and the wanton women, the daughter and her mother, mocked him there. The daughter and her mother carried the righteous man’s head and impiously dishonored his dignity. O shameless women, how you raged and behaved wildly and impiously, mocking and deriding the priest who performed two things at once! John accomplished two things at once in his mission: he completed his earthly course and revealed the Spirit. Between the two the herald stood and spoke the truth. He brought one to an end and gave a beginning to the one to come. With the seal of his word he [?] the course of the Law, and opened the book of the spiritual covenant. The skilled scribe among scribes exchanged one book for another, and proclaimed life in place of the penalties in the Law. The scribe who makes scribes wise revealed new [?] to us, and prepared a road before the one who comes to give life to humanity. Like someone drawing a picture, he depicted the mystery of the salvation of our lives. He anticipated it and called him the Lamb because of his sacrifice. Through the sacrifice of his death, death and wrongdoing were to be abolished. He announced these things before the events, as though they had already happened. O John, revealer of mysteries, uncoverer of hidden things, who revealed to humanity that the death of a man abolishes death! O great one, how great is the goodness that was [?] to you, for you revealed the mystery that had been hidden from all creatures! Glorious is the will of the one who chose to make you a man after his own will, and through your hands exercised the full power of his work. Worthy of praise is the one who revealed to you the mystery of his will. Let angels and human beings raise their hands, for he is worthy of praise.
For the commemoration of Peter and Paul.
Fourth discourse [?]. For the commemoration of Peter and Paul. Response: Blessed is Christ, who chose his apostles and filled them with the riches of his wisdom, my brothers.

Good one, who distributed the riches of your love to the members of your household, grant that I may be worthy of a small crumb from your gift. King who clothed the armies in the armor of the Spirit, direct my thoughts toward the goal of proclaiming you.

Skilled teacher, who gave understanding to humanity in its infancy, make my mind wise so that it may move toward your words. You who give life to mortal humanity through mortals, revive my senses to hear the sound of the word of life. Scribe who inscribed the book of the Spirit for bodily beings, let my tongue run together with my thoughts within the bounds of your word. Let the senses and impulses, the eyes and mind, meditate on you, so that [?] they may be kept from occupying themselves with empty things. I ask you for the Spirit’s help, you who enrich all [?]. Give me what is yours, so that with what is yours I may tell of your wisdom. You enriched the poverty of our lowly race, and through you the [?] world became wise and gained understanding. Your voice opened the road of life among mortals, and your command became a guide to us in our ignorance. Through the mission of members of your own race, you chose to reconcile heaven and earth, which had been divided because of our wrongdoing. You chose twelve men from the race made of dust, and gave them the power of the Spirit to overcome everything. Through them you humbled the tyranny of death and the Evil One, and through them you subjected the heights and depths to your authority. Your will hewed twelve stones from the mountain of humanity, and you made them foundations for the building of your love. Through the Twelve, as through the months that serve the year, you completed and perfected the establishment of immortal life. You sent them to the four corners, two by two, and they cultivated the earth and uprooted from it the forest of wickedness. You also chose seventy and filled them with the Spirit of life, so that they might breathe into the face of the world the breath of the life-giving Spirit. And when the heights and depths were revived by the sound of your command, they blossomed and bore fruits of praise to the name of your majesty. The harvest of the fruits of your seed, which you cast upon our earth, was abundant,

but the workers of the Spirit who would gather it were few. Your will directed the servants of your proclamation to implore you to send out workers to thresh your crop. You spread the riches of the power of your gift over every rank, and you invited good and bad alike to the banquet of your love. You chose from among the good to stir the good to zeal for the service of truth, and you called assemblies to give hope to those without hope. Through the righteous you revealed your justice, showing that you love truth, and through sinners you showed the riches of your kindness. Through those who turned willingly, you revealed our freedom; and through those who were compelled, you showed and made tangible your power over everything. The Twelve followed you willingly and through the power of signs, but your command compelled your persecutor against his will. Saul resisted the words of your proclamation, and against his will your command harnessed him to the yoke of your love. He was a zealous man, zealous against everyone for the sake of the Law, and he awaited the payment of the reward prescribed by the Law. He was an athlete who constantly strove according to the Law, hoping to win in an earthly race. He fought in an earthly way in the contest of hardships, not knowing that he could not be crowned without the Spirit. He fortified himself with defenses of the flesh as he went down to battle each day with the senses of the body. Everyone wore ineffective armor upon his limbs, and the will of his soul was hindered from winning. He bore within his soul the great banner of the Creator’s name, and in his mind he honored a single confession of faith. He considered all other acts of worship superfluous, for he accepted no foreign god, but only the One. With this aim he persecuted the proclamation, because he thought it was something alien to the God of all. The zealous man heard the new report of the revelation of the Persons, and he burned with zeal and grew fierce, seeking to avenge the insult to the Creator’s name.

He saw lowly people [?] something new on earth, and he put on armor to destroy them as evildoers. He could not bear to see the name of a human being triumph, while the Maker’s name was praised by every mouth. Zeal set him fiercely ablaze like fire, and he sought to burn the pure wheat as though it were a forest. “Why,” he said, “do they put a created nature on a level with the Creator? And why do they exalt another power alongside the divine Being?” “Why do they offer the worship due to the Hidden One to a bodily being? And why is a crucified man honored with the name of God?” “I cannot tolerate this great insult to the name of my God: people give the name of his majesty to the work of his hands.” “It is not right for me to neglect my duty and remain silent, lest I be accused by the Law that gave this warning.” “Moses revealed to me, ‘You shall have no foreign god,’ and he made clear to me that the [?] of things that come into being are not genuine.” “All gods that did not make and establish heaven and earth shall perish completely, and their memory shall no longer be recalled.” At this [?], the fervent man clothed himself in fierce zeal and persecuted the name of Jesus as though he were a foreign god. He persecuted his name so that it would not become established among the Hebrews, and he drove those who proclaimed him out from among the people. When he saw that the proclamation had gone out among foreigners, zeal inflamed him to block its way among the nations as well. He received authority from the blind leaders of wickedness and went out to persecute the light that had driven away the darkness of error. The zealous man set out on the road to the nations to persecute the light. Suddenly a ray flashed out, struck him, and threw him down. With a rod of light, the Gentle One struck that zealous man, showing him that he was being scourged by the very one he hated. He shot an arrow of light at him and struck his pupils. He took away his sight because he wished to persecute the Light of all. With light he scourged the eyes of the persecutor of light.

He struck him in the face and shook the persecutor of his name. He received the blow, and the sight of his outward eyes was blinded. Suddenly a hidden light dawned within his mind. He saw a radiant one whose light surpassed the orb of the sun, and he heard a voice sweeter and lovelier than all voices. “Saul, Saul,” he called him gently, as one who knew him, and showed that he knew of his zeal against his words. “Why do you persecute me, you who are circumcised in body but uncircumcised in heart? And why do you drive out the name of my lordship as though it belonged to a foreign god?” “Why do you threaten my heralds so fiercely and thirst for the blood of those who proclaim me, although they have done you no wrong?” “Why do you seek to tear down the lofty building of love and disturb the peace that came to reconcile a divided world?” “Why do you fight against the Mighty One who conquered death? And why do you shoot the arrows of your wrath at the one who conquers all?” “It is hard for you, man, to kick against the goads. You cannot wage war with your senses against spiritual beings.” “Your nature is too weak to journey to the height where I am. It does not allow you to ascend to me while you are flesh.” “Why do you persecute me as though [?], inflamed with zeal? And why do you revile my honored name before those who look on?” Why are you zealous for the Law, childish scribe? Leave childishness behind, and come near to maturity. I am not dead, as you imagined, but alive; through me the promised life and the peace of all are upheld. Although I died unjustly at the hands of insolent men, I am alive with a new life that has no end. The living voice spoke these things to the mortal man. Anguish seized him, and he trembled and was bewildered by the voice and the light. Through two witnesses the living one demonstrated his truth to the dead man: through the voice and the light he revealed his life and his authority. Through the voice he taught him that he was not dead, as he had supposed; and through the light he [?] the truth of his proclamation. The zealous man thought he was persecuting a man who had been killed, but he saw him with a crown reserved for him on high, reigning over all. In great glory he showed himself to the eyes of his persecutor, as a symbolic anticipation of the revelation at the end.

He showed a symbol of that glory to the mind, not to bodily sight, for the body cannot see that glory through the senses. The eyes of flesh did not see his very person, but a symbol of the revealed image that is hidden on high. He and those with him were alike in beholding the sudden light, but the meaning of the words was explained to him alone. He and they alike saw the brightness and heard the voice. For them there was the sound; for him, the explanation of what was hidden in the voice. Oh, the wonder that happened to Saul! He and those with him heard a voice that was both hidden and revealed. Oh, the hearing that was equal and yet unequal! One understood, while another stood like a deaf man. They heard a voice speaking in their own language, yet its meaning was hidden from their hearing and their minds. One heard the sound together with its meaning, while another heard a sound concealed from understanding. Saul heard and learned the meaning of what he heard, while to his companions it was like a marvel in the changing sound. He spoke intimately with him alone, in mystery, as with one of his own nature whom he knew would keep his Lord’s secret. The voice taught him that he was fighting against him in vain, and showed him openly that he ought not to struggle against him. He, for his part, accepted, listened, and assented to what he heard, and answered kindly the one who had called him. “Who are you, my Lord?” Saul answered the one who had called him. “Who are you, hidden yourself, while your voice is revealed through mighty deeds?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” the gracious one answered him. “I am the one who died, and the power with which his love clothed me brought me to life. “I am the one whom Abraham’s descendants crucified upon the wood, and I raised mortality upon the cross with me, to give it life through my life. “I am the one who descended in my own blood to the depths of Sheol and released from it the long-held prisoners whom death had imprisoned. “It is me you have reviled as a dead man who died and decayed. Look and understand that I am alive with a life that has no end.” Look, I have shown you the power of my victory in a single act. Stop; do not pursue a power stronger than you. See from where I have spoken kindly to you,

and have not held against you the disgraceful insult with which you reviled me. Enough! You have persecuted me mercilessly through my heralds. Restrain your sword and stop attacking my servants. The fervent man saw the flame hidden in the words, and the fury of his zeal cooled; he grew calm and peaceful. He came down from the height of foolish pride on which he had stood, put on the garment of humility, and humbled himself. He changed his voice from insults to thanksgiving and began to compose mournful words of heartfelt remorse. “Who are you, my Lord?” he said, calling him Lord involuntarily. And the voice, more serene than his own, answered him: “I am Jesus.” “Who are you, whose words sound terrifying and fill the soul with dread, whose command acts far more swiftly than lightning? Who are you, the man before whose command light runs, who scourges those who hate you with whips of fire? Who are you, dwelling in the realm above while your word is on earth, whose command rules heavenly and earthly beings? I did not know that you were in heaven, but thought you were on earth. I did not think you were among the living, but among the dead. Forgive me for sinning by persecuting your name and your heralds, and do not [?] me for withholding the glory that was due to you. Ignorance made me blind to understanding; my impulses grew dark, and I did not perceive the splendor of your light. But now that you have willed it, and your love has called me to know you, I will no longer serve according to the law, but in your love. The law and its observances are left behind: they made me blind, and it gave no reward for my willingness to bear its burden and its heat. Under your lordship my mind serves spiritually, and my impulses incline toward the goal of proclaiming you.” The Kindly One, who had seen him before he came into being, saw him chastising himself more severely than the scourge upon his eyes. He saw that he was ready to serve with him in his senses and impulses, sealed him with his name, and called him his own, a worker of the Spirit.

He saw him chastising himself for the sins he had committed, showed him mercy, and revived him with the hope of repentance. He encouraged him with a promise of forgiveness for the wrong he had committed against him, and gave him the hand of fellowship with his heralds. “Get up, Saul,” he said, “and go into the city to my heralds, for there you will learn hidden mysteries beyond your understanding. Get up, go in, and see those whom you persecuted and drove out from among the people, while the power within them triumphs among the nations. Go to the people you considered misguided, and learn from them the revealed truth of the Creator’s power. Go while the rod that struck you still rests upon your eyes. Show them the sign of my lordship, and they will receive you [?].” It is to them that I have given the key of mercy and of passing judgment. Go and appeal to them, and they will open the door of light for you. It is them that I have made stewards of the treasury of the Spirit. Approach them, and they will receive you at the door of my lordship. The zealous man obeyed what he had heard from the gracious one, and went in, blind, to the disciples, as he had been commanded. For three days he fasted, going hungry and afflicting himself. He pleaded that the light of his eyes might be restored to him. At the end of his fast he was granted a vision revealed by the Spirit, and was assured that a certain preacher would heal his affliction. He showed him a man whose name proclaimed his recovery, and at the laying on of his hand the suffering would flee from his pupils. He also revealed himself in a vision to the physician whom he sent to him, saying, “Go, raise up the dead Saul, who persecuted life. “Go, open his thoughts as well as his eyes, so that with his eyes and his mind he may see the light of my teaching. “Go, let him hear the voice of renewal and refreshment, and the senses of his body and the impulses of his soul will awaken.

“Go, give understanding to the skilled scribe of the covenant, and write [?]; teach him to recite my words spiritually in their newness. “Go, tell the runner who runs the race of the Law that there is no reward in the stadium of ritual observances. “Reveal and explain to the athlete who boasts in circumcision that the mark on his body does not give him the crown of victory.” Ananias heard that he was being sent to his persecutor. He was astonished and hesitated, wondering whether a wolf could be changed into a lamb. He said, “My Lord, I have heard from many people about this man, and how many evils he has made those who proclaim you endure. “How can I go to the persecutor who persecutes your name? How can I reveal the mystery of your love to someone who insults you? “How can I proclaim the voice of resurrection to someone thirsting for our blood? How can I sow hope and love in someone who disturbs our peace?” “Get up and go,” the Lord said to Ananias. “He is not a wolf, as you feared, but a lamb. “He wears the appearance of a wolf outwardly, but not in reality. Although he persecutes, he is not a persecutor but one who is persecuted. “He acts zealously, thinking that he is acting for the truth. He needs only a sign, and he is already drawing near to perfection. “He is a chosen vessel, selected and set apart for the hidden will. There is no flaw in the pure gold of his soul’s integrity. “With the trumpet of his voice he will proclaim my victory to the four corners, and in his deeds he will display my power before the eyes of those who see. “With his words he will dismantle the fence of the Law’s observances, and bring the nations into kinship with the household of Abraham. “With the thunder of his voice he will water the earth so that it bears fruit, and with his sayings he will revive its wounded who have died in sin. “I know how ready he is to endure sufferings, and it does not escape me that he will die every day for the sake of proclaiming me. “Before his love came into being, I had tested how steadfast it was. I know that he will not falter before terrors.” He is a good friend whose love is bound to his beloved, and whose warmth is not cooled by petty things. He is an athlete who knows how to win spiritually, and whose soul’s will is not entangled in earthly things.

He is a diligent soldier who constantly fights the adversary and never removes the hidden armor from his mind. Because I saw how steadfast his soul’s endurance was, I chose him and marked him with the seal of the Spirit, as he deserved. The disciple heard the testimony of the skilled master’s words, accepted it, and agreed that they were indeed true, just as they had been spoken. He took courage from what he heard about the persecutor and went to him, so that he might be further reassured by deeds. He entered and said to him in a gentle voice, as he had been commanded, “Brother Saul, our Lord sent me to come to you. “He sent me—the one who called you, ‘Saul, Saul’—so that through my coming to you, the light of your eyes might be restored.” The sick man sensed the lion of the Spirit who had been sent to him, and longed to meet him, for he heard a voice like that of the one who had called him. The physician, too, saw that the sick man was glad to welcome him, and had no difficulty applying the medicine of light to his eyes. He laid his hand on his diseased eyes and folded away from them the garment of darkness that the light had spread over them. Light had struck his sight, and his light had grown dark. Then the light that had made him blind returned and gave him light. O luminous one, who gives light to everything wherever he wishes, and with his rays darkens the sight of anyone who hates him! O wonder! Though the luminous one gives light to the eyes, the radiance of his light blinded Saul’s eyes. The light deprived the persecutor of light of his sight, then returned and gave him a double light, in his eyes and in his mind. When the physician of the Spirit laid his hand on him, darkness fled, and light returned and brought joy to his eyes and his mind. He saw and understood how excellent the things he had heard were, and [?] them upon his thoughts with the pen of the Spirit. He was baptized and cleansed, and took off the burden of resentments. He put on the garment of kindness that the Spirit had woven. He broke the seal with which he had been marked according to the Law,

and marked himself with the new seal of the name of grace. The persecutor turned around and began demolishing what he had built, arguing the opposite of his former words. From the Law he brought accusations against Judaism and showed how far it fell short of grace. Through deeds he proclaimed the Spirit’s help and demonstrated the power hidden in the preaching. The circumcised people saw the circumcised man attacking their name, and trembled in alarm, wondering whether the time had come for their people to cease to exist. The children of Abraham saw a son of Abraham who had left his people and begun uniting the divided nations in the love of Abraham. The circumcised and the uncircumcised stood amazed at his transformation, and both sides were filled with great apprehension about him. The people were amazed at how he argued against his own people, and the disciples too were afraid of him, wondering whether it was a deception. Through his deeds he demonstrated the truth of his preaching: his transformation was not merely outward but genuine. He truly put on the beautiful garment of faith, and was spiritually adorned with it, inwardly and outwardly. With love and compassion he devoted himself to the service of truth. He put on armor and took his stand in battle against error. He saw that his struggle was not against visible flesh, and he armed himself spiritually against the spirit. The King gave him spiritual armor to fight with, for he knew his love and his desire to wage spiritual warfare. He appointed him as a skilled commander over his armies, for he saw that he was armed against the passions of body and soul. Through his zeal he wished to demonstrate the greatness of his power: if a member of his household conquers through his power, how much more can he himself! He made him wage spiritual warfare against everything. He himself conquered through him, yet gave him a reward as though he were the victor. He set the world on one side and him alone on the other. All the ranks opposed to truth were defeated, and the apostle triumphed. He joined battle with spiritual and bodily beings. He drove away and terrified all the objects of worship, while his own voice rang out. Earthly and heavenly beings gathered to watch him,

as he struggled against all the fierce powers, hidden and visible. He would not leave the struggle, night or day, until the evening of death came and brought his toil to rest. He did not take off the armor the King had given him to fight with until he had devastated and utterly destroyed the ranks of the evil one. He neither dozed nor slept as he sailed the stormy sea, lest the wealth he had gathered sink among the waves. He was always awake, guarding his treasure against loss, and encouraging his companions with the sound of his words. His body and his mind were sound in faith, and with his words he healed bodily pains and the blemishes of the soul. With the clothes from his body he healed sick bodies, and with the breath of his mouth he drove wickedness out of souls. He raised up those who lay prostrate and gave a hand to those who had fallen. He applied the medicine of remorse to the wounded. He called to the lazy and roused them: “Get up and make an effort!” He took hold of those who had sunk low and raised them up through repentance. With everyone and in everything he made himself like others, so that he might give life to all. Through his acts of help he shared in the lives of people of every rank. His love overflowed, and he generously gave out the wealth of his words. He encouraged people of every degree to become rich from him. He left no people among whom he did not distribute his treasures, and no kingdom in which he did not store up the power of his wisdom. He made his voice heard everywhere like thunder, and people gathered around him from every direction to listen to him. The sound of his song was far sweeter than every other sound, as he sang of the Trinity in everyone’s ears. O [?], on which the Spirit’s musician played, bringing joy to spiritual and bodily beings! O flute that played every day without growing weary! Though it was weak, it was strengthened when he played it. O trumpet confined to one place, yet making its voice heard everywhere as though it were nearby! His limbs traveled with his mind to the four corners of the world, and he gathered them to hear the wonder of his proclamation. Through his deeds, his Lord’s testimony about him was fulfilled:

That he was a chosen vessel, selected and tested in the furnace of the Spirit. The Will to whom everything is revealed before it exists chose him and entrusted to his hands the spiritual treasure of his proclamation. He erased circumcision, the seal of perishable flesh, and sealed him with the Spirit so that he would serve spiritually. He changed the name by which he had been known, a borrowed name, and called him Paul, the obedient one, who was persuaded and persuaded others. Through his name he revealed his disposition, which matched his name, and through his deeds he fulfilled his name and his election. In every way he put off the name of Judaism, and in everything he put on Christ, the glorious name. More than anything, he loved the name that had changed his name, and he placed nothing beside the one who chose him, but him alone. He boasted in the name of Christ amid every affliction, and through it he fought and defeated error and those who served it. He made that very name the foundation of his proclamation, and upon it he completed the building of the people who believed in his name. His building is glorious and wonderful, and the height of his words is delightful. No one builds the building of truth better than he does. “I,” he said, “have laid the foundation of truth like a wise builder. Let everyone see how he builds toward its completion.” O builder who laid the foundation of faith, and upon it, as upon roots, established and built hope and love! O athlete who entered the contest against everything, and everything was defeated by the endurance of his faith! O warrior who was spiritually armed, who fought and directed his movements toward Christ, the goal! Who is capable of recounting in words the victory of your labors? Who can portray your beauties in writing? No mind can reach the height of your labors except one that imitates you in its senses and impulses. No one ascends to where you ascended, as you yourself said, unless he puts off mortality through the mystery of your way of life.

The summons drew you to the third heaven and spoke with you words that are hidden and cannot be spoken by a tongue of flesh. O man of flesh, who flew through the air while still in the flesh! O mortal, who was found worthy of the voice of the immortals! O you who were honored with glorious things higher than yourself, yet humbled yourself as though unaware that you had been found worthy of anything! O traveler who reached Eden without walking, and heard a voice that, though spoken, cannot be spoken! What have you said, chosen Paul? It is difficult to fathom. How does someone hear when it is not permitted [?]? Reveal to us openly what you have said, for it is difficult to understand. With what senses were you found worthy to listen to it, you alone? If it is not permitted to be spoken, why was it spoken? And if it was spoken, then it is permitted to listen to its sound. If you were found worthy to hear something that cannot be spoken, then you also received the meaning of what you heard. “Yes,” he says, “I heard and learned the force of what I heard. But it is difficult for people of flesh—for people of flesh—to hear in this way. “Even I, who heard it, did not hear with the senses of the flesh, but through the mystery of the speech possessed by the immortals. “Through the mystery of that voice with which they offer praise in that ordered realm, I heard what I heard, not through the body. “In the spirit I mysteriously heard the assemblies on high, who were spiritually praising the power of the divine Being. “Glorious and wonderful was the sound of the melodies of their praises, and the mind could never hear enough of that sweetness. “The ear of flesh could not take in that sound, nor could the tongue speak as they spoke. “Something new happened to me alone, though not for my own sake: I was found worthy to see that ordered realm in a mysterious way. “He wished to show the riches of his mercy in me first, so that through my hands he might give good hope to mortal humanity.

“On this condition I was found worthy of things higher than mortals, so that through me the human race might take courage in the hope of life. “For this reason the divine command drew me as far as Eden, so that I might go and see, and bring back good news of that ordered realm. “I knew that I went, but how I went I do not know, because the divine command did not wish to disclose to me how I went. “He did not wish to reveal to me whether my limbs traveled along with my soul. This too he did wisely, so that I might know my own nature. “He wished to show me things beyond the ordinary order, as to a close friend; but so that I would not forget my lowly nature, he withheld this knowledge from me. “That I heard a voice and its meaning is certain to me; but whether I was there in body and spirit, I do not know. “And if this eluded even me, who heard those things, who is left in doubt—the one who asks how I went? “I went and reached the place I have spoken of: believe it and hold it firm. And do not doubt that I heard the things I have recounted. “It was not boastfulness that urged me to recount the praise of my labors. The jealousy of fools compelled me to boast of things higher than myself. “For this reason I wished to disclose the things I saw: to give those without hope a hope in the blessings of the world beyond.” Who would not love the teaching of Paul, who heard and persuaded others, and did not hold back or deprive his companions of what he heard? Who would not study the books containing the words of the Spirit’s scribe, who explained hidden mysteries and brought them to light before his disciples? Who would not set the goal of his teaching before his mind—he who directed his movements and his limbs toward victory? Who would not polish away his soul’s ugliness through the beauty of his words, and see his own blemishes in the mirror of Paul’s virtues? Who would not build upon his confession of faith, against which the winds of harsh suffering blew without shaking it? Who would not put on the armor of the Spirit in his ranks—he who never slackened in the struggle until death? Who would not walk on the path of the one who [?] on the path toward the heights, who reached and arrived at the heights without discouragement? Who would not bind the movements of his soul with Paul’s faith?

And he committed hope to writing and taught a love that does not decay. How can anyone who reads his writings escape without repaying him, even with words in place of deeds? How can anyone be running toward his goal without offering him the crown of victory, as he deserves? Who has fought in the contest of truth like Paul, and who has deserved the crown of glory more than he? Who has gained wisdom in spiritual things like his mind, and who has spoken about things to come as he has written? Who has matched the goal that the King set, and who has bent toward victory as he did? Who labored as he did, without expense, and took no wages or human provisions? Who has run in the spiritual stadium without his soul’s desire becoming entangled in earthly things? He hired himself out for the work of the Spirit in the morning, and at the end of his life reckoned his toil as a single day. He began the race of preaching in his youth, and completed his course in chains and in his old age. Paul, an old man and also a prisoner for the truth, what mouth can describe you as you are? The mind is too limited to run swiftly beside you, and its wing is too weak to fly to you, to where you are. Only one knows how to award you the crown of victory: the one whom you loved above everything, as befits him. The will that chose you can reward your love—the one to whom everyone’s labors are visible before anything comes to be. His loving affection loved and cherished you and called you his own. He gave you strength to conquer through his power as though it were your own. It was not yours to conquer the passions without his strength, for mortal nature is far too weak to conquer by its own power.

It was not yours to learn the mysteries of hidden things, for created beings have no power to comprehend what is concealed. He revealed his love to you as to a friend whose love is true, and he disclosed to you the power of hidden things that are beyond you. He showed us your faithfulness through the money he gave you to trade with, and entrusted the treasury of his mercies to your hands as to someone trustworthy. Your love is faithful, and marvelous is the treasure entrusted to your hands. No one knows how to administer it better than you. You proclaimed the name of the divine Being in everyone's hearing, and you made known the equality of the Father and the Spirit. You made known that the Son is not younger than the one who begot him, nor is the Spirit less than the Father and the Son who comes from him. You taught us that the Self-existent One is not limited in his own being, and you showed us that he is not subject to suffering. Through the Spirit of revelation, you revealed the mystery of our salvation, which fulfilled and accomplished the hidden will in the visible reality of our body. On the harp of your soul, he sang of the distinction between two forms: the form of the servant and that of the Maker, hidden and revealed. Your tongue became like a pen in the Spirit's hand, and it traced letters in the human mind: the Word and the flesh. Your voice proclaimed the Word and the flesh among mortals: two, distinct in their natures and united together. They are distinct and united, hidden and revealed, and are called one: the Son of God, who joined to himself the man he assumed. Paul did not introduce a distinction between one son and another. Do not stumble, heretic, over the distinctions in his words. He distinguished the natures because they are distinct from one another, and brought them together in unity into one person. He distinguished them on account of the sufferings and the glorious deeds, and united them because of the love that admits no division. He differentiated them without splitting them apart from each other, and united them through the will that desired this.

He assigned to each what belongs to it, according to what it is, so that the Self-existent One would not be brought down to suffering by assuming what is ours. He gave the Most High a share in weaknesses through a borrowed name, and the lowly one a share in glorious deeds through the deeds themselves. If Paul, whom the Spirit chose, distinguished and united, who can dispute [?], heretic, with the chosen vessel? Paul has spoken. Who has authority to find fault with Paul? The Spirit who chose him condemns anyone who finds fault. Be silent, then, heretic, and do not dispute, lest you be condemned by the Spirit's harsh sentence. Be silent! Do not shout against the faithful, you workers of falsehood. You have disturbed people's peace enough with your disputes. I am convinced that you greatly hate the name of Paul, and I am not unaware that you find no comfort in the distinctions in his words. The medicine of his words makes the wound within you sting badly, and for this reason you hate him as a stranger. The enemy of humanity has blinded the eye of your minds, so that you cannot gaze upon the light hidden within his words. He made you drink the turbid cup of the gall of his wrath, and through you he disturbed the serenity of the peace that brought peace to all. He taught you to ascend to the heights, to the divine Being, and he showed you the hateful path of susceptibility to suffering. He alienated you from attention to Paul's words, because he saw that Paul proclaimed that the hidden nature cannot be circumscribed. It was his own device, which he discovered and taught to those who resemble him: to make the hidden one suffer and deprive the body of exaltation. In this, [?], he accomplished his will through your words and disrupted the orders that the Spirit had established through the heralds. He concealed his deceit in you as in a garment, and entered and hid within the flock as though he were trustworthy. He sent you like spies to the members of the household, and through [?] he dishonored the proclamation, like captors. Through you he avenged the disgrace of being mocked by the truthful, for you tore apart the sound body of the faith. Let us learn this from your hatred toward Paul: you have armed yourselves with cunning schemes against his words.

Oh, the impudence of the heretics and the devil, who all strive to disrupt the orders established by the Spirit! The insolent have committed a great crime together with the rebel: they have trampled on pure holiness and treated it with contempt through their blasphemies. For your own sake, O King who redeemed our race, have mercy on our race, which, after being freed, has turned back and become enslaved to the bondage of death. People have abandoned the path of your love, which is full of peace, and traveled along a path full of the danger of discord. They hated the heralds who proclaimed truth and faith, and loved the deceitful falsehood that the evil one brought forth. The name of Paul and his companions, the workers of the Spirit, is abandoned, while everyone weaves a crown of victories for the workers of deceit. No one brings testimony from the words of the truthful, for the fabrication of error has become firmly established in the minds of fools. If someone repeats a saying of Paul or of Christ, its sound is foreign and is not welcomed by the ears of the indolent. They have come to hate intensely the study of the words in the Scriptures, and the insolent consider attention to them superfluous. They say, "It is not good to study glorious things too much, lest the heart go astray through studying the words of the Spirit. Attention to words teaches inquiry and distracts the soul, and the mind becomes drunk on contradictions as though on wine. Moreover, the wise man cried, 'Do not eat too much honey.' See, they say, he showed that you should not hunger greedily for what is written. And the servant who knows his master's will and does not act accordingly receives severe lashes from him, because he knew and acted unjustly." Such is the teaching of the foolish master to his disciples: he traced the letters and taught them to recite them from Taw to Aleph. Such is the deceitful scribe's interpretation for his hearers: he kept them in darkness, away from knowledge of the word of life. Such is the murderer's bitter poison, which he cast among people, leading them astray from the path of the words of the Spirit. The Spirit opened the path of life through the mouths of the heralds, but the enemy, in his cunning, filled it with obstacles before the travelers. He instilled fear and frightened them away from learning, saying, “Do not travel along the path of the Scriptures, lest you go astray.” Come, herald, chosen vessel who proclaimed the truth! See the schemes that the Evil One has devised against your words.

Come, teach us from the wisdom that the Spirit placed in you, so that through it we may demolish the false structure that the deceiver built. Speak through us, so that we may repeat your words to the wrongdoers who have gravely wronged you through their slanderous insults. From the treasury of your writings, rebuke them, and through your sayings let us expose the falseness of their ideas. Let us repeat your words: “Every book written by the Spirit brings life-giving benefit to the person who labors to study it.” It makes the person who [?] it perfect and complete, and he becomes fit to serve spiritually. Come, falsifiers! See the benefit of the Spirit’s words: they perfect a person in spiritual things and give life. Let us also repeat what you used to impress upon your disciple: “From your childhood, the Scriptures have taught you the way of life.” Be ashamed and be silenced, you who hate the study of the Spirit’s teachings, at the words of the accomplished teacher to his disciple. Do not falsely find fault with the structure of his words, which is strengthened by the Spirit’s power and wisely built. The Spirit testifies that his structure is well constructed, and he himself rebukes the false structure of your ideas. Let the Spirit be the advocate in the case between me and you; his command exposes the hidden deceit of their thoughts. He himself will rebuke you because you have wronged his loving labor: he stood in the contest, won, and brought victory to his companions. Ah, you difficult people, who find such difficulty in what is clear! What light is as wondrous in its dawning as the name of Paul? What road is as easy to travel as his sayings? And who [?] along the path of his delightful words? What blessings are not stored up and hidden in his name! Whenever someone opens and reads Paul, he becomes rich and glorious. What medicine is not compounded and mixed in his letters? Help for every ailment is found in his instructions. What life-giving rule did he not establish?
