Even our Lord himself would have to stand accused, since he showed in his body the marks of the nails and the spear that struck him. He and his disciples laid out the path of this distinction and revealed and made known the nature of the divine Being and human nature. They distinguished the natures so that their order would not be confused, and they brought them together in the unity of one person. The preachers called the Word and the body one person, and the teachers of true religion directed themselves toward this same aim. Diodore and Theodore directed themselves toward the aim of their companions. Why, then, do fools find fault with them alone? There are other wise men who have studied this subject, and no one criticizes my interpretations except them. Only the heretics hated this discussion and refused to accept a single confession of the Word and the body. So the unlearned also agree with those who go astray, and follow their thinking along a path that is not true. The path that the heretics have trodden is not true, and I will show from their own books that it is not true. The Simonians considered the incarnation a dream, and explained the human experiences as an illusion.

The Borborites denied the Word and the body altogether, and concocted a fiction of unspeakable obscenities. The Menandrians went completely astray, saying that there is no divine Being, and gave the angels the title of creators. The Photinians called the three a single person, and confused the order of fatherhood and sonship. The Paulianists confined the Son within a beginning, and made his divinity begin with a human woman. The Marcionites fled from both these and those, and introduced into the designation of divine Being a being whose very name is ‘Stranger.’ The [?] did not even come close to making a convincing argument, since they removed the term ‘beings’ from their books. The followers of Bardaisan regarded everything as nothing, and tore down and built up a false structure that cannot stand. Valentinus surpassed every blasphemy with his blasphemy, and wickedly said that what Mary bore was not a body. Sabellius denied humanity and divinity, effaced the persons, and destroyed the order that exists in the divine Being. The followers of Arius separated the Son from the one who begot him, and called him a servant and minister like all created beings. The Eunomians called him offspring in name alone, and did away with the meaning of fatherhood and sonship. The Dimoerites confined our Lord to half a human being, and would not allow him to be complete, not even in his soul. Macedonius erased the person of the Holy Spirit, treated him as a stranger, and cast him away from the persons of the Father and the Son. The followers of Severus denied the body that he took from us, by saying that the one who suffered and was tested was not a human being. Here is the confession of the heretics who hate the soul. See, you unlearned people, how full their teachings are of blasphemies! Look carefully at how alien they are to the faith, and how fiercely they struggle to throw what is rightly established into confusion. You who possess reason, judge fairly, like a discerning person, how many differences there are between the righteous and the wicked. The men whose words I have defended are very righteous, and the truth they proclaimed among people is firm and pure. For their sake I have recounted the heretics, to reveal to people how far they are from righteousness. I wanted to expose their wrongdoing before the wrongdoers, to make them understand that they unjustly denied those who are upright. They called those who know the truth heretics, and for this reason I repeated the accusation against their injustice. My discourse compared the truth in them with the falsifiers, so that I might show people how foreign truth is to falsehood. It is manifest truth that he proclaimed on earth, O wise ones, but fools regarded it as the error of heretics. The truthful fought a great battle against liars, and the astonishing thing is that they were themselves given the name of liars. Theodore lived ninety years and a little more, and he never ceased or fell silent in his struggle against those in error.

The righteous man wore armor of steel throughout his life and fought against the bands of heretics. With the sword of the Spirit he laid waste to the followers of error and exposed the various tricks of their teachings. He fought skillfully against heresies and deftly untied the knots of error. Like an athlete he took up the contest against them, and he pointed out their guilt as though with his finger. He showed himself a wrestler in his maneuvers and dashed falsehood to the ground before the spectators' eyes. He regarded the various contests as an arena, and throughout his life he was never disappointed in victory. From his youth he began training as an athlete, and he neither rested nor stopped until death brought his race to an end. He counted the course of his life's years as a single day, and for him the day of youth was no different from old age. The days of the hard-pressed worker completed a grueling course, and he began and finished his service to his Lord with diligence. Love for his Lord compelled the upright man to fight, and he neither slumbered nor slept until he [?] toward victory. He longed for that victory of which Paul spoke: “I run toward the goal of the victory on high.” Oh, the victor who was worthy of the [?] of those who run well! Neither bodily weakness nor the sufferings of the soul held him back. Oh, the diligent man! How he [?] to acquire the treasures of life, and gave the enemy no opportunity to plunder his possessions. Oh, the wise man! How wisely he discerned hidden things, and not one concealed thing was hidden from his understanding. Oh, the merchant who traded with the talents of the Spirit! His profits multiplied wherever his preaching reached. The good servant received the talents of the Spirit from his Lord and diligently sowed their profit in everyone's ears. The fruits of his soul's labors flourished everywhere, and no people remained unrefined by the savor of his words. His insights shone like light among those on earth, and he drove away the error that lay hidden in people's minds. Through his sayings humanity saw the light of life and learned to look through visible things toward things unseen. People had ceased their inquiry, as though asleep, until the dawn of his words shone and awakened them. A cloak of sleep lay spread over the books of the Spirit, and he lifted it through the fine study arising from the stirrings of his soul. Readers of books used to study without understanding, until they read his writings and then became wise. They ought to call that brilliant mind the scholar of scholars. Without him there would have been no scholar who taught well. Everyone who became rich gained riches from the treasury of his writings, and from his interpretations they gained the understanding needed to interpret. What I too have learned to stammer, I learned from him; through his discourse I gained the ability to discuss the study of words.

His study became a guide for me to what is written, and he raised me to an understanding of the books of the Spirit. In return for the benefits he gave, I contend with his detractors, and I show that they unjustly denied his contributions. Men clothed in arrogance did him a great injustice, and I burned with zeal to demand an account from them for the disgrace they inflicted on him. The disgrace inflicted on him drove me to undertake a discourse, and for his sake I traveled the path of controversy. I saw heretics reviling him and his companions, and I resolved to pronounce a just judgment on their words. From the beginning my discourse was directed at their words, and once again I confine the subject of my discourse to them. I rebuke those who criticize the words of the learned: although they are ignorant, they provoke and revile those who have understanding. Great is the understanding that brilliant minds have revealed on earth, yet no one knows how to comprehend their insights. They wisely wrote everything they wrote in the books they composed, and no wise person can find fault with their interpretations. Only fools reviled them as though they were evil, because they are too weak to understand the force of their words. The idle are sick with the severe pains of ignorance, and they have no desire to hear news of healing for the soul. Those sick in soul, who have no understanding, are sick in their very souls. That is why they hate those who cut away the soul’s severe diseases. They know very well that their [?] cannot be healed; that is why they are clothed in anger that admits no reconciliation. The ignorant have developed fierce anger toward the learned because they distinguish the natural properties of the Word and the body. The Creator, the Father’s Word, took a body from us, and in love called it “Son of God,” according to his own rank. He gave it what was his, while he himself became no less than what he is, for his nature can neither be diminished nor increased. His nature is exalted above injuries and changes, and the properties of human nature do not approach it. The afflictions of human nature came upon human nature, not upon the nature that is high and exalted above injuries. Everything written about the man belongs to the human being: conception, birth, growth, suffering, and death. Trustworthy men revealed this distinction between the Word and the body, and fools contend with them over why they revealed things that were not evident. This is the reason that made them enemies of the righteous, and because of it they are detested and hated among earthly people. Indeed, they deserved to be loved for this, in keeping with the revelation of hidden things that they made known on earth. Anyone who reveals what has not been revealed deserves praise, and who opens a path for humanity's immaturity to seek out hidden things. The wisdom of the discourse found among the learned is for humanity's immaturity. And who would not reject the fools who deprived it of this benefit? Lovers of truth [?] twofold benefits: the word of truth and the excellence of their conduct. Glorious was the labor that marked the conduct of the wise.

No one knows how to recount adequately the various forms of their labors. Diodore, mighty in strength, toiled at his labors until his bodily senses were impaired by ascetic discipline. Theodore's story is far beyond telling: his eyesight grew dim from studying books, yet he did not stop or grow negligent. Nestorius too labored more strenuously than all who labor, because he gave his mind no opportunity to wander into error. See how diligently these righteous men pursued their labors, and see how great the wickedness of those who wronged them became! Look, people, at how much people have done against other people—ignorance attacking springs full of wisdom! The faithful were sweet springs for humanity's thirst, and everyone who drank from their springs forgot his troubles. The fools refused to accept drink from them, and now they are tormented by the conflict within their own thoughts. Woe to the blind who can see but are blind to understanding! They delight in the blindness of soul with which they are afflicted. The idle resemble bats in their [?], loving the darkness of the nights far more than the light. Woe to the intelligent nature that has made itself senseless and brought to an end the course of discernment that had been placed within it! Indeed, learned people, there is no remedy for ignorance, nor any reversal of the sentence pronounced by our Lord's word. Our Lord's word cut them off from within the church and cast them into exile among outsiders. He commanded us to regard them as tax collectors and pagans, and not to become entangled in their loathsome thoughts. Paul too cut off their practices with the sword of his words and handed them over to become companions of the devil. People who hate the truth resemble the devil, for they slander lovers of truth just as Satan does. Perhaps Satan occupied them with this business so that, by insulting the righteous, they would fulfill the desire of his inclination. He hates the righteous and habitually attacks the faithful; he has no desire whatsoever to see a righteous person. Now too he saw forms of righteousness in righteous men, and in his envy prepared himself for battle against them. The battle that fools wage against the wise is his own, and through their mouths he shoots the arrows of his wrath into the ranks of truth. He seeks to destroy the ranks of truth through the mouths of quarrelers, but the power of truth does not allow him to carry out his intention. Bitter in his malice, he merely displays the evil of his malice, and his soul’s desire does not reach fulfillment. If he could carry out his malice as he intended, there would be no mention of righteousness on earth, nor any righteousness at all. If his schemes had any opportunity against the faithful, he would have erased the names of Diodore and his companions from among the living. He has hated this company, and still hates it far more than anyone else, because he knows that they can untie the knot of his deceit.

All the schemer’s schemes are known to the wise, and they have exposed his falsehood before the eyes of those on earth and those in heaven. The forms of his error were hidden among the heretics; those discerning in soul exposed them before the eyes of all creatures. The vile one chose vile workers for himself against the righteous, but they were not strong enough to engage in battle with the faithful. As though with a sword, the righteous destroyed the camp of his falsehood, and a few remained to be witnesses to his guilt. The guilty one, full of sins, saw his condemnation, and now he grows bitter and vomits his gall upon ordinary people. He seeks to avenge the disgrace of the [?] on the innocent: Diodore, Theodore [?], and Mar Nestorius. No, guilty one, you have no strength to fight, for you have learned by experience the weaponry of the valiant warriors. Look, [?] them in the battle he fought with your factions: you fled and hid and could not stand firm on the day of combat. Otherwise, show which of your warriors defeated the faithful, and when, and where, and in whose days your victory occurred. Where is Simon, the firstborn, who took the lead in your abominations, and, one after another, everyone who became a disciple of his deceit? Look, all the divisions he brought forth on earth have vanished and perished, and nothing remains of them except a remnant to your disgrace. A small remnant of the heresies remains to your disgrace, lying in ambush like wolves for the gathering of the sheep. The heretics are always gathering where the sheep assemble, and they cannot conceal that they are despised and cast out as evildoers. The word of the righteous drove them out from among the sheep, and especially the righteous zeal of Diodore and his companions. Diodore and his companions brought down the arrogance of every heresy, and the volumes of their writings bear witness to their labors. The record of their victories is inscribed in their writings: when they began and when they finished the battle against them. Their battles began in the days of Valens, in the days of the man who supported the falsehood of Arius and his followers. He raised the bowed head of Arius and his followers and drove the righteous priests out from among the sheep. The faithful lived in that time—a harsh time—and they truly subdued the time and its harshness. The Lord of the ages sent them against those times, like a king who chooses warriors for fierce battles. It was a hard time for all three tireless workers, and it was the beginning of the conflict with the heretics. The party of Arius was fighting without restraint, and a belligerent king supported their struggle. The king and the people rose together against the righteous, yet they could not withstand the righteous. Oh, the victory that earthly people displayed on earth! They conquered the world and trampled mortality into the ground. Oh, those mortals who displayed the achievement of immortals!

They left the renown of their victory on earth for generations to come. Oh, those guides who opened a path whose toil is exhausting! They taught people to travel rightly toward the promised reward on high. The wise, who made others wise, journeyed toward the promised reward on high. This is the wonder: while they were on earth, they did the things of heaven. The conduct of these earthly people was full of great wonder, yet earthly people did not look carefully at their conduct. By their conduct they compelled me to recount their struggles, and the injustice done to them made me rebuke their oppressors. Their oppressors will answer for the injustice done to them, because they falsely condemned them when they were innocent. For this injustice I wanted to exact vengeance from the oppressors, and my mind compelled me to bring forth words of rebuke. The words of fools provoked me to answer back, and against my will I recounted the history of the conduct of the righteous. Let everyone whose conversation is upright love the conversation of the righteous, and train himself in their conversation throughout his life. Study with the faithful brings life that does not decay. Come, let us study the life-giving teaching found in their words. The faithful loved people's lives more than anything, and for people's sake they accepted mockery from the insolent. They saw that the Lover of humanity cared for humankind, and they set their purpose on imitating the purpose of his compassion. The champions of righteousness saw the purpose of his compassion. Come, let us rouse ourselves to examine the purpose of their conduct. Let us place their conduct like an image before our minds, and examine our souls to see whether they are ugly with hateful wickedness. Let us constantly scrub the filth of wickedness from our minds, so that we are not exposed in that scrutiny whose examination is just.
On the evil of the times; suitable for supplication.
Sixth Discourse. On the evil of the times; suitable for supplication.

I recount the terrible blows our land has suffered. Come, people of the earth, listen and groan over how much we have suffered. We have suffered greatly, in proportion to our wickedness, which has grown very great. Perhaps no generation has suffered as many blows as ours. In our generation, what is written about the Hebrews has been fulfilled: “I struck them, but they were unwilling to accept the various forms of discipline.” The Creator disciplined us harshly in all his discipline, but our mind looked without understanding at the severity of his blows. He disciplined us out of love, like a father disciplining his children, but our evil inclination took no pleasure in his loving correction. Our nature behaved like a brute in its shameful deeds and refused to accept the gentle yoke of serving its Lord. The Creator himself harnessed our soul as with a yoke, but it grew restive, kicked, and broke the yoke of the commands he had spoken. The beast that was our rational nature behaved like a beast and, worse than an animal, bit the words of those who taught it wisdom. Our thoughts barked like dogs at our shepherds, and our mind did not distinguish the master of the house from a stranger. A dog recognizes its master by sight and wags its tail for him, but our heart did not discern what is right, nor does it now. Because we did not exercise discernment as rational beings endowed with speech, the giver of speech raised his hand and struck us severely. That ruler, whose command is just, scourged us severely and thoroughly exposed our shameful deeds.

Through the blows we suffered, he portrayed the evil inclination within our soul, uncovered it, and displayed it before the eyes of earthly and heavenly beings. Heaven and earth became witnesses to our [?], and through our discipline they learned of our wrongdoing, which had been hidden. Those who speak and those who are mute plainly saw the severity of our blows, and they weighed our wrongdoing as in scales to see how unjust it was. The discipline of our days became like a mirror, and the evil of our shameful deeds overflowed far beyond the blows we suffered. Our evil deeds proved stronger than our countless afflictions, and our dull heart did not consider the weight of its wrongdoing. Because we did not reflect as befitted those with understanding, blows goaded us like animals without understanding. The divine command goaded us like animals, and what the wise man had spoken was fulfilled in us. With rod and goad the wise man disciplined foolish pride, and the same treatment was imposed on those who are mute and those who speak. All kinds of afflictions goaded our soul like an animal, yet it was not restrained from the evil of its shameful deeds. Famine starved us, but our proud spirit was not humbled. Sickness struck us, but our frenzy was not weakened. Death swallowed us, brought us in, and imprisoned us in the pit of Sheol, but our heart did not tremble at this terror full of terrors. As it is written, human corpses fell like dung, but our towering arrogance did not fall from its lofty height. The earth withheld its produce and gave us no fruit or crops, but the spring of our shamelessness did not cease flowing. The air underwent the various changes attributed to it, but the violence of our anger did not change from what it was. Thunder and lightning shook the earth in an extraordinary way.

Yet our inclination, that inner impulse, did not budge from its hardness. Hail shattered the vines and fig trees, along with all the fruit, yet the sight of this wrath did not frighten us. There were signs more terrible than other signs, yet our minds did not inquire into the reason for what they revealed. Locusts and crawling locusts caused damage such as we had never seen, yet we did not ask why punishments were so frequent. Lowly creatures without understanding ate our food, yet we did not inquire who had given us over as food. Our provisions ran out, our labor came to nothing, and our lives were lost. There is no one among us able to stand up for us and help us. Woe to us! Perhaps our race will perish under these harsh punishments, and no survivor will remain to us among those who dwell on earth. Woe to us! Perhaps what happened before will happen among us: the fire of Sodom and the chasm that swallowed Dathan’s household. The kinds of evil I have recounted are present among us, and the sufferings our land has endured bear witness that they are among us. From the sufferings of our land, I perceive that they are abundant among us. Now I am ready to set them out before my listeners. Come, listeners, hear the account of our various sufferings. Tremble and groan over the blows that have struck our wicked generation. Our wicked generation has acted far more wickedly than all other generations. Therefore its punishments are more numerous than those of all other generations. That Will which sees everything saw the ugliness of our wrongdoing and turned the face of its kindness away from our ugly deeds. He who is not wrathful showed us a wrathful face. The earth shook and nearly became a chasm. Our wrongdoing, in its wickedness, shook all creation. Nothing remained that was not shaken by our shameful deeds. The sight of our shameful deeds horrified the whole world and drove both heavenly and earthly beings away from us. The spiritual beings saw the shameful sight of our ugly wrongdoing. They grew indignant and fierce, ready to punish it with disturbances in the air. Those who see clearly looked at our insolence and examined it. They put on armor to humble our tyranny.

The same command that appointed them to serve us ordered them to put their hands to the decree of our punishments. The King who is above all wrote a decree of punishments and gave it to the companies of heavenly beings to bring to us. Like a bird, his winged beings flew at the command, and swiftly carried out the various blows against us. They saw that the sentence concerning the blows against us was urgent, and urgently they carried out the will of the one who sent them. The kinsmen of our race stretched our race out with straps of wind, and with the whips of hunger and thirst they tore our bodies apart. The bodiless beings took combs of pain in their hands and raked our bodies with the sharpness of their combs. They hung our people up like a robber before a judge, and our people began to wail because of the harsh punishments inflicted on them. Our people were beaten and torn apart from head to foot like a criminal. They wept and wailed, but the King’s servants would not listen to them. The King over all decreed against our people, who love wrongdoing, that our insolence should be scourged without mercy. The heavenly hosts scourge us without mercy, and perhaps they will not cease chastising us until the end. They have looked, and continually look, at the greatness of our wrongdoing. Therefore their hand remains raised above our backs. They know full well that we are not turning away from our hateful deeds, and therefore they clothe themselves in wrath to exact payment from us. The debt of our sins has grown enormously, beyond all bounds, and now they demand from us the various kinds of interest that have accumulated against us. Our humanity has incurred a bond of debt beyond that of other people, and because we did not repay it, now we are paying against our will. Our will acted unjustly in incurring the debt of our sins. Therefore our wounds too are more severe than those of every generation. Because we did not make an effort, as debtors, to repay the principal, now we are also paying interest upon multiplied interest.

Interest is demanded from us in proportion to our wickedness, and we deserve it, as wrongdoers who have committed great wrongs. We have committed great wrongs, and our conscience bears witness that we have committed great wrongs. Perhaps even the demons do not commit wrongdoing like ours. The demons do wrong and reflect that they have done wrong, and they know that they have sinned. We have neither reflected nor condemned our shameful deeds. Because we did not reflect, as befits beings endowed with understanding, now things that are by nature speechless are chastising us through their natural powers. Because we were unwilling to judge ourselves by our own judgment, now the righteous command, whose examination is just, judges us. The chief of judges entrusted our case to the justice of his command, so that we might know that he also possesses a justice that cannot be overcome. He examined the case of our wrongdoing with perfect justice and pronounced sentence in proportion to the evil deeds of those being scourged. He placed our wrongdoing in the scales of his examination, and because it weighed so heavily, he set scourges against it corresponding to its weight. He apportioned the scourges that fall upon wrongdoers according to the kinds of wrongdoing, and exacted payment for each with the scourge appropriate to it. He uprooted the love of money with the spade of poverty, so that it would not sprout again and bear the fruit of coveted money. He cut down the love of glory with the axe of humiliation, so that it would not devise ways to prick people with the sting of glory. He cut away oppression with the iron blade of need, lest the swelling it causes spread throughout the whole body. He applied the cautery of peacefulness to arrogance, so that it would not rise up and acquire the habits of a fanged beast. He bound falsehood with the weapon of a single word, so that it would not become accustomed to speaking excessive words. He put the bridle of silence into envy’s mouth, lest it bite people with the fangs of its hostility. He confined theft in fortresses that cannot be stormed, so that it would no longer rob people of their livelihood by taking their possessions. He struck adultery with the affliction of dimmed eyesight, so that it would not gaze lustfully at what does not belong to it. He silenced anger with the terrifying pronouncements of judgment, so that it would have no room to run wild. He justly disciplined all the passions with his righteous blows, and wisely showed his power in those being chastised.

Everything was terrified by his blows, and everything faltered; he made dread reign over everything that exists. Everything trembled at what happened to everything, and nothing remained that had not been tested by human sufferings. These things happened in the human dwelling place because of humanity, and because of human wickedness, rational and speechless creatures suffered evils. Because of humanity, the earth received harsh blows, and its womb dried up, no longer producing seeds and fruit. Because of human wrongdoing, it refused to bear the offspring of seed; though it was a mother, it became barren and bereaved. The unreasoning earth imitated human barrenness and closed its womb against the cultivation appointed for it. Its neighboring elements, water and air, imitated it, and no longer followed properly the smooth course of their changes. The silent elements, which had been orderly, moved without order and threw into confusion the world that had been ordered from the beginning. Human wrongdoing taught these insensible things to follow a course full of the terror of disorder. Humanity itself disrupted the order of all creation, and through its negligence loosened the bond joining the heights and the depths. In humanity, the heights and the depths had been bound together in a single harmony; because of humanity, everything deteriorated from what it had been. Human anger provoked the Power that never becomes angry, and he chastised the world with fierce, merciless anger. The chastisement in our days has been merciless, and perhaps human wickedness has never received blows like those inflicted on our wickedness. Otherwise, let us inquire into nature and Scripture, whether there has been a generation that the Righteous One chastised as he has chastised ours. Earlier generations received harsh blows, as it is written, and he made known to them the reason for the blows they received. As for us, he has scourged us with every form and kind of scourging, yet he has not revealed to us the reason for the severity of our blows. This is harder than anything else for those being chastised: while they are being chastised, they do not know the reason for the chastisement.

Our wrongdoing has concealed the reason for the chastisement from our minds. Our wrongdoing itself has blinded our soul to understanding, and it does not understand even as it is degraded by shameful deeds. It has imposed a barrier of silence on the soul’s power of speech and has kept its mind from attending to good things. It has not allowed the soul’s discernment to distinguish rightly; though the soul possesses discernment, it has acquired the habits of creatures without it. This habit has made it blind and without understanding. It has received blows but has refused to learn the reason for its blows. Our soul, so gifted in understanding, has received harsh blows; yet however many it received, the blows seemed to it as though they were not blows. How greatly the blows multiplied, yet those being chastised neither felt nor perceived them! He doubled the wounds, but those being struck took courage. How many earthquakes there were! The earth trembled and mountains fell, yet our heart did not tremble at the sound of the birth pangs of the earth that had been quiet. Dwellings collapsed and became graves for their inhabitants, yet the pride of our spirit was not humbled by the destruction. The earth was stripped of crops of every kind, yet our evil inclination did not cease its inclination toward hateful deeds. Trees dried up, leaves fell, and crops withered, yet the foul spring of our shameful deeds did not dry up. Locusts devoured us, crawling locusts stripped us, and crickets struck us, yet the bitterness of our soul was not frightened away from what it was. Violent storms blew in summer and winter, yet the fierce blast of our shameful deeds surpassed them. The air [?], and rain dripped down in hailstones, yet our wickedness did not change the course of its wrongdoing. The silent things trembled at the sounds of thunder and the sight of lightning, yet our sluggishness did not awaken from its sleep. Spiritual beings traced various signs across the heavens. We saw them and forgot them as though they were a dream. We were confident, we were secure, and we were at ease; even our hateful deeds did not expose our wrongdoing.

The powers on high displayed them to our unjust selves. We saw them, yet we did not see them with sound understanding. Everything that happened in the heights and the depths happened because of us, yet we did not ask what caused these changes. And because we were unwilling to inquire into the various kinds of punishment, the Creator signaled to his ministers to scourge us. The Watchers, our kinsmen, received a command concerning our wickedness, and they stretched out our heart for a harsh scourging suited to our heart. Because our heart felt no pain at the scourging that it suffered on our behalf, the righteous struck us in our limbs and in our thoughts. Perhaps those who think rightly considered this concerning our insolence: that the skin receiving the blows was not theirs [?], the one who had done wrong. A person is accustomed to give everything he has so that he himself will not suffer. Let the one who is afraid, then, receive the blows, and see—he becomes wise. Let him personally taste the harshness of the scourges, so that he may know how to preserve the proper order of his rational nature. On this condition our limbs were struck with severe pains, and now our contemptible body is being torn apart with wounds. In this way the righteous hasten to scourge us. They have not ceased, nor do they cease, striking us in summer and winter. In every way the righteous discipline the sluggishness of our heart, and when we do not repent, death comes and suddenly swallows us. Greedy death ravages us beyond all bounds, and without pity it tears our bodies apart with destructive fury. Like a captor, it pursues everyone in our race, and its captivity surpasses the captivity into which people take other people. People took us captive, and death took us captive—a double captivity. Yet captivity to our shameful deeds surpasses both captivities. Captivity to our wrongdoing surpassed captivity to people and to death. Perhaps it was what opened the road to captivity under these two captors. Woe to our people because of the captors who continually beset it and [?] it, yet it does not desist from its abominations. Woe to us, for we have become an object of mockery and contempt before all creatures. Those who can speak and those who cannot condemn the greatness of our disgrace. Woe to us, for an evil report has spread to the four corners of the earth, and there is no one in creation who does not recount the story of our wickedness. Even the demons, who are more wicked than we are, speak of our reputation for wickedness.

Although they are very wicked, they are greatly astonished at our evil deeds. If even the wicked are astonished at us because we have done evil, then our troubles have rightly grown severe and our pains have multiplied. Famine and diseases rightly pursue our lives. Perhaps they will restrain our wickedness from committing still greater evil. The Righteous One disciplines our wickedness with famine and diseases, and keeps us in order so that we do not run wild in pursuit of evil. Instead, let us ask what causes the severity of our afflictions, and why the food that sustains our lives is scarce and uncertain. Why is our time more troubled than all other times, and why is there no time when the course of our life is peaceful and good? Why are the seasons of the year gloomy in their changes, and why does none of their changes follow its proper order? Everything is disturbed, everything is confused, everything is gloomy, and the world has become like a graveyard for its inhabitants. Creation is clothed in deep mourning because of our evil deeds, and weeps for us as for a dead person whose mourning is bitter. The earth is bitterly distressed on our account. If it could, it would cry out like a mother over her beloved child. If it had a speaking mouth like those who speak, it would bewail our evil time with cries of lamentation. If the speechless creatures could feel the sufferings of our souls, they would never cease lamenting our humiliation. We have been brought very low, down to the earth, as it is written. Yet instead of the earth, our soul clings to mockery and contempt. Our evils blew like a whirlwind in our evil time and left us bare like trees in winter. Good words fell away from people's mouths like leaves, and people became inhuman in their deeds. Mortals suffered harsh torments to the point of death. They were scorched and withered by the distress of hunger's pains. The sword of famine came out against our people, who were engrossed in sin. It ravaged us and cast us down like animals, without burial. What was written concerning the people of old has been fulfilled among us: human corpses fall like dung. Look, human bodies have fallen without burial, and people have walked over other people without shame. Famine shut the door of compassion in the faces of loved ones.

One person trampled another as though that person were not human. Hunger forced nature by its overwhelming strength, and nature began transgressing both nature and Scripture. Because of hunger, degraded nature forgot its own nature and subjected itself to eating food contrary to its custom. Contrary to custom, people ate human flesh. Woe to us! What has happened to our nature, so full of suffering? Woe to us! Perhaps the end of the world is coming in our time, and everything written about the end is being fulfilled in us. It is written that women ate their children in a time of famine, and the beloved infants of their wombs became food for their bellies. Look, this happened at a time—in our evil time—and women ate their children and also the price paid for them. For paltry prices, fathers gave up their beloved children. They ate food full of anguish and died amid sobs. For a crust of bread, a mother received the price of her beloved child. Her eye streamed with tears, and her soul melted with grief. Alas for that food which nature bought contrary to its custom! Nature forgot the natural instincts that had been placed within it. Alas for nature, bound entirely by love for its own, yet selling its own for love of a single hour’s food! Alas! What has happened to our race, the head of all races? It has degraded itself through shameful things more contemptible than all else. Alas for our nature, called by the name of the one who formed it! It has become so low that even the lowly lament its abasement. Alas for the one exalted above all and more glorious than all in name and rank! Sufferings have trampled him, pains have humbled him, and death has swallowed him. Alas for the one who embraced the whole world in his body and soul! He has become more hateful than anything because of his wrongdoing. Because of his wrongdoing, speaking beings [?] and speechless beings alike have hated him. Now they batter him with harsh scourges of every kind. Harsh famine, countless pains, and swift death—and there is no comfort between one chastisement and the next.

Like waves, the scourges rush upon us one after another, giving us not even a little quiet or rest. The sound of wailing thunders through our land at every hour, and our life has become like a graveyard, night and day. Weeping in the streets, wailing in the houses, sobbing everywhere! Mouths wail, eyes shed tears, and ears ring. Everyone hears weeping and lamentation from every mouth, and there is no one who does not repeat a cry of woe. “Woe, woe!” people say to one another about humanity, whose good things have vanished, whose sorrows have multiplied, and whose sighs have doubled. At every hour, each hears the sound of sighing from his companion, and there is no utterance that is not mingled with human grief. Everyone is sorrowful, everyone is distressed, and everyone weeps. There is no face bright and cheerful toward another. Everyone is distressed at the sight of everyone else’s gloom, and everyone is stunned by the afflictions that have come to reign over the land. Everyone asks those they meet about the afflictions: “Is there perhaps any place free from afflictions?” Everyone, without exception, is filled with trouble upon trouble, and the heads of kings and the lowly alike bow before these troubles. The rich are distressed, the poor are distressed, the slave and his master alike; each goes out begging to gather what he needs to live. Beggars and those who were not beggars have gone out begging, and hunger has thrown the established order into confusion, sending people from one house to another. Hunger has taught freeborn people to beg, and now they go about asking for alms like beggars. The trade of begging has spread throughout the land, and there is never a moment when the cry of begging does not sound. People fashion mournful cries before their companions; weeping and lamenting, they make their listeners weep with them. Everyone howls like an animal alongside his companions; they moan and chirp like doves and swallows. The sound of their groaning does not even resemble a human voice, for hunger has altered their words and their tones. The unfortunate man varies his mournful cries about his need,

so that perhaps whoever hears his varied tones will feel sorry for him. Without concealment he cries out and begs with stubbornness and impudence. He swears and puts others under oath, saying, “Unless I receive something, I will not move away.” What has the wickedness of our inclination, that bitter inclination, done! It has uprooted freedom of soul [?] from us and planted impudence. The soul possesses freedom of soul from the time it is formed, and this is the wonder: hunger has conquered the one who does not hunger. Hunger has made the free soul [?], and she has become a slave serving the body's needs. The body's need has bound her under the yoke of the body's need, and she has begun fashioning mournful cries to ask for alms. Wickedness has committed a great outrage in our evil generation: [?] mournful cries to ask for alms. Wickedness has committed a great outrage in our evil generation, throwing the beautiful qualities of body and soul into confusion. Beautiful were the natural qualities placed within her, but wickedness, the tyrant among evils, has ruined them. Wickedness is the cause of the things I have recounted and am recounting; it is what has chastised us with famine, [?], and pestilence. It is what has stripped the beautiful earth of its good things, so that she has not given us fruit and grain as she usually does. It is what has brought forth locusts, crawling locusts, and crickets; it has altered the air and brought down fire instead of raindrops. There is no injury that has ever harmed us that it has not caused, and no loss that our race has suffered that it has not brought about. We should therefore have found fault with our wrongdoing, not with our God, who made us upright and free. Our freedom itself should have blamed its own lack of freedom, asking why the freeborn had become unfree. And because she did not exercise discernment as a discerning being should, let her blame herself: sufferings and losses have called her to a harsh account. Severe are the losses our soul has suffered in this time, and there is no weight whose heaviness equals our loss. The loss in every generation is small compared with ours, and the blows our soul has suffered bear witness to how much we have lost. No human tongue can describe the kinds of wounds we have suffered, and the mouth is too small to recount them as they really are. A speaker can only say that they happened; but how can a tongue set out how they happened and how great they were?

I too, who wished to speak of them, have said that they happened, but my mind could not grasp their full extent. Their multitude made me seek to investigate them, and I was greatly astonished and fell far short of what I sought. My thoughts mounted a chariot of words upon the road of words, and I wished to travel in the company of words toward the events. I wished to recount the kinds of events that happened in our land, but when I saw how numerous they were, my speech faltered. My speech itself was overcome with fear at the beginning of its words, lest it should begin and fail to reach the end. I saw the length of the discourse it was about to compose, and I was greatly afraid of arranging the various kinds of words. For words about wounds are terrifying when they are spoken, and the account of the severity of the blows is not easy to tell. The violence of the blows made me tremble to deliver a discourse about the blows, and my mind compelled me to weave a garment full of blows. Under the pretext of words, I wished to [?] those being scourged, so that they would not be exposed before the eyes of observers who see clearly. I saw that those who see clearly were very eager to look, and I painted a picture of the various kinds of blows for them to gaze upon. Come, observers who see clearly: look at our wounds, at how much we have suffered and how lightly we have treated our blows. Our mind resembled a wild beast in the face of our wounds: people try to subdue it, but it remains unsubdued to the end. The blows goaded our insolence as though it were a beast, and the more it suffered, the stronger it grew in its wildness. The Righteous One put a muzzle of hunger on the mouth of our wickedness, but our wickedness did not stop rushing into its evil deeds. With straps of stone he stretched out our body before the blows. It suffered much and treated much lightly, as though it felt no pain. What could feel pain became unfeeling in the time of suffering, and its nature forgot that it was a nature formed in mortality. The pains brought the one being scourged close to death, and the soul trembled, fled, and departed from its dwelling. The soul sat as mistress in the palace of the body, but the pains tore down the palace it loved, and it fled from it.

And if the soul fled from us at the time of our scourging, let everyone know also how many blows we suffered. Death is the end of life for those being scourged; therefore it is clear that our wound is more severe than other wounds. Perhaps someone who hears will say, “It is death.” But let that person hear that there is a death worse than death. Our death is worse than all the deaths that have been and are to come, for we have seen our death and thus died a double death. We have seen the sight of death in the punishment for our offenses [?], and before dying we have died at the sight of our harsh torments. Hunger and pain became guides for ravenous death, and it rushed to swallow us like a dragon swallowing an elephant. In every form, death has swallowed our mortal nature, and perhaps no living remnant of our humanity will remain. Every trial has passed over our soul, which possesses life, and perhaps the spring of life will run dry and our body perish. It possesses imperishable life within itself from the Creator, and through its vitality our noble body lives and moves. Had it not preserved us by the power of its vitality, the human race would have become as though humanity did not exist. We have become as though we were not human, through the punishment for all our offenses, and speaking creatures and speechless ones alike have been astonished and bewildered at our destruction. Heaven and earth weep and lament over our destruction, yet we alone are unaware of the destruction of our race. Because of our hateful deeds, the course of summer and winter is darkened, and the great order of the months of the year is confused and disturbed. Because of us, creation has put on mourning clothes and mourns for us as for a dead person whose mourning is bitter. The mourning on the day of our distress is more bitter than all other mourning, and the day of our death is more restful than the days of harsh torments. The days of our lives have vanished amid torments and pain, and in our lifetime there is not a day free from distress. From our childhood, pains have reared us, as it is written, and as we grew, the wounds upon our limbs flourished. From the very beginning of our race, pains have struck us, and troubles have served as a guide along the journey of our lives.

We have lived poisoned lives on earth from the day we came into being, and the cruel stings of envy have never left us. We have had evil neighbors in the land of our sojourn. They plundered our [?] and enslaved our lives with harsh labor. The enemies of our race led our race into unjust captivity and made us slaves to the desires behind their deeds. Our ancestors went out from Paradise like exiles and settled in a land full of thorns, pains, and death. Captivity by water overtook them even from this land. If only it had been captivity rather than merciless destruction! The captivity of the [?] waters destroyed us without mercy, swept away the dust from which our bodies were formed, and buried it in the earth. One captivity handed us over to another, passing us from one to the next, and gave us no time to remain long in the land of our sojourn. The first captivity carried us away from the beautiful land of Eden, and the second from the inheritance full of thorns. Another captivity carried us away from Babel through division and scattered our dust to the four directions, over sea and dry land. Three captivities, each worse than the other, took our race captive, and one of our race freed our race from slavery. An evil habit has been entrenched in our race from the beginning: it finds the bondage of slaves sweeter than freedom. The freeborn person has not loved freedom from the labor of slaves, nor does he desire to lift his head out of slavery. This habit has made him suffer harsh lashes, and now he is battered by wounds of body and soul. In body and soul he sins greatly and suffers greatly. Everyone is stretched out for harsh lashes, yet does not desist. The severity of his scourging has accompanied him through every generation, and especially in our own generations the blows have doubled. Look, harsh scourges surround us on every side. We suffer their blows, yet our various evil deeds know no bounds. Our evil and shameful deeds have multiplied beyond counting, and the scourging of our insolence has grown severe beyond measure. Our scourges were harsher than all the scourges of every generation, and at a command there was no respite between one and the next. A hidden command gathered them for an assault on our lives and taught them to wage war against our wickedness.

The scourges among us waged a great war against us and pierced our people with the sharp arrows of hunger and thirst. Like an army, diseases surrounded us on every side, and no body escaped being struck with wounds. Our whole body became a single incurable sore. Physicians recoiled from it and no longer bandaged it. Hunger and diseases battered his body and tormented his soul. They depleted his life of nourishment and vitality. There is no vitality at all in human life. Even if it exists, it does not, for there is nothing to sustain it. The food that sustains life has vanished from the mouths of the living, and the life of the short-lived hangs before his eyes. Everyone whose life is troubled looks toward the end of his life, pondering and fearing that his appointed time may have drawn near. In the evening he says, “Will I still be here in the morning?” And in the morning he asks his companions, “Has the sun set?” He passes through the day brooding over his troubles; as he counts the hours of night and day, his torment is doubled. Woe to miserable human nature! How deeply it is troubled, and how numerous are the sufferings of its soul and the pains of its body! Woe has accompanied this most wretched creature throughout every generation, and in our own generation it suffers more than in all other generations. In our own generation every human being suffers and is distressed. Woe is doubled, scourging is abundant, and torment is great. Great is the torment our eyes have seen and our ears have heard. Diseases pursued us, and people pursued us—both at once. Our bitter-natured humanity endured captivity to hunger and captivity to people, which is worse than hunger and every other evil. Captivity among the descendants of Hagar is harsher even than hunger, and the wound they inflicted was more bitter than diseases. The wound inflicted by the descendants of Abram is like a snake’s venom. Perhaps there is a remedy for the venom of reptiles, but there is none for them. If only the sons of the Egyptian woman were not called by Abraham’s name! For ignorant people are reproached by this designation. If only that righteous man had not approached that foolish woman! Perhaps those who stumble would then have ceased their stumbling.

If only they had a foreign name, foreign to Abram! They would have been called savages, like their father. The Creator called the ancestor of their tribes a wild donkey of the wilderness, for he knew that he could not observe the order of human life. It is fitting that the Egyptian woman’s son should be called a human beast. Let us remove from him the name of Abraham, who loved humanity. Abram loved humanity and loved his Lord. Therefore it is fitting that the righteous man’s children should be righteous. Abram is not to blame for fathering wicked and savage people. The wicked are to blame for not walking in the path of Abram’s love. Even I, who have reproached others, have spoken words deserving every reproach, because I said, “If only Abram had not approached Hagar the slave woman!” Fathers cannot shape the soul’s free will. It is the soul’s free will that makes people righteous or wicked. I have said these things to those who blame Abram, and I also say: if the Hagarenes took captives without cause, why did others do so? Are the Qadishites perhaps relatives of Hagar’s sons, that they plundered the world with a plundering that surpassed the Ishmaelites’? Did the devastation wrought by the Tamurites flow from Abram—the Tamurites who made Assyria, the mother of kings, into a wasteland? Let us not, then, blame fathers for their children, but rather the disposition that distinguishes between the two, good and evil. Let us always blame the evil disposition of Hagar’s sons, and still more that of the people of Qadish, those beastlike men. The nature of wild animals is not as savage as a Qadishite’s. What they did is evidence of their lack of peacefulness. The [?] of Hagar’s sons did not act as they acted, nor did the Tamurites wreak the devastation that those men wrought. Their devastation surpassed that of the [?] and the northerners. Perhaps there is no evil comparable to the evil they committed in our land.

Our land, full of wickedness, suffered these lashes, and our chastisement came through wrongdoers worse than ourselves. The Creator chastised us by the hand of wicked people worse than ourselves, so that when a wrongdoer is scourged by a wrongdoer, he may despise himself. Wickedness raised three rods against our evil: the Ishmaelites, the Tamurites, and the Qadishites. Our soul, full of pride, suffered three scourges from three peoples more arrogant than ourselves. The Creator is just in scourging our wickedness through wrongdoers, and it is right for us to acknowledge that, yes, our chastisement [?] came about justly. The authority that rules over all scourged us for our benefit, and wisely cut away the disease of our shameful deeds. Come, then, let us give thanks to that knowledge which bound up our wounds, and offer it gifts of praise, for it chastised us and won us over.
On supplication and fasting.
Sixth Discourse / Seventh Discourse / On Supplication and Fasting / Response (whichever is appropriate)

Physician who healed the sickness of our race with the medicine of his mercies, pardon our sins, as you have been accustomed to do for us. Good One who showed mercy to the evil of our inclination, though it was undeserving, fulfill the purpose of your kindness by turning our lives around. King who redeemed us from slavery to the Evil One and death, deliver our nature from the harm caused by the guilt of its sins.

Son of God who brought us back from captivity under the captor, set our lives free, so that we do not return again to slavery to the Evil One. From the beginning our race was harnessed under death’s yoke. One of us died and broke death’s yoke off us. Power who defeated the Evil One and death through a member of our race, give us strength to grow strong in the contest of our struggles. We are constantly thrown into the arduous contest against the passions of the body, and there is no time when the sting of our desires is quiet. A spring of animal passions flows from us, and with its turbulence it throws the course of our lives into confusion. The impulse dwelling within us is turbulent like a whirlwind, and it troubles our soul as a gust troubles the sea. It resembles the sea when it rages in its swelling pride, and it makes its desires roar like a whirlwind. Its surges race like waves through a person, and body and soul tremble before it, afraid of being drowned. The bodily impulse dwelling in our body is a second sea, and like a whirlwind it tosses the ship of our bodily existence. The ship of our mortality sails upon its turbulent sea, and the terror of its fierce winds shakes it. Our race, full of injuries, fears the harm it causes and constantly seeks a haven full of compassion and mercy. Everyone of mortal nature asks for compassion and mercy, hoping to escape the harms that constantly beset them. I saw that the kinds of harm afflicting it were exceedingly numerous, and I composed words so that I might travel with it to a peaceful harbor. It longs to reach the peaceful harbor of forgiveness of sins. Let your compassion be the pilot for the voyage of its life. Let the buoys of your mercy support its weight and lift it up, so that it does not drown in the passions of its soul.

Let it secure its life to your great name as to an anchor, and in you find shelter from the billows of turbulent passions. Turbulent passions constantly disturb its mortal existence and hinder it from journeying to the appointed meeting with your name. Lacking strength, it seeks refuge in your name. Give it [?], so that through you it may be lifted out of its pits. It lies submerged in the guilt of its sins, as though in the sea. See, it longs for mercy to lift it up. It looks to mercy to help it in the contest of its struggles, for it knows that its lowly nature is weak before these impulses. I too, whose thoughts are weak, looked upon its weakness, and I set my mind on traveling with it to the appointed meeting with mercy. Let mercy be like a guide ahead of his steps, and show him the path of forgiveness for which he waits. He waits for the forgiveness of sins, and walks fearfully, filled with dread. Forgive his sins so that he may be courageous on his life's journey. The guilty man has lived a short life, full of sins. Have mercy on his sins before the lamp of his life goes out. The course of this short-lived man's life is a lamp: it burns only briefly, and the oil of mercy runs out in it. The fire of temptations sucks up his life like oil. Suddenly he goes out, and the light of his understanding vanishes. Death violently sweeps through the cavern of his body, and he becomes a lifeless, decaying ruin. Lifeless, he remains in Sheol, subject to decay, until that voice bursts forth that brings the dead to life. He is accustomed to pondering this decay at all times, and he is distressed lest he depart under the guilt of his sins. He reflects on his sins; therefore he asks for compassion and mercy. Have mercy on his sins before he journeys to the home of his ancestors. The mortal man's ancestors journeyed to the house of death, and he too is likewise preparing provisions for his journey. The road of death is a great road for the children of Adam.

They travel it every day, and it never runs out of travelers. They are worn down every day by this unceasing journey, and worry that they may go to Sheol while still guilty. You who pardon sins, have mercy on the sins for which we are guilty, for the guilt of our sins has grown greater than that of all generations. We have incurred great debts, and our indebtedness cannot be counted. The interest on the record of our debts has grown beyond what we borrowed. We have borrowed an evil loan of wickedness from the Evil One, and now he charges us interest through shameful deeds. Our race began with shameful deeds from the beginning, and it longs to finish the days of its life in that same habit. Habit has conquered it and continues to conquer it throughout its life. It finds it hateful to hate the habit of its shameful deeds. Lover of humanity, have pity on the human being who hates his own life. Give him strength to overcome the onslaught of his desires. Give strength to him in his feebleness, for his strength is weak, so that he does not lose heart before temptations and tyrannical demons. The wrestler, weaker than all, is caught in two struggles: with the passions of his soul and with the demons that bewilder him in his weakness. Strengthen the impulses of this weak man who asks and pleads, and drive away from him the evil demons that thirst for his blood. My Lord, do not allow the desire of the wicked to be fulfilled, lest they exalt themselves and mock your great name. Good One, you called us by your great name from the beginning. Fulfill in deed the naming of our lowly race by your name. When you fashioned us, you placed the titles of your name upon our heads. Confirm them through deeds worthy of your name. Your name is glorious and cannot be expressed by those who speak. Let your name not be dishonored by the names that express our lowliness. If we have done wrong, we have wronged ourselves and have not diminished you. Neither loss nor gain comes near you. You are as you are, and you exist without change. Your command goes among all created beings without growing weary. The wrongdoing of the wicked and oppressive does not weary you, nor does the praise of the upright and righteous add to your glory. Reproaches do not disgrace the name of your righteousness, nor do exaltations raise the rank of your perfection.

Praise and insult are the same to you in view of your greatness, for the nature of your being admits neither of them. Your nature does not even have this name, “your nature.” For lack of names, we give it the name “nature.” No other nature brought you into being, you who bring creatures into being. Nor does a title belonging to things brought into being befit you. Then let created beings call you only as befits you. Let us not soil your name with borrowed names that are beneath you. No designation befits the name of your eternal being except this one: the Being who exists without beginning. It is fitting for everything that has been made to address you by this title, which you yourself taught the work of your hands to use in calling upon you. You revealed the name of your eternal being to Moses your servant. It is therefore clear that there is no other designation for your name. Glorious is your will—how greatly it loves the work of its hands! Through its own work it displays the power of its eternal being. My speech, which loves words, gazed upon this will and began to bring forth words of sorrow over sinners. My speech offers a sacrifice of words on behalf of those who speak. Accept its sacrifice, you who accept sacrifices and prayers. Its sacrifice is a plea full of cries. Have pity on its words, even if they are too contemptible to be accepted. Weak as it is, it begs you with loud cries, like the widow pleading with that ruthless judge. You composed the parable that makes known the weakness of our race, and portrayed an example in the widow whom the tyrant heeded. If pleading overcame the ruthlessness of that ruthless man, how much more will your own mercy incline toward sinners! If the ruthless man became merciful, as you showed, openly display the power of a miracle toward our wickedness. If the unjust man secured justice for the woman who had been wronged, how much more will you, the just one, judge justly the wrong done to us! We are wronged, my Lord, by temptations and by Satan. Settle the dispute between us with a judgment befitting your office as judge. Two adversaries have become the cause of all our evils: our evil inclination and the Evil One, who has hated us from the beginning.

The Evil One became our counselor, advising vile deeds, and people went out to pursue his vile deeds. Through his vile deeds he disfigured the lovely beauty of our image, and heavenly and earthly beings were driven away from us. They marveled at the beauty of our image before our folly; and after we sinned, they turned and wondered at our ugliness. Maker of our image in the likeness of his image, which is not made of parts, have pity on our image for the sake of your image, which is not made of parts. You have no image made of parts like mortals. And this is the wonder: you have given us a name that we do not deserve. You have called us by the name of your greatness, O Good One who is wholly good. Do not let the name of your goodness be changed by the evil of our wrongdoing. Far be it! This cannot happen, nor is it possible: that our wrongdoing, a mere gnat, should overcome the power that holds everything. What is the wrongdoing of demons and human beings compared with your mercies? Or what is the evil of all creation before your compassion? Your grace is greater than the creatures that came from you, and your compassion cannot be compared with the work of your hands. My thoughts, which love wandering, gazed at the mark of your mercies, and began to incline toward the mark of your great mercies. You fixed the mark of your mercies among the lines of the Scriptures. And now, for nearly six thousand years, it has not changed. Your will has dealt mercifully with every generation, and it has not diminished from what it is, right to the end. You pronounced a sentence of death on Adam because he sinned, yet Adam lived for more than nine hundred years after he sinned. You sentenced Cain to seven punishments of seven lashes, yet you did not carry them out exactly as you had decreed. You said, “I will wipe out everything I have made, without pity.” Yet behold, all creation remains, together with all who came into being. You cursed Canaan to become a slave and a slave of slaves, yet mighty kings arose from him and enslaved nations. You came down, without coming down, among the Babylonians to bring about [?], and you turned your weapons toward peace. You threatened the land of Palestine, saying that no one would remain in it.

Yet tens of thousands of its inhabitants remained without punishment. You raised your hand against the Egyptians and scourged them, yet there was no punishment without a little grace mixed into it. You swore that you would destroy the Israelites in the terrible wilderness, yet after you swore, you provided for them lovingly. We have seen that you disciplined lovingly wherever you disciplined, and there is no punishment into which you have not mixed kindness. We have considered your kindness and continue to consider it, and we do not cease pleading over our sins. We take refuge in your great love at all times, like children who constantly cling to their parents. We acknowledge your fatherhood alone, Father, and we do not lovingly call the one who begot us “father.” We know no other father but you, for there are no fathers whose love resembles your fatherhood. You alone are Father and Lord and also Judge, for all these belong to you together with your being, which has no beginning. Without beginning, you have possessed all that you possess as God, and there is nothing you have that has not always existed. To you, our Lord, [?] everyone’s eyes are lifted, and from you we ask for daily food and forgiveness of wrongdoing. Have pity on our lives, O fountain of immortal life, and grant us a time filled with peace and the nourishment we need to live. We have sinned greatly, and our wrongdoing has risen above our heads. We are close to drowning in the abyss of our sins. The number of our shameful deeds has grown beyond counting, and our guilt cannot be measured by any known measure. We have suffered many severe blows, yet our inclination has not stopped occupying itself with evil. The weight of our great punishment has [?] our hateful deeds, yet we have not tried to hate our wrongdoing—not at all. If our wrongdoing testifies against us, Lord, as it is written, show mercy and forgive, for the sake of your immeasurable compassion. Your mercy cannot be measured by those who measure. If that is so, what is our wrongdoing? A paltry gnat.

Our wickedness is a paltry gnat, however great it may be. Cast it like a drop of spit into the vast sea of your kindness. Do not be disgusted with us because we have sinned like sinners, for you understand the nature of our sinfulness better than anyone. You know us before our formation and after we came into being, and you understand our evil inclination and its tendency to turn aside. For you formed it, and you set it to the task of reflection. From you, then, it learned to reflect on what lies between good and evil. If you are the teacher and it is the pupil under your instruction, perfect your pupil according to the will of your greatness. Take a zealous interest in the little child who has become your pupil, and recite before him a lesson of words that will kindle his zeal. Write the letters of the name of your being upon his mind, so that he may read with understanding and keep his conduct in good order throughout his life. Repeat and trace out for him another lesson, that of love for humanity, so that he may bind his love to the Aleph of the Eternal One and the Taw of humanity. When a person has learned to read well, it is [?] for him to write and reflect on it through the freedom of his soul. You filled the soul with freedom when you formed it, and it has ample power to distinguish discerningly between the two. Discern, discerning soul, this distinction placed within your nature. Know your nature and your Maker, who placed both within you. You have both, O soul, mistress of good and evil. Judge justly which of the two is right. With your bodily palate you distinguish sweet from bitter. Discern your own nature just as you have distinguished what is not your own. It is fitting for you to see beauty, if you are beautiful. When the beauty of your soul pleases you, your judgment [?]. Every human being who possesses a soul is a discerning examiner [?], and it is easy for him to distinguish the ugly from the beautiful. Rightly, then, do speechless creatures bring us to judgment and condemn us, though they do not share our guilt. If the divine command has chastised us justly,

and changed the seasons outside the order of their succession, our punishment is just, and the scourging for our insolence is right. Indeed, we deserve to be scourged with double lashes. Our inclination deserves to be scourged with double lashes, for it knows that it has sinned but does not remember the reckoning of judgment. It has heard of the judgment that will take place at the very end, yet it does not tremble at the torment associated with the name of Gehenna. Woe to us! How much more tyrannical our mind is than a tyrant! The reckoning of judgment is certain for us, yet we do not regard it as certain. If it is certain for us, why does the evil inclination not tremble? And at whom does it scoff in the face of what is certain and proven? Your judgment is certain, greatest of judges, who [?] all. What shall we do, since we have treated your judicial decrees as false? We have listened to the proclamation of your righteous judgment as though it were false. If we had truly listened to it, we would not have sinned. We have sinned as we have because our nature clings to sin. Lord of all natures, have mercy on our nature, so that it may not be condemned. We are anxious about our sins throughout our lives, and now we are devising ways to seek release from our debts. Release us from our debts, Lord who has authority over our debts, and erase them from the record in the book of your judgments. Remove them from the archives of your judgment, and tear them up before the eyes of angels and human beings. Let no bond written in Adam’s name remain with you, so that Adam’s enemies may not boast over Adam’s debts. He wrote a bond of debt in Eden by eating the fruit, and because he did not repay it, Satan rejoiced over the burden of his debts. The interest on that commandment accumulated against his children, and they gave their bodies as pledges to ravenous death. Death took possession of their bodies as pledges, and now it ruthlessly wears them away in the hollows of Sheol. Sheol, the devourer, swallowed the children of dust, yet no mortal made of dust reflects on the dust of his fellow mortals. You who fashioned our dust, have pity on our dust that has become dust, and raise our dust from death and from sins. We die by two deaths, one worse than [?]: through the destruction of death and through the foul deeds of our evil inclination.

You who love our lives, restore our lives from both, and open before us the gate of death and forgiveness of wrongdoing. Death and wrongdoing have shut the gate of their deceitful schemes in our faces, and now they are plotting to engulf us without resurrection. You are the path of resurrection and the atonement for sins. You have taught us that death will cease and wrongdoing will fall silent. Through one of our race you marked out the road for the renewal of our race. Grant that we may travel toward the glorious appointed time when our lives will be renewed. Seal the gifts of our lives with the vitality of his life. We trust that you will not prove false to the promise of your words. The leaven of peace that you took from our race, full of sins, is now honored with the glories of your divinity. You made the firstfruits of our life more glorious than all, together with you. Honor our lives for the sake of the life of the one you chose. You showed him [?] a great, inexpressible love by raising him to the great height of your name. The one at the right hand of your divinity therefore pleads with you to be reconciled to us, because we have wickedly provoked you. The prayer that he offers you on behalf of sinners has been spoken. Now is the time that calls for the order of prayers. He is accustomed to pray lovingly for those dear to him. Receive his words with the love that befits your kindness. You lovingly cherish him in the rank [?] of your name. Fulfill in deed the plea he makes in words on our behalf. The head of our race prays with us on our behalf. Lover of our race, hear the one who belongs to our race, and have mercy on our race. Listen to our petition, which the Son, a member of our race, offers you. Extend to us a helping hand of forgiveness for sins, as we ask of you. Hear us, Good One, to whom the petition [?] of our words is audible. Persuade yourself, if our plea to you is too small. Our plea is small compared with the greatness of our guilt. Yet not to plead with you is itself a cause of guilt. We are all caught in a struggle of suffering because of our sins. To plead is perilous, but not to plead is doubly perilous. It is perilous to plead, because you have no need for anyone to plead with you. Yet we are afraid indeed if we do not plead concerning our wrongdoing.

You have no need of the pleading words of those who entreat you, since you hear everyone's plea before they plead with you. The wickedness of every generation was visible to you before all created things. But why do I speak of generations and times alongside your eternal being? Within your being you hold the limits of all finite things. Nothing exists in creation that does not exist in you. With you is the remembrance of the books that have existed and will exist. Nothing among created things is hidden from your knowledge. Our wickedness and the righteousness of watchful angels and human beings are plain to you. The repayment due to the good and the wicked is weighed by you. Although everything that exists and will exist is indeed in you, we cannot refrain from pleading over our sins. Because of our sins [?], we humble ourselves before your majesty. Forgive our sins and erase the record of our great wickedness. Have mercy, Compassionate One, on our wickedness, which has grown very strong. We are close to becoming companions of the people of Sodom. Let us not give wickedness a place to dwell in us, for if it dwells in us, Sodom's punishment will be small compared with our sentence. My Lord, let us not become companions of the people of Sodom in judgment, lest we leave behind a reputation for wickedness like theirs. Keep from our people a scourge like that inflicted on the people of Sodom. Do not make our land an image of the loathsome land of Sodom. The land of Sodom has been waste and void ever since it burned. It lies desolate and barren, without harvests of grain or fruit. May we never see that punishment, never at all; nor may its deeds even be mentioned in the course of our lives. Our human lives are short and full of sins. Lover of humanity, have pity on our lives, so full of sins. Do not condemn us according to the guilt incurred by our sins, for we have already incurred a few lashes on account of our offenses. You have disciplined our wrongdoing enough through visible things. Do not add twice as many lashes, lest we perish. Withdraw your rod from striking our bodies and our land, and rebuke the heavenly hosts so that they do not harm us.

Calm them so that they do not show us angry faces, and let them calm the air that has been disturbed because of our wrongdoing. Give a sign to the ruler who governs the course of the months of the year, that he may put peaceful restraints on the turbulent seasons. Call and warn the spirit who holds authority over the wind, so that the violent force of the air’s movements may be restrained. Give an order to the one who orders the silent seasons, that he may teach them to observe the proper order of their changes. Through their disorderly changes, everything has dwindled, and nothing remains that has not been impoverished from its former state. Human life is impoverished and lacks every good thing. Both the body’s nourishment and the soul’s activity are in turmoil. Rest of body and mind has fled from us, and humanity stands like a tree in the days of winter. The course of the months of the year resembles a gloomy winter, and there is no consolation to inspire hope as it should. There is no mention at all of anything restful and peaceful, but only the sound of dreadful things thundering through the earth. Only the sound of wrongdoing thunders among those on earth, while the voice of good things is silent, like a corpse without life.
