Every kind of goodness has died, like a dead person left unburied, and those who practiced these things have forgotten them as they forget the dead. Good things have died, and every kind of wickedness has come alive. Woe to us, for we have become dead to truth and alive to wrongdoing! We have raised dead wrongdoing to life through our wickedness, and in our cruelty we have killed the infants of righteousness. We have deprived our righteousness of offspring and have not allowed it to nurture the fruits of love. Our cruelty toward truth resembles Pharaoh’s, and perhaps our hostility is crueler than that of the Egyptians. Pharaoh drowned the bodies of infants in the river’s waters; we drown the soul’s life in the flood of wrongdoing. People put to death the life of the immortal soul—not that it dies, but that it becomes dead through wrongdoing. The death that comes from being dead through wrongdoing is worse than every other death. The voice of the one who gives life to the dead bears witness, for he declared these things:

“Death,” he said, “is not what kills the body alone, but what destroys body and soul together.” He destroys body and soul together on the day of judgment. Woe to us, for the day of judgment that brings these things about has drawn near! Woe to us! Our bodies have perished here through hunger and pain, and we are destined to be tormented in body and soul. Woe to us! We have worn ourselves out in poverty during this temporary life, and in the life to come we will be deprived of every good thing. Woe to us! We have lived, but have not conducted our lives well; we are to be raised, yet we do not live as befits our resurrection. We have lived on earth and have not been diligent during our stay here. How, then, will we fare in that way of life among the heavenly beings? So we have no place that is a place of work, except only that Gehenna where no work is done. Woe to us! Perhaps our lives will be spent there, in that labor filled with weeping and gnashing of teeth. May what I have said not happen to us according to our sins, and may we not be deprived of the good things both here and hereafter. May we not leave this world naked and go to find ourselves lacking glory in that order of existence. May we not be estranged from that glory which glorifies the good, and may they not cast us out like the man who was cast out of the banquet. You promised rich blessings to our race through one of our own race. May the promise of your words not be proved false through our slackness. We are very slack and idle in the work of truth, and we find it tiresome to labor even a little at good deeds. The gain of immortal life is great and abundant, yet we have no desire to take even a single penny from it. Fearful is the judgment that takes place there in that order of existence, and it does not forgive us even a single penny of our debts. It holds us accountable even for a word whose sound is idle, yet we have never reflected, nor do we now reflect, on that examination. That examination came to my mind, which occupies itself with words. It trembled and was terrified, and began composing a plea in words. I urged my foolish mind to compose a plea, knowing that it is too weak to put together ways of living.

Pleading is much easier for those who plead than hard work, and for this reason my mind chose what was easy. The lazy person has no desire to advance through hard work, knowing that the spiritual way of life is demanding. My mind too fled from spiritual labors, and now it is sewing itself a garment of words to cover itself with. It saw itself naked in its nakedness, and took words and spread them over its face out of shame. It chose to cover its nakedness with words, because it had heard that these had covered others like itself. It heard the voice of the wise man rebuking the lazy person and rousing the slack to work, as though waking them from sleep. “How long,” the wise man cried to the lazy person, “will you sleep and refrain from the work of righteousness?” He drew a picture of the ant for the sluggard who finds labor tiresome, so that he might consider it and rouse his mind to work. “Look at the ant,” he said to the heavyhearted person, “and learn from it the ways of diligence and vigilance of soul.” See how alert the lowly creature is in its work, and stir your impulses to the practice of good deeds. See how it prepares its food ahead of time, and you too prepare the provisions that are made ready for you. See that among them there are neither those who command nor those who are commanded, and urge yourself to labor before someone else urges you. My thoughts, which hate hard work, heard these words and put their hands to the work of persuasive words. Persuasive speech laid a foundation for those who labor, so that [?] they might build a structure of labors from words. I wanted to show a structure of labors to those who labor, so that they might build their conduct above my words. O builders of the structure of spiritual labors, build the labors of your conduct upon my words. Come, you who plead for forgiveness for every kind of wrongdoing; mingle my speech with your words in sorrow and tears.

Come, you whose conduct is as perfect as possible; sprinkle your labors like compassion upon sinners. Come, sinners who have sinned and done wrong as sinners do; walk along with words full of meditation about sinners. My discourse has pondered words about sinners, so that I might teach them a path full of grace and mercy. My mind mixes grace and mercy into the medicine of words, so that through words people may become worthy of grace and mercy. Into the drink of words I have mixed the medicine of forgiveness of sins, and I long for everyone to drink it and wipe away their wrongdoing. With this purpose I gave it the title “Supplication,” so that I might pray and plead concerning my sins and those of my companions. Come then, my companions, and join me in pleading with words. Together let us plead with the One who needs nothing, yet asks for supplication. He asks for supplication—not that he needs it, as my words might suggest, but to teach those who plead to plead with him. Like a teacher, his directing will stands above our heads and teaches us wisdom, yet the childishness of our souls does not become wise. You who make people wise, have pity on people slow of heart, who despise the books of your life-giving instruction. See how weak our nature is amid its weaknesses, and do not despise it when it constantly sins because of its impulses. You yourself formed it from dust as you pleased, and mixed into its clay the impulses of a weak inclination. Your directing will mixed a weak inclination with its dust, and without you it cannot strengthen the weakness of its clay. Insistent passions oppress its life throughout its lifetime, and do not allow it to be diligent in the work that brings it life. Like gnats, they constantly hover over its back and distract it from attending to good deeds. Night and day it is worn down by the pressure of troubles, and there is no time when it is wholly collected in its mind. Summer and winter it toils and struggles in want; it works continually, yet its need is never satisfied. Like a beggar, he too goes around seeking alms to sustain his life, constantly knocking at the door of the labors of every craft. Every day he seeks a new discovery of other labors, so that [?] he may find temporary nourishment to buy his life.

The weary man grows tired of devising new labors, and the more he toils, the stronger his poverty grows. Alas for the poor man, the son of poor people, who is poor and foolish and does not understand how to keep within the bounds of his poverty! Alas for the beggar who continually goes begging, summer and winter, yet whose own needs are not satisfied by alms! Alas for the hired worker who hires out his life to exhausting tasks, working every day, yet cheated of his wages through ignorance! Ignorance has made him both a victim of fraud and a beggar. The more he goes begging, the greater his toil and the smaller his wages. Adam’s dust has dwindled and been exhausted by hardships. You who formed his dust, have pity on his dust before it perishes! The particles remain together in his assembled body only briefly, and already the winds of suffering move them from one place to another. The whirlwind of suffering sweeps violently through him and heaps him up like mounds along the seashore. The sufferings of the man filled with suffering resemble water and wind. When they pass through him, he becomes like dust before whirlwinds. The whirlwind of suffering sweeps forcefully through his mortality and does not allow his dust to rest in one place. See, the dust of our clay is swept away and scattered everywhere, and there is no place in creation that has not been sown with our dust. See, we are scattered like seed in the earth’s bosom and made into food for crawling creatures and birds. One thing is lacking to the misery of our nature, bitter in its nature: that we should remain in the earth and our dust become a portion for the dust. No, merciful one! May this thing I have said not happen to us, and may the word born of empty expectation not come true. May our great hope in your greatness not be emptied, and may the truth of your name not be made false by our falsehood. You are faithful, and in you the truth of your name stands firm. Our falsehood does not harm you—not in any way at all. Stand firm, then, in the promises you have spoken to our race, and give us your hand so that we may rise a little from our fallen state. We have fallen deeply into countless shameful deeds, and unless your help reaches us, we have fallen forever. You exist forever, Lord, our Master and the Master of all.

Through you, heaven and earth and everything in them are sustained. Do not be disgusted with us, Lord, do not be disgusted with us because of the greatness of our wrongdoing. Instead, give your name the honor that befits your name. Honor your name through the salvation you bring us, so that the demons may not mock your name because of our wrongdoing. Because of our wrongdoing, the demons have mocked your great name. By forgiving wrongdoing, cut off the pretext of those who seek pretexts. Forgive our wrongdoing, and let its name never be remembered at all. Then the pretext of those who seek a pretext will be cut off. Put an end to this too: our offering you petitions at every hour. For we have wearied you with the wearisomeness of our words, though you do not grow weary. See, our words too have grown weak and have become inadequate for composition; they can no longer compose different kinds of petitions. See, articulate speech has grown weary of giving birth to words, and it has no desire to join with the mind. See, the mind too remains with its own thoughts and no longer wishes to meditate through the exchange of words. See, there are no words about forgiveness that have not been spoken. However much anyone speaks, he says the same things. See, they have been spoken and are repeated by every mouth. And what benefit is there, when no benefit comes from the toil of speaking them? See, our whole nature has given up on everything. Lord of all natures, have mercy on our nature, full of sins.
On Jonah the Prophet

Eighth Discourse: On Jonah the Prophet. It is recited during the Supplication of the Ninevites.
Response: Blessed is he who revealed his glorious deeds through his servants and fulfilled and completed his mysteries, my brothers.

The Creator placed great riches within the Scriptures and concealed them in a mystery until what had been decreed was fulfilled. He spread veils like a garment over the letters, so that eyes of flesh would not look with contempt on the treasury of the Spirit. He concealed his riches from ignorant childhood until it reached maturity; then he opened for it the door of his mercy. He laid awe upon those who knew his covenants, so that the power of wisdom might grow greatly in their eyes. He did not give the immature in heart authority over his hidden things, lest his precious things be despised through carelessness of soul. The heir was a child and could not manage his wealth, and he graciously gave us, as though to strangers, something from his channels [?]. Although he clearly disclosed his hidden things through his creations, he concealed the salvation of our lives in a mystery until the end. He chose one people and called it by his name as an heir, so that through it he might open the treasury of his mercy to all nations.

But when the son saw that he was called by name and set apart from everyone, senseless pride seized him, and he despised everyone. Childish in mind, he looked at the letters with eyes of flesh and did not examine the power of the hidden things through the movements of the soul. The child thought that the riches belonged to him alone, and in foolish pride he despised and scorned his fellow servants. He did not know that he was honored above all for the sake of all, because the one concealed within him reconciles everyone to the Lord of all. Even the righteous walked [?] along this path of the people's election, and they considered a journey to the nations unnecessary. The Law too strengthened their adherence to what was written, and through love for their people it made them zealous to hate the nations. They did not want the uncircumcised to become members of the household, lest the chosen people lose its inheritance. They were not pleased with his mission to the nations, and Jonah bears witness: when he was sent, he fled and hid. The Hebrew heard the sound of resurrection, that his dead were coming to life, and he was deeply distressed, lest they live and his people die. New tidings fell upon the ears of the son of the Hebrews, and anguish seized him at the new report of the nations’ return. He clothed himself in inconsolable sorrow over what he heard, and considered fleeing rather than being sent along the road to the pagans. The man circumcised in the flesh heard that the uncircumcised would live freely, and instead of tearing his clothing, he tore his mind with doubt. Revelation called him and spoke with him in a mystery: “Go out and gather for me the rational sheep into the fold of life. “Rise, go out, and proclaim the message of salvation among the drowned. With the sound of your words, awaken those asleep in wickedness. “Come, travel the road of proclamation to the dwelling of foreigners, and set before them a new path for worshiping my lordship. “Come, go and make peace with the angry who have departed from my household, and through grace reconcile them to righteousness. “Come, go and visit the sick who have long suffered the pains of wickedness, and with your words rebuke the fevers of their minds.

“Take medicine from the treasury of my hidden lordship, and bind their wounds with repentance leading to forgiveness. “Grind up compassion and mercy, and give their minds a drink. With the sweet medicine, wash away from them the filth of wickedness. “Take a lamp shining with knowledge of me and place it before their eyes. Drive away from them the darkness of error that has blinded them. “Grind those without understanding with the salt of knowledge of me, so that through your hands they may acquire the sweet taste of [?] the Creator. “First show them harsh words before deeds, and if they feel remorse, comfort them with the message of forgiveness. “Arm yourself with the strength of divine help. Enter the arena and trample down sin, which has killed humanity. “Take up the sword of the Spirit’s word on the tip of your tongue, and destroy wickedness, the tyrant that has rebelled against righteousness. “Uproot the structure of the gods’ names that error has built, and place the confession of one God in the minds of human beings. “Rise, go to Assyria, the city of kings that has rebelled against me, and instead of arrows, cast words of warning into it. “Call to her and shake her, full of pride, with the sound of your words. Cast into her ears: ‘A terrible overthrow is now hastening toward you!’ “Go and tell her: ‘Look, I am shaking the earth beneath you, and the report of the day of your downfall will terrify all the nations.’” The son of Amittai heard the voice proclaiming a terrible overthrow, yet he was still reluctant to travel the road to the nations. He considered the compassion of the one sending him, which overcomes his anger, and thought that perhaps he would speak words that would not be believed. “I know,” he said, “that you are merciful and that the wicked will live; your great love changes the severity of your anger. “If I go and proclaim terrifying messages to the Assyrians, I will be proved a liar, because you do not act according to your threats.” Two doubts hemmed in the road, the road before Jonah: that he might be proved false, and that the chosen people might be excluded. The messenger was considering the outcome of his journey.

His people's demand for an accounting and the uncertainty about his words frightened him. He chose flight, to avoid being sent on the road to the nations, lest his going break down the fence of the Law. Jonah arose to flee and hide from the Knower of all, and to live in a country where the receiver of revelations would not be stirred. The preacher's flight was not a flight from God; he changed his location with this intention: that he would not be sent. For he knew that the Creator's power is everywhere, and that the work of his hands cannot be hidden from God. He changed his location in keeping with the manifestation of prophecy, supposing that revelations dwelt only in Judah. The son of Amittai thought that if he went far away, God would leave him alone, and the voice of revelations would no longer urge him to go to Assyria. He chose a route across the calm sea to the land of Tarshish, so that the farther he [?], the farther [?] the Creator's voice would be from him. He hired a ship so that salvation for the nations would not be traded, and left his country so that the nations would not receive favor over his people. He fled from dry land so that the hearts of the uncircumcised would not be soothed, and traveled across the sea so that the voice of his pronouncements would not be proved false. The fugitive went down into the ship and slept because of his sorrow. A command went out like a messenger and stirred up the sea. The tempest became like a hunter and spread its nets, and Jonah fell with the sailors into the snares of the waters. With the rod of the wind, the command was whipping the sea: “For whose sake have you hidden a runaway servant from the Knower of all?” He struck the silent things and roused them against those who speak, and the mute taught rational beings how to deal with the Creator. The wind and the waters battered one another because of Jonah, to catch him for the work of preaching to the nations. The sea was stirred beyond its usual order against the son of Amittai, while the raging waves searched for him where [?] he was hiding. That storm was unlike an everyday storm, and the course it followed differed from its usual course. The scourging did not extend over the whole [?] of the sea; it was being whipped only around Jonah's ship.

A great wonder was appearing among the waves: though the sea was calm, it raged against Jonah and was tranquil toward everyone else. Oh, the command that gave understanding to things without senses, and stirred them up against the speaker who wanted to remain silent! Oh, how wise the silent things, deprived of intelligence, became: one part was tranquil, and another part raged beyond its usual order! The sea was tranquil toward the sailors as they traveled, but it grew bitter with harsh waves where Jonah was. The air was calm, the waves were still, and everyone was sailing along, while Jonah's ship was being battered by the tempest. The barrier set by the command divided the sea for the sailors, and they saw a marvel: though it was entirely calm, it raged against Jonah. That portion of the sea was being scourged with the lashes of the command, while the lash of the wind was crossing the boundary of the command [?]. It drove the ship down into the depths, yet it did not break apart; it raised it to the surface of the sea, yet it did not overturn. The command watched over it, while the rod of the wind scourged it. It rose to the heights and descended into the depths, but he did not destroy it. As his ship was scourged, the sailors suffered harsh blows, and they lost hope of escaping the raging waves. They advised one another that each should cry out to his god, so that perhaps they might escape the raging waves and remain alive. The captain woke Jonah: “Get up and plead! Pray and ask your God; perhaps he will give us relief.” Jonah had sunk into heavy sleep in the bottom of his ship, and he was unaware of the scourging of the sea on his account. The fugitive got up and saw that the sea was raging with waves, and he judged in his thoughts that the storm had arisen because of him. He did not pray with the sailors for the sea to become calm, because he knew he had done wrong and that, even if he pleaded, he would not be accepted. He refrained from praying, knowing, as one who had despised the commandment, that even if he called, the one he had despised would not answer him.

The sailors saw that their pleading had been in vain, and they decided to investigate the wrongdoing in their deeds. They attributed the turmoil of the sea around them to sin, for they saw that it was calm, yet it chastised them as it would an offender. Through the scourging of the sea they gained understanding, discerned, and knew that wrongdoing had caused the storm to disturb that portion of the sea. The blast of the wind became their teacher and made them wise. They considered among themselves that whoever had done wrong should reveal his sin. In the furnace of the lots they tested one another like discerning people, so that the deceit hidden within the mind might come to light. They cast lots to disclose who had sinned, so that he might pay the penalty for his wrongdoing, which had stirred up the sea. The command descended among the lots and selected them, and the lot of the Hebrew came up before the sailors. The uncircumcised asked the man circumcised in body, “What have you done? Reveal your deeds, tell us your people, and make your country known.” Jonah answered the sailors, “I am a Hebrew, and I am a servant of the God of all, who established everything. I fled and hid from God, who knows everything, and his command caught me in a strong snare made of yielding waters.” O herald who sought to conceal his proclamation, yet unwillingly disclosed and revealed the worship of his Lord! For this purpose he had been sent among foreigners: to go and proclaim one God, to put an end to their error. He fled from his people, and the nations caught him—the man who hated the nations. Unwillingly, he became a herald to the nations he hated. “I fear the one Lord,” he said, “who holds everything, and he governs the sea and the dry land according to his will.” The uncircumcised learned from the Hebrew that the good servant had fled and hidden from God, who knows everything. The sailors were alarmed when they saw the marvel that had happened because of Jonah. They tried to turn toward dry land, but the sea would not let them. The ship was held captive at sea, unable to move. Whenever they turned it toward dry land, the command held it back. The blast of wind shook it from every side.

The waves were armed against it like cavalry. The surf battered it and surrounded it like an army, while the blast of wind blocked its way like a wall. The sailors were caught between conflicting thoughts because of Jonah. They considered his death and his life, and how difficult both were. “What shall we do with Jonah?” they said in their fear. “Our deliverance is difficult, and your death is grievous. Do not blame us.” Jonah answered the sailors with discernment: “Pick me up and throw me among the waves, and see—the sea will become calm. For it is me that the ravenous lion, the mouth of the waters, wants. Give it its portion, so that it will not rage against your lives. It is against me that the great deep roars with the sound of its surging waters. The whirlwind too has come out after me and stirred up the sea. Because of my wrongdoing, a wall of wind has barred your way. It is watching for me to be lowered, and then it will dismantle the barrier of its waves.” The sailors cried out to God in great fear: “We beg you, Creator, do not hold us guilty for innocent blood. You are the Lord who rules over everything, on sea and dry land. You yourself wish this to happen; fulfill your will.” The sailors picked Jonah up and threw him among the waves. The surging waters grew calm, and the men marveled at the Creator’s power. They also made vows and fulfilled them afterward, on this condition—this condition: that they would become servants of the God of all. The fugitive fell into the snare of the waters, and the waves bound him. In silence, the mute waters were passing judgment on his discernment. After his scourging, the Judge pronounced sentence and broke the pen that had written the decree that he should descend to Sheol. He dug a grave for the living dead man inside a living body, to preserve the bodily man’s life within a living body. The command went down after the fish and drew it up to the surface. It rose, received the living man, and buried him inside itself. The sojourner entered the fish, a tomb within a tomb. The divine signal shut the door upon the living dead man. The fugitive descended into a prison filled with darkness, and the fish’s entrails bound his feet in damp stocks.

He fled from dry land, but the sea caught him and handed him over to the fish. It brought [?] into a tomb within a tomb—the deep and the fish. Oh, the marvel that happened to the son of Amittai! He descended alive into two tombs and did not decay. Oh, the dead man who was escorted alive to Sheol! Oh, the man of dust who was being buried in the [?] of a body! Who is this mortal, buried entirely, yet alive when laid low? Who is this prisoner, wholly confined, yet moving about in the grave? The mortal did not live by the strength of natural life. A command preserved him, as infants are preserved inside wombs. Human life cannot be sustained without air, yet this man of flesh lived without air, like spiritual beings. It was not his own doing that he fled and hid rather than be sent, for a great mystery had already portrayed in him what was to come [?]. The Knower of all did not bury him in the fish so that he would die. Through his descent he depicted the wonders that were to come. Through a human being he was going to give life to all, and through a human being he would free all from slavery. Through a human being's death he was going to destroy death's dominion, and he buried Jonah as a symbolic foreshadowing before the event. Our Lord's body would not undergo decay in Sheol, and he preserved Jonah without decay as a symbol of our Savior. For three days he buried Jonah in the belly of the fish [?], so that he would be a pattern of the hidden truth [?] when it was revealed. A living fish became a grave for the one who portrayed the mysteries, and a new grave received the body of the one who fulfilled the mysteries. Something new was happening symbolically to the son of Amittai: when the fish [?] his body, it kept him alive. The fulfillment of Jonah's symbolic mystery was also something new: the body swallowed by ravenous death did not decay. The symbolic mysteries of things to come are new and full of wonder: a body is buried in a bodily grave, yet lives and moves about. The son of Amittai opened a new path before the events, so that, when it was fulfilled, it would not seem strange to those who saw it. The wonders happened for the sake of the reality of the nations' salvation, so that, when human beings were saved through a human being, they would not doubt. Otherwise, let the man circumcised in flesh and uncircumcised in heart tell us:

What is the power hidden in the symbolic mystery that Jonah enacted? What made it necessary for him to remain in the fish for three days and live a life unlike ordinary human life? Suppose he was guilty of despising the commandment and his Lord's word: why did he not punish him with other afflictions, rather than with the fish? When did he chastise the members of his household as he did Jonah? Who else was confined alive in Sheol like the son of Amittai? At what time did he send his heralds to foreigners? When did he send a prophet to the nations outside his people? Why did he not prophesy in the land of Judah? Why did the voice set him apart from the people, saying, "Go to Assyria"? Son of Abraham, remove the covering laid over your face, and look at the truth hidden in the symbolic mystery that Jonah enacted. Take away the veil that Moses spread, and leave fear behind. See openly the King's image as it truly is. Look and examine the books of the Spirit with discernment, and you will learn that the mysteries were fulfilled in the Hope of the nations. Fix your mind on the new mystery portrayed by the son of Amittai, and see that all the mysteries were fulfilled in the one you crucified. Lift your thoughts to the great height of his preaching, and compare his journey with that of those who turned toward the nations. Let Nineveh be like a mirror before the eyes of your heart, and see how the voice of salvation went out to the four corners of the world. Travel with Jonah and descend into the deep in his company, and behold, you will reach the height above at your journey’s end. The son of Amittai descended and dwelt in Sheol as a symbol of our Savior, and the divine command preserved him, food for worms, in the fish’s belly. The buried man prayed with discernment in the chamber of the fish. He examined his thoughts, begged and begged, and pleaded to return to life. Hear the voice of my petition, God of all, and listen to my words. Bring my life up from destruction to life. I know that I sinned by not serving you on the journey to the nations. Now, through the life you have preserved for me, you have taught me that you love humanity.

You called me to go for the salvation of people; I am willing. Release me from my captivity so that I may go out and bring the dead back to life. I did not know that your love overflowed toward foreigners. I thought you had acquired just one inheritance and that you belonged to it. I thought that if the uncircumcised nations entered your inheritance, perhaps the heir you had chosen would go outside your house. I judged this according to the will of the Law: that the unclean nations should be excluded from its fellowship. Now that I have heard from its author that he calls the nations, I will not shut the door of my mercy in the faces of the wicked. Let my petition come before you, my God, and let me live by your word. Let my life be a sign of life to those dead in wickedness. In the anguish of my life I said that there was no salvation. If you are willing, I will once again see your face. Make me worthy to fulfill the vow of my lips in the land of the living, for if I come up, I will not remain silent: I will proclaim life. Oh, the prayer that was enclosed in a tomb within a tomb, yet broke through the barrier of the fish, the water, and the heights above! Oh, the prisoner who, in exile in the depths of the waters, stretched out his will instead of his steps toward the one who had imprisoned him! Oh, the buried man who spoke with the one who buried him, split open his tomb with the sound of his words, and returned to life! The scribe of the Spirit wrote a letter in the depths of the waters and gave it to the mind to enter and read before the one who knows everything. Spiritual stirrings carried it and delivered it to the Hidden One, and brought back to him a message of hope that he would return to life. The divine command goaded the tomb carrying a living dead man to bring the body buried in its belly up to the land of the living. The fish hurried as it came up toward dry land, for the command that had ordered it to swallow him compelled it to give him back. The pangs of the divine command compelled it to give back what it had taken,

so that the symbol would not remain in the tomb longer than the reality. The ship came up, carrying the mystery of the nations’ salvation. It laid its treasure on the seashore and returned to its own place. Where it had taken on its cargo when it set out to travel into the deep, there it came out, drawn by the command of divine power. It landed in the very harbor from which it had set out, for the captain who stood within it steered it there. Where the fish had swallowed Jonah, there it deposited him, for there he had heard that voice from which he had fled. The son of Amittai came out, saw the light, and heard a voice entirely like the first: “Go to Assyria.” Come, go and proclaim new good news to the uncircumcised nations. Since you have become a symbol, fulfill your symbolism through deeds. For this reason I buried you alive and opened a way before you: so that you might open a door before foreigners, allowing them to come to me. Through your resurrection I sought to raise those buried alive. Look, I have taught you how your life was saved; save those who are lost. Come, go and proclaim salvation and life to those long dead, and raise them through the living hope of repentance. Cultivate the soil of the hearing ear of their minds, and sow within it the good seed of reverence for truth. Uproot the weeds of idolatry that the evil one sowed, and sow the message that one [?] Creator rules over all. He himself taught him the way to the nations, though he was unwilling, and he himself taught him that he ought to have mercy on the nations. The son of Abraham gained discerning understanding and called the nations in keeping with the nature of Abraham’s household. He who was set apart from the nations began to travel to the land of foreigners. He journeyed along the road to his appointed destination in Assyria, as he had been commanded. The voice taught him how great the city of Assyria was: for three days he traveled within Assyria, proclaiming his message there. He also revealed and showed him that its greatness came from God, and that through his hand it had attained an abundance of wealth and people. He began to enter, going a day’s journey through its streets.

As he traveled, he began speaking in a voice full of menace. He proclaimed a message of wrath in everyone’s hearing, saying that the city of Nineveh would be overturned upon its inhabitants. He set a limit of forty days for the fulfillment of his words, to see whether they would turn back; if not, he would do as he had decreed. The Hebrew did not proclaim destruction alone, for he also mingled mercy with the destruction by setting a deadline. With terrifying words he frightened the hardhearted, to bring them down from pride to humility. With hard iron he cut into the disease of their deeds, so that wickedness would not remain like decay in the impulses of their souls. He applied a powerful medicine to the abscess of their minds, to remove from them the mark of wickedness that had killed them. The herald cried out like a trumpet in the city of Nineveh, and the waves of his resounding words shook the city that was full of pride. The mighty winds of the word of his mouth blew against her, and she trembled all over, for she was close to falling. His voice terrified kings, the lowly, and all the regions, and gathered them to hear the new message of his proclamation. He did not shrink before the authority of rulers, nor did he show favoritism toward wealth or the crown esteemed above everything. The people and the king heard his words and trembled in alarm. Though he was despised and scorned, his voice terrified the kings of Assyria. Crowds stood ready to hear his word. He cast the net of his proclamation and captured them. His word caught young and old alike, and with its swiftness restrained the course of every rank of society. The sound of his proclamation reached the king of Assyria. He abandoned his crown, scorned his authority, and honored his word. He issued a proclamation full of sorrow to all the people, that everyone should turn from his deeds to cries of supplication: “Let us hate wrongdoing, the ugliness of our souls, which has made us unclean, and let us love righteousness, beautiful both in its name and in its deeds. Let us curse sin, which has spread its darkness over our minds, and let us see with our understanding the light of the Hebrew man's word. Let us discipline ourselves by practicing fasting from pleasures,

and restrain the onrush of debauchery through chastity. Let us keep our mouths from food, the nourishment of the body, and keep ourselves from practicing oppression. Let even the animals fast from food with us, and let the speechless creatures weep with us because we have provoked him to anger. Who knows whether the God of all will have mercy on us, turn the fury of his anger away from us, and not destroy us?” The Good One, who saw them before they existed, saw that the wicked had repented and had turned his fury into reconciliation. He made them hate wrongdoing when they were unwilling, and his mercy awakened their capacity for remorse. He himself drew them by a hidden prompting toward knowledge of him, and gave repentance the reward of his kindness. It was not the Ninevites who opened the road of repentance. The Hidden One, in his love, revealed his hiddenness to the members of his household. Through them Jonah portrayed the wonders to come: that at the end of the ages he would show mercy to the nations through the second Adam. The herald saw that the Good One had mingled mercy with his anger, and he was deeply grieved that the sentence he had pronounced was not carried out. He cried out to him to follow the course of his own inclination as before, and began to repeat, “This was the reason that made me flee. Ah, Lord! Was this not what I said while I was still in my own land? That is why I fled beforehand, so that I would not be sent. For I knew that you are a God abundant in mercy, and that whenever people repent, your love is first to offer forgiveness. And now that I have become like a liar before foreigners, it is better for me to die than to be called a false prophet.” “Are you very grieved?” Revelation called to him and spoke with him. He answered his Lord that his grief had reached the point of death. The Hebrew saw that the uncircumcised had turned back, and he chose to die, because the [?] of the dead among the unclean nations did not please him. The pain of grief crushed his soul beyond measure, and he chose death rather than life, so that he would not be proved a liar. He left the city and went out to live alone, while he was [?] for the sentence he had pronounced to be carried out. He made himself a shelter to live in for a time,

with this expectation: perhaps what he had decreed would happen. The Knower of all saw in his thoughts that this was what he wanted, and his Lord drew him toward compassion through a trial. The command quickly made a gourd shoot grow. It spread its leaves above Jonah, and he rejoiced in it. The son of Amittai rejoiced in the leaves and fruit of the lowly gourd, for he saw the wonder of how it suddenly sprouted and bore fruit. He forgot his grief in the pleasure of his love for the fruit. Consider why it suddenly blossomed. The command bound him to the gourd in love so that he might gain further wisdom: when it withered, he would suffer greatly and learn its purpose. The same command that had suddenly given it to him and bound him in love for it then removed it. It suddenly withered, and he grieved over it. The command signaled to the fierce heat, and it suddenly blew. The gourd withered, its leaves were scorched, and its fruit fell. The sun blazed fiercely on Jonah’s head. He sighed repeatedly, his soul was grieved, and he asked for death. The heat that came upon the preacher was no ordinary heat. The command made it burn with extraordinary intensity. The same command that had stirred up the sea in an unusual way also made the sun’s rays burn beyond their ordinary measure. He taught him through the sea not to resist the journey to the nations, and corrected him through the gourd so that he would not grieve over people being alive. The gourd shoot became his teacher and made him wise. Against his will, it bound him in love to sinners. The speaking one became a pupil of the speechless one—the prophet became the gourd’s pupil. He learned his lesson and gained understanding from the silent one. The heat upon his limbs planted suffering in his heart, and through the trial he began to turn toward compassion. The mystery within the silent thing taught him love and mercy,

and explained them through revelation so that he would not grieve. The command addressed him in a single utterance in his own language: “Over what are you grieving? Over the silent thing that suddenly blossomed? Why are you bound in perfect love to weak things, yet do not draw near to the glorious things that human beings possess? Why do you love what is not yours and hate what is yours? And why are you angry at people being alive, as though you were not human?” Why do you not bring your thoughts to a fair judgment, and judge within yourself, with your own mind, these matters that concern you? Where has the watchful impulse of your discernment sunk, that you do not feel for your fellow beings as you do for yourself? You grieved over the destruction of a speechless gourd. How much more should I grieve over speaking beings fashioned in my own likeness! The outward heat distressed you in your outward body, but the hidden evil of human destruction crushed me. You felt pity and great sorrow over something insignificant. How much more should I pity the precious beings who turn to me! Look at the hundred and twenty thousand little children, and stretch your mind to take in the entire number. Have pity, son of Amittai, so that the great city is not destroyed. Imitate me by showing compassion toward your neighbors. What do you gain from the destruction of a land that wrath lays waste? No one gives thanks to the name of my Being amid the ashes. Direct your will toward the aim of my mercy, and bend it to conform to that aim. For this reason I called you to myself: that you might imitate me. I appointed you a lookout to turn the nations that have strayed back to me. Spread your words like nets to catch human beings. I am going to spread the net of love over all nations, and through your hands I have depicted the salvation of all by means of the Ninevites. I am stretching it to the four corners of the earth, so that they may worship my lordship. And look: I have demonstrated it through deeds to Nineveh, which turned back. I am going to appoint one of your race as commander, and through your triumphs I have made known my victory through him. Through a human being I am turning everyone toward faith in me. As a foreshadowing of him, I called the Ninevites through proclamation.

He gathers the nations and the people together in love for me, and before his coming I opened a road along the road to Assyria. Through him I am dismantling the barrier of the Law that stands before the nations. On this condition I called you and sent you among foreigners. The Hidden One comforted the son of the Hebrews through a mystery, so that he would not grieve at the return of the nations who had come to life through his hands. Through what was his own, he taught him to love his own as a discerning person should, and through his hands he revealed the salvation of the nations that was hidden within the people. He showed him a new way of proclamation, and through his hands he opened a peaceful path toward the appointed time of life. On this condition he extended the course of prophecy: he confined it within the people, then brought it out to the nations through the son of Amittai. Everything looked toward the fulfillment of his proclamation, and through his hands he revealed the beautiful image hidden in the mystery. Blessed is he who depicted for us, through the son of Amittai, the restoration of our lives. Thanksgiving to the Hidden One, who revealed his hidden nature through what belongs to us.
On Admonition
Discourse Nine: On Admonition, Suitable for Fasting and Supplication

Mortal nature is too weak to approach perfection, for flesh and blood cannot inherit the life to come. The inclination of his mind is set on evil from the beginning, and whenever his will desires good, his inclination drags him toward evil deeds. Although two opposing thoughts are planted in his nature, his inclination overcomes his nature.

It drags him toward temptations and subjects his free will to slavery to bodily desire. He is driven entirely by the compulsion of mortal passions. His will cannot carry out the good that he desires. Instead, his inclination forces him to do the evil that he does not desire. He is constantly caught in a struggle, fighting against his inclination. He fights against temptations with the weapon of his free will. Everyone is defeated by his inclination and enslaved to desires. The strength of his will cannot withstand the onslaught of bodily desire. More intoxicated than anyone is the man who [?] with himself. Who can rescue him from mortal passions? Victory belongs to the one alone who, with the weapon of the Holy Spirit, vindicated our guilty race, whose strength mortality had weakened. Both are fitting for you, my Lord, for your treasury [?]; your command is a sign of your compassion. Creation from nothing and renewal that cannot decay. I was not finding fault with your creation when I called our inclination evil. I was finding fault with our inclination—how evil it is, fighting against our will! You did not bind to our nature the good and evil that are in our nature. Rather, you entrusted both to our free will. It is our will that drags us toward mortal passions. And whenever our will chooses, it rises above the passions. It is our freedom that bows down to slavery to bodily desire. And if it chooses, it frees itself from subjection to temptations. Although our freedom has authority over both, our nature is too weak to be justified on its own. By the power of your love you justified us when our guilt grew strong. You assigned to our will the victory of mighty power. And if, when our wrongdoing grew strong, your love did not recoil from our wickedness, how much more now, when your mercies have shown compassion, will your compassion heal our sins! And if, while we were dead in our sins—while we were dead in our sins—

Christ died and brought us all to life, how much more shall we now be justified by the blood that sanctified our uncleanness! And if, while we were enemies, you reconciled us through the death of your Son, how much more now, through his reconciliation, shall we share in his life! Where our wrongdoing grew strong, the power of grace triumphed. Therefore the hope remains firm that mercy will show compassion to sinners. Our wickedness, my Lord, has fenced off the road that leads to your refuge. May your mercies dismantle the fence that our wickedness has built before us. The thick darkness of desires has covered our discernment. May your compassion remove the veil that error has spread over our hearts. The ignorance of our minds has blinded us to what is right. May the light of knowing you dawn, and may our blind souls see by it. The impulses of our desires have dissipated the salt of your teaching. May your compassion restore to our minds the sweet taste that we have lost. Your love needs no pleading, for you know before we plead. You are not appeased by words, for before we speak, they are already chosen by you. It was not anger over our offenses that made you angry when we acted wickedly. For you were examining our disposition before we came into being. The passions in our nature were revealed to your knowledge before we existed. Our hidden and secret things were readily accessible to your scrutiny. You knew that the disposition within us subjects us to desires, and you knew that through death our dust returns to its natural state. You were looking at our need for life before our dust was formed. You filled our race with life, with enjoyment that fills the span of time. You knew that two dwellings were suited to our nature. Earth for the infancy of our minds, and heaven for their maturity. The mystery of our salvation lay hidden in your knowledge, within your hidden being. When the time you had appointed arrived, you revealed your hidden will. You knew that you would take one from our race as its firstfruits. Through the sacrifice of his body, you would annul the sentence of judgment and death against us. The exaltation of our despised race lay hidden in your secret knowledge. After a time you revealed it as evidence of your hidden love. And if these things were revealed to your knowledge before we existed,

you were looking still more closely at our disposition, which does not stand firm against impulses. You brought us into being and honored us with reason. You turned us from wandering to the path of your hidden lordship. Through the weakness of our souls, the honor of your majestic image was diminished. Your help [?] raised us from degradation to greatness. Our wrongdoing turned you from mercy to severity. Your love became a mediator and reconciled us with his majesty. Peace and mercy are yours, for you reconciled us with him. Our nature has no refuge except your compassion, which sustains everything. For our sake you were called by names foreign to you. Although they do not befit your nature, you took them upon yourself because of your love. It was not that your nature was diminished by our weak names. You exalted the lowliness of our race by calling yourself by our names. For the nature of your being, there is no place to which you might travel or in which you might dwell. Yet because of your love for us, you came to us in your nature. Your hidden being cannot be encompassed by the sight of bodily eyes. Yet in our body, as in a mirror, we saw the glory of your majesty. Your nature, the limit of all things, neither descends nor ascends. Yet through the descent of your will, you honored us as though you had descended. Joy does not make you rejoice, nor does sorrow distress you. Yet you rejoiced at our return and kissed us in the person of the younger son. You divided the great treasury of your wisdom between two heirs, and you did not hold our weakness to account for squandering your possessions. The will of your being went out in search of us who were lost. When you found us, you announced your joy to the heavenly beings. With a robe of glory you covered the exposed ugliness of our wrongdoing. With the seal of faith you confirmed your promise to us. We have received the seed of your word; establish within us the fruit of life. Do not allow the deceitful one to sow his weeds in our souls. You called us your own children through love, not by nature. May the name of sonship that you bestowed on us be confirmed in us through our deeds. You invited us to the dwelling above,

and to kinship with spiritual beings. May the wrongdoing of our souls not drown us in the abyss of great torment. Hope in the greatness of your promises gives our souls courage. However strong wrongdoing may become, your mercy overcomes our ugly deeds. With oaths that cannot be broken you sealed your promises. You swore by your great nature, and by your nature you do not lie. On this condition you established our petition to your lordship: you ask for a sign of repentance and do not call past deeds to account. Trusting in your mercy, we plead with you, who have mercy on all. Open the door to our plea, which knocks at the door of your grace. Rebuke your justice, gracious one, so that it does not become embittered at our wrongdoing. May the love of your will appease you, so that you act as you are accustomed to do. May your knowledge not scrutinize our ugly deeds closely. Do not bring us under examination in that judgment which tests everything. For the word of our petition falls short and does not reach the height above. Stretch out to us the hand of your mercy, and through it we will ascend to forgiveness. For the wing of our mind is heavy and cannot fly toward your love. On the wings of your compassion, may we be lifted from the depths to your greatness. For the light of our knowledge is too dim to discern what is right. May the light of your knowledge shine forth, and by it may we see the blemishes of our souls. For wrongdoing has made us strangers to the inheritance of [?]. May we be fed like dogs from the crumbs of your mercy. For we have not borne the burden of the day while working in the vineyard of your knowledge. Our confession is not denied a share in service through grace. However great our folly may be, it is very small beside your mercy. Even if our wickedness has no equal, beside your grace it is like a shadow. Mercy and compassion are yours, and the wealth of your love has no equal. The multitude of your creations bears witness that you fashioned them with compassion. Your grace cannot be measured, nor can the treasury of your mercies be reckoned. For although its recipients draw from it abundantly, it remains just as it was.

From it spiritual beings become rich, and they cry out mightily in his service. Through the power of his word they are strengthened and carry out everything he wills. Through it the needs of mortals clothed in bodies are met, and with its help they are raised above the passions inherent in their nature. It is distributed in every region, to heavenly and earthly beings. It nourishes those who speak and those without speech, yet is no less than it was. Do not, then, close the door to the great wealth of your compassion. And let our petition not be held back at the door of our foolishness. My Lord, do not scrutinize the deeds arising from the evil inclination of our nature. For however much the flesh may conquer, even when it conquers it is guilty. Our whole constitution is a clod of earth, and our dust is kneaded with passions. The portion of life it possesses it drags along after its downward impulses. The waters of the passions soak the dust of our mortal body. The torrent of wrongdoing sweeps it away and brings it down into degradation. The power of life within the soul draws it toward good things. But the inclination of his heart brings him down into the great depths of evil. He is caught in battles with himself and struggles with his thoughts. With the bow of mortality he shoots arrows into his own limbs. He wins and loses continually and never ceases struggling. He is battered all over by the wounds of sins. The mortality within his nature stands opposed to his [?]. The susceptibility of his limbs to passion torments his mind. With these snares the inclination hidden in his limbs binds him, Binding him with a chain forged from desires. My Lord, may the key of your compassion’s command release him from captivity. And may your grace wash from him the filth that has stained his thoughts. May the prisoner whom his own will has bound come out into the spacious freedom of your mercies. May he be comforted in his sorrow by hope in the greatness of your promises. May your compassion be a guide to the stranger who lacks knowledge. Teach him the road he should travel to the halls of the kingdom on high.

May your mercies go out in search of the lost man who has forgotten himself. May your love bring him back to the assurance that comes from knowing the faith. May your command check the fever of the sick man laid low by wrongdoing. With the sponge of your kindness, may the blemishes of his soul be wiped away. Unless your help reaches him, he is nearer death than life. Unless your medicine heals him, there is no cure for his wound. Human medicines and bodily dressings have lost their power. Day after day the disease of our wrongdoing grows, spreads, and becomes stronger. Our diseases have defied the skill of earthly physicians. Both spiritual and bodily beings have raised a finger at our wrongdoing. Our nature has no physician to compare with the extent of your mercies. No one understands its wound as your hidden knowledge does. It was not because you neglected our pain that our folly became so deeply rooted. We concealed our wound, and gangrene took hold of our limbs. It was not that the power of your compassion had grown too weak to help. The sick were unwilling to apply the medicine of mercy to their sores. It was not because you recoiled from the sinner that we became defiled by sin. We ourselves found our sickness pleasant, so that the medicine of life would not sting us. We ourselves struck ourselves, bruising ourselves with the arrows of our mouths. Our body's wounds multiplied from the stones hurled by our lips. We forgot the knowledge belonging to our nature's discernment, and the speech of our understanding lost its savor through involvement in frivolity. Our laxity opened the gate of sight, hearing, and speech. Enemies entered and plundered the wealth stored in the treasures of the Spirit's words. Our sluggishness of mind did not hire us from early morning, and the day passed with all its hours, and we did no profitable work during it. Our greed did not allow us to gain mercy for Christ's sake. The lamp illuminating the hidden depths of our soul sputtered and went out. Laziness hid away the talent entrusted to us in the word of instruction. We did not distribute to the needy the silver of Christ's word.

In our wickedness we did not receive forgiveness for our great wrongdoing. Justice saw that we had not forgiven our fellow servants and was grieved. The word of instruction fell upon the rock of our hard hearts. When the sun of enticements grew hot, the seed in our soul was scorched and withered. The word of life was sown beside the path of our mind, and the enemy, like a bird, snatched it from among our thoughts. The ear of life sprouted among the thorns of our desires. The thicket of our hateful deeds grew up and choked the spiritual seed. The enticements within us did not allow us to walk along the narrow way. We traveled with the many along the broad road to destruction. The weight of sin's sleep submerged our nimble mind. We did not awaken from our slumber to receive the promised blessing. These things loosened the bond of our peace with your lordship. After reconciliation had taken place, our wrongdoing provoked you to anger. My Lord, do not let our corruption grow stronger or let us sink into sin. Draw us up from the depths of evil, as you drew Simon from the sea. You called us children and heirs through the wealth of your great promises. Do not let your pledges prove false, and let us not become strangers [?] to your wealth. Do not let the envious one rejoice over us when we abandon your inheritance. Do not let him boast that by his own power he plundered the wealth you gave us. Do not let the insolent one exalt himself, claiming that with his weapons he overcame your gift. Do not let him say, “I took them captive, and his heirs did not stand against me.” Let the unclean demons not rejoice over the humiliation caused by our evil deeds. Let the ruler of the air not say, “My authority still reigns.” May your love turn us toward supplication, and may the enemy be put to shame forever. Healing the pains of our iniquity is very easy for your compassion. It is easy for your grace to wipe away the black stains of our sins. Do not reject us because we have sinned, for you know before we sin. For flesh and blood cannot cleanse itself of foul things. And if our petition is not worthy to have its requests answered, have pity yourself, because you have made us children and heirs of your majesty. May gentle love persuade you and reconcile you to us despite our wickedness.

May your compassion be a mediator and bring us a sign of peace. We do not know how to pray as we ought for forgiveness. May grace plead on our behalf with supplication, as it is accustomed to do. Together with your grace, may the firstfruits of our race also plead with you, whom, for the sake of our salvation, you made equal to your majesty. Accept our supplication through the mediator whom you chose from among us. May an answer of reconciliation and forgiveness be returned to us. Because of our iniquity you afflicted him, so that through his suffering he might lift us from our humiliation. And now that he has ascended and been exalted, show us favor for his sake. You chose him for our salvation, to bring our mortal condition to life through his life. He who is equal to you in honor and in the authority of being—may the power of his authority make us worthy to receive forgiveness freely. He who became a temple for your hidden nature, for your willing indwelling. May we receive forgiveness freely. He who became a temple for your hidden nature, for your willing indwelling—may the will of his love dwell in us and cleanse us of foul things. Through eating his body, may the mire of iniquity be wiped from our hearts. May drinking his blood calm the turmoil of our minds. He gave it as a means of forgiveness and as a pledge of good things. May both be confirmed in us: forgiveness and the pledge of life. Through his suffering he abolished sin, and through his death he killed death. Let our killers not be awakened by the sound of our evil deeds. The aim of our petition is bound to the hope of these promises. Let our trust not prove false, so that the evil one who hates us may not rejoice. The faith of our minds has given us two guarantors: hope and love, which do not forget affection for those close to them. Our confession is strengthened by love, and our trust is placed in hope. And faith is the guarantor that his promises will not prove false. May mercy come to our aid because of these promises, lest the corrupter take us captive and make them false. Let our good things not be turned into evil things because we have sinned. Remain in your kindness, and turn us toward the will of your love. The riches of your knowledge have no need

of our petition and entreaty. For all goodness is yours. Have mercy and forgive, as you are accustomed to do. The creature has nothing that does not come from the Creator’s treasury. For even the very supplication that he begins to offer, he has learned through the help that comes from him. Yours is the power of wisdom that dwells in rational souls. From you they have received the gift of understanding and discernment. Through your treasury the wise grow rich, and through your help the righteous prosper. Your mercy brings back those who stray and increases hope for the lost. There is no good thing that is not yours, nor any gift bestowed without your command. Even in this, that we call upon you, it is you who called us and taught us. “Turn to me, and I will turn to you,” the Spirit declared through the prophets. “I do not desire your deaths, but the salvation of your lives.” A mortal has no thought that is not a desire belonging to mortal life. Nor does a person of flesh think spiritual thoughts. Communion with your love draws him from darkness toward the light. It removes from him the veil spread over his mind. In your light he sees light, and through knowledge of you he gains life. From you he learns to expound, and with what is yours he teaches others. Whenever he meditates on you, his wealth increases and grows. But if he abandons communion with you, his treasures are ruined and depleted. His wealth is bound to your grace, and his poverty to justice. If he acts righteously, he gains glory; if he sins, he is brought low. Yet although both things are perfectly clear—that through what is yours he rises and falls— the mortal clothes himself in pride and boasts of what is not his own. When he desires a little good, his pride lifts him to heaven. And when he is brought low by sin, despair cuts off his hope. If he acquires understanding, he despises and [?] anyone among people who is weak or deficient in his lowliness. For when he has gathered wealth through his labors, he scatters it through negligence of mind. Through our foolishness our wealth has perished, and through our negligence our treasures. We have diminished the honor of our image through a craving that loves evil things. Our wealth is in heaven,

but we think about earthly things. We have been invited to a wedding feast of joys, yet our mind wallows in the dust. All our labor is devoted to sin, and we occupy ourselves with empty things. The hours of night and day are not enough for our indulgence. Our human nature constantly labors in a field that is stingy with fruit. Though it cheats him of its crops, he does not cease his work. The body and the impulses of the soul are yoked under the harsh yoke of sin. The labor is pleasant to them both, and they do not realize how worn out they are. There is no idle limb that is not busy pursuing desires, nor any sluggish impulse that does not run toward passions. Thus the whole person is constantly at war with himself. His whole being is divided against itself, and he shoots arrows at himself. The heart is divided against the limbs, and the limbs against the mind. They deceitfully conceal their actions from one another. The limbs and the impulses of the soul constantly proceed without order, running in a stadium without reward or crown. The gaze of our eyes is wanton, and the hearing of our ears is deceitful. For the speech of our lips is deceptive, and our words are not truthful. The judge speaks with a double heart to [?] his neighbors. Our inward thoughts do not agree with our outward actions. Our tongue conveys peace, while deceit lies hidden in our mind. Kisses are on the tips of our lips, but a sharpened sword is in our thoughts. A false report enters and sends out a messenger of anger. It condemns the innocent and acquits the guilty. The eyes send out image-makers in pursuit of lust's prey. The greedy body feeds itself by mistreating its fellows. In the cage of the undisciplined eye, desire is placed like a bird. Instead of a sound, a [?] gesture stirs up undisciplined desire. Lustful desire lies hidden behind the covering of the pupils. It substitutes gestures for sounds, so that the prey becomes entangled in its snares.

O eye, torch of light, lamp of the outward senses! You have become a cause of stumbling for minds and bodily members. The heart signals to the tongue to speak falsely. Though an event has not happened, it describes it as though it has. The heart plays upon the harp of the mouth with the tongue as its finger. Yet the sound of the strings does not agree with the movement of the player's finger. It plays sweet melodies on it as on a flute. The first hearing is pleasant, but the outcome of the speech is evil. The mouth, too, is a pleasant spout that pours out the drink of speech. But the sweetness of its drink has changed and become the gall of evil. O advocate for the oppressed, who has turned and become an oppressor! He has sold the freedom of his authority into slavery to oppression. O tongue, messenger faithful to two kings! It has stirred up strife among the bodily members and turned against the soul. O speaking harp, whose melodies have become confused! O guide of the speechless, who has become speechless and forgotten his duty! The soul is [?] against the body, and the body does not agree with the soul. For there is one thought in the soul, while the mouth expresses the opposite. The laxity of our will has trampled on nature and the law. Nature and Scripture have become superfluous to our insolence. The course of nature has been halted, along with the utterances of Scripture. Nature proceeds neither according to its order nor according to the commandments of Scripture. In acquiring possessions there is oppression, and in marriage, corruption; in eating, gluttony, and in drinking, drunkenness. In looking there is wantonness, and in hearing, falsehood. Slander is on the lips, and deadly poison on the tip of the tongue. There is conflict in the love of money, and rivalry in gathering wealth, as people compete with one another to see who can oppress more. All mortals enter the arena of the love of glory. And when they thought they had won and risen high, praise ran up and condemned them.

There is no victory for their struggle and no reward for their labors. For they do not aim toward the goal set by the judge of the contest. Fasting is robbed by boasting, and prayer by praise. The work of almsgiving is made useless, and there are no fruits of forgiveness of wrongdoing. The body is sick with craving for flesh, and the soul with love of praise. The mind’s eye is blind and does not discern the truth. The outward senses are weak, and the inward impulses are feeble. Both have ceased running along the course of righteousness. The limbs and thoughts lie stricken with the severe fever of wrongdoing. Soul and body are submerged beneath the weight of love for evil things. O human being, full of passions, who will rescue you from your passions? Ask and plead, so that mercy may come to your aid, if possible. If mercy does not heal you, there is no cure for your brokenness. And if grace does not stand by you, your hope of righteousness is cut off. O Good One, who fashioned our nature and called it his image and likeness, save your image and the work of your hands, and do not let what you have fashioned be destroyed. You honored us with the name of your image; show us favor for the sake of your image. You called us children; do not let us be strangers to your household. Our nature falls short of this and is not worthy to bear the name of your image. Let our salvation be completed through you, just as our first formation was. Renewal is as easy as creation for your slightest command [?]. Your will is not hindered by the evil of our corruption. In mercy and love you fashioned us, without petition or pleading. Now too, in mercy and love, renew us, give us life, have compassion, and forgive. For our petition is not worthy to persuade you to grant forgiveness. Let mercy and love triumph in our renewal, as they are accustomed to do. No petition is needed by the giver who never becomes poor. Nor does the one who knows everything beforehand need pleading. He has heard the voice of our petition before it comes into being. And the plea rests within his knowledge before it is formed. He has looked upon us from eternity and has observed us at all times. Our affairs and everyone’s affairs have been revealed to the hiddenness of his divinity.

It is not petition that persuades the Power whose wisdom encompasses these things. He wants to show us that it is the will that sins and repents. Through petition he teaches us that it is not compulsion that makes us sin. Just as we have chosen to pray, it is also easy for us not to sin. The same inclination that acted wickedly and sinned is the one that chose and became righteous. The guilt belongs to it, as does the victory that accompanies the soul. This is the teaching that the Creator imparts to us through petition. So that our will may not be reproached in our restoration as it is in evil. And although he knows our nature well, and that both belong to it, he does not neglect our correction, because of his love for us. He attributes victory to our inclination, for the sake of our freedom of will. And since our will is free, he teaches us how to overcome. You, my Lord, have placed knowledge in our nature so that we may reflect on these things. You have taught us how our will has authority over our souls. In your knowledge you have instructed us, and in your kindness you have made us wise. Accept, then, our petition, on which the image of your wisdom is imprinted. We give you what is yours; accept your own gift from our hands. Take what is yours and give us what is yours, for it is fitting for you to give from what is yours. In prayer, my weak utterance gazed toward your hidden greatness. And it longed to be worthy, perhaps, of a tiny drop of your gift. I fixed the gaze of my poor mind on the abundance of your love. I considered asking whether it was possible to receive forgiveness freely. It journeyed toward the subtle workings of your compassion, accompanied by instruction. Show me the road I should take to the halls of perfection. Stretch out your hand to the drowning man who wishes to rise out of his wrongdoing. Through the strength of your help, may the child who has begun to babble grow strong. The longing of love awakens me like someone awakened from sleep. At the dawn of your command, may the sleep of wrongdoing be driven from my mind. The movements of my thoughts yearn toward the light of knowing you. Remove the veil of darkness spread over my understanding. The spiritual law has set victory as my goal.

May my impulses, together with my words, turn toward truth, the goal of life. At the spring of the word of instruction, I sought to quench my mind’s thirst. May the dryness of my thoughts be watered by the Spirit’s irrigation. With the silver of your word, I wish to trade, if I can. At the eleventh hour I am hired on the condition that I receive a denarius. Though I have not borne the day’s burden, may the evening of your compassion give me rest. Though I have not labored in deeds, may I become worthy of wages through words. Through the exercise of words, I wish to summon workers to your service. Hear my words, though they are contemptible, so that I may be a worker in your vineyard. I sought to gather those invited to the spiritual wedding feast. May mercy cover my limbs, which are stripped of modesty. May your love go out with my words in search of the lost sheep. And may they be gathered from every direction into the beautiful fold of your mercy. Act through my hands, as you are accustomed to acting through the hands of sinners. And may I become a source of benefit to myself and to lowly people like me. The partridge calls others toward death and hunts its companions for destruction. At the call of my words, may the dead who have died in their sins come to life. At the sound of my utterances, may the sleepers who have sunk into sin awaken. And may they shake off the burden of their sins at the announcement of a second dawn. May your own will plead with you on my behalf, for I cannot persuade you. May your love reconcile you with my sins, so that I may hear the voice of reconciliation. May the dew of your mercy and the showers of righteousness come to us, and may a shoot of repentance spring up among the roots of our mind. May spiritual seed sprout in our soul, a fallow field, and may our heart, which produces carobs, bear fruits of joy. May the sluggish hearing of our understanding be stirred by the sound of your commandments, and may our hearing become a path for the voice that brings understanding.

Through gazing at baseness, the lamp of our mind has grown dark. May your truth become a mirror, and may we polish away the ugliness of our soul in it. With the mouth that became a passage and a bridge for vulgar words, may we sing a song pleasing to you, thanksgiving without division. May the temple of our body be sanctified, and may the impulses of our soul be purified. May hope and love dwell in us in the completeness of faith. May our whole person pronounce judgment, body and soul together, and by a righteous sentence may the inclination that does wrong be condemned. May victory vindicate our discernment if it prevails, and may the impulse that falters in the contest be accused as guilty. May a voice of encouragement come to us, strengthening the camp of our body, and may our limbs gain strength in the struggle against the passions. For the weapon of our mind is weak before the impulses in our [?]. May the shield that faces hardships be armed with faith. By the strength of your help, may the tyrant, the corrupt inclination, be condemned—the one that fights against our soul with the weapon of our free will. My Lord, may your compassion, which seeks the lost, bring us back to the fold of life, and may the Watchers who serve your will look upon our restoration. May your gentle voice call us: “Return, repentant children. Strip off the wrongdoing that has made you ugly, and put on the garment of righteousness.” Our wrongdoing has stripped away our modesty and diminished our honorable name. May we be covered with the garment of your mercy, and may our lowliness be exalted through your name. Sin has killed our nature and veiled the face of our freedom. At the command of your power, may it be raised from wrongdoing, the grave of both. Through our sins we have been sold into slavery to mortality. With the silver of your love, may we be freed from bondage to sin. Our ugly deeds have disfigured the glorious beauty of the heights and the depths, and through our evil deeds heaven and earth have dried up and ceased to bear fruit. Through the severity of our wrongdoing, the elements have fallen into disorder. Because our mouth has dried up and ceased to offer praise, the seed has dried up along with the fruit. Because our mind has become barren of the fruits of righteousness, the earth has withheld its fruit and does not produce food for us. Because we have exchanged truth for falsehood and do not remain steadfast in truth, see, the changes of summer and winter proceed outside their appointed order.

Winter is gloomy beyond its appointed order, and summer goes beyond its proper bounds, as they discipline our wickedness with unseasonable cold and heat. Hunger and thirst scourge the insolence of our mind, yet our dull heart does not feel the scourging our mind receives. Our body is always bound in a chain of sufferings and pains, and ravenous death swiftly drives us to the abode of the dead. The rod of authority is raised and strikes us with oppression, greedily demanding from us the poll tax and new levies. Kings issue fresh commands, and rulers act without mercy. Along with the accumulation of wealth, injustice increases and grows stronger. And were it not for your overflowing love and the wealth of your abundant mercy, the world would long ago have been washed away in the flood of our grievous wickedness. Your love always overcomes the multitude of our evil deeds, and our disgrace is covered by the beautiful garment of your help. It is fitting for you, my Lord, to bear with the troublesome wickedness of our inclination. For the treasury of your mercy cannot be weighed, and your grace cannot be measured. You are our strong refuge and the helper of our nature. There is no time when our race has been condemned that your help has not acquitted us. Through all generations, as they run their course, your gentle compassion flows. It grows according to the measures of youth and old age. Your grace journeys with us and never stays behind wherever we are. It pursues our wickedness so that it will not return and dwell with us. Whom do we have like you, merciful one who loves our race? Who bears our troubles as your gentle love does? From whom can our need be supplied as it is from your treasury? For although we have not repaid your earlier gift, your giving overflows with mercy. The words of our petition look toward the purpose of your love for us. How eager you are to receive an appeal on behalf of sinners! Petitioners are subdued and silent
