because of the need in their lives, but your compassion cries out like thunder: “Rise, you lowly, and become rich without payment!” It is not our own will that carries us away into asking boldly for forgiveness. You encouraged us to offer even words in place of labors. May the words our mouths address to you be spoken according to your will. Though they are bare of deeds, clothe them with your help. Who can understand the failings of mortal life? And who can be cleared of hidden faults that are not revealed? You yourself cause understanding to dwell in us, so that we may gain wisdom about our hidden faults. You yourself teach us how to mix medicine for our sickness. Support our weakness, which cannot exist without your help. Do not neglect to help us, lest we perish forever. We have tested ourselves in contests of labor for righteousness. In every contest we entered, our limbs suffered bruises. And if there are members of our body that have not been battered, your help stood before them, and they were not struck by arrows from the evil one. Good and evil alike owe you thanks. For if they are made righteous, it is your doing; and if they sin, through you they receive pardon. It is yours to forgive wickedness and to bring righteousness to perfection. By your strength may the righteous walk, and sinners by your help. Do not charge our childishness with unwitting slips. Even when our inclination leads us into sin, it sins without realizing that it is sinning. Do not reckon against our weakness the wrong of transgressing your commandments. For if you demand repayment, no human being can avoid sinning, and no mortal can be found righteous. For he is formed from dust, and dust loves what belongs to it. The earthly man thinks about his dust and turns back to his dust every day. His life vanishes like a breath, yet he gives no thought to its end. Mortality rebukes him so that he will not exhaust himself with earthly things. Sufferings and pains discipline him, yet his fever is pleasant to him. May your compassion drive away sicknesses, for our nature loves pains. May its tastelessness be tempered with the sweet taste of your commandments.

May your command open for him the door that his weakness shut in his face, and loosen from him the chain that wickedness placed around his neck. May your gentle voice awaken the sleeper submerged in sin, and may he shout praise with the [?] to the one who has mercy on sinners.
On Human Nature
[?] Sixteenth discourse. It is recited during fasting and supplication. Response: Our Lord, turn toward your servants in your mercy; accept our prayer and grant our requests.

El, God, hear our supplication, which you have heard, and in your mercy answer the request in which our soul places its confidence. You who abound in compassion, show your love as you always do, so that the enemy of humanity may not mock the work of your hands. You who are richer than all, open your treasury to our need, so that we may not become destitute and hire out our soul to the deceiver. Mighty one of the ages, uphold what you have fashioned by the strength of your power, for it is shaken by the harshness of sufferings and demons. You whose being fills heaven and earth, fill us with your will, and may your holy name be hallowed in us. You whose nature is hidden from spiritual and bodily beings, reveal your power in us and show the riches of your kindness. Maker of all, who created the creation from nothing, have pity on your handiwork, so that it may not be destroyed because of our wickedness. You who freely feed and graciously give life to rational creatures and speechless animals, stretch out your right hand and satisfy our soul with your gift. You who lack nothing, from whose fullness all that you have fashioned is filled:

Open to our entreaty the door of your favor that is shut in our faces. You who are perfect in your being, whose everlasting existence has no beginning, fulfill in deeds the promises you have spoken to our race. You who paint the world with the unfading color of your love, wipe the filth of ignorance from our images. You who put bodies together and breathe a soul into their limbs, strengthen our resolve so that it may not weaken before terrors. You who, because of your love, honor humanity above everything, have pity on the image of your majesty, so that it may not be dishonored. By the name of your uncompounded being you [?] our composite nature. May your honored name not lose its savor through our tastelessness. In us you have shown your great love toward the things you have fashioned. Do not make us a sign of wrath to the work of your hands. In us you brought the great renown of your craftsmanship to its culmination, and in our composite nature you encompassed earthly and heavenly things. In us you have joined height and depth together as one body. Speechless in our bodies, articulate in our souls—a great wonder! My Lord, do not dissolve this union that your love has formed, and do not let the great bond that your command has fastened grow slack. My feeble speech looked upon this union and sought to follow the path of words bound up with it. My mind, deficient in understanding, struggled with this bond and marveled greatly at the skill of the command that bound it. My thoughts, limited in their reach, were bewildered by this structure, and they prepared words to build a discourse before the listeners. With this hope my speech journeyed after words, so that I might go out and bring the good news of your name to the work of your hands. With this intention I traveled among the lines of the Scriptures, to tell people the great story of your creative work. In this manner I drew words with the pen of my tongue, so that everyone might look upon the beautiful image of your workmanship. I saw that the image you fashioned obeys wisely.

And I sought to lift up its splendid beauty before those who behold it. In the image of our form I saw all creation bound together, and I called people to come and see everything in our nature. Nature drew me to see the natures bound together within it: how, and to what extent, a weak being can contain everything. In our very nature I saw the wisdom of your divinity, and I reflected that [?] is hope for humanity, however sinful. I saw the name of your Being dwelling in him as in a temple, and wonder seized me: how can one so lowly contain the Hidden One? He is very lowly, yet you have honored him beyond measure. Who would not marvel that you chose his lowliness above everything? And if your love chose him out of everything and called him by his name, let us therefore affirm that you do not reject what you have chosen. If your lordship made him lord over everything that came into being, who would not yoke himself to the service of his life? If your knowledge called him and brought him to an exalted rank, who would not acknowledge that his rank and his title of authority are secure? If you revealed your hiddenness to your creatures through his visible form, who would not turn his gaze away from everything else toward his constitution? If in him you disclosed the great mystery of the Son and the Spirit, who would not approach the wisdom hidden in his name? If in him you showed your kindness to the angels and to human beings, who would not love the refuge in his body, so that he might intercede on his behalf? If the Word himself, the offspring who comes from you, dwelt in him in love, who would not call him the one who encompasses the full extent of height and depth? If in him you brought to completion your care for everything, who would not hold fast to his care without ceasing? If through him you are going to judge the earth at the end of time, who would not fear the judgment that will be in his hands? And if through him you give blessings to the good and punishments to the wicked, who would not implore you to be an advocate on behalf of his sins? And if he rules over this world and the world to come,

who would not believe that he is a partner of the Godhead? I saw that our lowly nature had been raised to these ranks, and my mind urged me to turn my words toward its lowliness. The greatness of its rank compelled me to venture beyond proper bounds and travel a road whose exploration exceeds my words. I sought to approach your hiddenness through his manifestation. Stretch out your hand to me, as you did to Simon, so that I may approach and plead. My thoughts have descended into the sea of words offered on behalf of our lives. Let your command draw me up, so that I do not drown in unfitting things. I have approached to plead concerning my deeds and those of my companions. Strengthen my efforts so that they do not falter while they are being heard. My will knocks at the door of your mercy, desiring life for us. Open to us, so that we may enter and receive alms like the poor. Our lowly race is poor and in need of every good thing. Support its lowliness with a small crumb from your gift. It is far too weak to gather provisions for itself for a time, and it cannot cultivate the earth by its own strength without your strength. Its labor is full of great anxiety, however much it works, and there is no security in its provisions, however plentiful they are. Sufferings and pains accompany its toil in summer and winter, and every kind of harm constantly attends it—it and all that belongs to it. Its toil is great, and the reward it receives is small. Its weariness is great, and the food that sustains its life is paltry and precarious. It sows much and gathers little from the abundance. It is battered and worn out, and just as it begins to enjoy itself, death swallows it. It sows in anxiety and gathers its produce in fear. Its heart has no assurance that it will enjoy its toil and what it has gathered. It scatters its bread across the field so that it may return to it, yet it is anxious and distressed that it might perish and its life come to an end. It cultivates the earth and worries that it may blight [?] the crops. It travels along the road, while death sits waiting for it.

Like a woman giving birth, it awaits the crops as she awaits her baby, while the pangs of death strike its understanding at every moment. A great battle is constantly arrayed against its inclination. If it dozes and sleeps, terrors enter and plunder its freedom. The weak creature lies on two racks, one worse than the other: its bodily sufferings and the food needed for its life—a double scourging. It is scourged as though with straps by the hand of its own inclination, and there is no part of it that is not filled with endless suffering. It is troubled and distressed by its sufferings and its labors, and there is no time when it does not sigh bitterly. If the sun grows hot, its mind burns with concern for its crops. If the rain ceases, its thoughts dry up along with its plants. If the heat becomes excessive, thirst kills it; if the cold grows intense, it perishes from nakedness. If it becomes poor, it conceives despair and gives birth to grumbling. If it prospers, arrogance and haughtiness clothe it. If he becomes righteous, he grows arrogant and laughs at sinners; and if he sins, he despairs and decides that there is no longer any hope. If he becomes wise, he forgets the lowly nature of his dust; and if he boasts, he becomes a beast without understanding. In plenty and in little, his passions multiply and his wrongdoing increases. What can he do, and where can he flee, harassed throughout his life? Between excess and deficiency, he continually falls short. How can he preserve his life without suffering harm? It is very difficult for human beings to live well, and the race of righteousness is not easy for bodily beings. The body remains a body, however much it desires spiritual things. Even its desire is not its own, but belongs to another. Another dwells within it, in this perishable temple of dust,

and through that other's life it blossoms briefly before it decays. It is wholly subject to decay, however much a share of life exists within it. Even this share has little life with which to keep it alive. And if the life within it falls short of life, how can it live by a life that is perishable? Let your mercies come, my Lord, to help our lowly race, for look: the strength of its life has weakened and sunk low in the struggle against the passions. Stretch out your hand to the fainthearted contestant, for look: he has raised a finger in surrender and cannot openly engage in the contest. Call out and encourage the perishable warrior, for look: his arms have grown too weak to strike the target. Command the spiritual beings to help him, for look: his hand has grown weary of holding the bow of truth. Summon the heavenly legions to assist him before he falls and becomes a laughingstock to his enemy. Write and send him a letter bearing your name, which is greater than everything, and he will gain strength to bear his sufferings through hope in your name. Put your signature to the documents that save his life, and the passions and demons will be terrified to look at him. Rebuke the ranks of warriors who threaten him, and they will be terrified by the [?] of the name of your being. Send a single watcher, as in the time of the Assyrian, and the forces of the Evil One surrounding him will scatter. Send your command as you sent Isaiah to Hezekiah, and instead of figs let us lay mercy upon his sores. Let us hear that voice which came to Hezekiah: ‘Instead of adding life, look, I am adding forgiveness of wrongdoing.’ Yes, my Lord, turn us toward the health of good deeds, so that we may not be battered by the wounds of our shameful deeds. Go out in search of us, like the ewe that your love carried, and let us enter and graze in the fold of spiritual life. Make your face shine, and in your mercy seek us in our lost condition, so that the splendor of our dust, stamped with your name, may not perish. Rejoice in our plea, as in the [?] of the younger son, and speak to us of the life of hope portrayed in him.

We worked for the deceiver for nothing, and he robbed us of our wages; we lived miserably on the carob pods of desires. We have sinned and angered you—though far be it from you to have become angry or to be angry—and we are not worthy to call ourselves children of your name. Allow us to be like hired workers in the service of your house, and to receive alms like the poor from your table. And if it is possible, fulfill in deed the power of your parable, and reveal the mystery that you composed for our sake. Say to us, “You have now come to life from death, and you have returned to me from the destruction of ignorance.” Command your compassion to cover our disgrace with a robe of glory, and to place in our hand the pledge of life like a ring. Let your command give permission and prepare before us the sacrifice of your Son, and through eating it let us drive the bitterness of death from our limbs. And if anyone envies the salvation, the salvation of our lives, and our service, let your love soothe the bitterness of his disposition with the vitality of life. Call the angels and gladden them through our return. Let those who grieved because we sinned now give thanks because we have been made righteous. Reconcile those who were angry because of our wrongdoing, and turn them toward attending to the needs of our lives. Let them stir the air with power from you, as they are accustomed to do, and strike it so that it carries water upon its back. Let them put bridles of silence and reconciliation in its mouth, so that it does not rage beyond its appointed order through its changes. Let them be like charioteers upon its back, and direct it toward the surface of the earth in the rush of its course. Let them watch its course like spectators in a stadium, and weave for your name a crown of thanksgiving because you have gladdened us through it. Yes, my Lord, accept the composition of our words, even though they are lowly, and reward the meditation of our soul, even though it is feeble. Yes, my Lord, make the words of our mouth worthy of a word in reply, and let us hear from you, “Repent, sinners; there is hope.” Yes, my Lord, gladden the air, which is gloomy because of our wrongdoing,

and place a crown of droplets in its mouth, so that it may be reconciled to us. Yes, my Lord, let the sounds of our mouth be keys to your treasury, and let us open it and receive forgiveness of sins and food for this present life. My Lord, do not disregard the petition of our poverty, lest our hope in you grow weak through despair. My Lord, do not turn your face away from us in a time of anger, lest the tyrannical demons mock us as they are accustomed to do. My Lord, do not cast us away from your help as you would the wicked, lest the evil ones exalt themselves over our humiliation as before. My Lord, do not be merciless, for you are merciful. Far be it, my Lord! You have never been so; I have spoken according to our need. My Lord, do not let the name of your majesty be diminished because of our wrongdoing. Yet it is not diminished, even if we sin a million times. My Lord, do not be lacking in help or poor in treasure. Oh, what I have said about your being is false! My Lord, do not be like a stranger in your creation, or like a traveler who turns aside to spend the night in a place that is not his own. My Lord, do not be like a human being, for you are God, or like a man who cannot save, for you are the Savior. Even if our sins have grown greater than the sins of every generation, have mercy for the sake of your glorious name, by which we are called. If our foul deeds have disfigured the face of the clear air, do not show a face of anger, which does not befit you. If our wickedness has withheld good things from the mouths of our little ones, do not change the name of your goodness, which does not change [?]. You are wholly good and wholly just, and you hate wrongdoing. Neither your goodness nor your justice can be measured. No one knows how to call you by a name worthy of your name, for all names are too small for the greatness of your glory. If we call you good, the voice of your justice thunders on earth; and if, instead, we call you just, heaven and earth are full of your mercy.

If we call you hidden, your deeds are visible to the eyes of all creatures. If we call you visible, none of your creatures can see you. If we call on you to hear, you have heard our voice before we call on you. And if we plead with you to forgive, your love precedes both us and our wrongdoing. We do not know how to pray or how to praise, and we are afraid of saying words that do not befit you. How can we pray to the one who lacks nothing and is wholly perfect? And how can we praise the one who has remained in his glory from eternity? If he is glorified, then he grows greater through praise; and if he grows greater through glory that comes from us, he becomes perfect. If he is dishonored, his dishonor is greater than his praise. If he is made holy by our mouths, he gains additional praise. If he becomes angry, the wrongdoer’s insult must previously have been hidden from him; and if he is reconciled, we have shown him the path to reconciliation. And if, after some time, he does something out of regret, time has forced him to learn something he did not know. And if he does not know—something forbidden for any mouth to say—what greater knowledge does he possess than the things he has made? No, you earthly people, do not think earthly thoughts! There is nothing in Being that is less than Being. The very name “Being” declares his permanence; and just as Being exists, its knowledge exists with it. It exists before everything, and it is as it is. Nothing that happens or is going to happen escapes its notice. This is how a creature should think about the Creator, and this is how a rational being ought to repay the giver of speech. We owe a debt of love to our Maker. Come, let us arrange to repay a little of the great amount we owe. He does not seek repayment from us as though he were in need. He arranges occasions for us to grow rich from his treasures. A treasury of life without end is [?] in his nature, and he longs greatly to give from it to the members of his household.

He called our nature heirs to the love of his Son. For this reason he disciplines us and lovingly teaches us wisdom. Let us therefore endure the various forms of correction that come from his discipline, and let us not grow weary under the blows of famine and sickness. If the name of sons is firmly established in our minds, let us also affirm that our discipline is for our benefit. Let us accept the blows from our Maker without losing heart, and experience the cold of the changing seasons without grumbling. Let us ask him only this when the blows come: “My Lord, do not rebuke us in fierce anger according to our deeds.” Like the son of Jesse, let us plead aloud over our wrongdoing, and follow the path of his words to the appointed meeting of repentance. Yes, my Lord, may we be worthy of that utterance addressed to David, and return, like him, to the state of having our wrongdoing forgiven. Yes, my Lord, remove the offense of your servants as you did that of your servant, and let them hear the voice of forgiveness that the righteous man heard. David was righteous, but the Evil One envied him and made him wicked. Yet by confessing that he had sinned, he erased the name of wickedness from his heart. And if confession erased the name of the wicked and inscribed them among the good, then hope remains for the wicked to become good. Good One, who forgave adultery and murder with a spoken word, forgive the offenses of our shameful deeds, just as you forgave then. You are the one who forgave that lawless offense; now also forgive our disorderly sins. You are the one who revoked the sentence you had pronounced against murderers; now also withhold the blows you have prepared for our wrongdoing. You are the one who mingled mercy with anger throughout all [?], and did not allow our enemies to mock us. You are the one who stirred up your great love for the righteous and made them worthy to plead with you, although you have no need. In your love you forgave the sins of our people from the beginning, and granted the reward of your kindness according to the wishes of the righteous. For the sake of the righteous, you forgave the offenses of earlier generations.

And behold, it already stands forgiven by you before they plead with your kindness. You instilled zeal in human beings to plead with you, so that, when they have entreated you, they might consider themselves able to overcome wrongdoing. Moses prayed, and you forgave the sin of worshiping the calf. You said to him, “See, I have forgiven, just as you pleaded.” Joshua prayed, and you stopped the course of the sun and moon. You recorded in Scripture that Joshua’s word stopped their courses. Samuel prayed, and your command answered him with the sound of thunder. You credited him with the rain that came out of season. David prayed when he saw the Watcher destroying the people. The spiritual being drew back at his petition, though it was because of you that he drew back. Elijah called upon you, and you made the winds harsh, and the rain departed. You stirred the people to zeal, because the righteous man’s word bound and released. Elisha called upon you, and through his hands you restored the dead to life. You credited his prophetic ministry with the victory won from the mouth of death. Hezekiah called upon you, and you destroyed thousands of Assyrians. Although he was very [?], he triumphed by the Watcher’s sword. Daniel too revealed hidden things through the power of your help, and the Babylonians wove a crown of praises for his willingness. In every generation the righteous prayed, and you answered them. In our generation, which is bereft of righteous people, appease yourself. The pleading of your kindness is greater than that of all the righteous, and the treasury of your mercies cannot be compared with created things. Your love stirred the will of the righteous to plead with you. Now that the righteous are lacking, carry out your will without the righteous. The pleading and the words of those who plead belong to you. Why do you make the members of your household carry your grace? Let the goodness be entirely yours, as indeed it is, and do for us what you did at the beginning of time. Who persuaded you to create the creation when it did not exist? Who advised you to bind the world together in the constitution of humanity? Who was your counselor, advising you to call us your image? Who showed you how to complete your work by forming us? If you sought no help in bringing us and everything else into being, why do you seek help against our wickedness, a contemptible gnat?

Our wickedness is a gnat compared with the greatness of your divinity, and a mere handful if compared with the sea of your mercies. Your great compassion is a vast sea, greater even than the sea. Height and depth are very small compared with its greatness. Heaven and earth proclaim that your compassion is great: when they did not exist, you spoke, and they came into being from nothing. You created everything from nothing for our sake. How, then, could you neglect us in a time of wrath? And something far greater, beyond what speakers can measure: your love clothed us, raised us up, and placed us at the rank of your name. You gave us the name of your own being as a borrowed name. Now let us occupy its rank in our deeds themselves. Our dust has ascended to the exalted rank beside your own being. Let it not be brought down from its exaltation because of our wickedness. Our body sits at your right hand, clothed [?] in glory. Let its glory not be dishonored by the disgrace of our insolence. Let rational beings not despise it because of its weakness, for you have honored it with the great name of your divinity. Do not, Lord, let the demons, its tyrants, boast, saying, “Look, they became kings, but lost their grip [?] on authority!” Do not, my Lord, let the enemies of our people rejoice as they usually do, saying, “Where is the one who ascended to the exalted rank of the immortals?” They have scorned and mocked enough the name with which you honored us. Silence them, so that they do not exalt themselves against your lordship. Through us they wish to mock your great name, and then they intend to rise up against your greatness. Those who have become enemies of your name hate our image. Because they cannot revile you directly, they revile you through us. Do not, my Lord, fulfill the desire of the deceitful, and do not let the edifice of falsehood in which they boast be completed. Rebuke their lofty thinking so that it falls to the ground, and lift the head of our lowliness to the rank of your name.

Rescue our nature from the hands of the destroyers, for it has grown weak and wasted away in the bitter cold among their ranks. Spread your hand protectively over our feeble camp, for the number of those who love truth has dwindled. Let your face shine upon our lowly dwelling, full of troubles, for the beautiful light of righteousness has vanished from it. Appoint your command as guardian over our weakness, for it has squandered the treasure it received from your generosity. Call the spiritual beings and command them to help us, for demons and fierce passions have entered and plundered our treasures. Send the watchers to awaken us from our slumber, for we have sunk into our drunkenness as though into sleep. Send angels to bring peace to our turmoil, for all ranks are caught up in battles of discord. And if the powers on high are not sufficient to awaken us, appeal to our kinsman, and let him reconcile us with your majesty. He can help us in our turmoil, in the struggle of our labors, because he is your only Son and also our mediator. He knows how to plead lovingly on behalf of the guilty, because he has experienced the sufferings of mortality. For he has experienced everything that belongs to mortal nature, and he knows all the better how to help those who are being tested. You [?] him as the source of peace for all, to reconcile all. Fulfill in deed the choice that appointed him as the source of our peace. Now is the time for him to show among us the greatness of his rank, just as he showed it when our guilt grew strong. If you reconciled us through him while we were enemies of your name, how much more will our discord be reconciled through his mediation! If you rescued us from death and the devil through him, how much more will you deliver us from the stings of contemptible gnats! If he uprooted paganism and Judaism by his cross, how easy it is for him to restrain the passions that distress us! If he will judge everyone at the end of time, how much more can he soften the severity of the scourges before that time! If he has authority over the treasury of your divinity,
then he has authority to show freely given mercy to his fellow human beings. O good one, have mercy on our weakness, as is your custom, and give us alms through our kinsman, who holds your treasury.
Discourse on a single person.
Again, another discourse by Mar Narsai, on a single person. Refrain: Priest, seek mercy for the world that has taken refuge within our bones. My brothers.

Mortals heard the mighty voice proclaiming life, and they hated the world and its passing desires. The teaching of life fell upon the ears of earth’s children, and they left the earth and looked toward heaven, toward the spiritual beings. They heard the voice calling people to the house of God, and they threw off the burden of the world and looked toward the heights. The teaching of the Son of God dawned in their minds, and with discernment they hastened along the path to the heights. The discerning heard that there is a world that does not perish, and they despised this temporary world, whose course comes to an end. The righteous wisely exchanged one world for another: this passing world for the one that endures and does not perish. The discerning hated the temporary dwelling that is full of [?], and loved the world that is full of blessings and does not change. The saints wisely made a great [?], and exchanged the earth for the great dwelling of the heavenly beings. Oh, the reward of God's house—may it increase [?]! They exchanged mourning for the pearl of the kingdom on high. They gave nothing and acquired wealth that cannot be taken away; in exchange for a passing dream, they acquired reality and life without end. They heard the voice of the Son of God and hastened [?] to meet him. They became disciples of his teaching and good servants. They saw that his great treasury stood open before mortals, and they ran to him and passed from it spiritually. They heard his saying, '[?] Do not acquire anything on earth,' and withdrew their hands [?] from possessions and business. They abandoned their labors and came away naked from their businesses, eagerly running toward the possessions of righteousness. They left fathers, abandoned brothers, and renounced things that decay. They took up the cross of good labors and [?]. They left women and despised bodily pleasures. These embodied beings, clothed in suffering, lived [?] spiritual beings. The saints followed the good Lord, who is full of mercy, who in his great love called them to his teaching. The kind and merciful one was not ashamed to call even sinners to himself in great love. 'Come to me, you weary people carrying heavy burdens. Find rest beside me [?], and throw off the weight of your sins.' Oh, grace that is entirely full of compassion! Oh, poor one who has exalted the lowly people of the earth! He did not say, 'Throw off your burdens, and then come,' lest they grow too weak to make the journey toward life. He did not command, 'Cut away the burdens of your sins,' lest they lose heart and remain on earth in despair. 'Come with the burdens of your sins,' the compassionate one commanded, 'and I will forgive you and cleanse you of your offenses.' The earth is open to [?] and to sinners. The love of the master of the house overflows, and he calls everyone. After this good [?], who is full of mercy,

the saints followed, generation after generation, and inherited life. While he was on earth, and after he was raised to the one who begot him, he filled the path to the heights with companies of embodied beings. As he passed along the shores of the Sea of Tiberias, he caught fishermen and made them his companions. He took simple people and filled them with the wisdom of life, and sent them to the four corners to proclaim the good news. He stayed at a tax collector's house and emptied his house of business, enriching his life with the possessions of righteousness. He made another tax collector an apostle full of beauty. He gave everything he owned to the needy and followed him on his way. A prostitute heard of his fame and [?] her possessions. She grasped his feet and received from him forgiveness for her sins. Men followed him, and slaves and free people ran after him. All the shameless people who saw his radiance became modest. He welcomed tax collectors and did not shrink from sinners. He filled with crowds the road that leads to the heights above. Men and women ran and followed him lovingly, enduring the labors of righteousness for love of him. When he was exalted and sat at his Father's right hand, he further prepared the upward road for the children of Adam. He caught Paul while he was threatening his holy ones and made him a target for every trial for his sake. His light shone in the house of Cornelius the centurion, and he made his household a great church for the [?] of his name. He roused old men from soft and costly things and sent them out into the dust of the earth. He called young men away from pleasures and luxuries and equipped them with strenuous fasts and prayers. His summons peered in at brides in their bridal chambers. They left their mortal bridegrooms and went after him. He brought kings down from carriages [?] finery and made them run on foot along the upward road. He stripped them of silks and fine clothes and dressed them in the worn-out garments of poverty. He shone upon kings, and his love led them. He made them useful for his proclamation. He brought the people of palaces out into the thirsty wilderness and made them companions of the heavenly beings. He filled mountains and [?] with ranks offering praise. In the desolate wilderness he arrayed companies of the children of light. High cliffs and mountaintops are filled with his holy ones. From them thunder lovely voices telling of the power of his wisdom. The Son of God cast the fire of his love upon the earth and [?] the world with love for spiritual life. With the fire of his love he burned away the desire for earthly things and stirred the world toward that delight which does not perish. He lightened its burden of loads filled with [?] and harnessed it under his yoke, which is pleasant, sweet, restful, and peaceful. He placed upon its shoulder the burden of the Spirit, which is very light, and urged it along the road that leads upward to the royal dwelling. Along this road the holy ones traveled, generation after generation. They worked purely with God and gained life. Along this [?] road the holy man traveled; the blood of his Lord [?]. He worked diligently at the task of righteousness. From his youth

From his youth he clung to the path of righteousness.

And he walked uprightly, steadfast in holiness. He stretched out his neck and shouldered the yoke of the Son of God, laboring diligently at the task of righteousness. He threw from his shoulder the burden of the world, which is full of [?], and shouldered the burden of the Son of God, which is full of life. [?] our good brother from the snares of the foolish world, and like a bird he escaped from the traps of desire. He fled from the world, which strangles its children with its desires, and became a companion of the righteous who labored with God. He kept his mouth from earthly conversations, and his lips practiced spiritual songs. He freed his thoughts from earthly concerns and made them [?] for spiritual praises. He turned his gaze away from the affairs of this world and contemplated those blessings in the house of God. He blocked his hearing from listening to bodily sounds, and purified and cleansed it to hear spiritual sounds. He fenced off his heart from pleasures that [?], and flooded and filled it with every heavenly joy. He restrained his sense of smell from bodily scents [?] and delighted in the pure fragrances of righteousness. He cleared his mind of the filth of earthly things and raised his [?] to the lofty rank of spiritual beings. He gathered his soul away from bodily thoughts and flooded and filled it with every divine concern. He directed his understanding toward that knowledge of the Godhead and contemplated that life without end. He gave his limbs to strenuous vigils and prayers, and sanctified his senses throughout the entire course of righteousness. He bathed his impulses in the great light of crucifixion, and his whole being shone in Christ, the sun who is entirely light. He sanctified his soul, purified his body, and cleansed his thoughts, and his whole being became a pure vessel for the living One on high. The chaste man carried the cross of hardships on his shoulders and maintained a swift pace on the road to the kingdom. He carried his cross according to the command of the Son [?] of God, and he himself was crucified to the whole world and its [?]. Like an eagle, the blessed man flew above the traps and beat his wings toward the heights above, toward the assembly of the flocks. The holy man was diligent in the good labors of righteousness, and he rose in holiness without ever having enough. In that exalted rank of sons he [?] himself, and he worked diligently on the estate of the hidden Father. The diligent man did not work before his Lord like a slave, nor did he consider himself a hired worker as he labored. A slave works while being driven by authority; a hired worker, too, looks for his wages and receives his [?]. But a son works diligently as on his own property, and he is certain that he is an heir in his father's house. Both the slave and the hired worker wait for the sun to set, and both work as though under compulsion, not out of love. The heir labors greatly and fervently,

and for his possessions [?] diligently at all times. In this manner the holy man of whom I speak worked, and throughout his life he labored with God in purity. All his days he stood in the contest of righteousness, and in spiritual combat he drank his own sweat. The victorious man stood against the ranks of the passions and demons, fought the battle, won, and emerged a hero. He drew up his battle lines against enemies within and without, broke through their ranks, and emerged victorious from the contest. Through his endurance he overcame the dense ranks of the passions, and through his prayers the holy man drove away the host of demons. For he was a soldier of the immortal King [?], and he was wholly strengthened by the judgment of righteousness. He was clothed in the strength of orthodox faith, and the holy man was girded with the breastplate of righteousness. On his head was set a helmet fashioned by the Creator: the living cross, before which the evil demons tremble. He held in his hand the great bow of pure fasting, strung with the strong bowstring of good labors. He carried arrows of [?], with strong wings, and aimed at the battle lines [?] of the tyrannical demons. He held before his face the fiery hope of love for his Lord, and in his right hand a spear that embraces with pure love. His feet were shod with readiness, righteous and zealous, and he was like lightning against the ranks of his enemies. He was strong and courageous, ready and nimble, watchful and diligent. He was skilled and victorious, and his [?] ended in victory. Glory. Demons and passions turned their backs before the victorious man, and they were driven away before that soldier of righteousness. The ranks of the heavenly beings clothed in light marveled at him as he [?] the demons, the children of darkness. The assemblies of heavenly beings rejoiced in him and gave him strength in that battle against the powers, the offspring of vipers. [?] and he emerged victorious from the battle through strength. Behold, a crown of greatness is prepared for him in God's house. He was a sailor who steered his ship skillfully among the hazards of the troubled sea, full of storms. He gathered the wealth of righteousness through good labors, filled [?] with it, and looked toward the harbor of God's house. On the great sea sailed the merchant [?] of faith. He himself was the merchant [?], the sailor, and the helmsman. He took hold [?] of the rudder of faith, the mistress of treasures, and prepared fasts, his pure labors, and prayers. He spread the sail—a pure heart and a clear mind—on a lofty mast dyed with the blood [?] of the Son of God. The living Spirit [?] his ship in righteousness, and the fierce gusts of desires did not shake it. He flew over the waves, sped along, and passed over the hazards. With his merchandise he reached [?] the harbor of the heavenly beings. His ship is kept safe in the harbor, the garden full of blessings, until the day of resurrection dawns and he opens his treasures. Before angels and human beings he presents his wealth:

In the great assembly where all generations are gathered. There he opens the great treasury of righteousness before the King to whom heaven and earth belong. He presents the wealth of his good labors to the Lord of wealth and receives from him life and blessings without end. In the chaste assembly of the wise virgins, the holy man mingles with the lamps of his good labors. Because the bridegroom delayed coming in his glory with his angels, he slept and [?] until that coming dawned. During that [?] time, the holy man slept in righteousness. Now he awaits the bridegroom who is coming, and goes out to meet him. His vessel is full of mercy, that pure oil. His lamp is raised, and its flame shines, so that its light may be found. He is prepared and ready to come when he hears that the bridegroom has arrived. He carries his lamp and goes out to meet him with confidence. He enters with him into that delight which never perishes, and reclines at the wedding feast of spiritual life. He is a good servant, faithful, upright, and wise, whom his master appointed to provide for the members of his household. He received authority in the great house of the Godhead and distributed spiritual wealth to its household members. At the proper time he would give the portion of life in a spiritual way, and he did not fall short of the spiritual rule. He was watchful, diligent, eager, and upright in his ministry, and he weighed his provisions in the balance of righteousness. That thought full of deceit did not cry out within him: “The master of the house will come tomorrow; I will rest a little.” He contemplated that coming which is full of trembling, and the day of reckoning was always set before his eyes. He did not beat the male servants bought with blood, or the female servants, nor did he eat and drink with gluttons and drunkards. He conducted his life with proper order and modesty, and this wedding attendant completed his ministry in holiness. For he was awaiting his master's return, when his master would see his diligence: he was awake and ready, and his lamp shone in holiness. The blessing spoken by the pure mouth is reserved for him, and he will receive it before spiritual and bodily beings. He diligently traded with the talents he received from that immortal master and doubled their profit. He did not dig in the ground and hide the spiritual money, nor did he despise the authority of the master who had gone on a journey. He did not neglect the trade that is full of life, nor was he idle in pursuing the profit of righteousness. He diligently traded with the talents he received, and he is ready to hand them over with us, together with the profits, with confidence. When he presents the talents he received and their profit, his master rejoices and showers great love upon him. He hears from him that voice full of blessings: “Good servant, enter into the joy that never ends.” At that voice, spiritual beings fly to him, welcome him, and accompany him to the bridal chamber of light. The servants clothed in light look to their Lord's wishes,

and they stand ready for service in great fear. As soon as they hear that voice full of life, they accompany the righteous with fear and love to the royal palace. They become escorts for the righteous who showed proper reverence, and through their help they crossed the pit and inherited life. The soul of the righteous man is spiritually joined with them, and when they are raised, it enters with them into that delight. The reward for his labors awaits him at the gate on high, and his place is reserved at that feast which never ends. The holy man enters the banquet hall in fine garments, and he has no fear when the king visits those reclining at the feast. Blessed is our congregation, which has a father among the saints, and through his prayers our ranks are protected from harm. Behold, his images shine in the place of atonement, and his expiation is inscribed on the horns of the holy altar. His body is beside you, and his soul is among the heavenly ranks; his bones are in our land, and his spirit is in the garden filled with blessings. Behold, his good [?] have become a school for us, and his prayers are a high wall around the congregations of his children. Behold, his dust is a treasure for our poverty, and his prayers drive pains and illnesses away from us [?]. Blessed is our congregation, in which his radiant body is honored; and he has inherited the great dwelling established by the righteous. My beloved, let us take refuge in his prayers. Let us strive to be like him and travel with him to the land of light. We are children of a holy father full of grace. Following our father, let us lift our wings toward the house of God. In keeping with the promises, let us become spiritual servants, so that our father may live spiritually in the congregation of his children. Behold, his holy examples are good signs, set along the road that leads up to the heights of the house of God. Behold his footprints on the straight path of righteousness. Let us follow him and place our steps in his tracks. Following the good signs of his holy footsteps, let us run the race until we reach the spiritual gathering. Let us wisely direct our lives along our father's path, and enter with him into the delight prepared for him. Like a guide, our father traveled ahead of his loved ones, to show [?] the way to the heights clearly. Behold, the holy man rests at the end of the path of righteousness, and watches for his children to follow him in holiness. Behold, the merchant has reached the harbor where there is no fear. He lights a signal for his disciples, so that they may travel to him. He has come up from the sea with his spiritual merchandise, and watches for the ships of his spiritual household. The companion of the bridegroom ran the course smoothly [?], and behold, at its end he rests and is completely free from fear. The saint has reached that other resting place on his journey, and has prepared a place for the congregation of his spiritual children. Whoever follows the holy man along the straight path will rest beside him and fly with him to meet his Lord. Let us ask for his prayer and run lovingly in his footsteps,

so that, when we are raised and he is clothed in glory, we may cling to him. May the righteous man's prayer and your prayers, his diligent children, gather the scattered onto the path that leads to new life. May I be gathered with you at that time which terrifies the worlds, and may the king's servants not reject me as a stranger, away from your assembly [?]. When the fiery companies hasten to descend to earth before the King's Son, who comes to raise [?] our lowly race; when the assembled hosts of Gabriel's company take their places before that mighty one who descends to summon those sleeping in the dust; when the seraphim fly and soar before the coming of the Lord, who comes to plow life into the stones of the dead [?]. When the cherubim bear that chariot in solemn procession, on which the Judge of the living and the dead is exalted; When another trumpet sounds for the resurrection of the dead, and trembling falls upon them, and the dead stir within the dust; When the great horn of the royal house sounds and calls the generations out of the earth to resurrection; When the departed who died in Christ rise first, strip off and cast away mortality, and fly through the air; When all generations are gathered into that court of judgment, and trembling falls, and silence spreads over all creatures; When the sides are divided for life and for torment, and the ranks separate, some for [?] and some for Gehenna; At that time, may our entire congregation find mercy, and may we inherit life with our holy and righteous father. Make us worthy, our Lord, of that delight at the right hand; and with the saints, the children of your kingdom, we offer you praise. Refrain: Glory to you who have no forefathers, the Son whose coming the righteous awaited in hope.
Discourse on the Departed and on the Resurrection of the Dead

Discourse 11. On the Departed. Again by the same author, being his eleventh discourse. It is suitable for the Friday at the beginning of the fast, which is called the Friday of the Departed. Refrain: Blessed is the one whom the Lord of the world has mercifully chosen out of this world. My brothers.

I wanted to contemplate the splendid beauty of the human form, but while I was seeking to see its beauty, I saw its humiliation. I saw him crowned upon the earth, ruling over everything; then I turned and saw him cast into Sheol by everyone. I saw him giving commands, and speaking and speechless creatures obeying him; a little later I saw a worm crawling through his body. I saw him riding in chariots, fearsome in appearance; then I looked at him again, bowing his head at the entrance to the grave. I saw him adorned in garments of fine linen and silk; after some time I saw a spiderweb spread across his face. I saw the sound of his command terrifying his companions; then death rushed in and suddenly swallowed him, and his voice fell silent. I saw him building and enlarging his dwelling beyond measure; yet on the day of his death, no one allowed him to live in it.

I saw him preparing fine clothes for himself for a day of feasting; but death hurried and prepared for him in Sheol a bridal chamber of mourning. I saw him rushing to accumulate without ever being satisfied; yet at his departure he set out destitute of good things. The mighty man set out from his dwelling with nothing gained, and he took no provisions for the journey appointed for him. He left his dwelling just as he had come out of the womb. Naked he came, and naked he went: this is a great sorrow. The sorrow of the abasement of one more honored than all pierced my mind, and I grieved deeply over the humiliation of our despised race. I saw his exalted status depart from him like a shadow, and I saw his abasement and the humiliation of his soul lingering long. I gazed at his remains, lying in Sheol and turned to dust, and wondered how and when he would return to life. I wondered how life could spring from death, and how his lowly dust could return to its exalted state. Who will rebuild the temple of the body that death demolished? And who will bring the soul back to it, to sing praise within it? Who will open for him the gate of Sheol that is shut in his face? And who will bring him out of the strongholds of ravenous death? What power will breathe the breath of life into his nostrils and give a voice to his dead senses to sing praise? What command will go out, racing through the four corners of the world, and separate human dust from the dust of the earth? Who will separate the dust of human beings from that of the animals that ate them and then died, so that bodies became mingled with bodies? How mighty must that command be that orders them to rise! For the thousands of people who have become dust are beyond counting. How many thousands of heavenly beings will go out searching for those who perished in the sea, and the soul in every form [?]? From where will flesh and bones return and come, when there is no likeness [?] of a body in the dust of the earth? Is it the very dust of the earth that becomes a body? And who can separate dust from other dust of the same kind? I pondered these things foolishly, speaking in the person of fools, and repeated their words as though I myself were caught up in them. I repeated the thinking of fools from my own mind, as though thinking as they did. Paul listened to me and rebuked me along with them as a fool. The herald of the Spirit and chosen witness to the resurrection of the dead heard doubt about the resurrection of the dead, and grew zealous and indignant. He called me a fool, as I spoke in the person of doubting fools: “Why have you proclaimed the thinking of fools in people's ears? “Fool,” he said, “look at the nature of the seed that you sow, whoever you are: unless it dies, it cannot find life and bear fruit. “Look at the grain of wheat, the seed that you cast into the earth: first it dies, and then it lives, as a symbol of the resurrection. “It is the very same wheat that falls and dies like the body; it is the same wheat that sprouts from its decay in great splendor.

“In this same way the body dies and the body lives, and it is that very same perishable body that puts on glory. “It is the same body that acquires manifest senses like its former ones, and its own soul returns to sing upon the harp of its strings. “Everyone rises in body and soul, just as they are: the body with its senses [?], and the soul with its swift movements. “The body becomes immortal instead of mortal, and the soul takes off its clothing of sorrow, its filthy garments. “The very body that became dust becomes a body again; the very soul whose voice had ceased sings praise within it.” Paul bears witness to the body's decay and its renewal: it decays, and it is renewed by the power of its Creator. “This perishable body,” he says, “is destined to put on glory, and this mortal body to live an immortal life.” Do not grieve, nature worn out by mortality, and do not doubt the renewal of body and soul. Rise and listen to the voices that announce the resurrection to you, and gain hope that will be a source of hope for your mortality. Listen to the prophet who cries out in the Spirit to dead bones, whose voice proclaims fresh good news among mortals. Listen as he cries out like a trumpet to the silent ones and gathers the whole host of bodies for renewal. His voice proclaimed one renewal for body and soul, and he gave them the cup of consolation to drink, which brought the dead to life. Listen also to the voice of the one who renews mortal nature, who points out humanity’s renewal as though with his finger. Listen as he rebukes the doubting Sadducees and disputes with them on the basis of the divine laws. “You are mistaken,” he says, “because you do not know how to read the Scriptures, nor do you discern the force of the meaning of their words. In the resurrection,” he says, “there is no distinction between men and women, for their nature becomes immortal, like the spiritual beings.” See, our Lord has opened a new path for bringing the dead to life. Come, let us travel it toward the renewal of body and soul. See, he has proclaimed good hope to us through the sound of his words. Let us believe that he can fulfill for us the promise of his words. See, he shouted against Death, the ravenous lion that destroyed our race, and took three bodies of our kind away from it and restored them to life. See, he himself also descended into the lair of the devourer of humanity. He gave it his body, and it swallowed him and quickly expelled him. See, he rose and raised our entire nature from its fall, and breached the walls that Death had built to bar the dead. See, he came out and brought back captive humanity from the mighty one. He took away its armor, plundered its camp, and made it a laughingstock. See, he took captives, ascended, and reigned above everything. He is to come and renew everything through the sound of his words. See, the time is near for him to descend to earth just as he ascended, with a visible body and the hidden power of divinity. See, heaven and earth, angels and human beings await him, so that he may free them from bondage to corruption. See, all creation groans over mortals,

wondering when they will become immortal and free from suffering. Rational beings and speechless creatures alike wear mourning clothes, wondering when they will take off the hateful garment of mortality. Severe labor pains strike the earth like a woman giving birth, as it waits to bring forth human bodies from within its womb. Human beings and spiritual beings bear great sorrow, wondering when they will see the reality [?] of humanity’s renewal. The good servants wait hopefully for the master of the house, wondering when he will return from the banquet and give them their reward. The wise women hold their lamps in hope, wondering when the heavenly bridegroom will appear and they will enter with him. The heavenly assemblies await the fulfillment of hope, waiting for hope to dawn openly and dispel fear. They await that divine revelation at every moment, waiting for the gates of heaven to open so that they may welcome him. The ear of their minds is inclined toward that voice, waiting for it to [?], so that death may tremble and the Evil One be put to shame. The ranks await the command of the one they serve, waiting for him to give the order so that they may proclaim the sound of salvation on earth. All the courtiers stand at the king’s gate, waiting for him to come out so that they may welcome him with their hosannas. They weave a crown of victory with the movements within them as their hands, so that they may [?] the King of kings who conquered on the cross. The loving longing of their minds cannot be expressed—how greatly they yearn to see his glory and praise him! Fear and love reign together over their ranks, and they are deeply anxious lest they slacken in their readiness. They love greatly, long greatly, and fear greatly; like athletes, they are engaged in the contest for the promise of life. In spirit they run in the spiritual stadium to receive the reward of that victory which cannot be defeated. Look, the time of reward for their contests has arrived, and the time draws near for them to receive the prizes for their struggles. Look, the heavenly kingdom of the King on high has drawn near. Come, let us adorn ourselves spiritually and go out to meet him. Look, the gates of heaven are being lifted before his coming, so that he may descend to earth and bring up with him those who serve him. Great wonder, blessedness, and sorrow will mark the day of his revelation: wonder at his dawning, blessedness for the good, and sorrow for the wicked. In splendor and glory he reveals himself to the angels and human beings, and heaven and earth together are filled with his praise. His mighty signal lifts the veil from the face of heaven, and the light of his great radiance shines upon all and through all. Like lightning, his light shines in the four directions, and visible light is faint compared with his light. There is nothing comparable to the light that flashes from his face, nor any likeness for the swiftness of the [?] of his signal. Lightning bolts are slow compared with his command, however swift they may be, and the light of the sun’s orb is dark compared with his. The greatness of his glory cannot be expressed in human language;

and the mouth of every created being is too small to say how great it is. Fearsome and severe is the hour of his sudden dawning, and there is no bodily or spiritual being that is not terrified. Great astonishment suddenly falls upon created beings at the sound of the command, whose voice is far more terrifying than the sea. Like a messenger, his signal runs before his face and sets the heavenly ranks in position, troop by troop. In ordered ranks the spiritual beings resound before his majesty, honoring him with the sound of incomparable praise. A thousand thousands stand before him in awe, and ten thousand times ten thousand repeat his praise without ever having enough. His love rules over the thousands of heavenly beings, and they eagerly hasten to repay him their debt of love. The cherubim are yoked, the watchers escort him, and the seraphim cry out, “Holy, holy, holy is the King who dwells in glory!” They cry “Holy” spiritually, in the language of the spirit, like that unutterable speech that Paul heard. That sound with which they divinely praise the God of all cannot be uttered by a tongue of flesh. With hidden movements they openly sing praise to the Hidden One, and their sight is stopped before the bodily gate. They see the body being carried in honor on the chariot, while the invisible divinity is hidden within it. The Hidden One within the visible one suddenly commands their assemblies to cry out a song of praise for the renewal of all. They all cry out the sound of renewal in human ears, and the earth trembles at the fearful sound of their trumpets. They all become a thunder of voices, as many as they are, and the sound of spiritual horns matches their number. Their appearance is majestic, the speech of their utterances is glorious, and the course of their actions is far swifter than lightning. Above them all, Christ the King comes in glory, and they escort him with a song of praise worthy of his name. The chief of the angels carries the victory standard, the cross, and displays it to those in heaven and those on earth. The standard of his suffering and his victory comes before him, so that those who acted insolently and the tyrannical demons may be put to shame by it. Companies of watchers and angels run to meet him, and they gaze upon him with the hidden eye of their minds. The King descends with his standard to the earth where he was dishonored. He demands an accounting for his dishonor and gives gifts to those who welcomed him. The sound of the divine horn rings out before him, and the dead and the living gather and come to the assembly called in his name. The last horn cries out at the end, at the completion of the ages, and at its sound the gates of Sheol are opened before the departed [?]. A hidden command runs with that sound, and in the blink of an eye it raises and renews the bodies that have decayed. The voice and the command suddenly cry out in the ears of Death: “Return the captives, and give an account of the bodies that have perished!” A great groaning falls upon Sheol, the mother of the dead.

Terrible labor pains terrify her like a woman giving birth. The womb of the barren mother becomes a fountain of human beings, and she quickly gives back as much as she had heaped up. The command sprinkles the dew of mercy over the face of the earth, and bodies spring up from the dust like seed. The body rises whole and entire, with its senses manifest, and the soul returns with its wisdom, praising within it. No member of the body is left in Sheol, and none of the soul’s movements is lost without returning within it. Body and soul rise together in the blink of an eye. They strip off and throw away the garments of suffering and put on glory. The dead rise, and their nature becomes immortal. Then the living who remain alive are changed into that same likeness. One command raises and transforms the dead and the living, and no one is lost, either among the dead or among the living. The resurrection applies equally to all bodies and all souls. The good and the wicked rise together, in body and soul. The entire race descended from Adam returns to life. No one ever born remains in Sheol without being raised. Only one is missing there from their number: the one who, through a spirit of error, goes astray and leads people astray. He is the son of destruction, who alone among humanity perishes. Mercy does not deem him worthy to enter among the number of human beings. The divine command closes the gate of resurrection in his face alone. He is not shown the face of the King who commands them to rise. With a terrifying weapon, the command binds his body and the movements of his soul, and sinks him into the endless abyss of Sheol. In him a great wonder is revealed to rational beings: how a living nature is lost to life. Spiritual and bodily beings contemplate him: human beings contemplate his body, and watchers his soul, which suddenly come to an end. Something new happens in that renewal filled with wonder: everything is renewed, while one is destroyed without mercy. There is a great wonder on the day when the King of kings is revealed: he judges everyone, but leaves one without questioning. Joy and distress await the two sides on the day of resurrection: blessedness for the good, and doubled lashes for the wicked. The command holds crowns and lashes before the Judge: crowns for the righteous, and lashes for the wicked who lost the contest. The divine command holds glory and disgrace as though in a finger, giving glory to those who triumphed and disgrace to those who sank low. Like a ruler, the command goes ahead at the gate of [?]. It brings one in and sends another out into the outer darkness. It brings rational beings into the furnace of judgment and melts them down. It selects the gold—truth laid bare—and rejects the counterfeit. With the King’s seal it stamps the good for the King’s service, but rejects the wicked and throws them into Gehenna. He holds an outstretched staff in his hand and inspects his flock. He places the sheep at his right hand, as he promised. Great is the distinction made there among rational beings: although they are one in a single renewal, they are not one. The rational nature of watchers and human beings is one:

Yet they are not one, because their deeds differ. “On that day,” he says, “if two are in one bed, one is lifted up toward the heights, and the other is left behind.” If two women are grinding at the mill at that time, one is taken and the other is left as she was. Look, our Lord’s word has shown that separation: how he separates the righteous and the chaste from the wicked. He showed that this separation takes place among all ranks, and that he chooses both males and females. Although men and women have one and the same nature there, he showed that some from each group are left behind. Like lightning, the command passes through their ranks, taking one and leaving another from every rank. Although he separates them, the great order is full of distinctions, and according to their labors he assigns both reward and being left behind. He subjects human beings and spiritual beings to the same separation, testing alike the truth and falsehood of both sides. He brings the chaste, clothed in love, into the bridal chamber on high, and leaves here on earth the fallen who did not adorn themselves. Those who love the earth remain on earth, in the place they loved; those who long for what is above are lifted upward on the wings of the Spirit. On earth they receive doubled lashes, as they deserve, and there they pay the debt of the sins they committed. The earth becomes Gehenna for the children of earth, and they punish themselves through the things in which they sinned. Their own mind scourges them with discernment over why they neglected their duty during their life here. They themselves judge the wickedness within them that condemned them, and expose it [?] in the recollection of their thoughts. There they conduct a great trial against their sins, and before everyone’s eyes they expose the blemishes of their secret deeds. More bitter than all lashes are the lashes they receive, when the company of the righteous is crowned and their own company is put to shame. The wicked see a great wonder among the good: how lightly they fly toward the heights. It is a great wonder, and however much we say, it is greater than wonder: lowly flesh sprouts wings for flight. The command that fashioned it from dust in the beginning gives it the power of flight, so that it can fly through the air. He who breathed the breath of life into it, so that it became a living being, makes it a temple of the Spirit that does not decay. He who lovingly stooped down to what he had fashioned raises it from its lowliness and mercifully renews it. In love and mercy he fashioned it in the beginning and called it by his own name; in the same way he again confirms to it the promise of his words. From the beginning, when he fashioned it, he called it his image; and at the end he descends in his image and raises it from the dead. The hidden command descends in his image, no longer hidden, and gives immortal life to what is mortal. In the second Adam, whom he stooped to put on in love, he descends without change at the end of time.

The body that his loving will put on and called by his own name—he willingly clothes himself in it and descends to earth. He who ascended before the eyes of angels and human beings is the one who comes to judge human beings and spiritual beings. The watchers saw him ascending in a visible body, and they said that he would come in that same appearance, just as he ascended. At his appearing, his command descends swiftly, renews everything, and raises it with him to the place above. The hidden command cries out openly with an awesome voice, shaking the earth and terrifying the heavenly ranks. With his voice he commands heavenly and earthly beings: “Rise, be renewed, and put on glory that does not decay.” The voice of his command awakens earthly beings from their slumber, and they leap up and stand as though waking from a heavy sleep. A single voice, full of wonder, cries out on earth. Rational beings and speechless creatures tremble at it and obey it. Everything heeds it, and everything carries it out without delay. Through it the heights and the depths and everything in them are renewed. Rational beings ascend to a lofty rank beyond compare, and speechless creatures rest from their bondage in the service of human beings. The sun ceases its swift course, and the moon rests from the changes it undergoes every month. The stars fall, and the light of their rays goes out. The blowing of the winds in the air falls still and moves no more. Darkness comes to an end, and the succession of night and day passes away. Hours, weeks, and the months of the year are no longer counted. The spring in the womb of Sheol dries up, yielding no more fruit. Livestock perish, fanged beasts disappear, and crawling creatures come to an end. The sea rests from the battling of its violent waves, and human ships no longer sail upon its back. Everything is changed, and everything is renewed when human beings are renewed. Over everything and in everything, the light of the one Creator reigns. Everything is freed from bondage to human beings, and humanity itself dwells in a place where there is no fear. At a slight command everything is changed and everything is renewed. How swift it is, and how great its swiftness, cannot be expressed. That command is far swifter than anything else, and if anything is swift, it is very slow compared with it. There is no delay between the descent and the ascent—not even as long as someone takes to blink an eye, bringing eyelid to eyelid. On the chariot borne upon the back of the air, the King carries in honor the valiant soldiers who fought and conquered for love of him. His command harnesses a single spiritual chariot, and in it he seats both earthly and heavenly beings. It is his command that becomes both cloud and chariot, and it is this that carries and guides everything toward the heights. It is this that serves in place of everything for rational beings, and through it watchers and human beings are raised to the place above.

It is this that marches like a commander before their ranks, and it also gathers other ranks to the assembly of his name. The King marches toward the heights at the head of his army, with thousands of watchers at his right and at his left. With him the members of his palace travel to the place of light, to be heirs with him in the kingdom above. Very great is the contingent of his army, greater than all armies, and indescribable are the splendor and glory with which he is honored. With him is the whole rational creation: thousands of watchers and myriads of human beings. They all carry a crown of praise for the day of his victory and present it to him through spiritual movements. Heaven and earth recount his glory through the mouths of those who speak, paying him the debt of love with the sound of praise. In the greatness of his love, the gaze of their thoughts is [?], as they long for the moment when he opens the gates on high. They are very eager to see the way prepared for it, so that rational beings may enter and receive spiritual gifts. Their minds cannot have enough of the sight of the King, and the more they see, the more they long to gaze upon him. Before their movements, a command runs swiftly and draws aside the veil in front of the gate of the royal dwelling. The King opens the great gate before his entrance, and he enters and rests within the palace, together with those who are with him. The sight of that entrance is full of wonder and sorrow: wonder for those above, and sorrow for those below who are not raised up. Even the wicked gaze upon him who is better than all the good, and this is their sorrow: although they see him, they are deprived of him. The mind within them gazes sorrowfully, without having its fill, as the gates on high are opened and as they are shut. People see a new sight among human beings: although they are one, one is raised up and another is brought down. The spiritual beings too, the ranks of demons, see something new: although they are spirits, they cannot fly like spiritual beings. Wicked people and tyrannical demons stand in astonishment when they gaze at the gates on high as they are shut. They weep and loudly lament over themselves, for they see that the gate of forgiveness is shut in their faces. They weep in sorrow with resounding groans, repeatedly uttering cries of remorse. Sorrow scourges their inner nature with discernment, and remorse judges their own faults. They themselves wisely bring their sins to judgment, and test the falseness of their thoughts as though in a furnace. With the mind within them they weigh the burden of their sins, and in proportion to their wrongdoing they bitterly increase their sorrow. Bitter and harsh is the just judgment by which they are tormented, and the severity of its scourges cannot be expressed in human language. Great and deep is the abyss into which they fall, and it is very difficult to escape its harshness. Together with the rich man, everyone cries out to Abraham:

“Have pity, compassionate one, and plead for mercy to draw us up. Ask and implore the hidden Will, as you are accustomed to do, to sprinkle a little dew of mercy upon our misery.” “My children,” Abraham answered those pleading with him, “it is impossible to cross the abyss that lies between us and you.” Remember that you loved earthly things and the good things of this passing age, and did not [?] wait for the promise of spiritual life. Abram recounts these things to his children, but not aloud. In keeping with what is written, I have spoken the words as though they had happened. For they do not call upon Abram to give them life, nor can Abraham speak without the command. It is the command that has shut the gate of the kingdom before them, and it is the command that cries out through Abraham’s mouth that they have been left behind and tormented. It is the command that wields the rod, with blows not delivered by hands, and deals out lashes to those being punished according to their deeds. That same command also holds the treasury of good things above, and according to their love gives a reward to those who love love. The lashes of those who acted wickedly in ignorance are not equal, and the glory of those who proved strong in the struggle of their labors is greater. The command distributes good things and lashes according to people’s will, and brings joy or distress according to wickedness and righteousness. Although nothing in that delight is deficient, Paul said that one glory shines more brightly than another. Those above dwell in great glory that cannot be expressed, while those below lie in torment that cannot be described. The righteous—watchers and human beings—live in the place of light, while the wicked and the demons who acted wickedly dwell in darkness. The holy ones dwell spiritually in fellowship with the King, and delight with him in the imperishable court of the Spirit. Their delight is glory whose sweetness can never satisfy them fully, and their conversation is the sound of thanksgiving without end. They are clothed in glory and cry out praise in holiness to him who wished to share his holiness with the work of his hands. The righteous see the Hidden One, who is hidden and revealed in his glory. They do not doubt how they see while not seeing. In the visible one they see the glory of him who is concealed from all, and through the revealed one the vision of their minds descends. In the temple of the body they offer the sacrifices of their minds, but they are not permitted to gaze into the Holy of Holies. The holy place is the visible body of the firstfruits of our race, and the Holy of Holies is the invisible divinity. The holy place and the Holy of Holies are one in unity: one God in the temple of the body that he chose for his love. Human beings and spiritual beings offer one thanksgiving to the Hidden One in the revealed one, and also to the revealed one himself because of the Hidden One. By one love, all are bound to the one who was revealed; and he is, in his being, one lordship and one authority. There, over all and in all, the Hidden One [?] through the revealed one, and in his revealed state he judges all according to his promise.

For this reason too, he chose him out of all and subjected everything to him, so that those being judged might see the one who judges. For the children of the kingdom and the children of darkness needed to see who distributes gifts and deals out lashes. They also wanted to see something, however hidden it might be; and he who cannot be seen comforted them according to their longing. The one who orders everything has done all he has done wisely. The wisdom of his love—how great it is and what it is like—cannot be expressed. Wondrous is his creation, great is his renewal, and perfect is his love. However much we exalt him, our tongue falls short of his greatness. He showed his love by creating everything and renewing everything, and by bringing everything into the loving fellowship of his divinity. He invites and calls the members of his household to the wedding feast of his love, and makes them rejoice in that kingdom established on high. In the realm above he distributes the riches of his goodness, and sits granting a charter of freedom to the work of his hands. Human beings possess the riches of immortal life, and dwell without toil in a realm above suffering.
