The ships of their bodies rest in a peaceful harbor, and the waves of suffering no longer batter their minds. Through the power of grace they gain strength to sing praise to the one who, in his love, gave them a share in his glories. There what is written about the human being is fulfilled: he is a visible image that proclaims the Hidden One through his visibility. There human beings on earth see the one hidden from all, and no longer weary themselves seeking out hidden things. There one will reigns over all and in all, and no one imposes repayment for the debt of sins. There the Watchers and human beings become one in harmony. Strife ceases, envy comes to an end, and anger disappears. Love and peace reign over all and bring all into subjection, and one will governs everything according to its desire. The Hidden One holds the rod of anger in the hands of the visible one, and guides everything toward the hiddenness within the human image. Human beings and spiritual beings hasten to the gathering of humanity, and when they approach humanity's gate, they offer thanksgiving. They contemplate him as in an image, in the human image, and through his visibility they see the power of the might of the divine Being. The eye of reason does not see the divine Being, but the visible image that resembles the Hidden One. I said that it resembles him in the greatness of its rank, not in nature, for among passing beings there is none whose nature resembles the nature of the Hidden One. In love he made the work of his hands worthy to resemble him, and in grace he called it and established it in the rank bearing his own name. This is a divine means that cannot be explained: how wisely he honored what was his through what was his. This is the invention of that will which rules over all, and skillfully he bound the world to his divinity. Praise to him for his unfathomable wisdom, for he established everything and renews everything in love and mercy.
On Perfection of Conduct
65. On Perfection of Conduct. By the same author. The sixty-fifth discourse. On Perfection of Conduct.

One victor conquered sin, which had killed humanity, and gave human beings and heavenly beings a share in his victory. One hero went out to battle against the Evil One, and through his combat those on earth learned the ways of fighting. One athlete entered the arena of righteousness, and through his courage mortals gained good hope. One athlete roared in the arena of righteousness, and through his courage mortals gained good hope. One warrior joined battle with the mighty one, and through his endurance those made of dust braced their minds. Upon all and among all he [?] the help that came from his gift, and he invited and called the good and the wicked to the feast of his love. Like a hero, the mighty warrior cried out throughout creation: Behold, the world has won the victory! Let everyone rise and trample on his head. Rise and take courage, you earthly and heavenly beings, and gain victory through the victory achieved by my hands. Come, rest in my harbor, you weary ones who have grown weary among the crowds of people, and do not be battered amid the waves of desires. Come, heirs, take back your [?], which were plundered, and take possession of the allotments that were snatched from your lives. Come, strive to gain spiritual life, and despise labor for earthly things that do not last. Come, accustom yourselves to meditating on the blessings hidden in me, and hate and cast away the ugly habits of passing things. Sure and tested is the promise of life proclaimed through me. And without doubt it gives rewards to whoever believes in me. The Creator's power wished to reveal its might through my hands. Through me he dispenses the riches of his love to the work of his hands. The creatures he made owe him a debt of love, especially those endowed with discerning speech. Come, you who have speech, offer the thanksgiving you owe to the power of the divine Being, who proclaimed his might in the battle I fought. Come, contemplate the upright standard at the top of the wood, and learn how the battle against passions and demons [?]. Lustful passions have disfigured the beauty of your minds. Wipe the filth of your sensuality from your hearts. Tyrannical demons have seized the inheritance of your possessions.

Fight against them and take possession of the allotments of new life. Fight spiritually against your enemies, in the same manner that they fought against you and plundered your possessions. Put on endurance equal to the severity of the harsh passions, and subdue them so that you will not be subdued beneath their feet. Gain understanding equal to the craftiness of the cunning [?], so that you will not be [?] by their stratagems as before. Clothe the whole person in the armor of righteousness, so that the sharp arrow of the Accuser cannot pierce him. Let body and soul join battle against temptations, and let them aim diligently at the goal of the promise of life. Let the impulses and bodily senses aim at the goal of the righteous, so that together they may be worthy to receive the reward that does not perish. Now it is time to show the warriors the forms of combat, full of struggle against the passions. Let us openly state the subject of the discourse prepared for us, before listeners who love to hear about spiritual things. Let the radiance of the words of our mouth shine brightly before the eyes of spiritual people who clearly perceive the meaning of words. Without a veil, let us portray the story our soul has desired on the tablet of the mind that knows how to gaze upon things to come. I wished to speak about the dwellings of [?], and I wanted to tell of the structure that does not decay. I was greatly [?] at the victory of the King who conquered through the wood, and I longed to reveal his victory before his servants. My thoughts marveled at the contest and labors of the servants he chose, who [?] grew strong against the assaults of desires. I saw that his road and that of his household was narrow, and I resolved to follow their footsteps, even if only in words. I heard that promised blessings were hidden in its narrowness, and my mind urged me to hear them, even if only by hearing. I heard that the road traveled by this company was good, and I thought I might [?] help people benefit from it. Come, travelers who love the road of life! Travel with our account and receive a longing for new life. With love let us hear the account of spiritual life, and with understanding let us attend to the meaning of hidden things. With hope let us affirm what is said about things to come, for although they are hidden from it, they are far more certain than the sun. “These are the three that [?],” Paul said. It is therefore certain that through their power they can accomplish everything. The spiritual way of life is difficult for bodily people, but wherever these three are mingled with it, it is easy and orderly. Even our [?] explained and revealed the power within them, for they triumph over and overcome the assault on the soul and the limbs. For he said, “Everything that is difficult for human beings to accomplish is possible with God through faith.” Faith is a second sun for the eyes of the body. Come, let us see through it the splendid beauty of things to come. Its blaze is far brighter than the sun to anyone who gazes into it; while still on earth, he sees things soaring above in heaven.

The way of faith is full of great wonder. Come, let us marvel at it and learn the order described in it. The deeds it performs are full of abundant treasures. Let everyone approach and freely receive what they need for life. Let the wise also turn toward the door of its house, and behold, their needs are met without delay. Come, all ranks together with all degrees, and become equally rich from the treasury of faith, which has no limit. Through faith let us fulfill the mysteries of faith, and with its confidence let us place our trust in things to come. By its light let us see what is not revealed to bodily eyes; by conversing with it, let us awaken our soul with glorious things. Its discourse is full of great, inexpressible glory, and it gloriously bestows glory on those devoted to loving it. Through her the prophets were glorified in the mysteries of things to come, and through her the apostles triumphed by the power of mighty deeds. On her structure the righteous and the chaste built their labors, and the height of their conduct reached up to heaven. They began to build truth in an unstable world, and people began to build their labors upon theirs. On her foundation Simon Peter placed his confession, and received as his reward an imperishable crown of blessings. “Blessed are you, Simon,” said the mouth full of blessings, “for you have been found worthy to learn the mystery of hidden things from the mouth of the Hidden One. “It was not flesh and blood that revealed this to you so that you could make this true confession, but the Father, who has a Son resembling his own image.” He revealed to Simon the glorious image, free of composition, so that he might confess the Father who has a Son, the two resembling one another. Let everyone who confesses the Son confess as Simon did, and not doubt how the Word and the body are together. The apostles lovingly accepted and assented to what had taken place: that the Word willingly dwelt in a body to save our lives. For our lives he willingly dwelt in a body subject to change, and freed our lives from slavery to the Evil One and death. Through sufferings he completed what became the source of life for us. Through sufferings, then, [?] complete the course of our way of life. Let us learn from him through what sufferings he won victory, and how he scorned the promptings of desires. Let us hear from his heralds about his labor and endurance, and what labors he portrayed in his own person before their labors. Let them also recount the example of their own conduct: how they themselves stood firm against sufferings. In the [?] they fought against the promptings of fleshly desire, and in their minds they engaged in battle with their impulses. Through their capacity to suffer they overcame the watchers of suffering, and through weakness they gave strength to mortality. With food they fed their minds the [?] of the spirit, and through sleep they drove weariness from their understanding. Through nature itself they conquered nature and its promptings, and while they remained within it, they became like people who were not within it.

They heard that they were destined to live an immortal life, and they despised temporal life as though it were no life at all. They saw that they had been mystically renewed in baptism, and clothed their senses in the likeness of spiritual beings. They saw that the time to be rewarded for their struggles was approaching, and portrayed beforehand what was to come, before it happened. The faithful portrayed the world to come through their conduct, and set it on earth like an image before those who looked on. Like pigments, they ground together labors of every kind, and with [?] they sketched a representation of hidden things. Through fasting they showed that the body lives without food, and through prayers that the soul’s converse takes place in the spirit. Through keeping vigil they taught that mortal nature will no longer sleep, and through songs that it sings praise without weariness. Through contempt for possessions they made known the wealth hidden in heaven, and through humble things they opened a path toward glorious things. They fasted from bread, not because the food it provided was hateful, but to aspire to that way of life without food. They abandoned marriage, not because union with a spouse was unclean, but so that they might be as they are destined to be there. They scorned worldly pursuits, not because they were brought low by poverty, but so that they might be worthy to delight in what has no end. They subdued the brutish passions of body and soul, though they themselves had bodies and souls. They hated preoccupation with earthly things, though they were earthly, and loved contemplation of spiritual things, though they were far removed from them. He waged battle against every fierce force, hidden and visible, and they did not relinquish their hope of riches. They calmed anger, humbled pride, overthrew envy, and did not allow [?] to run as it pleased. The chaste placed chaste bridles on bodily desire, and though it was swift, they made it run at a measured pace. They sprinkled [?] water on the fire in their limbs. Its fierceness subsided, and it did not fight as it usually did. Their impulses rode upon their senses as upon horses, and they ordered the course of the whole person so that it would not go astray. They put a bridle of peace on the mouth, the horse of words, and the soul mounted its back like a charioteer. They disciplined the eyes in looking at visible things, and permitted only a measured amount of sound to enter the ears. They taught the hand to sow seeds of righteousness and gather glorious fruit for itself through its acts of charity. They trained the foot to travel the road to other people and visit them with spiritual gifts. They prepared the whole human body for the service of life, and occupied its life with the pursuit of a life foreign to it. They compelled its whole nature to resemble what was not its nature. It abandoned what belonged to it and began imitating what did not belong to it. The body's nature continually dwells on bodily things,

but they made it forget its own concerns and contemplate those of the spirit. The soul's nature is accustomed to thinking about natural things, but they turned the soul's attention toward glorious things. People showed other people a great wonder on earth: with their bodies they fought against their bodies. Children of ashes blazed a new trail in creation: they took their stand in battle against the slings of their limbs. Mortals acted in an unaccustomed way in their mortality: they portrayed renewal while bound by the cords of death. Who has ever seen perishable limbs engaging in combat with their passions while themselves susceptible to passion? Who has looked upon weak and wavering impulses taking their stand in battle against the enfeebling changes within them? To whom has strength been given as it has been given to human beings, who, though condemned, won a victory that cannot be defeated? A human being remains a human being, however much he triumphs through what is not his own. And this is the wonder: he triumphs through what belongs to another as though through what belongs to himself. Something new happened to the children of Adam, the soil of the earth: through their conduct they changed dust into spiritual gold. Adam, earth molded by a hand that is not composite, who made you forget your nature through what is not your nature? Your nature is dust, and your dust bears witness that your dust is dust. Yet the way of life you have now adopted rises above your dust, and like [?] turns the passions back against its susceptibility to them. You are subject to passions, and passions are woven into the tunic of your body. Who would not marvel at your susceptibility to passions, which you have made resistant to them? Come, you who are subject to passions; marvel and wonder at your brothers, who by their own wills conquered the passions within themselves. Come, mortals, and see how mighty mortals have become: they died without dying, and already came to life before they were to live. Come, people of earth, and see how wise people of earth have become: they judged their own deeds justly before the day of judgment. They set righteous judgment before their eyes like a goal, and devoted themselves earnestly to scorning the faults they had acquired within themselves. Before the examination, they entered into an investigation of their thoughts, accusing and rebuking the shameful things of body and soul. They made the [?] within them a judge between good and evil. They praised truth and condemned falsehood without showing favoritism. Without favoritism, the faithful judged what was right, and showed that human beings can judge truth justly. There is therefore no excuse for those who love excuses to make excuses, for there have indeed been people from among humankind who judged righteously. You have no defense to offer for your deeds, O human being, and you cannot say that the course of righteousness is difficult. It is very easy for you, if you wish, to become righteous, just as your righteous brothers became righteous in generation after generation. Direct your mind toward the conduct of your fellow human beings, and see in their deeds the truth of what I have said. Travel with the feet of the mind, accompanied by the books of the Spirit, and make your way well to the true assembly of those who labored in them.

Take the road from the very beginning of humankind, and place signs at the way stations of their lives. Enter the archives of the writings of the King of kings, and read the accounts filled with hundreds of human victories. Take up the scroll in which Abel’s story is recorded, and watch him offering a pure lamb and purity of soul. Cleanse your mind of the filth of foul deceit, and offer a sacrifice of purity of soul like his. Open your ears to hear the report of the day of his departure, and listen to the voice that demands vengeance for the wrong done to him. Let the voice of his blood be [?] for your soul’s endurance, and do not be distressed when you are wrongfully mistreated. When you have been comforted by the hope found in the death of the firstborn of the dead, turn the page and see his contemporary Enoch, who was taken away. Hear about a man clothed in perishable limbs who grew wings and flew through the air above the passions. See the new wonder that happened to a human being, which he accomplished for the human race through his being taken away. After his story, read in the passage in which Noah is depicted: through his gentleness, the fury of the sentence of judgment subsided. The transgression of the commandment decreed pains and sufferings for humanity, but through Noah the severity of the earth’s punishment abated. O soul filled with the rest of righteousness, in you people found rest from the turmoil of a life of toil! Let anyone who wishes to learn well learn from Noah that a human being can overcome the passions, even while subject to them. Noah, gentle in soul, was subject to suffering, as were his contemporaries; yet in that same human nature he won the battle against the passions and the waters. Shem too, in his [?], directed his purpose toward purity, and through his purity he became worthy to receive an exalted rank. Through his blessings he abolished the curses of the sentence of judgment, and people began to receive blessings in the Creator’s name. The blessings his father had given him flowed along with his descendants until they reached Abraham, the father of nations. The blessings flowing from Noah came to rest upon Abraham, and through him the uncircumcised nations shared in the blessing of the righteous man. Through the prompting of his will, the Maker of all fulfilled his purpose and gave humanity a share in the great wealth of his kindness. The Merciful One gave the wealth of his mercies through Abraham and allotted the riches of his great love to a member of his household. For a purpose he confined his will to his creation, so that humanity would be zealous to walk in the way of faith in him. The Lover of humanity instilled in one person zeal for another, to bind them together in love for his name, so that they would not forget him. His will journeyed from Abraham and settled upon Isaac, and he spoke with him words of love and [?]. Isaac rivaled his father’s devotion to his Lord and became heir to the promise of life that does not prove false. In faith the righteous man assented to the word of promise.

And when he saw that it was trustworthy, he gave it to Jacob to live by. Jacob was scorched by all the fires of harsh suffering, and he earnestly pressed toward the rank of Abraham’s household. He trusted the voice that called, “Abram, Abram,” and arranged circumstances so that he might become a companion of that voice. Full of endurance, he bore and endured every affliction, so that he would not be excluded from the promise given to his ancestors’ household. For twenty years the blameless man worked to earn wives, so that through those wives he might become worthy of the reward from God. The Creator appointed a good reward for human nature, and the faithful were zealous to pass it from one to another. They trusted the word of promise, although it was very distant, and contemplated it in its remoteness as though it were near. Through their labors they revealed the love in their minds: how greatly they loved the name of the Creator who honored them. Joseph’s toil is a clear witness to the manifest truth: he became a slave, but he was not enslaved to desires. Envy sold him from lordship into slavery, but he was not troubled over how or by whom he had been treated unjustly. 5. The Foreigner.
A member of the household of faith served among foreigners, and although he was a stranger, he received the authority of the rulers of the land. Let Joseph be a fine example for those who are oppressed: sufferings and people oppressed him greatly, but he neither succumbed nor sank into degradation. The son of Jacob overcame the assaults of women and of his enemies, and clearly showed that a person has control over his own freedom. His struggle cries out like a trumpet through every generation, so that humanity may hear of the human victory achieved in a human being. Moses too, Joseph’s companion, overcame the struggle of suffering. He was persecuted and endured the hardships of living as a stranger. The servant of truth hired himself out to worshipers of demons, but the purity of his soul was not stained by living in an unclean place. The faithful man served faithfully in the house of deceitful people, and he was not weakened by the deceitfulness of demon worship. After his toil, he saw the vision and heard a voice declaring new utterances among earthly beings. The voice that called creation into being in the beginning called the upright man, to proclaim through him the greatness of the power that had made his hands. Like a painter, he depicted the world through his voice, and [?] set it before speaking beings so that they might examine it. The upright man’s tongue became a pen in the Spirit’s hand, and he depicted created things in the form they had possessed from the beginning. He wrote a book of the Spirit upon his tongue for rational beings, and taught them about the world’s coming into being and how it was established. Like an orator, the eloquent man expounded his teaching in people’s hearing, and made them hear the name of the Creators who made humanity. The teacher of true worship took hold of the Spirit’s rod and began to discipline humanity’s childishness in true worship. The great, skilled man raised his hand against the Egyptians, and through their chastisement he cast fear upon all nations.

His mouth, the mouth of the Spirit, unleashed harsh scourges, to strengthen bodily beings more and more in spiritual things. His voice became like a physician among mortals, and he bandaged the afflicted people, who were being torn apart by the pains of error. Who would not marvel at the power of divine help, which through a human hand healed human beings of their pains? Through Moses he healed the sickness of wrongdoing among the members of his people, and showed that a human being can heal other human beings. The righteous were physicians in generation after generation, and their sayings were like medicines for the sores of wrongdoing. Moses handed over his craft to Joshua son of Nun, so that he might heal the Israelites’ pains with the medicine of his words. The disciple of the great [?] took hold of the Spirit’s iron blade and circumcised the people, removing the uncircumcision of body and soul. The fervent man clothed himself in fierce zeal against wrongdoing, and set them free, cutting it away from their limbs and their minds. These are the deeds of righteous people who lived among our race. Let us arise and follow the good example they displayed on earth. Let us look closely at the good course of their conduct, and let us walk as they walked in the land of our sojourn. They regarded their earthly dwelling as a temporary dwelling. Like travelers, they spent the night in the world and departed early. Job cries out that temporal blessings are not lasting, and concludes by saying, “Naked I came, and naked I shall go.” The righteous stood naked, without clothing, and showed everyone that there is no profit in visible things. They loved and cherished the Creator’s name more than anything, and set no visible thing alongside his hidden being. He contemplated unseen things as though they were plainly visible, and regarded visible things as though they were unseen. O earthly man, who left the earth while still earthly, and longed for heaven without having seen the dwelling above! O human being, clothed in perishable limbs, who made his body like diamond in the face of trials! Job was a human being, a man, O fellow humans! Though human, he overcame the assaults of turbulent sufferings. Trials battered his body and soul like waves, but he did not drown amid the storms of despair. He held firm hope like a rudder in the hand of his impulses, and anchored his soul in the peaceful harbor of his Lord’s word. The victorious rowed amid sufferings as though upon a sea, and fearlessly steered the ships of their minds. The sailors of faith looked toward the promise of peace. They believed and were certain that their rewards would not be withheld. Through faith they endured every suffering, hidden and visible, and left an example of their conduct for those who came after them. One after another they traveled along the paths of weary peoples, and arrived at the dwelling filled with blessings. Indeed, my lord Gideon too resembled Moses and Joshua.

Jephthah and the great Samson also labored in their service. Samuel lifted the wing of his swift course and surpassed them, attaining the rank of both prophecy and priesthood. From childhood he began the race of righteousness, and his endurance lasted through all the years of his life. He bore truthful witness about himself before God, declaring that his judgment had not been stained by favoritism. David, pure in mind, also saw the path of his service and prepared himself to walk in spiritual labors. He chose spiritually to [?] as a worker of the Spirit, and with spiritual beings he longed to fly [?] toward the heights. According to the will of the one who delighted in him, he [?]. Had he not briefly slumbered and slept, he would have been perfect in his love. Sin overcame the watchful-minded man like sleep. But although he sinned grievously, he turned back and became wise, so that he would not sin again. Through his sin he learned clever strategies against sin, and never again gave it an opening to enter his thoughts. Evil, however evil it was, became an occasion for good for him. He roused himself so that he would not sleep again and let it mock him. Trial became a skilled teacher for the discerning mind, and he guarded his treasure against being [?] by losses. Come, all ranks of the righteous, the [?], and sinners, and see how courageously the upright man confronted his transgression. Come, listen to his voice as he sighs over his downfall and bewails his wrongdoing in a thunderous voice. The righteous man composed mournful words in prophecy, and mournfully he wailed and wept over his transgression. “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” he said to his Lord. “You have put life-giving salvation far from me because of my foolishness.” O soul, who knew the ways of repentance, how resourceful you were in binding up the wounds of your guilt! O mighty warrior, who became guilty through sin, how courageously you struggled to remove the name of the guilty from yourself! O David, lover of righteous judgment, how carefully you examined the judgment of your own soul! No one knows how to judge his own transgressions in this way, as David [?] himself for the sins he committed. He sinned, and the garment of his soul was stained with innocent blood. Then he rose and washed it with streams of thundering tears. Once he sinned, although he had never intended to sin, and he multiplied beyond counting the sighs of repentance. He repented, pleaded, begged, and entreated over his transgression. He remained in his rank and uttered the words of prophecy. Through his mouth the Spirit of revelation proclaimed his exaltation—the same Spirit who had told him of the promise concerning his offspring. In his offspring he received the promise of life without end.

He believed and affirmed that it would happen, and it happened just as he had prophesied. The word spoken through the stirrings of his soul came to fulfillment, and from his offspring arose a man who gives life to humanity. His offspring is the one who became the source of life for us, and his offspring bears witness that he lives and has given life to those who believed in him. Is there anyone who perceives this salvation from the house of David and knows how to examine the conduct of the righteous who portrayed its likenesses? Is there anyone convinced by the revealing Spirit of prophecy, whose mind is alert to understand the explanation of its mystery? Is there anyone healed of the sickness of ignorance, whose heart is steadfast enough to receive the food of faith? Through faith the people of old looked to those who preceded them. They were zealous and imitated the example they received from one another. Hezekiah saw David’s example in his writings and undertook to portray it in his own limbs and mind. He carefully painted likenesses depicting his labors, and [?] perfection in his artistry. Josiah too showed great courage in following what was written, and of his own free will he longed for everyone to imitate him. The righteous were filled with a good concern born of love for the truth, and they longed to portray it in human minds. They left the good cargo of their conduct in the world, so that those in need of a livelihood might trade with it and gain life. They showed the ways of spiritual commerce, and people learned to trade spiritually. They built ships of love and fastened them in their minds, and launched them on the turbulent sea of bodily passions. They introduced a new craft among earthly beings, so that people on earth might cultivate heavenly things. The diligent practiced seamanship on the sea of the mind; without timbers they set sails amid the passions. They bound their impulses to their heads like a sail, so that they might become [?] of strength for the Spirit's course. They directed the voyage of their deeds toward the destination beyond, and gazed and fixed their attention on things to come as on a star. They secured their faith on high like an anchor, so that it would not be shaken by the harmful winds of the passions. Those subject to passions saw how difficult the passions were, and devised many useful means of overcoming them. They skillfully entered into battle with their passions, and calmly subdued the surge of their impulses. Like athletes they left the world, full of struggles, and rested in the harbor of the good hope of the promises made to them. With hope they completed the weary race of their struggles, and Hope himself strengthened them—the Hope in whom they trusted. As faithful people, they placed their deposits in his hands, so that he would preserve them for the day of repayment at the end. Come then, people, let us entrust our lives to the good Hope, so that they may not be snatched away by thieves, cunning men.

Let us store the treasures of our soul's labor in the land above, where there is no susceptibility to passions, the moth that eats them away. Like moths, the passions ruin the garments of our soul; let us shake them off by hearing of life free from passions. Bodily existence is soiled wool, and our lives are its [?]; let us wash it in the waters of the word of truth, the sweet spring. Our body is earthenware and glass, full of vulnerabilities; let us not bring evil habits near it, lest it break. The fragile vessels of our senses need only an occasion, and the passions habitually damage them as though they were earthenware. The stones of the passions constantly strike our limbs; if they were not fired by the Spirit, they would perish. What remains of our lowly clay is preserved by the Spirit's power, and through his help life wells up within its clay vessels. It is nothing without the power of the one who strengthens it; if he leaves it, it comes to an end and departs from life. It lives and moves through the vitality of immortal Life; if that Life lets it go, it returns to its earth and becomes dust. Our clay is dust, and our frame is kneaded with the waters of the passions; let us not add more water of the passions to it, lest we dissolve it. Let the strength of our conduct overcome mortality, so that it does not perish through the weakness of its mortal condition. Through faith let us firm up the softness of our weak clay, so that we do not grow slack and become water poured out. Through love let us wipe away the foul sweat of our susceptibility to passions, so that the smell of wickedness, which makes our beauty repulsive, does not grow stale within us. Through hope let us strengthen the building of our soul as with bonds, so that the fierce gusts of the passions do not topple it. Let us build truth upon the foundation laid by those who came before us, and order the course of the words of our mouth according to their labors. Let us imitate them in the practice of spiritual life, and let us paint in ourselves the likeness of their conduct.
For the First Sunday of Lent.

Tenth Discourse. For the First Sunday of Lent. Response: Blessed is he who, through his fasting, opened a path for us. That we may journey with the ants [?] to the place to which he has invited us, my brothers.

My mind advised me to plead my case against my thoughts, which loved distraction and hated the discipline of the word of life. My own inclination entered into judgment with me, reproaching me: “Why have you hated spiritual gain?” My thoughts stood up as advocates on behalf of truth, and condemned me severely for how greatly I had wronged what is fitting. My inner stirrings became accusers concerning the things in which I had sinned: “What is the reason you have shut your mouth like someone mute, instead of offering words in reply?” The discernment within me spoke to me as in a trial: “How have I wronged you, that you have blinded my senses to understanding?”

My wakeful mind called to me and roused me as from sleep: “Get up, you who are sunk in sleep, and shake off the weight of your laziness. “How long will you sleep and refrain from working? Hear the voice of the bird rebuking the sluggard. “Enough! You have spent the days of your life in emptiness. Stop being distracted and occupy yourself with the work of truth. “Come to work, even now at the end of the day, so that perhaps you may be found worthy to receive a wage through grace. “And if your senses lack the strength to perform deeds, at least offer words in payment, as a debtor is able. “See, I have warned you!” My mind called to me in secret and said to me: “Take care that you do not hear that pronouncement against the wicked servant. “See, I have shown you the path of life. Travel with the good; do not accompany the wicked who have traveled the broad road. “Rebuke yourself and reprove the faults of your companions. Teach them to hate wickedness, which kills human beings. “Train them in the practice of love and faith, and encourage them to acquire hope in the things to come. “Rouse them with the proclamation of the promise of the kingdom on high, and stir them with the sweetness of the promise of life.” With these words my own mind judged me as guilty, and I knew that it had advised me well to return to the path of life. Come, mortals, let us travel the path opened by the righteous, so that we too may reach the fulfillment of the life that has been promised. Come, let us imitate their conduct in the movements of our souls, and set the goal of their endurance before our minds. Let us learn from them what the Lord requires of his servants, and among which peoples the will of the one who orders everything finds rest. Let us question them as teachers of spiritual things, so that they may guide us from childhood to maturity. Let the labors through which they won their victories be like a mirror, and let us examine ourselves to see whether we are disfigured by the filth of wrongdoing.

In body and soul they gathered spiritual wealth; through their outward senses and hidden impulses they gained victory. They subdued their unruly senses through bodily suffering, and quieted their impulses through endurance amid provocations. They gave the body food in an orderly way so that it would not become unruly, and the mind ran in measured step with the body's members. The impulses laid the goads of fasting upon the body's members, and its senses and impulses ran together toward the promised life. Through fasting they harnessed the greedy body as though under a yoke, so that it would labor at the task of spiritual life. Perhaps they learned this secretly from a hidden power: that fasting is effective in cutting down desires. The Spirit's help taught them the power of wisdom, and they wisely guided body and soul. And if it is indeed the case that a hidden command made them wise, let us learn this from the son of Amram, who began with fasting. He was the first to blaze the path of desirable fasting, and at the end of his fast he received the riches of the Spirit of revelations. From him first ripened the life-giving fruit of fasting, and he sowed among humanity the delight of the food it provides. He labored at the spiritual work of fasting and received as his reward the provisions of the things to come. He was the first to descend into the arena of desires, and he wrestled with the impulses stirred by his craving for bread. For forty days he stood in the contest, night and day; and when he had won, the divine command gave him the crown of its hidden mysteries. O mortal who forgot his mortal nature and sought to resemble the immortals, who need no nourishment! O bodily man who scorned and mocked desires, and occupied himself with the conduct of spiritual life! O earthly man who despised earthly habits and, while still on earth, trained himself in the life of heavenly beings! O man of dust, whose clay was kneaded with the waters of passions, whose [?] seemed not too weak to overcome passions! First he tested his bodily members through fasting like an athlete, and knew that he could wrestle in body and soul.

The one watching his athletic struggle also saw that he was ready, and opened before him the arena of hidden things. He entered to examine the Spirit's treasuries with a spiritual mind, and touched hidden things that can be grasped only by the spirit. The divine command revealed to him the power of the Being who exists eternally, and his power was sufficient to form everything that came into being. Through the Spirit he revealed to him the order of the works of his hands. He saw with his mind and recounted aloud how everything was formed. In his hidden mind he read and pondered the hidden things, and he explained them aloud to his companions. The divine command wrote a new book upon his thoughts, and he in turn wrote it on tablets of stone to teach humanity. Three times he inscribed the letters of the book of life, so that whoever reads might meditate more and become still wiser. Once upon the heart, once upon tablets, and again upon tablets: twice by the divine command and once by the hand of mortals. Here is the spiritual teaching that the Spirit taught! Come, disciples whom the Spirit has instructed; read and understand. Here is the victory that the champion of truth displayed through fasting! Come, you who fast; fix his endurance in your minds. Here is the reward that the king gave the new soldier! Put on endurance of soul like armor, fight, and conquer. The Knower of all tested the good servant through fasting, and then gave him a reward surpassing his diligence. Why, indeed, did he keep the bodily man from food and make him live in the likeness of immortal life? In him he portrayed a mystery for embodied people clothed in suffering: they will live without food in the realm of the kingdom on high. For those with understanding, this is also the purpose of fasting: through endurance, people imitate the things to come. They are destined to live without food when they are raised from the dead, and he taught them to portray this in their present lives. Mortality will undergo renewal in that new order, and he depicted it symbolically before their eyes so that they might imitate it. Through fasting he revealed to them the renewal of their bodily members: they will strip off the garment of mortality, represented by food.

If fasting has revealed to us the mystery of our body's renewal, who would not hate earthly things and cherish it? If the formation of everything that came into being was revealed through it, who would not persevere in its laborious practice to become worthy of the mysteries? If it adorned the son of Amram with glory because he cherished it, who would not despise earthly things and submit to its testing? If a mortal acquired radiance through the Creator's mystery, who would not scorn everything else and long for it? Moses set up fasting like a mirror, but the eye of mortals was too weak to gaze into it. O bodily members that terrified other bodily members! O pupils from which the light of other eyes fled! O radiant man who drove away light by the strength of his own light! O lips, the doors of a mouth of flesh, whose opening made body and soul tremble and stand aghast! The face of the embodied man was fearsome and made bodies tremble, and the sound of the words of his mouth shook the senses and their movements. Come, see a wonder in a human body: he fasted and became so radiant that people were afraid to gaze at him. Through Moses' fasting let us gain hope for our renewal, for if we fast from evil deeds, our hope is secure. Let us keep our hearts, along with our lips, from evil, so that we may be glorious like the son of Amram, in body and soul. Let our minds fast, along with our bodily members, from everything hateful, and let us restrain our impulses from provocations just as we abstain from bread. A person is one human being, in body and soul, so that the whole person may be wholly devoted to the service of life. Let our impulses fast from pride, fury, and anger, just as our bodily members abstain from eating earthly things. Let us wash from our hearts the hateful envy that stains the soul, just as everyone washes the dirt from their bodily members. Let the mouth not fast from food while the heart goes unchecked. Let the outward senses not practice abstinence while the inner impulses run wild. Through fasting let us heal the pains [?] of our bodies and the defects of our souls, for it knows the remedy for things hidden and things visible. Let us show it the pains of our whole person, inward and outward, for its power is sufficient to heal the body and cleanse the soul.

It is a good physician who heals the wounded free of charge, compassionately binds up the fracture caused by wrongdoing, and grants life. It mixes kindness and mercy and gives them as medicines, and gives hope and love to drink in the cup of faith. Its cup is pleasant to anyone who drinks it in faith, for the sweetness of endless life is hidden within it. It is a sweet spring that flows continually for everyone, and those who drink it never grow tired of the sweetness of its drink. Come, minds dried up by the heat of wrongdoing! Quench the thirst of your thoughts with the cup of sweetness. Come, you who have become tasteless and strayed from your duty! Draw near to fasting and acquire the taste of discernment. Come, envious people troubled by foolish jealousy! Transform the anger of the inclination within you through the sweetness of fasting. Come, oppressors, whom the evil one [?] through his deceit! Give alms in return for the groans caused by your oppression. Come, sexually immoral people who have defiled the holiness of your bodily members! Receive cleansing by sharing in the practice of fasting. Come, thieves who have unjustly plundered treasures! Fast and humble yourselves, so that [?] you may be forgiven through repentance of soul. You arrogant people, bring down the stubborn pride of your minds, and clothe yourselves in fasting, a modest garment splendid in appearance. You gluttons, rebuke your swollen appetite with a measured voice, and shut the door of fasting in its face, lest [?] it grow ravenous. You who crave silver, scatter silver in the soil of fasting, so that it may yield the incorruptible wealth of righteousness. You who love praise, flee from praise, that deceitful trap, and expose its tricks through the soul-gladdening light of fasting. You who fast, abstain from praise as well as food, lest the love of praise enter and break your fast. Keep your lips from grumbling just as you keep them from bread,

lest a word from your mouth destroy the labors of your soul. Spread the veil of pure fasting over your eyes, so that you do not look wantonly with an ugly gaze. Withhold from your eyes the filthy drink that the body demands, and give them the modest cup of holiness to drink. The eye is undisciplined, and an undisciplined gaze lodges within it. Shut before it the door of a will devoted to modesty. Shine, women, with the brightness of fasting, like a mirror, and polish away the blemishes of your minds as you do those of your faces. Make the gaze of your thoughts modest, as you do with your clothing, so that the soul’s will may agree with the body’s appearance. Do not adorn yourself with outward clothes, daughter of Eve. Clothe your mind in modesty as you clothe your bodily form. Discipline the movement of your heart’s eyes as you do your steps, so that the immature in heart may not stumble because of your wantonness. Reduce the adornment on your limbs and adorn your understanding. Polish your mind as you do your face, with gentleness of soul. Take care not to become a cause of stumbling through the adornment of your face, lest you receive a double judgment because you sinned and caused others to sin. Hear from the law the accusation concerning the greatness of your wrongdoing: it condemns the wickedness of your inclination more than all other wrongs. Look, I have shown you from the law, from nature. Fear the scourges and ask for mercy while there is still time. Men and women, put on the strength of fasting like armor, for there is no distinction in the new mystery that he depicted for us with his hand. Fasting has revealed to us the single equality of that restored state: just as the body casts off corruption, so it also casts off its outward form. Let us fast purely, as befits the mystery of renewal, so that the truth of the mystery may not be falsified through our laxity. Let us fast equally in body and soul from everything hateful, so that the mind does not hinder the fast of the mouth. Let us not mix any wrongdoing into the sacrifice of our fasting, for if it is defiled, it is not accepted by the one who knows everything. The one who knows everything takes no pleasure in wrongful sacrifices, nor does bodily fasting please him without the soul.

The Jews fasted and offered sacrifices, but they were not accepted, because the worship of demons was mixed with their sacrifices. The Hebrews fasted with their outward senses, but not with their inward impulses; and the one who sees everything gave no reward for their tasteless fast. They humbled the body, but the heart did not come down from its pride. Outwardly they appeared pleasing, but he left them without a reward. The impudent falsely demanded a reward for fasting, and through the Spirit the prophet rebuked them for being utterly mistaken. “Why,” they said, “have we fasted, while you pay no attention to our bodily fasting? Why have we humbled ourselves, while you have taken no notice of our self-abasement?” What arrogance! A deceitful worker who is idle all the time demands wages from the owner of the vineyard as though he were diligent. What pride! A wild vine, devoid of fruit, brazenly disputes with the cultivator, saying, “Look, he has wronged me!” The revelation of the Creator’s mystery spoke through a human tongue and rebuked them because they had fasted and humbled themselves falsely. “You must not fast with a fast like this,” the prophet declared. “I do not want the humbling of the body alongside the pride of the soul.” “This is the fast that my will requires of those who fast: to untie the knots that wickedness has tied within their minds.” “If you want your fast to be free from blemishes, show your neighbor kindness with love and mercy, and see, I have accepted it.” See, the prophet of the Spirit has taught us the ways of those who fast. Let us not imitate the Jews, who fasted and gained nothing. See, the Hidden One has openly shown us how to please him. Let us cleanse our souls together with our bodily members in the sight of the Hidden One. See, through Isaiah he has revealed to us what his love desires. Let us always put ourselves right according to his will, doing what pleases him. Let us reject pride, which destroys the labors of body and soul, and love the goal of humility, which freely gives life. Let us uproot deceit, with its bitter thorns, from our minds, and plant within our thoughts the peace that brings peace to all. Deceit is a trap hidden in the soul as though in a pit,

and it hunts people like animals, to bring them to the destruction of death. Under the name of righteousness, deceit leads astray as though with bait, and entices the inclination to eat the bitterness of death. Let us therefore cut out the deceit hidden within our minds, and then approach the practice of fasting with purity of soul. Let deceit not hide itself in our fasting as in a garment, as the people of Jezreel did when they fasted and acted deceitfully. Let the Accuser not make use of our abstinence, as that foolish woman did against innocent Naboth. Here let us see the great crime committed by deceit: it concealed itself under the appearance of fasting and carried out murder. Tremble, you who fast, at the report of the murder committed during a fast, and fear that deceit may be concealed in your minds. See whether there is anyone who wants to act unjustly like Ahab, devising deceit to kill his neighbor and inherit his possessions. Even if the one who acts unjustly like Ahab does not kill, to the One who examines the heart he is a murderer because he has coveted. Reward and Gehenna alike are promised according to the soul’s will, and according to what a person desires, he is either justified or condemned. Omri’s son also desired and coveted what was not his, and the sword of his soul’s desire, which killed his neighbor, killed him. He killed Naboth through his will, not with a sword. Though he was king, he did not kill with his hands, but with his heart. In a covering of the sword [?], Jezebel concealed Ahab’s sword. Then she grasped it with the hand of deceit and killed the innocent man. She enclosed the murder in letters so that she would not be exposed, and stamped the king’s seal upon it so that she would not be found false. “Proclaim a fast,” you say, O foolish woman who hates fasting, “and seat Naboth at the head of those who fast and thirst for blood.” “Bring false witnesses against the truthful man, and let them spread the claim that he reviled the king and God as well.”

O will that constantly reviles the God of all, deceitfully pursuing dishonor under the guise of love! When did you ever love the Creator’s name, you foolish woman? And how did you honor the King’s ordinances according to the law [?]? O how crafty you are, cunning deceit that gives birth to murder! You have no equal except yourself or your schemes! O how deceitful you are, evil inclination [?] within the mind! Under the guise of love, you spew gall like a dragon. Come and see, you race of Eve, the wickedness of Eve, who proclaimed a fast and shed blood in the name of righteousness! Hear this and sigh bitterly, you wealthy women, over this crime that the king’s wife committed on earth. Women, give your husbands good advice, so that you will not be condemned like Jezebel, who counseled murder. Men, do not be persuaded by the advice of wicked women, so that you will not be exposed like Ahab, who coveted and was exposed. Let no one mix deceit with his fasting like the wicked, lest he be condemned by the sentence passed on those who shed blood. Let everyone show righteous zeal like Elijah, who rebuked deceit, exposed wrongdoing, and demanded an accounting for the bloodshed. Let those who love fasting imitate him in his fast—how strong he was! He abstained from bread and from provocations, showed zeal, and triumphed. He too resembled Moses in his forty-day fast. Night and day he fasted as he journeyed toward a peaceful meeting. At the completion of his fast, he was found worthy of a revelation like the son of Amram, and the voice taught him love and mercy, as it had taught Moses. Look at these people who fasted and brought their fasting to fulfillment through their deeds! Come, let us imitate their deeds, even if only a little. The word of the Hidden One has taught us through two men that whoever [?] receives a crown according to their labors. Let their conduct, then, be a goal for our souls, and let us imitate them with a sincere and pure will. Let us humble ourselves like the son of Amram, who hated pride, and rebuke wrongdoing like Elijah, who showed righteous zeal. They diligently carried the burden of the people. Come, let us also work, even now at the end of the day. And if our progress along the way falls short of those who came first, come, let us join those in the middle, whose example is easier for us.

If the labor of Moses and Elijah is difficult, here is Daniel, whose fast is easy and whose service is gentle. For three weeks Daniel fasted in body and soul, and he purified his heart, together with his bodily members, from hateful deeds. At the completion of his fast, he too received the reward of his labor: a spirit of revelation announcing the return of the peoples. O gift that is greater than those who receive it, yet is not diminished when divided into portions! O recipients who received their reward from a single treasury! They became rich, while its wealth remained just as it was. He made the members of his household worthy of the same reward, lest they become estranged if one were honored above another. They received the same gift equally from one treasury, because they had directed their wills toward one goal. We ought to imitate them in the practice of fasting and always run in the footsteps of their way of life. Let us journey with them with a spiritual resolve, so that they may bring us to the provision prepared for the renewal of all things. Let our body travel together with our mind along the road of fasting, with those who traveled lightly and reached the land of life. Let no one journey with the many on the broad road, lest he hear, along with the many, “Go to destruction.” Christ our head instructed us through his words to take the narrow road. Come, let us walk on it, so that we may hear him say, “Come and enjoy yourselves.” He himself first traveled on it through fasting, with endurance, and arrived at the completion of perfection. He too conformed to the condition of servants, fasted, and was tempted; and after his fast, hosts of spiritual beings attended him. For forty days, night and day, he stood in the contest, while the adversary watched his endurance.

He limited his fast to forty days, like those before him, so that no one would suppose that his nature was spiritual. In his fasting he conformed to the condition of his brothers and companions, so that he would not appear foreign to those who saw him, as though he were not human. He was human, from a humanity clothed in suffering, and it was fitting for him to resemble human beings in everything. It was not I who presumptuously called him human. Paul showed that his nature and ours are one. “The one who sanctified humanity and the humanity that was sanctified are one,” he says, “and therefore he was not ashamed to call them his brothers.” Elsewhere he again designated him as a human being, calling him one mediator and one human being. And if the heretics take offense at Paul's words, let us hear from him that he himself also called himself human. “Who,” he says, “do they say I am [?] a human being?” And, “Why do you seek to kill a man who proclaims the truth?” Look: both he and his brothers called his nature human. Why do the heretics blot out the name of humanity? They utterly hate the nature of our body, like Mani, and for this reason they quarrel with us like strangers. They too lie in that sickness of denying the resurrection, and whoever proclaims the resurrection of the body is repugnant to them. Even now I have seen the feebleness of their thinking, and my discourse has strayed from its journey along the road of fasting. From the beginning my discourse traveled along the road of fasting, because love for those who triumphed through their fasts drew me on. My thoughts ran swiftly over their stories,

so that I might set them like a mirror before those who fast. The fasting of the king's servants prompted my mind to recount the story of the king and his servants, who fasted and triumphed. I wished to show the power of fasting to those who fast, and I brought forward the King and his servants as witnesses to confirm my words. It is also right for anyone who judges according to the law to substantiate his statements with documents from the archives. Let us recount the King's judgments concerning every deed, and so the words of our mouth will be confirmed for our listeners. For discerning people, this is the purpose of daily fasting: just as we should abstain from bread, we should also abstain from wrongdoing. It is also a symbol of that incorruptible state in which bodies live without food, like spiritual beings. Among its purposes is also restraint from evil, so that when the body is subdued by fasting, it will discipline its course. The reason for the forty-day fast is that it is a means the spiritual physicians devised for humanity's health. For they saw that human nature was too weak for the daily course, so they accommodated it and gave it a short period as a kind of medicine. They confined fasting to a distinct period for humanity's immaturity, and bound people to perseverance through their longing for the feast. They established fasting as a foundation for the building of love, so that everyone might build the temple of their soul through their way of life. They completed the feast like a roof atop the building, so that everyone might rejoice in the temple of the spirit, which symbolizes the resurrection. The purpose of the feast is the resurrection of the body and the salvation of the soul, and they rightly taught that body and soul should fast together. In it is also depicted the victory of the King on high, who conquered and gave victory, arose and was raised to life, and raised everyone to life. At the completion of the forty-day fast, he marked his victory and taught his servants to remember him on the day of his victory. Through his fasting he revealed his victory to them so that they might imitate him, and through his victory he taught them to overcome the passions.

He limited the course of perfection to forty days, so that it would be easy for anyone traveling toward the appointed gathering beyond. He established the feast of his victory as a harbor of life, reached by those who travel along the path of righteousness. On the day of his resurrection he encouraged those who live in the body not to lose heart when their limbs grow weak. He showed them the mystery of the resurrection at the completion of the fast, so that when they battle temptations, they might rise with him. "Put your members to death, therefore," Paul proclaimed, meaning that they should put to death the deeds performed through their members. Let us therefore bury the passions of our body in the grave of fasting, so that we may be worthy of life at the completion of the fast, on the day of resurrection. Let our impulses and senses fast together with our lips, and let us lay the deeds of mortality as though in a grave. Let the eyes fast by not gazing lustfully, and the hearing also, lest it admit slander. Let the tongue fast, the advocate of the impulses and the bodily members, and let it offer praise as a pledge for its fellow members. Let the hands fast from acts of theft, and the feet along with them from running to take what belongs to another. Let the mind, the intellect, and the heart fast from thoughts, lest passions enter the soul as food enters the stomach. Let us fast from bread and from all passions, hidden and visible, so that the Hidden One may give a reward to our body and our mind. This is the fast that is chosen and beloved [?] the Creator: when body and soul turn away from everything hateful. This is what is right for someone who fasts with discernment: to cast away every shameful deed. This is the fast of which he said that it can drive out demons, and [?] the crown of victory like an athlete. Through this the heralds of the word of life also triumphed, and the power of the Spirit exalted them in the sight of those who watched. Come, you mortals whose strength is feeble; become strong through it, for its power can give strength amid weakness. Come, take up its armor and arm yourselves with it as befits it, so that through it you may conquer the enemy and his forces. With its armor let us fight the mighty one who fights against us, and with its help let us tear down the height of his rebellion.

Let everyone speak with the voice of those who fast and say to the rebel: “Go away, evil one! Your strength is feeble against fasting.” Let us shoot the arrows of fasting into the ranks of the devil, and look—his forces scatter away from our camp! Let everyone, in soul and body, offer spiritual praise to the one who, through his victory, opened for us a path to the heights. Response: Blessed is the one who through his fasting freed us from slavery to corruption.
On Our Lord’s Battles.

Discourse 12. On Our Lord’s Battles. Again by the same author, being his twelfth discourse: On Our Lord’s Battles. It is recited on the Sunday at the beginning of the fast. Response. Blessed is the one who through his fasting opened for us a path to travel toward life without end. My brothers.

Satan heard new voices among mortals: humans and heavenly beings were proclaiming peace for humanity. The rebel heard from Gabriel of peace for humanity, and anguish seized him: “What is this new thing that has happened?” The chief of the angels greeted a daughter of mortals, and the envious one trembled at the good news brought to humanity. “Peace to you, Mary!” the spiritual being cried in Mary’s ears. The evil one wailed, and the demons gathered at the sound of his wailing. “Our Lord is with you!” the angel cried to the daughter of mortals, and the devil’s groans multiplied at the peace granted to humanity. The messenger called the son of a human daughter “Son of the Most High.” The enemy was put to shame, and his forces sat in mourning. The man of spirit proclaimed these things among those on earth. The demons shook, and Satan, the head of their ranks, trembled. One spiritual being announced his conception to one woman, and on the day of his birth many cried out good news to humanity. “Good hope!” the spiritual beings cried out to those in bodies, and the rebel died at the sound of the good news of life for humanity. The sound of good news was being uttered by every mouth. People rejoiced, and spiritual beings brought sorrow to the demons. Simeon proclaimed openly that this was the one who was to come, who tests people as in a furnace through the dawning of his light. Anna the prophetess was recounting the ways of his salvation, and the Hebrew women were responding after her words. The voice of the son of barren parents thundered far louder than thunder, as he cried out that the time was fulfilled and the time had arrived. “The age of the Law has ended,” he prophesied, “and the time for a spiritual way of life has drawn near.” He called the pure one “the pure lamb,” [?], who cleanses blemishes, who wipes away wrongdoing through his sacrifice and gives life. The messenger called the one who sent him “Lord of mysteries,” and showed that he is both Lord and the judge who tests everyone. Human beings and heavenly beings proclaimed these declarations, and the Father impressed the seal of his voice upon them and confirmed them. The rebel, the hater of humanity, heard these declarations and was embittered by declarations that were strange to him. New declarations were being uttered by those who could speak, concerning a man who resembled human beings but was exalted above them. The rebel, too, regarded him as a human being, and was embittered by the declarations that were strange to him. The rebel, the hater of humanity, stood between two alternatives and did not know what to call him: a human being or God. If he were to call him a human being, the declarations about him exalted him beyond that; if he were to call him God, his bodily existence testified that he was human. The constitution of his body showed him that he was entirely human, while the power of his words proclaimed to him that he was divine. His conception and birth spoke of his humanity, while those who proclaimed him spoke of the divine Being who dwelt in him. Satan, too, pondered the power of the divine Being: how could he be human, and how could his power surpass that of a human being? The senseless one was astonished at the greatness of his power,

and was scorched by the two things present in one man. A womb conceived him, bodily organs gave birth to him, and knees carried him. This belongs to a human being, who possesses bodily senses capable of sensation. He was conceived through a voice, without bodily intercourse, and this is beyond a fleshly human being. He nursed on milk, was brought up, and grew tired from labor. These natural experiences testify that he possessed human nature. He was baptized like other people, by a human being, as someone in need. It is clear from this that he was in need with respect to his humanity. The Holy Spirit descended, and the Father proclaimed, “This is my beloved.” Here it was divine power that strengthened the man. One man, in body and soul, came up from the water, and the Spirit descended and remained with him without departing. The second Adam was guided by the power of the Spirit, and the adversary marveled at his hidden power. Severe labor pains struck the devil, and he considered whether to approach him or not. Like a woman in labor, he was distraught with bitter birth pangs, and he pondered what means he could use to bring his labor to an end. The rebel cherished hateful desires in his mind and longed to approach him as he would a mere human being. “Who, then, will let me approach him?” he pondered, “so that through sufferings I may test his feelings and see whether he is capable of suffering.” He looked upon the son of Adam as he had upon Adam, and hoped to lead this Adam astray just as he had Adam. He intended to fight him as he had Adam, but was afraid of the hidden one who was triumphing in him. The vessel of wrath counted him as one of the righteous and was embittered enough to dispute openly with him. For thirty years he was seared by his words, until he heard that voice: “This is my beloved.” This voice sent a tremor through his forces, and they began to cry out in the anguish of their minds. Those sunk in sleep started up at the Father's voice and gathered together to form a conspiracy against the mystery of our life. The rebel and his forces formed a wicked conspiracy to engage in combat with the mighty warrior who was stronger than he. The deceiver armed himself with the weapons of his deceit and began to stir up trouble, as he had that time in Paradise. He compared this occasion to that earlier occasion, not knowing that one occasion was unlike the other. He called the second Adam a son of Adam and, on that same assumption, tested him through bodily passions. He reminded the one who had a body of bodily passions and offered him various enticements as though to a friend. The lover of desolation longed to go out with him into the wilderness, where earthly beings could find no food to sustain them for a time. Like an athlete, he challenged him to combat, to see whether he had the kinds of impulses that resembled Adam's. He armed himself with all the passions of Adam, for he was concerned that he might escape his temptations. The voices concerning him were stirring him to combat.

And he devised a way to approach him skillfully. The craftsman skillfully inspected his weapons, gathered his stratagems, and then brought his various forms of combat against him. He arranged cunning stratagems like weapons within his mind, inspected his forces, and concealed the weapon of his deceit. He sought an occasion to display his various tricks and, to suit the occasion, devised stratagems that concealed other stratagems. Time brought his deceitful stratagems to readiness, and he was both eager and afraid to reveal his deceit. He fought within himself before engaging in open battle, and tested himself, considering, “Perhaps he will bring us low.” The warrior encountered a battle beyond his strength, and he wondered whether he would become a laughingstock to people. The hater of humanity pondered these things within himself, while the lover of humanity prepared the man to fight him. The Spirit armed the man who was one of us with the weapons of the Spirit, and sent him to engage in a contest with the mighty ones in the wilderness. He prepared him for combat to match the enemy’s preparations, and the champion went out where the leader of the combatants wanted. The champion of righteousness went out like a champion, equipped from head to foot with the weapons of the Spirit. The Power that chose him sent the heavenly powers with him, to be witnesses and spectators of his contest. The Lord of the world made the world a theater, with the heavenly powers as experts in the contenders’ combat. It was a struggle—a struggle on behalf of the world—and he fittingly gathered the heavenly beings to praise him. They had been grieving ever since the time when Adam was defeated, and they were waiting for Adam to conquer through Adam. Those who love our race were preparing for the day of victory, and longing for our race to conquer through a member of our race. For forty days one combatant stood against the other: the ruler of the air and a man who was one of us—a wondrous sight! A wondrous sight appeared before the spectators’ eyes, as spirit and flesh struggled without using hands. The embodied one fought without using hands; spiritually he grappled with the ruler of the air. He chose strenuous fasting as the weapon with which to fight, lest the devil think that his strength came from food. Without food he entered the battle against the mighty one, so that the demons would see that, although he was human, he was above humanity. Through endurance he taught those brutish beings that another power was with him, stronger than all. The leader of their ranks was considering the greatness of his strength; therefore he prepared every conceivable kind of combat. The rebel marshaled every kind of trap for human beings, lest he escape his tricks and he himself become a laughingstock. Great was the contest that suddenly confronted the warrior, unlike the contest he had arranged against all generations. Great fear terrified the bold-hearted one, and he was afraid to enter into combat with the embodied one. The embodied one also observed his fear and his impudence, and gave him an incentive to approach him through the outward sign of hunger.

For forty days the fasting one abstained from nourishment, and at the end his nature demanded its natural needs. He was mindful of Adam’s nature within his own nature; therefore he limited his fast to the fasting of his fellow humans. Satan, too, took courage from this limitation, because he had not exceeded the prescribed number of days that others had fasted. The rebel looked at the hunger of the embodied one's body. He approached him and saw that it was a body that hunger had overcome. He saw that his bodily senses had grown weak, as in every body, and thought to himself, “Now is the time to stir up the body.” He remembered that time in Paradise when he had seen Adam longing to eat the fruit. He looked at the son of Adam as though he were Adam, and in the same way presented him with a desire for fruit. He stirred up bodily desire in the embodied one's body, and troubled him as he would any bodily being, so that he would ask for food. Through food he had persuaded Adam's household to go astray with him, and he thought he could persuade the Son too, just as he had persuaded them. He first took up the enticement of bread as a battle, and began showing his adversary ways of persistence. “Speak a word so that there will be bread,” the crafty one said, “and it will become known that you truly are the Son of God. Command the insensible elements like a creator, and do something befitting the name by which he called you. Change the stones from the hardness established in them, and give them the nature of bread that can be eaten. Through deeds reveal the proof of the proclamations about you, and the greatness of your rank will become apparent to those who look on. Before many people the Father proclaimed, ‘This is my beloved.’ If you are the beloved, perform a wondrous deed and prove that you are loved. Thousands heard that voice declaring that you are the Son of God. Adorn your name with a deed that comes from you. Like your Father, do a deed resembling the work of his hands, and let those who can speak and those who cannot submit before the [?] of your authority. Speak a word full of wonder before those who look on, and let those who see the wonder of your powerful words praise you. You are in the wilderness, and there is no food at hand for the present. Command the elements to nourish you as their Lord. You are Lord, according to that voice that came to you. Accomplish your will completely through a word from your mouth. Attend to your need, just as your righteous companions attended to theirs, and do something to supply your body's need. Your companions too [?] a fast like this one of yours, and afterward obtained what they needed to satisfy their needs. Yours is a great one—you chose it because your name is far above theirs. Perform a miracle befitting someone greater than his companions. It is very fitting for you to make something by transforming something else, so that your deed may be a trusty witness to the word of your mouth.” The ruler of the air said these things to the head of our race, thinking that he would surely draw him down into his turmoil. This was the battle that the master of errors first undertook:

He went badly astray, and his claws did not [?] in the anointed body. This was the first contest staged by the veteran of contests, and the embodied athlete made him a laughingstock. In this struggle, the one proud of his nature tested his strength, and the nature clothed in mortality humbled his strength. The spirit brought the embodied one into a spiritual contest; the spiritual one was defeated, and the body, weighed down with senses, prevailed. He gathered the desires together into bodily desire and presented them like gifts to the embodied one. The contemptible one offered contemptible gifts [?] to the one skilled in understanding, who contemptuously returned them with insults to the one they suited. The second Adam flung the evil one's gift in his face, just as the Creator had also done with Cain's sacrifice. He trampled the deceiver's counsel like dung, and mocked and laughed at his foolish schemes. Wisely he gave an answer to the one lacking understanding, and from the Law he silenced the blasphemer's mouth. According to the Law, he pronounced the sentence condemning the evil one, so that he would know that he was judging him according to the Law. With one word he untied the knot of ten thousand words, through what is written: “A human being does not live by bread.” “A human being does not live by bread,” he answered the deceitful one, and the cunning devices of every kind vanished and came to an end. The Creator can keep a human being alive without [?] bread, and the utterance of the Creator's name suffices in place of everything. The shameless were ashamed of the confidence in which he had boasted, and he withdrew and fled to devise other schemes. He kept changing one scheme for another against the contestant, perhaps thinking that hope still remained for his deceit. The guilty one entertained an empty hope against the innocent one, not knowing that his hope of victory was cut off. The shameless one was fighting for victory, thinking that he had devices that could catch human beings. The deceiver set deceitful traps for the one whose soul was blameless, and concealed them beneath splendid beauty that captivated the eyes. In an eye-catching display he arranged every kind of beautiful thing: gold and silver, beryl and pearls. He arranged everything in an imaginary display, although nothing was there, and made these things appear, although they did not really exist. He regarded him as a human being, a man like one of us; for this reason he arranged images of what human beings love. The love of money is greatly cherished by mortals, and for this reason he reserved its pleasure for the second contest. In the first contest he fought against him with the desire for fruit, and in the second with the love of money, the sea of his swords [?]. He saw that human thought was drowned in this sea, and he spread its waves over the shores of dry land before our Savior. He covered the earth with a garment of silver as though with water, not knowing that the one skilled in understanding was mocking him. He was arranging his phantoms in an outward display, while the one who sees what is hidden openly despised his contemptible ways.

He arranged what looked like beautiful objects, although they did not exist, and brought them near the contestant to test his strength. He opened a theater whose curtains were full of evil. The fool entered and stood among golden things, although there was no gold. Arrogant in his thinking, he shouted shamelessly to the humble one: “Come, man, see something difficult to display! “Come and see men,” the Evil One said to the man who is one of us, “the whole world that I hold under his authority. “The world is mine [?], along with the glorious things within it.
