I give it to whomever I wish, if he worships me. “Only worship me as the lord who rules over everything, and take the world for yourself in exchange for an acknowledgment spoken by your mouth. “Acknowledge my lordship and lovingly call me ‘Lord,’ and I will give you a good reward: the world and its wealth. “I give you the world and its wealth for a single word; in return, offer me loving worship, with affection. “Take the world for yourself, man who belongs to the world, and pledge to me the word of your mouth that you worship me. “Give me your mouth for a little while as a pledge, and take for yourself something with unlimited [?] revenues. See— “how great is the exalted rank of the whole world, and how small is the price: the worship you pay me with a word! “See how abundant my love toward people is, O human being! I demand no costly things from those who love me. “It is love alone that I ask of anyone who listens to me. Listen to me and see how generously I treat anyone who listens to me.” The Evil One spoke these words to the one who shares our nature, and the one who shares our nature grew zealous against the deceiver’s schemes. The champion of good things clothed himself in good zeal, for the good one heard a slave demanding his master’s worship. The mighty one shot an arrow of rebuke at him. It pierced his heart, and the gall that had gathered within him came out. Evil gall had gathered within that evil-minded one, and our Lord exposed it with the plain declaration spoken by his mouth. He answered the adversary from the Scriptures and taught him his place, so that he would know that he was nothing. “Have you heard what is written, or have you not heard, you rebel: that the Lord is one, and that the worship of all belongs to him? “There is one Lord who rules over everything as God, and no one else has a share in his divinity. “The name ‘God’ does not belong to one who is not God, nor should a created being advance to the rank of Creator. “You too are a created being, you insolent one burning with pride. Know your nature, and do not exalt yourself above your Maker. “Know that you are a created being, a servant made by his Maker, and do not insolently seize your master’s rank [?] for yourself. “Be quiet, rebel, and stop your insolent speeches. Do not proclaim to me the hateful falsehood of your denial of your Lord. I know you and your deceitful speeches,

“and it does not escape me that you go astray and lead people astray. “Go away, deceiver! Go astray in your deeds as you usually do. Take the fantasy of your hoarded silver and strike yourself in the face with it.” You have given nothing, and you will gain none of what you intended. You brought forward [?], and your struggle was in vain. Go, fight your battle with yourself, and take as your reward the shame of your defeat. Go, defeated one, see how disgraced you are! Stop contending with the truthful, lest they expose you. Look, your defeat has been revealed in two contests. Go, prepare another contest for yourself, and be defeated a third time! Three witnesses lend their support in every matter, and for the third time I will condemn you in three bouts. The fighter withdrew from the arena after two bouts and changed the place and the methods of his combat. He fled from the wilderness, where he had thought he would win, and began to arrange a battle amid peace, in full view of spectators. He wanted to display his fighting skill amid peace, saying, “When I win, people will be witnesses to my victory.” Full of defeats, he was fighting for victory, unaware that he was multiplying his own utter defeat. The unclean one went up to the holy temple to fight, where everyone could easily see his defeat. The lowest of the low brought the Lord up to a great height, and stood there acting madly, with his accustomed madness. He said, “Throw yourself from this height into the depth below. If you remain unharmed, you are truly the Son. God called you the Son of God before many witnesses. Fly through the air, as befits the Son of God. Righteous are you, a man whose witnesses are the voices that came to you. Come down from the height, and look, the heavenly hosts will receive you. It is written of the righteous that they stumble on the ground without injury, protected by spiritual angels. You are one of the righteous, and your rank is even higher than theirs. Test your righteousness by the care bestowed upon your righteousness. Test your strength through the care of the heavenly beings, who will receive you in their hands, as it is written. They will not abandon you amid difficulties, however difficult they may be, because God has commanded them to guard you. Test through deeds the help of those who guard you, and then the company of the righteous will be encouraged to walk in righteousness. Blaze a trail through trials toward hardships, and show everyone the crown of reward that comes from your righteousness.” Oh, the crafty one—how craftily he hid his traps! Oh, the nimble one—how he leaped over the hidden traps! Oh, the cunning one—how cunningly he wove his schemes! Oh, the wise one—how wisely he cut through them! Oh, the fighter—how he fought to carry out his intention! Oh, the prudent one—how prudently he acted, to win in an orderly way! Oh, the spiritual being—how his schemes flew about in a spiritual way! Oh, the embodied one—how he sharpened his senses and brought them under control!

Oh, the extraordinary struggle that took place on earth, which harnessed the world to engage in battle with a spiritual being! A bodily being fought with a spiritual being, and human beings began to fight spiritually. By the Spirit's power, the bodily being overcame the mighty one, and the peaceful hosts marveled at the human being's victory. Company after company of spiritual beings stood watching this battle, marveling at how flesh could overcome a spirit. Among their companies they spoke of a great wonder: “What is this new thing that has happened among our companies?” They saw a mortal fighting with the mighty one, and they marveled and were astonished that mortality had defeated the tyrant. They watched the human being's victory and the evil one's defeat, and praised the Creator's power, which had given the human being victory. “Glory to the power that gave the human being victory,” cried the spiritual beings, “and reconciled the world with his majesty through a human being.” One human being fought with Satan. Satan was defeated, and the human being won and gave humanity victory. The human being won the contest he fought against the mighty one, and the mighty one was defeated in his battle with the human being. The heavenly hosts watched this battle and marveled at the extraordinary victory. They saw an unprecedented victory and defeat, and praised and magnified the one who had raised up the human race. The human race had incurred a debt and been held as a pledge by Satan. A human being arose and paid the debts of his fellow human beings. Through desire for fruit, Adam had been defeated by the evil one's counsel; through endurance, a son of Adam overcame the one who had overcome Adam. He avenged Adam's humiliation on Adam's enemy, humbled him, and stripped him of his tyrannical authority. Before the spiritual beings, he openly engaged him in combat, lifted him up and threw him down, and made him a laughingstock with a disgraced name. He entered the arena full of passions with him, and with the feet of his mind he kicked away the sharp goads. The rebel arrayed all the passions before the bodily being and divided them into three rounds of combat. The fool fought three rounds with the wise one. In all three, the son of Adam won and Satan was defeated. In the desire for bread he included every desire that human beings have, and the human being despised human desires. In the love of money he arrayed every sort and kind of money, and the champion of truth held them in check as though they were nothing. In the love of glory he hid all (all) the snares that catch human beings, but he leaped over them and passed beyond them unharmed. The champion emerged from the contest unharmed and was acclaimed by those who had watched his athletic struggle. The bodily champion triumphed gloriously, while the spiritual being, the ruler of the air, suffered utter defeat. The ruler of the air fought with a human being. The human being won, and the mighty one who had defeated humanity was defeated. Now that he has completed the various forms of combat and defeat, let us inquire how the battle came about and what caused it. Its cause is this: the contest that took place in the land of Eden.

For humanity had been defeated, and the Evil One had triumphed until now. The race of Adam was bound by the debt of its sins, and tyrannical demons were exulting over its debts. The one who had called humanity his own image saw its guilt, and he was not pleased to see demons trampling his image. That very image which had been defeated in Eden he now fashioned anew, in the same form as the first. Without sexual union he fashioned Adam from dust, and without the joining of intercourse he fashioned the last Adam. From the very race that had become indebted to sin, he abolished sin through the man whom he fashioned by the Spirit without sexual union. By the power of the Spirit he fashioned a man from a human woman, filled him with the Spirit, and gave him the name Son of God. God called that man the Son of God, and Satan trembled at the name of a man who was exalted above humanity. This title prompted him to come to battle, and he burned with impatience for an opportunity to carry out his intention. He was being roasted in the fire of his desire as though in a furnace, and he did not know how to quiet the flame. “Who would grant me permission to approach him?” he thought, while he shrank in fear from the divine command. “Who would let me bring various temptations against him? I would teach him that he too is a human being, full of desires. “If only someone [?] would bring him out into the wilderness, far from human society! I would go out with him and test his strength through human passions. “He is entirely human, drawn from a humanity full of passions. How can he trample passions underfoot when he himself is subject to them? “If only someone would cause the Creator’s power to withhold its help from him and give me an opportunity to approach him as I approached Adam!” The hater of humanity was pondering these things within himself, but the lover of humanity anticipated the desire behind his schemes. He saw that he was ready to engage in combat with the son of Adam, so he armed the son of Adam with the Spirit and sent him out against him. It is written that by the Spirit he went out from settled country into the wilderness beyond. It is therefore clear that he was being led by the power of the Spirit. The Creator’s power indicated to him where he should go, and when the enemy saw it, he went along with him to see the outcome. The Spirit revealed to him the mind of the spirit that was waging war and taught him strategies for countering the Devil’s strategies. He showed him that the enemy who had defeated Adam was fighting against him, and he anointed him with the Spirit so that the hand of that spirit would not strike him. He taught him whom he was to engage in spiritual combat and how to descend into the arena full of passions. By the power of the Spirit, the Spirit’s athlete accomplished everything he did, while the will of his soul adhered to the Spirit he had received. He fought the battle together with the Spirit, and the Spirit together with him, and he repaid the debt of that fall in Paradise. He repaid the Evil One for the fall that Adam had suffered, so that he would know that Adam possesses the power to conquer. The son of Adam triumphed and acquitted Adam of his sins.

Satan was defeated, and the army of demons was defeated with him. The son of Adam turned fiercely upon his attacker, and the enemy could not answer him word for word. Three times the crafty one questioned the wise one, and with a single word he exposed his absurdities. He engaged the athlete in three rounds, and in all three he was hurled to the ground as though dead. The son of Adam struck the son of Gehenna with three kicks. He howled and cried out, and the legions of his forces trembled. The bow of righteousness released three arrows, and in three stages he completed the contest with his attacker. He was to proclaim three names among the inhabitants of earth, and he proclaimed them symbolically in the contest he undertook. Through the mystery of the power hidden within him, he won the battle. He depicted it symbolically beforehand, to reveal it after his death. This was the reason for the contest he undertook with Satan: to save his race and reveal the mystery of the power of the divine Being. These things that came to pass had been mysteriously hidden within him: humanity’s salvation and the power of the incomprehensible divine Being. In the contest he undertook, he revealed both through the power of the one who chose him, and confirmed them through the victory he won over the evil one. Through the power of the one who chose him, he defeated the tyrant who had condemned humanity. The Good One allotted him that victory because of his endurance. Through endurance he overcame the habitual impulses of human passions, accompanied by the will of the one who chose him out of everyone. The hidden will dwelt in the [?] of his body’s constitution, and through him did what was fitting for the Maker of all. It was fitting for the Maker of all to do what was fitting, and for the man to perfect his love for the one who sent him. Human beings had been captive to the enemy of [?] from the beginning. A man went out and brought back the captives of his ancestral household. The lover of our race went out into the wilderness to visit his race, to the place where the captor who had taken his race captive sought him. The man rescued captive humanity from the rebel, plundered his army, and made him an object of ridicule and disgrace. He, a man, defeated the tyrant who had defeated humanity. By his victory he exalted human beings and humbled demons. He humbled the demons in the contest he undertook with the chief of demons, and took from them the armor they had taken from his ancestors. He left the enemies of his race stripped bare, so that they could not arm themselves to contend with humanity. The man fought a great contest against their ranks, and the spiritual hosts marveled at the might of his victory. The spectators of the athletic contest saw the might of his victory and gathered around him as around a king, to acclaim him. They wove a crown of victory and presented it to the human athlete. They praised and thanked the power that had strengthened him in the contest against the passions. The athlete of righteousness overcame all the passions, for the evil one too had summed them all up in three contests.

For the third [?]: Our fellow human prevailed against the mighty one, and [?] the enemy who used to exalt himself over the generations. He is the one who humbled that mighty one who had humbled our race, accompanied by the power that strengthened his humility. The Creator’s power enabled him to defeat the adversary, while the Creator remained hidden in the glory of his craftsmanship. In his constancy, the ever-present Hidden One remained constantly hidden, and his power, which came from him, was helping the man from among us. A man from among us was fighting Satan, not the Creator, as the dull-hearted imagine. For it was not the Creator who was fighting amid bodily sufferings, and they testify that they fought against a human being. The demons testify whom they fought in the wilderness: a human being whom hunger overcame after his fast. He became hungry after fasting for forty days, and the enemy knew that his hunger testified to his humanity. He saw that his bodily frame had been weakened by deprivation, and approached him to present him with bodily desire. He saw that his body had been weakened by hunger, which weakens the body, and supposed that perhaps he could lead him astray through a desire for bread. He was stirring a desire for bread in the body of the second Adam, in the same way that he had led Adam astray through bodily desire. His tricks failed, his schemes vanished, and his deceits came to an end. No place remained for him that was free from defeat. The rebel and his forces were utterly defeated, and the son of Adam won a complete victory and gave victory to his race. From now on, Adam’s race owes praise to the one who raised up Adam’s race through a member of that race.
On Our Lord’s Battles

Discourse 17. On Our Lord’s Battles. Again, another by the same author: the seventeenth discourse, on our Lord’s battles. It is recited during the fast. Again, another by the same author: the seventeenth discourse, on our Lord’s battles. It is recited during the fast.

Adam, the speaking image whom the Voice fashioned from dust—the honor given to his lowly clay stirred jealousy among the spiritual beings. The words that had been spoken concerning the formation of the mortal kindled Satan, the ruler of the air, with the fire of envy. The care devoted to his formation disturbed the enemy with envy. The title “image,” with which the image was honored, provoked him to wage war. “Who,” he said, “is this lowly being whose nature is dust, that he takes counsel about his formation and then brings him into existence? And that the one who is great and immeasurable, exalted above everything that has been made, calls the vessel fashioned from clay his own image?” His bitterness agitated the envious one, and he prepared himself for battle. He put on the armor of cunning to fight against the innocent one. From the beginning, the Creator was watching the preparation of his deceit. He gave him room to fight against his image, to put himself to the test. His image [?] was defeated by the crafty one’s tricks. And [?] him under the yoke of sin, and death enslaved his freedom. His childishness brought him a great downfall. He turned and accused his own will, because, though he was free, he had enslaved himself. He entered into judgment with his free will, accusing and rebuking his own thoughts. For if he had prevailed in the contest, he would have received a crown of glory. The mortal remained condemned for a full span of time, while the rebel reigned only briefly. The occasion of his folly became instruction for those who came afterward. The fall taught him much wisdom; he set out [?] for his own kind. Through sin they gained understanding, so that they might hate sin. The Creator turned his folly to our benefit and instructed our generations. Through it he disclosed our free will, so that we would not find fault with the way we were formed. Before forming us, he knew that this would help our nature. Thus, when a person was defeated through the choice of his free will, he would ask him for victory. And although victory belongs to him, he grants it to the authority of that person's free will. So that we might learn how much he loves our nature because of his image, he taught us wisdom through our free will from the beginning of our formation. And from our own nature he gave us a Savior at the end of the ages. When he formed the first Adam, he called us by the borrowed name of “image.” And in the formation of the second Adam, he confirmed that name in deed. From our own nature he fashioned an image resembling the first. This was to show that he did not reject our nature because it had sinned. With a threat he cast our nature into the exile of sin. And in mercy he showed favor to our race through a mediator of our own race. He did not send spiritual beings to us to bring us back to the knowledge of him. He himself reconciled us to himself through the mediation of our firstfruits, to confirm the name of “image” with which he had honored us from the beginning. He fashioned an image with bodily members, and the image of his being [?] dwelt in it. He did not fashion it from substances

that are apportioned in human seed. By the power of the Spirit he fashioned his work from the human [?] itself. He fashioned a body through the power of bodies and breathed in a soul through the power of the Spirit. He made him complete in everything belonging to human nature: conception, birth, and upbringing. He tested him through sufferings and afflictions, through hunger and thirst like everyone else. He prepared him to do battle with the mighty one on behalf of his race. He shared in everything belonging to Adam, in the likeness of the first Adam. Only sin he did not practice, for he triumphed through the power of the Spirit. The new voices that spoke at his conception, his birth, and his baptism greatly disturbed [?], and the ranks of his forces trembled. Because of the honor bestowed on Adam at his creation, he envied Adam and went to war. And at the praises of the son of Adam, he became embittered and inspected his weapons. Gabriel's voice distressed him when he spoke with his mother, saying that she was to conceive in a new way, without seed. The good news that spiritual beings proclaimed on earth on the day of his birth was lodged like arrows throughout the whole force of his army. He also heard the voice in the wilderness: “Look, the Lamb who cleanses blemishes!” And he prepared himself for battle, so that sinners would not be justified. The Father's utterance troubled him far more than the earlier voices, proclaiming, “This is my beloved,” and that he was the Son who fulfilled his will. The words his heralds spoke concerning the revelations were new. And the [?] concerning his appearing were higher than human beings. These things stung the crafty one, and the new reports shook him. He began to burn with envy far more than at the former time. His mind marveled within him at these things that had been spoken: although he saw a human body, he heard words that were above it. “Who, then, is this lowly one, this mortal clothed in suffering? The declarations about him are extraordinary and do not resemble those about his companions. Nature produces offspring from nature through marriage, but a voice sowed him in the womb, apart from human seed. He called the members of his race sons with the borrowed name of sonship; but with the name of his own sonship, he went further and called him ‘Beloved.’ He gave grace to a few, and it remained with them for a time; but this one received the gift with a promise that it would not be taken away. He is a human being born of a human being, and he resembles a human being in everything he is, however exalted his formation may be. I should not lose heart because of the different declarations about him. I must fight him with the weapon of the desire for food, for I am convinced that by his nature he is bound by desires.” With these thoughts the enemy consoled his troubled mind, as he sought to do battle with him in the wilderness. He recalled the desire for fruit by which he had brought down the first Adam, and he supposed that through the desire for bread he would overcome the second Adam. The Creator gave him an opportunity,

as on the first occasion, to do battle with the son of Adam. He brought the athlete out into the wilderness, as the murderer desired, and gave him an incentive through the fast of forty nights and days. He longed to tempt him with bread, using the enticement he had offered Adam. And when Grace saw his deceit, she armed him against him with forty days of fasting in the wilderness. He was seeking the weapon of his deceit and waiting to shoot at him the arrow of desire for food. For forty days he kept the athlete’s arena closed, while the spiritual beings assembled as spectators of the athletic contest. At the end of forty days, the combatants came down into the arena: the athlete of righteousness and the envious ruler of the air. At the end of the fast, he allowed the rebel to engage in battle, to display the strength of his victory through limbs that hunger had weakened. On the pretext of bread, he approached the body that hunger had worn down, hoping to draw him toward food through his provocations. “Now,” he said, “is the time when the Father’s care for you is needed. If you are truly the Son, demonstrate your sonship in action. You are in a wilderness, far removed from the settled life that supplies one’s needs. Your body is worn down by hunger, and no food is available to you. Command the elements, which obey, to supply your need. Turn stones into bread so that you do not perish from hunger. Speak a word with authority, as befits the declarations about you, so that your need may be supplied and the declarations about you confirmed. It is not difficult for the power you possess to make one thing out of another. For even the righteous of old commanded the elements, and they were transformed.” Oh, the schemes of the deceitful one, in which denial is concealed! As he drew his hearers away from the truth into his own error—oh, the schemes that deceit devised, which the faithful exposed! Oh, the snares that falsehood concealed, which the swift ones cut apart! The bodily athlete came down to contend with the spiritual one. The lightweight spiritual one was defeated by the heavyweight bodily one. Through abstinence from food, he fought against him by means of his impulses. The heavyweight, clothed in bodily limbs, dashed the lightweight to the ground. The spirit seized the limbs—the airy one seized the one with a heavy body. But the airy one could not maintain his hold on the bodily one, who possessed a composite nature [?]. The bodily one merely raised his voice against the spiritual one. The ruler of the air was terrified by the utterance of the one made of dust. A word overthrew the rebel, and his foot could not stand on the ground. “For the Creator’s word can keep people alive without food. I know that the Creator’s power supplies the needs of us mortals. But asking for help by putting him to the test is unnecessary. Go and learn from those of old who put him to the test when they craved food. The testing that arose from the doubts in their minds destroyed them. Do not offer me encouragement under the guise of a compassionate friend. I know that your counsel [?] brings death to anyone who listens to it. Do not offer me, with lamentation,

the deadly poison that killed Adam. Your table is falsehood. Go and enjoy what is yours.” The renowned warrior who had triumphed in battles against many was defeated. One of those liable to condemnation conquered him with a spiritual weapon. The rebel withdrew in shame from the first contest. He changed the place of combat and his weapon for the second encounter. He looked forward to an empty hope, going from one struggle to another. He thought that passions capable of ensnaring the unwary still remained: “If he has scorned bread and trampled hunger underfoot through endurance, I will wear down the strength of his endurance with the root of the love of money. So what if he has scorned hunger and despised the desire for food? He is a mortal, a son of mortals: after winning one contest, he loses another. Many have conquered through fasting, but mammon has defeated them. Many have scorned wines, but I have made them drunk with envy. I must fight him with the root of the love of money, from which evils sprout and bear the fruits of sin.” He wanted to fight him through the love of money. He longed to show him the splendor of possessions on a mountaintop. The Creator, who knew that this was what he wanted, granted him his desire. He brought the athlete up the mountain to grapple with the evil one. As was his custom, the rebel made images through an illusion that deceived the eyes. He showed the splendor of possessions, a crown, and royal authority. The enemy did not show reality and actual things to the one who sees everything. Rather, he gathered the world and its good things into an unreal likeness. Through an apparition he showed him images that were not real, while the one who sees everything mocked the deceiver’s claims. He kept displaying images, supposing that perhaps he might lead him astray. Christ, with his hidden eye, was examining his thoughts. He arrayed gold that did not exist and set up a crown [?] that was not real. He established ranks and authorities, though there was no voice appointing them. “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me. “For this authority has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I please. I ask you only one thing: honor me, if you are willing. “Worship me and receive crowns, and your authority will reign over everything.” The spirit seized the man of flesh with the bonds [?] of the love of money. But the spirit’s hand did not [?] the body anointed by the Holy Spirit. The man of flesh lifted up his will and brought the spirit down to earth. The heavenly throngs marveled at the man of flesh who conquered, who conquered the spirit. The athlete of flesh [?] above the mighty one’s weapons. The one with heavy limbs trampled the ruler of the weightless air. With his voice alone, the one clothed in a body shook the one with swift wings. “It is written that you must not worship another, but the Lord alone.” “Go away, enemy,” he told him. “Do not usurp the Creator’s name. A creature is not permitted to receive the worship due to its Maker.” By the word that named the Creator, he neutralized the gall of his wickedness. He poured out the cup that the devil had cunningly mixed for him.

“It is written,” he said, “that you must worship the Lord and serve him alone.” With this utterance he demolished the structure that deceit had built up. Through false worship he wanted to [?] him into following his reckless deeds. He reminded him of the name of God and rebuked him because he was not God. “Thanksgiving is due to one alone,” he said, “and you must worship him [?] at all times. “Rebel, do not seize for yourself the true worship that does not belong to you.” By the power of the Spirit and the name of God [?], the athlete of flesh triumphed. And he humbled the arrogance of the insolent before the spectators of the contest. One bout, through the craving for bread, he fought against the man of flesh; another through the love of money; and one after those two struggles. The wicked athlete withdrew from the contest in shame. He began devising tricks to change the place of battle. Only one hope remained for him, and on it he placed his confidence. He kept it for the end of the contest, so that [?] he might gain victory through it. “If hunger has not caught him, and the love of money has not bound him, “there is a hidden snare that he will not notice when he falls into it. If he has trampled the arrows of hunger and broken the bow of Mammon, “with the spear of the love of praise I will topple him from his height. I will prepare a cup full of deadly poison and give it to him. “Even if he tastes only a little of it, its [?] will loosen his limbs.” The envious one longed to [?] to the height of the love of praise. For he was convinced that the height of glory was a pit for anyone who climbed it. The Spirit brought the athlete up to the [?] that the rebel desired. He opened the arena of combat above the temple of atonement. The athlete entered the arena armed with the love of praise. He planted the standard of victory against the one whom the love of money had [?]. In the contest over the love of praise, he was confident that he would defeat the Lord. He did not know that he was becoming entangled in the fine snares he had laid. He concealed praise in a word, the soul’s messenger, and sent it to him. He addressed a message to him, with empty hope written in it. The rebel hid deadly poison in arrows of praise and shot them at him. The shield of salvation caught it—the shield the Holy Spirit had placed in his hand. “If,” he said, “you are indeed the Son, and the declarations about you are true, throw yourself down from here to the ground, and behold, [?] the sonship. For it is written that the help of angels accompanies the righteous person, and they protect him in hardships so that his steps do not stumble. Come down from the height to the earth and test the power of your authority. Look, spiritual beings will carry you and bear you in honor in their hands. Why do you hide your authority and shut out its praise? Reveal your glory and show your power, and then everyone will praise you.” O the traps concealed by deceit, and the snares spread by cunning, which the nimble one cut apart with the word spoken by his mouth! With a great array of weapons, the spiritual being fought the bodily one, but with a few words he overthrew him

and brought all his schemes to an end. He answered the crafty one’s schemes with a fitting reply. By the testimony of Scripture he silenced the impudent one’s mouth. “It is written,” he said, “You shall not put the Creator to the test through doubt, lest he close the door in your face and your requests go unanswered.” O the devices that deceit assembled, and the schemes that falsehood forged, which the Knower of all exposed in the furnace of the Spirit, the [?] of all! O bodily athlete, who entered combat with a spirit! O one subject to suffering, whom the mighty one who enslaved humanity could not defeat! O nature clothed in passions, which conquered the passions within itself! O captive who became mighty and led his captor into captivity! O warrior who fought and set the oppressed free! O offspring of a line of sinners, who freed his race from wrongdoing! Three times the bodily one entered combat with the spiritual one. Through movements of the mind, the one subject to suffering defeated the one not subject to suffering. He drew the bow and shot three arrows toward the target. With the third he proclaimed victory and the evil one’s disgrace. In the first encounter there were broken the mighty one’s bow and spear. Nothing among his weapons remained sound and intact. In another contest the warrior’s limbs gave way, and the spirit’s arms were broken in the struggle with the bodily one. With many weapons the rebel fought against the son of Adam. With the single weapon of the Spirit’s power, he defeated him and abolished his authority. With all his skill the mighty one struggled with the one subject to suffering. With a word alone the bodily one dismantled the structure of his schemes. The captor held the exile captive in three strongholds. The exile breached the rebellious walls of sin. In three traps he concealed all the passions of mortals. The nimble one passed beyond the passions that ensnare so many. Through the desire for bread he offered him desirable things of every kind. The rebel covered them with the appearance of bread, like a garment. In the love of money he gathered and heaped up every kind of evil. Under the name of crown and authority he adorned the ugliness of his thoughts. In the cup of the love of praise he crushed and mixed deadly poison. He spread glory like sweetness over his bitter cup. In three rounds he [?] all the passions, outward and inward. He set them up like a target in the struggle against our Savior. He arrayed the entire world on his own side, from end to end. The entire army was defeated by one who conquered through the power of the Spirit. He assembled and forged every stratagem and put them on like armor. The Son of David shattered them—his weapons—with a mere utterance. The rebel was put to shame with his armor, and his forces were scattered. The whole left side sat mourning the downfall of the mighty one. The accuser finished all his temptations [?] our Lord. He withdrew from him for a time, while he sharpened a sword for slaughter. The battle ceased, and the struggle between the one subject to suffering and the ruler of the air came to rest.

The spectators of the contest rose to acclaim the champion of truth. Wonder had gathered them all into the athletes’ stadium to see a new struggle between a bodily being and a spiritual being. They were watching an ever-new spectacle: two opposing combatants. For flesh had never endured [?] a single round with a spiritual being. The spiritual beings were studying the weakness of the one subject to suffering. With what weapon, they wondered, could a weak nature defeat a mighty one? For their fellow’s [?] was not as great as that of the one clothed in bodily limbs. For they knew that he had won victories in battle against many. They had gathered on this understanding: they would watch the outcome of the contest. Whoever gained the victory, they would offer him a crown of acclamation. They kept the crown of their acclamations until the contests were over. So that they might place it—their voices—on the head of whoever proved victorious. When they saw that the bodily being had defeated their spiritual fellow, They adorned the champion of righteousness with the crown of their voices. They offered cries of praise to the one subject to suffering in return for his victory. Their companies cried out, “Blessed is the power that conquered in the body!” Here their voices became peaceful toward our race, with whom they had been angry. They gained hope of renewal, that together with us they would rest from toil. The spiritual beings wove a crown for the bodily champion, for they saw that through his greatness he had dismantled the barrier between those at enmity. They shouted praise to him with hosannas as he came up from the contest: “Blessed is he who sustained the mediator for our peace and the peace of all! Give thanks to the Good One, who by his power strengthened your body in the contest. Blessed is he at whose command you brought low the tyrant who had taken Adam captive.” With love they were [?] toward him after his contest had ended. They served his hidden mysteries through revelations to earthly beings. Their companies ascended and descended to honor the son of mortals. They rejoiced at the sight of him, and the sound of [?] pleased them. They were greatly amazed at his struggle and marveled at his endurance. For although he belonged to the condemned race, he defeated the tyrant through his sufferings. It was not with human weapons that the suffering one won victory. His victory came through the power of the Spirit, and the Spirit crowned his resolve. In the name of the Son, who [?] in him, he triumphed and overcame sufferings. He was found worthy of great honor and [?] praised by the spiritual beings. Now that the contest is finished, let us ask whose struggle it was: that of the one capable of suffering, clothed in bodily limbs, or that of the nature that does not suffer? Who was it who grew hungry and was tempted, and whose need the evil one noticed? And to whom did the rebel offer the incitements of desirable things? Who was it who entered the contest and joined battle with the evil one? And who defeated the mighty one and was credited with the victory? The distinction clearly makes the struggle known to those who understand: it was a son of Adam who was tempted, in the likeness of the first Adam. It was he whom the Spirit led out into the wilderness, and he who grew hungry and was tempted. For nature was demanding from him

food to sustain his life. It was he whom the rebel was urging to turn stones into bread. For he saw that his limbs had grown weak and that fasting had loosened his sinews. It was to him that he showed images of wealth and great dominion. For he saw him clothed in the limbs of mortals who desire money. It was to him that he offered deadly poison in the cup of the love of praise. The evil one tempted the embodied one, not the power of the divine being. For he knew that the nature of the Self-existent One cannot be tempted with food. It was not to the Only-begotten that he was showing wealth and great dominion. For he knew that the wealth of mortals was contemptible beside the greatness of his glory. It was not for the one who knows hidden things that he was concealing snares of glory. For even the enemy himself knew that his schemes lay exposed before the divine being. He was not doing battle with the power that holds all things. For it was clear to him, a creature, that his strength was feeble before his Lord. Why would the Creator do battle with his own creation? And what use would victory be to the innocent over the guilty? He was not doing battle with his equal, to test his strength. For the nature of a creature is too lowly to be compared with the Creator. And if it was for the sake of salvation that he joined battle with the evil one, he could have brought back those who had gone astray at his command, without a struggle. When has the Creator accomplished his deeds through a struggle? And what opposing power dares to defy the divine being? How could rebels manage to stand against the Creator? And with what senses did the deceiver examine the purity of the divine being? How was the Ruler of all moving from place to place? And by what movements was he traveling wherever the rebel wanted him? Why was it not his own will that brought him out to do battle? For it is written that the Holy Spirit led him out into the [?], to go out and be tempted. Who is it who was tempted by the Spirit’s will and performed mighty works? For look: his will is subordinated to the will of the Father and the Spirit. How did he suffer hunger, he who gives life to everything by his command? And how did the rebel tempt him who possesses the fullness of wisdom? If, because he put on a body, his nature was tested through suffering, then he can be tested both in a body and without a body. And if the Only Begotten was tested through the things in which it is written that he was tested, then the Father and the Spirit also share in that testing, if their nature is one in the equality belonging to the divine being. It is impossible for one to be tested while another remains free from suffering. Everything that belongs to the nature belongs to the persons of the divine being. Whatever approached one, the whole nature shared in it. And if the Father’s offspring suffered the sufferings that belong to mortals, then the Father and the Spirit also tasted the suffering that approached the Only Begotten. But far be it! Let this not happen, and let those who understand not accept it: that the nature incapable of suffering

should be tested through these things that belong to us. It was our nature that was tested and received sufferings in its own nature. And the nature that was in him raised him victoriously above sufferings. It was one of our race who fought against the mighty one on behalf of his race. Through the Spirit’s power he triumphed and released the captor’s captives. Deaths were fitting for him, the humble son of mortals. And glorious things are fitting for the nature that assumed him, as befits it. And if the heretics quarrel with those who examine these things, as they habitually do, for us it is not [?] to bring the divine being down to bodily sufferings. Their quarrelling is a source of pride for us, and reproach from them is praise. Because they hate us for the truth’s sake, their voices do not distress us. The sounds of their torrents do not shake our resolve, nor do we accept a teaching that diminishes the Eternal One from his fullness. Our confession is tossed about within us like a [?] in the sea. And when their waves struck us, we secured it by the power of the divine being. Concerning the greatness of the divine being, they dispute why it was not diminished. And concerning the assumption of humanity, they fight over why it was exalted. Over the distinctions between the natures they arm themselves against those who understand. Against the nature capable of suffering and the nature incapable of suffering, they loose the arrows of their words. Through confusion and mixture they seek to obliterate the natures, while with their bitterness they disturb the peace that reconciled those who were at odds. May we never boast except in this distinction, as we confess that our nature is preserved with the Eternal One who clothed himself in it. In the [?] of the firstfruits of our body, we await the redemption of our bodies. And because it shares with the divine being, its honor is exaltation for us. Our entire race has been honored through the blessings of the [?] of his glory. His honor guarantees our peace with the Creator. We call him Son, together with the Word who clothed himself in him, without division. While we acknowledge that he shares nothing with the divine Being, we do not deny his nature or forget his humiliation. We do not deny his salvation or declare his promises false. We acknowledge his weakness and worship his glories. We honor the body that comes from us because of our love for the one who clothed himself in it. We acknowledge the hidden one through the visible one, and the [?] because of the hidden one. We offer a twofold confession to the one person of the one Son. Let his humiliation accuse those who deny the body belonging to our nature, and let his authority humble those who subject the Father's Word to suffering. The one capable of suffering rebuked them: he suffered in his nature and was tempted. And [?] suffering on behalf of all, except the Word who clothed himself in him. Through his temptation he showed his [?], for temptation approached his nature. Through his victory he made it shine out to us that he triumphed by the power of the Spirit. Because of Adam's folly, the second Adam was tempted. What the first lost in the contest, the last won through his victory. Through the condemnation of the first, his race was condemned, and they became barren. Through the victory of the last, those who came before and those who came after were victorious. Because of Adam's folly,

death entered and enslaved his race. Through the endurance of [?] Adam, death died and the dead came to life. Adam slipped and fell and [?], and the pains in his limbs grew severe. The second Adam rose [?] and lived, and through his suffering he gave life to many. The son of Adam fought the mighty one on Adam's behalf. He repaid him with the pains he had brought upon Adam through desire for the fruit. With the weapon by which the first was defeated, the last also triumphed. Where Adam was defeated through desire for the fruit, Christ conquered through endurance. The first Adam, who came from the earth, pledged himself to sin. The second Adam gave himself as a ransom and freed his race. Because of Adam, death entered, and sleep took hold of many. Through the second Adam, death was abolished, and he caused life to reign over all. Adam was freed through Adam, the earthly one through the heavenly one. He adorned with heavenly life the one whose frame death had dissolved. The rebel tempted Adam in battle on Adam's account. He saw him clothed in his nature and resembling his fellow in everything. The mighty one who had taken Adam captive fought with the Son. The rebel did not engage in battle with the power of the divine Being. Let those who hate the divine Being stop speaking of the divine Being's temptation. For someone of his own race has shown us that the temptation was his. Let him himself say to the heretics, the devil's disciples: "Do not hate the power of the divine Being like your master Satan. I am the one who went down into the contest and engaged in battle with the evil one. I overcame the one who had overcome everyone, through the power of the one who clothed himself in me from the womb. Do not bring the Only-Begotten down to the lowly condition of mortals. For even I, who went down into the contest, gained victory through his power." Look, one of our own race proclaims to us whose battle it was. Listen and hear, heretics: the divine Being is not subject to temptation. Let the prophet cry out in every tongue and rebuke the arrogant: “I myself am the Lord God, and I have not changed from what I am.”
For the Third Sunday of Lent.
Homily [?]. For the Third Sunday of Lent. Response: The Creator has promised us new life. And he gave a pledge of it in the life of Elijah, my brothers.

The son of sojourners marked out a path for me to travel in words, and I sought to journey through the deeds of his proclamation. The zealous man awaited me at the teaching of the Spirit’s words—he who bound and loosed as he wished and was not proved false. He restrained the clouds and dried them up like barren women; then he prayed again and made them pour down rain through a hidden command. He descended like a lion into the lair of voracious death and snatched a human body away from it with his Lord’s help. He fought a battle against the gods and their worshipers.

Error was defeated, and the hidden power triumphed through him. He won the contest through the power of divine help and, in the name of God, put those who were not gods to shame. And so that the mortal would not forget his lowly nature, he left him without help, and he trembled at the voice of a feeble rib. Through this event the son of sojourners learned two things: the lowliness of his own clay and his Lord’s love for humanity. By his journey he showed his zeal for the Hidden One, and at the end of his road he heard a voice full of compassion. In his fervor the zealous man traveled like an exile. He asked for death, lay down, and sank into sleep in his grief. The revelation called to him: “Rise and eat, son of sojourners, for the journey you have undertaken is too hard for you without nourishment.” “Look, a hidden command has prepared visible food for you. Take it and be nourished; recognize your own nature and have compassion on your kind.” The zealous man rose and saw that the table had been prepared by the command. He ate and drank, then sank back into sleep, still grieving. Twice the spiritual being called to the bodily man: “Rise, mortal, and nourish yourself with the food provided by the command.” The command that had powerfully sustained him through speechless creatures now also gave him food through beings who speak. Speaking beings and speechless creatures served him at his supper, and the man concerned for the truth lived without toil. He ate human food and drank the earth’s drink, and heavenly power attended to earthly things. Why, then, did he give him hidden strength through visible food? And why did he restrict the power of his help to something to eat? Through the food he gave him, he showed that he was a human being who needed food; and through his help he revealed that his power preserves humanity. Through the meal he taught that human beings live by food, and through his command he revealed that, if he wishes, he can sustain life with little. Not because it was difficult for him to preserve our lives without food,

but to make known that temporal life is bound to food. The arrogance of fools did not escape the knowledge of the one who knows everything: they were going to lead people astray through their outward appearances. The insolence of their thoughts was plain to him: although mortal, they seize the rank of immortals. Through Elijah he checked the love of glory beforehand, lest mortality should aspire to the heights of life. Through a day's food he gave him strength to live for days, and through a single meal he traveled many stages. The Tishbite rose and walked, sustained by the food, for forty days, night and day, until he reached Horeb. He said that he traveled by the strength of the food, not by human strength, teaching us that the power of his help rests within his works. The zealous man traveled for forty days, growing stronger, and each day [?] fierce battle against the insolent. He arrived and reached the shelter at the end of his journey, and heard a voice questioning him as though it did not know. “What are you doing here, Elijah?” he said to him. “Who drove you out of peaceful surroundings into this dreadful wilderness?” Oh, the greatness of the hidden depth of the God of all, who asks the Tishbite, “What are you doing?” By his command he preserved him so that he could journey toward him [?] to find rest, yet he sought to learn the reason for his journey as though he did not know. He asked him, “What are you doing?” as though he did not know, to open a path for the prophet to proceed toward his words. The righteous man answered the one hidden from all: “I have been deeply zealous, because your people have forgotten the great covenant of your hidden love. “They have discontinued the sacrifices they were obliged to offer to your name, and have offered them in the name of demons who are strangers to you. “They have killed your prophets and shed their blood without pity. I alone remain, and now they seek my life, as they did those of my companions.” The revelation called him, making the hidden will known to him:

“Come out, stand, listen, look, learn, and rest from your anger. “Look, I am producing wind, an earthquake, and flame, and I am shaking the earth before you according to your desire.” The command signaled to the things without senses and stirred them into haste. Fire and wind clashed with one another, and the earth shook. He held them in torment and shook them before the zealous man, who longed to add the fire of his wrath to the people's wickedness. Through earthquake and fire he exposed his inclination: this was what he wanted—to shake the earth and burn people with fire and wind. He showed him the wind, brought down an earthquake, and then fire, and made a voice heard: “I do not wish to do these things. “You, being human, wanted to destroy people as humans do. But it is not fitting for me to resemble you in destroying people.” After the fire, he made a gentle voice heard by him, teaching him about his will, that he loves humankind. Elijah trembled at the terrifying things he set before him, and covered his face in dread of the fearsome vision. The voice spoke to him a second time: “What are you doing?” And he answered as before: “I have been very zealous.” With a gentle voice he softened his soul's harshness, and set peace with humankind before him as a goal toward which he should incline. “Return,” he said, “on your way to the work of prophecy, for look, I have kept for myself seven thousand who obey me.” The zealous man thought that he alone was a prophet and righteous, but the voice taught him that he had companions in the fear of his Lord. “I have kept,” he said, “seven thousand who have not gone astray and bowed down,” making known to us that his command had guarded their minds. Through his help he preserved a few from those who had been sifted, and the flood of wickedness did not sweep them away into the worship of error. Through the remnant he preserved, who had not shared in the worship of Baal, he taught the righteous man the purpose of his mercy toward humankind. “Go,” he said, “and anoint one king and another for the people and the nations, so that they may crush the insolence of the wicked people. Anoint and appoint also a prophet of the Spirit to take your place, so that whoever escapes justice may be punished through him.” The zealous man turned from harshness toward gentleness,

and traveled along the path of kindness toward [?]. He anointed the prophet and appointed a king for the people and the nations, and in his proclamation he joined words to action. For this reason the divine command drew him all the way to Horeb, so that through instruction he might acquire love for his neighbors. He set out zealously to go and lodge a complaint against the insolent, but the voice taught him the way of peace toward humankind. He returned from Horeb to his own people, who hated peace, and saw that the people and the king were sick with the disease of wickedness. Because of wickedness he had abandoned the people and hated the king; when he returned and came back, he saw that the people and the king were gravely ill. He remained in the fever of Baal worship for a long time, and the disease of oppression that lay hidden in the soul broke out. The greedy king saw and coveted what was not his, and concealed the deceit hidden in his heart under the name of justice. He said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard for a good price in silver, or I will give you another vineyard in exchange, better than yours.” When his oppression, disguised as a purchase, was not complied with, his thoughts were troubled by senseless grief. Ahab lay down in sorrow and refused to eat because of the just judgment Naboth had given him in reply. Jezebel heard that the greedy man had been brought low before justice, and through her schemes she sharpened a sword against truth. “Why are you sad and your heart crushed?” she said to Ahab. “Why do you shrink back at the leaf-like rustle of the name of justice?” Why have you not pressed on toward acts of oppression? And why are you asleep when it comes to schemes for amassing silver? You are slack and feeble in doing wrong, and you are not fit to be king over Israel. “Get up,” she said, “eat and drink, rejoice and let your heart be glad, for I will give you Naboth’s vineyard against his will.” She forged a weapon of treachery within her thoughts, to shed blood legally, in the name of justice. She wrapped in a letter the sword that deceit had sharpened,

and bound falsehood beneath the clothing of written words. She wrote injustice and sealed the falsehood that deceit had transcribed, and fraudulent scribes interpreted them with partiality. O letter that was written in the name of justice, while deceit that gives birth to murder lay hidden within it! The foolish woman wished to commit murder in the name of justice, so that the wickedness of her treachery would not be exposed before those who saw it. She covered her injustice with the fine clothing of the law: whoever pronounces the name of God must die by stoning. On this condition she too wrote to the frauds: “Seat men who will give false testimony against Naboth. “Proclaim a fast,” she said, “and clothe yourselves in mourning like discerning people. Demand an accounting for the insult to the name of God and to the king of the people. “Let fasting and mourning be witnesses against Naboth’s blood, for anyone who reviles the king and the God of all deserves death.” The men of Jezreel, the elders and nobles, carried out the treacherous murder of the innocent man, just as it was written. They gathered the people, proclaimed a fast, and devised a treacherous scheme. Through false testimony they condemned the innocent-hearted man to death. O testimony that no voice had sown in ears! The heart conceived it through union with deceit and gave birth to murder. O mind, beautiful radiance of reason, whose light grew dark through false testimony against innocent blood! Those able to speak became more silent than the mute about what was right. They condemned innocent blood and did not consider what they were doing. The innocent man died by the sword of stones that deceit had sharpened, and the greedy man seized his household’s inheritance to make it his own. A revelation of the hidden command summoned the Tishbite: “Arise, zealous one, and demand an accounting for the blood that deceit has shed. “Show your zeal like a mighty warrior against the evildoer. Demand from his hands the blood of the oppressed man, and do not hold back. “Go and tell him, ‘Thus says the One who knows all: You have murdered and taken possession, but it is not secure as you supposed.

“‘According to the blood you shed, I will measure out your blood upon the earth, and on account of Naboth I will avenge the blood of my prophets.’” The good soldier armed himself with the armor of the Spirit, to go and fight the evildoer who had trampled justice. The zealous man saw the hard-hearted man who was eager for blood. He drew the sword of the word of the Spirit and held it out against him. “Look, you have committed murder by deceit and inherited the vineyard. But the desire behind your deceit will not reach its fulfillment.” Divine judgment forestalled your evil intention and shed your blood in return for the blood you shed, before the events took place. The Judge pronounced the sentence of death against you, and the hidden command, the executioner, drew the sword. “In the place where you shed Naboth’s blood, your blood will be poured out. And there Jezebel will become a sacrifice for ravenous dogs. And because injustice prospered through your hands more than through all who came before you, justice too will triumph over you through a harsh judgment.” The wicked man was put to shame by the righteous man against his will. He took off his crown, put on sackcloth, and walked barefoot. He grieved and pleaded over his lawless deed: he had coveted, grown greedy, seized, murdered, and trampled on the commandment. A message from the hidden command came to Elijah, teaching him how dear a soul is. “I have seen,” he said, “that King Ahab has humbled himself before me and clothed his mind in sorrow over what he has done. Because he has humbled himself before me and recognized that he sinned by shedding human blood, I will not bring disaster on his children during his lifetime. In the days of the king who loves injustice, like his [?], I will call the house of Ahab to account for the blood of my prophets.” The sentence of the hidden command against the wicked man was settled, and he prepared himself for battle with the Edomites. The insolent man was struck by a cruel arrow that the command had shot, and the righteous man’s word was fulfilled in him [?], just as he had prophesied. Wicked men hurled stone missiles at righteous Naboth, and the insolent man too was struck by evil men, just like Naboth. The wicked man died, and his hope of justice perished. He handed over his crown to an evil heir who resembled his father.

Because he ran swiftly along the path of injustice, he suddenly fell into the trap of suffering that the command had set for him. The fool sent messengers to inquire about his punishment, to see whether there was any way to heal his grievous injury. The messengers set out to consult what was no god, but the son of sojourners blocked the road before them. The zealous man exposed the deceit in the heart of the son of wicked people, showing how, like his father, he was bound by love for demons. “Go and tell that senseless man, accomplished in sin: ‘Is there no God among the chosen people who can heal your suffering? Because you have forgotten the God of all for the sake of things that are no gods, he will cut your life short, so that the demons you have loved will not keep you alive.’” The messengers returned to the wicked man who had sent them and brought news that cut off hope to the man who had no hope. He asked them, “Who turned you back so quickly?” They told him, “Your father’s enemy stopped us on our journey.” The sick man, laid low by two afflictions, mustered his strength and, like his father, sharpened a sword to destroy the righteous. He armed a force weak in battle against the truth, but his force was defeated by the power of the Spirit in the [?]. A captain of fifty went up, threatening Elijah, and in his arrogance he mocked him, the son of sojourners. “Come down quickly,” he said, “prophet of the Spirit, and do not delay, for the king wants to see your face at once.” When the prophet heard the insolent man's arrogant voice, he hurled arrows of fire at him, and he burned up along with his company. The fire of the hidden command licked at the men's horses, and the armor burned along with those who wore it, those clothed in arrogance. The disaster that had happened did not shake the wicked man. Again he sent a captain of fifty who was like the first. The insolent man went up to the zealous prophet with a proud heart and began issuing orders: “Come down quickly, for the king wants you.” The man whose arrogance had risen to the great height of prophecy came down in shame to humiliation, like the first. He persisted in his [?], dull-hearted and sunk in earthly things.

Again he sent a captain of fifty, for the third time. The humble man saw that the armor of arrogance had brought his companions low, so he put on the armor of humility to avoid condemnation. The humble man went up and began pleading humbly: “Let my life be precious, and do not crush me for the sin of having come.” Because he had not armed himself with arrogance like those before him, a revelation directed the zealous prophet: “Go down and go with him.” Elijah put on the hidden armor of prophecy, went down, and killed the murderous man with the sound of his words. “Thus says the one whom you angered by turning to a false god: ‘You will not come down again from the bed you have climbed onto and live.’” With the sword of the Spirit he cut off his hope of life, and in Ahab's house he confirmed his words through deeds. He completed and perfected the great height of prophecy and brought the ship of his preaching into a peaceful harbor. The Hidden One instructed him in one of his spiritual revelations: “Come, weary man, rest in the harbor of life, beyond death. “Come, enjoy a foretaste of the renewal of those who do not die, and remain alive in the new order of the kingdom on high. “Come in and see, as in a mystery, that kingdom to which you prophets have invited the people and the nations through your words. “Before these things happen, I am showing you the life prepared by my will for spiritual and bodily beings. “I will preserve angels and human beings in new, unending life, as they glory in the Spirit. “Through you I am giving the human race a sign of peace. Let your life be a pledge to mortal humanity. “Through you I guarantee to your whole race that they will live with you, and through your departure I confirm the promise of my words. “Through you I am opening a road to unending life, so that ravenous death will not cut short the number of your years. “Through you I am increasing good hope for the hopeless, so that they will not abandon their confidence in their liberation. “Through you I am showing that Adam's dust is not despised by me, for through your exaltation I have honored his lowly clay.”

Elijah heard that the command would take him away alive, and he sought to hide within silence what would benefit humanity. The zealous man thought this befitted his humility, so that lowly human nature would not boast of what was not its own. The all-knowing one, who saw him, saw his intention and revealed the mystery of humanity’s benefit to the human mind. It was also right that the source of our life should not be hidden, so that through what was clearly revealed we might be further assured of things to come. For this purpose the Creator revealed his servant’s departure: to bind people to the love of life without end. Nor was it because Elijah begrudged the benefit to our lives that he wished to hide his departure alive from our understanding. The zealous man considered whether the way to life might become a cause of pride and even reproach for those who came afterward. He proposed a journey and devised a pretext for his disciple: “My God has sent me on a journey that I must travel alone with him.” The command made his departure alive known to human understanding, and before anyone else it revealed it to Elisha, as a trustworthy man. “As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live,” he answered Elijah, “I will not forsake your great love, even to the end.” “The Lord has sent me to Bethel,” he said with a mystical meaning, “to the place worthy of having God’s name bestowed upon it.” The hidden command revealed to the prophets the reason for his journey, and they went out to meet him, to escort him in honor through the spirit of revelation. The seers of things to come addressed his disciple: “Do you know that today the Lord is taking your master away?” Through the spirit of revelation he answered them as one who knew: “This mystery has been revealed to me. Be silent about it.” He also used the journey to Jericho as a pretext with his disciple, but the disciple cut short his pretext by invoking God’s name and his master’s life. There too the prophets went out in the Spirit to meet the righteous man, prophesying about his departure from among humanity. “Do you know,” the prophets asked Elisha, “that today the Lord is taking your master away?” And he told them to be silent. The zealous man saw that the Spirit had revealed the mystery of his departure, and for the third time he offered his disciple a pretext: “The Lord has sent me as far as the Jordan, to go there and return.”

But the fervent-hearted man was not discouraged by these pretexts. The Spirit whispered within him that he should go out and see a great wonder: Adam’s dust being escorted in honor by spiritual beings. Elijah journeyed along a new road, away from humanity. He struck the waters, and speechless nature trembled before him. He raised his cloak, struck the river, and divided it in two; the unruly waters did not resist his word. Speechless nature feared the command hidden in the cloak. It ceased its flow and observed an order contrary to nature. Elijah crossed with his disciple as though on dry ground, and the river returned to flowing along its course as before. The worthy master arose to explain things to his disciple and to interpret for him the mystery hidden in the events. “Ask for whatever you wish, and I will give you the riches of the Spirit, before I am taken away to where the command has appointed me to go.” The disciple asked the modest master for a double portion of armor, so that he might go and fight against error with its help. When the master saw that he had gone too far and asked for something beyond his station, he withheld this from him until his departure; then he would give it to him. It was not out of envy that he withheld the gift from his disciple. The disciple himself had been very bold, and he set a limit for him. “If you see me when the command takes me away from you, receive the gift just as you have asked.” And he upheld the dignity of his rank. It was not doubt about his departure that divided his mind; rather, he considered whether he might still remain a little while. “If the hidden command takes me away from humanity, may the power of the Spirit be with you as you desire.” The master finished giving his disciple his words of instruction, and the heavenly companies arrived to take him away. They displayed an array of fiery horses that had been harnessed, and a chariot fitted with reins of fire. Wheels of fire could be seen beneath the chariot, and the horses had wings of fire, like flying creatures. That chariot which appeared was not fire, nor did the horses possess senses or riders.

For what was displayed was a vision, not a physical body: an appearance of fire and the shape of horses without physical composition. The spiritual beings displayed horses, as they were accustomed to do, and harnessed a chariot to exalt the son of sojourners. The hidden command urged them into action, so that through awe-inspiring things they might display a vision of humanity’s exaltation. The spiritual beings depicted a great mystery for those on earth: see, lowly nature is being raised to exaltation! Through the chariot they portrayed the honor of Adam’s dust, which the command would honor at the end, as the symbol indicated. Through one who departs without being swallowed by ravenous death, he depicted for us the mystery of new life without end. Through Elijah the Creator revealed to mortal humanity that hope awaits the hopeless at the end of time. He brought about his departure in a great vision, [?] spiritual beings, to show us our own departure to the heights. The chariot, too, which carried the son of sojourners in honor—the command was showing him its course [?] toward the heights. The bodily man became like a charioteer above the spirit, and flesh grasped reins of fire without being harmed. O bodily man, who rode upon spirit and commanded fire! O man of flesh, who was not scorched by the flame! O heavy one, who acquired wings for flight! O mortal, whom the hand of death did not touch! Through the spiritual beings, the command placed him above the horses, while his mantle remained with his disciple as a pledge. Through the garment from his body he gave him a sign of what he had asked for: that he had received a double measure of his rank, outwardly and inwardly. The man of flesh rode upon the wind and flew through the air, and the divine command directed him to the end of his journey, to the appointed place in Eden. The son of sojourners was taken to Eden, not to heaven; and the divine command kept him alive on earth, not in the firmament. For his feet of flesh did not tread the road to the heights, nor was that entrance opened to mortality. Only one from among mortals ascended to heaven:

The one who dwelt in him had opened the firmament so that he might minister in the Holy of Holies on behalf of his fellow mortals. He is the one who ascended with the Will that had descended to him, and he was raised above everything to bring everything to completion. Let us set the bounds of our discourse by his word, which cannot be annulled: no one from among mortals has ascended except him. The divine command drew the son of sojourners toward the heights, and after he had been raised up, it placed him in Eden, in a beautiful place. There he kept him with his fellow human being, Enoch, who had been taken away, so that they might remain there beyond suffering, as a symbol of the kingdom. Through them he showed us a sign of peace toward our race, and through their lives he promised life to mortal humanity. He held them as hostages of love to secure peace for humanity; and as long as they are in the land of life, our hope is secure. He promised us freedom for the soul and resurrection for the body, and entered them as guarantors in the written deed of our life. They put their signatures to the covenant for the renewal of our bodies, in that their limbs are preserved unharmed. He divided the span of this temporal existence into portions, so that he might sow hope for the resurrection of the dead in every generation. He took Enoch away during the ten generations that corrupted the established order, and through his removal taught them about his wrath. In the middle of the generations he took Elijah and kept him alive, and through his exaltation revealed the glory of the immortals. At the end of the ages he took one of us as the firstfruits, and through his sacrifice reconciled everything with his Majesty. He did not keep him alive apart from humanity as he did the servants, for the servants are on earth, while he is above in heaven as Lord. Enoch and Elijah are preserved on earth in the region of Eden, while he reigns over everything in heaven with the one who assumed him. He settled the good servants within Paradise as a pledge of that state which does not decay. The faithful did not receive their dwelling in Eden as their recompense, for the reward of their crowns is reserved in the kingdom on high. For the one who knows everything looked ahead to what would benefit our lives, and for our sake preserved in symbolic form the promise made to the righteous.

He is waiting for us, and then he will fulfill the promise of his words, so that together we may receive freedom for our bodies and salvation for our souls. See, the account of the righteous has opened a road to life for us. Come, let us journey, as in a symbol, toward its completion. See, through the taking away of two men, he has shown us that he transfers us to a state that does not perish. Come, let us set the goal of the righteous before us and direct ourselves toward it, and let each of us look at the steadfastness of their minds. Let us awaken [?] from our slumber at the sweet sound of their words, and drive the weight of desires from our minds. Let us wash our thoughts clean of the filth of hateful wrongdoing, and see ourselves in the mirror of their conduct. Like guards, we all surround the camp of our race. Let us not grow slack, lest the evil one break through our ranks. Let us always strive toward perfection by following their conduct, today and tomorrow, for the end of our lives is already approaching. Through faith the victorious overcame the passions within them. Let us take refuge in it in every struggle of body and soul. It is a shield that receives the enemy’s arrows, and the fiery sword cannot overcome its firmness. Through it human minds are tested as in a furnace, and the boiling of the passions reveals the impurity of the soul’s ugliness. Let the mind of our soul become gold in the furnace of its testing, and let us not grow slack before the incitements of our evil inclination. Let us look to Jesus and imitate him in our steadfastness, for he became the founder and perfecter of our faith. In place of joy, he endured the cross for our sake. Let us remain in the love of faith in him, so that we may reign with him.
Response: May our fasting be hyssop offered to Christ to cleanse our stains.
For the fourth Sunday of the Fast.

Discourse Twelve.
For the fourth Sunday of the Fast.
Response:
Come, mortals, let us cease from wrongdoing and love the life that does not perish, my brothers.

Mortals dwell in the temporary tent of suffering, and everyone stays only a short time in this life. Time runs on in a succession of changes that hastens it along, and with time people become like shadows. The world resembles a dream in its course and its changes, and mortal life vanishes like a vapor. A human being is a vapor, and temporal life is vanity of vanities. Time and life’s changes testify that they are a vapor. One time passes another and hurries like a traveler, and one time makes room for another so that it will not be delayed. The one who gives life its existence leads generation after generation onward, and death runs like a guide before every generation. Time journeys on without delay, and the generation with it. Though mute, it cries out to the one who can speak, ‘Do not delay!’ As it runs, time constantly rebukes rational humanity:

‘Why do you wear yourself out without benefit [?]?’ Like someone who can speak, the mute cries out to those with understanding: ‘Look and consider the changes of time and the passing of life.’ What age has maintained its course without change? And when have people remained alive without departing? Who has restrained the sun so that it would not change? And who has laid commands on death so that it would not approach him? Who has given silver and pearls and bought life? And who has concealed his body in a hiding place from sickness? What king has protected his life from harm? And when, after he died, has his crown endured without being ruined? There is no mortal called a human being who is not subject to death, and no creature of dust whose sufferings are not mixed into his clay. And if he is mortal, and his mind is clothed in garments of suffering, why does contemptible dust boast about a temporary life? Look, his departure cries aloud about his decay: a human being is dust, and his clay returns to ashes. The creature of dust lives on earth like a hired worker, and like a traveler he waits for death as though for evening. At birth he is hired, as though in the morning, to work the earth; and at evening death gives him rest, as though in sleep. He possesses nothing that does not decay when he decays, and he and his possessions are always returning to a lowly state. Why, then, does a mortal take pride in what is not his own? For neither can he help his possessions, nor can his possessions help him.
