Time changes his possessions during his lifetime, and he watches in silence; death leads him away to Sheol, and his possessions remain silent. Do not rejoice, owner of possessions, as though you had truly acquired them. For you are being estranged from what is yours, and what is yours from you. Call your possessions and make them stand beside you at the time of your death, and see whether any of them opens its mouth and pleads with death. Gather your slaves and clothe them in fearsome armor,

and let them shoot arrows at death’s ranks so that they will not strike you. You too, arm the impulses of your soul and go down into the arena. Engage sickness in battle, overthrow it, and cast it down. And if the strength of your limbs is too feeble for combat, prepare silver, give an offering, and save your life. No, rich man, no! These things I have described are not possible, and death is not appeased by a bribe so as to show you favor. If you wish, judge fairly, like a discerning person. Submit my words to your own examination and see that they are true. Look carefully with the clear eye of discernment, and see that the span of our lives is a mere breath and is subject to danger. Our lifetime bears witness to our departure, that [?], for it has already overtaken us with a single change affecting everything. Do not rejoice, human being, in temporary possessions, and do not exalt yourself over a poor person whose means of living are meager. Do not strike down in your arrogance the person embittered in soul [?], lest you yourself be struck down by the sentence of the one whose judgment is just. Do not deal ruthlessly with someone in need, lest you be drowned with the rich man in the abyss of Sheol. Remember his torment and his sufferings in Gehenna: how earnestly he pleaded, yet his words were of no use. Do not enjoy yourself alone, as though what you have were your own, lest you be excluded from sharing in the promised blessings. Do not indulge yourself excessively in earthly things, lest countless, doubled lashes be heaped upon you. Provide yourself with such comfort as is fitting for this temporary life, and give the surplus to anyone who lacks food. The wealth you have acquired is not yours but your Lord’s. Provide for yourself and your fellow servants as a steward. You are a steward, not [?], over everything you have acquired, and you will have to give the master of the house an account of your possessions. The master of the house is the God of all, who made everything,

and entrusted the wealth of his goodness to the work of his hands. He gave wealth to those who are rich in earthly things, to test whether they are faithful with what is not their own. He also made the necessities of this life scarce for the poor, to test them through deprivation as in a furnace. He could have given wealth to everyone just as he gave it to one person, but this would not have benefited rational beings. For before he made everything, he knew how to give, and what restraint was fitting for discernment subject to passions. He gave one person wealth to test his disposition with what was not his own, and he made another poor to train his life through trials. It was not that he needed to learn about them as though he did not know, but to reveal the power of the abilities he placed in rational beings. Through abundance and want, he wished to reveal the soul’s wealth: how far its discernment surpasses that of animals. To an animal, great wealth and poverty are alike: it neither grows proud nor is consumed with sorrow over having more or less. The human soul is a treasury of discernment, and it has the power to rejoice in much and grieve over little. The Maker of all placed his wisdom in the treasury of its disposition, so that, according to its judgment, it might administer the treasure entrusted to its hands. Our Lord clearly gave both to test us, so that at the judgment we ourselves would be witnesses against the wickedness of our own souls. You therefore have no answer, rich man, and you cannot be acquitted when you are called to account for why you acted unjustly. The Judge of all does not judge you because you acquired possessions, but because you were devoid of mercy and hated other people. The one who enriches everyone gave wealth for people’s sake, but you hid it and deprived people of their lives. Human lives depend on the necessities of this life, and anyone who withholds people’s livelihood is a murderer. Who would not weep over a rich man devoid of mercy, who through his wicked disposition has become a companion to a murderer? If nothing in all creation is greater than a human being, then neither is anything worse than a human being who hates another human being. Why do you hate me, rich man, as though I were evil?

And why have you become a hater of human beings, who are the image of the Creator? Why have you estranged yourself from peace with others, you hater of humanity, and made yourself devoid of compassion, like the Evil One? Turn away from the wilderness of arrogance, that desolate mountain, and dwell in the land of humility, which is easy to cultivate. Occupy yourself with the company of people who love peace, and subdue your inclination under the gentle yoke of humility. Sow your charitable gifts in the soil of humanity, which does not cheat you, and await the hoped-for fruit, whose nourishment holds hidden life. Give to the needy, stoop down to the distressed, and comfort the orphan. Let your face shine, and do not be sorrowful when you give. Take care not to give while you are sorrowful and your heart is distressed, lest you hear that voice which spoke to Cain. He too offered a hateful sacrifice that resembled himself, and when the Righteous One saw that his heart was gloomy, he rejected it and cast it away. Do not, then, sow the seed of your charitable gifts in despair, lest the fruits of your labors be deprived of their reward. There is no reward for fruits that come from sorrow, and hateful sacrifices are not accepted before the One who sees everything. Someone who gives while gloomy incurs two losses: he loses what belongs to him and confines himself under condemnation. Through his gift he brings a double judgment against himself, without understanding why he gives or why he incurs guilt. He gives and grieves the Giver who has given to him and to everyone, without understanding that he begrudges the Giver what belongs to him. For everything that kings and the lowly possess belongs to the God of all, and from his gift human beings and heavenly beings become rich. It is right to give him what belongs to him with pure love, so that we may not be accused over things that are not ours as though they were ours. And if wealth, life, and the payment of rewards belong to him, why does lowly dust boast because gold has been placed in it? Paul laid down that no created being should boast;

and if anyone boasts, let him take pride in the Lord alone. Let everyone attribute whatever he possesses to the Maker, apart from wrongdoing, which is ours and is practiced among us. For our inclination is the wrongdoer within us, not someone else's. Yet, although it is very unjust, whenever it wishes, it sets its wrongdoing right. It itself bears witness to the authority of its discernment, since by its own will it is acquitted or found guilty through what it possesses. Come, mortals, set the course of your wills in order, for it has now been revealed that our will has authority over everything. Let everyone blame his own will when he grows lax, and in his self-examination let him look at himself and rebuke his wrongdoing. Let our inclination act as a judge over all our deeds, and let us bring wrongdoing and righteousness before it for examination. Every rational person is bound by duty to know these things; and if he does not discharge his debt, his conscience rebukes him for his wrongdoing. Let us not neglect the power of the wisdom hidden in our souls and give rise to ignorant grumbling against our Maker. Let us not boast when our wealth and strength are abundant, nor be distressed when our way of life is lowly and our bodies are weak. Let us not exalt ourselves because of the greatness of a position of leadership, nor consider it degrading to submit to proper order. Let the one who commands temper his words with peaceful speech, and let the one who serves give thanks, as he is obliged to do. Let the one who is head be foremost among them in deeds, like the head through which the whole body receives light. Let the one who is under authority, in the position of the feet, always proceed like feet toward what has been commanded. Let the one whose mind is enlightened enough to discern well show the way to those whose understanding is darkened. Let the one whose mind is quick to hear and heed the truth raise his voice like a trumpet in the ears of the sluggish. Let the one whose sword of speech is sharp enough to kill wickedness lay waste the ranks of the enemy through his words. Let the one who is wise and knows the order of the word of life:

Give a sense of taste to those who are insensible to their duty. Let the one whose soul’s love is steadfast in faith prepare spiritual food suited to people’s immaturity. Let the one who is free from the stains of lust wash the limbs of his companions clean of foul things. Let the one who is holy, free from the impurity of fleshly desire, sprinkle his words like dew upon sinners. Let the one who is occupied with the proper study of spiritual things accustom his companions to hearing good things about the practice of life. Let the one who is learned and wishes to teach the unlearned measure his words according to their understanding, and teach in this way. Let the teacher say to his disciple, “Look at me and learn,” and let the disciple also attend to the purpose of his teacher’s words. Let the teacher not raise himself above his disciple in pride, nor let the disciple insult the teacher who makes him wise. Let the teacher take the place of the eye for the senses of the body, and let the senses follow the eye toward instruction. Let him fulfill the role of the mouth’s speech toward the limbs, and let the limbs listen to his voice without ever having enough. Let our love bind us to one another according to the order of the body, just as the body is held together through its senses and is one whole. The body is one and is not divided by the differences between its senses; though they are many, they agree in a harmony that cannot be torn apart. Christ is one, the head of the Church, the pure body; and in one love [?] that Christian bodies should remain. If the limbs are distinct yet agree in visible things, how much more should hidden impulses be joined together in hidden things. The feet differ from one another in their movements, yet the course of their work serves one body equally. No member envies another for its diligence, nor have they become greedy and taken more food than they need. Let us regard one another with discernment, following the order of the senses, and let each of us act like members of a body through our deeds. Let the resolute person encourage the weak with his voice and bind up his suffering with the medicine of hope that does not lose its strength. Let us restrain the frivolous person so that he does not behave frivolously, and let the lover of peace quiet the anger of hot-tempered people. Let the discerning person [?] the person lacking understanding to know the truth.

And let the diligent worker rouse the idle to the work of life. Let the person who owns possessions manage his wealth wisely, and let the person lacking property guard himself against grumbling. Let the person with healthy limbs not despise the constitution of someone who is afflicted, and let the person whose body is wasted not give way to despair. Let the person of splendid appearance not mock someone with an ugly face, and let the person of unattractive appearance not grieve over why he is like this. You who are skilled in conversation, keep your words free of boasting; and you who have few words, restrain your tongue from abuse. You who are quick-witted, take care not to rush into hidden matters; and you who are slow of understanding, do not delay in learning. You who love money, do not greedily take what belongs to another, lest the books of the Spirit call you a second Ahab. You who love praise, do not display your labors before spectators, lest you share in that pronouncement concerning the Pharisee. You who abstain from wine, take care not to mix anger into your drink, lest you become drunk on the drink of wrath and lose your understanding. You who fast continually, keep your mind from hateful things, lest you be disgraced by hunger both here and in Gehenna. You who devote yourself to prayer, pray in secret as you were commanded, lest empty praise empty your soul’s labors of their worth. You whose gaze is modest, do not stare at beautiful faces, lest you become entangled in the snares of bodily desire. Through an evil gaze, honored people have fallen from their rank, and mighty men have been defeated by the enticements of encounters face to face. The gaze of the eyes bound Samson, the mighty warrior, and beauty of face ensnared David, whose understanding was enlightened. And if mighty men and people of understanding fell through what they saw, who would not guard the gaze of his eyes against stumbling blocks? The eye is fragile, and a reservoir of [?] is contained in its spring. If they are breached, they flood the body and bewilder the soul.

Modest person, close the gate of your eyes and guard your pupils, so that the treasure you gathered with vigilance may not be plundered. Do not gaze for long at beautiful faces, lest you become ugly to behold at the wedding feast on high. You too, Eve, cover your face with modest clothing, so that modest people may not be caught in the snares of your evil gaze. Control the impulses of your soul and your eyes, so that those traveling on the road may not stumble in the path of your eyes. Look carefully and adorn yourself with modesty, lest you remain outside the door with the foolish women. Prepare oil and go out in the company of the wise women, lest the lamp of your love go out and you become a laughingstock. Do not adorn yourself with outward facial beauty, lest those well versed in the beauty of the soul mock you. Keep your steps and your eyes away from ugly deeds, so that they do not call you a slippery stone lying in the street. Look and understand that your eyes and the adornment of your face are a trap, and through you senses and impulses are caught as in a [?]. Your whole being is a trap hidden in the ground before people's steps, and no one knows how he falls into your snares. The snares of your desires are woven with cunning knots, and it is very difficult to escape your schemes. You resemble a partridge that calls its own kind to death, killing its companions with its songs and dying itself as well. Like a partridge, your appearance entices whoever looks at you, and with your movements you catch the young like birds. A twofold death is confined in the cage of your evil inclination, calling people toward destruction as though toward peace. The speech of your mouth is like bait set before the simple:

And when they longed to eat from it, they [?] in sin. No hunter is more skilled than you at catching people, and no bird calls as beautifully as your movements do. You are very cunning in the art of hunting people, and no one knows how to recount the varieties of your schemes. Your inclination is skilled at reading the books of the one who kills people, but your heart is childish when it comes to studying the wisdom of truth. He has been your skilled teacher from the beginning, and you have read and studied his writings, sinned, and caused others to sin. Leave off studying with the deceitful scribe who teaches falsehood, and come study the books of the Spirit, which impart life. Do not imitate your mother Eve, who listened to his advice, ate the fruit, and gave birth to death for the household of Adam. Look, once again you make the bitterness of death spring up through your schemes. You have killed us enough through the eating of the fruit your mother desired. Do not put us to death through desire for the flesh as you did through the fruit. Stop! Do not be a trap of wickedness for those who look at you, for people of every age have become entangled in the snares of your face. If only your face were as ugly as your mind! Then the simplehearted would recoil from your ugliness. If only you did not have so much facial adornment and so many pearls! Perhaps those who love adornment would neglect your company. Who, then, would put a restraint on your eyes and your steps, and bring you in and shut you up in a cage like the animals? Who, then, would bind your evil inclination in fetters forever? Perhaps the voice that disturbs people's peace would fall silent. If only someone would put the seal of silence on your tongue! Perhaps the destruction of the ranks of humanity would then cease. Blessed is the one who has stopped his ears and not listened to your words, and has become deaf to the talk of your shamelessness. Blessed is the one who, though he is with you, is not with you, and who has lived with you and guarded your soul from the harm you cause. Blessed is the one who has not lost sight of the purpose of his words while speaking of you, and has not been confused by the twists and turns of your shamelessness.

While speaking of you, I turned aside from the course my words were following, because I saw that the snares of your deceit had multiplied beyond counting. Speaking of you drew me away from conversation with everyone, because I saw that the whole world was bound up in the pursuit of love for you. It was not out of malice that I spoke against you, as you supposed. Nor did I condemn you, but rather your disposition, which sins and leads others into sin. I did not condemn even your disposition as something evil, but because, though it is good, everyone makes it evil for himself and his companions. Your disposition is not bound by nature like that of speechless creatures, nor are you alone in possessing impulses toward temptations. Your capacity for discernment is equal to a man's, and, if you choose, you are not inferior to him in putting it into practice. Men and women have the same discerning disposition, and the same strength and freedom of soul to overcome or be defeated. It is not womankind that is despised by the One who knows everything, but the disposition of brazen women that does not conceal itself. It is not conversation with modest women that leads people into sin, but the enticement of shameless women that bewilders the inexperienced. Union in partnership with faithful women is not impure; rather, the filthy drink of lawlessness is evil. A woman is pure when she keeps far from foulness, and union with her and the child born from her are holy and pure. She and her husband are equal in their labors and their reward, and together they inherit life in this world and the kingdom above. Here they differ from one another in their outward forms; there, there are neither males nor females, for their nature is one. And if they are one in the place that is free from harm, let no one separate what the God of all has made equal. Men and women have one nature and one Creator, and they ought to direct their actions toward one goal. For, it is said, man is not apart from woman in faith, nor woman apart from man in reverence for the truth. Let the man fill the place of the head for women, who are the feet, and let the woman walk in the order assigned to the feet below. Let the man be like a tongue, a harp with strings, and continually sow chaste words in women's ears. Let women listen faithfully to the sound of his sayings, and bear the fruits of purity of soul, hope, and love.

Let the words from the sower's mouth not be deprived of their due, and let the hearing not close itself against the seed of the word of life. You, man, sow the word of life in women's ears; and you, women, receive and listen to the testimony of men. We owe one another a debt of love. Repay it to one another and to the Creator alike, as is fitting. Pure love can repay humanity’s debt, and it makes us friends of the Hidden One and of the spiritual beings. Men, love the one confession of the one Creator; women, love the one equality of the one God. Confess rightly, as befits the understanding within you: one being and [?] authority, three persons. Confess that he is an equal, undivided nature, and that he has existed from eternity just as he is, without beginning. Confess that he is Father and Son and the Spirit who comes from him: one who begets, one who is begotten, and one who proceeds. Confess the Father, who was never not the Father, and believe in the Son, between whom and his Father there is no interval of time. Praise and exalt the Spirit, who is one in being and is not inferior or lesser in authority than the Father and the Son. Rightly name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: a nature that is equal and is not divided by difference. The God of all does not change from what he is, and the nature of his being is not confined within a boundary. His [?] cannot be seen by the eye through the outward senses, and he has no perceptible voice like bodily beings. He is wholly self-existent, wholly hidden, and wholly equal; he is wholly perfect in his divinity and his creative activity. His command established heaven and earth and everything in them, and from nothing he created everything hidden and visible. He appointed a time for the work of his hands as it pleased him, and when he wished, he brought his hidden love into the open. He created everything because of his love, not for his own comfort. He showed his power to his creatures, but not his being. He established everything from nothing by the power of his will, and at the end of the ages he renewed everything in the image of his image.

The first coming into being from nothing belongs to him, and the renewal that takes place in one also belongs to him. In the beginning he fashioned things from nothing as the Creator, and now he has renewed the work of his hands as the Wise One. He established everything and renewed everything wisely, as befits the power of his being, which is hidden from all. In the human form he completed his work at the beginning, when he created; and in a human being he renewed and gave life at the end of the ages. In the human constitution he enclosed everything as in a house, and in the human form his will dwelt as in a temple. (a) In humanity he bound together the whole power of his creative activity, and through a human being he renews everything and judges everything. He called the human form his image when he established everything, and in it he appears as in an image when he judges everything. Human beings and spiritual beings see the human form administering judgment, examining wrongdoing, rejecting and choosing. In the temple of his body, all worship the God of all, and in his visible manifestation, all see the One hidden from all. With the outward senses they see the visible body, and through its movements, the invisible divinity. In his body their questions come to rest as in a harbor, and they do not wear themselves out searching for the hidden one concealed within it. In his love, earthly and heavenly beings are joined together, and in him they offer one song of thanksgiving to the one Creator. Come, let us approach the temple of his body in faith, and in it offer the sacrifices of love that his love requires. Come, let us worship in him as in a divine sanctuary, and in him praise the God of all in a manner worthy of God. Come, let us see in him, through faith, the one hidden from all, and believe in him in what is revealed and what is hidden, here and there. Through faith the mind can know these things, and she reveals to it the concealed mysteries of hidden things. Through her aid it sees distant things as though they were near, and they are as certain to it as though they had actually happened. In her hidden treasury lies the treasure of the life to come, and from her both spiritual and bodily beings are enriched. Like an anchor she is fastened to the world in the sea of passions, so that it will not drift among the surging waves of desires.

Come, let us moor the ship of our soul to her as to an anchor, and preserve love amid the crashing of turbulent waves. Come, let us travel with her as with a guide who knows what lies beyond, and through her reach the fulfillment of the kingdom on high. Come, let us examine the inclination of our soul in her as in a furnace, reject wickedness, and choose love, the friend of truth. Come, let us uncover before her the defects of our bodies and minds, and with her medicines heal our inward and outward pains. She is a good physician who knows how to treat the wounded, and there is no remedy that is not compounded and kept in her treasury. She knows how to heal the rich and the poor, and both the righteous and the wicked need her help. Come, rich man, reveal to her the pains of your oppression; give alms and receive medicine that heals your wickedness. Come, poor man, take refuge in the strength of her help, and work with her without losing heart for the denarius of life. Come, righteous man, deposit treasures in the strongholds of her love, and place the seal of her truthfulness upon your mind. Come, sinner, write and present to her the repentance of your mind; put down sorrow and [?] as a pledge, and receive forgiveness. Come, dissolute man, make yourself chaste through her humility, and clothe your limbs in the garment of holiness. Come, thief, stop wandering astray and walk in her [?]; wait in the hope she offers, for [?] she will give you the record of your debts. Come, adulterer, sanctify your body through her holiness, and sprinkle your whole self with the pure [?] of the mystery of forgiveness. Come, humble man, walk in the company of her humility, and arrive with her at the peaceful harbor where there is no sorrow. Foolish Eve, come, become wise through faith, and gain understanding to protect yourself from your adversary. Set its purity like a mirror before your mind, and polish away the filth upon your thoughts with the splendor of its beauty. Take off the covering of ignorance, the outward adornment,

and adorn yourself with the beautiful garment of humility. Clothe your body and your mind in modesty, and instead of being a snare, become a mirror for human eyes. Set the judgment of the world beyond as a goal before your eyes. Look and consider the promised reward and the torment. Sure and discerning is the judgment awaiting the good and the wicked, and everyone receives without end what they deserve. The good rejoice without end, and the wicked weep. According to their labors, delight is apportioned and punishment is multiplied. Come, let us trade while there is still time [?] to trade, lest the time of the end arrive and we lose the fruit of our labor. Come, let us make [?] friends for ourselves here with temporary wealth, so that they may receive us into their dwellings, which will never be dismantled. Let us attend with love to our fellow human beings and to our Maker, for love can make human beings divine. Let us judge justly with our own minds concerning the sins we have committed, and let our inclination rebuke itself like a discerning person. Let everyone repeat this saying to the inclination of their soul: the word of the God of all is living, and his judgment is just. Let the mind speak with the tongue about things to come, and explain to it the mysteries hidden in the realm above. Let the mind show the body's eyes a beautiful image of that delight whose sweetness can never be exhausted. Let us see it with the mind and long for it with the soul's love, so that at the end we may receive its riches face to face. Response: Glory to you, forgiver of sins, a thousand times a thousand times.
On Poverty
Thirteenth Discourse: On Poverty. Suitable for Supplication.

Wretched is the age that has met me during my sojourn, and the acquisition of spiritual life is despised in it. Evil is the way of life that has become second nature to me among earthly beings, and it is very difficult for anyone who wishes to live well. Confused is the life that has taken my days captive, beyond all other days, and it has no order befitting rational beings. Dim is the light of discernment, the second light, and no one seasons what is tasteless with the word of truth. Weak is the structure of faith, which supports everything, and no one teaches how to build well the purity of one's soul. Cold is love, whose heat burns far hotter than fire, and everyone boils with fierce anger against their neighbor. Weak is the expectation of hope that holds fast to the gate of the kingdom, while the body is strong in the soul's impulses, in its desire for earthly things. Life and books that make people wise are despised and scorned, and the pursuit of discernment and the Scriptures has ceased. Attention to spiritual things is considered worthless, and everyone pursues earthly things without ever being satisfied. The practice of holiness, a pure vessel, is held in low esteem, while the distraction of frivolity, foul mud, is loved. Marriage, the proper order established by the Creator, has been thrown into confusion, and everyone runs along the ugly road of adultery. Falsehood, murder, and adultery have multiplied on earth, and the fruits of love have vanished and disappeared from humanity. Sorcery, divination, omens, and empty practices have grown strong in creation, and they have persecuted truth so that it cannot rule among human beings. The dominion of demons, cruel in their deeds, has spread, and they have harnessed the world to the harsh yoke of their blasphemies.

The company of those who serve righteousness has dwindled, while everyone constantly works the earth without stopping. Very few love the study of spiritual things, while those who cherish earthly things are beyond counting. Earthly people occupy themselves with earthly things night and day, and the mind has no opportunity to lift its gaze toward the heights. Those invited and called to the kingdom above seek the things below, and they long to remain here in an earthly dwelling. Mortality has bound them with the cords of passions, and everyone finds the prison of mortality pleasant. No one notices the harshness of the weapon of suffering, and no one hopes to escape its harshness. They long to remain in a worn-out dwelling full of fear, and they do not yearn for that dwelling which cannot decay. Temporal possessions are honored and loved more than their lives, while the delight of the promised life is considered unreal. No one looks forward to that hope full of blessings, except by speaking of it in words rather than deeds. In words they recount all the good things that cannot be expressed, yet although these things are real, they are not real in their minds. The reality of the world to come is regarded as a tale, and everyone fears without truly fearing. True things are not true to those who are untrue, and they deceitfully display modesty in their deeds. Their limbs bear the outward appearance of love and affection for truth, but the movements of their souls reveal and testify to impurity. The body is adorned like a tree bearing fruit, but in the mind there is no cluster of steadfastness. My beloved's vineyard flourishes with leaves as though it were fruitful, but among its branches are hidden carobs that cannot be eaten. The time that has overtaken me among earthly people is like winter.

And like trees, people are stripped of good things. The frost of wickedness has gripped the land of rational beings, and the workers have ceased their labor of doing good. The snow of wickedness fell on the impulses as on mountains; it blocked the road, and no one walks toward righteousness. Love of money battered the soul like hail, and the leaves of faith fell from the mind. Wickedness blew like a storm over the lake of the mind, and the helmsman, the skilled reasoning faculty, trembled and was bewildered. The fierce blast of habitual practices struck creation, and the thoughts that had not built the structure of love well tottered. Oppression set the earth ablaze with inequality; peace grew hot, mercy dried up, and compassion vanished. Love of truth entered and burrowed among the thoughts; like a mole cricket it struck and dried up the root of the soul. Pride, the tyrant, rebelled on the cliff of arrogance and began waging war against the ranks of humility. Gnawing envy lay in ambush on the roads before travelers and bit the world with the hard fangs of its bitterness. Like a caterpillar, despair crawled through the human mind; it ate the fruit, stripped off the leaves, and left only the root. The mind remained like a root, without deeds, and only a little vitality remained in it. The vineyard of Adam's vines, endowed with reason, was ruined and dried up, and savage demons trampled it like passersby. Not a single grape remained in it undamaged; and if one did remain, it contained no delightful wine. Woe to us, lest the owner of the vineyard bring us to judgment and accuse us of ingratitude, as he did the Jews. Woe to us, lest he summon the speechless elements of creation to bear witness against our wickedness, which has denied his love. Let us say, “Woe to us,” with the herald, the prophet of the Spirit, for people have become summer gleanings, as it is written. There is no cluster in our vineyard pleasant to eat, nor any early fruit to delight the will that planted it. Our Lord says, as in the voice of prophecy, “The godly have perished, and there is no longer anyone upright among human beings.” Deceit is in their hearts, and falsehood on their lips.

Like hunters, they conceal snares in their tongues. The person in authority brazenly makes unjust demands, and the judge too rapaciously demands more. The great man speaks as he pleases and is not contradicted; in his arrogance, he regards people as though they were not human. Whoever teaches does so out of pride and not out of [?]; whoever learns eagerly attends his teacher out of love of rank. Neither does the teacher aim at the goal of the master, Christ, nor does the student follow the discipline of discipleship. The light of teaching is dim for the students, and the taste of discipleship is bland in the mouths of teachers. The proud teacher teaches words, not deeds; the student, too, hears words, not their meaning. With eyes of flesh he instructs children in words of the Spirit, and shows bodily members the powers of hidden things. Flesh looks at spiritual things in a fleshly way, and the revelation of things to come is regarded as a shadow. Through bodily senses, a human being engages with what is beyond the senses, and gazes in bewilderment at divine mysteries as though in a dream. When truth is recounted in our generation, it resembles a dream; perhaps, to fools, a dream is more trustworthy than truth. A dream is trustworthy to the untrustworthy, even though it is utterly false; when it is recounted, they long to encounter it more than the truth. Truth cries out in the Scriptures, but no one listens; the ears of earthly people incline to hear earthly things. He runs continually among the letters, all alone, while a great crowd travels the broad road of wickedness. His radiance is brighter than the sun to those who see clearly, but those in darkness love darkness more than his light. His company is more desirable than gold and pearls, yet lovers of silver never even perceive that he exists. He is sweeter to the palate than honey and honeycomb, but to the wicked his drink is bitter and unacceptable. To those who love him, his company is dear and his food delightful; but to the unjust, even speaking about him is difficult. The prophet cries out that he is more precious than everything and sweeter than everything, but to the careless his taste is insipid and his company despised. David undertook to keep his words diligently.

But the sluggish of heart fled from him as from something evil. Evil people considered communion with truth evil, and recoiled from his drink as from medicine with a pungent smell. Mortals lie afflicted with the severe pains of lusts; that is why the word of truth bears so harshly upon their ailments. People sick in soul resemble someone sick in body who is afraid to reveal the severity of his illness to physicians. Sinners, too, are deeply afraid because of their sins, and do not approach the door of Truth, the physician who treats without charge. They are deeply ashamed to show him the sickness within them, and do not realize that an illness that has grown old is difficult to cure. In ignorance they conceal the sores of their deeds, and do not consider that after death there is no healing. They go astray in the hope of mercy that grants favor freely, and do not understand that if there is mercy, there is also justice. [?] that there is mercy, O human being; then accept that there is justice that cannot be overcome. If mercy prevails in judgment, there is no justice; and if the Just One judges justly, there is no pity. If he is just, let us therefore accept that his judgment is just, and learn clearly that he is just and good, but not without distinction. Everything created readily acknowledges that the Creator is just, and his love toward our race bears witness that he is merciful. With discernment we should call him just and good: good to the one who repents, and just when he calls the unrepentant to account. It is clear to us that our inclination has power over both, and, if it pleases, can change scourges into mercy. And if the store of the treasures of life and death is placed within it, why is our evil inclination so brazenly blamed? Our inclination holds the gate of the kingdom, if we so wish; it is what brings us in and what sends us out, according to its will. That voice which opened the way to the kingdom on high also cried out that the kingdom is within people and dwells in them. And if the kingdom, full of life, dwells within people, then no one is more foolish than a person who hates his own life. How could someone who hates the truth not be a hater of his own life,

when he abandons the path that guarantees life and walks in error? A person stands against his own inclination and against the truth: though he has understanding, he wrongs himself and his Maker. Mortals have committed a great wrong against the life within them, for they despised the law the Creator established to govern them. They abandoned the commandment that exalted them above everything, and cherished the love of the devil, who disgraced them. They despised the Name that honored them with its glories, and gave the honor of the name of majesty to what is not God. They trampled on the law—light, salt, and guide—which opens the way, gives flavor, and enlightens the mind. They broke through his commandments, the high wall against wrongdoing, and the wild beasts—evil habits—entered and ruined its fruits. Wild asses, bears, and lions—the various kinds of evil—rushed upon the vineyard of the law that people were to cultivate. Gnats, locusts, and flies—contemptible crawling creatures—gathered upon its leaves, knocked off its fruits, and scattered its produce. Like crawling creatures, brutish thoughts swarmed, clung, and reached the lofty heights of the law of the Spirit. Body and soul became unruly and were inflamed with desires, and they paid no attention to the shamefulness of their thoughts. Sexual immorality took on a dog's shamelessness against the truth, and however much the truth rebukes its debasement, it remains as it is. Theft took hold of the boldness of a ravenous wolf, and even if ten thousand voices cry out against it, it is not deterred. Unruly envy, which gives birth to murder, raged like a lion and raised its voice against judges and their rebukes. Oppression became like a shameless bear, and the more it drinks the blood of the oppressed, the more it thirsts. The love of gain hid snares in the sea and on land, and captured peoples and cities within its embrace. The love of glory stopped its ears against understanding, and like a viper despised the power within the Scriptures. Falsehood, the daughter of the Evil One, who fathered her in Eden:

She has surpassed her father in the art of slander. She resembles a fox in her deceitful dealings, and she slips into hollows in the ground so that she will not be exposed. Pride is a wild ass wandering senselessly through the wilderness; it has rebelled against the yoke of humility, which brings people peace. Gluttony is a devouring Sheol that is never filled. It has swallowed the world without realizing that it has eaten anything. Grumbling is a pest, insignificant in appearance but devastating in the damage it does. It passed over the field of discernment and ruined its fruit. Anger blazed like fire in the forest of the soul, and the senses and impulses burned together in its heat. Good things were burned and scorched as though by fire, and no fruit of delight remained in the vineyard of humanity. Agitations entered the inner judge like wild beasts, ate its fruit, and left it bare as in winter. The harsh winter of desires has lingered in creation, and the world has ceased its spiritual work. The darkness of error, a second night, has overpowered truth, and falsehood has risen to a high rank above what is true. Good deeds have dwindled like daylight in the winter months, and evil deeds have grown strong like the lengthening nights. In our generation there is nothing resembling summer in the work of life, and no one sweats in the face of agitations as one does in the heat. As in winter, the mind is confined within the temple of the body, and the frost of wickedness hinders its diligence. In passing things, summer is pleasant to earthly people; but in the things to come, they are content to remain in gloomy winter. For the work of wickedness, the succession of the year's months is too short; but for the practice of righteousness, there is not even a single day. In shameful deeds, summer and winter pass without anyone growing weary; but in upright deeds, half a day brings much grumbling. There is no having enough of gathering provisions for this passing time, but concern for gaining life is hidden away as something superfluous. Fools regard concern for the spirit as something superfluous, and, as though it were night, they remain quiet and idle when it comes to good deeds. The body, together with the mind, is sunk as though in sleep, and they do not awaken at the voice of admonition that brings life. The sleep of wickedness is dearly loved by the lazy,

and they take no pleasure in hearing the call announcing the morning. The children of poverty long to remain in poverty, and they have no desire for the great wealth hidden on high. In the realm on high, delight that never perishes is hidden; but earthly people love the earth far more than the heights. He has promised our human nature heavenly things that cannot be seen, but those made of dust wish to remain in the dust. He has fixed on high the living target promised by his words, but no one attempts, even in words, to aim toward it. By the power of the Spirit he explained things to come, and through his heralds he [?] them as though with a finger. As on a tablet, he depicted blessings and punishments in scrolls, so that eyes of flesh might be able to see hidden things. Like an image, he fixed his commandments in the Scriptures, so that people might see the truth of his name through visible things. Within the palace of the Scriptures he portrayed his hidden nature, so that everyone might enter and gaze upon his being through [?] letters. He wished to show the greatness of his love to the work of his hands, so he wrote a book and lovingly taught them to read. He depicted the power of his greatness in letters, not his being; he enclosed his activity in scrolls, not his hidden nature. For humanity's comfort he built the palace of the Scriptures, and brought into it a record of the mysteries of his hidden things. He made the spiritual law like a treasury, gathering and filling it with sentences of judgment against transgressors. He built himself a royal house on earth, full of every created thing, and authorized people to live in it in holiness. He stored within it the boundless treasure of the Spirit, so that it would suffice for those on earth and those in heaven. He made his beloved children, who are called by his name, its treasurers, so that they might distribute it wisely, as people of understanding. The guardians of the divine treasure became thieves and exchanged the wealth of glorious things for contemptible things. The members of the palace disclosed the secrets of the one who appoints kings, and raised their hand against the Creator who had honored them. The king's servants fled from the king who reigns over all, and conspired with the rebel to become his. The children of the kingdom abandoned the concerns of the royal house and began talking about the affairs of farming.

The bridegroom's invited guests hated spiritual delight and went out wandering along the roads to trade. The children of God, who had been worthy of the name of immortals, descended from their divine rank and stood upon the earth. The mortals who had been called immortals died, and gave up hope of ever returning to the name they had lost. In everything they betrayed the hidden command that had honored them. They despised his law and treated lightly his words, which cannot be undone. Through the law he tested them to show how much they hated him, and through the Scriptures he examined the falseness of their thoughts. Through his commandments he brought them into something like a furnace. He purified them, yet they were not purified of their foul deeds. Come, then, let us speak as an echo of prophecy: the Spirit refined us in vain in the furnace of the law. Let us recount our disgrace, as Jeremiah did to his people: discipline proved useless against our wickedness. Our faithlessness closely resembles that of the Jews, and our mind has rebelled against instruction even more than theirs. Our people did not hate the words of the Spirit as much as we do, nor did they doubt the things to come as we do. The Israelites did not despise and reject their teachers as the nations reviled and insulted those who know the truth. The Creator’s name was not blasphemed among the Hebrews as the pagans have reviled our faith. The people were children in relation to perfect conduct, and, considering their time, they were not greatly blameworthy for their insolence. The nations, who received the perfect worker of the kingdom above, returned to degrading practices far more than children did. They abandoned the incorruptible food set out in Scripture and went back to sucking the thin milk of observances. They constantly revile Judaism and paganism, without realizing how much more contemptible they are than both. They argue with them about why they stray from the truth, without noticing that they themselves stray more than those who are astray. The pagans honor their gods as good beings, while the honor of the God of all is despised by his worshipers. The teaching of every heresy is loved by its hearers,

while the teaching of truth is despised and insulted by its ministers. The Jews occupy themselves with observances that are not true; although utterly rejected, they are very diligent, like members of the household. The Manichaeans keep the order established by their teachers and do not relax their way of life, although it is false. The Marcionites repay their teachers with love, and although they are liars, they put on the appearance of truth. The followers of Arius are very zealous about what is written, and they build extensively on a foundation that is not sound. The Magi struggle for Magianism, a fabrication of demons, and honor it as something that exists, although it does not exist. There is no people in creation that forgets the one it worships or changes its worship of the lord it serves. Let the voice that chose him, then, awaken the son of Hilkiah, so that he may arise and astonish the mute elements as before. Arise, Jeremiah, and judge justly as you used to do, and summon heaven and earth as witnesses against our wickedness. The nations too have committed two evils, just like the people: they abandoned contemplation of spiritual things and loved earthly things. They abandoned the law, the sweet spring that pours forth life, and dug out the fabrication of falsehood—cracked cisterns. Among the nations too, his saying that the people were slaves has been fulfilled, for they abandoned the truth and desired dealings with worthless things. It is fitting that lions should roar against them too, for they themselves opened the demons’ mouths to blaspheme. The Babylonians and Assyrians roared against the Hebrews; against us, behold, the Accuser roars, a speaking lion. Nations more wicked than the people plundered them when they acted wickedly,

and because we have sinned, passions and demons are now trampling us. The people received punishment for their wrongdoing at the hands of the nations; but the scourging for our wrongdoing awaits us on the day of examination. Our punishment, then, exceeds that of the Jews: he scourged them by human hands, but will scourge us himself. His punishment is far harsher than human punishment. Paul bears witness that it is a terrible thing to fall into his hands. His word is living and far sharper than a sword; as with fire, it tests the falsehood within the soul. He brings to judgment the thoughts that desired evil and exposes them before angels and human beings. He brings a great case against our discernment, which wronged itself and his holy utterances. With righteous judgment he tramples down the wrongdoing of our insolence, which despised his words and did not shrink from violating his commandments. Wisely he inflicts scourges for our evil deeds, because we have trampled on the order established in nature and in the Scriptures. Skillfully he weighs our labors in the scales of his will: he rejects what is worthless and chooses what is perfectly sound. His command is full of harsh punishment and doubled scourges for the insolent who did not consider his sentences beforehand. He demands [?] for his great love and his threats, because he showed his love and his scourges beforehand, but they neither discerned nor understood. In proportion to his promises, he demands all the more from the members of his household, because they did not long to await the life to come. He recorded the promise of life without end in his books, so that people might see in the Scriptures what has no end. Through his prophets he opened a clear road full of peace, so that everyone might travel amid terrors toward the festivals. He set the Law like a mirror among earth’s inhabitants, so that they might look into it and see their own blemishes. Through the Law he showed two things to anyone who looks into it: promised blessings and grievous scourges for anyone who despises it. On account of both he brings us to judgment and scourges us. We desired blessings and hated scourges, as discerning people do. Our discernment ought to have chosen what is fitting; because we did not choose, he is going to separate us from his promises.

Our reason was required to pursue the truth; because it did not pursue it, now it is pursued in righteous judgment. Our indebtedness obliged us to repay him with praise; because it did not repay him, now repayment is exacted from it without mercy. For we deserve to be held doubly accountable, because we did not condemn our shameful deeds by judging ourselves. Who is as blind to understanding as we are, since we do not judge ourselves before the fearful judgment comes? Who has a heart of stone as hard as ours, since we have been softened neither by promises nor by threats? Harsh measures proved ineffective against our rebelliousness, and gentle measures proved excessive for the sluggishness of our souls. The heralds have grown weary in the Scriptures, and no one listens; the strength of their tongues has failed from crying out. Types and portions have come to an end, yet our wickedness remains. Visions and revelations too have ceased, while he remains as he is. The route of the heavenly messengers has been brought to an end, yet the course of our insolence has not ceased from doing hateful things. Only the speechless were sent as messengers, and now it is quite clear that even they have not ceased from this. Even the silent have sternly rebuked us, though entirely speechless; instead of using a voice, they have spoken to us through their changes. The sun that grew dark hid its light because of our hateful deeds, and the moon that became dim—our insolence turned it to blood. The lightning flashes that burned were kindled by the fire of our anger, and the thunderclaps that shook things grew stronger through the sound of our blasphemy. The earth that shook found our wickedness heavy upon its shoulders; as though crying out with a mouth, it rebuked us through its trembling. The summer that scorched the fruit with heat was inflamed by our envy, and the winter that lingered in its cold was prolonged by our grumbling. Our illnesses, which have multiplied, were born of our evil inclinations; and we ourselves urged hurried death to hurry and carry off our souls. The nation that fought against another nation—we drove it on; and the king who was brought low and defeated in battle—our sins defeated him. Through us the well-ordered structure of government has been thrown into confusion.

And through us the exalted rank bearing the name of priesthood has been dishonored. Through our contentiousness, strife entered and reigned over the earth; and now priests and kings fight against one another. Openly and secretly, everyone wages war against his neighbor, and there is no end to their fighting, night or day. All ranks are caught in the harsh frost of discord, and on every side traps lie hidden before those who walk. One mind dwells in anxiety and fear of another, and there is no one who trusts, nor anyone whose love for another is steadfast. Everyone speaks to his neighbor with a double heart, and the heart is anxious, since the words do not agree with the heart. His tongue is straightforward, his speech friendly, and his voice bright; yet his heart is crooked, his voice angry, and his appearance dark. The encounter of faces with [?] is radiant and cheerful, but the inward inclination is mourning and gloomy, as though over a dead person. The mouth lovingly kisses the mouth that is its counterpart, while the mind digs deep and treacherously hides traps. It is a great danger to journey toward the meeting place, the harbor of life, for the passions lie hidden as though asleep in the sea of the soul. Who can travel the road to the kingdom on high? Thoughts lie in ambush, concealed like robbers. Rightly, then, I called the age that has overtaken me evil, for it is evil, troubled, and full of danger for anyone traveling through it. Rightly I pronounced woe upon myself at the beginning of my words, for the sustenance of life has vanished and ceased in the years of life, in the years of my life. In my days the scripture has been fulfilled: the godly person has perished, and there is no one in creation who repents inwardly in his mind. I too have spoken words, but I have not done deeds, and I am far more deprived of good things than my companions. My thoughts, like those of my companions, are full of a forest of sins, and in my mind there is no fruit pleasing to the owner of the vineyard. I have put words together like a guilty man before the judge, hoping that mercy might bend toward my guilt at the judgment. Under the pretext of words, I entered to hire myself out at the end of the day, hoping that I might be worthy of a tiny coin in payment of wages.

I heard the sound of that voice calling to the hired workers, and it urged me to hire out my tongue in the work of words. The command that ordered wages to be given, a denarius apiece, said to me, “Get up and work diligently, lowly laborer!” May the mercy that hired our lowly race for the service of truth make me too worthy of payment—the denarius of life.
For the fifth Sunday of the Fast.
Discourse fourteen [?]. For the fifth Sunday of the Fast. Response: Good One, who reconciled the world to yourself, bring peace to our disposition, troubled by its envy, my brothers.

I was traveling on the king’s highway toward the goal of the kingdom. Blind envy met me, led along by the evil inclination. Envy stood at the crossroads, looking for evil things. It was asking travelers which road was good. It clothed itself in an appearance of compassion and asked as though out of love. But the gall of death was hidden

beneath the splendid garment of its lips. It wanted many people to travel with it on the broad road. That was why it asked: to seek companions for destruction. The evil inclination was guiding doubly blind envy. The blind was leading the blind to the appointed meeting at the gate of Gehenna. Envy hired a deceitful worker for the work of evil. He was to persevere in his toil throughout the hours of night and day. It [?] a counterfeit denarius for him, stamped with the image of death. It promised him torment if he led others astray and committed great wickedness. From the morning of the beginning [?], he began the work of injustice. He extended his bitter labor until the evening of the end. Envy does not grow weary of the long stretch from beginning to end. Nor do its workers ever grow tired or slacken in their labor. It grows young, ever young, day by day, like an eagle. As its ugliness is renewed, it pays out its bitter interest. It does not fear old age or weaken through sickness. Even someone old and feeble is young and strong when it comes to great envy. However old an envious person may be, in envy he is younger than a child. Even if he lacks knowledge, he is fully skilled in wicked jealousy. The envious person is doubly blind [?], deprived of the light of truth. As with night and day, falsehood and truth are alike to him. The envious person is deaf and senseless: he does not hear the voice of the commandment. He is deprived of hearing and speech by his own free choice, not by nature. The envious man is sick, wasting away in his inner impulses, not in his limbs. While he thinks he is entirely healthy, he is wasting away completely without knowing it. His soul is sick with envy, and he burns every day with jealousy. He does not sense the flame blazing within his mind. The evil inclination adds the fire of anger within his mind and feeds it with the wood of wrath, to burn one person by means of another. Its flame is far hotter than natural fire, and it burns the hidden soul,

not the outward body. Its edge is far more vicious than a sword or a double-edged blade. There is no counting the people it strikes down at every moment. It is accustomed to human blood and thirsts for the slaughter of humanity. It ruins the inner impulses together with the senses, soul and body alike. Those slain by the sword are many, but not like those slain by envy. [?] of the sword continually. What, then, is this envy, hidden yet revealed by its deeds? Though it has no existence of its own, it destroys living beings at every moment. My thoughts grew bewildered as I investigated it, seeking to discover its beginning and the root that bears its branches and bitter fruits. Who, then, cultivates the evil soil of its weeds? Who gathers its harvests and supplies its armies? With what weapons does it wage war against spiritual and bodily beings? Through which senses does it fight against the champions of righteousness? Who, then, assists it and secretly gives it strength? How does it grow mighty, though contemptible, and overpower the ranks of mighty warriors? My thoughts were astonished and amazed at its unjust victory: how does this contemptible thing triumph and bow the heads of champions? My mind urged me to examine and investigate envy: does it triumph through what belongs to it, or perhaps through what does not belong to it? My inclination secretly advised me [?] and showed me a path to follow. It became like a guide for me to the appointed end of the journey. The Spirit's help set before me a goal full of victory,

so that I might take aim at it through my inner impulses and strike down wicked envy. As though in a mystery, the great power of grace spoke with me: “If you wish to learn, take the road from the beginning. Travel with the books of Scripture, accompanied by the words of the Spirit. They will bring you to the harbor of what your thoughts have sought. Join the son of Amram and go with him to the beginning. He will show you where the bitterness of envy sprang from. Read the account of the sixth day and consider it carefully. There your mind will find an understanding of the cause you sought. See there the formation of humanity, and hear the voice that [?] the image.” And at the end of the saying, see the beginning of envy. The envious one heard the word “image”—he who is called by the hidden image. The gall of death stirred within him at the sound of the formation of the one made from dust. The fire of his passion blazed up within him, the tyrant, the ruler of the air. It burned entirely with envy, and he kindled a fire among humanity. He broke open the reservoir of his hatred and poured his gall upon human beings. He stained creation’s garment with the deadly poison of desire for the fruit. He loosened the bond that had been joined through the hidden knowledge of the Hidden One. He disturbed the peace that had been blended with the love and mercy of the Maker of all. He divided the dwelling of equals and separated them from one another. He made relatives strangers to one another. Through envy the evil one sowed his error among mortals. He made sin spring up in their senses, and they blossomed with poisonous fruit. He overthrew the honored image and cast it to the ground as something despised. He handed it over to death as a pledge, and rejoiced and laughed at its humiliation. Here is the beginning of envy. Read and understand, you who have knowledge. See his deceit and learn its cause: what he did from the beginning. Read his history thoughtfully, and you will understand his schemes. Listen to his deeds with discernment, and you will discover his secrets.

He ruined the beauty of the handiwork of the Craftsman who adorned everything. Then he reviled him as evil, saying that he had withheld his wisdom out of wickedness. He made the gall of evil spring up and caused the worship of gods to gush forth. He reviled the Eternal One through his handiwork, as though it had been fashioned imperfectly. Here is the foundation of the building of the deceitful one, the worker of falsehood. Look, builders of truth! Flee from the wickedness of his work. Here are the letters of the teaching of the foolish teacher of the left. Look, disciples of the right! Do not study foolishly. Here is the cup of his deadly gall, which he mixed and gave our nature to drink. Let no one [?] his drink, lest he be destroyed by death. Here is the broad road that the murderer laid out through his schemes. Take care not to travel in his company, you who journey on the narrow road. See, the scribe of the Spirit has revealed to you, O mind, the answer to the question you asked. Travel among the lines of the Scriptures toward the goal he has set before you. Put on the armor of the word of truth and fight spiritually. Shoot words instead of arrows against the deceitful ranks of envy. Mix spiritual eye medicine for the mind that the evil one has troubled. Temper the gall of evil with the sweetness of the sound of your words. Bring peace to the angry through the word of peace of the One who brought peace to all. Call them to the harmony that bound creation’s love together. Encourage the distressed with the promise of the kingdom on high. Repeat to them that saying: whoever endures will live. Read to those killed through envy the passage about Abel’s death. Let them hear the cry of the blood that cries out from the earth. Open the royal archives and read the judicial decrees. Show the punishment of murderers, recorded by the king’s pen. Go out to the plain with the brothers and see envy triumphing. The deceitful inclination of the insolent helps it win its victory. From this learn its tricks and the depth of its treacherous traps, and prepare subtle means

that expose its hidden schemes. Envy had clothed itself in the guise of love and went to battle against Abel. With a sign of peace it deceived him and led him out into the wilderness to be slaughtered. It saw the fruitful beauty of his victories, and sorrow clothed it. For it is ugly and does not wish to see someone whose mind is beautiful. Envy made the fruit of murder spring up in the land of curses. Through her the deed bore its first fruit, [?] the sentence passed on the tree. It gave the afflicted one a cup of blood [?], but she would not accept it. For she was sick from the lashes she had suffered through the transgression of the commandment. She retched and vomited out the blood, for she was not accustomed to drinking it. Nor did the blood itself remain in her: it cried out and rose from her bosom. O silent blood that cried out with the voice of beings endowed with speech! O heavy one, lifted up on the wings of the wind to the heights! O one slain and buried in the earth, whose voice spoke like thunder! O one covered and concealed, who went out in pursuit of his murderer! O blind envy, which doubled poison upon poison in its deeds! While it thought its deceit was concealed, it revealed righteousness as clearly as the sun. O deceitful one, who exposes himself unknowingly while practicing his tricks! O crafty one, who displays the emptiness of his mind while acting wisely! Envy [?] the innocent man and covered him with a garment of deceit. But the all-knowing command laid bare the covering of its craftiness. It exposed and revealed its ugliness through the sentence passed on the murderer. It showed generations and families the punishment for its injustice. Come, you envious people, and consider the great crime of envy, which shed innocent blood and concealed it from the One who knows everything. Come, you who hate your brothers without cause, as Cain did, and listen to the blood speaking and the hidden command answering it. Come and consider the punishment of the murderer who killed without cause. Take this example of justice and see how fitting it is for murderers.

Let the lashes inflicted on the deceitful one be an example to the evil inclination, so that it does not run wickedly along the paths of murder. Let the seven lashes inflicted on Cain be like a mirror for it. Let it secretly recognize itself in the trembling and shaking of his body. Let the mind say to the inclination, “See that you do not envy without cause, lest you become liable to punishment seven times seven, seventy times over.” Let everyone hate envy, for envy gives birth to murder. Let everyone flee from murder, for the punishment for murder is bitter. Envy is the root of murder, and from it its branches sprout. Whoever eats its fruit, the gall of death spreads within him. Envy brought forth in creation a new murder, the first of its kind. The envious began following in its footsteps with one purpose. Envy set a treacherous aim: to shed innocent blood. It taught the treacherous to shoot with the bow of deceit. It dimmed the soul’s light and blinded the movements of the mind. The whole person was darkened, deprived of the light of discernment. It made the rational faculty like crawling creatures without speech. The discerning mind forgot the wisdom of its rational nature. Envy armed the mind to fight against its loved ones. The person endowed with understanding did not notice that he was destroying his companions. With envy’s weapons the envious prevail and overpower the ranks of righteousness. In the night of its darkness they shoot arrows at the radiant one. It trains the envious person to engage in battle against truth. It teaches him methods of warfare, so that he may fight under the guise of love. Under the guise of love the envious person fights like someone full of zeal. Although he is an enemy of truth, he poses as a lover of peace. The envious person clothes himself in zeal, like someone demanding that duty be fulfilled. He displays his zeal deceitfully and undermines everyone’s duty. He harbors irreconcilable anger at the report of good things. Although the good person has not wronged him, he accuses everyone and grumbles. You hater of righteousness, why do you quarrel with the truthful? What wrong have the blameless done you,

that you slander them all? You who are blind by choice, why do you fight against the light? How have the rays of its splendid light harmed your blindness? If your own will has deprived you of truth, the light of both, why do you complain foolishly, when the light has not wronged you? Your wickedness shut the door against the light in your eyes. You yourself have deprived yourself of the light of righteousness. There is no justification for your treachery. Why are you envious? Even your alleged reason is no reason at all, but a deceptive pretense. To show you that you are indeed a liar and that your accusations are false, I will bring evidence of your wrongdoing from actual deeds. What is the reason you hated him, the radiant temple of revelations? When did he insult you as you insulted him? Where did he revile you as you reviled him? When did he repay you justly for the evil injuries you had lent him? Show openly how he wronged you, and then there will be grounds for your grumbling. Bring witnesses who will put their seals on the document of your falsehood. But far be it! Let it never happen that your deceit should overcome truth. You have no grounds, you wrongdoer, for opposing the company of the truthful. You envy the upright for no reason, though they have done no harm to your wickedness. Without cause you are constantly jealous, and you disturb the peace of the humble. The evil inclination incites you against the company of those who love righteousness. With the sword of the Accuser you destroy the ranks of those on the right. You deprived Abel of life so that he would not sow the word of life. You sold Rachel’s son so that his freedom of soul would not blossom. You drove Jacob from his fathers’ dwelling to another land. And you removed Jacob’s son from his brothers to the land of the Egyptians. Job, the diligent worker who labored in the vineyard of truth—you stripped him of his [?] and of the sound structure of his limbs.

It was you who carried off his possessions, and you who weakened his bodily frame. At your prompting his friends reviled him, and he became hateful to his relatives. Who would not flee your company, envy, you who hate your friends? Who would not hate dealings with you, destroyer of good things? Who is as blind as you, and who is deaf like you? For light is darkness to you, and a truthful report is deceit. You look and do not see, and you listen without understanding. You call good evil, and you name evil good. Among everything evil, there is nothing comparable that can match your wickedness. For you turn what is sweet into bitterness, and you make the sweetness of truth bitter. There is no people you have not divided through strife against one another. And there is no kingdom you have allowed to remain at peace for a single day. You tore apart the garment of harmony that had been woven with love for everyone. You exposed people’s modesty and made them contemptible. Alas for you, disturber of peace, who weaken everyone’s love! You have divided those who were equals into factions of every kind. Alas for you, killer of people, who destroy life through death! You have made rational beings fight against their own lives. Tell me, merciless accursed one, how have mortals sinned against you, that you have incited them through jealousy constantly to destroy their own ranks? In your gardens, King of righteousness, rescue our weak nature, which is captive to its bitter inclination and enslaved to it. Come, grace, to our aid, and stand in our defense as you are accustomed to do. For unless your help arrives, our nature will sink into envy. Spread the wings of your kindness and shelter our race from our inclination. For look, it seeks to tear us apart with the fierce fangs of envy. Envy made us strangers to the fellowship of your help. It drove us out of the inheritance that you gave us from the beginning. Envy sold our freedom, and we became slaves to sin. It brought us from greatness

down to the lowliness of mortality. The bitter inclination imprisoned us in the prison of curses. It shut the bolt in our faces so that we could not escape its bondage. Who is as blind as we are to the understanding of what is right? Our murderer lives within us, yet we are unaware of his presence. Who is as deaf as a human being, who does not heed the account of his own life? Everyone destroys himself through the envy of his evil inclination. The envious man has sharpened the sword of his mind against himself. When he thinks he is striking his neighbor, his sword turns back and strikes him in the heart. He thinks he is killing his fellow with the blows of his tongue, but he does not realize that the arrows scattered by his lips turn back upon him. He constantly stirs up strife to make room for his envy. He devises more and more pretexts to bring his deeds into the open. He casts zeal before the simple like grain before a bird. He spreads his deadly snares and entangles those of every size. The envious man leads his fellows astray with a deceitful appearance. He presents himself to people as someone who counsels good things. Everyone clothes himself in sorrow and wraps himself in the name of compassion. He speaks peace with his lips, while a sword is sharpened in his mind. He grieves and shows concern for his neighbor as though caring for a member of his own body. Yet he watches for a chance to find an opening to carry out his desire. Let the envious man who hates his brothers be called a second Saul. Saul offered comfort while deceitfully calling out, “My son David!” Saul poured out deceitful tears before the son of Jesse. His mouth was full of sobs, while his mind sharpened a sword. With his lips he called him “my son,” while hating him in his secret thoughts. His tongue spoke beautifully, but the speech of his mind was twisted. He called out, “Come back! Do not be afraid, my son David! I will not harm you.” Yet his thoughts were sharpened for murder like those of a robber. His eyes shed tears with sobbing, and his mouth cried out deceitfully. His face was cunningly downcast, while his heart longed for blood. The inward impulses signaled to the body's outward senses,

“Multiply and devise pretexts for deceptive appearances.” His mind was bold for murder, like an executioner, while his tongue softened its voice like a lover speaking to his beloved. O envy, how bitter you are! Nothing compares with your deceitfulness. The wickedness of the whole inhabited world cannot equal your evil. O deceit, deceitful through and through, with no room in it for honesty! O crafty one, who constantly dispenses gall in the guise of sweetness! O harp fitted with strings that stretch out deceitful schemes! O furious flute, whose voice sings of deadly poison! Sweet and enticing is the sound of its melodies as it sings deceitfully. And at the end of his melodies, the gall of death lies hidden for his listeners. The sound of his singing tickles every ear that listens to him. When his voice reaches the soul, he disturbs it and carries away its serenity. He presents himself in the guise of a friend when he first begins to speak. But the ending of his speech is worse than an enemy or a murderer. Let us see his wickedness in Saul: how greatly he poured it out upon David. Although it was as plainly visible as the sun, he concealed it under the guise of sorrow. Let the envious look at Saul, whose mind envy blinded. He did not see the beauty of the victories of Jesse’s son, or how delightful they were. Let the spiteful, who hate their brothers without cause, consider him. Because he became so intensely hostile, envy killed him at the hands of the uncircumcised. Let David be a mirror for those who are envied in their afflictions. He endured disgrace and persecution and received his crown through perseverance alone. Let those who cherish spiritual love imitate the purpose of his love. For he composed songs of lamentation, mourning tenderly over the man who sought to kill him. Let everyone learn from Saul alone the evil end of envy. And in David let us see how sweet the fruits of love are. Let us consider the two kings: one who envied, and another who was envied. Envy killed the envious man, and love kept the envied man alive. In Saul, envy showed us how greatly it hates those close to it. And in David, love taught us how greatly it loves its dear ones. Look, his hidden deceit has been revealed to us

by the death of Saul, the envious man. Let our minds not become entangled in the hidden snares of envy’s schemes. Look, Jesse’s son has taught us how to overcome envy’s ambushes. Like David, let us temper the gall of the envious with the sweetness of love. Let love speak through David’s mouth to envy, a second Saul: “How have I sinned against you, envious one, that you persecute me like Saul?” Let the envied person entrust the judgment of his wrongs to the one who examines hidden things. For he will condemn the envious person to punishment, as he did Saul. Through Saul’s death, the harsh punishment of the envious was proclaimed. And through the exaltation of Jesse’s son, the crown of victory for the wronged was proclaimed. You who are wronged by envy, do not be distressed by the sound of the envious person’s insults. Endure and remain silent like David, so that in the end you may reign with him. Do not boast, envious one, of lying slander. For your sword is destined to enter your own heart, as it did Saul’s. Do not think, envy, that through arrogance you have overcome the discerning. Against your will, you have vindicated them, for they stood firm against your schemes. You have been condemned from the moment you came into being, and no victory has been won by you. For your victory is disgrace, and your triumph is shame. When have your deeds succeeded except in a rotten stump? And where has your hateful deceit prevailed except in insolent pride? You are blind, deprived of light, and you do not perceive the truth. You hate good things and love evil things. You see the speck in your brother’s eye as though it were a beam. But the beam in your own eyes—you do not even think it exists. First remove envy, the fierce anger in your mind, and then take issue with your companion over the failing in his soul. Why do you strain out gnats, you fraud, while swallowing beasts? Why do you cleanse your bodily members while your inward impulses are unclean? Why do you quarrel with sinners as though you were a perfect example of righteousness? When have you shown your concern by seeking justice on behalf of truth?
