Shame on you, deceiver! How greatly you mislead through truth! For although truth hates deceitful people, you deceitfully carry its banner. Shame on you, doubly blind one, to whom light and darkness are alike! While light gladdens everyone, you are gloomy before its rays. Let the discerning marvel at you—how utterly you are deprived of truth! Let those who understand weep over you, for although you are alive, you are doubly dead. Your life is no life, for through your life you destroy life. If only you had died at the beginning, and death had been brought to an end by your death! You were the first to mark out the road of death for humanity. Had you abandoned your schemes, perhaps the rebel would not have reigned. Tell me, enemy of humanity, how has our human race sinned against you? You have been killing us from the beginning, and you are not satisfied with our ruin. Tell me, you who thirst for human blood, do you still crave our destruction? Rest a little from your destructive work, and leave a remnant of our race. Why are you ablaze with jealousy and burning against our salvation? Restrain the fury of your flame, so that you do not destroy us utterly. Who, then, will uproot your root and cut off the growth of your wickedness, so that you do not sprout again and bear fruit that makes the sweetness of good things bitter? If only your seed had been spoiled and your body had never been formed! If only the woman who bore you had not opened the door for you to come out! Your wickedness has harmed not only you but everyone alike. Even someone who accuses you encounters occasions for stumbling because of you. My thoughts about you have worn me out as I sought to expose the ugliness of your wickedness. Your bitterness overpowered me, and I stepped beyond the bounds of proper order. I was astonished at the multitude of your deceits, and I found fault with your maker. And while I thought I was offering no rebuke, I condemned myself to be rebuked. Oh, how your wickedness humiliates both those who love you and those who hate you! And if someone praises you, it is torment; and if reproaches are shameful. I reproached you, asking against whom you had armed yourself, when I saw the destruction of those you had slain.

My mind was troubled when I remembered that your wickedness does not come from nature. The Creator created you free and made you master of your will. Both alternatives are yours, so that you may distinguish truth from falsehood. My Lord, do not hold this against me: that I reproached so boldly and accused the evil inclination that brings forth bitter envy. Envy has no existence of its own; [?] I rightly reproached its prompting. It is our inclination that makes everyone envy one another’s good things. Our inclination gives birth to envy and nurtures it with cunning schemes. And when its wickedness reached its full extent, it threw the world into turmoil with one of its fruits. Nor does our inclination have an independent existence apart from the soul. It is the faculty of discernment within the soul, which acts in all sorts of ways. The soul is the ruler of the human being, holding authority over impulses and senses. It guides nature just as its will desires. Both good and evil are equally placed within our soul. It chooses according to its judgment, rejecting one in favor of the other. The soul rides upon the body like a charioteer upon a chariot. It guides the human being with the reins of his hidden impulses. The outward senses run like horses in a stadium. The mind tightens and loosens its grip, with the soul’s impulses as its hands. The body is harnessed and constantly runs wherever the charioteer wishes. The impulses and senses guide it as the rider wishes. In everyone, the mind calls out to the senses that carry it. It orders the whole body like a commander ordering his army. See, we have learned from our soul that our freedom belongs to our soul. Our human nature is not held captive, so that we should have grounds for complaint. See, our will has shown us that it is our will that sins and repents. It is not compulsion that leads us toward something in which our will finds no rest. See, our discernment has shown us that wisdom belongs to it. It distinguishes between being rightly zealous and being unjustly envious. To it belongs blind envy, deprived of the light of love. To it belongs foolish zeal, which does not recognize what is right.

To it belongs the spring that pours forth the medicine of life and the bitterness of death. It sows the sweetness of peace, and from it strife springs up. Let us therefore blame our will, not the one who fashioned our nature. For it is our will that disfigures the beauty of our soul, O freeborn one. Let us accuse our own freedom, not the giver of wisdom. For it is our freedom that deliberates about doing what is good or what is ugly. Come, then, let us bring a case against freedom, the companion of our will. Let us accuse our discernment on the basis of the laws of our nature. Let us say to the freedom of our soul: Why do you harbor envy within yourself? Why do you look maliciously upon the kinship of your neighbors? Why do you tear down the building held together by the sinews of love? Why do you loosen the bond fastened by the command of the one who brings peace to all? Why do you not judge justly, as befits your discernment? Why do you not rebuke yourself as you reproach others? Why do you not see your own ugliness in the clear mirror of the mind? Why do you not polish away your stains with love, which cleanses every blemish? Why is your voice so loud when you call a wrongdoer to account? Yet you are more silent than a mute when it comes to the charges against yourself. Why, envious one, do you reproach someone who foolishly envies? You who are utterly hateful, why do you hate someone who hates his fellow? You who are confused, how can you set right someone who is in turmoil? You who are full of blemishes, how can you seek to wash away the filth of others? Judge yourself first, and undertake an examination of your deeds. See that you are altogether guilty and held in bondage by your sins. You have been slain by the sword of your envy, yet you are unaware of your wound. You are dead and buried while still alive, yet you do not acknowledge your death. The torch of your mind shines brightly when it comes to seeing the faults of others, but you have become utterly blind when it comes to examining your own wrongdoing. You are cunning like a sophist when accusing your fellows, but you are an ignoramus among ignoramuses

when it comes to accusing your own shameful deeds. You act as an advocate for righteousness when you rebuke others hypocritically. Yet you are abusive when you are called to account for foolishly breaking the commandment. You condemn others arrogantly and acquit yourself in secret. You issue a dishonest verdict concerning yourself and your companions. There is no justice in your judgment. Envious one, be silent; do not rebuke. For it is not fitting for someone deceitful and crooked to judge. Who appointed you judge, you who are altogether unjust? You have been a liar since you came into being, and the gate of righteousness has never seen you. Envy always clothes itself in the appearance of a lover of righteousness, and with zeal on behalf of truth it stirs up its bitterness. He envies the virtuous person because he holds fast to the truth, and he also hates the one who falls short, while posing as a lover of purity. He slanders the person trained in discussing spiritual teachings, and scowls at the one who does not study, as though he cared about learning. He abuses the one who shows respect, saying that he flatters too much, and insults the one who is contemptuous, saying that he does not know how to show respect. He finds fault with teachers and heaps insults on pupils. “Look,” he says, “they have thrown everything into confusion, loving one person and hating another.” “They have dismantled,” he says, “the basic principles that lead to perfection.” “And their conduct does not incline toward the goal of uprightness.” Through these pretenses, Envy leads people of every rank astray. He throws the lowly and the leaders into confusion, those who command and those who obey. There is no place where Envy has not spread his snares of wickedness. There is no spot where he has not hidden treacherous traps devised by cunning. There is no people that is not enslaved to him under the cunning yoke of his service. There is no kingdom that does not bear the treacherous banner of his malice. On the sea and on dry land he has laid a net woven of snares. Over the mountains and over the heights its long ropes are stretched. With rich and poor alike he has deposited his stock for trading. Profits come to him from both those who envy and those who are envied. Those who envy sow his seed

in the souls of those who listen to him. And those who are envied bring forth grumbling at the sound of the enviers’ insults. The devil’s covering has spread over everyone and everywhere. The world sits in envy as though in a gloomy night. The light of righteousness has grown dark through envy, the darkness of error. The salt of proper conduct has been spoiled by the foolish zeal of the unjust. His messengers have ranged in every direction to announce his coming. They have troubled the whole inhabited world with the bitterness of their voices. There is nowhere for the humble lover of peace to hide. For Envy has driven harmony out of human dwellings. Where can the loving person live, whose love is bound to humanity? For jealousy has torn concord apart and divided the world against itself. The company of those who love truth has dwindled under Envy’s tyranny. Those who envy help him wreak destruction night and day. His armies do not sleep or take off the weapons of his deceit, for shedding blood is more pleasant to them than restful sleep. He waged warfare of every kind against the priests, generation after generation. He shed the blood of the holy ones with merciless savagery. He destroyed the prophets of old who bore revelations. He also killed the apostles, who brought forth the power of hidden things. He advanced and rose beyond humanity, against the source of humanity’s salvation. The murderer poured out his bile upon the Peace who brought peace to all. O envy, vicious dog, barking night and day! You bite every sort of person, those of the household and strangers alike. O tyrant who does not shrink from shedding innocent blood! O murderer who [?] the corpses of all whom he lays low! O deadly asp, who does not listen to the voice of charmers! Words of love do not enter the hearing of her bitterness. O murderous dragon, lurking in the depths of the mind’s inclination, constantly disturbing thoughts with the bitterness of his ways!

O oppressor who is never satisfied! O glutton who is never filled! His savagery spread and reached even the source of good things. He drove Adam from his inheritance and killed Abel, who was found righteous. He assailed Jacob because he was humble, and Joseph because he was wise. He envied Job when he saw him increase in the wealth of body and soul. He hated Moses, who was called God among those on earth. Why should I recount his anger against the servants who were found righteous? For he advanced and rose in tyranny even against the Lord of the servants. Through Judas, envy carried out his will against the source of our salvation. The insolent one imagined that he could cut off the source of our life. From this let us learn the destructiveness of envy, the hater of humanity: how utterly its wickedness is devoid of mercy and compassion! The deceitful one has no reason to hate the good. He is his own reason, and deceitfully constructs excuses. Even if there is a reason in the case of the servants, since the whole human race is guilty, what reason can be found in the case of the one who is pure and holy? Even if the guilty gave one another grounds for hostility, as guilty people do, how did the innocent one wrong you, that you shed his blood without cause? Look, it has been shown by your actions that you hate the pure without cause. With a reason or without one, you have poured out your venom upon humanity. You do not hate only the good, O envy, hater of humanity. Your bitter bile is poured out equally upon the good and the wicked together. It is not only into the knowledgeable that the sting of your blow pierces. For the scars of your deceit are found on the wise and the foolish alike. Against the righteous and the wicked you have drawn your bow, you deceiver. You strike every limb with the sharpened arrows of your jealousy. The gall of your wickedness has spread throughout the whole body of humanity. There is no sound limb that has not been torn by your bites. Oh, how evil your wickedness is, malicious and murderous envy! There is no evil thing as evil as you; and if there is, it is your disciple. Oh, how twisted your deceit is! There is no match for your cunning. If anyone is cunning and crafty, he has been schooled in the devices of your deceit.

No mouth can recount how many devices you use to lead people astray. Nor can the mind gather together all the inventions your deceit produces. Only one knows how to expose you and reveal the defects of your hateful deeds: The one you hated because he revealed your secrets before the eyes of onlookers. He can cut your root out of the soil in which our soul lives, and tear the branches bearing your fruit from the tree of our mind. Through the sweetness of his love, the gall of your bitter cup will lose its bitterness. Through the light of his dawning, the darkness of your hateful passion will depart. At the dawn of his word, those lying numb, submerged in jealousy, will awaken. They will begin the work of love, even at the eleventh hour. Come, mortals, let us take shelter in the bitter [?] fortresses of love. For look, envy has gone out like a captor in pursuit of our humanity. Come, let us flee to the country above, where anger does not reign. For look, jealousy has caught fire and set the whole inhabited world ablaze. Come, let us seek help from the mercy that has shown compassion to our nature. For look, the tyranny of our evil inclination has brought our nature low. Let us reach out to grace, so that it may help us in the struggle. For look, the whole human race has been defeated by the schemes of envy. Let us entreat the compassion that has mercy on all, so that it may reconcile us with justice. For look, the wickedness of our inclination has disturbed the sweetness of the peace of the one who brings peace to all. Our inclination has loosened the bond of our peace with the Maker. It is up to us, if we wish, to tighten what we have loosened. Our inclination has stained us with sin and defiled the purity of our mind. If it wishes, it can easily cleanse us through our soul’s repentance. Our inclination has disturbed us with envy and sown strife among us. It is for it to reconcile us with one another and with the Maker. I too have attacked our inclination and condemned it as evil, Because, although it possesses discernment, it has become deaf by its own will alone. I have called it names that disgrace its discernment. Envy, anger, and jealousy are its fruits. It is the father of envy, and jealousy is its offspring. If it wishes, they grow; if not, they do not exist at all. It is what rides upon the seeds:

Like a charioteer over horses, he drives the outward senses: eyes, ears, and tongues. At his signal the inward senses are harnessed, and the outward ones are under his authority. If he wishes, they proceed in order; if he wants, like wild beasts. His are both the power of wisdom and the lack of understanding. Whenever he wishes, he is a learned debater, and a little later an uneducated man. He taught me to speak with him about what his freedom has power over. He revealed to me that both shrewdness and childishness of heart belong to him. He signaled to me to restrain and rebuke the impulses that serve envy. He urged me to shoot words like arrows into the ranks of deceit. He informed me about the scheme put together by his cunning, and showed me deadly snares concealed beneath a generous appearance. I was roused by the sound of melodies as he sang songs of peace. Yet he was concealing strife beneath the garment of his lips. I heard him changing his tones deceitfully, like a bird. He greatly entices his listeners, like a partridge calling them to their death. I saw that he was remarkable in appearance, and I thought him altogether beautiful. But he turned against himself and revealed to me that his appearance was at odds with his deeds. O inclination, how wise you are, and how very cunning your deeds! Oh, how just you are when you wish, showing no favoritism even to yourself! You cunningly devise every kind of scheme whenever you want to cause harm. Yet perhaps no one is more guileless than you whenever you wish to help. I marveled greatly at your wisdom and at the authority of your freedom. How easy difficult things are for your will whenever it wishes! Students learn from you, and teachers become wise through you. The poor run to your door, and the rich to your treasury. See, the inclination of our soul has revealed to us that both are ours: To love the love that gave us life, and to hate the envy that killed us. Come, then, as discerning people, let us expose the deceit within our inclination. For the inclination within us has shown us that peace and anger are ours. Come, let us speak justly to our inclination, the master of our will:

“Do not exchange the sweetness of love for the bitterness of envy.” Come, let us repeat to it its own words and interpret for it from its own books: “Take care, inclination: do not disturb people's peace with your envy.” Cry out, you envious people, and say to the inclination within your bodily members: “Stop, inclination! Do not burn us in the flame of envy.” Recount to it the punishment of the rich man who was being cruelly tormented and was begging the man he had hated to give him relief from his burning. Let the envious, who hate without cause, remember that utterance. For that chasm is great, and it cannot be crossed to reach Abraham. Our Lord, overthrow Satan, who has thrown our race into turmoil through his envy.
For the sixth Sunday of Lent.
[?] For the sixth Sunday of Lent. Response: Give thanks to the bridegroom who has exalted his friends and brought them into the bridal chamber of his kingdom, my brothers.

Beautiful is the study of the Spirit’s words set down in the books, and good is the discourse in the Scriptures for whoever studies it. Wonderful is the teaching that proclaims the kingdom on high, and his love distributes good blessings to whoever loves him. A great treasure is hidden in the letters through which his words are studied.

Whoever reads with heartfelt love becomes rich forever. The written lines of his Scriptures resemble a ray of light, and whoever looks without doubt sees everything. Like a guide, his message runs ahead of the mind, and whoever loves the companionship of his love has reached heaven. Lovingly he calls people to draw near to him, and whoever draws near lovingly, he fills with his love. Like a teacher, he urges people toward his teaching, and he becomes a teacher to whoever accepts discipleship under him. I saw that the teaching of the skilled teacher was skillful, and my mind advised me to become his disciple, if he would accept me. Accept me, teacher who makes people wise through his teaching, so that I may engage my tongue in learning to study your words. My speech longs to become a disciple of the discourse of your words. Write out the alphabet for me as a model, so that I may study it. I saw correct characters traced in your Scriptures, and I greatly desire to proceed in the order of their meanings. Fulfill my longing, Good One, who is full of all good things, and give me what I need: understanding of the words in your Scriptures. I was wandering among the wonders recorded of you, and my mind pressed me to investigate the power within them. The kingdom on high, he says, is like ten virgins who were waiting to meet the bridegroom with their lamps. Five of them, the wise ones, took oil, he says, while the untrained ones made no effort to take oil. Time passed, he says, and the bridegroom delayed his coming. Sleep overcame them, and all ten fell asleep.

He said that at midnight a trumpet sounded, announcing the coming of the bridegroom from on high. They arose, he says, and put their lamps and their adornments in order, so that with their lights they might welcome the bridegroom who dwells in light. The foolish and the wise arose together on equal terms. Though they were alike, they were not alike in that same equality. The oil in the foolish women’s lamps had run dry, and they began asking their companions to give them alms out of kindness. “There may not be enough for us and you,” the prepared women replied. “Instead, go to those who sell it, if it can be bought.” They listened and went to buy oil that cannot be bought. The bridegroom came, and the prepared women entered, but those others did not enter. They remained outside the door because they had fallen short of their duty. They began knocking and knocking, trusting in their conduct. “Our Lord, open for us the door of the treasury in your kingdom, so that we may enter and receive the reward for the labors of our virginity.” “I do not know you,” the bridegroom’s voice answered them, “nor do I acknowledge at all the virginity you have kept for me.” Now that the living mouth has finished speaking, let us approach and examine the question hidden within his words. The saying he fashioned in the form of women is full of questions: why did he leave aside the company of men and speak of women? And if his saying looked to their nature, since that too is one and the same, why, when their virginity was equal, did he not make everything equal? Why did he make the virgins equal in name, yet divide them into two groups according to their deeds? Why, though they were clean of the stains of debauchery, did he set a boundary for them, so that they would not be admitted into the greatness of his love? Why did sleep overcome them all, and they [?] from labor, and in wakefulness too they were [?] in condition? Why, though they were all holding their lamps, was oil left only for the wise women?

If they practiced the conduct of virginity equally, why was there a distinction between wisdom and foolishness? If they were one, just as they were one in body and soul, why did not one graciously lend righteousness to her companion? Why did the wise women send away those who lacked understanding, when they knew that oil could not be bought for money? And if it was true that oil could be bought for money, why did they not sell oil themselves and receive the payment? And if those who were rich would not sell, who would take the sustenance of his own life and give it to another? But if the women who lacked oil went to buy it, why did the bridegroom not wait so that they might all enter together? Why did he answer them, “I do not know your deeds,” when he knew that they had kept themselves from impurity? And if they had not acted according to the will he desired, why did he not say, “Go to the fire and the darkness”? The difference in the pronouncement he made them hear has greatly troubled me: why was the punishment of those being punished not equal? At the lack of equality in the sentence he passed on them, my thoughts were bewildered: how did they not fall into the abyss of fire with the rich man? And if they remained on earth with the wicked because of the burden within them, how could they avoid being tormented with their torments? And if they did not enter and see the place they had been awaiting, what benefit did they gain from persevering in their virginity? Why did sufferings wear down their bodies and souls, while on the day of judgment they received disgrace instead of a crown? Why struggle with the impulses of the inclination within them, only to fall, despite victory, under judgment with the guilty? The outcome of their deeds is full of great sorrow: how they began but could not bring their good deeds to completion. Let us, then, begin to inquire into their labors, since the subject of the account in which they are depicted also deserves attention. Let us inquire how it is written that the kingdom was compared to them:

For look, they were unable to conform themselves to its likeness. Why does he not say of them that they resemble that glorious kingdom? For its glory precedes everything he created. “The kingdom on high was compared to virgins,” he says. What a great wonder! Who is compared to something inferior? The maker of comparisons fittingly made a glorious comparison with those who glorify him, for he can make the comparison, but they cannot compare themselves to the kingdom on high and its inexpressible delight. Yet it compares itself to them by calling them to its delight. With this purpose it was compared to us earthly beings: that through its likeness we might seek the likeness of glorious things. The likeness he presented closely resembles the truth and teaches it, yet no painter can portray its likeness precisely. Beautiful is the image that his command composed and placed in his gospel, and we ought to look carefully at the splendor of its beauty. Come, you who behold, and look closely at our Lord’s word, which portrayed humanity and the kingdom on high in an image of labors. The renewer of humanity portrayed human labors in his gospel and set them like a picture before those who behold. He called his gospel itself the kingdom that resembles the women, because it proclaims the kingdom on high to human beings. Through its nearness, people learn to seek what is above, and through its openness they see the beauty of hidden things. It was of the gospel that he said that it was compared [?] to virgins, in that it shows a way of life without marriage. He called the assembly that believes in him by the name of virgins, teaching us that he requires purity from his servants. He portrayed the image of his loving will in the form of women, because among women the appearance of modesty is [?]. He enclosed men and women within the folds of the word of his mouth, teaching that both groups can live in purity.

If he had portrayed the image of his word in the form of men, it might have seemed that he rejected women as a group. Wisely he portrayed females in the image of his word, so that the nature shared equally by all would not be divided into parts. He portrayed our whole nature and showed it to us through our own nature, so that it would be easy for us to look carefully at everything we possess. He revealed our good deeds and our shameful deeds in his parables, and portrayed and showed us the blessings and punishments that await us. He divided the course of our way of life into two groups, naming one wise and the other foolish. He compared the course of perfection to the wise women, and likened labors deficient in love to the foolish women. He called their labors themselves the lamps they had prepared. They were alike in having labored, even though they had not labored equally. The inequality of their labors caused the oil to run short. For if they had been equal, nothing that was equal would have been lacking. Through the oil that ran short, he portrayed and showed us the deficiency of their labors: they were guilty and were not anointed with love and mercy. Christ, who showed us mercy, called mercy by the name of oil, so that, just as he showed us mercy, we too might show mercy to our companions. He likened the person who shows mercy to his companions to oil, because, like oil, he soothes thoughts as oil soothes the senses. He painted the image of the shameless women without oil. [?] Their words did not soften the sore of wrongdoing. He blends oil into the way of life of the wise women, which showed kindness and mercy and anointed body and soul alike. Their conduct was anointed with the oil of mercy. Therefore they endured and were not entangled in the filth of the age. Painters too are accustomed to do this:

To preserve images from decay by means of oil. The painter mixes oil with pigments, so that by this means his image may endure without alteration. And if painters knew how to preserve borrowed images, how much more ought people to preserve the image of their own likeness! Our Savior condemned their carelessness about their images by calling them foolish women who had taken no oil among their provisions. He praised and exalted the diligence of the good people's will through the wise women, who mixed oil into their deeds. Within their number of ten he included all creation, and he greatly desires that they welcome him on the day of his appearing. He called the day of his appearing the coming of the bridegroom who is to come, and all the perfect he called virgins going out to meet him. The sleep in which he said they all slept alike is death, which makes the good and the wicked equal in the same decay. The cry that arose at midnight and roused the sleeping women is the commanding voice that calls at the end and raises everyone from the dead. He said that the bridegroom who betrothed us comes at midnight, because bridegrooms too take their betrothed brides at night. Through the rising together of those whose labors he recorded, he showed everyone the resurrection of all: everyone will rise. Through the lamps of the five going out together, he rebukes the merciless: unless they show mercy, they will not receive mercy at the coming judgment. Through the wise women's refusal to sell to the foolish women, he plainly revealed to us that there is no asking for mercy there. By recounting their words, “There may not be enough for us and for you,” he made known that our labor here is small compared with our reward. By sending them to buy oil wherever it could be found, he showed that there is an opportunity to show mercy, if only we had shown mercy. “While they were returning from [?], the bridegroom came”: this is the uncertainty by which we do not perceive when he is coming. “The wise women entered with the bridegroom, and the door was shut”: these are the righteous, who enter and rest in the harbor of peace. “The foolish women remained outside the door of the kingdom”:

These are the wicked, who remain on earth to be tormented. Concerning what is written, that the undisciplined women cried, “Our Lord, our Lord”: this is the hope that perhaps mercy will have compassion on those who have sinned [?]. They were thinking without understanding about their labors, hoping that the Kindly One would perhaps not disregard their conduct. “They cried out, and he answered them, ‘I do not know you’”: he did not wish to acknowledge a love that was not mingled with love for one's companions. “I do not know you,” he said to the undisciplined women, “because you did not know how to fulfill my will through compassion.” “The door was shut in the faces of those outside who had not entered with him”: this is the firmament above, which the divine command closed when the good had entered. The divine command becomes a testing furnace for the good and the wicked, and separates the righteous from the unjust through the burning heat of his love. Great is the separation that takes place there between one and another, and the distance between the height and the depth cannot be measured. The height of the righteous is lofty and exalted above all heights, and the abyss of the wicked is far deeper than all depths. The appearance of those who cherish love is more beautiful than anything beautiful, and the complexion of the deceitful is uglier than anything ugly. Nothing compares with the glory of the children of light, nor is there anything like the ugliness of the children of darkness. Brightness and darkness show everyone the labors with which each person occupied himself during life here. The body's appearance becomes a witness against the mind and reproaches it for the things it did deceitfully. From the body itself spring both glory and disgrace, and it itself dispenses blessings to itself and inflicts lashes. A person himself scourges his own soul for [?], and like a judge his mind condemns his shameful deeds. Everyone sees his own faults and those of his fellows, and no one hides either from himself or from his companions. A person gazes upon the whole of rational creation, and all gaze upon him in the same manner as his own gaze. Everyone examines a single person closely, and that person extends his mind toward everyone who sees him. Among those who have passed away, no one there hides from his partner:

Nor can his fellow and companion hide from him. Sight runs swiftly to the four directions and encompasses them within the gaze that is inside the body. Oh, the wonder that comes about in a person through his Maker: though bounded himself, he encompasses the height and the depth! He is confined, body and soul, to one place; yet he is far from everything, and everything is close to him as a neighbor. He is everywhere, although he himself is in one place. This is the wonder: he is beside everything, yet he is not beside everything. He resembles the Godhead in the manner of his presence, for it is everywhere, yet how it exists cannot be comprehended. Through his actions, that declaration is fulfilled in him: that the human being is the image of his Maker and closely resembles him. He resembles him in this: he is everywhere without being there, and he examines the hidden things within his own mind and everyone else's. Like the Creator, he examines the wrongdoing hidden in the soul, and by his examination distinguishes the ugly from the beautiful. Who can adequately describe in words the greatness of his rank—the child of dust whose command reigns with everything and in everything? Who knows how to portray his lowliness along with his greatness? For while something in him reigns over everything, something in him is more contemptible than everything. Who would not marvel at the division found in him? Part of him is on high and part in the depths, in glory and disgrace. Who would not rejoice, and who would not grieve, over both, when considering the blessings of the good and the torments of the wicked? Who would not say, “The human being is great, and the human being is contemptible,” when seeing him in the kingdom above and in Gehenna? I saw his glory and his disgrace portrayed on the pages of the books, and I rejoiced and grieved over his abasement and his exaltation. The divine command portrayed his image in two likenesses and taught him to meditate on his glorious and shameful qualities. Through the parable, he revealed to us the separation that will take place at the end, so that we might consider how to choose well before that day.

Through the virgins, he taught him the course of righteousness, so that he might cultivate purity of soul without neglect. Through the parable, he marked out for him the path of glorious labors, so that he might journey well toward the appointed meeting with life at the end. Through the wise women, he encouraged him with the hope of the kingdom above; through the foolish women, he terrified him with a harsh report. Through their virginity, he proclaimed that the human being can live in purity; through their labors, he showed that he possesses freedom of soul. Through the taking of oil, he showed that the human being has a compassionate disposition; through those who took none, he revealed that his cruelty is not forced upon him. Through the lamps that burned and those that went out, he revealed his freedom: if he had wished, he could have lit all ten of them. The will that lit five with the oil of mercy could easily have lit the other five, just as it lit the first five. The wise women and the foolish women have one and the same disposition; if it had wished, it could have become wise in its entirety. By dividing himself through a lack of compassion for his neighbors, he made known that he contains two things together: good and evil. When the foolish women asked the well-prepared women for oil, he reproved himself, showing that he ought to have had compassion on his companions. Through the wise women's unwillingness to lend to the undisciplined women, he openly condemned the soul's merciless cruelty. Their saying to them, “Go and buy from those who sell,” is entirely a rebuke to anyone who did not work in the time that has passed. Everyone can do good work as long as they are on earth, and it is easy for them to reach the rank of perfection. Because they did not work here with love, as was fitting, the lights of their lamps went dark on the day of the wedding feast. Because they had not generously shared the fruits of their labors with the needy, the wise women, in turn, withheld from them the gift of oil. Because they did not heed the voices of those who pleaded for forgiveness, they heard the response, “I do not recognize the labors within you.”

Because they closed the door of their spoken teaching before learners, the door of the royal house was closed against their requests. Because they kept their love apart from fellowship that benefits others, the king did not wish to make them worthy of fellowship in his love. Justice, in turn, repaid them for the debts they had incurred, and they received repayment in the same measure as their deeds. They condemned themselves before judgment, and by the verdict of their own thoughts they cut off their labors. It was not the judge who deprived their labors of repayment; they themselves were unwilling to repay his love wisely. It was not justice that [?] the door before their faces; they themselves closed it by not opening their love to others. If they had opened the door of their willingness before the needy, the bridegroom would not have kept them outside the door. If they had anointed the wounds of wrongdoing with the oil of the word, the oil of mercy would not have been lacking in their lamps. If they had poured out the love within them upon those in distress, their companions too would have poured out generously to [?] them. They themselves blocked the path of mercy before their own faces, and through their deeds they were unable to walk with the upright women. Let us learn from them about the conduct of life here, and in their repayment let us picture the repayment of judgment in the world beyond. For our sake he wrote the parable of their conduct, and for our instruction it runs through the written lines as though it were an actual event. I said this—“as though it were an actual event”—not because it does not exist, but because it did not take place in actual deeds as it is written. It did not actually happen in the way it was told, but it will undoubtedly happen in the future. For it is a parable, however much it bears the likeness of reality, and through its likeness it represents events that will happen later. It resembles a shadow in the swiftness of its movement, and it reveals the reality of events as a shadow reveals a body. In its written form it customarily runs ahead of events, anticipating what is to happen at the end.

It shows distant things as near to anyone who looks into it, and while they are far away, it tells of them as though they were close. Like a painter, it depicts matters that have not taken place and represents them in the form of an image and a likeness. The parable portrayed through the virgins resembles an image, and human nature and the conduct of human life are revealed in it. In it, the greatness of the love of the pure in soul is proclaimed, and in it, the stinginess of the merciless is despised. It called the pure in soul wise and possessors of oil, and it named the stingy foolish and buyers of oil. The oil is mercy, which those full of mercy sell. By not selling it, he showed that there is a time when it cannot be sold. He made known that selling itself has an appointed time, for only at its proper time can something be sold from one person to another. Selling has its place in this world of toil, but in the world to come, selling and buying cease. For this reason the wise women did not sell, so that the great order of that arrangement would not be disturbed. “Both worlds are arranged in order,” he too replies, “and their orders proceed wisely according to their arrangements.” The world of time is suited to selling and buying, but the everlasting world is suited to rest, stillness, and delight. Come, buyers and sellers! Buy and sell in the world where time has been given for buying and selling. Let no one overturn the great order of the two worlds by refraining from buying here and buying there. No one is permitted to bring commerce into the kingdom. If anyone dares, his audacity recoils upon him. If someone who despises a temporary kingdom receives punishment, how many times greater is the punishment of someone who despises the kingdom on high! On high is that kingdom which cannot be dissolved, and there is no place in it for conducting oneself in an earthly way. Earthly people are not permitted to enter there while bringing with them the buying and selling of earthly people. By barring the five virgins from entering, he set a boundary and barred everyone who lacks compassion. By giving no reward for the exhausting labors of their virginity, he showed that he rejects every way of life that does not spring from love.

They were virgins, and their conduct was steadfast; yet because they enriched no one through their labors, they were left wanting. Their practices brought no benefit to those who possessed them. Because they gave nothing from them, they did not receive the reward they hoped for. In expectation of a reward, they endured the [?] of desires, but they did not turn properly toward the example of the giver of the reward. He showed them a loving example so that they might resemble him. Because they did not resemble him, he withheld the crown from their heads. They strove to receive the crown of victory from him, but he rebuked them in the sight of angels and human beings. Oh, how evil is the wickedness of a disposition that shows no mercy! On the day of recompense, it makes labors count as though they were no labors at all. Oh, how hateful it is for someone not to share his prosperity with others! Even though he possesses good things, he himself is deprived of good things. Oh, how foolish it is for someone to enrich only himself! Even if he acquires the whole world, he has acquired nothing. Someone who acquires only himself has acquired nothing, because he himself cannot subsist without many others. Without the limbs, the soul cannot remain in the body, nor can it receive the reward for its labors without them. The soul needs the limbs, even though it is a soul. How much more, then, does one human being need another! Through other people a person completes the course of righteousness. If someone becomes righteous without other people, that person is not human. A person cannot be human without other people, and righteousness without other people is not righteousness. Do you want to be righteous and good, O human being? Do for your [?] what you expect to be done for you. Do you want to receive the reward for your [?] on the day of repayment? Pay your fellow the debt of love, and there—you have been repaid. Do you long to meet the heavenly bridegroom in garments of light? Let your face shine toward your companion, and there—you have welcomed him. Do you long to enter that delight with the wise? Teach wisdom to a fool, and there—you are entering at the head of the wise. No one enters until he brings someone else in with him.

For this is what that order requires of anyone who enters it. “Is someone with you?” the gate asks the one entering. If someone is, he enters; if not, he remains outside the gate. Come, you who would enter, who long for that entrance. Hear what it requires of anyone who wants to enter and see it. Come, you wise people, see the wisdom of the wise women, who discerned and knew to take provisions of mercy with them. Come, virgins, listen to that cry addressed to the foolish women. Wipe away from yourselves the name of foolishness, so that you will not hear it. You who love study and investigate the mysteries of hidden things, complete in action the study your thoughts have produced. You who explain to students the meaning contained in words, practice yourselves what you teach. You who are invited by the bridegroom and await the appointed time of that kingdom, stay awake from the sleep of ignorance.
Response. Glory to your mercy, Lord of all, for you freely show grace to sinners.
On the Raising of Lazarus

Discourse 20. For Palm Sunday.
The twentieth discourse, on the raising of Lazarus, to be recited on the night [?] of Palm Sunday. Response.
Blessed is [?], who on the day of his entry stirred the children to praise him with hosannas.
My brothers.

The evil one yoked the human race to the yoke of death and subjected them to his bitter bondage. He unjustly laid the yoke of his toil upon everyone, and without pity inflicted slavery on the good and the evil. He made the whole race mortal and subject to decay, and brought it into the fortresses of Sheol and imprisoned it there, never to come out again. Like a robber, he led all humanity into captivity and sold them into slavery to death, a [?] master. Because of death, mortals became slaves to death, while the poison of death was thoroughly mixed into their nature. Death lay quiet in nature as though asleep, until it heard that voice pronouncing the sentence of death. Transgression of the commandment called it and woke it like someone sleeping. It began to roar and demand the sentence, to fill its belly. Like a lion it rushed upon human beings and swallowed them, and like a wild beast it went in and hid in the caverns of Sheol. Sin called it and urged it to rush to the slaughter. She taught it to crush human beings without pity. Like a prostitute she went out and stood in the streets of Eden, and as though leading a child, she dragged Adam toward his destruction. She demanded a harsh payment from him for having prostituted himself with her. He gave his body, and she tossed it into the hands of death. Greedy death took the pledge from the prostitute, crushed it severely, and left not a shred of it intact. The will that had woven humanity's garment saw that it was torn and took pity on its handiwork, so that it would not be mocked by the insolent. Love drew him to have compassion on the work of his hands, and he returned to renew the garment [?] that had worn out through mortality. His will put on the garment of flesh like royal purple, and he revealed his glory in something smaller than his greatness. A human being is smaller than the Creator, beyond comparison, just as a woolen garment is inferior to the clothing of the one who wears it. In a woolen garment the king showed [?] the greatness of his rank, and the Father's Word revealed his hidden being in Adam's body. To abolish death, he put on the perishable garment, so that in human form he might rescue human beings from death's mouth. His will went out after death on feet of flesh. He ran, seized it, and took its human captives away from it. In human form he hunted the lion that hunts human beings, and in human food he crushed deadly poison and gave it to the lion to eat. His will journeyed with a human being toward mortals.

He proclaimed on earth the new tidings that the dead had come to life. Like a fisherman he stood over the sea of mortality, cast the net of the word of his mouth, and caught death. He first threw it flesh as food, like bait. It rushed forward and swallowed it, and then he pulled it toward dry land. The lover of humanity accomplished this toward our humanity through [?], so that through a human being he might abolish death for mortals. Skillfully he hunted down the world, that wild ass, subdued it, and yoked it beneath his lordship so that it would not run wild. His will laid a human hand upon sinners and trained them like beasts to carry his love. His will entered among sinners with bodily limbs and spoke gently with them through a mouth of flesh. Humbly he came among the people of earth, and like children he enticed them toward his teaching. Mystically he bound himself to them with bonds of love, and called them friends of his love and confidants of his mysteries. First he chose three friends for himself from among mortals, and then he spread his love abundantly over everyone. Jesus, it is said, loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, the three siblings, with human affection. He who loves everyone did not love them more than everyone else, but did so to stir people to zeal for loving his name. He stirred zeal in both groups of humanity by choosing for himself friends to love, both men and women. Through Martha and Mary he encouraged women toward purity, and through Lazarus he urged men to preserve love. Through the three he revealed the purpose of his love to our whole race, and he set their love like a mirror before those who looked. Through them the power of his greatness triumphed, as [?], and through them he tested the spiritual weapon with which he fought. He armed himself against death and iniquity, the tyrant. He shot two arrows at the target and struck it squarely. Sin and death were bitterly opposed to his righteousness. He grew zealous and mighty and subdued them against their will. He set up a target so that he might first take aim at iniquity. He shot and struck it by forgiving Mary's iniquity. Against cruel iniquity he had tested the weapon the Spirit had given him. Then he turned his gaze toward death, bound it, and cast it down. He maintained a great order in his battle with the insolent: he killed the first ones [?] who pronounced judgment, and rightly began by unleashing the arrows of righteousness against him. The sinful woman ripened and bore the fruits of righteousness. When death saw this, it lusted and became greedy to swallow human beings. In Mary, sin was defeated first, and its leaves fell away; and in Lazarus, death too swallowed a cruel arrow. Through two siblings, death and the Evil One learned his power. They were greatly astonished: what was this new thing that had happened? They thought it unheard of that a woman full of iniquity should hate iniquity, and that a dead man who had been buried should unexpectedly return to life.

The human race is accustomed to living in iniquity, and along the [?] of death their nature proceeds, one after another. Death, the ravenous lion, looked to this customary course, opened its mouth, and swallowed the friend of the one who gives life to the dead. It carried him down into the depths of Sheol to feed on him, not knowing that it would soon give back its food. Like a hawk it swooped upon the innocent doves, and like a fledgling it snatched the brother from his sisters. The doves of peace moaned and cried thunderously over the speaking fledgling who had become food for death. The chaste women clothed themselves in great mourning for their brother, because death had divided the united household where the siblings lived together. Before he departed, they sent word and disclosed the secret of his illness to the good friend who loved them out of his love. The innocent women sent this message to our Lord: “Look, our Lord, your friend is sick and near death. Come, save his life.” With faith and love they sent their appeal to him, as to a friend whose love for his dear ones is steadfast. He too looked toward the purpose of his thoughts when he said, “This illness is not for death, but for glory [?].” He called his friend's death “glory” beforehand, because, when he raised him, everyone would glorify his name. He heard. The lover of all, though his friend was sick and about to die, did not hurry to go and see him before he passed away. He restrained his kindly love with patience and did not allow it to rush quickly to bring healing. The Wise One who makes people wise acted wisely, and as one who knows what is to come [?], he revealed his power. For he knew that he would enter a contest with the mighty one and recover from him the captives he had taken from humanity. He was confident that he would conquer and bring down Death the tyrant. For that reason he delayed instead of going quickly. It was not fitting for him to go and fight against sickness, for that was nothing to his mighty power. It would have served no purpose for him to fight without cause, lest greedy Death think that he was looking for pretexts. It was not right for him to go out and stop the captor before he had gone out and taken captives, giving him no room to enter. This was fitting for the greatness of the power with which he fought: once greedy Death swallowed him, he would snatch him away from it. This is how a warrior ought to fight: he should engage the enemy within the enemy’s own fortresses. This is fitting for the spiritual athlete: to display his contest in the arena before the spectators. This is greatness: while his mighty opponent remains in his city, to enter as a captive and take from him the captives he has taken. This is worthy of great wonder and praise: to plunder human captives from inside Death’s own house. With this intent, the giver of life to all remained where he was until Death swallowed his friend and hid him in its pits. He framed his words before his disciples as though he did not know,

to let them know that he knew very well what was to come. “Come, let us go to the land of Judea,” he told them. They were greatly distressed, thinking that the time of his suffering had arrived. “Look, the Jews are very eager to kill you! Why do you want to go and cut off the hope of our lives?” He was going to snatch the dead man from Death’s mouth [?], while they thought it might swallow him like everyone else. He was preparing to enter a contest with the mighty one, while they thought that powerless men would defeat him. Since they had not learned the power of his greatness through the mystery, he framed an explanation a little clearer than the previous one. “Our friend has fallen asleep,” he told them about Lazarus. “Come, let us go and wake him from his sleep; let us call him so that he gets up.” “If he is asleep,” the childish ones said to the one who knows, “he will get up, as the natural course of sleep requires.” He spoke of the sleep of death, which is very harsh, but they said that he was sleeping the usual sleep, like everyone else. He saw that they were not stirring from the sleep of ignorance, and he woke them with the declaration, “Lazarus is dead.” “Lazarus has died, and I am very glad that I was not there, so that through his death you may gain strength of faith.” “I was not there.” Listen, Egyptian: who was it who was not there? The Word of the Father, who fills heaven and earth! How can we affirm that the heights and depths are filled with him, when he was not in Bethany, as he himself said? Flesh, composed of parts, cannot be everywhere. Indeed, it is impossible for a bodily being to be everywhere. And if he was both where he was and in Bethany, then it is established that he was not a visible body. And if there is no visible, bounded body, why was this said: “I am glad that I was not there”? Be quiet, insolent man! This is no time to speak with you. Do not hinder us from the smooth [?] of our journey. It was the bodily one who said that he was not where he was not. And this is how it is: whatever is made is not everywhere. The Self-Existent One is everywhere—everywhere and without limit—and his glorious nature was not far from Bethany. He remained for two days in the place where he was, so that during his delay death might attack his beloved friend. For four days he gave death room to delight in its food; then he shook it with the new voice that raises the dead. Christ the eagle came and arrived near Bethany. The innocent doves heard and went out to meet him. Martha went out first, alone, to meet him. When she met him, she wept and told him of her brother’s death. “If you had been here,” she said to him with a trembling voice, “greedy death would not have attacked and destroyed my brother. “If you had visited him while he was still alive here,

“the spring of vitality flowing within him would not have dried up. “If your pure body had come near his limbs, the bitterness of weeping would have been transformed by the fragrance of your body. “If you had seen him while he could still see the light of this passing world, he would have looked at you, and the suffering that afflicted him would have departed. “If he had heard you speaking as you usually did, the trumpet-sound of the speech of his mouth would not have fallen silent.” The simple dove said these things without understanding, supposing that it would be difficult for him to raise her brother. “If—if you believe,” he said to the believing woman, “you will see the great glory hidden in my words.” “Yes,” she said, “I am certain that you are the Messiah, and that you are the Son of that fountain which pours forth life.” She spoke according to an understanding shaped by the Law, not according to the truth befitting the divine name. She did indeed say, “You are the Messiah who comes into the world,” but without distinguishing the form of the servant [?] from that of the Maker. This was not revealed to human beings or to spiritual beings until the Spirit showed it to humanity in the form of light. Those who loved him called him Christ and Son, just as prophets and kings were called anointed ones by grace. It was with this understanding that Martha called him Christ and Son, not knowing that he was Son of the divine Being and son of humanity. She said these things in sorrow of soul and loving affection, and went in to call her sister Mary, saying that our Teacher had come. Mary heard the news of our Lord and went out to meet him. She fell down, worshiped him, and repeated her sister’s words. Mary bowed down, paying the homage of love to the one who forgave her wrongdoing, for her loving affection for him was greater than anything else. He asked them where they had laid his friend’s body, not to find out, but to make known that he knew where it was. He asked them as though he did not know, to make them understand. They answered, “Come and see the place of the tomb.” He went with them, walking in sorrow, and as he walked, tears poured from his eyes. Grief and weeping overwhelmed him over his loved ones, and he shed tears as nature demanded of him. Nature distinctly pressed its sting upon him, and the bitterness of his grief flowed through the channels of his eyes. For it was nature that wept over his friend, as he remembered the depths to which the nature of rational beings had sunk. He looked upon human nature and groaned bitterly, because death destroys its beauty and it becomes dust. He too was clothed in the nature that death had taken captive, and naturally he grieved over the abasement of his fellow human beings. He too was formed from that very dust, soaked in sufferings, and the poison of mortality stirred within his bodily constitution. His descent came from that very stock that gives birth to pains, and, as with everyone, [?] darkened him with its own.

Under this condition he wept with restraint over his friend, so that everyone might learn that it was the form of a servant that wept. Although the grief of his capacity to suffer greatly overwhelmed him, he shed tears in an orderly way, and with restraint he grieved and lamented. He placed modest restraints on his emotions and his eyes, and comforted himself with the good hope of the resurrection of the dead. The dull-hearted were astonished and amazed at his restrained weeping, but they did not understand what he was wisely doing. They said, “Could not this man, who raised other dead people, rebuke death and keep it from approaching the one he loves?” He disregarded it and remained silent, as though he did not know what they had said, and did not hold them accountable for the foolish murmuring of their thoughts. He approached the tomb, lifted his gaze toward heaven, and began to entreat the one hidden within him to reveal his power. “[?], you have heard me, and I know that you hear me. Reveal your power in me, so that everyone may know whose Son I am. “It was not to boast that I asked for his power to raise [?], but to reveal the power of your hidden being before the eyes of those watching. “It was not because I was anxious for help that I called upon you now, but to reveal that it is through the might of your power that I triumph.” Who was it who [?] over Lazarus, you who deny our body? And who was it who prayed and asked the Maker for strength? And who was it who shed tears tenderly over his beloved? And who was it who stopped his weeping in the hope of the resurrection of the dead? Who thanked whom for having heard him and for hearing him again? And to whom, and by whom, was this spoken petition being offered? The Father's [?] did not pray to the Father who begot him, for he is equal to him in his divinity and his [?]. The one equal to his Father did not ask for strength and help. And the one whose senses do not change did not shed tears of sorrow. The one exalted above suffering did not suffer human sorrows, and the one who knows everything did not [?], “Where is the tomb?” It was the son of Adam who [?] in sorrow over his beloved, and it was he who shed tears over the destruction of his fellow human beings. It was the form of the servant that saw his nature taken captive by death and begged and pleaded that he might bring his life up from destruction. It was the man who prayed to the Hidden One dwelling within him, asking him to restore a human soul from the mouth of [?]. The Hidden One was hidden within his limbs without [?], and through the might of his power he shouted at death, and death trembled before him. Through the strength of his help, he became indignant and rose forcefully against the insolent, who were about to see a marvel and despise him. “Jesus became indignant,” it says, as he grew forceful through the power of the Spirit. He stirred himself and shouted angrily at death. Against whom, then, did the sea of peace become indignant and rise forcefully? And against whom did the one full of gentleness raise his voice? He rose forcefully against the Jews who denied his power, for he raised a dead man who was rotting in the tomb, yet they were not put to shame. For he was looking at them before he offered his petition to his Father.

He prayed beforehand to shut the door against their words. They regarded him as an adversary of the God of all. For that reason, he attributed to his Father beforehand what was about to happen. The wise one built a wall of words before them and gave no room to the accusations in their thoughts. Through his thanksgiving he showed that he was in accord with the one who assumed him, and through his deeds he taught that he had the power to do everything. He raised his voice [?] and called to the dead man as to someone alive, so that everyone might hear that at his command the man would live and rise. The earthly one made an audible voice resound on earth, and ravenous death shook and was terrified at the sound of his voice. “Lazarus!” the mighty one shouted into death's ears. Anguish seized death: “Who is this who calls to the dead?” He heard a human voice calling to the dead as to someone alive, and he began to writhe like a woman giving birth when her time comes. The captor heard a new voice from a fellow captive, and he cried out and wailed: “What is this new thing that has happened? Something new has befallen me,” death said. “A man with a body is crying out and shaking the strength of my might in Sheol!” “Who are you, man?” death said to the voice that called to him. “Who are you, shouting so confidently, ‘Come out, dead man’?” Who are you, who scorn my might, have acquired strength, and seek to take the human captives out of my hands? Who are you, who seek to undo the order of mortality and open the gate that Adam shut in everyone's face? It seems to me that you are not one of those human beings clothed in suffering; you seem a stranger to the kinship of mortality. Have you not heard the story of human beings, from the beginning of humanity? Look: ever since they came into being, they have been placed under subjection to my dominion. Have you not asked why they became mortal, or [?] who sold them to whom, so that they became slaves? If you do not know the reason for your race's slavery, listen to me and learn how it happened from the beginning. Your father incurred a debt of sins through the evil one's loan, and when he did not repay it, he handed over his children in payment for his debts. The devil handed you over to me as collateral, and now all the generations of your descendants serve me. I hold human beings as collateral inside my fortresses, and unless they pay the bond of your debts, they cannot escape. If you seek to free your race from its pledge, pay their debts, and then you may take their [?]. The debt of sins incurred by their deeds cannot be paid off, for however much mortality pays, it remains mortality. [?] permitted you to cast strife into the ears of the dead and disturb them with a new voice to which they are not accustomed. Who appointed you guardian of mortality? The administration of life's end has been placed in my own hands. Who [?] litigation between me and human beings? For whether they wish it or not, they obey me.

I do not allow human beings to pass beyond my dominion until they pay the debt of sins incurred by their deeds. If you are just, judge justly between me and them. Examine and see that they are imprisoned with me because of their debts. Greedy Death spoke these things without speaking, for it was not he who spoke, but the meaning of mortality. I presented this meaning in the person of mortality: the cause of wrongdoing made [?] slaves to the evil one and to Death. “Give me what you took,” our Lord said, in keeping with what had been spoken. “Give me human beings, and I will pay the bond of their debts.” “Give up the collateral that your fellow tyrant brought to you, and I will pay the debt of sins in which you boast.” “Enough of your using the garment of our body for prostitution, making our limbs like a bed beneath your whoredom!” The second Adam gave these answers to Death, not aloud, but silently, in a mysterious way. “Come outside,” the man said to the man, “to the one who called you. Come out and be a witness to my words among the dead.” “Come, mortal whom Death swallowed like everyone else. Show human beings a pledge of the life that I promise.” “Come, departed one whom voices of despair accompanied to the grave. Take hold of the life of the dead that is proclaimed in me.” Come out! Proclaim good news to humanity, and encourage them not to be terrified by the sound of death. The mortal heard the voice of one capable of suffering, like himself, and suddenly stirred at a voice imbued with creative power. The soul heard the utterance of a soul speaking with it, and returned and entered the temple of its body to sing praise within it. His will plucked his lyre as at the beginning, and the dead senses acquired perceptible sounds. What a marvel was being proclaimed in Lazarus: he listened to the sound of a voice while [?] his bodily senses were silent. How did one laid in harsh shackles and imprisoned in Sheol break them without [?] human hands? How did one imprisoned in the defiant fortresses of mortality break through them, rejoice, and laugh at his guards? The mortal heard a new voice from one of his own race and began leaping like John in the womb of Sheol. A great marvel was performed for humanity through a human being: at a human voice, the buried dead received life. Who has ever seen a miracle so full of wonder—a human being commanding the dead, “Come out!” and meeting no delay? Even though human beings have raised human beings from the dead, it was not in the manner of what took place at our Lord’s hands. Both Elijah and Elisha raised the dead, but they prayed and pleaded at length, and only then accomplished it. For they were servants and pleaded with the Creator, and he honored them as servants because of his love. Christ, who is one of us, although he belongs to our own race, did not ask and plead like a servant and only then raise the dead. Even if he pleaded like a petitioner, it was not a petition. If you had examined him while he was amid the [?] here:

I do not diminish the spring of life that was flowing within him. Rather, these were words full of the power of his exalted rank. “You have heard me,” he said before his petition, and again, “You hear.” And indeed, if he had heard him, it was superfluous to plead that he should hear. “It is because of the crowd standing here,” he said, “that I have said these things.” Clearly, then, he did not stand to pray for the sake of praying. He pleaded and asked, because this is fitting for everyone who is created. Then he called to Death, and Death brought out and gave him the dead man he had requested. The buried dead man heard the voice calling him by name, stripped off mortality and cast it away, and clothed himself in life. Lazarus came out wrapped in his burial garments; though bound all over, he walked nimbly. The departed man came out with his bodily senses bound. He was completely tied up, yet his whole body ran. The crowds marveled at the mighty power of the one who [?] him, who did not undo his bonds until he had brought him out of the tomb. He commanded the onlookers themselves to remove his garments, so that they would not doubt and suppose that it was not he, but someone else. He commanded the Jews to roll away the stone from his tomb, to refute them through their having seen his body dead and decayed. They opened the tomb that they had closed at the time of his death, and they removed the garments that he had put on his limbs. The Knower of all was observing their doubt. That is why he said, “Remove the stone,” and, “Untie him and let him go.” It would have been easy for the command that raised him from within the tomb to remove his garments and then bring him out before the onlookers. He could have first rolled the stone away from the mouth of the tomb and then untied death’s bonds from his limbs. He raised the dead man who had lain in Sheol for four days, and he made those who buried him witnesses of his death and his life. The Jews gathered in crowds to look at the dead man running with his hands and feet bound. The onlookers saw a great wonder contrary to nature. Yet although it was a great wonder to them, his deed was greater still. For it was a wonder, and however much we may say, it remained a wonder: a buried dead man was stretching himself out like a living man. Who has ever seen a departed man like Lazarus, carrying his garments on his shoulders and bringing them out with him? Who has observed the dead senses of a dead body, bound yet not hindered from moving along? His whole body was completely bound with cloth bands, and a door was shut before his eyes, yet he did not stumble. He hurried and came swiftly out of his dwelling, and the crowds hurried to [?] him closely. Everyone’s eyes were directed toward his coming out, and they could not get enough of seeing the body that death had disgorged. Eyes gazed insatiably at his body, and however much they looked, they looked again to see whether it was really he or not.

They all set him before their eyes like a target, and however much they looked at his face, they looked again. As they faced him, their eyes marveled at his eyes, which had begun to see again, and their ears at his ears, which were listening to sound. They were very eager to listen to him closely as he recounted how he had heard the voice that called him. And perhaps those dead in wickedness asked the dead man who had come to life, “What order did you see in Sheol among the departed?” And [?] the dead man who had come to life answered the living who were dead, “The order in Sheol is silence and stillness without awareness: a great silence, with no life in the limbs, and a quiet stillness, with no activity in the movements of the soul. The body is silent like a mute, in keeping with its muteness, and the soul is alive in keeping with its life, but without activity.” The dead man dropped good news into the ears of the living, turning them toward the teaching that sowed life. Our Lord was sowing new life among mortals, and he showed it to them as a pledge through Lazarus. He pledged and promised [?] to all humanity, and he confirmed his word through three dead people whom he raised and brought to life. Three witnesses put their hands to the deed of our life: Lazarus, the widow’s son, and Jairus’s daughter. He took three hostages from Death, the destroyer of humanity, until he reclaims all his captives at the end of time. Through their lives he taught him the power of his might, so that he would not doubt the final victory. At the beginning he openly revealed to us the battle he fought with him, so that he would know that he would demand from his hands the human beings entrusted to him. He set him a limit from the day Lazarus arose: “Keep for me the captives who have come to you until I come. Look, I have shown you that these human captives do not belong to you, and that you have no authority over their lives as you imagined. You are [?] of their limbs until the time is fulfilled. See that you do not lose even a portion of a hair from their heads. And you too, captives who have returned from slavery, take heed! Keep in your minds the promise of the resurrection of the dead. See that you do not go astray as you did at the beginning, lest you tighten Death’s yoke upon your lives. See what a great battle I fought on your behalf against the two mighty ones who conspired together, Death and the Evil One. See how, through my own death, I descended into the depths of Sheol, broke its gates, and cut through its bars to redeem you. Look, Death has grown weak, and the Enemy is confined among the prisoners. Do not grow lax, lest their bonds grow loose. Look, I have shown you how they are defeated and how they conquer. Prepare the means suited to the battle in which you are engaged. Put on the breastplate of good hope that does not deceive, and take hold of the shield of faith that cannot be undone. Place the helmet of great love upon your minds, and take hold of the sword of the word of truth with your [?]. Fight and conquer the desires of the passions and bodily impulses,
and await the reward of [?], life without end.” End.
Another for the Feast of Hosannas.
Another for the Feast of Hosannas. Response: With the eye of the spirit the children looked upon you as you entered, and they cried out praise. My brothers.
The saving work of the God of all is a great wonder, and it constantly stirs those with understanding to praise.

No mortal mouth can express his glory, or what blessings our race has received through his grace. Our race was submerged in the mire of mortality and was subject to Death the tyrant as to a king. Everyone served the desires of mortality, and ravenous Death triumphed over our humanity. Our enslavement did not please the Maker of all. He sent his Son, who lifted our race from its fallen state. He uprooted all the passions from the [?] of our earthly nature and promised us adoption as children, full of blessings. After he had truly been exalted, as was fitting, he ascended to heaven and was deemed worthy of the seat at the right hand. As he pleased, he freed our race from slavery; after he departed, he left his remembrance in the holy Church. He established the chosen Church in the world in the likeness of a body, and within it the feasts like members, one after another. He was not pleased to leave his Church without festivals, lest it forget his work in the flesh. Just as our body's activity depends on its members, so the Church's ordering becomes known to us through its festivals. A body cannot do anything without members, and each member separately displays its own activity. If one member could sustain the whole body, the many members in it would be superfluous. And if one member is not sufficient for the whole body, neither does one festival show the Church everything. The feast of our Lord's birth cannot show what he did on the day when he was baptized by John.

Nor can the feast on which he was baptized reveal that victory over the Evil One at the end of his fast. Nor can all the glorious feasts within the Church show everything that took place on this day. On this day the prophetic declaration of old Jacob, King David, and Zechariah was fulfilled. On this day the word of righteous Jacob was revealed, the word written ages ago about our Savior. He said, “The scepter that rules over Judah shall not depart, nor the interpreter—that is, the prophet—from between his feet, until he comes to whom the everlasting kingdom belongs.” Then prophet and king will cease from Judah. His is the everlasting kingdom without end, and he is the fulfillment of the mysteries and the expectation of the nations. As Jacob, his father, prophesied ages ago, there has been neither prophet nor king in Judah from that time onward. So the Jew has no grounds for opening his mouth to say that Christ is not the king of whom old Jacob spoke. He cannot show that he has had a king from that time onward, and he has no basis for pointing to a prophet among his people. And if prophet and king have departed, as indeed they have, then he is the one in whom Jacob's word was fulfilled. Perhaps he says, “Because we have been scattered throughout all lands, [?] a prophet for us, nor a king to lead us.” When did you ever leave your land, you evildoer, without having prophets and kings before our Lord came? When you were in Egypt, Moses and Miriam were prophets for you; and in Babylon, Hananiah and his companions, together with Daniel.

He gave you these three in Babylon, together with Ezekiel, and Joshua the priest and Ezra the scribe, together with Zerubbabel. Why are you now deprived of prophets and kings, and not honored before God because of your evil deeds? The Spirit taught old Jacob to bless you [?], and he set the limit of your honor at the coming of our Lord. That honor which existed among your people has been taken from you, and you have not been raised again to the greatness from which you descended. When did captivity carry you off to other lands without a decree fixing the number of years you were to remain? He fixed four hundred years for you to remain in the land of Egypt, and seventy years in Babylon, after which you would be freed. And now that you suppose you are in captivity outside Zion, how many years have been fixed for you to remain before you return? Be quiet and do not cause a disturbance, you wrongdoer! Your honor has passed away. The king through whom you were honored has appeared. Do not doubt, you who are circumcised in the flesh but uncircumcised in heart. Come, consider Jacob’s words with discernment. See the signs he foretold concerning that king who was to come and remove prophets and kings from you. He will tie his colt to a shoot of the vineyard’s vines, and the colt will not run wild and break off any of the shoots. Through this sign he shows—he shows his power, which subjects everything; and, as with colts, he brings tyrants under his dominion.
