O humble woman, who gained the strength to overcome demons! At her voice, those who overpower people through desires trembled. O enslaved woman, who had been yoked to the service of error, yet freed herself from slavery to a cruel master! O desolate woman, whose soul’s dwelling the demons had laid waste! Her voice brought peace to the temple of her daughter, which they had been tearing down. O compassionate mother, how great is your love! You put on armor against the evil one who had taken your daughter captive. O woman, through the sacrifice of your faith you won the king’s favor, and he brought your captive back from her captor! Oh, how you believed, how you loved, and how you endured! Your soul’s perseverance never slackened in its trust. O human nature, how faithfully it observed the obligation of its bond! It responded and paid the debt of love befitting human nature. Natural affection pierced the Canaanite woman like a torment, and she suffered greatly for her beloved daughter, whom the demon was tormenting. She saw the crafty one tormenting her daughter with the distress caused by his treachery, and his bitterness spread through her daughter’s soul and her own mind. She considered the suffering of the daughter born of her own body to be her own suffering.

She was not comforted until the enemy departed into the wilderness. She sat in deep mourning, as though over someone dead, as long as the rebel raised his voice within the temple of her daughter. Her mouth was always filled with weeping and lamentation; she heard the frenzied sounds the demon uttered. She was tormented by bitter suffering night and day as she watched the writhing of the body and the terror of the soul. Her mouth did not cease its bitter wailing until her daughter’s body grew quiet and her limbs rested. The flow of tears from her eyes and her thoughts did not stop until she saw that the fountain of the evil one’s bitterness had dried up. She did not lay aside the armor of mourning from her mind until she heard the declaration that the demon had gone out. Though alive, she did not consider herself among the living until the voice of Jesus raised her as though from the grave. With his voice he raised her from sorrow and from the demon’s mouth, and she returned and saw both the life of this age and life without end. He cast the medicine of life into her soul like seed and made the fruit of faith blossom within her mind. She and her daughter came to life out of the death caused by the demon’s destruction, and she put on the imperishable garment of faith. Through her faith the pagan woman gained two benefits: the expulsion of the demon and belonging to the name of the Creator. Through the rod of the demon that scourged her daughter, she gained understanding and learned the proper way to walk on the path toward the Hidden One. The demon himself suffered twice the pain: while he thought he was administering punishment, he was scourged in return. The rebel fell unknowingly into the trap he had set, and his cunning recoiled upon his own head, as it is written. He sought to secure his own dwelling and ruin human beings, but a command overturned the edifice of his anger and brought peace to humanity. With the fumes of his anger he sought to spoil the sweetness of peace, but peace wiped his bitterness away from mortals. He made them drunk with his strife as though with wine, but whoever became accustomed to the Spirit’s drink vomited his gall. He subjected those made of dust as though they were slaves, but one of them arose and freed them from slavery to him. He treated the children of earth contemptuously, as worthless people, but a man of flesh [?] raised his voice, and he trembled before him. He was calm and undisturbed in the dwelling of humanity, like a king, but he heard the news of human authority and shook with terror. The pangs of death suddenly seized him, like a woman in labor, when he saw human beings driving out demons in the name of the Son of Man. “What is this?” one demon asked his fellow demon. “Look, our forces are terrified at the sound of human voices! “When has the strength of the mighty been humbled before the weak, as now, when those made of dust have driven out spiritual beings? “When have those sick in body healed their own limbs, as those clothed in bodies now heal sick bodies? When have slaves freed others from bondage,

“as Jesus now grants freedom to human beings? Perhaps what is written about the Son of Man has been fulfilled: that he will trample the head of our forces when he triumphs. “Perhaps this is the time for the fulfillment of the words of Balaam, our priest, and this is the one he called a star [?] of light that enlightens humanity. “Perhaps the message spoken by that spiritual being is true, who announced his conception and called him Lord and Son of the Most High. “What is happening at this time has never happened before: human beings call upon the name of the Son of Man, and demons tremble. “It has never been heard that the dead came to life without supplication, as this one awakens the dead as though from sleep.” The enemies of humanity said these things to one another when they saw a man turning human beings away from them. They saw that the cunning snares of their disturbances had been cut apart, and the prey they had hunted from Adam until now had escaped. They saw that even a bird with feeble wings had broken the trap and flown up beyond the terror of their injuries. In the Canaanite woman they saw their own downfall: how a feeble rib had overcome the strength of demons. Take courage, O weak race that has been defeated by sin! Put on spiritual armor, fight, and conquer. Take up the shield of faith in your thoughts, and place the helmet of life-giving salvation upon the head of your mind. Wisely arm your thoughts in secret, and learn the discipline of fighting against spiritual beings. The enemy who fights against your lives is not made of flesh, but is a spirit that wages war through hidden impulses. Prepare spiritual weapons to match his hidden nature, and fight and conquer through the perseverance of your minds. Keep us [?], Living One, so that we may see evil and turn away.
On the Prodigal Son.

By the same author, again his own: the twenty-third discourse. On the Prodigal Son. During this week of the Passion, a discourse is recited every night. Response: “Fitting for the Passion, my brothers.”

I wished to become a pupil under the instruction of the books of the Spirit, and I began to ponder what is written in [?] about a man and his sons. At the beginning of the passages, I encountered the account of the division of the possessions: a father who bequeaths the wealth of his love to his two sons. I heard the younger one saying to his father, “Give me my share, so that I may have control over my own course of life. Give it to me, give it to me, so that I may be master of my possessions and manage what is mine, as it is fitting for freeborn people to exercise authority.

Give it to me, so that I may gain the standing of a son among the servants, and everyone may know, may know, that I possess freedom by birth. If I am an heir, make my standing as an heir a reality, and test my judgment through the experience of how I conduct my life.” Although the father knew that his son would not make good use of it, he did not find it difficult to fulfill his heart’s desire. Although his son’s error did not escape his kindness, he did not intend to give more to the one who lacked judgment. Although it was his prerogative to give more to the one who deserved it, he gave the great wealth of his kindness equally. The merciful father divided the wealth equally between his sons, and he did not call to account the reckless one who had brazenly made the request. The rich man’s sons received their inheritance and took possession of their shares. With their division, they separated and became estranged from one another. The younger one gathered the wealth that had come to him from his father’s household, went far away, and settled in a country distant from those who knew him. Along with his possessions, he also withdrew his love from his father, and he became fond of living among strangers. He forgot his concern for the good things of his ancestral household and began to occupy himself with things unworthy of freeborn people. In soul and body he went away and became a stranger to his own people. Along with his possessions, his thoughts traveled in pursuit of error. The prodigal took all his wealth and went away with it, leaving no remnant of his love with his relatives. He left peace behind and fell in love with a desolate place full of danger. He occupied himself with wasteful living and debauchery. His thoughts conceived an ugly desire in the [?] of wrongdoing. His mouth gave birth to foul fruit, and his eyes nurtured it. Debauchery took captive the mind of the wise man’s son. Like an exile, he went away and was humbled before threats. He forgot his wisdom and despised his honored name. He did not remember who he was, whose son he was, or what his lineage was. He ate the food of debauchery with [?] and occupied himself with filthy drinking among the dissolute. His mind became drunk with the desires of body and soul, and his darting eyes followed his impulses [?]. He became dissolute and burned with desire for flesh, the food of death. He did not realize that by eating it he was destroying the possessions of his life. He lost his wealth and scattered his possessions among prostitutes, and he became destitute of both possessions and understanding. He indulged himself and ate, but his debauchery was not satisfied. He fell into debt, was taken as a pledge, and hired himself out for his daily food. The glutton hired himself out to a cheat to work for nothing, and the hateful man [?] him under the harsh yoke of his bitterness. He used him ruthlessly, without pity, and, as an insult, made him a herdsman of despised animals. He sent the one honored above all to tend despised pigs, and gave him food from his carob pods as though he were one of the dumb animals. The enemy who hired him made his life equal to that of the animals.

He bound the activity of his understanding together with the speechless beasts. His food was less even than that of the dumb animals he tended, and the sustenance of his life was scantier than he needed. For he ate miserable food without being satisfied, and he longed to fill his belly with carob pods. Severe anguish was added to his hunger, and he reflected that, although his food was contemptible, it was scant and insufficient. The anguish of his soul tormented him far more than hunger: how he had lost his wisdom along with his possessions. In his anguish and hunger, I wanted to examine discerningly what his case meant and why it was written in the Gospel. His story troubled me from the beginning, when I encountered it: was it a parable, or was it perhaps an actual event? I pondered whether his story was true or not, and whether he had received wealth from his father's household as it is set down. My thoughts stood divided over the reading of his story, and I considered whether to call it a parable or an actual event. I marveled greatly at the scribe of the Spirit who wrote his story. In his care, he recorded his remembrance and placed it among [?]. Like an image, he brought him in and received him among wonders, so that everyone might see who he was, whose son he was, and to whom he hired himself out. Therefore we ought not to doubt his story, for the herald of the Spirit has shown that his account is true. It is a parable, not a bodily event. Yet although it is a parable, its account is true and its meaning is great. Great wealth is hidden in his story, even though it is a parable, and the Creator's power and the work of his hands are revealed in it. The man of whom it is written is the God of all, who established all things, and his two children are the ranks of the righteous and of sinners. The wealth he distributed is the discernment he gave to rational beings, so that they might recognize the power of the Maker who honored them. The elder son represents the perfect, who cherish his love; the younger son represents those who long for the love of earthly things. The Creator gave the power of his wisdom to the good and the wicked, and placed understanding in the righteous and the unjust. The righteous lovingly guarded their treasures against losses [?], but the fainthearted squandered the wealth of their own free will. They are the children who remained in the house of our Father, their father, and paid the debt that human beings owe to their Maker. The younger son, who squandered the wealth that came to him and went far away, represents the wicked, who hated the love of spiritual things. They are those who went astray and departed from the truth, went far away, and settled beyond the peace of the Creator’s name. They are those who squandered the wealth and intelligence within them, and the nourishment of life vanished and was exhausted from their minds. They are those who ate and drank extravagantly, yet the foul desire of their thoughts was not satisfied. And they are those who worked for nothing alongside the deceiver:

They fell into debt and became poor through their desires and their deeds. For the one who hired them, for whom they worked, and who gave them no wages, is a murderer, utterly devoid of help. That freeborn son, who possessed authority, hired himself out to him, and it was he who stripped him of the possessions of discernment. It was that deceitful one who made him a herder of shameful things and gave him extravagance as food, without satisfaction. It was he who accustomed him to the foul drink of debauchery; he became drunk with sin as with wine, and his mind went astray. The sinner attached himself to the Accuser through his deeds and hired himself out to him in desires that brought no benefit. The pigs that, as it is written, he tended for nothing, without nourishment, represent [?] the practice of wickedness, which brings no benefit to the one who practices it. Again, the statement that he longed to fill his belly refers to the evil desire for shameful things that are never satisfied. The carob pods are forms of extravagance: the more the heart wanders in wickedness, the more ravenous it becomes. This is how sin always treats those close to it: it entices the heart to dwell on unseemly things. Like a prostitute, it displays the face of debauchery, and instead of entering the body, it enters and commits sexual sin with the mind. Its corruption is more loathsome than that of vile animals, and union with it is more unclean than union with a beast without understanding. The prodigal son who squandered his possessions committed sexual sin with it, and it defiled him through unlawful intercourse. Love for it separated his soul’s love from the one who begot him, and through association with it he forgot the companionship of his father’s love. It impoverished him in understanding as in possessions, and subjected him to the slavery of wickedness, [?] fetters. The freeborn man performed the work of slaves alongside his [?], and he yoked him with the animals in toil and the struggle for food. Without pity the evil one worked him, the exile, and felt no sorrow for his humiliation, despised and scorned as he was. In his ignorance, he too honored the one who dishonored him. He did not discern or understand how he had gone astray or whom he was serving. The impulses of his soul were sunk as though in sleep, and he did not feel the weight of his harsh labor. His heart was drunk with desires as though with wine, and he felt no shame at the ugly things that made his soul hateful. Like a dead man he lay in the wickedness that made his soul hateful. The moth of passions was eating into him, but he did not feel it. He rotted and decayed completely through desires, and no portion of life or health remained in him. He sank down and became silent under the grievous pain that had lodged within him, until nature called him [?] in silence and spoke with him. Like a goad, nature pricked his discernment. Suddenly he stirred and saw himself, made hateful by wickedness. He saw his body and soul decaying with the ulcer of wickedness. He grieved and sighed over his merciless ruin. He wailed and wept with the sound of thunderous sobs.

He said to himself, “Where are you, discerning faculty within me? Where are you, my understanding, endowed with the wisdom of discernment? You became mute and did not consider your own degradation. Where are you, my mind, kin to the Watchers who are always awake? Raiders came in and plundered your wealth, but you neither felt it nor noticed. Where are you, intellect, charioteer of the body, governor of the senses? Your swift running has ceased, and you have lost the contest. Where are you, soul, the spring that gives the body life to drink? Your wisdom has run dry, and the flow of your reason has ceased. “Where are you?” the dead man, who had died in wickedness, asked himself. “Am I among the living or among the dead? I do not know.” With great sorrow he sighed over his humiliation, and he began to revile the wickedness that had taken him captive and plundered his wealth. “Oh, this wickedness!” the sinner cried bitterly. “It has scattered my possessions and made me a laughingstock among my acquaintances. Oh, the hateful one, who is hateful and makes whoever follows him hateful! He has made me hateful and ugly-faced in the eyes of those who see me. Oh, the unclean one, who is wholly unclean and defiles everything! He has defiled my impulses through association with his shameful deeds. Oh, how bitter is the service of wickedness, and how heavy its yoke! How fruitless is the toil of anyone who hires himself out to its depravity! Oh, how blind ignorance is, and how harmful its company! It blinds the whole person to what ought to be done. Ignorance has made me blind and senseless. It scattered the wealth that came to me from our father’s house. It stripped me of [?] and understanding, and now I live on the wretched food of carob pods. How many hired workers there are in our father’s house who live at no cost! Yet here I am, perishing of hunger in ignorance.” “How many people eat the leftovers from my father’s table, while I lack food and no one gives me relief! I will get up and go to that father who is mine—mine and everyone’s—and say, ‘I have sinned against heaven above and before you. I confess that I have sinned, not a little but greatly, for I tasted your love and squandered the wealth of your kindness.’ I will say to him, ‘I have sinned, and I am not worthy to be called your son. From now on, make me like the hired workers, and let me live by your grace.’” The prodigal son said these things to himself and began to make his way toward his father with a repentant soul. Fear and love filled his heart as he traveled. Fear frightened him, while love encouraged him to be bold and ask. Fear of his sins frightened him away from returning, while love for his father urged him, “Do not delay.” Love’s affection proved far stronger than fear. It took him by the hands and strengthened his movements so that he would not grow weak. The lost one returned along the road by which he had left his father’s house, and he set repentance as the goal at his journey’s end. Mercies saw him as he traveled toward a meeting of peace, and they went out to meet him, to console him in his sorrow. That Will which had seen him before he left saw him.

And he hastened to meet him, embraced him, and kissed him lovingly. He saw him battered, distressed, and worn out by the toils of wrongdoing, and he pitied his degradation and his humiliation among strangers. He saw him torn by the wounds the Evil One had inflicted on him. He bandaged him with mercy and washed away the filth of wrongdoing. He saw that his body and soul were stained by habitual practices, and he sprinkled him all over with the pure waters of the mystery of forgiveness. He saw that his confidence in speaking was crippled, and he began to utter words full of encouragement for the soul. “This son of mine,” he said, “was dead, but he has come to life again and returned. He is the sheep that was lost from the pastures, and now I have found him.” The one whose understanding was childish heard the message of hope his father proclaimed, and he began to stammer loudly to his father. He heard that there was hope that [?] who had died in sin might live, and he began to plead that [?] he might be raised from his hateful deeds. “My father,” he said, “I have transgressed and sinned greatly without being rebuked, and I am not worthy to call myself by the name of heir. Someone who is not free has no right to the name of son, and it is not fitting for a worker of wrongdoing to be set free. Freedom of soul does not suit one whose soul is hateful, nor does it suit a commoner to hold the scepter of authority. I fall far short of being called an heir and a son, and I am not fit to receive the rank of the immortals. Let me work for my daily bread like a stranger and receive a portion with the hired workers in your house. And if I cannot be hired to work and receive wages, grant me the privilege of receiving alms by your grace like a poor person. For I know that I have incurred debts far beyond measure, and I am unable to repay the debt of my sins.” I know well that my wrongdoing is too great to be forgiven, and the sea is too small to wash away the ugly stains of my being. There is no other medicine capable of healing my grievous pains except the mercy of the Father who brought me into being through the work of his hands. With these words he mourned the deadness of his soul, and he did not cease sighing over his transgressions. He mourned deeply over his wrongdoing as over a dead person, and with sobs he wept thunderously over his sin. His mouth and his mind were filled with bitter weeping, and tears of sorrow streamed from his eyes. The sound of his sobbing astonished his father and the heavenly hosts. His father sent compassion and mercy to him to console him. “Be still, sinner!” mercy cried to him, but he would not be still. “Look, your father has ordered that the record of your debts be torn up. “Be still! Do not weep and torment yourself and the one who fathered you, for your father too has suffered and sighed over your sobbing.” His father saw that mercy had not been enough to quiet him, so he went out himself and pleaded with him to stop weeping. “Stop! Do not weep over the loss of your former possessions, for in your father's house there are great riches without limit.

“Stop! Do not grieve over the transgressions of your ignorance. Though your wrongdoing is great, I consider it nothing to wipe it away. “For I knew before you went out that you would sin, and it was clear to me that you would squander the wealth you had received. “Your return, along with your departure, was visible to my will, and I was watching you both when you were doing wrong and when you were repenting. “The mercy that showed you compassion went out with you to the land of strangers, and it advised you to return to the peace of your ancestral home. “Come near and enjoy your possessions as an heir. Take hold of the reins and manage what is yours wisely.” His father then gave orders to [?] concerning his exaltation, that they should crown him with the name and rank belonging to his father's name. “Bring out the robe that mercy has woven, and let him be clothed in it, so that everyone may know from his splendor whose son he is. “Put on him the ring bearing the seal of his father, who is more trustworthy than all, so that slaves and free people may see that he has returned to his rank. “Let him wear on his feet pure truth that cannot prove false, and let him trample the head of the enemy who plundered his possessions. “Slaughter the bull as well, so that he and those with him may feast on it, and let the enemy who gave him carob pods for food be put to shame.” His father's words were carried out [?], just as he had commanded, and slaves and free people began rejoicing on the day of his return. But his brother, who was older than he, was not there, for he was in the countryside, diligently doing his father's work. Then [?] he too came on the day his brother returned, and he saw that a great feast had been prepared on the day of his return. The brother who saw his brother's return was deeply upset. He became angry, went back to his work, and refused to enter. His father heard and went out to him to plead with him, just as he had gone out to meet his brother with love and mercy. “My son, do not be saddened that your brother has returned to his ancestral home, and do not refuse to share in the celebration on the day of his return.” He too turned to his father in response to his entreaty, and showed by his love how much he honored his father's will. “Look how long I have served you as a slave, yet you have never honored me with a young goat so that I could entertain my friends. “But for this fellow, who squandered your household's possessions among prostitutes, now that he has returned you have slaughtered an ox, although he does not deserve it.” “My son, everything of mine is yours,” his father answered him, “and as the elder you have authority over my [?]. “Today you ought to rejoice and give praise, because your dead brother has returned and has been brought back to life from his youth.” He too greatly distressed his father, even more than his brother did, by reproaching him for showing mercy to the wanderer who had returned. That kind man endured a great uproar from his children, and bore the difficulty of their thoughts beyond all measure.

Both distressed him through the discord of their actions: one through sin, and the other by demanding an accounting for the forgiveness of wrongdoing. One grieved him by ruining his life and squandering his possessions; the other reproached him for accepting repentance. In his wisdom he patiently bore with them kindly, and taught them to imitate him and gain life. Now that the story, set out symbolically, is complete, let us investigate what meaning lies hidden within its words. Let us investigate the meaning of what is written about the prodigal, who was considering returning to his ancestral home. In the younger son and his repentance he depicted the mystery of sinners, and in his dwelling among foreigners, the [?] of demons. Through his departure he depicted estrangement from God, and through his return, repentance leading toward righteousness. In his pleading words, when he counted himself among the hired workers, there is discernment judging itself for the sins it has committed. The hired workers are the unbaptized, who have only believed and have not shared in the mystery of spiritual birth. Again, his saying, “I am not worthy to be your son,” represents a scrupulous mind that judges its own actions rightly. The father who went out to meet his son and longed to encounter him represents the mercy that shows compassion to everyone who sins. By going out, embracing him, and kissing him lovingly, he showed how greatly he desires people to return to him. The splendid robe with which he clothed his body and covered his shame is baptism, which wipes away wrongdoing and grants freedom. The ring is the pledge of immortal life that the Spirit gives to [?] those who have acquired the name of daughters. The fattened ox is the great mystery of the body and blood of the one who, through his sacrifice, reconciled the world with his majesty. He fittingly called the sacrifice of his body a [?] fattened ox, for he was nourished with the food of the Spirit and a drink of wine. His slaughtering it on the day his son returned from wandering is also a sign of his immeasurable love for our race. By the voice that proclaimed, “My son was dead and has returned to life,” he taught us how greatly he rejoices in our repentance. By appeasing his son, who was reproaching him for showing mercy to the lost, he offered a rebuke to anyone angry at the forgiveness of wrongdoing. In that portrayal he was not accusing the righteous, but anyone here who finds fault with mercy for showing compassion. Before the judgment, he revealed beforehand what was to come, so that anyone angered by compassion might calm his disposition. He showed two things through his words to the elder son: that the righteous person who is constant in serving the truth should not be reproached. It is written in the Gospel that the one who was reproached was in the countryside, making known to us that he was always occupied with righteousness. The countryside symbolizes the practice of spiritual life, and he represented the things above through a likeness drawn from earthly things.

As for the young goat that he said his father had not given him to enjoy: his father had restrained him and kept him from taking part in reckless living. He called wrongdoing a young goat, because it wanders and leads people astray, just as young goats also wander, each one away from the flock. The young goat is very unruly at pasture, and its color is dark. It resembles wrongdoing, which smears the soul with [?] and darkens it. The friends of [?] represent human nature, which is stirred by enticements and demands its own, however much it desires spiritual things. For nature loves what belongs to it, since it is earthly, and it is placed, as though in a contest, between the two: the body and the spirit. His father lifted him out of the enticements of bodily desire and promised him the riches of the spirit to delight in. “Everything that is mine is yours,” he said to [?], making known to us that the promised blessings belong to him. In the parable he portrayed our whole nature as an image, and brought it in and placed it within the palace of the heavenly order [wrongdoing: ?]. In a form accessible to the senses, he represented the world through his two sons, and gathered the good and the evil to him for the wedding feast of his love. Through the younger son he drew sinners to repentance, and through the elder he encouraged the righteous with the payment of their reward. He called our human nature sons and heirs, masters of created natures, and became our Father—a great wonder beyond words. Oh, how far beyond anything the tongue can recount is this: that the Maker of all called himself a Father to humanity! Oh, how greatly the nature of the [?] of dust has been exalted, being deemed worthy to become an heir and a son of its Maker! Oh, what can we say, and how can we tell of what has happened—that he has become our Father, and we the heirs of his divinity? He has shown our race a great, inexpressible love, and every creature’s mouth trembles to tell how great it is. How can a mute mouth suffice to recount the greatness of his love, which made us, together with him, objects of worship for all creatures? How can we repay him the debt of love, when he has made even the spiritual beings rejoice in our repentance? “In this way,” he says, “the heavenly assemblies will rejoice over a sinner who returns and pleads for forgiveness for his wrongdoing.” And if the angels rejoice with us at our repentance, then severe is the reckoning for anyone who criticizes mercy. If the spiritual beings thirst to see us made righteous, then anyone who hates his brother deserves double punishment. Indeed, the heavenly hosts rejoice that we are alive, yet you are grieved that mercy freely shows favor to human beings. Indeed, the natures that cannot suffer have grieved over our [?], yet you are pleased that we should remain in Sheol without [?]. Indeed, they long for the time when we will reign together, yet you are angry with anyone who runs in keeping with their desire. Indeed, I too, a sleeper sunk in the sleep of wickedness, sprang up at the sound of forgiveness and rose to pour forth words. The story of the wanderer urged me to seek the power of wonders, and through his return my thoughts turned toward instruction. His story drew me to read in the book of his writings and learn the power hidden in the words spoken by the Spirit.

I went out with him as he left his father's house, and I returned with him to see his appeal to his father. I saw him squander great possessions among prostitutes, and then I watched him turn back to go toward forgiveness. I heard him put together sorrowful words about his folly, and I grieved deeply over my own wickedness, which resembles his. I heard him say, “I am not worthy to be called an heir,” and grief seized me because I had walked the road of the one who squandered his possessions. The path of my deeds closely resembles the one he traveled, and I too have squandered the wealth of life just as he did. I too worked for that [?] to whom he hired himself out, and like him I lived on the carob pods of [?]. Ignorance has made me too devoid of mercy, just as he also lost what was his through lack of understanding. May the mercies that favored him and brought someone out to meet him on the day of his return plead for me before the Judge who examines everything. May the voice that said, “My son was dead and has returned to life,” make me worthy to hear, “Come, sinner, receive forgiveness.” May the hand that spread a robe of glory over his nakedness cover my face, so that it will not be exposed before the eyes of onlookers. The command that gave him a pledge of life in the form of a ring strengthens my thoughts to await the promise of life. May the mouth that calmed the anger of his brother, who criticized mercy, rebuke the tyrannical wickedness that wages war against my thoughts. May the Watchers who rejoiced on the day of his return and praised his father become advocates for me in my guilt before justice. May the finger that depicted his ruin and the restoration of his life draw upon my mind the image of [?] that gives life. Yes, my Lord, let me share in the banquet of the dead man who came to life, and let what was spoken at the end of his story be fulfilled in me. Yes, my Lord, by grace make me worthy, together with him, of the feast of your love, and let mercy receive me at the judgment, as he was received.
For Thursday of Easter.
Discourse Nineteen. To be recited on the Thursday of Easter. Refrain: You who put an end to wars to the ends of the earth, put an end among us to the battles of the deceitful one, my brothers.

The mighty warrior went out to battle to bring back his captives from the Evil One. He put on armor of flesh to fight against the spiritual foe. The champion armed himself for combat with the strong one. He placed his authority upon his shoulder to show the power of his greatness. On the summit of Golgotha he opened the arena for his combat, so that angels and human beings might witness his contest. The enemy saw and was enraged that the champion had come down into the arena. With the devil’s weapons he prepared himself for slaughter. The rebel equipped himself with the appearance of armor, with [?] tricks. “Mortals owe me service as their master.” The champion of righteousness was watching the aim of his deceit. He was saying, “Look, the ruler is coming to plead his case.” “Now,” he said, “is the great trial in which the devil brings his case against me. As with everyone else, he demands an accounting from me for the reproach of death and sin.” The ruler of the world shouted

with threatening cries, thinking that he could terrify the Son of Adam as he had Adam. “Do you not know that the whole world and its authority have been handed over to me? Do you not acknowledge my might, since I have enslaved your entire race? You all serve me as slaves from beginning to end. Have you not heard about the battle I fought with Adam in Eden? How I prevailed and conquered the living image of the Creator!” With words full of deadly poison he tried to frighten the champion. He did not know that the champion was mocking him, laughing at his tricks. He thought that through death he would conquer him as he had everyone else. He did not know that through his death the champion would take the captives out of his hands. The insolent one fulfilled his desire and satisfied himself through death. But the dead man on the cross turned upon him, overthrew him, and abolished his authority. The one who was mortal by nature died, and the power dwelling in him raised him to life. Through the victory of his resurrection he brought the captives back from the Evil One. He stripped off mortality and cast it away, and was exalted above suffering. He tore up the debtors’ bond and through his blood reconciled those who were at enmity. He bound rational beings in love toward the Creator. His death became the source of life for mortals and immortals. Rational beings and creatures without speech alike gained hope and renewal. The authority of the rebel who had enslaved humanity was extinguished and destroyed. He began to wail, crying, “What have we to do with you, Son of David?” The heralds filled with the Spirit pierced him with their voices from every side, pursuing the deceitful one so that he would not disturb humanity’s peace. Those who reveal hidden things disclosed to the rebel the torment awaiting him. They cast into his ears the news that his flame would not be extinguished. When he saw that his authority had ended and torment was prepared for him, he became bitter, reckless, and mad, and turned entirely to opposition.

He saw that his schemes had been exposed by the light of Christ’s appearing. He began to act brazenly in public and to seize an honored name for himself. The insolent one calls himself Christ, an angel of light, and calls those who carry out his will angels of righteousness. He heard that Christ’s coming was to take place at the end of the ages, and the deceiver began to lead people astray in the name of Christ’s revelation. Long ago he conceived a plan, and he rages over it in his bitterness. His desire burns like fire to bring his will into the open. The command of the Creator’s power restrains his bitterness until the end brings the time appointed in his [?]. He knows how long the span of the ages must endure. He removes the command that restrains, and then the wicked one appears. At the end of the ages, he gives him freedom to display his bitterness. The insolent one rushes forward and rises to the lofty name of Christ. He imitates him in everything, in outward appearance [?] and not in reality, performing miracles like his through an illusion without substance. The rebel does not make his coming in spiritual form. Through a human being he accomplishes his deception among those who are perishing. The devil imitates the manner of Christ’s appearing: he chooses a human being for himself and through him brings his wickedness to completion. The rebel makes himself like the Word from the Father, who willingly came down to dwell in our humanity. He imitates that majesty which brought about the life of our salvation. He too clothes himself in a human being and through him hunts people down for death. He chooses one human being for himself from the very race of mortals [?]. He clothes him in a spirit of falsehood and through him performs deceptive miracles. He makes him drink the cup of his gall and intoxicates him with the fumes of his anger. With his bitterness he confuses the clear-minded, so that they will become like him. The insolent one accomplishes his entire will through that human being, stealing through him the honor, stealing through him the honor

of the majesty of Christ’s glory. He sends messengers ahead of him, thousands of demons, in every direction. They throw creation into turmoil with terrifying reports of his coming. They sow reports [?] full of terrors in the ears of all peoples. They leave their work and go out to see the deceitful one. Disasters and bitter reports race throughout the whole earth: “Look, the one awaited has now appeared! Go out and welcome the coming king!” The host of demons throws the inhabited world and its inhabitants into turmoil, as they gather from every direction to see the murderer. Terrifying visions are shown to [?] at night, and during the waking hours of the day there are reports that disturb people’s minds. The coercive power of the demons drags humanity toward the deceiver. As crowds upon crowds flock to the wicked worship of the rebel. That vessel of all error is borne in procession by thousands of demons, while rebels cry out to him, “Hail, king! [?], ruler!” He makes himself fly through the air, borne in procession among the clouds, and through a spirit of falsehood appears to the onlookers as someone flying. Unclean demons proclaim that unclean one holy, as though he were righteous. They weave praises for the insolent one as though he were righteous. He opens his mouth and speaks words full of peace. He draws humanity to himself under the guise of love and harmony. With false promises he draws people of every rank after his words. He promises revival and resurrection to the corpses of those who have fallen asleep. He raises the dead without bodies, through shadows and likenesses. He gives the lame the ability to walk, though they do not tread on the ground. Deceptive signs are falsely performed, and through a spirit of error the deceiver leads people astray by means of the son of perdition. He devises ever more schemes to lead people of every rank further astray. He hides all his snares deep down, to ensnare people of every stature in great numbers. He dissolves the authority of judges so that his own authority may reign. He abolishes kings and their crowns so that they may call him alone king. He removes levies and servitude, the poll tax and tribute. So that, once relieved of servitude, they may devote themselves to worship. He proclaims peace and harmony,

like a peace-loving king, so that under the pretext of peace he may entrap people of every rank in his snares. Messengers travel ahead of him to prepare halls for him. He moves from place to place in the manner of a king and ruler. The rebel is called God by his attendants. When he enters the holy temple, they worship him as Lord. The insolent one is honored as the Creator by the unjust. For the deceiver, the vessel of falsehood, calls himself the Messiah. That unclean lover of wickedness sits in the temple of atonement. He wickedly accepts unlawful worship from worthless people. “I am the awaited Messiah!” This is what the wrongdoer proclaims. “Let mysteries, symbols, and wonders now cease and come to an end.” He abolishes worship as well, so that he alone may be served. He removes the word of instruction so that his own word may be accepted. He silences the holy voices, the heralds of the Spirit’s words, so that they may not read aloud in the people’s hearing, nor the people listen to the message of life. “It was about me,” he says, “that the heralds proclaimed when they considered my coming.” Leave the spectacle of wonders and look at the true person. He stops baptism in water so that sinners will not be justified. He opens the spring of his foulness and stains the pure with it. “I myself justify sinners and forgive wrongdoing and sin. My words grant forgiveness to body and soul in place of water.” He abolishes the table of forgiveness so that it will not be consecrated according to the prescribed rite. He proclaims in everyone's hearing the abolition of the living sacrament. He removes the sweet spring from the lips of those who drink from it. He withholds that spiritual food from those who receive it. With insolent arrogance he shouts words full of blasphemy. “I myself am the truth and its interpretation. Leave the sacraments and honor the truth.” Oh, the calamity, bitter to hear of, that the rebel is going to bring about! He calls the sacrament of the body of the one who gives life to all his own sacrament.

Let the discerning now clothe themselves in mourning over this calamity. Let those who distinguish falsehood from truth pour out tears of sorrow. Let those who love study and learning compose songs of lamentation, for the deceiver abolishes discourse on the words of the Spirit. Let the unclean who were sanctified in the washing of baptism weep, for the rebel silences spiritual birth. Let all who share in the living sacrament grieve together, for those who belong at Christ's table are deprived of the medicine of life. Let the priests who minister in the sanctuary clothe themselves in garments of mourning. For the devil dissolves the rule governing their orders. Let all ranks sing songs of lamentation in every meter. For the sounds of praise cease and are no longer sung in the sanctuary. Who would not weep and groan over this bitter calamity? For the worship of [?] ceases and is offered to the devil. The insolent one throws all established practices into confusion on the day of his revelation. He dissolves rites and laws so that his own error may be honored. With lying signs he draws the simple to himself, and with changing apparitions he deceives the hearts of the knowledgeable. He abolishes the worship of the gods and dismisses pagan priests and diviners, so that he alone may serve as priest, king, and prophet. The things our Savior spoke of are fulfilled first: reports of tumults and wars. Then the lawless one appears. There will be earthquakes, pestilences, and calamities full of terror. Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom. The world ceases its labor during harsh and bitter winters. He stretches out the rod against everyone, and famine wastes mighty men. At a time of distress and upheaval, when tumults and wars grow intense, the insolent one brings about the revelation of his bitterness.

Because of this he astounds everyone, and error spreads among the mighty. Who see the season changing and the frosts melting away from the earth. He brings wars and battles to an end and increases peace for all nations. So that they may not be hindered in their pursuit of service to his bitterness. With these snares he imprisons humanity and binds it. So that when they see a counterfeit peace, they will accept it as genuine. Under the pretext of promoting peace, he draws all nations to himself. They abandon their occupations and escort him in honor as a king. Every order that is not troubled and goes astray after his teaching. Even the elect, if possible, he turns aside and draws into accepting his persuasion. The sorcerer, the murderer, makes use of love and compassion. The hater of all righteousness offers a greeting of peace to everyone. He hates only the elect, who refuse to obey him. He stirs up the crowds in anger against the righteous, so that they may not live. He moves from place to place, practicing deceit throughout his dominion. The rebel exalts himself above every object of worship and every god. It is not the error of idol worship that the deceiver dissolves and abolishes. He devises schemes to wipe the worship of truth from the earth. Under the appearance of peace, he weakens love for the Creator. Under the appearance of righteousness, his servants run before him. They bring good news of peace, saying, “Look, the savior has arrived!” Cities go out to meet him with songs and praises. They cry out to him with hosannas: “Glory to the king who has appeared to us!” He turns the joy of the church of the nations into great mourning, and the holy bride is corrupted by the false worship of the impostor. Lips that cried out praise and kissed the mysteries of the medicine of life cry out words of blasphemy and kiss the devil. Mouths that sang praises in the sanctuary, songs full of the Spirit, Defile the holiness of their mouths with songs to the deceiver. With the sound of praise, the brazen one steals the worship due to his Lord, bringing humanity down from the heights to the depths.

The rebel accomplishes his entire purpose through the son of destruction. Then the Creator gives a sign of mercy upon the earth. Elijah suddenly appears, restrains the deceiver’s onslaught, and stops him in his course, so that he may not go further and cause everyone to stumble. With this commission Elijah is sent at the end of the ages: to come and set everything right before the revelation of Christ. Elijah comes first to silence the voices of error and make the hearts of fathers cry out, so that they may be corrected by their children. The King sends a messenger full of peace to the inhabited world, so that through the plainness of his words he may temper the bitterness of the wrathful one. Like a lamp, he gives light through him to those in darkness, leading them to knowledge; and like a guide, he calls through him to those who wander, leading them to the way of life. At Elijah’s words, the voices of the deceitful one fall silent. The captives cut through his snares and turn back from wrongdoing. Elijah abundantly sows words of heartfelt remorse, and with the dew of his words he nurtures repentance among the people and the nations. In the same role in which John served before his earthly appearing, Elijah comes before that heavenly appearing. He chose for himself two heralds of flesh for his two revelations, to prepare for him on earth halls of love for him at his two revelations. To prepare for him on earth halls of love within the soul. John proclaimed his birth, and Elijah his revelation. Both have one aim: to bring the lost back to him. Elijah gives repeated warnings: “Look, the end has now drawn near! You who wander, turn back from error to the clear path of my words.” The insolent one persists in his stubbornness, going astray and leading people astray, until the overwhelming blow falls upon the face of the whole earth. He keeps the lawless one for that revelation, and then destroys him, so that humans and angels may see the judicial punishment he receives. Before that day, the signs that our Savior gave will appear. Everything written will be fulfilled, and the world will cease its course. The sun’s rays will be extinguished, and the moon will not give its light. The stars will fall like leaves, and the course of the heavenly lights will cease. Thousands of their ranks will move in procession,

those of the heavenly powers, as their ruling orders attend to the preparations for the King on high. Christ, the Lord of glory, will open the gate of the firmament. His revelation will suddenly shine forth and eclipse the heavenly light. Compared with the light before him, the light of the sun is darkness. Compared with his swift appearing, the flash of lightning is slow. Nothing compares with the glory in which his revelation is displayed, and nothing resembles the majesty in which the Watchers escort him. Thousands of spiritual assemblies proclaim the praise of his majesty, and countless seraphim declare his holiness from every direction. Their voices cannot be expressed in earthly languages, nor can mortals hear the melodies of their songs of praise. They shake the earth with their voices and heaven with their trumpets, as they run to the four corners to proclaim the message of salvation. The sound of horns makes the inhabited world and its inhabitants tremble, and terrifying trumpets cast trembling into the hearts of the drowned. Above them all, Christ, the Lord of glory, is borne in procession, while they cry out to him with their voices: “Holy is our victorious King!” The archangel bears in procession the living sign of the cross, and with indescribable glory displays it before the eyes of those who watch. The victory of the King who conquered by his cross goes before him, and spiritual beings proclaim him holy in place of the insults of the wicked. The tribes of the house of Israel are put to shame at the sight of him, and in mournful melodies they utter cries of lamentation. With great splendor he displays that sign on which he suffered on earth. When those who crucified him see the greatness of his glory, they will be put to shame before him. He himself, our firstfruits, is borne in procession with his sign by spiritual beings. Those in heaven and those on earth see the glory of his majesty. He appears in his own nature to spiritual beings and bodily beings. The one who ascended in the clouds is himself the one who comes at the end. At his ascension the angels announced beforehand his appearing: in the same form in which he ascended, he comes in his great glory. It is not the nature of the divine Being that changes place and travels in its own nature. It is the bodily one who comes to judge, the one who received judgment and authority.

It does not belong to the divine Being by nature to move from place to place. It is the will alone that travels. The self-existent Word descends with the body from on high, in a descent without change. Through this descent he renews rational beings and examines their deeds. He appears in great splendor, shining like lightning. He makes his appearance visible from one end of the earth to the other. The chiefs of the angels sound their spiritual trumpets. When their trumpets finish, the horn of resurrection sounds. The chief of the angels sounds the final horn of resurrection. With terrifying cries he commands the earth to give birth to the departed. Labor pains strike the earth so that it gives birth in return for the seeds. The command compels it, so that no dead person remains within its womb. The terrifying voice frightens Death, the master of the house of Sheol, demanding from him an account of the number of Adam’s children. No dead person is lost in Sheol, and no limb remains in it. It is one and the same voice that raises the good and the wicked alike. The resurrection is the same for everyone, but everyone’s appearance is not the same. It is the will that makes one body appear more glorious than another. At night the King on high reveals himself to those on earth, and he dispels the darkness with the light flashing from his body. Remorse falls upon everyone at the sound of the angels’ triumphant cries, and those on earth are terrified at the sight of the spiritual beings. The human heart is bewildered by the sound, which resembles that of the sea. Pains and pangs seize them, with a trembling that drives out their souls. The terrifying voice frightens the rebellious devil, and all his authority comes to an end at a single gesture, in the blink of an eye. He binds him with ropes of fire and throws him into the flame, while the onlookers contemplate his endless silence. But the man whom he chose for himself, and through whom he fulfilled his wicked desire, he removes from existence by destroying his body and soul. He does not allow him to remain with his master in torment. He utterly consumes him and removes him from life.

The Creator performs a new wonder upon the son of destruction: to the destruction of his limbs is added the dissolution of his soul. Through the destruction of his life, he shows rational beings a great horror: how the soul, whose nature is immortal, perishes from life. That vessel of all error deserves to become an object of terror. Because he led people astray from the truth, let people recount his destruction. To the Devil's disgrace, he destroys him, removing him from existence, so that, because his will dwelt in him, they may be tormented by the destruction of his life. Redoubled torments multiply for the rebel in Gehenna: the temple of his will is destroyed, while he himself is tormented forever. Before spiritual and bodily beings, he destroys that man. To those in heaven and those on earth, he shows the humiliation of the insolent one. First he binds the rebel and throws him into Gehenna. Then he opens the gates on high and gathers his chosen ones to himself. He makes a great separation when he gathers the chosen. The righteous fly to heaven, while the wicked remain on earth. Here what was prophesied beforehand by the pure is fulfilled. Some are taken and others are left, as the good are separated from the wicked. First the departed rise and cast off mortality. Then the living are transformed into the likeness of the immortals. Then the words of Paul the herald are fulfilled: the living whom the end overtakes do not sleep the sleep of death. The dead and the living are transformed and become like spiritual beings. He renews body and soul, and they no longer fear suffering. A single voice rouses the dead and raises them from the sleep of death. Along with the resurrection of the departed, the living undergo transformation. At a slight signal, all these separations take place. In the blink of an eye, heavenly and earthly beings are transformed. Swifter than lightning is that light which shines out suddenly. With the dawning of his appearance, he transforms everything and renews everything. The bodies of the righteous become capable of flight and spiritual. They are carried in honor upon the clouds as far as the gate of the firmament. Clouds of light bend down.

They carry the bodies of the holy ones, who are caught up to meet the bridegroom and enter heaven with him. He raises his commanding voice toward the gate of the firmament and opens the great gate of heaven before those who are entering. The King enters at the head of his army, together with all who loved his appearing. He shuts the gate of heaven against the wicked and unbelievers. At that time the demons and wicked people are terrified, seeing the glory of the elect as they are carried in procession on the clouds. They knock at the gate of justice, but grace does not answer them. They ask the Judge for mercy, but the Merciful One disregards them, because they loved the earth of curses and did not desire heavenly blessings. They are left in the place they loved, suffering harsh punishment. Sorrow and anguish of soul crush them far more than the punishments. There they judge their own faults and expose their deeds. There they gain knowledge and become able to discern their duties. They acknowledge that justice is right in the penalties imposed on them. There they see with understanding, through the senses of the agile mind. The crowns of glory with which the saints are rewarded in the kingdom on high. They weep and lament with sobbing as they look upward toward heaven. They see the path between them, which is difficult to cross to reach the good. “Open for us!” the oppressors cry to the Lord whose love they hated. A voice answers them, “I do not know your labors.” The laments that sinners utter there cannot be counted, nor can the sobbing with which they plead because of their torment be expressed. The earth becomes like Gehenna for the children of earth. In the furnace of their thoughts they examine the dross of their faults. With the vision of their minds they see the hidden things in their deeds. On the scales of their understanding they weigh the burden of their evil deeds. The punishment of torment is not equal for all those in Gehenna. For one punishment is more bitter than another according to the greatness of the wickedness. Nor, in the glory of those on high,

is the radiance of their splendor equal. For crowns of glory are given to the victorious according to their labors. Paul compared their splendor to the stars, those shining lamps. For one body shines more brightly than another, just as one star outshines its companion. Justice weighs out and gives each person a reward according to their labor. The glory of the diligent increases according to the love within their minds. Instead of earth, they have the expanse of the upper surface of the firmament. Their canopy is the heaven above, which was established from the beginning. They dwell in a radiant place where darkness does not reign. Nothing compares with the sweetness of their spiritual delight. They do not toil in their rest, nor grow weary as they recline. They exult spiritually in blessings that never end. Their labors are their songs of praise, and their occupation is their worship. And there is no tiring of the melodies with which they sing praise to the divine Being. There is no desire of the flesh there, nor any change of mind, for soul and body are raised above passions and changes. In the great glory, the outward forms that distinguish them fade away. And males and females are equal in the garment of light in which they are wrapped. There the distinction between slavery and freedom ceases, for there is one who alone reigns and extends his authority over all. There God is wholly present in the souls of rational beings, while all proclaim him holy, both spiritual and bodily beings. There every authority ceases, for only one authority is named, and he subjects the rebel’s entire force beneath his feet. The devil and sinners cry out to him from the darkness: “Your judgment is just, O Judge, and the sentence of your justice is right.” The good proclaim him holy in the light, with praise that never loses its vigor. For they are strengthened by the power of the Spirit to render praise to his majesty. The knowledge of his faithfulness is made known over all and in all. And the good and the wicked alike clearly acknowledge that the divine Being is one.

There the divisions and schisms that disputes brought forth cease. And one God is believed in, in three equal persons. They learn the power of the divine Being, who is high and exalted above suffering. And with unveiled faces they see the firstfruits that he took from us. They see him as an image through the sight of the outward senses. And with the mind they contemplate the divine Being, who has no image, through the sight of the outward senses. And with the mind they contemplate the divine Being, who cannot be seen. In him they offer thanksgiving as in a temple of atonement. While at the doorway of his body they worship the nature that cannot be bounded. They become his partners in the inheritance of great glory. For through their kinship with him they are honored with his glories. It is not to the height of his authority that they are raised through kinship with him. For he is honored together with the eternal Being by spiritual and bodily beings. His heirs are given the name of immortality. And from the light of his great glory their bodies are clothed with glory. Let us remember these blessings and despise the desire for gain. Let us long for that light and see our ugliness in the light. Let that day be like a mirror for us, and let us look into it. Let us use it to polish away the blemishes of our souls before the examination of justice. Let us awaken our slumbering minds through the vigilance of love for the truth. Lest the thief come and snatch away our soul’s wealth. Before that day, let us prepare oil for the light of our lamps. So that terrors do not bind us with the harsh ropes of sin, And we are hindered from traveling the smooth road of righteousness. For the gate of the kingdom is narrow, and the road of life is constricted. Through purity of soul, let us acquire wings for our heavy limbs. Since the day of the coming is hidden, let us guard our treasures with fear, lest he come suddenly and come upon us like a thief. Let us order our conduct here in purity, like the wise, and through knowledge of the Spirit acquire spiritual gains. For the chasm lying between those above and those below is formidable. Let us travel with love as our companion, so that it may lift our weight. With the anchor of faith, let us secure the ships of our minds, so that the waves do not drown us:

The waves of the devil’s doubts.
Response: Glory to your power, our Savior, by which you defeated the devil.
On the Explanation of the Mysteries
[?] Seventeenth Discourse: On the Explanation of the Mysteries

My thoughts pondered the mysteries of the Church in a mystical way, and I wished to reveal the meditation of my heart through the words of my mouth. With the words of my mouth I wished to speak of their greatness, and in verses to draw a picture of their glory. My mind gazed intently upon their glory, but trembling seized me, weakened me, and left me unable to act. Unable to act, I stopped and stood still because of the blazing heat, and I began to cry out sorrowfully with the son of Amoz. With the son of Amoz, I pronounced woe upon my unclean self, which in its uncleanness had directed its mind toward its Lord’s mysteries. I pondered these things and turned back in fear, but the Spirit, by his prompting, encouraged me to enter the Holy of Holies. He allowed me to enter the Holy of Holies of the glorious mysteries and reveal the beauty of their glory to those initiated into the mystery. Come, then, now, you who are initiated into the divine mystery. Hear the account, wondrous in its words, of the mysteries of the Church. “A mystery for me, a mystery for me, a mystery for me and for my own,” the prophet cries.

Now listen with understanding to the mystery being revealed to you. Truly, this mystery is lofty and exalted, which the priest performs mystically within the sanctuary. The Church mystically depicts the glorious mysteries and shows everyone, as in an image, the things that happened. Through the mysteries she commemorates the things that happened at the Son’s death, and she also reveals his resurrection from the dead before everyone’s eyes. A mystery [?] what has happened and what will happen; but the Church symbolizes in her mysteries only what has happened. The Church celebrates her mysteries in secret, away from outsiders, and the priest performs them mystically within the sanctuary. She gives only her baptized, sealed children the joy of sharing in these revered mysteries that she celebrates. Therefore she calls out to the hearers through the deacons, telling them to bow their heads and receive a blessing from the priesthood. Bow your heads, you faithful, baptized hearers, and receive a blessing through the laying on of the pure priest’s hand. After they have been blessed, another proclamation addresses them: “Everyone who has not received baptism must leave here.” “Go, you unbaptized; do not share in the Church’s mysteries, for only members of the household are permitted to share.” Again another proclamation is made in a different form: “Everyone who has not received the seal of life must leave here.” Anyone who has repented and returned from heresy that distorts the faith must not share in the Church’s mysteries until he is sealed. Again, anyone who has denied his faith and returned to his madness must not share until he is absolved through the Church’s seal. Again another proclamation is made in a different form: “Everyone who does not receive the body and blood must leave here.” Anyone who has been placed under restriction by the priesthood and forbidden to receive may not remain even at the time when the offerings are presented. Anyone forbidden by the rule to receive the holy sacrament is not even permitted to stand in the place where the offerings are presented. A sick person who is not well and is necessarily unable to receive may not even stand in the church where the mysteries are consecrated.

They all leave the church sorrowfully, and they stand in deep mourning in the church’s courtyard. They call those who remain in that delight blessed, and pronounce woe upon themselves because of their separation. Through her dismissal, the holy Church depicts those who go out into the darkness of Gehenna. The king saw a man who was not wearing garments [?], and he gave the order, and they bound him and cast him into the outer darkness. The Church likewise examines her congregations at the time of the mysteries, and casts out anyone who is not adorned with clean garments. After these things, a cry addresses the hearers, telling them to go and inspect the church’s doors and keep watch over them. “Go, hearers, diligently watch the outer doors, since you do not share in the Church’s mysteries as members of the household do.” The prodigal son who squandered his possessions remembered these things and humbly asked to be like the hired workers. Let us put anger and resentment away from us at that time, and look upon Jesus as he is led to death for our sake. He goes out to his suffering in the paten and cup with the deacon: bread in the paten and wine in the cup, the symbol of his death. These men carry the symbol of his death in their hands; and when they placed it on the altar and covered it, they represented his burial. These bear not the image of the Jews, but that of the watchers who ministered at the Son’s suffering. He was served by angels at the time of his suffering, and the ministers ceremonially honor his body [?] in mystery. Now the priests enter the sanctuary in procession and stand there in great glory and splendid majesty.

The priest chosen to perform that sacrifice bears the image of our Lord in his own person at that time. He served as mediator between us and his Father, and in the same manner the priest serves as mediator. Listen, priest, to what a height you have reached because of your rank! Tremble before our Lord and honor your rank as befits it. See that you have been raised above the cherubim, above the seraphim! Let your conduct rise above nature, as befits you. See that you have been entrusted with administering your Lord’s treasures! Be without blemish and beyond reproach, as you have been commanded. In this role the priest stands at that time, and nothing compares with the greatness that he approaches. All the priests in the sanctuary bear the image of those apostles who gathered at the tomb. The altar is undoubtedly a symbol of our Lord’s tomb, and the bread and wine are our Lord’s body, embalmed and buried. The cloth above them also represents the stone sealed with the signet ring of the [?] and the guards. The deacons who stand on either side waving fans symbolize the angels at his head and at his feet. All the deacons who stand in attendance before the altar portray the watchers who surrounded our Lord’s tomb. The sanctuary also represents Joseph’s garden, from which life flowed to human beings and angels. In another way, it represents that kingdom which our Lord entered and into which he brings all his friends with him. Its revered altar symbolizes that throne of his great glory, upon which he appears to watchers and human beings on the day of his revelation. The sanctuary symbolizes these things below and those above; it commemorates what happened and portrays what takes place spiritually. As soon as the priests and deacons stand together, they begin to recite the faith of the fathers.

We believe in one God, the Father from eternity, who holds all things by the hidden command of his divinity. He made and established everything visible and invisible, and brought the creation above and below into being from nothing. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He is the only-begotten in his divinity and the firstborn in his body, for he became the firstborn from the dead of all created beings. He is begotten of his Father and exists without beginning; he did not come into being or come to be made along with created things. For he is God from God, Son from the Father, of his Father’s nature and equal to him in all that belongs to him. Through him the worlds were revealed, and everything that came into being was created; in authority, worship, and glory he is equal to his Father. For our sake he came down from heaven without change, to redeem our race from slavery to the Evil One and death. By the power of the Holy Spirit he formed a bodily temple from the daughter of David; he became human and made his temple divine through union. His body was conceived in the temple of Mary without sexual union, and he was born in a way beyond the ordinary course of human birth. He suffered, was crucified, and accepted death in his humanity alone, while Pilate held the governorship. He was in the tomb for three days like every dead person, and he rose and came back to life, as is written in prophecy. He ascended on high, to the heaven of heavens, to bring everything to completion, and sat in glory at the right hand of the Father who sent him. He will come at the end of time to renew everything and to judge the living and also the dead who died in sin. We also confess the Holy Spirit, who exists from eternity, equal in essence and divinity to the Father and the Son. He proceeds from the Father in a way that cannot be fathomed and gives life to all rational beings who were created by him. We also confess one universal Church, belonging to the fathers and the apostles, sanctified by the Spirit. We also confess one washing and baptism:

In it we are baptized for the forgiveness of sins and adoption as children. We also confess the resurrection from the dead and that we will live a new life forever and ever. Three hundred and eighteen priests set their seal to this; they established it as the rule and anathematized everyone who does not confess according to their confession. The Church confesses according to the confession of the fathers, and [?] she also serves their faith at the time of the mysteries. At the time of the mysteries her children thunder out their faith, reciting it with mouth and heart, without doubt. After the faith has been recited in the proper order, the Church’s herald then directs them to pray. “Pray,” he says, “in remembrance of the fathers, the catholicoi and bishops, together with the teachers, and with them the priests, the deacons, and all the orders, and everyone who has departed from this world in faith, that they may be crowned on the day of [?] from the dead, and that we may inherit life with them in that kingdom. Pray, my brothers, for the offering that we present, that it may be acceptable before God, to whom it is offered, and that through the hovering of the Holy Spirit it may be sanctified, so that it may become for us a source of life in the kingdom on high.” With these words the Church’s herald urges the people, telling them to pray before God with a pure heart. The priest then offers the mystery of the salvation of our lives, filled with trembling and clothed in fear and dread. The priest trembles, is greatly afraid, and shakes exceedingly because of his own sins and the sins of all the children of the Church. He is the eye of the whole body of the Church, and he recalls in his mind all the deeds of his companions. He is also the tongue of the whole body belonging to Jesus. He is its representative and speaks in its defense. Trembling and fear for himself and for his people fall upon the priest at that awe-filled moment.

In an awe-inspiring role, in an awe-inspiring rank above the seraphim, the son of dust stands as mediator in great fear. The awe-inspiring King is mystically slain and buried, and the awe-inspiring watchers remain in fear to honor their Lord. Ranks of watchers surround the altar at that moment, as Chrysostom, who saw them, testified. With this meditation, the priest stands to perform his priestly ministry, attentively, with great fear and trembling. Like Jacob, he bows three times and three, and then approaches to kiss the tomb of our Lord. Jacob honored his brother Esau by bowing, and the priest honors Jacob’s Lord by bowing. He kisses the holy altar with love and affection, trusting that he will receive holiness through his lips. He asks for prayer from the ministers who surround him, so that through his humility he may receive mercy from the Merciful One. He now prays before God with an aching heart and confesses his own sins and the sins of the body of the Church. The priest asks for hidden strength and assistance, so that he may carry out God’s gift according to his will. The people assent to everything the priest says before God, and they seal his ministry with “Amen.” By saying “Amen,” the people join hands with the priest, and through their spoken response they participate with him in his prayers. Then, at that moment, the priest blesses the people with the words uttered by the life-giving mouth. “Peace be with you,” the priest says to the children of the Church, “for peace has abounded in Jesus our Lord, who is our peace. “Peace be with you, for death has been abolished and corruption undone through one of our own race, who suffered for us and gave life to us all. “Peace be with you, for sin has passed away and Satan has been defeated through the son of Adam, who conquered and gave victory to Adam’s children.

“Peace be with you, for the good Lord has been reconciled to you through the death of his Son, who suffered on the cross for our sake. “Peace be with you, for you have been brought into peace with the angels through him who received authority over the angels and reigns over all. “Peace be with you, for you have been united, the people of Israel and the nations, and through Jesus the dividing barrier and all hostility have been removed. “Peace be with you, for new life is reserved for you in him who became the firstborn of all creatures in life without corruption. “Peace be with you, for you have been invited to the kingdom on high through him who entered beforehand to prepare a place for us all.” The people lovingly answer the priest and say, “With you, and with your priestly spirit.” By “spirit” they do not mean the soul within the priest, but the Spirit that the priest received through the laying on of hands. Through the laying on of hands, the priest receives the power of the Spirit, so that through it he may be able to celebrate the divine mysteries. The people call this grace “the priest’s spirit,” and pray that he may be at peace with it, and it also with him. This shows that the priest himself [?] needs prayer, and that the whole Church must intercede for him. Therefore she cries out that he may be at peace with his spirit, so that through his undivided peace the peace of all her children may increase. For through his virtues he greatly benefits the whole Church, while through his evil deeds he gravely harms the whole community. “Peace be with you,” the people say to the pure priest. “May you be at peace with your spirit through the harmony of your conduct.” “Peace to you [?], through whom the mysteries of the Church are celebrated. May your spirit be at peace with you through your conduct.” “Peace be with you, for great is the gift bestowed on you. May the peace of your spirit increase through your spiritual achievements.” Then the herald of the Church commands all the people to give peace to one another in the love of our Lord. First the priests exchange peace within the sanctuary, and then the people also exchange it in the nave in the same manner. Whoever gives peace to his brother in the church ought

to cleanse his heart of every grudge, anger, and evil inclination. This is the peace in which the angels and human beings will be united on the day when the glorious Bridegroom comes to judge all. This is the peace in which there is neither deceit nor hatred, but which is entirely light within light and perfect love. Blessed is the one who lovingly gives peace to his brother, for he receives perfect peace within his mind. Peace is the name of Christ, who reconciles all, for he is the one who reconciled those on earth with those in heaven. Blessed is the one who brings his heart to peace at the time of the mysteries, for all his sins and evil deeds are forgiven him.
