Here it is fitting to recall the Lord’s saying, in which he warns us most earnestly about resentment. “If,” he says, “you remember that your brother holds a grudge in his heart, leave your offering and go and be reconciled with him; then make your offering.” “First go and be reconciled with your brother,” our Lord said, “and then offer the sacrifice that you are presenting.” Although the priest is appointed as mediator to make the offering, he must offer it with the agreement of all the people. Therefore, whoever presents this offering must forgive the offenses of his fellow servants, and then make the offering. But if the person against whom he holds a grudge in his heart is far away, let him forgive that person’s offenses in his mind before God. If a priest tramples on this commandment of the Lord of all ages, let him know that he has neither prayer nor offering. While the kiss of peace is being exchanged in the church, they read the book containing the two lists of names, of the living and the dead. The Church commemorates the dead and the living at that time, to make known that the living and the dead benefit from the offering. The people then add, “On behalf of all the catholicoi,” words that follow what the book that was read proclaimed. “On behalf of all the ranks who have departed [?] from the holy Church, and on behalf of those who have been found worthy to receive this offering.

On behalf of these and on behalf of your servants everywhere, accept, Lord, this offering that your servant has presented.” Then the herald of the Church cries out and exhorts everyone to give thanks to the Lord and petition him with purity of heart. He says, “Stand properly; consider in your minds what is taking place. Great is the mystery in which you are serving, O mortals! Look, the awesome mysteries are being consecrated by the priest’s hands. Let everyone remain in fear and trembling until they are completed. The priest alone has already drawn near to pray. Pray with him, so that your peace may increase through his mediation. Lower to the earth the gaze of the eyes of your hearts, and direct upward the hidden gaze of your thoughts. With watchfulness, petition and plead with the God of all at this time, which is full of trembling and great fear. Let no one dare to utter a word with his mouth, for whoever speaks oversteps and violates the commandment. Let whoever prays pray in his heart and not with his lips, and seek mercy in his mind and not with his tongue. Stand in silence and reverence, for the peace that surpasses all understanding is here with us.” At this time the priest uncovers the mysteries that are worthy of worship and puts aside the veil that lies over them. This does not symbolize the resurrection when it is removed, for the stone was not rolled away at the time of the resurrection. After the resurrection [?] the angel rolled away the stone, and the priests lift the veil from before his mysteries. Then, before anything else, the priest blesses the people with the formula that he pronounces aloud to the faithful. He says, “May the grace of Jesus our Lord, the love of the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with us.” May that grace which our Lord gave us through his coming grant us confidence before his majesty.

May the love of the Father, who sent to us the Son [?], open for us the door of mercy on the day of his coming. May the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, of which we have been deemed worthy, sanctify us and cleanse from us the filth of our sins. Then he carefully prepares the people and says, “Let your thoughts be above at this hour, where Christ the King sits at the right hand. Do not occupy yourselves with empty thoughts about earthly things.” Look at him who is now mystically slain on the altar, who sits on high and asks for mercy for sinners. The people respond: Toward you, Lord, our thoughts are directed, God of [?], Isaac, and Jacob, the glorious King. The glorious King whom the righteous and the fathers praised: they were glorified in him, and in him they give praise without end. The priest continues: This acceptable and pure offering is now being offered to the Lord, the Lord of the heights and the depths. This is the Lord who took away and takes away the sin of the world. He is now being sacrificed to wipe away and forgive your sins. Look, he is being offered on behalf of angels and human beings, so that all together may delight in him in body and soul. Look, he is being offered on behalf of sinners and the righteous, so that through him they may be cleansed of the stains of their sins. Look, he is being offered on behalf of the departed and the living, so that all peoples may find mercy through his sacrifice. Look, he is being offered to the God of all as a pledge, to save us from the torment of Gehenna. The people respond: It is fitting, right, worthy, and proper to present this offering on behalf of all creatures. From this point the whole [?] body of the church falls silent, and everyone cries out to pray inwardly. The priests are silent, and the deacons stand in silence. All the people are calm and at peace, quiet and still. The altar stands crowned with splendor and praise,

and above it are the Gospel of life and the adored wood of the cross. The mysteries are arranged, the censers spread fragrance, and the lamps give light. The deacons hover and wave fans like the watching angels. Deep silence and tranquil peace rest upon that place. Radiance and glory, splendor and power fill it to overflowing. The pure priest, the tongue of the church, opens his mouth and speaks with God in mystery, like a member of his household. He recounts the praise of that incomprehensible Being, who is the cause of everything perceived by the mind and by the senses. That Being cannot be comprehended, examined, or searched out, and cannot be known by bodily beings or by the watching angels. One essence, one lordship, one authority, one will that does not change from what it is. One Creator, who established the heights and the depths by his command. The watching angels in the heights and human beings in the depths praise his name. One God, who made his existence known through Moses, and through Jesus our Lord revealed and showed us his Trinity. The church learned from our Savior three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one Being. Three persons [?], among whom none is before or after another, and there is no distinction except in their particular properties: fatherhood, being begotten, and proceeding. One will, one praise, one lordship. The mystery is entirely hidden, concealed, and veiled from everyone, and the watchers are dazzled as they contemplate its hiddenness. The priest continues: All the watchers stand in awe to praise the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The angels also offer worship to that Majesty, and the commanders of the heavenly hosts continually send up praise. The cherubim give praise; the seraphim proclaim holiness with their holy acclamations, and the authorities and dominions with their songs of praise. All cry out together, saying to one another—and the people respond—“Holy is the Lord who dwells in light.” “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord,” the people respond, “heaven and the whole earth are full of his praises.” The cry of “Holy” three times signifies this:

But the word “Lord” makes known that the nature of the eternal Being is one. Holy is the Father, who possesses the distinctive property of fatherhood: he is the cause and the begetter, and is not begotten. Holy is the Son, who possesses the distinctive property of being begotten: he is begotten of the Father from eternity, without a beginning. Holy is the Spirit, who possesses the distinctive property of procession: he proceeds from the Father and exists beyond time. The whole church cries out these words and returns to silence, and the priest continues to converse with God. He gives thanks for the mercy and grace shown to us in the one manifestation of the Word, who was revealed in a body taken from us. The Creator, whose glory is worshiped, took a body from us, so that through it he might renew the image of Adam, which had worn out and become corrupted. The Holy Spirit built a temple endowed with reason in Mary's womb, by a will in which the whole Trinity concurred. He was laid in a manger and wrapped in swaddling cloths as a human being, and the watchers praised him with their songs as God. He offered sacrifices according to the Law as a human being, and received worship from the Persians as God. Simeon carried him in his arms as a human being, and called him the mercy that has mercy on all, as God. He kept the Law perfectly as a human being, and gave his own new law as God. He was [?] in the Jordan by John as a human being, and heaven was opened in honor of his baptism as God. He entered the wedding feast in the town of Qatne as a human being, and changed the water into wine as God. He fasted in the wilderness for forty days as a human being, and the watchers descended to serve him as God. He slept in the boat with his disciples as a human being, and rebuked the wind and calmed the sea as God. He traveled and withdrew to a deserted place as a human being:

And he multiplied bread and fed thousands to their satisfaction as God. He ate and drank, walked and grew tired, as a human being, and drove out demons by the word of his mouth, as God. He prayed and kept vigil, gave thanks and worshiped, as a human being, and forgave offenses and pardoned sins, as God. He asked the Samaritan woman for water, as a human being, and revealed and disclosed her secrets, as God. He reclined at the table in the Pharisee’s house, as a human being, and forgave the sinful woman her sins, as God. He went up Mount Tabor [?] with his disciples, as a human being, and revealed his glory before their eyes, as God. He shed tears and wept over Lazarus, as a human being, and called him, and he came out through his great power, as God. He rode on a colt and entered Jerusalem, as a human being, and children praised him with their hosannas, as God. He approached the fig tree and showed that he was hungry [?], as a human being, and his power suddenly withered it, as God [?]. He washed [?] the feet of his twelve disciples, as a human being, and called himself Lord and Teacher, as God. He ate the Passover prescribed by the Law, as a human being, and exposed Iscariot’s treachery, as God. He prayed and sweated at the time of his suffering, as a human being, and shook and terrified those who arrested him, as God. The guards seized him and bound his hands, as a human being, and he healed the ear that Simon had cut off, as God. He stood in court and endured mockery, as a human being, and declared that he would come in glory, as God [?]. He carried his cross on his shoulders, as a human being, and revealed and disclosed the destruction of Zion, as God. He was hung on the wood and endured suffering, as a human being, and shook the earth and darkened the sun, as God. Nails were driven into his body, as a human being, and he opened graves and brought the dead to life, as God. On the cross he cried out, “My God, my God,” as a human being, and promised paradise to the robber, as God. His side [?] was pierced with a lance, as a human being, and at his command the curtain at the entrance was torn, as God. They embalmed his body, and he was buried in the earth, as a human being, and he raised up his temple by his great power, as God.

He remained [?] in the tomb for three days, as a human being, and the watcher angels praised him with their songs of praise, as God. He said that he had received all authority, as a human being, and promised that he would be with us forever, as God. He instructed [?] Thomas to touch his side, as a human being, and gave them the Spirit as a pledge, as God. He ate and drank after his resurrection, as a human being, and ascended on high and sent the Spirit, as God. This, then, is the confession of the apostles and the fathers, and whoever does not agree with their faith has no hope. This is the truth that the fathers proclaimed and taught. Profess it with them, so that you may receive immortal life. Our Lord Jesus departed from us to the place above, so that at his coming he might bring us up with him to the kingdom on high. Because he went to a place beyond our knowledge, he wished to comfort us with his body and blood until his coming. And because it was not possible for him to give his body and blood to his church, he commanded us to perform this mystery with bread and wine. Blessed are the Christian people! What they possess, and what a hope is kept for them in the heights without end! For when the time came for the suffering of the one who gives life to all, he ate the Passover prescribed by the Law with his disciples. He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “This is truly my body, without any doubt.” He took the cup, gave thanks, blessed it, and gave it to his apostles, saying, “This is my true blood, which is for you.” He commanded them all to take it and drink from it, so that it would atone for their sins forever. That he gave thanks and blessed is written in the Gospel, which is full of life; but the chosen apostles did not tell us what he said. Theodore, the great teacher and interpreter, handed down that our Lord spoke as follows when he took the bread: “The nature of your divinity, Lord of all, is worthy of all praise, all thanksgiving, and all acclaim.

For in all [?] you have fulfilled and completed your plan for the life and salvation of human beings. And although they were very wicked in their deeds, in your mercy you did not neglect to help them. To accomplish the salvation of all and the renewal of all, you took me from Adam’s nature and joined me to yourself. Through me all pledges and promises will be fulfilled, and through me the mysteries and types given to the righteous will be accomplished. And because I have been without blemish and have fulfilled all righteousness, through me you uproot all sin from humanity. And because I die without guilt and without wrongdoing, through me you decree the resurrection of the body for the whole human race.” With this intention the Son of the Most High gave thanks to his Father, and he spoke these words when he gave his body and blood: “This is my body, which I have given for the sins of the world; and this, in turn, is my blood, which I have willed to be poured out for sins. Everyone who eats of my body and drinks of my blood in love lives forever and remains in me, and I in him. Keep doing this in remembrance of me within your churches, and receive my body and blood in faith. Offer bread and wine as I have taught you, and I will perfect them and make them body and blood. I make the bread and wine body and blood through the hovering and action of the Holy Spirit.” Thus the giver of life to the worlds spoke to his disciples, and he called the bread and wine his body and blood. He did not call them a type or a likeness, but definitely body and truly blood. And although their nature is immeasurably far from him, yet in power and in [?] it is one body. Let the heavenly watchers and human beings continually give you thanks, my Lord, Christ our hope, who gave yourself up for us.

Our body, which the priests break in the church, is one in power with that body which sits in glory at the right hand. And just as God is united to the firstfruits of our race, Christ unites himself to the bread and wine that are on the altar. Therefore the bread is certainly the body of our Lord, and the wine is his blood, as the Lord’s own and truly. Thus he commanded those entrusted with his mysteries to eat his body, and thus he instructed the members of his household to drink his blood. Blessed is the one who believes in him and affirms his word: if he is dead, he will live, and if he is alive, he will not die in his sins. The apostles received their Lord’s command with care, and they diligently handed it on to those who came after them. Until now it has been preserved in the Church, and it will continue to be preserved until he brings his mysteries to rest at his appearing and revelation. With this intention the priest gives thanks before God and raises his voice at the end of his prayer so that the people can hear. He makes his voice heard and with his hand makes the sign over the mysteries set before him, and the people respond with “Amen,” assenting to the priest’s prayer. Then the herald of the church instructs the people, saying, “Pray in your minds. Peace be with us.” Give your attention at this time, in mind and thought, for see, the great peace is being accomplished in the fulfillment of the mysteries. The priest begins to plead fervently before God that in his love he may be pleased with the living sacrifice being offered to him. He lists the orders of the Church one after another, on whose behalf the Church offers the mysteries worthy of worship. First he remembers the glorious Church in every place and asks that they may be of one mind and faith. He remembers the priests, the visiting clergy, and the deacons, and pleads that they may live in holiness and purity. He remembers the martyrs, the confessors, and the teachers, that their names may be remembered in the Church at the time of the mysteries. He remembers the kings and judges in every place, that they may judge uprightly throughout the whole world. In his words he remembers all who mourn and all ascetics, that their prayer may be accepted before God every day.

He remembers the upright and the righteous in every place and asks that they may perfectly keep the covenant they have made. He remembers the children of the holy Church in all their ranks and asks that they may guard their faith carefully. Then he also remembers the departed in every place, who have died and passed away in faith without doubting. He remembers himself, who has been deemed worthy of this mediation, and asks for mercy upon all creatures together. He remembers those who generously give alms to the poor and asks that they may receive a double reward for their charitable gifts. He remembers the fallen, sinners, and offenders, and asks that they turn to repentance and receive pardon for their sins. He remembers those for whom he offers sacrifices, that they may find mercy and forgiveness for their sins and offenses. He remembers pagans, unbelievers, and those who have gone astray, and pleads that they may come to know the faith of the holy [?] Church. He remembers the whole world together with its inhabitants, that wars, demons, and conflicts may cease within it. He remembers the weather and the crops of the entire year, and asks that the crown of the year may be abundant and blessed. He remembers his own country and all countries together, and asks that there may be peace and tranquility in their dwellings. He remembers those who travel on the seas and among the islands, and asks that they may all be saved from storms. He remembers those beset by troubles and persecutions, and asks that there may be relief and rest from their afflictions. He remembers those confined in prisons and in chains, and asks that they may be released from their bonds and harsh torments. He remembers those who have been cast into exile, far away [?], and asks that they may find respite from hardships and trials. He remembers those who languish in sickness and pain, and pleads that they may obtain bodily health and healing. He remembers those whom accursed demons torment, and asks that they may find mercy and compassion from the Lord. In his words he also remembers the enemies of the holy Church, that their offenses may be forgiven before God. He remembers the sins of the entire body of the Church:

And asks that they may be deemed worthy of forgiveness [?] of sins and offenses. The priest remembers all these before God, imitating Mar Barsamya through his supplication. With this intention the priest prays before God, and asks him to be pleased with the sacrifice he offers him. The living sacrifice within the Church is offered on behalf of all, and this sacrifice helps and benefits all creatures. Through that supplication which the priest makes on behalf of all ranks, all his sins and offenses are forgiven him. After these things, the priest gives thanks before God, as our Lord Jesus taught his Twelve. “Behold, we celebrate,” says the priest, “and commemorate the suffering, death, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus.” The priest says these things in [?] and supplication, straightens himself up, and stretches out his hands toward heaven. The priest looks toward heaven with confidence, and calls upon the Spirit to come and perfect the mysteries he has offered. He asks the Spirit to come and hover over the offering, and that God may give it power and efficacy. The Spirit descends at the priest’s entreaty, however sinful he may be, and perfects the mysteries through the mediation of the priest who consecrates them. It is not the priest’s goodness that brings the mysteries worthy of worship to completion; rather, the Holy Spirit completes them through his hovering. The Spirit hovers not because of the priest’s worthiness, but because of the mysteries placed upon the altar. As soon as the bread and wine are placed upon the altar, the mystery portrays the Son’s death and also his resurrection. Therefore the Spirit who raised him from the dead now descends and brings to completion the mysteries of his body’s resurrection. In this way the Holy Spirit completes them through the priest’s hands, and without a priest they can never be completed. The Church’s mysteries are not completed without a priest, because the Holy Spirit has not given permission to complete them. The priest received the Spirit’s power through the laying on of hands, and through him all the mysteries within the Church are completed.

The priest sanctifies the womb of baptismal water, and the Spirit grants adoption as children to those who are baptized. Without a priest, a woman is not betrothed to a man, and without him their wedding is not completed. Without a priest, even a dead person is not shrouded, nor do they lower him into his grave without a priest. Unclean water is not sanctified without a priest, and if there is no priest, the whole house becomes unclean. The Holy Spirit accomplishes these things through the priest’s hands, even if the priest is entirely steeped in sins and offenses. What priests accomplish, they can complete even if they are sinful; those who do not hold the office cannot complete it, however righteous they may be. The righteous do not bring the Spirit down through their purity, nor do sinners prevent his descent through their sinfulness. Here the Long-suffering One bears with the priest who has sinned, and through his hand completes the glorious mysteries that cannot be expressed in words. In the world to come, he judges him severely and takes away from him the gift that was given to him. Because he did not honor the greatness of his office as he should, he is despised there and becomes an object of ridicule before all creatures. Listen, priest whose deeds do not match his office! Tremble and shudder at the torment in Gehenna. Your reckoning is harsher than every other reckoning, foolish priest, because you did not serve as you should in the office that came to you. In the world to come there are no ranks or degrees; rather, Christ alone will be all in all. The priest calls upon the Spirit, and he descends upon the offering; the priest bows down trembling, with fear and overwhelming dread. Then, at that moment, the Church’s herald cries out: “Stand in silence and fear. Peace be with us.” Let all the people be in fear at this moment, when the mysteries worthy of worship are completed through the Spirit’s descent.

Then the priest makes his voice heard by all the people and makes the sign with his hand over the mysteries as before. He makes the sign now not because the mysteries need the sign, but to teach, through this final sign, that they have been completed. The priest makes three signs over the offering, and through them he brings it to completion and perfects it mystically. The priest bows three times before God, and in these bows he worships openly before his majesty. In one he praises, in another he gives thanks, and in another he prays, calling upon the Spirit to descend and overshadow the offering. Our Lord remained three days in the bosom of the earth, and on the third he arose and returned to life in great glory. In the same likeness, the priest bows three times, and in the third he symbolically represents the resurrection of our Lord Jesus. The priest also kneels three times, and through these acts he portrays our Lord’s stay within the tomb. He kneels three times before the descent, and afterward he no longer kneels, because the mystery of the resurrection has been completed. The priest completes the mystery of the resurrection when he completes the mysteries, and he no longer symbolically represents the mystery of his death by kneeling. The three hundred and eighteen priests gave the command that there should be no kneeling on Sundays or on any feast days. Therefore no one is permitted to kneel during the mysteries except the priest, who portrays a mystery by kneeling. Even the priest himself is to kneel only before the descent; after the descent of the Holy Spirit, he must not bow down. Then the priest takes the living bread in his hands, raises his gaze toward the heights, and acknowledges his Lord. He breaks the bread in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, and unites the blood with the body and the body with the blood. He makes the sign over the blood with the body and mentions [?] the Trinity, and he makes the sign over the body with the living blood, using the same invocation. He unites them—the body with the blood and the blood with the body—so that everyone may acknowledge that the body and blood are one. Then the priest, after all the rites have been completed,

blesses the people with the words with which our Lord blessed them. He now begins to break the body, little by little, so that it may be easily distributed to all who receive it. The priest has symbolically represented the Son’s resurrection by completing the mysteries, and very fittingly he breaks his body so that they may distribute it. For our Lord too, when he had risen from the tomb in glory, appeared to the women and the disciples ten times. At one time he appeared to Mary Magdalene alone, and at another to Luke and Cleopas as they were traveling along the road. At another time he appeared to the company of eleven in the upper room, and on another occasion beside the Sea of Tiberias. He appeared to them all and assured them of the resurrection. He also showed Thomas his side, where the spear had pierced him. On the Mount of Olives our Lord blessed his twelve [?], parted from them, and ascended in glory to the heaven of heavens. And now he appears to the members of the Church in the [?] of his body, and they believe in him and receive from him the pledge of life. Then the church’s herald cries out and raises his voice: Let us all approach with reverence the mystery of the body and blood. In faith let us remember the suffering of Jesus our Lord, and in that faith let us also contemplate his resurrection from the dead. For our sake the only Son of the God of all took on a complete human being and fulfilled his saving work. He suffered on the cross, died, was revived, rose, and ascended; and in his love he gave us [?] and his blood as a pledge. Through them let us remember all the kindnesses he has shown us. Let us give thanks, worship, and praise him at all times. Now, with pure love and faith, let us approach and receive the treasure of spiritual life. With one pure, sincere prayer and heartfelt sorrow, let us share in the revered mysteries of the holy Church. Let us make a commitment to repentance before God, and let us feel remorse and sorrow for the hateful deeds we have done.

Let us ask the Lord of all for mercy and forgiveness of sins, and let us also forgive the offenses of our fellow servants. The people respond: Lord, forgive the sins of your servants, and cleanse our conscience of division and quarrels. Lord, forgive the offenses of those who praise you, and purify our souls of hatred and slander. Lord, forgive the sins of your servants who have acknowledged your name, and make us worthy to receive this holy gift in faith. Lord, forgive your servants who call on your name every day, and grant us, Lord, to be yours according to your will. My Lord, may these divine mysteries give us confidence and the freedom to stand openly before your majesty. Then the priest prays and asks God to sanctify us and blot out our sins through his grace, and to make us all worthy to stand before him without blemish, and all of us to call him confidently, “Abba, our Father.” Then the people respond and earnestly recite the prayer that his living mouth taught his beloved children: Our Father, who dwells above in heaven and in every place, may your holy name be sanctified in us by all nations. May that kingdom which you promised us come to us, and may we enjoy [?] through a pledge, here and now. May your loving will come to pass, find rest, and be fulfilled in us, and may we be worthy to carry out all our deeds according to your will. Just as all desires cease in us in heaven, so on earth too may we desire only what accords with your will. Give us bread and everything our bodies need during this time of our temporary stay in this world. Forgive our debts and pardon the sins by which we have become guilty through our laxity, our susceptibility to suffering, and our weakness. For we too have forgiven from our hearts everyone who is indebted to us, and we hold no grudge in our hearts against anyone. Do not bring us into temptation or into testing, for we are weak, and without your strength we are nothing.

But deliver us from the wickedness of the deceitful evil one, and do not allow him to approach us through his schemes. For yours are the power and the kingdom, and to you glory is due forever and ever. Then the priest says to the people, “Peace be with you,” and the people answer, “And with you, priest, and with your spirit.” The priest began with the Lord’s Prayer at the beginning of the mysteries, and with it he concludes again now that all the mysteries have been completed. “Peace be with you,” says the priest at this time, reminding us of our Lord’s resurrection from the dead. “Peace be with you,” our Lord said to his Twelve when he appeared to them and brought them the good news of his resurrection. “Peace be with you,” our Lord said to those who shared his secrets, “for look, I have risen, and I am raising all creation.” “Peace be with you,” he said to his brothers, his companions, “for look, I am ascending and preparing a place for all of you.” “Peace be with you,” our Lord said to the Twelve, “for I am with you forever, without end.” The priest gives this peace to the members of the church and strengthens them in love, hope, and faith. When the children of the church have prepared themselves to receive the mysteries, the priest cries out, “The holy sacrament is fitting for the holy [?].” The holy sacrament is fitting for all the holy, sanctified by the Spirit of adoption, through their agreement with the fathers. The holy sacrament is fitting for all the holy whom baptism has sanctified, according to the law of the church. The other groups, those who have been expelled from the church, must not share in receiving the divine mysteries. The people answer, “One is the holy Father, who has existed from eternity, without beginning or end.” He has made us worthy to gain holiness by grace through the spiritual birth of baptism. The Father is one, and the Son and the Holy Spirit are also one: one in three, and three without change. Glory to the Father, to the Son who is from him, and to the Holy Spirit,

the eternal Being who exists forever and ever, without end. Then the priest himself receives the holy sacrament first, to teach the people that he too, though a priest, needs mercy. The priest who consecrated them needs to receive the adorable mysteries, so that he too may be worthy to share in the pledge of life. The priest receives the mysteries before the bishop if it was the priest who consecrated them and not the chief priest. The priests and deacons receive them from hand to hand, and then the people: men and women, young and old. As the priest comes out, he blesses the people and says, “May the grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.” The holy sacrament comes out on the paten and in the cup, in splendor and glory, accompanied by priests and a great procession of deacons. Thousands of watchers and ministers of fire and spirit go before the body of our Lord and honor it in procession. All the children of the Church and all the people rejoice when they see the body coming out from within the sanctuary. And just as the apostles [?] in our Lord after his resurrection, so all the faithful rejoice when they see him. Great, my brothers, is this mystery, and it cannot be expressed. Whoever can comprehend it, let him comprehend it, if he is able. “A mystery for me! A mystery for me!” cried Isaiah, wondrous [?], concerning the revelation of God that he saw in the temple. If I wished to write something about this [?], all the sheets of paper in this whole universe would not be enough for me. Meat is suitable for the mature and fully grown, but milk for infants until they reach maturity. “Whoever eats my body remains in me, and I in him,” he says, “if he carefully keeps all my commandments.” “Whoever eats my body and drinks of my blood while unworthy eats and drinks to his own condemnation, without benefit.”

The person approaching to receive the body stretches out his hands, raising his right hand and placing it above the other. The recipient crosses his hands in the shape of a cross, and then receives his body above the cross. Upon the cross our Lord Jesus was mocked, and by that same cross he flew and was raised to the heights above. In this symbolic manner, the recipient approaches and receives, and the priest who gives it says to him, “The body of our Lord.” He receives in his hands the adorable body of the Lord of all, embraces it, and kisses it with love and affection. He brings in and hides the leaven of life within the temple of his body, so that his body may be sanctified by receiving the body of our Lord. It pardons his sins, cleanses his blemishes, heals his pains, and washes and scrubs away stains with the hyssop of his mercy. While the body and blood are being distributed to all the recipients, the Church cries out in honor of the mysteries and says these words: “Look! The medicine of life is being distributed in the holy Church. Come, mortals, receive it and be forgiven your sins. “This is truly the body and blood of our Lord, which the nations received and through which they were forgiven, without doubt. “This is the medicine that heals pains and foul sores. Receive it, mortals, and through it be cleansed of your sins. “Come, receive freely forgiveness and [?] through the body and blood of him who takes away the sin of the whole world.” After the whole congregation has shared in the body and blood, they continue, saying with joy and gladness: “Our Lord Jesus, King adored by all creatures, remove every harm from us through the power of your mysteries. “When you appear at the end of time for the salvation of all, may we go out confidently to meet you with hosannas. “And may we give thanks to your name for your grace toward our race, for you have forgiven our sins and blotted them out through your body and blood.” And here and there may he be worthy to offer to your divinity

fitting praise together with thanksgiving, forever and ever. Then the church’s herald cries out in his proclamation and urges the people to give thanks, saying: “All of us who have been deemed worthy of the gift of the mysteries, let us give thanks, worship, and praise the God of all.” The people answer: “To him be praise for his gift, which can never be repaid, forever and ever. Amen and amen.” Then the priest prays and gives thanks to the God of all, who has made our human race worthy of the glorious, inexpressible mysteries. He asks and implores him to strengthen us to please him in our thoughts and words, and also in our deeds. Then everyone, both in the sanctuary and outside among the congregation, prays the prayer taught by that life-giving mouth. With it they begin every prayer service, morning and evening, and with it they conclude all the mysteries of the holy Church. For it is the prayer that embraces everything, and without it the whole prayer is [?]. Then he comes out and stands at the entrance to the sanctuary, stretches out his hands, blesses the people, and speaks. At that time the priest blesses all the people after the pattern of our Lord Jesus’ blessing of his twelve. On the day of his ascension, the high priest raised his hands, blessed his twelve, and gave them his priestly blessing; then he was taken up. The priest represented [?] the mystery of his resurrection in the completion of the mysteries, and the mystery of his appearance before his disciples in his distribution. As the pure priest stretches out his hands toward heaven, he bestows a blessing on the whole congregation and says: “May he who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in heaven now also bless us all through the power of his mysteries.” In this blessing with which the pure priest blesses us, he depicts the mysteries of the blessing that is to come upon us. When we have been raised from the dead and have put on [?], we will be taken up to heaven with the Savior. There all sufferings will cease for our humanity,

and we will delight in desirable blessings without end. In this world, where we live amid every kind of suffering, may he preserve our lives from hidden and visible harm. And just as he has graciously made us worthy to receive his mysteries, may he make us all worthy to become temples of his divinity. With every breath, let us give thanks, worship [?], and praise him for his gift, which no fleshly tongue can express. These things the pure priest bestows through his blessings, and with his right hand he marks the congregation with the living sign. These are the glorious mysteries of the holy Church, and this is the order in which they are brought to completion by the priesthood. Blessed is the one who purifies his heart at the time when the awe-inspiring mysteries of our Lord’s body are consecrated. The Watchers on high call the children of the Church blessed, because they have been deemed worthy to receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus. Glory to your name for your indescribable gift! Who is able to repay your divinity with praise? Come now, you who share in the mysteries of the children of the Church; learn the order by which you should approach the priesthood. Do not approach as the apostle Paul [?]. With a pure heart approach the body and blood of our Lord, which cleanse you from the stains of the sins you have committed. They do not recoil from a sinner who wishes to repent, nor from an unclean person who mourns and grieves over his uncleanness. They receive the unclean and sinners on this condition: that they pledge not to return to their deeds. At that time, pray lovingly with the priest,

so that the giver of life and forgiver of sins may receive you. Take care, then, not to go outside the church at the time when the awe-inspiring mysteries are consecrated. Who would willingly exclude himself from that banquet to which Watchers and human beings have been invited? Who, though assigned a place among the children, would place himself among the outsiders whom the Church has expelled? This is the time when we ought to stand like angels, at that moment when the Holy Spirit overshadows us. This moment gives life to whoever stands during it; this moment distributes gifts to whoever receives it. Blessed is the one who believes in him and receives from him, for if he is dead, he will live, and if he is alive, he will not die in his sins. Here our ship has reached its resting place, and our fishing has ended. Let us therefore be silent, for what it gathered was our aim. I asked beforehand that you not condemn my weakness with reproaches. Now, in love, correct my shortcomings if you find any. Glory to your name, for you have brought to completion with us what we began in you; and thanksgiving to your Father and to the Holy Spirit forever and ever.
For Wednesday of Holy Week.
[?] By the same author. Discourse twenty-seven. [?] Wednesday of Holy Week. Refrain: Blessed is he who by his death killed sin, and by his humility calmed anger. My brothers.

A human being is a vessel of clay in which the treasure of life is placed. The greatness is not his own, but belongs to the power of his Maker. In a lowly vessel are placed the precious things of Adam’s household. Though it is very lowly by nature, glorious things are kept within it. In a vessel that breaks at a blow, treasures are placed, O mortals. And in our body, which gives rise to suffering, dwells the eternal Being who does not suffer. A human being is lowly clay, lowly by nature like clay. But his Creator made him a precious vessel, so that he might become a dwelling for him. His form was glorious and beautiful, although he was dust. But when he listened to the words of his deceiver,

he sank into the lowliness of his nature. [?] The Creator was not pleased that the evil one should mock his handiwork. So that the envious one would not boast that he had conquered Adam by his own strength, he took the vessel that had been corrupted, made from the dust of mortal Adam. He fashioned it with the Spirit instead of water, so that its structure would be firm. Since death had broken its nature and ruined the wall of its form, he cast it in a spiritual furnace, so that it would not again be corrupted by sin. The Creator took his image, made it a temple, and dwelt in it, so that the envious one would not gain power to ravage the King's temple. The self-existent One chose one from the mortal race and dwelt in him. In the composition of his frame, he bound him to love for creation. From the very dust of Adam's family, he formed an image like Adam. He perfected him through the sufferings of mortals, by the power of his divinity. By the power of the Spirit he fashioned him, without the seed of sexual union, so that he would resemble Adam, the first image, in everything. Just as through Adam death entered and corrupted his race, so through Adam, the second image, he would release those held captive by death. The man, the second Adam, shared in everything that belonged to Adam. Once he had been healed through sufferings, he redeemed mortals from death. For nine months, according to the natural order, he dwelt in a fleshly womb; and amid the pangs and sufferings of childbirth, he came forth from his mother's womb. He suckled milk like an infant, to show that he belonged to our race. He offered sacrifices like everyone else, to render thanksgiving. He underwent circumcision in his body, so that the promise would be confirmed in him, that the nations would become heirs to the riches of Abram's blessings. He grew up like a child, because he truly was a child. By the power of grace, he advanced toward perfection. He approached baptism in water, to open a path for mortals. Although he was pure in his own person, in his own person he purified the unclean through his baptism. The Father's only-begotten Word was with him from the beginning. He was with him and dwelt in him, but did not share in his afflictions. He himself grew in wisdom and grace according to his nature, while the self-existent One remained in his own nature, without alteration or change. The man, the second Adam, lived among people, to bring them back from error to the knowledge of the life they had lost. He healed bodily ailments without human medicines. He cleansed the soul's blemishes by the power of the Holy Spirit. With clay that blinds the pupils, he opened the eyes of the blind. From the clothes upon his limbs, the afflicted woman received healing. He gave limbs to the lame and the ability to walk [?] to the paralyzed. He opened ears that were closed, and they heard the sweetness of his words. He drove away visible ailments and healed hidden sins. Through visible things he showed [?] that he had authority over hidden things. With his voice he commanded death

to return the dead it had swallowed; and as he finished speaking, the dead returned to life. The three dead people who were raised were reliable witnesses for him, proclaiming the resurrection and declaring that from now on death was abolished. By his word he drove out demons, making them leave their dwelling places. The rebels cried out to him, “Do not torment us, Son of David!” Even they, unwilling though they were, proclaimed his authority beforehand: he would call hidden things to account in the righteous judgment of his examination. By healing the body he showed that he also healed people's sins. Through the three [?] whom he raised, he proclaimed resurrection to the broken. Through the demons he drove out of people, he dismantled the deceiver's authority. He restored the captor's captives by taking people out of his hands. The envious one cried out in bitterness; he shouted and wailed with weeping, because a mighty warrior had gone out to battle to take the captor's captives away. The tyrant gathered the forces under his authority against the victorious one, thinking that through death he could overcome the one who gives life to the dead. In the battle against Adam, he put on the serpent as armor and fought. Now, against our Savior, he fought through Adam against Adam. Abraham's descendants, who had been freed from slavery to the Egyptians, became armor for the deceiver. He put them on and fought against our Lord. At the Passover festival, the tyrant stirred up the soldiers he had chosen, so that these brazen men would help him with the swords of their tongues. The descendants of Aram became the deceiver's agents against Adam. Through their hands he fulfilled his desire, just as he had through the serpent against Adam. It was not his wish to proceed with the killing during the festival. Christ carried out in action the plan of his incarnation. At the festival he gave himself for slaughter so that many would see his death and, when he rose from the grave, would be witnesses to his resurrection. The living Lamb of God prepared himself for the Passover sacrifice, so that through the sacrifice of his own person he might reconcile the world to its Lord. He celebrated Passover according to the Law, and at Passover revealed his own Passover. He distributed his body to his disciples as a pledge of life for mortals. The Son of Adam showed his love for his fellow human beings in action: he gave his body as food before the suffering of his crucifixion. He prophesied about what was to come, about his suffering and his humiliation. He revealed and made known the treachery of Judas, who would betray his master. In the power of the Spirit he was stirred against the wickedness of the brazen man, whose bitterness was not softened by the sweetness of the mystery he received. He made him a participant in the mystery, yet he did not abandon his murderous intention. The giver of life to all washed his feet, yet the ungrateful man was not restrained. He knew the treacherous man was a murderer even before choosing him. He sheltered him with his gentle love and did not expose his treachery. The deceitful man went out at night to betray his master to the brazen men, because the deceiver was urging him on, to accomplish his will through his hands.

The envious one had longed to kill him since before the day of his birth. Through Judas as an intermediary, he brought his intention into the open. Judas became like, like a messenger for the envious Accuser, who sent him to the gathering of insolent men to hunt down Life for death. The thief sold for a price the one who buys the worlds back from death. He received his payment—a noose—and sold Life to the abode of the dead. O seller of Life to death, who did not consider how he was selling! He gave away an incomparable gift and received a paltry price. For thirty pieces of silver he sold [?] the liberator of our nature. And the prophet’s word was fulfilled, which he had foreseen in the Spirit ages before. The giver of life to all fulfilled everything in his own person for everyone’s sake. He prophesied about his humiliation and about the will of his disciples. “You will all stumble,” he said, “when the time of suffering draws near. You will leave me alone and will not comfort me in my afflictions.” Simon boasted of his love and said to our Lord, “I will never deny you, nor will I falter before suffering.” With “Truly,” the giver of life to all answered the fervent man’s boast: “Three times you will give way to denial at the time of suffering.” He showed his disciples that he endured suffering willingly, and that no compulsion forced him into the humiliation of the cross. “Get up; let us go,” he said when the time of suffering drew near, making known that he willingly gave himself over to his enemies. He went out to pray alone and took his disciples with him, so that through his prayer he might teach them that mercy is needed in affliction. Three times he prayed in anguish, and this was what he said in his prayer: “If it is possible, let me not drink the cup of all-devouring death.” Our Savior prayed in anguish before his suffering, as one subject to suffering. Sweat formed drops on his limbs from his dread of the cross [?]. An angel appeared to him from heaven, encouraging him not to falter in the contest from which he would gain victory. With words full of encouragement, the angel strengthened him. “[?] of the cup of death gives you a crown after your victory. Do not falter amid weaknesses, O fleshly one of Adam’s race. “For the cross brings you to glorious things at the end of your contest. Endure sufferings, you who are subject to suffering, and drink the cup [?] of Adam’s household. “For you will be exalted on high after suffering and humiliation.” Now let the erring ones come—Eutyches and [?]— and let them show, as they are accustomed to do, whose prayer and suffering these are. Who prayed before the suffering, O wise man lacking understanding? And whom did the spiritual being [?] strengthen? Reveal and explain your understanding to me. I know that, as is your habit, you ascend to the heights above, and your violence drags down into suffering the eternally existing Word who is from the Father. O unspeakable crime! O wickedness that cannot be forgiven! The awesome one who holds creation—they made him weak in the contest. O insolent will, how brazenly it has dared and exalted itself [?]! For he who made his angels spirits

was being strengthened by a watcher! To whom was the Word praying, O you who are devoid of [?] understanding? For he possesses authority by his very being, like the Father who begot him. How did that power which bears the dew [?] recoil from suffering? From whom was he asking help, he who is the giver of good things? Who helped him in creating, when he brought everything into being? Now, in the suffering of the [?], did he call an angel to help him? Restrain your blasphemies, insolent man! We have no use for your interpretations. Our confession is good seed; do not mix your weeds into it. Do not bring the Father's Word down to the sufferings that belong to mortals, nor exalt the Only Begotten beyond the help of what he created. Who has spoken like this wicked man? Who has been so insolent as this misguided man? They thought the Power that strengthens living creatures was weak on the cross. Do not go astray, you insolent people! The Word is not less than his Father. Nor was the Creator asking a spiritual being for help. It was the bodily one who was praying, who needed help. The one subject to suffering feared suffering, for sufferings accompany his nature. Our fellow human being was pleading for himself and his companions, for he knew that he needed help at the time of suffering. He was the one who feared suffering, because he saw that his nature was mortal. For this reason the angel strengthened him at the time of suffering. He truly prayed and feared, not merely in an assumed appearance. And the angel truly strengthened him as one who was [?]. If he did not truly pray, then he was not a human being. Then our hope is in vain. Do not sink our nature into the abyss of death, you insolent people! Let [?] be exalted in honor with our fellow human being. The one subject to suffering prayed in his suffering, and the Self-Existent One accepted his petition. He surrendered himself to his captors to fulfill his Father's [?]. The crowd of insolent men [?], and Judas was like [?]. He approached and greeted the Merciful One; the deceitful man kissed the Gentle One. O false disciple! O friend whose love is treacherous! He carried a sword in his mind and kisses on his lips. “Do what you have come for,” he said to him, calling him a false friend. “Do as you wish, insolent man! Why do you kiss me in pretense? With a kiss, then, you betray me—a disciple selling his master! “Why do you conceal beneath a greeting the sharpened sword of your mind?” “Whom are you looking for?” the Calm One said to the crowd of insolent men. He threw them to the ground to show the power of his majesty. The disciples took up swords when they saw that the insolent men had [?]. Simon burned with zeal, intent on fulfilling his promise. By cutting off the ear, he thought he was fulfilling his love for his master. The All-Knowing One answered him, “Enough now of your help.” The Gentle One showed his love, as was fitting for his coming. He put the ear back on the head of the body, yet the crowd of insolent men felt no shame. They dragged him to the court, and he went to drink like a guilty man. His disciples abandoned him and fled,

and did not remain with him in his suffering. Simon followed him to see the outcome of his interrogation. His love stirred him to zeal, and he entered the court with his master. The guards asked the innocent man, “Are you also a disciple?” His fervor cooled, and he forgot all his promises. The suffering of death shook him, the chief of the Twelve. His resolve weakened and failed through his threefold denial. In the morning our Savior looked at him as he came out of the court. With his look he rebuked him: “Where is your zealous boasting?” Simon sighed and [?], because his Master reminded him of his promises. He had promised, “I will not deny him,” yet he swore, “I do not know him.” The Master did not punish the chief of the disciples for his folly. For this reason he allowed him to falter, so that his word would be fulfilled. He made the chief of the apostles the foundation of the structure of his teaching. Through his denial and his soul’s repentance, he blazed in him a path for the lost. They brought the innocent one before Pilate as though he were guilty. They stirred up the judge against him, saying that he wanted to seize the kingdom for himself. Pilate therefore questioned him as he judged him: “Are you a king, as they have said— the members of your people and your companions?” But he gave no answer, for silence suited his humility. Thus his word would be fulfilled in deed: he did not open his mouth in his humiliation. Before Pilate the unjust descendants of Abraham were shouting, “Crucify him! He deserves death, for he has stirred up our people and agitated them.” The judge, who was not one of the people, acquitted him and declared, “He is innocent.” But the people who knew God covered up justice with falsehood. The unjust accepted responsibility for his blood, so that they would be held accountable for it. They laid the reproach of killing him upon their children, so that they too would be condemned by it. The judge washed his hands and cleared himself of his killing. The unjust took him and went out to disgrace him on the cross. They devised a treacherous plan together with their master, the Accuser: that he deserved to die on the cross as a transgressor of the Law. The insolent planned to [?] insult him alongside robbers, so that those who saw him would count him among criminals. They raised him onto the wood and nailed him there, to make him a spectacle for onlookers. While he was fulfilling his own task, he was openly proclaiming his death. He was mocked by the priests and ridiculed by the people, he who was the dwelling place of the Godhead. And the Godhead was shaking the natural world because of his humiliation. Heaven and earth and everything in them wore garments of [?] over that holy body, which was being dishonored by the unclean. The sun fled and hid its light, and the moon turned to blood, so that the unjust would not delight

in the beauty of their radiance. An earthquake made the earth tremble and split cliffs and stones, as the silent things rebuked the hard hearts of the insolent. The Spirit tore open the front of the doorway and disgraced the temple of atonement. He showed that he was abandoning and forsaking it by tearing its garment of modesty. The tombs of the righteous were opened, for the command stirred them, so that the dead would become heralds of the resurrection of the one who gives life to the dead. The insolent pierced him with nails—[?] Joseph, upon whom the Word had ridden. The Word stirred the silent things to enter into judgment with those who could speak. They crucified him between robbers, as though he were a doer of evil. Though unwilling, they set their seal on the marvel of prophecy. Wonder drew the robber on the right to repentance. He rebuked his companion to make him stop his blasphemy. With a voice full of groans, the robber pleaded, asking forgiveness, that mercy might make him worthy on the day of judgment. With the hidden eye of his mind [?], he saw the kingdom of heaven. He said to our Lord, “Make me worthy to see your kingdom.” Oh, the wonder that was being proclaimed to those on earth through the robber: he asked for a kingdom from the crucified man who was crucified beside him! But the giver of life to all did not deprive the robber of the reward for his words. He answered and gave him his reward: a kingdom in return for his confession. He fulfilled in deed for him the [?] that he had promised him. For through his soul he brought him with him into Paradise at the time of his death. Oh, the wonder that was being proclaimed at Golgotha through a mortal! The body nailed to the cross was opening a road to [?]. Oh, the dead man whose death proclaimed the resurrection of the dead to the departed! Oh, the prisoner upon the wood who loosened the bonds of sin! The body, the clothing of the Only Begotten, was suffering the pains of death. Yet he did not abandon it or depart from it, even at the time of its humiliation. The mortal entrusted his soul to him when he was in distress. “Into your hands,” he said, “I place my soul. Return it to its dwelling in peace.” He bowed his head on the cross and surrendered his soul to the Creator. The departure of his soul bore witness that his death was not forced. Now is the moment that shows to whom suffering and death belong. The one who shares our nature teaches us that the Word does not share in his sufferings. “Into your hands,” he said, “I place my soul.” Let us ask whose soul it is: that of the Word, the Only One from the Father, or that of our fellow human being, the son of Adam? The Godhead has no soul. Heretic, do not go astray! For the life of the Godhead is not sustained by a soul. It is the soul of the mortal, the one who was clothed in bodily members. When sufferings approached his members, it departed from him in distress. There was a soul in that body which the Word chose as his dwelling. Its departure bears witness that it left him at [?] the suffering.

It was one capable of suffering who suffered the harsh pains of the cross, as he cried out with groans, “My God, my God, do not abandon me [?].” It was not the Word who pleaded with his Father, with whom he is one. The divine one has no God. Eutyches, with whom are you arguing? It was not the Word who bowed his head and surrendered his soul on the cross [?]. The fountain of life does not die. Restrain your blasphemies, insolent man! It was not into the Eternal One that the nails and the spear in the side were driven. The Only One has no bodily members. Heretic, do not be insolent! It was the man of flesh whose body was [?] on the wood of the cross. He was the one offering supplication, for he needed help. It was the bodily one who bore death, because he was mortal by nature. He pleaded with the Only Begotten that [?] his soul [?] for him. He bowed his head on the cross and entrusted his soul to the Creator. When his soul departed to Eden, his body remained inside the tomb. The Father's Word did not abandon the dwelling [?] the pure one that he had chosen for himself. Although he had been in him from the beginning, he did not suffer in his wounds. He never departed from him, neither during his sufferings nor on the cross. Nor did he taste suffering in his own nature through the sufferings he endured in his bodily [?]. Death swallowed the mortal one, but he saw no decay among the dead. For prophecy did not allow death to lay hands on his body. They pierced him between his ribs with a spear, and blood and water flowed from him. No bone in his body was broken, in keeping with the mystery Moses wrote down. The insolent men divided his clothes and cast lots among themselves. The prophetic word of his father David was fulfilled in deed. They took his body down from the cross, brought it into a tomb, and laid it there. His death did not corrupt his body, for he did not linger among the dead. For three days the Giver of Life remained inside the tomb. He contended with death in judgment, dismantling and abolishing its authority. The Word who had clothed himself in him was with him as he lay inside the tomb. He did not suffer through his sufferings, for his nature is above suffering. The Word had the angels honor his holy body. The spiritual beings awaited the signal of the one who gives life to all. The Father's Word [?] fulfilled his promises to him. After death had dissolved his body, he raised him on the third day. O dead man whom death swallowed, who turned and killed his killer! He broke death's bitter sting and dispelled its gall from humanity. O man of dust who fought against the spirit and ruler of the air! He exposed the demons through his victory and put them to shame in his own person. One of our own race fought against death and the devil. Through the power of the one who clothed himself in him, he defeated the two robbers who had exalted themselves. It was the battle in which Adam had been defeated, and all his nature had been defeated with him.

The divine Being clothed himself in the son of Adam and through him won victory for his fellow humans. On the third day he stripped away the mortality of his nature. He killed sin in his flesh and gave victory to mortals. Through the power of the divine Being who dwelt in him, he entered the contest and triumphed. By his power he overcame death and abolished its authority. He was with him when he suffered, but did not share in his wounds. After he had been tested in everything, he brought him to perfection through his personal suffering. Through insolent men, death tore down the outward temple of his body. The Word rebuilt it and dwelt in it—a building that would never again be shaken. It was of this temple that he said, “Tear it down, and I will raise it.” He was teaching his hearers that the dissolution affected the body alone. The divine Being cannot be dissolved, for the divine Being has no beginning. The dissolution belongs to the mortal body, and it alone tasted death. By the dissolution of his body he taught that he was a human being capable of suffering. By rising on the third day, he revealed the power that raised him. Our mortal nature was too weak to be its own savior. The divine Being clothed himself in our nature and through it freed our whole race. The exalted One humbled himself in his love to raise up mortal Adam. With the weapon by which Adam was defeated, the self-existent One [?] gave victory to the son of Adam. He wished to exalt the lowly one, not himself to descend to lowliness. He exalted the earthly one and raised him to honor alongside his own majesty. Adam’s race owed [?] for transgressing the commandment. And what its mortal members did not repay, the self-existent One repaid through the son of Adam. The mortal one died in his nature, while the self-existent One remained in his [?]. Through the power of divine being, the mortal one conquered and rose again. It was not the Creator who suffered the sufferings of death on the cross. It was the son of Adam who, through his suffering, paid the debt recorded against Adam’s household. He fulfilled the saving plan through him, the bodily one, on behalf of mortals. In his death and resurrection, our entire nature died and came to life. He made him a garment for his hiddenness and a mirror for us mortals, so that, through the movements of the soul, we might see his hiddenness in the [?] of our body. For the reconciliation of rational beings, he took him as the firstfruits from us all, so that through him he might bind together the love that Adam had undone by transgressing his commandment. He honored the entire nature of rational beings by assuming him. Those who are [?] to us by nature he made sharers in his honor. This greatness, which came to rational beings through a member of our race, the wicked and contentious denied through the distortions of their words. They do not allow our nature to be honored with glorious things, nor do they permit it to be exalted with God, who assumed it. The heretics conceived and gave birth to two unforgivable wrongs: they brought the self-existent One down to dishonorable things, and they deprived our body of life. They are haters of the body and are divided against divine being: they assigned a beginning to the self-existent One and denied the body its assumption. Their war is against divine being, which they subject to suffering through their words.

And their struggle is against humanity, which they do not deem worthy of greatness. They quarrel with the scribes of the Spirit’s words—every one of them—and [?], those who show us the distinction between the two natures that became one. The heretics do not listen to the heralds of the Spirit’s words, who cry out like trumpets about the exaltation of the member of our race. Let the chief of the apostles come and expose the falsehood of their words. Together with the Jews, their companions, let him accuse these blind men. Let Peter speak to the arrogant, to the arrogant—the new Jews who have arisen: “God made the body he assumed both Lord and Messiah.” Who made whom Lord, Simon, firstborn of our confession? Explain to us the force of your [?], so that through it we may refute the heretics. “The self-existent One, the Father’s Word,” he says, “took our nature and dwelt in it. He made it Lord and Messiah, in honor alongside his own majesty. “This Jesus whom you crucified—listen, you latter-day Jews—the self-existent One made a partner in glory and exalted his authority.” He, the firstfruits of our nature, rebuked the arrogant by showing his disciples the constitution of his body after his resurrection. Let us listen. Let them listen to him along with the disciples, even if they deny his humanity. For a spirit has no limbs, as he showed his disciples. “Touch me,” he said, “and examine the body and bones that I have.” “And proclaim this among all nations: that I rose with a body and bones.” See, he showed us this plainly after his death and resurrection: that it was the bodily one whom death wronged, and the Word does not share in his sufferings. And if they do not say so plainly, they make the divine Being suffer through their words: that it was the Creator who was displaying flesh and bones in his own nature. Let the accusation and the demand for an account of these things I have recounted turn back upon them, because [?] they caused confusion and proclaimed a distinction that proclaims a body belonging to the divine Being. They honored the Creator who has no beginning with two beginnings: one from the womb of a human woman, and another from inside the tomb. Oh, the [?] of these insolent people! How brazen and arrogant they have become! For they confined the incomprehensible divine Being within a womb and a tomb. Come, my brothers, like discerning people, let us distinguish [?] from falsehood, and wash the garment of our confession clean of the soot of heretics. Let us cut the rotten and diseased limbs away from our body. For look, the sickness of their words is spreading, and gangrene has taken hold in [?]. Let us drive away from the sheep the wolves that have ravaged the flock. They disguise themselves in the appearance of lambs, though they are strangers to the truth. Let us not mix the weeds of their statements into our truth. They cause divisions to sprout in everyone concerning the confession of the divine Being. Let us bind the love of our minds to the faith of the apostles. For they strengthened our humanity through the confession of faith. On Simon’s confession let us build the structure of our faith, and let us walk in Paul’s company, for he blazed a trail to heaven. In agreement with the Twelve,
let us confess with them, as Simon did, that the Creator made the body he took from us Lord and Christ. The end.
On the Robber
Discourse Twenty. On the Robber, to be recited on the Saturday of the Resurrection. Response: Thanks be to him who blazed a trail to the kingdom through a shedder of human blood, my brothers.

The Creator created a new creation on the summit of Golgotha, and displayed the power of his craftsmanship in a crucified man. Those on earth and those in heaven saw a crucified man, and gathered around him to see the wonder being spoken of concerning him. All creation gathered from every direction to examine the craftsmanship displayed upon the wood. The Lord of the world skillfully portrayed the world, and raised it up and placed it upon the wood for everyone to see. On the panel of a visible body he portrayed all creatures, so that beings with speech and those without speech might examine his craftsmanship in it. In a human being he brought the work of his hands to its limit at the beginning of time, and in the Son of Man he completed his handiwork at the end of time.

He chose a man for himself, to renew the worn-out world through him. He polished him through sufferings and displayed his beauty before the eyes of all creatures. He fastened him to the wood like a mirror before the eyes of those watching, so that they might look at him and see their own blemishes. He raised him up just like the serpent Moses raised up, to heal humanity from the bites of tyrannical demons. The demons had bitten the human race destructively, and he hung a man on the summit of Golgotha to give life to humanity. He lovingly turned everyone's gaze toward him, so that whoever looked with loving affection might wound the demons. Speaking and speechless creatures gazed lovingly at him, at the crucified body. They grieved over his suffering and gained hope in humanity's salvation. The world gazed lovingly at him, at the salvation of its life, for it saw that the time had arrived for its old age to be renewed. It saw him in great disgrace, standing among robbers, and grieved deeply over his unlawful humiliation. Speechless and speaking creatures alike marveled at his love, because he agreed to die for the renewal of their natures. A hidden sign taught them to marvel at the crucified man, with whom the world and its wickedness were crucified. Oh, the wonder of the Creator's inexpressible power, who crucified [?] the world and its desires in one man! Created things saw a great marvel in one man: they were crucified with the mortal who was upon the wood. The robber on the right marveled at this wonder, and anguish seized him over his unlawful conduct. The sinner clothed himself in great sorrow over his sins, for he saw creation mourning in grief. He saw the elements of creation grieving at the time of the suffering, and he grieved and sighed over his countless [?] abominations. He saw the heavenly lights wrapped in mourning clothes and was greatly astonished at the change in their order. He saw an earthquake shaking the earth as though it were about to fall,

and he trembled and was terrified at the harsh blows dealt to his mother. He saw hard rocks splitting and the people terrified, and instead of his clothing, he tore his soul over what had happened. He saw wicked men mocking the man crucified with him, and he pondered the reason for his death and the reason for their mockery. He reflected wisely and considered with discernment that it was because of this man that the heavenly lights had darkened and the earth had shaken. "Why have darkness and an earthquake come together?" he pondered. "And on whose account have two such terrible things happened in a single hour? Who has shaken the speechless elements of nature from their roots? Look, they are in turmoil like a woman in childbirth overcome by pain. Who has changed the brightness of the light into darkness? And who has shaken the face of the earth with trembling? Who has put restraints on the swiftly running sun? And who has turned the bright moon into gloomy blood? For whom are the voiceless elements of nature mourning so unusually? For whom are they weeping as for a firstborn son bitterly mourned? Why does the earth shed tears with a thunderous sound? For whom do the eyes of her face pour down tears of dew? Could this crucified man, crucified with us, be righteous? Is it because of him that the voiceless elements of nature are clothed in mourning? Could envy have crucified him unjustly, though he was innocent? Could the devil have driven nails into him, though he did not deserve it? Could the priests have envied him and hated him unjustly because he performed mighty deeds beyond their rank? Why do they threaten and insult him as though he were evil? Look how brightly shines the renown of the help he distributed throughout the earth! Why does he drink down insult and mockery like a guilty man? The dead whom he raised bear witness to his innocence. If my own wickedness has crucified me in keeping with my offenses, why is he who did no wrong being condemned unjustly? If the sins I committed against justice have bound me, why does he who is innocent bow his head upon the cross? If the snares I buried in the ground have caught me because I sinned,

why does he whose words gave life to sinners die? I have heard reports of the power of the signs he performed on earth. People have unjustly repaid him with the pangs of death. These were the things the man on the right was pondering within himself. Like a judge, he examined what he saw happening on the cross. With discernment he entered into a just judgment within his own mind. He condemned his own wickedness and declared innocent the righteous man crucified with him. As though in a furnace, he tested the truth and rejected falsehood. He displayed the beauty of the truthful word before the eyes of those watching. Although the anguish of his bodily sufferings was piercing him severely, he did not give in or retreat from the struggle against wickedness. The weapon of truth was in his debt in the hour of suffering. He fought heroically and won an extraordinary victory. A fierce contest suddenly broke upon him on the summit of Golgotha, and he resolutely gave himself to the struggle. He exposed himself to death, although he was already dying. He scorned and despised every suffering as though he felt no pain. He fought two battles as he hung high upon the cross: against wickedness and against the mockery of insolent people. Like an athlete, the bandit took his stand on the cross. He engaged in battle with his own evil deeds and the mockery of the people. Wickedness and the people stood arrayed against him like an army, but he alone overcame sin and the crucifiers. Oh, how astonishing was the battle fought by this weak-willed man! At the moment when hope was cut off, he gained the victory. At the hour of death he entered battle stripped of armor. Naked, he overcame every suffering, outward and inward. The people were armed with mockery against our Lord, hurling insulting words like javelins. From unclean mouths came mockery of the one who sanctifies the perfect. Insolent people reviled him as though he were a wrongdoer. The robber on the left also mocked him, hurling arrows of insult at him even more than the people did.

The insolent man attacked insolently with a foolish fist; instead of a sword, he drew his tongue to pour out insults. “If you are the Messiah who is to come,” the wicked man said, “save yourself, and save us too from torment. “If you are a king and David belongs to you, give the command, and your armies will arm themselves against those who crucified you. “If you are the Son, and you are the Son of God as you say, come down from the cross, and then your claim to be the Son will be confirmed. “If the mighty deeds you performed among humankind are genuine, show your power on your own behalf, and you will be believed. “If you are innocent and people have crucified you on the wood for nothing, call upon God, and let him exact vengeance for the disgrace of the wrong done to you.” Oh, how that unruly dog barked at the gentle one! The vile man did not shrink before the Holy One. Oh, how that insolent mouth blasphemed against the humble one! The accursed man felt no shame, either for his wrongdoing or for the suffering of the one he insulted. Oh, how the hidden Command endured his insolence and did not fiercely consume him with the fire of wrath! At the sound of his insults, the man on the right grew zealous and fierce. He forgot his own sufferings and began to fight against the insults directed at him. The righteous man fought a just battle with the wicked man, and wisely shot arrows of remorse into him. The wise man spoke the name of God to the godless man: “Do you not fear God, whose judgment is just? Like a [?], he spoke with the man condemned to death: “Why have you poured out the wickedness of your mouth against the innocent one?

“Why do you insolently mock the one without blemish and increase the lashes decreed in judgment for your wrongdoing? “Do you not know that our own wickedness hung us on the cross, and our insolence has made us die without mercy? “The hidden Command has justly called us to judgment, and has paid us the wages of a shameful death according to our deeds. “This man is innocent and holy, clean of every stain.
