Though he had done no wrong, the people, blinded by envy, crucified him. “Why do you want to share in the guilt of blood unjustly shed and include yourself in the sentence passed on murderers? “Is the blood you previously shed without cause not enough for you, that you must add doubled wickedness to what came before? “Is temporal death for your wrongdoing not enough for you, that you must also die the hidden death that has no end?” Oh, the new teacher who proclaimed truth on earth, and with the words of his mouth exposed and rebuked tyrannical wickedness! Oh, the wicked man who exposed the wickedness he had habitually practiced, and proclaimed the truth that he had not known how to contemplate! He rebuked his companion for unjustly reviling the Just One, and turned to plead concerning his own transgressions, [?]. The memory of his wickedness arose in his heart at the time of suffering, and he began to pass judgment on himself for the sins he had committed. The man sleeping in wickedness stirred from his sins as though from sleep, and saw that he was stripped of good deeds as though of clothes. He saw his body and soul exposed and naked, and he grieved and sighed bitterly over his transgressions. In great sorrow he painfully scourged himself, and with resounding sobs he wept over his misery. All alone he made a place for dancing on the cross; his movements became lamentations, and he composed cries. He mourned for his soul as for a dead person atop the cross, and shrouded and buried himself in heartfelt remorse. He mourned doubly over his soul and his torment, for he saw that he would die and then be raised again for the punishment of judgment. He rightly pondered two thoughts concerning two deaths, and anguish seized him because his sins had bound him to two judgments. The judgment beyond terrified him far more than the judgment here.

And he considered death on the cross to be nothing. He kept remembering that torment without end, and inwardly in his mind he saw it as though with his eyes. He inwardly saw the splendor of the kingdom on high, and he yearned and wondered whether mercy [?] would make him worthy to enter. He fixed his mind intently on the promised blessings, and became bold like a poor man driven by his need. The bold man took on great boldness, just as before, in the same manner in which he used to raid so boldly. He did not cover his face to conceal his thievery; he put on a brazen face and began to break into the royal palace. On these terms he boldly asked our Savior whether he could plunder the spiritual treasury. His former habit dragged the greedy man into greed; he trampled every [?] and went in to seize plunder, as was his custom. He began to say to the owner of the treasury, “Remember me, my Lord, in that kingdom hidden on high from sight.” Give my poverty a single spiritual coin, so that by grace I may live on a tiny morsel of your gift. Forgive my transgressions, wipe away my sins, and cleanse my blemishes. In your mercy, erase the record of the debt I owe to your justice. Rescue me from my lost condition, have mercy on my need, and raise me from my state of death. Make me an example of the abolition of death and the undoing of wickedness. Through me, open a path of repentance for the generations to come, so that they may follow me in heartfelt remorse toward forgiveness. Let the light of faith in you shine within my darkness, and drive from my soul the darkness of wickedness that lurks within me. Bring me back to you from the captor who took me captive away from you. Free me from my slavery, so that I may serve with you and belong to you. I belong to you, but I have been carried captive away from your dominion. Rescue this member of your household, and let everyone know the power of your lordship. Enough! Until now I have served among strangers, and my days have been spent in the useless service of my error. The day has ended, and the sun of my life's Sabbath has set. If your help does not reach me, I will become nothing.

My Lord, do not let me perish from the company of Adam's dust, or be excluded from the fellowship that brings the dead to life. Sprinkle over my deadness the dew of mercy hidden in your words, so that [?] I may be refreshed on the day of resurrection and offer praise in return. Make me worthy to walk with the few on the path of the righteous, and to enter and rejoice in that delight which never decays. Who revealed this to you, you who are dead in your sins, so that you know these things? Who informed you that a crucified man is king over all? Who showed you that a human being has authority on high, and how he can exercise dominion over the things to come? Who taught you that he can absolve a person's wrongdoing? And where does he get the power to grant immortal life? Tell me, man, when has one human being raised another from the dead? And when have earthly people distributed the kingdom on high? Granted that one human being has raised another from the dead—that is written down—but we have never heard that human beings distributed the kingdom on high. Who misled you, wandering in the confusion of desires, into thinking that a crucified man gives life and forgives wrongdoing? Look, son of error, perhaps your mind has wandered into error. Examine things carefully, and only then ask for things beyond your reach. Perhaps the weight of your bodily sufferings has made you lose your way and become confused, and your mind, as though in a dream, has wandered among things that are not revealed. It was not the robber who went astray in his petition. The composer of these words went astray and mocked him in keeping with his deeds. The speaker recalled the magnitude of his wrongdoing and his shameful deeds, and wanted to mock him: where could a man lost in error have obtained the truth? Who, then, taught this utterly ignorant man to know the truth? Who marked out a path for him to travel toward the heights? Who copied out a new book for this false disciple? Who became his teacher in the study of things to come? Who explained to him the meaning of the revelation of hidden things? Who told him that there is a kingdom that will never pass away? Who became a counselor to this man wandering in error, so that he could bring himself to his senses at a time of terror? With what eyes did this seer of hidden things see that dwelling which no eye of flesh has beheld?

With what ears did this dull listener to wrongdoing hear that voice which cannot be heard through senses made of clay? With what mouth did this babbler, stammering far from the truth, utter that song of praise which cannot be spoken by a tongue of flesh? With what palate did this tasteless man taste the sweetness of life? How, and to what extent, was he able to receive spiritual food? Granted that he conceived of a kingdom hidden on high, what authority does a crucified man have over its delights? Granted that he hoped mercy would show favor to sinners, how can one human being help another? Granted that he believed this man could accomplish the things he imagined, who put into him the thought of these things that he could not see? The man of flesh did not ponder fleshly thoughts, nor was it his own impulse to ask lovingly for the things above. A hidden prompting secretly drew him to see hidden things, and it raised him toward the revelation of secrets. The power of the Spirit spoke with him spiritually, and it explained to him the secret mysteries that were hidden from him. It made the power of wisdom concerning things to come dwell in him, and it revealed to him that there is a kingdom and a sentence of judgment. It told him, “The crucified man who is crucified with you possesses the kingdom on high and the judgment to come.” It revealed to him that he can blot out a person's wrongdoing and write in his name a certificate of freedom in place of slavery. He wished the debt certificate of the guilty to be torn up through this demonstration: if a guilty man has gained acquittal, who should doubt? He opened the kingdom on high to those on earth through his entrance: if a robber entered first, who is left behind? He revealed the exaltation of our race in the promise he made to him: if one of our race possesses the kingdom, blessed is our nature! He showed the remission of our sin through his soul, which entered Eden, for we too are destined to enter the kingdom on high with him. As in a picture, he portrayed our wrongdoing and our repentance in him, and raised him up and fixed him on the summit of Golgotha for onlookers to see. Under this arrangement he forgave his wrongdoing at the time of the Passion, so that we might learn that he suffered on the cross for our sake. In this way he chose for himself a man more sinful than everyone, so that through a sinner he might show his power, which can accomplish everything.

He promised the kingdom to a man who shed blood and was full of wrongdoing, to open a path of repentance for those who had acted wickedly. He came to pay the debt certificate of Adam's race, and first he set free one debtor who owed a great deal. He wished to renew the nature worn out by mortality, and he accomplished this in a man who was entirely dead in hateful wrongdoing. He gave a sign to the elements and made them mourn over his humiliation, and they showed that he is the Lord and the Son of God, who is [?] over all. Through things without speech and through those able to speak, he proclaimed his power, and like heralds the creatures cried out about his authority. He made insensible things mourn as though they had senses, and gave those with senses the understanding of the Spirit. He clothed the sun and moon in mourning garments, and compelled the robber to declare the greatness of his power. Through the changes they underwent, speechless things cried out as though they had mouths: “We are suffering because of the man who hangs among us.” Through its earthquake the earth spoke with the children of earth: “My children, how greatly you have hated the blood that binds up my wounds!” The robber's voice thundered through creation more loudly than thunder: “Look, mortals, at the life hanging [?] on top of the cross!” Heaven and earth had already listened to the trumpet of his voice, but the people alone stopped their ears to avoid hearing. The signs took place to rebuke the dull-hearted people; because of them the heavenly lights grew dark and the earth shook. He pressed the robber about his wrongdoing, and the robber turned from his wrongdoing, so that he might see, repent, ask, and plead for his folly. He revealed his divinity in his humanity before the eyes of all creatures: although he suffers as a human being, he is the Son of God. The Jews crucified the embodied Son of God, not God, the Word of the Father, who is begotten of him. They drove material nails into the body's frame, not into the divine essence, whose nature is above injury. The robber saw the visible body upon the cross, not the hidden nature, which cannot be seen except by the mind. The Spirit of revelation showed the man on the right, in his mind, that the man whom the people were mockingly insulting was the Son of God.

Truth spoke through him to shame the people and defeat the demons, so that the enemy and his followers would be put to shame by his proclamation. At the sound of his confession, the rebel who had taken Adam captive was ashamed, for upon the cross he was stripped of the captives he had taken. He put him to shame through a single man whom he turned toward himself; the rebel could not stand against him and prevent the man from acknowledging him. He exposed him through the promise he made to the robber, and, for the robber's salvation, sealed the word of his mouth with “Amen.” He swore by “Amen,” the word that is the seal of truth: “Today you will be with me in Eden, in the fellowship of the soul.” “You will be with me in the land of Eden,” he told him. But why in Eden and not in heaven, where he had asked to be? The robber sought the kingdom above, not Paradise. He asked him for the promised blessings, not trees. The robber too could have said, “What is this? I asked you for the kingdom, not Paradise. If you are the Lord, and the heights and depths belong to you, why do you hesitate to fulfill the promise of your words? I asked you to let me inherit the imperishable things above. Why are you giving me an earthly inheritance whose dwelling is poor? Paradise too is a part of the earth, however beautiful it may be, and the food of its fruits is perishable, however sweet it may be.” He who discerned the truth in his mind did not entertain these thoughts, for the prompting of the one who had mercy on him did not allow him to demand these things. The one who revealed to him the mystery of the invisible kingdom also placed the bridle of silence upon him, so that he would not doubt. In faith he asked for the kingdom from the one who had [?] him. Because it was far away, he brought him into Eden while it was still being gathered. He could not enter with him at this time, lest the great order of that arrangement be disrupted. That entrance takes place in due order at the end of time, when angels and human beings enter together, a great assembly.

Since he did not allow him to enter with him, because it was not fitting, he brought him through hope into the mystery of entrance into the kingdom. He brought him into the land of Eden in soul, not in body—in that person who can receive spiritual things. He gave his rational faculty a pledge of things to come, so that he would know that the hope into which he had entered would not prove false. He gave the mortal man a pledge of life in Eden, to undo the death that had enslaved Adam and his offspring. Where the head of humanity had sinned and death had killed him, there he brought the man who had walked in the turmoil of robbery. At his Father's bidding, the thief entered to dwell there. The enemy saw him and wailed and wept, for this displeased him. Into the place that the transgression of the commandment had fenced off against Adam, Adam entered through the robber who entered with our Lord. The soul of our Lord and that of the robber entered together, and he opened the gate before the souls of [?]. A fence of wrath had been set up against us to keep us from entering. Our Lord broke through it and brought us in with him through his own entry. To shame the demons, he opened Paradise to mortals, so that those who rejoiced when we left might now grieve at our entry. By what he did, he exposed and shamed the ruler of the air, who had driven Adam out of the inheritance his Lord had given him. The envious one imagined that Adam would never return to his place. Suddenly he was put to shame when he saw him in Eden in two souls. Two entered first, one righteous and one sinful, so that he might know that both the good and the wicked would indeed enter. He grieved and groaned over the robber more than over our Lord: how had a shedder of blood breached the wall he had built? The proud-minded one had thought that by his scheming he had fenced off Paradise. When he saw that they had opened it, anguish and despair seized him. He saw that a road to Eden had been opened for people to travel,

and he wailed and wept because he was left alone amid shameful things. “What shall I do?” he said to himself in bitterness of soul. “The king whom I cast into exile is crying out for his kingdom.” “Where shall I go?” the evil one asked his evil inclination. “Adam has taken possession of the heights and the depths through his offspring. “At first I drove him [?] out of Paradise so that he would not inherit, yet no place remained on earth that he did not inherit. “I would have been content with the earthly inheritance he acquired on earth, rather than have this new report reach me that he is ascending on high. “I would have preferred him to possess the earth twice over, rather than be called an heir of the heights and a son of the kingdom. “I would have been at ease if he had inherited the heights and the depths together, without being raised to the lofty rank of divinity. “This man whom I crucified upon the wood is one of his race, yet here he is promising heaven and earth to his companions. “He hangs on the cross, with nails driven into his body, yet he swears with an ‘Amen’ that he can give the kingdom on high. “He is caught in the struggle of suffering and is close to death, yet a despised man has come forward and begs him, ‘Give me life!’” The accuser received redoubled lashes from that utterance: “Remember me, my Lord, when you come.” The more the robber pleaded upon the wood, the more bitterly he himself was racked. While the Giver of life to all was promising, “You will be with me,” he was perishing fiercely in the fire of his own inclination. While he was swearing and sealing his word with “Amen,” the other was howling like a woman in labor overcome by pain. Envy was struck as though by an arrow by these events, and the robber’s voice stung him more than anything. And if the robber, who had been his disciple, stung him so, what will he do when heaven and earth cry out against him? If his confidant exposed him and revealed his trade,

where will he go when the watchers and human beings jeer at him? If a murderer received the promise of the kingdom on high, how will he bear to look when our whole race enters? O robber, who cut off the enemy’s hope and gave and created hope for the hopeless through the forgiveness of his wickedness! O you who became guilty and pledged yourself to shameful deeds, yet received back the record of your debts freely through a single word! O you who were utterly defiled by loathsome wickedness, yet sprinkled your whole self with the pure waters of repentance! O you who plundered and seized earthly possessions throughout your life, and on the day of your death plundered heavenly blessings! O you from whose wickedness travelers on the road hid themselves, who opened the road of repentance before sinners! O idle man, who spent his days in emptiness, who spoke a word and received as his wages the kingdom on high! O how fully, and in what way, can I paint a picture of the forgiveness of your wickedness? With “Amen” the Giver of ranks confirmed the rank that came to you. My tongue is too feeble to portray your story, O breaker through foundations, and I do not know how to reveal the hidden devices of your trade. You were utterly brazen and conducted your life cunningly. You sinned as you wished, then turned back and pleaded as you pleased. The one who forgives your wickedness alone knows the recesses of your heart, and the one who knows you was not repelled by the enormity of your wickedness. Wisely he portrayed your story on the tablet of his sufferings, so that everyone might learn to journey through sufferings toward the things to come. Response: Glory to you, who bring the erring back to knowledge of the greatness of his glory.
On the Mysteries of the Church and on Baptism
Discourse Twenty-One: On the Mysteries of the Church and on Baptism

Our Lord opened for us the sweet spring of baptism and gave our race the sweetness of immortal life to drink. In the heat of wickedness our understanding dried up and its fruits fell away. He sprinkled his gift like dew and refreshed our soul. The fierce thirst of mortality killed our body. He buried it in water, and life stirred within its mortality. The grime of the passions had smeared the beauty of our discernment, and he painted us anew with the incorruptible pigment of the Spirit. Skillfully he compounds the medicine that renews our race, with oil and water and the power of the Spirit, who is mightier than all. The master craftsman introduced a new craft: that human beings should form human beings without sexual union. The divine command devised an invention that had never existed: that we should bring forth human beings from within water, without seed. Where has anything like this ever existed or happened—a womb of water giving birth to infants without mating? Who has ever heard of one kind giving birth to something not of its own kind, as now a speechless nature gives birth to rational beings? Although the waters brought forth creeping creatures and birds, it had never been heard that water gave birth to a human being. This is a marvel, and however much we speak of it, it remains full of wonder: that a womb of water should conceive and give birth to fully formed infants. It is entirely new, and great is the manifestation enacted in it: the course of conception and birth takes place in less than an hour. Its order proceeds outside the order established in nature,

and it is not delayed by growth that takes place little by little. Come, listener, hear the wonder of the new birth: its conception and its delivery take place in a single hour. Come, observer, see the artist who forms infants: while the word is still moving in the mouth, the child comes out of the womb. Come, discerning one, discern and consider carefully the power of the divine Being, which gives strength to weak things. Come, mortals, look at the nature afflicted with mortality: it strips off its sufferings in baptism and puts on life. Come, let us examine carefully the mysteries of our renewal and learn what is hidden in the visible waters. Come, let us approach the priesthood, the salt of the earth, and see how it compounds human beings with spiritual things. Let us enter with it where it enters to grant forgiveness, and incline our minds to listen to the voice that speaks with it. Let us listen to how the power of the Spirit speaks with it and teaches it to impart power to ordinary water. The hidden command communicates hidden mysteries to it, and it explains them aloud before the listeners. He practices the craft of the new birth before it and shows it how to form a spiritual image. The priest becomes like a pen for the hidden power, and through the priesthood’s hands it writes names over the water. O writer who writes the Spirit on a fluid tablet! The ink of his words is not erased by the dissolving waters. Oh, how great is your craft, mortal man! No one knows how to contemplate it in a manner worthy of its greatness. Oh, how fine is the pen of your mind for depicting mysteries! No artist can make images like yours. Hail to you, priest, who ministers spiritually on earth! The spiritual beings are not authorized to imitate you. O priest, how great is the rank in which you serve! The ministers of fire and spirit tremble before it. Who can express how great your rank is? You have surpassed the heavenly beings by virtue of your authority. A spirit’s nature is subtler and more glorious than yours, yet it is not permitted to depict the mysteries as you do. The angel is great, and however we put it, he is greater than you.

Yet when he is compared with your ministry, he is less than you. The seraph is holy, the cherub splendid, and the watcher swift, yet they cannot keep pace with the freedom of the word from your mouth. Gabriel is glorious and Michael great, as their names testify; yet they are all subject to the mystery entrusted to your hands. They gaze at you when you approach to minister, and they wait for you to open the door for their songs of holiness. Bearing sounds of praise, they stand at your right hand, and when you have completed the mystery of your salvation, they cry out in praise. In love they submit to the will hidden in your mysteries, and they honor you because of the office exercised through you. And if spiritual beings, who are not subject to suffering, honor your office, who would not weave a crown of praises for the greatness of your rank? Let us marvel continually at how exalted the greatness of your rank has become: it has subjected the heights and the depths to its authority. The priests of the Church hold authority in the heights and the depths, and they command heavenly and earthly beings. Between God [?] and human beings they stand as mediators [?], and by their words they drive wickedness away from humanity. The key to divine mercy is placed in their hands, and according to their desire they distribute life to human beings. A hidden power empowered them to do [?] this, so that through visible things they might show his love to the work of his hands. He showed his love in the mystery he entrusted to earthly beings, so that through his gift human beings might show mercy to one another. He entrusted the power of his gift to the hands of the Church’s priests, so that through it they might strengthen the weakness of human beings who had become guilty through sin. Through his ministry the priest pays humanity’s debt; with water he erases the record of his race’s debt and renews it. In baptism he casts bodies as though in a furnace, and as though by fire he destroys the undergrowth of mortality. He puts the Spirit’s medicine into the water as into a furnace, and cleanses the human image of its filth. With the Spirit’s heat he scours away the grime of body and soul, and in place of clay they acquire the appearance of heavenly beings.

He prepares a basin of water and sets it out like a furnace; then he approaches and reveals the power of his craft. Splendid garments cover his body outwardly, and the robe of the Spirit adorns his soul inwardly. Adorned in every part, he stands before those watching, so that through his adornment he may reveal to human beings the things to come. He becomes like a mirror before the eyes of his companions, so that they may look at him and gain hope of being glorified. Through the garments he wears, he sets a goal before their eyes, so that they may long to be adorned spiritually. Through the adornment on his limbs, he teaches this: the mystery in his hands clothes in glory whoever approaches it. In his hands is placed the treasure of life hidden in the water; unless he comes forward and distributes it, it is not given. He extends the key of his word and opens the door of the gift, and through the sound of his voice the King distributes presents to his servants. He too stands as though beside the sea, like Moses, and instead of a staff he raises his voice over the silent waters. With the word of his mouth he strikes the waters, like the son of Amram, and they obey his voice far more than the voice of the son of the Hebrews. They listened to Moses, but although they listened closely, they were not sanctified. They obey the priest of the church and acquire holiness [?]. The Israelite merely divided the sea; he could not cleanse his people's wrongdoing through the power of the miracle. The priest's miracle is great and has no equal among those that have occurred: it gives things without sensation the power to forgive wrongdoing. He fixes his gaze on that command which created the creation, and from it he learns how to create a new creation. He too imitates the manner in which the world was brought into being, and makes his voice heard like the one that cried out over the earth in the beginning. Like the Creator, he too commands the ordinary waters, and instead of light, the power of life shines out from them. The Creator's voice created the heavenly lights from nothing, while he creates something from something through the Creator's power. The creation he creates in the womb of the waters is not his own, but belongs to the command that created the creation from nothing. That command which spoke, and rational and speechless beings came into existence—

He commands through it, and human beings become a new creation. The very voice that the waters heard when they brought forth swarming creatures is the one they hear from the priest's mouth, and they give birth to human beings. The offspring they produce now is greater than the former offspring, just as a rational human being is superior to a speechless creature. Like seed, he casts his word into the womb of the waters, and they conceive and give birth to new offspring in an unaccustomed way. His mouth interprets the Spirit's words to the silent waters, and they gain the power to give life to rational beings. The speechless waters hear a new utterance from those who speak, like the utterance Mary heard from Gabriel. He too brings good news to human ears, like the news the angel proclaimed at the Son's birth. He fulfills his office in the angel's place, and does more than the angel, for through the sound of his words he gives hope to those without hope. He stands as mediator between the Divine Being and human beings, and through his words he confirms the covenant between the two sides. With sighs he implores the Hidden One, who is hidden and revealed in his love; and power from him descends upon him and brings his words to fulfillment. In the name of the divine Being, with the three names, he consecrates the water, so that it may suffice for the complete cleansing of the unclean. He cleanses human impurity with water—not by the water, but by the power of the name of the divine Being that overshadows it there. The power of the divine Being dwells in the visible water, and through the might of his power it brings the strength of the Evil One and death to an end. The Evil One and death are abolished in baptism, and the resurrection of the body and the salvation of the soul are proclaimed in it. Body and soul are buried in it as in a tomb, and they die and live in the mysteries of the resurrection that will take place at the end. It symbolically carries out the rite of burial for a person, and the voice of the priesthood is like the sound of the trumpet at the end. In the watery tomb the priest buries the whole person, and he raises him through the life-giving power hidden in his words. He stands fully armed at the entrance to the tomb of baptism, and there he performs the mystery of death and resurrection. With a clear voice he proclaims the power of what he is doing:

how a person dies in the water and returns to life. He openly reveals and shows the person being baptized in whose name he dies and comes to life so swiftly. He invokes the name of the divine Being and says three times: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one equality. He repeats the names in a clear voice and says this: “So-and-so is baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.” He does not say, “I baptize,” but, “He is baptized,” because it is not he who baptizes, but the one designated by the names. The names grant forgiveness of wrongdoing, not the human being; and they sow new life in mortality. In their name the person being baptized is immersed as though in a tomb, and they call him and raise him from his state of death. Three times he lowers his head in their names, so that he may learn the order: [?] they are three. The bosom of baptism becomes a symbol of our Savior, following the pattern of the three days in the tomb. Our Savior was among the dead for three days; likewise, for the person being baptized, the three times correspond to three days. He truly dies, symbolically sharing the death that the Giver of life to all died; and he truly lives, after the pattern of life without end. In baptism he strips off sin and death and casts them away, after the pattern of the clothes that our Lord left in the tomb when he came out. Like an infant emerging from the womb, he emerges from the water; and in place of clothes, a sponsor receives and embraces him in this way. He resembles an infant as he is lifted out of the water, and everyone embraces him as they would an infant. In place of [?] swaddling bands, they put clothes on his limbs and adorn him like a bridegroom on his wedding day. He too fulfills the customs of the wedding feast in baptism, and by his adornment he depicts the glory prepared for him. Through the beauty of his garments he proclaims the beauty of the world beyond: here is the symbol, and there the reality that does not deceive.

He is invited and called to the kingdom on high that will never pass away, and he depicts beforehand a symbolic demonstration that it is real. He puts on garments as a symbol of that glory which does not perish, so that he may symbolically resemble what is to come. Symbolically he dies, rises again, and is adorned; and symbolically he resembles immortal life. His birth is a symbol of that birth which will take place at the end, and the conduct of his life is a symbol of life in the kingdom on high. He begins to walk along the path of spiritual life, and like spiritual beings he lives on spiritual food. His symbolic birth takes place spiritually, and the nourishment prepared for him also corresponds to his birth. His birth is new and utterly foreign to earthly beings, and the greatness of the food that nourishes him is beyond measure. He suckles the divine mysteries like milk, and like a newborn he is led by stages toward the things to come. The spiritual mother prepares spiritual milk to sustain his life, and instead of breasts she places the body and blood in his mouth. With the body and blood the Church gives life to the children of her womb, and reminds them of the great love of her betrothal. Her betrothed gave her his body and blood as a pledge of life, so that she might receive the power to give life from her own life. He showed her that he gives life to her children through the food of his body, by means of the parables he had previously composed symbolically. He called the sacrifice of his body the fattened calf, and symbolically slaughtered it beforehand through the return of one of her children. In her children was fulfilled what is [?] in the story of the wanderer: his love went out and received them in baptism. With love and mercy he went out to meet them and received them, and embraced them as people who had been dead and had returned to life. He explained the meaning of his parables and revealed it before their eyes, and gladdened them with spiritual food and drink.

He gave the ring as a pledge—that is, the power of the Spirit—and clothed them in the glorious robe of baptism. He sacrificed himself, who was spiritually [?], and fed them food in which life is hidden for the one who eats it. He shod them with the good course of a virtuous life, so that they would not stumble on the deceptive path of mortality. He invited and called the heavenly beings on the day of their renewal, and gladdened those who had been grieving over their sins. The womb of water gave birth to them spiritually, and the power of his grace fully supplied all their needs. Angels and human beings rejoiced, and still rejoice, at their repentance, for they brought the words of the parables into actual deeds. Heaven and earth rejoice that they have returned to their Father and recovered the shares of their livelihood that had been plundered. Demons unjustly plundered humanity’s inheritance, but one man arose, pronounced judgment, and exposed them. He pronounced a just judgment against the deceitful ones and took away from them the plunder that he recovered from his Father’s house. Through Adam, the deceiver who sows error in the world led people astray. But a son of Adam became zealous and demanded redress for the disgrace of his whole race. The fervent man clothed himself in great zeal for his ancestors. He agreed to die rather than let them be called slaves of the wicked. Like an athlete, he descended into the contest on behalf of his people. He joined battle with Satan, overpowered him, and defeated him. On the summit of Golgotha he fought against the murderer and made him a laughingstock before angels and human beings. With the wooden spear he overthrew him and cast him down from his confidence. Through the very one he thought he was wronging, he suffered death and was torn apart. The arrogant one boasted about the death of human beings, but through the death of one man his boasting came to an end. One man died on the cross on behalf of mortals and taught them to walk in the way of his death and his life. People portray his death and his life in baptism. When they have died with him, they rise and are brought back to life in a mystery. They walk with him on the new way that brings the dead to life,

and on earth they imitate the conduct of heavenly beings. By eating his body they drive death from their bodies, and through his living blood they give their minds life to drink. They nourish body and soul with the food of his body and blood, and through the power of his gift they overcome Satan and death. Through the power of his gift they bathed and were cleansed of their sins, and they gained strength to fight against the passions. Those clothed in passions put on hidden strength from the water and began lightly to trample the enemy’s power. Like athletes they came up from the baptismal [?], and angels and human beings welcomed them lovingly. Earthly and heavenly beings shouted the announcement of their victory. The demons heard, trembled, and were terrified by the new sound. The heights and the depths wove crowns for them through human hands, for they saw that they had won the great battle against the mighty one. They received from the King gifts greater than their labors, and he gloriously honored them beyond their capacity. He seated them at table within the palace of his hidden mysteries and set before them a table of immortal life. He prepared a beautiful bridal chamber on earth, as a [?] of the one above, so that they might delight in it in a mystery until the end. He built himself a sanctuary so that they might hallow his holy name within it, until they are raised to the holy place hidden on high. He chose priests for himself to minister there in holiness and, in place of sacrifices, to offer the sacrifice of the mystery of his Son. They all offer the mystery of his Son according to his will, and through it they atone for the wrongdoing of those who call upon his name. He placed the silver of his word in their hands through various means, so that they might trade with it and gain spiritual life. People cast human beings as though into a furnace, and scour away from them the hateful filth of foul wrongdoing. Suddenly they gain a beautiful complexion from within the water, and the light of their minds blazes brighter than the sun. They become rays of light on earth through the light within them, and the world shines with the beautiful flames of their conduct.

They suckle the Spirit after their birth in baptism, and their nourishment, like their birth, is lofty and exalted. Like fledglings, they raise the wings of their conduct, and enter and rest in the beautiful nest of the holy Church. Like an eagle, the priest hovers over them and prepares the food of perfection for them to feed on. He prepares the living sacrifice and sets it before their eyes, and invites them to contemplate it with heartfelt love. He begins to depict the awesome mystery spiritually, and mixes words like pigments before those who watch. With the pen of his word he draws the image of the crucified King, and shows his suffering and his exaltation as though pointing with a finger. His voice proclaims death and life in the people's ears, and he distributes and gives forgiveness of wrongdoing in bread and wine. First he shows mortal humanity the mystery of death, and then reveals the power of life hidden in his words. He prepares a bier with the sacred vessels, as for a dead person, and brings up and lays down the bread and wine as though laying out the deceased. He enacts in mystery the day of the King's death, and stations the ministers in splendor in keeping with the representation. He stations two deacons in order, one on either side, to guard the mystery of the King of kings. Awe and love rest upon the movements of their minds as they contemplate the bread and wine as though contemplating the King. They are clothed in a radiant appearance that shines from within upon their faces, and through their garments they show the beauty of their minds. With their stoles they portray the sign of the messengers of peace who were clothed in beautiful garments in the chamber of the tomb. The disciples saw two angels in our Lord's tomb, honoring the place of his body as though it were his body. And if spiritual beings reverently honored the place of his body, how much more should bodily beings honor the mystery that has honored them! In the likeness of those two watchers, two deacons now stand to hover over the mysteries.

The priest serves as the mouth on behalf of every mouth, and like a mediator his voice speaks with the unseen One. He calls upon the hidden One to send him hidden power, to place in the bread and wine the power to give life. He turns the gaze of every mind toward the unseen, so that through visible things they may look upon hidden things. “Minds on high!” he cries out to those on earth, and they answer, “Toward you, Lord, who are hidden on high.” He goes on to explain the reason for looking upward and what it is that he calls people to share in. “Look,” he says, “people, at the sacrificial offering made on your behalf, which the Eternal One lovingly accepts for your lives.” “Look attentively at the bread and wine on the table, which the power of the Spirit changes into the body and blood.” “See the visible things with the outward senses of your bodies, and picture the hidden things through the inward movements of your minds.” “Remember your deaths through the sign that is full of death and life, and praise and magnify the one who gives strength through weak things.” With their voices they seal his words as with a seal: “The sacrifice of our life is fitting, right, proper, and holy.” Like a pen, he writes words with the tip of his tongue, and they add their signatures with the response, “Yes, they are true.” They bear witness to the words spoken on their behalf, and, instead of a seal, they seal the mystery of their lives with “Amen.” He writes out a document of thanksgiving through his words, and they pledge themselves: “Yes, we will pay our debt of praise.” With their voices they pay the praise set down in his writings, and he brings it before the divine will. Along with the offering, the priest raises up the people's prayer, and he sanctifies the people through participation in the living mystery. With deep feeling he prays for himself and for everyone, that his words may be an acceptable sacrifice before the Most High. As he makes supplication, he imitates the spiritual beings in his words, and in holiness he teaches people to cry, “Holy!” He repeats to the people the cry of sanctification uttered by those who dwell in peace, so that they may cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord!”

The very words that the seraphim cried three times he makes heard in the people's ears at the time of the mysteries. Like Isaiah, he too is filled with awe when he makes it heard, remembering how greatly humanity's lowliness has been exalted. The revelation that the prophet saw symbolically, he contemplates by faith in its actual fulfillment. Isaiah saw a burning coal approach him, held by a fiery seraph in a fiery hand. It approached his mouth without actually approaching it, yet it truly wiped away the iniquity of his body and soul. The seer did not see a vision perceptible to the senses, nor did the spiritual being bring a physical coal near him. In the coal he saw a symbolic revelation of the body and blood, which, like fire, destroys the iniquity of mortal humanity. The priest explains the power of that mystery which the prophet saw, and in his hand, as though with tongs, he holds fire in the bread. He takes the seraph's place for the people, as the seraph did for Isaiah, and through his actions he wipes away iniquity and gives life. The spiritual seraph did not hold in his hand a spiritual vision [?]; and this is the wonder: a hand of flesh holds the Spirit [?]. The one with swift wings could not bring the food into the belly, yet the one with a heavy body stretches out his hand even to the trembling ones. He nourishes body and soul with the food of the sacrament’s power, and turns mortal human beings into immortals. His voice abolishes death’s authority over mortals, and dissolves and removes the evil one’s dominion over them. Through food the evil one killed us in the beginning and made us slaves; and through food the Creator has now chosen to give us life. Through the hand that wickedly plucked the fruit in Eden, he wisely held out to us the fruit of life. In Adam he cursed us and gave us as food to ravenous death; and in the Son of Adam he opened for us the spring of his kindness. In our own nature he fulfilled his will and revealed his love, so that the declaration that called us his image might be confirmed for us. He granted us the ability to give a pledge of life in our mortality, so that, according to our will, we might sustain ourselves through the power of his will.

Through the power of his will, the priest distributes life in bread, drives away wickedness, and makes the Spirit dwell within our bodily members. The power of the Spirit descends to the mortal man, dwells in the bread, and sanctifies it through the greatness of his power. What a wonder! Although everything is full of him, the Spirit, he does not draw near until the man of dust gives the command. What a gift! Although it has been given from the beginning, it is not received until the son of dust makes his plea. The Spirit is beside everything and in everything, in the heights and in the depths. He is hidden, and the priest reveals him through his words. He stretches out his hands, together with his mind, toward the heights above, and invites him to descend and fulfill his soul’s request. The Spirit, who does not travel, does not descend in his nature. Power from him descends, acts, and accomplishes everything. His power overshadows the visible table and gives the bread and wine the power to bestow life. His power strengthens the priest’s hand to grasp his power, and the weak flesh is not consumed by his flame. The bodily man holds the Spirit in the bread in his hands. He lifts his gaze toward the heights and then breaks it. He breaks the bread, places it in the wine, makes the sign, and says: “In the name of the Father and the Son and the Spirit, whose nature is equal.” He completes his words in the name of the Being in three persons, and raises the sacrament as though raising a dead person, in a representation of the reality. The Lord of the sacrament truly rose from within the tomb, and without doubt the sacrament acquires the power of life. The bread and wine suddenly acquire new life, and suddenly grant forgiveness of wickedness to those who receive them. He makes the bread and wine one through their communion, just as blood is mingled with the body in all its senses. He puts wine and water into the cup before he consecrates it,

just as water is also mixed in the blood with its constituents. With these things the priest completes the sacraments of perfection, and then makes his voice heard, full of love and mercy. He concealed love and mercy in the sound of the word of his mouth, so that the creature might call the Creator its own Father. The voices of those who obey follow the course of his voice, as they prepare to call the hidden, self-existent One “Our Father.” O incomprehensible gift bestowed on humanity, which freely received a name that the world cannot encompass! Children of dust call the Maker of all “Our Father.” They ask him for holiness and the kingdom on high. May your holy name be hallowed in us, Maker of all, and may the pledge of life without end be confirmed in us. Together they ask for holiness and the help of the Spirit, for the hidden will, temporal nourishment, and forgiveness of sin. Through their petitions they show the love in their minds: how eagerly they desire to share in the things to come. With a voice of thanksgiving they conclude the words that complete the mysteries, and they ascribe holiness to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Holy is the Father, and holy are his Son and the Spirit who comes from him. Holiness and praise are due to them from every mouth. After the proclamation of holiness and the offering of praise, they direct their minds’ gaze toward the gift. With their senses and inward movements, they eagerly press forward together to approach the bread and wine, within which forgiveness of sins is hidden. Through faith they gain the power to see hidden things, and they honor the holy gift in their cupped hands as they would a king. They affirm that the King’s body dwells in the chosen bread, and through it resurrection of the dead is proclaimed to whoever eats it. He too says “The body” when he gives it to him, and he calls the mixed wine in the cup “The blood.” He gives the bread and says, “The body of Christ the King,” and gives the wine to drink, saying likewise, “The blood of Christ.” He believes that the bread and wine are the body and blood, and this is firmly established for both the giver and the receivers. With it he proclaims forgiveness of sin and resurrection of the dead. Although these are not visible, they are very clear to faith. Faith shows the soul a hidden vision

and teaches it not to doubt because of visible things. The eyes belonging to the body’s senses see bread and wine, but the soul’s inward movements see the hidden power that is mightier than all. We should look upon the mystery of our salvation through the soul’s inward movements, and set faith before our minds as our goal. Let us receive the bread and affirm that it can forgive sin. Let us drink the wine and confess that drinking it imparts life. Let us honor them as the body and blood of the King, so that they may bring us to the glorious things of the kingdom. Let us believe that they can give life to us in our mortality, and direct our minds toward the fulfillment of the hope contained in them. With our hidden mind let us look in a hidden way upon the things we see, and let us not doubt the renewal present in visible things. Let the beholder look not at the bread or the wine, but at the power that consecrates the bread and wine. Bread and wine are set before the body's eyes as a sign, so that it may share with the mind in things unseen. The body cannot see hidden things along with the mind, or contemplate concealed things as thoughts do. For its sake the gift was given through bread, so that through visible things it might gain hope for hidden things. To it and to the soul is promised the delight concealed in the mystery; and for its comfort there are the visible things of food and drink. See, it is accustomed to finding relief from its sorrow through visible things; and so that it should not grieve, its Lord comforted it with bread and wine. Through bread and wine he set before it a goal directed toward things to come, so that it might yearn for the renewal prepared for it. Come, mortals, let us yearn for the goal hidden in our mystery, and let us not abandon the expectation of the life promised to us. Come, let us take refuge in the power of his spiritual help, so that he may assist us in the struggle against animal passions. Come, let us make every effort to approach him in holiness, so that we may receive from him medicine suited to our wounds. Let us continually apply him like medicine to our senses and impulses, so that we may drive away bodily weakness and slackness of soul. He is good medicine whose potency is compounded with grace, and no illness, hidden or visible, can resist him. The physician on high compounded it and gave it to those on earth, so that with its help they might heal the ailments of their minds.
Let us all apply it in faith to our blemishes, so that from it we may obtain resurrection for the body and salvation for the soul.
On Baptism

Discourse Twenty-Two: On Baptism.
Response: Blessed is the spring that flowed over the Jordan! Adam drank, and his thirst passed away, my brothers.

Who can repay the debt owed to the maker of all, who came in his love to give humanity spiritual birth? The mouth—and the depth [?]—is too small to join us in thanking the Creator's power, which renewed our image and wiped away our wrongdoing. As in a furnace, he recast our image in baptism, and instead of our clay he made us spiritual gold. He wished to paint us spiritually, without pigments, so that the beauty of our image would no longer be ruined by mortality. O painter who paints images on a panel of water, whose artistry is not hindered by opposition! O craftsman who breathes the Spirit without hands and sows immortal life within mortality! O command, for which all difficulties are easy, which gives strength to weak things through the power of its greatness! O will, whose bidding precedes its action, which saw in its knowledge what it created before creating it! His bidding foresaw this will that he revealed toward us, and he contemplated it before creating us, at the beginning of our creation. Before it was fashioned, the image of our renewal was drawn before him; and throughout his existence it was in his heart to accomplish this.

He accomplished it with wisdom, as befits the one who knows everything; wisely he fulfilled his will and displayed his power. He made a second creation for the creation he had made in the beginning, and shook from it the old things of mortality. He wished to wipe the filth of wrongdoing from mortals, and at his command he placed the sponge of the Spirit in the hand of our body. Who can measure the purpose of his love toward our race? He made our lowliness master of his wisdom. From our very clay he made treasurers of his hidden things, and from it he appointed stewards to give life. He chose [?] for himself as mediators between himself and us, and sent them as messengers to humanity. It was to them that he gave the great seal of his divinity, so that with it they might seal the work of renewing everything. It was to them that he entrusted the wealth of the Spirit, which cannot be contained, so that they might distribute it lovingly, in keeping with its greatness. He taught them a spiritual art, so that they might draw the image of life on the surface of the water. O bodily beings who portray the Spirit without hands! O mortals who [?] life in mortality! O priesthood, how far you have been raised above everything! You have taken hold of the reins in the heights and the depths through the power of the one who chose you. O wonder, whose marvel is too great to recount: mortality gives itself life as though by its own power! O will that lowered itself to its creatures and placed its wealth in the hand of flesh, so that flesh might enrich itself! O Creator, who came and [?] his creative power, and placed a drawing reed in the hand of his handiwork, so that it might draw for itself! Who would not marvel at the greatness of the love of his kindness? He made our clay a creator of creation, in his own likeness. Who would not give thanks for his care toward our race? He raised our lowliness alongside his incomprehensible being. To our very nature he gave authority, together with its renewal, to create for itself a new creation of beings who do not die. He breathed the power of life into our body, which produces suffering, and it began to interpret spiritual things that it cannot see. He showed our soul the art of his creative power, and it acquired the power to create a creation like the Creator.

Through the word that comes from him, it forms human beings in the bosom of the water and fashions them spiritually, without hands. This is a means whose explanation is beyond recounting; the hidden will can recount it as it truly is. Through purity of soul, the mind can contemplate it, and with understanding rather than eyes it sees its majesty. Its subject is sublime and cannot be expressed in bodily terms; its investigation is exalted and cannot be grasped in an earthly way. The account of the renewal of our image is spiritually composed, and only through the Spirit can the mouth explain its matters. In a heavenly way he compounds medicine for the pain of our wrongdoing; unless the mind rises to the heights, it cannot see it. For the Master of teachers, salvation is prepared [?] as the subject of our lives’ study; unless the learner follows his example, he does not understand. Come, disciples of the great Christ, let us look carefully at the spiritual writings concerning baptism. Come, heirs of the covenant written in blood; see the channels of your benefits with the eye of the spirit. Come, contemplate your channels with loving devotion, and praise and exalt the one who enriches humanity from his treasures. Come together, pure children of baptism; let us picture the voice that cries out in the waters, and they receive power. Come, let us examine discerningly the hand of flesh that buries bodies and swiftly raises them to life. Let us prepare ourselves to see a wonder in the temple of holiness [?], and the heavenly powers attending the mystery of our salvation. Now is the time that demands orderly conduct from those watching. Let everyone fix the gaze of his mind on what is being said. See, the priest prepares to enter the Holy of Holies, to open the door of the heavenly kingdom before those who are entering. See, he approaches the door of the royal palace to receive power to accomplish the mysteries that take place through his hands. See, the heavenly King stretches out to him the hand of the Spirit and places in his hand the seal of his name, so that he may seal his sheep. See, he clothes [?] him in the glorious robe of the immortals,

so that with it he may cover the shame of human beings who sinned and were exposed. See, he has arrived to attend to the flock entrusted to him; he raises his voice and calls his sheep by their names. See, the sheep, lambs, and ewes gather, and he places upon them the life-giving seal of his Lord’s word. See, through their own words he brings them as though into a furnace, and requires from them a single confession of the Creator’s name. The divine command holds him spiritually like a pen, and he registers and inscribes body and soul in the book of life. As with a rod, he drives away from them, by the word of his mouth, the darkness of error that blinded them to understanding. He raises his voice and says, “Renounce the evil one and his power, his angels, his service, and his error.” First they renounce the dominion of the evil one who enslaved them, and then they acknowledge the power of the Creator who set them free. The one who approaches the Church’s mysteries declares two things: renunciation of the evil one and faith in the Maker. “I renounce the evil one and his angels,” he cries aloud, “and I have no fellowship with him, not even in speech.” The priest stands as a mediator and asks him, “Whose servant do you wish to be from now on?” He learns from him whom he wishes to call Lord, and then enrolls him among the firstborn in heaven. He turns his face away from Satan and his angels, and then traces the image of the divine Being on his forehead. He renounces the Evil One as an evil being whose dealings are evil, and his angels as enemies of the word of truth. The Evil One and his followers hate the word of truth, and whoever loves truth ought to hate them. Let him repeat with the son of Jesse, “I have hated those who hate you, Lord,” and ask him to avenge the insults against the Creator’s name. Whoever approaches baptism has a battle to fight against Satan, his angels, and his service. His angels are people clothed in falsehood, who serve him through abominable practices full of wickedness. One of his angels is Mani, the deceitful wolf, who dresses like the lambs of the flock and leads the flock astray.

Another of his angels is Valentinus, who denies the truth and, through his denial, conceals the resurrection of the dead. Arius, whose thinking is depraved, is also his angel. He is afflicted with the disease of inequality, which is worse than a lion. Eunomius, the cunning serpent, is also his angel. With his bites he destroys the souls of those who listen to him. Among his angels is the foolish Apollinaris, who builds falsehood into the structure of truth without concealing it. Among his angels is Paul, whose thinking is perverse, who fires his sling against the power of the Father’s Word. Let us also count Eutyches among his angels, the madman who went mad in his love of attributing suffering to the one who cannot suffer. The peddler learned the craft of adulteration: he mixes, for everyone, the living nature with the sufferings of the body. The enormity of his wickedness far exceeds the wickedness of his associates, and he helps the Accuser much more than his companions do.

Through these people the enemy of humanity leads human beings astray, and through them he pours the gall of his deceit into people’s minds. They teach the forms of service involving abominable practices, and also expand it with deceitful inventions. The service in which they take pride is his service, and the mysteries spoken of in it are his, not those of truth. The heretics make a stir for him in every form, and through his cunning they go astray and lead others astray with their madness. We ought, therefore, to flee from them as from unclean people, and not become involved in their abominable deeds. Let us call them and the Evil One unclean and wicked, and turn our faces away from their mysteries, which are full of wickedness. The invention of the Evil One and his followers is full of wickedness, and the diseases of wrongdoing are hidden in it, in the deceptions of his craft. His inventions are the circus, the stadium, and the theater, and the tumultuous sounds of the [?] that he composed and wrote. His deceptions are omens and divinations of every kind: twitching eyes, ringing ears, and encounters along the road. The disciple of truth renounces these things when he becomes a disciple, and then approaches the confession of faith. He reveals the sincerity of his soul in an audible voice: “Look, I have moved away from the evil one to the Creator.” He puts the demons to shame by the sound of the words from his mouth: “Listen, rebels! I have no fellowship with you.” He gladdens the assemblies on high with the declarations of his faith: “Come, spiritual beings, rejoice with me, for I have escaped destruction. Your companion I am, and a fellow worker in your activities. I long to serve that Lord whom you serve.” The wanderer who has returned to take refuge in the King of kings calls himself a fellow servant in the kingdom on high. First he appeals to the stewards of the holy Church,

asking them to bring him to the King's gate so that he may speak his words. The stewards are the priests, the ministers of the mysteries, who have the treasury of the Spirit to administer. The wanderer, a child of exile, approaches one of them, asking them to free him from enslavement to the evil one who took him captive. Like an exile, he stands naked, without a covering, and shows him his suffering and hardship among his captors. “In your protection, O King!” the captive cries to the King's servants. “Approach the King and plead on my behalf, so that he may look favorably on me. “Go in and tell him, ‘One of your servants has returned from captivity, and now he begs to see your face in love.’ “I am utterly captive to the servant who has rebelled against your lordship. Free my life from his bondage, so that he may not overpower me. “I am your servant, good Lord, and the son of your maidservant. Why am I serving the evil servant who is hostile to you? “For a long time I have wickedly served him who is wholly wicked. Rescue me from him, so that I may be yours, for yours I am.” The wanderer puts these words together on the day of his return, following the pattern of that story of the younger son. For his sake the parables were enacted in deeds, and it was fitting for him to speak his words as they are written. He is the one of whom it is written that he wandered away and departed, then returned and came back. The day of his departure and his repentance is recorded in the Gospel. On this day what is written truly comes to pass, and abundant mercies go out to meet him and welcome him. The heavenly hosts await his repentance and honor him as one who was dead and has returned to life. The devil alone grieves over his return, because he has escaped his snares, broken his traps, abandoned him, and fled. The sinner has fled from the bondage of his bitterness and taken refuge in the good Lord, whose love is sweet. The exile has returned from his exile to his Maker, and now he begs to enter and see the King's face. Through his petition he brings a case against his captor and accuses him on the basis of the divine law. He gives the King's servants the pen of the words from his mouth, and they write and present it before the Judge.

He asks the priests for an advocate ready to face the judgment, and they plead his case while he remains silent. The priest stands as though in court at the time of the mysteries, and brings charges against the Accuser on behalf of sinners. The sinner too stands like a poor man who has been wronged, asking and pleading for mercy to help him at the judgment. He stands naked and stripped before the judge, so that his humiliation may move mercy to cover him. Without a covering he pleads his case against his accuser, so that the king may see him and quickly take up his case. He bends his knees and lowers his head in shame, for he is ashamed to look upward toward the judge. He lowers his [?] and approaches sorrowfully to ask for mercy, remembering his slavery to the Evil One. In kneeling at the time of the mysteries, he depicts two things: his fall, and the payment he makes as a debtor. He now recalls that fall in Paradise and pleads his case against Satan, who led his father astray. He is afraid of him; that is why his face is turned toward the ground, until he hears the voice of forgiveness and then takes courage. He waits for the priest to bring his words before the judge and return to him a deed of freedom through oil and water. He also brings a guarantor with him to the court of law, to enter and testify to the readiness of his soul's love. With heartfelt love he gives assurance that he will remain in love of the truth, and his companion guarantees that the testing of his soul is indeed trustworthy. He becomes a guide for his words and deeds, and shows him how to conduct a spiritual life. He calls him by name and presents him before the guardians, so that they may name him an heir, a son, and a member of the kingdom. The priest asks for the lost one's name in writing, and brings it in and places it in the archives of the king's scribes. He stations him like a sheep at the entrance to the sheepfold, marks his body, and joins him to the flock. He holds the sign of oil in his hand before those watching, and openly proclaims the power of wonders.

As through a symbol, he shows the eyes of the bodily senses the hidden power concealed in the visible sign. O dust that marks the sheep with its Lord's mark, and seals them in his hidden name with a visible sign! O earthly being who holds the Spirit on the tip of his tongue, and cuts away the wrongdoing of soul and body with the word of his mouth! O mortal in whose mouth a great spring has been established, who gives immortal life to his fellow human beings to drink! O poor man, son of poor parents, who suddenly became rich and began distributing riches of the Spirit that his fathers did not possess! O earthly being whose dust bears witness to his lowliness, who has received power to create a new creation himself! The Good One taught the members of his household a new creation, so that they might renew the handiwork of his creative power. Human wickedness tore down the lofty work of his hands, and he gave human beings authority to build it again. He saw his handiwork grown old and worn out through mortality, and devised for it a means of immortal life. He saw that the foundations of his house were shaking because of its susceptibility to suffering, and he laid its foundations in the depths of the water and made them firm. Through yielding water he wished to make frail bodies firm, and through the Spirit’s power to strengthen wavering impulses. His command mystically prepared a furnace of water, and instead of fire he heated it with the Spirit, through the power of his will. He made the creature itself a craftsman responsible for its own restoration, so that it might cast itself in the furnace of water and the heat of the Spirit. Come, see the wonder in mortality: it dies and comes to life through the working of this wonder. Come, let us contemplate the mystery of our death within the water, and see the marvel that is mystically performed in us. Come, let us approach the keepers of the Church’s treasures and hear from them how they give life through water. Let us enter with them into the mystical Holy of Holies and learn from them the meaning of the mysteries of death and life. Death and life are the mysteries of baptism, and both are accomplished together in it through one priesthood. Through the priesthood the Creator wished to reveal his power:

And to it he entrusted the great wealth of his kindness. He appointed priests as stewards over his channels, so that, as faithful servants, they might distribute wealth to the members of his household. He gave them the seal of the name of his incomprehensible Being, so that they might seal human beings with the holy name. Everyone places the stamp of his name upon his flock, and human beings mark [?] other human beings threefold. The priest holds the iron of oil on his fingertips, and with its sharpness marks the body and the senses of the soul. A mortal polishes the oil with the words of his mouth and sharpens it like iron to cut away wickedness. He recites three names in order, one after another, and threefold he completes and perfects the mystery of our salvation. O weak one, how great is the marvel performed through you! The mouth is too small to tell how mighty its manifestation is. O earthly one, how high your limited nature has been raised! The mind cannot ascend with you to where you have reached. O human being—it is to the priest that I have said these things—how great is the authority you have received, that you can give life! The priest gives life to his companions through his ministry and opens a road for his fellows toward the things to come. Serving as a mouth, he speaks for the impulses and the limbs, and on everyone’s behalf he utters words of forgiveness of wickedness. He first sets out oil and water as foundations, and through his utterances the name of the divine Being completes and builds. With liquid oil and weak water he casts the body, and transforms it from dust into pure gold. [?] would not marvel at the power our poverty has acquired, enriching itself from the gift beyond comprehension? Like a treasurer, the priest stands at the door of the sanctuary. He inserts the keys—the words of his mouth—and opens up life. He places three names upon the oil and consecrates it, so that through its holiness it may sanctify human uncleanness. In the name of the hidden One he marks the visible body, and the penetrating power of the name enters as far as the soul. Oh, the wonder that a human being performs through what is not his own! He marks bodies [?], and what is within feels it.

He too attends to the bodily members like a physician: he touches what is outside and detects the suffering of the inward parts [?]. He applies the remedies of his craft to the body and the soul [?], and by divine power heals both the visible and the hidden. He divinely prepares the medicine entrusted to his hands. Through its power he heals every ailment, and it is not diminished. He has opened the doorway of the holy temple as his shop. He attends to illnesses and binds up the wounds of his fellow human beings. With the outward mark he touches the hidden wounds within. He bends down and applies the medicine of the Spirit through the sign of water. With an audible voice he proclaims the power of his hidden mysteries, and with his tongue he distributes spiritual wealth. He makes words sound in the ears of the flock as he marks it, and it listens with love as the three names are proclaimed. He concludes his words with the name of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, and confirms the one being baptized in their names. He traces the three names on his face like a shield, so that the tyrant may see the image of the divine Being upon the human being’s head. The purpose of the mark upon the forehead is to put the demons to shame, so that when they look at the human being’s head, they may shrink back from him. Because of them, the mysteries of oil and water take place, to serve as armor against the onslaught of their attacks. The oil with which earthly beings are anointed is armor, so that they may not be seized by spiritual beings in the hidden battle. It is the great seal of the King of kings with which they are sealed, so that they may contend in the spiritual arena. They receive a spiritual seal upon their foreheads, so that it may shine before the eyes of angels and human beings. Like eager workers they stand at the King’s gate, with the priest at their head, like an army commander at the head of his flock. At the time of the mysteries he arranges their ranks as for battle, so that they may shoot sharp arrows at the enemy. He fits together arrows of words and places them in their mouths, so that they may strike terror into the evil one who enslaved them. He sets a target before their eyes so that they may practice upon it, and stretches words upon their tongues as upon a bowstring. They enter a trial at the beginning of the battle to which they have been summoned, as they are examined through the confession of their thoughts.

The priest truly stands at the head of their ranks and shows them the target of truth, so that they may aim well. They renounce [?] the evil one, his power, and his angels; then he draws the King's sign on their foreheads. They renounce and confess, doing both together without division: renouncing the evil one and confessing from the heart in the name of the divine Being. Through the priesthood they establish a covenant with the divine Being, promising that they will no longer turn back to Satan through their deeds. They give [?] a spoken pledge of their intentions, and he brings them in and calls them [?] the divine will. He holds [?] the kingdom's register in his hands, and he has authority to enroll people through the palace. He calls the King's servants by their names and has them stand. He brings them forward one by one and impresses the seal of oil on each one's face. With his spoken declarations he proclaims the power hidden in his words: whose they are, and whose name it is with which they are sealed. “So-and-so,” he says, “is a servant of the King of kings above and below, and he is sealed in his name so that he may serve according to his will.” In his hands he mingles the name of the divine Being with the oil, and he makes the sign, saying, “The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” “So-and-so is marked,” he says, “with the three equal names,” between which there is no distinction of greater and lesser. The priest does not say, “I mark him,” but, “He is marked,” because the seal he applies is not his own but his Lord's. He is a mediator whom grace has chosen to minister; although the power is not his own, he drives away evil and gives the Spirit. Through the visible oil he shows the power present in the names, which can invisibly strengthen human weakness. He repeats the three names while applying oil over the whole person, so that tyrannical demons and persistent passions may not harm him. It is not the oil that protects a person from harm; it is the power of the divine Being that [?] gives strength to weakness. The oil is a sign proclaiming divine power, and through the invocations it secretly strengthens the servant. Through his power, body and soul gain strength and no longer fear the harms of mortality.

Like athletes, they go down and take their stand in the stadium, and they engage in combat with the feeble, degrading impulses within them. The oil of anointing imparts this strength—not the oil itself, but the Spirit who empowers it. The Spirit empowers the anointing with soft oil, and it becomes vigorous through the rite performed with it. Through its vigor it strengthens the body and the impulses of the soul, and they courageously engage in contests against the evil one. The demons see the mark of his name on the person and tremble before him, because in his name they see the glorious name. The name of the divine Being looks out from the mark on the forehead, and the eyes of the deceitful ones are ashamed to look at it. A second sun has risen from on high over the person's head, and with its rays it drives away the errors of a second darkness. Come, human being, praise and exalt the one who honored you, who through his gift made your body a second sun. Come, debtor, repay your liberator with thanksgiving, for he redeemed you and freed you from slavery to the evil one and death. Come, mortal, give praise to the power of the divine Being, who placed your strength within you so that you might sow life in mortality. Sing with every mouth, race of earthly Adam, to the one who raised you from the dust to his greatness.
[?] on the holy Sunday of the Resurrection.

Another by him, likewise his own. Discourse thirty-one. It is recited on the holy Sunday of the Resurrection. Response: Blessed is Christ, who on the day of his resurrection won victory for our nature and condemned the tyrant. My brothers!

The King on high put on an earthly appearance to bring humanity’s captive soul out of the strong man’s grasp. His will came forth in human form and shone upon humanity. The evil one saw him but did not recognize him because of the power of his hiddenness. The Creator took the form of a servant to set everyone free. He [?] his glory beneath the clothing of mortality. He chose a commander from the very race held captive by the evil one and armed him with a spear, so that he might go out and redeem his own people. He gave him divine armor with which to fight, so that when he triumphed he might gain the title of victor through its power. The bodily commander put on the King’s armor and placed the helmet of life-saving deliverance upon the head of his mind. He put on the armor spiritually, in keeping with its hidden nature, and girded his soul rather than his limbs for battle. The bodily one armed himself with the movements [?] of the soul, for he saw in the spirit that his adversary was spiritual. In the spirit he fought the spiritual being, the ruler of the air, so that his earthly limbs would not hinder him. In body and soul he bore the armor the King had given him. He put it on with love, in the senses of the body and the [?] of the soul. The mortal fought a hidden battle through hidden power. He won victory for body and soul and set them free. His race had been held captive by the evil one and by death, the rebellious tyrant.

He had given himself to the battle on behalf of his people. He went out into the wilderness to battle the evil one and defeated him. Then he prepared himself for battle with ravenous death. He engaged the strong man in combat over the craving for bread. He bound him and threw him down through endurance arising from [?]. The spiritual being was defeated by the bodily one through the Spirit’s power. The body, which sufferings had trampled, overcame the ruler of the air.
