The despised body [?] rejoiced and laughed at the strong man, and [?] took away his armor so that he would no longer fight against mortals. “Go away, evil one, to your partner,” he said to him. “Go and prepare other armor for yourself, on account of death.” Go, prepare death’s snares for yourself by means of mortals, for on your own your strength is too weak for the battle. Go, gather the children you have begotten through cunning, and arm them with slander, as you are accustomed to do. Call your companions in falsehood to help you, for you are a liar, and through lies you [?] conquer. With a word he released the crafty one from battle for a time, so that he might go and devise a deadly scheme under the guise of a lawsuit. He knew how to plead his case according to the law, and he sought to win by recalling former events. He recalled the transgression of the commandment in Paradise, and took refuge in that offense as though it were testimony. He took courage from the desire for the fruit, as from a guarantor, for it had guaranteed him the enslavement of humanity [?]. He held up to him the signatures of Adam and Eve: “Look, your ancestors signed and agreed. Read and understand. Adam wrote me a bond in Eden when he became indebted to sin, and because he did not repay it, he pledged his children in place of interest. From the beginning I acquired authority over mortals. It was not in secret that they signed and submitted to slavery as debtors. Your race became my captive not through force but through debt. They willingly agreed to become slaves. It was not Adam and the people of his generation alone who became indebted to me, for the whole human race is included in the bond of mortality. And if you are made of dust and share in the sufferings of the body, look at your nature and know that you are included in the bond [?] of my dominion. There is no bodily being possessing limbs who is not mortal; and if he is mortal, he is subject to slavery to me and to Death. Or show me that you are not mortal, and I will leave you alone. But if you are mortal, your nature settles the dispute raised by your words. Show the document the king gave you declaring that you are not mortal—though I do not accept even this for someone made of dust. You are a bodily being. Why are words needed in court? The body’s [?] is entirely the corruption of mortality.” These were the things the devil was thinking as he employed evasive arguments against the body. He held on to mortality as though it were a defensive barrier, thinking that through it he would defeat him, as Death does. The hateful one secretly said these things within his thoughts, but the searcher of hearts saw them as though they were out in the open. And because he saw the evil one’s meditation with his hidden eye, he exposed the ugliness of the evil schemer to the observers. He spoke the hidden things openly and aloud: “Look, the devil has come to plead his case. Look, the ruler and master of the world demands of me

that I pay the dues of mortality like other mortals. Under the guise of a lawsuit he spoke against me as against a human being: ‘You are a human being; pay like someone found liable by the court.’ With evasive arguments he disputed with me too, as he did with Adam: ‘You are descended from Adam, a root swept away by the river of my cunning.’” Why are you proud of the words that have come to you? Do not boast about what is not yours, for you are dust. The enemy of our race looks upon my nature as something lowly, and he does not [?] the power that clothed me from the womb. The revelation of my descent to humanity is hidden from him, and he does not know the creation that came into being through my hands. I too silently conceal my greatness from him until he fulfills his treacherous desire through the death he brings upon me. Now, in judgment, I reveal hidden things to him: that he unjustly [?] against mortal humanity. If mortals are indebted to him because they sinned, who can bring a case against me, since I am free from blemishes? And if Adam incurred a debt and was held in pledge because he listened to his advice, who can wage war against me, whom he has not overcome even by a gesture? It is clear, then, that the enemy rules unjustly by force, and does not justly wield his scepter over mortals. Although it is quite clear that I am free from his bondage, I willingly accept the death brought about by his deceit. He threatens me with death and frightens me like death, but through death I overthrow him from his dominion. He wages war against me with the weapon of mortal sufferings; through my own suffering I teach him that his power is weak. By the very thing through which he thought Adam and his sons were held in pledge, I erase his deed of ownership over mortals. With death he sealed the record of the human race’s debts, and through death upon the wood I tear it apart. Before spiritual and bodily beings I annul the sentence in which he boasts as though victorious. I show heavenly and earthly beings the salvation that brings life and the renewal accomplished in me. I call heaven and earth as my chosen witnesses, and with the hidden name I seal the promise of my words. Speaking and speechless beings, be mediators between me and the evil one, for without a judgment the enemy incites ravenous death. And if he acts unjustly, thirsts for injustice, and is eager for blood, [?] justly, rebuke his injustice, and expose his deceit. Look, I accept his unjust sentence, and I show that death has not overcome me by force. Look, I descend into the depths of Sheol as into the sea, and readily proclaim the news of my victory. Look, I fulfill the types and mysteries that the righteous depicted, and I pay Jonah his reward, for he died for my sake. Through deeds I reveal that descent: he went down and came up and symbolically proclaimed my victory. As a symbol, the fish swallowed Jonah without his dying; in reality, death swallows me but does not cause me to decay. Let the gatekeepers of Sheol now raise the gate before me, so that I may enter and bring Adam’s captive people out from the mighty one. I will go down with the blood of the new covenant, my own blood, and free the prisoners whom death has confined in the pit of Sheol. With my blood I write and seal humanity’s salvation.

For death is the witness that confirms the covenant. On the wood of the cross I write it with my own blood, and I erase the record of the debts they incurred through sin. The giver of life to all descended and plunged into Sheol, the dead sea. The power of his descent [?] the dead waters. With the breath of life he stirred those who had no sensation, and thousands of the dead began journeying to the assembly of the living. With silent movements the mighty one cried out against greedy Death, and anguish seized Death at the new report of the return of the dead. “Give me the [?] of Adam’s children that the evil one gave you. Enough of subjecting my freeborn children to your harsh yoke!” Death the tyrant trembled and was terrified at the sound of his words, and reluctantly brought out the captive people [?]. The prisoners came out of the lifeless pit and proclaimed the hope of the resurrection of the dead to those without hope. The dead brought new tidings to the living who were dead, but the living rejected the new message spoken by the dead. There were messengers among the [?], who [?] the dead alive, and he made everyone hear the news of the voice of salvation. At the voice of the departed, those dead in wickedness were comforted, as they saw the renewal of the body and the [?] of the soul. The dead were telling the [?] about the new thing that had happened: how death had conquered Death and raised the dead. A great wonder was being spoken of in the land of Judah, as a dead person met a living person who knew him. It was not those who had died long ago who came to life through the cross, so everyone recognized his brother and his relatives. For he did not raise people from the distant generations of old, lest the eye of flesh prove false in its testimony to the truth. From the very generation of those living this earthly life, he raised some to be witnesses to his proclamation. O mighty one, who descended to Sheol by the road everyone travels, and blocked the road along which people journey to the abode of the dead! O buried one, whom Death swallowed but who did not decay! O embodied one, whose bodily structure did not come apart! O athlete, who wrestled with the mighty one, made him think he had fallen, then turned, threw him down, and raised his own race! As he willed, he fell in body and soul like the guilty. Then he arose and returned to life, raised the body, and freed the soul. On this condition he wrestled with the mighty one: that through his victory he would free his race from slavery. By his death, the giver of life to all conquered the conqueror of all. By the very means through which Death thought humanity stood condemned, Death was brought low. Through death, Adam and his children wrote him a deed of slavery. [?] And through death, Adam freed Adam and his children. The second Adam died a mortal death for Adam. The son of Adam arose and gave life to Adam and his descendants. The embodied one, who was held together by the sinews of the spirit, died. He arose and returned to life through the power of the craftsman who dismantled him and rebuilt him. At the resurrection of his body, those on earth and those in heaven rejoiced, and he gladdened those who had mourned because of his death. The spiritual beings rejoiced because by his death he had conquered ravenous death. They descended and bore his body into the tomb in triumph, like a victor. His body had become a royal palace for the heavenly beings, and they sang a song of victory to the one who conquered death. They cried out praise to him as he rose from within the tomb:

“Blessed is he who by his death killed death, which had destroyed humanity!” They had mourned deeply over his [?], as over a king, but on the day of his resurrection he clothed them in splendid colors. He displayed the heavenly beings in white, to teach them about the renewal brought about by his hands. The watchers showed those on earth a wondrous sight: the splendid clothing that bodies will wear on the day of resurrection. Through the splendor of their clothing he instructed them, sowing the message of salvation in their ears with a sign of peace. “Why do you seek the living one among the dead?” they said to the women. “You will live, for he has risen, come back to life, and conquered death.” At a hidden command they rolled the stone away from the entrance of the tomb. They opened the door before the women's eyes, and the women entered and saw. Why, then, did the watchers remove the stone that had been sealed? Was it difficult for him [?] death, to lift the stone? Look: he accomplished the resurrection, which was exceedingly difficult, with a command. How, then, did he not lift the stone, which was easy? His body escaped from the mouth of death, that terrifying lion, yet he summoned spiritual beings to lift an insignificant stone. It was not difficult for that command which raised his body to lift the stone from the doorway so that he could come out. He removed the stone for the sake of bodily eyes, so that they might see the tomb and the body's burial cloths and gain hope. To reassure people, he opened the tomb before those who looked on, so that they would not doubt his resurrection and wonder whether he had not risen. That he rose is certain, and this is far more [?] than the sun. The spread of his proclamation to the four quarters bears witness. Although his resurrection is plainly revealed to everyone through his deeds, it is not certain to those who are sluggish in heart and blind in soul. Here is evidence of his great power, showing that he rose and came back to life: he abolished my errors and loosened the bonds of mortality. He rose on the third day so that the promise of his words would not prove false, and he fulfilled the mystery that the son of Amittai depicted in the belly of the great fish. The prophet spent three days in the depths as a symbolic foreshadowing, and he fulfilled that foreshadowing through actual deeds over three days. In Jonah there was a symbolic foreshadowing: he died without dying and remained alive. Here there was the actual deed: he truly died, yet did not decay. The son of Amittai emerged unharmed from the sea, just as he had descended, and depicted a demonstration of death, life, and the conversion of the nations. With this stipulation, the divine command sent him after the nations, to depict a symbolic foreshadowing of what took place at the end of the ages. So too the firstfruits, who stood in place of all, died for the sake of all. He rose, came back to life, and proclaimed life to the people and the nations. He came out of the tomb [?] and left his garments as witnesses that he had now taken off mortality and put on glory. In his wisdom, he made two things known through the garments he left: that he no longer needed them, and that they would serve as witnesses against those who denied him. The impurity of Jacob’s descendants was plain to him: they would cover the place where his garments lay with the waters of slander. Through the garments he left, he exposed the deceit of their thoughts: how could those who stole his body have left the garments in the tomb? His body had been embalmed with myrrh and aloes and carefully laid to rest. It would have been easy for those carrying him to move him in his garments. But if they stole him like fugitives gripped by fear, how did they unwrap him and fold the garments so calmly? Foul envy blinded the slanderers.

They did not consider the clear light of his body’s resurrection. They wished to cover his proclamation [?] with a garment of silver, but he tore apart the garment that deceit had woven, and its weavers [?]. With silver they bought from Judas the work of death, and after he rose, they denied his resurrection through deceitful silver. What can deceitful silver do against the manifest truth, when it speaks like a herald through the mouths of silent things? Stones and tombs, [?] the curtain, cried out to those who could speak: “Rise, you who are sunk down, and receive the good news of the resurrection of the dead!” And if silent, mouthless things proclaimed his victory, then the deceit of silver is futile and cannot be believed. Those who could speak and those who were mute became his witnesses against those who denied him, and set their hands to the testament of his death and life. The skilled scribe, mighty in spirit, recorded the victory. He gave proof through the curtain, which he split in two. He showed that he had abandoned the temple’s sacrifice for the people’s atonement, and no longer wished through blood [?] to reveal [?] for humanity’s reconciliation. Through the curtain he revealed his threat against the insolent: if a silent thing suffered a blow, how much more should those who speak fall silent! Human understanding deserved the scourge of wrath, but he raised the rod and struck the linen curtain instead of the mind. Within his mercy he restrained the sword that his judgment had decreed. He raised his hand to bring down his rod, but his love held him back. I do not seek vengeance for his death as against guilty men, for it was not fitting for the giver of life to humanity to destroy human beings. He said, “I have come for the life of human beings, not for their destruction,” and he confirmed his words through his deeds. He died for everyone and gave life to all, as he had promised. He fulfilled and completed his work on behalf of all. The second Adam died in his nature as mortals do. He raised mortality up with himself and gave it life through his own life. He gave over the structure of his bodily temple, which the wicked destroyed, and the Father’s Word rebuilt and completed it according to his promise. He descended in a nature subject to suffering and plunged into Sheol. He brought up with him a catch of human beings into new life. He broke open the pit that Death had built before the dead and opened a path for mortality toward life. He raised his voice like a commander before his soldiers: “Rise and take courage, for I have conquered Death and the Evil One. “I engaged in a hidden battle in a visible body. I defeated the mighty one in the contest and plundered his wealth.” I argued a just case against him before the judge, and then I secured his condemnation because he had unjustly taken our race captive. He brought out an unjust document and displayed it before the laws, though it had not been sealed with the signatures of trustworthy witnesses. When the falsehood concealed in his words was exposed, the king rebuked him and ordered him to be sent into exile. Now that I have won and the mighty enemy of our race has been condemned, I also give my companions a share in the greatness of my victory. Mortals, the Spirit has given me the power of life. With it I arm the nature capable of suffering against sufferings. Look, spiritual armor [?] has been forged for those who are flesh. Put it on, mortals, fight, and win a spiritual victory. Under death’s sentence [?] you were condemned and brought low. Come, receive the record of your debts without payment, and gain life. By my own death I trampled down the deadly one who destroyed human beings.

Through my victory the evil one of the air was condemned and exposed. O victory that conquered tyrants while being conquered! O downfall of the bodily one who fell and raised others up! The mortal one fell—the temple of flesh built by the Spirit—and the will of the angel who had dwelt in it rebuilt it anew. Who was it who fell under death, you friends of death? Who was it who paid the record of debts as though he were a debtor? For who was the mortal [?] who died by nature and truly rose? Whose resurrection was it that even the silent became its heralds? Reveal, then, the aim of your thoughts, so that we may [?] in response to it. Whom do you wish to call the [?] who conquered death? To which nature did both suffering and victory belong? Reveal this and explain it to us, you investigators of truths. If the Word, the Father’s offspring, suffered in his own nature, then our nature did not suffer with him in his death. And if our despised nature did not die and also rise again, then the hope of the resurrection of the dead is false and empty. If death swallowed the nature incapable of suffering, how, then, did he suffer—in his own nature or in ours? If he tasted suffering in his own nature, this is impiety. Did he suffer in his entirety, or did he suffer and undergo trial only in part? Indeed, there is nothing, whether incapable or capable of suffering, that suffers in one part while another part continues without end. If the Only Begotten fell under death in his own nature, then he abolished the immortality belonging to the name of divine Being. And if he fell as you say, and not as we do, who raised him from his fall and gave him life? For him to raise his own fallen self is difficult; and if another raises him, he is needy and deficient. If the Spirit and the power of the Father remedied his fall [?], then it has become evident that he is far beneath divine Being. And if he is inferior to divine Being—it was not I who said it—why do we contend with Arius as an outsider? This is why the church drove him outside its gates: he belittles the Son and places him beneath the one who begot him. And if this is so—that it is wrong to speak this way—weave a crown for the interpreter who translated well. It was to you that I said, “Do this”; we cannot. A great chasm between us and them cannot be crossed. We do not consent [?] to the heretics’ torn garment, nor do we pour good wine into the wineskins of error. We do not give the pure holiness of our faith to barking dogs who do not understand the power of the divine being. Why should we [?] the pearl of our soul’s confession before minds that love dung like animals? We do not walk the road of confusion with those who go astray, nor do we travel the false path of susceptibility to suffering. We do not bring the One exalted above all down to humiliation, nor do we put to death that Life which gives life. It is the evil one who fell into Sheol, the abyss beneath death, through the mortal who died in his own nature to abolish death. Death was striking the vessel fashioned from dust, and the Teacher of all fashioned it anew in a spiritual way. He is the one who dwelt among the dead for three days; he rose on the third day and raised our race. Blind envy blinded the slanderers,

and they did not look at the clear light of his body’s resurrection. They wanted to [?] his proclamation with a garment of silver, but he tore apart the garment that deceit and its weavers had woven. For silver Judas sold him into slavery to death, and after he rose, they denied his resurrection with deceitful silver. What can worthless silver do against manifest truth, when it [?] like a herald through the mouths of the silent? Stones, tombs, and door curtains cried out to those endowed with speech: “Rise, you who have sunk down, and receive the news that the dead have come to life!” And if the silent and the mouthless cried out his victory, then silver’s deceit is futile and is not believed. Those endowed with speech, [?], became his witnesses against the deniers, and set their hands to the testament of his death and his life. The Spirit’s skilled and mighty scribe, who [?] victory, gave a sign in the door curtain that he split in two. And he showed that he had abandoned the temple of sacrifice for the people’s atonement, and no longer desired [?] blood to reconcile human beings. In the door curtain he revealed his threat against minds: if he confounded a silent thing and it was silenced, how much more those who speak! The discerning mind deserved the stroke of wrath, but he raised the rod and struck the garment instead of the mind. He held back the sword of his judgment within his mercy. He raised his hand for his rod to descend, but his love restrained it. I do not seek vengeance for his death as the guilty do, for it was not [?] for the [?] of human beings to destroy human beings. He said, “I came for human beings to live, not for their destruction,” and he confirmed his words through his deeds. He died for all and gave life to all, as he had [?], and he fulfilled and completed the deeds of the Almighty. The second Adam died in his nature, as mortals do, and raised mortality up with him and gave it life through his life. He gave structure to bodily matter, which the evil ones had torn down; the Father's Word perfected and rebuilt it according to his promise. He descended in a nature subject to suffering and plunged into Sheol, and brought up with him a catch of human beings to new life. He breached the wall of death before the dead and opened a road for mortality toward life. He raised his voice like the master of an estate before his workers: “Rise and take courage, for I have conquered death and the Evil One. I fought a hidden battle in a visible body; I defeated the mighty one in combat and plundered his wealth. “I argued a just case against him before the judge, and then condemned him because he had unjustly taken our race captive. “He brought out a fraudulent document and displayed it before the law; it had not been sealed with the signatures of witnesses [?].” He is the one who descended to the lowest regions of earthly beings, and he is the one who ascended above everything to raise everything up. The insolent drove nails and a spear into the frame of his body, and by renewing it he erased the record of bodily sufferings. He descended upon the lion in its lair with the armor of the Spirit, and rescued the flock of Adam's race that was being torn apart. He shouted in Sheol like a mighty warrior and shook its foundations. He broke its gates, cut through its bars, and brought out its plunder. The gates raised their fronts as he came out, and the heavenly spirits praised the might of his victory. [I am five [?] of [?].] Heaven and earth became mouths for him in place of those who denied him:

Because the living denied him, the departed cried out, and the mute confirmed it. The hosts on high [?] to honor the earthly one; they honored his death and proclaimed his life to his companions. The Watchers brought hope of life to the abode of the dead: “Rise and take courage, you who are made of dust, because death has been abolished! “Cry out and say to the destroyer of your limbs, ‘Where is your sting, serpent, who killed us through eating [?]?’ “Repeat this and taunt him as you laugh at his wiles: ‘What can he do, now that Life has cut down the tree of affliction?’ Speak his name in a riddle, like Samson: ‘The body you swallowed is a spring that brings forth life. “‘From within the eater, spiritual food came out for us; and from the one who terrified us and brought forth suffering, sweetness flowed.’ “Let heaven and earth rejoice with us, those who speak and those who are mute, for a sacrifice from among us has reconciled the Lord with his creatures. “Our race offered a single firstfruit to the Godhead, and through him he gave a sign of peace and the renewal of everything. “Let earthly and heavenly beings give thanks with us: blessed is he who showed his love for his creatures in our body.” The end.
For the Friday of the Confessors

Discourse Twenty-Four. For the Friday of the Confessors. Response: Thanks be to the Power who strengthened his martyrs, so that they triumphed and conquered through the power of his love, my brothers.

Mortals heard the cry of victory from the top of the tree and gained hope of engaging in spiritual combat. One from the race that had incurred guilt through sin conquered on the cross; at the sound of his victory, the guilty rose and put on armor.

The second Adam won victory in soul and body, and the members of his race through the senses of the body and the movements of the soul. Hear, people of the earth, the voice that cried out on earth: “Rise up and take courage! I alone have conquered through the cross.” There had been no hope of victory for those in the flesh, but the promising voice of one who had triumphed gave them courage. Mortal nature could not overcome the passions, but when it saw a body grow weary on the wood, it gained courage. The weak body could not hate life, but when one man in the flesh despised it, the body rallied its senses. Earthly people did not know how to journey to the heights, but one earthly man blazed the trail before their eyes. They had not been confident about engaging in battle against the bodily senses, but he showed them how through abstinence from food. They did not know how to trample silver under their feet, but one man taught them by binding it and trampling it on the ground. The deceitful trap of the love of glory lay buried and concealed, but one swift man set it in motion [?] and exposed its deceit. The body and the impulses of the soul were occupied with earthly things, and there was no radiance of spiritual things among earthly people. They struggled in the athletic arena, but no one brought back a crown of victory in return for their labors. They were always going down to engage in battle with human concerns, but whenever they fought, they were defeated in the contest, and the reward remained unclaimed. But when the condemnation of the human race grew severe, and the tyrannical demons cheered and laughed at their sufferings, the Merciful One took pity when he saw his image being mocked, and he anointed it with the Spirit to confront the passions of the flesh. With the power of the Spirit he armed his image as with armor, so that through the Spirit’s power it might go out and conquer the spiritual beings. He tested the bodily warrior in everything, so that through his testing he might train the body for victory. Using him as a target, he taught his fellow servants to aim toward the ordered life of the kingdom above. He set up his victory like a mirror for the contestants,

so that they might imitate him in their impulses and senses, moving toward perfection. Through his sufferings they learned to engage in battle with incitements, and through his endurance they scorned and despised desires. They saw his body fastened with nails by unjust men, and they surrendered their bodies to every affliction in imitation of him. Through his death they received the good hope of the resurrection of the dead, and they hated life and loved death so that they might live with him. While they suffered, they remembered the hour of his death, when he forgave the insult against him and pleaded with his Father for forgiveness. They remembered the words he cried out on the wood: “Father of mercies, forgive the offense committed in ignorance.” They imitated him as they suffered the afflictions of this passing age, and they exchanged a life lasting only a time for one without end. Those in the flesh crucified their bodies to desires, and earthly things became dead before their eyes. They died to creation while living in it as though they were not alive; they themselves also regarded creation as though it were not alive. They walked on earth according to the pattern of spiritual conduct, and through their labors they fashioned an image of an order that does not perish. Through temporary sufferings they purchased the kingdom without end, and through things held in contempt they gained the exaltation of the rank above. They entered the arena and joined battle with the mighty one, and with visible limbs they seized a spirit. A hand seized an incorporeal spirit, and the swift-winged one was defeated and bound before the heavy one. O perishable nature, defeated every day, which prevailed and conquered the warrior who conquers every day! O ashes, whose dust bears witness to their lowliness, which conquered the spirit whose name proclaims his lightness! The rebel saw the second Adam and was defeated; he cried out and wailed over this unaccustomed victory. He saw the powers being driven away by the name of Jesus, and anguish seized him at how a body could drive away a spirit. He heard that demons were departing at an audible voice, and he trembled and was terrified that beings incapable of suffering had fled from a voice. The insolent one stood in doubt about what had happened, wondering whether it was perhaps a dream or apparitions. For he thought that in his tyranny [?] he could not be humbled.

And he also thought that mortals could not be saved. But when he learned through deeds of humanity’s salvation, he fell from his height and began devising hideous schemes. He took off the armor of tyranny in which he had fought, armed the captives themselves, and set them to mock one another. He set the world fighting so that it would wage war against itself and be defeated, while he himself became like a spectator watching warriors. He enticed the inhabitants of earth into conflict and stood there mocking as they were defeated by one another. He clothed mortal nature itself in his armor, and it began tearing its own perishable self apart. He spread a veil and blinded their understanding, so that they would not consider why human beings were striking one another. He clothed them in the lying spirit of his contentiousness and made them act like champions of the truth. He gave them the cloudy dregs of his bitterness to drink and intoxicated them with desires as with wine. He cast zeal for the name of God into their minds and made them avenge insults against the errors they had brought forth. The rebel heard that the proclamation of the Creator’s name had demolished the wicked structure of the names of gods that he had built for himself. He saw that one confession of one God was being proclaimed, and he hired workers of falsehood to help him. He saw human nature faltering in the struggle against sufferings, though through endurance it had begun to soar above sufferings. Anguish seized him: how could the body, which hates death, turn and ask its destroyer to come near it? He lay among [?], crushed as he wondered why those who love life were hating life. Why had earthly people despised earthly things, and on whose account had they scorned pleasures, contrary to their custom? Why had earthly people trampled on fleshly desire, and on whose account had they despised their comforts like people above such things? Why had nature, bound by desires, become estranged from them and yoked itself to a way of life foreign to it? This had never happened or been heard of among mortals: that mortal nature should hate life and love death. The race of Adam's children has no other hope

except a lifetime that runs its full course and a life within time. Human beings had not hated human things as though they were not human, nor had the children of dust become strangers to the work of the earth. Earthly people had never performed the work of the spirit, nor had perishable beings borne fruit for those who cannot suffer. Earthly people had not traveled the road leading upward, nor had the body, with its heavy wings, flown with spiritual beings. Their mother is the earth, and on the earth they are born upon the dust. Like infants, they suck the milk of earthly things. They fall far short of spiritual training and cannot take the mature food of the word of life. Something new had suddenly happened on earth to the children of earth: they hated the earth and their kinship with earthly things. The hater of humanity was tormented by these sufferings, for he saw human beings beginning to treat the passions lightly and trample them down. The envious one saw that human beings had come to hate his love, and he added to the fire of his evil intent to destroy them. He saw that those made of dust had armed themselves against his power, and he too changed his weaponry to shackle human beings. The ruler of the air armed himself with cunning devices, for he saw that the simple had learned strategies against his schemes. He armed the children of earth themselves against one another and divided them from each other through strife. The rebel divided the very nature formed from Adam's clay, and from it drew reinforcements for the ranks of his forces. The deceiver summoned the simple themselves to help him, and sent them like spies among their companions. He taught them methods of combat involving cunning strategies, and occupied them with the practice of wickedness so that they might pour out wickedness. Lowly human nature became reckless and raged against its own members, and began tearing itself apart without understanding. They entered the bodily contest against flesh, and lowly dust joined battle with what was formed from the same substance. The rebel stood with his followers on his left, and the unseen Power with the children of truth on the right. The powers on high gathered, it is said, as spectators of the athlete, to watch human beings fighting against spirits. Demons and human beings drew up for battle with senses and impulses:

Those capable of sensation with the body's senses, and the demons with impulses. The spirit clothed the impulses within them with a hand of flesh, and through visible limbs they fulfilled their desire. Those incapable of suffering laid hands on those capable of suffering, and tore the body to shreds—the garment outside the armor. The enemy's hand pounded the garment of flesh [?], but suffering did not reach the impulses within the limbs. The rebel seized the senses of the visible body, but the sharp edge of his deceitful sword did not reach the mind. Cunning struck the lowly chest containing the treasure of life, but the impulses hid the spirit's riches in the strongholds of the soul [?]. Judging by outward appearances, the insolent one thought [?] that he had prevailed and won, but he did not perceive the hidden strength within the soul. Although the body, weak in its limbs, lost the contest, the soul was not defeated by his wiles. The envious one planted the arrow of his anger in the weak body, but the steadfast mind met them with the spirit's shield. The visible limbs suffered blows the whole time, while the impulses, incapable of suffering, remained unchanged. Not even the body was brought low by being torn to shreds, for although it was capable of suffering, it forced nature beyond its usual order. For it was a marvel through its endurance in the face of sufferings, and it was exceedingly strong while being mercilessly cut apart. O you who can suffer, whose nature bears witness to your corruptibility, who forgot your nature and matched the strength of those who cannot suffer! O dust, scattered grains of sand, which gathered itself into a spiritual structure! O mortal being, wholly molded in mortality [?], who transformed his clay into a constitution foreign to his name! O clay, weak in body, molded from earth, which suddenly became a pearl endowed with beauty! O glass, brittle by nature and prone to breaking, which sufferings struck as though it were diamond, yet it did not break! The despised stone that had not been set in the building of truth became the topmost stone in the King's temple.

The clay that the waters of suffering and vulnerability had swept away hardened itself and became pottery that rebuffs sufferings. The fainthearted one strengthened himself like a warrior and sought to mock the mighty one who had trampled his nature. Who, then, taught the heavy-bodied one the ways of combat, and who urged him to engage in battle with spirits? Who showed the short-lived one how to hate his life, and who brought him the good news of life without end? Who roused the sluggish sleeper from his stupor, and who laid out a road to the heights for the lover of the depths? When did people of flesh—people of flesh—love spiritual things? And where did earthly people become like heavenly beings? Who revealed the reward to the one who had no hope? And who told him about the renewal of body and soul? A sign from the one who had placed the fire of his love within him spoke in him, and secretly taught him to join battle with terrors. By a hidden power he strengthened himself for the struggle. Through it he became courageous, threatened his adversary, and treated him with contempt. Through the Spirit of revelation he gained the understanding to hate his own life, and through it he became wise enough to exchange one life for another. They compared one life with the other and weighed them like discerning people, and the scale holding life here proved lighter than the one holding eternal life. They weighed the endurance of life here against the kingdom on high, and their sufferings did not outweigh the reward of things to come. The sufferings of body and soul are small beside the promises, and fire and sword cannot be compared with the crown of glory. The body cannot provide enough for reconciliation through its sacrifice, nor can the soul, through its endurance, bring about peace. They reckoned that gift which brought about peace as grace, and did not boast that they had gained victory through their sufferings. The king’s servants remembered that saying: “When you have done everything commanded, do not boast.” They remembered that herald who proclaimed to the nations: “The sufferings of this time are not equal to the promised blessings.” They marveled at his own labors, at how glorious they were, and were astonished at his words, which were full of fear.

“I am afraid,” he said, “I who sowed the word of life, lest I myself be excluded from the treasure of life.” And if the [?] whom the Spirit chose was full of fear, who can boast that his labors will make him worthy of blessings? If the athlete of righteousness humbled himself, who would display the beauty of his labors before onlookers? The athletes also considered the meaning of his words and understood that suffering is small beside the reward. For this reason they endured sufferings gladly, because they looked toward crowns far more splendid than their labors. They laughed at swords, scorned the iron combs, and trampled on fire. They mocked and ridiculed the cunning of the Evil One and death. They broke the sword with the unyielding sharpness of their resolve, and shattered the instruments of torture through endurance of soul. They overcame the fire through the burning warmth of the love within them, and its fierceness cooled and grew feeble before their clay bodies. Oh, the nature that destroys bodies, defeated by bodies! Oh, the devourer that became food for those it would devour! Oh, people of flesh, always burning with desires, who stilled the fury of the flame through their endurance! The athletes overcame fire with the fire of their resolve, and the impulses within them were not distressed by the blaze. In them that written saying was spoken and fulfilled in deeds: “If you pass through sea and fire, I am with you.” They entered fire and water and were tested by persecutors. The fire cooled, the waters grew calm, and they stood in a spacious place. O creatures of dust whom the flame set ablaze, who became vessels for a treasure of life that cannot be stolen! O ashes continually soaked in the waters of suffering, through whose limbs sufferings passed like fire! A garment woven from threads of perishable wool washed itself in the flame and was not scorched. Let us call those embodied people asbestos, for they washed the filth from their limbs in the flame.

For that substance is a perishable body, like all bodies, yet a garment made from it is not destroyed by decay. Those embodied people also possessed a perishable body, yet the garment of love they wore was not destroyed. The fire of the waters of suffering washed away the body's filth. The body became beautiful, and the soul shone at the voice of renewal. Mortals heard the voice of renewal speaking on earth, and they dismantled the body built of passions so that it might be renewed again. They saw that the structure of their limbs was small and weak, and they took the initiative to dismantle it through the readiness of their minds. They themselves dismantled it, not the coercion of their persecutors, for it would have been easy for them to drive sufferings away from their bodies. They contemplated the filth of the perishable body and brought it into the furnace of sufferings to melt it down, so that it might acquire beauty. It was not coercion that constrained the freedom of their minds. They themselves judged, as discerning people, that this was fitting. With a devout mind they saw that their bodies were frail, and they cast aside the body of weak clay and acquired the spirit. Like wise people, they judged and considered both sides: death lasting only a time was preferable to death lasting forever. The stirrings [?] of the soul and the senses of the body entered into debate: which was right—to suffer a little or to suffer severely? “Which is easier,” the stirrings said to the body's senses, “temporary sufferings or torment without end?” “Whom should we fear,” the soul said to the temple where it dwelt, “the killer of one person, or the killer of both?” And perhaps the mind recited the meaning of that saying: “Do not be terrified of the killer who kills the body. Rather, fear all the more, and tremble as discerning people, before the one who can cast soul and body into the fire.” They contemplated that torment without end and that judgment whose scrutiny penetrates the stirrings of the soul. “The word of the God of all is living,” they read and pondered, “and his judgment is far sharper than a two-edged sword.” The victorious ones wrote the books of the Spirit on the tablet of their hearts, and spiritually they pondered hidden things. When scourges came upon them, and sights met their eyes, and their limbs trembled,

their thoughts read of things to come and comforted them. Again, when the terrible sword flashed above their bodies, they placed the salvation of life upon their minds like a helmet. When the flame blazed up in the [?] of wrath, endurance descended like dew upon their limbs. The victorious ones traveled the road to Babylon in their thoughts, and there they saw the fire defeated and the body victorious. In their minds they saw how high that blaze rose, and how a hidden command struck down its towering flame. It was very terrifying when it was unleashed upon the wood of wrath, but the end of its burning was contemptible and despised: it was defeated. Very fierce was the command that gave it food, but weak and feeble was the force of its action outside its appointed order. The destroyer of everything subject to corruption forgot its nature, and the force of its fierceness grew weak. The mouth of the [?], which in its greed had never been satisfied—they threw it a log, but it did not open its mouth to its food. The victorious ones pictured before their eyes, as in a mirror, what the Babylonians had arrogantly done. They stood there and watched with the eyes of their hearts, as the nations gathered to see human beings destroyed. They awaited the outcome of that event and saw it through, as fire was kindled by the fire of tyranny. Perhaps they too gave this answer to their killers: “We are not concerned to spend our breath over our destruction. The command that restrained the mouth of the flame will itself rescue us from the torment of your afflictions.” They heard the promise that cannot prove false and took courage: whoever endures to the end will live forever. The hope of life strengthened them in their afflictions, and they did not weaken while suffering at the hands of unbelievers. A wondrous vision appeared before their eyes, and the heat of love was checked by love. Through affection for divine love, the affection for love implanted in mortal nature was being uprooted.

O will, possessing the freedom of discernment, whose force overcame the bondage imposed by the Creator! O loss, bound entirely to temporal life, which the love of immortal life overcame! O one whose nature is pledged to death because of his folly, who began paying off the bond of debts through bodily sufferings! O one sold to the devil through eating the fruit, who proclaimed people free through endurance of desires! With everyone and in everything they fought bodily battles; they prevailed over everything, defeated everything, triumphed, and won. Through the sufferings of the body and the stirrings of the soul they gained victory, and they despised and scorned the desires of body and soul. Through endurance they surpassed the Watchers, the second nature [?]; they trampled nature itself and rose above its stings. As for bodily desire, the spring that flows continually, they cut off its flow from their limbs so that they would not lust. They buried the love of money, the mother that gave birth to every evil, in a grave, so that it would no longer bear fruit for death. They imprisoned the love of glory in the strongholds of humility and shut against it the gates of love, in which they were fortified. They subdued with a word of peace the mighty power of envy, the tyrant that [?] and prevailed over all the passions. They bound anger, that untamable wild beast, and shackled it with gentleness as with a chain. They brought pride, the lion that prowls in the thicket to destroy people, into the cage of humility and imprisoned it there. They cut down the evil inclination and uprooted it, so that it would no longer sprout again and bear bitter fruit. They humbled the arrogance of the desires arising from impulses and sensations, and subjected them to a will that loves truth. With the armor of the Spirit they fortified all the powers within and without, with which the soul's will fought as though they were its own. Through what was not its own, the will triumphed as though through its own resources, and the victory won by that power was credited to it as though it were its own. It was not within its own power to overcome the passions embedded in it,

but belonged to the Power that gave it strength to overcome its passions. The Spirit gathered the fire of love within the mind, kindled it, and burned up the hateful forest of desires [?]. Through the promise of immortal life he stirred the will, and love spurred it on to go and fulfill his own will. Through hidden movements he [?] and reached toward the height above, and with his understanding he saw that imperishable dwelling. On the wings of the Spirit, earthly people flew and entered heaven, and there they heard the sound of praise that cannot be expressed. The victorious ones journeyed in the company of Paul, the chosen vessel, and reached the place where praise is offered spiritually. The command that chose him brought them near through their will, to hear a voice that cannot be expressed by a fleshly tongue. With him they ascended to the third heaven in their hidden understanding, and concealed the beauty of their victories under his example. They always imitated the upright purpose of those who had triumphed, and [?] very greatly through the perseverance of their minds. Abel's death was always portrayed before their eyes, and they contemplated his murderer as he was being tormented. Their thoughts were awakened by the voice of his blood as it cried out against his murderer to the One who sees everything. The silent man brought a great accusation against the insolent man and entrusted it to the divine command, to enter and present it before the judge. The judge saw the accusation made by the blood, grew indignant and fierce, and pronounced judgment on the murderer according to his crime. He stretched out the shedder of blood for seven harsh lashings, so that through his sentence he might frighten people away from murder. On this condition the chosen martyrs surrendered their bodies, and they did not demand redress from their tormentors for the humiliation of their sufferings. They discerned meaning in the blood that cries out like a speaker, and gladly poured out their blood so that it might acquire a voice. Through the harsh scourges inflicted on the insolent, they were exacting vengeance for death from the executioners who condemned them. They did not reproach their persecutors, asking, “Why this treatment?” For they were convinced that suffering itself was a cause of life. They did not grieve over the destruction of their limbs,

for the resurrection of the body was always pictured before their eyes. They were not distressed over the separation of body and soul, for they saw that through death they were passing into life. O mind, how steadfast it was, and how it scorned nature, which it blinded and silenced at the separation of the two parts! O freedom, how greatly you despised bondage and regarded the love implanted in nature as though it did not exist! O struggle that the soul waged against itself! It prevailed and defeated the tyranny of violent impulses. It joined battle with the impulses, and the impulses with it; then it, together with the impulses, surrendered to the power of freedom. The power of discerning freedom triumphed in the contests; the hidden command of the Maker of all sustained it. With the armor of the Spirit, freedom conquered nature and its passions, like a valiant commander who conquers through the power of the kingdom. By the power of this armor, bodily beings fought against spiritual and bodily beings, in [?] and openly. Through their struggles they gained experience of the power of its help, for everyone who fought with it gained victory, was exalted, and reigned. With the hidden eye of remembrance, they contemplated that athlete who put it on and fought against the mighty one. Job’s suffering was always set before their eyes, and they imitated his endurance in pursuing victory. They set up his struggle like a [?], to see in their minds how a bodily being fights against a spiritual being. They contemplated the visible and the hidden as though both were visible, seeing the body triumph and the spirit suffer defeat. The proclamation of the victory of despised flesh encouraged them to join battle with the mighty one through the senses of the body. The answer Job gave his wife was the answer they gave the devil, whose hope was empty. Job regarded the rib of his companion as a foolish woman, who gave her [?] to the name of the one who spoke through her. The foolish one committed adultery with the foolish woman through the desire stirred by the impulses; but the righteous man uprooted the thicket that had sprung up in the soil of his companion. Together with the righteous man, the victorious ones cried out, “Go away, evil one!

Go act foolishly with foolish women, as you are accustomed to do! You will not debase the chastity of our souls through your hateful companionship, and we will not receive evil seed into our thoughts.” Go, arm yourself with bodily beings against us, for without flesh your strength is too weak for combat. Go, gather your companions to yourself, [?], to help you, for from the beginning you have used us to wage war against our humanity. Through a rib of our body you engaged the head of our race in battle, and through his own member you killed Adam as with a sword. With Eve's bow you also shot the arrows of your deceit at Job, but he caught them on the pure shield of faith. You placed the harsh shackles of fleshly desire on Joseph, but he cut them apart with the agility of chaste impulses. And because you learned through experience to conquer with our weapons, now you seek to fight against us with what is ours. You are deceitful, and in human guise you lead human beings astray. Without a human being, you do not wage war against humanity. Through human childishness you carried out your bitter design, and through it you make fellow human beings taste the bitterness of death. Come with the army of flesh assembled for you, and engage our limbs in battle through beings of flesh. Enter and hide the ugliness of your soul in visible flesh, and carry out your design through beings of flesh against [?]. We do not fear your schemes, however harsh they may be, and we do not flee from the sound of your deceitful bow. We will take off our armor for you if we do not defeat you, and we will give you no room to shatter the ranks of truth. We will not cease fighting as long as it is day, until the evening of death comes and gives our bodies rest. If you want to learn the purpose of our resolve, carry out your will by bringing death upon us, and see our deeds. If you wish to test our strength through deeds, bring out the scourges, kindle the fire, and sharpen the sword. For neither height nor depth counts for anything with us, nor can the heavenly powers defeat us.

Nor can any other created thing, even if it wages war against us, loosen our soul's love for him who created us. Oh, how valiant the athletes of righteousness became! They conquered on earth and began to mock the heavenly beings. They overcame [?] and humbled his power through their sufferings. They cheered and laughed even at death, which everyone fears. They hated their lives and despised earthly comforts, and they prepared body and soul together for the wedding feast on high. They saw in secret that banquet which never ends, and adorned their minds with perseverance as with garments. Their thoughts were always full of fear and love as they remembered the man whose soul's garments were repulsive. They watched him as he left the banquet and contemplated how bitter his torment was. They remembered that dismissal of the foolish women, and they never ceased gathering the oil of mercy. Although the wealth of sufferings they had gathered on earth was very great, they were afraid that the fuel for suffering might run out. With the eyes of their minds they examined the Scriptures, and they advanced toward the goal of perfection. For they were convinced that toil without love was useless, and that no one could enter the gate of heaven except with it. Paul’s words led them to consider this: he declared glorious deeds worthless without love. If prophecy, which is greater than everything, remained on earth, how could lesser labors ascend to the heights above? If he regarded the gift of tongues as brass, who would dare [?] face the scrutiny of righteous judgment? He called mountain-conquering faith nothing. How, then, can we be satisfied that something lesser amounts to anything? If sufferings together with almsgiving proved useless, who can gather the riches of great love? The victorious sailed toward the harbor of love through the movements of their souls, and in it, as in a harbor, they deposited the treasures they possessed. They saw that no good things could compare with its greatness. They despised everything and loved love above everything.

Through their sufferings they experienced its unconquerable greatness, and in their afflictions they sought no other help besides it. It was fitting for them, who knew love, to love it, and fitting for love to help those who shared its secrets. Because they loved it greatly and did not slacken in their communion with it, it loved them and helped them beyond their strength. Because they set out from it and did not fall short of it in their deeds, it brought them to the harbor of life without end. Theirs is victory, together with an imperishable reward, because they hated life and loved the hope that does not deceive. Theirs is praise from every mouth as victors, but ours is reproach because we do not resemble them in our purpose. They left to unworthy heirs the [?] from their sufferings, and these scattered them on earthly desires. They gave the wealth from their labors to the lazy, who did not use it to relieve the poverty of human life. Lax children received an inheritance of spiritual things and sold it for nothing, receiving no spiritual payment. They were not truly heirs to the wealth of the Spirit. Their love was deceitful, and they loved truth falsely. For love of earthly things they attached themselves to the truth, and for the rank of leadership they put on the religious habit. Out of love of glory they adorned and built tombs for the righteous, and out of love of money they made them places of business. The ministers of the sanctuary set snares for silver in the sanctuary, so that a catch of elusive silver might fall prey to their love of money. For the sake of silver they covered the walls with deceptive silver, so that everyone would see the beauty of the silver and bring silver. Out of love of money they honored the bones with their outward senses, while in their minds they kissed silver insatiably. Out of love of money they honored the bones with their outward senses, while in their minds they kissed silver insatiably. They gave dead bones a bodily voice to demand money from humanity in the theater. Those who hated money and cut the snares that money spread—love of money made them a catch for money. Through the power of bones, greed wanted to swallow much, and through spending money it enjoyed authority to drive out demons.

It did not drive them out in truth, but through deception; the rebellious spirits fled from the sound of money, not from truth. Love of money hired them as workers for its vineyard, to labor at the task of wickedness as though they were serving truth. The demon serves love of money through the body's senses and ministers to it through desires, as to a master. Come, discerning one, [?], and marvel with discernment at how far love of money has flown on wings of money. It yoked humans and demons together under the yoke of its toil, and neither height nor depth could fill its emptiness. It defeated the clever and the simple through its tricks and gained the rank of mastery over everyone. Even the champions who triumphed and conquered in the contest of truth—it overcame them under the guise of love for their bones. It demanded from the bones of the chaste a payment for [?] love, though it loved them only in appearance, not in truth. For the sake of money, the greedy magnified and honored money, and demanded payment for a deceptive appearance as though it were genuine. The [?] of the righteous did not seek to be honored, nor were they concerned with our songs and our worship. Those whose souls were radiant had no need of incense from us, nor did those clothed in glorious light need lamps that last only a time. To honor the righteous with the soul's love was [?], just as they themselves loved God with the impulses of their souls. In secret, like discerning people, they pleased the one who sees in secret; and he, the hidden one, honored them both secretly and openly. Our firstfruits, too, who opened a living path to the heights, pronounced blessed the one who believed in his name without seeing. We ought to have directed our inward impulses toward his purpose, rather than displaying beauty before our companions through outward appearances. It was not fitting to honor ourselves through the honor given to the righteous, nor was it right to demand from them payment for our labor. They freely gave the gift through which they had become rich, and we ought to have ministered in the same way.

Gluttony entered and settled among mortals, and because of this human life is troubled and worn down. Love of [?] spread snares among earth's inhabitants, and everyone fell into the traps of oppression. Empty glory humbled itself under the name of sweetness and gave the children of [?] the gall of death to drink. Hateful envy blinded the soul to knowledge, and the world grew dark and began groping along walls at noon. Understanding departed from the rational mind, and the stirrings of [?] ceased within the understanding. And if the help of the command does not reach us, then the promises made to our race have also come to nothing and proved false. Come, you debtors, let us pay off a little of the record of our debts, lest the weight of our wrongdoing grow heavier and sink us. Come, let us take refuge in trustworthy harbors—in the righteous—so that they may help us with love and mercy before the Judge. Come, let us make friends here while we are alive, so that they may receive us into their dwellings that never pass away. Come, let us trade spiritually alongside the diligent, so that we may deserve the wages of the workers who bore the day's burden. Let our mind judge the sins we have committed, as discerning people do, so that we may become companions of those who endured scourging with love. Since we cannot endure bodily sufferings, let us suffer a little in the stirrings of our soul instead of in our limbs. Since our strength is too feeble to stand firm before threats, let us call upon the [?] who felt compassion for our nature, so that they may help us. Response: Blessed is the Lord whose servants sleep, while he makes their commemorations great.
On the Martyrs
Discourse Twenty-[?]. On the Martyrs. Response: Blessed is he who has made the commemoration of his helpers great, here and above in heaven, my brothers.
Everywhere Jesus raised up witnesses to his [?], and in every region he received the standard of his crucifixion. Throughout the whole world he made the sun of his proclamation rise.

And with its rays he swept darkness away from the inhabited world. He cast the net of his teaching into the sea of humanity, and enclosed within it all nations together with all kings. He left no city on earth in rebellion against his teaching, and no corner of the earth remained where he was not victorious. His proclamation had wings and flew over the earth, and in its swiftness it took possession of districts in every region. His word ran swiftly over sea and dry land, and he harnessed the world to the gentle yoke of his teaching. People received his proclamation with great love, and for its sake they endured tortures and every kind of affliction. For love of him, children abandoned their parents, regarded them as strangers, and followed him. For his sake, parents also disowned their children and handed them over without pity to every kind of death. He brought a great division upon the earth on the day of his coming, and severed the love of parents from [?].

Brother handed brother over to death for his sake, and there was no household free from strife. A daughter would not accept her mother's errors, nor would a mother be persuaded to acknowledge her daughter. Jesus is the cause of all this division, just as he himself clearly taught us. “Do not suppose,” he said, “that I have come to bring peace on earth. For I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.” I have come to proclaim new good news to humanity, and whoever is persuaded and accepts me becomes hated [?]. Whoever acknowledges me and my words renounces his father, and whoever accepts me and believes in me leaves his mother. He renounces everyone in his household, and they too renounce him. He sets his body against the world, night and day [?]. He carries his cross on his shoulder and goes out in my company. He [?] all his family and kin and follows me. If he is rich, he despises his wealth and becomes poor. Once he has emptied himself, he is worthy to become my disciple. If he is wise and approaches the simplicity of my teaching, let him first renounce the wisdom of the world and then come. If he is a ruler and wishes to come under my authority, let him become my disciple with the humility befitting my lordship. I have come to open a narrow gate for humanity. It is very constricted, and it is not easy for everyone to enter through it. Only the small can enter through the gate I have opened, and those who are lightly burdened can travel the road I have laid out. The gate is narrow, and the road is constricted and very difficult. It is not easy [?] for everyone to walk along it. Not everyone who wishes to come finds it easy to come, for a person masters my instruction through great toil. Not everyone who calls himself my disciple can fully practice the discipleship I require. I have come to teach humanity a life of toil, and the one who hears and keeps my word is worthy. He renounces his brothers and makes himself a stranger to his sisters. He leaves houses, villages, and possessions, and then approaches me.
This is the seed our Savior sowed among humanity:

The martyrs received it with a love befitting [?] discipleship to him. For his sake they became strangers to everything they possessed, and they regarded the world and its good things as nothing. They hated comforts and loved being without peace [?]. Though they were on earth, they were not on earth but on high. While they were alive, they were dead [?] to the whole world, for they lived for him, not for the world, which does not endure [?]. They hated their lives and loved death without being compelled. They themselves accepted the death that everyone fears. The blessed journeyed along the road of death [?] without dread or fear. Though its taste was exceedingly bitter, they did not shrink from it. The steadfast weighed this temporary life against eternal life. With discernment they rejected the former and chose the latter. They used the accurate scales of the mind and carefully weighed the passing world against the eternal one. They did not slacken in the contest they had entered, nor did they falter or give way before the severity of sufferings and torments. They were not enticed by wealth and the gifts that fill this age, nor were they held back by either family or ancestry. They deliberately set this one goal before themselves: to choose death for Jesus’ sake and reject life. They saw that Jesus’ death had become the source of our life, and they gained strength to scorn every kind of death. They saw him hanging on the summit of Golgotha for our salvation, and with the blood of their necks they repaid him the debts they owed. They gazed at our Lord hanging on the cross with robbers, and they understood that he had accepted death for humanity’s sake. They saw the robber who received forgiveness of his sins from him, and they considered that his mercy was also revealed toward them. They saw the elements transformed on the day of his resurrection, and they understood that he was their Lord and the Lord of all. They saw the forces of nature crying out without words, because they had recognized that he was Lord of the heights and the depths. They saw the mute forces of nature crying out to human beings endowed with speech,

and they knew and understood why he had tasted death. They too ran and took refuge in him like the robber, and they asked him for forgiveness of sins and new life. They regarded this passing life as nothing, and they believed that this world was like a single day. The Son’s workers hated the world and everything in it, and they hoped to inherit new life in the kingdom above. They hated and rejected all beautiful things and possessions, and they longed for the world to come and the promised blessings. They rejected perishable gold, which brings no benefit, and hated silver, which cannot save any of its owners. They cast away every form of idol worship and cried out praise to the one God, who is exalted above the heights. They hated and rejected the glory of this passing existence, and they loved and cherished the glory above, which does not perish. They abandoned the idols that the evil one had set up to lead humanity astray, and they approached and bowed before the Judge in loving worship. They left behind here every possession and every beautiful thing, and they ran after the pearl more glorious than everything. They recognized the master of the house from his buildings, and like trumpets they sounded praise to the one who fashioned everything. They abandoned the muttering of sorcery that the evil one had poured forth,

and they cried out praise to the one Creator and Maker. They understood that the sun and moon are created things, and that it is not right for them to seize the rank of divinity. They understood that it was not fitting for them to be called gods, or for the worship due to God to be offered to them. They saw the Son, who opened the path of life for our race, and as though crossing a bridge, they passed over death into the land of life. The hour of death is very frightening and deeply distressing. How desirable this temporary life is to a human being! Temporary life is dearly loved by human beings, and even the righteous are deeply distressed when they depart from it. Look at Hezekiah, who was told of his approaching death:

He turned his face to the wall and wept sorrowfully. The king who heard that he was going to die wept bitterly, until he heard the good news of life from Isaiah. If a righteous man feared and trembled before the cup of death, who finds it easy to endure sufferings without [?]? The martyrs endured the sufferings of death without trembling. They died a temporary death with Jesus so that they might live with him. The death of Jesus made death into sleep. By his resurrection he rendered it powerless and stripped it of its authority. Where does the frail body, born of the earth, get the power to stand firm, hold out, and heroically overcome sufferings and torments? Where does our miserable race, so full of suffering, get the power to fight courageously and overcome the sufferings of death? There is no strength in the frailty of Adam’s dust. Where does it get the power to endure sufferings without difficulty? Who gave the body this ability to hate its own life? How can it scorn the cup of death? By what strength did it overcome scourges and instruments of raking torture? Who strengthened its frailty so that it would not give way? The death of Jesus gave a helping hand to those who live in bodies. In it they take pride, and through it they mock the dominion of death. If Jesus had not died and come to life, who, being mortal, could hate life, which is loved above everything? If Christ had not imprisoned death in the tomb, humanity would have had no hope of new life. Jesus invited our entire race to new life, and the martyrs ran and went to him, to the place where he had gone. He went first to prepare a dwelling on high, and then his friends ascend with him to the royal dwelling. With this hope the martyrs die without [?], and for this reason they scorn life without distress. The righteous looked forward to delighting in another world. For this reason they die here so that they may live there. Let everyone run to these righteous ones and contemplate them, for through their deaths my error came to an end and truth triumphed. Through them the teaching of the proclamation also triumphed, for they bore witness to it not with words but with death.

For even when someone merely believes, the confession made by his words is not deprived of its reward. Paul cries out: “If you confess the death of Jesus and also believe that he rose from the tomb, you will inherit life.” If confession by the mouth alone gives life, how much more will the martyrs inherit, who believed and were also crowned! If the robber entered Paradise through a word alone,

what place do the martyrs enter, who held their lives in contempt? Christ alone is capable of giving this reward, and he repays the martyrs with crowns for their torments. Who is capable of praising these righteous people except that good Lord for whose sake they died? Look, their deaths shine everywhere far more brightly than life, and their festivals are exalted in every region. Look, people hurry from everywhere to their feast days, and every day their commemorations shine in the four quarters of the world. Walls cannot protect cities as the prayer of the martyrs protects the whole world. No king can offer help [?] as the prayer of the martyrs can help us. No ruler rescues those who seek refuge in him as the martyrs [?] rescue from afflictions. Who would not rejoice in these righteous people and be glad at heart? Who would not honor their commemorations and their festivals? These became sacrificers of their own selves, and offered themselves as offerings to the King they loved. These hated the whole world and its desirable things, and loved suffering and death for Jesus’ sake. These renounced family, wealth, and power, and for Jesus’ sake did not wish to live this temporary life. Through these the pagan faction was defeated and brought low, and the teaching of Jesus prevailed and triumphed among unbelievers. These did not bear witness through the testimony of words alone: they doubly sealed and confirmed what they had received. With words they testified to the teaching that was proclaimed, and through their deaths their words were also confirmed.

The martyrs cried out all these things before their persecutors: We are certain of Jesus’ death and also of his resurrection. We confess that he truly died and truly rose, and the good Lord does not separate us from his lordship. We have seen him himself risen from the grave in great glory, and he cannot be exchanged for another lord, for we are certain of him. If you doubt our words, persecutors, our deeds bear witness to our words, if you are willing. It is not in words alone that we confess the lordship of Jesus: look, we are ready for every suffering for Jesus’ sake. It is not merely with spoken words that we confess him, for through death we bring our love for him to completion. The sword cannot sever our love for Jesus, and no affliction can put a blemish on our faith. The champions sought all these things before their persecutors, and they did not tremble or bow down before the persecutors of righteousness. The martyrs cried out loudly before the judge: We do not worship the sun and the moon, which are created beings. The one God, who created the heights and established the depths—we serve him and offer him the debt of love. We acknowledge him as the exalted Lord, ruler of all, and offer him songs of praise at all times. The Lord of the heights, who came down to earth to give life to the world—we confess him without division, as it is written. That Savior, who came down and redeemed Adam’s race—to him we sing songs of praise night and day. That Savior, who died for our sake so that we might live with him:

We worship him and offer him our bodies as sacrifices. “Whoever denies my word and loves his life,” he says, “let him take up his cross and come after me, and delight with me.” They put the tyrant kings to shame with their replies and cried out to them, “We do not worship any created beings. Let the sword come, and let fire come with its flames, and let us see whether they can separate his love from us. Until now we have testified in words about the one we love; from now on, let action bear witness to our words. Perhaps there is [?] for proving verbal testimony false;

But who can invalidate a deed? A deed, then, is a witness that cannot be proved false. Let it now come and testify about Jesus. Look, we enter every affliction for his sake, and we are ready for every scourging because of our love for him. And if you say that you do not accept verbal testimony, then accept testimony given through deeds. Our body bears witness, and so do our limbs as they are cut off, that Jesus, for whose sake we are being destroyed, is true.” The martyrs endured temporal death in the hope of life, and their commemorations will never cease. The memory of their persecutors has faded, but theirs endures, for Jesus, for whose sake they gave their bodies, is one. The pagan kings who tortured them have come to nothing, while the righteous, who endured every torture, are glorified. The renowned kings have no memorials on earth, while the festivals of humble people are exalted. In this, the human race has no claim even to renown, for although they were human, they rejected human life. The frail human race loves life and has no strength to rouse itself against sufferings. Our body is dust, and where could it get [?] in the dust? For it is a child of ashes, and nothing is weaker than it. This earthly race is more wretched than anything, yet from it came the martyrs who scorned every kind of death. They offered their necks to death by the sword for Jesus’ sake, so that they might receive from their Lord a reward for their labors. They are convinced that the Creator does not wrong them, and they are certain that they will receive from him the reward for their labors. In the hope of that new life they endured every evil, so that they might enter and dwell in the harbor of light in the region [?] above. Trusting in the kingdom on high, they offered their necks, so that on the day of judgment they might receive from him the crown of victory. For the confession of our salvation they gave up their bodies.

Look, they await the day of his appearing, when they will receive their reward. They sought to inherit that Jerusalem which is on high, and for its sake they despised the pleasures of life below. They longed to enjoy that spiritual delight, and therefore they renounced the idols and confessed the Son. They long to share in the way of life of the royal household, and for its sake they rejected gold, silver, and loathsome attachments. They long to cry out with the Watchers, “Holy, holy,” and therefore they loved and cherished the dwelling above. They long to eat from the table that is full of life, and therefore they scorned earthly morsels [?]. They long to drink from that spiritual cup.

For its sake they gave up drinking earthly wine. The martyrs long to receive crowns of glory, and for their sake they gave up the perishable glory of the earth. The martyrs long to rejoice with the Bridegroom; for his sake they rejected all the pleasures [?] of this life.
