One gave up his life by the sword at the hands of persecutors, and is destined to receive an imperishable crown [?] of glory. One was cut apart limb by limb by the persecutors, and this was the marvel: half of him was alive, while half was struck down [?]. One ended his life under torture, another under the scraping instruments; another in prison, another amid afflictions, and another under torture. Hail to the athletes of righteousness who triumphed and were victorious! Hail to the victors who conquered and brought victory to the race of Adam! Hail to the invited guests of the imperishable Bridegroom on high, who surrendered themselves to every affliction and every scourging! Hail to the rays of the great Sun of Righteousness, who were not lost in the gloom of loathsome darkness! Hail to the lamps of righteousness, who gave their light, which shone upon the earth and rolled up the darkness, the cloak of error! Hail to the valiant ones who did not weaken in their afflictions, who overcame nobles, kings, and rulers! Hail to the consecrated ones who stood in the arena against the Evil One and defeated all the bands of the children of darkness! Hail to the race of Adam! How greatly it has been exalted!

It has become master over what is on high and what is in the depths. The tyrannical demons wailed and cried out with a voice of lamentation: “Woe to us, for the great crown of our dominion has been abolished!” “From now on, the dominion of our rulers has ceased, and we can no longer open our mouths because of what has happened. “From now on, our disciples have abandoned the teaching of our words, and look—the whole world has become disciples in the name of Jesus! “All creation has been filled with the words of the Spirit, and everyone runs to take refuge in the Galilean. “Look—the whole world has become disciples in the name of Jesus, and even those instructed in the teaching of our words have taken refuge in him!” Let our whole race rejoice and be glad in these righteous ones, and let the weakness of our entire body be strengthened through them. Thanks be to the Lord who made his servants victorious in the contest of suffering! To him be glory, and to them praise, from every mouth.
On the Martyrs
Discourse 30. On the Martyrs. My brothers.

O Power who descended with the athletes into their contests, through you I am strengthened to recount the beauty of their victories. O Son, for love of whom the martyrs endured [?], give me words adequate to recount their praises, O you who intoxicated people with your love, so that they trampled on death. Give me your love to drink, so that through you I may speak their praises, O slain one who paved the road of suffering for his armies. May your suffering stir me to tell their stories with discernment, O slain bridegroom at whose wedding feast the demons lay cast down.

Grant me to mingle the account of your slaying into your banquet. Through you, my Lord, I will approach the telling of their sufferings, for only through you can their victories be known. You are the beauty of everyone who has drawn near to perfection, and you are the crown of all who have triumphed in their contests. Through your own suffering, the martyrs dared to face their sufferings; because they saw pain in you, they endured their afflictions. Grant me, our Lord, to weave the beauty of their [?] from your treasury, which is full of riches for anyone who approaches it. These are the ones who bore the weight of your suffering on their bodies and, through their wounds, raised your image upon the cross. These are the ones who scorned the sword and the flame, and for your sake trampled on [?] in the burning fervor of your love. These are the ones who defied the sword as they were being killed and joyfully offered their limbs to be cut off. These are the ones who ran toward slaughter with great eagerness and received the sword like a gift full of blessings. These are the ones who became food for fire and wild beasts, and did not tremble or shrink back as they were being destroyed for your sake. These are the ones who left the world and their kindred for your sake, and hated homes, brothers, and families so that they might draw near to you. A true friend wins glory only through sincerity; unless he dies for his friends, he does not love. This is love, and there is no other greater than it: that someone should joyfully approach death for his friend.

Someone who loves amid a pleasant life, splendor, and pleasures has no love that is proven in the eyes of the discerning. Fire tests pure gold to see whether it is good, and death, through sufferings, tests love [?] to see whether it is genuine. Unless gold enters the furnace and is refined in it, there is no way for the king’s image to be stamped upon it. And unless someone approaches affliction even to the point of death, the image of divine love is not formed in him. Gold receives an imprint [?] in the furnace so that it becomes an image, and through sufferings a person establishes the image of God within himself. Gold receives ten thousand blows upon the anvil; then they fashion it into an ornament for a crown, with the beauty it has acquired. So too the martyrs gained beauty through their wounds, and now they are woven into the King’s crown in glory. Human tyrants became skilled craftsmen who forged people through sufferings and placed them in the kingdom. They put the martyrs’ body into the fire like gold and made from it a wondrous crown for the great King. They forged it with lashes and gave it beauty through wounds. Fire tested it, and it received an imperishable form. They received blows like gold and acquired beauty like jewels, so that they might adorn the bride in the wedding hall. The slain Bridegroom invited them to the wedding hall, and they brought their blood with them as their offerings. Look, I see a banquet of light filled with the maimed.

Severed necks, bodies sawn apart, and flayed bodies. Slaughtered heads and mangled remains [?] from every torture—the great wedding hall is filled with them. The virgin bride rejoices greatly in these calamities, and the disfigured sights of their severed limbs are dear to her. This one is scourged, that one split open, and another slain; this one is torn to shreds, that one flayed, and another lifted up. Some are bound, and some are killed by persecutors; one is torn apart, and another is ripped to pieces by wild beasts. For one, the scent of his burning rises from the fire like incense; another is torn apart as evildoers rip him to pieces. One was stripped bare, another torn to shreds, and another cut apart. They all unjustly endured every kind of affliction. A great banquet of crucifixion, the mistress of sufferings! Whoever entered it pressed out the wine of pain for himself and drank. The guests whom the heavenly Bridegroom called, who had entered with him—a sharpened sword met them in his wedding hall. Blazing fire together with a sword thirsty for blood, the striking of stones, and the gnashing of lions’ teeth. With the great smoke rising from the blaze came the fury of the pagans, whose waves resembled those of the great sea. The saints became accustomed to sufferings of this kind, and joyfully endured pains without complaint. It is easy for love not to complain when afflicted, for it bears everything and endures everything, as it is written.

In their love, the martyrs endured pains and sufferings, afflictions and scourging, while being abused by the wicked. The cluster of grapes of life, which the Jews pressed with a spear, made the martyrs drunk with its wine so that they could bear their afflictions. They drank deeply of that wine [?] of the crucifixion, until they did not even feel the fire during their struggles. The wine they drank from Golgotha made them walk joyfully upon the flames. They anointed themselves for the contest with blood from the side of Christ the King, and the enemy’s raised hand slipped off them. The wretched one who fought and brought Adam down among the trees struggled to bring the martyrs down before the judges. The spirit of falsehood, which sang deceit into Eve’s ears, enticed them in order to make them deny their faith through its cunning. But they did not accept the evil counsel or the hateful speech, for they were shrewder than the serpent that had led them astray. They had gained wisdom from the skillful teaching of Jesus and had been trained in shrewdness and innocence. In his gospel he commanded and taught them to resemble both doves and serpents. In innocence they resembled doves, as they had been taught; and while being killed, they remained quiet and guileless among their killers. If a dove had anger in it, it would not live with someone who threatened to kill its young. And because this quality is beautiful, the disciples also acquired it,

so that they would not become angry when being destroyed by the wicked. The serpent is shrewd, guarding itself against harm and living cautiously every day, like the wise. For in its shrewdness it knows that wherever it is caught, they will crush its head, and therefore it flees from its attackers. For if [?] it is caught and struck, it hides its head and surrenders its whole body to suffering and blows. For discerning people, faith is the head of the soul; and the martyrs guarded it at their trial so that it would not be struck. Their only concern was to guard their truth with the shrewdness of serpents full of venom. They carefully held fast to faith, the head of life, and surrendered their limbs to cutting and hacking. The serpent’s life is in its head, and if they crush it, it loses its life; therefore it hides its head [?]. The soul’s life depends on faith and is preserved in it; and if faith is harmed, life is lost. And it is necessary to guard the faith against stumbling blocks, just as a snake hides its head from blows. So the martyrs guarded the faith with reverence, and while they received blows from the judges, it received none. The martyrs perceived another life that was to come, and for this reason they gave their bodies over to endure suffering. Through the sufferings they endured and the blows they received, they stirred the earth to recognize that God has another world greater than this one.

They endured suffering because of the pagans until the pagans believed and acknowledged that there was something hidden which they perceived. The persecutors saw how joyful they were in the face of death [?], and wonder moved them greatly to offer praise. And they began to reflect: “If there were no other life, these people would not treat their own lives with such contempt. They take pride in something great and hidden as they are killed, and for its sake they run toward the sword with a pure heart. These people perceive a good hope, glorious and hidden, and therefore they scorn every blow and threat. Who is this Jesus for whose sake they die, and why do these people take pride in his name as they are killed? Why do they lovingly acknowledge him until death, enduring suffering and not denying him in their afflictions? They say that he was crucified and proclaim that he was killed. Why, then, do they take pride in him and worship him before everyone? Why do they worship him if he is a human being [?] sufferings? And if he is not alive, how can they die for his sake? There is great power in the one who was crucified by the Jews, and in his love he makes human beings worthy to believe in him. Whether he is God or a human being, the Son of God, there is power in him that draws people to faith in him.” Because of the afflictions the martyrs endured at the hands of their persecutors, the pagans who saw their torments said these things. And because of these pagans who honored [?]

Through their sufferings they gathered a people to the proclamation. The spectators marveled at how they endured every blow, and they convinced the whole world that they were not being beaten for nothing. Through their afflictions, the martyrs became his witnesses [?], testifying that he has another life to give to those who love him. With their blood they wrote the faith in the God of all, and through their deaths they became teachers of the truth. It was not their words that were accepted by their hearers, nor [?] the action of their faith, how true it was. From the blows and sufferings they endured in their bodies, everyone knew that the toil of their trials was not in vain. Look, their testimony is depicted in their own sufferings, and their teaching is written in the lashes on their bodies. Everyone agrees to accept their testimony, because they sealed it with their blood and accepted their sentences. The martyrs died in the hope they had seen: that there is a resurrection. Blessed is Christ, who crowned his martyrs in their contests. Its conclusion: Glory to you, Lord of all, for those who [?] in you are not put to shame.
On the Renewal of Creation
Homily Twenty-Six. On the Renewal of Creation, suitable for New Sunday. Response: Blessed is he who built us and then destroyed us, and will build us again and never again destroy us. My brothers:

One Creator created creation from nothing, and he renews it [?] from lowly things into glorious things. One will fashioned the world, worn down by [?], and he frees it from bondage to hardships. One is the Lord who began a work that involves no toil,

and he brings it to completion in a perfection that lacks nothing. One is the Nature that brought everything into being, rational beings and those without speech, and in the harbor of his love he gives his creatures rest, so that they will not be worn down. One is the command that nourishes the world with visible things, and he will give life to visible things through things unseen. One authority orders the course of Watchers and human beings, and from his treasury he distributes gifts according to their wishes. One is the Hidden One, whose nature is hidden and whose work is revealed. Though he is hidden, his works cry out about his hiddenness. His works testify to his incomprehensible hiddenness, for ever since they came into being, they have been unable to behold his eternity. He exists eternally, and his existence has no beginning. He willed that the works he made should endure without end. He wished to give the works he made a share in his eternity, so that, by enduring, they would become witnesses to his eternity. It is an everlasting wonder that the Self-existent One and his work should endure, so that, just as he is everlasting, his creation too should be everlasting. The Creator of creation did not create it for a limited time, but so that, through its endurance, it would preserve time itself. The ages have moved along with the created order ever since they came into being. The ages pass, but creation does not pass out of existence. The ordered course of its enduring existence proceeds without end. Even if it comes to an end, its renewal accompanies its end. My mind drew me to turn to its end, for I saw that it was far more wonderful than the time of its beginning. Its end is wonderful because its renewal follows it. It was this renewal that I said was more wonderful than the beginning. Its beginning was wonderful, for it was suddenly fashioned from nothing. Its renewal, which happens suddenly, is also very wonderful. Just as it suddenly came into being from nothing, so at the end it becomes something more wonderful than it was at first. It is wonderful that the Good One renews the creation he made, so that, in its renewal, it may endure with him without end. From the beginning he desired that it should exist without end, and on the day of completion he fulfills the longing of his love. He had this desire from eternity, without beginning:

That it should exist first until time is fulfilled, and then forever. He knew this desire before everything existed. It was not through some new decision that he wished to establish things and then established them. He was also fully aware of the renewal that would follow his building. No new thought compelled him to renew what he makes old. There is no deliberation in that mind which cannot be comprehended, nor any act of willing in that will which does not first refuse and then desire. He had thought of what he did before doing it, and he had desired that purpose which he willed and which brought things into being. It was not through some new decision that he did everything he has done and will do, since everything that came into being was already present to him before it existed. Long ago he gave a beginning to the work of his hands, and gloriously he renews his handiwork at the end of the ages. He who is glorious in his work established times and orders for his works, and his creation cannot say how glorious and orderly he is. Glorious and orderly is the arrangement he made for the two worlds: to one he assigned a definite span of time, and the other is forever. In one he established an order in which everyone continues in toil; the other he made to give the weary rest without labor. In one he stored up kinds of training full of toil; the other he filled with activity that involves no weariness. He looked upon them both with the hidden eye of his [?], and arranged them as seemed fitting to the one who knows everything. He knew that the dwelling of time would be dissolved, and he encouraged it beforehand through the renewal he promised it. Through promises he stirred its desire and drew it toward knowing him, so that, once it knew him, it would believe that he could raise it from its fallen state. As though taking hold of someone who had fallen, he grasped it with a hand of flesh, supported it, set it upright, and lifted its gaze toward the heights. With a human hand the Lord of the world took hold of the world and cried out to it, “Rise and regain your strength from your sickness!” He gave it, as medicine, some of the earth from which it had been formed. It drank of it and shook off the bitterness of mortality. The dead world came to life and was raised in a mystery, and it learned the manner in which it would again be raised in actual fact. He opened a path for it to await the preparation of the heights, and sent one of its own ahead of it as a guide.

He dispatched one [?] from the world to another world, to prepare a perfect world for the weary world. Like a high priest, he commanded him to enter the sanctuary above, to make atonement there for the sins of the weary world. The Lord of all took from all a pledge of peace, so that, while that pledge was with him, all would believe that they would return to him. He fixed a time for his return from the presence of his beloved, and now the inhabitants of earth and heaven await him. The world, worn out by sin, awaits that delight, so that it may receive release from the debts it owes to its God. Every day it awaits that messenger whom it sent ahead [?], so that he may come and announce to it the renewal of its old age. Suddenly the light of the world dawns from that world and drives away from it the darkness of earthly labors. With the light of his face he removes the mourning of its sadness and lifts from it the heavy burden of being subject to suffering. With the sound of the trumpet he rouses it from the sleep of its ignorance, and it starts up and rises as though from the bed of its grievous pains. Suddenly, without delay, he renews it completely, and no place within it remains without renewal. The whole creation is renewed in that renewal: heaven and earth and everything contained within their boundaries. Speaking and speechless creatures rest together from their labors, and they no longer grow weary through the hardships [?] of their needs. That world gives everyone, together with everyone else, rest from every burden. Among those who enter it, there is no one whose weariness does not find relief in its rest. It is that rest which is described in the books of the Spirit, and in it the weary voices of prophecy find rest. In its rest there is no toil to wear down anyone who rests there, nor does anyone any longer fear a change from good to bad. In that renewal there is no change between good and bad, nor does anyone, while awaiting one hope, look for another hope. In it all the expectations of the Watchers and human beings are bound together.

In it the first things and the last things reach their completion. In the harbor of its peace the heavenly hosts rest, and they are no longer worn out by governing heaven and earth. In it they rest from their labors on behalf of human beings, because human activity and deeds also cease. Human beings rest from the weariness of human affairs and no longer depend on the use of earthly things. The liberation of human beings gives the spiritual beings rest from toil, and human beings and the peaceful ones share one way of life. The spiritual beings are occupied with exhausting labors on behalf of humanity. When human beings are set free, both those who command and those who receive commands rest. Because of humanity’s need, they now give commands and also receive them. When humanity has become rich, they no longer give commands or receive them. There humanity reigns in the wealth of immortal life, and those who serve the needs of its life also rest with it. The weary one receives perfect rest that never changes, and created beings no longer toil or suffer exhaustion on his behalf. The whole creation rests with him, and he with everything; rational beings and speakers alike remain in stillness and silence. His sufferings of soul and body cease. He no longer struggles, nor do passions struggle against him. Sin is extinguished, and death is extinguished for him; the fierce battle that wages war against him comes to rest. In his rest even the rebels who opposed him without cause find rest, and they share with him the one will of the one Creator. One will reigns there over all and in all, and there is no opposition, no hindrance, nothing at all. One reigns in accord with the will that crowned him, and he judges by the will that gave him judgment. The Son, who shares our human nature, received all judgment from the Father, and he gives gifts to the good and punishments to the wicked. On the day of his revelation he displays the power of his supremacy, subjects everything, and renews everything by the might of his authority. Creation awaits the renewal that will take place through his hands, and now she groans, wondering when the time of her renewal will come. Like labor pains, sufferings strike her vulnerable nature,

as she waits to give birth to children of immortal life. Like a woman in labor, she bears the burden of mortality, and that very day will ease her sorrow and take away her mourning. At a hidden command she suddenly puts on the garment of renewal, and like a bride she stands in glory that does not decay. In great glory she sees how glorious she herself is, and the eyes of her soul never tire of looking at her own face. Those who rejoice in that joy never have enough of it, especially human beings and the peacemakers who served well. Human beings and the watchers rest there in that delight, and they become heirs of blessings without end. The watchers rest from service that has learned to cease, and they are no longer worn out by the continual course of changing times. The movements of their thoughts rest from change, and they no longer desire hateful desires as demons do. The course of those who turn aside from their ranks comes to an end, and they all submit to the one will that established them. The demons cease the lawlessness of their blasphemies, and instead of insults they offer praise, even against their will. They no longer marshal mocking accusations against human beings, nor do they arrogantly revile the name of the divine Being. One loving will belongs to all toward everyone—to the peacemakers and the inhabitants of earth, to the good and the wicked. The good and the wicked acquire a love that does not grow cold, and although their deeds distinguish them greatly, they are united in love. In perfect love, watchers and human beings unite together to offer one song of praise to the one [?]. The good and the wicked cry out praise wherever they are, and there is no end to the sound of the praise offered by those who praise. Praise is the occupation in which they continually persevere, an unbroken continuance without interruption or toil. Everything that happens there happens without toil, and no mouth, as long as it is mortal, can say how. How can mortality [?] describe in words the way of life of that immortal order? How can a tongue of perishable flesh portray that beauty which has no equal?

That way of life has no equal in this way of life, nor is there an illustration that shows it accurately. Only its own true likeness resembles it, and only it can recount the vastness of its great glory. Its glory stirred me to describe her splendor [?] in words: how glorious she is, and how she glorifies those who are worthy of her. I saw that those who offer praise are destined to be glorified, and wonder seized me at the greatness of that indescribable glory. The glory of that day cannot be expressed: how another creation comes into being in place of the one that exists. It is not that creation becomes another creation there, nor that something else takes the place of what existed before. The very thing that came into being out of nothing in the beginning is what comes to have an existence more glorious than its former one. It is the same nature of spiritual beings that gains glory, and in their nature they remain the same, without alteration. It is the same race of bodily beings that inherits life, and in their own nature they gain immortal life. The resurrection of those who rise brings rest to body and soul, and without ceasing they sing praise to the one who renews all things. Those who are renewed give thanks to the one who renews [?] all things, because nothing at all is left without being renewed. Everything is renewed [?] without losing its original nature, and everything is transformed, and its transformation has no end. Rational beings grow rich in blessings beyond words, and speechless things also rest in an order that cannot be disturbed. The heavens remain in the same pattern [?] in which they were established, while their pillars neither shake nor are shaken. The sun and moon cease the course they continually follow—not that they cease to exist, but that they rest from their courses. The speechless things, which have no understanding, rest from their courses and become again that light which existed in the beginning. The light gathered in their spheres returns to the light, and the light remains in its own nature without end. Not a single ray from the luminaries is lost, nor is anything diminished from the beauty of its radiance. Nothing in its nature loses anything belonging to its nature, nor does it remain what it is without transformation.

That change compels everything to be transformed, and once transformed, it remains in an order that does not change. The blowing movements of the swiftly moving air become still, because earthly beings have no need for its blowing. As though entering a harbor, it rests from its changes, and it does not weary the spiritual beings who move it. There is no need for its subtle substance to become dense, nor for it to receive liquid water and sprinkle it on the earth. The very nature of liquid water also becomes completely still, and it no longer rages wildly as it did before. The blowing of the winds does not wear down the delicate body, nor does that delicate body flow according to its fluid nature. Perishable natures are not worn down by their changes, since nothing needs the change that comes from the elements. There are no elements in that spiritual way of life, nor does anyone serve or receive service from a companion. There is one Power that preserves everything without assistance from anything, and by his mighty power earthly and heavenly beings are upheld. By his power he strengthens rational nature so that it does not change, and speechless nature so that it maintains the order of stillness and silence. Speechless beings remain in stillness and silence according to their natures, and they are not required to honor those who possess speech. Those who possess speech possess strength without need, and there is no need for the assistance [?] of silent beings. What use is the rising of the sun to someone who does not toil? And what benefit is the moon’s course to someone who is beyond time? What benefit comes from the rays of the shining stars to someone who does not need illumination from the heavenly lights? What purpose does the blowing of the moving air serve for someone who suffers no suffocation? And what are cold and heat to someone who experiences no suffering? What purpose does the falling of rain and dew serve for those who lack nothing? And what are times or seasons to those who are beyond time? What purpose do the changes of summer and winter serve for someone who does not change, or the counting of months and days for someone whose life has no end? What purpose does the growth of crops and fruit serve for someone who does not eat? And what are creeping creatures and wild animals to someone who has no struggle? What purpose does anything edible serve for someone who does not need the strength that comes from food?

What purpose do envoys and messengers sent to humanity serve where the inclination is bound [?] by loving affection? Humanity is bound by loving affection in that order of existence, and has no power to turn toward the opposite. Together with humanity, everything rests from every toil, and in that same structure everything is preserved without destruction. Let no one say that anything among all that came into being perishes [?], for everything remains and is preserved in its own nature. Light remains in its own luminous nature, not under restraint, but in the order in which it was established. Air remains in its own subtle nature, not blowing, but in unchanging stillness. Darkness is preserved in its own dark nature, not according to the order of this present distinction, but in [?]. There is no distinction between light and darkness, because there is no sun to separate night from day. There is no daytime, because there is no toil for those free from toil [?]; nor is there night, because there is no sleep for those who do not sleep. Humanity lives without sleep, toil, or suffering, and therefore does not need the ordering of night and day [?]. These things came into being and were established to meet the needs of human life, and in humanity’s delight the course of its servants comes to rest. The earth rests from the labor of summer and winter and is not worn out giving fruit to the one who cultivates it. It remains in the order it had when it first came into being, and its structure is neither dissolved nor destroyed. In the very structure in which it was formed when it did not yet exist, both it and the natural elements within it are preserved. Along with it, the weary elements rest from their weariness, and along with it they maintain an unchanging order of stillness. Along with it, the exhausted seeds rest from sprouting, since the food they produce is no longer needed by those who eat it. In it, the sprouting of all trees also ceases, and they no longer sprout or wear themselves out growing. In it, the element of fire is hidden wherever it exists; although its usefulness ceases, it itself does not cease to exist. Over it [?] the waters lie spread out, resting as they are,

neither flowing nor stirred by the gusts of air. In it, the various kinds of things that flow from it are stopped up, and they remain still and silent, without being used. Every fashioned thing that came from it returns to it. Gold and dust, the precious and the despised, are buried in it. Everything is in it, everything is upon it, and it is together with everything. Through its preservation, everything is preserved from destruction. In it sleep all those able to move over its surface: creeping creatures, wild animals, and winged birds as well. In it, the speechless creatures cease their living activity—not that they disappear, but that they cease reproducing. The speechless species suddenly cease reproducing. This is a rest that gives the world repose, not destruction. There is no destruction in what perishes, none at all, for everything returns to the earth and is concealed in it. Among rational beings and speechless creatures, none perishes completely except one rational being and one speechless creature. The one who perishes entirely, body and soul, is the human being who becomes an instrument of the devil. He alone is lost from the life of rational beings, and he is pledged to the resurrection of the dead that takes place for the body. That lost one perishes completely, body and soul, and his destruction becomes a spectacle for all creation. All creation examines his destruction and marvels at the mercy that mercifully preserved it from destruction. Through that one who perishes, it learns the power of the one who brought it into being, who formed it in mercy, preserved it in his love, and renewed it by grace. Through his destruction, it sees a sight unfitting for it to see: a living soul whose life comes to an end and ceases to live. The soul acquires incorruptible qualities in its very coming into being. [?] What a wonder that the source of its life suddenly runs dry! The nature of the spirit does not undergo corruption, not at all. Who would not marvel at what happens through the Creator’s power? It is the Creator’s power that destroys the soul of one human being, so that people may learn how evil human wickedness is. The wickedness of that man’s evil teaches everyone

that unless people lived by mercy, they would not remain alive. Through his mercy toward everyone, he shows the power of his grace; and through one who perishes, he proclaims the truth of his justice. Through the destruction of body and soul, he teaches two things: that he is good and that he is just toward speaking creatures and silent ones. Rational and speechless creatures learn together about both: neither his goodness nor his justice can be overcome. In justice he condemns the guilty one who made himself guilty, so that his compassion may not become disorderly. Through the one who perishes, he shows everyone a great order—not merely to put on a display, but to make known that he deserves to perish. He does not do this to display the power of his justice, but to shame Satan [?], who thinks that through him he can conquer everyone. That man perishes utterly, to Satan’s [?] shame, so that he cannot boast that through a human being he began and brought his work to completion. He led people astray from the beginning of humanity, and through a human being he completes his deception [?], yet does not achieve completion. The desire of that bitter soul is not fulfilled, because the shrine in which he seeks to hide is destroyed. In a tower of flesh he sets up the instrument [?] of his bitterness; but his tower is demolished, and he himself is bound with ropes of fire. He falls into a fire whose heat is hotter even than fire, and into darkness whose gloom surpasses that of dark places. In the severity of his torments, creation sees something new: although he feels no pain, his sufferings are multiplied and his torment doubled. Earthly beings and heavenly beings [?] marvel at his torments—at how brazen he was, and how just is the punishment for his wrongdoing. Wickedly he sought to usurp the glorious name for himself, and Justice, with perfect justice, pronounced his sentence. The Creator is just, and just is the judgment by which he passed sentence: he chastises a few and spares many, to teach everyone wisdom. In justice he acts, chastising the wicked who despised his commandments; and wisely he gives gifts to those who keep his love. Wisely he destroys one human being out of all, and mercifully he gives life to everyone through his life. He gives a sign to rational and speechless creatures, so that they may see that his power can accomplish everything, as the Lord of all.

He is Lord over all, and all rational and speechless creatures belong to him. To him belongs the name of self-existent Being and Godhead. It is a marvel [?] for the self-existent One, who created the creation from nothing, to preserve the order of his creative work without confusion. It is a great order by which he renews his creative work, so that through its renewal he may depict a demonstration of his kindness. In his kindness he shows everyone, through the renewal of all things, so that everyone may learn the providential care of the Lord over everything. Through his providence everything came into being from nothing, but the works he made were unwilling to acknowledge his providence. He wished to give understanding to his works at the end of time. That is why he brings about that renewal and a just judgment. Through the renewal they learn the power of his creative activity: he is the one who created, and he is the one who renews creation a second time. Those who were unwilling from the beginning to know the one who established everything will learn the power of his divinity on the final day. This is the purpose of that renewal at the end: that creation may learn the power of the Creator [?] who created it. Great is the lesson creation learns in that renewal. It marvels within itself at how much greater it becomes than it now is. It considers the time of that training as nothing when that order is compared with this one here. It even thinks to itself that it does not exist, although it certainly does, when it contemplates the permanence of what lasts forever. It fixes its mind on that endless permanence, and its soul's love cannot get enough of its delight. Astonished at its delight, my mind too moves in bewilderment, and [?] to gaze clearly on the splendor of its beauty. “Look closely,” my mind counseled itself, and it began to travel a road it had never seen before. My thoughts journeyed along the new road of the renewal of everything. They were astonished and amazed at how wonderful the things beyond are. They stood in amazement, although they had not truly seen what they saw. They grew weary and gave up, because they could not see the vision they sought. Good hope encouraged them not to lose heart.

And they began aiming at the goal they sought to portray. I set a target for the speech of my mind, so that it might aim toward it [?]. And now I seek to aim well, if that is possible. The mind can see beautiful things clearly, and nothing prevents it if it is willing. I wished to recount beautiful things before those who are beautiful, so that they might aim to look closely at beautiful things. I have recounted, as best I could, the beautiful things of the day of renewal. And I recount them again, to stir people to [?] them. Who would not love the repetition of words full of wonder? And who would not meditate on glorious things that bring him glory? Their subject is full of wonder and glory for anyone who meditates on it. That is why I have meditated, and still meditate, on the thoughts they contain. I long to meditate on them without ever having enough, so that perhaps I may keep my heart from dwelling on ugly things. Through experience I gained experience in thought, and I learned that good meditation is good for the one who practices it. Come, mind, meditate rightly on things rightly ordered, and lovingly repeat the words about the renewal of everything. Come, look closely at how beautiful the renewal of everything is, and praise and exalt the one who renews our aged condition. Our Creator looked upon our old condition before creating us, and at our formation he foreshadowed the day of our renewal. As one comforts a child, he wished to comfort the childishness of our soul, so that it would not grow weary in the old age of this troubled world [?]. In the form of an image he depicted invisible likenesses and showed them to the hidden [?] mind concealed within our soul. He showed our mind the renewal that will come at the end, and although it was very far away, he placed signs of it in things close at hand. Through things close at hand he showed us the power of distant things, and through visible things he taught us the order of hidden things. Through what is revealed he revealed to us the hidden nature of his divinity, and he made a tongue of flesh the herald of his secrets. With a tongue of flesh he spoke to us about things to come [?], in the manner in which flesh is accustomed to hearing bodily things. He taught the person of flesh a spiritual mystery.

Flesh spoke, and people of flesh listened to a new language. A person of flesh [?] spoke a new language with people of flesh, and perhaps someone listening asks, “Who is it that spoke?” Do you wish to hear who spoke, O listener? Listen to me and learn that it was a man who spoke [?] with humanity. It was a man: the Spirit spoke within his soul, and he spoke with humanity. He listened to hidden things and interpreted them through human beings. He became a mediator between humanity and the Creator, and through his service as an envoy he reconciled the Lord with his creatures. Through his mediation he ended the strife between all and among all, and proclaimed on earth the good news of a peace that does not change. This is the man who reconciled everything with the Lord of all, and he is the one who opened a new road for the renewal of everything. He made known to us the renewal that will take place at the end, and he showed us the path along which faith travels. He taught us that our old condition is renewed in him, and he drew [?] a pattern for us, so that we might become like him through a mystery. In his own person he showed what concerns us, so that we would not doubt the hidden things he promised us. He was the first to take off the garment of mortality, and in his very nature he ascended and was exalted above death. As though pointing with a finger, he showed humanity the renewal of his body: “Look [?], mortals, at the body that has become immortal!” Divine power raised him on this condition: that through his resurrection he would depict an example of the renewal of everything. He renewed all creation together with him in a mystery, and through him he will truly renew it at the end of time. Through him takes place that renewal which is beyond words, and through him even that judgment which cannot be expressed is pronounced. The Lord of all chose him from among all as the firstfruits, so that he might take his own place before the work of his hands. Through his visible presence he fills the place of the Self-existent One for all, and creation rests, as in a harbor, in the senses of his body. In him the free movements of reason are bounded, and they do not strain to pursue an inquiry into the hiddenness of the Hidden One. He becomes for all a holy temple of the One who holds all, and in him the worship of all is offered to the Lord of all. All creation enters with him into the presence of the Lord of all,

and offers him one undivided thanksgiving. This is also the purpose of his election and exaltation: that he should become a haven that gives creatures rest from their labors. He gives the weary world rest from its weariness, and with the breath of his mouth he drives the cloud of sufferings away from it. On the day of his revelation he reveals the power of his might, and creation sees the power of the divine Being displayed gloriously in him. Suddenly the light of his dawning shines upon all creatures, and there is none among created things that does not marvel and take refuge in him. The Lord of all turns all inhabitants toward him, so that they may watch as he judges all and renews all. With ease he gives his signal for what is to happen, and at once the deed [?] his signal without delay. He cries out a single utterance on earth, and all hear it; before it is finished, everything is completed, at rest, and set in order. He too follows the pattern of that command which suddenly called creation into being in the beginning, and renews all through the power of the Lord of all. That very power which made everything from nothing is the power by which he renews heaven and earth, rational beings and those without speech. He gives rational beings and those without speech rest from toil and change; they no longer labor or suffer weariness through arduous tasks. He himself began with that renewal which cannot perish, and he brings it to completion in a perfection without end. He was the first to enter a life beyond harm, and he acquired the power to give life to others as well. The mortal inherited the possessions of the immortals, and he gives human beings and spiritual beings a share in his inheritance. It is written that we have become heirs with him, and we are indeed becoming so. Therefore the promise expressed in his words is reliable and cannot prove false. The spiritual beings saw revealed truth through the earthly one, and they rejoiced and praised the One who revealed in him the truth of his hiddenness. The heavenly hosts raised a cry of praise on earth to the Hidden One, who openly showed his love to the members of his household. He revealed his great love to [?] through a human being, and taught them that among created things there is none greater than humanity.

He made the human being ruler over the rulers among the works of his hands; and behold, the ranks of ministers [?] in him [?] nature. Creation bows before his dominion as before a lord, and honors him because of the power gloriously displayed in him. The Creator's power willed to raise him to the height of his own name, and behold, he is called by the name to which no other can be compared. No created thing bears the Creator's name, nor does creation as a whole. This is the wonder: that a creature was deemed worthy of the Creator's name. The Creator honored his creation by what he did: he took a certain portion of it and honored it with his glory. That man in whom these things happened is a portion of the whole, and through his honor the whole is honored together with the Lord of all. His soul is a portion of the spiritual beings who are not subject to suffering, and they are close to him in kinship and exaltation. His body is a portion of all corruptible bodies, and they are related to him through their bodily stock and renewal. There is a portion of all created things in him, the firstfruits of our life, and in his exaltation there is also the exaltation of the whole creation. How, then, can anything among created things perish? For everything is gathered together and preserved in one of our race. How is it possible, while the firstfruits dwell in glory, for the body from which the firstfruits came to remain in dishonor? No, listener, do not divide the love that embraces all, and do not tear the complete body apart from its unity. Do not doubt how this can happen. Believe that the Creator's power is capable of everything. Everything hidden and visible is easy for the Creator's power, and he is not hindered whenever he wishes to do something. The Creator himself was pleased to act in this way, and according to his loving will it was already accomplished before he acted. It was not only recently that he chose one man for the renewal of all, for he had chosen him before he created the creation in the beginning. What he did was present in him together with his own existence—not that it already existed, but that it was not hidden from him. Without a beginning, this decision stood firm with him, and it was present to him just as it is after time.

And if this is so—and it is indeed true—let us not doubt the deed that has existed from eternity. The Being who brought everything into existence exists from eternity, and hidden in him were all the things that came into being whenever they came into being. From his own perspective, the world was created before he created it, and it was renewed before he announced its renewal. He renewed it a second time according to his loving will, desiring our life, and taught us the order of his constancy and his work as Creator. Through these things that he did for our sake, he taught us how much he loved us and how greatly he honored us through his glorious deeds. He loved us and created us, though he knew that we would hate him; and he renews us, fully aware that we are unworthy. We are unworthy—and however much we say it, we are unworthy—to receive a rank high and exalted above created beings. The Creator's nature cannot be compared with created things. Who would not marvel that he made us his equals through the greatness he bestowed? His will chose one man and took great delight in him, and he placed his will in the hands of that man's will, so that he might govern everything. He placed the divine will in the hands of his will, and there is no will that is not willingly brought within his bounds. Through him the temporal world and the everlasting world are sustained, and he governs earthly beings and those who dwell in peace. He nourishes all from the treasury of the one who delighted in him, and he orders everything according to the will of the one who establishes order. He orders everything and gives life to all, [?] a member of our race; though he is a human being, he holds a divine rank. His nature teaches that the rank he received is higher than himself, and he himself also bears witness that his rank is higher than his created constitution. Come, then, let us marvel at the rank that has reached our lowly race, and let us give thanks to the one who raised us to the height of his name. Come, let us marvel at the mighty authority of the one who shares our humanity, who renews everything and judges all as Lord of all. Come, let us marvel at him when he appears from where he is, when he suddenly shines forth and veils the light with his own light. Come, let us remember that descent by which he comes down to earth, and then returns and ascends with the whole creation accompanying him. I said that the whole creation ascends with his ascension,

because [?] and speechless beings are bound together in his body and soul. Come, let us prepare ourselves for what he has prepared for us, and let us await that hope which comforts us. Let us lovingly preserve the pledge of life belonging to that renewal, so that we may not be put to shame when heaven and earth are renewed.
On the Ascension of Our Lord
By the very same author. Discourse Thirty-Six. On the Ascension of Our Lord. Refrain. Blessed is Christ, who on the day of his ascension raised us up and seated us with him in heaven. My brothers.

I marveled greatly at our lowly clay, at how great it had become: though it is dust, it proclaimed its authority and reigned over [?]. My thoughts were astonished at the lowly clay, at how high it had been raised, for it became a [?] very well suited to glorious things. I examined mortality, which brings forth sufferings, seeking to understand how it suddenly became a spring that sends life flowing to all. My mind troubled me over the [?] clay of which our body is composed, for it had acquired wings to fly toward the heights. Lowly nature silently beckoned to me: “See the wonder—how greatly the lowliness of Adam’s dust has been exalted!” Susceptibility to suffering, which brings forth sufferings, called and urged me: “Look at the frail nature clothed in glory!” Weak clay, which [?] sufferings, called me and roused me: “Rise and contemplate the son of dust who has reached [?]!” The discernment within me rebuked me as though I were mute: “[?] your mouth; give thanks to the one who has exalted your race!” My inner inclination whispered to me silently and mysteriously: “[?] words; give praise to the bridegroom on high!” My mind advised me: “Lift your gaze toward the heights; [?] the firmament, which has opened its gates to the new king!” My thoughts were stirred by the voice of the spiritual herald, who cries out in the Spirit and shows us the image of victory. I heard the new book of the New Testament being interpreted through revelation to bring our lives to perfection. I saw the twelve chosen witnesses gathered together.

They were asking about the restoration of the kingdom on high. The members of the royal court gathered around the King to ask him, “At what time will you reveal the crown of your sovereignty? Reveal and explain to us whether the promise in your words is near: ‘I will give a reward to Abraham’s descendants,’ as you promised.” The skilled Teacher saw the thinking of those who were children at heart and restrained them from their [?] questioning. The children asked about the kingdom in a fleshly way, and the [?] of all brought them up to maturity. “It is not yours to know the time when the ages will end. Do not yearn to [?] the power of hidden things. This is your task: to carry out the powerful work of proclamation and to be witnesses to the new way that I myself have opened. I want you to put your signatures to the covenant that I established in blood for Adam’s children. I am sending you as envoys to the four quarters, to bring the nations back into kinship [?] with Abraham’s household. I am clothing you in the Spirit’s all-conquering armor, to join battle with the strong one who enslaved humanity. Through you, as through light, I drive away the darkness of error. By kindling them, I illuminate the blind world. Through you I uncover the veil of wickedness that the evil one spread, and I tear apart the hateful garment that he wove in Eden. I set you like mirrors before those who look, so that people may see themselves and hate wickedness. Through you I open the treasury of the Spirit, which enriches everyone. Go out and give the reward—life’s deeds of freedom—to mortal humanity. Through you I complete and fulfill mysteries and prefigurations. Explain the power of wonders and make it shine in everyone’s ears. Through you I open the way of the Spirit for those on earth. Show them the path of restoration that does not decay. Through you I reveal severe judgments and abundant mercy. Admonish and rebuke, so that you yourselves will not be found guilty when judgment is pronounced.” The Teacher finished giving his disciples the appropriate instructions and began to travel along the new road leading upward. He accomplished the will of the one who sent him by saving humanity, and completed the work of his visitation on behalf of all. He bore victory before the eyes of spiritual and bodily beings, and beings with speech and without speech carried him in procession with fitting love. Earthly and heavenly beings gathered to accompany him as he journeyed to receive the kingdom on high. A hidden command harnessed the chariot with swift runners of wind and commanded the air to carry the King who had conquered and ascended. It spread linen cloths—clouds of light—over the chariot. The King sat down, and the command placed a crown on his head. Beings with speech and without speech yoked their voices beneath the chariot [?], and openly escorted the Hidden One, the Eternal One in a body. The charioteer directed the fiery steeds toward the heights and taught them to travel along a road that had never been trodden. The command sounded like a trumpet in the ears of the deaf, so that they opened the gates for the King to enter in glory. He raised a signal toward the gate, the garment of water, and opened the gate that was constructed from sheets of water. By a word, the command opened a new gate for the new King, a gate through which no human foot had passed.

He alone blazed the road to the kingdom on high and entered to minister in the Holy of Holies as the high priest. It fell to him to minister spiritually in the sanctuary on high, in a pure place that is not defiled by earthly things. Hail to our nature, which became great in name and deeds, which ascended and reigned above rulers and authorities! Hail to our [?], who attained the rank of headship and subjected speaking and speechless beings to his authority! He walked the earth and took captives from the mighty one; he led them away and ascended to a place secure from harm. He humbled the rebellious tyrant and cast him down from his oppressive rule, and clothed his armies in spiritual armor. He taught them the strength of spiritual combat, so that they would direct themselves toward the goal by which he himself had conquered. He showed them the ascending path, the road to the heights, through the sign of his body, which was being borne in glory above the air. He encouraged them to gaze at him with delight, so that they might see his glory and gain hope in his promises. He made the air solid like a chariot before their eyes, set his visible body upon the wind, and reached the heights. He sent to them some of the spiritual beings who attended him in glory, and they astonished them with the white garments they wore. He showed them the heavenly beings clothed in light: if his messengers were wrapped in light, how much greater must his own light be! A garment of light formed a barrier before them, so that they would not strain themselves while trying to see what was not permitted. Two thoughts stirred those earthly men, and for two reasons they were gazing toward the heights. They looked to see whether they could see the gates opening, or whether perhaps the constitution of his body was being changed. For they were pondering how a body could ascend to the [?], and how something possessing a bodily constitution could enter through a closed gate. Amid this uncertainty, he sent the spiritual beings to them to dispel the anxiety and doubt in their minds. They suddenly stood before their eyes and astonished them, for they had not approached them by walking, but appeared suddenly. They addressed them explicitly as Galileans and showed them that they knew the one who had ascended. Why are you standing and gazing at the heights above? Why are you straining yourselves over something difficult for bodily [?]? Learn from us, as those who are trustworthy concerning hidden things, that this Jesus will come in the same way that he ascended. In the appearance in which you saw him with your bodily senses, in that very appearance he remains, unchanged in body and soul. In that same appearance he remains in indescribable beauty, and he will come at the end of time to judge all. In that same appearance of the visible body and the hidden [?], he ascended and reigned in accordance with the will that chose him from among all. Whatever disputes the heretics may raise about that appearance, I confess it and do not deny the testimony of the Watchers. I do not make liars of the spiritual beings, the chosen witnesses, nor do I alter the clear imprint of the sound of their words. I do not disregard the utterances of the King's servants, nor do I constrain the stewards of the hidden command. True and trustworthy is the record of the ascension of the firstfruits of our race.

The spiritual beings also set their hands to it, sealed it, and ratified it. They too followed the course of the words of the one who ascended, who revealed and declared in what nature he rose from the tomb. They touched [?] and saw the place of the spear and the places of the nails. They knew and understood that a spirit does not possess flesh and bones. He showed flesh and bones to the witnesses of his death, so that they would not doubt his resurrection, thinking that it was a likeness and not he himself. He showed his confidants the nails and the spear in his body after he had become immortal and no longer subject to suffering. After his death he showed something new, beyond the usual order: he ate and drank with his heralds and strengthened their certainty. He compelled his nature, whose susceptibility to suffering glory had swallowed up, and showed it in suffering, accepting food like someone in need. It is certain to us that he showed suffering without being subject to suffering; but how he showed it, he alone knows. We do not contradict his utterances that he ate and drank. How he ate is clear to him who testified that he ate. By what he did, he confirmed beforehand the promise of his words, for he said that he would eat with them in the kingdom on high. Otherwise, let those who efface the body and make the Word suffer say how we are to understand that he showed sufferings and ate and drank [?]. Come, interpret for us, you new scribes of the proclamation: whose was the body that underwent sufferings and that hands touched? If the hidden one became visible and became flesh, why did he show us sufferings in his body after he rose? Was his nature perhaps subject to suffering before his coming, so that he showed sufferings to confirm its susceptibility to suffering? Far be it! My own will did not give birth to this audacity. The foolish zeal of those who mingle the natures compelled me, and I said it. It was not from my own desire that I ventured to ascend to the height above. I want to bring them down to earth, because they have been so presumptuous. Pride did not seize me so that I would ponder hidden things. I wanted to curb [?] the boastful words of their blasphemies. It was not the rank of a teacher that I sought to seize for myself. Those childish in heart read perversely, and I was displeased. They reversed the purpose he had adopted at the beginning of his victory, and for this reason I shot the arrows of my words against them. They wanted to put stubble and chaff into the building of truth, and my thoughts grew hot as in a fire, so that I might burn them. They ought to show through their actions how they are constituted, and make known the aim of their thoughts and how they think. If they belong to the body of the church as its members, why do they hate the name of Christ, the head of the body? Why do they reject the name “Son of Man,” which is set down in the Scriptures, and why do they erase the honorable name that our race received? Why do they mix the hidden nature, which cannot be mixed, and why do they mingle the hidden things, which cannot be mingled? The hidden nature is not [?] with the visible body; [?] does not acquire a limit in what is limited. There is no place for the one who holds everything to journey away to, for his nature reigns outside everything and within everything. For this reason I fight with the weapons of my words, to destroy the ranks of those who make the Word suffer and those who [?] the body. They lower the Word to the susceptibility to suffering of lowly flesh,

and exclude the body from the honor it has with the divine Being. The watchers proclaim that he ascended and became king in that very nature of his, but the mouths of those whose hearts are slow to understand are shut. They revealed to the apostles that he would come again in it at the end of time, yet they do not listen to the proclamation of the spiritual beings. It was one of our race who ascended and became king with the divine Being; it was not the divine Being that descended to earth and then ascended. It was our own nature that rode the wind and bridled the air. Rational and speechless beings carried him and honored him for the sake of the Hidden One. It was he who opened a new path through the flowing air and grew wings for flight, though this was not in his nature. It was he who opened the gates of heaven before earth's inhabitants and entered to serve as priest in the Holy of Holies for their lives. He did not enter to serve as priest according to the order prescribed by the Law, but with the blood of his own new covenant. He did not come to minister in earthly things like the priests; he entered heaven to make atonement for everyone through the sacrifice of himself. He entered once and was received in the Holy of Holies, and no further time limit was set for his dwelling there or the greatness of his rank. He entered and appeared before the All-seeing One, as was fitting for him. He gave him rank and placed on him the crown of the name of divinity. By the power of his hidden command, he brought him to the rank above, to that greatness which cannot be compared with that of created beings. He subjected everything to him, and he became king over everything through the power of the one who assumed him. He received authority to judge spiritual and bodily beings. In his judgment he examines the discernment of rational beings, and blows [?], and words and signals of the eyes. Through the visibility of his body I see, in hidden movements, that hidden reality which is [?] from everything, while everything is revealed to it. They contemplate him with the outward senses as one who is visible, and with the mind through the power of the divine Being hidden within him. Watchers and human beings are yoked together under the yoke of his love, and they honor him as the image of the hidden King. In his body, bodily beings see their own limbs, and spiritual beings see their own selves in the movements. They repeat praise spiritually with the voice of their senses and proclaim him holy with the delight of their minds. At all times they worship, in the temple of his body, the one who is hidden within him, and offer him the hidden sacrifices of their thoughts. In the harbor of his body, the movements of their thoughts find rest when they grow weary from searching for the Hidden One who cannot be comprehended. For this reason the Maker of all chose him from among all, so that through the manifestation of his body he might meet the need of all. The creature needed continually to seek what is hidden and to learn the power of hidden things and their manifestations. And because the hidden nature cannot become visible, he set a limit to their questions through a visible image. They continually run in the stadium of the name of Being, and when they reach the gate of his body, they gain the victory. He gives to the athletic striving of their minds the crown that the Hidden One holds out in his hand in return for their labors. Through the hand of his body, the owner of the vineyard gives [?] to the workers who have labored in hope of new life. Through him the talents of the Spirit are returned to the good servants,

who received the money, managed it well, made a profit, and grew rich. From him the wicked servant hears that declaration: “Why did you hide the talent that I placed in your hands?” With him the wise women enter the bridegroom’s bridal chamber, arrayed proudly in a robe of glory that does not perish. He answers the foolish women who have no oil: “Go and enjoy the fruits of your labors, as you [?].” At the sound of his words, those who keep his love gain hope and go out to meet him, to receive their reward in return for their labors. With him they fly toward the heights on the wings of the Spirit, borne in procession upon the chariot of the air’s back. By the visible sign through which his own body ascended, the bodies that became a dwelling for his love are raised up. A cloud carried him like a chariot as he ascended, and a hidden command guided it like reins. In the same way, clouds of light carry bodies by that command which commanded the air and [?] his body. In him he depicted our weaknesses and our glories, and set them down in writing on the tablet of his body. Through him he showed us how grievous our fall had become, and through him he made known to us how exalted our salvation is. In his conception he depicted our formation from dust, and in his birth, how the earth bore us without intercourse. Through his growth among earthly things he revealed that he was one of us, and by enduring sufferings he showed that his nature was that of mortals. By his death he proclaimed the reconciliation accomplished through him, and by his resurrection he undid sin and abolished death. Through his ascent [?] he opened a road for us to ascend to the heights, and in his triumphal procession he exalted our body from the dust. His earthly appearing was like morning for us, and the course of his journey toward the heights was the day’s completion. He set out in the morning and lashed the [?] of our body with sufferings, and rested in the harbor of the heights above as though at evening. Through his ascension we opened gates that had been shut, and he brought us with him into the Holy of Holies, where entry had not been permitted. Our ashes rose with his exaltation to the divine Being, and our dust sat in the rank of a king and gained authority. He took hold of the scepter of sovereignty and reigned over all, and began commanding what was not his own, like the Creator. O dust, how greatly it was exalted through what was not its own! O mortal who dispensed life from what belonged to others! O earthly one who left the earth, the mother of his body, and entered to dwell in the bosom of a mother who was not his by nature! O creature of dust who abandoned his place, a temporary dwelling, and ascended to a place whose permanence has no end! O descendant of Adam’s race, fashioned from the earth, who acquired the rank and the title of divine authority! The heavy one mounted the wings of the wind [?] and flew through the air, astonishing the assemblies on high with his lightness. The assemblies of heavenly beings stood in great amazement as they watched a body flying in an unfamiliar way. The Watchers wove him a crown of glory as he ascended, for they saw that he had opened a road for human beings to their assemblies. They became messengers to the disciples who were grieving, and gladdened them through the white garments they wore. Through his ascension they gained love and compassion for our race.

And they began traveling along a road of peace toward our humanity. They were deeply grieved at our fall from glory [?], but when they saw us rise through one of our own race, they rejoiced again [?] and were comforted. Transgression of the commandment [?] blocked the road between us and them, and with his blood he annulled the sentence that had fenced in our debts [?]. Through his mediation, peace was made for all by the Lord of all, and through his ascension he confirmed the peace of the renewal of all things. He freed the captives who had been imprisoned in the fortresses of [?], and comforted them with the glories he received and inherited. He himself became a mirror of beautiful things, and wove them into splendid crowns for his victorious head. At his conception, glory to the God of all from his creatures, and peace on earth and good hope for those without hope! At the offering of sacrifices, a voice proclaimed consolation: “Look, he is appointed for judgment and as a sign of peace.” His baptism proclaimed his greatness like a trumpet, and the Father’s voice announced his love and the greatness of his rank. His fasting proclaims his victory in the wilderness, where through bodily senses he defeated the conqueror of all. At the time of his death, even silent things became speakers, for a hidden command compelled them, and they gained power. The sound of his [?] killed death and trampled sin, and the dead cried out in death’s ears, “Where is your sting?” On the day of his ascension he called earthly and heavenly beings and showed them a new road for traveling to the heights. Spiritual and bodily beings went out to accompany him, to see how his body flew in a spiritual manner. The sight of his body was delightful to earthly beings, and communion with his soul was greatly cherished by those at peace. The fleshly eye could not get enough of gazing with its bodily senses as he was borne in procession on the chariots [?]. The spiritual beings would not rest or leave him; they strove to see how they might excel in love for him. Even the season in which he ascended was beautiful and delightful; the course of his journey surpassed the sphere of the sun. Along with the victory of the great sun, he won his victory and spread the light of his proclamation to the four quarters. In the month when light conquered darkness, he cleansed away sin and drove away error, the hateful garment woven by the Evil One. In June, light and Light triumphed—the servant and the Lord—and darkness was defeated along with darkness, the [?] of error. The luminary stood at the highest step in the course of its journey and placed darkness at the lowest step, as though in a grave. The Sun of Righteousness also ascended to the height above and cast error and its heralds [?] down into the depth below. By the three hours that light took from darkness, it cut short darkness's course and limited its [?] at the lowest step. Our King also gave three names to his Twelve, and through them they cut off the road of death that the Evil One had opened. His rays descended like rain upon the whole earth and watered her bosom; her fruits ripened [?] in his warmth. The Creator sprinkled the dew of mercy through our firstfruits.

And the fruits of righteousness sprouted in the soil of our soul. In the month when fruits and seeds shout for joy for this temporary life, he brought forth early fruits that bestow life without end. His conception was in Nisan, the month that is the firstborn of the year, and his birth was in Kanun, the month when light plunders darkness. He fasted and was tempted in the gloomy month devoid of fruit, and from the temptations he brought forth early fruits of his soul's endurance. He sacrificed himself at the time when Adam incurred guilt by eating, and through his sacrifice he reconciled the Lord and his servants and made them glad. In the month when Adam's guilt grew strong in Eden, in that very month the second Adam, who conquered death, triumphed. At the time when the foolish [?] heir left his inheritance, the diligent one entered the land of life that does not perish. Through victory he paid off the bond of our debt and enrolled us with him as children [?] and heirs of the riches he received. He brought back our captives from the [?] who had taken our race captive and brought them up to a land that the weapon of his deceit cannot conquer. He placed our spiritual [?] wealth in the height above, where it cannot be ruined by the harm caused by desires. He drew the mind toward the treasures where our soul is placed, so that we might travel among what belongs to us and not hesitate over what does not belong to us. He showed us what belongs to us, so that we might love what is ours like discerning people and not become entangled in what is not ours like fools. He [?] our soul through the promises of things to come, so that the bodily senses would not bind us with desires. He set up for us a milestone of peace on the road he himself traveled, and taught us [?] and how we should journey to the heights of life. Through two roads he showed the course of the two sides, so that everyone might travel whichever one he wishes by his own free choice [?]. He called the road of life narrow because of its toil. And he called the road of destruction broad because of its pleasures. He himself completed the course of the road of life, so that whoever journeys after his words would not grow discouraged. Look, the king has set out on the new road of the King on high. Let us travel with him so that bandits do not strip us. Look, he has raised a standard for his armies at the [?] of heaven. Let us bow before him with movements of the soul instead of bodily limbs. Look, he has opened the gate of the arena into the kingdom. Let us take our battle position against temptations in the hidden mind. Look, he has forged spiritual armor for soul and body. Let us take up the sword of the Spirit’s word on the tip of our tongue. Through his sufferings he cultivated the soil of our body, overgrown with thickets. Come, let us sow good seed in it and bring forth life. With his blood he cleansed the blemishes of our soul and our limbs, so that we might not be stained by the desires of our evil inclinations. Through his sacrifice he reconciled the heights and the depths with the one who sent him. Let us not weaken the peace of all through our negligence. Through his ascension he raised up our body, weighed down by the senses. Let us gain wings through the movements of [?], to where he is. Paul cries out like a trumpet in his authoritative writings that he took us up with him in [?], which he reached at the right hand. We died with him, and he brought us to life with him, for he is [?]. He took us up with him as limbs belonging to the head of the body. Our heart believes that he arose, was raised from the dead, and gave life to all [?]. We are certain that he ascended and reigns [?] above all. With the love of our souls, let us preserve the love that is fitting for him.

And let us not doubt his promises because they are far off. Together with the spiritual beings, let us continually bear witness to his ascension: he is destined to come in the same appearance in which he ascended.
On the Feast of Pentecost

Discourse Twenty-Seven: On the Feast of Pentecost.
Response:
O mortals, let us repay our debt to the one who exalted our race through the power of his wisdom, my brothers.

The Creator opened the treasury of the Spirit before mortals and enriched them from the treasures of his mighty power. The one who enriches all placed his wealth in a vessel, and although it was lowly, he kept a treasury of glorious things in it. He made weak clay the treasurer of his hidden things. He fired it with the Spirit and placed the Spirit in it—the glorious in the lowly. As on lyres, he sang hidden things on the strings of his body, and through his voice he spoke to earthly and heavenly beings. The command rang out like a trumpet through a tongue of flesh, and spiritual and bodily beings gathered around him. A fragile reed became a flute for the living Spirit and delighted all with the sweetness of its songs. The power that gives life to all dwelt in that which gives birth to suffering, and it began to pour forth life to all through the breath of its lips. The sick man who had long lain in the pains of sin began to heal the body's pains and the soul's defects.

The tree that had dried up in the fierce heat of desires suddenly sprouted and bore delightful fruit. The vineyard that had cheated the laborer [?] of his labor and produced wild growth suddenly brought forth a ripe cluster of grapes for wine and yielded praise. The heir [?] who had recklessly squandered the wealth he received returned to his father. His father [?] went to meet him and gave him his wealth. In love and mercy he hurried [?] to meet our lives, and embraced our race through the firstfruits he took from us. He covered our shame with a robe of glory woven by mercy, and gave the power of the Spirit as a pledge, like a ring. He invited and called us to the wedding feast of unending life, to the banquet full of inexhaustible blessings. Through the mystery he betrothed us to fellowship in his love. He opened his treasury and confirmed his words through deeds. He chose one member of our race as the firstfruits, sanctified him by the Spirit, and accepted his sacrifice as redemption. He made him a treasury of hidden and delightful things, and promised through him to enrich everyone from his gift. Through him he promised the members of his race an inheritance of life, and made him a spring to give his own people drink from his life. He filled him with the undiminishing power of his divinity, so that he might give strength to feeble mortality. He pledged and promised to the servants of his proclamation that he would enrich them from the fullness of the power he had received.
