As he was going to the one who sent him, he encouraged them: “Look, I am going, and I am sending the promise of my Father.” He called the riches promised in his words “the Comforter,” who can comfort the poverty of a sorrowful soul. He called him “the Promise,” so that they might receive hope in their minds of the time when they would see his riches openly distributed. He also called him “the Power” hidden in the heights above all, who can prevail over and conquer everything by the might of his greatness. “Remain in the land of Judea, where I suffered, until I place the power of the Spirit in your limbs.

“Remain in Zion, according to the declaration of prophecy, that from her would come forth the one who can forgive sin.” He wished to abolish the sin of the nations on account of the people, and gave as his reason that he turns away sin for Jacob's sake. In Zion he showed that his light and his sentence of judgment were present, enlightening everyone and bringing accusations through his examination. In the place he chose, called by his name, and established his laws, there he explained the power of wonders and the hidden meaning of mysteries. He invited and called the tribes of the nations to Mount Zion, and gladdened them with a feast of sacrifices prescribed by the Law. In Zion he also explained the wonder of that banquet to which earthly beings and [?] gather. There he commanded those who cherished his love to wait for him, so that he might repay them for the love they had shown him. He bound them by the promise of a spiritual reward, so that they would not grow slack when they parted from one another. He mystically placed the seal of the Spirit upon them and marked them with the breath of his lips, so that they would belong to him. Through the breath of his mouth, he showed them the power of his gift, for from him comes the payment of the reward—the riches he promised. He breathed into their faces and strengthened them with the promise of his words. He taught them to forgive sins and to judge wrongdoing. He placed in their hands the key of mercy and the sentence of judgment, to open the gate for both groups, the good and the wicked. He set out to receive the kingdom on high that had been promised to him, and instructed them: “Remain in Judea and proclaim my victory. “Remain there, in the place where I endured suffering and humiliation, for there I will give those who humiliated me a demonstration of my greatness. “Before many people [?], I endured suffering at the hands of insolent men, and in everyone's sight I will display my power [?]. “Where the lowly jeered and laughed at my humility, there proclaim my unconquerable might. “Those who considered me contemptible, full of suffering, and rejected by everyone—I will teach them through the works of my wisdom. “Those who denied me the glory that was rightfully mine as one who was innocent—look, they are being refuted as every tongue sings to me.

“Because they did not praise me with the lyre of David's composition, I will sing [?] of my victory on twelve strings drawn from their tribes.” He arranged them like a twelve-stringed lyre, so that they would praise him with twelve voices, as though with strings. Because they had not offered him the song of thanksgiving they owed him, he played his victory on the lyre of his Twelve. Twelve voices proclaimed his victory like trumpets. Because the tribes had fallen silent, he made the strings of their limbs ring out. At the joyful festival he sacrificed himself as a lamb, and at the festival of Pentecost he marked his victory. He set everyone free through the mystery of the deliverance from Egypt, and distributed his riches like the tablets on Mount Sinai. At the festival when he inscribed tablets of stone, [?] of stone, he traced spiritual letters in the movements of the soul. On the day when he bestowed an inheritance on those of the flesh, he distributed spiritual riches to those of the Spirit. At the time when he wrote the covenant full of death, he sealed the promises of the covenant that gives life. Amid the wonder of the sounds and horns on Mount Sinai, he suddenly made the voice of the Spirit who renews everything ring out. There, a voice full of terror frightened the servants; here, a voice gives hope to soul and body. There were fire, smoke, and violent shaking; here was light distributed in the sign of fire. There, servants ministered to servants with terrifying voices; here, he calls with a gentle voice full of peace. There was the adornment of earthly things for earthly people; here is the beauty of spiritual things for heavenly people. There the mediator too stood in great fear, conveying words to the people whose hearts were divided. Here the head of the Twelve [?] is calm and rejoicing, establishing peace in the minds of his companions. Moses cries out, “Fear and terror fill my thoughts,” while Simon proclaims hope, love, and faith. Moses tore the garment that the bridegroom sent to the bride, while Simon clothed the Church of the nations in a robe of glory. Anger overcame the bearer of the betrothal gifts, and he broke the tablets.

He exposed and revealed the disgrace of the king’s bride. Here the bridegroom’s friends cry out like trumpets and show him the hidden beauty of the holy Church. Those who were fleshly heard the sound of [?] and recoiled from it; here those who were spiritual heard it and yearned to meet it. They cried out to Moses, “You speak to God,” for the Creator’s voice was not pleasing to those who were without God. In the spiritual bridegroom’s bridal chamber, everyone longs for the moment when they will hear fresh good news from the Creator’s voice. With this hope the laborers went out and hired themselves out in the vineyard, to receive as their wages a pledge instead of a denarius. The eager workers heard the promise of the King on high and readied their movements and their limbs to put on armor. Suddenly a sound rang out like a trumpet before the kingdom, and the command gathered the armies to meet the King. He sent out a sound, shook the earth, and displayed fire, rebuking and encouraging with terror and mercy. Through the shaking he showed his fierce anger against the insolent, and through the fire he revealed his wealth that cannot be diminished. “Suddenly,” it says, “there came a mighty sound like wind,” and the marvel of its force filled the human dwelling. They saw tongues dividing like fire, and a hidden command placed them upon their heads. Through the sign of fire he gave spiritual wealth, which would not diminish even when many received it. In a radiance of light, the King distributed to the armies spiritual provisions that do not perish. Through tongues like fire he revealed his wisdom and taught them a new book that they had not known. In that vision he also depicted the power through which they would triumph: like fire, they would destroy the forest of mortality. He armed them with hidden armor as for battle and put into their hands the sword of the Spirit to destroy wickedness. He varied his wealth into portions of every form, so that they might distribute it according to the capacity of its recipients. They were sent to peoples whose languages they had not known.

They wrote books and recited them spiritually. They wrote spiritual letters on the tablets of the heart, and the fleshly mouth expressed the power of knowledge. Their limbs became like strings for the finger of the Spirit, and the hidden one played upon the tangible one—the Spirit upon the body. O instrument that possessed the voice of mortality, which changed its voice and sang life into the ears of the dead! O lyre whose strings are corruptible flesh, which composed what is free from suffering, [?] contrary to its custom! O flute of fragile reed, singing of sufferings, whose voice drove susceptibility to suffering away from those subject to it! O uneducated men who scoffed and laughed at the sophists, and men of few words who brought the course of rhetoric to a halt! O fishermen who caught perishable food, who caught the food of ravenous death for life! O poor men in need of shelter, asking for alms, who suddenly became rich and distributed life from their treasuries! Those of little strength went out to battle against the mighty one, and with visible limbs they defeated the tyrant. Those childlike in understanding acquired spiritual wisdom and gave flavor to human wisdom, which had grown tasteless on earth. Those blind in heart, deprived of light and groping about on earth, became torches, drove away the darkness, and gladdened the earth. Bodily men, carrying the weight of earthly things, became spiritual and acquired wings for flight. Earthly men, sons of dust, offspring of the earth, began taking aim to shoot at the target of heavenly beings. Those who caught speechless creatures went out to catch rational beings. They cast the net of preaching and enclosed the earth in it. They caught people of every language from the sea and from the dry land, and invited them to eat spiritual food. They kindled the fire of preaching in the forest of wickedness and burned the thorns of desires that the evil one had caused to grow. Through the sign of fire they received authority to cultivate the earth. They burned the forest and sowed wheat, good seed. Through the radiance of fire they acquired knowledge of every language and gave the foolish nations a sweet taste. Through the power of the Spirit they gathered all the nations to see a wonder, as they beheld the unprecedented thing that had happened.

They were astonished and marveled to one another as they heard different languages from a single people. Mortals saw a great wonder within mortality, as thirsty nature poured forth streams of water. There the divided nations received a single harmony, for the unfamiliar sound of conversing voices bewildered them. Syrians called out to Greeks as to speakers of their own language. Fury subsided, anger ceased, and peace reigned. Ethiopians spoke the same words with Romans, and in one language they sang praise to the one Creator. The Medes gestured to the Alans, asking, “What is this?” And the mouth interpreted and relieved them of their questioning. The uncircumcised asked the circumcised people, as members of the household, whether this had ever happened among their tribes. The people told the nations, “I have never seen it, nor has this happened among our people until now.” Abram received in one language and handed it on to his children, and in it the wonders of prophecy were also composed. The hidden command resolved the questions of both sides and taught them that this was the mouthpiece of what had happened then. The command that gave languages and divided the nations was itself what spoke in one language with many. The scribe who taught new writing to that infancy was the one who brought it to maturity through what happened here. The pen that inscribed words upon the heart of that dullness was the one that increased the heart’s understanding and interpreted clearly. The key that opened the doors of the soul filled with pride was the very one with which humility opened the treasury of the Spirit. There pride seized the mind, urging it to journey to the heights, but the voice overthrew it and cast it to the ground, so that it would not be presumptuous again. There the presumptuous drew up for battle against the Hidden One; here the Hidden One willingly descended to those who knew him. Fear of the waters that had washed the earth terrified them, and they began building a wicked structure in which they might escape. Their heart was united in [?] in the wicked building, but the voice split that unity, scattered it, and cast it away. The command became like evening for them and gave them rest, so that they would not wear themselves out at something too difficult for their lives.

They had presumptuously desired to journey to the heights, but the One who knows everything bound them to earthly things. He gave languages with the appearance of anger, though he was not angry, but so that he might put bridles of fear into the mouths of the presumptuous. He made the discipline by which he scattered them serve their benefit, and in it he depicted mysteries of what happened here at the end of the ages. May he be blessed by every mouth for everything he has done, for he knows beforehand, before the ages, and acts accordingly. For he knew that through one sacrifice he would atone for everyone, and he depicted beforehand the forgiveness of sins in the sacrifice of the lamb. He was certain that he would give the Spirit through tongues, and he depicted its pattern in what had happened among the people of old. He revealed the power of his being to his creatures and taught them that both the former things and the latter things belonged to him. He distributed riches and gave tongues in the sign of fire, and taught them that he was the one who made the division both here and there. There he divided and occupied them with earthly things; here he divided and trained them in spiritual things. There he concealed why he divided them; here he explained and revealed the significance of both that event and this one. There he raised the rod and frightened them like children; here he opened the door of his mercy to maturity. Although it was indeed he who [?] there and made wise here, he varied these things through accommodation and through force. He inspired fear there and gave encouragement here, like skilled practitioners, and ground them like medicines for the soul to drink. There he concealed the power of hidden things so that they would not be despised; here he disclosed and revealed the riches of his great glory. He showed his glory in those who received his proclamation, raising them beyond their rank in the eyes of those who saw them. He revealed his hidden things through the structure of a visible body, and made the voice of his mighty power heard through a tongue of flesh. Movements and senses became mouths for his hidden nature, and he completed and perfected his work through soul and body. The one who lacks nothing wished, through those who lack, to fill the deficiency of bodily and spiritual beings. O needy ones who distributed the riches of the one who lacks nothing!

And visible beings who proclaimed the Hidden One through manifest senses! O children of the earth, born on earth and dwelling on earth, who opened a road to the kingdom above through their words! O nature that returns each day to the nature of its dust, yet through love became a dwelling for the Spirit who does not change! The Creator wished his love to dwell in a temple of dust, and through one subject to suffering he showed the riches of his mighty power. The one hidden from all revealed his hidden nature through what is visible, and through the poor he distributed the riches of his kindness. Through the mouths of the weak he [?] the mysteries of his hidden things: that he has an offspring who resembles in every way the Father who begot him. Through a tongue of flesh he proclaimed the Spirit who has his being from him; and just as the Son is equal to him in nature, so too is the Spirit equal. On the harp of words, you angry people, hear the equality that the persons of the Son and the Spirit have with his being. They were hidden with him, [?] existing without beginning, and he disclosed them in the image of a human being, to exalt his image. Through the visible image he disclosed the revelation of the Son and the Spirit, and showed them to heavenly and earthly beings. Through a mouth of flesh he yoked spiritual and bodily beings together through worship of the name of the divine Being, three persons. “Go out,” he said, “make disciples of all nations and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son who is from him, and of the Holy Spirit.” And if earthly beings were baptized and sanctified in the name of the divine Being, what benefit, then, did this designation bring to heavenly beings? Let us call Paul, so that we may learn from him as from a treasurer who, with the key of the divine command in his hand, opened the treasury of the Spirit. “Through the Church,” he says, “the God of all revealed his wisdom to the intelligent powers who had not known it.” And if spiritual beings learned the power of the hidden nature through the Church, who would not confess one divine Being, as the Church declares? If the authorities of the peaceful ones gained wisdom through her, who would not learn from the wisdom she learned and revealed? The Church [?] from her bridegroom, the greatest of the great, and wrote a book for the children born of her to study. The apostles received the power of the Spirit, became rich, and grew great; from it they provided for the poverty of the human race. Freely they received that gift, full of blessings;

and freely they spread it before those who would receive it, as they had been commanded. The heralds went out after the savage world; they subdued it and harnessed it under the gentle yoke of the Creator’s name. With love they heard that command, “Make disciples and baptize,” and carried it out in words and deeds without hesitation. They proclaimed and [?] the name of the divine Being: three persons, one equality that cannot be split by division. The diligent workers mounted the horses—the rebellious nations—and harnessed them beneath the chariot of the King of kings. With the armor of the Spirit they overcame all the powers bearing the name of gods, and taught people to call upon the name of one God. They uprooted paganism and Judaism, which had borne no fruit, and planted truth, a fruit pleasing to the owner of the vineyard. They burned the forest that the Evil One had made grow in humanity’s field, and made the seed of the word of life flourish within souls. They uprooted the law of idolatry that error had built, and laid the foundations of the building of truth belonging to one [?]. They drove away the thick darkness that had spread over humanity, and toil advanced toward the radiance of righteousness. Twelve torches shone in creation, which had been dark; it took off its mourning clothes and put on the garment of faith. Like the months in their order, they served the earth through every change, and broke up spiritual food to suit people’s understanding. They went out onto the paths and among the roads, as they had been commanded; they gathered both good and bad and filled the banquet hall. By sea and land they traveled among people to give people life, and in everyone’s ears they sowed the good news of the resurrection of the dead. They spread the net of preaching to the four quarters, and it gathered and filled itself with a pleasing and beloved catch of people. Like springs, they watered the earth that was full of life, and the dead pit of its dryness brought forth life. They cast lots and divided the nations and lands, and each of them journeyed to the region to which the divine command had appointed him. Simon made a new voice heard in the land of the Romans and taught them the understanding of the lordship of one Creator.

The mother of cities fell to the chief of the disciples, and, as in a head, he set the eyes of faith within it. Like a trumpet, the son of thunder cried out to the Ephesians and gathered them to [?] the wonder of his preaching. He explained his name through the deeds of his zeal, for everyone was stirred by him as he cried, “Come, receive life!” At the thunder of his voice, the human heart was watered and softened to yield fruit: hope and love. Matthew cultivated the land of Judea with the sound of his words; he cast the seed of life within it, and it brought forth glory. The afflicted land, which had been troubled by divisions, he supplied with a stream of explanation of the mysteries, and it gained strength. The circumcised people, who had boasted in the mark on their flesh, saw the nations being marked by the Spirit, and he shattered their mark. He perfected the people, supplying what they lacked, and gave them spiritual food: the three names. Like a child, the people had been practicing the name of the Father; and when they grew wise, he taught them the three equal persons. The heralds sowed [?] in everyone's ears, and a single confession of the Creator's name sprang up on earth. The voice that called Mark drew him to the Romans, and there he explained the power of the deeds proclaimed in the preaching. He brought news of the new king to the king's ears, and the king marveled that there was a king above his own head. The king and the people listened to his choice words, and they accepted and acknowledged that there is a king who reigns over all. Luke poured out the stream of his words in the land of Egypt, and like the Gihon he spread the good news of life over everyone. He spoke Syriac with the Egyptians, who were strangers to him, and they gathered around him when they heard his speech, which resembled their own. He imitated their voice, like a bird calling to one of its own kind, and enclosed them within the snares of his preaching. He spoke in their own language and let them hear the sound of salvation, and awakened them, as though from sleep, to the service of life.

For this purpose he enriched them with the power of languages, so that everyone might receive good hope in the speech of his own mouth. Through the gift of languages he taught them to travel the road of preaching to all [?]. With new speech they laid the foundations of the building of truth, and from all nations they built and completed a single confession of faith. Paul, the chosen one, sought pure gold—truth—in it, and charged everyone to consider how to build wisely. Everyone cries out against the heretics, the deceitful workers: “Do not build with straw and thorns in this building!” It was fitting for him to warn the members of the household, and he knew how to recognize the brushwood of a wicked building. Like a commander at the head of the army, he constantly gives encouragement, so that no one takes off the armor of the Spirit and is condemned. He teaches us ways to fight spiritually and shows us that our enemy is spiritual. “Put on truth,” he says, “put on the helmet of salvation and life, and grasp in your minds the sword of the word of the Spirit.” See, the soldier of the Spirit has taught us the ways of combat. Come, let us prepare to put on armor according to his order. See, the king's servants have opened the road of preaching. Come, let us travel it toward the appointed gathering of life without end. See, they went out and cultivated the thorn-covered land through their sufferings. Let us uproot from it the brushwood that has sprung up among the wheat. See, they have opened the gates that had been shut in people's faces. Come, let us strive so that they are not shut through our own negligence. Look, they have woven a garment of faith in the depths of the water. Let everyone cover the sores of his body and the blemishes of his soul. Look, armor has been forged for the warriors of righteousness. Let us not grow weak before the devil’s schemes. Look, they have taught us how to conquer and by what he is defeated. Let us meet his arrows with the renowned shield of faith. Look, they have opened a treasury full of blessings before those who would receive them. Let us receive freely and give freely, live and give life. Look, a spiritual stream has sprung up for those on earth. Let us give our souls and our companions a drink of its sweetness. Look, the Sun of Righteousness has risen amid the darkness.

Let us drive the error of the darkness of the Two from our minds. Since we cannot attain perfection like the heralds, let us offer words in place of deeds, like Shmona. Since our speech falls short of reaching the height of their conduct, let us journey with them through the soul’s love, whose wing is swift. Let us cry out with them in one thanksgiving to the one Creator, who has enriched everything with the gift of his mighty power.
On the parable [?] workers for his vineyard.
By the same author, likewise. Homily sixty-eight, which he composed on the parable of the man who went out in the morning to [?] workers for his vineyard.

The sound of the trumpets of our Lord’s dawning rang out on earth, and the world awoke as though from the sleep of apathy. Mortals lay in apathy as though asleep, and our Lord’s voice awakened them against their will. Those sleeping in wickedness did not want to hate wickedness, nor did they long to see the Sun of Righteousness. The children of error loved the night of error, and they had no desire to listen to the sound of truth’s dawning. They were imprisoned in the vast darkness of ignorance, and the prison of shameful deeds was pleasant to them. Evil habits had grown old among the children of Adam, and they loved and cherished shameful things as though they were beautiful. Laziness held them fast in the silence of error, and they did not desire to acquire the wealth of good deeds. They had been without the practice of good deeds ever since they came into being, and without the labor of loving truth they journeyed [?] through the world. They went about their affairs lazily, and they were needy and deprived of every good thing. There was no gleam of goodness or of doing good in their dwelling, and however much they sinned, they kept sinning without ever being satisfied. Wickedness was mingled with wickedness in the course of their lives, and there was no place free of hateful deeds.

They conducted themselves as though they were not human, until one man came and made them wise. One man arose from among people sick in soul and healed them of the sickness of ignorance. With the medicine of his words he revived them from their sins and showed them the path of resurrection through good deeds. He occupied them with meditation on good things, so that they would no longer return to contemplating wrongdoing. He separated the workers of wrongdoing from wrongdoing and encouraged them to draw near to righteousness. The good friend occupied them with good pursuits, and like laborers he hired them for good work. A man from among humanity came to the service of humanity. He raised his voice and made them hear the different forms of his work. He framed the labor of his preaching in a parable, and through a mystery he called rational beings to the summons of his love. My thoughts heard the sound of his summons calling humanity, and they stirred from the silence in which they lay, as though from sleep. In the sluggishness in which the movements of my mind were [?], they rose to listen to the voice proclaiming good wages. At the sound of wages my mind, [?] labor, awoke and began composing a discourse about the different ways of succeeding. As though in a dream, it saw the truth being explained, for it supposed that it could perform works of labor by arranging words. It heard words from that mouth which expounds life, and drew near to listen to a voice filled with laborious work. The lover of our race called our nature to labor, and sent to us one of our own race to call us to him. With parables he caught us like a hunter catching a winged creature, and brought us inside, enclosing us within the words of his preaching. He scattered the bait of [?] on the ground before our minds, and gently drew us toward the food like a fledgling. He set a trap of parables for our hearts, which love to wander, so that they would no longer wander among desirable things as before. He knew that we had grown accustomed to wandering in error; therefore he enclosed us within the snares of his teaching. His love skillfully caught us like prey, and shut us in behind the gate of the teaching that filled his mouth. In the morning he went out to catch us for his teaching, just as a watchful man goes about the land seeking laborers. In the morning everyone who hires a laborer among earthly people [?] does so, and according to the same custom our Lord also called us to the service of his love. He [?] morning at the beginning of the parable of his preaching, and, as though in the morning, called us to the work of tending his vineyard. He compared the former time, before his own, to night, and the time of the parable of his teaching to daytime. He represented the course of this ordering of things as a single day—night and daytime—as Moses called it in Genesis. He divided the time of all generations into two periods, assigning the hours of night to one and those of daytime to the other.

He called the period of [?] night because of error, for people were blind to goodness as though in darkness. He called his own time daytime because of truth, for in it people saw the truth clearly, as though in the light. The revealed Truth proclaimed his message in human ears, and people listened to him as to a man proclaiming truth. He called himself a man, one of us, and called his proclamation the kingdom hidden on high. “The kingdom on high is like,” said the King of [?], “a man who went out in the morning to hire workers.” He agreed with the workers on a denarius for a day’s work and sent them to work in the spiritual vineyard. He went out again at the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, and hired them on terms of payment like those of the first workers. At the eleventh hour he hired them as he had in the morning, and made them equal in receiving the same wage. In the evening he called the steward to pay the wages, and he gave the last workers a denarius each, as he had been commanded. The first workers saw the gift he gave the last and thought he would give them more, in proportion to the time they had worked. They too received a denarius each, like their companions, and began rehearsing kinds of [?] complaint in their thoughts. They began to grumble, astonished at the gift, asking why he had made them equal in the payment of wages. “We,” they said, “have borne the burden and heat of the whole day, yet these who were hired for one hour have received as much as we have. “The wage is not fair when compared with the work, and the labor of one hour is not equal to that of a whole day. “We have toiled at the work all day without slackening. What is this, that the labor is greater but the wage is equal?” The master of the house saw the workers who had begun to grumble. He called one of them and reasoned with him in front of his companions. “My friend,” he said to him, kindly calling him his friend, and showing him the purpose of his great love for humanity. “I am not unjust in paying the wages, as you suppose, nor do I cheat anyone who has worked for me with love. “I agreed with you on one denarius, and you yourself are a witness. Take your denarius and stop speaking words full of complaint.” Here end the words that our Lord spoke in mysteries. Let us seek and investigate what is hidden in their interpretation. Every discourse in parables requires investigation, for unless investigation sheds light, the words are not illuminated. The investigation that examines words is a second light, and, as with a light, it reveals the light of the words’ meaning. There is no [?] greater than the light of the Spirit’s words, nor any wisdom possessing power like their wisdom. They cannot be weighed against beryls and pearls, nor compared with anything regarded as precious. Everything is inferior when compared with their beauty.

Every beautiful thing is as though without beauty before their [?]. They are far more desirable than anything desired among earthly beings, and [?] their loveliness has taken the world captive, drawing it to desire them. Their loveliness has taken earthly and heavenly beings captive. They despised everything they had loved and came to love studying them. I too loved studying them, though I did not love them. I loved them in words, while remaining far from deeds. A desire stirred me to weave [?] without deeds, so that perhaps my mind might turn from words to deeds. He enticed me like a child, to occupy me with instruction, so that through instruction I might learn the power within instruction. I sought to approach the school of the Teacher of teachers, because I saw that the discourse of his word surpassed all instruction. I heard a good discourse spoken in people's ears, and I wearied myself to understand and make known the discourse I had heard. News of the wage he gave the hired workers reached my ears, and I wanted to be hired, even briefly, at the end of the day. In the morning I heard that he hired workers to work in his vineyard, and stipulated a denarius for one hour and for eleven. My thoughts, weak in [?], were astonished at the equal wage: what was this, that the wage did not correspond to the work? Who among [?] stipulated a denarius for twelve hours, and what worker toiled in this way and received in this way? There is no rich man who hires workers at every hour, nor any hired worker who hires himself out at any hour partway through the day. The report of this work is unlike that of any other work, and it has no counterpart in all the work done among earthly people. Its uniqueness compelled me to labor in investigating it: why does its pattern differ from every other pattern? Its likeness enticed me to paint its likeness with the pigment of words, so that through words I might reveal to people the forms of its images. I saw the image of his labors outlined in the Scriptures, and from what is written I sought answers concerning what is not written. In the Scriptures I saw the name of the kingdom running through them, and with it [?] a man who hired workers for his vineyard. He likened the man who proclaims the truth to the one who hires workers, and called his proclamation the kingdom that is on high. He called the good news that he proclaimed on earth the kingdom on high, because it shows the path to the kingdom to those who seek it. Our Lord's word laid out on earth the path of the kingdom [?], and taught people to travel with it to where the kingdom is. He was about to reveal the heavenly order to earthly people, and he depicted its images among earthly people before it came to be. It had been appointed for him to engage people in spiritual labors [?], and he engaged them bodily before the deeds themselves. In bodily form [?], the embodied one traveled ahead of embodied people and showed people how to travel [?] along the path of spiritual things. He depicted spiritual labors [?] in a vision perceptible to the body, and people began [?] toward the goal hidden on high.

Oh, the wonder that took place on earth among earthly people: though they were earthly, they loved the occupation of those who are not earthly! Earthly people heard a new voice from [?], proclaiming on earth new good news that had never been proclaimed. With the promise of wages he urged on the children of earth, and they ran to him and received them lovingly. His love drew him into fellowship with those of his own race, to hire them for the work of spiritual life. He taught them the forms of spiritual service, so that through their labors they might gain immortal life. By this he indicated that he went out in the morning, at the beginning of his appearing, calling his appearing itself the morning and the beginning of the day. He called himself a man, since he is also a man, and he called his teaching a kingdom full of life. The morning was the beginning of his preaching, and the morning workers were the twelve apostles who were hired to work with him. They were hired in the morning of the proclamation, and they were the ones who bore the burden of the whole day. The preachers of the word of life bore a great burden, because the beginning of the pruning work of proclamation was hard. Hard was the time that all the chosen apostles endured, and very fierce was the battle with pagans and Jews. Judaism was strong in its observances, and paganism too was fervent in its love of demons. The pagan nations were bound by love of demons, and love of demons was firmly established in their [?]. The champions of righteousness fought two battles, against paganism and Judaism, those towering cliffs. Judaism held its head high, and paganism too sheltered as though within fortresses. The names of gods who were not gods were strongly defended, but the apostles cast them down to the ground through the name of one Power. Men of earth proclaimed on earth the name of one Power, and all the names of those who were not gods trembled and were terrified. The men of God uprooted from the earth those who were not gods, and sowed the name of the one God like seed. They cleared away the forest of idolatry like dung, so that the seed of life would not be hindered in its growth. The good workers were persistent in nurturing the seed, and they watered it with words of the Spirit, like dew. With words of the Spirit they cultivated the vineyard of humanity, and they waited for it to yield spiritual fruit. With fear and love they approached its cultivation, so that they would not be despised by the master who had hired them. Like pruners, they cut every kind of evil away from it, so that the foundation of the roots of its faith would be firm. Through faith they strengthened its faith, so that the scorching heat and frost of desires would not harm it. They greatly desired to protect it from harm.

And they were diligent in ensuring that it did not lack the watering of the Spirit. They cultivated it with [?] and supported its branches with words. Its leaves blossomed, and it bore the fruits of purity of soul. The vineyard that had been barren bore pure fruit, and human beings and heavenly beings marveled at the goodness of its fruit. Great was the wonder at the changed season of the vineyard of the nations, which yielded good things instead of the carobs it used to grow. It bore various kinds of carobs in the time of idolatry, but when it gave itself to spiritual service, it bore blessings. The [?] of apostleship cultivated it spiritually, and drove out of it wolves, bears, and [?] evil. All kinds of evil beings had trampled it like wild animals, but in defiance of them, all kinds of good things flourished that could not be overcome. They made a high fence around the divine vineyard, so that tyrannical demons would not harm it with their attacks. They built a tower of praise in its midst for glorifying God, to guard the fruits of praise gathered within it. The disciples also made a winepress of baptism, so that in it they might cleanse the blemishes of bodies and minds. They richly stocked it with every kind of good thing, so that whoever worked in it would lack none of its blessings. The power of the Spirit gave them the wisdom to do these things, and he gave their minds strength to cultivate human beings. The owner of the vineyard sent them to work in his vineyard, and, according to his will, they fulfilled his will through their work in his vineyard. The workers completed all the [?] of the owner of the vineyard. They began and finished with a single purpose, without interruption. They did not lose heart in their work, because they saw that the reward was far greater than their labors. The labor was small when compared with the reward, and twelve hours were no match for a single denarius. The good master had agreed on one denarius for the good workers, and they worked very diligently to cultivate the vineyard of rational beings. The workers of righteousness cultivated the rational vineyard and guarded its fruits so that they would not be ruined by harmful attacks. They made the three names a wall around the record of his life, so that the structure of his mortal life would stand firm. They knew that the composition of his body could come apart. Therefore they placed the three names upon him like bonds. With bonds of the Spirit, the builders built the structure of humanity, and they secured its foundations in the name of the Being who cannot be undone. They first laid the name of the Being as a foundation, and upon it they completed the entire height of humanity’s confession of faith. They established throughout creation one confession of one Creator, and they proclaimed one name on earth to their hearers. In this name they made disciples, taught, and baptized people, and they brought the whole world under the authority of the one who rules over all. From every dominion they gathered the divided nations,

and taught them to honor one authority. Under one authority they yoked every power in the heights and depths, and within it they embraced all creatures, rational and speechless. Within the hearing of their words they embraced everything: earthly beings and [?] beings without bodily composition. Oh, those mortals, clothed in a corruptible body, who enclosed the world within the words of the Word dwelling in them! Oh, those earthly beings, bearing the burden of mortality, who ascended and subjected the heavenly hosts to their word! Oh, those fishermen, who caught food to feed the body, who caught rational beings and fed them food, the food of the Spirit! Oh, those uneducated men, ignorant of every field of study, who instructed the world with a rhetoric it had never seen! Oh, those who were created with one language and one manner of speech, who spoke with everyone according to the speech of their own languages! In every language, [?], men of few words, spoke, and explained to all peoples the power in their words. By the power of their words they astonished even peoples skilled in speech. How much stronger than every power is the power within them! Every people, all together, was overcome by the power in the fishermen, and no people remained that had not submitted to the power within them. The wise were defeated, the learned were put to shame, and the eloquent fell silent. The voice of uneducated men thunders through the earth like a trumpet. Pride was brought low, arrogance fled, and self-exaltation ceased. Humility is lavishly praised in every language. All the teachings that demons invented became as though they had never existed, and the one teaching that uneducated men [?] stood firm in truth. The meditations of poetry and rhetoric fled, and they could not offer the fishermen an answer to the word of truth. The brilliance of the philosophers, proud of their reputation, was extinguished. The light in the words of those more uneducated than anyone shone brightly. Those more uneducated than anyone taught something greater than everything, and priests, kings, and their rulers raised a finger in wonder. They set up one authority like a target before all peoples, so that every tongue might turn toward the gathering place of his name. They proclaimed throughout the earth the name of the Being who exists and exists, and repeated a second and a third time the Trinity that cannot be divided. They assigned three names to the persons, as they had been commanded, and joined them to the one authority of the name of the divine Being. Along with the divine Being they also numbered the mystery of embodiment, without the Trinity becoming a group of four. Within one designation they confined and enclosed the name of humanity: the Son of God and [?] humanity, one person. They wrote ‘one person’ in the sign of the name ‘Son’: the Father's Word [?], who exists from eternity, and the man who is from us. They are two in [?], since there are two natures, and one person, according to the number that does not change. The number of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit does not change.

Nor is the nature of the divine Being mingled with human nature. The nature of the divine Being remains in its own distinctiveness alongside humanity, and humanity too is preserved [?] alongside the divine Being. The natural properties belonging to the natures are not mixed, especially the nature of the Maker with that of things made. The insolent mixed the nature of the Maker with that of things made, and I marveled greatly at how presumptuous the human mind had become. The human mind compelled me to change the course of my words. I left my subject and traveled the path of the Word and the flesh. Without understanding, the insolent mixed the Word and the flesh, and my discourse grew zealous to distinguish things that cannot be mixed. This zeal has possessed my mind in all my discourses, and it does not let me walk along any path apart from it. The path of the parable of the laborers who were hired had been laid out for me, but when the path of mingling crossed mine, I turned aside from my subject. I left my discourse to rebuke a discourse of invented words, and I turned to follow the path of the discourse from which it had departed. Come, then, recount the subject entrusted to you, and follow the path that the workers opened up by working in the vineyard. I long to travel in the company of the workers who worked well, so that I too may share in the payment of the reward promised to them. Their promises attracted me to hire myself out alongside them in their labors, so that perhaps I might have a gleaning of words for the harvest of life. For the sake of life they toiled in the service of the vineyard’s master, and they bore the burden of hard labor throughout the day. They were hired in the morning, as the terms of their wages required, and they continued their labors as the hours of the day ran their course. All day the diligent workers toiled at their tasks, and at evening they rested from their labor and received their wages. For the sake of their wages, the weary workers endured every hardship. Those who came first and those who followed them directed themselves toward one goal. One after another they approached the task in which they had been instructed, and all alike performed the work that gains life. The apostles were hired at the morning hour of our Lord’s appearing, and they bore the burden of cruel mockery from the people and the nations. Those of the third hour were another generation that arose after them and followed the path of the exhausting labors of apostleship. Those of the sixth hour, in turn, were those hired some time afterward, who portrayed the likeness of that way of life in their own conduct. Those of the ninth hour were the righteous who lived from generation to generation and accepted the burden of insults like those who came first. Those of the eleventh hour are those who come at the end of the ages and possess a love that does not weaken before his [?]. The affection of love joined them to those who came first, and they received their wages in keeping with the readiness of their minds. In their minds they greatly desired to do much work; therefore they received wages greater than their work. The master of the house gave payment for the intention of their love,

so that through their love he might encourage people to cherish love. He encouraged people with the generous wages for a single hour, so that they would not grow slack even if their lifetime were short. It is love he seeks in [?], whether few or many, and according to their love he gives wages to those who cherish love. Because of love he honored the workers who came last, and he gave them payment without demanding labor expressed in deeds. The little labor of one hour was very slight when compared with the total of twelve hours. O love, how precious you are among those who love! You have given wages for little labor as though it were much. The labor of the workers hired for one hour was little, but love placed it alongside the weight of twelve hours. Who has ever weighed things this way in an equal balance, with the scale pans for twelve hours and for one hour rising together? The reckoning of much and little came out the same; and this is the wonder: the weight of the stones did not [?]. Here let anyone who knows how to look carefully marvel at how much greater the greatness of love is than everything else. The greatness of love overruled the reckoning of much and little, and made the exertion of a whole day equal to that of a single hour. The image that love presented in this deed resembles what Moses did at the gathering of the manna. Moses commanded that a measure of manna be gathered for each person, but the belly’s great appetite gathered much beyond the measure. Through the measure he tested the greedy inclination as in a furnace, and exposed and revealed the self-indulgence hidden within it. When self-indulgence grew greedy and gathered much, it came to the measure, and its toil became as though it had not toiled. Oh, that gathering, gathered without ever having enough! When they measured it, much and little became the same. Oh, the command that guides everyone and teaches everyone wisdom, and brings abundance and scarcity to equality! The great toil of the whole day was very much, and the little toil of a single hour was very little. That command, which tests labors [?], examined them and weighed them in the same manner as the measuring of the manna. I have compared the wages for much and little with the measuring of the manna—not because they are identical, but because they resemble one another as an illustration. The toil of the diligent was not like the great amount [?] gathered by the greedy, nor was the labor of the victorious like the little gathered by the upright. There they gathered out of love for their bellies, to sustain their bodies; and in this way they persevered in hard toil under an agreement for wages. Under an agreement for wages, both the first and those after them toiled; and according to love they received repayment for their intentions. The owner of the vineyard looked, and still looks, at the soul’s willingness; and it was this willingness that he rewarded under the name of a denarius. Under the name of a denarius, he gave them rest from their labors and comforted them after the distress of the sufferings they had endured.

He called the rest of the resurrection of the dead “evening time,” so that, when they rose, they would rest from the labors of mortality. At night the toil of the earthly world comes to an end, and in it the way of immortal life dawns anew. In that life he gives wages to the weary workers and weighs their labors [?] according to the willingness of those who toiled. According to their willingness he promised repayment for much and little, and gave for little as for much—a denarius each. The last received a denarius each before the first, lest they be saddened on account of their one hour of labor. The labor of a single hour is little compared with that wage; and who would not marvel at the greatness of the love of the one who gives the wage? The first marveled at the greatness of the love of the one who gives the wage, and [?] that he would give them more in proportion to the time spent working. The weary workers were thinking in terms of time, and were expecting wages greater than what had been promised. As promised, they too received a denarius each, and they were deeply displeased because their expectation was not fulfilled in the payment. Foolish grumbling gave birth to an impulse of envy: why had there been equality in the payment of wages? They blamed the master of the house for the equality: why had he made [?] the little equal to the much? “Why,” they said, “have you made the last workers, who worked one hour, equal to us, who [?] bore the burden and heat of the whole day? Why have you given wages to those who were not hired as we were, and equated a whole day’s exertion with one hour? We ought to receive more, since we worked harder. For it is only just that payment should correspond to the labor.” The one who paid the wages saw the complaint directed against his love, and answered to persuade the complainants [?] lovingly. The kind man lovingly answered the complainant and called him his friend [?], though he was not [?] worthy of this title. “My friend,” the master said to his servant, “I am not wronging you, nor am I being false to the terms of the wages I agreed upon with you. I agreed with you on one denarius, and you yourself are a witness. Take what is yours, and let no complaint be made against the greatness of my mercy. If I am good, and my will is inclined to give generously, why are you displeased and complaining out of turn?” The complainant did not actually bring a complaint against the one who paid the wages, nor did the master actually rebuke the hired workers as it is written. The matter did not happen as it is written and as we recount these words, nor did their speakers utter them as accounts of actual events. They expressed them in terms of mortal ways of thinking, to restrain the insolence of complainers so that they would not complain. He restrained complainers through the form he gave the words, so that anyone who complained might hear the words and cease complaining. For this purpose he presented the workers [?] as grumbling—not because they had grumbled, but so that no one would give rise to grumbling. He taught people through the representation [?] of grumbling and the voice of accusation, so that they would not complain when people were shown mercy through grace.

Through grace the master of the house made the members of his household equal, and he did not calculate when he gave them equal wages. He did not give the workers equal wages without reason, but because he saw equality in their serene and pure hearts. The one who sees hidden things saw equality of love, and gave recompense [?] for the little labor along with the much. The time was short for the workers hired for one hour, but he assessed the wages according to the willingness that stood ready. “No one hired us,” they answered when questioned, as though saying, “We were not there at the time for labor.” And perhaps, if it had been fitting, they would have said to the master of the house, “If we had been there at the beginning of the day, we would have worked hard.” He gave wages for this readiness of will, and showed that readiness of love deserves a double wage. The last received a double wage along with the first: one denarius [?], the fullness of life that does not perish. He called the promise of immortal life a denarius, which becomes the reward of the righteous in return for their labors. They justly receive wages for their labors, and each one's reward is doubled according to his willingness. The last and the first received their reward according to their willingness, and they learned how well the master had arranged matters for his servants. All generations learned a great lesson from this arrangement: not to grow slack when they are hired to serve in the fear of truth. He gave hope to the generations to come through the equality of the wages, and encouraged them still more by having the last receive theirs first. It is said that the last received their wages before the first—not that they actually received them first, but to strengthen the fainthearted. A single signal gives everyone their wages together, and there is no delay between one gift and another. For there is no earlier or later there at the time of judgment: there is one judgment, one recompense, and one decision. At a signal, all the repayments appointed for that day will take place, and nothing can compare with the swiftness of that command. Suddenly he issues a single command to those under his command, and everything stands ready as though it had been commanded from the beginning. Come, then, let us heed that command, whose authority is great, and keep good order before that day which sets everything in order. Come, let us hire ourselves out with the hired workers for every kind of good deed, and cultivate our souls as the righteous cultivated humanity. The righteous cultivated humanity purely, as they would a vineyard. [?] Come, let us too cultivate our souls with good deeds. Let us occupy our souls and our bodily members with good deeds, and not grow slack in the work of goodness. Let each of us perform the work of life in body and soul, with the outward senses and the hidden impulses of a single human being. Our soul together with our bodily members is one human being.
With one mind, let us repay kindness to [?].
On the Rich Man and Lazarus
Discourse Twenty-Eight: On the Rich Man and Lazarus

Our Savior painted a picture of a story on the tablet of his words and set them within the palace of his proclamation. He arranged the words of his mouth like a portrait and called them events, as though they had actually happened. He carefully matched words with words and stamped them with the seal of parables so that they would not be despised. In every detail he made them resemble what had happened, and clothed them in the splendid garment of the name of stories. Under the name of stories he concealed the power hidden in his words, so that they would not be despised by the minds of the fainthearted. He took account of the spiritual dullness of the fainthearted as he painted a picture of the deeds of the good and the wicked. He showed the good and the wicked the beauty and splendor of his words, and urged them to hear words full of wonder. Great wonder lay hidden in the words of his proclamation; they were revealed, yet were not clearly seen. They appeared as though they had taken place in actual deeds, yet they were not visible, because the action within them was far away.

Action makes up for what words lack, and, as though by a light, reveals the beauty of beautiful things. The words of the proclamation are full of beautiful things, and the power of their sayings is hidden as though in a treasury. Great power is hidden in inquiry for the one who seeks, and unless he seeks with loving devotion, he cannot find it. Loving devotion called me to read in our Lord’s book, and from the reading the parable drew me toward understanding. The reading itself stirred me to investigate the words, and from the words there came to me a desire to study their hidden meaning. I saw that the hidden meaning of the words was covered in a garment of words, and my mind stirred me to uncover the meanings presented in the words. I entered through the doorway of the Scriptures and stood there; as though looking at a picture, I saw in the letters the image I was seeking. I wanted to examine the beautiful design within the wonders, to learn why the name “wonders” was set over the letters. I saw the name “wonders” running among the letters, and I wanted to know the meaning as well as the name. I saw two persons portrayed in the pigment of words, and although they resembled one another, one image did not resemble the other. The name “rich man” and the name “poor man” were inscribed over them, and they were [?] in their names and deeds. The name “rich man” was inscribed first, at the beginning of the line, and at its end was the name of the poor man, who was destitute and needy. The image of the one who [?] wealth was portrayed in splendid clothes, and that of the poor man in shabby attire made up of patches. The appearance of the one who was not beautiful was splendid in its features, while the face of the one beautiful in soul was disfigured. The various pigments in the ugly man’s portrait were bright, while those of the beautiful man were darker than darkness. Oh, the wonder that was visible in the two images:

They were beautiful, yet in truth they were not beautiful! That rich man was not as beautiful as he appeared, and that poor man was not as disfigured as his ugliness suggested. Outwardly, the appearance of the humble man was ugly; inwardly, the proud-minded man was ugly and disfigured. The ugly man, ugly through and through, was ugly in his soul; and the wholly beautiful man was splendid and desirable in his mind. Outward beauty brought contempt upon the man ugly in soul, while bodily ugliness praised the man beautiful in soul. That poor man, ugly in appearance, was ugly in his body; but the man with splendid limbs was repulsive and disfigured in his mind. The splendor of beauty was visible upon his limbs, but within his soul was an appearance uglier than everything ugly. The man ugly in mind displayed himself in clothes of fine linen and reveled in countless luxuries. His clothes were splendid, and his finery was desirable. He never had enough of indulging himself in his abundant luxuries. His wealth was abundant, and the provisions for his life were lavish. There was no room between one indulgence and the next. Luxuries were piled high upon luxuries, and the various kinds of finery never left their places. That pleasure-seeker enjoyed every kind of luxury, and the more he enjoyed himself, the more he longed to enjoy himself again. No kind of delicacy ever left his table: while the first was being taken away, another was already before him. The house of that self-indulgent man was like a festival, and the sound of merriment boomed like thunder. That poor man was tormented by the sound of his merriment, and he added cries of mourning to his afflictions. The sufferer's distress matched the merry man's pleasures, and his laments were as numerous as the other's songs. One was singing, while the other was weeping bitterly. Who would not marvel at one soul's joy and another soul's sorrow? One was dancing, while the other stamped his feet as though mourning the dead. Who would not be bewildered by these unjust circumstances?

One acted wickedly, while the other labored to live righteously. Who would not say that their rewards were unjust? That wicked man reveled undeservedly, while that humble man suffered unjustly. No equality could be seen in their conditions: they experienced opposite extremes of pleasure and suffering. That wicked man did not deserve such pleasure, and such suffering was not fitting for that humble man. The evil age reversed the fortunes of the good and the wicked, honoring one and disgracing the other in ways they did not deserve. The lover of truth suffered undeservedly, while the lover of falsehood indulged himself in splendid things. The glutton lived amid good things and luxuries, utterly devoid of mercy. He had no pity on the poor man lying at his gate. At the wicked man's gate was the beloved man, who lived in poverty for his name's sake. He longed for relief, but no one eased his need. He was destitute and lacked every good thing. His misery was doubled by poverty and sickness. He was worn down by two very grievous afflictions: poverty, which humbles a person, and loathsome sores. He was covered all over with loathsome sores, densely packed together. There was no healthy spot free of blemishes. The body of that distressed man had become a fountain of sores, and foul pus flowed from him, sickening the soul. Drops of pus poured from his limbs, and the stench of decay coming from him distressed him. Ravenous dogs drank the pus from his body and fed on the delicacy of his wounds. The ravenous creatures came to the smell of his decay. They visited him and were themselves cared for by his sores. Oh, the man who, though human in body and spirit, is cut off from the visits of other people! Oh, the embodied man whose body is repulsive to others with bodies, and from whom the eyes of his fellow human beings turn away!

Oh, that soul which lodges itself in a dead body and dwells there without life in its limbs! Oh, the limbs which, though they exist, do not exist, and which the soul moves with a lifeless life! Oh, that soul! How long it bore the body's weight without giving way in that exhausting and bitter struggle! Exhausting and bitter was the contest the righteous man endured, and the endurance of that mind had no equal. Who has ever seen a contest so exhausting, and who has ever beheld a contestant like this one? Who has fought a battle in a body [?] when there was no body? Who has held the battle line with senses, yet without senses? That warrior had no senses to hold the battle line, for they had fallen silent from the ravages of severe pain. The man whose mind was sound was tormented by bitter pain, and although he suffered, through endurance he did not suffer. He did not suffer because he looked toward the end of his toil, yet he suffered greatly whenever he considered the ruin of his body. He was tormented in body and soul in the contest of his sufferings: his body by pain, and his soul by the anguish of weariness. Weariness wore down the unwearying man as he saw his own various torments and his neighbor's pleasures. He contemplated the abundance of that rich man's good things and longed for them, but no one relieved his need. Oh, how needy was that man who was not truly needy, though needy in name! And how abundant was the wealth concealed at the end of his toil! Oh, how comfortable was that rich man, distinguished by his titles! And how greatly multiplied was the torment that befell him! Oh, how ruthless was that cunning man, possessed of cruelty, who looked upon that torment without pity! Oh, how tyrannical he was, and harder-hearted than a tyrant, since he would not relieve the humble man even with his crumbs! Oh, how dismayed the humble man was in his lowliness as he looked upon the abundance of that [?]! The sight of those good things wore him down far more than his pain did.

He suffered doubly and shed tears. His mouth was full of lamentation and weeping, night and day [?], and he sighed at the sound of that debauched man's revelry. The more the debauched man indulged in desirable things, the more the other's mourning over his pain and need increased. The more the cruel man hardened himself in his tyranny, the more the other humbled himself amid insults. The more the arrogant man exalted himself in the greatness of his possessions, the more the humble man was brought low at the sight of his own lowly condition. The more the splendor of that unlovely man increased, the more the ugliness of that beautiful man's suffering grew. While the delicacies of that tomb for food were being laid out, the man who lacked food was being clothed in every kind of endurance. While all kinds of good things delighted the glutton, pain and hunger tormented the holy and pure man. Oh, the contest—how worn down its contestant was! Oh, the luxury—how feeble was the man enjoying it! Oh, the sickness—how healthy was the man who lay in it! Oh, the health—how sickly was the man who dwelt in it! Oh, the sight of two images facing one another: pleasure without limit and distress beyond measure! That rich man enjoyed himself without ever having enough, and that poor man suffered torment without measure. I considered their inequality, how great the difference was, and how intense were the wicked man's pleasure and the righteous man's suffering. I saw pleasure and suffering woven together in the account, and I drew near to see a spectacle full of inequality. The inequality compelled me to pursue an inquiry in words, and now my mind is weary from bringing forth words about what it has investigated. Come, my mind, approach the investigation of what you have sought, and openly display the forms of explanation prepared for you.

What is the reason for the designation of rich man and the designation of poor man? And why has the record of their deeds been written down? Did their deeds actually happen as they are written, or will they perhaps happen at a later time? Did it really happen that the rich man rejoiced and the afflicted man grieved, that the one lived in splendor and the other was degraded until death? Did their time come to an end, along with gladness of heart and sorrow of soul? Did death dismiss both pleasures and afflictions? Did that poor man depart and go to Abraham's embrace, while the rich man remained tormented in the abyss of Sheol? No, listener, this did not happen as actual events, nor was it carried out as the words of the account describe it. No rich man enjoyed himself and lived splendidly amid pleasures, nor did pain and deprivation wear down a poor man. The account in what is written took place in words alone, and the writer wrote these various parables for instruction. The lover of humanity fashioned parables to instruct people, so that through parables he might draw humanity to his teaching. Like a painter, he blends the words of his proclamation, and he portrayed the world in two images of two classes. He portrayed two persons and two classes in his gospel: wealth in good health and poverty bearing the righteous. He portrayed healthy wealth in the figure of that rich man, and he named poverty after Lazarus, a poor man. He designated the side of poverty by the name Lazarus, and attached to his name an unconquerable steadfastness of soul. By the name of the rich man he designated those who live at ease and the children of wealth, and in his pampered life he portrayed the pampering of those who indulge themselves. Through his lack of compassion he illustrated the greed of the merciless, and through his wickedness he exposed the disposition of the deceitful. Through his great arrogance he humbled the arrogance of the proud and taught them not to boast about human things. Through his self-indulgence he exposed and laid bare gluttony, so that it would not grow greedy and bring still more doubled lashes upon itself. Through that greedy man he decreed doubled lashes for the greedy: if they show no mercy, they will receive no mercy, just like him.

That greedy man was not merciful throughout his life, nor did he humble himself to show compassion to the one at his gate. It was written that the poor man lay beside his gate, so that everyone might know how evil greed [?] is. By mentioning that greedy man he rebuked greed, and by mentioning that poor man he comforted those in need. By mentioning the poor man he bandaged the pain of poverty and applied unconquerable patience to it as medicine. Through his poverty he portrayed the life of poverty, and through his endurance, the ways of a mind that does not give up. Through his own endurance he encouraged the souls of those in pain, and by mentioning his sores he lightened the burden of their suffering. Through his being needy and longing for food without eating, he signaled to those in need to stand firm in deprivation. Through his lying abandoned and despised before that greedy man's gate, he called those despised by others to look upon his own humiliation. Through his patience he imparted patience to others, so that no one would give rise to hateful grumbling on the day of trial. Through the foulness of his sores he called to the sick as though with a voice, urging them to enter resolutely into the struggle against pain. Through the pus of his body being licked away by dogs, he offered encouragement to the discouraged to acquire hope. Through everything he endured in his poverty and the severity of his pain, he sowed good hope among the weak so that they would not give up. He wanted to strengthen human weakness through a human being, so that people would not give up when tested by things that weaken them. Through Lazarus he called the whole company of the poor to come and see an image of their lives in one poor man. He painted his story like a portrait before the poor, so that through its images they might form [?] hope in their minds. He set his endurance before their eyes like a mirror, so that they might look at it when tested by lesser afflictions. In that man's parable he embodied all the pains of those who suffer, and in his endurance, all the minds that overcome suffering. He carefully portrayed his trial for those undergoing trials and crowned them with the crown for his labors that was awarded to him. He wove a crown of reward for the weary who imitate him.

And he decreed harsh lashes for the wicked who hate the good. In him and his companion the master painter depicted every class: in one, the poor, and in the other, the class of those who possess wealth. He rebuked those who possess wealth, rebuking them through the reproof of that rich man, so that they would flee from his mercilessness. He condemned his mercilessness through a rebuke in words, so that everyone might learn to rebuke himself with heartfelt repentance. Through his death he revealed the day of death that terrifies the wicked, and through the departure of that poor man, the rest of the good. Death is restful for anyone worn out by hardships, as the saying that granted a reward to Lazarus's name testifies. “Lazarus died,” the writer wrote about Lazarus, and the heavenly hosts carried him up and placed him in Abraham's bosom. The poor man, who resembled Abraham, ascended to Abraham and rested in the harbor of the man who had given rest to the weary during his lifetime. Righteous Abraham relieved that diligent man's toil—not that he himself gave him rest, but the one who gives rest on the day of resurrection. It is not Abraham who gives the weary rest from their labors, nor is he the one who grants a reward to those who resemble him. It is the Lord of all who gives a reward to exhausted workers, and by his judicial sentence punishes the wicked who showed no mercy and lived in comfort. The recompense did not actually take place as it was told, nor did the lashes of the judicial sentence fall upon the wicked. What happened symbolically will take place at the end, and at the consummation the power hidden in its symbol comes to rest. The poor man who rested from his toil was portrayed symbolically, and in the same way so was the rich man who remained in Sheol. The rich man is said to have remained in Sheol in torment because the wicked are destined to remain in the place below. The wicked remain in the place below to be punished. That is why it is said that the rich man remained and stayed in Sheol. That merciless man who had no compassion remained in Sheol and was not raised with Lazarus to the place above. The weight of [?] hung upon the soul of the heavy-hearted man, and he could not fly through the air with the one who was light. The body of the man whose flesh was wasted grew wings of spirit.

Like a bird, he flew from the earth toward the heights. The limbs of the man clothed in [?] became like lead, and he sank into Sheol like lead into the depths of the waters. The splendor of his clothes became snares for that proud man. They caught him suddenly and gave him as food to ravenous death. The man who devoured his companions became food for the devourer, unable to escape from the mouth of death. Death swallowed that devourer of pleasures, and no rebellious part of him remained among the living. He fell from the height of his pleasures into the depths of Sheol and began to wail over the afflictions that had suddenly surrounded him. A great groan suddenly wrung him over what had happened to him, and he marveled and was astonished at the change in his circumstances. An evil time had finally overtaken him without his realizing it. Because he had not discerned the time, that evil time rebuked his pride. He looked at him without understanding during his time of prosperity, and his soul despised him, contrary to proper order, on the day of torment. On the day of his torment, the senseless man pleaded, not knowing that the time for the soul’s repentance had passed. The misguided man, mistaken in all his judgments, deceived himself, thinking that an appeal made with words would stand him in good stead. The ignorant man wanted to put together a verbal appeal, and he began making a plea that could bring him no benefit. “My father Abraham!” the ignorant man cried out to Abraham. Abraham answered him with words that rebuked his ignorance. The pressure of suffering compelled the arrogant man against his will, and he uttered words far removed from his deeds. The thoroughly unjust man called righteous Abraham his father, without looking carefully enough to distinguish injustice from righteousness. The son of sin called himself a son of Abraham, thinking that he could deceive Abraham and Abraham’s Lord. The [?] recalled his family relationship with the house of Abraham, but did not consider how his evil disposition made him foreign to that family. His evil disposition made him hateful to Abraham, and he heard words full of reproach that cut off his hope. The arrogant son of Abraham relied on Abraham. That was why he repeatedly called on Abraham to come and help him.

The accursed man saw that poor man in Abraham’s embrace, and begged and pleaded that he would come down and relieve his distress. “Send my brother Lazarus to me,” he said to Abraham. He did not shrink from using names that did not belong to him. The names he used were foreign to his evil disposition, and the character of his deeds was utterly foreign to their actions. His disposition tormented that man of bitter disposition, and he sought, through Abraham’s name, to ease the harshness [?] of his lashes. The invisible flame tormented him severely, and he [?] for mercy to relieve his burning. The accursed man asked for the water of mercy through Lazarus, to lighten the burden of the flame upon his tongue. The tip of his tongue was tormented far more than the rest of him—that tongue which had served as an advocate for words against the truth. The man whose mind was battered had fought against the truth, and the truth itself shut the door against his words. The truth would not persuade Abraham to have mercy on his son, and Abraham too answered him with a declaration that cut off hope. “Remember, my son,” Abraham said to his son who was unlike Abraham, “that the day of judgment has ended the course of your day of good things. “You thoroughly enjoyed those bodily pleasures. Go out and suffer torment in proportion to that [?] of your desires. “Remember that [?], when your good things of every kind were plentiful. Compare it carefully with the retribution that has met you. “Judge fairly: the examination that tested your falseness is just, and it has wisely given you a reward equal to your labor. “The chief of judges has pronounced judgment against your wickedness, and no one dares reverse the word of his sentence.” By the decree of his judgment he set a boundary and barred us from communicating with you, and none of us can go down to where you are. There is a great chasm between us and you, and no created being can cross over to its other side. Abraham expressed these things, not through an actual deed,

but in words corresponding to the meaning conveyed through him. Abraham spoke according to the meaning, though he did not actually speak. And in accordance with the words, that rich man heard what he heard. The rich man heard a terrifying report from Abraham, and he began devising other schemes in the hope of escaping. The misguided man devised other schemes according to his own thinking, not knowing that the door was shut against his schemes. With the pretext of his brothers he fenced around the pretext of his foolishness, and turned to making a plea full of deceit. The merciless man said that he had five brothers, and made a show of being deeply concerned out of love for his brothers. He spoke deceitfully when he said that he had five brothers, for he had no intention prompted by brotherly love. On behalf of his brothers, the man who was no son of Abram pleaded with Abram that someone from the dead should go and proclaim the punishment of judgment. “No one knows the punishment of judgment that has seized him, and someone from the dead must go and testify to the living. Those unfamiliar with the things here need witnesses, lest they too come into this torment in which I lie.” Tell me, accursed man, when and where were you merciful, that now you are so concerned to keep people from torment? A poor man lay despised at your gate, and your heart did not [?] at the humiliation in which he lay. When, wicked man, did you show your love toward those in distress, that we should now believe you take no pleasure in people's destruction?
