The envious man put on an appearance of compassion for humanity. He pleaded and begged, but his words were futile. The [?] of the schemes he devised was futile, for he heard a word that demolished the towering words he had built. The son of Abram heard a word of sorrow and despair when he was told, “There is water [?]; let them persuade them.” “They have the great Moses and his companions there,” he said. “Let them teach them what is fitting there and here.

Moses and the teaching of his companions are sufficient to instruct people, and there is no need for someone from the dead to explain things to the living. The dead cannot persuade the living as the living can, nor will the living listen to a report from those who are not alive. A great barrier has been erected before those who have departed, and none of them can break through its strength. Strong is the wall that death has built before the dead. Why do you weary yourself over something for which a plea is so difficult?” That rich man's petition was a plea that persuaded no one. His words came to an end, but the lashes decreed by his judgment did not end. A double judgment was added to him when his words ended, and he fell silent in Sheol, where stillness and silence reign. Now that the rich man's voice and his pleading words have fallen silent, come, let us approach the meaning hidden in his story. The meaning of the words is hidden in the plea concerning him, and only through words can the covering of words be unveiled. Words are spread over the story of the man who multiplies words. Let us reach out with words and lift the garment covering the face of the words. His words have wearied me from the beginning of the account of his words, as I sought to know and make known the reason for the arrangement of his words. This is the reason: instruction for humanity is hidden within his case, and no other explanation is needed to make his case known. His luxury [?] and his torment are recorded for humanity's instruction, so that people may learn to observe the order of the two worlds. The parable of the two men has shown me both worlds: one man rich and one poor, reality and its representation. The reality and representation of the two worlds are hidden in the two men, along with the dishonorable and glorious things of this world. The world of time proclaims the rich man's time, and the world [?] to come reveals the poor man's toil. The other world is represented by poverty in this world, and the wealth of this world by poverty in the everlasting one. Whoever is poor here without losing heart is rich there, and whoever possesses wealth and is proud in spirit is poor there. Whoever loses his life, as it is written, is found there; and whoever finds it in this order of things is lost in the other.

That rich man had acquired great gain on earth, but on the day of his death he lost his good things and inherited misery. Lazarus was known as a man who lacked everything, but in the other world he acquired good things that never pass away. The decay of his body prepared imperishable blessings before him, and wealth without end [?] welled up from the depth of his poverty. His finery doubled the misery of the man dressed in fine linen, for from his luxuries he acquired the luxury of the flame. Opposite things happened to the two men—and perhaps not just to the two, but to everyone who resembles them. These things happen to those who possess wealth or poverty, and they receive a double recompense for their deeds. Whoever is rich and lives indulgently has his torment doubled, like the rich man; and whoever is needy and afflicted has abundant comfort, like the poor man. The poor man's story gives courage to those in poverty, and the rich man's judgment curbs the greatness of wealth. The words that [?] heard from Abraham are the very words heard by wealthy people who live in such indulgence. In the peaceful harbor where Lazarus rested from his troubles, those burdened with afflictions find rest. Through Lazarus our Lord gave rest to weary laborers, and under the rich man's name he diverted indulgence from its course. He exposed wealth when indulgence accompanies it, and wove praises for neediness that does not lose heart. Greed remained in Sheol, in the torment of fire, while poverty ascended and rested in Abraham’s bosom. Abraham gave relief to the poor wherever he was, and he was compassionate and full of mercy toward wrongdoers. In his earthly dwelling he gave rest to human beings and spiritual beings, and in the dwelling above, through Lazarus, to all who suffer. For Sodom he pleaded that the threatened punishment should cease if righteous people were found there, yet he could not show mercy to the rich man in his distress. “It is not possible to cross over to you,” he answered the distressed man. This was an act of mercy, not of merciless vengeance. It was not merciless vengeance that exacted payment from the greedy man, but a judgment full of justice and faithfulness.

The poor man did not inherit delight through favoritism, but a reward worthy of his diligent labors. For the two men described deserved what befell them, and no one knows how to examine their case as their judge does. Just was the judgment that judged the two of them with two verdicts: torment for one, and blessedness with Abraham for the other. He invited and called all who are distressed to Abraham, and cast all who live at ease into torment with the rich man. Through the man who lived at ease, he defined and revealed the limits of temporal life; through the man who suffered, he taught everyone endurance of soul. He encouraged sufferers by naming Lazarus, who was afflicted, and portrayed the pampered through the punishment of the pampered man. Everything that happened was brought about for our benefit as human beings by the one who brought it about, and he wisely arranged these things as in a treasury. He concealed these events as his hidden mysteries, and taught human beings to seek them lovingly. The lover of humanity cast the fire of his love into human beings, and showed them how to reveal the blaze of his light. He skillfully fashioned the power of his teaching so that it would be firmly established amid the soul’s movements, without being shaken. He planted it in the soul like a sapling deep in the earth, and sprinkled his sayings like dew upon seedlings. He took on the role of a farmer in his punishment of wrongdoers, and pruned the various kinds of evil from them like shoots. The wicked bore branches of various kinds of wrongdoing, and he cut them off like boughs from trees. He cleared away the thicket of shameful deeds as one clears a forest, so that the good seed he had sown in human beings would not be ruined. He came to the wounded like a physician, and applied to each of them the medicine suited to that person. He cut away the swelling of wickedness with the iron blade of the sentence of judgment, and strengthened weakness with the hope of things to come. He applied the cautery of the name of Gehenna to greed, and gladdened the merciful by mentioning their lamps. He encouraged diligence with a reward whose blessedness is doubled, and rebuked the lazy through the one who was rebuked.

He gave everyone, one and all, a taste for good things, and seasoned them as with salt through the sweetness of his words. He gave people sick in soul the sweetness of his words to drink, and shook from them the hateful burden of shameful deeds. Here are his good medicines, which healed our dead race. Come, let us lovingly consider the power within them. Here are the commandments of the skilled teacher who made our souls wise. Come, let us strive to keep the order in which he arranged them. Here is the path of peace that he himself showed humanity in his own person. Come, let us walk in it according to the bounds his love established. He has set before us two orders of existence: the present and the future. Come, let us long for that order which has no end. He has told us the good news about his kingdom on high. Come, let us adorn ourselves in garments fitting for the day of his banquet. Everything is prepared and kept for us. Come, let us strive to receive wealth that never dwindles. There is nothing that has not been explained to our minds. Come, let us stand firm in understanding the words explained to us. The kinds of hidden things that had not been revealed have now been explained. Come, let us meditate on the power of their explanations. The proclamation has sped out to the four corners of the earth. Let us listen with everyone to the good news that brings life. The heralds of the proclamation sowed the good news and brought the fruits of righteousness into bloom among mortals. Come, mortals, let us cultivate the fruits of righteousness while there is still time to nurture every kind of goodness. With love let us cultivate the field of our souls’ free will, so that we may reap immortal fruits of which we will never have our fill.
On the Formation of Adam and Eve
Discourse Twenty-Nine. On the Formation of Adam and Eve, and on the Transgression of the Commandment.

A king is honored through his image, when far away as though nearby. Through his image, Adam, the Creator wished to enlist the service of rational beings. The Creator placed his image in the world, the royal city. Through the visible image he makes known his hidden power. The Creator adorned creation with his image when he fashioned it, so that in their love for Adam they might imitate his love. He made him kin to the angels through a spiritual soul. And he joined him to the speechless creatures through the composition of his limbs. It says, “The Lord God formed Adam from dust of the earth.” “And he breathed into him the breath of life,” and made him living and rational. It says, “The Lord God saw, and behold, everything he had made was complete.” Only Eve was lacking, to be a delight to Adam. The Lord God cast stillness upon Adam, and he slept. He took one of his ribs and fashioned a woman in his likeness. He took a bodily part from Adam and made a human being like Adam. He restored Adam’s bodily parts so that he would lack nothing. Adam saw a new wonder: a human being who had come from a human being. For she was complete in everything, in body and soul, like him. The Maker extended revelation within him as far as he could receive it. And he made him understand how she was formed, that Eve was a part of his flesh. Adam prophesied and said, “Eve is bone of my bones. She shall be called woman, for she sustains temporal life.” In Adam’s formation he showed

that he appointed Adam as head, while Eve, in the second rank, fulfills her service to the man. Eve is equal to Adam in nature and formation. She is inferior to him in authority, for Adam is the head and she is his feet. The Creator formed them outside the dwelling of Paradise. He placed them in the region of Eden, where the heavenly lights rise. The Lord God, it says, took Adam, the image of his glory, and placed him in the Paradise of Eden, to be an heir within it. He also laid down a commandment for him, suited to him at that time [?], so that he might know the power of his nature and learn the Maker’s authority. The Lord, it says, commanded Adam and set a boundary for him at the tree, so that through this the discernment of his nature might become known. “All the fruits of Paradise I have given for your enjoyment. Only from one shall you not eat, for it brings forth death from its fruits. But if you keep my commandments and do not act presumptuously toward the tree, I will give you the fruit of life once I have tested your freedom.” He laid down this law equally for both of them, so that they would not blame one another when they transgressed the commandment. O source of all wisdom, who knows everything before it happens! Though he knows the one he has formed, he lays down a commandment for him as though he did not know. Inquiry into these things has prompted me to recount the purpose of the tree: how can something speechless possess knowledge of wisdom? And if he knew that Adam would not keep the law he was laying down for him, why did he make him mortal, a mortal against his will? And if he had not created Adam, the head of our nature, mortal, why did the all-knowing one, who knows everything, not prevent him from doing this? Hearing the words of the scriptural reading greatly confuses simple people: that Adam’s transgression of the commandment made our race mortal. And if Adam’s wrongdoing condemned Adam and his children, why did this escape the all-knowing one, who knows everything? Why was he preparing created things so well suited to mortals? And why males and females in nature for its perpetuation? But far be it! It is not fitting to say this about the Creator’s will: that he did not know we would sin,

and that anger changed his will. When he formed us, he knew that he was making us mortal. His creation bears witness to his knowledge, for it was created for mortals. He made us rational and discerning, provided for us, and filled us with his wisdom. He wished to bring our discernment into the open through a test. Adam had been formed and adorned equally in body and soul. His discernment was hidden until he transgressed the commandment. The commandment became like a furnace and brought Adam into a test. His discernment was revealed, showing that he was not deficient by nature. He called it the tree of knowledge, although it was mute by nature, because the knowledge hidden in Adam was revealed through its fruit. Adam was unworked gold before he ate from the tree. After he ate the fruit, he displayed the beauty of his forms. The fruit became like a furnace, and Adam was like gold within it. The power of eating blew upon him, and he received a taste of knowledge. Through the tree of life he disclosed to us the ordering of the world to come. He set it in the place of a reward for the excellence of Adam’s will. Longing for the tree’s fruit enticed Adam in his childlike state, so that, when his soul ate from it, the fruit of life would renew him. By speaking of two trees, he represented both worlds to us. As though to children, he wished to disclose his hidden nature through a symbol. Through the tree of knowledge he bound him to earthly wealth, and through the tree of life he disclosed to him that heavenly wealth. Adam, still a child at that time, could not learn this. Therefore he enticed him through the tree, so that he would become capable of knowledge. He who created Adam and everything else knew everything about Adam. In forming the mortal, he wished to reveal his services. He barred him from one tree and stirred him to desire the other. Whether to eat or not to eat was left to Adam’s will. He placed the innocent ones in the dwelling of Eden and honored them.

He subjected everything that came into being through him to the authority of his image, Adam. “The Lord God created,” it says, “the livestock and the wild animals.” He brought them before Adam so that he might give names to his possessions. His maker [?] gave him power, and he gave as many names as he could. Through this, he taught him that he had made him master of everything that had come into being. The Creator’s image is a marvel: how excellent his formation is! His dominion extends over everything, and all that came into being was subjected to him. The lives of [?] and rational beings are equally bound to him. Through their kinship with him, they honor him like a king. The heights and depths are for his dwellings; the sea and dry land for his provision; winds and breezes for his life; summer and winter for his comfort. The creatures rejoiced in him and obeyed him as their master. And the angels were [?] in his service, rejoicing. Creatures both speechless and rational gathered around him in love. And they rejoiced that the nature they all shared was included in his honor. One alone found no rest under the rule of Adam’s love. Harmony did not please him, for he had swallowed poison from an arrow. It was not pressure from others that had forced him to become an adversary. For he had been created good by nature, like the angels who belonged to his rank. There was no cause for his envy and no occasion for his bitterness except Adam’s greatness, for he saw him honored by everyone. His gall stirred him to envy, and he became entirely hostile. He grew angry with the Creator because he had honored Adam’s image. He was destroying himself in his thoughts through the evil desire that burned within him. He was devising every sort of scheme to bring his tricks into the open. This was his hateful desire: “Why is Adam honored? And why are creatures both speechless and rational bound together in love for him? As for me, who am the ruler of the air and of all the spiritual ranks, he did not honor us even with a word when he fashioned our nature. But when fashioning this contemptible thing, the dust and ashes of the earth, he said, ‘Let us make a human being in our image, and let him be honored in our likeness.’ He made him like a lord on earth

and called him the image of his hidden being. He is honored by everything that came into existence, like the Creator within his creation. He even subjected heavenly and earthly beings to his honor! He is a mortal molded from the earth, and lowly in his judgment, like the earth. Yet the authority of his word makes him king over those above and those below.” The fire of his envy blazed up, and the fury of his jealousy burned. He sought to peer in at them and bring his thoughts into the open. He did not show them his tricks as he is accustomed to do now, because at that time he was not permitted to appear in human form. He made the serpent his garment, put it on, and concealed his ugliness, so that they would not suddenly be terrified by a sight unfamiliar to them. The innocent ones were calm and quiet, observing the order established by their Maker. They looked upon one another with beauty, in the purity of their minds. The deceiver began to speak aloud through a lyre of flesh: “What is the reason you are forbidden to eat any fruit?” First he questioned them as though he truly wanted to learn, for he was aware that by his own nature he could not know hidden things. He had not heard the commandment that the Creator had laid upon Adam’s household. That is why he questioned them: to learn what had been said and then lead them astray. The serpent spoke to Eve, the crafty one to the innocent-minded woman: “Has the Creator perhaps forbidden you the desirable fruits of Eden?” The innocent woman said to the deceitful one, “We have not been forbidden the trees, only that one tree over there, for death is hidden in eating from it.” The deceiver found an opening and began to sow his weeds. He brought forth the fruit he desired: exile at the very outset. “You certainly will not die,” the serpent said, misleading Eve. “You will become like gods, knowing hidden things.” Oh, the hater [?] of humanity, who disturbed the peace of creation! He was not content merely to lead them astray, but even brought forth gods. Here his wickedness came to light,

and he condemned himself by his own words, for he envied Adam and his children and introduced many self-existent beings. “You will become gods,” he said, “and there will not be just one God. That is why he forbade you that tree and called it death. “Come, enjoy its fruits, and look—your eyes will be opened! “For life is hidden in this food, which will make human beings gods.” The woman saw the tree, it says, and saw that it was altogether desirable and pleasing to look at. She took some of its fruit and ate, and also gave some to her companion with her. It says that she ate first, to win for herself the name of a god, since she had been persuaded by the claim, “You will become like gods.” She gave it to her husband afterward, so that she would become a god first. The empty hope of the devil’s promise deceived her. Their eyes were opened, it says, through eating the fruit, and they saw. They found fault with themselves—a sight full of disgrace. They had not known shame before eating from the tree. But once they had transgressed the commandment, they saw that they were naked and exposed. They joined fig leaves together to hide themselves from one another, for sin had suddenly brought exposure and disgrace upon them. Discernment had been hidden in their innocent minds. Once they ate from the tree, they became able to discern what was proper. That is why he called the tree from which they ate the tree of knowledge: the knowledge in their minds came to light through eating from it. It was not that the tree gave knowledge, for it did not possess this by nature. Rather, because of it they learned what it meant to transgress the commandment. They made a covering for their bodies from the leaves of that very tree. Because of it they acquired knowledge, and with its leaves they covered their bodies. But he who knows hidden things did not neglect his repentance. Even when he gave him the commandment, he knew that he would sin. Toward evening the Creator made the sound of his footsteps heard, as he came to call them to account for the offense of transgressing the [?]. O nature that is not made of parts,

who is not confined by his works! He gave his footsteps a sound as he came to rebuke Adam. O source of all wisdom, who holds the sum of all things, who asks, as though he did not know, where the member of his household is hiding! He made the sound of his footsteps heard to frighten them because they had sinned. He asked, “Where are you, Adam?” while showing that he knew where he was. “Where are you, Adam?” the Maker said to the image he had fashioned. “Where are you, heir of Paradise? Why are you hiding your offenses?” O Good One, how he loves the image of Adam, made of dust! With tender sounds he seeks him in his lost state. “Where are you, honored Adam, whom I made master over the earth? What have you become, exposed one, modest one who has stripped off his splendor?” “I heard your voice and hid myself,” Adam answered his Maker. “I am ashamed to look at your face, because I am stripped and exposed.” “Who made you naked?” the Master said to his servant. “Who stripped off your covering, honored one who has disgraced himself? Did the sight of the tree entice you to eat? And has the boundary I established made you naked, without clothes?” “The woman gave it to me, and I ate,” said childish Adam, thinking that he was showing himself to be free from blame. God said to Eve, “What is this that you have done?” She shifted the blame onto others: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” But he did not question the crafty one as he had questioned Adam, for he had no excuse for his envy, allowing him to say, “Someone else deceived me.” Then the Creator who had fashioned them began to pronounce judgment. He began first with the serpent, because it had been the cause of the evils. In the curses upon the serpent, he was cursing the devil. He was pointing to his downfall, indicating that he was removing him from his authority. He had been ruler of the air and commander of his companions. But because he deceived Adam and Eve, he fell to the earth and was brought low. God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this and deceived them, you are cursed more than all crawling creatures, and your movements will be bound within you. Dust will be your food, and your movements will be upon the earth.

Because you drove the heir out of his glory, you will be struck down upon the earth. From now on you will be an enemy to Adam and all his children.” “For he will trample your head into the ground, and you will strike him when he sins.” After the serpent, he turned the sentence of judgment toward Eve. For she had first accepted its advice and stretched out her hand toward the fruit. He cursed her with pain and wailing and bound her with the pangs of childbirth. He placed her in subjection to her husband, so that she would meet his needs. Oh, how wise are the Creator’s ways of dealing with his creatures! What he had established in nature, he imposed as correction. Last of all, the Creator cursed Adam, the image of his glory, for the severity of the sentence had been softened through the serpent and Eve. The Lord said to Adam—the Maker to the image he had formed—“Because of you, I am cursing fruits, seeds, and trees, because you listened to your wife’s voice and ate the fruit of knowledge. You must work the ground, and only then will it give you fruit. You are dust from the ground, Adam, and to the ground you will return because you sinned. Because you despised the commandment I gave you, speaking and speechless creatures will despise you. Look, now you have become a god, just as the Evil One deceived you into believing! Command the forces of nature to obey, if his prophecy is true!” The Creator spoke these words, mocking him. “Look, Adam has become like one of us; now he has become a god! Let him leave Paradise, the heir who did not appreciate his own honor, lest he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life.” But the Creator spoke these words to teach him, so that his folly would appear great in his own eyes and he would deeply hate sin. And if transgressing the commandment made him a stranger to his dwelling, how much more ought he to honor his Creator and never sin again! How glorious Paradise was, and how much delight was found within it! As he left it behind and went out, he was reproached for his sin. Like a teacher, the transgression of the commandment taught the simple man much wisdom. The sentence of judgment and the correction made him hate sin. Through the tree was removed

the veil over his mind. Through his desire for its fruit, he came to recognize the freedom within him. Adam began to prophesy through the power the Creator had placed within him. By revelation he spoke of the future of his race. Adam called his wife Eve, the bearer of life, for she was destined to become a mother and give birth to human beings in successive generations. The Lord God made tunics for Adam and his household by stirring their thoughts to cover their bodies. The Creator clothed them in tunics of skins by placing within them the knowledge to meet their needs. Everything he decreed and imposed as correction was done to teach them. For their comfort he supplied the needs of their bodies. With his voice he commanded them to leave the beautiful dwelling of Eden. So that they would not enjoy the fruit of the tree that gives life. “Lest,” he said, “Adam return and take some of the fruit of life. Let him go out to the place where he was formed and cultivate the ground of curses.” For one day those made of dust were heirs in the dwelling of Paradise. At the evening of that day they moved as strangers to another land. In the morning they [?] their formation, and at the ninth hour [?], condemnation. On the very day on which they were formed, they ate, sinned, and went out. Through the Spirit the prophet wrote for us that they spent one day in the land of Eden. For he said, “At the evening of the day,” not at the evening of another day. Adam left Paradise and settled in the land around it. The man made of dust grieved because he had become a stranger to his dwelling. He fenced Paradise off before him with the sharp edge of the sword of the spear. He also stationed a guardian for it, a fearsome cherub to guard it. O wise Creator, how greatly he loves what he has formed! He kept contemptible things away from it, so that they might honor him with glorious things. He greatly honored Paradise by stationing a guardian for it. So that Adam would recognize his folly and turn back to seek his honor. He made him aware of his sin so that he would honor his Lord’s command. So that, when he worked the ground with all his strength, he would know what he had lost. Adam left Paradise with sorrow yoked to him.

And [?] began boasting, “Adam has become my slave!” The spiritual hosts grieved when they saw the humiliation of the honored one. They all clothed themselves in sorrow because the freeborn man was laboring in slavery. They had rejoiced in him when he was formed and had delighted in seeing him. For they saw that their nature was akin to that of his soul. They were clothed in loving sorrow because death had come to reign over Adam. They were distressed as they saw his soul separating from his body. All creation mourned over Adam’s beautiful form. It had been bound to him in love, but sin loosened the bond. The spiritual beings turned their faces away from him like strangers. And the elements were unwilling to act to sustain his life. Even the animals rebelled against him, and the creeping creatures fled and hid in the earth. All his possessions despised him because he had despised his Lord’s word. By his own will he became a stranger to the dominion that had been given him. The lowly creatures grew insolent and greatly despised the honored one. Creatures without speech and those endowed with speech clothed themselves in mourning over his downfall. Only one rejoiced: the one who had been distressed by his honor. He gave the mortal a dwelling near Paradise, so that he would always remember both his inheritance and his folly. The Creator devised these means to discipline Adam, and through the harshness of his correction he was drawing him toward understanding. These things had always been hidden in the knowledge of the one who created everything. He brought them to light because of the transgression of the commandment. He had created Adam mortal and prepared a dwelling suitable for him. He made the sin of transgressing the commandment the cause of mortality. Through this affair of Adam's household, he was teaching wisdom to all humanity: If sin brought about death, let us henceforth hate it, because it has ruined us. The sentence was severe for him and greatly disciplined the simple man. Since sin had cast him into death, he was to learn who could give him life. The commandment taught him much wisdom and made him recognize his own nature, so that the man made of dust would not become proud

and forget his limited nature. When forming him, the Maker stored up every kind of wisdom within him. He made him master of his own freedom, so that he could conduct himself according to his own will. He planted pleasant impulses within him: desire and love, as part of his nature, so that from the spring of his body the whole human race would continue to exist. Adam, it says, knew his wife, and Eve, the living one, conceived. She bore a child and called him an acquisition from God. See the wisdom of our nature, which the Maker stirred within it: the gift that he gave at the beginning, it regarded as his own possession. Eve rejoiced in acquiring Cain, her firstborn. After him she bore another and gave him a name meaning “breath.” She named Abel “breath,” because his life would vanish like a breath, while through her prophecy she rebuked his brother, who would destroy his life. Eve and Adam, it says, saw that they had acquired offspring endowed with speech. Though they had become mortal through sin, they acquired life through their children. Abel became a shepherd, and Cain a worker of the soil. They offered the first fruits of their labors to the God of all. Abel offered a lamb, and with his offering he offered his willing heart. Cain offered plants from the ground, but willingness was not mingled with his offering. Their offerings revealed the intentions of their thoughts. And [?] rebuked the deceitful man by returning his offering to him. That Maker who had rebuked Eve and Adam when they sinned— he himself wished to bring the intentions of Abel and his brother into the open. His knowledge became a balance and weighed them both. The upright man's intention weighed heavily, while the deceitful man's intention weighed little. He lovingly accepted the offering of Abel, whose heart was pure. But he rejected and cast aside Cain's offering, because his mind was not pure. Through fire the Creator revealed whose offering had been accepted. The fire took hold of Abel's offering and consumed it, but it did not approach Cain's. Cain clothed himself in deep mourning, and his face became very gloomy. He became embittered against his Maker because he had rejected his offering. The Lord spoke openly to Cain in a gentle voice: “If you make your will good, I will accept your gift.

But if the bitterness of your thoughts is not tempered with sweetness, your sin crouches at the door and is not wiped away from your limbs. Look, envious man, I have given you your offering; why are you distressed? You have authority over what is yours. Go and manage what is yours with your own hands.” Cain’s will did not change after he was admonished. He did not accept correction through the reproof offered to him. He was reproached for his arrogance, like the Accuser. He added anger to anger, and his mind gave birth to murder. For the insolent man thought that, by killing the innocent man, he would cause distress to the Creator because he had rejected his offering. Through Abel he sought revenge for his grievance against the Maker, like his master Satan, who insulted his Maker through Adam. Cain spoke to his brother—the envious man to the innocent man: “Come, let us go to the plain and see the beauty of the earth.” The man burning with envy composed words of love, so that, under the pretext of love, he could go and vent his anger on the guileless man. The guileless man trusted the crafty man, as Eve had trusted the deceitful one. The innocent man went out with him to the plain, unaware. Cain the murderer attacked and violated the affection natural to kinship. He killed his brother out of envy, intending by his murder to distress God. Oh, the heart that gave birth to murder, a deed new upon the earth! Oh, the insolent will that opened a road to the abode of the dead! Through Abel the road was opened, and death began to travel along it. Adam learned through the deed that he too was mortal. Through Cain the Accuser fulfilled the desire born of his envy. He took comfort for a long time when he saw that death had gained dominion. The master taught his pupil falsehood and denial. He hid the murdered man in the earth, so that he would not have to confess when questioned. For the murderer thought that Abel’s blood could be concealed. He did not know that the one who had rejected his offering could see him. Cain hid the murdered man and concealed his intention along with him. He sought to hide his deed from the one who knows hidden things.

Suddenly the Maker spoke and called aloud to the murderer: “Oh, envious and deceitful man, how has the innocent man wronged you?” “Where is your brother Abel?” the Lord said to Cain. He answered him evasively, though he knew why he was calling him. Oh, the all-knowing one who asks as though he does not know what has happened! Just as he had questioned in Paradise, so he questioned the murderer. In Eden he questioned Adam, saying, “Where are you, Adam?” even as he saw him. And here he asked Cain about Abel, “Where is your brother?” although he knew. He asked as though he did not know, so that perhaps the insolent man would repent. For if he confessed his wrongdoing, he would also grant him forgiveness. Cain, the first disciple, equipped himself with his teacher’s weapon. Both the teacher and his disciple lied, and justice bound them. “Where is your brother Abel?” he said, but the wrongdoer was unwilling to confess. Instead, he answered wickedly, “Am I indeed my brother’s keeper?” He spoke to his Lord with a clenched fist, but the murderer did not escape detection. “If your beloved has perished, whom am I obliged to hand over to you?” Justice bound Cain’s voice with terrifying ropes. Because he was unwilling to confess voluntarily, he disclosed it and confessed when he was exposed. “What is this you have done?” the Lord said to Cain. “Your brother’s blood cries out to me, bringing its case against his murderer. “From now on you are cursed from the earth, and the earth beneath you will not prosper. “Because it received innocent blood, it will receive curses along with it. Your body will be tossed with trembling in return for the body your hands destroyed. “You will become a terror to those who see you, because your heart did not tremble at murder. For you began the first bloodshed and presented the first offering to death. “For seven generations I will demand the innocent blood from your hands, “because you opened a road to the abode of the dead, along which the multitude of humanity would travel. “I will make an example of you, showing that I demand blood in return for blood.” The threats were put into effect, and trembling clothed the murderer. His body shook upon the earth, and quaking convulsed him entirely. With repentance that was not voluntary, he pleaded with the Creator. He asked for death for himself, so that he might escape the scourges.

Cain said to the Lord, “Look, you have driven me from the earth. You have clothed me in trembling and quaking, which are very terrifying to those who see me. “I ask one thing, if you are willing to deal with me according to your mercy: “that through death your curses may be released from my limbs.” “Not so, murderer,” the Lord said to Cain. “Your wrongdoing will not be punished in this way, by death alone. For seven generations I will prolong the scourges that punish your wickedness. “The punishment for your murder will be spoken of throughout the whole world.” The Lord placed a mark on Cain so that he would not die at human hands. He made this the sign: that his command protected him. He kept the murderer alive as a warning to the generations to come, so that, when they considered the punishment [?], they would flee from murder. For a time, Eve and Adam had been comforted when they had children. Then grief over their children entered. They wept for Abel, who had been killed [?], because death had destroyed his features. And they mourned over Cain, because a disturbance had been caused in creation. The Creator bound them together through the love inherent in natural affection, so that the delight found in nature would ease the distress of hardships. Through this arrangement the Maker taught us wisdom from the beginning, so that through the pains and sufferings of death we might acquire love for him. He occupied us with earthly things in our earthly condition, so that, when we became aware of our exhaustion, we would ask for life without toil. He nurtured our infancy with milk, with weak things suited to our strength, so that, when we reached maturity, we would possess the knowledge of life. He did not give us free control over wealth while our understanding was still infantile, for as long as an heir is a child, he cannot manage his possessions. Through the vitality of the soul, he granted us that our temporal life should be sustained. And when we become immortal, he will preserve us through the power of the Spirit. The Creator of our nature understood everything belonging to our nature, and wisely guided us from lowly things to lofty things, so that, when we learned and understood who had brought us to these things, we would give thanks to the Power that established everything, for how greatly he loved our nature.
On Humility
By the same author. Discourse sixty-[?]: On Humility.

With a word of peace the Lord of the world captured the world; he subdued it and harnessed it under the gentle yoke of his kindness. Through humility he humbled the might of the heights and the depths, and taught them to walk in the way of humility. They cast a net of peace over all, and it caught everyone; he nourished them with the gentle food of the word of his mouth. He cast the fire of his love upon the earth full of thorns; the thicket of mortality vanished, and life sprang up. With the light of his name he drove away the darkness of ignorance; people saw the power of his being and believed in his name. With the sound of his commandments he purified the world, which lacked understanding, and it acquired a taste for the sweetness of the life of the one [?]. With the waters of mercy he washed the people whom wickedness had made ugly, and bestowed on them the [?] beauty of righteousness. With the fire of the Spirit, the Maker of all recast his image,

and renewed it, shaping it spiritually so that it would no longer be corrupted. He overlaid it with the spiritual gold of the name of his being, and placed it on high so that it would not be ruined by harmful things. By renewing his image, he revealed to his creatures the power of his wisdom, for he wisely enabled his own to grow in the knowledge of him. In wisdom he arranged that through his image he would renew everything and bind human beings together with spiritual beings in the peace of his name. He opened a new path of humility before his servants, for he himself first traveled along it and came to his creatures. The Word of the Father, who is entirely the likeness of his Father, desired through humility to bring peace to the divided world. The Creator took the likeness of a servant from among mortals, and humbly revealed himself, hidden in what was visible. For he did not show the nature of his being to the eyes of those who saw him, lest they think that pride had deceitfully carried him away. By his own will he clothed himself in the appearance of a servant and appeared in it, while his nature remained what it had been, without change. He concealed his being, which his creatures cannot comprehend, and revealed his glory and showed his power through the humble one. He came to teach humility to the members of his household, and humbled himself through the humble one whom he assumed for his name. In what belongs to us he showed his humility and the power of his wisdom, not in his own nature, which is neither diminished nor increased. In the likeness of a servant he humbled himself in proportion to his greatness, and did not boast in the glories of his hidden majesty. He established humility in himself like a mirror, so that people might see themselves and hate pride. He humbled himself to the point of death for the sake of humanity, and crucified with himself the mortality that had oppressed his race. He died for all and gave life to all through the power of the one who assumed him. He reconciled the world with the will that brought peace to all through him. For this reason he humbled himself and descended to Sheol, to raise humanity from the lowliness of mortality. And because he surrendered himself to death and gave life to all, the Creator also honored him with the name that is above every name. Through humility he triumphed and was exalted above death, and he also taught us to overcome the passions through humility. If the humble one whom the Most High put on humbled himself, who would rise up in pride—a fool who destroys himself? If the rich one impoverished the wealth of his glories, who would boast in what is not his own as though it were his own? If the freeborn one humbled himself and [?] slaves, who would not [?] slavery to corruption for his liberator? If the righteous one counted himself among sinners, who would not lavish his own labors on behalf of his members? He himself opened the path of humility for us. Come, let us humble ourselves, so that we may not be estranged from the promise of life. He showed us that through humility he gained victory, and raised himself and his companions out of humiliation. He taught us a living example for us to imitate:

Let us bend our [?] and our limbs toward humility. In humility he sowed his teaching in the soil of humanity, and people brought forth the sweet fruits of humility. Through humility he captured the unruly world, brought it in, and confined it within the fortresses of humility. In humility he cast his net into the sea of humanity, and it gathered a catch of humility, caught by mercy. With [?] he proclaimed his words in everyone's ears, so that the sound of his teaching would not be difficult for his students. He called his good news an easy yoke before his hearers, so that people's minds would not grow slack in carrying out its work. “My yoke,” he said, “is pleasant to anyone who works humbly, and the burden of my words is very light for anyone who carries it.” And if it is difficult [?] for a time in the face of its threats, look: the encouragement of receiving the reward outweighs the hardships. “Let anyone who grows weary of the work imitate me, for I myself cultivated the soil of human beings and spiritual beings. Let anyone who is discouraged by hardships imitate me, for I gladly trampled down the sting of voracious death. Let anyone who bends toward the gentle goal learn from me, even as he struggles toward an exaltation that cannot be brought low.” Through humility the humble one conquered the proud world. Come, children of dust, humble yourselves and receive exaltation. Through humility he took captive the tyrant who had enslaved humanity. Come, let us weave him a crown of victory through humility. Through humility he trampled down death, which had trampled down our nature. Let us likewise trample down its threats through humility. Through humility let us bind our love to his lowliness, so that we do not fall away from the promises of riches. Through humility those perfected in his love fulfilled his will, and he gave them a share in the glories that he received when he was exalted. Through humility Abel offered a gentle lamb, and the disposition of his soul was far humbler than his offering. Humble in soul, he [?] his will together with his offering, and his sacrifice and the disposition of his soul rose up to acceptance. Humility placed [?] above death, and he grew immortal wings toward life. O mortal, entirely food for mortality, who rescued himself from the mouth of death, that voracious lion! Peaceful Noah also subdued his inclination through humility, and through his endurance he won the battle against the warring waters. O weighty one, who submerged his [?] in the waters of suffering! The waves carried his weight, and he did not sink. Abram too traveled along this road of humility, and arrived and reached the fulfillment of his reward. He entrusted himself to humility as to a teacher, and learned from her to meditate on the Creator's name. O disciple, who learned and taught himself and his household, and explained the mysteries of the name of the Eternal Being to his fellow human beings! O rich man, who acquired wealth and humility,

and did not exalt himself over earthly possessions [?] as though they were his own! He called himself worthless dust before his Creator, and because he made himself small, his Creator made him the beginning of the promised life. Let Abram be a mirror for those who acquire wealth, so that they do not exalt themselves above the humble because of their wealth. Do not boast, owner of possessions, in possessions that last only for a time, for time itself rebukes your pride through its changes. Time passes, and wealth passes away with its possessions. Pride comes to nothing, and the lofty neck descends to Sheol. Why are you proud of what is not yours, mortal? Why do you boast of earthly things that do not help you? You are dust, and [?] returns to ashes. Reflect on your nature, [?] renewed from its corruption. Know your nature and humble yourself before the One who sees everything. Wear yourself out and plead that he may raise your dust from its lowliness. Put humility over your limbs like a garment, so that your body may wear the [?] garment of the resurrection of the dead. Acquire humility, a great wealth that never grows poor, so that your body may wear the splendid garment of the resurrection of the dead. Acquire humility, a great wealth that never grows poor, so that you may be worthy to receive the wealth of life without end. Look at Abraham, who acquired wealth and humility. He grew rich and gained possession of earthly and spiritual things. Imitate Jacob, who humbled himself in earthly matters and acquired the rank of humility and seniority. See the wonder that humility performed through him: it reversed the order that the Creator established for human beings. His humility forced nature outside its established order and gave the rank of seniority to the younger. Who would not love humility, endowed with strength, which by its power overcame the forces of nature and their authority? Who would not flee from pride, weak in strength, whose power dwindled in Esau’s hands before the humble man? Esau’s pride brought him low; he was defeated and impoverished, and surrendered the rank of seniority to one younger than himself. Let everyone flee from pride, that treacherous armor which cannot give victory in battle to the one who wears it. Let everyone put on humility, that good armor which gives strength even to the weak and grants a reward. With this armor of humility Joseph too fought, and through endurance he won the battle against lustful desires. Moses too put on humility like armor, and those clothed in the armor of sorcery were defeated by his voice. He anointed his mind with humility like an athlete and put to shame the contestants whom error had anointed. Through humility he purified his body and sanctified his soul, and his mouth proclaimed the revelation of hidden things. The discerning man loved humility more than anything, and through it he was raised to a lofty rank above everyone. Here is the testimony to his humility within his own books: “The man Moses was very humble, more than anyone.” The One who sees everything saw him clothed in a modest garment, honored him with glory, and he became a god among mortals. O humble man, who wisely humbled himself and received a reward greater than the labor of his humility!

O descendant of earthly beings, a lowly nature, who put on glory foreign to the [?] of mortality! O poor man, whose life is troubled and whose years are few, who has acquired spiritual wealth and the name of God! Let us see in Moses how high humility was raised, so that it could lend a hand to the victory of him whose power can accomplish everything. Let those who serve humility contemplate him, and let them not slacken in the struggle against pride. Let the humble person arm himself against pride, like an athlete who guards himself against his opponent. Pride is an enemy and adversary of humility, and the humble person must not grow slack. Humble one, guard the strongholds of your soul against arrogance, lest it attack and plunder the treasury of your humility. Rouse the impulses of your discernment and guard your treasures. Drive the sleep of laziness from your thoughts. Put on the armor of humility against pride, and hold the sword of peaceful speech upon your lips. Do not allow the enemy to scrutinize you, lest he take courage for battle and advance to kill. Pride is a foolish murderer without understanding, and no one considers the pledge of death in its insolence. It is a tyrant [?], not softened by the sound of lamentation, and like a lion it roars continually to crush people. It was pride that broke Cain, the firstborn of arrogance, made his body tremble, and led his soul astray from uprightness. It spoke through contemptible Ham, and he dishonored his father. Then it bound him in the harsh chain of the righteous man's curse. Its counsel made careless Esau lose his rank, and through association with it he learned to deny his obligations. With it King Pharaoh armed himself against Moses; and because he [?] greatly, he descended into the merciless abyss. The insolent men who coveted the priesthood also served it, and they descended alive into Sheol, contrary to the natural order. In the strength of his arrogance Sennacherib threatened Hezekiah. He suddenly stirred the voice of justice to cry out, and it made him a laughingstock. Pride spoke blasphemously through the mouth of Rabshakeh, but the voice of prophetic proclamation shut his mouth. Foolish pride took the foolish King Rehoboam captive, and because he despised counsel, he became a stranger to the inheritance of the tribes. The Babylonian, too, subdued nations with the weapon of pride, but his pride turned and bound him under a yoke with the animals. He raised his rod over all the nations and disciplined everyone, but he did not understand who was using him to discipline his companions. Because he did not credit the power of victory to the one who gave him victory, that one rejected him and cast him into exile among the animals. See the repayment that pride gives to those who love it! You who are weak, flee from the service of this murderer. See, its hidden deceit has been exposed by the testimony of the Spirit. Let no one be led astray by its words while [?].

See, it has been shown that its path ends in shame, and it drowns in the pit whoever travels with it. Do not walk the path of pride, O human being. Abandon arrogance and go in the company of humility. Do not boast of temporary possessions that do not [?]. Look at the many who amassed wealth and left it on earth. Do not exalt yourself because of a title of authority that passes away. Look and consider those who wore crowns and now lie in Sheol. Which king has been rescued by his crown from the mouth of death? Who has given wealth and bought life without end? No, human being, do not boast and deceive yourself, for there is no death that does not return a person to his nature of dust. A human being possesses life for a time, not forever. Here is the proof of how short his life is: the gate of death. A person must therefore live as befits his life and guide his life toward its end in a fitting way. Let the creature of dust consider the lowliness of his clay, how humble it is. Let him humble himself so that even his own clay does not reproach him. Humility befits your name, O creature of dust. Why do you exalt yourself with things that do not befit the name of ashes? You belong to the same race as righteous people, O human being. Walk the path of humility that the righteous have trodden. Travel with those of old in a company full of [?] and peace, and see [?] the company of those who labor in humility. Imitate David: see how greatly he humbled his own will and did not boast of the greatness of his labor in humility. See how the word of peace chose him for a lofty rank, yet he did not grow lax when he was deprived of his authority. He was anointed by the Spirit to be king and herald, yet he went out [?] from among the people like an evildoer. His will was made a holy temple for the Spirit of revelation, yet he was constantly persecuted by the spirit of falsehood dwelling in Saul. A hidden prompting continually played upon the lyre of his soul, and he drove demons away from the envious man who persecuted him. Whenever Saul grew inflamed and raved under the frenzied demon, the son of Jesse played the lyre of the Spirit, and the crafty one departed. Whenever the murderer raged within the envious man, David cried out through the Spirit of revelation, and the rebel trembled. And again, whenever he raved in his torment, burning with envy, he sharpened a sword to shed his helper’s blood. The foolish sick man, laid low with the pain of a demon and wickedness, began insulting the spiritual physician who had mercifully tended him. Saul lay afflicted with two senseless diseases: blind envy and a frenzied demon that deceives people. David gave him spiritual medicine suited to his illness, but because he rejected it, he rotted, wasted away, and died in his sin. Let the proud of heart, who are haughty and blind, look at Saul: envy blinded him, and pride killed him by the sword of the uncircumcised. Let the humble who love peace also look at David, so that they do not lose heart at the sound of insults from the insolent.

Do not be distressed, you who are humble in spirit, when you are insulted. Look at the son of Jesse, whom Saul repaid with reproach and dishonor. Do not repay someone who harms you according to his offense, lest you be reproached by the voice that says, “Forgive.” Bind your love to the gentle yoke of humility, and do not slacken in spiritual work. Travel with those who are full of the Spirit along the road of the Scriptures, and place [?] among the ordinances of humility. Read and understand the power of the wonders of the proclamation, and learn the parables and the explanation of hidden mysteries. Look for the passage in Matthew that is directed against pride, and see there two men praying before the One who sees everything. Look at the foolish, arrogant Pharisee who boasted about himself. Because he raised his voice, his pride left him without a reward. He was not lying in what he said, for he did not [?]. But because he wanted to display his labors, he went down ashamed. See how foolish pride rewards the person who clothes himself in it: it strips him of the work of his righteous labors. The Pharisee was righteous in the things he recounted, his fasting and his almsgiving. But because he mixed pride with his alms, he nullified his alms. The tax collector [?] who heard the boastful voice that destroys the reward looked at himself and lowered himself into humility. He saw that no labors give a person grounds for boasting, and he lowered his eyes so as not to gaze toward heaven. He bowed his head and hid his face from those watching. He began to plead like a debtor who had incurred a debt and been held as security. He restrained his limbs together with his thoughts before the One who sees everything, and began to scourge himself with contrition of soul [?]. He saw that he was entirely stained with the blemishes of wrongdoing. He poured out tears and washed his body and the impulses of his soul [?]. He raised his hand and scourged himself with the rod of sorrow, and discerningly condemned himself for the wrongs he had committed. With a sobbing voice he pleaded before the [?]: “Have mercy on me, for I have sinned! Woe to me, for I have wronged your love!” At the sound of his sobbing, the Judge [?] and the King’s ranks marveled, and he sent mercies to quiet his weeping. “Be still, sinner!” cried the mercies sent at the hidden command. “Look, the King has ordered us to blot out the record of your debts. “He has sworn with an ‘Amen’ that your wrongdoing is forgiven because of your humility. Go, rejoicing in the forgiveness of wrongdoing that mercy has given you.” Come, you humble people, and see how greatly humility has been exalted! It has received the rank of authority, immersed in “Amen.” Come, look discerningly at the man full of blemishes, who [?] his blemishes in the baptism of his self-abasement. Who has won a victory like that of the man who was wholly guilty? The One who sees openly placed on him a crown woven with “Amen.” Who has been justified like the sinner whose very name was wrongdoing? Through humility he erased his name together with his debts. Who would not aim at the gentle goal of humility, which teaches a person the ways of victory even if he is untrained?

Who would not meditate on loving communion with humility, which is full of peace and urges the sinner to ask for mercy? It taught the simple tax collector the ways of supplication, and traced out contrition of mind for him in place of letters. Come, let us study the books of its words, which possess power. Let us read with understanding and gain strength to overcome wrongdoing. The strength of its help can justify the guilty, and a multitude of wrongs counts as nothing before its pleading. Paul bears witness and praises the power of its help: it raised him up, and he attained the rank of leadership. The Will to which everyone cries out looked upon his humility and chose him beforehand to teach through his preaching. His voice proclaimed gentle sounds in people's ears and awakened them to hear the voice of the word of life. With kindness he cultivated the soil of rational humanity, and it yielded fruits of righteousness for the owner of the vineyard. He taught humility, urged and established it, and made it his own; he yoked people to the gentle yoke of humility. Through his gentleness he imitated the Master who chose him, as he proclaimed one confession of one Creator. Through humility he uprooted paganism and built up truth; Truth itself called him a wise man who builds well. Come, you humble people, build the structure of your conduct upon the foundation of humility that Paul laid. Learn from him how one ought to begin, and what works we should lay upon the rock of faith. Let his voice be like a mirror before your eyes, crying out and proclaiming that everyone should watch how he builds. Whoever builds with genuine gold—his work endures; whoever builds with straw and stubble—his work burns. See, he has shown us how to build the structure of truth; let us examine the judgment that tests the works of both sides. Humility can teach one to build well, and through it a person's building is completed, even if it is deficient. There is no deficient person who is not made complete by its perfection, and no unlearned person who is not made wise by its understanding. It is a peaceful harbor that gives rest to the soul and the body's members, and safely preserves the labors of righteousness. Through it the temple of the body and the will of the soul are purified, and a person becomes a pure dwelling for the hidden power. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall I look, and whom shall I choose as a dwelling for my hidden will, except the gentle and humble person who hears my words?” O Creator, from whom heaven and earth are filled, how can a lowly human being be large enough to become a dwelling for your love? “Yes,” he says, “I am in the heights and the depths, and they cannot contain me; yet in the humble person I am pleased to make a dwelling for my will. “My will loves humility far more than sacrifices; although I have no need, I long to see the sacrifices of its love. “Humble Noah offered it to me along with his offerings, and my will found rest in it,

“and I accepted visible sacrifices from him. Through it Moses the stammerer became wise and gained understanding, and with his stammering he interpreted the hidden things of my will. “Through it chosen Paul prepared himself to face sufferings; and when it saw that he could engage in battle [?], it anointed him with the Spirit.” See, the hidden sign has shown us whom he desires, and how he dwells willingly in the person in whom he dwells. The Maker of all chose a dwelling for himself in the humble in spirit; although everything belongs to him, he left everything and took up residence in the gentle person. The humble in soul is more worthy of blessings than all who have ever lived, for he alone is worthy that the Hidden One should dwell within him. If nothing is greater than the power that established everything, then neither is anything greater than a dwelling fit for his name. Who would not adorn the temple of his soul with humility, so that it might become a dwelling, and the will of the Despised One might dwell in it? Who would not hate companionship with senseless pride, which continually repays those who honor it with grievous injuries? For everyone, it is said, who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever is puffed up with arrogance in his heart will descend into disgrace. The proud-minded person is utterly abhorrent before God, and the conduct of his life is despised and hated by the One who sees in secret. Take care, you who are betrothed: do not grow lax in little things, lest you become hateful to the Hidden One, who hates pride. Endure lowliness for a little while, so that you may live long, for a reward is reserved for the humble according to their labors [?]. Listen to the voice of the giver of reward toward the humble [?], who makes the punishment severe for anyone who oppresses the lowly in soul [?]. For anyone, it is said, who causes a little one to stumble and oppresses him—it would have been better for him to be drowned in the depths of the sea. He called the lowly in soul, who makes himself small, a little one: someone who does not boast of the glorious achievements of his great labors. He called Lazarus this little one in the written account, for he was afflicted by two pains that brought him low. He was tormented by sickness and poverty; he longed for relief, but no one eased his distress. And he who had lacked earthly things during [?] time became rich and enjoyed [?] without end. Lazarus rested in the harbor of life, Abraham’s bosom, and opened a road for the humble to ascend to him. Come, you humble people, travel in the company of the humble in soul, and rest with Lazarus in the harbor of Abraham’s bosom. See, our Lord’s parable has opened a road like a guide [?], so that whoever walks humbly may not lose heart. Like a lookout, the parable cries out in people’s ears: “Rise, take courage, and travel on the road of humility!” Like a trumpet, it makes its voice heard by all the proud: “Take care, people! Do not become arrogant like the rich man.” Look at the possessions of that accursed man, which remained on earth: his wealth did not travel with him to Sheol as he had expected.

See how he pleaded but was given no relief from torment. He asked to return and testify to his brothers, but permission was not granted him. A command barred the road before him on every side and shut the door against his petition, so that it would not be accepted. See, through Lazarus and the rich man he has shown us how dearly humility is loved and how deeply pride is despised. See, he has taught us about the recompense of that rich man, and with what blessings he gives rest to the weary according to their labors. Let Abraham’s bosom [?] be the goal of our soul’s desire, so that we may become like him through perseverance in our faith. Let us call him Father through deeds, not through names, so that he may open the gate to the harbor of his love and receive us.
On the Coming of the Antichrist

Discourse 35. On the Coming of the Antichrist, or the False Messiah. And on the Revelation of Christ Our Lord. It is recited on the Sunday that begins the Fast of Saint Elijah. Response: Come, let us arm ourselves with the armor of good deeds, so that the arrows of the evil one may not wound us. [?]

We have heard a disturbing report of what is coming at the end of the ages, and it is very difficult to describe its turmoil. A great calamity is going to be spoken of among the earth’s inhabitants, and no mouth can express how bitter its report is. The evil one announces evil news among mortals, and there is no one who is not troubled and whose mind is not bewildered. What is going to be told deserves weeping, and it is fitting that we compose choked cries to accompany its announcement. Let whoever listens with discernment listen in sorrow, and let whoever pays careful attention shed tears in grief. Let us grieve in our minds and pour out tears in our thoughts; instead of garments, let us tear our inner impulses over what is coming. The devil is going to devise a cruel deception, and he is cunningly arming himself against our lives. He wishes to raise a rebellion of wrongdoing against righteousness,

and he is preparing to place the Creator’s name upon his own insolence. Arrogant in mind, he seeks to ascend to an exalted rank, and brazenly slings a burning coal at the divine Being. The fool puts on deceitful impudence like armor, and wickedly aims a missile against the truth. Though covered in wounds, he calls himself the Victor, and seizes without cause a sound of praise that does not befit him. “I am the Messiah,” he says [?], without denying it, “and in me the mysteries and symbols depicted by the righteous are fulfilled.” He urges people to receive him as righteous, and he goes astray and leads others astray until he is exposed by righteousness. He leads people astray through errors and displays mighty deeds through illusions, until that final cry rings out. The insolent one brazenly casts contempt upon all [?], and rushes upward to an exalted rank, though he does not truly ascend. The chosen herald Paul marveled at his insolence and depicted it beforehand in his writings, so that everyone might see it. He called the [?] in which he appears “rebellion,” for he raises a rebellion and prevents the truth from being spoken. The report about him had gone out from the beginning of the proclamation, and people began asking questions about his coming. The apostle had heard his disciples’ question about him, and instructed them not to be alarmed by the report of him. “Do not accept,” he said, “that the time of the end of the ages is near, and do not be persuaded by either a letter or a revelation.”

The all-knowing one has revealed: unless the rebellion comes, the course of earthly life will not be completed. Unless the son of destruction comes to stray and lead others astray, the manifest truth of the renewal of all things will not be disclosed. Unless he displays the evil of his disposition before the eyes of all creatures, the [?] of his insolence will not be confirmed by his deeds. The Maker has set a limit to the time for the work of his hands. Until it is completed, he does not let the deceiver loose to deceive. The barrier of the divine command stands before him like a wall, holding him back from the [?] advance of his rebellion. He has long been intensely eager to fulfill his desire, but God does not let him loose until the appointed period he decreed is completed. The crafty one waits for the command that set his limits and restrained him, waiting for the appointed period to end so that he may reveal his deceit. He stokes himself like a furnace with the wood of fury, waiting to increase the fire of his anger and burn humanity. He habitually hides deceitful snares night and day, and sits watching for prey to come to the [?]. Like a hunter, the one with a twisted mind waits patiently, constantly watching for his purpose to reach fulfillment. His inner disposition resembles that of a partridge, a cunning partridge; and more than a partridge he desires and longs for the day of completion. If he had not been confined by a hidden command in a harsh cage, he might have rushed out and swallowed our race at any moment. If it had been up to him, they would have perished long ago,

had he not been restrained by that command of the one who called us his image. It is this that struck him so that he would not rise beyond his appointed bounds, and it still restrains him until the day fixed in God's knowledge. Wisely he restrained him within the bounds of his hidden command, and wisely he opens the way before him, so that he goes out and leads others astray. The day of his revelation brings benefit, even if it causes loss, so that everyone may learn how evil are the calamities he brings upon humanity. Through his evil he teaches two things to those among humanity who are watchful: his own destructiveness and the power of the Creator who restrained his anger. The Good One points out his love for us as though with a finger: had he not restrained him, he would indeed have destroyed us from the beginning. If he has now done such harm at the end of time, how much harm would he have done if God had let him loose from the day we came into being? He made his disposition a testing furnace for us and for everyone, so that through his evil he might assay the gold of our discernment. Through him he teaches us the kinds of warfare waged against the truth, and through him he makes known to us the help by which he protects us. He has kept him for the end, the great [?] who is insolent toward him, so that humanity and the heavenly beings may see the evil of his disposition. Before that day on which he renews the creation he made, he gives him room to bring his wickedness into the open. It was not because the Creator desired harm [?] that he let him loose, but to reveal his destructiveness and the weakness of our souls. He uses it to accuse us maliciously, as in a court, because we are not vigilant in the struggle of suffering for the truth.

It is a great contest that he is preparing to wage against us, and by every means he seeks to lead us away from the truth. He saw our nature victorious and cast aside his valor. Now he is embittered at how suddenly he was defeated and exposed. He saw that one of our race rebuked him and made him a laughingstock. Now he devises ways to avenge his disgrace on that man's relatives. He saw him raised to the lofty rank of bearing the name of the divine Being. Now he plans to surpass his rank through sorcery. He saw the Watchers and human beings subjected to his authority. Now he cunningly devises a rebellion against his power. He had heard that he was to come at the end to judge everyone, and he prepares the weapons of his wickedness so that he can come in his likeness. He heard that he would descend to earth in the glory of the heavenly beings, and he too prepared bands of demons to escort him in procession. He heard that he was destined to be tormented under an endless sentence, and he defiantly shook his fist at the power that torments him. He saw that the sentence fixing the time of his downfall was approaching. Now he raves like a murderer at the hour of his death. He knows for certain that he will not escape justice. Having lost hope, he mocks and despises everything that inspires fear. He considered that there was nowhere he could hide on the day of testing, and he eagerly sought to fulfill his desire wickedly. The greatness of his wickedness made him act unjustly without pity, and his arrogance made him commit evil beyond all bounds. The insolent one went outside the order of [?].

And he sought to exalt himself above the Maker and the work of his hands. The boastful one spews abuse against the power that gave him power, and he does not understand that he is humiliating himself through his arrogance. The wicked one fights against the will that honored humanity, and through a human being he vomits his bile against the divine Being. Through a human being the Creator redeemed humanity, and through a human being he too wishes to destroy humanity. The God of all chose a human being for himself and through him set everyone free. He too has emboldened one human being to enslave everyone. The Creator called the human being he chose Messiah and King. In the same way, he gives these titles to the human being who becomes his dwelling. He formed him in the womb without sexual union to redeem humanity. Perhaps he too spreads this claim about that deceiver. He took the firstfruits from the lineage of Abraham's family, and [?] it is a Jew who becomes a vessel for that deception. He too imitates everything that happened in the second Adam, and he performs mighty works without truly performing them. In the same form in which he came into the world bodily, he too comes into the world in a human body. The deceitful one chooses a single human being from humanity and makes his dwelling in him, just as the hidden one dwelt in a human being. The enemy of humanity dwells in a human being to lead humanity astray, and calls him the Son of God, as has happened before. The crafty one calls the son of destruction the Son of God. He snatches the name of God into his hand and attaches it to his own name.

He places the honored name like a covering over his own baseness. He strives to ascend to a lofty rank, but [?] does not permit him. In foolish arrogance, the captive raises an outcry against the divine Being. In contention he seizes the titles of divinity. Like a captor, he passes through the earth, full of arrogance. He takes people captive to become slaves to his rebellion. At the head of the exiles, he leads people out of their minds, and instead of possessions, he plunders the riches of their thoughts. He takes the mind captive and strips the understanding bare. Instead of the body, he mocks the soul and humiliates it. He skillfully wages war against hidden thoughts, to subject the whole person to his desires. He skillfully arranges the occasion prepared for him, and crafty demons make ready a time suited to him. Through the craft of demons he deceives those watching, and shows their eyes shadows that are not real. By deceiving the eyes, he sets apparitions before their pupils. He makes the senses rest on nothing as though it were something. He depicts on earth likenesses of things perceptible to the senses, and makes them appear as though they existed, although they do not. Demons become a vision that seems to exist although it does not, and confirm it through images that are not real. They themselves become blind, deaf, epileptic, and stammering. The son of destruction heals them by deception, although he does not heal. They cry out like people in distress before his recklessness.

He rises and stretches out his hand to heal. The one sick with sin does not give true healing. He longs to destroy the soul's health through the promises of his words. The impostor clothes himself in the appearance of that physician who came into the world. He calls to people, 'Come, be healed'—that is, 'Die.' The healing of the deceitful physician is full of bitter death. Under the appearance of goodness, he distributes harm to those who obey him. The false Christ imitates the appearance of Christ and draws crowds of nations to himself, so that they may acclaim him. Like a righteous man, he raises his voice to sinners: 'Come, receive your debt certificates free of charge'—that is, 'Incur guilt.' Full of arrogance, he lowers his words like a humble man, and humbly sows his word in people's minds. Perhaps he even says deceitfully, like our Savior, 'Look at me, for I am gentle, and rest from pride under the appearance of my gentleness.' Perhaps, wholly unjust himself, he proclaims forgiveness of injustice. The evil one, whose depravity has no equal, rebukes the wicked. Perhaps he abolishes the divinations and omens of Chaldean astrology, so as to establish his imposture beyond disturbance. Perhaps he becomes an opponent of his own craft and is incited to [?] his evil inclination against his Lord. Perhaps he denies his kinship with his fellow conspirators and is incited to seize an honored name foreign to his own. Perhaps he rebukes the priests whom he installed in his house of worship, incited to establish the belief that he is to be worshiped.

Perhaps he says, “Why do you follow my error?” so that no one may recognize that he deceitfully leads people away from the truth. Oh, how skillful is the enemy of humanity and of the Creator! Yet he cannot overpower the Power who gave him power. Oh, how insolent is the tyrant who rebels against the divine Being! Yet he cannot subjugate the One who truly and eternally exists. The rebel rebelled against the divine Being in his spiritual pride, and he despised and scorned the command that created him along with everything else. Though dead in his sins, he calls himself by the name “Living,” and displays his wealth before his spectators as though he were God. Anointed with sin, he says, “I am the Messiah and King,” and calls his servants apostles of righteousness. He sends demons like heralds to every land, and they go out spreading the hateful news of the day of his coming. They pour disturbing sounds into their listeners’ ears, and there is no hearing that is not disturbed by their deeds. “The time of mysteries and symbols has ended,” the accursed ones cry, “and the reality that was spiritually depicted in the Scriptures has arrived. “Rise, go out, and welcome the revealed truth, children of the promise!
