Receive the good things that the Good One promised to satisfy your desires. “Stop studying and discussing the fulfillment of mysteries, and seal up the books of bodily observances. “Why do your minds need a display of symbols? Look closely and examine the reality itself. “Cease the labor of righteousness, with all its toil,

“and rest in the harbor of the things to come that are hidden in my own person.” Oh, what a mouth, uttering unspeakable wickedness! How it exalts itself, without concealing itself even a little! Oh, what a shameless creature, whose disposition is far more shameless than a dog’s! He barks continually and does not understand at whom he is barking. Oh, the fighter who fights against himself when no one is pressing him, and casts strife between earthly and heavenly beings! The wrath of this wrathful one troubles angels and human beings, and he spews his gall upon spiritual and bodily beings alike. He dwells in a human being just as he dwelt in the serpent in the beginning, and through him he bites human beings as he did Eve. As in a building, he conceals his nature within a bodily form, just as he concealed himself in the serpent in Eden, went astray, and led others astray. The body becomes an instrument for his subtle nature, and through its limbs he expresses sounds [?] full of wickedness. He and his legions enter and dwell in an unclean temple, and there they receive the worship of wickedness from the impure. He summons all his forces and assembles them around his body, so that the lawless may come and escort in procession the one who is more lawless than they are. The embodied demon makes all the demons run before him, so that they may proclaim the utterly false one as true. All the demons throw the earth into turmoil on the day of his appearance, so that the news of his deception may spread quickly. Everywhere and in everything they spread the snares of his traps, so that through his cunning they may catch the foolish world.

Woe to our nature because of the one who assumes our nature—how insolent he is! Through us he leads us away from the truth without our noticing. Woe to our race because of the robber to whom we are blind! He plunders it, and his deceit goes unrecognized. Woe to our family because of the one who belongs to the family of spirits! He mocks it, and his mockery [?] is pleasing to its mind. Woe to us because of that evil neighbor within our borders! He oppresses us every day, and his appetite for oppression is never satisfied. Look, for nearly six thousand years he has kept oppressing us, and he is still intent on taking even the [?] of our lives. He seeks to take our lives away from us at the end of time, but the Will that called us his image does not give him free rein. With this intention he came to us in a man from among us, so that through our own nature he might catch our nature as in a trap. That man becomes a trap for that hunter, who enters and lies hidden inside our body to catch us through it. He saw that the Good One had delivered us from his wickedness through a man, and now he devises a way to bring us back to himself through a human being. He saw that he could not fight us by himself, and he hired a man through whom to wage war against our freedom. He puts the sword of his bitterness into a man's hand and mercilessly lays waste the ranks of humanity. He enters and lies hidden inside a visible body, and through it he shoots the arrows of his wrath into human nature. The deceitful one does not wage war against us openly.

Nor does he violently compel our will to submit to him. Through a man he addresses deceitful cries to our freedom, and like a hunter he coaxes us toward the gathering place of his schemes. It is a man who raises his voice on earth and cries out to humanity: “I am the man who saved humanity, and I will save it again.” “Come, receive life [?] through my hands,” the deceitful one cries, although his gift is nothing but endless death. He desires our death and longs to kill us at every opportunity. If the command did not stand as a barrier before him, he would destroy us. The hidden command has confined his fierce wrath within bounds, and whenever it gives him free rein, it restrains him again so that he does not destroy us. He gives him free rein to fulfill his desire, which thirsts for our blood, and he restrains him to make known his love for our race. From within our own race he sends his command and restrains his wrath, so that he may see and be ashamed that there is someone within our race who comes out to confront him. A messenger from among us is sent against his wickedness, and he quiets his tumult with the sound of his words. Like a ray from the heavenly sphere, he suddenly shines forth and drives the darkness of his abominations away from humanity. Like a commander, the Tishbite [?] to confront him, and takes the human captives away from him by the power of the Spirit. By the power of the Spirit, the prophet of the Spirit comes at the end, to go out and fight against the rebel who proclaims falsehood. He fights spiritually against the deceitful one, and shows him that the power of the Spirit is present in our flesh.

When he thinks he has fulfilled his desire among those of flesh, a man of flesh [?] and exposes his deceit. On the day when he thinks, “Now I have already become king over everyone,” one man raises his voice and strips him of his power. A man from among us goes out against the one filled with pride, and engages him in battle openly, before the eyes of all creatures. The Spirit arms a warrior from our camp and sends him to do battle with his insolence. In our flesh he fought against our free will, and it was defeated by him. Yet through that same flesh of ours he too is defeated, and everyone mocks him. In the flesh that he saw being corrupted by its desires, Elijah in turn shows him his might. The body that escaped the corruption of ravenous death does battle with the rebel who brought death in. A great battle takes place on earth at the end of the ages, in which two men of flesh fight with two powers. Truth and falsehood put armor upon their senses, and shoot the arrows of their words at one another. The Tishbite is girded entirely with truth, while the son of destruction is wrapped in the guise of deceit. The man of the right hand wears the breastplate of righteousness, while the son of destruction [?] the rags of hateful wickedness. The prophet of truth wears the helmet of faith, while the deceitful worker has covered his head with a helmet of falsehood. The righteous man fights valiantly in the name of righteousness,

while the wholly wicked one hurls words of falsehood. The evil one fights deceitfully through his evil companion, while truth triumphs truly through Elijah’s mouth. Falsehood is the entire armor of the son of destruction, while the Spirit equips the proclamation of the one whose mind is pure. Through the Spirit, the prophet of the Spirit cries out like a trumpet, and those engaged in spiritual service listen to his voice. The deceitful messenger speaks error among liars, and they obey him, just as [?] Eve obeyed the serpent. The prophet comes to undo the deceiver’s deceit, so that his error will not become established in human minds. He comes at the end to [?] fulfill what is written: to turn the hearts of those whose hearts are dull toward understanding. The voice of the herald of truth confirms the word of truth that cried out beforehand: “Look, Elijah has come and is coming.” “Elijah,” it is said, “is coming to proclaim the way of truth.” It is therefore clear that through him everything written will be fulfilled. The chaste man comes to confirm the words of prophecy. He shows great zeal and openly exposes falsehood. Like an athlete, he comes down and stands among the demons, entering into battle with the mighty one and his forces. All the demons wage fierce battle against him, and he against them all, but they cannot overcome his valor. The power of the Spirit strengthens his body and the impulses of his soul, and he does not falter in the struggle on behalf of his Lord.

That command which gave him victory in the contest with the priests of Baal [?] will also give him victory in the battle against the rebel. On this condition he gave him strength in the days of Ahab: that he should prepare the way for that final victory. The slaughter he carried out among the priests of Baal was a pledge of this slaughter that he is destined to exact from the demons’ camp. The divine command that chose him for prophecy traced a mystery in him, and he is destined to fulfill the truth of its words through deeds. As a symbolic act, the prophet of truth kills the false prophets, for just as it happened then, so it will happen at the end of time. With his own hands he slaughtered the worshipers of demons, to the demons’ shame; through him the chief of deceit himself will also be exposed. The righteous man exposes that deceiver’s deceit and disgraces him before angels and human beings. When his deceit grows strong, he fights against him and accuses him of boasting deceitfully of his fist. He alone puts the arrogance of his tyranny to shame and makes known to him the Creator’s power, which is placed within our nature. From the beginning the Creator saw his evil inclination and placed the strength of his help within us beforehand, so that we might fight against him. Through Elijah our whole race fights against him and, through our weakness, condemns his might. The sight of the chaste man confronts him like a barrier. He exhausts all his arrows against him without wounding him. Through the son of perdition, all the demons aim at the pupil of his eye.

Yet not one of the stratagems of their schemes reaches him. The battle waged by the son of sojourners is a great marvel: he stands alone against thousands and does not falter. The power of the divine Being who strengthens him deserves wonder: how one human being defies so many! How mighty indeed is that help within his limbs, since powerful demons cannot wound him! [?] How [?] are the mind and the words of this mortal man’s mouth, which silence the tumultuous cries of that camp! Come, let us marvel at that struggle before it happens, so that when it happens we may not lose heart at the dreadful report of it. Come, let us thoughtfully marvel at a man of our own race who does battle with spiritual beings stronger than himself. Come, let us carefully examine the armor he wears, against which the ranks of warriors wear themselves out, while it remains undiminished. Who has ever seen a human being like Elijah, surrounded by thousands of demons who cannot strike him? Who has considered the man who defeated ravenous death and then trampled down the deceitful one who brought death in? Death and the Evil One are put to shame by him, a mortal, and cannot trample down the lofty rank with which he has been honored. Great terror suddenly falls upon Satan when he sees him coming with a sickle against his army. [?] strike his armies at the sound of his words, whenever they hear him raising his voice against their ranks.

It is not his bodily voice that the unruly spirits fear, but the power concealed within his words. Great mourning overwhelms those endowed with intelligence when they contemplate the light of this mortal’s words. On the day of their victory, the lowly are defeated by a son of the lowly, and they marvel at him, at how their plots [?]. All together they gather in agreement around one man and help him, yet they cannot defeat one man. I have called Elijah, a son of sojourners, “one man,” and I have named another “the son of destruction,” who will perish utterly. One man and another engage in combat against each other: the prophet by [?], and the son of destruction by Satan’s power. For that man who comes to deceive is a human being, and the enemy of humanity carries out through his hands the deceptions of his name. He cannot deceive human beings without a human being, and so he chooses a human being for wickedness, to act wickedly through him. He commits great wickedness through the hands of that man, and through him he exalts himself against the Maker and the work of his hands. His mouth spews grievous injustice against the divine Being. [?] And with his lips he insults the name that is [?] above all. The uncleanest of the unclean wants to seize the holy name, and the slave of slaves longs to receive the worship due to the Lord. The dwelling place of demons enters and sits in the holy temple, raving and saying, “I am the Messiah and the Son of God.” His ministers also wickedly shout this:

“Yes, he is God!” Oh, the master and his disciples! In God’s name he goes astray and leads astray those who are deceived by him; and although he hates God, he conceals his own ugliness under God’s name. The ugly one seeks to beautify himself through the pure one—not to become beautiful, but to disfigure the splendor of his beauty through his arrogance. The ugly one does not disfigure the beautiful one, who does not change; rather, he disfigures himself by what he brazenly does. It is insolence for a servant to seize the Maker’s name, and utter wickedness for molded clay to despise its molder. The accursed one raves against his molder in an accursed manner, and gives the accursed one the rank of ruler. The deceiver calls the ruler of the air the head of everything, and he sanctions people's worship of him, the murderer. The murderer is the one who dwells in him, the destroyer of life, and he urges him to kill people with the sword of injustice. He holds the sword of injustice in his hand, which is full of injustice, and unjustly devastates the ranks of humanity. Under the appearance of peace, the hater of peace steals peace away, and he sows his message in people's ears as though it were life-giving medicine. He proclaims peace on the day of his appearance, though he is disturbed by envy, and in the guise of a friend he displays a deceitful face. The unclean one abolishes all the teachings he sowed in the earth, and then cunningly builds the structure of his deception. The great master of error skillfully establishes his teaching, and no one knows how to discern his craft.

He abolishes pagan priests, diviners, and burnt offerings, and compels people to sacrifice their wills to him. He deposes kings and removes the ranks of authority. He alone calls himself king and lord. He yokes the necks of the free [?] under his lordship, and they offer him their thoughts instead of tribute. They weave a crown of praises and place it on his accursed head, and with their words they crown him as a king. Only the righteous are not yoked under his authority, nor are they persuaded by the sound of the deceiver's disturbances. He buries tens of thousands of snares deep down to catch them, and by every means he approaches the righteous to catch them. The accursed one incites his followers against the righteous, and through his servants he shoots arrows at those who cultivate truth. Through the hands of the nations he grapples with the righteous, and through visible bodily members he oppresses the upright. Though bodiless, he uses a body to wage war against those with bodies, and with the sword of speech he destroys those endowed with speech. He wages a great war against everyone who will not submit to him, until he hears that voice which destroys him. He draws up his battle line against everyone who does not acknowledge him, until he is put to shame by the command of the ruler of all. Arrogant in mind, he mocks everyone and despises everyone, until the King over all [?] and exposes him. News of his turmoil flies to every land,

until the heavenly powers cry out and silence him. He spreads his cunning snares in every region, until he sees the peacemakers coming out to meet him. He remains on earth, gains renown, and leads the earth's inhabitants astray, until he fixes his gaze on the [?] and trembles before him. He and Elijah draw up their battle lines against each other, until the appointed span of this age's existence is completed. The righteous one remains in the contest with the wicked one, until the hidden command opens the gates of heaven. The truthful one is engaged in battle with the liar, until the throne [?] is set up to judge everyone. Earthly and heavenly beings are caught in this turmoil, until a single command gives rest to all the ranks. The Watchers and human beings cry out together in their thoughts, longing for the war of wickedness to end. The righteous and the chaste bear a greater burden of suffering, and are distressed by the wickedness of the evil one far more than anyone else. Severe labor pains constantly strike their thoughts, and like a woman giving birth, they await the children of the resurrection of the dead. Heaven and [?] and everything in them are clothed in mourning, waiting for that renewal which will never change. Creation weeps for herself as for someone dead, waiting to live with that life which cannot decay. Her suffering lies before her eyes like someone dead, and she gazes at it, waiting to see it in new life.

The sound of groaning cries out on earth from every mouth, and speechless creatures weep bitterly over those who speak. All alike await a single hope; until they rest in [?] his love, they find no rest. They long to hear the sound of that horn at the end, and unless they hear it, they find no consolation for their sorrow. They have only heard [?] that it is destined to sound at the end, but the day of its announcement is hidden and concealed from all creatures. Only one knows the day on which it will be heard: he in whom is hidden the will of the Hidden One, to whom everything is revealed. He, together with the Hidden One, knows the day of its revelation, and whenever he wishes, he reveals his power and makes it known. His command waits for the full span of this temporal existence, until it is complete; then he fulfills the promise of his words. Suddenly he shines upon the inhabited world like lightning [?], and covers the heights and depths with the light of his words. A great, indescribable light flashes from him, and light becomes as though it were no light in comparison with his light. He opens [?] by his descent, and then comes down. He summons and calls the powers on high to escort him in honor. All together they gather to him from every place and escort him with the love befitting the greatness of his rank. A thousand thousands cry out his praise without ever having enough, and ten thousand times ten thousand repeat his praise without interruption. All of them bear praise and holiness in the movements within them,

and offer him a crown of victory befitting his name. “Blessed is the Victor!” all the ranks cry out, rank to rank, and they shake the earth with the sound of their declarations of holiness. “Glorious is the one who gives life to all!” cry the ordered rows of their ranks, and they astonish the world with the wonder of their utterances. The blast of their trumpets is filled with great wonder, and no mouth can describe its intensity. 4. Very terrifying is the appearance of the faces revealed in it, and the light of fleshly eyes is too weak to gaze upon it. Flashes of light come from the fiery beings, and sight is bewildered when it gazes at the power of their faces. Their appearance and the sound of their speech are full of fear and love: fear for the wicked and blessedness for the good. Blessed is whoever loves. Blessings and punishments [?] in the form in which they appear: blessings for the righteous and punishments for those who have sinned. Woe to those who have not repented. They sow in the earth the good news of the renewal of everything, and like seeds they gather bodies to the threshing floor of life. They gather and stand before a single person, waiting for him to exercise his power over their dominions. They are all harnessed under his authority as under a yoke, and the taste of his name from every mouth is sweet to them. The King of kings sits upon a chariot of spirit, and countless thousands of spirits are harnessed to it. [?] the number of the hosts who escort him, and the sound of the holy praise of those who hallow him has no [?].

In great splendor he reveals himself before the eyes of all creatures, and human beings and heavenly beings join in praising him. The standard of his suffering and his victory comes before him, and creation marvels at the crucified man: how greatly he has been exalted! At that time the demons and those who crucified him are ashamed, for they see the standard they mocked being carried in honor. Demons and Jews stand in great astonishment as they gaze at the man whom they [?], who has become king over all. A grievous calamity suddenly falls upon Satan, for heaven and earth cry out the praise of the name he reviled. There is bitter mourning without consolation for the son of destruction, who perishes completely before the eyes of angels and human beings. The name he denied makes a terrible voice sound toward him and excludes him from life, body and soul. The unjust one, who brought destruction upon himself, perishes utterly and completely, and no remnant of him remains among the immortal [?]. Christ the King cries out a single utterance [?] toward him, and he completely [?], and the pride of his deceitful master is put to shame. The Watchers and human beings see something new on the day of his destruction, and they marvel greatly at the power of the Maker, whose power can accomplish everything. The Lord shows his servants something new through the work of his hands: although it is something, he can make it as though it were nothing. From nothing he created everything as he pleased, and when he pleases, he turns something back into nothing. He did well to bring everything into being from nothing.

And he does well to destroy the son of destruction [?] without pity. Through his destruction, the Good One teaches rational beings wisdom, for they ought to have kept the order of their created nature. The accursed one departed from the order of created existence; therefore he destroys him and removes him from life. His destruction brings doubled mourning upon his master, and the loss of his life adds a severe punishment to him. It would have been a relief for him too to perish completely with his disciple, rather than to be tormented severely without end. The command of the one who created him deals wisely with him, and no one knows how to express the greatness of his loving compassion. The deed he performs there is full of great love: he does not burn up the company of the wicked as he did that one man. Through the one whom he destroys, he shows that he is both just and merciful, for just as he destroyed one, he could also have destroyed many. He does not desire the destruction of the son of destruction for destruction’s sake, but to reveal his justice and kindness. He makes both qualities known to both companies, the good and the wicked: although he is very good, justice too is mingled with his goodness. Every act of discipline arising from his knowledge is carried out for good, and those who know his love know only to praise him. Rightly he disciplines those who hate the wealth of his kindness, and rightly he wins over those who keep the mystery of his faithfulness. [?] The just judge examines wickedness and righteousness, and at his command he makes rational beings stand before him with their deeds.

Through one man he brings everyone into the furnace of testing, and into his hands he entrusts blessedness for the good and punishment for the wicked. For this he set him apart from the beginning of his formation, so that through him he might distinguish the ranks of the righteous and the wicked. For this he appointed him when he formed him without sexual union, so that through him he might renew creation, which had grown old in mortality. By his command he renews all creation through him, and gives it wisdom to know itself and its maker. Like a maidservant, he makes it stand before him on the day of his revelation, and it honors him with a voice of praise beyond comprehension. He brings out the whole world with its inhabitants to meet him, so that it may weave for his name a crown of praises worthy of his name. The holy name of the offspring who comes from him is hidden in his appearance, and through him it is hallowed by spiritual and bodily beings. The glories of his revelation and the sight of his embodied form cannot be expressed; the mouths of those endowed with speech are too small to tell how great it is. Thousands of Watchers and angels bear his banner. They honor him and are honored through him, each according to their worthiness. In the heights they stand ready when he appears, and welcome him with the pure voices of their songs of sanctification. Like [?], he looks down from the heights upon the face of the earth, and the world shines with the rays of his mighty light. The sun flees, the moon also hides its rays, and the course of the morning star and its companions ceases. The air rests from its swift movement.

And the sea stills the turbulent battle of its waves. Speechless things return to that substance from which they came, and the world becomes as it was at the beginning of its existence. The nature of speaking beings alone endures and is not destroyed; it alone [?] into the furnace where its inclination is tested. For the [?] of all, the judge of all comes at the end, and a single cry rings out on earth, filling the void. His voice runs like a messenger through the four quarters, and creation stirs as though awakening from a heavy sleep. He sows the power of life in the earth by the word of his mouth; the dust stirs and acquires senses that can perceive. Like seeds, bodies sprout from the dust, and the vision of their minds shines far more brightly than the sun. The whole body returns to immortal life, and not even the tiniest part of a hair is missing from it. It rises altogether, whole and complete, wherever it fell, and not even a fragment of it remains in the earth. The command of the one who formed him searches out [?] from within the dust and skillfully puts him together so that he will never perish again. He brings a case against Satan and Death on his behalf and demands from them reparation for his humiliation and their dominion over him. He casts into a dark prison the demons who assailed him, and binds the evil spirits with chains of flame. He binds his enemies and puts a gag of silence in their mouths, but releases him from the chains of mortality.

With the waters of mercy he washes away the filth upon his limbs and adorns him with an imperishable robe of glory. He cleanses the corruptible one of corruption and death, and instead of leaving him a corpse, makes his body fly to the heights above. The spiritual hosts marvel at his heaviness: how can a dense nature fly, contrary to its accustomed ways? He himself also marvels endlessly at this: by what power has his weakness acquired the ability to fly? Perhaps mortal nature says to itself, “Am I the same nature, or has another perhaps been substituted?” If it were possible for him to think this, perhaps he would think it; but he cannot, because ignorance is uprooted. The one who raises his mortal [?] from the dust himself strengthens him so that he will not doubt his transformation. With his renewal he acquires a strength mightier than everything, and passions cannot gain control over his thoughts. I too marveled at the greatness of the power given to him, and turned my discourse away from his course toward his greatness. From the beginning my thoughts traveled through the story of the deceiver, and I wished to reflect on the account of the son of destruction. I wanted to arm myself against his arrogance with the weapon of words, but when I saw that he was destined to be exposed, I left him alone. I examined his haughtiness to describe it in the sound of my verses, but looked ahead and saw how harsh his downfall would be. I marveled greatly at his lawless insolence,

and was utterly astonished at his endless torment. His impudence called to me and urged me to recount his deceit, but my heart was distracted by the sentence prepared for him. The severity of his scourges softened my words against his cruelty, and I said to myself, “Why am I mistreating the evil one who is doomed?” Let us then stop accusing [?] him, for he is already accused [?], and let us counsel our soul not to grow slack in the struggle with him. A great raider [?] is preparing to draw up his forces against our people. Come, let us forge weapons for ourselves that will overcome his plundering. He is preparing arrows of wrath to shoot into the camp of our race. Let us hold up against him the pure shield of faith. With the sword of his evil inclination he longs to destroy the vitality of our lives. Let us place the helmet of good hope upon the head of our mind. With the spear of his fury he intends to uproot the building of our soul. Let us put on love like armor, so that we do not grow weak. With every skill he devises schemes against us, seeking how to defeat us. Come, let us arm ourselves so that the arrows of the Evil One do not wound us. Its conclusion. Glory to your power, our Savior, by which you defeated the devil. Another. You who put an end to wars [?] at the ends [?] of the earth, put an end among us to the wars of the deceitful one.
On the Revelation of Our Lord
Discourse Twenty-Three. On the Revelation of Our Lord and on the Way of Life in the World to Come

The good hope of the world to come has wearied my mind, and I sought to [?] when the world of time would come to an end. Time gave me a sign concerning that world which brings the ages to an end: “Look, human being, at how one world dismisses another.” Swiftly that world dismisses the world of time, and there is no delay between the one and the other, not even the time of a gesture. Like a shadow, the world filled with time passes away, while the world in which there is no toil endures without time. There is no toil in the world that comes at the end of the ages, nor anyone who trades, nor anyone who neglects to gain. The world that brings the toiling world to an end is without end, and boundless is the span of the enduring life within it. There is no numbering the course of life or the years of its life, since there is not even a reckoning of days by the sun and moon. It is one day that undergoes decay [?] in that way of life, and there is no change that interrupts the course of its permanence. My thoughts recalled its endless permanence, and rose to tell of its vastness, which excludes an end. It brings this earthly way of life to an end and gives rest from the weariness of the peaceful and of earthly people. It is a great harbor, filled with peace, in which there is no fear. In it the ship of the world, worn out by hardships, comes to rest. Crushing toil has worn out the world and its inhabitants, and now it longs to rest from its weariness in the harbor of peace. I long to speak about that world which gives rest to the weary.

And I yearn to reveal in words the various aspects of its story. I strive to reveal the various aspects of its story to people, so that they may paint in their minds an image of its loveliness. The mind can paint an image of what has no bodily composition, and the understanding can see things that are not visible to eyes of flesh. I am not recounting visible things in plain words. Come, you who can speak, and hear hidden things through visible things. Come, hear the account of the age that brings the temporal world to an end, reveals hidden things, and displays them before the eyes of those who see. Come, consider the day that is the end of days and allows no further day to come after it. Come, look closely at the splendid beauty of its glorious wonders: it is marvelous and glorious, and delights people with its magnificent beauty. Listen carefully, like discerning people, to the report about it: when it will happen and how it will unfold in its great order. A great ordering will take place on that great day. It will bring the world to an end and usher in a world without toil. The day of that revelation exchanges one world for another, and there will never again be another day like it. Our Lord also revealed the greatness of that day in his clear words: that day is more terrible than all the days that have been or will be. The powers on high will be shaken on that day, as it is written, and will honor it as a day without equal. The king's standard is carried at the head of the ranks of the peaceful ones, displaying the victory of his might before the eyes of all creatures. In the heights, the heavenly powers stand ready to welcome the King of heaven with a great procession. First come these things that are said to happen on earth; then that revelation will appear, disclosing hidden things. There will be disasters, earthquakes, famines, and plagues, and people will destroy their fellow human beings in their conflicts. Lawlessness will increase, deceit will prosper, and sin will grow strong. Love will diminish, and hope and faith will grow faint.

The detestable deceit of deceivers will openly triumph and condemn the evident truth of the truthful. The evil one will find an evil time suited to his wickedness, and it will help him carry out the designs of his bitterness. The deceiver will spew out all his bile before those who go astray. He will stray and lead others astray until the day of his appointed time. That liar's time is bounded by a known period, so that he cannot boast that he establishes his deception according to his own will. The Creator's power will bring forth [?] from him at the end of the ages and bring into the open the intention that was hidden within him. The God of all will bring the wickedness of his evil into the open and display it before the eyes of earthly and heavenly beings. For this reason he does not restrain him from his wickedness: so that everyone may know how evil the deceiver's wickedness is. The wickedness of his evil killed our race from the beginning, and he has extended his wrath until the time when the ages end. The herald, the apostle Paul, looked toward that very time and revealed and made known the hidden mystery of his lawlessness. The truthful man laid bare the mystery of lawlessness to expose deceit, and showed that he would reveal his wickedness through a human being. Through a human being the murderer of humanity fulfills his desire, in that guise in which he went astray and led others astray in the land of Eden. The enemy of humanity chooses a man from among humankind and speaks through him as the Creator speaks through a man from among us. The one whose mind is bent on battle enters and dwells in a temple of flesh, imitating the Father's Word in the temple of our body. That wholly evil one conceals the wickedness of his evil within a man, and through that very man he seizes the rank belonging to the Creator's name. The wicked servant calls himself by the Creator's name and boldly says, “I am the Messiah, the renewer of the ages.” Paul, who heard clearly, had heard this blasphemy, and disclosed it beforehand, before the blasphemer uttered his blasphemy. The factions of every teaching hear the sound of his blasphemies and praise him as the master of falsehood. The report of his deception goes out to the four quarters, and diverse peoples of every language flock to him.

He speaks with them using every form of deception, and they eagerly listen to his fraudulent words. He devises cunning schemes and conceals them before their eyes, and, like grain used as bait, he scatters words full of wickedness. He displays various kinds of false signs on earth, and establishes his deception through illusions and tricks that deceive the eyes. The deceiver fulfills his every desire among those who are deceived, until the son of sojourners comes out to do battle with him. The son of sojourners comes out to meet the son of destruction and puts an end to his assault by the power of the Spirit. The Spirit arms the man of flesh with the Spirit's armor and sends him to do battle with Satan. Humanity and heaven behold a great wonder as demons and human beings fight against one man. He alone holds the battle line against many, and the warriors are defeated by him in their contests. Like an athlete, he comes down and stands among their ranks. He raises his voice, and the forces of the evil one tremble before him. Creation becomes a stadium for his athletic contest, and the world gathers to see the battle of one against thousands. There he stands in the middle of the theater of combat, and earthly and heavenly beings gaze upon him. Oh, the [?] contest that takes place on earth, in which thousands of spiritual beings are defeated and a human being is victorious! Oh, the victory that takes place in a world full of sins, when truth triumphs and the faction of error and its children is defeated! Oh, that voice with which the righteous man cries out before the wicked, making the assembled fighting forces of demons and human beings tremble! The son of sojourners makes his word flash like a sword, and the enemy flees, unable to stand defiantly before his utterances. The words of the man full of zeal become sharp arrows, and he pierces the camp of demons surrounding him. Thousands upon thousands and myriads upon myriads gaze upon him,

and they flee and hide like foxes in their dens. He wages a terrible struggle against the forces of the Evil One, until the King on high appears and helps him. The King on high looks down from the height of his royal dwelling and quiets the battered world, putting an end to its turmoil. Like lightning, his light [?] among those on earth, and creation sees a new sight revealed to it. Human beings and the peaceful heavenly beings see a new sight: the gates on high opening before his appearing. The sound of the peaceful heavenly beings’ trumpet suddenly rings out, and the world cannot bear to hear the sound of their songs of sanctification. They all become thunderous voices, every one of them, and honor the King who reigns over their ranks. They display a great array and an awe-inspiring sight on earth, and their minds’ attention is fixed on the command. They long for the King’s command and yearn to fulfill his words; the word of his mouth is sweeter to them than every good thing. By the word of his mouth he destroys the deceiver, the son of destruction, and utterly wipes him out, body and soul. That man suddenly suffers complete destruction, and his entire being is utterly deprived of life. The demons witness a great calamity in his destruction: how the spirit of life, the life of the soul, perishes. Creation stands in amazement and dismay at that time, and the terrible labor pains of the new birth terrify it. The sound of the trumpet shakes the earth and its inhabitants, and after all these sounds comes an awe-inspiring voice commanding them to rise. The King over all suddenly utters a single cry, and everything is renewed and swiftly transformed. First all the dead rise from the dust, and then those who are alive are transformed into the same likeness. The dead rise and the living live in one likeness, and there is no difference between one and another, not even in the slightest indication. It is one signal that raises the dead and gives life to the living, and both the righteous and the wicked rise with the same appearance. The command of the one who [?] over all raises the good and the evil.

Only then are they separated from one another by the scrutiny of judgment. The scrutiny of judgment separates the righteous from the wicked and opens the way to the kingdom on high and to Gehenna. Everything that happens on that day takes place at a slight signal, and the speed with which it happens cannot be expressed. Nothing compares with the swiftness of that command except the likeness of that deliverance through which the worlds came into being. That command which created creation from nothing is the very one that commands and renews it in the blink of an eye. In the same manner in which he commanded and it came into being from nothing, he commands it to become something better than what it was. The renewal he brings about for it at the end of time is better than the formation he accomplished for it at the beginning of time. The greatness at the beginning is nothing when compared with the glory at the end. Its end is immeasurably more glorious than its beginning, and speakers cannot express the nature of its glory. Only one knows how both came about, and in him were hidden the world's coming into being and the renewal of the worlds. The things that came into being were visible to him as they would come to be, and their renewal at the end was also pictured before him. He maintained a great order in their creation and their renewal, and the mouths of those endowed with speech are too small to say how great it is. He alone knows the things that have happened and those that are to come, and they were present in his beginningless being. Without a beginning, they were hidden in him while still uncreated, and he created them and renewed them as he pleased. He was pleased to show his love toward created things, proclaiming his power through their formation and their renewal. Through his creatures he taught his creatures about his hidden nature. Had he not created, his works would not have known his power. It was not because he was in need that I said this—that they would not have known—

but because there would have been no works to bear witness to his greatness. Through his creative activity he showed his power to the works of his hands, so that from his handiwork they might learn his love toward the things he fashioned. He did this for our benefit: he made us, and then returned and renewed us, so that through both we might learn the power hidden in his handiwork. He displayed the greatness of his love in our creation and our renewal, and taught us how closely his love is bound to the works of his hands. He revealed his will to the works of his hands at the beginning and at the end, and from his own handiwork he made a mediator for his creatures. Through the mediation of one human being he renewed the world, not because he was in need, but to exalt what was his through what was his. He exalted what was his by [?] one for himself from among all, and through his hands renewed the world that had worn out through mortality. Mortality had worn down the handiwork of the one who fashions everything, and through a mortal he renewed the world that had died through sin. He chose one mortal from the whole race of mortals and made him lord over earthly beings and [?]. He established the human form as his image when he fashioned it, and now he has given him the exalted name of his divinity. In his name he comes at the end to renew everything, and through the might of his power he turns everything back to the knowledge of him. He silences the name of error among mortals and quiets the slander of demons against the truth. He brings Antichrist, the chief of those who go astray, to an end, so that he no longer goes astray and leads people astray through his strife. He is the one who opens the gates of heaven on the day of his revelation and draws to himself the whole race of rational beings. He is the one who distinguishes the good from the wicked by his judicial sentence and gives recompense according to their deeds, whether good or evil. It is he who makes that separation between one person and another: one is raised up, and another is plunged into the abyss below. “Two,” it says, “will be engaged in the same labor,”

and suddenly they are separated from one another in the blink of an eye. Oh, how dreadful is the dreadful hour of that separation! There is nothing comparable to it that resembles its terror. Oh, how repulsive is the hideous appearance of those left on earth! Nothing is disfigured like their own persons. Oh, how bitter is the remorse by which they are judged! There is no one to comfort them or offer reassuring words. It is a harsh torment with which they are tormented in body and spirit, and its pain is harsher than all the torments of those who suffer torture. Weeping and wailing, gnashing of teeth and the sound of groans; fire without a nature, a worm without a body, and darkness without [?]. These things are said to torment the company of the wicked; and if this is true, the torment is worse even than these things. How could it not be bitter for the wicked who did not turn away from wickedness, when the gates of heaven are shut in their faces? How could it not be bitter when they look at the company of the righteous flying through the air, while they themselves sink into the depths of the earth? The earth becomes the dwelling place of the children of earth, and they weep and wail because they have been left out of the blessedness of those in heaven. They constantly see the blessedness of the good in their minds, and they long for it, but the desire within them is not fulfilled. Remorse for their sins wells up from within them, and they themselves become accusers of their own thoughts. The understanding within them adds to their torments, and as they are tormented, they are tormented yet again, without end. Their thoughts there become a spring of torments, flowing constantly over their own persons without interruption. With discernment they reflect on discernment, and they never tire of condemning their ugliness. The knowledge that the good acquire in the dwelling above is the very same knowledge that sinners acquire in their earthly dwelling. They are equal in knowledge, since their resurrection is also the same,

and there is no difference in their minds’ love of what is good. There is no difference either in resurrection or in knowledge, for they rise together and together know the various forms of wisdom. Only in place are the companies separated from one another, and the wicked are not permitted to mingle with the good. Their unworthiness separated them from equal standing and deprived them of delight together with the righteous. Their deeds estranged them from the blessings of the good, and they were not worthy to share the inheritance of those in heaven. The earthly remain on earth, for they loved earthly things; and the righteous become heavenly, for they desired the things of heaven. The righteous, who love truth, ascend above to heaven, where Christ, the King of righteousness, is. Christ the King does these things on the day of his appearing. He is the one who gives gifts to the good and punishments to the wicked. Through him, things unknown and hidden are revealed, and the scrutiny of his judgment shows everyone the nature of their deeds. All rational beings stand naked and exposed, and there is no thought that is not revealed and laid before his scrutiny. The day of his appearing will be a testing furnace. He chooses and rejects according to the scrutiny of his righteous judgment. He makes a single utterance heard on earth before all creatures, and creation stirs as though waking from a heavy sleep. The dead, who have no sensation, hear the sound of his command. They take off the garment of mortality and receive life. Bodies subject to decay receive life without decay, and the suffering of death never again approaches their limbs. The nature of mortals suddenly becomes immortal, and it marvels at itself because of the renewal it suddenly receives. The Son of Man raises the whole human race, and the dead and the living put on the garment of immortality. All the senses of the dead body receive life, and none of its limbs remains in Sheol.

The very same body that fell and decayed in mortality is the one that rises and receives immortal life. The very same soul that put on the body and did everything through it is the one that returns and dwells in it without departing. The human being rises in body and spirit, complete in every respect, and with his limbs and the impulses of his soul he pays for the wrongs he committed. In the very same nature in which he did good work and committed hateful deeds, he receives gifts of [?] and double punishments. In that same bodily and spiritual constitution, body and soul are renewed with everything they possess. In the same form in which Christ, the head of our life, rose, the visible body and the hidden soul rise. Our life-giver and renewer rose in body and soul, and in his resurrection he pictured for us the pattern of the day of our renewal. This is also the reason for the resurrection of the firstfruits of our life: to confirm us in the hope of immortal life. For just as through Adam we became mortal, so also through the second Adam we become immortal. The second Adam opened a path for us to new life, and he himself was the first to open the gate of the kingdom above. Our firstfruits entered the kingdom above in body and spirit, and he promised us that we would enter with him just as he himself entered. With this pledge he comes down to us at the end of time, to raise our race to where his royal dwelling is. Like the sun, the light of the day of his appearing dawns, and with its great brightness it obscures the light [?] of the sun. The powers above race through the air before his coming and escort him in procession as a king who reigns over [?] all. He is king over all because of the King who gave him his rank; and, like the Creator, he creates a new creation a second time. By the Creator’s power, the second Adam creates a creation—not by creating, but by giving rest to what has been created. He gives great rest to speaking and speechless beings, and they no longer toil amid the weariness of this world.

There the various agitations of body and soul fall silent, and they no longer feel the hateful desire for shameful things. There the various agitations of body and soul fall silent, and they no longer feel the hateful desire for shameful things. There the slaughter of the fierce warfare of tyrannical demons ceases, and they no longer wander astray or lead people astray through the mystery of error. There ravenous death stops swallowing, and sin no longer pierces people with the sting of wickedness. There mortal nature mocks death and the Evil One, and people say, “Where is your sting, ravenous death?” There is equality there between the angels and human beings, and they are not divided in their thanksgiving to the one Creator. There they offer one undivided thanksgiving, and in their minds they repeat “Holy” threefold: “One Being, who is always three.” However often they repeat it, they repeat it again without ever having enough. Through the mediator who is one of us, they utter the thanksgiving of their hearts; and they also count him with the divine Being in name and rank. He is the one who comes to accomplish these things without end, and as mediator he fulfills the order of the hidden nature. It is not the divine Being who comes to us by moving, for that Being undergoes no movement from one place to another. It is not the Creator who passes judgment on those being judged, but Christ, who also [?] all judgment. He is the one who comes by moving from one place to another and opens the gate of the Holy of Holies before those entering. All creation gazes at him when he appears and glorifies him together with the Power who gave him glory. Glorious is his revelation, exalted his manifestation, and discerning his judgment; the mouth of all creation is too small to recount his glory. Human beings and spiritual beings shine in wonder at his glory: how he commands and renews everything with a slight gesture. With a slight gesture he commands the earth, and it gives birth to human beings, like that gesture which commanded it in the beginning, and it gave birth to Adam. Every soul hears the sound of his command, wherever it is,

and returns and enters the temple of the body from which it departed. He too follows the pattern of that command by which he breathed it into Adam, and gathers it from every direction into the limbs. He too follows the pattern of that command by which he breathed it into Adam, and gathers it from every direction into the limbs. He joins body and soul together, forming one human being, in the form that humanity had at the beginning of time. The whole of creation becomes perfect and complete through that perfection in which Christ [?] himself was also perfected. In Christ everything is renewed and everything is perfected, and he subjects everything to the authority of his headship. Through his hands the hidden will reigns over everything and in everything, and there is no mind in which reverence for the truth does not dwell. He turns everyone toward the divine will and invites them to join the good in the kingdom above. He brings the angels and human beings with him into the kingdom above—all those who have loved the day of his divine appearing. Wicked people and tyrannical demons remain on earth, while payment is demanded of them for the debts they incurred and for which they were held in bondage. All become free from death and suffering—the children of the kingdom and the children of the earth alike. In this alone the company of the wicked is equal to the good: they put off mortality and the passions. There the soul’s impulses and the body’s desire cease, and the spring of shameful deeds dries up and stops flowing. One spring wells up from all humanity: love for human beings and perfect love toward the Creator. There they all alike call upon one Creator, and understand in him three in one and one in three. There the good and the wicked study a book [?], and explain the Creator’s power in his work of creation. All these things truly come about through our renewal, for nothing is lacking in the immortal creation. There is one thing in which they fall short. In this they are equal, but not in everything.

The great boundary between the righteous and sinners. A great boundary is established there between the two sides, and no one can cross its deep chasm. A mountain stretches from the earth toward the heights, and its extent cannot be measured by those who measure. Its vast distance astonishes the minds of those on earth. They gaze at it but cannot cross its great boundary. A crushing desire continually crushes their minds: they long, but the desire within them is not satisfied. This is the desire that lashes them more severely than whips: they see glory but cannot approach the gate of glory. Oh, how great is the glory of those who are glorified, and how contemptible the humiliating disgrace of those who are tormented! Oh, how bitter is the torment in Gehenna, and how sweet the delight of the kingdom above! Oh, how hideous is the hideous appearance of the children of darkness, and how beautiful the beautiful appearance of the children of light! Oh, how harsh is that declaration, “Go to Gehenna,” and how lovely the declaration, “Come, receive the kingdom above”! Oh, that hour when the righteous are separated from the wicked, and one is raised up while another is plunged down—it is a great anguish! A terrible groaning suddenly falls upon sinners when they contemplate the power of flight that the righteous acquire. It is a great wonder what exhausting labors accomplish: they cause wings for flight to grow on those who perform them. The righteous acquire spiritual wings on the day of resurrection, and like spiritual beings they fly through the air toward the heights. They journey spiritually along spiritual paths [?], and this is the wonder: suddenly they acquire the power of flight. It is a great wonder, whose marvel cannot be expressed: although the good and the wicked are one, they are not one. The good and the wicked have one nature on the day of resurrection. What, then, is this—that part of it flies and part remains behind? Iniquity is the cause of this distinction between one and another, and it sinks the company of the wicked into the abyss of iniquity.

It is righteousness that gives the righteous the power of flight, and through it chaste bodies are raised to the heights above. It is sin that binds the limbs of the unfaithful, who did not travel the path [?] of the kingdom on high with their companions. The weight of iniquity dragged its bearer away from righteousness and sank them into the hateful abyss of their deeds. There the good and the wicked rise as though from sleep, and they marvel and are astonished at the swiftness of that separation. They all cast off the body's weight and the soul's passions, yet although they cast them off, their individual appearances are not alike. Their appearance distinguishes them from their companions, and through it they learn the different kinds of conduct that distinguish good from evil. There they learn the different kinds of good and shameful deeds, and no one asks or is taught how a person lived. The garments of the soul's labors are spread over the limbs, and from what is visible everyone learns the nature of what is hidden. The scrutiny of judgment brings deeds and words into the open, and people look upon the blemishes within them as though in words [?]. The blemishes within them bring a case against the guilty and condemn them together with their own sins. Oh, how exact is that scrutiny which examines everything! Even the guilty acknowledge its judgment as just, for its judgment is true. Oh, that power which strengthens mortal humanity to know itself and rebuke its own blemishes before the eyes of onlookers! Oh, the wisdom people learn at humanity's renewal, making humanity's childishness wise with the wisdom of truth! It is the wisdom of truth that makes them wise through the power of its insights, and it teaches them to accuse every kind of hateful deed. With love and anguish they judge themselves and acknowledge as just the sentence passed upon their sins. They continually plead their case against their sins with discernment,

while they are scourged by the soul's remorse more severely than by lashes. Remorse of conscience is harsher upon them than any scourging, and it is harsher still when the gates of heaven are shut. The sorrow of that time cannot be expressed, when they contemplate the separation that happens suddenly. They contemplate it with the eyes of both body and mind, and they weep and lament doubly over their separation. The heavens are high, and the earth is an abyss that cannot be crossed. Perhaps they repeat that utterance addressed to the rich man. They understand that saying precisely, and they know [?] that the door of forgiveness is shut in their faces. The King opens the gates on high before those entering, and they enter and rest in that delight which never decays. The children of the kingdom see wonder and glory there, and they are astonished and amazed at glorious things that cannot be expressed. That delight cannot be expressed in human language, nor can spiritual beings describe it as it truly is [?]. The mind cannot fully explore the splendor of its beauty, for as it gazes, its vision wanders in wonder from one thing to another. Its account is bitter to the eager seekers who sought to investigate it, for after seeking it, they returned to seek it as though they had never sought it. The search for it impelled even me, weak as I am. I sought to know, but fell far short of knowing. I fell far short of recounting the different good things of that delight which the Good One has prepared for those who cherish his love. I thought I could paint the image of his love in words, but the words grew dull, and my portrayal was not sufficiently precise. Who can paint images of things that have no likenesses? Who can supply a comparison for a likeness that has no comparison [?]? That spiritual order has no likeness, just as the Self-Existent One has no equal among the works of his hands [?]. There is no equal to the Godhead that made everything, nor is there any likeness resembling that dwelling of the heavenly beings.

The earthly dwelling does not resemble it, although it too is a dwelling, for the form of life in this one passes away, while that one does not pass away. Even this world, which I said passes away, is not itself perishable [?], for it is not the world that passes away, but the order operating within it. He dissolves the order of this earthly way of life and establishes the reign of that unchanging way of life. That way of life does not change from what it is. Paul bears witness to this, calling it a house that never decays. Our firstfruits entered this house as High Priest and promised us that he would bring us in with him on the day of his appearing. On the day of his appearing, he opens the door of the Holy of Holies and brings in with him those who have loved the day of his appearing. I wished to speak of this day before my hearers, and now I hope to reveal its beauty before those who are beautiful. Its beauty attracted me and still draws me toward recounting it. When shall I give rest to my weary speech in a peaceful harbor? It is a great harbor, filled with peace without end. In it the ship of the world, battered by sufferings, comes to rest. The sea of sufferings has battered earthly life, and now it gains relief by resting from its weariness in the dwelling above. From the beginning the Creator made one dwelling and another, so that when someone grows weary, we may give him rest from his weariness in the one that endures. To the one that [?] he invited and called us who endure: the human race and the spiritual beings without bodily composition. Here and beyond, he anchored the hope of rational beings, so that when they recline at rest, they may receive the reward they have awaited. He promised a good reward to those who await good things, and entrusted the treasury of the promises he had spoken to one human being. He appointed one human being as treasurer over that dwelling, and made him a distributor of gifts and a bestower of precious things. Into his hands he placed the entire treasury of his loving will, and gave him the rank and exalted name of his divinity.

In his name he comes at the end to judge everyone, and like the Creator he renews the world that has worn out through error. Evil error has battered the world from the beginning, and the world has forgotten the name of the Creator who established everything. Christ will undo that error on the day of his revelation, and turn everyone back to the knowledge of the one Creator. There he makes the Creator’s name reign over all and in all, and created beings no longer go astray by giving that name to what is not God. They continually hallow this name in their minds, and there is no end to their constant hallowing. Spiritual and bodily beings occupy themselves with this, and the more they contemplate, the more they long to contemplate well. This is the work of that spiritual way of life: hallowing and praise, with a constancy that never has its fill. Those who offer praise never have their fill of that praise, for there is no weariness or discouragement there. There the evil inclination of those prone to stray comes to an end, and the stirring of desires also grows quiet and still. Sin is uprooted, death is dissolved, and conflict is at rest. The sting of wearisome passions and tyrannical demons is abolished. There is no remembrance of evil there, none whatsoever, and no one thinks about or even ponders anything hateful. There the whole creation becomes a new creation, and the old name is erased from every mind. There distinctions of classes and ranks are also abolished, and no one asks who is a slave or who is free. There is no distinction between being Jewish and being uncircumcised, and no one is despised or despises another for ugly defects. There is no defect in that renewed order, nor even any mention of defects, because mortality, full of defects, has passed away. Where there are no mortals, there is no mention of defects or injuries, because the new nature does not admit the old things.

The old things have ceased in Christ, the King of all, and he has renewed the world as a new and immortal world. In that world there are no names or words belonging to mortality, nor any remembrance of desires or earthly things. One remembrance remains constantly in every mind there: the name of the Creator and undivided love for humanity. Human beings and spiritual beings are bound together in love and compassion, and they do not slacken in their enjoyment of love’s goodness. Love alone endures in that order, and the soul’s inclination is bound by it and does not grow slack. Our inclination has no power to grow slack there, nor is it permitted to entertain two conflicting thoughts. Only a spring of good things flows from it, and it does not remember any kinds of evil at all. There is no evil, nor even the name of evil, in the land above, nor in the minds of the wicked who dwell in the land below. The understanding that the good possess in the kingdom above is also possessed by the sinners in Gehenna. The righteous and sinners alike possess one understanding, and there is no division between one mind and another. With one mind they praise the name of the one Creator, and they love and honor him without interruption. There is no interruption or weariness at all, nor does anyone slacken in the delight afforded by the name of grace. Only goodness is spoken of in that way of life, and they continually meditate on it and recount it. There they possess the great wealth of a great intellect, remembering the first things and the last. The course of life in both worlds is depicted before their eyes, and they forget neither the things that have happened nor those that are to come. They know precisely the things of earth and those of heaven, and they explain the full meaning of each world. They understand how created things came into being from nothing, and what cause renewed them at the end of time. They know how to traverse the great expanse of the four quarters.

And in their minds they encompass its height and depth. They see faults, examine wrongdoing, and judge truthfully; not one of the things that have happened or are happening escapes their memory. Their vision runs swiftly along with their movements, and they are not hindered by the progress of the sluggish [?]. They look equally upon distant and nearby things, and they see visible and invisible things together. Suddenly they acquire a wondrous vision in their senses and movements, and they see their own faults and those of their companions. Everyone recognizes those he knows and those he does not know, and no one asks who someone is, whose son he is, or where he comes from. They all receive one knowledge that does not pass away, and there is no tongue that does not explain the Creator’s power. All languages come to the same level there, and no one needs to learn anything from another. Human nature sees the whole of its own nature, and in its understanding it grasps the full extent of all humanity. Beginning with Adam himself, human beings begin to count Adam’s race, and each encompasses the whole of human nature within his mind. And who, I ask, has counted the number that people count, when even the number of spiritual beings is encompassed among them? In that state, the human being becomes the sum of everything, and the saying is fulfilled in him: he is the image of the Hidden One. Like the Creator, he discerns there the kinds of hidden things, and his sight reaches far enough to see the nature of spiritual beings. It is a great wonder, a wonder difficult to believe, that a nature possessing [?] sees what has no bodily composition. And perhaps his soul also sees itself as it is, and comprehends its own uncompounded nature through an image in its mind. If anyone objects that this is difficult to believe, I ask him: Does Christ see spiritual beings? And if he does not see the nature of spirit, which has no bodily composition, how does he judge those who are to be judged, if they are hidden from him?

And if he does not judge the spiritual beings who sinned, what then becomes of the written statement that he judges everyone? It would be a great disgrace if he received the authority to judge everyone but were unable to see the natures of those being judged. For we are certain of the judgeship he has undertaken, and there is no doubt that he sees those who are to be judged. And if he sees what has no bodily composition, however he sees it, then this sight is also given to us. For we will see the nature of spirit and our own souls, and the soul will marvel at the wonders that come to it. It is a great wonder that our nature sees what has no material constitution, and our sight moves swiftly over all created things. And if the listener finds this difficult to believe, recount another sight he will see, far greater than these. Christ the King, who reigns over everything and rules everything—we will see him clearly, just as he is. So, my fellow human being, will we see the King over everything, but not see the servants of his sovereignty? Yes, we will see Christ the King and the spiritual beings, and nothing in creation will be hidden from our understanding. There is only one whom we truly will not see: the one whose glorious nature is exalted above those who see. Him alone we will not see, nor will anyone at all, because no created eye can see him. The divine nature cannot be seen by the beings it has formed, neither by mortals nor by spiritual beings without bodily composition. Even spiritual beings are created, however exalted they may be, and they cannot see the nature that formed them. We are able to see their nature, and they ours, because we are equal in sharing one created condition from the Creator. The Creator gives us a wondrous sight, and in that state we gaze with the eyes of the spirit. There people see a great wonder in one another, and nothing prevents them from seeing the heights and the depths. They stand in the heights and see where sinners dwell.

The gaze of sinners, too, races toward the height above. At this sight the company of the wicked suffers greatly, and it silences them more effectively than the torments of Gehenna. The torments of earth’s children increase twofold when they contemplate the great glory of those at rest. If someone asks how those incapable of suffering can suffer, I ask him how the nature of demons suffers. If he then says that demons do not suffer there either, I say to him, “What, then, is the examination of judgment?” If there is judgment, there is also suffering for those being judged; and if [?] suffering, judgment and the very name of justice are nullified. If there is no judgment and no justice that examines people, then the striving of the righteous and of the angels is futile. If [?] earthly beings and those at rest, the Creator did not act justly in what he did. It is not just that he imposed the discipline of toil on rational beings, then turned and placed the good and the wicked on an equal footing. Why, then, did he multiply the different warnings against evil, only to make them false by exacting no account from sinners? Oh, the invention born of presumption is not true! Yet I too have presumptuously found fault with the just decree. The scrutiny of that Judge who judges all is just; he truly gives blessings and inflicts torments. His examination is full of blessings and torments, as it is written, and there is not a letter in his books that has not been inscribed justly. Presumption has declared these truths false, because it is accustomed to raising presumptuous objections. The accounts of the day of judgment are utterly true, and they will be revealed in actual events just as they have been stated. The day of judgment reveals the force of their meaning, and the fools who presumptuously criticized them will be ashamed. Perhaps they will learn in their own persons the force of just judgment, when they are condemned for the guilt of their objections. Stop, you presumptuous people, your criticism full of arrogance, and listen carefully to the account of the judgment that will take place at the end. The judgment is just, and the manner of its justice cannot be expressed. Both the righteous and the wicked testify to its justice.

Good and wicked alike acknowledge his justice, and in their own minds they confirm the sentence of his judgment. Their minds become a furnace of testing there, and they judge their own persons without overlooking anything. The word they heard judges them, as it is written, and it calls them to account for the warnings they acknowledged and then turned around and denied. The chief of judges solemnly declared, sealing his words with “Amen,” that everyone whose speech is unjust will come to judgment. The judgment is just; just is the one who examines everyone on the day of judgment, and in his justice he separates the righteous from the wicked. “One is taken and another is left”: this is what he does. One goes to heaven, and one remains on earth—this is a great sorrow. Where the body is, it is said, there the eagles will be. The body is Christ, and the eagles are the righteous who enter with him. The righteous enter where the body, Christ, is, and he makes them rejoice in that delight in which there is no toil. There is no toil in that spiritual delight, and in it body and soul are spiritually nourished. Body and soul rest there from their labors, and they no longer toil either bodily or in their souls. In spirit they are nourished by that nourishment without nourishment, and they have no need of what body and soul require. They live spiritually a life without end, and with the angels they converse and work at spiritual things. There they meditate on spiritual things like spiritual beings, because the exhausting toil of earthly things is not there. It is a great rest in which those worn out on earth rest there. They remain in it continually and never grow tired of its continuance. They continually marvel and wonder at their rest: how refreshing their rewards are, and how glorious! And perhaps, together with Paul, they repeat Paul's words: “The sufferings of this time are not equal to the gifts of our glory.” Our sufferings are small when compared with our reward, and this passing world is nothing beside our glory.

Glorious and excellent is the reward that the children of the kingdom receive. They cannot describe it, nor can it be described as it really is. With their senses and inward movements they see the glory of the glory within them, and in body and spirit they glorify the one who glorifies them. They constantly see the one who glorifies them, and they offer him sacrifices, to him the pure sacrifices of their thoughts. They see with their eyes and minds that judge who is from among them, not the divine Being that has never been seen and cannot be seen. A creature that has been made cannot see the Being who is, because the nature of the divine Being is exalted above those who see. Visible beings see that high priest who is from among us, the one who fulfills the high priesthood [?] for our lives. In this manner the herald called him an apostle and priest, and faithful and [?] to the one who made him, greater than Moses. On this condition the Lord of all chose him from among all, to take his own place [?] for the work of his hands. He takes the Lord's place for human beings and spiritual beings, and when they see him, their movements come to rest in the harbor of his body. In the temple of his body their gaze rests as in a temple, and in it they pray to one divine Being, to one Creator. The work of his hands longed to see the Creator himself, and since this was impossible, he gave them rest in the image of his image. He fashioned the image of the second Adam as an image, and raised him up and set him in the kingdom on high, in his own place. He takes his place for heavenly and earthly beings, so that they will not exhaust themselves searching for the hidden one who cannot be comprehended. The creature searches for the hidden one, asking where he is and how great he is; and through the visible one he checked the rush of its soul's searching. He built it as a house in the city of his kingdom, so that the temple of his body might accommodate those who worship him. Created beings, who came into being through the Maker, worship the Eternal One; and he, like a temple, is honored with the title of Creator.

Along with the Maker, he is honored in name and authority, since he is called the Son of God, like God. We call the son who is from among us the Son of God, and we count him with the divine Being without distinction. We understand one Being to be three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one equality. We count him within the number of one person, together with his being like the One who exists without beginning. This is the reason for the greatness of that man's rank: that through his greatness he might raise created beings toward the Creator. In him all creation is honored along with the Maker, for when it worships him, it knows that it too is worshiped in him. He who receives the worship of all is a part of creation, and [?] when it is worshiped along with the Creator. Along with the Creator, creation receives loving worship. This is the wonder: while it worships him, it is worshiped in him. The Creator performed a great wonder for the things he fashioned: he gave them a share in the glories of his divinity. He revealed the greatness of his love to his works through this that he [?], so that they might know how much he loves the work of his hands. The one who fashioned everything dearly loves the work of his hands: he made them heirs of the glory of his body. He made human beings heirs of glory along with the man. They glorify him and are glorified in him through the Maker's power. It is the Maker's power that made him glorious and worthy of praise; and if he had not known [?], he would have exalted those of his own kind. God gave him the rank of his divinity and made him Lord and Judge of all creation. He is the one who judges spiritual and bodily beings. He is the one who distributes gifts to the good and punishments to the wicked. He is the one who brings the children of the kingdom into the kingdom on high. He is the one who leaves the children of darkness in the outer darkness. In the harbor of his love he gives rest to the weary who cherished his love, and in Gehenna he torments the wicked who despised his commandments. With his glory he glorifies those who praise his proclamation, and through his judicial sentence he humbles the pride of those who revile him. In his royal dwelling the King on high brings joy to those who love him, and before everyone's eyes he makes the light of their conduct shine.

Light shines from them, the children of light, and they marvel and are amazed at the glorious light of their own persons. The glory within them reveals the labors of their lives, and the appearance of their persons shines in proportion to their labors. Although they are all clothed in incorruptible glory, they are not all equal in appearance as they stand. The glory within them is lesser or greater from one to another, just as the radiance of one star is less than that of its companion. The soul’s disposition does this within that arrangement: it increases or diminishes the different degrees of glory. It is this disposition that also reveals this among the wicked: the lashes of those who are punished are not all equal.
