The lashes grow stronger according to the will that committed great wickedness, while torment is lessened according to the soul that judged itself. What our soul’s disposition accomplishes is a great wonder: it glorifies us, and it disgraces us on the day of resurrection. It raises us to the kingdom on high, which is above everything, and it sinks us under the weight of sins into the earth below. Our Lord, the Lord of all, therefore spoke rightly when he said that he does not judge, but that a person judges himself. Every human being judges himself on the day of judgment, and from him spring the different kinds of blessings and the severity of the lashes. He places the crown of victory on himself in the sight of those watching, and he brings shame upon his own face before [?]. Honor and dishonor belong to it, and it makes us children of the kingdom or children of darkness. Since it is clear that our disposition has authority over both, let us not complain about the severity of the lashes reserved for us. Let us blame our disposition as an adversary that distinguishes between the two: why did it not live up to the light of its discernment? The great light of discernment is within its nature, and its rays spread toward the four directions more powerfully than the sun’s. It is a second sun, constantly running its course in the heavens of our soul, showing us the different kinds of good and shameful things. Through it, as by a light, we see the two ways of life, and through it we learn the reason for this world and the world to come. Look, people, and see how great is the understanding within a human being:

It knows how to consider things far away and things nearby. Come, consider how unrestricted is the freedom of his soul, and how he has authority to do beautiful things or shameful things. It is very easy for him to judge himself accurately, to choose the good and reject the evil according to his discernment. It is a testing furnace for beautiful things and hateful things, and it purifies us of ugly blemishes better than a furnace. Come, then, let us purge our various hateful deeds in the furnace of our soul before the day of testing at the fearful judgment arrives. Come, let us seat our soul’s disposition as our judge and bring before it the case concerning the sins we have committed. Come, let us hire repentance as our advocate and bring our arguments before the judge who examines everything. Let us make the mind an admirable [?] for what is said, and let us set out the passions of body and soul one after another. Let the mouth mediate between one and the other, and let the impulses cry out to the bodily members, “Listen carefully!” Let the soul say to the bodily senses that carry out its actions, “Take care! Do not behave mindlessly like animals.” Let the eye be a guide to visible things, and let it mark out a path before the limbs so that they may walk properly. Let it shut the gate of wisdom, the soul’s treasury, so that the various kinds of evil do not plunder it like robbers. Let the whole body preserve the order proper to its bodily nature, and let the hidden soul express the various kinds of wisdom through it. Let the senses be like horses serving the soul’s activity, and let her be above them like a charioteer upon a chariot. Let her place the reins of discipline upon the visible senses, and let them proceed properly toward the appointed meeting of love and faith. Let soul and body preserve the order of a single human being, and let them not fall away from conduct befitting a human being. A person is one human being in body and spirit, and must know the reason for his name and [?]. His name is explained as body and soul, a twofold vessel: one bodily and one of the soul, a dwelling for all things.

By his constitution, the human being is a dwelling for all things, and in him the creation of speechless and speaking beings is brought together. And if, as he is, he contains the sum of all things, then good things too ought to be brought together in him. Let him portray a good likeness in his own person for those who see him, and let them contemplate him as a divine image. God called him the image of God at the beginning, when he created him, and gathered to him rational beings [?], so that they might be established in him. Come, human being, see how greatly your nature has been exalted: though you came from dust, you have acquired the title ‘God.’ Come, consider the greatness of the rank given to you, and give thanks to the one who has honored the lowliness of your clay. See that your frame was made from clay when you first came into being, and now reign over earthly beings and [?]. From you comes the King who reigns over all creatures; heaven and earth and everything in them obey him. One of your own race has become King and Lord and Judge as well. See that you do not wrong the one who has honored the lowliness of your clay. See that you are destined to enter a judgment whose examination is just, to pay there the debt of the sins you have committed. See that everyone’s faults are revealed there before the eyes of all, and people look upon one another’s faults as though in sunlight. Hear that the wicked who desired evil remain on earth, and refrain from wrongdoing so that you do not remain on earth with wrongdoers. Hear that the good ascend to the heights of the kingdom on high, and enter with the good into that delight which is full of blessings. See that the righteous and the chaste are destined to see Christ, and cleanse your soul of foul things so that you too may see him. See that those whose souls are foul do not enter where he is, and purify your soul of foul things so that you may enter and see him. Hear the sound of weeping and gnashing of teeth in Gehenna, and tremble and shudder at that report, which is terrifying to hear. Hear that this spiritual delight never ends, and count everything as nothing; enter and delight in what has no end. See, I have set out for you the kinds of good things and the names of evil things. Flee from evil and cherish goodness, for engaging in it is good. See, I have shown you that the toil of the world will surely pass away.

Do not toil in it beyond proper bounds, lest you be put to shame. See, I have taught you that there is another [?] in heaven. Love to occupy yourself with it, so that you may become an heir with its heirs. See, I have laid out a road for you to travel to the assembly above. Accustom yourself to travel well toward the heights. See, I have told you that the road to the heights demands toil. Prepare yourself for toil and make ready to travel with the travelers. You have heard the report that there are two roads in the world. Take care not to travel with the idle on the broad one. You have heard that it is written that the road of life is very narrow. Discipline yourself [?] and receive immortal life. All these things, and many more than these, are recorded in the writings of the books of the Spirit. What I too have recounted, I recounted from what is written, so that everyone may know that my thoughts have followed the path of the Scriptures. The Scriptures showed me how to walk in the path of their words, and they taught me to teach the truth of their meanings.
On the parable of the seed and the weeds.
69. On the seed and the weeds. By the same author [?]. The sixty-ninth discourse, which he composed on the parable of the seed and the weeds.

Christ called the word of his teaching good seed. He called the teaching of the [?] the weeds that grew with it. He compared the world to a [?] and called himself the master of the house. And the good seed of his teaching was received by the soil of the soul. The one who sowed the weeds is the enemy of our nature. He sowed the word of his teaching and made schisms and divisions spring up. He said that the people fell asleep because they neglected their duty, like a farmer who grows slack, so that brushwood increases within the field. The righteous servants who saw weeds among the wheat brought a question to their master: “Did you not sow good seed?” The master, who knows [?], answered the servants: “An enemy has done this to ruin the seed of my teaching.” The servants burned with zeal and said to the good master: “Let us go and gather the weeds, so that they do not hinder the growth of the wheat.” But the master, who is gentle, said to the zealous servants: “Let them grow together until the end comes,” “lest the wheat be gathered with the bitter weeds.” He was pointing to the possibility of change, since perhaps they would turn back from wrongdoing. No, my Lord, your knowledge is not mistaken: weeds do not change, for their bitterness belongs to their nature, and they cannot [?]. “This seed,” he says, “is rational and has control over its own will. “It can easily change according to its free choice. Receive proof of this from those who came before them.” They were bitter weeds, but they were transformed and became wheat. Abraham was a weed, and by his own will [?] he was transformed. He became a delightful fruit, and through him the bitter became sweet. Zacchaeus the tax collector was a weed who gathered plunder from others. By his own will he became wheat; he turned around and sowed charitable gifts. The robber was a weed, nourished on human blood. When he saw the wonder on the cross, he mingled with the wheat. The great Paul was a weed who battered the wheat as it grew. He was zealous against the truth, but turned around and stood for the truth: a farmer who abundantly sowed his teaching in the four regions [?]. He cultivated the soil of souls and filled the world with his fruits. Look at the weeds that were transformed and became choice wheat! Come now to those who went astray and would not return to knowledge. Marcion was the first weed that sprouted in the wheat field. He drank the rain of instruction but persisted in the bitterness of his own will. He was a dog that broke loose, went mad, and barked against his Maker. He proclaimed three principles: the Just, the Good, and also the Evil. Mani was another weed, clothed in the appearance of wheat. He was a wolf lurking in the flock, showing himself as a lamb; a dragon that sucked in gall

and gave it to those close to him to drink; a deadly root growing among the wheat. He resembled a brightly colored bird, changing into every form. He was an associate in sorcery and a kinsman in magic. He broke apart the order of our nature and deprived the body of life. He invented out of his own mind the claim that resurrection belongs to the soul alone. The whole sum of his teaching rests on two principles. He called them Good and Evil, according to the deeds of each. Bardaisan, however, was wheat that turned into a weed. When the Church saw his transformation, she uprooted him from among the wheat. He had been one of the flock’s lambs, but he turned around and bit the flock. The harvesters drove him away and threw him out, and he mingled with the wolves. The difficult questions he sought to overcome, he turned and hurled against himself. He was a debater against his companions, whose teaching turned into [?]. He turned to investigating everything and introduced many self-existent beings [?]. While he thought he had flourished, he perished and became a stranger to the truth. He was wheat whose growth changed—Paul, who became a weed. Through a woman he was brought low, like Samson grinding at the mill. He too had been invited [?] to the feast, but he went out and became a stranger. He cut off his hope of life and spoke wickedness against the Most High. He said that the Son had formerly been with his Father without an individual existence, like the mere sound of a word, which has no individual existence by nature. He assigned a beginning, from Mary’s giving birth onward, to the one who is equal to his Father and is not younger than him in existence. What can the insolent man do when John rebukes him, saying that in the beginning the Only Son [?] was with his Father? He was there in the world, and the worlds were established [?] by his hands. He himself came to his own, and his own did not receive his word. Those who heard his teaching he made heirs of his glory. He gave them a share in honor, in the name of immortality. Here is the demonstration of [?], like the sun before those who understand. And seers are weighed, as in a sieve, by the words of the Spirit. Valentinus, the weed, denied the resurrection of the body, and he regarded the writings containing the Spirit’s words as foreign to him. But this is his great wickedness, in which he openly boasts: he claims that the Word himself underwent a change and did not take a body from Mary. Arius, who denied the truth, had grown in the wheat field, and he concealed himself beneath an outward appearance. So that his bitterness would not [?]. For he was a wolf wearing a disguise, and he hid among the flock. When the shepherds became aware of him, they drove him out from among the flock. He brought his thoughts into the open and revealed the falseness of his thinking. He poured falsehood out of his heart, and his lips spoke wickedness. He called the Son a creature of the Father, and the Spirit something fashioned by the Father.

He claims that the Father alone exists, and that the Son and the Spirit are his [?]. The Father, he says, is without beginning, while the Son and the Spirit come after him. And because he created them, there is a span of time between him and them. But if he made the Son a creature, as the blasphemer says, What prevents everything from being called a son of God? Gabriel and Michael too were fashioned by the Father’s will. Although they are spirits, they are [?] with respect to the title of Being. And if the fashioning of the Son and their own fashioning are entirely alike, Then he possesses only a borrowed name, and in his deeds he is far removed from it. Another weed, his companion—his name is harder than [?]. But the discerning person recognized him from the fruits produced through his [?]. He too corrupted the confession, departing from the truth of the faith. He sought to demolish the building whose foundations cannot be overcome. He claimed that no soul was taken together with the body by our Savior. Instead, the Word took a mortal body for himself and dwelt in it. When he realized that he was being exposed, he brought his [?] into the open. He devised another trick by which to conceal himself for a time. He changed his position and confessed this too: that our Lord took a body and a soul. But he claims that he left out only the mind, since it too is a third distinct entity. Why, then, did none of the Scriptures tell us about this? Above all, why did Moses not tell us—the one who wrote about our formation? Perhaps this contemptible man has become wiser than the son of Amram! And he has discovered something extra: the mind, a third distinct entity. Look at the seed of the murderer, which he sowed in the souls of his [?]. He disturbed the earth with his weeds and caused divisions in heaven. At first Satan had sown weeds among the wheat. He raised up schisms and divisions like battle lines against the truth. When he saw that his army had been defeated and that truth had triumphed [?] through its ministers, He devised another trick and went in and lay hidden among the wheat. He saw that he could not win openly, and he began to wage war from ambush. He acted like a member of the household and like a teacher of truths. He saw that the good news had been poured out over all peoples and languages, And had taken hold of [?] in every region and bound the [?] of paganism. He put on the appearance of a disciple so as not to display his falsehood openly, because he knew that his teaching was abhorrent. And was not accepted openly. He saw that [?] was radiant, illuminating the eyes of souls and bringing the stubborn to conviction. He [?] a path to the kingdom and concealed the ugliness of his thoughts beneath the splendid garment of the name of light. He entered and hid in ambush. The simple did not notice him. He spread a covering over the soul and blinded the light of knowledge. He silenced the mind’s awareness of the senses, so that it would not understand what is right. He darkened the light of the eyes,

keeping them from reading the Scriptures. He stopped up the ears that hear, so that they would not listen to the words of the Spirit. The tongue, the fountain of words whose flow had never ceased, he made stammering and crippled, so that it would not speak of spiritual things. The heart, the king of the members, the harp of all wisdom—he stripped it of its treasures and threw some of his carob pods into it. Oh, how subtle his schemes are, and how deep his tricks! Oh, deadly poison, with sweetness mixed into it! “The meaning of the divine Scriptures is not good,” they say, “and whoever reads gains nothing except to learn arrogance.” “He read a great deal,” they say, “and grew weak. He began investigating and probing deeply. He studied the Scriptures extensively, went astray, and departed from what is right.” Oh, the unspeakable injustice that the evil one proclaimed through the mouths of the idle! Learning, the light of the soul—they [?] turned it into darkness. Fools filled the well-trodden path of the Scriptures with obstacles. “Do not listen to an explanation,” they say, “and do not pay attention to a word that is expounded. “Be like a blind person toward Scripture and like a deaf person toward interpretation [?]. Flee from the [?], so that their teachings do not lead you astray. “This alone is enough,” they say, “that we believe without investigation.” Where did you learn this, you who hate the words of the Spirit, that you have trodden a new road and wandered onto a deceptive path? Satan answered them through the errors he sowed in their ears, so that they meditate on maxims and recount absurd dreams. It was not enough that he led them astray through stumbling blocks while they were awake; he also shows them visions, so that they will be believed as true. Oh, the enemy of our nature—how skilled he is with snares! Paul bears witness to this when he makes his tricks known: “Our struggle,” he says, “is not against a fleshly being like ourselves, but against the rulers of the air, the spirit that wages war against flesh.” At the beginning of the battle, he used to devise every kind of scheme and renew his weapons every day, because he was fighting against knowledgeable people. But now, they say, stratagems are no longer [?] for his craft. If he merely gives a sign, fools carry out his will. If he wishes to catch us through the [?] of the love of money, our will has already [?] him, and gold is written on our hearts. If he introduces the love of glory, a poison pleasing to the eye, we desire it far more than he does, and perhaps he learns it from us. If he fights against us through lust, its leaven is embedded in our nature, and he merely offers advice. Then the deed comes out into the open. The three chief sources of all the passions are those we have mentioned. Once he had enslaved us through these, he stood there like a victor. With these passions he fought against the beginning of our nature. He was confident that through them he would win, as he had in earlier times. [?] For the rebel knew this and had learned it through experience:

that the whole nature of mortals is bound by these passions. He put them on like armor in the battle against our Lord, for the insolent one thought he could lead him astray as he had Adam. Here his tricks did not stand, nor did the devices of his craft, because his opponent was secretly armed with the armor of the Spirit. After that victory which our nature won with our Lord, which the heights and depths perceived and which was proclaimed in every region, look—we have given him our obedience, and he has entered and settled within us as he pleased. He has become like one of us, and the members of the household do not treat him as a stranger. The soil of our soul is cultivated for him, and our obedience also submits to him. He sows the seed of his teaching, and its fruit comes a hundredfold. We have uprooted the seed of Christ’s teaching from our minds, and we have heaped up the evil one’s seed, and his weeds are pleasing to us. In name we are insiders, but in our conduct we are outsiders. We are called servants of Christ, but we serve the enemy. The hateful desire for sin—its drink is very sweet to us. Money, the root of evils, has its root planted within our hearts. The love of glory is deadly poison, a trap that kills from ambush. We are caught in its snares, yet we do not notice its bonds. Envy is a murderous sword that kills the soul along with the body. It dwells within us like an army commander, and our affections pay it honor. Pride destroys good order; it is a friend who kills those dear to him. We wear it like a garment, and our mind is adorned with it. Our tongue has become a messenger for the falsehood that the devil brought forth through a promise, and it serves its purposes. We have forgotten the order of our discipleship and departed from our duty. Everyone is his own master, conducting himself as he pleases. Rebellious scribes have sprung up among us, teaching from rebellious books. They are far from the duty that the Scriptures taught us. The path that the earlier generations laid out was clear through faith, which they all [?] alike. But Satan, through his weeds, made grievous divisions spring up in it. All the teachers [?] drank from a single spring of instruction, and like channels [?] reaching toward the four corners, they watered the earth with their words. They were like light in creation, and they illuminated the world with their flames. Through their words, like a flood, they turned difficulties into clear explanations. They put on armor against the evil one, so that the ranks of truth would not be broken. Through their own sufferings they closed the breaches in our nature. But when the end of the warriors’ lives arrived, and they lay down in restful sleep after the toil of their service, Satan entered stealthily and sowed the weeds of his teaching,

and disturbed the entire flock with the bitterness of his weeds. He saw that the hunters had fallen asleep. And he began openly to uproot, causing many schisms and divisions. The one harmonious body of the church, made up of many, he divided into parts through the differences in his teachings. The field that diligent workers cultivated through the sufferings of their afflictions, he befouled and filled with his weeds, making a hateful thicket grow in it. Among the lost sheep gathered by the great Shepherd of shepherds, wolves entered disguised as lambs and tore apart the bodies of the flock. The sweet spring of the Law, which used to water the soil of the soul—he altered its utterances so that the heretics would not accept them. And who would not be distraught over this: the temples that the Holy Spirit adorned became a dwelling for an unclean spirit, because they gave a hearing to the wicked. The captives who were brought back through the cross from the captivity of the devil turned back and became enslaved to the evil one, willingly and not by force. The guests whom grace invited to the banquet of the heavenly Bridegroom—look, they have gone out and become strangers, so that they will not enjoy the wedding feast. Who would not grieve over this? We have been false to the hope of life, and we have exchanged the reality of things to come for earthly things. And who can put right the ugly things of our days? Evils have become entrenched in us through long-standing habit. Our disease has grown too strong for medicine, and physicians have fled from it. The knowledgeable cannot offer treatment for the diseases of our soul. Teachers have clothed themselves in arrogance, and students in stubbornness. They have made the easy, pleasant yoke harsh for those who bear it. New things have sprung up in our days from ignorant teachers, who lay down laws for us to observe hours and days. They abandoned the road that the righteous opened and the knowledgeable also traveled. They went off wandering through the wastelands of error taught by the wicked. They reduced the whole Law to the observance of days, and revived Judaism for us through the new laws they handed down. They rejected the Scriptures of the Spirit and the glory of their words. From the inventions of their own minds they established foreign laws. They stopped speaking about love, hope, and faith. Instead, they are constantly occupied with recounting empty, foolish dreams. And if a knowledgeable person rebukes them and restrains the fabrications of their words, they sharpen the sword of their tongues, and all of them kill him out of envy. They say, “This man pries into things and disputes with God. He teaches a new doctrine and does not believe that the dream is true.” Who is teaching new things, you who are blind to knowledge: the person who recounts what Scripture says, or the person who establishes a fabrication for himself? They have obscured the light of knowledge and have refused to be persuaded. It is beneath the arrogant man

to humble himself and come to the truth. And on every side, look, Satan’s wishes are being fulfilled. He has made schisms spring up among outsiders and disputes among insiders. No knowledgeable person has recounted the misery of our days. For the evil one has choked Christ’s good seed with his weeds. But who will rouse [?], so that he may rise and weep for us with his lamentations? For he knew how to recount the evils of sins. Look, he rejects fine gold and openly accepts counterfeit metal. Those who deserve honor are despised and scorned, while the fool’s prestige flourishes. Come and see, righteous son of Amoz, the injustice of the nations, like that of the people: they have called evil good and named good evil. They have mixed sweet with bitter, and falsehood with truth. For arrogance confuses the proper order, so that what is right is not discerned. Rise, worker of souls, great and glorious Paul. And see the field of your teaching, which the evil one has filled with his brushwood. Architect who [?] and completed churches in the four corners of the world, come and see your lofty building as unskilled people tear it down. Sailor who traveled the sea and guarded his ship against the waves, rise and see the ship of the Church, which [?] winds are battering. Simon, chief of the apostles, fisher of fish and people, come and see the net of your teaching, which the evil one has torn with his disputes. You used to catch a thousand a day through that power of apostleship, but the devil, in his envy, has scattered many of them. The twelve apostles are lights; the world shone with their flames. Rise and drive away from our humanity the darkness that the evil one has spread. Messengers whom the King sent for the peace of the whole inhabited world, come and heal the divisions that the devil has stirred up in the churches. Cultivators of the land of the nations, who uprooted the brushwood of paganism, rise and cleanse the Church’s field of the deceitful one’s weeds. Salt that seasoned those who were tasteless, so that through it they acquired a pleasant flavor, may the minds that the evil one has corrupted be seasoned by their words. Come, my brothers, let us return to the road that Truth opened through the apostles. Let us not wander along the path of falsehood, where there are many stumbling blocks. Come, let us approach the persuasion offered by the words of the Scriptures. Let us heal our own defects with the words that the Holy Spirit caused to be written, and take medicine to bind our wounds from the medicinal root of their words. For they know the sufferings of our nature and can heal its wounds. Let us cry out about the pain of our nature to the skilled physicians, and let us not be ashamed as we confess the ugly blemishes of our sins. Let us draw near and ask for mercy from the great sea of mercy, who has poured out the treasury of his gift upon the wicked and the unjust. Let us pour the tears of our eyes over the wounds of our sins. Let us put our recklessness to shame because of the snare in which we wander. Let us drive pride away from us,

and uproot envy from within us. Let us plant love in our minds, together with hope and faith. Let us uproot from within us the weeds that the evil one has made spring up in his envy. Let us receive the good seed that the word of life has sown in us. Let us cultivate the soil of our souls and uproot the brushwood of our sins. Let us prepare our hearing for the Spirit’s life-giving teaching. Here are the medicines of the Scriptures; come, let us draw near to them. With tears of heartfelt repentance, let us heal the pain of our wounds. Here are the apostles, the physicians who bandaged the wound of our humanity. Let us show them the pains of our souls, so that they may help their sick. Here is our Lord, the sea of mercy. Let us draw near and ask for help, for this is the purpose of his coming: that sinners should turn to him. How shall we appease justice, so that it does not accuse us in the court of judgment? For there is no place there for tears, repentance, or pleading. The time is near for the coming of the bridegroom who invited us to his wedding. Let us prepare clothes for the feast, so that we do not become a laughingstock there. Now is the time to trade with the talent our Savior gave us. Let us not bury the silver of his word, so that we are not called wicked servants. Let us put oil in our lamps, so that we do not run short when he comes, and so that, with the five wise women [?], we may enter the bridal chamber with him. You who have sunk into sin, rise from the sleep of your sickness. For the great dawn has drawn near, and it rebukes the lazy. Workers whom idleness hired at the end of the day's work [?], look forward to the wages of his gift, so that you may be made equal to those who came first. See, he has opened the door of his compassion. Let us call upon mercy to come to our aid, so that it may help us in the struggle, in the battles against the accuser [?]. The parable of the seed of the weeds itself urged me to speak the truth, for I saw the teaching spring up from the seed of the deceiver's word. While I wanted to denounce the bitterness of his weeds, the sickness of those inside grew far worse than the wrongdoing of those outside. Those outside split the flock, went out, and became strangers. Those inside wandered after them, yet think they are still inside. They abandoned the path of the Scriptures, where peaceable people are settled. They went out wandering along paths full of the threat of bandits. They suffered blows, and their bodies were battered, yet they did not realize they were being struck. For the deceiver led them astray with the greedy enticements of his disturbances. Zeal concerning these things stirred me to tell of the suffering caused by our wounds. Perhaps reproof itself will awaken the sleepers who have sunk into sin. Through rebuke I sought to check the violence of our fever. For a sickness that has grown chronic through habit must be healed with strong medicine. Christ, who renewed your creation, do not disregard our petition. In mercy you called us your heirs; do not count us among strangers.
On the Feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross

Discourse Thirty
On the Feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross
Response:
Blessed is Christ, who by his cross gathered his Church and scattered those who crucified him, my brothers.

Through a crucified man, the Creator revealed to the whole world the name of his being and the great power of his divinity. Like the sun, he raised him up and placed him atop the wood. From him the whole inhabited world, which had been darkness, was illuminated. Through a crucified man, he captured the savage world, brought it in, and confined it under the laws of his proclamation. On the summit of Golgotha he raised the standard of his victorious power, so that through it he might gather together those in heaven and those on earth. Through a human being, humanity stumbled; they became guilty through sin and fell into the abyss of mortality. Through a human being, the Lord of all chose to give life to humanity. He fastened him to the wood so that through him he might abolish humanity’s sin. Through his crucifixion he purified our entire race along with himself, so that through him he might free mortal nature, which gives birth to suffering. Through his death, ravenous death, the killer of humanity, died in him; and through his resurrection he distributed life to our entire race. For our sake the Lord of the world came into the world, and in the robe of our body he showed his compassion toward humanity. In the judgment in which Adam was condemned in Eden, within Paradise, the second Adam was victorious and became king on the summit of Golgotha. Through his crucifixion he put the rulers and authorities to shame, and through the stripping of his flesh he exposed them before the eyes of those watching. For since, in the wisdom of the God of all,

the whole world did not understand the power of his wise works, the Creator chose, through the simplicity of preaching, to give life and salvation to humanity through a crucified man. It did not gain wisdom from the created things that his command established: the heavens above, in their vast extension and expanse, spread out from water like a canopy above humanity, displaying by their continued existence the glory of the one who established everything. The heavenly lights, too, appointed for the seasons and to give light to humanity, display his power through their shining and their ordered courses. The air, then, through its changes and mixtures, shows humanity by its movements that there is one Maker. At times it thickens, and clouds form from it; from it lightning and thunder also appear with great force. Fierce thunderclaps sound across the heights; hail is formed, and snow quickly gathers. The earth, through its surface, its produce, and its springs, brings forth and displays forms of every kind before the eyes of those watching. His command set a boundary of sand to restrain the sea, and placed within it a firm ordinance so that it would not rage uncontrollably. The earth is preserved and is not dissolved by the onrush of the waters, nor do the waters themselves disappear into the earth. The established order of all creation is preserved as it came into being, and the elements within it do not consume one another. Through wisdom the world did not understand its Lord, nor did it recognize the Governor who holds everything. Human understanding is lodged in the mind, yet through it they did not come to know the one Creator who established everything. All creation displays his glory like a book, and teaches humanity a single teaching about the one self-existent Being. The whole world, in its dullness of heart, did not understand, nor did it gain wisdom from created things so as to know its Lord. For this reason, at the end of the ages, the Creator chose to raise humanity to life through the simplicity of preaching. Through a crucified man, despised by unbelievers, the Giver of life to all chose to give life to humanity through his crucifixion.

His death was despised and his suffering scorned by the insolent, yet through the lowliness of his proclamation he saved the lost. The eloquent were put to shame, the wise fell silent, and the rebels fell; the crucified man yoked them under his dominion. Where are the philosophers among the Greeks, who used to boast of the subtleties of their teachings? For they supposed that the world was enlightened by their studies, but the cross dawned and overshadowed their ideas. When they understood the mighty greatness of the crucified man, they abandoned their own teachings, and all ran to follow him. Their assemblies and teachings disappeared from the inhabited world, for at its dawning the cross dissolved them from the midst of the earth. Thus the word of Paul, the herald of the Spirit, was fulfilled: even the wise among the Greeks came to nothing and perished. The Hebrews too, who exalted themselves because of their Scriptures, were stripped of their positions by the cross on which they crucified him. He abolished the laws and teachers of the Jews, and by his great power scattered them to the four corners of the earth. The Jews, they say, slow of heart, asked for signs like those they saw in the days of Moses, when he delivered them. Let us ask the Jews: What did the whole world gain from the signs that Moses [?]? The righteous man, they say, brought ten plagues upon the land of Egypt, yet he did not turn even one Egyptian from his stubbornness. The report of his mighty signs spread throughout the whole land, yet not a single person drew near to his teaching. Not only did the uncircumcised nations fail to turn to him, but even his own people did not keep his laws. He performed signs and displayed mighty deeds [?] the Creator, yet the stubborn people provoked him in the shadow of death. They reviled Moses, went astray after idols, and worshiped carved images; they all perished by the sentence pronounced by God. See what the cross accomplished at the end of the ages: although it was considered contemptible, it drew the world after its glory. The Jews ran and hid themselves at his proclamation, and [?] of them—look—were scattered to the four corners of the earth. All the nations together took up his yoke, and now they worship him, the crucified man, with sincerity of heart.

At its dawning, the cross became a sign of peace for our nature, and [?] placed it in the harbor of immortal life. As foreshadowed by righteous Noah, he relieved the weariness of the battered world, and through his crucifixion rescued humanity from destruction. Through righteous Noah the world was given rest from evils, and a change came upon the whole world through [?]. The true Noah, Christ our King, who brings peace to all, placed the world in the peaceful harbor of his crucifixion. His living cross became like an ark for our nature, and through it we were rescued from the flood of the sentence of judgment. Come, let us consider the greatness of the mighty deeds accomplished by the cross: how, through its revelation, it gave hope to humanity. The human race had fallen into countless evils and had become estranged from the worship of God. For they had no knowledge of the Creator’s name, and so they assigned his praise to the work of his hands. In their error, people served and bowed down before created things, without recognizing the Creator who had fashioned them. They worshiped carved idols and honored images that had no awareness, withholding glory from the Maker who had created them. All the demons were praised by unbelievers and honored as God by those who had gone astray. Praise of the God of all had ceased from the mouths and tongues of human beings. For their tongues were busy with empty things, praising evil spirits and extolling unclean demons. It was not enough for them to honor the tyrannical demons with the blood of animals and offerings of grain. Rather, they became so wanton in this desire that they appeased those murderers with the blood of their own children. Beaten-down people shamefully served evil spirits, and with innocent blood they satisfied those who thirsted for blood. Our race lay in this deep abyss of wickedness, and accursed demons trampled it in their rebellion. Human nature had lost all hope of good things, and in despair it served as a slave to its desires. For this reason, the one who knows everything abandoned them

and handed them over to the deceptive desires of their hearts. Through their lust they defiled and degraded even their own bodies, clothing themselves in shame through their debased conduct. In the rites of demons they corrupted the order established in nature, and they had unnatural intercourse like animals. Male and female defiled the marriage bed through disorder and defilement with sexual perverts. They committed adultery and sexual immorality contrary to the established order, with lawless depravity and degradation. The wicked carried out all these things in the rites of demons, and the [?] light of reason grew dark for them. The streets and cities were filled with unclean altars, and in every house they set up carved idols and arranged images. The gods they bowed down to were beyond counting, and the goddesses they worshiped were beyond all order. There was a great division between one group of priests and another, and each person cherished his own error through the wickedness of his inclination. Disputes and divisions multiplied among the nations, and countless wars intensified throughout all generations. From the wickedness of the accursed demons, evil deeds [?]; and they became accursed, shedding the blood of their fellow human beings. The sin the world committed long ago cannot be told, and the wickedness it practiced throughout all ages cannot be described. Words are too few to tell the kinds of wickedness that all people committed before the coming of the crucified King. Through his appearing, the Crucified One abolished all these things from among the people and also from among the nations throughout the inhabited world. Look, all the nations worship him together in unity—the one God who turned them back through the crucified man. They all renounce the names of the gods through which error led them astray, and acknowledge Jesus, who gave them life through his victorious power. In their own languages they all cry out one confession of praise to him who, through his cross, made peace reign in the heights and the depths. Hail to the Crucified One, who killed death through his crucifixion and proclaimed peace to all who were far away and to those who were near. He is our peace, who made the two one in unity and broke down the barrier that stood before humanity.

He abolished all laws through a single command of his, and through the sacrifice of his body reconciled everyone to God. Hail to the Crucified One, through whose appearing mortals received life, and through whom spiritual and bodily beings were brought into peace. Hail to the Crucified One, who changed and abolished all blasphemies and uprooted error from the people and the uncircumcised nations. Hail to the Crucified One, who changed and abolished all blasphemies and uprooted error from among the people and the uncircumcised nations. Hail to the Crucified One, who made the human race worthy to become, from here on earth, heirs in the kingdom on high. This is the Crucified One who washed creation clean of its filth and wiped away from it the foul smell of abominable deeds. This is the Crucified One through whom the human race was gathered into one church, the peaceful harbor of the one God. If you want to learn the power of the crucified man, consider in your mind how far the proclamation of him has reached. Look, then, in the east: see how the power of his rays has shone forth, and Persia, which was darkened by idolatry, has been illuminated. Now let the mind rise toward the west, and see there the greatness of his power through those who worship him. He caught all the kings and warriors in his net and established them firmly on the foundation of faith in him. Look in your thoughts as far as the south and consider what the Crucified One accomplished among its inhabitants when he shone forth. Ascend in your understanding also to the whole northern region, and see the power of the victorious name of the crucified man. Look and marvel at all the teachings that existed on earth, and how the crucified man brought them to an end and swept them away. Before the [?] rays of his living standard, the objects of worship fell, the demons fled, and their servants were put to shame and brought to nothing. Chaldean astrology held sway for four thousand years, yet it could not subject everyone to its teaching. Although, through its antiquity, it had firmly established its [?] on earth, the Crucified One, when he shone forth, uprooted it, cast it down, and exposed its falsehood. Thus the law of Moses, the firstborn of prophecy, also held sway for a thousand and five hundred [?] years. Although prophets, priests, and kings were his heralds, not one of the nations turned and came to his teaching. It has now been a thousand years since Magianism also began and established the rites of its confusion among the idols.

For it did not succeed, although kings rose to support it, together with judges who aided it with their furious threats. With dreadful tortures and cruel deaths they killed beyond measure, yet they could not turn a single person toward their teaching. Although they acted insolently and waged war against the people of Jesus, countless people from their own ranks turned and believed in Jesus. They tasted the sweet spring of baptism in the Church and became advocates for the confession of our faith. The tortures inflicted by accursed, bloodthirsty men failed, and the children of the holy Church multiplied beyond number. Thus the whole error of Magianism maintained its hold through the rulers and cruel kings who arose from it. The cross, however, in approximately five hundred [?] years brought all the nations near to its teaching. Its power stopped the fountain of Chaldean astrology and exposed the wickedness of its deceit before the eyes of those watching. It leveled to the ground the city of Zion, which did not receive it, and put an end to prophet, priest, and ruler within her. It demolished the temple among the crucifiers, that wayward people, and raised its own temples in its place throughout every land. It abolished the law with its bodily observances and trained those who were children in understanding through the power of its wisdom. It silenced the mutterings of Magianism, the fabrication of error, and uprooted the altars that error had built for the devil. It cleansed the air of the dark smoke of sacrifices and purified the waters from bathing in the name of demons. It showed the children of darkness the manifest truth and instructed them in the glorious light of its proclamation. He showed the might of his power when he appeared to save our lives, and through his crucifixion he filled creation with the fame of his victory. The cross, which by his judicial sentence had been a curse for humanity, underwent a change and freed humanity from curses. The cross, considered a disgrace by the nations and the Jews, removed disgrace and condemnation from the guilty.

Sin was extinguished and death was undone through the crucified man, and endless life sprang forth for the race of Adam. The heavenly bridegroom opened the heavenly bridal chamber through his cross and brought earthly people up to delight in it. All creation bears the likeness of this standard and points to his standard as though with a finger. All creation carries our Lord’s standard and honors it, and in its structure it bears the mystery and likeness of his glory. This brings shame to the faces of enemies who refuse to be persuaded, and joy to all the children of the holy Church. The whole world, through its forms, bears the victory of the crucified King, who was revealed at the last to save humanity. The world confirms his pattern through its regions, and serves this mystery through its very existence. Like the cross, whose pattern is formed with four sides, the world shows in its own body that it bears his sign. The year stands upon four elements in the likeness of the cross; if it is hindered in one of these, it cannot be completed. Even the luminary whose light illuminates the whole world cannot complete its course without the arrangement of the sign of the cross. Through the ascent and descent of its degrees, in four months [?], it displays the sign of the crucified man. On the twenty-fourth of June, opposite December, these are in the heights and those in the depths, on the two sides. On the twenty-fourth of the month of March, opposite September, the two sides together bear an equal measure. On the twenty-fourth of the four months [?], the sun displays the sign of the cross through its descent and its ascent. East and west, north and south, opposite one another, together bear the complete pattern of the crucifixion. But if one is separated from its companions, an astonishing dissolution overtakes them all, leaving them unable to stand. Look at the bird flying in the air: how it depicts the cross with its body and displays it before the eyes of the foolish. It stretches out its head, extends its feet, and spreads its wings; then the clear air carries it aloft upon its back.

This is the mystery: everyone who acknowledges the sign of Jesus flies and ascends on the day of resurrection to the heights above. Whoever is not baptized and does not mark the cross upon his face remains on the earth, and the door of mercy is shut in his face. Trees too, together with plants of every kind, bear the four-sided sign of the crucified body. Let us therefore approach the books of the Spirit and see his sign, revealed through the righteous from generations past. Abram testifies how he received the promise of the land from God, whose love overflows upon those of his household. Abram [?] received the land as an inheritance through promises that, being established in faith, he would become its owner. He left his land and his ancestral home in Ur of the Chaldeans, and followed the voice that called him toward what had been promised him. The all-knowing one, whose love is true and does not prove false, promised to give him the whole land of the Amorites. Through his revelation he [?] Abram so that he might see the land, commanding him to walk through it as its owner. He therefore instructed him to travel its length and its breadth, so that through this he might reveal the sign by which he would inherit it. He traced a cross through his footsteps as he took possession of it, so that through this he might be shown that by this sign he would inherit the land. See, Jews, how the founder of your lineages traced the great pattern of the sign of the cross in the land he inherited. The land Abram inherited bears the likeness of the heights above—that order of things which is to be revealed through the crucified man. The King on high made heaven a second resting place, and there he wished to bring the ship of the world to rest in a harbor of blessings. Everyone who traces the sign of the cross on his forehead enters that kingdom which will never pass away. The miracle concerning Isaac also resembles this: his birth came from old age and barrenness. He went up as a burnt offering, like a lamb, according to the command; but before he died, the lamb from the tree rescued him. Mortals were condemned by the sentence of the Evil One and death, but the living Lamb set them free through his crucifixion.

The ram suspended in the tree redeemed Isaac, and the living one who was crucified redeemed creation with his blood. The aged Jacob also saw in a revelation a ladder set on the earth, with its top high in heaven. This revelation is a symbol of the crucified man, for through the cross people ascend to the heights above. Jacob gave his blessing as he had learned from the revelation, and displayed the symbol of the crucifixion through Joseph's sons. Joseph placed both his sons before his father: Manasseh on his right and Ephraim on his left. He crossed his arms, one over the other, in the shape of a cross, and through the sign of the cross he raised one of Joseph's sons and lowered the other. Our father Jacob raised Ephraim with his right hand, and with his left he lowered Ephraim's brother, who was the firstborn. See, this symbol was explained through the crucified man, who exalted the despised nations that were baptized in his name. The people who had been the firstborn among the nations in splendor [?] were brought low through the cross and became despised because of their insolence. The aged Jacob marked his blessings with the cross itself, so that everyone might learn that without the cross they are not brought to completion. When he had finished everything he said, he rose from his bed, gave thanks to his Lord, and offered him worship over the top of his staff. This is a clear symbol, which our Lord himself also enacted in his own person, completing and bringing to its end the whole course of his proclamation. He bowed his head over the top of the wood and gave up his spirit, and through the cross he brought to completion the mystery of our human salvation. Come to the staff of Moses, the prophet of the Hebrews, and see how it held the symbol of the crucified man. For when radiant Moses laid it on the ground, its power to act lay fallen and inactive. But when it was raised toward the heights in Moses' hand, all created beings obeyed it, both those capable of speech and those without speech. Whenever it was raised in Moses' hand over the land of Egypt,

it multiplied signs beyond number against the Egyptians. The Creator performed great wonders through the righteous man's staff, which bore the symbol of the wood of his crucifixion. Moses raised the staff in his hands toward the sea and split the sea with it, and the waters stood like a wall. The people walked through the depths of the water in an extraordinary way, and suddenly received complete freedom beyond their expectations. As for the Egyptians who dared to pursue the people, he raised his staff and drowned them in the middle of the sea. So, as soon as the cross was raised on Golgotha, all the demons drowned in the cross as though in the sea. Like the Egyptians, the rebels drowned in the crucified man, and his great power drove them out of the world. The King who is worshiped abolished Judaism and Samaritanism, together with paganism, through his cross, and reigned over all. When there was a great battle against the Amalekites, Moses raised the staff in his hand against Amalek. When the staff in his hand sank down, Amalek grew stronger; whenever it was raised, the people gained the upper hand in victory. The hands of Moses, the chosen one, were, it says, steady in faith, and through the raising of the staff in his hands, his people were victorious. Joshua son of Nun defeated Amalek as a symbol of Jesus, and put them to shame through the strength of his weapon, Moses' staff. Jesus our King, the Son of God, conquered through the cross. Through his crucifixion Satan was defeated and death was abolished. Moses, who was a servant, carried a symbol of the crucifixion, while Jesus, who is the Lord of the symbols, carried the cross. The son of the Hebrews traced these symbols with his staff, and they reached their fulfillment in the crucifixion of the Son of God. With a bitter piece of wood Moses sweetened the water at Marah, and the people drank and were refreshed from their thirst. The cross of Jesus sweetened the nations that had been bitter, and gave them the sweet taste of the Creator's name.

What shall we say about the serpent that Moses raised in the wilderness, which displays the symbol of the revelation of the crucified man? That serpent which was made was of bronze, and through its being raised up it saved the people from venomous snakes. Through the stretching out of the lifeless serpent, the Hebrews lived, and through it they were delivered from the bites of snakes. The serpent bore the great symbol of the crucified man, and through his crucifixion he heals the diseases of those who suffer. He too was raised on Golgotha in the likeness of the serpent, to save humanity from the sickness caused by the demons' venom. Adam's race, which the serpent had bitten among the trees, looked upon the cross and gained immortal life. Look at Elisha, the [?] of the Spirit, and what he accomplished when he raised the Shunammite woman's only son. It is said that the prophet lay down over the boy, extended his legs, and stretched out his hands in the shape of a cross. Elisha rose from the dead boy when his flesh grew warm, and began to trace the cross of Jesus by walking. He walked through the house, once along its length and once across its width, so that by this sign he might deliver the dead boy from the hand of death. The prophet stretched himself over the dead boy again three times. Then the dead boy sneezed, came to life, and stood on his feet. Three times he traced the Trinity upon the boy—a great symbol through which all the dead are raised. The statement that the prophet stretched himself out over the dead boy is a symbol of our Lord, who was to be stretched out upon the wood. Through these symbols the prophet was able to revive the dead boy, to show us that through this mystery the dead rise. Greater than all these, then, is what happened when the iron belonging to the company of prophets fell into the depths of the water. For it is written that the prophet cut a piece of wood and [?] there. It sank, and the iron floated upon the water. See the reversal that was displayed through Elisha, who, through the symbol of his Lord, multiplied miracles among the Hebrews. Like the iron, our nature had sunk into the abyss of death. The cross descended, and our race rose above death.

The Son of God descended with his cross into the sea of Sheol, and the dead rose from the whirlpool of mortality. Through the wood of the cross, mortals who had incurred guilt through the tree gained victory; in place of the guilt that came from the tree, they received life through the cross. Whoever dares to dispute these mysteries should know that his quarrel is not with us. It is against his Lord, who traced his mysteries throughout all generations. The outsider fights against him by opposing his symbols. Let us now speak against the pagans and address the Jews, who in their wickedness join together in mocking our proclamation. Those who are astray supposed that the holy Church worships wood and honors it as God in place of God. Because they themselves worshiped created things instead of the Creator, they rose up unjustly and reviled us over the wood of the cross. These afflicted people go astray through the deception of the devil, and bitterly spew out wickedness against the faithful. The Church does not worship visible matter, but the sign of the crucified King, who conquered through the wood. But if the Church worships wood, as they supposed, why is the cross also made from other materials? From materials of every kind, small and great, and precious ones too, the Church makes the visible image of the hidden King. Through his living sign she gains victory and holds fast to a refuge, and she kisses it with pure, unwavering love. The Church has not gone astray through trees or images, nor through matter and materials that came into being for humanity. When she bows before the living sign wherever it is traced, she worships our Lord, not perishable materials. The wanton people of the Jews worshiped idols, honored images, and reviled the Lord who redeemed them. This is what they said before the calf they made at Horeb, as they worshiped it and honored it as God: “This is your Lord, O Israel,” the wicked said, “and this is the one who redeemed you from slavery in Egypt.” The people honored carved figures and images, as recorded in the Scriptures; and now their wrongdoing stands accused by the books themselves. The heart of the idle people ran wild after demons.

And for this reason they loved idols instead of their own life. All the pagans strayed from the clear and pure path, and worshiped stones, animals, and even trees. They honored them as God with their acts of worship, and served them with lusts full of wickedness. They saw the heavenly lights that the Maker of all created by his power, and went astray and bowed before these silent things as before God. The followers of error descended into this wickedness and did not hold back. They worshiped and served what had been given to human beings. The followers of error descended into this wickedness and did not [?]. They worshiped and served what had been given to human beings. Far be it from the Church to acknowledge these things as unbelievers do! Far be it from her to take on the hateful likeness of the followers of error! She gloriously praises the [?] of our Lord, through which she was betrothed, and honors it as the seal of the King of kings. Whatever belongs to the king is honored above everything because of the king; even if it is something lowly, it receives honor because of the king. Although the wood of the cross is lowly by nature, because of its purpose it is greatly honored on account of Jesus. The cross of Jesus is a seal upon our faith, for through it his saving work on our behalf was completed. Even a denarius bearing the image of an earthly king is received by the people of his dominion as they would receive the king. Because of the king's imprint, it is honored above everything, and whoever rejects it rejects the king to whom it belongs. In the same way, the venerated sign of the cross bears in its appearance the great image of Christ the King. People kiss the king's [?] and the figures in his writings, and honor it as they would the king. Lowly clay, and paper too, are insignificant things, lowly by nature and considered of no account by those who understand. For when the king writes his words on paper, everyone honors it like [?] and refined gold. Lowly clay, a loose clod from the earth, gains glory when earthly kings stamp it with their seal. When the king's decree is sent out with the imprint of his own hands, everyone stands and kisses it as they would the king. By the seal bearing his name, the king confirms the promise of his words.

And nothing is sent out by him without his seal. How much more reliable, then, is the seal of Jesus our King, who sealed his words with the great seal of his cross! He walked on earth and completed all his saving work, and through his crucifixion demonstrated the truth of what his words had promised. But if the seals of temporal kings are honored on earth, how much more should we honor the cross, the seal of the King on high! If the nations kiss and bow before the seals of kings, it is all the more fitting that everyone should honor the cross. Kiss and bow down before the sign of Jesus for Jesus’ sake, so that through it you may be freed from the harm caused by the devil. The cross is our Lord’s seal; it has won the victory. Through it death fell, and error vanished from the inhabited world. The King who is worshiped established this sign in his church, so that people might approach it as they would the image of the King of kings. Through it the uncircumcised nations are sanctified and circumcised, and they become a people belonging to the great King who reigns over all. All who wish to be baptized are marked with it, and without his sign they are not called the church of Jesus. The priesthood too is marked with it to celebrate the mysteries, and in its name it completes the rites and mysteries in the holy church. All the sanctuaries, together with the fortresses, are marked with it, and when they have been sanctified by this sign, the Spirit dwells in them. The priest impresses the seal of Jesus upon the holy sanctuary, so that it may become a harbor full of life for the human race. Through this cross the mysteries of the church are also sanctified, and in its name they become a pledge of immortal life. The cross accomplishes all these things in the holy sanctuary, and through it he forgives and sanctifies human beings. Through it the truth of Jesus is revealed to those on earth, and through the image of his sign they receive blessings that never perish. Through it unclean demons are driven from their dwellings, and from its rays they flee and hide like bats. Through this sign the assault and power of demons are brought to an end, and through it all illnesses and injuries are healed. The righteous took up this weapon and became mighty through it.

They overthrew the evil one and pierced him with the spear of the sign of the cross. They became warriors and took up the lance, the cross of Jesus, and Satan and his angels were defeated before them. This is the great banner in every land, and it made the glorious martyrs victorious in their contests. This is what made the beauty of its light shine throughout the whole world and gathered human beings to see its glory. Like the ark, it is with us at the head of our camp, and it guides the ship of the church to a peaceful harbor. Before the ark cities trembled and fortified towns fell, and all the kings of the Amorites were defeated and brought low. But when the cross of Jesus began to reign over creation, the foundations of the fortress of Sheol trembled, and it fell to the ground. Through it the dead rose and the fainthearted were sustained, and by its appearance it gave hope to those without hope. It brought low the strength and might of the demons who kill human beings, and made them weak and contemptible before those who venerate it. It showed its glory to [?] and to those on earth: its sign in the heights, and the image of his crucifixion on earth. Constantine saw the cross above in heaven, shining like the sun with great glory. Inscriptions were also written in order on its arms: “By this sign you have conquered, King Constantine.” He carried this sign and went out at the head of his army, and the enemies who fought against him fell at the sight of it. The king and his armies raised a shout of praise to him who, through his cross, put an end to wars in every region. The king’s mother searched for the revered wood, and it was revealed to her by the fragrance that rose from within the earth. The sweet fragrance of fine spices wafted from the earth, and the people and the nations gathered there saw its glory. For this reason Helena, the king’s mother, also built [?] splendid sanctuaries in its honor and celebrated its festivals. From the day when the revered wood had been hidden, people walked as though in darkness, until it shone forth.

Now that it has shone forth, it has spread its light in the four directions and gladdened with its beauty those at peace and [?]. O wood, while you were hidden in the earth by wicked people, the divine command displayed you above in heaven, in the realm of light! Who would not marvel at the mighty deeds our Lord performed? He came in his love and brought peace to the world through his crucifixion. In the temple of his body he shone upon the cross on Golgotha and illuminated the world with the splendid light of his glory. His rays flew like the sun’s in the four directions, and the darkness of idolatry vanished from creation. At his dawning, heaven and earth and everything in them rejoiced, and through his heralds he filled them with the riches of his glory. This is the shepherd who endured the cross for his flock. Believe in his name and bow before his sign without doubt. Come, mortals, take refuge in this king, and continually trace his cross upon your bodies. Carry out your deeds and conduct yourselves in his name, and do not approach to taste anything without his cross. With a pure heart, believe in and acknowledge his living sign, and it will guard you from transgressions, hidden and open. His cross inspires awe in those above and those below, and whenever all the demons see it, they tremble before it. The holy Church celebrates this sign with praise, honors it, and receives grace and mercy from it. All the righteous glory in it and take refuge in it, for it has freed them from slavery to mortality. See, they bow before it and honor it with songs, and the assemblies of the Watchers and human beings praise it. Come, together with the spiritual beings, let us offer one thanksgiving to him who exalted our race through his cross. To him be praise!
On the Bronze Serpent
By the very same author. Discourse thirty-nine: On the Bronze Serpent. Also suitable for the Finding.

The Lord established a covenant of love with Abraham and promised him that he would deliver his descendants from slavery. His offspring was destined to be enslaved in the land of Canaan, and he showed him beforehand that he would free it by the power of his greatness. He showed the power of his greatness to the Egyptians in Egypt.

Despite their unwillingness, he fulfilled his purpose toward Abraham. With power and wealth he brought them out of Egypt, and settled them without fear in the dreadful wilderness. He made those who hated peace dwell in a desolate place, so that through the wilderness he might bring peace to the desolation of their minds. For the sake of peace, he made them dwell in the wilderness outside, so that they might perhaps turn away from involvement in shameful things. He saw that in peaceful surroundings they did not turn away from hateful deeds, and he drove them to a place far removed from human society. By a change of place he hoped they would change their deeds—not that their [?] concerning wilderness and peace had escaped him. Evil habit had accustomed them to unbecoming things, and they did not follow the beautiful example he showed them. He longed to delight their minds with good things, and gave them abundant life and mighty deeds, so that they might perhaps change. He fed them with manna and quails without their having to toil, and made drinking water flow from the flint rock and refreshed them. He stretched a cloud of dew like a tent over their heads, and set up a pillar shining with light like a lampstand. Light shone in their dwelling place night and day, and with the visible light was the light of truth. Those who hated their own souls enjoyed both lights. Although they were greatly honored, they were not [?] as befitted their honor. The visible light was beautiful to the eyes of the body, and truth was still more beautiful to the eyes of the soul. Body and soul gazed upon the two lights, yet although they saw, they did not truly see. They lived in great peace there where they had settled, and there was no wilderness whose desolation was as harsh as that of their minds. By its peacefulness the wilderness rebuked the sin within them: it had become peaceful, but they did not call their evil deeds to account. It too had been evil before the people dwelt within it, but through the people he made peace reign over its evil. Its peace was desirable, and people longed for its peace. There was no one to disturb or impair its tranquility. The venom of the crawling creatures that lived in it had lost its strength. Although it caused harm, it did not harm as much as its harmful nature allowed. Abraham’s offspring was bitter there, though suffering no harm, and did not recognize who was protecting it from harm. The wrongdoers did a great wrong to the grace among them, and when the wilderness saw this, it returned to its former habit. Evil habit compelled it to resemble what it had been, and its unworthiness drove away its peace, so that it would have no peace. The sound of blasphemy awakened the unrest that dwelt within it, and hateful grumbling opened its mouth to bite. The bitterness of leeks pierced the vessel holding the crawling creatures’ venom, and the crawling creatures rushed to subjugate rational beings. Sin opened the gate of command before the silent creatures and emboldened them to rise against those who speak. “The people sinned,” it is written in the book of the great Moses, “and the Lord stirred up the snakes to bite them.” Scripture attributed the mute creature’s bite to God, to make those being punished know the power of his dominion. His power gave wisdom to the snakes, which have no understanding.

He quieted them and roused them as he pleased. He pleased to place the seal of silence on their mouths, and again he pleased to release them to bite. This thing that I said pleased him was not pleasing to him; the people’s wickedness compelled him to change. That commanding will, which is altogether beautiful, saw the people’s ugliness, and it did not please him to look upon their ugliness. He saw the festering sore of wickedness in the camp where he dwelt, and at a word he gave it as food to lowly crawling creatures. Contrary to its nature, the silent creature cried out to rational humanity: “Look at me—not at me, but at the power that bound me and released me. “The power that guided me restrained me from harming your understanding; and when you did not recognize it, it released me to strike at your ignorance.” The crawling creatures put on the armor of wrath against those endowed with understanding, and began shooting the arrows of their venom into the people’s ranks. The bold creatures drew their tongues like swords, and mercilessly thrust them in as destroyers of life. They waged a fierce war against body and mind: they killed the one and drove the other from its dwelling. The silent creatures exacted retribution for wickedness from those who speak, and silenced their blasphemy against the Creator. The Creator himself taught the creatures without understanding to exact vengeance from those with understanding for the insults against him. The creatures without understanding showed great discernment, discerning much; and [?] those endowed with speech do not discern as they did. Through their discernment he taught wisdom to the senseless people, and through their venom he cleansed the bitterness of their thoughts. Their hearts were full of the evil gall of idolatry, and the Good One tempered it with venom worse than their own gall. His power wisely tempered gall with gall, and the snakes’ venom overcame human bitterness. He displayed great order through something that has no order, and through its confusion he set in order what the human inclination had thrown into confusion. His command placed the scourge of wrath in the mouths of the silent creatures, and with a mouth instead of a hand he scourged those being punished. He stretched out the hard-hearted people for severe beatings, and made venomous creatures, which are cut off from him, their scourgers. He handed them over to merciless executioners, so that through their cruelty he might soften the hearts of those hardened in wickedness. Like avengers they went around inside the camp, searching out wickedness wherever it was hidden. Like guilty people, the evildoers hid themselves, for they knew that the crawling creatures were exacting payment for their debts. The debtors were condemned and could not stand before their creditors. They raised their fingers to the master of the debt: “Have mercy; do not destroy us.” The merciful one had compassion, not because of persuasion but because of love. He called his servant and taught him to provide a remedy for his people. “Make a serpent,” the Lord said to Moses his servant, “and set it up as a sign and a reminder, to heal the people. Fashion bronze in the shape of serpents, so that it resembles a living serpent in every respect.

Make a dead serpent in a form resembling the real thing, so that by its lifelessness it may silence the venom of serpents.” The humble man obeyed the command spoken to him. He believed, assented, prepared, and made a forged serpent. The man endowed with speech forged the likeness of mindless reptiles. He raised it and hung it within the camp of the people's tribes. He hung the fashioned image in the midst of the people, so that those who were bitten would look at it and inquire into its purpose. By holy ordinances he placed the life-giving remedy in their midst. He turned everyone's gaze toward it, so that they would contemplate it. Like a mirror, he fastened it to a wooden pole before their eyes, so that its appearance would be visible to both body and mind. Moses showed his people a new sight, and through that sight he showed them how to be healed. “Look and be healed!” This was proclaimed aloud. They were astonished and amazed that a sight could [?]. At first they stood in doubt as they looked, until they learned through experience and then believed. Through experience they gained understanding and became wise. They believed that the speechless thing could restrain the venom of reptiles. Through trials they learned what the forged serpent could do. They trampled serpents confidently through the power that came from it. They saw that looking at it brought the assault of their afflictions to a halt. They despised and mocked the weapons that had bitten their [?]. The bitter bites became as nothing, because the sight of the serpent neutralized the venom in them. Whenever a living serpent bit a living person, he looked at the dead one, and its venom withdrew from his limbs. When the venomous snakes raged venomously, the still, lifeless image stilled them. They grew weary and weak from [?] the venom within them. Although it was bitter, its bitter taste was not perceived. However much they multiplied and bit bitterly, the venom seemed like no venom at all to the body's senses. As long as a person's eye was fixed on the dead one, the venom of the living ones seemed not even to exist. The eye remained constantly fixed on its appearance and never tired of contemplating its silence. O silent one, whose silence astonished those endowed with speech and drew their gaze toward the power hidden in its appearance! O lifeless one, entirely devoid of life, who brought people to life out of the death caused by the venom of reptiles! O voiceless and senseless one who raised a voice, who rebuked the deaf and quieted them from their struggle! O one who does not see those who see him, or whom they resemble, yet became an image that drives away people’s sufferings and pains! O one who did not discern the mighty greatness expressed through him, yet restrained the venom of undiscerning serpents! O one who does not even know that he is what he is, yet taught people to contemplate the Creator’s power! Ah, you serpent! No, you are no serpent, for you are not even a serpent, yet you were able to become a source of life to whoever looked at you. Was it your appearance that neutralized the venom of crawling creatures?

Or was it perhaps another, unseen appearance? Was it from you that mercy flowed to the people, or perhaps from the one who created the people and everything? Did the healing that came from you happen by chance, or is a mystery of the true Physician perhaps hidden in you? How is it that, although you are silent, you are more formidable than living beings? By what power do you overcome the living and bring the dead to life? The inquiry about you is full of questions, unfeeling serpent, and a great [?] is hidden in the help that flows from you. The inquiry about you called me to investigate the questions concerning you, and it urged me to travel in words along the path of your story. Your story pressed me to recount your story before listeners, and now I dare to reveal the power hidden in your silence. Come, listeners, investigate with me the cause that I have sought to know, so that, through what we know, we may learn how to investigate hidden things properly. Let us investigate why the hammered serpent was fashioned, and, once it was fashioned, how and through whom it did what it did. By what power did it overcome the serpents through its appearance and blunt the force of the deadly venom they were injecting? How could a dead image without life drive sufferings away from perishable limbs? How, moreover, did it restrict its healing to the eyes alone, while the other senses did not benefit from its help? Why was the mercy coming from it distributed through looking, rather than its body itself being brought near the wounds?
