If the power that overcame the serpents belonged to it, why were those who had been bitten not brought near it? If it had no power to give people life, why [?]—entirely, entirely, wholly a dead image without life? What use was an unfeeling thing to those endowed with feeling? What benefit did silent bronze bring to those endowed with speech? If the nature of silent things could accomplish this, why did the sacred vessels in the sanctuary not accomplish it? The books were beautiful, and the ark was glorious too. Why did healing not come through seeing them? The deed of the forged serpent involves one of two things: either it is something, or [?] something is hidden in its appearance. There is some cause behind its role and its healing, and it seems greater than all the causes found in the Law. The books could not accomplish what the sight of it accomplished, nor could sacrifices, burnt offerings, and the blood of calves. You saw the deed accomplished through the unfeeling object; it was higher and more exalted even than Moses, who fashioned and made it. How could it not be greater than Moses and his book, since it accomplished something that neither Moses nor his law accomplished? Those who had been bitten looked to Moses and his book, but they received no help against the bites of the snakes. The appearance of Moses, greater than all, was awe-inspiring; yet to the snakes he was more contemptible and despised than anything. Even if the whole of Moses had been laid upon the bites, he would [not] have healed them unless a person looked at the serpent. The sight of the mute object carried far more weight with the vipers than Moses and the divine law.

It is therefore good to investigate what its purpose was, whom it concerned, and why it became great and was honored above Moses. I have marveled greatly at its lofty rank, and I marvel still: how did it dispense life-giving healing when it was itself dead? Its very deadness compelled me to speak about it, and here I stand like a woman giving birth, in labor with its story. Like an infant, its story pressed upon the womb of my mind, seeking to come out and proclaim the power of the revelation hidden within it. A revelation of divine power is disclosed in it: that power was destined to accomplish something new on earth, just as it had accomplished something through it. Through it he symbolically opened a road before the events themselves, so that people might easily travel toward their life. Human life is hidden in the sight of it and in its healing, and a likeness at hand of something hidden, destined to [?]. Healing flowed spiritually from its stillness, and perhaps this is how it happens for people through a human being. God was destined to [?] among human beings, and not [?], to give life to human beings. He accomplished this beforehand through the serpent that healed people. He depicted the mystery of the one who was coming in the appearance of the silent object, so that when he came, his appearance would not seem strange to people. For people were destined to marvel at the novelty of his power, and he empowered the serpent so that they would not doubt the one who was coming. By the sight of it alone he gave healing to those who were stricken, so that no one should demand in faith a sight of [?]. The Hebrews too were healed through faith, not through a medicine that could be seen and handled. Through that same faith he was destined to give life to people among humanity, and through faith he established a [?] of faith in him. It was appointed for him to undo death through human death, and he taught people to ask for life from something wholly dead. On the summit of Golgotha they were destined to hang him upon a wooden cross, and he taught Moses to hang up his symbol in the midst of the people. When the wickedness of the nations increased, he became a blow against it; and in that same likeness he revealed the likeness through the occasion of wickedness. Because of wickedness, vipers rushed upon the Hebrews; and for [?] wickedness, he armed the serpent against suffering. Through something incapable of suffering, he freed those who suffer from their sufferings, so that no one might object when he saved through one capable of suffering. Through a dead thing that had no claim to life, he gave life to the people, so that when he raised the dead through a dead man, no one would question how. He rebuked the one who judges beforehand through the deed he performed, so that, if he judges, he might judge what happened then, and this likewise. He exposed the doubter beforehand through the healing brought by the serpent: if something silent gave healing, how much more one who speaks! He rebuked the contentious one [?] through the sight that drove away pains: if this happened through bronze, how much more through a human being! Why, man, do you marvel at the salvation of human beings? Look, through bronze a wonder like this took place. Why, circumcised man, do you not accept the revelation of your mysteries? Look, what happened among the uncircumcised nations is depicted in you. Are you certain about the serpent, which healed you freely, yet unwilling to accept that a man gave life to human beings? Did the sight of something mute save you from the mouths of mute creatures, yet you do not acknowledge the salvation brought through one who speaks?

And if not, explain and tell me the reason for the serpent: what it is, whom it concerns, and why you were healed through it. If you are certain that it healed your pains as it did, why do you doubt a healing greater than that? The salvation brought through a human being is far greater than that brought through a serpent, just as the greatness of a human being surpasses that of animals. Be silent, then, Israelite blinded by envy, and do not deny the plain [?] with your falsehood. Be still, you too, heretic, servant of two! Do not confuse the course of our discourse with your contentiousness. To me, the measure of your contentiousness is the same as the Jew's. That is why I have joined the name of your wickedness with that of someone like you. The confession of your faith and the Jew's is one, for you have defiled the mystery of the incarnation just as he has. He does not accept the salvation of human beings that came through a human being, nor do you acknowledge that the Self-existent One saved humanity through a human being. Humanity has been saved through a human being, you quarrelsome people! Moses bears witness: he raised the serpent as a symbol of your salvation. “Just as Moses raised the serpent in the wilderness,” he says, “so also must [the man,] the Son of Man be lifted up.” The very same command that healed the people's pains through the serpent also gave life to human beings through a human being. The same will that exalted something mute through its help also exalted a speaking human being above all. As a symbol of the exaltation of the one who speaks, the silent thing was made great; through his authority it acquired authority to drive away pains. Both its making and its raising were appointed for this: to open a path for the exaltation of humanity through a human being. The Creator's power exalted humanity through a serpent and a human being, and healed its sickness through something mute and someone who speaks. Through the serpent he healed the visible pains in the limbs, and through a human being he healed both visible pains and those concealed and hidden. Life-giving healing was distributed through the gaze of the eyes, and salvation for humanity through faith in the mind. The power in the silent thing was less than that in the one who speaks, since it could not wipe away sins and stains. It could cleanse only bodily defects; the guilt of sins was difficult for it to forgive. The unfeeling physician healed half the human being. It was not its task to perfect the human being, because it was not human. A man was destined to perfect humanity through the Creator’s power, and he first sketched a portrayal of his perfection through something inferior to him. He sent the serpent as a forerunner before his coming, so that through something that inflicts harm he might heal the pains of those who had been bitten. He accomplished this through a serpent and a man to put the demons to shame, so that through the very thing by which they had afflicted humanity he might give humanity life. Through a serpent the leader of their ranks deceived the head of humanity, and through a serpent he healed the pains caused by serpents. He was pursuing them through the mystery of the healing that came from the silent thing, to let them know that the time when they would be exposed had drawn near. Perhaps they were distressed when the serpent drove away diseases, just as they howled when Christ drove out Legion. Perhaps they lamented when they saw the healing worked by the mute thing, as at that time when [?] they were being scorched before Jesus.

Perhaps they pondered in the hateful meditation of their minds: “What is this new thing that has happened among mortals? How did it happen that the serpent, through which death entered, turned around and gave life to mortal humanity through the sight of its face?” They put on mourning over the serpent and over our Lord, at how they healed diseases and sins without medicines. They mourned especially over our Lord, because body and soul were being healed through the [?] of his mouth. They were amazed and astonished at him and at the serpent, at how closely the symbol resembled the reality through its deeds. And if the demons were amazed and astonished at the reality and the symbol, let the Jewish heretic remain outside the gate. Let the worthless stand outside the gate of faith, since they do not wish to enter with us into the confession of the truth. Let the symbol, together with the reality, scorn the arrogant and shut the gate of its truth in their faces. Let the serpent in its silence dispute their words, because they do not allow the man who is one of us to be exalted. Was the lifeless serpent exalted and honored? Why, then, do you bar the second Adam from exaltation? Did bronze fashioned by human beings heal humanity? Why, then, does the man fashioned by the Spirit’s power not heal? Then grant him the power to help, as you do the mute thing, and let him stand in the rank he has attained alongside the divine Being. His rank is higher than that of the [?], you quarrelsome people, and whoever diminishes the loftiness of his rank will suffer double punishment. Because of its rank, the weak, forged serpent became great; without that, it would not even have been counted as anything that exists [?]. It would have been nothing if something had not been hidden in it, and its healing would not have been believed without something. The something I spoke of is Christ, the reality above all; compared with him, everything is considered nothing. Paul testifies that it was a shadow of something [?]. He says that the Law possessed only a shadow, not the reality expressed in bodily acts. The substance is Christ, who is real and complete in body and soul; his shadow is the serpent that served as a symbol of his salvation. The mute creature served among the Hebrews as a symbol of his salvation, and its silence cried out like a herald about his coming. To those with discernment, the speech of its silence was clear, for it conversed with its hearers without a sound. Instead of ears, eyes listened to its proclamation. O herald without understanding or speech, who made the new tidings of humanity’s renewal heard on earth! O messenger, crippled in speech and movement, who swiftly overtook those endowed with speech! O creature through which the Creator’s power spoke, though it did not speak! People listened to it, though they had never heard its voice. O unattractive serpent, how beautiful is your story! Though you are ugly, through you people were made beautiful, freed from ugly things. O ugly creature that made humanity ugly from the beginning, you turned back and restored the beauty you had disfigured in the land of Eden. You are ugly, serpent, and all the more so because you are made of bronze.

The good that comes from you is not yours, but belongs to the Good One. In his love, the Good One made you a vision of beautiful things, so that through you he might rebuke the hateful one who made people ugly through your agency. So when someone praises you, it is not you that he praises, but the [?] who reveals his power even through weak things. The Creator’s power gave life to the people through a mute symbol; he also gave life to the dead nations through the living reality. Let us truly acknowledge that his power accomplished both this and that. The former things and the latter things belong to him. Blessed is he who, through his cross, opened for us a road to the kingdom on high, and through it saved us from slavery to the Evil One and to death.
On the Incarnation of Our Lord Christ

For the Dedication of the Church. Another by the very same author. Discourse Forty. Composed by him on the incarnation of our Lord Christ, and suitable for the Dedication of the Church. Response. Church of the nations, worship your betrothed, who planted you on earth and enrolled you in heaven. My brothers.

The Church is full of discernment, possessing treasures and wisdom. The teaching that flows from her [?] to the four quarters. The nations, divided in language and far from harmony, she yoked together under one yoke, which teaches love to those who bear it. The great mystery that was hidden from ages and generations—its reality was explained and made known to those above and those below. The Son, who [?] with his Begetter, hidden and concealed like him—the Church first [?] learned of him that he who is born of the Father is eternally existent. The Spirit, who is from the Father and is not inferior to him in being, distributed his wealth within the Church, and she received it like a [?]. In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit—three holy names—I received power and authority, and learned that their being is one. Israel proclaimed one God, as [?]. And the Church learned the explanation, so that she might confess three persons. The Son was hidden with his Begetter from those above and those below. Through mysteries and wonders, the prophets wrote down indications of him. But when the time reached its fulfillment, as [?] in his knowledge, God sent his Son to come and renew our created being. He set out from where he was and came to where he was. He set out from the Father without moving, and his will came into the world. For in his nature he cannot move from one place to another. Times and ages are within him, and created things do not contain him. He came wholly by his will, and remained wholly in his nature. For his nature is everywhere, while his will goes and comes. He came to the dwelling of mortals to renew our image, which had worn out. From our lowly nature itself he made himself a temple and dwelt in it. Without seed, the Spirit formed it within a womb, without sexual union. So that through him he might renew created things and reconcile those above, he sent a messenger of peace to announce his conception on earth. Through the gate by which death had entered, life entered, and death departed. “Peace to you, full of grace,” the angel said to Mary. “My Lord is with you, daughter of mortals, for from you the Savior will dawn.” Here is the point over which the contentious heretics stumbled. They made it into an arena

for the combat of their questions. They say, “The Word himself changed and became flesh, as it is written. He did not take a body from Mary; rather, his own person became flesh.” But if the Word changed, then he became composite. And if he became composite, his formation had a beginning. And if he began through being formed, he is like everyone else in being created. He is then the Maker in name, while far removed from the deeds. May this blasphemy recoil upon the heads of the heretics, who tore the garment of the confession of the apostles’ faith. [?] You who are hard to persuade and blind to understanding! Why this dispute, and about whom is this quarrel? What will you gain from this, by making the Being who does not suffer subject to suffering, and calling him who is equal to his Father a creature of flesh? Listener, do not be confused or fall into doubt because of what you have heard. Come, draw near to conviction; listen and learn correctly. The Word himself did not change and become flesh in his own person. Rather, the Word put on flesh to free mortals through it. The Word himself did not become flesh; rather, he assumed a human being, who was complete in every respect, in body and soul alike. It was a human being who experienced conception, birth, and growth, hunger, thirst, suffering, and death that lasted for a time. But sin had no power over him, and Paul bore witness to this. For he was a dwelling of the Godhead, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Nor, again, should the listener suppose, because I called him a human being— That I speak of two sons, as the wrongdoers have invented. There is one Son, the Son of the divine essence, who is equal to the one who begot him. He was hidden in his Father’s bosom until the time of his coming. Because of his love for us, he took a complete human being and made him one with himself in lordship and authority. From the day when the Spirit formed him within the womb without sexual union, he was Lord, heir, and ruler, equally in the heights and in the depths. Mortals could not gaze upon him in his own nature. Therefore he took a human being, to conceal his radiance in humanity. In this he exalted us: he clothed himself in our lowly nature and raised it with himself to heaven, to the honor at his right hand. He had called our nature his image in the beginning, when he fashioned it. But this image was corrupted through the devil’s counsel. Now, in his mercy, he wished to renew our image, which had worn out. He took the firstfruits from us and raised them to himself in glory. This is our entire confession, which we learned from the books of the Spirit: God does not change and is not subject to suffering. The sufferings belong to the human being, that one of our race who can suffer, who was given a share in glorious things because of the love of the one who assumed him. Conception and birth belong to the human being; circumcision [?] and sacrifices belong to the human being. Hunger [?] and thirst belong to the human being; weariness and sleep belong to the human being. Prayer and suffering are his own, apart from God the Word. The child Jesus grew in stature and in discerning wisdom, and increased in favor

with God and humanity. To whom, then, do all these distinctions belong? To the Creator, who cannot be brought low, or to the human being who is of our race? No, contentious people, do not be mistaken! This growth belongs to the one of our race, who came to perfection in union with the Word. It was not that his authority was deficient from the day of his birth, but that it was fitting for his exaltation to accompany his growth. Let us speak of his temptation and his struggle with Satan. It says that at the end of forty days he became hungry and was tempted. Come, interpret this [?] for us, you new scribes who have challenged us. Explain its meanings to us: whose are the hunger and the temptation? Here they took refuge in silence and raised a finger to acknowledge the truth, for the plain meaning of the reading itself exposes the wickedness of their words. For the evil one would not have dared to bring temptation against the one who knows everything, whom he knew could not be tempted. Rather, he brought temptation against the one who had bodily limbs, whom he saw longing for food at the end of his fast. And, as with that first Adam, he was eager to tempt him through food, because he saw him clothed in Adam’s nature. He thought that he would accept his word. In all these things, it was the one of our race who was tempted, not the Creator. For the Creator’s nature is above sufferings and temptation. He grew weary from the exertion of the journey, and sat down and rested from his labor. He asked the Samaritan woman for water to relieve the suffering of his thirst. Here the weariness belongs to the human being, and the hunger and thirst are his own. While the Word dwelt in him, he himself was being tested. Using water as the occasion, he turned the woman who had gone astray toward his teaching. Through the knowledge of his divinity, he brought her deeds to light. But he said to his disciples, when they brought him food: “I have other food that you do not know about.” And this food was to do his Father’s will, to show how greatly he longed for sinners to repent. He slept in the boat, and they woke him. He arose, rebuked the sea, and calmed it. Sleep belongs to a mortal, but calming the sea belongs to the Creator. He said, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and I am glad that I was not there.” In his humanity he was not there; in his divinity he was there. As he went to awaken him, he shed tears of sorrow. The man of dust [?] grieved over the man of dust who shared his nature. Whose tears [?] are these, you foolish people who have strayed from the way, if not those of the one clothed in bodily limbs, who was covered in every respect? He was stirred in spirit, it says, and called aloud to Lazarus: “Come out, dead man, and see for yourself the dwelling of life that you have cast off.” Here it is the Creator’s voice that called Lazarus, and he came to life. As he raises sleepers [?] from sleep, he raises the dead from the dust. He openly spoke these lowly things about himself when he said to his disciples, “I am going to my Father and my God.” Let the writers of fabrications tell us: Does God have a God, and does the hidden Being [?], through whose [?] everything came into being, have a maker?

He called God his God because he is his Maker and the Maker of everything. And he called the Exalted One [?] his Father because he had been made worthy of this by grace. “Now, behold,” he said, “my soul is troubled by the sufferings I endure, and I am sorrowful to the point of death because of the harshness of the cross.” Whose soul is troubled, you [?] without understanding? Is it that of the eternal Word who is from the Father, who is equal [?] to the one who begot him? Do not be mistaken, you insolent people! The eternal Being is above suffering. These are the sufferings of the man, that suffering one who shares our nature. These things belong to the man who became a son by grace, not to the united Word, who has been with his Father from eternity. But I did not say that the Word acquired sonship by grace, lest Arius boast that perhaps I am aiming at his purpose. “My Father who sent me,” he said, “is greater than I in being and authority.” It was not fitting [?] for the creature to be compared with his Creator. He is greater than him in being, because his nature has no beginning. Anyone who has a beginning is lesser in his constitution than the eternal Being. We therefore have a high priest who is faithful to his Maker, like Moses in all his house, and greater than that son of Amram. Who is this high priest, and whom do you call his Maker, to whom he is faithful over his house and who rules over the work of his hands? Jesus is the high priest, and his Maker is the hidden eternal Being. Because he became a dwelling for the Creator, he made him lord over his possessions. “There is one mediator [?],” it says, “between God and human beings: the man Jesus,” who was exalted and became king and ruler. Here he calls the one who was descended from David the mediator. Through his death he became the mediator and reconciled us with the Creator. He tasted death in his own nature, apart from God the Word. While the Word dwelt in him, suffering did not touch his nature. Suffering and death belong to the one capable of suffering, who has death in his nature. Resurrection and life belong to the Creator, who has life in his nature. Everyone who came into being is alive in him, and he gives life and light. He is a spring full of life, whose flow never ceases. For he does not diminish in his nature, nor does he grow beyond what he is. He does not fall under sufferings, for his nature is above sufferings. The sufferings belong to the one who shares our humanity, who was made low, grew great, and was exalted. He was made low when he tasted death for a time, and grew great when he came into lordship. But let the listener not think, because I have distinguished the lowly things in this way, that I am speaking of two persons: the Word and the temple he chose for himself. I confess one Son, and I proclaim two natures: the worshiped and glorious nature of the eternally existing Word who is with the Father, and our nature, which he took as he had promised and pledged. He is perfect in his divinity, equal to the one who begot him, and also complete in his humanity, with the body and soul of mortals. Two that came into unity, with one love and one will: the united Word from the Father and the [?] of a servant that he assumed.

Because of the love of the one who assumed him, the one assumed shares his honor. He humbled himself in the names given to him, though he did not diminish in his nature. The one made of dust became, by grace, an heir [?] with the Word, who honored him in everything in his nature and subjected the heights and depths to him. The Word took on the lowly attributes of the one made of dust through a borrowed name. The mortal one, too, was honored with the glories of the Only Begotten. He was not honored with these glories for [?] a time, but from now and forever, for his dominion has no end. Once he offered himself to God as a sacrifice. He became a high priest in heaven, and his priesthood does not come to an end. He entered the heavenly Holy of Holies to make atonement for everyone, and the whole mortal race found salvation through him. He did not enter with the blood of animals, according to the order of the high priests. Rather, his own self became the sacrifice, and he poured out his blood for everyone. To him he said, “Sit at my right hand,” until everything is subjected to him. He reigns over everything that came into being, together with God who assumed him. His also is the coming that is to take place at the end. With the sign on which he suffered on earth, he is glorified when he comes. At the sound of his word, the dead [?], from Adam onward, are raised. Those who loved his appearing fly in the clouds to meet him. With the breath of his mouth he destroys the one who comes to deceive in his name. With the rebuke of his word he brings the devil’s dominion to an end. He is escorted in glory by a thousand watchers and by myriads of angels. Countless seraphim proclaim the holiness of his majesty. Heavenly and earthly beings see his body openly revealed, while his divinity is hidden behind the doorway of his humanity. Mortals look upon him openly, face to face. Like an image, through his visible appearance he draws everyone toward the hidden one. He does not do these things apart from the one who assumed him when he comes. He is with him without change, from beginning to end. There is one Son and one person: two kinds that became one. United are the Word who is from the Father and the form of a servant that he assumed. Because the two natures [?] became one in union, the listener must not therefore suppose that he became a mixture in his nature. The divine being is not mixed, nor is the Creator changed. His nature is hidden and concealed, and beyond all changes. Nor did change approach his holy dwelling, the form of a servant that he assumed, for its nature is preserved with the Word. In thought, however, the glorious deeds are distinguished from the deaths. They are attributed to the one Son, whose two natures became one. The human weaknesses belong to the one who was born of Mary. The glorious deeds [?] belong to the Word, the eternal offspring of the Father. He willed, because of his love, that our race should be honored through him. Here what we call his image reached its fulfillment. Not in the image of his nature, but in the image of his honor. For he has no composition, nor any shape or likeness. The Creator is without composition and cannot be bounded by sight. The prophets gave him names suited to human understanding.

Although he neither becomes smaller nor grows greater, they said that he became smaller and also grew greater. Although by his nature he is everywhere, they said that he descended and also ascended. But the fools who heard these things did not understand [?] them correctly. They attributed these weaknesses to the Creator as belonging to his nature. And the presumption through which they strayed from what was right was not enough for them. Instead, they devised schemes and armed themselves against the truth. Come, then, listener: become a disciple of Scripture. Walk in the way of righteousness, and do not stray onto the path of falsehood. Believe in the Father without beginning, the self-existent one who precedes all created beings. His being cannot be bounded by the thought of created things. Confess the Son [?] who is from the Father, begotten from him without suffering. He is Lord, self-existent, and Creator, equal to him in his nature. Glorify the person of the Spirit, who is of that same nature. He is not inferior to the Father and the Son in lordship or authority. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit share equally in one nature. Three holy [?] persons, one being without beginning. The prophets proclaimed this nature through mysteries and wonders. The distinction of the persons was kept to be revealed through the Son. And when the time came for the manifestation of the one who had been hidden through the ages, he revealed this distinction to us, so that we might confess three persons. Here is the true confession, without the weariness of lengthy explanations. It does not carry a burden of words that would confuse the listener. The Son’s descent to us was not a journey or a change of place, but an act of love and will, while he was not diminished from what he is. For I said in what I recounted that the Creator is not diminished. Nor does he [?], nor does he come, for by his nature he is everywhere. It is the bodily one who became lowly and was exalted through the suffering and death of the cross, and was honored afterward in the resurrection and ascension. He became the true dwelling of the Godhead, without separation, and was honored together with the divine being in lordship and authority. “The Father,” he says, “judges no one,” for he has entrusted all judgment to him, to examine those above and those below in his judicial sentence. He is the one who rewards the diligent for their labors, and by him the wicked are condemned to scourging and Gehenna. For this reason he chose him out of all and made him a temple for his glory, so that mortals might look upon him as he examines their deeds. Because his glorious nature cannot be subjected to sight, he comforted us through the visible one, as though we were seeing him. Here we look through a mirror, in mysteries and riddles; there, with unveiled faces, we shall see him in person. Not the person of the Word—this cannot happen—but the one who belongs to our own race, the firstfruits of our nature. For a mortal cannot see God and live. Paul also testifies to this: no one has seen him or can see him. For this reason he took a human being and made him the image of his glory, so that mortals might be comforted through him in place of the hiddenness of his [?]. Thanks to you, O Good One, for your gift! How greatly you have loved our nature and honored it with your glorious gifts, although our nature was unworthy. Through the firstfruits you took from us, our whole race was honored, and together with us were renewed:

Heaven and earth and everything in them. And although the spiritual beings are far higher than we are in their natures, through us they learned of you and acknowledged your name, and together with us they were renewed. “Through the church,” he says, “the Creator’s hidden wisdom was revealed” “to the heavenly authorities”—wisdom that had been [?] from the beginning. Through us the spiritual beings learned that the Father has a Son who is hidden. And together with us they received the confession that the Spirit is self-existent, like the Father. Through us they also learned the distinction between the two natures that became one: that of the self-existent Word who is from the Father, and that of the human being who belongs to our race. Together with us they received the knowledge that everything is renewed in Christ, and through our liberation they gain relief from the bondage of their labors. “Creation itself,” he says, “is also freed from slavery together with us,” when we receive deliverance from the mortality of our nature. Come, you who have gone astray; return to the path while there is still time for reconciliation. For the creatures are waiting for us, so that together with us they may receive renewal. The spiritual beings are looking toward us, so that together with us they may obtain transformation. They await deliverance according to the Maker’s promise. Love for those who love learning stirred me to say these things, and zeal against those who spoke presumptuously compelled me to distinguish the natures. Although I have carefully distinguished the natures, the glories from the humiliations, I have made no division in my confession, for I confess one Son. I believe in one lordship and acknowledge one authority, as I worship equally the Word and the dwelling he chose for himself. I confess the King who put on the purple robes of Adam’s body, and I worship the Lord who joined our nature to his greatness. I distinguished these things from those, not with a divided mind, but so that fools should not imagine that the Son is a creature, as they supposed. These are the people who prolonged their arguments and brought the self-existent One down to lowly things, and deprived our nature of the honor of the one who assumed it. For their thoughts are sick, and their minds are diseased. They do not accept words of truth, because they have blinded their conscience with sin. They cannot attain maturity, for they are mere children in understanding. Like newborn babies, they crave bodily food. They laid the foundation of their words on sand and did not consider it. They began building a structure of hay and chaff for [?]. They are drunk with murderous envy against the holy Scriptures. They conceal their hatred under the name of God, in which they wrap themselves. Simple people without understanding are led along after their words. They have abandoned the path of righteousness, and now they wander after falsehood. Truth, which is brighter than the sun, is dark to their minds. Their confession is established in falsehood, a night of suspicion [?]. Faith is the anchor that holds the ship of the Church. Fools abandoned it and drowned in speculation as though in the sea. The sweet spring of teaching, whose waters nourished the righteous, they rejected as though it were bitter; and the drink of the evil one [?] pleased them. They are sick and laid low with fever—in their minds rather than their limbs. Yet they boast as though they were sound, unaware of how diseased they are. They stand against righteousness as though they were champions of the Law.

They clothe themselves in arrogance as though they were enforcing what is right. They have not yet become disciples or studied the Scriptures. Yet in the impudence of their minds they want to become teachers. Come, submit to the truth, you quarrelsome people, and learn what is true. Put away your stubbornness and take up the yoke of humility. It is not out of envy that I wish to demolish the structure of their words, but to turn your minds toward the truth, if possible. For you are untrained when it comes to learning, yet you want to teach. You have treated the one who teaches within the Church as a stranger. You have wronged prophecy and rejected the words of the Spirit. You have produced a new fabrication from ignorant teachers. Here what is written in the Gospel has been fulfilled in practice: if a blind person leads a blind person, the end of his road is a pit. How does someone blind to knowledge differ from a blind person? Though [?] he does not know the truth, he promises to teach his companions. A sick person overwhelmed by fever in body and soul alike now promises health to bodies diseased by sin. Do not follow your own will, you fool who lack understanding. Humble your mind a little and listen to the words of the Scriptures. Teaching is a sweet spring that gives life to those who listen to it, and a light that turns souls toward the level path of righteousness. I do not wish to boast through these things that I have recounted and said. I call the truth, which I honor, as a witness to my words. I do not seek to exalt myself over my fellow members. For I am a member of the body, and I suffer in their pain. It is fitting for those who have understanding to follow this pattern: the injury [?] of one member they should regard [?] as belonging to the whole body. Christ, the head of the members, made his Church one body. And he despised temporal death for love of his bridegroom [or: his members]. Here is the physician who knows hidden and [?] ailments. Come, you who are sick, receive healing, so that you do not die in your sins. Awake, you who sleep in sin, and throw off the weight of your offenses. For dawn is approaching, awakening those who sleep from the sleep of death. You sick who have lingered in the fever of the soul’s hidden diseases, here is mercy, a freely given medicine [?], which heals bodies and souls [?]. Members of the household who have strayed and gone out, return to the road while you are alive. Do not rely on being called members of the household in name. For what does a sinner gain by being called righteous? A borrowed name is an accusation when it is far removed from deeds. What did Judas gain from the apostleship he acquired [?]? And what benefit did he gain from the power of the mystery of the body that gives life to all? Because he did not set his mind right, he became a stranger to his calling. And [?] changed his will; envy killed him instead of a sword. Let us not boast of names, but turn to deeds. For deeds can justify even someone who is far removed in name.

Come, you who have strayed, [?] in the ocean of our Lord’s body. For he can take hold of our souls [?] and bring them into heaven in hope. Since the gift bestowed on our race cannot be repaid by deeds, let us repay it with gratitude, with thanksgiving free from doubt.
On the Construction of the Tent of Meeting
Homily 41. On the Tent of Meeting. By the same author. The forty-first homily. Which he composed on the construction of the Tent of Meeting, and which is suitable for the consecration of a church.

The Creator made a second creation through Moses, to teach humanity that he was the one who created the creation in the beginning. His will portrayed a twofold world before the member of his household, so that he might proclaim the power of his craftsmanship to the heavenly hosts. His power gathered the heavenly hosts on Mount Sinai, so that they might see his power as they had seen it when creation first came into being. In the same form in which he had created the creation before their assemblies, he drew the patterns of the Tent of Meeting and showed them to his servant. Through the Tent of Meeting he wished to make known [?] his greatness, and in its construction he depicted the structure of the heights and the depths. He fashioned it on earth in the form and likeness of the two worlds, earthly and heavenly, a twofold light [?]. I marveled greatly at the twofold wonder of the one who orders everything: he created something when there was nothing, and he renews it. He created all creatures from nothing in the beginning, and then returned a second time and renewed them through Moses. He summoned angels and human beings to look at the vessels of his work, so that they might be witnesses to his renewal and his construction. On the mountain he drew an image that did not exist as though it existed, so that in nothing they might see something brought forth from nothing. With skill he drew forms that had no composition, so that through their composition he might confirm his servants in his creatorship. He depicted the truth of his name in a vision and showed it to them, so that they would not doubt his existence, which has no beginning. First he laid down his name as a foundation for the building of his work, and upon it he completed heaven and earth and everything in them. Again he placed his name like an iron tool in Moses’ hands, and he carved out words and built upon them the truth of his name. Through words he taught him to establish his power in writings [?], and through signs he made them firm as though with roots. The builder of true worship built a house out of something, and patterned it after that structure made out of nothing. The world had been created out of nothing by its Maker; and he too imitated him with nothing and made something. The command sketched for him the beautiful [?] dwelling that the world had become, so that he might imitate it and make a tabernacle resembling the worlds. That will which created creation out of nothing showed him a splendid vision resembling something. “Look and make,” the Creator’s power said to him, “according to that spiritual pattern which I have drawn before you. “Look: carefully draw the splendid image of the two worlds, and place it on earth before those who see, so that they may contemplate it. “Make one tabernacle according to the pattern in which I made heaven and earth, and when it is constructed, divide it into two without division. “Put a curtain between the one and the other, and separate them,

“just as the outstretched firmament separates the two structures. “With a garment of water I divided my work into two dwellings. You too, make yourself an upright garment and divide your work. “Stretch curtains over the earth and secure them, and surround them with worked boards in place of a wall. “Let there be one tabernacle and another within the tabernacle you construct, according to that pattern of one world and another within a single world. “My will fashioned one world and another—the temporal world and the world to come. You too, fashion one tabernacle and another according to that same pattern. “I filled the temporal world with a time of passing things. Look carefully, and place everything opposite its counterpart. “In the outer tabernacle place earthly things, and in the inner one place the order of spiritual things. “Arrange and make spiritual and bodily things, so that the work of your hands may resemble the work of my hands.” O Maker who made the worlds out of nothing, who teaches his servants to imitate him in making something! O Artist who drew created things when they did not exist, who returned to depict them again and traced them before the son of Amram [?]! O you whose eternity is hidden in his eternity, whose power uttered clear sounds before his servants! O you, yes you, man formed from the earth, whose mind rose to imitate your Maker! O Moses, frail clay drawn from the waters, who, though a creature [?], guided creation like the Creator! O stammerer, crippled in speaking a word with your mouth, whose word surpassed the course of human beings and heavenly beings! With the divine voice the slow man ran, and his tongue flew over things he could not see. The word of the Spirit spoke with him spiritually and fashioned his mind to bring words to fulfillment through deeds. Through deeds he completed everything shown to him, by the might of that Power who is perfect in his being and his work as Creator. He made the temporary tabernacle on earth as he was commanded and divided it in two, corresponding to the division between the heights and the depths. He arranged his work according to the order [?] of the worlds, this one and the one to come, and gathered into it and filled it with a representation of life here and there. Through his arrangement he showed people two ways of life and taught them to observe the order established in both. In the outer part he instructed them in bodily things, and in the inner part he gave them understanding of spiritual things. He placed bodily and spiritual things in the two parts, corresponding to the human being's composition of body and spirit. He permitted the body to enter the outer part at any time, and everyone's soul to enter the inner part through the high priest. Everyone entered with the high priest in thought, since the body could not enter as long as it was earthly. That inner tabernacle was depicted [?] spiritually, and the high priest too entered it through spiritual mysteries [?]. The likeness of the outer part was depicted symbolically, and continual entry also corresponded to it.

The body was permitted to see only what belonged to it [?], and was restricted from contemplating spiritual things. That outer tabernacle was filled with bodily activity, and bodily things [?] and sustenance for the body were placed in it. Lifeless sacrifices were offered as its burnt offerings, and rows of bread were arranged on its table. A golden lampstand, a portion of [?], was fixed in it, and above it were the forms of the heavenly lights and the numbering of the days. The entire course of the year's duration was contained in it. The power of [?] was hidden in the figures depicted on it. The tabernacle extended toward the four quarters, corresponding to the inhabited world, and was arranged according to the order of the months of the year. Its arrangement was full of great order [?] for anyone who looked at it, and its regulations too were established in correspondence with the world. The order of its course moved along with the world, and its objects too were arranged according to the changes. In the north were placed the altar of sacrifices and the table of bread, which signified the forgiveness of sins and the changing of the seasons. The rows on the tables were filled with the changing of the seasons, and the months of the year revolved among their rows. The twelve months were represented in six rows, and each row was constituted by two months. The months bring about the sprouting of seeds and the growth of fruit. And [?] the rows were also arranged in this order. Human life is sustained by bread insofar as a person is earthly. That is why bread alone was placed on the table. The rows were arranged on the north side in this configuration, so that they would face the arrangement of the heavenly lights. The lampstand faced them with its flames, symbolizing the heavenly lights, and they faced it like seedlings awaiting the sun. The command that established the Law placed it in the south, facing north, in the same configuration as the sphere of the sun. It revolved with the sun, not on [?], but through the ordered activity of its rays. The entire arrangement of the heavenly lights was represented in its arrangement. The number of days and the succession of months were embodied in it. The week of days was depicted in it, and it itself represented the Sabbath, with seven lamps above its top, corresponding to the number of days. The arrangement of its flames was numbered according to the number of days, and it was arranged in the likeness of a complete week. Six branches faced one another on it, while it stood in the middle, like the days when everything was made, with the Sabbath at the end. The work of those six days was represented in it, and it was holy like the Sabbath day, which the divine command made holy. A second week was counted out in the tabernacle of meeting, and its flames were like the heavenly lights in the expanse above. Its light appeared only in the outer tabernacle, just as the sun gives light only in this dwelling here below. The light from it was not needed in the Holy of Holies, just as the dwelling above has no need of a heavenly light.

That inner tabernacle was modeled on the dwelling above and, in its likeness, was set apart from the entrance. Although it was on earth, it served as a likeness of heaven. Its furnishings also spoke of things to come. The incense altar and the incense holder placed in it foretold the thanksgiving of a pure soul. The high priest also entered it with fragrant incense, and once a year he made atonement in it for himself and for the world. In it he received forgiveness of sins and the spirit of revelation. Both his entrance and his departure were full of fear and love. He was full of fear because he feared on account of his sins, and he was full of love as he entered to receive mercy. Mercy and judgment were revealed through its furnishings, and they were consulted about events that had happened and were happening. The jar and the staff were reminders of things past: the food of manna and the choosing of priests from the house of Levi. The ark symbolized the heavenly ministries, and the seraphim symbolized the perfection of immortal life. The golden object whose name was interpreted as “atonement” represented the forgiveness of sins accomplished through our Life-giver. That object itself was called “atonement,” not because it made atonement, but because it was a symbol of the one who makes atonement. The mystery of atonement lay hidden in the arrangement prescribed by the Law, awaiting the time when the one who forgives sins would reveal it. The mute plate longed for the speaking plate, waiting for him to come and fulfill its mystery through deeds. It longed for the forgiveness of sins accomplished through deeds, because it had no power over the sins of human nature. Its power was too weak to wipe away human wickedness, and it could not release mortals from death. It possessed only the name of the atonement brought by the one who atones, and it gleamed like lifeless images. It clothed itself in borrowed names without deeds: the plate of [?], and also the atonement that was a symbol of atonement. Through its titles it prophesied about the one who was coming, and pointed, as though with a finger, to the day of his revelation. By the name “plate” it spoke of his bodily nature, and by “atonement,” of the power of the divine Being dwelling in him. There was no power to forgive sins in its silence, nor could a human being give life to humanity. The Creator’s power empowered both the symbol and its fulfillment, and through his mighty power he gave life through mortality. Human mortality was proclaimed through the plate’s silence, and through the revelations [?] that occurred in it, the Word in the flesh. A spirit of revelation breathed in it despite its silence, like the divine will in a man of our own kind. Through it the priest of the people learned the mystery of hidden things, just as we learn the power of the divine Being through one of our own race. The mute object was placed in the Holy of Holies upon the arks, just as its Lord was destined to dwell on high. Mute cherubim honored its silence, in the likeness of the heavenly hosts honoring the source of our life.

The hammered gold was honored because of the source of our life, and its [?] also looked toward the atonement within it. Otherwise, let the [?], the minister of mysteries, say what the reason is for this atonement found in a silent object. Why was it placed in the Holy of Holies as something holy, proclaiming the mystery of hidden things and the forgiveness of sins? Why did the priest depend on its silence when he entered, and why was he taught through it to disclose mysteries? Why did the cherubim not speak, though they were mute? For it is written that the voice of revelation was conveyed from it. Why did even the priest not enter into its presence at all times, and when he entered, why did he enter with [?] alone? Why was a voice conveyed to him from a mute object, and not from on high, where the power of the divine Being is? Why was absolutely everything done through the mediation of a lifeless plate, and why did a speaking being bow his head before a silent object? Look, O Jew, at the force of the testimony contained in your Scriptures, and see that my thoughts have carefully investigated the [?] of the mystery. The account of the tabernacle of your sacrifices is also full of questions: why was one place called holy and another called holy? Why was the outer one served with the blood of animals, but the inner one with incense alone, and only once a year? If the symbolism of that entry was full of benefit, why did he not perform it every day, so that he might benefit every day? Every day those burdened with sins need forgiveness, and at all times they need to listen to the [?] that wipes away wrongdoing. No, Hebrew, it is not as it is written: another power is hidden in the letters and in the voice that sounded forth. Your outer sanctuary signifies the earthly dwelling, while the inner one is a symbol of the spiritual order. The altar of your sacrifices symbolizes that sacrifice offered for our lives, and your mercy seat is a shadow of the forgiveness of our sins. The voice that used to speak to you from that plate is the power of help that flows to humanity through a human being. The wooden cherubim that hovered over the mercy seat represent the heavenly beings who serve the source of our life. The high priest's entrance once a year depicted that entrance made by our firstfruits. The mystery of our salvation was destined to enter the sanctuary on high, and that entrance was rehearsed through the high priest's entrance. The priesthood of your people was a herald before his coming, announcing that coming through the sacrifice of sheep and the blood of calves. The tabernacle of your time was a guide through its divisions, displaying two orders: that of this world and that of the world to come. But why a tabernacle and a [?] for a single way of life? And why a sanctuary and a Holy of Holies, one visible and the other hidden? Why, in one, a pouring out of animal blood, and in the other, incense and the likeness of spiritual watchers? Why did you [?] before the door of your Holy of Holies, without entering and looking upon its glorious things? Why, too, did your priest not enter continually? And when he entered, why did he not bring sacrifices in with him? Your sanctuary bears witness that what I have said is signified in it.

And your Holy of Holies confirms my words through its rites. In its entirety it intimates the proclamation of our life, and through its symbols it points, as with a finger, to the truth that has appeared. The radiance of your Scriptures longed to receive his great appearing. Now that he has appeared, why do you prevent people from looking at him? Look at the [?], how bright its radiance is! It pursued the darkness of idolatry, destroyed it, and brought it to an end. Come now, fool, remove the covering from your mind and see the world walking in the light of his proclamation. Come now, arrogant one, descend from the height of [?], and look at creation honoring the banner you rejected. All creation cries out his praise without ever having enough, and the four quarters weave a crown of victory for his name. All the righteous were comforted by the mystery of his coming, and the books of the Spirit spoke of his revelation. The priests had their regulations arranged according to his order, and kings were honored in their dominions through his rank. Through the greatness of his rank, the Law and its observances were exalted; without him, it would not even have been named. It was honored in his name through the Spirit of revelations, and the revelations spoke of his revelation. The priest worshiped him symbolically before that plate; the plate itself served in his place. With the blood of animals he depicted in blood the sprinkling of his blood; and the one I speak of was shown to be the one who makes atonement. Through the promise to the righteous, his [?] was confirmed, and through their sacrifices his suffering and death were glorified. That expectation prescribed by the law pointed to him, and Moses bore witness, having built the tabernacle as a symbol of his revelation. The symbol of his revelation filled the tabernacle [?], and, as though with a finger, it pointed him out through [?]. Both sanctuaries and everything in them looked toward him, waiting for him to come and perfect them through his holiness. The dead sacrifices longed for holiness from him, waiting for him to sacrifice his living self and release them. The lamb, through its sacrifice, explained his [?], and raised its voice louder than thunder through the mouths of those who ate it. Through the eating of the speechless animal, the eating of his body was revealed; and through its lowly blood, his precious blood was explained. The sprinkling of its blood protected the people from harm. If the blood of a speechless animal was enough to protect them, how much more the blood of one who speaks! The Good One was going to redeem human beings through the blood of one who speaks, and he sent a speechless animal to prepare the way before his coming. He willingly gave everything a dwelling in the pattern of his body, and he established the tabernacle and called it the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. The tabernacle was designed as a symbol of the formation of his body and soul, and service was performed in it both bodily and spiritually. Bodily and spiritual things were placed in it, in keeping with the fact that the watchers and human beings were to [?] toward him. He was bringing all the people to the harbor of his peace.

And, as with an anchor, he bound them by their hope in him. Its watchful gaze was directed toward the [?] of his dawning, and it looked at the splendor of his light as at a star. A well-ordered arrangement filled the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies, and it was laid out on earth toward the four directions, corresponding to the world. The [?] took the place of the sun within it, and by its lights the requirements of the sacrifices were fulfilled. The sun ripens fruit with its heat and makes seeds sprout; likewise it did so in the tabernacle, the second world. It and its lamps were fixed in the outer tabernacle, corresponding to the sun, whose course is bounded within this dwelling here. The likeness that the son of the Hebrews made was very close, and no one could make a better likeness than this. “Look,” he said, “and make it in the form of the pattern that I drew before you.” And this is the wonder: although nothing resembles anything— There was nothing like the pattern he drew for him on the mountain. Who would not marvel that he made a likeness according to a pattern that has no likeness? With his mind he contemplated what he had seen spiritually; and it is full of wonder that he saw it in inward stirrings and completed it in [?]. The seer of hidden things saw a vision of light, and it was far beyond the understanding of earthly people. The measurements of the tabernacle of time were very numerous, and its divisions too were crowded together and intermingled. He made measurements of things that do not exist as though they existed, and established its arrangement according to divisions that were not real. He made it in an orderly way, according to the patterns he saw on the mountain, and [?] precisely traced its likenesses without alteration. Oh, how precisely you portrayed your images, son of the Hebrews! Their likeness resembles that nothing that was shown to you. Oh, how splendid [?] the Spirit [?] in your words! And [?] its color to the beautiful color that portrayed the worlds. Oh, how beautiful is the path you opened among earthly people! And [?] that voice which spoke with you opened it through your mouth. Oh, how true is the name of the divine Being that you proclaimed on earth, exposing and revealing the stubbornness of those who are not gods! Oh, how swiftly the word of your mouth ran, you who were slow of tongue! It traversed the worlds and set down the order of the one who establishes the worlds. Oh, how subtle your mind is, man, for seeing hidden things! You [?] its movements to contemplate what cannot be seen. Who would not marvel at your word, Moses, drawn out of the water? In place of water, you filled the earth with words of the Spirit. Who would not say that the Spirit interpreted well through your mouth, since, as he prepared you, you explained his mysteries among earthly people? Who would not acknowledge the power that strengthened the movements of your soul? It was he who created creation in the beginning and made it known through your mouth. Who would not believe that he placed within you the power of curses, and that, at his command, speechless elements fulfilled your word? Who would not call you a god on earth, as you were named, since deeds were accomplished on earth together with your word? The title given to you is fitting, mortal man, and the word addressed to you was fully fulfilled through deeds.

The name of God was bestowed on you as a borrowed title, but the one you called the great prophet proved to be so through his deeds. All your words were fulfilled as they had been prophesied, and not a single letter fell short of fulfillment. The very one you called the great prophet fulfilled your words and sealed your [?] with the seal of blood from his limbs. Concerning him the Spirit spoke hidden mysteries through you, and they were waiting for him, for the time when he would come and reveal them. The structure of the tabernacle of time also pointed toward him, who was destined to become a pure temple for the power of the divine Being. For a span of time the tabernacle served the Creator's name, but he is served in holiness within it without end. The hidden one willingly dwells in the sanctuary of his body, and in it he is hallowed by spiritual beings and bodily beings. All creation worships its Maker in his body and cherishes it as a divine temple. His body is the Holy Place, and the movements of his soul are the Holy of Holies. The Holy Place and the Holy of Holies were depicted in his likeness. The tabernacle of time was called holy and holy, as though someone were saying that it was destined to become body and soul. In the outer tabernacle, bodily existence was revealed, and in the inner one, the hidden soul was proclaimed. Through body and soul, a human being becomes a complete human being. In that same likeness, the tabernacle was depicted in two tabernacles. Moses fashioned that structure according to the structure of a human being. Come, let us see in it the human structure that was made by a human being.
On the vision of the seraphim that Isaiah saw.

Homily thirty-[?]. On the vision of the seraphim that Isaiah saw. Suitable also for the Consecration of the Church. Response: Blessed is he who revealed worship to us through his faithful ones, my brothers.

Glorious is the Creator, who exalts his servants through his revelation and distributes his riches to the members of his household through visions. He is worthy of glory: although he has no need of praise, he gives his glory to those who praise him so that they may praise him. His glory is within him, and no glory is added to his glory. If he is praised, his glory exalts those who praise him. He is entirely glory, and his works are filled with his praise. He lacks nothing, and from his bounty he provides for everything. He is without composition, yet he regularly appears in likenesses. He is without a voice [?], yet makes his voice heard in sounds perceptible to the senses. In every form he shows himself to the work of his hands, and in every likeness he depicts his mysteries before their interpreters. He shows the greatness of his love in visions of various likenesses, so that through gentle enticements he may draw human beings to approach him. He showed Adam a vision suited to his bodily senses, and called to him as to a child, so that he would modestly cover his naked body. He spoke with Noah through a bodily voice and taught him to make a place of escape for himself and for all. He called Abraham and spoke with him in his own language. He stamped him with his name, so that his children would call upon his name.

He placed his strength in Jacob’s hands in the form of a man, and showed him how to engage in hidden combat through the outward senses. He spoke with Joseph in a language resembling that of the Egyptians, and gave him the power to understand hidden things. He revealed his greatness on Mount Sinai before the eyes of the son of Amram, and filled him with the Spirit to recount his works. He depicted an example of his kindness before Elijah, so that he would know how to imitate the purpose of his mercy. Now too he clothed himself in a splendid form and stood in the sanctuary, to reveal to human beings the incomprehensible greatness of his glory. He wished to show himself to human beings in great glory, and brought one human being near him to gaze upon him. He revealed his greatness before Isaiah’s eyes in the holy temple, and stationed ranks of peacemakers to proclaim his holiness. He moved down from the heights and dwelt in the depths, though not in his nature. He stood upon the earth, not in reality but in name. He gathered the watchers, called the angels, and signaled to the cherubim. He clothed them in an appearance filled with manifold wonder. The flying ones soared, the fiery ones sped along, and the swift ones ran. They thought he had arrived, and his command had preceded them to the earth. Trumpets sounded, ranks were ordered, and legions were arrayed. Instead of armor, they put on the power of the Spirit to strengthen themselves. They set out, moving across the heights without taking steps, with the power of the divine Being among their ranks, without any change of place. The King's army set out with the authority that makes kings reign, and no road was worn in the air beneath their feet. The command of the hidden Power and the heavenly armies descended, and no one perceived the sound of its descent except one. One human being from among humanity saw [?], and he stood and contemplated the greatness of his power and his attendants. One human being saw his appearance, not with physical sight, but with the mind, as far as a created being can see. With his hidden mind he saw the invisible vision, and in thought he entered the holy temple with the Watchers. The command of the one who rules over all entered the holy temple, and his attendants stood to serve him in holiness. They adorned a throne of glory and set it up for him as for a king. They raised a fiery veil between him and themselves.

The attendants spread a veil of glory before their eyes so that they would not gaze upon the face of the King who dwells in glory. Their wings became coverings for their persons, and they concealed the senses they had suddenly acquired, contrary to their usual state. The incorporeal beings displayed senses to a bodily eye, and hid them from the glory of the majestic vision. They wrapped their wings around their faces like cloths, so that they would not be blinded by the blaze of the vision's splendor. The splendid vision appeared before their eyes, and they were afraid to look at it with their eyes fully open. It was exceedingly fearsome, and nothing was more fearsome than it. Yet it was lovely, as the sound of their cries of holiness bears witness. Their wings served as intermediaries between him and themselves. Through them they offered him the holy gifts of their thoughts. They suddenly brought forth six wings, without bodily composition, and distributed them among the parts of their forms. With two they covered their faces, which had no physical shape, and with two they concealed the feet they had, although those feet did not exist. With two they raised their wings to fly swiftly, and they began reverently crying out holy acclamations. “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord,” their ranks cried out, and the foundations of the holy temple shook at their cries of holiness. With three equal cries of “Holy,” they proclaimed one authority, and through all three they revealed one lordship over everything. They called the nature that holds all things “the Lord of Hosts,” and thus declared that the divine Being [?] in a threefold manner. They proclaimed the Trinity on earth through their cries of holiness, and according to their appointed order they offered the thanksgiving they owed. Three times they repeated the praise in a wondrous voice, and opened a path for humanity to invoke three names. Three names were hidden in the name of that acclamation of holiness, and the Watchers were the first to reveal them through their cries of holiness. But why did they proclaim “Holy” only three times, neither adding to nor subtracting from the number?

If their service is continually to proclaim holiness, why did they not proclaim “Holy” without growing weary, as they are accustomed to do? They were obliged to proclaim “Holy” without number. What, then, was the reason they stopped and fell silent instead of paying what they owed? Even if a thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand had offered praise, their praise would have been too little for the glory being praised. Even if heaven and earth had shouted with all their hosts, they could not have praised him as his wondrous greatness deserves. Even if all creation had stood with its companies, it would have fallen far short of offering the gifts of praise. The Creator is immeasurably greater than created things, and they fall immeasurably short of his greatness. If this is so, as their differences testify, why did the watchers limit their proclamation of “Holy” to three times? The spiritual beings did not simply fall silent and cease praising, nor did they withhold, or now withhold, the payment they owed. Through their proclamations of “Holy,” they revealed a great order on earth: three persons are hidden in the being of the hidden Nature. They learned that there is one divine Being when creation was established in the beginning; afterward they gained an understanding of the revelation of the persons. The Hidden One revealed a hidden mystery to them, not openly, but so that they would seek it, each making his own search into the mystery. They repeated the praise three times in a mysterious way, but they did not understand the power hidden within their words. They spoke words without understanding their meaning. They proclaimed “Holy,” but could not grasp the reason for it. They marked out a road of peace for creation toward the Creator, so that it might travel rightly to meet the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. They arranged three proclamations of “Holy” and placed them along it like milestones, so that whoever traveled by their proclamations would not become confused. “Holy is the Lord!” they cried over the earth, and the earth shook.

They taught it the order of the power of the divine Being, who has no limit. They taught them to proclaim the holiness of the power of the divine Being, and through Isaiah they taught a great wonder. The son of Amoz saw a great wonder among the heavenly beings: how glorious they were, and how fearful as they proclaimed “Holy.” The Hebrew's thoughts were astonished at the wonder within them, and he gathered his mind from every direction to attend to the vision. The seer was amazed at the wonder of the vision and its ministers: how greatly they feared the revelation that spoke with him. Their dread amazed him far more than his own did, for although they were spirits, they feared the spiritual vision. “Who has stirred these mighty beings?” he wondered. “And from whom have these majestic beings hidden their faces? Who has gathered them and stationed them in company after company, laying a yoke and dread upon them, so that they stand there terrified?” To whom do the voices cry out in holiness and fear? At whom can they not raise their eyes when confronted with the vision? Why do they hide their faces within their wings? Concerning whom do they utter three cries and repeat no more? The prophet stood in doubt about what he saw, for the wonder of the vision made him uncertain. “Does what I have seen really exist, or does it not? Is it appearing to me alone, or perhaps to others too? “Is it a body, and am I looking at it bodily? Or is it perhaps an unreal shadow? “Did I enter bodily and stand within the sanctuary? Or did I perhaps see it in my mind without seeing it? “It exists, and it does not exist,” the Israelite pondered, like his father, who was granted a vision resembling his own. Israel too was granted a vision beyond his capacity, and he was given the name Israel: he saw God. The vision of Israel’s son resembles his father’s vision, and it is one power that displayed its might there and here. That authority which placed itself in Jacob’s hands also showed Isaiah a wondrous vision. The seer, the son of seers, saw a great wonder. He stood and contemplated without his senses, as though using his senses.

He contemplated the beauty of the vision without ever having enough, and the more he looked, the more he continued looking with delight. The sight of the vision was deeply pleasing to his mind, and his understanding had never expected to gaze upon its splendid beauty. The more he contemplated how terrified the seraphim were, the more fear and love increased within his mind. The more their wings were drawn over their faces, the more he sought within himself a way to hide. The more the sound of “Holy, holy” was heard, the more he considered himself unworthy even to listen. As the vision appeared in the Holy of Holies, he reflected, “The awesome Creator has come to dwell among his works.” He saw the vision that appeared to him in the Holy of Holies, yet the holiness of those who proclaim holiness could not encompass its extent. The vision he saw was far greater than all visions. The sight of the spiritual beings, which could not take it in, bears witness to this. Their voices [?], their wings grew weary, and their minds were bewildered. Though they strained, they could not contemplate the radiance of the vision. They grew weary and exhausted from covering their faces, and although they covered themselves thoroughly, they were not concealed as they ought to have been. The vision filled whoever looked upon it with fear and love; with wisdom it made them tremble and filled them with awe. Under the influence of both, the seer stood contemplating. He was afraid and filled with longing, wishing both to approach and to hold back. Severe labor pains struck his understanding, and he labored to give birth to the vision that had appeared to him. Like a child, the vision pressed upon his mind, seeking to come out through his senses and proclaim the greatness of its power. His mind received the good seed of the spirit of revelation, and he marveled greatly that, though unworthy, he had been found worthy of such a thing. He recalled [?] the lowliness of his lineage and the greatness of his wickedness, and thoughtfully marveled at what he saw. Sorrow for his sins was piercing the mortal man, and he shrank from raising his eyes toward the vision.

Whenever he longed to gaze intently at the splendor of its beauty, he looked at himself, grieved, and sighed over his offenses. Whenever he longed for the voices of the Watchers crying, “Holy,” he remembered the uncleanness of his people and covered his face. Whenever he longed for the voices of the Watchers crying, “Holy,” he remembered the uncleanness of his people and covered his face. When he considered that the vision was spiritual in nature, he despaired and concluded that he was losing his life. The prophet lay in a struggle of suffering before the revelation, longing to hear a voice announcing forgiveness of wickedness. Sorrow for his own wickedness and that of his people was piercing him, and he sighed bitterly within his mind. “Woe to me, wretched man that I am,” the righteous man said to himself, “for I am defiled by the abominations of the people's wickedness. “Woe to me, for the appearance of my face and my thoughts is ugly, yet I have stood to gaze at the beauty of the vision of the power of the divine Being. “Woe to me, for I am lowly clay kneaded with sins, yet I have been found worthy to see the command that fashioned our lowly clay.” With a just judgment the righteous prophet accused himself, and before judgment he condemned himself so that he would not be condemned. The righteous man stood like a guilty man before the revelation, and before receiving a blow he confessed, “I am guilty.” As though with straps, he stretched himself out with remorse of soul, and scourged himself before the lashes reached him. He sentenced himself to harsh lashes when no one had called him to account, and wisely discerned the duty a person owes. On behalf of the guilty he condemned himself, though he was not guilty, and with his sighs he lifted [?] the blows away from the insolent. He became a good advocate for his people before Justice, and by his supplication he quieted wrath and drove anger away. The Judge and the members of his order marveled at his advocacy, at how well he knew how to devise winning strategies. The command hidden in the vision heard the plea of his words and sent him comfort through a spiritual messenger. The vision sent a spiritual man to the son of Amoz to sound in his ears the good news of forgiveness of wickedness. The Watcher brought the Hebrew man good news, full of peace and containing a sign of atonement for sins. The spirit carried atonement for sins in the hand of his movements and gave it to the prophet, so that through it he might be cleansed of stains.

The command directed the spiritual being to approach, take a glowing coal with fiery tongs, and bring it to him. He commanded the fiery being to take fire [?] with fire [?], and with it destroy the forest of wickedness that had sprouted in humanity. A thicket of wickedness sprang up from the yield of Adam’s sins, and the Hidden One sent a heavenly being to clear it away. He showed him a sickle of fire to reach in among the wheat and reap the thicket, leaving the crop unharmed. Like a reaper, the spiritual being approached the son of Amoz and reaped away his wickedness with the sickle that the divine command had placed in his hand. He saw a burning coal lying on the holy altar, approached, and took it in his fiery hand, as he had been commanded. With fiery tongs the fiery being grasped the fire, brought it near, and placed it on lips of flesh. Oh, the wonder that took place for the son of Amoz! Though he was flesh, he was not burned by the burning coal. Fire could not grasp fire without something between them, yet lowly flesh held it in its mouth and was not scorched. The one not subject to suffering suffered from the radiance of its fierceness, while the body, full of suffering, did not suffer when it drew near him. Oh, the fiery being who could not grasp the manifestation of fire! Oh, the body that the flame did not hurt! It was not fire that the Watcher grasped with fiery tongs, nor was it a coal that approached the prophet. He did not see in bodily form the vision shown to him, nor was the vision appearing bodily. The Creator did not confine himself within the holy temple, nor did the seraphim spread out wings perceptible to the senses.
