The spiritual beings did not cry out with a sound perceptible to the senses, nor did Isaiah listen to the voice with his bodily senses. The revelation came spiritually upon the man of flesh, and he saw what he saw with his mind, not with his eyes. With the eyes of his mind he saw the invisible sight, and in his understanding he heard a voice imperceptible to the senses. Through hidden stirrings the hidden command spoke with him, and the revelation spoke subtly with his thoughts. Through inward stirrings the spiritual being also brought the coal near to his inward stirrings,

although there was no coal at all, but only a vision. For it was a vision that was truly seen, not in bodily form but in a vision without material composition. Without hands the spiritual being grasped a coal that did not exist, and without tongs he brought it near a mouth clothed in a body. With tongs that did not exist he grasped the invisible coal and brought it near the mouth of the visible man, without being seen. With a bodiless voice the bodiless being spoke with the embodied man, revealing and showing him the forgiveness of wickedness that he was receiving freely. “Look, this has touched your mouth,” said the Watcher, “to take away your wickedness and loosen the bonds of your soul’s sins. “Look, your wickedness is forgiven, and the record of your guilt is erased. Rise, go out, and proclaim the message of forgiveness to your fellow human beings. “Look, the hidden command dwelling in the vision has permitted me to bring you the medicine of mercy without hands.” Look, show me how I may heal the pain of your soul, and how I may erase the record of debts charged against your limbs. Teach me how to scour the filth of sins from you with fire, and explain to me how, through it, I may reveal the truth of faith. Why, then, did he purify the pure soul with a sign of fire, when fire causes pain to those who feel pain? Why did the Watcher take hold of it with tongs rather than with his hand, when the power of a spiritual being is stronger than that silent thing? Why did he take fire from the altar of burnt offerings, when it was the sacrifices that purified, not the fire? The Israelites were purified through sacrifices of sheep. Why, then, did he not take something from the sacrifices and bring it to him? Through the blood of calves, those [?] in soul received atonement. Why, then, did he not put blood on his mouth and atone for his sins? It had never been heard that anyone sprinkled fire on bodily limbs, nor that a spiritual being without senses took hold of fire. This atonement is very foreign to what is in the Law, and nothing in it resembles the ritual order handed down by Moses. Moses and Aaron used to sprinkle blood on sinners—not on the mouth, but on the ears and thumbs. What the spiritual seraph did for Isaiah was something new,

and it has no parallel in the entire ritual order of the Law. Come, explain to us, priest who [?] ministers with blood: what is this that the Watcher did for our fellow human being? Come, show us, Israelite who has seen God: what is the power hidden in the vision your prophet saw? Come, explain to us, you who atone for wrongdoing with the blood of animals: why did the spiritual being not erase your brother’s wrongdoing with blood? Why did he not sprinkle blood on his ear or his palm, as Moses and Aaron taught concerning those being healed? Why was the great ritual order practiced among you changed, and why did the Watcher teach you to walk a path you had never seen? Look for some [?] in the vision your prophet saw. Perhaps it is not a symbol, but the reality that supersedes symbols. Through its departure from the usual order, the symbol proclaims the revealed reality; it marked out a clear path in advance of the events. The abolition of the sacrifices prescribed by the Law is depicted in the burning coal, and its meaning is filled with a forgiveness of wrongdoing more real than that. Great wealth that can never be exhausted is hidden in its appearance, and the promise of life high above the earth is revealed through it. The voice of the heavenly beings proclaims pure holiness, and never before had they been heard proclaiming holiness in this way. The Trinity fills the cry of their proclamations of holiness, and they teach humanity to proclaim holiness threefold. They joined three voices together and cried out three times; they taught the order that exists within the divine Being: three in one. They pointed them out to earthly beings as though with a finger: “Look, mortals, and proclaim holiness fittingly, following the sound of our voice.” They proclaimed three equal persons in their cries of “Holy,” and, as faithful witnesses, declared them through the mouth of Isaiah. They revealed the truth within them to the prophet in a mystery, and he took it and stored it in the Scriptures as in a treasury. In the treasury of the books he placed the mystery that had been disclosed to him.

He sealed it in silence until it would be explained through events. He laid silence like a seal over the proclamation of holiness, so that fleshly eyes would not gaze upon these things and despise them. The pure holiness was being kept for revelation at its appointed time. Therefore the prophet concealed it in silence from those who looked. Revelation disclosed it beforehand in a mystery through the mouths of spiritual beings, and showed humanity that it must await the order appointed for the end of the ages. He was to reveal the mystery of sanctification at the end of the ages, and he placed it beforehand in the Scriptures as a pledge. The spiritual beings, too, proclaimed holiness in this refrain and fell silent, so that everyone might ponder why it was repeated three times. The forgiveness he gave the prophet, too, he gave through a word, so that when people turned away from forgiveness, they might consider why. The coal itself, which [?] iniquity, is full of questions: how did it approach a mouth of flesh without burning it? Who, then, gave it the power of forgiveness, though it had no understanding? And how did a lifeless thing bring to life someone who was dead in his sins? Fire is lifeless, however much heat it possesses, and it has no understanding, however brightly it glows. Within it is the mystery of the gift of bread and wine: although they are lifeless, they give life to those who receive them. The Good One was to give humanity life through bread and wine, and beforehand he gave life to one human being through a vision of fire. He shut the door against the doubting mind, so that if the life given through bread seemed difficult to accept, it might look at the coal. So the coal, an insensible substance, erased sins, but human flesh and blood cannot forgive sins? So you accept as true the word that forgave iniquity; why do you hesitate over forgiveness accomplished through actions? So you wish to grasp the appearance of a shadow; why do you not grasp the body, the reality behind the shadow? The mystery of forgiveness given to the son of Amoz is a shadow of this reality, which forgives everyone through bread and wine. A figure of the truth was depicted in the sight of that revelation, and it was urging humanity to approach its interpretation.

[?] depicted it as a visible image, and brought it in and placed it in the Holy of Holies prescribed by the Law. In accordance with the Law they traced spiritual likenesses, yet even so it differed greatly from the Law. The colors with which it was painted were very bright, and the blood of speechless animals was not mixed into them. The sacrifice depicted in the image did not resemble the uncomprehending sacrifices, nor did the praise of those who praised him resemble the praise of Moses. He was exceedingly glorious, and no glory resembled his glory; even the glory of the holy temple grew dim at the sight of him. In the holy temple the watchers portrayed the true image, and they acclaimed him as a king with shouts of glory in his royal dwelling. The son of Amoz marveled at the splendor of the glory of those who praised him, and the world and its glory became as nothing in his eyes. He considered the world as though it did not even exist in comparison with his glory. Indeed, it is just as he thought, and far more so. The prophet thought that he was in another world, and he stood up to accuse the people’s wrongdoing in his own person. He entered into a just judgment against himself on behalf of every human being, and he saw that all human nature was imprisoned under sins. He fashioned a cry of woe in the sound of his words, like a lament, and loudly mourned the sufferings of humanity. “Woe to me!” he said—that is, “Woe to human nature, which wrongdoing has confined in the prison of mortality!” The nature of mortals is more afflicted than all other things that came into being, and the fleshly armor in which it fights is weak. The Judge saw that he judged himself rightly, and in his mercy he had compassion on the lowliness of all human nature. He saw him accusing the shameful deeds of his race in his own person, and he sent him to be an advocate in the trial of wrongdoing. He saw that he showed no partiality toward himself by making light of his wrongdoing, and he set him ablaze with the Spirit so that through him he might cleanse the people’s wrongdoing. He saw that he knew how to judge justly, without [?] leniency,

and he gave him the rod of prophecy to discipline the wicked. He tested the genuineness of his faith as in a furnace, and he made his mouth a revealer of hidden mysteries. He made himself heard aloud [?] to the member of his household, as they considered who was worthy to proclaim his words. “Whom shall I send, and who will go?” the revelation cried out. And the righteous man lovingly answered, “I will go.” Whom, then, did the Knower of all ask, as though he did not know? For he already knew who was suited to his task. He asked so that the one to be sent, eager in mind, would hear and choose for himself to carry out his Lord’s command. With love he agreed to proclaim the truth in the ears of the wicked, and of his own will he chose toil on behalf of sinners. “I will go,” he answered the revelation that spoke with him, “and I will declare the truth of your name without concealment. “I will proclaim the power of your being among those on earth, and I will abolish the name of the gods that error has made. “Give me the seal of your great name, which cannot be falsified, so that by your name I may erase the borrowed names that are not true. “Write me a document bearing the signature of your eternal nature, so that I may read it before everyone and everyone may know that everything belongs to you. “Place in my hands the straight rod of the spirit of your will, so that with it I may strike down the deaf idols that demons have set up.” Oh, the prophet, glorious among the prophets! How he suffered to bear the burden of the proclamation entrusted to him! Oh, the messenger, swift of mind! How his mind raced, so that before he set out, his will had already reached the place to which he was sent! Oh, the seer of beautiful things! How clearly he gazed, and his thought soared toward a revelation beyond his strength! Oh, the upright man! How well he knew how to judge discerningly: he looked at himself and condemned the wrongdoing of the whole world! Come, let us set ourselves a target like that of the son of Amoz, and aim toward it by accusing ourselves of our shameful deeds. Come, let us sigh over our hateful deeds as he did, and judge our wrongdoing before the coming judgment judges us.
Let us confess that we have sinned, as he confessed before the revelation, so that we may be worthy to hear the voice of forgiveness, as he heard it.
On the Church and the Priesthood

Homily Thirty-Two. On the Church and the Priesthood. Suitable for the fourth Sunday of the Dedication of the Church.
Response: Bridegroom who invited us to the bridal chamber of his kingdom, do not separate us from it.
My brothers.

The Creator built a holy temple for those on earth, so that in it they might spiritually offer the worship of love. He adorned and established a sanctuary and a Holy of Holies: a sanctuary on earth and a Holy of Holies above in heaven. In the earthly sanctuary he commanded them to serve as priests symbolically, and in the heavenly one through the actual deeds themselves, without division. In his unfathomable knowledge he distinguished two ways of life, and filled them with riches both temporal and unending. He called the earthly dwelling an earthly sanctuary, and that dwelling hidden on high the Holy of Holies. Through both sanctuaries he showed his love to the members of his household and taught them to proclaim his holiness symbolically. He wished to give the works of his hands a share in the holiness of his name, so that through it they might be made holy when they proclaim the holiness of his holy name.

It is not he who benefits from the sounds of their proclamations of holiness, for he is holy, and in his purity he makes the unclean holy. Through various means he encourages his own to become like him, so that he may make them heirs to the glory of his Son. With this provision he built the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies, and urged people to serve as priests in it for the sake of their lives. He granted them permission to abandon the wrongdoing of their deeds, and gave their free will the authority to act righteously. He appointed them stewards of the treasure within them, so that they might increase the wealth of righteousness as much as they wished. He made the inclination within them a treasurer of glorious things, so that it might enrich itself and its companions with glorious blessings. He pledged and promised a treasure of life without end, and placed it high above, in a place concealed from those who see. In secret he showed it to the hidden [?] concealed within the soul, so that it might examine it with the eyes of its impulses and see its beauty. He placed a desire for spiritual wealth on earth, so that earthly people would long for it and hate earthly things. He showed them a new path by which to journey toward him, and one innocent man, who conquered through the Spirit, opened it through suffering. Like an athlete, he traveled ahead along the path of life, and arrived and reached the final goal of perfection. He counseled the members of his race and promised them that they would be [?], and that through his mystery they would journey with him in perfection. He taught them to serve as priests after his own example: he in heaven, and they on earth, in a mysterious way. He gave them a rank higher than the rank prescribed by the Law, and instead of sacrifices, he taught them to offer love. He fulfilled the Law through the law contained in the words of his proclamation, and gave priesthood in place of [?], to grant forgiveness to all. First he chose twelve priests for himself, corresponding to the number of the tribes, and instead of one people, he called all nations to belong to him.

He placed in their hands the power of the Spirit to overcome everything, and they uprooted error and sowed the truth of the Creator’s name. They forgave wrongdoing and cleansed blemishes through his help, and taught people to hate the wrongdoing in their deeds. On earth they ministered as priests the mystery of the establishment of the kingdom on high, and through visible things they depicted the wonders of things to come. Through them the word of life was proclaimed among mortals, and people began to travel along new paths. They began to serve as priests spiritually, just as they had received from the high priest who sanctified them. They served as priests according to his purpose and grew great through his [?], and handed on the ranks of their ministries to their disciples. For this purpose he gave priesthood to new priests, so that human beings would be priests who forgive wrongdoing on earth. Priesthood came into being among mortals for the forgiveness of wrongdoing, because mortal humanity constantly needs forgiveness. Sinful passions arise within human nature, and they cannot be cleansed without the medicine of holiness. A person cannot travel along the road without stumbling, and when he stumbles, he needs the mercy that heals his wrongdoing. Mortals lie afflicted in body and soul by the pains of wrongdoing, and they need a physician who knows the illness within and without. Priesthood came into being to heal hidden and visible illness, so that it might heal wrongdoing through spiritual skill. The priest is a physician of hidden and visible things, and through his skill the healing of body and soul is easy. With the medicine of the Spirit he cleanses wrongdoing from people’s thoughts, and people take off the garment of wrongdoing and put on truth. With the tips of his lips he opens a path toward knowledge, and, as though with fire, he tests truth and rejects wrongdoing. He is the Lord’s messenger and minister, as it is written, and through him care for humanity is carried out. Like a limb, he is chosen from the body of his own race, and, as its head, he is bound to lead his companions. He fulfills the role of the head for the impulses and the limbs.

Through him people discern wickedness and righteousness. Through him they see truth and falsehood as though with an eye, and like a mirror he displays the image of beautiful things. Like a tongue, he explains the truth before students and brings the power of hidden things to light before ordinary people. Spiritual teaching is hidden within his lips, and he continually sprinkles the dew of mercy on the soil of humanity. He abundantly sows hope, love, and faith, and harvests fruits—blessings [?] that never perish. He brings the sound of the word of life into the outward senses, and the mind listens to the sound of words of kindness. The impulses need the fragrance of sweetness that revives the dead, and they refresh the dead body with the sound of resurrection. Like a trumpet, he constantly cries out in people's ears: “Look, people! Do not neglect [?].” Like a guide, he shows travelers the way: “Come, mortals, travel together toward the promise of life.” He constantly sails through the sea of humanity by means of his words, and earnestly warns everyone to guard the wealth of their soul. He stands aboard the ship of the Church, keeping watch night and day, and guards it against the damage caused by the wind of the wicked. He is a helmsman highly skilled amid the waves, and knows how to sail toward the appointed place of life without [?]. With the [?] of the Spirit, the ships of reason; he directs their course toward the harbor of life hidden on high. Because of his hope for things to come, he endures hardships, and everyone fears that the oil in their lamp might run out. He received a talent of the Spirit from his Lord to trade with, and he must place the silver of words on the soul's money-changing table. He learned from the King the art of forgiving wrongdoing, so that he would not be reluctant to forgive his fellow servants. The treasure of the Spirit is entrusted to his hands to administer, and he ought to provide wisely for those who look to him. His Lord gave him rational sheep to lead, so that he might pasture them in the life-giving meadows of the words of the Spirit. He is charged with leading sheep, lambs, and ewes, and people of every age—men, women, and children. The command that called him into his presence appointed him to serve humanity,

so that he might uproot error and sow the Creator's name throughout the earth. “Go out,” he said, “make disciples, proclaim, and baptize all nations: one Being, one Creator, three persons.” He must proclaim the three names in people's ears and initiate them in the name of the Being hidden from all. For this purpose priests are appointed on earth to serve as priests: to turn people from error to knowledge. Through [?] their words, people see the light of life, and through their labors they taste the sweetness of truth. He is like a mediator between God and human beings, and through him the soul’s sacrifices are offered before the Lord of all. Through him the riches of the Spirit are distributed to earthly people [?], and they cry out for strength to be strengthened for the service of truth. Everyone opens the gate of mercy before those who look on, and freely bestows forgiveness of wrongdoing on his fellow human beings. In water and the Spirit he casts them as though in a furnace, strips them of wrongdoing, and clothes them in garments of righteousness. He calls upon and implores the hidden Power to descend to him and give what is visible the power to give life. Those being born [?] become like a womb, and the power of grace is like seed that brings forth life. Body and soul descend together into the womb of the water, and they are born again, purified from uncleanness. Oh, how great is the wonder shown toward our race: through sinners it chose to make sinners righteous! Oh, the incomprehensible gift of the God of all, which through the poor distributed its riches to those who are poor! Oh, the decree—how powerful it is over everything he created—which gave the work of his hands authority to become like him! Through a human hand he opened his treasury to human beings, and people grew rich from the treasures of his divinity. He gave the keys [?] of his mercy to earthly beings [?] as to trustworthy people, and at all times they faithfully open the treasury of his mercy. A mortal holds the keys with [?] his lips, and with a tongue of flesh [?] he opens and closes the gate of hidden things. He buries people in the womb of the water as though in a grave, and brings back to new life those dead in wrongdoing.

By the Creator’s power he buries the dead and gives life to the dead, and spiritually brings people to birth as though from a womb. He raises spiritual infants by the power of the Spirit, and when they have grown, he offers them the food of maturity. With the food of [?] he nourishes bodily human beings, and the nourishment of those who are born corresponds to their birth. He continually prepares a living sacrifice before those who eat, and mixes and gives them the power of life to drink, for body and soul. He prepares and sets a table of life before their eyes, and depicts the mystery of death [?] and life in bread and wine. Through visible things he reveals the power of hidden things, and people live by eating bread and drinking wine. The outward senses see bread and wine, while the hidden movements within receive the power present in the visible things. The priest stands like a tongue to interpret, and his voice proclaims death and life to human beings. In bread and wine he reveals the body and blood of the King who died for everyone, came to life, and gave life to everyone through his cross. The bodily man stands in fear to minister, and asks for mercy upon himself and his race, that he may be worthy of mercy. He calls upon the Spirit to descend to him with power from him, to put power into the bread and wine to give life. Life dwells in the visible bread and wine, and they become food for short-lived mortals. He concludes his words in the name of the Being in three persons, and teaches people to cry out “Holy” with the spiritual beings. After his words, the people respond, “Holy, holy, holy is the [?], hidden from all and revealed to all.” He stretches out his hands and breaks the spiritual bread, and traces the symbol of the body and blood of him who died and rose again. With his hands he gives the King’s body to his [?], empowered by the strength of grace to give life. He gives the bread and says, “The body of Christ the King,” and gives the wine to drink, calling it “The precious blood.” O man of flesh, who carries fire without being burned! O mortal, who distributes life although he is mortal! Who permitted you, lowly dust, to hold fire? Who made you a distributor of life, son of the poor? Who taught you to hold fire in handfuls of flesh?

And who revealed to you wisdom hidden from you? It is not yours to perform these things that are above you. It is the helping power of the God of all that has raised your lowliness. He made hidden power dwell in you and strengthened your movements; and through you he [?] the power of his hidden mysteries to ears of flesh. Through his help you acquired the gift of giving life, and although you are dust, you hold a treasury of spiritual things. The priest of the Spirit has been made treasurer of the Spirit’s treasury, and spiritual things have been placed in his hands to distribute. A mortal holds the keys of heaven like a ruler, and binds and releases by the word of his mouth like the Creator. He binds wrongdoing with the chain of the word of his mouth, and in turn releases when someone turns away from wrongdoing. The command of the Creator’s power sets its seal upon his words, and he binds the wicked [?] the good when they have been justified. What a great wonder is the great love of the God of all, who gave the works of his hands authority to resemble him! His command alone rules over everything he created, and it belongs to him to bind and release as he wills. In grace he gave human beings the authority of his command, to make his love known—how greatly he loves the members of his household. He acts wisely when he shares what is his with his own people, so that through incentives he may draw his own people to belong to him. With glorious things he encourages people as though they were children, so that through his words they may acquire the rank that bestows life. Under the name of priesthood he opened the treasury of his great wealth, so that everyone might receive forgiveness of wrongdoing through a fellow human being. He is ready to gladden earthly people with the holiness of heaven, and he gave [?] as a pledge of the promise of his words. In the earthly sanctuary, the priests symbolically imitate that dwelling, and like a mirror they display an image of things to come.

They are set like guides on the road leading upward, and no one travels without them to the appointed gathering beyond. They serve as light on earth for those in darkness, and, as with salt, they give flavor to those who are tasteless. They continually cast the nets of their spoken words and catch people, drawing them from death to life. Through them, those dead in wickedness, whom error has buried, are raised, and through their words the dead see the light [?]. Through them the dead and the living are judged in both worlds, and the examination of human beings and angels is reserved for their authority. They judge spiritual and bodily beings, and demons are put to shame by the radiance of their conduct. If the radiance of their conduct accuses wickedness, how can people who have rejected their words be acquitted? If spiritual angels are judged through them, anyone who despises them deserves a double judgment. Everyone owes them a debt of love, for they ask mercy on everyone's behalf from the one who shows grace to all. Let their hearers repay them with the reward of love, for they [?] the necessities of spiritual life. Like fathers, let them show their love toward their children, and with spiritual food let them nourish their inner impulses rather than their bodily members. Our Lord calls them shepherds of rational sheep, and the nourishment, too, is spiritual, corresponding to the flock. The utterance addressed to Simon was spoken to them: they are to shepherd the rational sheep, lambs, and ewes. Priests of the churches, hear the words of that examination, and show the love that Simon showed toward our Savior. Shepherd purely, according to the command of the good shepherd, and care for the flock with the great love that befits his love. Look and consider how he bought the human flock with his blood and, upon the wood of the cross, wrote its deed of freedom from slavery. See how much he suffered from oppressors on behalf of his flock:

He scorned and disregarded every suffering so that it would not perish. He desired those who cherish his love to imitate his purpose and to follow in his footsteps along the path of his proclamation. The Father promised and pledged a reward to anyone who loves him: that he would be with him in the delight of life without end. Who, then, is the one whose love is true, whose disposition is wise, and who knows well how to guide his fellow servants? With an “Amen” he swore to the one who possesses and practices these things that he would entrust to his hands all the wealth of the kingdom above. Along with the reward for the one who managed his wealth well, he decreed punishment for the dishonest who received it and withheld what they owed. But if the wicked servant says that judgment is far away, his master will come and hold him accountable for his wrongdoing. Come, then, servants bought with blood more precious than everything; listen to the word of the one who frees our race from slavery. Come, consider the force of the meaning hidden in his words: along with reward, there is also torment without end. He encouraged the good with [?] the reward of things to come, and filled the insolent with dread of severe punishments. Let us therefore fear his words as true, and not grow careless, lest we be condemned with the guilty. His judgment is true, and the assurance of his words does not deceive. Let us not doubt his promises, lest we perish. Priests ought to observe these things more than anyone else, just as the rank they hold is more glorious than anyone else's. Anyone who knows his master's will and does not do it deserves lashes in proportion to the knowledge he possessed and disregarded. But whoever defrauds others insolently defrauds himself of the good things promised to him. He promised his own will the reward of things to come, and he is punished as someone who knew and yet sinned. A priest who sins faces a grave accusation and severe punishment. Both his torment and his exaltation are proportionate to his rank. I wished to praise the greatness of the rank called priesthood, but sorrow pierced me when I saw it diminished through ignorance. I marveled when I saw the greatness of the glory of those who excelled,

and I grieved and was distressed at the disgrace of those who sank low. Just as their authority had been greater than every other rank, so it became immeasurably lower than every other rank. The treasury of the Spirit had been entrusted to them to administer, but the fools despised it, not knowing how to discern the power of its greatness. The hidden command placed the keys of heaven in their hands, but the accursed priests shut the door before those entering. They had been authorized to forgive people's wrongdoing, but the wrongdoing of those who granted forgiveness became far worse than that of the defiled. The high priest called the priesthood light and salt when he bestowed it, but its light grew dark and its flavor became tasteless through those who received it. He summoned and called it to give life to mortal humanity, but look: it has itself died through shameful deeds. Good seed had been entrusted to it to sow in the earth, but the laborers ceased their work in the word of truth. It had gone out to meet the spiritual bridegroom, but the [?] fell asleep, and the light of their lamps went out. The oil of mercy ran out from the vessels of their deeds, and they received no mercy because they had not shown compassion and forgiven wisely. He called those who have no compassion foolish virgins: they guarded their bodies but were not purified from quarrelsomeness. What will someone gain by keeping his body pure if his mind is not cleansed of hateful things? What benefit will the [?] clothed with the title of priesthood receive if the inward deed does not [?] the outward title? The title of priesthood means a great work, not authority, and whoever approaches it is bound to act. Paul teaches whoever desires it how to approach it: whoever desires the office of elder desires work. The priests rejected the words of Paul, the chosen vessel; they desired authority and hated the labor that brings life. They loved the title because they loved earthly things; they despised deeds of worth and honored falsehood. They honored falsehood more than the truth that had honored them; through deceit they appeared admirable and received praise in the eyes of onlookers.

They received the gift that cannot be sold for earthly things, then took it and sold it for deceitful silver to those who were unworthy. For dead silver, they did not give the gift full of life; and dead people received it, people who had died in sin and had not been forgiven. They placed the staff of spiritual affairs in the hands of fools, and ignorant men stood at the head of the flock to lead it. An ignorant shepherd raised his staff over those like himself, and a man childish in understanding became the head of an infantile people. The weak man thought he was tending sheep, not rational beings [?], and he led them through earthly things as though they were speechless creatures. The fool imagined that he exercised dominion on earth, and he began demanding taxes from the flock like kings. He did not know the purpose of the title of his authority, nor had the flock gained an understanding of how to live. A blind man, blinded to knowledge, took hold of the blind, and they began traveling the road of error without understanding. Without knowledge the fool led his companions, and he traveled the road without knowledge, as though in darkness. In him was fulfilled what is written in [?]: that the priest would be without knowledge, just like the people. The priest [?]—they agreed with one another in improper things, lost the way, and stopped running toward righteousness. Justice too, seeing that they had strayed beyond proper order, sharpened her sword against the wickedness of their deeds. She saw the wickedness of the priests [?] and the flock and was grieved; she shut the door so that mercy could not plead with her on our behalf. Human supplication stands outside the door of mercy, while mercies are held back before the door by the just command. Come, then, people, let us plead over our wickedness while we are alive, so that we may not be condemned by a sentence without end. Come, let us build ourselves a fence of mercy before Justice, so that perhaps she may be reconciled and erase our wickedness from her book. Let the priests act as mediators through their words:

And let them offer the sorrows of their minds as a bribe. It is their duty to offer sacrifices of love and to make atonement for the wickedness of others and of themselves. They are authorized to open the door before sinners, like treasurers of the great treasury that has no bounds. They shall be like a tongue to interpret, and shall breathe out their spirit before the Judge who examines wrongdoing. Let the priest proclaim this message to his flock: “Repent, sinners, so that mercy may heal all your sins.” Let him continually sow the hope of life in everyone's ears, and apply the medicine of repentance to the soul's pains. Let him suffer for everyone and grieve for everyone with discernment, and, like Paul, regard his companions' sufferings as his own. A bond has been drawn up against him for the debts of his fellow human beings, and he is obliged to repay the debt of love to the one who honors him. Mercy has raised him to a high rank above his companions. In keeping with his rank, let him demonstrate labor worthy of his title. His title declares that he has been appointed to serve as priest on behalf of others, and he ought to live up to his title through his deeds. The silver of mercy is entrusted to his hands to distribute. If he hoards it, he will hear the declaration that he is an evil servant. The man who received a talent and hid it also thought he had escaped, but the decree of hidden judgment caught him through his own reply. His master too called him an evil servant, in keeping with his wickedness, because he received freely but did not give freely as he had received. Let priests listen discerningly to that declaration, and invest the silver of the word of life in their hearers. Let the hearers also receive the seed of their words, so that they may not be condemned with the defrauders who received and then withheld what they owed. Let them listen lovingly to the voice of correction in their words,

so that they may not be reproached when they are punished for their sins. Let everyone gladly accept the correction of his conduct, and let him himself implore the physician to apply medicine to his sore. The priest is a physician who heals the pains within the soul, and whoever is sick in mind ought always to run to him. He knows how to apply spiritual medicine to thoughts, and he cuts away wrongdoing with the surgical blade of divine mercy. You who are sick in soul, come, draw near to those who have knowledge, and reveal the blemishes of your minds to the hidden will. You who travel on the road, come, join the wise, and journey well toward the appointed meeting with life without end.
On the Dedication of the Church
Discourse Thirty-three. Again on the Dedication of the Church. Response: Church of the nations, worship Christ, who planted you on earth and enrolled you in heaven, my brothers.
The Son of God held a great wedding feast for his Church, and invited and summoned all nations to the day of her banquet. The radiant Sun betrothed the daughter of darkness to himself,

and shed his splendid beauty upon her face, and she clothed herself in light. The rich one who never becomes poor loved the daughter of the poor. He entrusted his great wealth to her hands, so that through it she might be exalted. Christ the bridegroom, in his great love, stooped down from his heights. He willingly became a bridegroom to mortals and exalted them. The Lord on high stooped down from his heights toward those below. He became a bridegroom to the defiled nations and made them holy. The bridegroom, the Son of the Most High, betrothed the Church of the nations to himself. He united her to himself in his love and raised her head among her enemies. An exiled woman, abandoned, crushed, and brought low, became the companion of the Son of the Exalted One who dwells in the heights. A dark woman, wrapped in the darkness of demon worship—the Light loved her, called her to himself, and filled her with light. The Son of God called and gathered the woman who was scattered and distracted by empty things, and made her his own. The lover of all loved that wayward daughter of foreigners. He gathered her to himself and sowed the teaching of life in her ears. The finder of all sought that lost woman who had been lost among the powers of error. He led her and brought her into the sheepfold of life. The honored one betrothed the exposed and disgraced woman to himself. He made her chaste through his radiance and covered her shame with the robe of his glory. The Holy One chose the companion of demons and servant of evil spirits. He showered her with his love and washed her great wickedness away from her. He saw that she was black, covered in grime, and ugly in appearance. He brought her down into the water, washed her, and cleansed her of her filth. He prepared for her a bath full of life. He washed and bathed her, and cleansed her face of its ugliness. With living water he washed away the filth of the stained woman. He poured holy oil over her head and made her face joyful. With oil and water he washed her body and purified her soul.

And he gave her the name “Holy Church, full of beauty.” He stripped away her reputation for ugliness along with her offenses. He clothed her in beauty and gave her the title “Chosen Church.” The glorious bridegroom called her by the beautiful name the prophets had given her in their revelations, on the day of her bathing. The prophets of the Spirit called her “Church” in their utterances, and in her they sang praise to her Lord from all nations. The righteous prophets gave her the name “Great Church.” The bridegroom came and confirmed her name in baptism. He washed her with water, marked her with oil, and showered her with love. He took a robe of light and clothed her in it in holiness. In his living name, and in the name of his Father and of the Holy Spirit, he sealed the bride and perfected her spiritual beauty. He placed a crown of light on the head of the glorious woman. He broke his body for her, mixed his blood for her, and gladdened her heart. Through his suffering he freed her; through his slaying he redeemed her; through his death he purchased her. Through his resurrection he poured spiritual life upon her. He built her a bridal chamber from the rays of his Father’s light. He who pours out life invited the ages and generations to her wedding feast. The Church, the bride of the crucifixion, clothed herself in light, and from her rays her beloved ones shone—the children of her inheritance. The bridegroom’s love cannot be expressed by speakers, and the bride’s affection cannot be set down in writing. The bridegroom’s love for the bride nailed him to the wood, and the bride’s affection drove her to the cross after the bridegroom. What bridegroom endured the cross for his bride except Christ, whose great love cannot be expressed? And what bride loved a bridegroom hanging on the wood except the Church, whose story surpasses what speakers can tell? For his Church the Son of God died on the cross, and because of his death the Church loved him and joined herself to him. The slain bridegroom and the redeemed bride joined one another, and now ages and generations rejoice at their wedding feast. The bridegroom placed his beloved bride in the lofty heights and showed her beauty to those in heaven and those on earth. He invited the ages and called the generations to the wedding feast of life.

He seated them at the banquet before the king’s daughter, the holy bride. Righteous prophets, glorious apostles, priests and kings, and slain martyrs he called to the wedding feast of the holy Church. The wedding feast is great; the bridegroom is Christ, and the bride is the Church. The wedding companions are apostles, prophets and martyrs, priests and kings. All peoples, ages and generations recline at her banquet, and all delight in the body and blood of the bridegroom, Christ [?]. The bridegroom’s body is living food at his Church’s wedding feast, and his blood is spiritual drink in his banqueting hall. It is a great wedding feast at which all the ages recline, and the heavenly hosts move about there to serve. It is a living banquet, with life flowing between its rows, and its guests drink the new life that the bridegroom has mixed. The song of the Spirit now rises loudly at the wedding feast of life, and its delight overflows with joy beyond expression. The banquet guests sing of the bridegroom’s beauty without ever having enough, and with their songs of praise they honor the holy crown. The voices of human beings and angels mingle, and the banqueting house is filled with songs of the Spirit. The chief of singers, King David, carries his lyre; he plays and sings of the Church’s blessedness and the bridegroom’s beauty. Christ the bridegroom and the Church the bride are on his lips, and now the wedding companions take spiritual delight in his song. “Listen, O Church, bride of light,” said [?] David, “and I will tell you of the beauty of the bridegroom whom your heart loves. “Christ the bridegroom is more beautiful in appearance than other human beings, and mercy is poured upon his holy lips. “He is blessed forever; his splendor and glory overcame tyrants. His arrows are sharp, and he killed his enemies by his cross. “By his death he cast down sin, death, and Satan too, and he returned victorious from battle, his bow held high.” His throne is established at the right hand of his exalted Father. His dominion is clothed in righteousness and does not change.

With the good oil of his divinity he anointed his humanity, and with joy he poured it over his life-giving body. The garments of his bodily existence are perfumed with sweet fragrance, and he dwells in the heights at the right hand of his hidden Father. My Lord is the bridegroom, and the Lord said, “Sit at my right hand until I make all your enemies a footstool for your feet.” He is the high priest and the living sacrifice that atones for sins, and he remains unchanged in his high priesthood and his priestly service. In the splendors of holiness he was begotten of his Father beyond time, and in his humanity he was born of Mary in holiness. All kings worship him with their offerings, and all nations serve him in everlasting servitude. His holy name endures forever, together with his dominion. His name existed before the sun and does not change. In him all nations are blessed, and they praise him, for from among them comes the holy Church, the bride of light. David marveled at the bridegroom’s indescribable beauty, and he began to sing his exalted praise with the children. He saw him on earth, clothed in our body, and marveled at him. He began to cry out and proclaim his glory and his dominion. “O Lord, O Master, how glorious is your name throughout the earth! See, in heaven your praise thunders from the heavenly beings.” David sang these verses full of wonder to the holy Church, the betrothed of the Sun of Righteousness. He filled the ears of the bride of light with the bridegroom’s beauties, and kindled the fire of his love as a blaze within her mind. Isaiah stood up and began to cry out at the wedding feast of life: “Emmanuel is the bridegroom whom the Church has loved. Beyond the natural order, the virgin bore him without sexual union. He is the Lord, mighty in power, who does not change. His dominion brings peace and tranquility to all nations, and there is no end to his great peace or to his kingdom.” The aged Jacob raised his voice amid the rejoicing:

“This is the bridegroom for whom all the righteous waited. This is the one who came and brought an end to the prophets and the kings of the people. This is the bridegroom who suffered on the cross for his Church, and with his purifying blood washed the robe of his bodily existence. This is the bridegroom whose teeth are far whiter than milk, and who shines all over with the glory in which he clothed himself at the resurrection.” All the prophets, the heads of households, stood up with their songs, and the bridegroom’s beauties filled the ears of the bride of light. One was crying out, “Look, he comes forth from Ephrathah to shepherd the people, save the nations, and reign over all.” Another proclaims, “The Messiah comes and endures death. He uproots Zion and builds the Church through his crucifixion.” Another sings: “Arise, shine, bride of light, for your great light has come: Christ the bridegroom.” Look, his light has dawned, brightened your eyes, and made your face joyful. Look, his glory rests upon your head and adorns you. The kings of the earth come to you with their offerings, and look, the hosts of the nations run lovingly to you. Another cries out with joy: “Rejoice, daughter of the nations, in place of the daughter of Zion, for look, Christ the king comes to you and makes you glad.” Righteous and upright, humble in his love and full of salvation, he loves you in place of the Hebrew woman who plotted his piercing. The singing grew strong, and the voices of prophecy multiplied at the wedding feast of the Church, the betrothed of Jesus, the beautiful bridegroom. The diviner heard the sound of rejoicing and began to proclaim: “He is the great star, the bridegroom on high of the holy Church.” He is the exalted head who arose from the offspring of the house of Israel, and he is the head of all the nations, to which I belong. David changed to other melodies in his songs and began to sing of the beauty of the bride purchased with blood. Look, the king’s daughter stood in glory at the right hand of the glorious bridegroom, who came and redeemed her through his [?].

O king’s daughter, whose glory comes entirely from the royal house! In her chastity she is radiant, adorned, and full of beauty. The beauty of the king’s bride is not outward. Within, she is adorned with the beauty of the bridegroom who died for her. Through his love, the love of the bridegroom, the Church is adorned and full of beauty, and faith, hope, and love are poured over her face. Her clothing is adorned with the fine gold of faith, and upon her head is placed the beautiful crown of holiness. She is the daughter of the nations who forgot her people and her father’s house, and inclined her ear to the voice of the bridegroom who died for her. The bridegroom saw that she was truly burning with love for him. He longed for her lovely beauty and made her his own. She worshiped her Lord and followed her Savior in love, and look, the kings of the earth seek her favor with offerings. The son of Jesse saw the perfect love of the bridegroom and bride, and added melodies to his songs concerning the Church. The great Church drawn from the nations will surround you, bridegroom, and for love of her you will return to the heights above. Before you is the one song of praise of the great Church, and in her all the families of the nations you redeemed will worship you. Through you the feet of the nations stand upright, and within your Church they bless you in righteousness. In your great Church I will thank you, my Lord, rejoicing, and among the thronging assemblies of the nations I will sing to you. Our Lord, I proclaimed your righteousness in your great Church, and I did not restrain my lips from proclaiming your salvation and your faithfulness. My Lord, I have not despised your righteousness and your faithfulness among the nations, your great Church purchased with your blood. You are worthy of worship, bridegroom, for you remembered your Church, which you acquired long ago. My Lord, do not withdraw the right hand of your love from within your Church. Your faithfulness is now proclaimed, beautiful bridegroom, in the great church, whose beauty shines among the saints. God stands in the great church among the saints. He is great and awesome, glorious and exalted above those around him. You who are ordained in the church, praise him in the church, the church of the nations—Christ the bridegroom, who redeemed the church of the nations by his cross.

I will thank you, my Lord, uprightly and with all my heart, in your great church, where those upright in praise [?] are gathered. “Praise the Lord with a new song,” he said, “for his praise now rises from the righteous in the great church.” The son of Jesse saw the assemblies of the nations in the holy church and taught them a new song at the church’s wedding feast. All you nations, come, clap your hands in the church, your mother, and sing praise to him who in his mercy redeemed your lives. With these beautiful strains of the church, the son of Jesse sang at the banquet that the Son of God prepared for his church. Now glorious voices thunder within the holy church: the prophets [?] and apostles, who sing [?] within her spiritually. The voices of prophecy and apostleship mingle, and the church is filled with the glorious thunder of lyres. Now great Paul’s voice rings out like a trumpet. He cries out and proclaims the lofty beauty of the holy church. Her spiritual orders are woven upon his tongue, and her life-filled beauties are depicted in his verses. The song of the herald of the nations rings out in the holy church, and angels and human beings marvel at his melodies. All the apostles sing with him in their own languages at this wedding feast that Christ the bridegroom prepared for his church. The bridegroom’s good news thunders with life at his church’s wedding feast, and from it the bridegroom’s attendants drink new life. Great is the wedding feast, wonderful the banquet, and sweet the drink. The bridegroom rejoices, the bride exults, and delight runs high. The chief priests and radiant priests, the church’s invited guests, fill their mouths with songs of the Spirit at the wedding feast of life. O church, betrothed to the Sun of Righteousness! Your glory now rises high, and your crown shines among the stars [?]. Your wedding feast, full of delights, continues through the generations, and the peoples and nations in every region delight in it. The holy church, purchased with blood, is established on earth, while her lofty head is in heaven, with God. Every day her great banquet and its delights increase through the nations that come from every region to rejoice within her.

Her building rests upon the foundation of faith, and the blasts and words of all her adversaries cannot shake her. Kings threatened her but could not shake her firm resolve. Now the head of the blessed church is crowned with victory. The holy church stood between the crucifiers and the pagans, and she clothed herself in glory on her right and on her left. She overcame teachings and destroyed the factions of those in error [?]. Now her head is held high, and her adversaries lie beneath her feet. Her gates are open to everyone who comes to take refuge in her. She is full of light, and her children resound with songs. Kings hurry and run to bow before her footstool, and all the nations gather at her gates with offerings. Her walls are high and cannot be overcome by persecutors. Look, the promise of her great peace is recorded in the Gospel. The church of the nations is redeemed through slaughter and purchased with blood [?]. Beneath the wings of the cross of light, her beloved ones dwell. Our Savior built her upon the rock of faith, and the gates of Sheol and the barriers of death cannot overcome her. Her foundation is laid upon the confession of the chief of the disciples, and her walls rise high in good hope and pure love. She is established on earth, yet her completion is in heaven. The authority of the bride of light embraces the heights and the depths. A church on earth and a church above, yet one church: the holy church and the church of the firstborn that is to come. For she is one church whose beauty shines in both worlds, because the bridegroom who betrothed her has exalted her name in both worlds. She shines on earth and gathers the nations into her house of refuge. And look, in heaven her walls extend in courses of fire. In the world that passes away, she is a harbor for every generation. In the world to come, angels and human beings rejoice in her. As soon as this course of mortal life ends, her beauty shines in the lofty realm of the immortals. Here she delights in the body and blood of the bridegroom, her Lord, and there she rejoices in his glorious radiance, wrapped in flame. Here, through the sacrifice of his body and blood, she makes atonement for her children.

And there she reveals his human nature to all her beloved ones. Here and there, the church and her children will delight in him. Here she resounds with the books of the Spirit that the righteous wrote, and there she rejoices in their very persons, clothed in light. Here are the books of prophecy and apostleship, and there are the children of light gathered together in person. Here they thunder through their books within the sanctuary, and when they are raised, they gather to her in the realm of light. Above she is exalted in that glory which cannot be expressed, and the assemblies of her children delight in her together with the spiritual beings. My mind marvels at the lofty beauty of the holy church, and I have no words adequate to speak of her splendor. Her story is beyond the wise and the eloquent, and she is the fountain of all the wisdom [?] in the house of God. She is wrapped in light and clothed in light, the bride betrothed to light. She is bathed in light, and her beautiful light cannot be described. Worlds and nations have honored her from the beginning, and the books of the Spirit thunder about her throughout all generations. The Lord of the prophets laid her foundations and established her building. In his blood he wrote the document of her peace and victory. The apostles built her through their life-filled preaching. They died for her and raised her walls through their deaths. Priests and kings increased the beauty of the lady of treasures, and all the peoples thundered with their voices in songs to her. Great are her bridal gifts, and splendid is the wedding feast of the King's bride. Her treasuries are full of great wealth that cannot be exhausted. Inside the upper room, when she entered the house of God, the bridegroom bestowed on her his body and blood and his great love. The apostles, the bridegroom's attendants, also gave her their bridal gifts: the sufferings and deaths they endured at the hands of persecutors for her sake. The prophets offered their revelations concerning her, and through their books they danced before her spiritually. The martyrs lovingly offered her the blood from their necks, and the priests came and offered their ranks in the sanctuary of atonement. Kings gave her their dominions as a bridal gift,

and, wearing their crowns, they bowed joyfully before her footstool. Men and women, old and young, and people of every stature brought and offered her voices of praise as a bridal gift. Great is the wealth of the Son's holy Church, and from her all the ranks and gatherings of her children become rich. Those who have passed away, those who now stand, and those yet to come—the ranks of their dominions are bathed in her great beauty. Her lofty temples blaze with light full of delight, and her sanctuary of atonement is clothed in splendor and holiness. Within her is established the altar, the symbol of the tomb of Christ the bridegroom. Within her is placed the cross, the sign of his death that pours forth life. Within her the body and blood are distributed for the forgiveness of sins: the living sacrifice of that high priest who bought her with his blood. The tent of meeting, whose time had ended, pronounced her blessed, for she brought the blessings of God's house to fulfillment without end. The priests of the prefiguration gave honor to the priests of the reality, for the prefiguration passed away, and they honored the reality of the holy Church. The speechless sacrifices prescribed by the Law bowed from afar before the rational sacrifice of the Church, the bride betrothed to the Son. The dead sacrifices reached their fulfillment in the living sacrifice within the sanctuary of the Church, the mother of truth. The synagogue went out because she hated the bridegroom to whom she had been betrothed. The Church entered and became the bride whose love is true. The synagogue crucified him, and the Church of the nations received life through his crucifixion. Now she delights in his body and his blood, which forgives sins. See, the dowry of the bride of light is upon her lips: the body and blood of the living bridegroom, the Son of the Most High. See, the King's bride rules in the four quarters of the world, and the dominion of the glorious one embraces the heights and the depths. The four quarters bear the name of her who is full of beauty, for her bridegroom and Lord gave her a name in four letters. Blessed are you, Church, for your Lord loved you and redeemed your life. He poured out great peace upon your paths and your ways. Blessed are you, Church, for the Sun of Righteousness loved you. He shed magnificent light in your palaces and filled you with glory.

Blessed are you, Church, whom the incorruptible light has chosen; he has exalted you and set you on high, far above, in the heavens [?]. Blessed are you, Church, whom the bridegroom, the good Lord, has betrothed; he has invited both worlds to your wedding feast, which is full of blessings. Blessed are you, Church, whom the Son of God has purchased with his blood; he has redeemed your life from slavery to the worship of idols. Blessed are you, Church, in whom [?] the Father has delighted and whom the Son has betrothed; the Holy Spirit has perfected your spiritual beauty. Blessed are you, Church, whom kings’ daughters have called blessed, because the bridegroom who owns heaven and earth has loved you. Blessed are you, Church, for look, your bridal chamber [?] is prepared in heaven, and the promised blessings are arranged within it, without dominion [?]. Blessed are you, Church: although your lowly origin is from the earth, look, your beauties [?] are portrayed in heaven, in the house of God. Blessed are you, Church: the Lord of blessings has poured every beauty upon your head; he has loved you, betrothed you, and made your name great. Blessed are you, Church, whose festivals resound in the four quarters of the world; his holy name is exalted in you, as he promised. Bride of blessings, accept my words as an offering, and shelter my life beneath your wings from harm. Our Lord, grant that I may not be excluded from that blessedness which the Church and her children await on the day of your appearing. Praise [?] to you, bridegroom [?], from your Church, purchased with your blood.
On “In the Beginning” and on the Being of God
Discourse Thirty-Four: On “In the Beginning” and on the Being of God

I heard “In the beginning,” which Moses wrote before everything else, and I wished to travel along the path of his words toward the beginning. I saw that he had inscribed five letters at the head of the line, and my mind advised me to meditate on the opening of his book. He hewed the letters like stones with the [?] of the Spirit, and built upon them the great house of the heights and the depths. He ground the divine message like pigments in the words of his mouth, and painted the creatures he had not seen as they were [?]. He composed, like a picture, the world that came into being in the beginning, and took it and set it before viewers so that they might look at it. The painter [?] made a great design through his art: he painted created things, and then the image of the Creator’s name. He first showed the king’s array to the king’s servants, and then lifted the curtain at the doorway of the royal palace. He laid the expression “In the beginning” like a foundation, and above it he built “God created,” like a builder. “In the beginning,” he said, “God created heaven and earth.” On this side [?] is creation, and beyond it is the Lord of creation. He mentioned creation before the Creator, and then the Creator—not because creation was earlier, but to make known the time when it came into being. He made its coming into being known by writing “In the beginning” first, and revealed concerning the Creator that he existed without a beginning. The Being who brought creation into existence is without beginning, and he continues without end in his enduring order. The mind can say only that he exists, that he exists; but as to how he exists, the door is shut against its investigation. No eye made by his hands can see his nature, nor can his creatures contemplate him as fully as they desire.

He is without composition, without limit, and invisible; he does not change from what he is into its opposite. His nature is above changes and above those who see, and among created beings there is none whose mind can adequately express his greatness. The Nature above all holds [?] in the heights and depths, and everything that came into being from him is contained within him. The creation that he made from nothing is filled with him. This is the wonder: when nothing existed, he created everything. At his command the great world stands upon nothing. Look at the marvel: everything is set upon nothing! Through the power of life he reaches beings both rational and speechless, and in these very beings is the demonstration of the greatness of his power. Created beings cry out about his incomprehensible greatness, and through their actions they reveal the power of his creative activity. Oh, his identity cannot be grasped by investigators! However much they investigate, the inquiry into him lies beyond the limit. He has no limit, nor can words bring inquiry into him to an end. The person who pursues an inquiry about him grows weary. Stop, investigator! Do not overreach yourself in investigating the Hidden One. Know your own nature and acknowledge the greatness of your Maker. If you wish to inquire, pursue an inquiry fitting for the Limitless One: how he is one equal nature in three persons. Inquire how there is a beginning in the nature: fatherhood, being begotten, and procession. Yet even here, let us not investigate how it is through probing inquiry, but through the love that befits the learner. It is fitting to inquire into the divine Being with love, and beautiful to meditate on his hiddenness without probing. Therefore, the person who seeks to learn properly is not blameworthy, but rather the person who strings words together in contention. I entered the house of the laws of the King of kings to learn, and to see the order of the royal household that is invisible to me. I did not enter where I entered to scrutinize the Hidden One, but to hear a new discourse about his hiddenness. A man wrote a new discourse with the pen of the Spirit, and I sought to learn the force of the meaning hidden in his words.

A herald expounded “In the beginning” among [?], and I wished to know the reason for his proclamation. At the beginning of his statements I saw the expression “In the beginning” appear, and after it the name of the Creator who created in the beginning. I heard the name of God, who created creation in the beginning, and my mind urged me to inquire lovingly into his name. His name increased within me the fire of his name, so that I might know his name; and now I am ready to call him by the name that befits his name. The son of Amram called him God and Creator of creation; and look, I too am justified in calling him what he called him. I agree with the Hebrew that he is God of all; and I praise the work of his hands for declaring that he is the Creator. I am certain that he is the self-existent One without beginning; and I speak no falsehood in saying that his enduring existence has no end. I accept that the nature of his being has no limits; and I believe that he does not fall within the scope of sight. My mind bears witness that he does not change from what he is; and my [?] cries out that he is not subject to weaknesses. That he possesses, along with his being, knowledge of what happens is written in my mind as on tablets, and cannot be erased. That he knew how everything would happen before it happened—I proclaim this before earthly beings and the peaceful ones. That within his nature there are equal persons, equal with him—let heaven and earth cry out with my mouth that this is so. That he is Father, Son, and Spirit, one being—let those who speak and those who are mute put their signatures to the document of my words. That he is Father, that the Son is offspring, and that the Spirit is self-existent—let human beings and spiritual beings walk along the path of my confession. That between the Father, the Son, and the Spirit there is no [?] or sign—even if there were another creation, it would be too small to confess this. They are not split apart from one another by distinction; among created beings there is no one who can say how great that equality is.

Although they are three, they exist in unity; no tongue can adequately praise that being. When I said “three,” I did not mean three self-existent beings, but three persons who are equal in being. I said that there is one being, and I say it again; and within that being are three persons who are not divided. To distinguish the persons, the numbering [?], one after another, so that everyone may know that the order of their persons is real. The order of their names proclaims a manifest truth: everything the Father has, the Son and the Holy Spirit also have. Their nature and authority are one, and their will is one; there is no distinction of greater or lesser between one and another. Within the divine being there is nothing inferior to the divine being; for wherever there is divine being, there is no further rank of greater or lesser. The Father's fatherhood does not precede his offspring; nor, again, is the Son's creation [?] inferior to his begetter. The Spirit is not less than either the Father or the offspring, whether in being or in authority over every creature. They are one, even though they are placed one after another; they are three, even though the nature within them is one. They are three because of the order of their names; and again, they are one because their nature is equal in its nature. One is not distinguished from another by separation and division, but by name [?] and number, without confusion. Here is a demonstration of what I have said in the way they are constituted: there is something which, although it is one, has something within it. Look at the orb of the great sun, which shines on everything: although it is one, there are light and heat in it. The sun’s orb and its rays have one nature. Neither does the orb precede its rays, nor do its rays precede it. Light and heat are contained in it, and it in both of them. Although they are one, they are three in their distinct properties. The sun’s orb, its light, and its heat are three; yet the three are also known as one, without separation.

The orb has never been seen without rays, nor have they shone out from its bosom without heat. It is as it is, in the order of its unity, with the powers that accompany it in an unbroken constancy. Like a child being born, radiance comes out from within its bosom. Yet although it comes out, it does not come out by being severed from it. In the manner of the Spirit, it possesses the power of heat, which dwells within it and comes out from it without changing place. Praise to you in the heights and depths, hidden Being, who created the worlds above and below by the command of your power. Look: in created things there is a demonstration of the power of your divinity. They travel and dwell without moving from one place to another. The two powers in the orb travel without traveling, and dwell with everything without moving from their place. The power of their activity passes over everything and through everything, and its swiftness is not hindered by the distance it extends over all things. If the sun, a created work, is so wonderful in its construction, who would not marvel at the power of the Maker, who cannot be bounded? His extent is not confined by the limits of finite things, nor can those who inquire comprehend what they seek concerning him. If anyone wishes to pour out words of contradiction, let him pour them out, then, and explain to us these things that belong to us. Let him explain how the soul dwells within the limbs, hidden from everyone, while the power of its activity is evident. How does it, too, possess two powers in its nature, which are both within it and outside it without separation? How does its life-giving power run through all the senses, without its swiftness being hindered by solid bodies? How does the word that comes from it travel outside the body, without becoming distant either from the soul or from anyone? How is the whole inquiry both within it and outside it? And however much we inquire, the investigation concerning it cannot be comprehended. Who has ever seen it through the perception of the outward senses? Who has grasped it and examined it with eyes of flesh? If there is something within us that is beyond our examination, why do we weary ourselves pursuing an inquiry that cannot be pursued? The hidden inquiry concerning the divine Being cannot be pursued. Whoever pursues it, even if he searches, only goes astray.

Let us seek through faith alone, so that we may believe—and even this not through investigation, but through love. Through love it is possible to inquire into the hidden nature: how it exists and has within it three equal [?]. Whoever seeks him rightly seeks him as the Father, and it is fitting to confess that he has a Son and a Spirit who comes from him. It is fitting for created beings always to acknowledge the Creator’s power, for when they did not exist, he fashioned them out of nothing. Nothing existed when he fashioned everything out of nothing, and because he willed it in his love, everything came into being out of nothing. He alone existed before everything and beyond everything, and when it pleased him, something came into being for him—something great. The things that came into being were present with his being, not by nature, but traced within him in love. The worlds that came into being afterward were pictured within him, and he had counted them: how many there would be, how they would be, and when they would come into being. It was not a new thought for him to fashion things afterward, nor was it within time that he considered time and then made it. He established an order for the work of his hands, determining when it would come into being, although from his perspective it was already made and complete before it existed. From the beginning that has no beginning, he had resolved to reveal the power of his creative activity through the work of his hands. The all-wise one wisely made everything he made, and no one knows how to fathom the power of his wisdom. The fountain of love lovingly revealed his love, and none among created beings can repay the debt of his love. The one full of knowledge skillfully fashioned the world, and no tongue is capable of describing his craftsmanship. The beginning of his creative work is full of great wonder, and the world is too small to look closely and [?] at it. Even if there were worlds multiplied a thousand thousand times, they would be far too small to behold creation as it was being fashioned. If the heavenly hosts had been created before its formation, they would have been astounded as it was fashioned out of nothing. If they understood how everything suddenly came into being, their power to marvel would have failed them. How great, then, was that command! He commanded, and they came into being, and its swiftness was not delayed by any great interval.

How, then, did heaven and earth arise out of nothing? And how could that nothing bear something? It was not nothing that bore the weight of what came into being, but the prompting of that command: he commanded, and it came into being. The hidden will that rules over everything suddenly commanded, and everything stood upon nothing, when nothing existed. He stretched out heaven like a garment above everything, and spread out the earth like a foundation beneath everything. He made spiritual beings possessing immeasurable power, and numbered them, though numbering them is exceedingly difficult. He gave a sign, and the mass of air was fashioned, light-winged; it suddenly flew and occupied its domain in the four quarters. He made the waters flow, gathered up the fire, spread out darkness, and covered his work with the hours of night as with a garment. He covered the earth with a garment of darkness when it first came into being, like a painter who paints an image and then reveals it. At evening the Lord of the world painted the world; at morning he removed the covering that lay over it. Like a picture, he assembled and made heaven and earth, and called the rational beings [?] to come and see the splendor of its beauty. All night he concealed the beauty of his craftsmanship, and did not wish to reveal how he spoke and everything came into being. A great silence lay over everything while he arranged everything, and both the rational beings and the speechless beings were still. For twelve hours he prolonged the silence over everything, and when it was over, he made his voice heard: “Let there be light.” The Lord of creation cried out with a new voice within creation, and the ranks of heavenly beings trembled at the greatness of his voice. He sounded his voice like a trumpet throughout the inhabited world, and the spiritual beings gathered and came to listen to him. For their sake, the one who has no voice made a voice heard, to teach them that his command had formed them and everything else. Through a sound [?] he instructed those endowed with speech, so that they would know that he had formed everything from nothing.

He made them hear a voice resembling the movement within them, and roused them to contemplate the formation of light. They had been as though sunk in sleep all night, and they stirred from their stillness through the sound that rang out on earth. Great astonishment had lain upon them before this voice, and they had been wondering how they had come into being when they had not existed. In their inward movements they were thinking about themselves and everything else: who could have fashioned their existence and that of everything? The Creator’s voice, which rang out on earth, became their teacher and taught them a new book that they had not known. As though for little children, he wrote a sound in place of letters, and taught them to read the written words: “Let there be light.” He set the voice before their eyes like a model to copy, and they began crying out, “Blessed is the Creator who created light!” “Let there be light!” cried the one who has no voice, and the word went into effect without delay. Suddenly beautiful light dawned from nothing, and it pursued the darkness like a mighty warrior pursuing someone weaker than himself. Darkness fled and hid in the narrow recesses at the ends of the earth, and the Watchers marveled at the greatness of the power that had given it strength. They marveled not at it, but at the power of its light: how it had overcome the darkness and driven it away so swiftly. Swiftly darkness fled from the inhabited world, and swiftly the radiant light entered and reigned on earth. Like a bridegroom, it reclined in the bridal chamber of the heights and the depths, and illuminated the world with the beautiful hue of its radiance. In gathering after gathering, the spiritual beings stood to see its beauty, and they could not get enough of praising its Maker. The sight of its light was pleasing to their minds, and more pleasing to them than its light was the command that had made it. They contemplated the splendor of its beauty without ever having their fill, for it too joined them in glorifying the works [?] of his hands. He created it, bringing it into being from nothing as he pleased. Then he turned and praised it—not for the sake of praising it, but to teach. He praised the light to teach the heavenly hosts: if he himself praised it, how much more should they give praise!

They praised and marveled, acclaimed and exalted its maker. They gave thanks and worshiped, believed in and acknowledged the power of the divine Being. Through the shining things, the spiritual beings learned the power of the divine Being, and they all agreed that everything came into existence through one power. He extended the light’s rule for twelve hours, then turned to the darkness, telling it to come and enter the place where it had been. The spiritual beings marveled at evening just as they had at morning: how the light departed in the same orderly way that the darkness had departed! The watchers saw a marvelous sight: mute natures maintaining order like rational beings. In darkness and light they contemplated the Creator’s power, and how wise he was in ordering the works of his hands. Through these silent things, they too acquired great discipline, and bowed their necks to bear the yoke of the Creator’s name. One day [?], night and day [?], in darkness and light.
