Suddenly he made a voice ring out, like that first voice. Like a messenger, the command went out from the Hidden One: let there be a firmament, a heaven resembling that first one. It was put into effect, and the firmament came into being amid the waters. It stood in the middle, like a canopy above the earth. He fashioned it from the element of water and made it solid, so that it could bear water upon its back. [?] And a portion remained on the earth equal to the one above. Here too the spiritual beings saw a great wonder: a garment of water carrying water and rising swiftly. They wondered and marveled at the craftsmanship of the command that spread it out: how effortlessly he stretched it over [?] the regions! It was worthy of wonder, and they marveled with understanding at how he hardened the fluid waters so that they carried water. Did he perhaps stretch it out below, over the surface of the earth, and then raise it? In that case, the angels, the light, and the air rose with it. And if it reaches from the edges, as it does, nothing remained that he did not enclose within it on high. Otherwise, how could this solid vessel have been raised, with dense substances passing through it, without its splitting apart?

The inquiry into how it came into being and was raised is very difficult. No one knows it except the commanding will that spoke and brought it into being. My mind wore me out investigating how it happened, but I could not grasp it. Still it wears me out, suggesting that perhaps I might grasp something. As far as my thoughts could reach, I reflected as a created being can reflect: perhaps he stretched out this vessel in the place above. And perhaps the command took up the whole portion of water, and after raising it, his commanding will hardened it, and it supported itself. Perhaps, when it rose, he suddenly stretched it out above everything, while everything below remained on the earth as it had been. Its formation took place swiftly, without delay, and no mouth can say how swift it was. The command that stretched it out on high was very swift; even the swiftest thing is much slower than it. That utterance which he spoke, and the heavens above came into being, formed it in that same manner, from nothing. The first came into being from nothing at a slight signal, and this one from something, just as swiftly. He established a beautiful order for his creation, [?] in his being, and wisely created from something and from nothing. He taught the works of his hands through the order of his creative activity, and for their instruction he extended his work over six days. He could have created everything he created in a single hour, but his works would not have learned the power of his greatness. He delayed creating the creation for its benefit, so that he might complete what was his in the perfection of his divinity.

At the beginning of the day he made the heavens and the angels, the earth and water, darkness, fire, and air. At morning time he fashioned light from nothing, and the Watchers learned that they too had come into being from nothing. On the second day he made the firmament from within the waters, and taught them that it was also easy for him to create from something. On the third day he gathered the waters into the basin of the seas, and made known to them that his command ruled over the things he had formed. On the fourth day he made the lights, the sun and the moon, and taught them to observe the order of his creative activity. On the fifth day he made the waters fruitful, and they brought forth swarming creatures. He made known to them that even silent things fulfill his word. On the sixth day he created speechless kinds of creatures from the earth, and stirred them to contemplate their differences. As though pointing with a finger, he showed them the power of his being: “Look, angels, I have the power to do everything.” As though with a pen, he was writing a book in their minds, and teaching them to read the writings of the formation of all things. Like a superintendent, his command stood at the head of their ranks, explaining to them the meaning of his hidden things. He depicted the world like an image before their eyes, and set them there to examine it closely. The King of kings built creation like a palace, and brought them in to see the beauty of his royal dwelling. Through visible things he taught them the [?] of his being, so that they would not wear themselves out investigating his hidden nature. He was hidden from them, and they did not know the greatness of his power. He made it known to them through the things he formed, one after another. Like a guide, his command ran ahead of their assemblies, leading them toward knowledge of his hidden love. His love revealed to them how much he loves the work of his hands, and how deeply he desires to protect his handiwork from harm. Lovingly he created everything hidden and visible, and without toil he accomplished his will and displayed his love. He made his power dwell in the heavenly powers that came into being from him, and strengthened them to preserve the order of his creation.

He appointed them as rulers over everything he created, so that they would know how to govern heaven and earth. They too submitted with great love to his loving will, and gladly placed their necks under his command. He commanded like a king and arranged the ranks of their authority, and each took up the task shown to him. One he commanded to stir the air like an army commander and make the waters race above the back of the unbound wind. Another he authorized to draw flashes of lightning swiftly and make the sounds of harsh thunder ring out powerfully. To another he entrusted the sun's sphere to guide its movements, and he runs continually, night and day, without swerving. To another he entrusted the little moon with its changing phases, and he keeps it in order throughout the duration of time, so that it does not fall into confusion. Some set the speechless stars in motion to travel in order, and through their courses they teach wisdom to human beings endowed with speech. As they were appointed to govern the dominion of the nations, they labor continually to maintain their rule. Some stir up wars on earth against the guilty, and others keep harsh conflicts away from the innocent. Some subdue rebellious nations through their companions, and others hold back the power of the wicked before the [?]. Some chastise fiercely with thunder and lightning, and others gently bring down rain and dew. Some strike through the changes of summer and winter, and others protect bodily beings from harm. Some each guide a single human being and watch carefully over him, so that tyrannical demons do not harm him. They all diligently serve the hidden will, and follow the course of their activities according to his will. They continually strive to conform to the purpose of his love, and never slacken in their expectation of receiving their reward. Like athletes, they have been engaged in the contest ever since they came into being, and together with everyone they await the victory at the end. Wondrous is the contest in which beings not subject to suffering struggle, and the greatness of its toil cannot be expressed by a tongue of flesh.

How great must be the strength within them to uphold everything! For nearly six thousand years have passed, and they have not slackened. How they labor across the heights, night and day! They have neither grown weary nor weakened from traveling with the heavenly lights. How they bear [?] the weight of time within themselves, yet no weariness arises in their minds! How they burn with loving devotion toward the Creator! They have neither grown cold nor turned away from readiness to do his will. Let us marvel at the power of his will far more than at the power within them, for he can strengthen the work of his hands to preserve order. Let us praise his power, the strength behind his household's endurance, and continually weave a crown of thanksgiving for his help.
On the ordering of creation, also making known about
Discourse thirty-[?]. On the ordering of creation, also making known the persons of the Trinity.

The son of Amram opened a great treasury for us through his prophecy: the great power of the Creator when he began his work. This had been hidden from everyone: how he began creating, and by whose power heaven and earth and everything in them were established. The Creator wished to make his mighty work known to rational beings. He chose Moses as his pupil and taught him a spiritual book. On Mount Sinai he showed him a vision full of wonder. And he let him hear a voice [?], as he drew him to instruction. The Creator wished to reveal

himself to Moses in a human manner. Because of this, Moses longed to see his nature. “If indeed you have chosen me as your pupil and you love me, show me the glory of your nature, so that I may gaze upon your hidden radiance.” “You are greatly mistaken, Moses,” the Lord said to him. “No mortal sees me, for my nature is beyond those who see. I called you to me for instruction, so that you might learn that I am the Creator, not so that you might learn about my hidden being, which created beings cannot fathom. I am the Lord and God, and this is my name: ‘I am, I am.’ By the power that comes from me, I established heaven and earth and everything in them. Since mortals do not understand that my lordship rules over everything, I am making you a messenger and mediator to teach them. Through you I wish to reveal my being and the things I have fashioned. Through you I wish to give wisdom to the whole race of crowned beings. See, Moses, I am revealing to you the hidden mysteries of the things I have fashioned. Go down and proclaim among mortals that I am the maker of everything that has come into being.” In forty days the teacher completed the new pupil’s instruction. The mortal’s mind was able to grasp the whole of everything that had come into being. He caused the power of the Spirit to dwell in him and sang wondrous [?] through him. At the sweetness of the melodies, those above and those below were amazed. The sound of his voice became like thunder, and both speechless and speaking beings heard him. His words, like trumpets, proclaimed the Maker’s power. “In the beginning,” he said, “the Creator began and created everything that came into being.” In his knowledge he determined the times of beginning and ending. Though he himself had no beginning in his being, since his nature is without beginning, creation, at its appointed time, [?] as he himself knew. For it was not a new thought that drew him to create created things. Rather, this had been established from eternity in his knowledge, together with his being. Nor did he establish heaven and earth and everything in them for his own rest. Rather, in love and mercy he revealed his will to created beings. For he is good by nature, and his nature is full of blessings. In his goodness he willed and brought everything into being from nothing.

For it is fitting for the Creator to proclaim his power through his works, and for created beings to gain knowledge through contemplation of his creatures. His being has no beginning, and his dominion has no end. But his works have a beginning, and his creatures have a time and an order. His being cannot be comprehended by the thought of created beings. Nor can he be encompassed by sight, for his nature is above this. His being cannot be measured to determine how far he precedes the beginning. There was no time when he did not exist, for he existed before everything. He existed without beginning, a self-existent and perfect nature. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three persons, one power. The perfect Father, without beginning, who begot the Son without suffering. And the Son, who is from him and like him, with no interval of time between him and his Father. And the Spirit, who is from that same nature, a self-existent and real person. For the very equality of his nature testifies that he is self-existent together with the Father. The Father's offspring resembles him, for he has been with his Father from eternity. And because he exists with his Father, periods of time do not confine his begetting. The Father's offspring resembles him and exists with him like radiance. For just as radiance exists with fire, the offspring exists with his Father. The radiance of fire is with it, and there is no fire without radiance. For fire is seen together with its radiance, and the radiance is revealed together with it. In the Father his offspring also exists, and the Son is with him without beginning. There is no Father without his offspring, nor a Son without the one who begot him. The Son who is from the Father does not subsist like radiance, without a person of his own. Rather, he is a real person and an image resembling the one who begot him. The Father is not called the Son, nor is the Son named the Father. For the distinction between their names proclaims the reality of the persons. The Spirit is a person from the Father, equal to him in everything. Just as the Son is equal to the Father, the Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son. The difference between their names does not impair [?] their equality. The names are assigned according to order, while the persons are equal in being. In our soul he drew for us an illustration of the three persons of the Being.

The Son and the Spirit are from the Father, as with speech, life, and the soul. Along with the soul are born speech, power, and vitality. The Son and the Spirit exist with the Father, without beginning. Two powers accompany the soul: speech and vitality are with it. And two powers are with the Father: the Son and the Spirit, without beginning. The Son is begotten without beginning, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father. One is begotten and one proceeds; there is one equality in nature. The Spirit is from the Father, but is not called by the name of offspring. For he is not foreign in nature, nor is he [?] of names. Eve was formed from Adam, yet she is neither his daughter nor his sister. Although she is from him in nature, she is called only his wife. In our nature, as through mysteries, he drew for us a pattern of his Being. Whoever doubts the begetting should see its illustration in our own nature. Through our very nature he taught us wisdom, so that we might understand his greatness. For if our own nature is not clear to us, how much more hidden is the inquiry into him! His creatures cannot be comprehended, and his works are too difficult for us. How, then, shall we dare to investigate his Being, which has no beginning? A creature cannot investigate the Being of its Maker. However much it seeks to learn how he began, it finds him without beginning. However much thought seeks to investigate his Being, it finds him in this one way alone: that he is unlimited in his nature. Let this suffice for our inquiry: that we examine only his works. As for inquiry into his Being, let it be honored by our silence. Let us hear about the things he fashioned, and praise the work of his hands. For a creature owes thanks to the Creator for everything he has created. That he began creation in the beginning—this we have heard from Moses. But how and by how much he precedes the beginning, let us not inquire. Rather, let us inquire as people of understanding, with an inquiry fitting for creatures: what was the reason that he made heard

a voice concerning the things he fashioned? In the beginning he began and created heaven and earth first, and five other natures, which he did not call by their names. Yet they are included in this statement, within the creation of the beginning: fire, water, darkness, and angels, speaking and silent. In this statement, “In the beginning,” he included the fashioning of the angels. And he, the Creator of everything, created them from nothing. In this creation of the beginning, [?] that he made a voice heard. For there was no creature to hear and receive instruction. But when he began with the natures that came into being one after another, he wished to make his creative work known to the angels through a voice. This is the reason for the voice: that he might teach the spiritual beings. For that Lord who orders all things is the one who established their hosts. O voice, mightier than all, that spoke in the beginning! He was drawing the spiritual beings toward himself in love. Darkness covered the heights and the depths alike. The earth was submerged in water before it received its ordered form. In the beginning the earth had neither visible form nor order. He calls it unformed because it was not yet adorned with trees. “The wind,” it says, “was moving above the waters of the depths.” He calls the gentle blowing of the wind “the wind of the air.” The Creator’s word served as a means of instruction. He made his voice heard by the angels: “Let there be light that illuminates everything.” O voice that brought light into existence out of nothing! O light, whose previously nonexistent nature was formed as soon as the command was heard! The light drove away the darkness that had spread over the created things. The spiritual beings were all amazed at the power that had given it authority. After the word that created light, he made another utterance heard, praising what he had fashioned, for he had fashioned it beautifully. O wise craftsman, how careful he is in his workmanship! He set a limit for the light, determining how far it should exercise its rule. He separated light from darkness so that neither would encroach upon the other.

He established a law for their courses through the hours of night and day. He called the light “day,” and the darkness he called “night.” He gave them names corresponding to the activities of their hours. There was evening and also morning—a day, as it is written. He called it the first day, because there had been no other like it. He also made night the beginning of the first day, to preserve the order of his creation, since darkness came first. The first day was completed: night and [?], one day. Then he proclaimed another command: “Let there be a firmament from the waters.” O voice possessing authority, whose word is accompanied by action! O power that compressed fluid things and made them solid! He created the firmament from water, so that it would carry water above it. He called it by the name of heaven, that first heaven of the beginning. He made the firmament in the middle like a nearby canopy, so that it would be close enough to see and would separate water from water. O balance that does not waver, which divided the waters equally! Half was for the earth’s use, and half he compressed into the firmament. O craftsman who orders everything, whose knowledge cannot be comprehended! Before he began the work, he knew what would be needed for it. He was going to suspend the luminaries, whose nature is fire, in the firmament. He stored up waters above it so that it would not be scorched by fire. The Creator also knew, before he created everything that came into being, that another dwelling would be needed for rational beings at the end of time. For this reason he created the firmament like a canopy in the middle, so that in the end it would serve us in place of the earth as our resting place. There was morning as well as evening, and the second day was completed. He turned and praised his creation, which he had beautifully fashioned. Then came the evening of the third day, no different from the first, for it was the same power that commanded something to come into being, and it came into being. “Let the waters be gathered,” he said, “and let them become seas in one place. Let the surface of the earth be revealed,

so that it may be suitable for habitation.” What a command, which does not delay! What a word, which needs no repetition! As soon as his will gave the command, the waters were gathered into seas. The earth shone and rejoiced, and a command went out concerning it. “Let the earth bring forth,” he said, “and make grasses, crops, and trees spring up.” The command became reality, and the earth was adorned with fruit. Crops and trees came into being, and the Good One praised his creation. There was evening and also morning: the complete third day. Another command went out, and he commanded that there should be lights. “Let there be lights,” he said, “in the firmament above the earth, so that seasons, months, and years may be known through their courses.” The word went into effect, and suddenly the lights came into being. He established an unchanging law for the course of night and day. What a craftsman, who [?] everything, whose will rules over everything! From something or from nothing, it is easy for him to make everything. From light he created the lights, from that first light, dividing it into portions for the moon, the stars, and the sun. He did not fasten them in the firmament, so that their courses would not be hindered. He hung them like lamps and ordered the course of their hours. The fourth day was completed within the bounds of evening and morning. Another command went out, that moving creatures should come into being from the waters. The waters brought forth living creatures of countless kinds: swarming creatures, fish, sea monsters, and deadly animals. What power! Difficult things are easy for him, according to his will. From the waters he formed and made countless kinds. From the waters he created birds, a nature that swims through the air. Although it comes from the waters like the swarming creatures, the air supports it and carries it along. O Good One, how great is his love! His command watches over his creatures, and when their formation is complete, he equips them with blessings. “Produce offspring,” he said, “and multiply on the earth, in the sea and on dry land alike, while your kinds are preserved

in succession, one after another.” On the fifth day he completed the creation of the swarming creatures and the birds. On the sixth day he began to create wild animals and livestock. He said, “Let the earth bring forth and produce living creatures of every kind.” Fanged beasts, livestock, and crawling creatures were offspring of the earth. What a mute nature it was that brought forth animals from within its womb! Though it was mere dirt, lowly in appearance, it gave birth to beauty of every kind. It did not give birth by its own nature, but through the power of its Maker. The one who spread out the earth in the beginning commanded it, and it gave birth to animals. On the sixth day livestock and wild animals were created together with Adam, so that those suited to his service would receive their formation along with him. On the sixth day the formation of everything that came into being was completed. The Creator showed his power through his works: he spoke, and they came into being. On the seventh day the Maker rested from his works of creation. He blessed the seventh day and called it a holy day. For that power does not grow weary, nor can his will be hindered. Something came into being from nothing; in six days, everything [?]. It was not because it was difficult for his will that he did not create everything at once. For it was all the same to him to make everything in one day or in many [?]. He established an order for his creation, as he himself knew. To instruct rational beings, he completed everything in six days. For the angels were watching his work of creation and examining it. Whenever he spoke a word and it came to pass, the spiritual beings cried out praise to him. He did everything with knowledge, that wise one who knows everything. From something and from nothing he brought created things into existence. He created light from nothing to reveal his greatness. He also created our soul from nothing, to show that he has authority over everything. From light he created the heavenly lights, the sun and moon as lamps. The hosts of angels shouted praise to the power that forms everything. The Creator had these purposes in view as he formed everything. He took his time over his works to teach rational beings about his power. He endowed the seventh day with holy blessings,

so that it would not be a stranger to him because he did not choose to create anything on it. That day too was a day like the preceding days. Since no work of creation took place on it, he called it holy so that they would not despise it. The indication of its holiness is this: that he rested [?] from labor, so that when we hear the name of the world, we may learn who the Creator is. This day was destined to instruct the descendants of Abraham [?], so that when they observed it by refraining from labor, they would learn what its reason was. Over everything that came into being through him, he uttered a declaration [?] as it came into being. He himself praised his creation, because it had been beautifully formed by him. Until this point there was uniformity: a single utterance for everything that came into being. But at the completion of his works, a new utterance was spoken. He said, “Let us make a rational human being in our own image and likeness. Let him rule over everything that came into being, which was prepared for his sake.” Oh, how wise the Craftsman is! Oh, how abundant is the love of the Good One! He created and adorned everything, and only then fashioned the heir. He built a house for the one made of dust, stocked it, and filled it with good things. He subjected speechless and rational beings alike to his service. In every way he honored the mortal: in his formation and his authority, in calling him his own image, and in subjecting everything that came into being to him. For all the things that came into being and were formed, he made only an utterance heard. But here, in the formation of Adam, there is counsel and a new intention: “Let us make a human being in our likeness, and let him have authority like us.” So that through the image of his visible form he might proclaim his power to created beings. “Through him I reveal my hiddenness to intelligible beings.” “And through him I make my lordship known to speechless and rational beings alike.” “I set him up as an image for created beings to contemplate.” “So that through love for him, everyone may come to know me through him.” Adam’s formation is a marvel, different from that of other created beings. For everything that came into being he made by his word, but concerning him he said in counsel, “I will make him.” Glorious is the formation of the one made of dust, and hidden mysteries are concealed within it. For he did not say, “Let him be like me,” but rather, “In our image and likeness.”

Oh, the mortal, in whose formation hidden mysteries are concealed! Oh, the one made of dust, who revealed three persons to us through his formation! In the formation of Adam’s image, he taught us as through a mystery. By saying, “In our image and likeness,” he made known to us three persons: the beginningless being of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In Adam’s image, everything that came into being was honored, as in a mystery. Otherwise, whom was he addressing as equal to his greatness? For when he said, “Come, let us make in our image,” he was not speaking to angels. By the expression “our image,” he taught us about the distinction of the persons; and by “our likeness,” about the equality of their nature. He said, “Come, let us make a human being, and let us bind everything that came into being to him, so that through their kinship with him they may lovingly supply his needs.” God made Adam in his image, dust from the earth. He breathed into him a soul for life, a living and rational nature. Oh, the love shown to our race! Oh, the honor of our formation! For the life that he made dwell within us, he willingly breathed into us out of his love. Oh, the nature that is not composite, whose being cannot be measured! When he fashioned our nature, he made us with hands and mouth. He did not make us like the animals, which came into being as males and females. For Adam came first in his creation, and then Eve from his rib. He fashioned Adam first, and then the woman from Adam. So that he might learn the power of his Maker, who adorned his created form. “The Lord God,” it says, “formed Adam from dust of the earth.” He placed him in the paradise of Eden, to be its heir. In a beautiful and delightful dwelling he placed Adam as his image. So that created beings, through one close to them, might lovingly call upon their Maker. His image resembles the Creator in name, not in nature. For he gave him authority over everything he had fashioned, like the Creator over what belongs to him. He becomes a father when he begets, and he begets a child who resembles him. Like the Father, who begot the Son in his nature, which has no beginning. He himself becomes a father in time, and in time he begets a child. The Eternal One begot outside time, and there is no interval of time between him and his offspring. He makes something from something, and fashions it when it does not yet exist.

Like the Maker, who brought everything into being from nothing. He makes something from something, and in this resembles the Creator. Everything that exists looks toward the earth, but his gaze is toward heaven. With a single gesture of his gaze, he seeks his dwelling on high. In these ways the one made of dust resembles the Creator symbolically. For through speech and life, he too commands the elements. He figuratively gave the first Adam the designation “image.” But the image became a reality in Christ, the second Adam. Here the saying, “Come, let us make him in our image,” reached its fulfillment. For the Creator took his image and made it a dwelling for his glory. In Christ the promises made to Adam became a reality. The one whom he called his image became corrupted, but was restored and renewed in Christ. In connection with Adam as his image, he described the greatness of paradise. So that Adam might know the honor given him by being placed in a glorious land. “The Lord God,” it says, “made a paradise in Eden toward the east.” He made trees grow within it that were very suitable for food. One of the trees he placed in the middle of paradise. He called it the tree of life, so that through it Adam might gain life. He planted another tree and called it “the one that knows what is right.” For the knowledge hidden in Adam is brought to light through its fruit. He spoke of the spring that flowed out of paradise and watered it. From its abundant flow, four streams branch out in every direction. The first river is Pishon, which winds around the land of Havilah. There are gold, beryls, stones, and gleaming signet stones. The second river is Gihon, which waters the land of the Cushites. Through the irrigation it supplies, it gives life to the Egyptians and Midianites. The third river is the Tigris, which serves as a messenger to Assyria. All the peoples around it delight in the sweetness of its water. The Euphrates is the fourth river, which passes through the middle of the land. It gives itself to the canal diggers so that they may irrigate the lands with it. It was not to praise Paradise that the prophet recounted these things, nor to extol the greatness

of the rivers within it. He magnified the power of the Creator, for whom difficult things are easy: how the spring of Paradise passes through the sea toward us. Waters pass through the seas, yet the waters do not mix with the waters. This bears witness to his greatness, for his power established everything. O the command that keeps water within water as though in a [?]! It does not mix the waters of Eden with the turbulent waters of the deep. His mute and silent works cry out continually about his power, teaching rational creation that the Maker is there in his works. The account of Paradise revealed to us teaching full of life. The story about the tree brought us to understanding. Through such means the Creator wished to give wisdom to our rational nature. As with children, he accommodated himself to us and made known to us the freedom within us. Through the things he fashioned, he taught the spiritual beings that he is the self-existent One and the Maker. He gave us wisdom through nature, which revealed within us his hidden being. In the beginning he fashioned the earth and the heavens when they did not exist. Along with the power of that beginning, the intelligible powers came into being. He created the lights while making his voice heard by the hosts of spiritual beings. By bringing light into being, he taught them that it was he who had adorned their own beings. He made the firmament from water and set water above it. He adorned it with luminous forms, an adornment suited to rational beings. He gathered the waters from the earth into the reservoirs of the seas and the depths. He adorned the earth with crops and trees to sustain the lives of humans and animals. The waters teemed with living creatures, and the earth brought forth every kind. Through the silent things he fashioned, he imparted much wisdom to rational beings. He made our nature from the earth and breathed into us the breath of life. Through his love for our race, he bound together mute creatures and rational beings. All these things he fashioned had been hidden in his knowledge from eternity. He brought them into the open and showed his love for his creatures. His will, however, together with his being, preceded the things he fashioned. Before creating, he knew how many natures he would make. He knew that two created realms were suited to rational beings: an earthly dwelling for mortals, and heaven for immortals. He knew the thoughts

of rational beings before they existed. The hidden things that would happen in time were already revealed to him. He contemplated everything that came to be before it came into existence. The works that would come into being from him were already defined in his knowledge. It was not to meet a need of his that he brought creation into being. He revealed his hidden will, showing how much he loves what belongs to him. He is the spring full of life, for he possesses life by his very nature. From nothing he fashioned everything and gave life to [?]. His wealth is his will, and his great treasury is his thought. Though the recipients had not asked him, he opened his treasuries and enriched everyone. His love extends over his creatures, and every day he cares for what belongs to him. His command preserves all beings, rational and speechless alike. He established a law for mortals, so that if they keep it, they may live by it. He appointed his spiritual host to attend to their needs. These things were ordained from eternity to take place according to his will. With knowledge beyond comprehension, he appointed times for his works. All of them [?] proclaimed his hidden nature through the visible works of his hands. The sun and moon tell of his greatness as they follow their courses. The things he fashioned owe him thanksgiving for his gift. Because he adorned them in mercy, let them lovingly give thanks to him for who he is. No need of his is met by the thanksgiving of created things. Thanksgiving benefits us; he himself has no need of it. Who praised his nature when he existed from eternity? Who offered him praise before he created creatures? His glory is inherent in his nature, and his exaltation belongs to his very being. He neither diminishes nor increases, for his nature is above such things. It is us he exalts when he calls and brings us near to the knowledge of him. So that, when we know him, he may give us the kingdom in return for thanksgiving. With heartfelt love let us thank him, the Maker, for the things he fashioned. For he fashioned everything for our sake. To him be thanksgiving from all [?].
On the Formation of Creation
Discourse Thirty-Six: Again on the Formation of Creation

The self-existent One, who adorned the heights and depths by his powerful command, wished to make his handiwork known through a spoken utterance. In the beginning he fashioned heaven and earth, water and air, the hosts on high, light, and darkness that [?] over everything. He created creation from nothing with the slightest command, and covered its face with darkness as with a garment. The Creator performed a great wonder at the beginning of his works: he built a house, sealed its windows, and filled it with darkness. He wished to make his handiwork known through its causes, and he delayed his works to instruct rational beings. The hosts of the peaceful ones were being created in the beginning, and for their instruction he uttered the words, “Let there be light.” “Let there be light illuminating everything!” cried the Creator, and he gathered the heavenly beings to hear the wonder. O trumpet of the Creator’s voice, which suddenly rang out and startled the heavenly hosts with the sound of its tones! O command whose fulfillment accompanied its utterance! O craftsman whose labor in everything he made was a mere gesture! “Let there be light, a beautiful garment adorning everything, and let the heights and depths and everything in them be clothed in it!” The deed was accomplished along with the command, and light came into being. It drove away the darkness and brightened the air, which had been gloomy. The ranks of the heavenly hosts cried out, “Blessed is the Creator, who created and adorned the beautiful light and gladdened everything!” He himself praised his creation, for he had made it beautiful, and his voice testified to the greatness of his power, which can accomplish everything. O utterance that made something out of nothing! O command that the absence of anything could not delay! Through an utterance, the Creator wished to teach them:

the spiritual powers, about his existence. They had not perceived that he existed eternally, before his creatures, and they did not know who had fashioned their own beings. Through the voice that said [?], “Let there be light,” they gained understanding, and as the deed was accomplished, they cried out praise to the Maker of everything. By this means, he who has no voice made a voice heard [?], to teach the spiritual beings the power of his hidden being. The voice that spoke on earth in the beginning instructed them, and [?] them that one Creator had created everything. They joined their voices in perfect love and bowed down before him. Together they raised holy cries to the King of the heights. The coming into being of the light taught them the Creator’s power and yoked them beneath the gentle yoke of voicing thanksgiving to him. One day, night and daytime, was completed when the light ended, and darkness began to make a path for the second day. He established a great order for both in their respective dominions, so that neither would encroach upon the other in their courses. On the second day, the command went forth that there should be a firmament, and he divided the waters, half to the heights and half to the earth. “Let there be a firmament amid the waters, solid water, and let it carry waters above its back without being shaken!” O command that hardened the waters, whose nature is fluid, and made them a solid substance to carry waters! O balance that divided the waters, that enormous mass, and gathered them into two seas, in the heights and in the depths! He stretched out the firmament like a roof over the house below, so that it would serve as the ground for the house above. His gesture wove it like a white garment, and he traced figures upon it: the sun and the moon [?], lamps of light. He hung two luminaries, lamps of light, in the firmament, so that with their flames [?] they might gladden the earth to sustain humanity. From that first light which came into being, he made the luminaries, and from it he allotted to the sun and moon their smaller flames.

He set a portion of the clear light in the great orb, and placed a quarter of the light in the thin orb of the moon. He gave the larger and brighter portion to the day, and the smaller and dimmer one to the quiet night. He fixed the course of the sun and moon in twelve [?], so that when one finished, it would give its companion room to proceed. He established the great sun’s journey in two directions, so that the ordered course of the little moon would not be disturbed. It travels its course by day over the dwelling place of humanity, and gives the little moon room to travel its course. With an unceasing course it journeys onward in two directions, making its circuit of the heavens night and day. When it rises toward us, it is like a bridegroom, and with the white gleams of its orb, its radiance gladdens the earth. At evening it moves away and journeys on like a military commander. When darkness notices that it has departed, darkness enters and takes control. The little moon makes its course through changes, and in a single month it ascends and descends twelve degrees. The moon’s light does not hinder the great sun when it encounters it in the dominion of the heavens, along the path of its rising. For human life, the Creator [?] desired a great house. He set its foundations in the flowing waters and made them firm. He stretched out its roof from the fluid substance of the yielding waters, and piled waters above its back like a vault. He hung the lamps—the sun and moon—in the roof of his house, poured in the oil—the command of his power—and lit them. Glorious is the Creator, whose works are wonderful and whose thought is great! Before making his creation, he knew beforehand what it would need. The one who prepares everything made a twofold dwelling for creation. He adorned and built two [?] for the two worlds. He made the lower one suitable for mortal life, stocked it, and filled it with fruits suited to bodily beings. He made the upper one a beautiful dwelling full of blessings,

so that spiritual beings might delight in it spiritually. For earthly beings he made earthly things, and to heavenly beings he promised heavenly blessings. The one who knows everything contemplated the two dwellings; even before heaven and earth existed, he was looking upon them. For his loving will preceded his creation, and the works he made were pictured before him through his will. He completed and built heaven and earth as a spacious house, stocked it, and filled it with great riches for whoever would dwell in it. He gathered the waters and made the seas into a great reservoir. The command of his power paired them, and they brought forth swarming creatures. The womb of the yielding waters brought forth solid bodies, and from the heavy waters came birds whose wings are light. He commanded the earth, and it conceived species and families: peaceful livestock, beasts with teeth, and creatures of every kind. He tilled the earth and cast into it the seed of life. The seeds sprouted, trees arose, and fruit blossomed. The Creator's power completed and finished everything that came into being. Then he molded the heir and master of all possessions. For everything he made, he spoke aloud concerning its formation; but when he molded Adam's dust, there were both speech and deliberation. For everything that came into being, he said something, and it came to be. But when forming the human image, he said, “Come, let us make.” He stretched out the heavens without calling another power to help him. He also spread out the earth without consulting his counselors. He made the hosts of the [?], fire and spirit, and did not disclose the mystery of the power [?] of his being in the persons who were with him. In Adam's formation there was new deliberation and thought, as the One on high made the voice of his thoughts heard. He said, “Come, let us make a human being in our image and also in our likeness, and let him rule like a king over everything that has come into being.” What is this change you make, O Creator—new [?] and thought concerning Adam's dust? Whom are you calling to help you in forming your image? Who has been your counselor in everything you have made? O dust, whose ashes are lowly but whose formation is exalted, in whose molding hidden mysteries are spoken! O mortal, who revealed and made known through his formation:

Three persons, one being without beginning. Through the composition of Adam's image, the Father made known that everything came into being with the Son and the Spirit as his equals. He concealed the mystery of the revelation of the persons from everything that came into being, lest the spiritual beings imagine another power. In Adam, his image, he revealed to the prophets, as in a mystery, that the Son and the Spirit are equal to the Father in [?] being. By saying “in our image,” he proclaimed and taught their equal nature; and through one likeness he revealed and made known to us three persons. In Adam the heir, he taught and revealed the Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in one equality. This power, hidden from all, created everything; and when everything had come into being, he fashioned the human being. The Hidden One uttered a single word concerning everything that came into being; but in forming Adam's image, he changed his manner of speaking. He said, “Come, let us make a rational human being in our image, and through the kinship of his soul and body let him bind everything together. Let him be kin to the heavenly beings through the life of his soul, and also related to bodily beings through the composition of his body. Let him be an image that proclaims my hiddenness through his visibility, and let him rule over everything that has come into being, to make my lordship known. Through him I reveal the being of my hidden nature, and through him I teach the spiritual beings about my authority over all. I honor his formation above everything I have created, for with hand and mouth I mold him and breathe into him.” With a hidden hand I honor his lowly dust, and from my living mouth I breathe into him the spirit of life. O Being without composition, hidden from all, who for the sake of the lowly one humbled himself by using the names of bodily parts! The Lord took lowly dust from the ground and fashioned Adam, a rational image, from dust. He breathed the breath of life into his nostrils from the breath of his mouth, and Adam became a living soul, a rational vessel. He fashioned his servant alone, without a female companion, teaching him that his formation was new in every respect.

He completed and perfected the rational vessel, which the Living One [?]. There was no counterpart resembling Adam in whom he could find comfort. He cast the stillness of sleep upon the childlike Adam and sank him into deep sleep. He took a rib from among his members and fashioned the woman. He restored that part of his body as it had been before, and from what belonged to him he fashioned a body resembling his. From a human being came a human being resembling him, complete in body and soul in Adam’s likeness. He lay sunk in sleep and did not feel the division of his body. He awoke from his sleep and saw a human being resembling his own body. Through the Creator’s Spirit, revelation sounded on the harp of his soul, and his mouth spoke new words of prophecy. “This time she is bone from my own members. She shall be named after me: the man’s woman, who establishes a household.” He also called her by a name in which the meaning of her role could be discerned, showing that she was the mother of the living, the one who gives birth to the living. He gathered to him all the species that were on the earth, so that he might place the seal of his word upon them and they might belong to him. He called them by their names [?], as he was able, and learned of the power that had subjected everything to him as to a master. He fashioned those made of dust in a lowly place, and then placed them in the land of Eden, wonderful and desirable. The heirs entered Paradise and took possession of their allotted lands. Through the commandment he had a deed of his lordship written for them. He placed authority over Eden’s desirable fruits in their hands, but forbade them the tree that brings forth death. He called Adam his image and set a boundary for him, so that he would not approach and take the fruit that imparts knowledge. “Do not eat from the tree that brings forth death. Keep the commandment, for I am giving you the fruit of life.” The Creator placed two trees there to test his image. He created them: the tree of life and the tree of death. He placed two orders of existence in the trees as symbols; through them he disclosed to us earthly life and the kingdom above.

The commandment stood like a ruler guarding them, lest the childlike Adam dare to reach for their fruits. Through the commandment he revealed and made known to him, as in symbols: “I will give you new life if you do not sin.” Although he knew that Adam would indeed sin like a sinner [?], he wished to test him through the commandment as though he did not know. Although he knew that he had placed mortality in his nature, he wished, through the fruit, to make him fear what would come afterward. Through the commandment concerning the tree, he stirred the innocent man and brought his discernment to light through a test. The commandment became like a furnace for testing the man, and desire for the fruit was like heat over the gold. He blew the air of desire for the fruit into Adam’s gold, polished it thoroughly in the fire of eating it, and revealed its beauty. The Maker of all created Adam as fine gold and concealed his beauty under ignorance as under a covering. Through the commandment he brought him in, as into a furnace, and tested him [?]; through the trial he polished away his tarnish and revealed his beauty. He secretly gave the commandment to Adam’s household, so that the assemblies on high would not hear the commandment spoken. This mystery took place in secret among bodily beings, and he did not include the heavenly beings in the stipulation concerning Adam. The ruler of the air had not heard this commandment, and he did not know why they were forbidden the fruit. Envy disturbed the serenity of his soul, and he suddenly grew dark when he saw Adam made lord over everything that had come into being. Jealousy set him ablaze, set the devil ablaze like fire: “Why has dust been made king on earth? Was it not enough for this son of ashes that he called him his image, without also subjecting the heights and depths to his authority? Was it not enough for the dust of the earth that he formed him with his own hands, without also laying the yoke of laboring for him upon spiritual beings? As for me, a spirit holding authority among the ranks of those like me, he did not wish to speak even a word about our formation. But this contemptible one, dust of the earth, a son of ashes—with great deliberation and thought he adorned and formed him. He also called him his image, exalting him as a lord,

and yoked the heavenly beings [?] to the service of his life. If I approach him without a body, he does not see me; if I approach him without a vehicle, he does not answer me.” At the beginning of time, that envious one was not permitted to change himself and lead the man astray through different forms. He chose the serpent to conceal his bitterness in it, and the deceiver played it like a lyre with strings of flesh. He drew the serpent along and acquired a vehicle for approaching the woman, so that when she saw that it was a creature of flesh, she would accept his advice. The deceiver played deceitful notes on a flute of flesh: “Why have you been forbidden and stopped from eating? Has the Creator perhaps placed a restriction on the trees, so that you cannot enjoy their fruits as the animals do?” Eve spoke with a bodily voice to the creature of flesh: “We are permitted to enjoy all the fruits. He restricted and forbade us only one, because it produces death. He said that he forbade us its fruit for this reason: so that we would not die.” The cause of death, which had been hidden from spiritual beings; and the crafty one rejoiced that he had found a place to plant his deceit. He tilled the soil of hearing, of the [?] of the frail rib, and the accuser cast his seed into her mind. “It is not deadly poison that is hidden in the tree,” the serpent explained. “The fruit gives eyes full of light to whoever eats it. The tree possesses great power through its food, and it can transform human beings and make them like gods. A great spring of divinity is hidden in the tree, and if you drink of its sweetness, you will gain high rank. That is why he forbade you to eat from it: so that you would not become like him, lest you reach the great height of his divinity. He is indeed jealous, unwilling for you to become his heirs or to be called by the great name of his divinity.

Approach the fruit, eat from it, and see the light! Then you will possess the power of wisdom like gods.” The woman saw, it says, that the fruit was desirable and beautiful to look at. She took and ate, and then gave it to her husband, and he ate. She was the first to listen to the advice and pick the fruit, and her mouth hurried to eat so that she might become a god. By eating the fruit she wanted to seize the name of God for herself, gain a rank above her husband, and become the head. In their craving for food, the mortals imagined they would reach the heights, but the working of the command brought them down to the depths of Sheol. By eating the fruit, those made of dust gained understanding. They looked and were ashamed that their limbs were exposed. The food became like a mirror for the movements of the soul, and the mind made the outward senses modest with garments of leaves. Those childish in heart gained discerning understanding and covered the naked flesh of their limbs. From the tree they had eaten from, they made a covering; the leaves of the very tree that had stripped them naked covered them. Toward evening, [?] the voice of the Creator, as he made the sound of footsteps heard within Paradise. O spiritual one, who made a sound without bodily limbs! O all-knowing one, who asks his own image, “[?] are you?” He knows where he is, yet questions him while seeing him. He makes his voice heard and calls to him, to turn him back toward himself. “Where are you, Adam, the visible image that reveals my hiddenness? Where are you, the heir whom I made master over all my possessions?” With tender tones he sought the lost one, calling repeatedly in a sorrowful voice, “Adam, Adam!” “Where are you, Adam?” the Creator cried to the one made of dust, and the creature answered his Maker in a sorrowful voice: “I heard the sound of your footsteps and hid out of shame, so that you would not look upon my nakedness, for I am exposed.” “Who stripped off your glorious garments, king of the earth? Who left you naked, without a covering?” The shamefaced man seized upon an excuse, blaming the rib taken from him, supposing that he would not be condemned by the sentence of judgment. The woman you gave to be with me—she gave me the fruit, and I ate.

If it had not been for her, I would not have transgressed your command. He bore with Adam for a long time, as with a child, and asked the woman, “What is this wrong you have done?” Like Adam, she too shifted the blame onto the serpent: “The serpent advised me, and I ate the fruit against my will.” But he did not ask the serpent who had led it astray, for it was not the serpent itself that had deceived, but the one speaking through it. The Creator pronounced a harsh sentence upon the offender, bound him, and threw him into prison by means of curses. “You will be more accursed than everything I created that moves upon the earth. Your swift movement will be hindered, so that you can no longer deceive. Worthless dust from the earth will be your food, and you will not enjoy the sweetness of fruit. You will be an enemy to the human beings you deceived, all your days, and they will be your adversaries without reconciliation. They will trample your head and strike you as they overcome you; but when they sin, you will strike them through your cunning schemes.” Through the sentence upon the serpent, he condemned the devil; and through the curses upon creatures of flesh, he cursed the deceitful one. He did not wish to disclose the angels at the beginning of time, lest the error associated with the name “gods” increase upon the earth. In this way he concealed the story of the devil, so that no one would think him powerful and capable of everything like the Creator. He too had been created with the spiritual beings clothed in light, and had dwelt with the holy ones in the heights. He possessed and exercised leadership over the authority of the air; but when he envied Adam, he fell from his rank like lightning. It was him that he cursed with the words, “You will go upon your belly on the earth,” so that he would no longer ascend swiftly to the heights.

He humbled him further and decreed that worthless dust should be his food, as he wallowed upon the earth among those made of dust. It was him that he called the enemy of humanity, the murderer; and it is he who strikes the human heel with the sting of wickedness. He chastised the deceitful one with harsh lashes in proportion to his wrongdoing. Then he raised his rod against the woman who had listened to his advice. With the pains of childbirth he scourged Eve, who had plucked the fruit; and because she had exalted herself, he bowed her head beneath her husband. Last, he cursed Adam, his image, with a sentence of judgment, for the harsh lashes upon the serpent and Eve had tempered his bitterness. “The earth is cursed because of you, king of the earth. It will sprout thorns and yield them to you when you cultivate it. By the sweat of your face you will eat bread as you wear yourself out, and even your possessions will despise you, because you despised my commandments. You are dust, taken from the soil, and dust you will become. Because you undid my words, death will undo the dominion of your life.” O Knower of all, who knows everything before it comes into being, who displayed his wrath in his sentence of judgment as though he did not know! He created Adam from dust and called him his image, and made his dust in the likeness of the dust of mortality. From the beginning he placed this in the composition of his body: that he should travel the road of mortality and ask for life. It was not out of anger that he decreed curses and the pains of childbirth, nor in remorse did he bring death upon mortals. The natural conditions that he had placed in mortal nature he turned into a fitting provision for humanity’s help. He knew Adam’s dust before Adam came into being, and that death would dissolve and undo the composition of his body. It was clear to him that the palate would sin through desire for the fruit, and he knew the evil inclination of Adam’s discernment. Through experience he wished to make his rational nature wise,

so that his discernment would not remain without training. Through the commandment he arranged means for Adam to learn that he ought to observe the order established by his Lord’s command. Through the tree he uncovered Adam’s hidden discernment, and through the eating of the fruit he revealed the power of his rational nature. The tree did not possess the power of discernment, nor did a silent thing enable a rational being to know these things. The death that enslaved Adam was not hidden in the tree, nor did the commandment make those who came afterward sinners. The composition of Adam’s body proclaims that he was mortal; Eve’s companionship, too, was full of suffering. The whole world, through its arrangements, bears witness to this, as do fruits and seeds for the perpetuation of seeds [?] mortality. He called the tree a possessor of knowledge, not because of its nature, but to test Adam’s wisdom by means of its fruit. He called the other tree a giver of life, not because of anything of its own, but because he depicted it as a symbol of the kingdom filled with life. Through [?] he attached to it judicial sentences full of fitting provisions, and he gave the other to innocence as a pledge of life. Adam, still a child, was not capable of strict discipline, nor could he listen to an account of the kingdom on high. Through simple things, as though through milk, he gained training; then through the tree God made two arrangements known to him. He represented earthly life by a fruit-bearing tree, and through the tree of life he depicted the arrangement of the kingdom on high. He promised paradise as a reward for the labors here, and guarded its fruits with the restraint imposed by the voice of his commandments. Glorious was its spring, whose flow watered the four regions; like a conduit it passes through the sea without mingling. What a command, keeping the waters as though in a vessel and not allowing Eden’s spring to mingle with the great reservoir! What fluidity of waters, with waters dividing waters! Though they are one, the waters have become strangers to the waters. Eden’s spring does not possess this authority by nature; it is the Creator’s power that keeps waters within fluid waters. He who created everything out of nothing by the power of his greatness:

He signaled to the yielding ones that they should not mingle with their companions. The son of Amram, who recounted these things, also magnified his power, for even difficult things are easy for the power of his will. On this condition he divided the waters of Eden: that they should bear witness to the greatness of his almighty power. He sent them like heralds to the four quarters, to proclaim his greatness while remaining silent. In India the great Pishon proclaims the Creator’s power, and enriches the land with beryls and pearls. Gihon spoke to the Cushites through the sound of its torrents. Though silent, it exalts his nature and waters the earth. The Tigris cries out like a trumpet to the Assyrians: “Behold the Creator among the silent things! Listen, you who can speak!” The Euphrates makes its voice heard like thunder in its mighty flow, and like a trumpet awakens the crops with the sound of its irrigation. Moses did not praise the greatness of the rivers; he magnified the Creator’s power, which is capable of everything. Although his will is his treasury and his command is wealth, he delayed the works of his hands like someone in need. For six days the Maker of everything fashioned everything, and on the seventh day he who completes everything rested from his labor. It was not difficult for the mighty power of him who created everything, with a single command, to [?] and make everything that came into being. His works did not need six days; it was to teach the spiritual beings his power—that he had fashioned everything. He was teaching them, as he created the beautiful light, that the Creator can make something out of nothing. The sphere of the sun and the formation of the moon also make known to them that he can transform something and [?] something. Their ranks cried out as they saw the great wonder: the deed came into being with the command; [?] was delayed. Through his works they learned the power of his creative activity, and they believed that he alone is without beginning. At his command they received authority to carry out everything, and their companies took charge of the affairs of earthly beings. He entrusted great wealth to them as faithful servants:

And he made them guardians of mortal beings. They received spiritual authority over everything that came into being, and his powerful command strengthened them to offer praise. He made the devil the chief who stirs the air, and, as to a commander, he entrusted his fellow servants into his hands. Because of his authority, pride seized that rebel, and in his arrogance he wanted to exalt himself above the Creator. When the evil one could not harm the power of the divine Being, he wanted to insult the Creator’s image in place of the Creator. By dishonoring Adam, the rebel attacked the Creator, thinking that he was hurting the one who had fashioned him in his image. He led Adam astray through desire for the fruit, so that he would eat and die, and, when Adam died, he would grieve God through Adam’s death. Through Adam’s death, the rebel thought he would snatch away the glorious name—the name of existence itself—from the God of all. The rebel sought to gain [?] by leading Adam astray, but a command overthrew him like lightning from his position of authority. The envious one fell from his greatness and was stripped of his glory. While he thought he would find comfort, his pain increased. Through the sentence Adam received, the rebel thought that death would immediately dissolve the fabric of his body. For the evil one’s desire did not succeed as he wished, and Adam did not die when he ate the fruit, as he had expected. For his life continued for nine hundred [?] years and more after that time, and a spring of life flowed through his body to sustain his frame. The warning in the sentence disciplined him like a child, and through that warning he came to hate sin, the cause of his death. Mortals did not acquire new properties through the sentence. The Creator had placed within their very nature these things that happened. His Lord’s command became his teacher and made him wise, inscribing signs in his mind to serve as a warning. He hated sin, which had become the cause of mortality, and came to love the Creator, who had disciplined him and made him his own. These things concerning Adam were already known to the Creator. He did not introduce death as an afterthought, against his own will. For Adam’s benefit, he spoke of them as new things, so that through experience Adam would learn his Lord’s will. Everything that came to be, he designed [?] in Adam according to his will.
And into his constitution he bound love for everything that came to be. For everything that happened, Adam owes praise to the Creator who showed his love toward the things he had made.
On the Creation of the Angels
Discourse Thirty-Seven: On the Creation of the Angels

The creation of the one who formed everything is full of great wonder. The power of the universe, whose master is hidden, cannot be described. A hidden power lies concealed in the investigation of his craftsmanship, and it cannot be explained unless he himself explains [?]. Searching for him is lofty, investigating him is mysterious, and finding him is difficult. However much we seek him, we must still seek him earnestly. The wealth of his wisdom is deeper than every depth, and the well-ordered arrangement of his creative work cannot be encompassed. His command is broader than his immeasurable creation. He has set a limit for everything, but he has no limit to confine him. His gesture is swift, his power mighty, and his strength immense; the mouth is too small to recount the ways of his might. A discourse seeks to speak about the one who spoke: how he spoke, and his floods arose out of nothing. From nothing he created everything, when nothing existed; and upon nothing he set everything that came from nothing. He issued a single command over everything, and with that word everything came into being from nothing. His command swiftly ran over his creation, and at once the work stood before him at the signal of his command.

The work did not delay at his signal, not even for an instant, nor was it slow to display the power of his greatness. With a signal he beckoned creation to appear, and suddenly it was formed, without knowing how it had been formed. Suddenly he spoke, and speechless beings came into existence along with speaking beings. They were astonished and amazed at their natures, which had suddenly come into being. The rational beings marveled still more at their nature: how fully it was constituted, and how much authority it had over the freedom dwelling within it. Their assemblies stood in wonder and amazement when they were formed, and they marveled insatiably at the reason within them. They were astonished at their rational nature: how articulate it was, and how swift was the power of understanding that moved within it. They examined themselves and everything with discernment, asking who had brought them and everything into existence when they did not exist. With the intelligence within them, they pondered whether they had arisen by themselves, or whether some other power had formed them. “What, then, is this that has happened?” they signaled to one another. “Are we self-existent beings, or have we come into being from another being?” “Did we already exist as we now exist, or did we not exist? Have we come into being just now, or does our origin lie far behind us?” There was great inquiry among them when they first came into being, and they marveled greatly at their own formation and that of everything. They contemplated the vast expanse of the heights and depths: how great must be the command that had made them so great! They marveled at the darkness of the created world; although it was very dark, to them it was not as dark as it really was. In its darkness their sight was [?]: how it sped along without being hindered by its gloom! Within its gloom they beheld a wondrous sight, and they never tired of pursuing inquiry into what had happened to it. Very great was the wonder in which they were immersed, and they labored without end to discover its cause. They struggled in the contest of wonder over the formation of everything, longing to learn the cause that had wearied them. They persisted in the arena of the worlds’ coming into being, never resting from the struggle of searching for the hidden one.

They longed to see openly the hidden one who was concealed, so that, when he was revealed, he might relieve the weariness of their minds. With this hope, their expectant thoughts labored to hear something that would resolve the inquiry that had worn them out. Their ranks stood facing one another in terrible labor pains, and like a woman giving birth they were in anguish to bring forth what they sought. All night they labored in pursuing this inquiry, until they heard [?] a voice crying out, “Let there be light.” At dawn they heard a voice that was not a voice, speaking in a way suited to the hearing of their minds. The command that had formed them cried out spiritually, and they too heard spiritually, with the hearing of the spirit. Those attentive listeners heard an inaudible sound; and although they heard it well, they could not hear it as it truly was. They heard the one who makes everything hear crying out, yet not crying out, for even his voice was unlike a bodily voice. Those who heard his voice were astonished at its sound: how he made the voice of his will heard while his nature remained hidden. They marveled that his voice was revealed while his very self remained hidden, and they were afraid to inquire into his hiddenness. They remained in fear before they saw light come into being; but once it was formed, they rested in the harbor of its brightness. They rested in a peaceful harbor when the beautiful light came into being, and they rejoiced and praised its Maker, who had made it well. They cried out praise to that voice which had created light, and gloriously repeated the praise of the one who made the voice heard. “Glory to the one who made a voice reach our hearing without sounds, and through visible deeds showed us the power of his hiddenness!” Through his deeds the spiritual beings saw the one hidden from all, and they rested from fear and from investigating his hiddenness. In that silent coming into being, they contemplated the coming into being of their own selves: just as it had come into being, they too had come into being from nothing. Light came into being from nothing, like everything else, and the spiritual beings in their ranks marveled at its formation. They stood in order before that Order which had arranged them,

and under his glory they joined their voices to sing praise. Their assemblies cried out lovingly, “Glorious is the Creator, who through the things he has formed revealed that he is the Maker of everything! Worshiped by all is the one who makes everything from nothing, who through what exists taught us the power of his divinity.” In divine fashion they proclaimed holiness before the God of all, and in keeping with his glory they offered him the praise that was his due. Like debtors, they paid the thanksgiving they owed, and praised and exalted his creative power, which had formed things so well. The creation that had come into being greatly pleased their minds, and they marveled greatly at its Maker and Preserver. Wisely the wise contemplated the wisdom of the Hidden One: how skillful it was in forming and preserving. Through his acts of wisdom, the wise learned spiritual things, and through his understanding they gained understanding to investigate hidden things. He brought them into a school like little children, so that they might study the name of Creator and his creative power. They studied the name of Creator and his creative power, and they were astonished at the variations in the sounds of his voice. They were amazed at that utterance, “Let there be light,” and perhaps they reflected that they too had come into being through an utterance. That utterance stirred up inquiry in their minds. They searched carefully and learned well about its beauty. Come, then, let us pursue with the spiritual beings the inquiry they pursued, and learn with them the reason for the voice and the force of its meaning. Come, let us gain understanding through the power of the understanding that enlightened them: how and about what he instructed them through an utterance. Why, indeed, should there be a voice for him who by his nature is without utterance? For he is utterly hidden from perceptible sound. He whose nature is without composition is without utterance. If this is so, a hidden reason lies in the sound of his voice. Through his voice he taught that he himself had fashioned everything from nothing, and that heaven and earth and everything in them belong to him. Within two visible [?] he enclosed everything,

so that no one would think that within his creation there was anything created by another. First he created heaven and earth, water and air, and along with their formation came the formation of the spiritual beings. He created heaven like a wall and spread out the earth, and within them he enclosed everything, rational beings and speechless beings. He desired a great city as a dwelling for the work of his hands, and stocked it with everything useful for the needs of his handiwork. He nourished rational nature more abundantly with good things, and revealed and showed it the power of his being and his creative activity. To the rational beings he revealed through creation that he was swift, yet for their instruction he prolonged his work over six days. In six days he taught them the order of his power and made them skilled scribes of the work of his hands. They learned skilled scholarship from the creation before their eyes, and in their skill they began to bring order to the beings without discernment. Through their discernment, the beings without discernment gained understanding and yielded themselves to subjection under their authority. The silent beings submitted to the authority that he had given them. Though without perception, they perceived and knew that there was a Creator. Through the speaking beings, the silent beings learned to keep order; and through the silent beings, the speaking beings marveled at the Creator’s power. Both orders benefited from one another through one Lord, and they offered thanksgiving to his lordship, one through the hands of [?]. Rational beings and speechless beings became a source of good for one another, and they benefited greatly through reverence for the Lord who had fashioned them. They learned that they were one creation under one authority, and they did not waver in the thought that there might be another ruling power. Their very formation strengthened them through the Creator’s power, and through actions they learned the workings of their own actions. Now that rational beings and speechless beings have submitted to one authority, come, let us contemplate that authority which instructed them. Come, let us consider the varied wonder of his creative activity: although he is one, he is not one in the things that are visible. Let us listen intelligently to what is recorded in the Scriptures, and let us examine the book and its writings with understanding. Scripture revealed to us how we and everything else were formed, but it did not choose to reveal to us how the spiritual beings were formed. Moses did not write about their formation in the book he wrote, until he reached Abraham and mentioned them.

He did not tell us about their appearance at the beginning of his account, until he described their mission to Hagar. He did not inform us that they had been entrusted with anything to administer, until they showed their care for the Egyptian woman. He did not tell us that they were our relatives and companions, until they themselves taught proper conduct to Sarai’s servant. He passed over the great account of their deeds in silence. As though they did not exist, he left them unmentioned and said nothing about their formation. He imposed silence on the deeds of those who attend to our lives, and concealed them beneath a covering of ignorance. Why, then, did the one who recounts everything neglect to mention them? For he explicitly mentioned in his writings everything that came into being. Why, then, did he conceal that clear account of how they came into being, and not reveal it before us as he revealed our formation to us? Why did he not say whether they came into being along with everything else or after everything else, just as he said that humanity came into being last? Why did the one who revealed everything to him not reveal to him that among created beings there is a creation beyond the reach of harm? Their nature is beyond bodily harm, even though humanity is said to be above everything. Why did he not show him the power of rational understanding within them, or tell him about the freedom of their wills? Why did he not teach him that they are spirits and are not composite, so that perhaps we might have learned that their nature and the nature of our soul are one? The craftsman who gave them their nature examined that nature, and when he saw that they were beautiful, he concealed them from those who would look upon them. He saw that their splendor surpassed that of everything he had created, and that if it were revealed, people would be led astray by its splendor. He considered the error concerning them before they came into being, and forestalled it with the silence he imposed on their formation. He saw that the human inclination longs for whatever is desirable. That is why he concealed the desirable account behind silence. He imposed silence on the desire of Adam’s descendants, so that evil desire would not be stirred up in their minds. He placed the restraints of ignorance upon their minds, so that, once they knew, they would not throw the course of his creative work into confusion. The swift course of their thoughts was visible to his commanding will,

and he forestalled them before they began to travel into error. He erected a fence of silence before the brutish, so that they would not trample the work of his hands with their blasphemies.
