From eternity he heard the sound of their blasphemy, before they came into being; and once they were formed, he quieted it with the silence surrounding the heavenly beings. He silenced them like the mute concerning error, so that he would give error no room to reign on earth. Through the silence within them, he quieted error's strife, so that it would not run wild and trouble people with its turmoil. He knew that it was savage and killed people. For this reason he bound it with silence as with a weapon. He brought it into the prison of oblivion and confined it, so that the name of its wickedness would not be remembered among earth's inhabitants. Through Moses he erased the name of its wickedness from his books, so that people would not dwell on accounts of its ugliness. It was striving to divert the name of his Being to itself. Therefore he wiped the hateful name from his law. It fraudulently stole the power of creation for itself and proclaimed a fiction about beings that were not real. Though feeble in strength, it made itself strong through the angels' strength, and concealed its ugliness beneath their beauty. It called them beings who had brought creation into existence, and said that creation depended on their help and that the world was preserved by them. It raised them to the lofty rank of divinity and named them creators of everything and guardians of everything. It was not that the angels were being exalted to this height, but that error was taking refuge in their names. Nor, again, was error itself, in its own person, causing turmoil, since it possesses no actual substance that exists through actions. The demons' will and the human inclination desired this, and he restrained their wickedness—he who restrained the angels together. The Good One, who is entirely good, saw the wickedness of the wicked and concealed the goodness within the spiritual beings so that it would not be disgraced. He kept the creation of those pure in soul from disgrace,

and placed it in silence as in a treasury, so that it would not be exposed to savagery. With the seal of silence he sealed the treasury of his household, so that wicked servants who stirred up rebellion would not destroy it. The company of demons was stirring up rebellion against his Being, and intensified its rebellion against the fortress he had built to confront their desire. He built a lofty fortress through silence concerning the spiritual beings, and carefully placed their creation inside it. That command which gives wisdom to all acted wisely, concealing goodness from the wickedness of the wicked. Oh, evil, how wicked is the inclination of your insolence! Even the Creator conceals from you the goodness of his bounty. Oh, error among those who go astray, how insolent you are! The one who orders everything takes care to protect his works from your abuses. Oh, hateful thing, whose appearance makes anyone who looks at it hateful! The Good One concealed the beauty of his handiwork from its eyes. Oh, contemptible thing, the sound of which is contemptible to its hearers! From the beginning it drove the Creator of creation away from itself. From the beginning he saw how repulsive its appearance was, and turned his face away, so as not to look toward it when forming the Watchers. And if the Creator did not wish to look upon what is hideous, who would dare to gaze at it with a loving face? We should not look toward it with a loving face, lest we become hideous in appearance, resembling it. Its likeness has hidden the likeness of the Watchers from our minds. Were it not for this, their likeness would have been revealed to our eyes from the beginning. And if looking at it is so evil, just as it itself is evil, who would not turn his heart’s gaze away from dealings with it? Flee, then, people, from dealings with evil wickedness, so that you may not be deprived of fellowship with good goodness. See what it has done from the very beginning of time: it has not allowed us to see the created nature of the heavenly beings. Their created nature is more beautiful than the creatures that came into being with them, and the order of their activity bears witness to how beautiful it is.

Their appearance is delightful, and their actions move swiftly. Who is able to look closely at their ordered ranks? The one who establishes everything arranged them in a beautiful order, so that through their ranks he might order the wild world. He assigned them to order the world through their rational nature, so that creation would not be confused and without order. He did not arrange them because he lacked the ability to order everything, but to make known that his creation too is arranged in order. He established them together with the silent creatures, so that they would not exalt themselves and forget his rank as Creator. He brought them into the school together with beings without speech, so that they would not boast as though they needed no instruction. Through an audible voice he made them hear the power of his hidden being, so that they would know that there is a Being hidden from them. As with little children, he taught them about his being the Creator, so that they would not be bewildered by the splendor and glory of their own beings. With a slight gesture he spoke, and they came into being like everything that came into being. In creating them, he placed them on the same footing as everything else. They are servants [?], even if they are said to be spirits, and from one Power they received the nature that enables them to fly through the air. The Creator’s power strengthened them to perform mighty deeds, and he made them good servants of his activity. He supplied them with the vitality of immortal life and abundantly enriched them with freedom of soul. He placed the elixir of life and freedom of soul in their nature; by nature he made them alive and made them free. He honored them with life beyond the reach of harm and enriched them with freedom that cannot be overpowered. He placed the great wealth of discernment in their hands, so that they would not need to borrow anything from the silent beings. Without needs of their own, he settled them in a needy world, and without weariness he occupied them with the needs of our lives. He called them fire and wind through the mouth of the son of Jesse, yet the perception of their minds is far swifter than these. Like fire and like wind they fly through the air, and they are hindered neither by fire nor by wind. They stand between opposing elements, and they are harmed neither by cold nor by heat.

Like everyone else, they are enclosed within the numbered days and months, but they have no need of a change from one to another that is better. This world is counted as a single day in their eyes, since it is one and the same day that returns throughout all days. It is one day that has been running through the world from the beginning, and they run along with its course without interruption. Their thoughts are not interrupted by the [?] of time, for the Lord of time has strengthened them to keep watch over time. Oh, the mind that has acquired heroic endurance and does not weaken before the opposing forces surrounding it! Oh, the might of the divine power at work in the spiritual beings, which sustains the world and governs it through the members of his household! Oh, the creatures made by the one who made everything, who do what surpasses the power of their own beings! Oh, the nature that came into view after not existing, and, once formed, began to resemble its maker! Oh, the gift that cannot be limited by its recipients, yet has given itself to be contained by those who take hold of it! Oh, the greatness that comes from divine greatness, which has revealed its thought in something small among its creatures! The nature of the heavenly beings is something small, and this is the wonder: in its smallness it governs everything. Their nature is small compared with the size of massive bodies; they cannot be compared with mountain peaks and lofty mountains. They are [?] than the sphere of the sun and moon, and yet these cannot run their courses without them. Oh, the nature that makes light run its course through its own brightness, and bears something immeasurably greater than its own strength! Oh, the radiant beings who fly through the air alongside the heavenly lights, whose radiance is not affected by darkness! Oh, the flying beings who possess wings that are not made of assembled parts, who fly and soar without growing weary in their tasks!

Oh, the creation that comes from the immortal Creator and possesses immortal life like the Creator! Oh, the Creator, alive by nature and exalted in his being, who has given his servants a share in the glories of his divinity! Oh, how constant is the permanence of his everlasting being! He has given his creation a permanence that is never cut short. Oh, how great is the abundance of your love, maker of all! For [?] you have made your handiwork a companion in the greatness of your glory. Your creation is glorious, but it is not [?] like you—far from it! For you are the Creator, and by grace you made it the work of your hands. Your creations are filled with the splendor of your glory. They exist in you, yet they are not mingled with your being. You exist, and you exist outside what is yours and within what is yours, and your everlasting being cannot be grasped by those who investigate. You cannot be grasped by the speakers who speak about you, because no word is adequate to say how you exist. Who can recount the praise of your glory? Even if someone can, praise from us is superfluous to you. Whoever praises you praises you needlessly, because your glory is higher than praise and blame. Glorious praise and contemptible insult are equal to your being; the sound of acclaim and the sound of blame are the same to you. You sought praise from your creation as an opportunity for it, so that whoever praises might become glorious through praising. No one praised you before creation came into existence. It is clear, then, that even now you are not made glorious by praise. The Watchers did not sing you praise before they existed, for if they had not existed, they could not have delighted in your glory. For those who praise, existence came first, not praise. Glory, then, to the cause of the glory of those who praise! Oh, how glorious is that Being who glorifies his works, who made them possessors of glory through his own glory! How glorious is the making of the heavenly beings! This is the wonder: though they did not exist, they came into being and were glorified. It is a wonder how beautiful beings came from nothing, and how their beauty became beautiful without any material. Material of some kind serves as a cause of whatever comes into being.

And who would not marvel that the Watchers became beautiful without any material? That command which spoke, and they came into being, took the place of material; it fulfilled for them the role of craftsmanship. The gesture itself became material, labor, and craftsman; it began and completed the work without seeking any other help. He had no help from Matter, Mani’s invention, nor from the Archon, the falsehood concocted by Bardaisan. Evil, begotten by one full of evils, did not help him, nor did the gods who are no gods, whom the crafty one named. The crafty one brazenly called demons self-existent beings, and the erring one falsely said that Matter created everything. False is the Manichaeans’ invention of two powers, and impudent is the speculation of Bardaisan’s followers about the seven beings. Two did not fashion creation in the beginning, you Manichaeans! Nor did seven elements create it, you followers of Bardaisan! Evil does not exist, evil Mani—whom are you denying? Nor do the Archons invented by your companion possess authority. Stop, you impudent people, your quarrel with the Creator! Do not insult his truth with the names of false beings. You are liars, and your hearts are full of falsehood. The self-existent beings your minds have begotten are not real. There is one self-existent Being, who exists and is as he is. He is the one who fashioned creation in the beginning from nothing. The self-existent Being has no need to ask his creation for help, nor can his creation rise to the level of his being. Beyond everything is the self-existent Being who exists without beginning; on this side of him are heaven and earth and everything in them. He is outside everything, and he is within everything; the might of his power is not bounded by the work of his hands. The matter of the Manichaeans is contained within his creation, and the eternal beings of the followers of Bardaisan serve his command. Everything is bounded by him, since his nature is sufficient for everything.

He has no limit that bounds his craftsmanship. He exists forever, existing in his own being, and alongside his power there is no other power foreign to his name. He created the creation, which is full of countless kinds; though they are many, they were numbered in his knowledge [?] before they came into being. He made the spiritual beings spiritual, and he appointed them to serve before his will. Paul bears witness to the service in which they continually engage, in that he called them all by the name of servants. “Are they not all spirits and servants?” he says. And he yoked them to the expectation of the salvation of our lives. At their very coming into being they received this from the Maker, and the Maker himself ordered and established them for this. For the order of his service, he set them to laborious tasks, so that, when they grow weary, they may know that they are created beings. The labor in which they toil proclaims that they were made, and points out to people, as though with a finger, that they are not eternal beings. The course of their activities cries out like a trumpet: “Look, earthly beings, how weary is the order of those at peace!” The weariness within them joins them in bearing witness to their labors, and they themselves confirm its testimony: “Yes, it is true.” The labors of the Watchers, and the Watchers themselves, are a trustworthy witness that they came into being like everything else, to govern everything that came into being. They are beings that came into existence, not makers of created things; they were made servants of the things created by the Maker. O service of the one Maker, full of wonder, which reveals him, though he is not revealed as he truly is! Oh, how much greater is his creative work than our understanding, and how far short it falls of his immeasurable greatness! Beyond measure it is greater than we are, yet lower than he is; for behold, it was measured by him before we applied measurements to it. Its extent was measured by him before it came into being, and the weight of its mass was weighed by him in the scale of his command. The existence of the spiritual hosts was manifest to his command; their number and the purpose for which they would exist were reckoned by him. The whole creation had been created by him in his will, and he created it a second time in actual deeds whenever he wished.

He possessed this will from eternity along with his being, and he brought it into the open at the time that [?] the wisdom of his love. With great love he fulfilled the will that he had desired, and wisely arranged the order that he had marked out for himself. Heaven and earth were drawn upon the palm of his hand. Oh, what have I said? Not upon a hand, but in his command! The ages were inscribed for him in the book of his eternity, and I rightly said that they endured in his eternity. He had measured the earth and its dust in his fist. He has no fist, even though the prophet said that he does. The high mountains and the rocks within them were weighed by him; they were weighed by him on that balance which is not held in hands. He held the wind and its gusts in the handfuls of his power, and he had bundled up the mass of waters in the cloth of his command. He had established a clear boundary between the elements and had commanded how they should proceed without encroaching on one another. The path traveled by the sun and moon was known to him, and he had determined the course of the hours of light and darkness. The stars were numbered and arranged before his knowledge, and each had been assigned how it should travel. The deeds of the Watchers and human beings were also clear to him, and the good and evil of their deeds were known to him. The ranks of demons were distinguished by him from the angels, and he knew that they would indeed separate themselves from their companions. All these things, and others like them if there were any, were hidden in him, visible to him, and numbered by him. It is therefore not right to call him by names that imply weakness, for his creatures display the power of his might. Let us not boast and imagine that a boundary encompasses his extent, for even what he has made cannot be encompassed by our minds. Let us not babble and introduce another power alongside him, for even the Watchers, who are spirits, are his handiwork.

They are his handiwork, and he fashioned them like everything else. David bears witness when he says that he made his angels spirits. He called them "his angels," not simply "angels," so that everyone might learn that they belong to him because they were created by him. They are his creation, and all of them are bound under his command. His being their creator and maker has not escaped their notice. Those who go astray erred and called them hidden, self-existent beings. Perhaps the upright among them grieve over this injustice. It is a great injustice to give the Creator's name to servants, and perhaps the good servants are indignant over this offense. Perhaps only the demons rejoice, though they do not truly rejoice; for even if they rejoice, they rejoice only briefly and then turn to grieving. For a short time the demons rejoice and human beings go astray, but afterward indescribable regret comes upon them. Regret scourges the insolence that did not repent, and greets with love the angels who grieved here. They grieve greatly whenever human beings go astray in their name, and they rejoice greatly when the Creator's name is hallowed. The Creator's name is beloved in the movements of their minds, and they greatly desire that everyone should hallow his holy name. They will reverently proclaim his holiness in one accord, never relaxing the harmony in which they persevere. All the good servants remember that they were made, and they do not grow weary of rendering praise to their maker. Indeed, by their very constitution, they do not allow the wakeful mind within them to cease or fall silent from praise. They possess a wakeful mind in the nature with which they are endowed, and for this reason Scripture calls them Watchers. They are Watchers who have never slept and never sleep, and through their wakefulness they awaken people to learning. In the school they stand at the front like teachers, and through their teachings they make humanity's childishness wise. From that great Teacher who made them wise they acquired wisdom, and they direct everyone toward the goal of his teaching. They are occupied and labor night and day in meditation on his word, and, keeping pace with the passing ages, they seek out communion with him. Communion in divine love is dear to the Watchers.

Come, let us be their companions in the meditation in which they persevere. They serve the hidden will every day without interruption. Come, let us persevere in constancy toward our Maker. For our salvation they have toiled and labored ever since they came into being. Let us help them, even a little, through the labor of our lives. For our sake they stir the air through all its changes. Let us stir our minds to understand the order of their changes. On our behalf they run in the spiritual arena. Let us praise them, so that we may be worthy of the reward of their crowns. To help our souls, they engage in the contest alongside their companions. Let us encourage them to strive still further for our victory. Through their struggles they bring the demons' warfare against us to an end. Let us give thanks to the good Lord who armed them. They drive demons from our camp so that they will not harm us. Let us praise the Name that bound them in love for our souls.
On the Conduct of the Angels
Discourse Thirty-Eight: On the Conduct of the Angels

I saw the temporal world running continuously, and I wanted to learn who sets its silence in motion. I saw that its running and its silence were wisely ordered, and I said to myself, "Who, then, taught it to proceed in order?" I marveled greatly at its changing seasons, ground up like spices, and I wanted to know who grinds it and transforms it. I entered among its changes and stood as though in an arena, to observe closely how they overcome and are overcome. My thoughts wished to travel along with its course, so that I might know where its path begins and its running ends.

Its running and its order made me inquire about it, so that, once I had investigated it, I might understand and inform those who inquire about it. Its [?] wore me down like a hungry person longing for bread, and I yearn to fill my mind with its crumbs. Its beauty drew me to approach it and examine it, so that perhaps the ugliness of my speech, full of passions, might be made beautiful through it. Through words about it, I long to share in its beauty, and I am ready to reveal the desire of my mind. Desire for the world has stirred my mind beyond its usual order, and now it compels me to give birth to words like infants. Like a woman giving birth, my mind labors over the subject of it: when will it bring forth the infants of this discourse before its listeners? The question of the world is the question my mind has brought forth: who moves it and changes it, although it is mute? Who changes summer into winter and winter into summer? Who turns its cold into warmth? Who makes the orb of the sun rise in the morning? Who hides the beauty of its light in the evening? Who makes it race swiftly across the heights? Who holds it so that it does not come loose and fall to the earth? Who makes the moon small, just one day old? Who brings it to youthful maturity halfway through the month? Who silently lays commands of order upon it, so that the great order of night and [?] is not disturbed? Who makes the stars run in order, one after another, and shows them the path of their unceasing journey? Who sets the mute air in motion to serve us? Who makes its silence cry out with bodily sounds? Who hardens and thickens its thin substance? Who makes it carry masses of water and sprinkle them upon the earth? Who raises it like a rod above the sea and subdues the sea's unruly impulses through its storms? Who stills its turbulence when it grows violent? Who in turn makes it violent when it has grown calm? Where is its fierce blast when it is not blowing? From where does it suddenly come with violent force?

Who kindles the fire of lightning from its trembling? Who makes the sounds of thunder heard out of its stillness? Who blends its cold with warmth, so that the water it provides may nourish the earth's fruits? Who preserves it when it mingles with dense bodies, so that it is not destroyed by elements foreign to it? These things made me inquire about their changes: does the power to change belong to them, or to others? Do these mute things possess reason in their own natures? Or is it perhaps rational beings that move those without reason? Do those who possess reason have the power to do this? Or, again, are they enabled and strengthened by the Creator's power? The shepherd of these things placed reflection on them in my mind, and I reflected that it is one who does these things by the power of his will. There is one power that exercises its might through spiritual beings, and he orders the works of his hands through the works of his hands. Through rational beings he moves the natures that have no perception, and through spiritual beings he fulfills his love toward created things. From the beginning he entrusted the world to their intelligence, so that they would preserve the succession of the seasons without confusion. He made the angels treasurers of his kindness, so that they might distribute the treasure of his mercies to those on earth. He appointed them stewards over his service, so that they might give the members of his household their provisions at the proper time. He entrusted the infant world to them as to a teacher, so that they might teach it wisdom, bringing it from infancy to maturity. He entrusted its flighty course to their tutelage, so that they might discipline it away from shameful deeds. The Mind appointed tutors for the fool, so that they would not allow him to go about as he pleased.

He was utterly lacking in understanding, ignorant as he was; therefore he appointed those shrewd in mind to serve him. He entrusted to their authority the wealth that he needed, so that they might attend to his needs day by day. The greedy one longed to eat and gorge himself wastefully, so he put the food into the hands of the upright, for them to provide for him. He wished to restrain his wastefulness through the hands of the upright, so that he would not eat wastefully and die miserably. The Good One, Lord of the brutish world, is wise, and in his wisdom he taught it wisdom through the speech of speaking beings. He appointed rational beings to serve the speechless world, so that through their intelligence they might teach its brutish nature wisdom. Through these rational beings, the Ruler of all orders everything, and there is nothing among created things that does not complete its course through their hands. He entrusts to them the course of both speechless and speaking beings, and in their language the Hidden One speaks with his creatures. Through their mediation he reveals his love and also his threats; he gives blessings and inflicts lashes on those who are punished. Through their service as messengers, the Lord of all does everything; he chooses and rejects as his will has deemed fitting from eternity. He sends them as messengers to those on earth, and they return and report to him what he knows. He requires from them the count of human beings and the changes of the seasons, and they are very diligent in maintaining the order placed in their hands. Through them he carries out the work of his providence; sometimes he disciplines and sometimes he wins over, so as to help. Through them he rescues those who cherish his love when they are afflicted, and through them he disciplines the contemptuous when they become arrogant. Through them he governs the authority of kings and the division of nations, and through their diligence he orders seasons and brings seasons to an end. His command rides upon their movements like a charioteer, and they are harnessed like horses and fly through the air. O spiritual chariot of the God of all, in which spiritual horses are harnessed with spiritual reins! O charioteer who holds the world, but not with hands,

who makes the hosts of peacemakers race across the heights! O charioteer whose riding transcends all riding, who sets a course in motion without visible limbs! Who has ever ridden on something that cannot be ridden, with a nature harnessed beneath him that is not subject to the senses? Who would not marvel at the great course of the great mountain? For look: its single course has lasted a little less than six thousand years. Who would not say that the one who created everything is the one who makes it run, and that his power strengthens the weakness of his handiwork? His power makes the heavenly beings run under his command, and by that same command he makes the world run beneath his servants. Oh, what a marvel, whose wonder is doubled by another marvel: the world is harnessed beneath its Creator and its fellow servants! The Watchers are harnessed beneath the command that established them, and the world is harnessed beneath the authority of those whom he empowered. Under the yoke of his love, creation is harnessed beneath the spiritual beings, and their powers are above its back like a charioteer. With spiritual reins they hold the incorporeal air and guide it according to the will of the one who guides everything. Everything, all together, is harnessed and subjected to their powers. They run with everything and keep everything free from harm. He divided the world into the allotted regions of their authority, and each of them carefully attends to the work entrusted to his hands. There is one who holds the sun in hands that have no bodily composition, and shows it the path of a journey that leaves no footprints. The Watcher runs swiftly alongside the speechless sun and directs it so that the path of its journey will not become confused. Alongside its unrestrained movement, the swift mind constantly flies, setting the limits of its circuit around the earth, night and day. There is one who carries the moon on his incorporeal shoulder and guides it through its changes as though it were a child. He carries it with his mind, [?] the one without understanding, and guides it so that it will not move about like a beast. He sets arrangements and stages before it as before a pupil, so that it may know how far to descend and ascend. There are those who hold the radiance of the stars like torches, and with their rays drive away the darkness of the nights.

The beings endowed with speech prepare a level road in the air for the speechless ones. They remain constantly upon it and do not slacken in traveling along it. Rank upon rank, the insensible beings travel along the road, with the heavenly beings at the head of their ranks like guides. The ranks and their arrangements resemble a king’s encampment, and the spiritual beings are commanders of armies beyond numbering. There are those appointed to stand over the moving air, and they move it through the hidden movements of their thoughts. The bodiless beings set the bodiless air in motion, and make it something that can be ridden, although its nature cannot be ridden. The incorporeal beings hang upon the incorporeal air and divide it into portions as though it were a solid body. The incorporeal beings make a body out of what is not corporeal, so that in its bodily form it may carry the mass of corporeal waters. They weave dense garments from its thinness, so that their density may keep the waters from pouring out. They spread clouds in the space between the heights and the depths, and above them they heap up water like a canopy. With water and wind they roof the house that our lives need, and from its roof they bring down water and sprinkle it on the earth. Some give thunder its power and its terrifying voice, and shake the earth with the sound of its swiftness. In the air itself they make cisterns of water, and produce a sound when water is poured into water. The sound of the wind suddenly passes through the reservoir of water and scatters the mass of water in the clouds. The cloud, a waterskin of wind, is full of liquid water; when the sound of thunder passes through it, it bursts and pours out. O the struggle of two mute things and one speaking being, within which is hidden the cause of peace for Watchers and human beings! For the sake of peace, the Watchers teach the mute things warfare, lest their harmony destroy the peace of fruits and crops. Skillfully the rational beings teach the mute things combat.

And from the air itself they forge the weapons with which they arm themselves. They forge arrows of fire from it when it grows dense, and send them across the heights with violent force. They strike its surges with violent force, as though striking iron, and bright sparks come out of it. It suddenly shines brightly amid the light, and swiftly reveals its light and hides it. The sight of its light fills anyone who looks at it with wonder, for its end comes with its beginning, without delay. It does not allow anyone looking at it to take a good look: even as he looks, it withdraws its light from his pupils. O swift thing that swiftness itself cannot see! Even us who have seen it, it does not allow to take a good look. Let us, mute one, look at the beauty of your silence! Do not hurry us along with a swiftness that is not your own. It is not lightning's own power that makes it run swiftly; a rational being makes its silence race, while it itself is unaware. It is a Watcher who swiftly lowers the clouds to the sea; they carry water and do not sink under its weight. Like a ship, the cloud carries a store of water; it rises and stands across the heights, and then opens. The spiritual being holds the oars of wind and guides it, so that it does not sink under the weight of the water [?] inside it. O sailor who speeds his ship of air through the air, and instead of oars carries it by spiritual movements! By movements the spiritual being carries the wind of the air, and when it is shaken, it gives a sound that shakes the earth. He grips the edges of its swiftness as though gripping a garment, and drives it down toward the surface of the earth against its will. O swift one who has no desire to remain on earth, who continually travels across the heights like a nobleman! Oh, how great is the good providence shown toward our race, which compels natural beings to act outside their established order for our sake! The air naturally possesses the ability to fly, and this is the marvel: it rises to the heights and descends to us. An angel’s power constrains its power of flight and brings its lofty course down to our lowly places. One angel has been appointed commander over its host,

and he directs it through changes of every kind of form. One exercises leadership over its changes, while he has fellow servants with him who obey him. A holy one has been appointed in place of Satan, who went astray and fell, and the servants with him take the place of the legions of tyrannical demons. He and those with him bring order to the unruly air, while other companies govern what has been entrusted to them. The authorities’ jurisdictions are divided into ranks, and they proceed in an orderly way in carrying out their tasks. There is one entrusted with ordering kings and their dominions: at one time he establishes a king, and at another he removes him from power. There is one who assigns battle to warriors, and according to his testing he grants victory to the good and disciplines the wicked. There are those who guard people daily against harm and drive the forces of tyrannical demons away from them. One angel accompanies every human being as a loving companion and is with him from the day of his birth until his death. The living one runs alongside the life of the short-lived person, and on the day of his departure he stands constantly beside his bed. He separates the soul, his kinswoman, from the bodily members, and he takes her wherever the Creator has commanded. He is bound and subject to the command of the [?], and it is not his own prerogative to perform what is accomplished through him. It is not he who grants the span of life and its short duration, nor does he have authority to add an hour or take an hour away. Nor does he govern a person’s life by force, and he cannot compel him either to do good or to do evil. A human being possesses freedom of soul in his likeness and, as a discerning being, can both sin and act righteously. The freedom of soul within a human being is not constrained, nor is it directed to do anything without its consent. The soul of a human being and spiritual beings have one nature. It cannot be overpowered unless it overpowers itself. From the beginning it possesses within itself a complete personhood [?], just as the constitution of the peaceful ones is also complete. They are its kin, and it belongs to their own stock,

and in their actions they always show love for their kinship with it. It is that utterance which called humanity by the name of the Hidden One that they honor through the honor they show to human beings. Through humanity they show their great love for the Creator; for this reason they labor to provide our sustenance and to serve us. For our sake they are greatly worn down and continue to toil, and they find no rest until they rest in the harbor of [?]. For our sake they are engaged in the struggle of the changing seasons, so that through their changes we may remember life without end. For our sake they labor and toil at arduous tasks; though they do not grow weary, they labor with us so that we may find rest. For our sake they stir the air with the movement within them, so that through its breezes the crops that sustain our lives may flourish. For the sake of our lives they arrange the course of the months of the year, so that we may not go astray and lose the order of our discernment. For our sake they show the sun and moon their path, so that we in turn may not lose the path of our journey toward the Creator. For our sake they divide the hours between light and darkness, so that they may not doubt the Creator who created them. For the sake of humanity's rank they received authority over ranks and orders, and showed that they both command and are commanded, so that humanity's rank might be exalted. To honor humanity's dignity, they honor the orders of their authorities; and for the sake of humanity's order, order reigns among their ranks. Great order dwells among the orders of those who arrange things; and although they are one, some command and others are commanded. The great herald of the nations considered their authority and called them by names expressing the authority of their dominions. For our benefit he wrote that they rest [?] and also suffer birth pains, until we strip off our susceptibility to suffering and put on glory. All creation [?] labors with them, and they with it, until the day of birth from among the dead arrives. Together with the silent creatures they are occupied and toil over that created being for whose lost condition there is hope. Creation hangs upon the hope held out to humanity, and the Watchers even more so, since they understand the greatness of the hope prepared for it. With good hope for the salvation of our lives, they wait every day.

And they are certain that they will receive it through their deeds. Because of this hope he wrote that they were subjected to futility, and the world received the promise of a reward on the day of its renewal. The toil that the Watchers undertake on humanity's behalf is real; here is proof of its reality in the changing seasons. The seasons bear witness to the labors of those who maintain peace; without a mouth, they cry out in silence about how greatly they toil. The speechless elements cry out in silence to humanity: “Look, human being! For your sake the Watchers toil.” For your sake both rational and speechless beings are subjected to toil, yet humanity itself does not perceive how greatly they toil on its behalf. Look, human being, at their labor, even if only a little, and exert yourself in contemplating the goodness of the Watchers, your kinsmen. See how greatly they have toiled and continue to toil on your behalf; as they nurture you, they also grow fruit to meet your needs. The growth of fruit and the sprouting of seeds belong to them, and at their word the course of the months of the year is ordered. They move swiftly through the air, and the beauty of their labors is pleasing to them. Gladly they attend to everything and guard everything, and through their activity they offer praise to the one who ordered everything. They cry out praise when they are sent out on their tasks. This is the wonder: along with their work there is also praise. Each of them accomplishes two things at once without distraction: service on behalf of humanity and praise to the Hidden One. O workers who carry out divine work, who are not hindered from accomplishing two things at once! O servants of the Lord of all, who serve everyone, whose love is perfect toward the Creator and toward his creatures! O messengers of the immortal King of kings, who through their missions preserve the lives of mortals! O peacemakers and lovers of peace, the peace that belongs to everyone and is among everyone, who uphold humanity’s peace through the love within them! O heralds of the Creator’s power toward his creatures, whose voice the deaf elements obey without a sound! O how far beyond telling is the speech within them, for even silent things obey the voices of their proclamations! Without a sound, each of them speaks with silent things.

And although there is no speech, they accomplish through deeds what words express. In secret they speak with the insensible elements, and these give out perceptible sounds like beings with senses. As though with hands, they grasp the air by its four corners and spread the rush of its swift movement toward the four quarters. With its gentle breezes they refresh human beings and animals alike, and with its moisture they water the earth so that it may yield fruit. Skillfully they treat the ailments of the sick world with cold and heat, two opposites. They continually temper its cold with heat, and then apply it like medicines to its debilitating ailments. O the bodiless healing practiced by those without bodies, which spiritual beings prepare and which benefits our bodies! The Lord of the world gave their skill to the world, for he saw that they knew how to treat the ailments of its weakness. From the beginning he placed the power of his will in their nature, so that they would be able to care for the world, sick with sin. From him they learned their skill, and then they excelled; the power of his help runs [?] with them until the end. The power of the Creator [?] runs swiftly with them, and with it they travel without any measurement of footsteps. Subtly he gives his signal without a sound, and they obey his voice without bodily hearing. He speaks with them according to the hearing he has given them, so that they can listen with the mind to the hidden voice. With their minds they listen to that utterance which is all this, and with understanding they contemplate it in wonder. Oh, how great is the vast wonder among the spiritual beings! The mouth of all creation is too small to recount its wonder. Oh, how sharp is the mind, [?] the faculties of the mind, capable of listening to a voice subtler than all intelligible things! Oh, how swift is the understanding with which they perceive! Though there is nothing visible, it is certain to them. Oh, how hidden is that hidden reality above them!

And how plainly its activity is revealed before their eyes! Oh, how firm is the hidden certainty of their thoughts! They do not grow slack in seeking that hidden reality. It is hidden from them just as it is hidden from all creatures. And this is the wonder: however hidden it is, to them it is as though revealed. By faith they see a sight that cannot be seen, and without sight the understanding of their thoughts is directed toward it. By faith they listen to a voice without an audible utterance, and receive it without bodily senses. By faith they completed the [?] of faith, and believed that it is possible to believe [?] the Creator. By faith they completed the course of faith, and believed that it is possible to [?] in the name of the Creator. By faith they arose to set the power of the elements in order, and through it they overcame the fierce force of their conflict. By faith they undertook service to humanity, and did not doubt that voice which called humanity his image. Faith yoked them to the labor of sustaining his life, and they nourish him so that they may not despise faith. Faith sent them to his kindred, and through it they contemplated the hidden nature of his spiritual soul. They believed that it is spiritual and not [?], just as they themselves are spiritual and immortal. Its kind belongs to that kind which [?] kinds, and it too is without composition and invisible. Its lineage proceeds from that lineage without succession, and it too comes into being in that manner, from nothing. Oh, the nature of the human soul and of spiritual beings, who possess immortal life like their Maker! Alas for human beings, whose soul within them is immortal, yet in their disputes they have called the one who created it dead! Alas for the injustice whose wrong is plain even to the blind, which contentious people conceal under the appearance of love! Oh, the error that the deceiver poured forth among the children of error! It resembles that deception in Paradise. The aim of the deceit in that case and in this is one and the same.

And it is the same deceiver who practiced deceit there and led people astray here. [?] This error about mortality resembles that error about envy and wickedness. He said that it was out of wickedness that he forbade eating the fruit; now he has misled people with love, saying that he consented to die. “Out of love,” he says, “the maker of humanity died for humanity.” Here is an error filled with errors beyond measure! The measure of this error is harder to determine than other measures. However long we make our account, words fall short of it. Its enormity compelled me to multiply my words about it. I left the discourse about the angels and spoke about it. I saw that its enormity had disturbed humanity’s peace. That is why I mingled the account of it with the account of the peacemakers. I saw that the heavenly beings are exalted above all suffering, and I grieved deeply that fools make their maker suffer. Over the suffering attributed to him I grieved deeply and was filled with sorrow. I left the road and traveled along the road taken by the foolish. Return, my soul, to your discourse, to the path of the discourse about spiritual beings. Do not stumble on the false trail of those who love suffering. Proceed rightly [?] in the orderly account of those whose understanding is sound, and carefully pursue a fitting inquiry into their activities. Inquire, then, how they can move insensible natures, and by what power they overcome the mighty force of the elements. How do they give bodily form to air, which has no body, and then turn its bodily form back into a spiritual one? How do they mingle its coldness with heat, then separate it again and restore it to its original order? How does their subtle nature pass through its subtle nature, while the weight of the sun and moon hangs upon them? How far does their gaze descend in their activities, without disturbing the balanced order of the heavenly lights? How far do they fly from where the earth’s circuit lies, and how do they reach the other circuit at [?] evening? How do they measure the hours of night and day, without ever having departed, or now departing, from the order they received at the beginning? How many thousands are there in their legions? They are with everything, everything is with them, and everything is in their hands. Who can count the stars and number human beings?

For every star and every human being has one with it. Who knows how to examine all changes carefully? For not a single change occurs without their involvement. Who understands the authority of kings and the governance of nations? For the ordering of their affairs is entrusted to the activity of these beings. Who has heard David’s words about their holiness, in which she called them those who proclaim holiness and offer praise? In a single utterance the Holy Spirit revealed them, and showed that they are able to praise by the very fact that they offer praise. Who can grasp the order of their activities? There is no number to the portions that they count. He alone counts and reckons them before they come into being, and [?] he already held the full measure of their deeds. He knew how many they would be and what they would be like, and they were arranged before him before they rose to authority. They had been tested in the furnace of his examination before they came, and both their genuineness and their falseness were revealed to him. It was clear to the divine will how many of them would remain with him, and how many would depart from the purpose of his command. The tyrannical demons had been banished by him before they went astray, and the watchers on high were entering his household. [?], the ruler of the air, had been removed from his authority, and Gabriel’s company stood in the place of his rank. They were honored by him with order and rank in later times, and there was no order whose ranks were incomplete. These whom I have mentioned were with the eternal Being—not in actual existence, but in the mystery of things to come. They existed as future things, not as accomplished works; they were known and were given according to his knowledge. They were known to the knowledge that created them for the time when it knew they would be needed, at the time when they would be of help. When it was of help, the Creator created the creation he created, and through the angels showed it the way to journey toward him. Through the angels he taught the world about his lordship, for through them he guides it and makes it wise until the end. Throughout its existence he cares for the life of the short-lived one, and does not allow it to do anything without them.

The world has nothing hidden from the angels, nor do the angels have authority outside its course. As they run, they run a race crowned with victory, and they eagerly desire to arrange it without blame. The Lord of the world occupied them with the world’s labor, so that they might become rich through the poor one whom they nourish. For their own need they constantly supply the needs of its life, and when they give to it, they receive from it like people in need. They are not supplying any need of the God of all through it, for the world’s course is of no use to its Maker. The power that created creation from nothing is not too weak to govern the work of his hands without the watchers. He and his servants are honored through it; he sustains it through their hands, and raises and lifts its lowliness up to his greatness. The assemblies on high repay his kindness through their deeds. Yet why do I say that they repay it? They cannot repay it. The repayment is small when compared with grace. Why do I call it small—small, when it does not exist at all? The payment of a reward counts for nothing before the Creator; and if it exists, it exists by grace, not through labor. The watchers do not deserve repayment [?] because of their labor; rather, by grace they receive a reward from grace. I said that they receive blessings freely—not freely, but because the world cannot supply anything equal to the blessings. Very beautiful too are the labors of the heavenly beings, and no one can portray the beauty of their thoughts. Their beauty made them possessors of beauty; had they not been so, they would not have pleased the giver of beauty. The greatness of their love brought them near the King, and the King himself was greatly pleased to exalt them. Oh, the wonder of the greatness befitting the Maker: created servants have acquired the authority to act as makers! By the Maker’s power they move everything, through the Maker, and they do not forget that it is through his mighty power that they master everything.

They did not forget the name of the Maker through whom they are empowered, but human beings went astray and became confused in their thinking about them. Created beings who went astray called them by the name of the Maker, and attributed to their authority the authority of a maker. They divided up the great name of divinity among their names, giving one of them a share in creatorship. No, you who have gone astray! Do not become confused and stray so far. The self-existent One is one, and everything else came into being from him. There is one Creator, to whom creatorship belongs, and one Creator, to whom the name of self-existence rightly belongs. The name of Maker does not befit servants, you transgressors who have gone astray; nor does it befit the Maker to give his rank to the work of his hands. The spiritual beings take no pleasure in this error. And why am I saying that they take pleasure in it and do not take pleasure in it? Through their actions they reveal the power of the Maker, and if it were possible, they would cry aloud that the self-existent One is one. They knew the one Maker from the beginning, when they were formed, and they know no other power besides him. The love within their thoughts is bound to the will of his love, and they are very careful not to fall away from communion with him. They are always occupied with the concern with which he occupied them, and there is no time when their thoughts do not meditate on it. Good meditation is established among them night and day, and however much they meditate, they continue meditating on it without ever having their fill. Through good hope they were bound to the blessings beyond it. This is the wonder: however much they move, they never grow slack. The good among them never have their fill of love for blessings, but our inclination has forgotten the love of blessings through its own laxity. The Creator promised good blessings to them and to humanity. Blessed is the one who keeps the memory of those blessings in his mind! He invited our race to the kingdom on high along with their assemblies. Blessed is the one who is found worthy and enters with them where they enter! Come, mortals, let us become companions of the immortals, and let us become fellow heirs with them of the promised blessings.
On the excellence of the soul and how it governs.
Discourse Thirty-Nine. On the excellence of the soul and how it governs the body, which is its home.

The beginning of wisdom is true knowledge of the power of the Creator, who created out of nothing everything hidden and visible. The beginning of understanding is to understand his work as Creator: he created creatures not for his own ease, but out of his love. The beginning of insight is to contemplate the greatness of his power: he bears the world and governs it according to his will. The beginning of knowledge is to know his love toward the things he has made: though they do wrong, he does not take revenge on those who wrong him. The beginning of righteousness is to acknowledge the justice of his discerning judgment: though he overlooks much, not even a wink of the eyes escapes his notice. The beginning of goodness is to delight greatly in his kindness: though he overflows abundantly, compassion is mixed with the severity of his lashes. The beginning of discerning judgment is to distinguish clearly what befits rational nature, the mistress of speechless creatures. The beginning of everything is to acknowledge the order established in nature, so that the nature of rational beings may accord with the reason within them. The beginning of the law is to meditate on the law of the Spirit, to fulfill everything written by the mouth of the Hidden One. The beginning of repayment is to repay love to the Maker of everything, who honored the human image above everything and gave it a name. Everyone owes a debt to his Maker, who gave him a law and made him master over his possessions. He owes many times more praise than all other things that came into being, for he alone is designated by the name of the One exalted above everything. It is his duty to know the power of the command that created him:

He arose and took counsel concerning his formation, and thus fashioned him. It is fitting for him to acknowledge the justice of his Fashioner’s power, who fashioned him with his hand and breathed a soul into him from the breath of his mouth. He skillfully assembled and made him a vessel of dust: a visible body and a hidden soul, one human being. In the likeness of an image, he depicted in him the power of his creative work: speechless creatures in his body, and rational beings in the structure of his soul. In his body he encompassed the nature of everything visible, and within his soul the ranks of the heights, which are without composition. He made him a kinsman of [?] and earthly beings, and, as in a temple, made [?] and speechless creatures dwell in him. He wisely pitched him on earth as a dwelling of love, furnished him, and filled him with the power of wisdom for the one who dwells in him. In his soul he placed the great treasure of his creative power, so that from it he might seek everything needed for his life. The human soul is a treasury of hidden things, for within it is encompassed the power of the Creator who cannot be encompassed. Hidden mysteries lie concealed in the investigation of its formation, and they are revealed only through the power that created it. In the account of it there is a mystery revealing the name of the divine Being, and its structure is depicted in a threefold way, with word and power. Its likeness corresponds in some small measure to the revelation of the Persons: its nature to the Father, its word to the Son, and its life to the Spirit. Its nature does not resemble the hidden Nature in its actual essence, but symbolically, as an illustration of its dignity. It is far inferior to the immeasurable Being, just as the shadow of a body is inferior to the body itself. He is the self-existent One, and his enduring existence has no beginning; but it is created, and its composition is confined within time. The Creator’s power gave it the power of reason, so that it might live and give life to the lifeless body in which it dwells. He placed it in the body like a spring flowing with life. Through it the mute senses are watered so that they may bear fruit. Watered by its reason, the composite body sprouts and gives a voice of thanksgiving to its Maker. Through the power of its life, he lives and walks in this temporal life, and with it he awaits the inheritance of immortal life.

By its light he sees the glorious light of the Creator’s name, and, following its steps, he travels and reaches the divine Being. Through its skill he acquires discernment to distinguish rightly, and, as a rational being, he orders the course of his reasoning. It is a second sun in the [?] of the perishable body; by its rays he works the land and travels along the road. Its understanding is salt for the blandness of his desires; through it he is seasoned, and thus the human being becomes useful. Its thought [?] is wealth for the poverty of his lowly dust, and through its wisdom he provides for his life like a rich man. Through the speech that comes from it, he raises his voice above created things, and through its authority his authority extends over [?] and throughout everything. At its prompting he commands earthly beings [?] to obey him, and through its understanding he draws heavenly beings down toward him. Through its lightness he crosses the sea as though on dry land, and the weight of his body does not sink among the waves. Like an anchor, it hangs from the ship of his bodily existence and protects him from harm so that he is not destroyed. At its direction he travels like a sailor guided by a shining star, and it sets his course toward a peaceful harbor. Through its skill he teaches mute creatures to serve him, and through its understanding he brings order to what has no order. Through its shrewdness he outwits the speechless creatures, and through its devices he puts bridles on wild beasts. Like a charioteer, he rides upon the wild world and controls it so that it does not run wild as it moves. The soul has yoked all creation beneath his authority, and it has seated him like a king upon a chariot. With the reins of its movements, he holds heaven and earth in his hands, and directs his sovereign will wherever he wishes. O human being, whose name is dust, beneath everything [?], how high you have been raised from your lowly clay, above everything! O Creator, greater and more exalted than all creatures, how far your loving will has descended to our lowliness! Your command raised our lowly clay above everything, and you placed in our hands the scepter of your command, to govern everything.

You placed the power of your wisdom in our nature, impoverished of life, and it began to pour out streams of words in your likeness. Yours is the treasury of words within the soul, and through you she learns to make her words resemble your word. Your word touched her in the beginning, when you created her and everything; she stirred and rose at the sound of your command and acquired life. You mingled life with her constitution when you fashioned her, and clothed it in the garment of a visible body. Your will built her a temple—the body—and she entered and stood like a king within a palace. She arranged the visible senses like a lyre, and the finger of her skill played upon them with speech and hearing. The mouth became for her like a flute that consumes breath, and through it she sang the sound of sweet melodies. Through a hollow reed she constantly sings delightful sounds, and cheers the one weary of life with the vitality of her [?]. Through the breath of her life, what is dead sings praises in sweet sounds; it boasts of another who speaks through it as though that power were its own. It is like a reed, devoid of voice and life; but when the living soul sings through it, it acquires life. The soul is its life, and she preserves it in the life of [?]. When she lets it go, it returns to its own nature and becomes dust. Of everything it possesses, it has nothing that does not belong to her, and it cannot endure without the power of her activity. She sits within it like a mistress, though it does not see her; and it serves like a slave, remaining silent before her freedom. The Creator therefore fittingly built it as a house, and then she entered to dwell in it like a king’s daughter. In forming a human being, the divine command first assembles the body; after a time it fashions the soul and settles her within it. The Builder designs a royal dwelling in the substance of flesh, and when it is complete, he summons its inhabitant to [?] within it. With the body’s sinews he builds a bodily house, and between its arteries he lays moist blood as mortar. He lays the seed like a foundation in the womb where the body takes shape, and brings it step by step toward completion, like a building. The seed becomes [?] for the body, and thus it comes into being; from the body itself springs a body resembling the body.

The soul has no seed by which to produce another, nor does her nature spring up within the limbs from her own substance. The hidden command fashions her from nothing, in the same manner in which he fashioned Adam’s soul through the breath of his will. Her nature comes into formation from nothing, since she is akin to the Watchers and spiritual beings. She too is a spirit, like the spiritual beings who are not composite; her nature and her formation correspond to the way they came into being. The spiritual beings came into existence from nothing in the beginning, when they were made; and throughout all generations her existence proceeds from nothing. In the formation of Adam, she was formed after the body; and that same order continues every day for her and the body. The master of painters first fashions the form of the limbs, and then breathes into it the breath of life, and it becomes a soul. He weaves a garment of flesh with a spiritual hand, and then spreads it over the soul like purple robes. Within darkness he assembles the body and creates the soul, just as he created in the beginning and placed it in darkness. Through the formation of a human being, he shows humanity, as in a mystery, the manner of his creation out of nothing. He continually proclaims the greatness of his power in our formation, through the fashioning of body and soul that takes place every day. In the composition of the body he shows the creation of perceptible things, and in the coming into being of the soul, the coming into being of the intelligible hosts. He continually renews the whole creation through our formation, and makes it rejoice like a woman giving birth on the day of our birth. In us both speechless and rational natures are discerned, through the power of the Maker who renews their natures in us. They continually see a great wonder in our formation: human beings sprout from seeds in the likeness of human beings. They see the seed that human beings cast into human soil, and though it is lowly and despised, it changes and becomes a glorious vessel. They see the body being assembled like that first body, and also the soul dwelling within it, like Adam’s soul. Our existence bears witness to that utterance of the sixth day, as it is spoken every day: “Let us make humanity.” It is that very same command that formed Adam which forms the body and breathes the breath of life into its nostrils. He creates a living spirit in the body when it is assembled.

And immortal life stirs within its mortality. For nine months he dwells in a house [?] darkness, and after a time [?] he comes out and sees the beautiful creation. Out of darkness a human being emerges from within another human being, shows light, makes a voice heard, and pours forth words. The hosts on high marvel at his birth, at how precious he is, just as they marveled on the first day when light came into being. Like a shining light, he brings joy to the earth that had been sorrowful, for he too drives the darkness of suffering away from his mother [?]. A human being comes out of the womb with body and soul: a visible body and a hidden soul, a twofold vessel. His composition is skillfully fashioned in two forms: the body is dust and the soul is spirit—two that are one human being. People call body and soul one human being, because of the love of that Creator who joined them together. There is one body and one soul belonging to one human being, and there is one command that daily forms a human being within a human being. From the body itself the command forms another body, and all souls are like the soul of one human being. Body closely resembles body, and soul resembles soul, just as the coming into being that occurs every day resembles the first day. The Fashioner of all does not create humanity afresh, for human beings flow from the human being he created in the beginning. From one body came all bodies that have existed and now exist; souls too have one nature, like that first soul that came into being. One is the command that created body and soul in the beginning, and its power runs with the things it fashioned until the end. His fashioning is the same every day as it was at first; the body bears witness, since body resembles body, and soul resembles soul. Like a herald, the soul cries out within the limbs: “Look, people, how closely human beings resemble one another!” She is confined within the body and cannot be seen bodily, yet her voice is far brighter than the sun to the body's eyes. The appearance of her dignity is hidden inside the body, and she keeps it modest so that it will not be despised in the eyes of those who see it. She dwells within it, yet inquiry into her is hidden from it. Although she is visible to it, it does not see what she is like or how great she is. Her nature is within her, and her activity is outward, in deeds.

And although it is very much within her, it is distinct from her, and she in turn from it. The constitution of her subtle nature is not mingled throughout it: it is one thing, and she is another, without mixture. Among the hidden organs she is concealed in one place, and the power of her life is spread over the senses, both inward and outward. She sits in the heart as in a shrine in the middle of the house, so that all the senses may listen to her loving conversation. The mistress of the house sits in her home, in the middle of the house, and the body's senses gather around her like children. The body, childish in understanding, drinks the milk of her movements, and she continually raises it as though upon her knees. Like a nursing mother, she bears the cries of its childish heart, and according to its capacity she gives it food to nourish it. She too grows along with its dimensions, though she does not grow; and her love babbles like a child in its infancy. Her constitution is complete from the beginning, even while she is being raised, but she cannot make use of her completeness without the body. The speech of her rational nature is within her from the day she came into being, but the swift course of her movement is hampered according to the condition of the limbs. She knows how to sing the sound of sweet melodies, but to the extent that the flute of flesh is weak, she too is weak. She follows an order in playing beautifully on the lyre of her own being, and she is afraid to stretch the body's strings lest they snap. She possesses a power of discernment to rely on, but the body's senses do not respond to her so as to play beautifully. She wisely guards her treasures outside silence [?], until the infant body grows up and inherits its possessions. She too acts toward the limbs as parents do: as long as their heirs are children, they are not given control. She resembles the God of all in the silver [?] of her activity, for he leads a person step by step from low things to high things. Along with its growth, she ascends to the stage of youth.

And as it grows old, she descends to the level of weakness. When it is healthy, the judgment of her discernment is sound; and when it is sick, her understanding is too weak to do what it should. In its days of prosperity, her mind is at rest and her voice is clear; and on the day of its mourning, her thought is gloomy and her voice is faint. She is satisfied when it is satisfied, although her nature does not receive food; and she hungers when it hungers, although she has no need of nourishment. She stays awake during its toil, while it occupies itself with earthly things; and she sleeps when it sleeps, although her wakeful intellect does not sleep. She rejoices in its life, although it is dead and without life; and again she grieves on the day of its departure, although she herself is alive. She longs for its love, although it is utterly devoid of understanding; and she hates its sufferings, although she does not suffer through its susceptibility to suffering. It is through love that she suffers with her beloved, not by nature, for her nature is above all bodily sufferings. Through love she bears the painful hardship of its mortality; and like a woman in pain, her voice laments on the day of its sickness. Through love she is harnessed within its senses as though under a yoke; yet the laborious service of its desires gives her no pleasure. Because of her love for it, earthly love is dear to her; and although she is a spirit, bodily things give her pleasure. Because of her love for it, she descends with it to lowly things, although she does nothing foreign to her name. Her nature has no fleshly desire for sexual intercourse; but when flesh desires flesh, that desire comes to her from it. It is not hers to eat material food as the body does; yet if it hungers, she hungers with it and eats with it. Her wakeful intellect has never slept, nor does it sleep; yet when its senses are submerged in sleep, her thoughts wander. The body sleeps, and she sleeps with it, although she does not sleep. Her voice sleeps, but her mind is awake and her intellect flutters. Sleep belongs to the body, as do food and sexual union; and only figuratively is her nature said to share in what does not belong to her. The passions belonging to her nature and to the body's nature are distinct; yet because of love, they are said to be one human being. Hers is envy, a crab crouching among the thoughts; and hers is wrath, likened to a venomous asp. Hers is pride, a wild ass that rebels against subjection;

and love of glory, a fox strutting among lions. Hers is grumbling, a moth that gnaws the garment of love; and slander, a snare that catches the pure in heart. Hers is resentment, hers is anger, and hers is murder; and she devises ways to repay injuries to whoever harms her. Hers is sorrow and remorse for her deeds; and she pleads, asking for mercy for her sins. Food belongs to the body; sleep and sexual intercourse belong to the body; and it is the body that is bound to earthly things according to its needs. The sufferings and pains of mortality belong to it, and it in turn returns and becomes dust on its appointed day. It is with the soul, yet is not mingled with her subtle nature; and the soul is within it, yet does not become [?] with its bodily structure. It carries her in its senses, yet does not perceive what she is, since it does not know her; and she carries it, yet it does not discern her lightness. Like horses, its senses are harnessed under her authority, yet it does not understand the cause of its being harnessed. Like a charioteer, her will rides above its body, and the ship of its bodily existence is directed wherever she wishes. Through its movements she holds the course of its actions as though with reins, and she keeps it in order so that it does not stumble into desires. She places speech from herself in its mouth like a muzzle, and does not allow it to bite itself or its companions. She constantly raises the rod of judgment over its childishness and reminds it of the threats and punishments of the world beyond. She holds in her hand a book recalling blessings and punishments, and instructs it in hidden things that it cannot see. “Be afraid, mortal!” she cries through its mouth, warning it that endless torment is reserved for the wrongdoer. In love she urges herself and her partner not to slacken in the struggle for truth. Like a lookout, she cries to the senses and thoughts: “Get up! Apply yourselves diligently to doing good things!” “How long will you sleep, body, while the inclination is awake? Get up, rouse yourselves, and see the dawn of righteousness!” With the sound of threats she awakens herself and the limbs, so that they do not sink into desires as though into sleep.

She drives the sleep of wrongdoing away from herself and her beloved, so that they may stay awake to gather the fruits of reason. Night and day her meditation is engaged in rational thought, and her movements cause the power of life to flow without end. The Lord of natures placed a spring of life in her nature, and he no longer cuts off the flow of life from her living being. The leaven of the life of the immortals is hidden in her created being, to draw the dead body toward life. The power of her life flows through the drums of her mortality and brings forth unfamiliar words that are foreign to it. Like a speaker [?], the mute one speaks with what is not its own, and bears the fruits of reason on the branches of its body. The silent one bears the soul’s fruits at the tips of its limbs, and from it wafts the fragrance of a life it cannot see. The finger of life constantly plays upon the structure of its body and gladdens the sorrowful world with the sound of wisdom. O lyre whose strings are perishable flesh, which, though it is flesh, sings spiritual melodies! O flute made from a [?] reed full of knots, through which clear sounds pass without disturbance! O tunic full of the moths of base passions, which the living soul, kin of the Watchers, wears! O living being who, though needing no covering, is wrapped in a perishable garment and takes pride in it! O winged being whose wing is lighter than a bird’s, who nests in a body and has no desire to fly away from it! O you who are confined in a prison full of darkness, yet find pleasure in the harsh fetters of suffering! O command that confined a living being in a dead house, so that clay breathed the breath of life and acquired a voice! O craftsman who depicted a living being in a frail garment and set a seal over her face so that bodily beings could not see her! O artist, how wise is your creative power! In the human being you revealed your greatness to the work of your hands. As on a tablet, you depicted the world in his body and soul, so that heaven and earth might contemplate you through his visible appearance. In him earthly and heavenly beings see you.

Although you are far away, in him you are worshiped as one who is near. With body and soul you fashioned [?] the image of our likeness; and above all creatures your command [?] in forming him. You pitched him on earth as a tent of love with two cords, so that earthly and heavenly beings might dwell in him. With body and soul you built and completed the temple of his life, so that beings with speech and those without speech might offer one thanksgiving in it. Your will wove the garment of his body from dust, and like a seal you imprinted yourself upon him, O realm of life. Through the life of his soul, the dead world lives and walks, and by her light it journeys toward its appointed meeting at the harbor of peace. Like a lamp, the soul hangs in the temple of the body, burning with the oil of rational and immortal life. Her life fills the dead body with an order of light, and when she withdraws it, darkness reigns over its limbs. Her word is a lamp and shows him the light of life; at the top of his frame her voice burns like a torch. By her light he sees; by her voice he [?]; through her speech he expresses himself; and through her skill he practices every craft on earth. By her strength he fights the battles of his desires, and with her help he overcomes the passions of his mortality. Through her he triumphs in the contest of righteous labors, and she gives him a crown of victory in return for his endurance. She teaches him to engage in spiritual battle and encourages him not to lose heart before the adversary. She holds the crown of immortal life in her mind and entices him as one would a child: “Come near and receive it.” She goes down with him into every struggle against desires, and, as with athletes, she anoints his senses so that they cannot be seized. Death alone can separate her from companionship with him, and she cannot engage in battle with the one who leads her away. The executioner of the hidden command suddenly peers in and terrifies her like a woman giving birth on the day of her delivery. Terrible pangs strike her too at the time of death, when she is driven out from within the body like a newborn child. Like a captor, death enters the palace where she lives and strips her out of the body of her lowliness.

The mistress of the body leaves her house naked, and like an exile she moves from it to another country. Her mind bears great mourning on the day of her departure, as she sees dreadful death destroying her dwelling. With the sound of lamentation she weeps for herself and her beloved, because he is decaying and the sound of her songs is ceasing. She weeps thunderously in silence over what has happened to her, for she no longer sings sweet songs on the harp of her love. She is greatly distressed when his senses are cut off from her, and a worm sings within his limbs in place of her mind. She grieves deeply over her separation from her beloved, even though she knows very well that the hope of returning to him remains. The command that created her gave her the power to know these things, and it placed within her the power of the wisdom of [?]. The command that brought her in and confined her within the limbs brings her out, just as she entered, without harm.
