She is not brought low by the suffering of the body's pains, nor does she decay when the garment that covers her decays. She is far above death and harm; she cannot be seen or physically grasped. She is a living spirit, and her wing is light for flying through the air. She is not caught in death's snares as the limbs are. One of the Watchers comes down to her on the day of her departure and takes her to the place appointed by the Creator. Like a guide, the spirit leads the spiritual soul until she enters the dwelling chambers to join her companions. The angel who guarded her in this life shows her where she is to live until the resurrection. All souls are appointed to dwell on earth, some in Eden and some in the place to which he was sent. The souls of those who love truth dwell in the region of Eden, and those of the wicked in places beyond it. The righteous dwell in Paradise in spirit, not in body, longing for the establishment of the kingdom on high. [?] He wished the children of the kingdom to dwell in a spacious place, so that everyone might learn that the hope they await is certain. It is not that they receive a reward there for their labors, but that he might reveal the distinction that will be made at the end.

Nor is the place outside a punishment for the wicked; rather, it makes known that they will not be raised to the heights. He gave Paradise as a pledge to confirm his words, so that through humble things he might establish the power of his glorious things. In keeping with the infancy of temporal life, he honored its time, so that through it he might draw people toward the things to come. Paradise too is a part of the earth, however beautiful it may be, and its fruit is perishable food, like all other fruit. Through his story he stirred up zeal among mortals and urged them to long for immortal life. On this condition it opened its entrance before our Savior: that he should first prepare the way for those who would enter. The first Adam closed its gate in humanity’s face; the second Adam opened its gate, and the robber entered. Two souls entered it first, as a mystery, in the same manner in which Eve and Adam had left it. Two lived in it at the beginning of the earthly creation, and two entered it in a firm mystery that cannot perish. Breaking the commandment through desire for the fruit drove two out, and keeping the commandment in righteousness brought two in. Sin fenced it off from sinners who resemble Adam, and righteousness opened it to Adam and the robber. With the righteous one, a sinner entered Paradise, to lend a hand to the idle so that they might become diligent. Through the robber he showed that it is possible to become righteous, since the enormity of his wrongdoing did not prevent him from entering. Through the one soul that entered with him, he revealed to everyone that, if they are willing, they are not prevented from entering.

The souls of our Lord and the robber entered first, and then the way was prepared for the journey to the land of Eden. All souls that have endured suffering enter Eden, and there they rest as on a bed of delight. As though asleep, they rest there from their activities and do not exercise the rational power within them. They rest completely from concern with good and evil, and they do not struggle in the contest of righteous labors. It is not that the power within them has ceased to live, but that the bodily instrument that conveys words is absent. It is not that the stream of discernment has dwindled and dried up, but that the tree of the body, which needs watering, is absent. It is not that the mind’s wisdom has diminished and its treasures have run out, but that the steward into whose hands it could give them is absent. It is not that the intellect has ceased its swift course, but that the body, the mount that carried it, is absent. It is not that the impulses, those rays of light, have had their flames darkened; rather, the pupils are unavailable for seeing clearly. It is not that speech, the trumpet of sounds, has fallen completely silent, but that death has closed the mouth that conveys words. The freeborn soul has not forgotten her freedom and therefore fallen silent; rather, because the body she loves has fallen silent, she has shared in its silence. She is gripped by mourning for her beloved, who has parted from her, and she makes no use of earthly pleasures. She wisely keeps silence over his departure until she hears the voice that calls to his mortality. For she cannot do anything without him, just as he too is nothing without her. The Maker of all fashioned them into one human being. Can half a human being be complete without the other half? The soul is half a human being, however alive it may be, and its activity cannot be sustained without the body. The Creator [?] wished to call both it and the body his image. How, then, can it give shape to deeds without the body? He granted it the body through which to display the power of its wisdom,

and did not permit it to do anything even while the body sleeps. When the body sleeps, it too sleeps with it, though it does not sleep. Until the body rises, it is not awakened to its work. If it could do nothing while the body slept, how can it do anything now that the body is submerged in the sleep of death? If it did not sing through the body while its structure was intact, how can it sing now that the body has become worthless dust? If, while it was in the body, its movement was crippled by the sleep of suffering, how much more must it be still now that it has left the body's limbs! I said that it rests from activity, not from life, for its nature cannot lose the power of life. Its wealth remains within it, even though it has left its home. It is poor: it has nothing through which to manage that wealth as before. Speech remains within it, even though it rests from activity. It has no tongue through which to express the power of its wisdom. The mind remains within it, an eagle endowed with flight. There are no limbs to serve as wings for its swiftness. Discernment remains within it, a pilot skilled among the waves. There is no sail to catch the wind within its folds. Its impulses remain within it, its wind-catching folds. There is no sailor to attend carefully to their appointed times. Everything belonging to its nature remains within it unchanged: nature, speech, and the power of life, though they are silent. They are silent, but not entirely in the same way as the body. Rather, they rest from activities performed through the senses. They rest, but not in an insensible stillness like the limbs. Rather, they are awake and also think, but there is no work. The soul remains without work when it is taken away, because there is no tool of its craft for it to use. No carpenter can work without an adze, nor can a smith practice his craft with his hands without a hammer. No sailor travels on the sea without a ship, nor does a fisherman catch fish without nets. The soul has no ship made of bodily timbers. That is why it rests from voyaging on the sea of reason. It has no adze of flesh stained with blood. That is why the assembling of timbers by its discernment has ceased. Its skill remains within it, just as when it was in the body,

like a craftsman whose mind retains his skill. For so it pleased that Craftsman, the master of craftsmen, that without the body the soul should not trade in earthly things. He promised her and the body recompense and a sentence of judgment; together they will inherit the blessings above and the scourges below. She and her beloved await that recompense together; and as long as the body lies silent in the grave, she too remains silent in life. She now rests in a restricted life, without movement, in the same condition as infants while they are in the womb. The power she possesses is the very same inside the womb and outside it; and as long as the door of departure is shut, she too is held back. She is the same in the womb, in sleep, and in the grave; and she wisely observes her own appointed order and his. She cannot sin or act righteously except through him, nor can she produce movements and words without him. If she could act righteously on her own, the wicked of earlier generations would already have paid their debt. If Adam’s soul could readily pay for its sin, there would be no further matter arising from the transgression in [?]. And if the record of the debts [?] of those who have departed had been paid off, there would be no judgment or claims against the people of former times. The Scriptures cry out like trumpets that judgment stands firm,

and nature testifies that the soul alone performs no works. Therefore body and soul are obliged to pay for their sins before they separate from one another and their work ceases. Therefore everyone ought to act righteously before ravenous death comes and swallows up the body. Come, mortals, practice righteousness while you are alive, for after death there is no working of either good or evil. Come, let us plead, in body and soul, with the mercy that formed us, that it may rescue us from torment without end.
On the blessings that Noah gave his sons.
Another by the same author. Discourse [?] and one. On the blessings that Noah gave his sons.

I saw in the Scriptures the mystery of the good things intended for humanity, which the prophecies [?] disclose through the Spirit in symbols. The Spirit of revelation revealed it spiritually to the son of Amram, so that he might reveal to humanity the mystery hidden in their limbs. The mystery of their liberation was hidden in their limbs, and it was passed from one to another through their line of descent. Within them was laid the treasure of life that they needed, and through their [?] the life within them was preserved. The Creator [?] the vitality of life in Adam’s dust, so that when it decayed, his mortality might live through its life. Along with his dust flowed the vitality that came from his limbs, until it became a fountain of immortal life. In a mystery it flowed unseen before those who watched; although they saw, they did not see the power of its vitality. Radiantly [?] it showed its flame in Adam and Seth, and a little later in Enoch, Lamech, and his son Noah. In Noah the power of life in human nature was revealed; through him the sentences pronounced in paradise were softened. Lamech prophesied that through Noah the weary world would find rest, and that through his purity he would cleanse the earth of curses. His father's word was fulfilled in him through his deeds: he brought rest to the earth through the blessings with which he blessed his sons. His limbs became a dwelling of peace for the peace of humanity; he preserved the lives of his fellow creatures from harm. In the harbor of his body rested the succession that carried the treasure of life; he gave it to his sons so that they might carry it to those who came afterward. He wisely guarded the treasure of his ancestral house, and with understanding he opened its hidden riches before his offspring. The Spirit taught him to guard his wealth carefully, and also taught him to set his sons upon his paths. His power strengthened the weakness of the impulses of his soul, and he poured forth a discourse of righteousness from his mind. His limbs became like conduits for the flow of the Spirit, and like channels he poured forth the waters contained in blessings. Streams of words flowed from his mouth, the mouth of the Spirit, and the hearing of his offspring served as the soil. The righteous man sowed good seed in the field of his sons, and he worked earnestly so that they would receive it with purity of soul. His heart was pure, and the words of his mouth were sincere. With joy he raised his voice to bless: “Blessed is the Exalted One,” cried the member of the household of faith, “who strengthened my impulses to bless my children in his name. Blessed is he who stored within me the wealth that nourishes the work of his hands, and made me a spring that pours forth life for humanity. Blessed is he who revealed through me his kindness, for he loves humanity, and demonstrated through my hands the truth of his name: that he is the God of all. Blessed is he who dismantled through me the barrier of wrath that he had prepared for his servants, and through my life kept alive creatures both speechless and speaking.

Blessed is he who established me as a sign of peace before those who see, so that they might imitate me in calling upon his name with purity of soul. Blessed is he who caused the power of the wisdom of his divinity to dwell in me, so that I might pour forth from my mouth [?] that gives life to humanity. Blessed is he who made me a second Adam for Adam's descendants, and made me resemble the one at the beginning through the order he established for me. Blessed is he who created through me a second creation after the one that had existed, so that the world might proceed according to the order of his creative work. Blessed is he who established me in the exalted rank of one who bears his image, and extended my authority over the towns in likeness to his own. My tongue is too small to bless the name of his Being, who gave my mind the power to understand things to come.” With knowledge of the future, the righteous man blessed his offspring. For this reason he blessed the name of his God, and then his sons. “Blessed,” he said, “is the Lord, the God of Shem.” Here is knowledge of the future! But why “of Shem,” and not “your God,” O righteous man? You are older than your offspring, righteous father. First place the name of your God upon yourself, and then upon your children. What you have done in the mystery of your blessings is something new, righteous son of Lamech; perhaps an indication of something new is being revealed in it. Blessed is our God! The true prophet prophesied about Shem and gave his sons a share in the abundant riches he bequeathed to his son. “May he enlarge Japheth,” he said, “and may he dwell in the tent of Shem the elder; and let Ham become a servant to his brothers, serving them.” For Shem, “Blessed is the Lord”; for Japheth, enlargement; and for Ham, servitude: three conditions, distinct yet equal in a single utterance. For one, the name of the Lord; for another, expansion; and for another, servitude—all three from one mouth, in three expressions. The eloquent speaker divided his pronouncements into three measures and bound them together in the even [?] of a single utterance. The righteous father placed three rods in his sons’ hands. He made one longer, and of the other two, one longer than its companion. He placed the youngest and the middle one beneath the eldest, and in two different ways made them dependent on his inheritance. Through the form of his words he concealed the power within his utterances, and he placed the name of blessing upon the firstborn without blessing him. Shem the firstborn has no blessing, if anyone examines the matter. For his father said, “Blessed is the Lord,” not “Blessed is Shem.” Nor, again, does the curse he pronounced upon the youngest fall directly upon him. For he cursed Canaan, who is Ham’s son, and not Ham himself. He gave Shem’s blessing to the name of the Creator, who is above all; and the curse due to Ham he gave to Canaan, his firstborn. Your words are difficult, righteous man, and your discourse is obscure. No one grasps the meaning within your blessings. Your meaning is hidden and greatly perplexes those who inquire. Investigating your words is not easy for anyone who seeks. Your blessings do not attach to the names of those being blessed, nor do your curses distress the souls of those being cursed. You sought to bless Shem, but [?] you named it with God’s name; and when the blessing flowed forth, you immediately gave it to its Lord.

You wished, again, to curse hotheaded Ham, who burned with sin; yet when you inflicted suffering, you made his son suffer the pain that belonged to him. No one knows what to call you according to your action: from what appears, neither one who blesses nor one who curses. It seems to me that you have no control over your own will, and that it is not you who are speaking, but someone else. It seems that another forces your pipe to play as he wishes, and forcibly draws your mind wherever he directs it. [?] Remember, righteous man, that the words you spoke are higher than you; and if you are required to reveal them, they are beyond your understanding. [?] They are beyond your understanding, not because they are difficult, but because they are hidden. This is the marvel: you recount something [?] hidden from you. A great mystery is hidden in your utterance, righteous man; and [?] is destined to exalt the lowliness of your [?] despised race. Your pronouncements are full of the sweetness of life, son of mortals; and [?] their sweetness wipes death away from humanity. The discourse your heart poured forth is a marvel—its dust [?]—for you mixed curses with blessings and concealed them. You resembled the God of all, O man, in the freedom of your [?]; for good and evil are equally subject to his command to change. His sign taught you to imitate [?] his likeness—the one of whom I speak, whom you resembled through the variation of your words. The word is his [?]; it spoke through the word of your mouth, and he expressed through you distinct [?] with a single meaning. A single meaning [?] is hidden in the word of the righteous son of Lamech, and the petition in his sayings is directed toward a single aim. The aim [?] of truth—Truth set it before the lover of truth, and he directed himself toward it as befitted [?] reverence for truth. Manifest Truth signaled to him to reveal the truth of his name, so that people might see his truthfulness through a human mouth. The word of truth, which had been far away, descended into Noah’s mouth, and through his lips it uttered sounds suited to human understanding. It traveled with humanity from Adam, the head of humanity, and its course did not rest until it reached the harbor of his body. In his body and soul dwelt [?], which rebukes humanity, and like a spring he poured out its stream upon the heads of his children. Christ dwelt mystically in him, the one of whom I speak, and he gave him to his sons in the form of water contained in blessings. To his firstborn he entrusted the treasure of life that had been hidden in him, because he saw that he knew how to keep its riches unharmed. He subjected his brothers to the authority of his leadership, so that through their subjection he might give them a share in the treasure of life. He distributed life from his own life to the children of his womb, and taught them to preserve the mystery of life within them. They see the life within them mystically, lest, when it is revealed, they despise it as unseemly. On this condition he established Ham and Japheth under the great Shem, so that even unwillingly they would honor the mystery in the elder.

He honored the birthright, not to honor what belongs to nature, but to exalt the one who renews nature when it has grown old. He apportioned honor full of righteousness not to nature, but to the mystery of the one who brings mysteries to completion through his perfection. He did not distribute his words into three measures without distinction, but to build up his children’s understanding through a single word. He spoke a word, and although he certainly spoke it, it was not he who said it. He was very careful to say it in proper order, in accordance with what he said. And he was very careful [?]. The master of the word is the Being who rules over [?], and its bearer is righteous Noah, the keeper of mysteries. The Creator looked upon his faithfulness; the Creator who revealed everything to him looked, and revealed and showed him the great mystery of humanity’s salvation. In the testing of his soul, he saw that he was steadfast in faith, and gave him the ability to recount words of faith. He too received his Lord’s word in faith. He raised his voice and proclaimed the truth that had been disclosed to him. With love he received the mystery of the revelation disclosed to him, and he shone brightly through the greatness of the goodness shown toward humanity. The righteous man stood in great wonder at the beginning of his speech: how was it possible for a human being to see [?]? Like the son of Jesse, the ancestor of the son of Jesse also marveled that lowly nature [?] had risen to the summit without a step. With wonder like that in the song, “O Lord, our Lord,” Noah too stood when the mystery was disclosed to him. David marveled and composed words on a harp of words; Noah wondered and brought forth a discourse that pours out life. He marveled and wondered discerningly at the life he was to bring forth, at how far it rises above the life of fleshly human beings. The wise man marveled at the giver of life, not at life itself, and turned his words from the gift toward the giver. He opened his lips and wanted to say, “Blessed is my firstborn son,” but changed his words and said, “Blessed is the God of Shem.” He had prepared himself to bless his son, but wonder overtook him, and he blessed the Name that is full of blessings. “Blessed is God,” the righteous man said to the righteous one who created him, and included his son within the words addressed to his Lord. [?] The righteous man mingled his son's blessing with the blessing of his Lord, because he believed that God's name was entirely blessing. “Blessed is my son's God, who delighted in him and called him by his name; and blessed also is my son, within whom his Lord and his son are hidden.” He marveled at the one who was hidden in his son, [?], and said, “Blessed is the Lord, who is to reveal his lordship in my son.” His Lord revealed what was to come to the good servant—not openly, but in a mystery, in a symbolic way. From his offspring was to come the liberator of humanity. At this he marveled: who was to set whom free? From Shem was to arise a king who would reign over all. In anticipation of this, he subjected his brothers to the yoke of his name. Otherwise, why did he not give separate blessings, either to Japheth, whom he enlarged, or to Ham, whom he made a slave of slaves?

Why did he not give Japheth an inheritance as he did the righteous man, but instead granted that he should expand and grow within his brother's inheritance? Why, when he cursed Ham, did he not drive him away to a distant land, but instead enclose him within the inheritance of the blessed brothers? Why did he not separate him by a judicial sentence, as he did Cain, and forbid him to mingle with his relatives? Why did he not make the curse upon him take effect as it was pronounced? And why did he not serve his brother, as it is written? Scripture teaches that Ham's offspring did not serve in slavery, either under the descendants of Shem, the blessed firstborn, or under the descendants of Japheth. Ham's descendants are said to have been the first to exercise rule. Nimrod, who is a descendant of Ham, bears witness that this is true. Nimrod received dominion and temporal kingship, and Scripture establishes his might before the Lord. “Nimrod himself,” it says, “became a mighty hunter”—as though someone were to say, “He gave him dominion.” And if the Lord made Nimrod a mighty warrior, then the curse did not hold true as it was pronounced. The Egyptians and the Canaanites are also descendants of Ham, and Scripture shows not that they were enslaved, but that they enslaved others. The Israelites, the descendants of Abraham, are descendants of Shem, yet contrary to the law they served as slaves to the descendants of the cursed one. Where, then, was the statement fulfilled as it is written? For look: events turned out contrary to what was said. They turned out contrary to what was said, not contrary to the truth. In its meaning, however, both the statement and its speaker are true. Plain truth dwells within the account that the righteous man expounded, but understanding is needed to show it to the mind's eyes. Without understanding, the sight of its beauty cannot be seen, and without effort, its truth cannot be examined. An account that labors over hidden things requires effort, and if someone makes the effort, it is easy for him to see it clearly. It is very clear to anyone who works at it lovingly, but very dark to anyone who does not labor in the truth of his love [?]. Through love, everyone can see it as it is, and with understanding it is easy to recount it to others too. I heard it with love, and I long to recount it in discourse, so that those who love love may consider it and cherish it. Lovely is the account that the righteous man expounded concerning his loved ones, and everyone ought to contemplate it lovingly. The meaning hidden within it is full of benefit for humanity. The righteous man too marveled at this: how greatly it benefits people! The Wise One considered its benefit and expressed it wisely, so that its preciousness would not be despised in the eyes of fools. The eye of fools is accustomed to despise whatever is plainly revealed. Therefore a covering of words is laid over every utterance. The revelation that spoke [?] Noah considered the disposition of fools, and concealed the utterances of his mouth beneath a garment of words.

The Hidden One could have disclosed the mystery that he revealed to his heart, and it would have been easy for him to show plainly [?] his love. Yet he did not show it—not because he was unconcerned with humanity’s benefit, but because people were incapable of benefiting from it. Not even to Noah, who distributed the riches of the mystery with his own hands, did he show its power precisely as it is. The man of flesh saw the shadow of the truth in his son’s body, and thanked his Lord, who showed him the mystery before the events took place. He set the figure before his mind like a mirror, and eagerly embraced it with insatiable love. Without ever having enough, he repeated that utterance: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Shem, who has blessed us in his name.” He contemplated his son’s rank as though in an image, and called to his two brothers, “Come and look!” The blessing and the curse signaled to his sons [?] that they should fix their minds’ gaze on the mystery he had seen. He taught Japheth to broaden his understanding and the impulses of his soul, so that he would be able to receive the riches flowing from Shem. He admonished Ham to bow the shoulder of his arrogance, [?] the yoke of the service of life hidden in his brother. Through the blessing and the curse, he urged them to keep his word, so that when it was fulfilled through events, they might gain its riches. Before the events, he longed to do what was fitting, so that when they were revealed, he might be adorned with the splendor of his children. He looked ahead to the splendid beauty of the mystery he had seen, and urged his sons to depict it before their eyes. With the eye of the mind, the seer saw the beautiful mystery, and he yearned to see it in the flesh without a covering. The man of flesh found comfort in his son’s body, and believed that consolation was hidden within him. Shem was set before his eyes like a mirror, and the more he looked, the more he looked again, never having enough. He fixed the gaze of his eyes and his mind on Shem; like someone [?] by physical love, he occupied himself with his story. He repeated the account of the blessings in two ways, and he did this out of love for his child. He made Canaan a slave of slaves twice. This is a sign of the recompense for a father's love for his sons. Out of love for his son, the righteous man bound his sons, so that they would be yoked under the authority of his Lord and his son. Through Ham and Japheth he subjected the world to his Lord and his son, as one who knew that everything was contained in their line of descent. Everyone together was destined to serve the offspring descended from him; therefore he yoked his sons' necks beneath his son's yoke. He made his sons serve the king who would come from his line, and stamped them with two seals expressed in different words. The son of Lamech placed a seal of words upon Ham and Japheth.

He varied them according to the number of the pronouncements. He gave both of them portions of blessing and cursing. Although they differ greatly in name, they are equal in force. The force in both is one, and their meaning is one, since the one who distributed the two together was also one. The righteous man distributed two together, from one to two: the good that came from Shem to shameless Ham and modest Japheth. To the slave he assigned a share as to a slave from his master's household, and to the freeborn as to someone needing support. From the treasury of wealthy Shem, Ham and Japheth also became rich, and they were subjected to him, one willingly and the other by force. Out of love, Japheth accepted the seal of service to his brother, while Ham's father compelled him by force to serve his brother. Under the name of freedom he gave freedom to the humble in spirit, and through slavery he yoked the arrogant beneath the free. Paul also did something like this in his writings, subjecting slaves and the freeborn to the Lord Christ. Every slave, he says, is a freedman, released from childhood; and the freeborn person is also a slave of the Lord Christ. And if Paul yoked the classes [?] beneath one Lord, who would dispute Noah's statement, saying that it is not so? And that it is so, as it is written, Scripture [?]; the righteous people of later generations also lend their support. After Noah, Abram received the promise of life, and he sealed the document of the covenant through his two sons. He fathered two sons from his own body, full of blessings, and gave them a stream of words to drink like Noah's. To Isaac he handed over the leadership he had received from Shem, and he yoked Hagar's son to serve like Ham. The righteous man looked to Noah, who blessed one and subjected the other, and he too agreed to fulfill the words in deeds. Isaac [?], the son of the promise, also aimed at this same goal, and closely followed the likeness in words and deeds. Like Noah and Abram, the father of these words acted toward his sons, and in the same manner repeated blessings full of wonder. He honored Jacob with the rights of the firstborn, although he was not the firstborn, and placed the elder below him, in the rank of Ham's household. He said to Esau, 'If you return, you will be set free.' But from what, then, was he setting him free, since he was already free? Esau was not subject to Jacob throughout his entire life, nor did his descendants perform slave service for the Israelites. The words of the righteous in the Scriptures are set down in wonder, and no one knows how to marvel properly at their meaning. The power of understanding strengthened them to understand how to portray the meaning of words on a tablet of words. Like painters who paint images of things to come, they painted likenesses of invisible things by means of visible things. O seers who saw something they did not understand! Though it was not visible to them, they recounted its likenesses before those who could see.

O heralds who disclosed mysteries before the events, and before he came revealed the mystery of his dawning among earthly beings! O guides who prepared the road for the King's coming and placed along it milestones—words filled with signs of peace! The words of those sailors of peace were words of peace, and in the harbors of their sayings they gave travelers rest. They built an inn of love in the Scriptures for people's journey, so that they would not be worn down by despair, the desolation of the two [?]. They agreed together upon the one will of the one Creator, and they were not divided over the expectation of the hope they fulfilled. They heard good news proclaimed in their own tongues, and gained hope to await the hope that was to come. Noah first prepared the road before their eyes, and they all [?] in the footsteps of the word of his mouth. With his mouth, that nimble mind walked along the road of hope, and with his tongue he traveled the path of the promise of life. O traveler whose mouth walked in place of his feet! Without his walking, his tongue measured out the earth. O guide who showed the road without walking and set along it milestones that cannot be measured by footsteps! O man who traveled calmly in the promise of life, your word reached the chamber of the Giver of Life! The Giver of Life was mysteriously hidden in your offspring, and beforehand he showed you the power of his life in one of your children. In your firstborn dwelt the [?] of immortal life, and your mind marveled as it contemplated the life in your son. Your thoughts stood in great wonder at the fruit that came from you, for in the branches of his body you saw the life of humanity. With your mind you gazed upon that life which gives life to all, and you called your sons to gaze upon it with delight. With gladness your word gazed at the mystery in Shem, and toward his promise you gathered the [?] of his brothers' gaze. By the splendor of his beauty he amazed the sons of your womb, and, though they were unwilling, they painted his likenesses before their eyes. They contemplated the word of your mouth as though looking at an image, while it portrayed the image of their life in the name of God. Your [?] held the name of your God like a pen, and with it traced the utterance, “Blessed is the Lord.” Blessed is the Lord whom the Lord, the master of painters, portrayed through you, so that you might portray in your sons the image of the thanksgiving [?] they owe him. You bound your children to the debt of love toward your Lord, so that they would repay with gratitude the Good One who fashioned them. The Good One hid good leaven in you out of his goodness, and you placed it in the bodies of your sons to preserve them. Wisely you acted toward your children, O wise man, for you concealed within their limbs the wealth that would meet their needs. O wise man, guide your impulses wisely in doing this, so that the life of your race may flow along with your descendants. Love your race; place within it, within your race, a treasure of life. Hide it in your earth, so that it may be preserved until the end of the ages. Like merchants, the senses that transmitted it carried it, and lovingly passed it from one to another until Mary.

Oh, the wonder bestowed by the Creator on humanity: though mortal, man became the guardian of the life within him! Oh, how deep is the knowledge of the one who orders everything! He placed within his creation riches suited to its needs. O Craftsman, who made everything from nothing, who stocked and filled his handiwork with his wisdom! From his wisdom he placed the wisdom of truth within our nature, and it taught our race in its ignorance to know his name. It revealed to Adam the hidden reality that it portrayed visibly, and made him aware that he had a master, the Lord of all. It bound pure Abel in love for his Lord, and through visible things he offered the thanksgiving fitting for the Hidden One. Through it, beautiful Enoch learned to make himself beautiful; and because he was so beautiful, he remained in the beauty of the immortals. It told Lamech about the child who would come from him, who would give the earth rest and remove the mourning of human sorrow. It spoke a new language in him too, in Lamech’s son, and his mouth uttered new sounds of humanity’s renewal. Everything that this knowledge said was from God. It made everyone wise, and it continues to make everyone wise until the end. From his wisdom the people of old learned to become wise, and it also teaches the others who come afterward. More than anyone, Noah became wise through it, to disclose its mysteries. It, in turn, called him above all others and drew him into its intimacy. As to a friend, it revealed to him the mystery of its secrets; he too, in love, [?] its faithful command. As a lover of truth, he faithfully maintained reverence for truth; and it, in truth, repaid him with a reward greater than his labor. It paid a good reward to the righteous man who labored with it. He benefited from it and gave it to his sons, so that they might find shelter in it. It placed in his hands the provision for immortal life, and he too placed it in his sons’ hands, so that they might live by eating it. The righteous man ate its life-giving food and fed it to his sons. The medicine of his life blossomed within our nature, preserving it in [?]. The life that came from Noah flowed with our race from Noah onward, and it endures until time has completed its course. Life began to flow from us from the beginning, and it remains with us in an intimacy without end. The Power that created us created life within us and concealed it. When he wished, he revealed it before everyone’s eyes and in everything. In our very formation he buried life from his own life, and after a time he revealed his will, which had been hidden within us. In what is hidden and what is visible he showed his love for our humanity, and wisely accomplished his will through our hands for everyone. Through our hands he completed his ministry toward all and in all. Come, let us thank him above all, for he loved us above all.
On the Tower of Babel and the Division of Languages
52. On the Division of Languages. By the same author. Homily Fifty-Two, on the Tower of Babel and the Division of Languages.
The Creator gave human nature a sign of peace, so that people would not be terrified by the flood that destroyed humanity.

He established a covenant of love with those of flesh, promising that he would not again become angry and punish their deeds with water. Through a visible sign he showed them the greatness of his love: how deeply he loves the children of his [?] and hates wrongdoing. He stretched the sign of the bow across the clouds before their eyes, so that they would look at it and hate the wrongdoing that had destroyed them. Through the bow he revealed to them his severity and his kindness: he is the one who chastises and the one who cherishes, both at once. He showed them a curved bow without a string, to teach them that he would not shoot arrows of water at them. He displayed the bow without a hand and without a string, to let them know that he had no desire to shoot at human beings. He did not stretch it across the air and make its appearance magnificent in order to shoot, but to place fear and love in the human mind. He set fear and love in the clouds like a mirror, so that they would look into it, hate wrongdoing, and choose love. The appearance of blood and the radiance of fire were depicted in it, showing how threatening it was to wrongdoers. Peace, [?], and the power of his being were hidden in its appearance, for its wielder and the arrows of his wrath were in proportion to the bow. As though pointing with a finger, he showed them through stern signs: This is what I held in my uplifted arm on the day of the flood. On this I stretched the command of my will [?] like a bowstring, and I began to aim against the tyrannical wrongdoing among you. I [?] this in the hand of my will like a mighty warrior, and shot terrifying arrows of water into the ranks of humanity. With this I reaped the field of the wicked, full of undergrowth. The waves became my gravediggers and carried out my will. I am the one who reaped the animals along with humanity and made them a bridge of [?], subject to decay. I am the one who also left a remnant with Noah, my friend, and kept the speechless kinds alive with Noah to serve humanity. I am the one who preserved the lives of all in dead wood, so that they were not drowned amid the billows and terrifying waves. My will stood like a sailor within the ark and guided it as though with [?] to a peaceful harbor. My hidden will drew it to safety as though with ropes, brought it out, and set it in the midst of the earth unharmed. Look, I have brought you to a [?] harbor, as I promised. See that you do not scorn my commandments as the earlier people did. Look, I have shown you the severity of the lashes the wicked suffered. Desist from wrongdoing, so that you are not scourged like wrongdoers. Look, I have taught you the ways of righteousness and the name of grace. See that you conduct yourselves wisely with both. Look, I have established a covenant of peace between me and you. Do not break it through laxity in wrongdoing, so that I become angry again. Look at the bow stretched out for me across the heights. It has no string, nor any hand to wield it. Look and consider: a bow is useful for the day of battle, but I have made it a sign of peace between me and humanity. I desire peace, not war with humanity.

That is why I have put no string on the bow I have displayed. Look, I have shown you the desire of my will, which loves humanity. Do not force me to act in anger against my will. Let heaven and earth be witnesses between me and you that I have no desire to kill people who are not guilty. The Hidden One secretly proclaimed these words to humanity and wrote them in the covenant of the sign of the bow. Noah himself and his sons considered them, as it is written in the book. But after a time his descendants went astray, following error. For a considerable time peace remained among the earth’s inhabitants. But a little later strife entered and reigned on earth. The remnant that had survived the waters returned to its corruption and began to walk the path of turmoil, like the people of earlier times. They abandoned the inheritance of the commandment of peace that they had received from Noah, and forgot the sign that the Creator had given between himself and them. They left the place and the neighborhood around the ark and began wandering about to choose lands for themselves. They journeyed from Corduene, where they had emerged into a peaceful harbor, and set their course toward Babel, whose name means confusion. They journeyed away from the peace established by the Creator, whose love is rich, and went out seeking an inheritance of land whose embrace is poor. In their desire for land, the earth’s inhabitants went away from peace to take possession of [?] in good and beautiful regions. They were all united as they traveled toward Babel: one people, one language, and one purpose. One will led them as far as Babel, and within Babel they conceived a desire for trouble and wrongdoing. The insolent boldly conceived an ugly desire, like Adam, who desired and coveted [?] and rank. Foolish pride drove the children of Adam, and they too went astray in the same error as their father. The thought Adam had—to become God—also came to his children: to seize divine rank. His descendants too boldly followed Adam’s path and sought to raise a wicked rebellion against the Creator. Those made of dust, the children of ashes, rebelled against their Maker and prepared weapons to fight against their own life. The wicked wickedly put on the armor of wrongdoing and began shooting arrows of pride against the truth. The fools had put on foolish pride like armor, and they set arrogance like a helmet upon their minds. They imagined they could subdue the heights and the depths beneath their hands, and ascend to the lofty rank of divinity. The ignorant thought their thoughts ignorantly, and did not look carefully at the outcome of their deeds. Without understanding they set out from the place where they lay, and without order they sought to begin a wicked construction. What, indeed, was the desire that burned in their thoughts? What did they intend by undertaking toil beyond measure? Why, indeed, did they raise their thoughts toward the heights? And why did they travel a road too difficult for mortals? An evil desire tormented those dull-hearted people, and they sought to raise wings from the earth toward the heights. Their lack of sense roused them as though from sleep, and they began exercising their thoughts on things that were not fitting.

Their senses sank, as though asleep, away from what was right, while they rose like diligent workers and devoted themselves to earthly labor. They abandoned the divine service that brings life, and undertook toil that brought no benefit to body or soul. They despised the unbreakable oaths of the God of all, and treated as false the sign full of peace that he had shown them. They thought, “He is lying and will not keep his word as he promised. He will turn back, bring terrifying waters, and destroy us.” The fools considered the one who is more trustworthy than all to be untrustworthy, and so they began building a rebellion against the Creator. On these terms the proud-hearted came to an agreement [?], and undertook toil that would not reach completion. The fools without understanding conceived this idea: to build a house in which they could escape the flood [?]. They armed themselves with this thought as with a weapon, intending to draw up battle against the Maker in the heights. Those senseless people conceived three very foolish ideas, and because of them prepared weapons with which they imagined they would win. One was to escape a flood that might come; another was to engage in battle in the heights against the creators. The third was that, once they had fought, won, and taken power, they would leave a glorious name on earth as victors. The children of the condemned one were fighting for victory, not knowing that they would surely be condemned like their father. They desired and planned to conquer with the weapon of arrogance, and brought the hidden deceit of their thoughts out into the open. “Come,” they said, “let us mold bricks from clay and burn them, and build a tower whose top reaches the heights above. “Come, let us struggle at this work and at saving our lives. Come, let us make a name for ourselves in creation greater than anyone else’s, “so that coming generations may recount the exertion of our strength. Come, let us show ourselves mighty in battle against the Maker’s name, and wage a terrifying battle against him in the heights. “Come, let us arm ourselves with weapons fit for warriors, and shoot arrows at the God of all, who destroyed our race.” Come, let us avenge the blood of our companions, whom he destroyed with the sword of unrestrained waters. Come, let us do to him what he did to the members of our people. Let us demand from his hands the blood of our kind that he shed without cause. Come, let us present our rightful claims to him, as in a court of law: “Because of whom did you destroy the speechless creatures along with humanity?” Let us boldly fight him with judgment and weapons. Let us take his rank and his title of authority, and let it become ours. Let us mold bricks and burn them in flames, so that they will not soften when water is poured over them. Let us build a fortress and occupy it. Let us fill it with weapons and [?], so that it will suffice for the day of battle prepared for us. Let us broaden its foundations and enlarge them in proportion to its size, so that waves of water and gusts of wind will not shake it. Let us make it firm and build it skillfully, as befits us, so that our craftsmanship will not be disgraced in time to come. Let us build the whole of it with fired bricks as though with stones, and instead of clay let us put lime between its courses.

Let us mix lime and bricks together in the structure we labor to build, so that the changing seasons of cold and heat will not damage it. Along with our building, let us also strengthen our resolve, and let us not falter before the one who comes to fight us. See that none of us neglects his companion at the moment of crisis, lest our adversary scatter us throughout the whole earth. Oh, the arrogant, who unwittingly spoke clearly and prophesied, announcing beforehand their scattering in time to come! Oh, the blind, who, though unable to see, saw accurately! They looked and understood what was to come as though it had already happened. Oh, those who were united in a single purpose in their wicked building, who set their hands to the discord of their own languages! They themselves proclaimed their condemnation in words not their own, and revealed and made known their migration to every region. They put their hands to it, wrote, and agreed that they would be scattered, without considering the sentence that their own mouths had made plain. They wrote their own indictment with the unrestrained pen of their tongues, and did not stop or turn away from the foolish scheme they had conceived. They dug deep and laid foundations as though they would last forever, not knowing that the time of their overthrow was near. They fired bricks, burned lime, and began to build. Along with their building, their thoughts rose higher. As the building rose toward the heights, their hearts rose still higher in arrogance. As its dimensions increased day by day, the wickedness within them grew beyond measure. Their hearts were wakeful and did not sleep, night or day. Though they were [not] growing weary, they did not realize how hard they were toiling. They were very eager for their anxiety to come to an end, and waited for the time when they would see their labor completed. Their desire to build could not be satisfied, and they did not let their senses or movements slacken from the work. The Maker, who sees things before they exist, saw that they were laboring in vain, building and multiplying sins. He saw that even if they built, they could not build as they had hoped, and he restrained them so that they would not wear themselves out in toil and wrongdoing. He had pity and showed mercy, as he is accustomed to show mercy, and began to speak words of love and of menace. Love, then, threatened the insolent with discipline, and in mercy cut away the pain of their minds. For he truly pitied that senseless toil, and under the appearance of wrath he gave them relief from the flood. The voice he made them hear was full of the appearance of anger, but within it was hidden an inexpressible love. Suddenly he made an audible declaration to the person of the Word that he and those with him were preparing to descend. The Knower of all was consulting those who shared his counsel, and, as though seeking help, he called them to descend with him. “Look,” he said, “human beings have become one people with one language, and they have gathered together to fight against my will. Look, the children of Adam have attacked my sovereignty, like their father,

and they seek to ascend to the exalted rank of divinity. Look, mortals feared death from [?], from destruction by water, and built a fortress in which to shelter from the flood. Look, those of earth have prepared weapons and formed a conspiracy to ascend and stir up conflict in the heights between me and themselves. Look, they have made an agreement not to separate from one another until they conquer and the heights and depths become theirs. Look, without intending it, they have prophesied about their own scattering, and it is fitting that the word they spoke should be fulfilled in deeds. Come,” he said, “let us descend and divide them from one another, so that they will no longer understand the speech and utterances of one another’s languages. Come, let us silently stir up conflict among them without their noticing, and steal from them the sword of speech in which they take pride. Come, let us descend together to earth without changing place, and wage war against beings of flesh without [?]. Come, let us give them the distinct speech of every language, and then they will be divided, and the warfare of their schemes will cease. Come, let us sound among them a new voice that they do not understand, and cast some of them into exile in other lands.” O Creator, what is this that you are saying? For the utterances your command makes heard concerning your being are new. Whom are you calling to descend with you to the earthly realm? And whom do you ask to be a helper to your might? With whom did you take counsel, so that he might join you in speaking to humanity? And to whom do you say, “Come with me; let us descend and divide them”? Who was your counselor at the beginning, when you created? And to whom did you [?] the hidden mysteries of your divinity? Who helped you when you were creating heaven and earth? And who strengthened you to give strength to the work of your hands? Whom have you ever called or brought near to speak with you? Whom have you considered worthy to pronounce judgment according to your discernment? Your voice resembled that earlier voice on the sixth day, when you were shaping Adam’s image with the finger of your command. Only there did you make a voice like this heard: “Come, let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness.” The voice is one, and the meaning of that utterance and this one is one. There, “Come, let us make”; here, “Let us go down”—alike and true. One command proclaimed both that utterance and this one, and one nature formed humankind there and divided it here. He called his fellow counselors when he said, “Let us go down,” and when he said, “Let us make.” They are the ones who made humankind and divided humankind. It was the Father who called the Son and the Spirit at Adam’s formation, and he summoned them to divide what they had created. In forming humankind and dividing humankind, the Creator wished to reveal the mystery that makes known the persons hidden with him. It is clear [?], then, that among created things none is greater than humankind, for hidden things concealed from everyone are revealed through it. Otherwise, let us ask why he said “Come” only at the formation and division of the foremost creature. If he did not call the Son and the Spirit who are from him on both occasions, who, then, is equal to him, that he should consult him?

That utterance was not fitting for the heavenly beings: “Come, let us make together,” and “Come, let us go down together,” as though they were his partners. Had he said, “Go, descend, divide humanity’s language,” it might have seemed that he called and sent the spiritual beings. But “Come, let us go down” was indisputably addressed to the Son and the Spirit, the persons who are with him. Formation and division alike belong to the Son and the Spirit. Together with the Father, they created everything and divided humanity. They formed, and they wisely divided: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, equal in nature. They are the ones who now descended without moving from their place, to take away speech and give speech to human nature. In humanity’s division they outlined the mystery of their persons, and at the end they explained it through the gift of tongues. They called one another to the formation and to the division, so that everyone might learn that the nature of all three is one. They descended to divide, not by a descent involving movement, but by a command whose swiftness cannot be expressed. He sent [?] a command like a messenger to the insolent. It suddenly cried out and terrified those sailors of pride. It was the command that descended and took from them the weapon of speech, and clothed them with another weapon, another kind of speech. With a harsh sword it cut apart the speech of their tongues and placed in them speech that differed from the first. It took away the first to teach them that it had fashioned everything; then a second [?], to make them know that it ruled over everything. Gently it fought against them, as they desired, and instead of the body, it battled with their conversation. Skillfully it engaged their movements in battle and bound them with the harsh cords of their tongues. Wonderful was the battle that the Hidden One fought against earthly people. No mind can recount its marvel, however much it may recount. What, then, was that sword he held in his hand, which struck speech instead of limbs, while the body felt nothing? How did the hidden command enter their thoughts, seize and carry away the treasure within them, without their noticing it? How did he snatch away the powerful speech of their mouths and make them babble and stammer at one another? How did he cut off the living spring of their original speech, so that words no longer flowed along the banks of the mouth as they had gushed forth before? How did he interrupt the flow of a single language and open a path for the mind to travel through new sounds? How, and how fully, can we tell how that event took place, when he cut off speech and made speech spring up through a change of sound? Let us ascribe its power to that command which accomplished this, for he himself knows how he accomplished it so easily. It is clear to him how he plundered human speech, and how he then gave another treasure different from the first. The wealth of speech, both the new and the original, belongs to him. He cut off speech and grafted speech into that same nature. The plectrum of his command suddenly struck the lyre of the soul,

and it began singing new sounds foreign to it. That command which breathed into it in the beginning, so that it sounded its voice, spoke with it in another language, and it listened to his voice. He did not change its nature and make another nature; rather, speech underwent a change by his judgment. The command dyed speech with another pigment. It took on a new color, changed its sound, and marveled at itself. That Voice who said, “Let us go down,” descended, he and those with him, and threw into confusion the ranks of people who had been at ease. He descended without descending, for there is no place through which he must travel. His command descended and fulfilled his word, while he remained as he is. He descended while remaining beside all and in all, without limitation, so that by his coming [?] he might bring people down from their pride. He descended and shook [?] their arrogance and their thoughts, and took from them the armor of pride they had been wearing. Great astonishment suddenly fell upon the insolent, and they sat marveling at what had happened. They stared at one another in bewilderment, wondering whether these were really the same people or perhaps some other apparition. They spoke to one another in sounds foreign to the speech within them, and the ear could not grasp the meaning of the sound. For they heard with their ears without understanding, and they also watched the mouth's utterance without comprehension. The helpless people stood in doubt about what had happened, examining the body's nature to see whether it was no longer the same. The body's appearance was unmistakable to bodily eyes, but the sound of speech was utterly foreign to the hearing of the ear. Eyes and ears were astonished at one another: one could see, while the other was blind to understanding. The mouth silently marveled at its fellows: how they spoke distinct languages that it did not know. Amazement and astonishment lay upon their movements and limbs, and the soul marveled at the body, and the body at the soul. The soul was astonished at the body, which heard and remained silent, and the body marveled at the soul because of its unfamiliar speech. The soul was still more astonished at [?], wondering who had changed the sound of the melodies of its speech. “Am I myself, or am I not myself?” it said to itself. “Perhaps my former self has perished, and [?] in another.” Oh, what a very great marvel, entirely full of wonder: the soul hears the sound of its melodies but does not understand! Oh, the new things that were happening among mortals: though they possessed soul and body, they were inarticulate. Oh, speakers who lost their speech and sprouted languages! From the single speech of one tongue they acquired many. New sounds were being spoken among earth’s inhabitants, and people marveled at one another because of the change in their voices. They called to one another, person to person, but no one responded. Speech became like no speech at all to those who spoke. The [?] called out to the Greek to answer him a word, but he gave him no reply, no word from his mouth to his companion’s mouth. The Roman spoke with the Egyptian in the tongue of the flesh [?].

But he could not interpret the speech of his fellow mortal. The Mede gestured to the Alan who was [?] nearby, but he remained silent and paid no attention, as though he had not heard, for he did not understand. The Indian approached the Hun to speak with him, but his words were superfluous, and he was not understood. Each person spoke to himself in his own language, and himself explained its meaning to himself—the meaning to which he had assigned an expression. They grew weary and exhausted as they shouted to one another, but they gave no answering word, voice responding to voice. They were tormented with painful labor like a woman giving birth, but the soul could not give birth to the child of speech. Something of speech was turning within the soul like a child, but the gates of the mouth were shut against its coming out. The command that had brought speech to birth in the soul’s mind was the very one that shut the door in its face, so that it could no longer come out. He silenced speech within their thoughts and awakened speech. It was the same speech that fell silent, the same that [?] in another form. It was one language that was divided into portions, and from it the languages of the nations sprouted like shoots. Like a vine, it spread its branches into every land, while its power remained unchanged at the root of the soul. Speech remained like a root among one people, and that people alone continued to use the original language. The hidden command divided them as though by lots, and each person spoke the portion of language that had fallen to his name. Love and compassion were mingled in that division [?], and although he thoroughly divided them, he did not sever the love implanted in nature. For one portion fell to fathers and their children, and a man, his wife, and his children spoke one language. The one who orders everything did this with wisdom and love, so that nature and the order of life together would not be destroyed. With great order he divided them and made them equal, like a father who bequeaths to his children the wealth he has acquired. In the guise of [?], he gave the wealth of his kindness, to instill fear in the heirs who had received the power of his wisdom. Although that voice saying, “Come, let us go down,” was full of wrath, he distributed peace to humanity through his descent. He had promised a sign of peace to Noah and his descendants, but he changed his voice into a guise of wrath to frighten humanity. The voice was clothed in the guise of a sword and an executioner; but after raising it as though to kill, he held it back in mercy. It was not to kill that he raised his sword and showed it to them, but to make known that he took no pleasure in seeing wrongdoing. It was not because they had built a wicked building that he divided them, but to drive out the wickedness within them through division. What he did had been determined by him from the beginning, and he did it wisely, as he is accustomed to doing what is good. For before he established speech in the soul, he knew that after a time a flood of words would flow from it. He had allotted this division before everything,

and he contemplated it before heaven and earth existed. No new thought drew him toward division, nor did anger overcome him so that he descended and gave them different languages. He is accustomed to frightening the members of his household with an appearance of anger, as he did from the beginning with Adam’s household. For there too, on account of the fruit, he introduced death, to teach them [?] restraints, generation after generation. He also said that he brought about the flood because of wrongdoing, to place bridles on human nature so that it would not become brutish. Because of wrongdoing he cursed Canaan and made him a slave, so that no one would insolently mock the father who begot him. In this same manner he now descended to those made of dust, so that through the appearance of a voice dividing humanity, he might bring humanity peace. His will descended for the sake of peace, as did the one who descended, and he brought peace to the people who had gathered as though for wrath. He saw that they were eagerly and insolently building a rebellion, and he descended and demolished the wicked building before it grew strong. He saw that they were hastening to reach the heights and ascend to him; he made his voice heard and scattered them so that they would not be crushed. Like a king, he decreed judgment against the offenders and cast them into [?] in the lands. The command of his hidden will went forth like a ruler and bound them in the harsh armor of their languages. He placed another language in their mouths like a chain and confined them in the prison of their languages. He sent them to different lands as though to fortresses, so that they would no longer raise a wicked rebellion against his lordship. His will held a new language like a rod and drove them out of Babylon as though in anger. How closely this command against the insolent resembled that command which drove Adam out of Paradise! As though in anger, [?] he drove them out, just as he had Adam, so that through Adam and through them he might make the earth peaceful for human life. With this provision he scattered them among different lands, so that life on earth would not be disturbed by widespread slaughter. Had they remained in one place, as they intended, they would have multiplied greatly and rushed toward bloodshed in their craving for land. Had they stayed in the land of Babel, at the tower of rebellion, they would have rebelled there against righteousness, as they desired. Had he not issued a decree for their scattering, wrongdoing would have increased twofold in their dwelling place. It was right, then, that he confused them and scattered them, so that their gathering together would not increase wrongdoing and disturb the peace. They went out from Babel to divide up the earth to which they had been sent, and each of them set out for the land that the divine command had assigned him. The divine command became a guide for them and showed them the paths to travel in every direction. That [?] which divided them accompanied them; it journeyed with them to the lands where they would live. The divine command became like a teacher to those childish in understanding, and taught them how to live in the earth to which they had been sent. A skilled scribe wrote on the tablets of their minds and taught them to read well through the word within them. They read and pondered the writings of their thoughts.

They explained the meaning hidden in the speech of their tongues. They became masters of the new speech their hearts had brought forth, and established rules for the conduct of earthly life. Along with speech, they gained an added ability to live in an orderly way, and began to practice what was good for body and soul. What happened under the appearance of wrath was therefore for our benefit, and the Good One wisely carried it out in response to our wickedness. It was entirely full of love and mercy, though no one knew it, and it was a cause of peace for human beings and spiritual beings. The division of languages gave [?] of peace, and earthly and heavenly beings were enriched by it. The spiritual beings saw the love that the Good One showed our race, and gained hope that there was hope for us in our lost condition. They saw that the threatening voice had changed to gentleness, and that the scourges had turned into comfort for those being scourged. That voice saying, “Come, let us go down,” had been full of harsh scourges; but mercy transformed it, and they came down and distributed gifts of peace. The Lover of humanity distributed peace under the appearance of wrath, lest the children of destruction suppose that he loved wrongdoing. He mixed a pledge of life with the voice and gave it to them to drink, to portray the mystery of what was to come at the end of time. In this division, which had the appearance of wrath, he portrayed the mystery of the gift he gave the apostles in the appearance of fire. Through what happened, he announced beforehand what was to come, so that when it was revealed [?], it would not seem strange to those who saw it. He was [?] to reveal in human language the persons who were with him, and he gave tongues resembling tongues as a pledge. The voice that divided humanity opened a path of peace for us, so that we might travel to the appointed meeting, to the haven of the Godhead’s peace. He revealed and taught us the distinction of the persons of the Son and the Spirit: together with the Father, they divided the nations and gave them languages. They brought about that division as an expression of wrath, and they in turn bestowed the power that came from them in the appearance of fire. From both events mortals learned the power of the divine Being, for the first things and the last belong to him. They owe one thanksgiving to him, the one who orders everything, who showed his love and made them wise in his hidden mysteries.
On Righteous Job
Homily Forty: On Righteous Job and the Trials He Endured

For humanity’s benefit, the Creator recorded the memory of human beings, so that through the remembrance of the righteous who triumphed he might make people wise. Although the will of the righteous was plain to him as the one who knows everything, he did not wish to hide the wealth they had gathered through their labors. He recorded the remembrance of their names in the book of his words, and through them, as guides, he opened a path to life.

Like seal impressions, he fixed the names of the victorious in his Scriptures, and wove them into a beautiful crown for the head of victory. He laid their labors like a foundation in the books of his words, so that people might build their conduct upon their labors. He fixed their labors like the heavenly lights, the sun and the moon, so that by their radiance they might shed light upon the hidden soul. He placed the names of the righteous in his Scriptures as milestones of peace, so that everyone might know how to walk amid the soul’s labors. Through their conduct they became a mirror for the eyes of the heart, so that everyone might polish away the ugliness of his [?] through their labors. The Creator did not weave praises for the righteous who loved him; he set up their conduct as a goal for those who came after them. He watched them as they suffered bodily pains, and observed their endurance as they received blows. His power strengthened their minds in their contests, and with his help they won victory in their battles. These beings of flesh did not wage war against flesh. They entered the contest against the ruler of the air through the movements of their souls. The Creator wrote down their triumphs and placed them in the archives, so that everyone might learn about the battle between flesh and spirit. In this battle against spiritual beings, Job too triumphed, and through his endurance defeated the accuser in the contest. Because flesh defeated the ruler of the air and the spiritual being lost, the Creator recorded humanity’s victory and the demons’ defeat. He wrote the remembrance of righteous Job in the book of his words, and called him a man, so that everyone might learn that he was a bodily being. He made known his [?] and identified his people, showing that he was an Edomite, so that everyone might know that he was a being of dust, formed from the earth. He recounted his conduct: he was blameless, upright, righteous, and perfect, and greatly honored his Lord’s word with purity of soul. He mentioned his possessions and his abundant wealth, which flourished in the land; yet his possessions did not bind him to earthly things. He showed the splendid crowns of his children, ten in number; his affection for his children did not weaken his love for his Lord. He praised and exalted his care for his children: through sacrifices he made atonement for everyone, in case they had sinned.

He introduced the subject of the love of the righteous through the story of Job, saying afterward that the righteous continually come to pray. “There was a day,” he says, “when, as was their custom, the sons of God came to stand before God in purity of soul.” He introduced the account of the Accuser, who came with them and stood among them before God, though not to pray. The Creator revealed the two dispositions of the two sides: the will of the righteous and the desire of the evil one against the righteous. He did not say that they came in a physical or visible way, for bodily beings cannot see the One hidden from everyone. He wanted to disclose the thoughts of the righteous and the wicked, and why they constantly press toward the gate of the Most High. The righteous do not see the Hidden One simply by coming, nor can Satan speak with the divine Being. And if the righteous see the Hidden One through purity of soul, how could the Accuser look upon God? It is therefore right that we should not picture the meaning merely according to the words we hear. Let us investigate what lies within and not stumble over outward appearances. In this sense he said that the sons of the Righteous One came to fulfill their vow of purity of soul to the One who sees everything. The evil one came to accuse righteous Job, not to offer sacrifices of love like the righteous. He wanted to expose his deceitful thinking through the case of Job, teaching us that this is his constant occupation against the righteous. The hostile one saw the great wealth of righteous Job, and envy troubled him: why was Job prosperous and flourishing on earth? The envious one heard the reputation of his blameless and upright conduct, and the voices of everyone recounting Job’s labors stung him. The Accuser was tormented by the Creator’s voice, which continually proclaimed Job’s righteousness and integrity. News of his labors and his charitable deeds spread throughout creation, and his good deeds struck him [?] like arrows. Angry jealousy set that envious one ablaze: “What is this—that he has virtuous conduct as well as possessions?” The Accuser was burning in the fire of rage, wondering by what means he could bring his hidden deceit into the open. He plotted secretly with himself and constructed an argument by which slander could discredit Job’s labors.

In this sense he said that he came before God: to accuse righteous Job of not being righteous. He spoke with himself, not with the Hidden One, and said, “I have roamed the earth and spread my nets to catch people. Job alone has cut my nets and broken my snares. He has not become entangled in my traps and wicked knots. He is prosperous on earth, his body is healthy, and his mind is strong. The fame of his good deeds shines in all four quarters.” His Lord’s command does not allow me to approach and test him, for he is like an athlete, clothed and armed with the strength [?] of his help. The Creator’s power has kept me from approaching him to fight him. Were it not for that, I would perhaps have overcome him like anyone else. But who will give me an opportunity to strike him through his possessions, so that everyone may learn that he belongs among mortals clothed in suffering? In his prosperity his mind is sound, along with his limbs; but if he were distressed over his possessions, he would lose heart. Poverty and deprivation have not humbled him, and therefore he does not stumble into grumbling words. Greedy death has not snatched a company of people away from him. If grief for his children had broken him, he would have conceived insults. The evil one accused Job on account of his prosperity, saying that his wealth had woven him a crown of victories, not his own will. The Creator exposed the schemes that he devised against the righteous man by having it written that he questioned him as though he did not know. The Creator did not question the evil one to learn his course, nor did the rebel see or speak with the one who knows everything. The Creator is accustomed to using such expressions, and he continually questions his creatures as though he did not know. He asked Adam, “Where are you, Adam?” although he could see him. He asked Cain, “Where is your brother?” although he knew where he was. In his anger against Sodom, he declared, “I will go down and see whether they have acted according to the report that has reached me, or have carried it out.” Here he asked the evil one, “Where have you come from?” while teaching us that he roams the earth and leads people astray. Through the question he wished to reveal the evil one’s deceit, for he continually fabricates accusations against the righteous. “Look, you have set your heart on my servant Job.” He exposed his thought:

“There is no one like him, blameless and upright, who honors me.” The evil one’s answer to the Creator was not an audible voice. Through his reply, the Creator wished to record for us the thought behind his deceit. “You,” he said, “have stretched a merciful hand over his possessions, and through your help he enjoys health and prospers on earth. “Through your power his name shines throughout creation as a blameless man. Withdraw your help, and see: he will become more contemptible than anyone. “Through your power his name shines throughout creation as a blameless man. Withdraw your help, and see: he will become more contemptible than anyone. “A garment of mercy is spread over Job as a covering. Lift your right hand, and see: the ugliness of his soul will be revealed. “The gold of your word coats the counterfeit ugliness of his soul, and through it his hidden copper passes for genuine beneath its coating of gold. “Let me test him through the loss of his property, as in a furnace, and expose the counterfeit weakness of his soul, showing that he is not steadfast. “In his prosperity his mind is sound, and he does not lose heart. Through the abundance of his property his spirit is uplifted, as though he were steadfast. “He belongs among mortals clothed in suffering, molded from dust. If the river of my cunning flows over him, his clay will dissolve.” Open a door for me so that I may reach him through my cunning. I will stun him with bad news, and his heart will tremble. There is no mortal who is not distressed by the loss of his possessions, and no one subject to suffering who is not weakened by bad news. The devil was thinking these things within himself; that insolent one was not actually speaking with his Lord. The substance of the words is recorded in the Scriptures as though they had taken place, but the Hidden One never spoke with the rebel. Through a sign, through hidden impulses, he gave the evil one room to act, as he does with spiritual beings when they are sent out. The sign subtly revealed to the devil: “Look, everything Job possesses on earth is handed over to you.” The rebel saw that the Good One had left a member of his household unprotected, and he gathered his forces as though for battle against Job. The insolent one thought he could terrify him through his possessions, and through the loss of his property he sought to weaken the structure of his soul. Agitated by envy of the righteous, he did not know that news of loss could not disturb the serenity of Job’s soul.

The weak-minded one regarded him as someone subject to suffering, not knowing that through endurance he could overcome his sufferings.
