He does not uncover the hidden things of [?] like the Creator, nor does he examine the soul’s thoughts like the One who knows everything. If he had been certain before the struggle that he would suffer defeat, he would not have descended into the fierce contest with the righteous man. Without knowing, he armed himself and entered the battle. He began to shoot the arrow of his wrath at the righteous man’s possessions. There was a day, it says, when Job’s children were gathered together, and an evil messenger brought news of a raiding band that had attacked. A messenger came to the righteous man with an urgent voice, to stun his steadfast heart suddenly with terrifying news. “A raiding band attacked,” he said, “and carried off the oxen and the donkeys. The farmers and herdsmen died in the savage assault.” The evil one contrived a pretext to mislead him by speaking of a raiding band. The demon made it appear that captors had attacked and carried them off. “I alone escaped from the raiding band that attacked,” he said, “and I have come to recount the merciless disaster that happened.” While the first was finishing the news of the raiding band’s attack, another arrived, bringing news of the sheep that had perished. “Fire from above suddenly fell like lightning, and the sheep and shepherds burned in the flames. I alone survived there,” he said, “to bring the news that the Creator has treated your possessions unjustly. Your Lord has repaid you with terrible destruction in return for your righteous deeds: he sent down fire and consumed the sheep without mercy.” Oh, the crafty one, who buried traps and concealed them so that they would not be recognized by the one who walks in innocence! He stirred up the air, gathered fire, and burned the sheep. Then he proceeded to revile Job’s Lord for the wrong he himself had done. “He himself,” he said, “heated his fire, and the sheep burned. He took no account of the pure sacrifices you used to offer.” The report of the burning of the sheep and shepherds had not yet ended when another came carrying news of the camels that had been lost. “The Chaldeans formed three bands,” he said, “coming from three directions. They carried off the camels and killed the men, and I alone escaped.”

The rebel shot three arrows through three reports, but not one hole was pierced in Job’s armor. He dropped three distressing reports into his ears, but the serenity of his soul was not disturbed by the evil one’s turmoil. He changed his three barbs and struck him with three reports, but the gall within Job’s body did not burst. Three times he put his tested metal into the furnace of trial, and the gold of his soul displayed its beauty—how brightly it shone! He took the oxen captive, burned the sheep, and drove away the camels: three snares, which the swift-winged one cut through. Three times the wicked athlete went down into the arena, and all three times he came out ashamed, without a victory. His schemes proved useless against the blameless man, who was not entangled in the traps of his craft. The accuser lost the three contests he had staged. He changed his weapons and renewed the battle, hoping that perhaps he might win. That envious one was ablaze with the fire of his fury, wondering by what means he could shake the athlete into grumbling. The heat of his anger stoked his bitterness, and he burned with eagerness to bring his fire to bear on Job’s children. As the report about the lost camels ended, he brought a fresh report, bitter to hear, wrenching the affections and troubling the soul. “Your seven sons,” he said, “prepared a feast with their sisters and gathered together in harmony at their eldest brother’s house, as was their custom. “A violent wind suddenly blew, unlike anything usual. It shook the house’s foundations, and the house fell and buried them. “The roof fell and buried all ten of them, mingling their blood with their cups where they reclined at the feast.” The rebel put on an appearance of compassion to deceive Job, and with the news about his children he presented himself as a friend. “Never,” he said, “has such a thing happened to the righteous, nor has the Good One given such a reward to anyone who loves him. “In your case, Job, the Creator has reversed the order of his mercies. He mixed no mercy with the wrath he brought upon your possessions. “It was not enough for him to burn your sheep and take your camels captive: he poured out his fury upon your heirs and killed them.

“The Creator did not act justly when he robbed you of the fruits of your labor. Even if it was someone else who attacked your children, he could have stopped him. “If his love for you is genuine, why did he neglect you? And if he rewards people’s labors justly, why has he wronged you?” Oh, the deceitful one! The destruction of human beings was not enough for him, and he began to pour out the gall of his anger against the Creator. “He himself,” he said, “made the wind of wrath blow and killed your children. By attacking you, he sought to distress you through your heirs.” In the battle over Job’s children, the rebel thought he would defeat him, supposing that his love for his children would compel him and give rise to grumbling. The devil saved the fierce battle for last, knowing how firmly people's love is bound to their children. The rebel fought three battles against the righteous man, and in the fourth he exhausted his arrows and stood ashamed. He had pinned his hope on this struggle and was waiting to hear just one word of abuse and defeat Job. For his heart's desire did not reach fulfillment, and that blameless man did not gratify him with a word of abuse. O champion of righteousness, how much he endured! He did not weaken through the adversary's tricks. O mortal, clothed in bodily limbs, who conquered suffering! O flesh that fought a battle against a spirit! O son of Adam, dust of the earth, who forgot his nature! His affection for his children did not cool his love for his Lord. O mind yoked to the sufferings of mortality, which did not weaken into grumbling through grief for his sons! O adamant, against which the evil one worked harshly, yet which did not soften at the [?] reports! It was not that the mortal forgot his nature amid the sufferings he endured, nor was it because he hated his sons that he did not grumble. For he did feel grief over his sons and his possessions, but he found comfort in love for his Lord and did not weaken. Job wisely weighed one love against another, and his love for his Lord overcame his love for his sons. He grieved deeply over his possessions but did not grumble. He mourned his children and soothed his grief with love for his Lord. He tore the garment covering his body and shaved his hair, but he did not tear his heart with doubt about his Creator.

“I came out naked when I was born,” said the righteous man, “and naked I will return, without clothing, just as I came.” “My God gave to me and took it back; his command has authority. May his name be blessed by his possessions for all that he created.” The blameless man offered words of thanksgiving in place of his heirs, and his Lord set his seal upon his endurance, because he did not [?] or grumble. The struggle involving the death of his sons and the loss of his possessions ended, and he began preparing another weapon to destroy the body. He was tormented by the fire of his anger against Job, wondering what trap he could deepen to bury Job's agility. “It is a great sorrow if Adam's dust defeats me, and a son of ashes mocks and laughs at a spirit. I carried off his possessions, and he encouraged himself by trusting his Lord. I killed his sons, and he blessed the name of the one who gave and took away. Now I know that he does not weaken through outward things, and that he does not feel the pain of his children as he would his own. Now I must approach and demolish the temple of his body, for unless he suffers in his limbs, he will not weaken.” These were the wicked schemes he was devising within himself; he longed to bring his treacherous desire into the open. The Creator revealed his hidden treachery through what he caused to be written: that he too came with the righteous before God. Through a question, the divine command exposed his deceitful thinking, and he condemned himself by saying, “I have been roaming the earth.” “Have you set your heart on my servant Job?” he said to him. “He is blameless and upright, and there is no one like him who honors me. “He does not abandon righteousness and integrity, yet you provoke me to destroy the good servant through your hands.” The deceitful one answered the Creator’s hidden command: “The skin that was struck by the arrows of my blows was not his own. “A man,” he said, “will give everything he owns to preserve his life, for it is his life alone that a person loves above everything. “And if you want to learn this,” the insolent one answered, “stretch out your hand and strike him a little, and see—he will deny you! “If you strike his limbs with the rod in your hand, he will stand before your face and revile you openly.” The Knower of all looked upon the desire in the accuser’s soul,

and handed Job over to him, so that he might enter into combat with him over his body. “See, Job is delivered into your hands,” the Hidden One declared to him. “Only his life—you are not permitted to take it from him.” The evil one realized that the Good One had withdrawn his protection from a member of his household. He drew his bow and loaded it with fiery arrows of his wrath. The evil one went out, it is said, and struck Job with a malignant sore, from the top of his head down to his feet, without mercy. With a foul sore he melted his body as though in a furnace, and with its fierce boiling he scoured from him the filth of the passions. He emptied out the arrows of his fury in the fire he kindled, while Job’s body grew ever more beautiful in the flame. Two opposing combatants descended into the battlefield: the ruler of the air and the bodily man clothed in limbs. The bodily man defeated the spiritual being through strength of will, and the spiritual being was defeated by flesh through faintheartedness. The athlete of righteousness stood in the stadium, and the man of flesh engaged in combat with the spiritual being. The spectators of the athletic contest, the hosts on high, gathered together, and all marveled at the bodily man who defeated the spirit. Oh, the unprecedented battle that took place, contrary to custom: the one who receives the blows is awarded the crown of victory! The bodily man received blows from the spiritual being, who tore his body to pieces; yet through his wounds he won victory like a true champion. The rebel tore down the structure of his body, but he built up his soul. He wore away his limbs, but he strengthened his inner movements through endurance. The evil one and Job had set up a target in the arena: whoever hit it through strength of will would receive the crown. The bodily man aimed his will at the target they had set up, while the spiritual being scattered his arrows short of the target. Oh, the archer who excelled and won in every battle! A single man of dust brought him down while sitting unarmed. Oh, the mortal, the lowly nature that demons trampled upon! Though fallen, he stood firm and threw them beneath his feet. O athlete in the flesh, whom spirits seized! Though heavy in body, he rescued himself from those who are light. O sailor who travels the sea in a harsh winter! The turmoil of the waves did not drown his faith.

The Evil One tossed him about in the sea of his body and his mind, but he secured the ship with his endurance so that it would not sink. Reports blew against him like whirlwinds, but he did not lose heart. Grief over his children's death struck him, but he did not waver. The Evil One battered the field of his body with a hailstorm of pains, but his mouth yielded a song of praise instead of blasphemy. The Accuser carried off his possessions to capture his heart, but he sheltered the wealth of his inner self within the truth. Because he did not lose heart at the loss of his possessions and the sufferings of his body, his Lord wove him a crown of victory in return for his afflictions. Because he blazed a path toward righteousness through his own discernment, his Lord made him a path for people to travel by imitating his labors. Because he took up the banner of truth's victory against the Evil One, his Lord inscribed his memory like a portrait within his books. He wrote down his memory as a mirror of the soul's beauty, so that everyone might polish away the ugliness of their own soul through Job's beauties. The Good One praised the righteous on this condition: that through their labors they should become an image of hidden truth. It was not earthly praises that he wove for his athletes; he instilled in people on earth a zeal for righteousness. Through Job's sufferings he opened an arena for athletic combat and allowed flesh to engage in battle with spiritual beings. His victories became like heralds in everyone's ears: “Endure, people, and do not lose heart amid bodily sufferings!” Everyone proclaims his victory like a trumpet: “The time is short, the suffering small, and the reward great!” Through the sufferings he endured, he speaks with everyone and in everything: “The sufferings of this present time are not equal to the glory to come.” Let Job be a mirror for the weakness of our souls: although he was a bodily being, through bodily sufferings he defeated a spiritual being. Let us always travel the path of his labors without grumbling, and through his endurance let us set a goal for our faith.
On Joseph, When His Brothers Sold Him
Homily eighty-[?]. On Joseph, when his brothers sold him. It is suitable for the Passion and is recited on Tuesday. Response: Whichever is appropriate.

Love for the righteous called me to journey along the path of the righteous and to travel in my mind along the beautiful road of their conduct. Love for them drew me toward instruction like a child: “Rise, idle one, and journey in the company of the diligent!” The splendid radiance of their conduct set a target before me, so that I might aim toward it with my verses, if I can. My thoughts marveled at their spiritual victories: how strong they were, and how they did not lose heart before afflictions! I pondered the mortality in which they were clothed: how the lowly body conquers and overcomes its sufferings. Earthly nature cannot conquer by itself. How, then, did bodily beings become strong in the spiritual contest? Flesh cannot triumph through the strength of its limbs. Who, then, gave victory to one whose strength was weak? The command that formed him from dust and called him its image caused the power of [?] to dwell in him and overcome his passions. The Lord who made him to be lord over his fellow creatures gave him strength in his weakness and made him victorious through his power. Through the strength of divine assistance, the athletes triumphed. The Good One gave the strength of his assistance to their willing efforts. Through his own power he gave victory to the members of his household who cherished his love, and lovingly assigned the greatness of his strength to their labors.

He placed the utterance of his hidden prompting within their impulses and urged them to trade with the silver of his words. He stipulated a denarius for Abraham, Isaac, and his son Jacob, so that they would work spiritually in the vineyard of his love. The Creator chose three laborers to work in his vineyard, and through their number revealed an indication of the name of his being. He taught them to work with him according to his will, and they [?] his silver on the table of the soul’s impulses. They gathered spiritual fruits through their words, passed their labors on to their children, and died without dying. Abraham handed his course over to Isaac so that he could trade with it, and Isaac showed the path of his labor to Jacob, the chosen one. Jacob brought forth twelve fruits from his own limbs and presented them as firstfruits to the Most High. He fathered twelve from the common root of his body, and although he himself was impartial, the heart of the offspring that came from him was [?]. Some of them resembled him and walked in the path of his toilsome service, under the agreement for the wage called the denarius of the promised life. Joseph labored spiritually after his father’s pattern and stamped himself with the Spirit’s seal for battle. Rachel’s son wished to serve in the spiritual rank, and he resembled his ancestors in his love for the Creator. He imitated them as he ran his course toward righteousness, and on their paths he pursued the quest of faith. Love set before him a goal for his spiritual labors, and in hope he inclined toward the expectation of things to come. He girded himself with faith as with armor, and in his mind he held the sword of his Lord’s word. His father too saw that he was armed in his own likeness. He poured out love and anointed him with affection so that he would become still more courageous. He anointed him with affection as with oil for entering the contest, and through love for his Lord he overcame the passions of bodily desire. Why, then, did the righteous man divide his love among his children and anoint one with the oil of love far more than his brothers? Why did he break the harmony of love implanted in nature and cast discord among the twelve fruits of his body? Why did he honor one member and call him his own?

And behold, the entire bodily substance from which his children were formed was his own. Why did he split the bond of equal affection and give one an inheritance of love surpassing that of his brothers? The nature is one, righteous man, and the birth is one; and one is the command that fashioned your offspring with the substance of your seed. I know that the nature is one, and my own nature bears witness; but the soul’s will does not correspond to its constitution. It is the soul’s will that changes equal love, and it causes a person to hate one and love another. The great power of discernment rides upon nature and directs it like a charioteer wherever it wishes. The power of our will constrains love by the strength of its resolve, and draws it like a towrope into a peaceful harbor. This power secretly signaled to me with discernment: “Look carefully and see nature, which is equal and yet divided. It is equal in its nature, for the nature is one, as is the command that formed it; yet the will of its soul is split and divided through its freedom. A person therefore has authority over his will insofar as he is rational, and in his freedom he chooses or rejects whomever he wishes.” The righteous man’s love for his children revealed and showed me that the discernment within us has authority over impulses and desires. It was not that righteous Jacob’s love was divided and split: the power of his will directed his love, not his natural disposition. The inequality of his children’s wills divided his love, and he loved and hated through the discernment of his own soul’s will. He planted zeal for righteousness in his children’s minds, so that, if they became righteous, they too would be loved like Joseph. Joseph’s love made him dear to his father’s will; and because he loved truth, the righteous man loved him more than his brothers. His love placed the youngest of his brothers above his brothers, and raised him to the rank that lay hidden in the recompense of his reward. The love he showed toward his father and toward his Maker brought him in return a crown of victory woven for him by mercy. Nature prompted him to love his father and his Maker, and by his conduct he repaid God and his father.

Through the evenness of his love, he divided the love implanted in nature; and his soul’s affection compelled the natural impulse to love more. The love Joseph received from his father resembles Christ’s love for John, who loved his Lord. Our Savior also fathered twelve spiritually, and honored one of them with his love far more than his companions. Following the pattern of Jacob, who fathered tribes equal in number to the months, our Lord also chose disciples to teach humanity. He appointed them according to the number of Jacob’s sons, so that the symbols belonging to the people might correspond to the salvation of the nations. As a symbol of our Savior, Jacob fathered twelve tribes and depicted the wonders of the company of twelve whom Christ chose. In his love for Joseph he resembled our firstfruits, whose love abounded toward the will that loves love. Through his love for his son he portrayed a type of the Bridegroom’s friend, for he too loved one of his children as a figure of John. Love made chaste Joseph beloved by his father; it also raised the apostle above his companions. Joseph’s love drew his father after his love, revealing and making plain that love repays love with love. Let anyone who asks for mercy therefore look at Joseph: he loved his Lord, who repaid him with a love greater than his own. His father too increased his love for him for this reason: he saw that the love of his soul was bound to his Maker. He loved him far more than his brothers and stirred his brothers to jealousy, so that they would run to the Hidden One’s door and be loved by him. Although there was one father and one Creator of body and soul, the willingness of one member sprang up, while the many sank low. Joseph was diligent and constantly remained at the Hidden One’s door, so that he would return love and [?] to him as a reward for his labors. In love and mercy, his love was bound under the Lord’s yoke, and through his father he honored the word of the Hidden One. He sought to please his father by honoring him, repaying his love with the love that he always rendered to his Maker. The willingness of his soul came early and bore its first fruit before the Law,

whose words were destined, after a time, to lay down a warning. It is therefore clear that the Law did not teach the righteous; rather, they became a law for the practice of truth. The herald of the word of truth also explained it well: the Law was laid down for the wicked, not for the righteous. The righteous first became a law to their own minds, and by their conduct they showed the path of the Law. The impulse of discernment predates all laws; it is the teacher that writes and instructs the rational mind. This impulse wrote a book for Joseph upon his mind. He read it with understanding and interpreted the book of worship of the Hidden One. He learned two things from the law of discernment: a person owes a return of love to his Lord and to his father. He too, as a discerning man, returned two things in his love: loving reverence to the Lord who sustained him, and to his father. When his father saw that he was diligently repaying what he owed, he too repaid him with a reward of love in keeping with his willingness. He loved him in secret because he saw that he was hidden in his love, and honored him openly because he had kept his senses chaste along with his will. He adorned his body with clothing in keeping with his willingness, and in his thoughts he honored his soul, full of love. The Creator too loved him far more than his brothers, because he saw that the love of his soul was bound to his hidden being. From his hidden being he gave him power to see hidden things, and strengthened the movements of his mind to contemplate things to come. The Hidden One expressed the sign of his power through the movements of the soul and openly made known to him the power of his hidden being, for everything is revealed to him. In his dream he revealed to him his exaltation and his brothers’ humiliation, and secretly showed him that he would raise his scepter over those who hated him. Joseph saw a dream in secret and showed it to his brothers, teaching them about his authority to rule and judge. “I saw,” he said, “that you and I were working the land, binding sheaves in the field to provide food for the season. I saw my own sheaf rise and stand upright, and I saw your own sheaves bowing down to me.”

Through the sheaves he showed him the famine that would advance and strike everyone, and through their bowing, the subjection of his brothers, who bowed before him. Eleven sheaves bent their heads and bowed to one; it stretched out its hand, ruled them, and overcame them. Oh, the wonder that was being shown through the sheaves: famine and abundance were being revealed through the twelve! Oh, the number of eleven months that fell into debt and became poor! The hidden sign made them dependent on one [?]. Oh, the food that asked for food while itself providing nourishment, in twelve sheaves that were pleading with a sheaf! Oh, human nature, entirely alike yet entirely divided! From it come both famine and food, deficiency and completeness. It is one nature, entirely alike in everything it possesses, yet entirely divided through the will exercised by its power of discernment. From one spring the members flowed like fountains; eleven dried up, while one overflowed with the stream of his love. Like the Gihon, he displayed his flow in the land of Egypt, and the irrigation supplied by his power of speech brought far more joy than the silent river. The Gihon dried up, for wrongdoing had stopped its great flow, but Joseph made a sweet abundance flow through food. In the dream he saw, he revealed both things to his brothers, [?] they might deny the revelation conveyed through the sheaves. The revelation of mysteries proved useless to their evil disposition, and they rejected the hidden things he had revealed through the sheaves. Joseph’s brothers gained no benefit from his revelations; instead, they grew more bitter in spirit against his dreams. In their envy they hated him all the more because of his fine qualities: why was his mind as outstanding as his beauty? The more they hated him because of his exaltation, the more his Lord made him a spring pouring forth the power of hidden things. Again, in a second vision, he revealed another mystery through him, crying out mightily like a herald to proclaim his authority. “I saw a dream,” the humble young man recounted to his father and his brothers:

“There were the heavenly lights, the sun and the moon, bowing before me! Together with the orb of the great sun and the lovely moon, I saw eleven stars harnessed to the yoke of bowing to me.” His father saw that his dream was a sign of his renowned authority, and he marveled greatly, for what it revealed was greater than himself. He explained to his son the meaning hidden within the wonder: “Are your mother, your brothers, and I to come and bow before you?” The righteous man stood in great amazement at what he heard [?], and pondered deeply, fearing that envy might hinder love. He wisely examined his brothers’ disposition, fearing that bitterness and wicked deceit might undo the dreams. While Jacob was considering the righteous man’s case [?], his sons’ inclination was secretly devising deceit. The insolent men grew envious and bitterly hated the man whose soul was [?], because they saw that he would become great through spiritual revelations. He was growing up with his brothers, and his brothers with him. Yet while he was even-minded, his brothers’ hearts were divided and torn. He was bound by love for his father and for them, while they, sons of deceit, were tearing down the structure of love. He was bound to his father in harmony over their needs, while they were destroying the love between him and the father who had begotten him. Blind envy blinded Joseph’s brothers, and they did not see the light of righteousness hidden in his dreams. Envy became like a veil before their eyes, and they did not realize that the purpose of the dream was to help them. Dead envy is dead without being dead, and alive without being alive: dead to truth and alive to sin, both nonexistent and existent. What evil is more wicked and insolent than its wickedness? And who is as deprived of light as its folly? Jacob called and said to his chaste son Joseph, “Come, go and see how your brothers and the flock are doing.” The innocent man set out as his father had commanded him, his mind as guileless as his bodily movements. They saw him coming, cheerful, righteous, and generous, and sharpened the sword of their thoughts to kill him. “Look, here comes the dreamer of dreams!” the insolent men exclaimed.

“Come, let us remove him from among the living and put an end to his dreams. Let us silence his life so that he no longer dwells on glorious things, lest he become king and enslave us, just as he saw.” The innocent man approached and greeted those men full of anger, but they did not answer him as brotherly love required. They accepted from him provisions for their temporary life, but plunged his body into a deadly plot to kill him. He greeted them with love and affection and kissed them, but they did not return his greeting as they should have. They ate the bread their father had sent them and began devising cunning schemes to destroy him. When all his brothers saw him, they said, “Look, the dreamer of dreams [?] and revealer of mysteries has arrived! This is the heir whose fragrance is sweet to his father. Let us observe mourning for him in our midst and before his father! This is the one destined to become master and enslave us, so that we bow before him as before a master and become his subjects!” Joseph’s brothers were plotting together, discussing what means they could use to drive him out of his father’s house. When Joseph saw that his brothers were gloomy, he approached them and asked them, “What is troubling you? Has a lion attacked the flock and carried off sheep? Or have wolves attacked the pregnant ewes and torn them apart? Has a band of raiders cut off some of the sheep and driven them away? Is what happened today the reason you are troubled? Do not be troubled if such a thing has happened, for there is great wealth in our father’s house, without limit.” The contemptible men behaved disgracefully at these words and angrily answered him with wicked words: “Son of a thief, why are you speaking soothing words? Look, ten men are distressed because of you! Call those dreams you have dreamed all your days, and let them rescue you from the troubles that are now coming upon you!” Judah ran and drew his sword to kill him, while Reuben prepared an empty pit in which he could be hidden. His brothers threw him in while he wept and raised his voice:

“What have I done? What is my offense, that you have repaid me like this?” Joseph prayed at the bottom of the pit and called to his Lord: “You who judge in truth, judge justly between me and my brothers!” Joseph looked up and down, but there was no one to help. Yet God had arranged for merchants to come to him. Justice itself had brought them toward the pit, so that they would come and find relief there from the midday heat for his sake. The merchants approached the pit and rested in the cool during the midday heat. The evildoers ran toward the pit to feed them. They brought Joseph up out of the pit, took him, and went away. They began looking for a traveling companion to go with them on the road. The evildoers approached the merchants and asked them, “If you want to buy a slave, we have one with us: a young boy, handsome in appearance and very desirable, who is intelligent and knows how to serve [?] and people. We will bring him, and you can see him. Set his price, give us the money, take the slave, and go in peace.” The insolent men rushed at the humble one to sell him, just as the Jews also rushed at our Savior. Joseph’s story closely resembles that of our Savior, whom wicked men hung on a tree although he had done no wrong. The insolent men dealt ruthlessly with that innocent one. Without pity they caught him and brought him to the merchants. The merchants saw Joseph’s beauty and desired him, thinking that they would ask a great deal of silver for him. The insolent men answered, “We want twenty pieces of silver for him. That is not much—only a day’s food. Give it to us and take him.” When the boy Joseph saw that they had decided this about him, and that he was being estranged from his father’s household and his brothers’ household, he knelt and bowed before his brothers, weeping. His tears streamed onto their shoulders as he pleaded with them. Let me die here at your hands now, rather than be sold and become a slave [?] in a foreign household. I implore you by the God of Abraham's household: do not send me to lands I do not know. As for Jacob, look, I grieve because I am leaving him.

His old age cries out against you, and my youth cries out along with it. Reuben, firstborn and beloved heir, have pity on your brother. Do not bring our aged father down to Sheol in misery. Simeon, listen to me and have pity on your brother now. Do not let me be sold and become a slave in a foreign household. Valiant Judah, lion cub [?], let your compassion flow. Do not afflict our aged father with bitter misery. Reuben knocked him down, Simeon shoved him, and Judah shouted at him. Naphtali too prepared and brought shackles for his hands. Zebulun said, "There is no need for a heap of words. Bind the boy, hand him over, and be rid of him." When the young Joseph saw that there was nothing more to say, he lifted his eyes toward heaven and said: Who could make me like a bird, light of wing, so that I could fly, alight, and see the face of that old man? Who could give me the voice of thunder, mightier than all, so that I could cry out suddenly and our father hear my thunderous voice? Who will go and whisper in that old man's ear [?]: "Look, the son of your vows is being tossed about in foreign lands [?]"? Who would reach such great heights of shamelessness and display that tunic before Jacob? The wrongdoers took Joseph's tunic and slaughtered a young goat. They soaked the tunic in blood and sent it to his father. When that tunic was brought before Jacob, they said to him, "Take it and see whether you recognize the tunic. We do not know whether it belongs to your son, whether it is your beloved's. We found it in the wilderness as we wandered about. It looks like Joseph's tunic, but we do not know. If it really is his, do not be angry that we brought you the news." Jacob saw Joseph's tunic stained with blood. Anguish seized him, and he wailed and wept bitterly. Who has broken the staff of my old age, the one who supported his father? Now I have fallen, and there is no longer anyone to hold me up and help me. Who has extinguished his father's lamp, whose light was wonderful? In my grief over him, I stumble as though in darkness.

Who has plucked the lovely flower with its sweet fragrance, and woven and given me a crown of thorns for all my days? Who has decorated a bridal chamber of mourning for me at this time? Instead of dancing, here I am leaping about and weeping. He tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and sat in mourning. He spread Joseph's tunic before him and gazed at it. How I can bear your departure, I do not know. And how did you leave your father's house, son of my vows? If a wild beast tore you apart on an unsafe road, then, along with your tunic, your death too was investigated [?]. Perhaps a raiding band separated my [?] from his father's house? Yet no one has heard that a raiding band came to this land. Perhaps envy separated my beloved from his father's house? There is hope in justice, which demands what is its own. Jacob sent for his sons and brought them back from the flock. He questioned them about Joseph, asking what had happened to him. He cut off his white hair and threw it down before their eyes, weeping, pleading, and begging them. “I put you under oath by that God who cannot be deceived: what happened to Joseph, who came to you at the pasture?” They answered him, falsely protesting their innocence and declaring to him under oath, “We do not know.” They wept deceitfully before their father, and old Jacob believed their claim: “We do not know.” Jacob lifted his eyes and looked up to heaven. He prayed before God and begged him: “You are God, who answers the righteous according to his goodness. Answer my beloved, and protect him wherever he is. Spread your wing over him so that he may take shelter beneath it from harm. While I am still alive, grant me the privilege of seeing his innocent self. Before I go down to the dead, grant me the privilege of seeing him. Let me place my lips upon his lips, and then let me die.”

The merchants entered the land of the Egyptians with Joseph, rejoicing and marveling because of him. “Peace has accompanied us on our journey from the day this slave joined us to travel with us. The works of the Lord are present in this boy's [?], for we are protected from harm because of him. We know for certain that he is not a slave, and it is not right for him to be subjected to slavery like a slave.” The merchants approached Joseph and pleaded with him: “Eat, Joseph, and drink with us, and put aside your mourning. Do not grieve over the circumstances that have befallen you. You are freeborn, and we have no doubt about that.” Potiphar came out and saw Joseph with the merchants. He was captivated by his lovely appearance and began to say: “Is this boy perhaps a slave? Give him to me, and I will very gladly pay a generous price for him.” The merchants said, “If he wishes to go with you, who will stop him? His price is twenty pieces of silver; let him go with you.” The merchants received Joseph's price from Potiphar. They approached Joseph, kissed him, and pleaded with him: “Do not grieve over this, young Joseph, and do not be angry that we have accepted your price, for we are in need.” Joseph said, “Merchants, go in peace. May the Lord bless your journeys forever.” Justice herself called Potiphar out of his house to come and buy a slave who would rule over the Egyptians. Potiphar took the slave and left the marketplace. He entrusted his whole household to him to manage. He handed over to him all the treasure under his authority and instructed him: “See to it and manage it wisely, as you think best.” He ran to bring the news to his household, saying to them, “Come out and see the handsome slave we have acquired!” “His appearance is beautiful, his complexion marvelous, and his face striking. He resembles a rose and the lilies in the season of Nisan.” The foolish woman saw Joseph’s beauty and desired him.

Desire for his body blazed within her like fire. Like a lioness she sprang upon the innocent man, to bite into his body and soul with her shamelessness. She painted her eyes with very bright, gleaming kohl, braided her hair skillfully, and stood before him. She polished her body, applied her perfume, and hung gold ornaments on herself. She stood before him openly and shamelessly. She put on fine linen and silk, hung three girdles about herself, and positioned herself opposite him, trying to unsettle him as she said: “Look at me, Joseph! I am beautiful and very lovely. I am desirable. Forget your people and your father’s household.” She invited him to eat, but he was not pleased to eat with her. She mixed wine, but he scorned her and rejected her shamelessness. Whenever she called and he did not answer her, she stared at the ground. Whenever she spoke to him and he did not reply, her mouth let out a wail. Whenever she looked at him, he raised his gaze toward heaven. Whenever she beckoned to him, he shook his head and went out to his work. Whether he came in or went out, stopped or set off, she accompanied him. She would not agree to leave him even for a little while. That foolish woman began to speak openly, her shamelessness unabashed before those who heard her: “Joseph, do not despise me, for I am your mistress. Do not become angry, for you are unquestionably our slave. “If you comply and do what I have told you I desire, I will make you master of my property and possessions. “If you are afraid of Potiphar, the master of the house, I will devise another way for you, and you will have nothing to fear. “I will send him poison and kill him wherever he is. You will be my husband, my master, and my heir as well. “I will tell you another secret, just between you and me: I have a great treasure that has no limit.” Joseph heard these words, and his soul trembled. He began shaking out his clothes and crying, “I do not want it! “Wealth for which blood is shed is no benefit to me. I will not acquire an inexhaustible store of ill-gotten possessions.

“I renounce wealth that brings wrongdoing upon anyone who looks at it, and inexhaustible treasures that yield blood. “I will not forge a wicked plot against an innocent man, nor will I defile the pure marriage bed.” “I have a glorious King who dwells on high. If he sees me do this, he will despise me.” Joseph raised his eyes and looked toward heaven. He prayed before God and pleaded with him: “You brought me up from the pit into which Reuben threw me, and you rescued me from the sharpened sword. You brought me into the land of the Egyptians by your great power. Stand by me now, and help me against this Egyptian woman.” Joseph went into the chamber to pray. That foolish woman followed him in and shut the door. She embraced him and kissed him, weeping before him and pleading with him: “But I have loved you! Look, do not reject me, son of the Hebrews! If you will not agree and do my will in what I tell you, I will shut you in the great dungeon of the prison. But if you agree and bow your head to my words and pleas, I will make you ruler and lord over all Egypt.” Joseph looked above and below, but there was no one to help. Yet help was made ready for him by God. With his bodily strength he shook off the seductress and threw her down. He let go, cast her aside, opened the door, and escaped from her. The lioness saw that the ram had escaped her, and she began roaring with strangled cries inside the chamber. The slaves and the free people heard her loud voice. They all gathered and asked her, “What happened to you?” That foolish woman began speaking without concealment, feeling no shame before her companions for her disgraceful conduct: “The slave whom the master of the house bought and brought here is insolent! He took me for a prostitute and wanted to make sport of me. I was sitting in the chamber like a modest woman, and he opened the door to come in to me and dishonor me. I saw him open the door to come in to me, and I began shouting and howling at him like a jackal. When the deceitful slave saw that he was trapped,

he left his garment, opened the door, and went out as though he were innocent. See how this slave has repaid his good master for the honor he gave him and for entrusting his whole household to his hands!” Potiphar said, “Who is your witness that he did this? I do not want to judge him unjustly. His garment is in your hands, and it cries out that you are guilty. I do not want to believe you, because you are not truthful.” The Egyptian heard his wife’s words, became jealous and enraged, and confined Joseph in prison as an adulterer. The righteous man fell into the cruel pit that deceit had dug for him. His body sank, but his love did not sink beneath the harshness of his sufferings. Joseph entered the dwelling of those in darkness and brought them joy. He lightened their burden of suffering and anguish of soul. Joseph alone did not deserve this [?]. Blind envy, without understanding, had imprisoned him for no reason. The chaste man was imprisoned and lived among vile men, like our Savior, pure and clean, among robbers. Two offenders, servants of the king, were with the righteous man, like the robber on the right and the one on the left. The servants had been thrown into prison because of wrongdoing, like the robbers whose deeds brought them to crucifixion. Joseph alone was imprisoned there without any fault, as a symbol of the Giver of life to all, whom envy crucified though he had done no wrong. Both Egyptians dreamed different dreams at the same time: in one was deliverance, and in the other, death upon a tree. The extraordinary dreams they saw saddened them, and the Hebrew came in to cheer them with the meaning of his words. He saw that they were saddened by the memory of the dreams they had seen, and from their faces he understood the distress in their minds. He questioned them as though he did not know, though that was not so. He learned from them and taught them through the spirit of revelation. In the drink of the vine and the wine from it, he saw his deliverance; and Joseph gladdened him, as with wine, through the imagery of his words. The baker too saw his punishment in the king’s food, and the righteous man taught him that through food he would become food. The righteous man explained that the three branches represented three days,

and the three baskets, three days of life and death. Oh, the wisdom that the Hidden One causes to dwell in the members of his household! In their exile he reveals the power of his hidden command. Joseph’s words were fulfilled in deed, just as he had interpreted: the cupbearer lived and the baker died, in accordance with their accounts. The cupbearer forgot the upright man, forgetting him like an ungrateful man, until a dream roused the king, and then he remembered him. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, saw a dream and was astonished. He questioned his servants, but they gave him no interpretation of its meaning. He saw fat cows beside the river. They were very beautiful and pleasing to the eyes of those who saw them. First he saw seven fat cows, and after them seven very bad ones. He saw the weak cows rush forward and swallow the fat ones. They went inside and vanished, and nothing remained of their bodies. Again he saw seven ears of grain growing at the top of a stalk. They were plump, like the first cows. At the end of his dream he again saw ears of grain, which were blighted; their appearance resembled that of the weak cows. He saw ears of grain swallowing ears of grain, food swallowing food, like the cows, when flesh swallowed its fellow flesh. King Pharaoh was astonished and amazed at the dream he had seen, for it was unlike all the dreams that come through the mind’s wandering. He summoned magicians and those skilled in divination and questioned them, but the divine command hid the force of its meaning from their eyes. The king was distressed and sat mourning, without understanding, because he saw that the power of his dreams eluded the magicians. The king’s cupbearer saw the king’s distress and remembered. Though unwilling, he began to recall his offense. The servant disclosed to his master his offense and the dream he had seen, and told him about the Hebrew who had interpreted his dreams. He said, “My lord Pharaoh became angry with his servants because they had done wrong, and confined them in prison, in the house of the chief of the guards. “My companion and I saw dreams full of distress. We presented them to a certain Hebrew, and he interpreted them.

“The meaning of the interpretation sounded utterly certain to us, and his word was fulfilled through events involving life and death.” Pharaoh awoke, as though from sleep, to the prospect of the Hebrew, and hurried his attendants to summon Joseph. The dream he had seen drew him to seek its significance and, like hunger, urgently drove him toward understanding it. The son of Ham sent and summoned the son of Shem—the slave summoned the master—so that the blessed one might come and reveal the meaning of the wonders to the cursed one. The son of Abram came before the Egyptian and saw that he was dejected. With the sound of his words he drove distress from his soul. The son of Ham recounted to the son of Abraham the dream he had seen, and also told him that his dreams had defied his magicians. Through the spirit of revelation, Joseph began to interpret it for him and to make the meaning of hidden things shine before his mind. He said, “Listen, king, and learn the might of the Creator’s power, for it belongs to him to disclose dreams and visions. “It is not mine to reveal the meaning hidden in your fortunes. He has disclosed it to me so that I may teach you the meaning of his hidden things. “Hear the meaning of your dreams from him through me as an intermediary, and know and understand that his command makes the members of his household wise. “The seven cows are seven good years, and the weak ones are seven bad years of famine. “The seven full ears of grain are also years, and the seven dried up by the hot wind are seven years of famine. “Through the fat cows he revealed abundance, and through the weak ones that swallowed them he disclosed famine. “In the same declaration he also depicted the full ears of grain: although they were very good, they were destroyed by the weak ones. “Through the ears of grain in the field he portrayed both abundance and famine, and taught people that they cannot live without his command. “If bread itself gives life by its own nature, why is its power not the same in abundance and famine? “It is not bread that sustains mortal life by its power; rather, the divine command gives its power through the agency of bread.” Joseph disclosed the abundance and famine that were to come through the power of that command which gives life and brings death through various means. “Look, great abundance is coming,” the righteous man revealed,

“and famine will come after the period of years I have spoken of. “Just as the cows that were weak swallowed the seven, so famine will swallow abundance and destroy it.” For this reason he repeated the dream twice: the matter was pressing hard and was about to happen. “Now let Pharaoh find a man,” said Joseph, “who knows how to provide for famine during abundance.” The Egyptian who wore the crown fell before the Hebrew, and the son of Ham bowed unwillingly before the son of Abraham. “There is no man wiser or more discerning than you,” he said, “and no one knows how to administer things with wisdom like yours. You shall be master and ruler over my household, and the word of your mouth shall govern and judge slaves and free people. Only in the title of kingship shall I be greater than you; you shall have authority to administer things as you wish.” The king of Egypt fulfilled his promise and made him master. He honored him with royal garments, like a king’s son. Jacob’s son rode in the chariot of the king of Egypt, and Abraham’s son began giving orders to the sons of Canaan. The dreams he had dreamed in his father’s house were fulfilled in reality, and his scepter inspired awe, like the sheaf that stood upright. The work of interpreting his words also reached its fulfillment: abundance and famine appeared, just as he had declared. The famine was the means of fulfilling that utterance addressed to Abram: “Know for certain that the children of your offspring will become slaves.” Let us understand that Jacob’s son was also sent for this purpose: to go down and prepare the land set apart for Abram’s offspring. Although his brothers maliciously cast him out as though he were an evildoer, it was the command of the one to whom everything is revealed that brought this about. The wicked fulfilled the desire conceived in their hearts, while the one who knows everything fulfilled the purpose of his providence. The things he accomplished through Joseph were revealed to him, and, like a wise man, he explained them through a member of his household. Famine reigned throughout the whole land and imposed its law, and it brought Abram’s sons up against the Egyptians. The harsh famine brought Jacob’s sons into subjection.

Unwillingly they went down to pay the debt owed to the dreams. Because they had not paid the righteous man a reward for his labors, they repaid him the principal together with interest on two occasions. Twice they paid what his two dreams had foretold through the stars and the sheaves, which had symbolically portrayed them. The Hebrews went down to the Egyptians to buy bread, and the justice they had wronged in Joseph caught them. She bound those who had sold him before her beloved, and drew the sword of her harsh punishment against their necks. The man slain by envy recognized those who had sold him, but did not repay them with harm matching their deeds. The righteous man assumed the guise of justice toward his brothers and brought them, as into a furnace, to be tested by his words. “You are spies,” Joseph said to the buyers. “You men have come down to spy out the land, not for bread.” “By Pharaoh’s life!” The chaste man grew angry and terrified them. They trembled and were dismayed, for there was no longer any hope of escape. “We are honest men, not wrongdoers,” the envious men replied. Yet as they sought refuge in the name of the Divine Being, it caught them. They disclosed that they were eleven and had one father. “One has been lost,” they said, and through him their number had fallen short of the number of the months. “Ten of us came down to buy food, and one young brother remained behind. Investigate and see that it is just as we have said.” They had fallen into the trap they themselves had set with their words, and a hidden command bound them on every side. He required them to act according to their words, just as they had declared, and showed that he was righteous and that he too feared the God of all. “Let it be as you have said,” the righteous man replied. “Give proof of your conduct, and you will be delivered. “Go and bring me your youngest brother, whom you said you have, and I will release you to go with your brother to your father. “Leave a pledge appropriate to the situation in which you find yourselves, and take food to the hungry people in your homes.” He detained one of them and bound him in irons for a time, and supplied them with silver and food in their loads. They set out from Egypt and returned to their father. They told him what had happened and the condition that had been imposed.

The righteous man was astonished and amazed at their words. He reproached his sons: “Why did you disclose this? “Why did you reveal the number of my children, how many they are? The man may even demand from you the one who has been lost!” They stopped talking, but the famine did not relent in its severity. It forced them to return to Egypt against their will. They took their brother, as they had promised, so that they would not prove false, and prepared gifts for righteous Joseph, hoping that he might be appeased. They took some of the good produce of the land of Canaan, balm and honey, and a double [?] in addition to the first payment they had made, which had been returned. They set out, traveling amid the predicament that had trapped them, afraid that it might come to its conclusion through these events and destroy them. They were full of dread as they traveled like guilty men, fearing that pleas and words might not be enough to bring about reconciliation. The closer they came to Egypt, the more distressed they became, and their thoughts were bewildered by what had happened. They reached the country, and the pangs of death reached them. They suffered and were dismayed like a woman in labor overcome by her pains. They prepared gifts and went in to plead for reconciliation. They also brought Benjamin in with them to confirm their words. Eleven speaking sheaves fell to the ground, and the dreams the righteous man had dreamed were fulfilled in actual deeds. Against their will, the envious men paid the debt of love and fulfilled the mystery that revelation had foreshadowed through the sign of the sheaves. He spoke with them wisely, as a wise man who saw fit to join deeds to words and reality to the vision. He asked them about their father, whether the righteous man was still alive. Then he saw his brother and said, “Is this the one you spoke of?” He restrained his compassion and forced himself to test them, so that through the trial he might learn the purpose of their thoughts. He honored them with the courtesies they desired and showed them that he knew the order of seniority, from the oldest to the youngest. He ordered his steward to lodge them with a show of affection, to place a cup at the opening of their sacks, and to practice divination concerning them.

He ordered his own cup to be placed in his brother’s sack, so that by all these means he might test the love of his deceitful brothers. They set out from his presence rejoicing like innocent men. While they were still eager, the command raced after them and terrified them. Mourning enveloped their minds like clothing. “Why have you repaid honor with shameful injury, instead of continuing in conduct fitting for freeborn men?” He searched them as though he did not know what had happened, and found the cup where he had placed it, with Benjamin. They returned weeping, with mourning spread over their heads, for mourning had turned their hearts’ joy into sorrow. They fell down and rolled on the ground, pleading about what had happened. They confessed and said, “There is no acquittal for our guilt.” The righteous man saw his brothers’ suffering and suffered with them. He could no longer endure the sorrow that crushed his soul. For the love of a discerning being, implanted in nature, compelled him, and tears brought relief to his sorrow. He wept before them because of how much they had suffered without knowing, and showed his love by not repaying them for their deeds. Compassion spurred him toward reconciliation like a [?], and he let them know that he was the one whom deceitful envy had sold. “I am Joseph, [?] a slave through the envy within you. But see, the hidden will, to which everything is revealed, has raised me up. “I am the one you envied, whom deceit drove out of peace. But see, through me the God of all has brought peace to a divided people. “I am the limb you cut off from your own bodies. Come, let us show one another compassion, even now, and return to unity. “I am the one who saw eleven sheaves and one of my own. See, the meaning of my words has been explained by your bowing down to me. “Go to righteous Jacob: ‘Joseph is alive! Come down quickly, and you too must pay the debt owed to the dreams.’ “Go and tell him: ‘The staff that supported you is alive. Come, take the staff of my own person in your hand, and be comforted by it.’ “Go and tell him of my honor and authority among the Egyptians. Give his soul rest in the harbor of the news that I myself am alive.

“Go and tell him that my God has made me lord of Egypt. My authority reigns and governs slaves and free people alike. “Reveal and show him also the hidden power [?] my movements, and he caused the true wisdom of hidden things to dwell in my understanding. “Go and tell him: ‘The famine will continue for five years. Come, and I will feed you, so that you and your household do not perish.’” Joseph also comforted his brothers with these words: “My God sent me to provide you with food during the famine.” In this way he urged his father Jacob to come, so that by his descent he might bring to fulfillment the words spoken to Abram. Through the promise of prophecy he persuaded his brothers not to delay coming to his loving presence. He laid the fear of famine upon them and frightened them, saying, “The scourge of famine will remain for another five years.” With these words he stirred them to come down to him, and he inscribed them on their minds as on tablets. Pharaoh, the Egyptian king, heard about what had happened and rejoiced greatly at the news of the Hebrew man's family. Pharaoh summoned Joseph and said, “Do this: bring your people and give them rest among the good things of my kingdom. “Give your brothers provisions and send them to their father's house, so that he may come, see, and rejoice that you are alive and in authority.” Joseph's brothers accepted and agreed to what had happened, and they set out joyfully for the country where they lived. The tribes of the righteous man arrived and reached their father, carrying the wealth of the time and a sign of peace. The gifts sent by Joseph and King Pharaoh brought him joy, and they gave him the good news that his son was alive and in authority. He was astonished and amazed at what had happened so unexpectedly. He hesitated and said, “This is a very great thing, if it is true.” He saw the wagons Pharaoh had sent, and his mind was at rest. He gained hope that what he had heard would come to pass. “It is a great thing that Joseph is alive,” said the righteous man. “I will go down, see him, and rejoice that he is alive before I die. “I will go and lay the sorrows of my eyes to rest in the harbor of his body, and cast off my grief through conversation with the words of his mouth.

“I will go and repay the debt of the dreams that I owe him, and fulfill for him the longing of love that he saw in the sun. “I will go and see him honored among the Egyptians, and the promise to Abram and Isaac will once again be confirmed in me.” Israel traveled along the road on which the Hidden One had sent his father traveling. He entered the land of Egypt with his descendants, and the promise began to unfold. They saw one another, father and son, righteous man and righteous man. They repaid one another's love and fulfilled the mysteries conveyed through the dreams. The righteous man bowed before the righteous man, he together with his children, and was yoked in service to his lord and son. Through the bowing before Joseph, the Creator yoked crowns and plows, as a symbol of our Savior, who received loving worship from everyone. In this way he honored the righteous man through his family's bowing before him, so that no one would be astonished at the worship of all offered to our firstfruits. Through Joseph he taught the worship of all offered to a human being: heavenly watchers and human beings together worship the human image. The Hidden One was to take a human being and accomplish everything through him, and in the person of [?] receive from everyone the worship of all. In this way he also depicted wonders in the lives of the righteous, so that we would not regard them as strange when the truth of his revelation was made known. He revealed his sacrifice through the sacrifice of the ram that rescued Isaac, showing that he too would thus redeem his own people through the sacrifice of his body. He showed through Joseph that the worship of all is offered to him. He portrayed his greatness and traced his mysteries in righteous men and kings. He revealed him at the end and through him comforted everyone, those who came later and those who came before. Who would not marvel at the conduct of the righteous and their endurance? Through their labors they opened a road toward the divine Being. Who would not assent to the mysteries and prefigurations embodied in them, and acknowledge the power that strengthened them through the things to come? Who would not give thanks in keeping with their frame of mind? They believed, loved, hoped, and submitted to what they awaited. Who would not knock at the door of love, through which they entered and became kings, and himself become a king by following the chaste example they displayed on earth? Let anyone who desires to be chaste look at Joseph, and watch himself so that he is not defiled by bodily desire.

Let anyone running the spiritual race consider him, and put restraints on his bodily senses so that he does not become brutish. Following his example, let him do battle with temptations, so that the fire in his limbs may be extinguished through his soul’s endurance. Let him go down with him into the arena full of sufferings, so that he may rise with him to victory and the payment of the reward. Glory to the Lord, who through his love fulfilled and completed the mystery of the wonders that his servants saw in the name of the divine Being.
On the Flood

Discourse 16. On the Flood. By the same author, again by the same author: the sixteenth discourse, on the Flood. To be recited during the fast. Refrain. Blessed is he who, in exchange for an earthly dwelling, has graciously given us a dwelling in heaven. [?]

Wise and glorious is the Creator, who fashioned everything from nothing. He showed his power in his works: he spoke, and they came into being. His riches were hidden in his knowledge before his creatures were formed. His love revealed them according to his will, and he poured out his gift upon all. He fashioned everything in order and made nothing deficient. For he is perfect in his nature; its maker is perfect and complete. The time when he would create the creatures was determined in his knowledge. The appointed time was hidden along with the hiddenness of his nature. He revealed his hiddenness through his works and showed his power in what he fashioned.

The assemblies on high cried out to him, “Glorious is the Creator in everything he has created!” Through the fashioning of his works he taught rational beings that there is one power that fashioned everything, and nothing came into being without him. He made and joined rational and speechless beings into a single body. He bound together everything he had fashioned in the composition of his image, Adam. He made the image a mirror for his creatures to look into, so that in the visible image they might see his hidden nature, which cannot be [?]. Through his image he taught rational beings how much he loves his creatures. Through the sentence passed on wrongdoing, he showed that he loves righteousness. He rebuked Adam for despising the commandment and rejected Cain because he had killed. He showed his love and his justice: he disciplines and wins people over without destroying them. He showed them his justice, which hates wrongdoing and sin. He showed them his goodness, how greatly he loves those who repent. Like children beside [?]. With the rod for transgressing the commandment, he scourged the simple. Through suffering, the humbling of the mind, he taught them their duty. The Merciful One comforted them through spiritual revelations. He came down to them in various ways and forms. Through one man whose conduct was pleasing, he turned them toward his love. Through the hope offered by that man's being taken away, he softened the bitterness of the angry. Through Enoch, who was pleasing and was taken away, he showed his love toward them. For it was not human nature that he hated, but wrongdoing and sin. In life he [?] the spark, to proclaim through it the abolition of death. Through his being taken away, he promised life that would have no end. He showed them his love through Enoch, but they despised the hope of his [?]. Through the wrongdoing of their deeds, they dragged him from mercy to anger. Through Enoch he quieted his justice and changed his anger into a respite. But through their wicked desires they sharpened his sword for vengeance. Human wrongdoing increased on the earth like the waters of the deep. The whole earth was flooded with sin before the flood of justice. They burned with bodily desire and threw the order of nature into confusion. Like animals, they attacked and mistreated one another. Like lustful stallions, they neighed after one another's wives. Neither the woman stayed with her partner nor the man with his wife. They strayed from the path in their desire, which craved gain. Their minds were clothed in oppression as in garments. The [?] of sin grew strong, and wickedness rose like a mountain. The storm of wrongdoing, like the sea, disturbed humanity's peace. The mist of error spread and covered the face of inhabited places. The rays of light from the eyes of the mind flickered and trembled. They sank into the sleep of wrongdoing and did not realize that they were sinning. Though their minds were not asleep, their impulses slept along with their limbs.

Only one man did not sink into the [?] of wrongdoing with the evil one. The movements of his soul were awake, and he drove away the sleep of sin. Noah alone kept his soul pure and did not defile his body with wrongdoing. His impulses were like gulls, and he did not sink into sin. The [?] of the oppressors' wrongdoing did not disturb the clarity of his soul. He did not stumble as he walked through the darkness among the wicked. The movements of his mind became wings for the weight of his limbs. Discernment carried him above the waves of sin. And he who kept his mind pure and cleansed his soul of wrongdoing was found worthy of spiritual revelations that expose the wickedness of evildoers. He spoke with him through revelations and testified to the purity of his soul. He revealed to him that he would wash the earth clean of wrongdoing with a flood. “Human wickedness has stained the beautiful garment of creation. Look, I am washing it with a flood and cleansing its filth. You alone,” he said, “have purified your thoughts of hateful things, and your mind has not been defiled by the mud of the earth’s wrongdoing. Because you have not joined your love with the wicked in the fellowship of their thoughts, you alone will escape the demands of justice.” He revealed and made known to the blameless man the wickedness of his people: “Look, justice is scrubbing away the mud of your deeds.” He revealed to him the wrongdoing of the sons of Seth, who had mingled with the daughters of Cain. Though they were separated from one another by the Creator’s decree, the offspring of righteous Seth mingled with the lineage of Cain the murderer. The exalted descended into lowliness to associate with evildoers. What their eyes saw ensnared those rational beings and bound them. The beauty of lovely faces ruined the beauty of their minds. “The sons of God saw,” it says, “that the daughters of men were beautiful.” They desired them and took them as wives, and fathered mighty men of wickedness. It was not greatness of bodily size that [?] wished to make known. They recorded for us the greatness of their wrongdoing, for they became mighty in [?]. The beauty of Cain’s daughters opened an ugly spring of sin. It engulfed the sons of the righteous man [?] in a flood of bodily desire. The murderer’s daughters mixed a cup and made the pure drunk with its [?]. They troubled the minds of the wise through the appearance of their faces. When the exalted abandoned their dwellings and descended to the land of sighs, the wrongdoing of their deeds rose up and brought justice [?] down to earth. Because they did not remain near the beautiful dwelling of Paradise, a flood of wrongdoing swept them away, and wickedness increased upon the earth. He regretted having made human beings, because they had corrupted and overturned his ordinances. It was not that regret had overtaken the one who encompasses the whole of all knowledge. He made his voice heard to bring them to repentance, so that perhaps they would turn away from wrongdoing. Words full of threats were being spoken to them, so that, if possible, the sleepers who had sunk into sin might awaken.

The Creator’s voice sounded like a trumpet in their ears: “Look, I am wiping from the earth the people who have thrown my ordinances into confusion.” He brought the end upon the earth, and the blaze of wrath went forth. He made his voice heard: “My spirit will no longer dwell in human beings forever.” He spoke again, a second time, to gentle Noah and told him to make a wooden ark in which to take shelter during the flood. “Make an ark of gopher wood for him [for yourself], and coat it with pitch so that it does not sink, so that it may withstand the waves when waters mingle with waters.” He showed him its length and width, and what its measurements should be. He taught him how to divide it into compartments suitable for him and for the animals [?]. “Make its length three hundred cubits and its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits, with provisions inside its compartments. It shall have three stories, so that creatures of every kind may live in it: wild beasts, livestock, winged birds, and human beings.” Oh, the Lord who sustains everything and teaches the righteous practical skills! 100. Although he could have rescued him, he taught him how to provide for the necessities of life. He could have preserved the blameless man along with all the other creatures he kept alive. It would have been easy for him to shelter everything without an ark. The construction [?] of the ark was intended to bring the insolent to repentance, so that they would be reproved by a visible sign and judge their own deeds. Through the work on the silent house [?], he wished to teach rational beings wisdom, so that the living would ask the lifeless why they were being put to work. The mute were crying aloud [?] to rational beings, “Turn back from wrongdoing! Look, through our construction repentance is being proclaimed, if you are willing!” Like a herald, the sound of work on the ark was crying out, “Rise and escape the burden of your sins, you sleepers submerged in sin!” The sounds of the ark’s construction were useless to you [them], for the weight of evil had blocked the hearing through which understanding enters. Noah alone listened and waited for the end, while the insolent mocked him, saying that his construction could not be trusted. He built himself a complete house according to the command that had taught him wisdom. Revelation spoke with him, telling him to prepare provisions for himself. He brought in and stored food for himself and for every kind of creature. Although the divine command was protecting him, it taught him to attend to his needs. It was not food for eating their fill that the righteous man gathered and stored, for he knew that food would not suffice without the divine command. They were nourished with only a little, to sustain the life of their bodies. The command of the Creator’s power preserved them with little. Noah, it says, did as he was commanded. Then the Creator spoke with him: “Enter [?] the ark, you and your sons, and your sons’ wives along with your own. Bring the wild animals in with you, and the livestock and birds, to preserve offspring on the earth, so that the different kinds may continue through successive generations. Bring in males and females,

two by two from the unclean kinds, and seven by seven from the clean [?], males and females together.” The blameless man did not know how to distinguish the unclean from the clean until the command showed him through the number prescribed for each kind. He brought in a greater number of clean animals, which he would need when he came out, since God would permit him to eat meat and offer some of them as burnt offerings. Oh, the command that gathered the fierce and savage kinds, made them peaceful toward one another, and subjected [?] them before Noah! That command which had brought them silently before Adam itself subjected and governed them under the yoke of the blameless man’s word. They were coming, species by species, drawn along by the command. Males and females were coming, clean and unclean, in haste. Bridles of peace were placed in the animals’ mouths, and they were quiet. The lion and the ox were yoked together under the yoke of the Creator’s command. The bird lowered its wings and descended from the heights to the depths. Doves and hawks were hurrying to the gathering at the [?] of the ark. A great peace reigned at the door of the righteous man’s house. Species that devoured one another kissed one another in love. In Noah, the authority belonging to the honor of Adam’s image was renewed. The species that had rebelled against Adam returned and submitted to Noah’s hands. The command went out like a messenger and gathered them from every place. It yoked the different species together in harmony, and they made peace. He set a deadline of seven days while the animals were gathering. This followed the order in which he had established everything and rested from his work on the seventh day. There he delayed his work to teach the heavenly hosts. Here too he delayed, to show that he had no desire to destroy. For a hundred years, grace had been crying out like a herald: “Sinners, turn back from wrongdoing before justice comes forth!” After the long delay of [?], he set a deadline of [?] days. For [?] years and for [?], he had been waiting for repentance. “Seven days from now, my command will be carried out, and I will gather grace inside the wall of justice. Seven days from now, I will shut the door of my mercy, and I will break open the sea held above the surface of the firmament.” When Noah was five hundred years old, a revelation informed him of this. In the six hundredth year of his life, there came to an end the appointed period that he had fixed. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, justice sharpened her sword. With water as her weapon, she [?] all the forces of the inhabited world. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, the sea crossed its boundary. The vault above was altered, contrary to the order of its appointed position. In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, the flood came upon the earth. Noah entered with his sons and their wives, and all the species of animals [?]. The sound of the waters shook the inhabited world and its inhabitants. The tumult of the waters above covered its face with darkness.

Noah and those with him were waiting for the command that had gathered them, so that he would close the ark’s door with the key of his powerful command. That entry was a marvel: they were to be sheltered from the flood. Rational beings scorned the warnings and despised the work on the ark. But creeping creatures believed and entered, so that the flood would not overcome them. They were all matched as they entered, males and females together. None entered beyond the required number, nor was the number deficient. For the insolent people were watching the species gathering at Noah’s door. They did not consider why they had abandoned desolation and loved peace. Through all these things the Creator proclaimed repentance in the ears of the sluggish. Through the construction of the ark’s beams and the gathering of the wild animals, throughout the full span of years, revelations cried out like trumpets. Like a rod of discipline, the sound of the flood was crying out. He set a limit of seven days before their lives would be cut off. A marvel to the seven days, but not to the heart [?] of those who drowned. Noah entered and brought in the animals, just as the revelation had commanded him. The divine command closed the ark, and the Creator’s power sealed it. The speechless entered, while those who could speak remained outside, having chosen to be deaf. Justice rebuked them through the silent creatures that had obeyed the command. After seven days, in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, the voice of justice cried out throughout the inhabited world. On the seventeenth day he marked out the calamity of his sentence, and the decree of retribution went out against every rank. The springs of the deep burst open, and the floodgates above were opened. With the sword of water, the divine command laid waste the whole inhabited world. The waters of the deep rose [?], and those above descended to the earth. In a watery trap, justice bound the wickedness of the evil. Deep encountered deep, and torrents pressed against torrents, against torrents. Waters called to waters to strike the heads of the insolent. The speechless deep roared like a speaking creature as it rose. With the sound of its waves it rebuked those who could speak but had despised the command.
