The rain above contended with the wicked through the sound of its descent, because wickedness had brought it down from the heights to the earth and disturbed its serenity. Because wickedness had brought it down from the heights, waters pressed against waters as they rose toward the heights. Those above [?] with those below, like a messenger of justice. The voice of command was urging [?] the waters above to descend to the earth, and the dreadful command was driving those below toward the heights. The descent and ascent of the silent creatures accused those who could speak. Though speechless, they obeyed the command and rose and descended to exact retribution. [?] It was completely filled, and the mountains were filled with sounds of choking cries. The heights and depths moaned with choking cries of every kind.

The little children were tossed about as their lives came to an end. They pleaded with their fathers, but there was no one to help those in distress. They climbed toward the heights, but the flood brought them down. They descended toward the depths, but the deep roared against them. On every side the battle of the waters hemmed in the weak. Not a single survivor remained among the whole host of humanity. For forty nights and [?], rain came down on the earth. The deep rose upward, as waters pressed against waters. In forty days the waters reaped the crop of weeds. With a harsh sword they cut through the stiff neck of wickedness. In forty days wrath stripped the barren vineyard. Like workers in a winepress, the waters trampled humanity and the animals. As it rose, the deep proclaimed the Creator’s great power: his command had stirred it up, and it rebuked rational beings. The waters grew mighty above the earth, and the high mountains were covered. Wild animals, livestock, winged birds, and human beings perished. The waters destroyed every stage of youth and old age. Because their deeds had been alike, the waters made their deaths alike. The flood gathered and buried every kind in a single grave. With a garment of water they covered humanity and the animals. Noah and those with him were saved out of all [?] humanity upon its surface. It was the command that guarded their lives, not the silent timbers. The deep carried the ark and lifted it high on its waves. It was borne along upon the waters, and the command held it secure. It passed over the heights, above the towering cliffs. Surging waves struck it, but its structure was not shaken. The waves battled beneath it, while it passed calmly over them. The blast of a mighty wind shook it this way and that. Water and air clashed with one another beyond their appointed order. Amid their battle, the ark remained in peace and rest. The deep carried it upward and bore it in procession upon its shoulder. The waves bowed before it and made room for its journey. O ship without sails, which crossed sea and dry land! No helmsman guided it through the turmoil of the surging waves. O vessel that carried the whole world in its entirety! Its voyage did not require sailors to guide it. The command was its sailor, and the decree its helmsman. In place of a star, the divine will guided it to the harbor. Its voyage was secured by the [?] of faith, and [?] was unfurled. Grace, instead of wind in the linen sails. For forty days it traveled in darkness like [?]. For the sailor stationed within it had no need of a light. At the end of forty [?], justice sheathed her sword. At one hundred and fifty, a sign of mercy appeared on the mountaintops—after one hundred and fifty days.

The command went out like a messenger, carrying a letter of peace that mercy had written to wrath. At one hundred and fifty, the waters subsided, and the mountaintops appeared. The command flew silently and gathered the waters into the deep. For one hundred and fifty days the ark crossed the sea, and its voyage was directed toward the expanse and the middle of the earth. From the place near [?], it set out at the beginning of its voyage. It brought its journey to an end on the summit of the mountains of Kardu. The command for its construction also had the journey’s end in view: that it should carry Adam’s family across, so that they might settle peacefully in the middle of the earth. Beyond the sea had lived that generation which corrupted the earth. Until then, the middle of the earth had not been visible to mortals. The sea had formed a barrier before them until the flood came. The command broke through its barrier and brought them across to the middle region. In the neighborhood of Paradise they had spent [?] generations. The whole earth was empty of humanity and animals. It was like a wasteland from sea to sea. No human voice spoke in it, and no animal’s foot trod upon it. Grace also prepared the ark on this condition: that it should be a bridge for Adam’s family and carry them across to a spacious land. Through the occasion of the flood, they opened up a road along which no human had passed. It had been established in the Maker’s knowledge that he would do this. It was not out of anger that he drove them from the place where they had been living. It was not out of regret that he cast them into the region in the middle of the inhabited world. For this wealth had already existed in his knowledge before created things. He brought it into the open through various occasions, for the instruction of mortals. So too, in this act by which he destroyed his creations and covered them with water, it was not anger that made him act suddenly, without knowing what he would do [?]. Before the flood, he knew what had happened and what was to come. He knew concerning his creation that [?] death would dissolve it. Wickedness ruined his creation without escaping his knowledge. Before he created sinners, he knew that they would indeed sin. He knew that he would leave a remnant of humanity and of every kind. For this reason, he arranged them and brought them into the ark, pair by pair. He knew that insolent minds would raise the question whether he had destroyed his creation and made another because he hated it. Before he destroyed it, he was looking at the thinking of those who sow falsehood. He struck down beforehand the growth of the weeds of their thoughts. From the first creation he left a remnant of everything, to show that the creation his hands had made was not evil. He saw everything that happened before it came into being. It was not out of regret that he destroyed everything; because of his mercy, he showed compassion and spared a remnant. He displayed his justice, showing that he is just [?], good in his deeds. He showed that he was just when he punished, so that they would not suppose that he loved wickedness. He mingled mercy with his justice.

So that they would not call him a destroyer, he showed his power in both things: in punishing and in sparing. He proclaimed the authority of his lordship: his will disciplines those who belong to him. With the whips of the raging waters, he scourged the wickedness of the insolent. With the rod of [?] the wicked, he maintained order for the living. The waters carried the remnant whom mercy rescued from wrath. He brought his remedies through their midst, so that his seed might bear fruit in every region. In the seventh month, the ship entered [?] [and came] into the harbor. On the seventeenth day, it came to rest on the mountains of Qardu. In the second month, on the seventeenth, it had set out from its place. In the seventh month, on the seventeenth, it entered the harbor. For [?] months it was confined and kept safe in the harbor. It did not open the storehouses of its wealth until the second month. In the second month, the master of the ship sent a messenger to go out and see whether the fury of the waters had subsided from the earth. The unclean raven was sent, greedy and fond of food. The craving for flesh captured it, and it did not return to bring an answer. He sent a second messenger, from a peace-loving kind. The dove went out, inspected the encampment, and returned to him. He waited another seven days and sent the messenger again. The dove came back carrying news of peace in its mouth. It showed its olive leaf to the one who had sent it, a sign in its hands, like a pledge of reconciliation [?], showing that the Judge's anger had subsided. The righteous man rejoiced and was comforted by the letter of peace it brought. He sent the messenger again, for he saw that its promise was confirmed. Three times the dove went out, and on all three occasions it reassured him. He opened the door of the ark and saw the earth—the earth—and was comforted. He saw light and heard a voice through spiritual revelations: mercy had become the mediator and had calmed the Judge's anger. Look, grace has persuaded him to open the door before you. Come out, prisoners, and take comfort in the beautiful sight of the earth. After six hundred years of Noah's life, at the end of the year that followed them, the command instructed the righteous man to go out onto the earth with those who belonged to him. "Come out," he said, "you and your sons with you, and your wife with your sons' wives. Bring out with you the birds, the livestock, and the beasts of prey." The righteous man received the command, went out, and brought out every kind. None of those confined remained behind without going out to the dwelling place of the living. The same number that had entered it came out from there unharmed. For the command had guarded them all and sustained their lives. The prisoners came out rejoicing because their lives had been preserved. In the second month, the command had confined them in the prison. In the second month he opened the door of mercy before them. On the seventeenth day, justice buried them. On the twenty-seventh of Iyar, grace raised them to life. In Iyar he brought about the flood,

at the height of the dry season, lest the insolent should suppose that an abundance of rain had happened by chance. In Iyar he brought about their departure, in the month that is beautiful and adorned, so that the sight of crops and fruit might gladden the hearts of the distressed. Oh, the depth of the great riches of the wisdom of the God of all! He prepares for his creation a season suited to its revival. In Nisan he fashioned the creatures and adorned the earth with trees. People and animals found a beautiful, adorned bridal chamber. In Iyar he opened the ark, in the month in which he had shut it upon them. He prepared a table of nourishment, a beautiful season before them. In Nisan he brought the congregation of the house of Israel out of Egypt. He erected a bridal chamber for her in the wilderness and wove her a crown of flowers. In Nisan he also renewed the creatures through our firstfruits, so that in the season when he had fashioned them, he might renew his corrupted creation. In a joyful season he also fulfilled and completed his purpose for Noah. He brought him out in the month of flowers and made everything rejoice with him. All kinds of creatures went out with Noah and dwelt with him on the earth. He offered some of them as firstfruits to the command that had preserved their lives. Noah built an altar of freewill offering and offered sacrifices of reconciliation. The Creator accepted his sacrifice together with the readiness of his will. The self-existent One, who needs nothing, smelled the pleasing aroma. The Nature that never becomes angry was soothed from the heat of his anger. He said, “I will not [?] curse the earth again because of humanity, for I know that the human inclination is set on evil from youth. From now on, throughout all the days, sowing, harvest, and crops, summer and winter, will proceed in their ordered succession.” He blessed the earth in its changing seasons, as it yields fruit for people. He blessed people with conception and the birth of offspring: “I will cast the fear of you upon all, upon wild animals and livestock. I will yoke all species under the yoke of human authority.” And along with the blessings of childbirth and authority over everything, he taught them to eat animal flesh as they ate plants. He showed them the distinction to observe in slaughtering animals: once they had poured their blood onto the ground, they could then eat their bodies. He said, “Only do not eat the blood, for the blood is the animal’s life. Do not eat flesh together with its life, lest you become liable to punishment.” The people of earlier times did not know to eat animal flesh, until the command was revealed to Noah: “Eat, and [?] eat.” The promise was a law that he established for the natural order. If the earlier generations had known it, Noah would have observed it all the more. By establishing a law for him, he showed that the law was new. If it had been established for the earlier generations, he would not have renewed his covenant. In connection with the killing of animals, he warned them against murder. Whoever kills a human being, his blood shall be shed in return for that person. The human being is the image of his Creator and lord of all creatures. In proportion to the greatness of his honor,

severe is the punishment for killing him [?]. The perfect teacher laid down new laws for his disciple. He wrote them on his heart with the pen of the command of his will. He entered into a covenant with him again and confirmed peace with oaths: “I will never again wipe human beings from the earth with the waters of a flood.” “This is the sign of the covenant that I am establishing between myself and the earth: the sight of the bow appearing amid the water in the clouds.” This sign had existed since the ordering of everything. He did not wish to show it to earlier generations until he revealed it in the days of Noah. He gave [?] it to Noah as a sign of peace, to remain until the end, so that whenever mortals see it, they may be comforted by the sign of peace. He made the simple wise through the new laws that he wrote. He gave them understanding to cultivate the earth with [?]. Noah began to work, it says, and planted a vineyard, which bore fruit. He drank some of its wine and became drunk, and went astray through the unfamiliarity of its strength. He had not experienced how drinking it confuses the mind, nor did he know how those who drink it should use it. Noah drank and forgot himself, and wine [?] the honored man. The insolence of contemptible Ham’s will mocked him. The righteous man cursed the insolent one because he had openly mocked him. He bound him under the yoke of slavery, to frighten others through him. Through curses directed against the insolent, he instilled fear in many [?], so that they would not be like accursed Ham and become accursed as he was. The righteous man’s word did not bind him to slavery by nature. There is no slavery in nature [?], except that of an evil will. Ham’s will mocked the honored man who had lost himself in his wine, and he made him a sign to the insolent, so that they would show respect before those deserving honor. The Creator recorded the story of honored Noah, who was exposed, to teach the knowledgeable through him not to boast of their strength against wine. Alongside the purity of his body, he recorded the error into which he fell through wine, to give an emphatic warning that those who drink it should use it in moderation. He showed that the one who preserved clarity of mind was worthy of revelation, to encourage the pure through him, so that the word of life might dwell in them. He recorded for us the victory of his endurance: how steadfast he was among the wicked, and how he was not enticed into [?] through association with his own people. He preserved him in the waters of the flood [?] and made him a new beginning for creation. He brought peace to the desolate earth through the [?] of the propagation of his race. He brought him out of the ark and hid the ark from him, so that his descendants would not go astray over it and call it God. With this intention, righteousness hid it from those who might see it, so that what had been a means of life would not become a cause of error for others. He hid the ark in the earth, in the same manner as he acted in the case of Moses. For he knew that the Hebrew people would go astray over his tomb. All knowledge belongs fittingly to him who comprehends the full extent of all wisdom. Things that have happened and things yet to come do not escape his knowledge. Before everything existed, he examined it, and before it came into being, he knew everything. His works were encompassed by his knowledge before they existed.
He who knows everything deserves to be praised by everyone. Though he knows the evil of our inclinations, he gives us time through various circumstances.
On the choosing of Moses and on the fire he saw.

Discourse Forty-Two. On the choosing of Moses and on the fire he saw in the bush. And on the deliverance of the Israelites. To be recited on the Thursday of Passover. Response: Blessed is he who, by being killed, killed death, and raised our nature to life on the day of his resurrection, my brothers.

The son of Amram saw a new sight on the mountaintop: fire in the bush, and the bush in the fire, yet it was not burning up. He saw a frail substance standing in the mouth of the blaze, yet its heat did not harm the bush’s moisture.

The flame’s mouth was open like a lion’s, and the bush lay before it like food, yet it did not touch it. Sheol the devourer, which grows hungry again however much it eats, became a faster on Mount Horeb, contrary to its custom. The confounder of order, for whom everything was equal before its enormous belly, observed order before the divine revelation. It appeared divinely before Moses’ eyes, and though it could harm, it did not harm what was vulnerable to harm. It appeared in the form of fire to the son of the Hebrews, and though it was fire, it was not a fire that burned. He saw the likeness of fire dwelling among the bush’s branches, and he marveled greatly at who had put a bridle of silence upon it. In that wild thing, whose impetuosity had never been subdued, its fierceness was harnessed under a command as though under a yoke. The hidden will rode in a visible form and placed bridles of flame in the mouth of its chariot. On the mountaintop he halted his swift chariot, and the fire under his control neighed like horses. Moses heard the neighing of the fire from the mouth of the bush, and he wanted to learn the reason for the vision that had appeared to him. “I will turn aside and see this great sight,” said the discerning man, “and why the bush burns without burning up.” The command that had fashioned the vision secretly called him: “Come near and ask what the cause is and why this is happening.” He gently encouraged him to approach the vision, then in turn filled him with fear, so that he would not approach without being sanctified. “Moses, Moses!” he called him, speaking as one who knew him. “Take off your sandals, and then approach the place where I am. I am holy, and the mountain has been made holy by my presence. Do not defile with the sandals on your feet the place that I have made pure.” He regarded the sandals on his feet as unclean—not because they were unclean, but to magnify the greatness of the vision before his revelation. He taught him to approach the revelation in holiness, so that he would know how to sanctify the members of his people. On this condition he showed him the vision of the flame:

that he should add the fire of the Creator’s name to the forest of error. Through fire he revealed the power of his greatness, whose strength can accomplish everything; and through the bush he disclosed the wealth of his kindness. He portrayed the mystery of his severity and his kindness in the vision, and [?] them like an image before his household servant. He was sending him to the Egyptians and the Israelites, to punish and to deliver according to the discernment of his righteous judgment. Through the fire he showed how easy it was for his command to scorch Egypt; and through the bush he showed that he takes no pleasure in human destruction. From within the fire he spoke with the man whose speech was halting, saying to him, “I have authority over everything and in everything. I am the one who created creation in the beginning out of nothing, and by my power the created world, made by my hands, stands firm. I am the one who chose Abram, Isaac, and Jacob, my servants, and honored them with the great title of my glorious name. I am the one who promised the land of Canaan to their descendants, and I have come to fulfill the promise of my words to them through deeds. The cry of their suffering among the Egyptians has risen to me, and I have come down to rescue them from the oppression of their oppressors. I know the pain in their hearts and how bitter it is. Therefore I have ground the medicine of the vision to heal them. I know the injustice of their taskmasters and how unjustly they have acted. Therefore I have drawn the sword of the Spirit to destroy them. I am giving you the weapon of my word, which cannot be overcome. Go, use it to humble the sons [?] of Ham, the slave who enslaved free people. Go, tell the slave of slaves, who was cursed by his father, ‘Enough of your enslaving the children of the righteous man whom his father blessed!’ Go, proclaim personal freedom to the son of Shem, the firstborn, and throw off him the yoke of slavery imposed by the contemptible Ham. I have remembered the promise of my true words to Noah, which Canaan’s descendants have made false in their arrogance. I am the one who blessed, and I am the one who cursed, according to their dispositions; and I am the one who promised that the sons of Shem would be slaves to Canaan. Wisely I blessed and cursed the two sides; and the accursed one who reversed them—I will overturn him through my blessings. Reveal, then, the power of my blessings to the Israelites,

and reveal and show the lash of my curses to the Egyptians. Go, bring good news to the children of my friends, and remind them of the promises I made to him. Sow the name of the God of their fathers in their ears, and they will awaken at the sound of the assurance of their freedom.” The Hebrew heard of his people’s freedom, and his soul found relief. But then he grew troubled again, fearing that it might be a report without deeds. “Here I go,” the humble man answered the voice that called him, “and I will proclaim to the Israelites the good news of your name. “Look, I am proclaiming God's name in the people's hearing, and now they are asking for his precise name. What shall I say?” “There are countless names of gods in creation. If I bring them the name ‘God,’ they will say, ‘Which one is he?’” “First they demand the name from me, and then the deeds. How shall I name you before the questioners who ask for your name?” The Creator saw that he was pressing his inquiry about his name, and he revealed and showed him the name of the Being who has no beginning. He taught him to reveal the name of his being before the Hebrews: that he exists without beginning and without end. “I am not,” he said, “designated by a name bestowed by fools, but by power and by deeds of creation. “I am the One who exists, and this is the name of my incomprehensible being. No one has given me a foreign name apart from what I am. “If you wish to learn the name that proclaims my lordship, I am called God alone, and also Creator. “But ‘I am who I am’ is the name of my being.” To make it certain, he repeated the utterance twice. The son of Amram heard the name of the Being who exists and is hidden, and wondered how the people would believe in something hidden. “Go back and say”—he repeated and told the messenger—“that I am the God of your fathers, of Abram and Isaac.” These things he heard seemed excessive to the stammerer, and he did not want to go, lest he go and not be believed.

“Look, the people will not believe my words,” the stammerer replied, “nor will Pharaoh listen to the utterance of the name of the Being.” The Creator saw that he was trying to put together excuses, and he shut the door against the excuses of his ignorance. He saw that his faith had grown sick through doubt, and he applied the medicine of the power of signs to his mind. “What is that in your hands?” he asked, as though he did not know. And he said, “It is a staff,” not knowing what he had questioned him about. He questioned him so that he would acknowledge that the staff in his hand was a real thing, so that, when it was transformed, he would not suppose it was unreal. “Throw it on the ground,” he said [?] to the owner of the staff. He threw it on the ground, and it became a snake and began to writhe. The Hebrew saw the transformation of his staff and trembled in terror. He was afraid of it, lest it bite him and his life come to an end. The voice speaking with him saw that he had lost courage and encouraged him to grasp the snake as he would the staff, without being afraid. He steadied his trembling and grasped it in his hands as he had been commanded. The snake changed back and became a staff as it had been before. Again he said to him, “Put your hand inside your robe, against your chest.” He put it in and brought it out, and saw that it had become leprous, like snow. He commanded him to put his hand back inside a second time. He put it in and brought it out, and it returned to what it had been before. Through his staff and his hand, he taught him the power of the One who acts through his hands, who chastises and delivers, who assails the wicked and silences him. Through the staff he showed him the harsh blows that would fall upon the Egyptians, and through his leprous hand, the ugliness of the wrongdoing among his own people. They were clean when they came in from paganism—[?] the leprosy of two—and after they mingled with the Egyptians, they became leprous with sin. Through their departure from Egypt they were being cleansed, as depicted when his hand became leprous and then became clean again. Like the staff, the Egyptians too had been silent, but after a time they became vipers through sorcery. For their sake he changed the staff, and it became a snake, so that through his discipline he might draw them away from evil.

With two signs he opened a path for the one being sent, although the difficulties were plainly visible before his mind. His thoughts about his journey stood divided, and he returned to devising another excuse: his stammering speech. The voice rebuked him: “Who made a mouth for a human being? And who gave a mouth the power of speech, so that it pours forth words? Does the staff that became a snake not teach you that it is easy for me to have you proclaim my greatness through your stammering? Why do you marshal excuses and arguments against my will? Look, whether you wish it or not, you will certainly go. Go! Do not be troubled that these things you have heard might not happen. Direct your thoughts toward the outcome and see that they are true. I myself will be the word dwelling in your stammering mouth, and I will speak to the Egyptians and the Hebrews.” The son of Amram saw that he had exhausted his arguments and would certainly have to go. He took his wife and sons with him, intending to go and remain there. With this [?] he journeyed from Midian to the land of the Egyptians: if he could, he would deliver them; otherwise, he would remain with his relatives. The one who searches the heart saw that he had [?] to hide himself, and he exposed and revealed the secret scheme within his heart. With a show of anger he met the doubting man on the road. He raised his sword and cut short the schemer’s scheme. He flashed a sword against his life as though to kill him. His wife saw it and interceded with her son’s circumcision. She held up the circumcision like a barrier before the command, and kept the sword from her husband so that it would not approach him. “I have a bridegroom of blood,” she said, according to her understanding, “and I am a kinswoman of the faith of Abraham’s household.” The daughter of diviners held Abraham’s seal in her hand, so that Abraham’s Lord might see her and be reconciled to her. The one who knows everything saw that she had taken refuge in Abraham’s household. He accepted her plea, restrained his sword, and refrained from killing. Although he raised his hand, he did not raise it to kill, but to expose the scheme Moses had devised in his heart. Like a raider, the command fell upon his camp, took his company away from him, and sent him off stripped of everything. He gave the shepherd only a staff to hold in his hand,

so that with it he might display the power of signs to the people and the nations. He placed the sword of the Spirit in the warrior’s hand, so that he might go and fight the sorcerers clothed in error. Like an exile, he entered Egypt, from which he had departed. He raised his staff and spoke the word in his mouth, and she trembled before him. He entered and told his people the vision he had seen. They found relief, yet found no relief, because they did not truly believe. Pharaoh too heard the name of God and trembled, yet did not tremble, because he thought there was no God who could overpower him. He gathered the tribes and taught them the message of the promise. Then he went in to the king to make God's name known to him. “The Lord over all has sent me to you as an envoy, to free his people from bondage so that they may serve his name. The Israelites are children of his divinity, and they owe him the love due to a father and a master. He told me, ‘Go and say to King Pharaoh: Send me my firstborn son, whom I brought forth through the [?] of my hands.’” “My firstborn son,” said Moses, the firstborn of the spirit of revelations. But the promise conveyed by his words found no acceptance in Pharaoh's ears. “Who is the Lord, and who are his people? I do not know. Nor can anyone free Israel from slavery. Go away, Moses! Do not mislead your people, lest you add a double yoke to their necks. Go away, fool! You have babbled enough before a sophist. Do not speak any further, or you will be disgraced.” Moses did not tremble at the Egyptian's threats, nor did he shrink from proclaiming the Creator's power. The son of Abraham answered the son of Ham the slave, saying, “I am an envoy whom the Hidden One has sent to the dwelling of mortals. He gave me a document bearing his name to bring to his people. Read, understand, and see that what I have said is true.” Moses unfolded the decree bearing the name of the One Who Is, and began reading its first syllable: the transformation of the staff. The Israelite threw down a staff before the Egyptian, and it became a snake—not merely in appearance, but in reality. Pharaoh did not tremble at the transformation of the staff into a snake, for he was accustomed to the illusions of sorcery.

For he thought that, like the sorcerers, Moses was deceiving people with illusions and showing human eyes an unreal apparition. He summoned sorcerers to come and deceive with their appearances. They threw down staffs, but the magic they had planned did not succeed. They too did something resembling what Moses had done, but not in reality. Truth rose up and swallowed their appearances. The real snake swallowed the counterfeit, which vanished and came to an end. The counterfeits could not hide from the real one. The sorcerers thought that Moses was deceiving people with their own sorceries, since he had been trained in their craft from his youth. The hardhearted hardened their hearts and did not heed his words. So he returned and brought another document announcing another scourge. He raised his hand in the Creator's name and struck the river, and the river's fresh waters became bitter blood. The severity of the scourge turned the waters into blood, so that Pharaoh would learn that the silent things had been struck on his account. O Creator, whose judgment of the work of his hands is just, why do you punish those who have done no wrong instead of the guilty? Pharaoh deserves a double punishment because he has not obeyed your words, not the speechless creatures, who do not understand you or even know who you are. Raise your rod and strike the offender for his wrongdoing, so that he will not offend again and mock you insolently. O mind, do not presumptuously find fault with that knowledge whose judgment is just in its ordering. He rightly punishes the voiceless creatures instead of those who speak, to make them know the greatness of his love for humanity. He said this: “[?] hardened Pharaoh’s heart”—not that he hardened it, but that he bore with him patiently. He could have punished him and ended his life in a single hour, but this would not have suited his kindness. He kindly bore with the senseless fool until he himself sank his own soul into the abyss of wickedness. The dull-minded man had gone out to the river to offer sacrifice. Moses met him and showed him the punishment he was about to suffer. Before inflicting punishment, the treasury of punishments revealed his punishments, to teach those being punished that their blows came from him.

He raised his hand and struck the earth, and it filled with locusts. Countless frogs came out and covered its surface. The insolent man saw this and grew stubborn, and he summoned the godless men. They falsely produced frogs, though there were none. Moses’ frogs were truly real, with bodily form, but the sorcerers’ were like a shadow that has no substance. The land of the Egyptians stank because of Moses’ frogs. The rebel suffered, and he begged and pleaded, but not sincerely. “Choose a time for yourself,” the humble man answered the arrogant man. He said, “Tomorrow.” The righteous man prayed, and the frogs disappeared. The rebel turned back, and his heart strayed from correction. Moses returned and showed him a punishment full of lice. He revealed it to him beforehand, saying, “Look, I am doing this,” and then carried it out, so that he would know that it was not deception but truth. Through a speechless staff, the earth received a blow from one who could speak, and lice swarmed over people and animals. The lice that the Israelite produced clung to their bodies, until even the Egyptians wailed because of their viciousness. The Egyptian suffered a harsh punishment from the Hebrew. The sorcerers were defeated and raised a finger before God. “This is the finger of the God of all,” they told Pharaoh. But the hard-hearted man did not listen to those followers of error. The Creator sent to him again, for the fifth time: “Send my people to me, or else receive another punishment. “Look, I am sending against you a swarm of every kind, mixed and intermingled, destroying everything without mercy. “And to establish the truth of my word, which goes ahead of its coming, look: I am making a distinction between my people and yours, so that it will not approach my people. “Look, I am giving great order to its confusion, and though it lacks discernment, it will show more discernment than you.” The swarm of flies [?] and covered the face of the whole earth, destroying crops and the fruit of every tree together. At last the rebel felt the pain, though he remained stubborn, and called Moses to hold back his hand from striking. “Stop your scourges, son of the Hebrews! You have punished me severely. I will let the people you requested go with you.” Moses lifted the rod of punishment away from the insolent man.

But he went back to lying and did not release the people as he had promised. The Lord said to Moses his servant, “Open the storehouse and bring out scourges against the insolent who have despised my warnings.” Dreadful death went forth with the word of the son of the Hebrews, and suddenly all the livestock in the land of Egypt perished. The animals died, but the wicked man's wickedness did not die. The Lord saw this and raised his hand through a member of his household. He commanded him to strike the stiff-necked man with a terrible boil, so that through his body he might humble his soul from its pride. The man of earth scattered ashes toward heaven and disturbed the air, and boils broke out on human beings. With boils that blistered, the insolent, clothed in arrogance, fell, yet they were unwilling to strip away the terrible boil of their thoughts. They suffered severe scourges, and their limbs were ravaged. While the plague of blisters still persisted, another followed it. To suit their sickness, he prepared a caustic treatment, severe cauterizations, to cut away from them the disease of wickedness that had ravaged them. He signaled to the air, not [?] through Moses' hands, to rain down hail, and with the word the deed took place without delay. The man made of dust raised his right hand toward heaven, and hail came down, mingled with the fire of wrath. Hail and fire, two opposites, mingled with one another. They came down and fought against the wicked on behalf of the Creator. The silent things waged fierce battles against the wicked, exacting payment from them for the reproach and dishonor they had brought upon God's name. Oh, what a battle, unlike other battles, for enemies embraced harmony for its sake! Who has ever seen two opposing elements, alien to one another, embrace harmony contrary to their custom? Who exercised authority over created things like the son of Amram, who compelled the forces of nature and subjected them by the word of his mouth? Here the saying addressed to him, “You shall be a god,” was fulfilled. Like a god, he commanded the forces of nature, and they obeyed his command. The deaf things heard him and had no difficulty carrying out his words, while those endowed with speech rebelled on the cliff of contentiousness.

In response to their rebellion, he varied the scourges, using every kind, and swiftly arrayed them one after another. After the hail he brought fierce and devastating locusts. They covered the earth as with a garment, so that it could not be seen. They were exceedingly powerful; [?] their like, nor would there be again. Without pity they devastated and destroyed fruit and crops. The land of Egypt was ruined and stripped of every good thing, yet the hearts of its children still persisted in tyranny. The Lord of all also raised his hand against their pride, and after the locusts he struck them with the plague of darkness. For three days there was darkness where they lived, and the hours of night could not be distinguished from those of day. The darkened people sat in the great darkness of ignorance, deprived of light and understanding. At the end of the plagues, the divine command raised a hand through Moses and struck them with the death of the firstborn, whose mourning was bitter. At night the angel of death passed through the land filled with wickedness and killed the firstborn of humans and animals alike. The spiritual watcher flashed a sword before their eyes, and the soul trembled, departed, and fled from the limbs. Swiftly he flew over their bodies like lightning, and like a thief he broke into their limbs and snatched away the soul. All the firstborn of free people, slaves, and the poor died, and not a house remained that had not been plundered by sudden death. He stirred up bitter wailing throughout Egypt, and they wailed and wept loudly over their firstborn. They raised mournful voices and [?] over the departed; they grieved and groaned loudly over their children. The night of mourning saddened them over their firstborn, but it gladdened the Israelites with the sign of deliverance. With the lamb’s blood he marked out the deliverance that would set them free, so that the angel of death would have no power over their firstborn. Speaking beings sprinkled silent blood on their doors, and the watcher saw it, turned aside, and passed by their houses. O mute [?], by what power did you overcome the spiritual being?

And how did fire and spirit bow down and fear you? All Egypt trembled and shook at his severity, but you, silent one—by what power did you overcome the mighty one? What you accomplished was not your own doing, weak blood. The watcher saw in you the sign of the one who was to come, and he drew back before him. Speaking blood was destined to set all the nations free, and he depicted beforehand in you the sign of his coming through the departure of the people. The sign of the truth set the children of Jacob free, and he taught them to hand it down until he comes. On the fourteenth day of the month of Nisan he established its commemoration, so that they would not forget this deliverance that set them free. From the beginning he was intent on the mystery of this day, and he knew it before he established creation in the beginning. On it he delivered the children of Abram from slavery, and he set it down in writing before their eyes so that they might contemplate it. The rebellious were astonished at the power of the Israelites’ deliverance; they raised a finger and acknowledged victory in the name of the Creator. Pharaoh, it is said, called Moses and said, “Get up and leave here! Lead your people away, so that they may go and worship before their God.” “Get out from among my people,” the son of Ham said to the son of Abraham. Though unwilling, he begged and pleaded for his offense. He who had resisted the truth from the beginning was humbled. Thus, at the end of the plagues, he pleaded for the people to leave. He hurried them to depart quickly. This was not his own doing, but that of the command that was compelling him. The hidden command was urging him to send them out, so that the day of the mystery being commemorated would not be delayed. The Hebrews left Egypt in haste, and there was no time for the dough of their provisions to rise. They went out rejoicing because they had plundered the wealth of their persecutors. But Pharaoh changed his mind and grieved greatly because he had been left poor. Foolish jealousy inflamed the senseless fool. He armed his army and hurried out after the people. The rebel led all his people, and they went out with him, so that his forces might receive judicial punishment along with him. They owed retribution for the infants they had destroyed, and the hidden command gathered them together for a single destruction. With the sword of water they had ruthlessly killed infants,

and he prepared them for that same retribution, in keeping with what they had done. With horses and weapons they went out to hunt down the Israelites, and swiftly pursued them as far as the sea. The Hebrews saw their persecutors and were dead with fear. They gave up hope, thinking that escape was no longer possible. They saw the terrifying sea roaring before their eyes, and King Pharaoh behind them like a dragon. They turned to Moses to appeal to him, not with love, but with grumbling and doubts in their minds. “Why did you bring us out of Egypt to die here? Slavery to human beings would have been far better for us than death.” Moses prayed when he saw the foolish people grumbling, and the Lord answered him—the one who answered him before he prayed. He made darkness like a wall behind them, and before them a great light like a pillar. For the eyes of the persecutors he made the darkness doubly dark, while for their own eyes he doubled the light during the hours of darkness. All night the darkness grew dense behind them, and all night the pillar before them shone. That night was a night of darkness and lights: light for the people, and double darkness for the Egyptians. Both sides camped in fear before the wonder, and both the people and Pharaoh longed for victory. Moses took courage through hope in the power of the signs, and kept his gaze fixed on the Creator in [?]. The Creator, too, came down to him alone, and, as though teaching a child, instructed him in hidden things. That command looked upon him, having seen how earnestly he pleaded, and spoke with him as with a friend whose love is steadfast. “Why are you praying?” the Lord said to his servant. “Raise your hand and divide the sea, so that the people may cross. With the staff with which you disciplined the hardhearted Egyptians, scourge the turbulent sea, so that it may learn order. Through you I teach order to the speechless and to those who speak, so that they may know the power of the Maker who fashioned them. Rebuke the sea, and let the turbulent rush of its waves fall silent, so that the Israelites and the Egyptians may see my greatness.

Cry out to the speechless one, and see, it will obey you like one who speaks. Proclaim my name to it, and see, it will understand the power of my being.” The stammerer stammered to the silent one as he had been commanded. The speechless one heard him and carried out his word in deeds. It made a broad road through its midst so that the people could cross, and the waters stood packed together like a wall. Moses was performing a great wonder—yet it was not Moses, but the command of the Creator’s power speaking through him. Through the seer, those watching saw a new sight: speechless nature keeping its order without breaking it. Fetters of silence were laid upon the brute, and it no longer kicked with the feet of its waves as it had before. The same command that gathered the waters in the beginning divided them and [?] them to keep their order. The silent waters heard the voice that had created them, and they made room for the people to cross between their waves. In the visible staff they saw a hidden power and feared it. They stood like servants on the right and on the left. Those who could speak also saw the speechless waters obeying the command, and they gained confidence in the power of the Maker, whose power can accomplish everything. The feeble people saw that a road had been opened through the waters, and they began to travel confidently between the surging waves. Abraham’s descendants traveled through the depths as though on dry land, and as they traveled they could not get enough of walking there. The travelers saw a new and unfamiliar way of walking. It was real, yet to their minds it did not seem real. They looked at that crossing as though in a dream. “It is there—and it is not there,” they thought about its strangeness. The Egyptians too stood in doubt at this wonder. “Is the sea divided, or is it not?” they wondered. The hidden command that had brought this about drove them onward: the people to cross, and the Egyptians to drown. It was not with confidence born of faith that the Hebrews crossed, nor did the Egyptians feel afraid as they entered between the waves. The command led them forcefully like blind people, and they could not discern or understand the power of the miracle. He spread ignorance over Pharaoh and his army.

The fools entered and stood among the snares without realizing it. Like a hunter he lured those childish in heart, and surrounded them on every side with snares of water. The contentious man entered with his entire army, and they stood in the deep. The fool did not consider that his sins had bound him with harsh cords. The divided sea remained in its appointed state until morning, and at daybreak he signaled to Moses to raise his hand. The Egyptians saw a terrifying sight at that moment, and they urged on the wheels of their chariots, trying to escape. When they entered the middle of the sea, it was not of their own accord that they entered; nor was it their own decision to falter and become afraid. A hidden command brought them in against their will, and it also cast dreadful panic into their minds. The Hebrew turned his face and looked at the deep. The waters surged and covered the horses and their riders. Weighed down by their sins, they sank like lead. Not one survivor remained among them, safe and unharmed. They all perished because they had agreed with one mind to drown the Israelites’ babies in the waters of the river. The wicked died with water as their shroud, without receiving burial, just as the infants had died without burial. The Examiner of all dealt with them just as they had dealt with others, and he exacted from them repayment for the destruction they had inflicted on their fellow human beings. The Hebrews saw their corpses on the seashore, and they reminded them of the corpses of the infants that had floated on the river. The children of Abraham rejoiced and took comfort in the Lord of Abram, who fulfilled and completed the promise he had spoken to Abram. They praised and exalted the power of the Creator who had freed them. They believed in his name and loved and honored Moses his servant.
On Samson the Mighty Man
Homily Forty-Three: On Samson the Mighty Man

In the Scriptures I saw a picture of the righteous man’s victory, painted on the page of the Law in two forms. At the beginning of the passage I saw beautiful pictures, but at its end I saw signs that were not beautiful. In the first account I read of the triumph of his great strength, but in the second, of disgrace, dishonor, and weakness. The beginning of his story was very wonderful to anyone who examined it, but the end of his story was deeply shameful to anyone who heard it. Inconsistency could be seen in the righteous man’s story, and the path he traveled in the course of his life was confused. My thoughts were bewildered by the inconsistency in the struggle of his labors, and I wanted to learn why there were two different outcomes in one life. My mind carried me away to investigate his glory and his disgrace, and desire brought me inside the gateway of the books of the Spirit. I entered and stood among the written letters, and began to linger over the account in which the Nazirite man is described. I saw the designation of his election marked at the beginning of his story, and a spiritual being declared it before human beings. I saw a man of the spirit announcing his conception and birth, and defining his chosen status in the name of the Creator. In the Creator’s name, the spiritual one called the bodily man to be a servant and minister of his Lord’s word. He placed the holy name on his head like a seal, so that he would know whose he was and whom he served. The command chose him for the service of the King hidden on high, and equipped him like a soldier with the armor of Nazirite consecration. He armed the bodily soldier with Nazirite consecration,

so that everyone would know that his armor belonged to the spirit, not to the flesh. He was destined to fight spiritually against the adversary, and he gave him spiritual armor beforehand, so that he might triumph through it. He was destined to wage a great struggle against injustice, without lowering his dignity before ranks higher than his own. He sent an angel to announce his conception and birth, and placed on his head the great crown of Nazirite consecration. He chose him as a commander from a fainthearted people, so that through his courage he might strengthen them in good hope. The people had grown weak in their trust in God, and through Samson he strengthened their heart in true reverence. He placed the power of his help on his head like a crown, and authorized him to judge his fellows without reproach. He called and appointed him to judge the people and contend with the nations, so that on every occasion he would beat down injustice and keep it from rising. The divine bidding sent him against the injustice of the people and the nations, and sent him as a mighty warrior to fight at the forefront of the battles. He first saw his own will directed against the nations, for he saw the falsehood of demonic teaching flourishing among them. He saw the teaching of demons triumphing among the uncircumcised nations, and he grew zealous and roused himself to wage a fierce struggle against them. The resolute soldier prepared himself for the struggle against the nations, and devised occasions for fighting on behalf of righteousness. He made it his purpose to fight for righteousness, and in all his actions he bent himself strongly against injustice. He gave himself to battle like a mighty warrior, for he wanted by every means to exalt the name of righteousness. His heart wisely devised cunning strategies, and under the guise of love he exposed and revealed falsehood. The wise man, skilled in warfare, put on the guise of love, and like a spy he went among the uncircumcised and probed their words. He betrothed himself to a woman from among those who hated the name of his God, so that through one woman he might humble the error associated with the name of the gods.

The hidden divine bidding strengthened his resolve to act wisely, and he said to his father, “Get me a wife from among the daughters of the uncircumcised.” His father and mother, it says, did not know that this was from God, so that he might exact vengeance from the Philistines for his fellow countrymen. Through a daughter of the nations he exacted his people’s vengeance from the nations, and skillfully bent his will toward his Lord’s purpose. He set out from his people to hurry and betroth himself to a daughter of foreigners, and his Lord placed a target for him on the road to test his strength. A lion cub met the speaking lion on the road, and he tore apart its tough body and flung it away like a young goat. He tested his strength against the lion’s strength, for he was a mighty warrior, and learned that he could confront the battle line of the uncircumcised nations. Without a sword and without a staff he killed the lion, and learned that he had no need of the help of weapons. He entered the home of the uncircumcised, became betrothed to a woman, and gave a pledge. Then he returned to his people, intending to fulfill his promises. The thought of the woman pressed upon him, but it was not really about a woman: his soul’s desire was to take action against the Philistines. He was very eager to fulfill his Lord’s command, and longed to avenge the disgrace of his people. The nimble man quickly called out to take a wife, and prepared gifts in which reproach and disgrace were concealed. The mighty man set out along the road to Timnah to make his journey, and turned aside to see whether the lion’s carcass was still there. He saw the destroyer of men lying ruined on the ground, with a swarm of bees nesting in its remains. He saw lowly flying creatures mocking that strength, and believed and was certain that he would likewise mock the Philistines. He saw honey flowing from a body full of harm, and gained hope that he would deliver his people from oppression. The chosen Nazirite stretched out his hand toward the unclean body, and took food full of life from the bitter one. The pure man ate unclean food and was not defiled. He also gave some to his parents to eat, but did not reveal where it came from. He wisely concealed the secret of his great strength, so that it would not be held in contempt when repeated in the mouths of [?].

He held a feast and invited and summoned the uncircumcised men of Philistia. At their banquet he composed a riddle about the killing of the lion. For he thought that by killing it he was killing them. That is why he composed the riddle about the lion and the food that came from it. He set a riddle full of understanding before ignorant men, and they could not explain the force of the meaning hidden in it. Samson said, “From the eater came food, and from the bitter one flowed sweetness, contrary to the usual order.” Those uncircumcised in heart were astonished and marveled at the Hebrew man: how wise he was, and how concealed was the question posed by his words! He left them in great amazement at the way he put his words together, and bound them in ignorance as though with a weapon. They harassed his wife so that she would learn it from him and teach them. Yet even when she had learned it and taught them, they could not overpower him. His betrothed wore him down to make him disclose the secret of his riddle to her, and his resolve gave way under the harassment of that daughter of pagans. She harassed him beyond measure with her distressing words, and he revealed and showed her the secret he had concealed from his parents. Out of distress he revealed and disclosed to her what was hidden in his heart. She in turn disclosed it to the deceitful men of her people. On the seventh day the guilty men defeated the mighty warrior, and before the meal the food hidden in his riddle was revealed. “What,” he said, “tastes much sweeter than honey? Or what is more bitter and harsh than a lion’s mouth?” The wise man saw that the schemers had overcome him through a woman. He grew zealous and fierce and armed himself for battle against them. He killed thirty men in revenge for the explanation of his riddle, took their clothes, and satisfied those fools. Through a woman and his riddle he blazed himself a path toward battle, so that he might advance successfully toward the victory promised by his Lord’s word. Through a woman and a riddle he provoked them to battle, and on every occasion he revealed the strength hidden within him. Through various pretexts he stirred up fierce battle against them and taught them that he was not fighting them casually. The hunter who feared the truth caught three hundred foxes.

With creatures that cannot speak he waged war against those who can. Through lowly foxes he humbled those full of pride, and they could not withstand the resolve with which he fought. His opponents clothed themselves in furious zeal over their losses and began seeking revenge for the disgrace he had brought upon them. They prepared for war against Israel, hoping to capture in battle Samson, who had humbled them. They thought they would exact vengeance for their blood from Abraham’s descendant, not knowing that they would be caught in the trap they had hidden. Foolish pride incited those dull-hearted men, and they prepared weapons to fight against Israel. The crafty foxes, whom lowly foxes had subdued, began threatening the kingdom represented by a lion. The ranks of the Philistines shouted aloud, “Either come out and fight, or hand over mighty Samson to us!” The feeble people heard the sound of gnats buzzing in their ears. They grew afraid, humbled themselves, and bent their shoulders to submit to slavery. They abandoned their trust in the name of the Creator who had exalted them, and surrendered their desire for those impure in soul to mock. They neglected to make an appeal worthy of the strength within them, and returned an answer full of the reproach of revilers. They pledged to hand the righteous man over to the uncircumcised, and the fools were not ashamed to condemn their deliverer without cause. “Do you not know,” the wavering men said to Samson, “that the Philistines rule over us at this time? “Why have you brought this trouble upon us with our enemies? Now they are devising ways to wipe us out with their wars. “Come down and appease the Philistines whom you have angered, and put an end to the war you have stirred up against our tribes.” “Swear to me by the Lord,” the righteous man said to his fellow countrymen, “that you will not strike me, and I will go down without hesitation.” The fools bound the leader of their people as though he were a criminal and handed him over to the uncircumcised in heart to mock him. The mighty man went down and stood among the ranks of warriors. He neither feared nor cowered, though his death lay plainly before him.

He went down courageously, bound, to his killers, and did not doubt the help that accompanied him. The endurance of Manoah’s son was full of great wonder: he did not falter before the killers who threatened him. His heart had put on faith like armor, and he was strengthened by good hope in his Lord’s promise. His hope rested on that Power which gave him strength. For this reason he went down, bound, to his killers. He took courage through the power of that sign upon his head, and he took greater pride in the hair of his Nazirite dedication than in armor. The uncircumcised saw that his body was bound, as they desired, and the fools thought that they were now about to end his life. The fools considered the man who lived in his God as good as dead, not knowing that they themselves were [?] the pit they had dug. At the moment when they thought they were now about to end his life, he suddenly rose and drove them out of life. They raised a sharpened sword above his head, but the strength of the help within him raised it over their own heads. They stood eagerly ready to mock him, but the awesome Name showed its power and put them to shame. The power of the Spirit stirred the mighty warrior’s soul, and he broke apart and cast the visible armor off his limbs. Scripture testifies to the power of the Spirit hidden within him: before its greatness, the chains were like threads. He snapped the hard iron like threads and threw it away, then stood and fought without a weapon, using a worthless bone. The hidden command made ready the shaft of a worthless bone, and with it he laid waste the warriors’ ranks as though with a sword. The man whose soul was holy held an unclean bone in his hand, and the armored men could not stand before his right hand [?]. The wicked saw a terrifying sight in the righteous man’s hand, and they fled and hid from the terror [?] of what they saw. The Hebrew held a bone like a sword, making it flash, while the ranks of the uncircumcised were thrown into panic. The sight of the bone was exceedingly terrifying—not the sight of a bone,

but of the Power that was revealing its own appearance through the bone’s appearance. Cruel death was dealt out through its hardness, and the blow it delivered was far sharper than a sword. The hardhearted were terrified by its hardness—or perhaps not by it, but by the one who held it. The bone and the hand holding it were exceedingly terrifying, not by their own nature, but through the Power that held them. A hidden Power held the hand, and the hand held the bone, and it laid waste those who were full of pride and dull of heart. It was far sharper than a two-edged sword, and whenever it struck, it grew sharper still for maiming bodies. Its edge alone came near the uncircumcised bodies, and they were swiftly scorched as though by fire. The Nazirite merely raised his hand against the ranks, and they fell before one body reached another. O bone, how extraordinarily victorious you were! I am not speaking to you, but to the hand that held you. O hand, how immeasurably strong you became! It was not you, the hand, but the command that spared your frailty. O man, how great was the strength of your bodily senses! It did not belong to your body, but to the power that strengthened your movements. O Samson, a name in which his God's name is hidden, how clearly you explained the power of your name through your deeds! Did your hand not grow weary, man holding the bone? Or did that bone not wear out in that battle? How mighty the bone was in your hand, and you through the bone! It did not break, nor did your hand grow weary from it. How did it withstand the onslaught of a thousand men? By what power did it subdue the strength of those who possessed might? The man killed a thousand men with you, insignificant bone! And this is the wonder: the man did not grow weary, and you were not destroyed. The deed accomplished with you was full of great wonder, and no one knows how to tell of its greatness. Samson, the skilled reaper, held it like a sickle and reaped the field of the Philistines in a single hour.

O reaper who reaped bodies with a sickle of bone! Its iron did not grow blunt among a thousand speaking sheaves. The swift man cast down a thousand sheaves in a single stoop, and he did not straighten himself until he had completed the count of a thousand. He began with one and finished with one the battle he fought, and not even a part of his limbs was injured. He remained entirely unharmed in body and soul. His strength did not waver, nor did his confidence slacken. Like an athlete, the athlete came up from the battle, and on his head lay a crown consisting of the count of a thousand slain. At the end of the battle, the mighty warrior grew thirsty and distressed, and he began asking for a drink to sustain his life for a time. “O Lord,” he said, “you have made me victorious through your powerful help. Give me a drink to match the victory you accomplished through my hands. “You gave me victory in the fierce battle against those thirsting for blood. Do not neglect me and let my victory perish at the hands of the uncircumcised. “Give me a drink, just as you also gave me victory, lest I die and fools revile your great name.” The good Master heard the plea of his righteous servant and gave him a drink from within the bone with which he had won the victory. With an insignificant bone, the Master gave his servant victory in battle, and from it he gave him a sweet drink to refresh himself. A sweet drink flowed from the bone, contrary to nature, and the righteous man marveled, for this was the power of the Creator, for whom everything is easy. The bone was unclean and also devoid of water, but the will of the one who rules over everything overcame both. Where did the water flow from within that dry thing? And who made what was wholly unclean into a fountain of life? The same command that made water flow from the flint stored within it moisture that had not been there. The same will that made the rock a spring of water also made the unclean bone a source of drink for the righteous man. The same angel who nourished the Israelites on their journey gave water from a silent thing to a speaking mouth. One of the Watchers moistened the womb of rock and bone and brought forth flowing infants from them, contrary to the usual order.

The spiritual being took some of the moist elements and coupled them with the elements of dryness. He subtly joined them to one another, carrying out what he was commanded, as was his custom. By the same method by which he carries water above the wind, he subtly placed it in the rock and the bone. This unusual event is difficult for us, but for the heavenly beings, in their ranks, it is very easy. They received great power from the Power that established everything, and activity in the heights and depths is easy for them. They accomplished this event, along with all the other things that happened; they accomplished it through the power of the Maker who empowered them. Through the Maker’s power, water flowed from the bone for Samson, and with his help Samson conquered and triumphed without a sword. Without a sword, the innocent man conquered those full of sins, and without doubt he received drink from the mouth of a bone. The pure man drank pure water from an unclean mouth, and by his drinking he showed that nothing is unclean. Indeed, nothing that came from the Creator is unclean, for he showed that even what was unclean to us is pure. Let everyone skilled in faith consider Samson’s drink and have no misgivings that anything in food or drink is unclean. The bone was unclean according to the commandment of the law [?], but it was entirely clean according to the divine will. The hidden will declared things clean and unclean according to its purposes. Who can judge the Lord who rules over everything? His loving will acted lovingly toward his servant, gave him victory in the contest, and gave him drink as he pleased. Wonderful was the contest that the Hebrew man waged on earth, and Satan and his forces were astonished at its wonder. Astonishment seized the ruler of the air, blinded by envy, at the battle that a human being fought through the Maker’s power. The hater [?] of humanity was struck, in his envy, by the arrows of his own thoughts when he saw Samson overcome the army he had assembled. He counted the slaughter carried out among the Philistines as his own, and regarded his servants’ defeat as his own disgrace. More than anywhere else, his name was glorified among the uncircumcised.

And when he saw that he had been put to shame among those deceived by his name, anger clothed him. Satan clothed himself in furious zeal against Samson and began devising cunning schemes to fight him. The crafty-minded one devised schemes against the righteous man when he saw that he could not fight him openly. He dug deep and hid snares of desire along his path, to catch in them the swift-footed Nazirite gazelle. The shameless one put on the weapons of his craft and began to creep in through women, as was his custom. He sent a woman like a spy to the blameless man and tested his strength through the weak rib through which he had tested Adam. With a woman's love he bound the righteous man as though with a weapon, and through her harassment she weakened his mighty strength. Samson, who loved reverence for truth, [?] a woman for himself, and through his love for her he loosened the bond between himself and his Lord. The son of Abraham entered into a loving relationship with a pagan woman, and through his intimacy with her he forgot the fellowship of his ancestors' household. A woman led the captor of nations away as a prisoner, and like a captive she yoked him beneath the yoke of her desires. With every kind of maneuver she wore down the heart of the sound-minded man, so that he would tell her what strength enabled him to triumph. Beyond all bounds she pressured the resolve of the discerning man, until he revealed to her the great mystery [?] of his Nazirite consecration. “I am a Nazirite,” he said, “and the great Name is hidden in my Nazirite consecration. If I remove the crown upon my head, I will be brought low. “My God gave me a crown of victory—the crown upon my head. If I shave my hair, the strength of his help will depart from me.” The foolish woman saw that he had weakened and revealed his whole heart to her. She acted treacherously and disclosed the secret of his abasement to her own people. She called him and put him to sleep on her lap like a little child, and began to plunder the treasure of strength hidden in his head. Like a simpleton, the wise man sank into the river of sleep, and he did not awaken or notice the plundering of the treasure of his Nazirite consecration. As though from a drink of strong wine, he became dazed and silent, and was given over entirely to sleep beyond all bounds. The woman full of wickedness cruelly shaved his head.

Along with his hair, the strength of his help was taken away from him. The cunning woman called and awakened him as though out of love. The man sunk in sleep stirred and saw that his crown had been taken from him. The uncircumcised seized the man pure in body and consecrated in soul, and cruelly blinded his eyes without pity. Those blind in mind made the enlightened man blind. They brought him into the millhouse and made him suffer like an accursed man. Contemptible foxes made the brave lion grind at the mill, and in darkness they silenced the voice of his might. Beyond all bounds they mocked and jeered at him and his Lord. When his Lord saw it, he took pity on his humiliation and struck them down. The worshipers of false gods held a great festival for the god of their delusion, and summoned Samson to mock him before one who was no god. The righteous man whom wickedness had blinded came among the uncircumcised, and the humble-minded man began to dance before those contemptible people. The shameless men demanded a dance from the chaste man at their banquets, and he danced in silence, sighing over his humiliation. The discerning man felt great anguish in his mind when he saw how humiliating was the enslavement of his dignity. He saw the worshipers of the flesh mocking him at the demons’ festival, and he called to his Lord to restore to him the strength he had lost. “Please, my God,” the righteous man said to his God, “hear me and answer me, and avenge for me the disgrace of my eyes. Have pity on my lowliness, overlook my folly, and forgive my sins. Do not hold against me the sin I committed concerning the secret of your gift.” With mournful cries the righteous man pleaded concerning his folly. His Lord heard him and gave him strength as before. The help that had accompanied him returned and settled in his senses, and he began to test its reliability by putting it to the trial. The mighty man grasped two pillars with his two hands and brought the house down upon its inhabitants, with himself in their midst. “Let me die,” he said, “with the Philistines, the uncircumcised in heart.” His words were fulfilled in deeds, just as he had said. The righteous man died a suffocating death with the wicked, and he was not buried as human custom requires. The mighty man died mightily among the weak, and his victory on the day of his death doubled the victory of his lifetime.

Those who died on the day of his death, it says, were far more numerous than those during his lifetime. He began and completed the sword’s purpose against the wicked. From the beginning his will was directed against the wicked, and although he sinned greatly, he did not desist and neglect his duty. He sinned by revealing the secret of his gift before a foolish woman, and he suffered and sighed bitterly over his folly. Let the righteous man’s folly become a rod for disciplining our souls, and through its disclosure let us scourge the wickedness hidden in our hearts. Let us look carefully at his diligence and the laxity of his soul, and let us not boast when we acquire virtues. The nature with which we are clothed is weak and full of passions. It shines briefly in [?], then fades again. We ought to guard our lives from harm with fear, and freely guard the treasure of our souls’ freedom.
On David and Saul [?]
55. On David and Saul. Again by the same author, his own work: the fifty-fifth discourse, composed by him on David and Saul.

My mind found splendid company in the conduct of the righteous, and eagerly sought to journey with it through the discourse of words. It saw that the path of the labors of their minds was straight, and prepared words to contribute material to their benefits. It saw that in their conduct they resembled the King’s purpose, and [?] words for the lyre of the mouth, to incline it toward the truth. The merchants of the word of truth traveled on the path of truth, and through trials they gathered spiritual wealth. [?] My thoughts journeyed amid the [?] wealth of their conduct, to see the beauty of their victories and whom they resembled. The sound of their endurance awakened my mind as if from sleep. I went out to see how human beings overcome sufferings. Love for them drew me like a child toward their labors, and I wished to paint an image of their beauty with the pigment of my words. I wished to meditate on the writings in the books of Kings, and I saw a tablet on which the history of kings was inscribed. I saw king after king depicted between the columns, and the imprint of each one's name distinguished him from his companion. The crowns upon their heads did not resemble one another, nor did the scepters they held agree with one another. For one, the tablet of his story ran with the blood of eyes [?]; another proclaimed the name of his authority like a burden. In the book of the Spirit, Saul was inscribed as something superfluous. Then the divine command read him correctly and erased his name. It was not through a mistake that the writer wrote his name. The one who inscribed it did so to teach through his name, so that no one would go astray. He placed him as a sign at the crossroads of the Spirit's tablets. This was so that people might see and not wander into the error of his way. On the page of the book he painted the image of the feeble king, to show through him how ugly the ugliness of injustice is. At the head of the column concerning the choosing of kings, he inscribed Saul, so that whoever reads might look carefully and then read. On the second tablet he wrote of the choosing of chaste David, and depicted before the spectators the victories of his soul's purity. The hidden command anointed both of them without making a mistake, and chose and rejected according to the testing of their conduct. He chose them while knowing their deeds before they took place, and showed his love, which overflows even toward the wicked if they are willing. Through Saul he showed how greatly he hates an evil disposition, and through the son of Jesse he revealed his will: that he loves the righteous. Saul's injustice caused him to be rejected and cast out of the kingdom, while David's love became for him a crown of leadership.

The command erased [?] Saul's name from the archives and wrote, in place of the unjust man, David, who practiced justice. The hidden command laid its hand upon his authority and sealed his rank of leadership with an oath. The God of all, who does not lie, swore and confirmed that David's throne would be established forever, without end. His offspring [?] would continue its course alongside the shining sun and moon, and would not be hindered from passing on the royal name. He said, “Once I have sworn by the holy name, and I will not lie: David and his descendants will reign as long as my enduring existence [?].” “I give him a kingdom in time as a pledge, and at the end of the ages I will confirm it through deeds.” “I will repay him with a good reward for his endurance: a kingdom in time and a kingdom on high that will not pass away.” “Because he did not become proud and despise my commandments like Saul, I will exalt him before the eyes of all who see, through the child descended from him.” “I do not give heaven and earth to be governed [?], and his scepter will rule over those above and those below.” “From the beginning I make him a sharer in the name of my being, and I appoint him heir and lord of everything I have created.” David received the promise of life at the beginning of his reign. He believed and affirmed things far away as though they were near [?]. Through visible things he saw hidden things that cannot be seen, and through earthly things he depicted the wonders of things to come [?]. In expectation of the reward of things to come [?], he endured hardships, and out of love for the Creator’s name he kept the commandments. He heard that God is the God of all and that he established everything [?]. He placed nothing alongside his lordship that did not acknowledge him. From the divine commandment he learned of God’s being, and in his thoughts he affirmed that God’s everlasting existence has no beginning. He meditated on the law of the Spirit night and day, and pondered its hidden things evening and morning. He was nourished like an infant on the milk of its words, and through their meanings he advanced toward perfection. It was always set before his mind like a mirror, and in it he saw the beautiful image of good things. With his outward senses he saw earthly things in it, and with his mind he contemplated things without end. Through his love he captured an image of the Being without composition [?], and although it was hidden, it was revealed to him through faith. Through faith he contemplated things that were not revealed, and they lay before him as though they had actually taken place. He pointed out the Creator’s power as though with a finger: “People, see the God of all through the things he has made.” Through silent things he taught rational beings: “You who have discernment, look at the silent course and give praise.” With the sweetness of his voice he stirred the crowds of listeners to offer praise to the Power that had empowered their very beings. He invited and called speaking and speechless beings to give thanks to the Hidden One, like debtors who had received life and owed thanksgiving.
