With the sound of thanksgiving he trained humanity in its infancy, and from [?] he led it upward to the heights. On the harp of words he composed melodies to offer praise, so that through the horns everyone might listen to the revelation of mysteries. With [?] he enticed them as though with bait, and then he cast the net of life over his listeners. With the Spirit’s snares he caught the wayward people and enclosed them within the strongholds of the word of life. He put bridles of love on the brutish person and disciplined the course of his impulses, turning them away from evil things. Like a charioteer, his voice rode upon every mouth, driving them along the smooth road of the Creator’s name [?]. His voice was beautiful as he proclaimed in everyone’s hearing: “Hear this, all you peoples, and listen to my words.” He longed to bind all the nations under the yoke of love, so that they would serve under the lordship of the one Creator. With the Spirit’s weapons he fought against error, tearing down the name of paganism and building up truth. He wore zeal for the one Creator like armor and fought against the gods that human beings had made. With the sound of his words he exposed the godless, saying that they possessed [?] but had no understanding of God. In every battle he prevailed, secretly and openly, and in the Creator’s name he was exalted above every god. In every land the power of his victory was exalted, and among all peoples the triumph of his labors was recounted. There was just one who mourned his victories: the hater of humanity, who took no pleasure in a human being’s triumph. He was clothed in sorrow at the splendid qualities of the chosen king, seeing that love for him triumphed and conquered everyone. The rebel clothed himself in furious jealousy against David and wanted to multiply cunning schemes against him, as he had against Job. There he kindled the fire of wrath among the righteous man’s possessions, so that [?] he might hear cries of blasphemy from the righteous man. Here he laid a snare for the lion who terrified the nations, so that, if he fell, he could raise his voice against the righteous. Everyone was secretly at war with the righteous man, and he buried countless snares deep, seeking a way to prevail. The Evil One devised an evil scheme against the son of Jesse and caught the handsome man in a trap, as he had Adam. He showed enticing grain to the eagle with swift wings, and it left its lofty height and came down to the ground to take the food. Desire took captive the king who took nations captive, and he went out like an exile and became enslaved to debasement. The tyrant imprisoned him in a dwelling of debasement, so that he would no longer [?] his forces with the sound of his victory. With a frail rib he shattered him and threw him down as with a weapon. He shut the door of denial in his face so that he could not escape. With the very chain he had laid on Adam, he bound the righteous man.

And, as with the fruit, he stirred his loins with the beauty of a face. With fruit he killed the king who first reigned on earth, and with enticements he cast David down into the pit of wickedness. Adam was lovely and David handsome; [?] they would sin. Through his cunning, the Evil One debased them, though they were cleverer than everyone else. He clothed the lovely kings in garments of wickedness and stained them with desire for food and desire for the body. He mixed deadly poison into food and bodily desire and made them drink the murky [?] of its bitterness. He mixed a foul cup with sin and gave it to David. He drank from it, and his mind went astray, though he was wiser than everyone else. He enticed him like a child and drew him toward pleasure. He laid a snare before his pupils and caught him through his eyes. The weak eye saw beauty that appealed to the bodily senses, and through flesh it ensnared the fleshly [?], its own companion. Flesh longed for flesh with fleshly desire, and, like someone hungry, he yearned to eat the fruit. The hunger of the eyes tormented chaste David, and he devised a way to satisfy the desire of his loins. The impulse within signaled to the eye outside: “Look and see how pleasant the food of flesh is.” Her eye was fixed on the other eye, never satisfied, and she delighted in looking again, to complete her gaze. Bodily desire captured the eye, as it had Eve, and it could not get enough of looking at the face, just as she had looked at the fruit. Eve marveled at the fruit, at how delightful it was; and David’s eye marveled at bodily sensations, at how desirable they were. The fruit, through being eaten, erased the hidden commandment from Eve; and the beauty of a face blinded David’s understanding. Nothing seemed more beautiful to Eve than that fruit; and before the son of Jesse no beauty was set that could compare with hers. One trap caught them both, David and her: David through a face, and her through [?], body and body. The cunning hawk saw a bird that desired food. It lay in ambush on the ground and suddenly caught her through an ugly glance. The foolish dove swooped down to take food into her belly, and the enemy stretched out the birdlime of wickedness and plucked her wings. The son of Jesse went up to gaze at the beauty of the land, and the rebel placed a wanton sight before his eyes. He released his inclination from the restraint of love for truth, and bound his mind to the face of a rib, soft in body. As he looked, he did not consider whom he was looking at, nor did he remember that utterance: “Do not covet.” That harp which sang truth forgot its wisdom and began to pluck the strings of the body, heavy with sensations. The flute of the Spirit, sweet in melody, changed its voice, and fleshly sounds, full of sorrow, rose up. The hater of wickedness desired and coveted what was not his, and tore down the fence that the law had set before the covetous. David’s guest lodged with David without his knowing. He spared what was his own, wronged another, and offered it to another.

He sent and brought the ewe that the righteous king had raised, and made her a sacrifice to the deceitful wickedness that had lodged with him. David ate the food of wickedness with the deceiver, and entertained himself with the adversary over a filthy drink. He who caught nations in the Spirit’s unbreakable snare—his eyes caught him in the slack snares of his own household. He who put the bridles of chastity into the mouths of the dissolute debased himself through an ugly gaze of fleshly desire. He who sealed the tablet of fellowship with the imprints of his words erased, by his gaze, the handwriting of the Spirit’s finger. He who bound people not to wrong their fellows moved the boundary that the Creator had set in human nature. He who rebuked the covetous so that they would not sigh for what belonged to others spurred his inclination to violate his companions’ wives [?]. The clear eye through which people used to see the Hidden One suddenly grew dark, and [?] darkness over those who saw. The sound of the trumpet that proclaimed the name of the Divine Being ceased its peals, and people no longer listened to [?] life. He who explained the [?] of hidden things to the ignorant—his understanding fell silent, and he did not discern his own conduct. The beautiful radiance that used to show the path of righteousness flickered and went out, and its course toward righteousness ceased. The salt that gave a pleasant taste to tasteless things became tasteless itself, like [?] that had not been crushed. The pen of the Spirit, which the skilled scribe had moistened, surrendered itself into the hand of his inclination to write falsehood. He who awakened spiritual beings with the sound of his songs to sing praise fell asleep in sin, and his senses sank into the sleep of wickedness. He who invited the mute to give thanks to the God of all silenced his lyre, and wickedness severed the strings that stirred it. He who fought fiercely in battles, defeated kings, and plundered nations was defeated by a rib, weak in strength and lowly in body. The athlete who had triumphed with the crown of his struggles was overcome by his adversary, who trampled his valor into the ground. He who stood in the ranks with spiritual and bodily beings was seized by wickedness, bound, and thrown aside like someone contemptible. The pure mind that breathed forth divine revelations defiled itself with foul vomit that harmed his companion. The lion cub who killed a lion and tore apart a wolf trembled before a beast whose teeth were blunted and whose fang was lowly. The lion and the wolf had not shaken his confidence, but a bear at peace suddenly growled, and he trembled before her. The son of Jesse lusted, and his inclination became filled with the desire of his flesh. He began to dwell on shameful things that did not befit him. He saw that his hidden offense had been exposed by an obvious pregnancy, and he began devising cunning schemes that would bring about destruction. He abandoned the contemplation of spiritual things in which he had been occupied and occupied himself with reading the book of the murderer. The evil one wrote a deceitful [?] book upon his thoughts, and he began, like an uneducated man, to sound out things that did not befit him. He practiced the crooked script of the great deceiver, seeking to devise [?] how to shed blood.

He [?] and became proficient in the writings of the master of falsehood, and he too learned to wield the pen wickedly. With deceit he sent to a member of his household, like a spy, and summoned him into his presence under the appearance of affection, while deceiving him. Uriah saw the deceit concealed beneath the words, and he too concealed the distress of his heart beneath the appearance of his words. He heard the king command him to go and enjoy himself at home, but he scorned comforts [?] under the appearance of affection for his master. “No,” he said, “by your life, good king and [?] king, I will not change my great love for you with time.” The son of Jesse saw that [?] had overcome him, and he conspired secretly with his thoughts to write wickedness. His limbs grasped the [?] that the evil adversary had fashioned, and he began tracing innocent blood upon the paper. The pen of the Spirit held a pen of death in his hand. He reversed the order and began writing from [?] to aleph. When the Holy Spirit wrote through him, his script was upright; but once the evil one’s finger grasped him, it threw his order into confusion. He impressed deadly poison into a letter and gave it to Uriah, so that he would go and drink it far from the king, without the king being exposed. The innocent man took the sword that the deceitful adversary had forged, and went and carried it to the executioner to cut off his own head. O messenger who carries death on his shoulders and bears it like a gift to prolong his life! He went along proudly with the king’s seal placed in his hands, not knowing that death lay concealed inside the seal. Uriah set out from the king’s presence with his death beside him. He walked along with his killer, happy and cheerful. He arrived at the camp of his lord’s servants, entered, and presented himself before the commander who led his people. He greeted him and gave him the king’s sealed message, in which death was depicted. He rejoiced that he had been found worthy to convey the king’s word. The poor man thought he would receive gifts for his service as a messenger. He did not know that he was surrendering his life like a condemned man. The commander opened the king’s seal that had been placed in his hands. He was greatly astonished that a righteous man had strayed from the path. He read the letter and saw the treachery hidden within it. He sealed it again and concealed the treachery within his thoughts. He saw death raging within the bounds of the writing. His heart understood that the king had pronounced a sentence against him and sent him away. David confined him inside a cage of writing and sent him to Joab: “Look, and release him cunningly.” “Inspect the people,” he said, “and arrange the ranks of the troops. Under the guise of [?], conceal the treachery so that it will not be discovered. Place Uriah at the head of the army like a victorious warrior, and turn away from helping him, so that he will be thrown into confusion and die.” Joab fulfilled the king’s wish as he had been commanded. Uriah died, the innocent man perished, and injustice triumphed.

The commander wrote and informed David of everything that had happened: “Your servant is now dead. Fulfill your heart’s desire.” The son of Jesse heard that Uriah was dead and was relieved of his anxiety. He did not know that Uriah’s death would increase the anxiety in his own life. The righteous king accomplished his desire through adultery and murder. He sent for his companion’s wife and took her as though he were acting justly. The wise man thought that he had acted wisely in what he had done. He did not know that it was foolishness before the One who knows everything. The king thought to himself: “Who can uncover the king’s secrets? And who [?] the head that is set above the body?” His thoughts wove cunning schemes like a garment, and he concealed his wrongdoing from those who saw and from the One who sees everything. Who concealed from his mind the image of the Hidden One—that vision which had been secretly depicted before his memory? Who silenced the sound of the trumpet of his prophecy—the man who said that the Hidden One is present in the heights and the depths? Who cut the strings of the harp of the Spirit and silenced the singing of its sweet melodies? Who hindered him as he ran so well along his path, so that he stopped and sat idle, abandoning his spiritual labors? Who caught the swift gazelle in the snares of wrongdoing and gave it as food to the insatiable desire of the flesh? Who confined the fearsome lion inside a cage, so that contemptible foxes jeered and laughed at his humiliation? Who put a bridle of silence on him amid the thunder of voices, when he had been [?] glory to the Hidden One with the spiritual beings? Who confounded the wisest of all through terrors, so that he became a child, though he gave flavor to the tasteless? Who broke the arms of the mighty warrior, so that he fell short of the goal toward which he had aimed with the movements of his soul? Who blinded the clear eye of his faith and darkened his mind, preventing it from seeing the Hidden One through its movements? Who put to death the body and soul of the man who was wholly steadfast, so that he became feeble through the blows his inclination inflicted on him? David had fallen into hateful wrongdoing as into an illness, and the king was ashamed to expose his [?] before onlookers. The physician on high saw a member of his household lying in wrongdoing, and sent his companion, the prophet, to him to heal his pain. He sent him a spiritual physician to heal [?] the spirit, to drive out wrongdoing and bring the spirit back to the temple of his soul. With the sound of the harp of prophecy, he wished to awaken the sleeper who had sunk beneath the weight of wrongdoing as though into sleep. The exalted [?] gave spiritual medicine to the spiritual physician, [?] to go and heal the body that wrongdoing had ravaged [?]. Nathan came to the son of Jesse as he had been commanded. He reached out his hand, examined the painful spot, and saw that it was severe. He saw that it was not fitting to approach him with a harsh incision, lest suffering reach his soul and drive it mad. He wished to mix a gentle medicine through parables, so that the thick blood of wrongdoing might be softened by spiritual medicine.

Nathan began combining words like medicinal ingredients, while David was sunk as though in sleep and did not understand. “There were two men,” he said, “living together in one town, one rich and the other poor—a king and his servant. “The rich man owned many sheep and cattle, while the poor man owned just one ewe. “A guest came to that rich man, who owned much, and he slaughtered the poor man’s ewe before him. “Judge justly, according to your discerning judgment. Condemn wrongdoing and vindicate truth, as you are accustomed to do. “See that you show no partiality in the case [?] before you, for I have brought it to you relying on the promise of your just judgment. “A hidden command sent me to you by a sign, to learn from you how wrongdoing is undone and truth is vindicated.” The son of Jesse heard of the injustice people had committed in the land. He became indignant and furious with the oppressor who had wronged his neighbor. Without knowing it, he passed a just judgment against himself: “[?] the Lord! The man who did this deserves death.” He pronounced a just sentence against himself according to the law, and sealed [?] his tablet with the living name, the name of the Creator. He decreed the punishment of a harsh death against the oppressor and put his hand to the sentence ending his own life. What will you do now, son of Jesse, after your words? Look, you have been condemned by the sentence your own mouth pronounced. Look, you have decreed death in your writings and deposited them in the archives; you have signed an accusation of wrongdoing, declaring that you deserve death. The prophet of the Spirit saw that the king had condemned himself by his own words, yet his heart was dulled, and he did not realize that he was judging himself. Nathan raised his voice and spoke openly: “You are the man who did this, O king and prophet! You are the one who seized what was not yours, although you had plenty; you are the one who shed innocent blood through your schemes. You have beautiful wives who wear crowns, yet your loins were not satisfied until you seized your neighbor’s wife. The desire of the flesh took you captive, David, beyond all proper bounds. Your eye coveted, your will coveted, and your inclination killed. Why did you forget that utterance in the Scriptures: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,’ lest you be exposed? Why did you erase from your mind that saying: ‘Whoever sheds blood, his blood shall be shed in return for the blood he shed’? Why did you hide your transgression from the one who knows everything, and not remember what you yourself proclaimed—that he examines the heart? Did you not say that he is everywhere, in the heights and in the depths, and that the work of his hands cannot hide from its Maker? Where is your voice that used to proclaim in people’s ears: ‘Blessed is the one who has not joined with evildoers’? Was it not I who chose you as [?] and rejected the wicked man? Why did you not remain faithful to the calling for which you were anointed? You sinned and hid from justice like a fugitive, not knowing that it was following close behind your wrongdoing. You felt shame before people, but felt no shame before my name, which is [?] above all.

You covered your wrongdoing with a double garment of unjustly shed blood. Because you hid like a fugitive from correction, look, I am revealing the shame of your wrongdoing before everyone’s eyes. Because you shamelessly acted like a fool with your neighbor’s wife, look, I am handing over the wives of your bed to dishonor. Because you killed and shed the innocent blood of someone who had done you no wrong, the sword of death shall never again depart from your children. Because you brought truth low and raised high the horn of shamelessness, from now on your offspring shall not raise their heads before their persecutors.” The son of Jesse saw that the divine command had caught him—the command to which everything is revealed. It rebuked his wrongdoing and exposed his sin against his will. He saw justice burning fiercely against him, and lowered his voice like a debtor who had incurred a debt and been made to give a pledge. He saw the scheme he had devised in his thoughts exposed. [?] He condemned himself for having sinned unjustly and hidden himself. In a loud voice he accused himself of wrongdoing before the one who knows everything: “I am the one who coveted and [?], killed and concealed my transgression. I am the one to whom the guest of wickedness came, pressing upon my mind; he goaded me and dragged me toward the pleasures of shamelessness. I am the one who [?] to hold to a lawful spouse, and stained my bed with unlawful corruption. I am the one who hid snares to catch the innocent-hearted, and I am the one who shed innocent blood that had done me no wrong. The evil [?] hid a snare for me in the outward senses, and iniquity caught me in the trap of the face of the beautiful [?] rib. Iniquity blinded me to the understanding that comes from discernment, and I did not notice that I was walking along a false path. Now I am in debt and cannot repay the loan, and ten thousand labors do not match my guilt. The waters of the great sea are too little to wash me, and my own iniquity cannot be atoned for by earthly things. My guilt is great, and the sin I have committed cannot be measured. The sea is too small to wash away the filth of my own iniquity. The divine Will saw him—he who had seen him before he sinned—for it was he who scourged him like a judge scourging someone condemned to death. He saw that he was humbled and that his heart had lost its confidence, and he gave him a hand, lest he give up hope of living. He gave a sign to the physician who had come to heal his pain, to apply soothing words as medicine to his wounds: “Speak gently with him through the sound of your words, and let the good news of life freely bestowed fall into his ears. Make it known and tell him: ‘There is medicine that heals iniquity, if you pay its price with repentance and the sufferings of the soul.’” The Spirit spoke with the son of Jesse through Nathan as through a lyre: “Look, mercy has persuaded the Hidden One to be reconciled to you. Look, it has come to me in a mystery that your iniquity is forgiven, and you will not die for your guilt, as you supposed. Look, the command has restrained the executioner of the law, so that he should sheathe his sword because of divine mercy. A dreadful death had been prepared for you by the law, but he showed you favor, lest the enemy boast over your death. It was he who caught you through his enticements, to rejoice at your [?].

And if you die, his arrogance against the righteous will increase. ‘I will give his arrogance no room to grow, so that he does not become accustomed to shedding blood on the pretext of iniquity. Through you I am opening a new path to repentance, so that the Evil One may be put to shame when [?] are shown mercy through grace. In you I am painting a beautiful image of the name of grace, which will become an advocate for sinners at the end of time. Through you I proclaim good hope to the hopeless: mercy is greater than human iniquity, and they are given life freely. I know the evil inclination of human nature, which is far too weak to stand firm against temptations. In you I place the leaven of life that gives life to humanity, and from your line I raise up fruit that wipes away iniquity. On this condition I have wiped away your guilt with the medicine of mercy: that I might open a path before him who comes to forgive iniquity. From you will shine forth the one who erases the debtors’ bond, and look, I have revealed the mystery of his coming through his father’s iniquity. By the law of his words he abolishes the decrees of vengeance, and he transcribes and writes compassion and mercy within his books. With his blood he writes a charter of freedom for his fellow human beings, and he erases the covenant of humanity’s slavery.’” For this reason I did not give death [?] to kill you because of the iniquity that [?] servants. Because of iniquity, mortals became slaves to death. See, I am tearing up the record of your debts by delivering your life. See, son of Jesse, how much I have loved you and shown you favor. I set aside my law so that you would not become a slave to death. Yet I did not annul my law or its claim. I gave mercy as a bribe on your behalf and appeased it for you. Nor has justice forgotten what it remembers. The record of your iniquity is inscribed in its book, together with all who have sinned. Here I erased the record of your offense from the law, not from that hidden book inscribed in my knowledge. See, your iniquity is forgiven for the duration of this life, according to the law. Go, prepare sacrifices of love for yourself for the life beyond. See, I have shown you the path of compassion that mercy has opened. Travel it with diligence, and teach others to walk with you. See, I have given you a helping hand of hope so that you may return to life. Support the lost and encourage them with the message of forgiveness. See, I have delivered you from the law that threatened you. Deliver the oppressed from the oppressor; show grace and have compassion. The sinner, who was dead in his sin, heard the voice of forgiveness. He sprang from death as though from sleep and returned to life. He saw that he had advocates at the judgment to plead his case concerning his offense, and he began to beg to return to his former position of leadership. He was afraid that the document of his forgiveness had not yet been sealed, and he implored the divine command to sign it on his behalf. He turned to composing sweet melodies on the strings of his harp,

so that perhaps he might regain confidence before his Lord. He remained afraid, even though he had received forgiveness for his iniquity, and he did not stop gathering advocates on his behalf. It was clear to him that, although he had received release from his offense, he was not yet worthy to cry out and sing praises in the Spirit. He also begged for this with the sound of sighing: that [?] might play upon the harp of his soul as before. The Creator saw him longing to speak through his [?], and restored to him the power to reveal things to come. He received the gift that had rested upon him before his offense, and he began to sing sweet melodies in the Spirit. How long will you forget me, Lord, as though I were an evildoer? How long will you turn your face away from a member of your household? How long will you put sorrow among my thoughts, while I see the contempt of the fools who mock me? My God, my God, why have you abandoned me to my persecutors? My help has gone far away because of the hateful speech my lips uttered. For I know that iniquity has taken my victory from my head, and because of this the enemy pursues my life without compassion. It is not hidden from me that my afflictions are because of my offense. I am certain that my sins have stirred up [?] against me. It is not that the help that accompanied me has diminished or grown less. It is I who have fallen short of readiness for the love of truth. I acknowledge that I have sinned and that I am being punished because of my offense. It is not about my wanderings that I plead, but about my iniquity. This alone I beg of the divine command that punishes me: that my correction may not be harsh, but compassionate. Do not, Lord, rebuke me severely in anger, and do not show me a face of wrath without reconciliation. Discipline me with gentle lashes, as befits your kindness, lest the pain of my correction give rise to hateful grumbling. The righteous man carried great sorrow in his mind, even though he had heard that voice saying, “Your wrongdoing is forgiven.” O righteous man, to whom the divine will handed the record of his debts, and who returned and placed it under judgment like a guilty man! O athlete who lost in the contest and whom the divine will upheld, yet who would not put on the crown of forgiveness without victory! O ever-watchful man, who sank briefly into the sleep of wrongdoing, yet did not weigh the labors of his praises against his wrongdoing! Come, sinners, see the sinner who sinned and found relief, and knock, as he did, at the door of mercy belonging to the righteous divine will. Come, righteous people, see the righteous man who fell into sin, and guard the treasures of your minds against the thief. Come, discerning people, see the seer who looked and became blind, and close the eyes of your thoughts to hateful things. If the seer of hidden things became distracted in his looking, who would not lay a modest covering over his eyes? If the holy man defiled himself by looking at a face, who would not restrain his wandering eyes from stumbling blocks? If a rib with a frail body overthrew the mighty man,

who would not arm the impulses of his soul against the serpent? Let David be like a mirror before those who look, and let the ranks of the righteous and the sinners look into him. Let no righteous person boast [?] as though he already reigned, and let no sinner give up as though he were already lost. Let the righteous man guard his soul’s treasures against pride, and let the sinner also bind up his wound with repentance. Let everyone direct his impulses and senses toward the goal of truth, so that we may be worthy [?] to receive the imperishable crown of victory.
On Solomon, His Election, and His Judgment
56. On Solomon. By the same author. The fifty-sixth homily, which he composed on Solomon, his election, and his judgment.

King David received the authority of an everlasting kingdom and gave it to his son, so that the promise expressed in his words would not prove false. The son of Jesse saw that the promise lay hidden in his line, and he warned his son not to grow careless and lose his rank. He heard that the scepter of his rule extended forever, and, looking ahead to the future, he gave his crown to his son. While still alive, he gave him the crown that the King over all had given him, because he saw that the Evil One was preparing to seize his exalted rank. He sealed his crown with the seal of oil, lest it be transferred and the Evil One see it and rejoice in mocking his Lord’s promise. The prophet-king sealed his crown with holy oil, so that the cunning schemes of deceitful people would not harm him. The righteous man knew that his son would grapple with the Evil One, and he anointed him beforehand so that the Evil One’s hand would slip off him. He gave Solomon the crown and the rank of ruler, so that his name might be fulfilled in deeds that brought peace to people. Great peace lay hidden in the name proclaimed for him, and David revealed it through the crown and rank he entrusted to his hands. Revelation called his first name “Beloved of God,” and his other name “Lover of peace among people.” These names were given to him prophetically, one by Nathan and one by David, the distinguished prophets. Nathan [?] called him Jedidiah: “The Lord loves him.” David named him Solomon: “Peace that brings people peace.” In accordance with the Law, they gave these names to the keeper of the Law, so that he would first love the God of all, and then his servants. His names are full of love for truth and love for peace, and the son of Jesse sought [?] to perfect his son in both. The wise man acted wisely at the end of his life: he made his son king and taught him the power hidden in his name. The righteous king handed over his crown and rank to his son, so that the promise of his words would continue with his descendants. The faithful man loved his Lord’s promise more than anything, and his Lord in turn repaid him with a love greater than his own. Through deeds he confirmed his words to the member of his household, honoring his son with true wisdom like his father’s [?]. The wise son resembled his father at the beginning of his reign. Like the one who fathered him, he pursued justice and humbled wickedness.

He armed himself courageously against wickedness and went down like an athlete into the contest of righteousness. The young boy took hold of the scepter of authority and raised his hand to scourge tyrannical wickedness. He stretched a harsh snare for the wicked among his people, and the wicked among the nations feared his severity. The wicked were astonished at the severity of his blows, and the righteous were astonished at how closely the speech of his mouth resembled that of his father David. From his mouth they heard the true wisdom that had been in his father. Good and bad alike feared him and obeyed his commands. The decree that chose him cast dread into their minds. Though unwilling, they accepted his election and honored his rank. That same decree strengthened his impulses with the power of wisdom and adorned his mind with a treasury of sayings about hidden things. He opened his mind like a treasury among a needy people and enriched them with discernment in judging between good and evil. The people needed the discernment of his judgment, and he drove the darkness of partiality out from among the people. The decree that chose him first tested him in a case involving death. When it saw that he was pure, it displayed his beauty before the eyes of those watching. Through contemptible prostitutes it tested his truthfulness, and through deeds it explained his name: he was a lover of peace. Two foolish women lived together [?], though they were not alike. They conceived and bore [?] infants alike through lustful intercourse. The women who were not alike conceived alike at the same time, and they reached the appointed course of childbirth established in nature. Their unlikeness uncovered the concealment of their deeds and brought them into the testing furnace of righteous judgment. The contemptible women lay down carelessly, as they were accustomed to do. The weight of sleep held them fast, and they neither stirred nor noticed. One slept and carelessly killed her son; the other was sunk in sleep and did not wake at her infant’s distress. The woman full of wickedness slept and killed, then rose and stole; the woman full of compassion lay down and was quiet, then rose and was astonished. Sleep overcame the lazy woman beyond all measure, and she did not wake at the sound of her baby struggling. The weight of her wickedness fell upon her infant and silenced his life; and when she woke, her wickedness did not wake. Only her body stirred from its heavy sleep, while her soul sank beneath the immeasurable weight of wickedness. The cruel, wicked woman wanted to make use of her son's death; in place of her infant, she conceived and gave birth to a double wickedness. The foolish woman saw that she had become [?] through her negligence; she conceived deceit and gave birth to wickedness to remedy her disgrace. She saw that she had been deprived of raising her fruit endowed with speech, and she wove a garment of theft to cover herself. Like a raider, she suddenly fell upon her companion, snatched the living infant from her, and put down [?]. The woman full of wickedness wanted to exchange one infant for another; wickedly she took the living one and put down the dead one.

The shameless woman took the living one and put down the dead one; as she schemed to remedy her disgrace, her shame increased. She wanted to adorn the ugliness of her soul with a living infant, and with her dead son she wanted to disgrace the beauty of compassion. She denied her own child [?], saying that he was not hers; and the one who was not hers she called her own, though he was not. Her lap embraced the child who was not hers until morning, and she did not know that the light was coming to expose her. Morning woke the loose women, and they rose to care for children who were not theirs as though they were their own. The theft had overturned the order of motherhood: although the children were theirs, they were not truly theirs. Both women were falsely carrying children who were not theirs, until morning exposed the falsehood. Morning revealed the falsehood in the infants' faces, and through their features it exposed and uncovered the deceit. The mother of the living infant looked at the infant's face and saw that the dead child lying in her lap was not hers. Astonishment seized her at these lawless deeds: her infant had been stolen, and another infant lay in her bed. The corrupt woman acted lawlessly against her companion, and like a robber she stole the living infant from her. The shameless woman's mind put on the armor of insolence, and she began denying that the dead infant was hers. As though entering a contest, the two fell into suffering and insolence, and they fought over the right to the living infant. The living child's mother fought with the [?] of love, and the dead child's mother with the deceitful weapon of denial. Compassion compelled the living child's mother to demand her own, while insolence incited the shameless woman to seize what she had no right to. The foolish women waged a great battle over their infants, and their quarrel did not subside until the king and the people heard. The son of David heard the news of the killing that reached his ears. He became zealous and resolute, determined to explain his name through his deeds. The command of the Ruler of all had chosen him to bring peace to people, and he too began to bring people peace in keeping with his name. He wanted to demonstrate through deeds the peace signified by his name, so he summoned and called the tribes of the people to hear his judgment. All the tribes gathered to listen to an unprecedented judgment, so that they might see the power in the son of David while he was still young. The Power that had placed the strength of wisdom in him gathered them, so that through visible things they might see the power of hidden things. Gathering upon gathering, people of every rank stood to listen to him, waiting for him to open the gate of his mind. Like hungry people, young and old longed to hear a word from the mouth of the youth who had suddenly become king. In the [?] of longing, people of every age stood at the time of judgment, waiting for the king’s heart to give birth to the judgment concerning the infant. The king himself was also gripped by the labor pains of truth, eager to reveal the infant’s hidden identity before those watching.

His mind, which gave birth to proverbs, stood like a woman in labor. It suffered birth pains to bring forth a word that was not premature. He gave orders to a servant, and the foolish women entered and stood in court. They began to plead, one out of love and the other shamelessly. The mother of the living child told the story gently, while the mother of the dead child struck her forehead with her fist. The woman who loved her infant pleaded sorrowfully for her infant, while the woman who had killed her son cried out wickedly, without concealment. The son of David marveled at the shameless woman and how bold she was. He looked and considered how to quiet her agitation. He saw that she was bold, with the hard forehead of obstinacy, and that without witnesses her falsehood could not be checked. He saw that if he said the dead infant was hers, she would contradict him, king though he was, since it was not his. He considered that if he ordered them to give the infant to the prostitute, the people would think that he had acted [?] out of favoritism in the [?]. He saw that if he settled the women’s dispute without a test, the wisdom of truth dwelling within him would not be revealed. He wisely examined the case brought before him, and through a test he investigated it and exposed it before the eyes of those watching. As a test, the wise man, the son of wise men, ordered a sword to be brought to settle the dispute between the two women. He would bring the wayward women into the furnace of the sword and see which was the mother of the living child and which the mother of the dead child. “Let the sword be a clear witness concerning the infant whose identity is hidden, and let it disclose to us whose the living infant is. “Let it reveal to us the secrets of the deceitful impulse and tell us how one infant was exchanged for another.” The Hebrews stood in great astonishment at the king’s command. They marveled at this unprecedented judgment, so unlike customary practice. His hearers stood in doubt because he had asked for a sword. They wondered whether his judgment was sound or not. The dull-hearted thought the words he spoke were a joke, but lovers of truth reflected that truth lay hidden in the command. The son of David saw the disagreement in their thoughts and called for a sword to test them, together with the [?] prostitutes. He brought them into the testing furnace like [?], and purged from them the hateful alloy of discord. The sword was brought, and the executioner stood in the courtroom. The king commanded that the living infant be cut in two. “Cut the living infant in two,” the son of David commanded, “and give his limbs, half to one woman and half to the other.” “We are fighting over his life,” the shameless women cried. “Let his life perish, and then we will be at peace, free from the struggle.” They were embroiled in a struggle over which would win possession of his life; together they received from him an equal [?] that would end the struggle. The mother of the living child saw the king’s terrifying command and thought that perhaps he truly intended to kill her son. She saw that the executioner had raised the sharpened sword, and her compassion rushed forward and seized his hand to keep him from killing. Nature stirred her to assert the claim of the love implanted in nature,

and taught her to hold back the terrifying death commanded by the king. “No, son of David! Your judgment is not just,” she cried in the courtroom. “You have not acted justly in commanding that the living infant die. “Investigate thoroughly, righteous king, and only then put someone to death. Do not rush to shed blood without an examination. “Look, righteous son, at your righteous father, and be like him. Honor the truth that is [?] in your name, as your father did. “See that you do not undo the just boundary your father established, and do not learn to wrong people by showing favoritism. “Do not give injustice room to grow when it sees you walking in the path of deceit. “Do not destroy the living infant when he is innocent, and do not stain yourself with innocent blood, free from guilt. “Give him whole to the shameless woman, and let him be hers. Do not divide him into useless portions. “I cannot watch him die as he is cut apart. If I must see it, death is far better for me than life.” Oh, how zealous nature was, asserting the claim of its love! It did not weaken when its enemy attacked. Oh, how heroically it fought against the sword! It did not allow the ranks of its ardor to be broken. Oh, how fiercely it fought out of love! It did not falter or bow before the king’s command and power. Oh, the compassionate prostitute! How clearly her compassion was revealed when she gave the infant to the shameless woman, if only he might live! Oh, the foolish, scheming woman! How merciless she was, asking that the living infant die so that she would not be exposed! Oh, how unyieldingly she possessed a heart of stone! She did not soften when the sword faced the child. Oh, how the shameless woman cried out before the son of David: “Let him be neither mine nor yours! Let him die [?], as decreed.” Solomon, the peacemaker who brought people peace, marveled at her shamelessness. From her very shamelessness he learned of the deceit hidden in her heart. The son of David marveled at the love and compassion of the child’s mother. From her anguish he discerned and understood that she was his mother. “She is his mother, and her love testifies that he belongs to her. Give him to her alive, so that she may rejoice in his life, just as she asked.” The prostitute won her case, and the king made her infant a crown for her. The shameless woman’s insolence was put to shame, and she went away empty-handed. The onlookers wove a crown of praises for the just king, who wisely acquitted the one rightly and condemned the other rightly. In a hidden [hidden] case, the righteousness of his insight was revealed. The people testified that his judgment was true and his examination just. Through this judgment they learned that he had the power to administer justice. They feared him and honored his position as ruler. As in a [?], he tested himself by examining the women, and showed his people the beauty of his soul’s purity. The Creator too, who saw that he had emerged pure from the test [?], adorned him with a vision and spoke with him about the power of his wisdom. In a vision of the night he spoke with him, whose mind was awake:

And he commanded him to ask for zeal for truth in righteous judgment. “Ask,” he said to him, as though he did not know what he wanted, “and I will fulfill your soul’s request in deeds.” “Give me a discerning heart and understanding,” answered the son of David, “so that I may seek out truth and expose falsehood without contempt.” The son of David asked the Creator for righteous judgment. The Creator filled him with understanding and confirmed his words. First he gave him wisdom of heart to hear cases, and then he added worldly riches and abundance. He adorned his position as ruler with two kinds of riches: wisdom of soul and the splendid adornment of material things. The son of David grew rich in spiritual and material things. In spirit and in body he became beautiful and splendidly adorned. In body and soul he pleased God and human beings. He built and adorned a holy temple [?] for the worship [?] of his Lord. He built a house for the one who fills heaven and earth. Although he does not dwell in things made by human hands, he dwelt in it out of love. Through visible things he showed his love toward the member of his household: although he is everywhere, he chose for himself a dwelling in a temporary house. He revealed the greatness of his love for the great David through David’s son, and fulfilled in deed the promise of his words, just as he had promised. He promised an everlasting kingdom to the son of Jesse. He made his son king and gave him riches and wisdom of heart. All the nations marveled at his great wealth and the wisdom of his soul. News of his administration of justice spread throughout the regions of the earth. News of his administration of justice reached every land, and among all the nations the [?] of his judgments were recounted. The kings of the nations longed and yearned to hear his judgments. They sent gifts to persuade him to let them see his face. The wonder of his name terrified those who possessed great wealth, and they trembled and were bewildered by the greatness hidden in his name. The name hidden within him cast fear upon those who possessed power, and against their will they bent their necks beneath the yoke of his name. The Egyptians were afraid, the Cushites were astonished, and the Indians were amazed. They carried and brought splendid gifts to present to him. Those far away were eager; outsiders gathered, and those of his own household crowded together to hear from him the wisdom of truth that had been given to him. Truth was openly [?] at the gate of his house, and [?] the Creator’s name was praised [?] during his rule. The God of all was praised by every mouth, and those who were not gods were scorned by every tongue. Through the gifts of kings, the King over all was honored, and the idolatry of demon worship was despised. “Blessed is God, who dwells among his people!” all the nations cried out. And the rebel trembled because the sound of his gods’ names had ceased. All the nations paid their debt of praise through the son of David, and anguish seized him because people offered praise through a human being. The Creator’s name was glorified through a human being, and envy set him aflame: why should a creature of dust be exalted? The envious one clothed himself in great mourning at the honor given to his Lord.

And he began devising cunning schemes to bring his name into contempt. The deceiver’s heart prepared the weapons of deceit to wage war against the Creator through a human being. The rebel mustered all the weapons of his bitterness to raise a rebellion against the righteousness of David’s son [?]. He summoned and called his entire army to battle, to bring down by every means the exalted worship of truth. He gathered his demons, mustered his legions, and summoned his servants, so that they might [?] him in the fierce battle he had undertaken. He deepened his pitfalls, concealed his means of harm, and spread out his cunning devices to catch the man through whom the Creator’s name had been honored. The deceitful one wove a net of wickedness for the upright man, so that he would become entangled in it, his mind would go astray, and he would lose his rank. With the cunning knots of the daughters of Eve, he bound his prey, so that he would not escape the [?] of his bitterness. Like a robber, the envious one lay in ambush along the path of women, for he saw [?] that King Solomon constantly passed that way. The captor and his accomplices lay in ambush along the king’s road. Suddenly he sprang out, caught the king, and stripped off his splendor. He snatched from his head all the splendor of the Creator’s name and left him naked, without the covering of true worship. He set his father’s trap for him, the lion who terrified the nations; and just as he had caught David, he caught him too through the love of women. Through the love of women, the evil one caught the man of discerning mind, and through his dealings with them he kept his attention away from righteousness. With the rope of women, he bound the strength of the mighty warrior and brought him in and confined him in the prison of ignorance. In ignorance the cunning one bound the man wiser than all, so that it was not easy for him to fight against his deceits. He sent women like spies and tested his free will. He persuaded them to persuade him to make light of his mysteries. The cunning serpent hid his bitterness in women, and through their tongues error pierced him as with a sting. The scythe dealt a grievous wound to the man whose soul was sound, and the venom of its [?] spread through all his senses. Like a dragon, deceit peered out from among the women. It bit him in his soul and made the hair fall from the head of his mind. Like hail, he spewed his gall over his limbs. It spread and reached even the hidden impulses of his soul. The rebel scattered filthy grain before his eyes, and with his delicacies he lured him like a bird into his turmoil. The debased one spread shameful snares of debauchery, and with them he caught Solomon through his flightiness, to bring him down. Alas for the swift one whom wanton eyes hunted down! He was led in and imprisoned under the harsh laws of idolatry. Alas for the mighty man whom lustful ribs overcame, who removed the weapon of the Creator's name from his mind! Alas for the handsome man, greatly loved in body and soul [?], who disfigured his beauty through the ugly union of debauchery! Alas for the wise man at whose knowledge even spiritual beings marveled, who occupied himself with foolish women, and they made him a fool! Alas for the learned man who disclosed the mysteries of hidden things,

at whose wisdom the tyrannical demons rejoiced and laughed! Alas for the wise man who healed the sick in soul [?] with his words, who made his own soul sick with the loathsome disease of idolatry! Alas for the truthful man who silenced ceaseless error, who abandoned the path full of truth and walks in confusion! And so on. Alas for the upright man who raised the head of righteousness [?], who bowed the head of his integrity before deceivers! Alas for the trumpet that amazed the nations with the sound of its melodies, whose beautiful sounds were silenced by deaf idols! Alas for the harp that proclaimed the wisdom of truth, whose soul's strings the cunning demons cut! Alas for the flute through which his Lord's will sang, which the demons broke, so that it could no longer give voice to the spirit of revelation! Alas for you, king, more glorious than the kings who have been and who are, who made your rank contemptible before [?] earthly and heavenly beings! Who would not marvel at the degradation of the one more honored [?] than all, who himself dishonored his dignity through unseemly things? Who would not grieve over the abasement of the man exalted in knowledge, who abandoned the study of [?] and expounded falsehood? Who would not mourn the change in that great sea, whose wisdom ebbed away and whose fountain of discernment dried up? Who would not weep over the craftsman who composed proverbs, who became a proverb himself? Now the mockery of him is recounted everywhere [?]. Who would not fear unwitting slips, since he slipped without knowing it and fell into shameful deeds? Who would not be alarmed about the hidden things within the soul, when, without his noticing, passions raid and plunder his wealth? Who would not be watchful in the battle against his deceit, since he has buried countless traps deep before his mind? Who would not guard his soul's treasures against captivity, continually watching the door of his storehouses by night [?] and day? If the passions plundered the wise man’s wisdom, who can guard his treasures against thieves? If the swift man was caught by the pipes of female demons, who would not flee from the company of Eve’s daughters? If the mighty man fell into the trap of their disturbances, who would not flee to a love beyond their schemes?
On the departure of Enoch and Elijah.
Again by him, by the same author. Discourse Fifty, which he composed on the departure of Enoch and Elijah.

Sin and death fell upon Adam like bands of raiders. They stripped him and left him naked, without possessions. The ancestor of our race went out of Paradise naked, and the kindred of his soul sat mourning over his departure. The spiritual beings sat in deep mourning over the human being, for they heard that death was destined to dissolve the structure of his body. They considered the sentence passed upon his wrongdoing and grieved over how the [?] image had perished. The Creator called him a “[?] image” when he fashioned him. When they heard the news that he was returning to his earth, they turned and sighed. His return to his earth saddened the heavenly beings, and they lost hope that he would ever return to life. They were [?] to his living existence when he was fashioned, and they grieved greatly over his separation from their company. The destruction of his body caused them extraordinary sorrow: how could they be parted from the company of the rational image? They marveled at his power of speech, at how glorious it was that his soul uttered articulate sounds through the senses of the body. The sound of his songs delighted them before his wrongdoing. When he transgressed and sinned, they were stunned and astonished at his fall. Sin overthrew the image, the brother of the heavenly beings, and gave him like a log to ravenous death, which tore his body apart. They looked at him as at a corpse, the corpse of an infant, and never ceased grieving over his death. They counted him dead from the moment he ate the fruit, and still more after that declaration, “You will return to the earth.” That command sent the earthly man back to the earth, and he went out to dwell beyond the pastures of Paradise. The mortal man lived outside the place where he had dwelt, and a wall of fire was drawn around it before him so that he could not enter. The spiritual beings gazed at the wall of fire and were astonished at what the desire for fruit had done. The desire for fruit drove Adam out of Paradise. The demons rejoiced, and the hosts of heaven grieved. All creation sat mourning over his departure and sorrowfully bewailed the death of her child. The world became like a house of mourning over the human being, and the sound of lamentation for him was spoken by every mouth. Speaking and speechless creatures bewailed his mortality and never ceased sighing over his destruction. His guilt erected a fence of fire before him. He longed to enter his own place but could not.

The divine command cast him into exile, and like an offender he wandered in a land of thorns. The king of the earth fed on thorns and thistles, and he sighed doubly over his humiliation. His labor was exhausting, his running wearisome, and his food scanty; the changing seasons troubled him throughout his days. Speaking and speechless creatures grieved over the sufferings of his soul, and recounted his various afflictions in sound and silence. His various afflictions were spoken of in sound and silence, and generation passed on to generation the sorrow of his life. Through experience he learned what mortality meant, and death began destroying his children without mercy. The death that Adam had brought in began among Adam’s children, and swallowed Abel, the beloved firstborn of righteousness. Through the righteous man’s death, death became king over mortals, and human beings became slaves to death and to the Accuser. The sentences pronounced against the guilty were fulfilled in action, and mortal nature was condemned and [?] through mortality. Sin took Adam’s body as a pledge and gave it to death to feed on it greedily. The devourer greedily ate its food, and the robber mercilessly tore his captive apart. The destroyer’s devastation passed through all humanity, and no one remained whom death’s claw had not wounded. Heaven and earth mourned over his destruction; they sighed and [?] in anguish. The pangs of death struck all creation, and it waited for the time when it would give birth to the hope of [?]. The Creator, who sees everything, [?] these sufferings, and suddenly announced good hope to those without hope. The Creator sowed good hope in the ears of [?] through one who had not been subjected to slavery to death. He carefully preserved one human being from destruction and comforted the world in its sorrow over humanity. To comfort humanity, the Lover of humanity took Enoch away and kept him alive, so that through him hope might be preserved for humanity. He proclaimed hope through the taking away of that pleasing man. Because he was so pleasing, he made his goodness a source of hope for humanity. “The righteous man was pleasing,” it is written about the righteous man in the book of Moses. Because he was pleasing, he preserved his goodness in the treasury of life. As in a portrait, he painted an image of his good deeds, and anointed it with immortal [?] so that it would not decay. Sufferings erased the splendid beauty of Adam’s image, and in Enoch he renewed that form which death had ruined. The Creator undid death’s destruction through Enoch’s life and comforted human beings so that they would no longer grieve over guilt. Adam’s children mourned over their destruction, from Adam himself until Enoch pleased God. The children of mortality were tormented by death’s scourges, and there was no hope proclaiming hope to mortal humanity. For six generations he prolonged the scourging of those being scourged.

In the stillness they heard a voice announcing life. In the seventh generation, mortals heard the good news of life, but although they heard it clearly, they could not grasp it precisely. They certainly heard that voice concerning Enoch’s life, [?] and they wondered what it meant and why he had kept him alive. They all heard the good report of the righteous man’s being taken away, but they did not know how to discern the [?] of the resurrection of the dead. They did not learn openly the reason for the abolition of death. Rather, its report was full of mystery, and its power was concealed. The spiritual beings heard this in a mystery, and in a mystery they pondered its meaning. Through this mystery, those who loved humanity cast off their sorrow and began rejoicing at the good news of humanity’s renewal. They had been sitting in deep mourning over humanity, and when they all heard the news of his life, they rejoiced and were comforted. Enoch’s life comforted the [?] and encouraged them to continue in the ordered course of their duties. The transgression of the commandment had weakened their love for humanity, and they were unwilling to change the movements of the air. They considered the [?] on humanity’s behalf to be wasted labor, and they were reluctant to continue on the path of caring for it. A hidden command compelled them to labor greatly, and they accepted and obeyed that command which subjected them. The spiritual beings who minister to humanity obeyed the hidden command, especially from Enoch’s being taken away onward. Enoch lifted the sentence of mortality and reconciled humanity and the heavenly beings through his being taken away alive. His life cut off the path of death symbolically, before the time when it would actually be cut off in deeds. The Lord of the world took him to himself as a pledge of peace and kept him alive so that he might proclaim life to his fellow human beings. The children of the rebel raised a rebellion against the Lord of all. He humbled them with the harsh lashes of mortality. Through death he scourged that stubbornness which stirred up rebellion, yet in mercy he showed it favor by preserving the life of one human being. He chose one human being within a single span of ten generations and kept him with himself as a pledge on behalf of the debtors. The whole race of Adam were debtors. They made promises, but they did not pay the debt of their sins. On this condition he took Enoch as a pledge: that they should remember to repay love to the Maker of all. They had owed a bond of debt from the beginning, and because they had not paid it, they paid it through Enoch against their will. He became a worthy guarantor for his fellow human beings, so that they might pay the bond of debt incurred by their deeds. Through the harvest he taught them to repay love, and his gracious love stirred him on behalf of the righteous. It was not the righteous who compelled him to make peace with humanity, for before he made peace, he already knew the works of peace. In his love he had foreseen the peace he made in Enoch’s time,

and he had also prepared his being taken away before he took him away. He knew this deed that he performed at the beginning of time, and what was to happen at the second time was [?] to him. All times lay open [?] before the one who orders the times, and their changes were arranged before they came to be. He knew the error of Adam and his children before they went astray, and he was preparing to undo death and remove error. Through events he revealed his will: he desires our life. He gave us hope through the departure of a few people. He took Enoch away and kept him among the immortal living beings, and through his departure he gave hope to [?] generations. The people of earlier times gained good hope through Enoch’s life, and his departure became like a guide for those who came afterward. His descendants walked on the path of life in the hope of life, and they began recounting the mystery of their lives from generation to generation. Lamech explained this mystery splendidly as he recounted the various good things intended for humanity. Noah made the sound of his blessings heard like thunder, showing that the time for humanity’s renewal was drawing near. Through his blessings the righteous man revealed his Lord’s will: he was preparing to save humanity through a human being. All the voices bearing hope converged upon Abraham, for in the harbor of his love the expectations of twenty generations came to rest. Twenty generations passed from Adam to Abram; their courses reached the peaceful harbor of one man. Abram was one man, and his love for his Lord was undivided. Because of his love, he made him a harbor for his companions. Abraham became a peaceful harbor for the members of his race, and in him the ships of the Spirit—divine revelations—came to rest. Beginning with Abraham, people embarked on the love of truth, and the Creator also revealed his will toward humanity. God had one will toward humanity, and he made it known through the righteous by means of events of every kind. He told Abram that through his offspring he would bless the nations, and told the son of Jesse that from his line he would establish a kingdom. One after another, they handed down the promises expressed in his words, and there was no time when he did not show the various aspects of his will. To the good he showed the great [?] of his kindness, so that they might sow good hope in people’s ears. In every age he sowed the seed of humanity’s salvation. How abundantly he watered it with various revelations in place of drops! Through revelations he instructed human beings and heavenly beings, so that they would know how to walk in the path of the name of Being. He opened a great road through prophecies for people to travel toward him, and he showed it still more clearly through the son of sojourners, the prophet and priest. He chose a prophet and priest for himself at the midpoint of the ages, to show humanity the various aspects of his will. He entrusted all the power of his activity to his hands, so that he might guide and win over the members of his people through reverence for the truth. He made him a divine steward on earth, to feed his Lord’s servants from his Lord’s household.

The righteous man distributed a fair ration to his Lord’s servants, and wisely provided food in famine and abundance. With the scourge of [?] he disciplined those who rebelled against his Lord, and taught them not to rise up against the Creator. The rebellious children of Abraham had become stiff-necked, and the son of sojourners subdued them as though with a yoke. The voice of that zealous man was a harsh yoke, and he subdued the brutish against their will. Against their will they chose the lordship of God's name, and without finding rest they rejected and cast aside the worship of demons. Through the [?] of the Creator's name, they loved the Creator, and because of the uncleanness of idolatry, they hated involvement with it. The mouth of the son of sojourners had become a spring of scourges, and he gave them all kinds of fierce blows to drink. He held his Lord's command like a rod, and with it he disciplined the troublesome people who loved wandering astray. By every means the righteous man subdued the troublesome, while by every device they broke the yoke of his words. The flow of prophetic words is a harsh yoke, and it skillfully subdues people through fear of the truth. Through his prophecy Elijah became an outstanding farmer, and because he had labored much, he rested in a harbor beyond danger. The diligent man rested in a peaceful harbor beyond danger, and opened a path for those who [?] well, so that they might travel with him. The righteous man traveled on a smooth road without stumbling blocks, which had been opened for righteous Enoch through the beauty of his soul. The Creator saw the beauty of that beautiful man's soul and preserved him alive, so that the beauties of his soul would not be destroyed. Elijah became beautiful with this same beauty of good deeds, and he did for him [?] what had been done for the beautiful man. He deemed those pure in soul worthy of the same reward, and gave ravenous death no power over their bodies. He raised the good servants above death, to put zeal into people's minds so that they might become good. Through the two men whom he took away to himself, he taught people not to doubt the pledge of the resurrection [?] of the dead. He had a treasure of life stored up to reveal to humanity, and he showed it beforehand through two men, Enoch and Elijah. Enoch and Elijah became guides for humankind, so that people might travel on the road of immortal life. He took Enoch away in the first course of ten generations, and the son of sojourners in the second, in the middle of the ages. In the middle of the ages he brought about the departure of the good servant, so that he might be a reminder of the first things and the last. The Lord of the world divided the world into three periods, and in each period he took one man and preserved him alive. In the first he took away Enoch, a righteous man, and in the second he led away Elijah, the chosen prophet. In the third, what can be said about him is beyond us, and no mouth can express how glorious his departure was. His will advanced as though by steps toward the completion of the ages,

and he raised people step by step from lowly things to glorious things. The time when he took Enoch away was humbler than that of Elijah, and that of the son of sojourners was lower than that of Christ. Of Enoch's departure he said only that he was taken away, and did not disclose to us where he took him or where he placed him. Moses hinted mysteriously to us about his departure, but did not explain to us the reason why he was taken away. He spoke these things about Enoch in baby talk, as though to children, because the way of life at the beginning of the ages was still childish. Enoch's age was far more childish than Elijah's, and the forms of one departure were less impressive than those of the other. The people of early times heard a simple voice concerning Enoch's story, but concerning Elijah they heard the many voices of prophecy. Many voices were speaking about Elijah, saying that the time was near for him to be taken away from humankind. One prophet would tell his companion the report he had received, and they passed their revelations from one to another. The day of his departure was announced from one to another, as they wove him a crown of praises from their revelations. The athlete of the Spirit was praised by the voice of revelation, and the prophets of the Spirit celebrated his athletic achievement. Like an athlete, he moved from one place to another, and although he knew, he concealed the day of his departure. The modest man did not wish to reveal his glory, lest the cunning snares of empty praise should catch him. He wisely managed what had been concealed, until the spirit of revelation overtook him through the heralds [?]. The spirit of revelation compelled him to reveal hidden things, and unwillingly he disclosed the time when he would be taken away. He devised pretexts for his disciple, saying that the Lord had sent him on a mission, speaking in mysteries. In mysteries he showed him the mystery of his departure, as is fitting for those entrusted with divine mysteries. The God of all was giving wisdom to the good servant, so that he might arrange his departure to immortal life. The mortal man was being transferred to life without decay, and he wisely honored that life before mortals. He was ready [?] to travel a long road on which there is no [?], and he stretched his mind to match that immeasurable expanse. With the eye of the Spirit, the seer saw that delight, and to his mind the world became as though it were no world at all. He saw another world in an incorporeal vision, despised everything, and loved what does not decay. He saw how great was the way of life to which he was being transferred, and he marveled and wondered at his Lord's love—how greatly he loved him. The righteous man saw how great [?] his Lord's love was, and how he glorifies the members of his household with splendor. Glorious was the day on which the sojourner was taken captive, and splendid were the forms of revelation concerning the course of his journey. He saw a wondrous vision depicted above the earth: the form of fiery chariots racing through the air. He saw [?] of fire yoked to wheels of fire. Above them stood a fiery charioteer. He saw fire bound to fire with reins of fire.

He marveled at the greatness of the glory that had been shown to him. He marveled at the great glory of the day of his departure [?], and could not get enough of gazing closely at the beautiful things. He saw as much of spiritual things as a human being can see. Then he recovered from his amazement and returned to speaking with his disciple. He revealed to him [?], “I am truly being taken away,” and instructed him to ask for something that it was fitting for the master to give. “Ask me,” the renowned master said to his disciple, “and receive something that will remain with you and bring you glory.” The disciple asked for a double measure of prophecy, and his master taught him how to ask and how to receive. The petitioner asked, and the giver gave two in one. Then the prophet began traveling along a road he had never seen. The man made of dust sat upon the spiritual chariot. He grasped reins of fire in his hands and was not scorched. Like a steed, the spirit moved [?] beneath the man made of dust. The body guided the spirit, and the spirit guided the body. The prophet of the Spirit flew by the Spirit wherever he went, and it seemed that he was ascending toward the heights. The divine command drew him upward—not to heaven, but to a place higher than the earth. Elijah did not ascend to heaven on the day he was taken away, but to the place where Enoch, his fellow human being, had been taken. The same command that had taken Enoch away took him away too, and assigned them one place so that they would be together. There was one reason why they were taken away from humankind, and it was fitting that they should be in one place and share one way of life. He distinguished them only in glory when they were taken away, in keeping with the course of life from childhood to maturity. The age in which beautiful Enoch was taken away was still a child, and the manner of his departure was less glorious than Elijah’s. The Tishbite’s age was more mature than Enoch’s, and the forms displayed on the day of his departure were also more glorious. Through spiritual forms he distinguished them, to reveal to humankind the distinction that would exist at the end. He depicted the final day through the spectacle of the righteous being taken away, especially on the day the Tishbite was taken away. He was going to raise the human race to the heights above, and he depicted that ascent beforehand in the taking away of his servant. The course of that chariot directed the gaze upward, to where the whole human race was destined to be raised. It is in this sense that the Tishbite is said to have ascended: not that he actually ascended, but that he might depict the mystery of the ascent. He depicted the mystery of the ascent in the spectacle of his being taken away: that mortal nature thus ascends in the mysteries of his ascent. The righteous men Enoch and Elijah opened the road of life for us, and came to rest in the harbor at the end of the road of the deathless. They are preserved in life without decay in the place to which they were invited, and in their natural state their life is reckoned as somewhat diminished. The righteous live in a somewhat diminished way where they are, through the power of that Spirit for whom even difficult things are easy.

By the power of his command, those made of earth are preserved in the land, no longer subject to the hardships of earthly beings. In that nature, full of [?], they dwell and live; and this is the wonder: they are not harmed by injuries. It is a great wonder how they live human lives and are not worn down by the battering of grinding waves. Within them are the kinds of turmoil that trouble human beings, but the command that transferred them brings these to rest. That command quiets the various kinds of turmoil within them, and they do not slacken in their occupation with praises. Glorious is their occupation, and beautiful the course of their conduct. Who is capable of recounting the meditation in which they persist? The meditation practiced by those who meditate beautifully cannot be expressed. Paul bears witness, for he once went and listened to their discourse. Mortals take part in that discourse of the immortals, and with bodiless beings they sing praises in spiritual voices. Earthly beings are destined to become like spiritual beings. To confirm everything, he transferred two bodily beings beforehand. To confirm everything, he transferred those two men, so that through their transfer he might strengthen people’s confidence in things to come. He received those pure in soul as hostages of peace, so that humanity’s peace with its Creator might stand firm. The nature of mortals has been a weak nature from the beginning, and they habitually wander among desires without restraint. The One who sees everything saw the ugly wandering of their thoughts, and took from among them two dwelling places to be beside him. As a sign of peace, he transferred them from among human beings, so that people might preserve their love for him in his hiddenness. Two faithful men continually confirm humanity’s peace, and he fortifies it through the good meditation of their thoughts. He loves the human image; indeed, the lover of humanity loves it. By every means he seeks this: that human beings should live. For the sake of human life, he spared two mortals from death, so that through their lives they might remind people of their own life. Immortal life is promised to the whole human race, and two guarantors are witnesses to this [their lives became a guarantee for their mortality]: Enoch and Elijah. Their lives became guarantees for our mortality, so that we should not slacken in our confidence in the life that has been promised. The Good One prepared incorruptible life for human nature and recorded it in two books, with three witnesses. Enoch and Elijah put their signatures in the first book, and in the second, one guarantor and chosen witness. The Creator chose a chosen witness from among mortals to testify to the good things awaiting those of his own race. All testimony on earth is given through human testimony, and people customarily seal a bond of debt with three witnesses. The Creator wrote a bond of obligation between himself and humanity, and sealed it according to an earthly and [?] order. He appointed three witnesses to testify in it, in the bond guaranteeing our life: Enoch, Elijah, and third, Christ, who is one of us. Christ, who is one of us, sealed the bond guaranteeing our life with his blood, so that the promise of life might be confirmed for his entire race. Through his death he freed us from slavery to the Evil One and death, and through his resurrection he promised us immortal life. After his death he became immortal in his nature.

So that his life might serve as a chosen witness to the human race. The Creator chose that man to give humanity life, and raised his rank to the lofty rank of his divinity. His rank is not [?] within the order of his divinity, but within that order which has no equal. The rank in which the firstfruits of our race [?] has no equal, and his headship cannot be compared with that of created beings. He did not treat him as a servant who would become great through allotted gifts, nor did he make his departure like that of Enoch or Elijah. He removed Enoch and Elijah from among human beings and settled them in another place on earth. Enoch and Elijah, earthly beings, dwell on earth, and they are preserved on earth in that same mortal nature. Those faithful men entered the region of Eden to dwell there, where Adam, the head of our entire race, had lived. The second Adam broke through the [?] that stood before humanity and brought human beings into the place that had been fenced off by a judicial decree. By a judicial decree, human beings had been barred from that place, until one man undid it and gave humanity assurance. One man, Christ, who is one of us, entered it first and granted all human beings entry there through their souls. Enoch and Elijah alone had entered in body and spirit, and they remain there until the time of the one who brings the ages to an end.
