The one who brings the ages to an end entered it first in spirit, not in body, and he departed from it and ascended to a place more glorious than it. Our firstfruits ascended to the place on high, higher than the heights, to the Holy of Holies, where no human foot had entered. The priest who is one of us entered before the Divine Being to serve as priest, in a place free from those who suffer harm and those who cause it. With his own blood he served as priest once among earthly beings, and the sacrifice of his holiness was sufficient for all creatures. On behalf of all creatures, the Creator chose him from among created beings and accepted his death as a ransom for his mortal creatures. Human wickedness stained the world with abominations, and the Good One in turn cleansed it through the death of one man. [?] Through the very thing by which death entered and ruined humanity, life entered and abolished death from human nature. Adam [?] the road of death through his desire for the fruit, and death spread throughout the whole nature of Adam's race. The transgression of the commandment subjected humanity to slavery to death, and people despaired that the human race would ever live again. To give humanity hope, the Creator chose three men and made them witnesses who testify to humanity's life. Enoch and Elijah testify on earth to humanity's life, and the [?] of our life confirms our life above in heaven. Two faithful men testify on earth to our renewal, and one in heaven confirms the words of those above and those below. Two, Enoch and Elijah, give assurance on earth as servants, while one dwells in heaven as a king and commands on earth. I did not count the king who reigns among servants, nor is his authority like the authority of earthly people. I did not call him an ordinary man, like [?]:

Nor did I call his departure like the departure of mortal human beings. Let the heretics not rejoice as they usually do, for I am not accustomed to giving grounds for their accusations. I know that they devise pretexts like hunters, and I am not unaware how cunning they are at hunting words. The hunters of the words of faith hunt words, but when they catch them, they fly like a bird out of their hands. Our faith cannot be caught in the hands of fools, because they cannot grasp its power with their minds. They are far too weak to [?] a single contest openly, and the course of their statements is devoid of understanding. They cannot catch words with words as they imagine, nor can they give a clear explanation of hidden things. The sound teaching of faith is hidden from them, and when it was revealed through the mouths of the knowledgeable, they were bewildered and astonished. I have repeated the sound teaching of faith [?], and I am not unaware that they handle it ignorantly. No, you simpletons, I did not arrange my words ignorantly. They do not flow for you because you are not trained in the discipline of words. You do not know how to walk the path of faith, and you have not measured the words placed within its meanings. Without understanding, you stumble as though over a stone, and you do not know how to distinguish the ugly from the beautiful. I spoke rightly in the discourse in which I spoke about the man: he who was exalted above humanity was a man. It was a man who proclaimed hope to humanity, and the utterances that Enoch and Elijah sowed on earth were confirmed. It was a man who ascended and reigned above in heaven, and opened a path for human beings to become heavenly. It was a man who became a witness to the document of our life, and put his hand to it and sealed it with his blood so that it could not be falsified. He was a man, and again I say that he was a man. And if the heretics are enraged, let them shout loudly. Let them shout loudly until Legion hears and howls with them, like that voice before our Lord. Legion howled bitterly over his downfall, and the voice of the disciples closely resembles that of their master. The foolish heretics resemble their foolish master, and they do not understand that they condemn themselves by the sound of their own words. They resemble a mole, always burrowing in evil study; and when they heard the sound of the word of truth, they became wild and frenzied. The sound of their frenzy does not let me leave them alone, nor does it allow me to pass them by without rebuke. Their thinking stands like a target before my thoughts, and urges me to strike them with the arrows of my words. I long to strike them with words [?], because they do not stop disputing against my words. In the study of words I had a subject to ponder, but when I pondered it, the noise of the heretics hindered me. “Leave me alone, people!” I cried to them in every way. But whenever I thought they would finally be quiet, they became agitated and enraged. Even now, in this matter, I have seen their agitation.

And I let my discourse rebuke their blasphemous words. My discourse fought against the blasphemies of the blasphemers, then left that subject and proceeded along the road of confronting the obstinate. It rebuked the obstinate with an exchange of words answering words, and I soothed the uneducated by persuading them of the truths. I spoke these truths truthfully: what is the reason that death rules over human beings of our race? I saw human beings of our race raised above death, and I composed words to reveal in words the things that are not revealed. I wanted to speak about unrevealed things before my hearers and inform them, so that they would know the kinds of hidden things. The kinds of hidden things were concealed in the account of these matters that I related, not to the mature, but to children and those without knowledge. To those without knowledge I revealed the reasons for the departure of human beings: what was the reason that they departed from us to another place? Enoch and Elijah departed [?] from us to another place, and by their departure they depicted for us a pattern of the transformation of our lives. The one who loves our race promised us new life and sealed it with three seals, three human beings. I called all three of them human beings, not in respect of rank, but according to the order of human nature. The three of them have one nature, in body and spirit. Their rank is not equal, [?] for servants are not like the Lord. Enoch and Elijah are servants, even though they live. Christ, who is one of us, is Lord over all, even though he is human. Enoch and Elijah are kept on earth until the resurrection; Christ is in a place exalted and [?] above mortals. He is not dead, since he has become immortal, and he alone received this on behalf of mortals. On behalf of mortals, the Creator chose him from among mortals, so that he would fulfill the order of servants and of the freeborn. He too is a servant, insofar as he is a work of the Maker; yet he is also Lord, because he received divine rank. He is divine because of his rank, which is higher than all. He was exalted and became king, not by his nature, but by his rank. That man, who shares our humanity, was exalted in his rank, and all this was because the one who took pleasure in him willed it. The God of all willed that they should call him by the name of his own majesty. And look, foolish people, you [?] at the greatness of our rank. You fools, why are you distressed over our exaltation and unwilling to receive [?] the king who is one of us? Human beings, rejoice that you have become divine through the man who became God with God. The Word, the Son of God, dwelt in a man of our race, called him by his own name, and gave him the rank belonging to the name of the divine Being. He gave him names and deeds that are above him; and although he gave him much, he does not forget that he is one of us. He is one of us, and for the sake of our lives he ascended and was exalted. We owe thanks to the Good One who exalted our race. Let the whole mortal race say, “Thanks be to the Good One, who exalted our race through one human being whom he took from among us.”
On Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael

Discourse Forty-Four: On Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael.
Response: Martyrs, ask for mercy upon the world. Of “He who offers refuge” [?]: “In your bones, my brothers.”

The children of the promise went down as captives to the land of the Babylonians, but they did not abandon their confidence in the promises made to them. Lovers of peace journeyed in adversity to the region of the wrathful, but the love of truth did not grow cold in their minds.

Bearing the mark that the Creator had inscribed upon their senses, they settled among pagans but did not imitate their customs. Those who possessed good judgment went in and mingled with the foolish, but the sound judgment of their minds did not lose its sense of duty. Clothed in the armor of the Law, forged by the Spirit, they stood among the ranks of warriors and did not falter. Running the race of righteousness without contempt for it, they lived among the defiled but did not stop or neglect their labors. Athletes who grappled in combat amid struggles tore their captors’ hands away from their bodies. Children of Abraham, the chosen friend whose love was steadfast, they entered the contest, won, and came out like their father. The innocent, children of the innocent man, entered the contest of suffering. They awaited and fulfilled that utterance addressed to Abraham. They resembled Abram in awaiting a hope that does not deceive. They believed and affirmed things far off as though they were near. They set his trial before their eyes like a target and leaned strongly toward the help that comes from God. Righteous Abram did not waver over his son’s death, nor did Abraham’s children fear their own deaths. In their minds they watched him as he offered up his son as a burnt offering, and they gave their bodies to the flame to resemble him. They clothed their impulses in faith as in armor, and believed that the power of his help could overcome the fire. Through faith they scorned and despised the Babylonians, for they saw that the promises voiced by Chaldean divination were feeble. Through faith they chose to die a temporal death rather than be deprived of the expectation of what was promised to the righteous. They considered it easy for faith to overcome death, and they were not thinking of escaping the burning. They remembered that if they died, they would travel the road of death like everyone else; and if they did not die, they would surely die eventually, as mortals do. They looked toward death, scorned and despised earthly things, and chose, before death came, to die a death filled with hope.

Hope was like a guide to them on the road of suffering, showing them the path of endurance in which there is no fear. In the place of terror the steadfast stood clothed in hope, and courageously endured the sufferings inflicted by their tormentors. The Babylonian roared like a lion to terrify them, but they regarded his voice as the sound of a gnat buzzing in the air. His command hissed like a serpent, threatening them, but they regarded his fury as a mole that burrows and cannot hurt. Skilled in sin, he made a great statue with [?], to ensnare everyone through it into the error of the Chaldeans. The spirit of revelation had shown him a statue, great and glorious, and he wanted to erect an idolatrous statue patterned after the one he had seen. He saw that the statue he had seen was skillfully adorned, and he sought to exalt his sovereignty in proportion to its greatness. The dream depicted the image of his dominion for him, so that he might understand it. But he went mad and devised an interpretation contrary to the truth. He had seen the dream, but then forgot it, so that he sought to recover it. Once it had been interpreted, he turned to scheming to lead people astray through its vision. The prophet revealed to him that he was the head of fine gold, and he planned to rise to a lofty rank by constructing the statue. He showed him that he would perish by a judicial decree from God, but he raised a rebellion rather than submit to the words of the Spirit. The fool put on the armor of arrogance against the truth and began to wage an unjust war against righteousness. His heart, full of injustice, prepared an unjust war, to destroy the ranks of the children of [?] with the sword of his injustice. He gave the command, and the statue he had fashioned in his mind was constructed. He summoned peoples and provinces to worship his counterfeit. He fashioned it in his heart, and then gave orders, and people fashioned it. He shaped it in his mind, and then the image-carvers [?] shaped it. The demons advised him to shape a statue according to their desire, and they showed him how to make it and how high to make it. They also instructed the craftsmen who assembled it, so that they would fulfill their wishes through the splendor of its appearance. The deceitful ones devised a mystery together with the Chaldeans, to lead people astray after error through the form of the statue.

They set its height at sixty cubits, it is said, so that its appearance would astonish everyone, even from far away. They also made it six cubits wide, as they wished, so that its structure would be stable in proportion to its height. Perhaps the demons had given the Chaldeans this advice: to enlarge the statue so that the king’s dominion would become much greater. Perhaps he said, “Despise the teaching of Judaism, so that the exiles will not rise up against the kingdom.” Perhaps the statue was also constructed with this intention: to catch the lovers of truth through it as in snares. For they knew the love that the righteous had for righteousness. That was why they enlarged and spread out the snares of the great statue. They placed the fashioned gold on the earth like a trap, so that through its splendor people would come to hate the beauty of the soul’s splendor. The beauty of the righteous stirred up jealousy among the Chaldeans: why had the truth within them grown great and triumphed? The demons kindled the fire of wrath in embodied demons, so that through it they might destroy the name of the God of the children of Abram. As if with firewood, they stoked the anger of the tyrant king, so that the command he spoke would blaze more fiercely than fire. They gave the king of wrath a cup of wrath to drink. He drank, became drunk, and lost his reason in the fumes of delusion. He completed the image, full of ruin, according to his desire, and established a festival for people to celebrate in wickedness. He issued a command that entirely abolished reverence for the truth, and wrote a decree by which falsehood was upheld. He sent messengers to every region, to all the nations, and they began proclaiming news full of ruin for the soul. “Listen, nations, to the king’s command!” the heralds cried. “Come out eagerly and complete the ruin of your own selves!” “This is what the foremost king, the head of gold, has commanded:

‘Come, render me loving homage through the image I have fashioned. You owe me loving homage and must render it to me. Pay your debt, so that you are not scourged like debtors. I have chosen to bring you into a testing furnace by means of the image, to see who most loves the authority of my lordship. Through what I have done, I have sought to test my lordship over everyone, to learn who boldly resists it. Now I issue my command and seal the document containing my word. Set your hands to it and add your seals after mine through your worship. Now I declare and bear witness before everyone and in every place: anyone who scorns the command I have spoken shall burn in the fire. See that you do not despise the command I have established in the land, lest you be condemned by a merciless sentence.’” The rulers went out and gathered the nations for the festival of the image. They fulfilled and carried out the king’s command as they had been ordered. Everyone bowed his head, whether out of love or fear. Those endowed with speech honored and worshiped a mute thing without understanding. The command of the [?] drove them on swiftly, and they did not delay in bending the knee before the silent thing. The command became a hailcloud over their heads and battered them fiercely, without mercy. His anger blew like a whirlwind through their ranks and sank the ship of their thoughts in false worship. All the Babylonian ships sank in sin, and only three Jewish ships remained watchful. The threat battered all the ears of grain in the field of Assyria, but three Hebrew ears among them were not broken. The scourge caught hold throughout the vineyard of Nimrod’s descendants, but the vines of Abraham’s household remained firm. The Chaldeans saw the beauty of the fruit on their branches and were grieved that their fruit too had not been ruined. The insolent clothed themselves in angry jealousy against the blameless, because they had defied the command of the king who had honored them. Jealousy over them stirred up the wicked, those with malicious hearts: “Look, O king, how greatly the captives you honored have scorned you!” You honored them above everyone, but they despised you more than anyone. You gave them authority, but they raised their heel to trample you. The troublemakers stirred up the old man against the wise men.

He raised his voice and shouted in anger that would not be appeased: “You exiles, children of captivity, who have denied my authority! Why have you rejected my command before my armies? You gluttons, who ate your fill of bread from my tables! Why have you repaid the one who honored you with evil deeds? You Jews, whom I named after my gods! Why have you scorned worshiping the image that my will has honored? You [?], who did not appreciate the honors given to you! Why have you insulted the exalted rank of my kingship over all? You fools, whose house of worship did not save them! Why have you mocked the festival I held for my great god?” The pure men did not tremble at the threats of that arrogant man, nor did they abandon their confidence in the true faith. They did not seek help against the onslaught of his fierce anger, nor did they lower themselves to appease him, even with a word. “There is no need for persuasive words,” they answered the king, “and we do not need to waste our breath on your threats. Do as you wish and satisfy your anger as you are accustomed to do. We cannot go astray into the error of worshiping your image. Heaven and earth cannot persuade us to do this, and neither angels nor human beings can overcome our courage. Far be it from us to forget the great name of the house of Abraham and to despise the covenant between the Creator and our ancestors! Far be it! May we never bow our heads before a speechless thing and call that which is no god, fashioned by deceit, a god! Far be it from us to become slaves to a slave made by slaves, and to say that something made can take the place of its Maker! Neither height nor depth nor angels, nor any other creation, if there is one, will change our word. We have warned you: stop talking and show your deeds! Test our resolve in the fire of your anger, and see that it is firm.” The Babylonian heard these words, which utterly nullified his image, and became bitterly agitated beyond all restraint. The gall of his bitterness surged through his thoughts.

He summoned his servants and equipped them to kindle the fire. “Heat the furnace sevenfold,” the accursed man commanded, “so that I may kill in it the children of captivity who have scorned my commands. Mix with the wood anything that can make it burn more fiercely, and exact payment from the Hebrews for the insult to the image of my god. Bring forward all the peoples who have come to the festival for worshiping the image. Let them come and see the burning of the men who despised my majesty. Before the crowds I will humiliate those who humiliated me, so that everyone may see and not rise up against my words.” The Chaldeans fulfilled the desire of the king, who was eager for [?]. They kindled the fire and summoned the nations as they had been commanded. The [?] and the Tibetans gathered, crowd after crowd; the Medes and the Alans stood there, company after company. A great crowd gathered to watch the Israelites, to see the marvel of human endurance overcoming fire. Everyone's eyes were turned toward the furnace, but its heat prevented them from looking steadily at it. The ruthless man commanded the serpents who were more ruthless than he, and they bound those mighty men in their clothes. They bound them in the splendid garments covering their bodies, so that the fire would quickly consume their limbs. In anger those wrathful men did this to the innocent, seeking thereby to appease the fierce rage in their minds. Those spiteful men ruthlessly carried the men who were full of peace and wickedly threw them into the midst of the fire. The faithful men went down and stood calmly in the furnace, and the fiery Watcher welcomed them as chosen men. The Creator sent an angel to his faithful men to protect them from the harm of the flames. The spiritual being made a dewy breeze inside the furnace and tempered the fierce heat with coolness. The fiery being took a rod of fire in his hand and drove the fire away so that it would not approach their limbs. Fire saw fire and was terrified; it shrank back and hid. For all its fierceness, it could not bear to look at the sight it saw. The burning flame saw a terrifying sight in the hand of the spirit. It forgot its proper order and began moving outside its appointed bounds. The Watcher placed fiery bits in the mouth of the fire,

and regulated its confused course so that it would not blaze wildly. The discerning flame kept its appointed order before the discerning men and did not greedily devour much, as it usually did. Who has ever seen a marvel like the one involving the righteous: a greedy mouth with food placed inside it, yet not touching it? Who has ever beheld the flame, that devouring Sheol, [?], though it had never been satisfied since the day it came into being? Who has put a piece of flesh into the mouth of a deadly lioness, and she did not touch it, just as the fire did not touch the bodies of the chaste men? Oh, the nature that, contrary to its habit, forgot its own nature, abandoned its appointed order, and followed a path unsuited to it! Oh, the devourer that grows greedier the more it eats, yet decreed a fast and closed its mouth to food! Oh, the burning flame whose fierceness increases the more it burns, yet whose fury cooled at the height of its strength! Oh, the ravenous flame that grows greedier the more it consumes: it consumed much, yet its voracity did not grow greedy! Oh, how much can we say, and how can we describe what happened—a grain placed in the mouth of the burning flame, yet remaining unharmed! Oh, how bold the chaste righteous were to look upon its fury! Their bodily sight was not harmed by the blaze. Oh, how the eyes of flesh endured the sight of the wonder! Even the spiritual beings were astonished and marveled at the greatness of its wonder. The flame rose forty-nine cubits, and as far as it rose, so far it descended, without measurements. Who, then, cast a measuring line into the air and went up to measure it? For nothing can be measured without something to measure it with. What hand held a measuring rod above the fire and measured a line from the furnace to the very end of its blaze? The command that placed restraints of silence upon its mouth measured it through the spirit of revelation, by the mouth of Daniel. He who told it to maintain its order contrary to its usual nature revealed to his servant how many cubits it rose into the air. At that time it displayed its blaze more fiercely than on any other day, so that the accusers who had kindled it without cause might examine it. It argued its case against them by rising toward the heights,

so that people saw how high it rose while maintaining its appointed order. “Look, Chaldeans!” the silent one cried to those who could speak. “Though I am fire, I have become no fire before these beings of flesh. You offered me flesh as food to feed upon, and here it lies before me, frightening me so that I dare not approach it.” The fire in silence and the Watcher facing it examined the case. With discernment they acquitted one side and condemned the other. They protected the righteous and punished the wicked harshly, so that everyone might learn that the Maker’s power dwelt in his servants. The blaze saw the Maker’s power in the work of his hands. It drew back from him and did not approach him as it usually did. Its habit is always to harm whatever approaches it, but here it remained silent and did not injure bodies that could be injured. The righteous rejoiced within it as upon a bed of delight, while it, like a maidservant, performed a service remarkable even for servants. The furnace became a beautiful bridal chamber for those beautiful in soul, and the Watchers and the fire attended upon them. As though in the sanctuary of the Holy of Holies, they stood in prayer and offered there the pure sacrifices of their thoughts. With great suffering, the chaste men prayed fervently. With loud cries they pleaded and begged for their lives. With a holy voice they offered thanksgiving to the one who had preserved them alive, and with discernment they composed the words of their songs. “Blessed is the Creator!” the holy men cried in holiness, “who preserved our lives from the injuries of the flame. Blessed is he who revealed in us the sign of his mercy that his judgment decreed, and through us displayed the strength of his greatness, whose power can accomplish everything. Blessed is he who, through us, opened a path for people to know him and made us witnesses to the greatness of his power among the Babylonians. Blessed is he who armed the fiery Watchers with the armor of his name and did battle with the blaze in place of our limbs.” Blessed is he who taught order to the fire, which was indiscriminate in what it consumed, and through its discrimination put the pride of the undiscerning to shame. The Babylonians, whose own order was confused, marveled at the fire’s order: who, indeed, had placed the bridle of silence on that savage thing? Its stillness prodded the sluggish man’s heart toward understanding, and he began to search for traces of the power that had overcome his power.

Great dismay fell upon the king and the armies when they saw that the fire had no power over the food they had given it. They saw that it was bound and would not approach the Israelites, yet its mouth was unbound to destroy their accusers. They saw that within its own house it was calm and had ceased its activity, while outside it raged and roared savagely. They saw that its fierceness had been restrained inside the furnace, yet it came out and displayed the strength of its power against those who had prepared it. By its discrimination it turned the image’s festival into mourning, and the sound of the [?] turned into lamentations. All Babylon was rejoicing at the festival the king held; but when it saw that the king’s words had not been fulfilled, it wept and mourned. The armies mourned with the king, for they saw that his proud heart had fallen from its confidence. The fool had been confident that he would become still greater through the image, but when he saw that captive youths had scorned him, he was ashamed and humiliated. The foolish man supposed that his authority would rise as high as the image he had raised, but when the exiles mocked him, dismay seized him. Dismay seized him when he looked and saw the youths in the fire, walking about without their limbs being burned. “Are they really the same men, or not?” the contentious man wondered. “Are they walking about alive, or is it perhaps not real?” “Something new has happened among the Babylonians, something I have never seen. If it is real, the hope we looked forward to has proved false.” “We expected to become great through the greatness of the image we made, yet now we have become smaller than everyone, for three men have overcome our power.” “We threw three men into the furnace to die, yet now I see that they have trampled death down, stood up, and made a mockery of us.” “We gave three men as food for the flame, but they bound its mouth to keep it from their bodies and unleashed it against our people.” “We cut three shoots from the vine of Abraham’s house, yet now I see that another, a glorious one, has sprung from them.” “The fourth one’s appearance is full of great majesty, and the radiance of his face is unlike that of created beings.” “His appearance outshines even the appearance of the flame, and perhaps it was because of him that the fire acted with discernment.” “Perhaps he drove it away from the captives’ bodies and taught it to go out and destroy the ranks of our armies.”

“Perhaps he gave discernment to the undiscerning fire, and at his command it acquired authority to preserve life and to kill.” “What is this that has happened in our land and in our days? Look, our own scourger is scourging us like evildoers!” “We sought to scourge the captives because they despised us, but our scourger has turned against us and is scourging us fiercely.” We hoped to use fire to exact repayment from them for our humiliation, but now it has come out and demands repayment from us for their blood. Come, let us approach the furnace, even though it is terrifying, and plead with them to plead with it not to destroy us. Come, let us take refuge in the true faith to which they hold, so that perhaps we may escape the burning flame. Come, let us all lovingly ask them to come out of the furnace quickly, so that the fire may subside. With fear and affection, the king and his counselors approached and begged and pleaded with those undergoing torture, who had shaken us so greatly: “Come out of the furnace, servants of the God of all, and turn away from us the fury of the fire that threatens us. Come out, righteous men, who serve the truth without disdain, and be our advocates at the judgment before righteousness. Come up, chaste men, from the contest of righteousness. You have labored greatly and have condemned Assyrian Babylon. Come, innocent men, rest from your struggle against our wickedness, for our guilt has now been exposed before all creatures. We wickedly waged an unjust struggle against you, and when the Righteous One saw it, he turned our injustice back upon our wickedness. Your God is righteous, and his love for his servants is steadfast. In accordance with his righteousness, he vindicated his servants and condemned our injustice. The fabrication of Chaldean religion to which we hold is false. If it were true, where is its power, which did not stand up for us? From what has happened, let everyone learn with certainty that there is no god able to deliver except the One. Let what he has done be a sign of his might: none of the gods has the power to help except him. Let all the nations and their gods look at this and see how contemptible the delusion of their idols is. Contemptible is every god who cannot deliver his worshiper, and honored above all is the one who has shown his power through his servants.

You are servants of the God of all, who rules over all, and here is the testimony to his divinity among the members of his household.” The arrogant-minded man spoke these things unwillingly, because he saw that the power of the Maker whom he had mocked had overcome him. His mouth had poured great mockery upon the Maker, but he turned around and praised him before all the nations, unwillingly. In the land of Judah he had mocked and laughed at his lordship, and in his own land he repaid him with destruction worse than his own. In the house where he placed his trust, he overthrew him and cast him down from his confidence, showing him how feeble was the power of the help in which he had boasted. He thought that by his own strength he had conquered God's people and put an end to their festivals, but God rebuked him in his own country, showing that the victory had not been his. When he uprooted the holy temple, he thought that its burning coals had gone out. But through his servants, God taught him not to boast insolently. Through his deeds, he wisely passed judgment on his insolence, so that he would not think that God himself was fighting against his injustice. He bade his servants trample him like something contemptible, so that he would know how feeble was the power in which he boasted. Perhaps his prompting stirred his heart to make an image, so that through an image he might portray his hidden nature before his eyes. Perhaps he himself spurred him to summon rational beings to worship a mute thing, so that, when they struggled, he might make known to them the power of his greatness. Perhaps he himself urged the accusers to kindle the fire, so that, when it was defeated, he might proclaim his power through the members of his household. Perhaps it was with this intent that he did not call him to account from the beginning, so that his rebuke would not be without benefit. He did not do, or now do, these things I have mentioned by compelling anyone; rather, he let them be and did not call them to account from the beginning. He could have demanded an accounting for the insult to his name and to the members of his household, but he let it pass and remained silent until the wickedness of the wicked was revealed. Through the wickedness of the wicked, the power of his greatness is regularly glorified, so that he may reveal to humanity the great wealth of his patience. In his patience he bore with the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, and when he saw that his wickedness exceeded all bounds, he rebuked him in due order. Like a fisherman, he stood over the sea of his patience and offered him bait as one does to a fish, until he caught him.

He placed the net of his love in the hands of the members of his household, and instead of spreading it through water, he spread it through fire over the Babylonians. The divine fishermen stood amid fire and water, and skillfully caught Babylon, the catcher of nations. Like fish, they first thrashed about in their struggles, but when they saw that they had fallen into the nets, they were ashamed and fell silent. They were greatly agitated as they swam in the waves of falsehood, and when his command drew them onto dry land, they lost their lives. The rational fish gave their bodies as food to the fire, and they wailed and cried out as they roasted in the flame. The Babylonian, a fish on dry land, cried out in a loud voice: “Come, fishermen, come up out of the sea of flame! Come up, you men who catch people without using your hands! You have caught enough of your captors as food for the fire.” Crowd after crowd, the nations made ready to watch as the chosen witnesses came out from within the fire. Group after group, people of every rank, men and women, stood to gaze at the greatness of the power that had given them victory. In great amazement they gazed at what had happened. It was real, yet to their minds it was not real. “It is real, and it is not real,” those without understanding pondered. “Are these really the men, or a shadow resembling a body?” Those whose hearts were divided fell into bewilderment, and as though in a dream they marveled at the truth plainly before them. The righteous truly remained in the fire without harm, but until they came out, the truth was not confirmed for those who would not believe. The faithful came out, truly steadfast, and the unbelieving saw them and were then convinced. They came out with their limbs and clothing intact; not a single part of their heads or their garments was missing. They came out with the truth within them shining more brightly than gold, and its radiance lit up the eyes of those who saw them. They came out clothed in visible garments and hidden glory, praising the living Name that had glorified them.

They came out of the fire, trampling it beneath their feet. This was the wonder: not even its smell [?] had touched them. The prophet bears witness—he who was a witness in the mouths of wild beasts—for he testified and said that the smell [?] of fire had not touched them. Wonderful was the contest that these earthly people undertook on earth, and the mouth of earth’s inhabitants is too small to tell how great it was. Great was the victory won through the endurance of the captives, and the song of a fleshly tongue is too weak to express its beauty fully. Their Lord alone knows how to paint the image of their beauty and recount the endurance of their minds. He is the one who proclaimed the power of his greatness through their tongues and recorded in his books the day of victory on earth. He set their victory in the Scriptures like a mirror, so that those running the race of righteousness might look into it. Through their labors they stirred up zeal in those who came after them, so that they might aim at the upright goal of their conduct. He made their captivity among the Babylonians serve a useful purpose, so that through their sufferings he might give flavor to those who were tasteless. He acted well in leaving them unattended so that they became slaves, in order to reveal through their subjection the glory of his might. He wisely remained silent when they entered the furnace of testing, so that through their testing he might expose the falseness of Chaldean religion. He skillfully composed the account of their victories, so that whenever it was recounted, everyone might learn how to triumph. He mightily helped them in the contest of suffering, so that he might give hope to those who are tested through suffering. Just, too, was the punishment that his command inflicted on their persecutors, so that no one might dare to rise against his friends. His judgment is righteous, his testing is just, and his command is wise. No one knows how to recount adequately the ways of his wisdom. He sent the people whom he had chosen for his name into captivity among the Babylonians, and through their subjection he humbled the errors of Chaldean religion. His providence brought about a double benefit: through his people he taught the nations that he is Lord over all. Through what he did, his command taught wisdom to the people and the nations: he disciplined them and won them over, each through the other. As though wielding a rod, he raised them up against one another,

and scourged the people through the nations, and the nations through the people. Come, then, let us learn the power of his wisdom through his discipline, and acknowledge as his the great glory that befits his name. Response: Glory to the Power that strengthened the martyrs, so that they triumphed and were victorious in the contest.
On the Rebuke of Priests
Discourse Forty-Five: On the Rebuke of Priests. It is also appropriate for a time of hardship.

This evil age has forced me to speak about its wickedness, and its disorder has made me speak about its confusion. I saw that it was out of order, with the order of its course disrupted, and my mind hurried to examine its confusion. I saw it going wildly along a path of error, and I was greatly astonished at its lawless audacity. It was behaving savagely like vicious animals, and it allowed no one to approach it. Its turmoil bewildered my thoughts as though in a dream, and I thought that perhaps its course was a dream and not something actually happening. I thought the change of times that occurred in my days was a dream—not because it was a dream, but because it was far more deceptive than a dream. Its disorder forced me to call it the bewilderment of a dream, and, as in a dream, it distracts people from their duty. It has sunk the world into a kind of sleep through its heaviness, and no one wants to shake off the burden of wickedness. The darkness of its ignorance resembles the darkness of night, and it is very difficult to walk rightly in its gloom. The time of this age is darker than all other times,

and perhaps there has never been another age darker than it. It has extended its dominion over everyone and everything in darkness, and in its bitterness it has overcome the light of discernment. Travelers have stopped journeying toward the meeting place of peace, because the age has risen like darkness before their eyes. People of every rank have ceased attending to good things, and everyone has shut his mind up within himself as though in winter. The discerning have wrapped their thoughts as though in a garment, and have gone inside and hidden themselves so that they might not be battered by the age’s bitter cold. Apathy has seized them like a fever, and they have been unwilling to interpret hidden utterances in people’s ears. All orders have fallen ill with the same sickness of ignorance, and no one applies a word of truth to his companion’s pain. The pain of their [?] resembles an inflamed swelling, and no one knows how to dress it properly with faith. The illness into which they have fallen is more severe than every other disease, and there are no medicines capable of healing its wounds. The sickness of this age has penetrated the hidden soul, and now it is eating through human nature like a woodworm. All orders and every rank lie in its decay, and this is the astonishing thing: everyone is sick, but no one notices. Kings are sick, and the crown upon their heads is rotten. There is no authority whose office is healthy and whose conduct is orderly. Priests are sick, and the rod of their commandments is weak. There is no rule with which spiritual health abides. The priests, the healers of souls, are spiritually sick, and in their souls they lie in the fever of bodily passions. Ugly passions of every kind peer out from them, and each is more rotten than his companion and corrupted by shameful deeds. Envy bites, pride kicks, and rage scorches. Even when there are no grounds, grounds are tied into knots that cannot be undone. Wrath rages, strife burns, and hatred threatens. Everyone is intent on destroying his companion as though with fire. Traps are laid with cunning, snares with deceit, and ambushes in secret. Who can escape these afflictions?

Swords are sharpened, arrows pointed, and spears held ready. Perhaps not a single human survivor will remain unharmed. Battle is prepared, conflict made ready, and ranks drawn up against one another. And this is the tragedy: who is fighting against whom! Come, beings that speak and those that are silent, and marvel at the fierce battles the priests draw up against one another. Come, spiritual beings, look and consider with discernment how strong our insolence has become in this age. Come, nature of [?], sigh over yourself. Wail and weep over your lawless evils. Your evils have grown strong without restraint, contemptible nature, and you have walked without discipline along the paths of insolence. Your will has rushed insolently against the truth. Look: the evidence of your insolence is in the leaders of your people. The leaders of your people have torn apart the harmony established within you. They have divided you into factions of every kind. The sowers of peace have disturbed peace with their disputes. They have stirred up strife between earthly and heavenly beings. The [?] have stirred up evil strife between each and all. Now the troubled world is fighting against itself. They have put on evil zeal like armor against one another, and without pity they have hurled words like arrows. The learned have shot arrows of insult into their own members. They have not understood whom they are striking with their words. Blind envy has blinded them to understanding. They have not realized whom they have hurt by the injuries they inflicted. Foolish pride has led them away from understanding. They have neither discerned nor recognized what befits their great name. The love of money has bound them to earthly things. They have not longed for the promise of life in the world to come. Rapacity has set them ablaze with the fire of cravings. The world's good things have become too few to meet their needs. The love of glory has caught them in the snare of glory. Like a bird, they have fallen from the heights of their way of life. Gluttony has entered and burrowed into their thoughts. They have gathered from everyone, but the desire within them has not been satisfied. Those who lacked nothing have become deprived of everything. Although everything was theirs, their hands have been emptied of everything. They have come to need what is their own, those who possess the wealth of their [?].

And now they plead for alms like beggars. Their envy has made them dependent on everyone, and their contentiousness has kept good things from their mouths. They debased themselves with things unworthy of them, and they diminished the high rank in which they stood. They were called shepherds of rational beings, but they abandoned human beings and went wandering after dumb animals. Those endowed with reason loved irrational creatures more than rational ones, and acquired speechless animals as property for their own profit. Through love of earthly things they forgot concern for spiritual things, and exchanged the wealth of precious things for worthless things. The heavenly bridegroom invited them to the kingdom [?] of heaven, but they treated his truthful words as lies. Truth will be a witness at the judgment between him and them, and will call them to account for the insult to his truthfulness. With righteous judgment he will rebuke the deceitful priests who despised his gift and dishonored the mysteries of his glory. He will pronounce judgment against the schemes of the deceitful, who hoarded his wealth and did not use it to provide for people's needs. He gave them his word so that through it they might distribute life to human beings, but they hid it beneath the clothing of their deeds. He addressed to them the same utterance that he addressed to Simon. They heard it but remained silent about the meaning hidden within it. It was to them that he entrusted the care of his human flock, but they ate the flesh of the fat sheep and despised the weak. It is fitting to repeat concerning them the prophetic saying: “Woe, priests, ignorant and foolish shepherds!” The shepherds tended our nature unnaturally, and without compassion scattered our lives on the mountains of error. Our humanity became like a flock without a shepherd, and beasts—evil Watchers—came in and ravaged our race. Rational beings wandered along the paths of ignorance, and no one turned their minds toward what is written. The shepherds fell short of the goal of reverence for truth, and the flock went astray on the false path of their deeds. By their deeds they threw the path of faith into confusion,

and by their schemes they filled it with the danger of discord. They cast discord like a stone before those walking along the way. Danger increased, and no one traveled faithfully. They shifted the landmarks of peace and removed them from their places, and the dwelling of hope and love was thrown into confusion. Like bandits, minds lay in ambush for other minds, and people stripped their fellow human beings of good things. The treasury of faith was full of great riches, and people plundered it, not with love but with deceit. The deceitful joined in a scheme with the deceiver, and with their pronouncements plundered the undivided confession of faith. The insolent conspired in wickedness with the rebel, and disturbed the peace of the Creator's name that existed between us and them. Wicked priests became partners in discord and raised a rebellion, refusing to heed the word of peace. The word of peace placed them in a haven of peace, but they drove peace out from the midst of peace into the wilderness outside. Peace, the Creator’s name, wanders in the wilderness outside, with nowhere to enter and stay among those who know him. Like a poor man, he is driven from his rightful home, while falsehood enters his inherited house and plunders his possessions. Strife has seized the domain of peace and lives in it, raising its voice and shouting arrogantly against righteousness. The wilderness is not as frightening to the bandits who live there as disputes are to those who side with peace. Those who inhabit the wilderness are not as alarmed by wild beasts as those who love love are shaken by deceit. A great tragedy has occurred in our generation, with its bitter impulses: the cause of peace has become a cause of every evil. The priesthood came into being among earthly people for the sake of peace, but the priests turned the order of peace toward strife. It was given to us to serve as light and salt, but its light grew dark, its taste became insipid, and it turned back to the earth. The one who gave it called it the forgiver of wrongdoing and the giver of life, but its wrongdoing increased, and the fragrance of life faded from it. The divine command gave it the keys of heaven, but it neither entered itself nor opened the door to those who repent.

The priests shut the door of mercy in people’s faces and did not accept the remorse and tears of those pleading with them. The priests hid the word of life from mortals and did not extend a hand to those dead in wrongdoing so that they might live freely. Without compassion, they pronounced condemnation on sinners and did not apply the medicine of repentance to their sores. They approached the work to which they had been appointed with negligence, and rendered the thanksgiving they owed under compulsion. The herald of the Spirit called the priestly office “work,” but they turned it into a title of earthly authority. They regarded the orders of the church as earthly and, like outsiders, demanded recognition of their ranks from people. The priest sits like a judge at the entrance to his house, and like a ruler he raises his voice and demands payments. The ignorant man raises the title of authority over his hearers, without realizing that his office is far removed from authority. Your office is not one of authority, fool! Why are you deluded? You are a slave and a servant of your fellow servants. You are not appointed to exact payment, man! What are you demanding? Mercy called you to the King’s gate to show favor freely. The great treasure entrusted to your hands is not yours. Why do you boast about what is not yours as though it were your own? Mortal, you are the treasurer of the King over all. Do not boast when you give from your master’s household. Your master gave you resources from his treasury to distribute. See that you do not wrong your fellow servants by showing favoritism. Listen to your master’s voice accusing the wicked servant. Manage things well, so that you do not become his companion in judgment. The Creator is going to examine his servants with righteous judgment. Woe to anyone who hid his master's money from the moneylenders! Amid tumult and trembling comes the scrutiny of his judgment. Woe to anyone who did not lovingly show mercy to his fellow servants! With fire he tests the deeds and words of body and soul. Woe to anyone who did not build pure labors into the building of truth! Without neglect, he pronounces judgment on every rank, and he is not intimidated by the authority of priests and kings. For priests, he makes his punishment all the more severe,

in proportion to the gift and the greatness of the power they received from him. He makes their punishment doubly harsh, without mercy, because they were given authority to forgive, but did not show mercy and forgive. Before angels and human beings he brings them to judgment, because they were honored in the sight of earthly and heavenly beings. In the sight of earthly and heavenly beings he honored them, but they treated that honor with contempt through things unworthy of his dignity. Above the assemblies of heavenly beings he honored them, but these mortals did not discern and understand the rank to which they had ascended. He raised them to a lofty rank, higher than the Watchers, but they did not consider how greatly lowly humanity had been exalted. The rank they received testifies to how greatly they were exalted above all, for even the spiritual beings who are higher than they are stand lower than they do. The Watchers are not authorized to ascend to the rank they received, nor are they capable of carrying out its ministry in their own persons. Awesome are the assemblies of heavenly beings and their authorities, yet when compared with the priesthood, they are far inferior. Gabriel is glorious and Michael is great, as their names testify. Yet even so, their titles are inferior to the priesthood. The name of the priesthood is a title greater than everything else; and if anything is greater than anything else, it is beneath the priesthood [?]. The priests despised the lofty rank that honored them, and disfigured its beauty with the ugliness of their deeds. In every way they despised its honorable name, until contemptible people scoffed and laughed at its degradation. They sold for a price that gift which cannot be sold. Though the world cannot supply its worth, they fixed a price for it. They exchanged for passing things the rank that cannot be exchanged. Though nothing is comparable to its name, they assigned it an equivalent. O shameless greed that cannot be restrained, which set a price on what is difficult to put up for sale! O priesthood, which exchanged its name for paltry things! Though everything belongs to it, it gave away what was its own without gain. With what was not its own, it foolishly bought what was its own. And now it is mocked between buyer and seller. One wrongs it by giving it away for a contemptible price, and another despises it by acquiring it for worthless things.

Between buyer and seller its disgrace increases, because they do not perceive what power is hidden within it. You ignorant people who cannot distinguish good from evil, why have you sold height and depth without knowledge? You arrogant people whom foolish pride has led astray, why have you exchanged heavenly things for contemptible dust? A pearl is not sold without experts, yet here is the absurdity: fools have sold the priesthood. Engraved gems are found only in the treasuries of kings, yet here is the marvel: the Holy of Holies is [?] in the marketplaces. Worldly offices are not granted without discernment, yet no questions are asked about the administration of the wisdom of truth. This alone the priest asks when he grants it: whether there is gold. Otherwise, he makes no examination before selling. The priest considers the size of the gift and then grants it; if the gift is large, he too increases what he grants and gives it generously. The buyer, too, trades in it according to his losses, devising ways to recover through his profession what he has lost. Its seller regards its service as a profession, and its buyers, too, deal in it as merchandise. No broker trading in earthly things is like the broker who buys and sells spiritual things. There is no dispute over perishable possessions like the struggle that people wage over things unseen. Kings and tyrants have not waged battles against one another as priests have attacked priests like robbers. Like robbers, priests have [?] the priesthood, and in their contentiousness they have trampled one another without pity. Through their contentiousness they have disturbed the world that was at peace, and now it fights night and day without end. Through their divisions they have torn the garment of faith, and countless faiths have multiplied on earth. In their envy they have caused, caused divisions among the churches. Now everyone is divided, and no one agrees with what his fellow says. The assembly that Christ gathered through his suffering is one body, but the priests have divided it into countless parts.

One is the body that became a sacrifice for our reconciliation, but fools have destroyed it by mixing one with another. One is the nature of the One who is, and he is as he is, but the senseless have mixed him with the fashioned work of his hands. The sacrifice for the salvation of our lives was complete in body and soul, but the wicked have made him deficient in soul and without a mind. The Word, the Son of God, is one with the one who begot him, but pride has divided that equality, though it has not divided it. The nature of the divine being is without limit and invisible, but the reckless have confined it within bodily members, though they have not confined it. The natures, distinct in their being, became one person, but the dull of heart do not understand how they came to be in him. I said that they came to be in him not by nature but by love; even so, one remains distinct from [?], just as it is distinct. The Creator is distinct and is not mixed with the work of his hands, and creation is lowly beside the greatness of the power that created it. A creature remains a creature, however great it becomes through its causes; and the Self-existent remains self-existent, however much he is diminished by a borrowed name. The Maker was diminished by a borrowed name—though far be it from him to have been diminished! For even this expression, “a borrowed name,” is presumptuous. It is presumptuous for someone to attribute change to the Self-existent, and arrogant to say that he is diminished [?], even in name. Self-existence can never be diminished from what it is—not through borrowed language, nor in deeds, nor in any way at all. The inclination of the wicked has sought to diminish the hidden nature, and no one is to blame for this disgrace except the priests. If those lying in wait had properly established a single confession of faith, fools would not have built straw into the building of truth. If the priests had directed their impulses toward the right goal, the dull-hearted would not have hurled insulting words. If the priests had loved the unity of the body of Christ, divisive schisms would not have sprung up within the churches. If the priests had trained their minds in spiritual things,

people’s love for the things to come would not have grown cold. The priests have become for us a cause of life and a cause of death. If they had remained in the order of life, it would have been a blessing for our race. The cause of death has now prevailed through their deeds, and now everyone is eager to kill his fellow without mercy. From them people learned to envy other human beings, and now everyone is clothed in angry zeal against his neighbor. They began by taking revenge for insults, and now everyone threatens to exact vengeance for an insult from his fellow. They disrupted the sound order that once prevailed among us, and now our way of life is confused, and we have no order befitting human beings. They ought to have made people wise in their childishness and, through their words, given understanding to those without understanding. They ought to have walked uprightly toward the promise of the world beyond and, through their labors, shown the path to the kingdom. The Creator promised the kingdom on high to human nature, but the priests blocked the road to the heights, and no one travels it. Travelers have ceased their journey in good deeds, and no one travels along the path of the hope of faith. And if anyone does travel, whether out of love or by natural inclination, the coldness of the priests does not let him proceed uprightly. The great danger of their conflicts hangs over everyone, and no one trusts even someone whose love is sincere. Everyone has been cast into division and discord, and no one trusts his fellow, even in a word. If anyone does trust, his trust is no real trust, for snares are laid on every side in the path of his trust. People catch one another with words as though with snares. Perhaps silence and quiet would be more fitting than conversation. Speech is the sign of the rationality present in our nature. But what are we to do, since envy has prevented its exercise? The priests’ envy has reared up like a savage lion, and now it bites reason with the fang of anger. The priesthood, a destroyer of people, has acquired the fangs of a wild beast and has begun biting and kicking people without understanding. The peace of human beings and spiritual beings was bound up in it.

But now angels and human beings are afraid to approach it. A great tragedy has occurred in our generation, so full of sins: from what we trusted, terror and despair have sprung up for us. Our hope and faith were placed in the priesthood, but now it has fallen, and with it has fallen the confidence of our souls. Like a foundation, it supported the structure of our lives; then the winds of lust blew, and it shook and swayed. It was not the priesthood that shook and swayed, as I said. Weak priests trembled at the sound of the wind of temptation. It was not the priesthood itself that was shaken by the things I have recounted about its ministers. Their minds grew small, and they fell short of their duty. It was not the priesthood itself that disturbed the message of peace that dwelt within it. Those at its right hand were unwilling to remain in the structure of its love. It was not the priesthood itself that treated its dignity with contempt before outsiders. The guardians of its treasury belittled its [?] through their actions. I saw its mysteries treated with contempt as the mouths of fools spoke, and amazement gripped me at who was insulting whom with [?]. Through my verses I wanted to avenge the reproach of its humiliation on the insolent people who despised its nobility and dishonored its ranks. I saw dull-hearted people mocking the greatness of its ranks[?], and I became intensely zealous to bring forth bold words. It is boldness for anyone to find fault with those in authority. And I, who have found fault, am not unaware of how I have done so. Zeal for the priests compelled me to find fault with their deeds, because they abandoned the path of faith and made a path of falsehood. My words reproached their lawless deeds, and although I have indeed reproached them, I do not despise the order they hold. It was not out of envy that I reproached them as I did, nor was it out of malice that I accused them concerning their deeds. Truth bears witness that I have not hated them and do not hate them. I hated the wrongdoing within them, which brought wicked strife upon us. They are greatly loved by me because of the rank entrusted to their hands, and greatly hated by me because of the wrongdoing they have spread over the earth. I love them because of love, love, and because of their order; and I hate them because of wrongdoing and partiality. I do not encourage anyone to exalt himself above their ranks,

so that they may not be despised, however evil their conduct may be. With discerning love, let us pay them the debt of love. Even if they are unworthy, let us not withhold what is fitting. The greatest of the great established a rule concerning their ranks, and he does not permit us to despise the order prescribed for them. Let anyone who despises them despise their lawless conduct, without neglecting the duty appropriate to their name. The honored name that is above all has been placed upon their heads, and we must not despise them as though they were evil men. The keys of heaven are held in the hands of their minds, and no one enters that dwelling without them. On this condition, let us honor them lovingly, as treasurers and guardians of the love of spiritual things. With this intention, I too refrained from accusing them, so that no one would venture to mock their great name. My accusation is not the accusation of a [?]; rather, it expresses an intention full of love and bears witness to pain. Love [?] bears witness that I rebuked them lovingly, and it permitted me to plead my case against them according to its laws. I pleaded my case lawfully against the priests of the Church, because I saw that they had strayed from the lawful rule. My discourse has traveled along the path of its words from the beginning, and I will not stop recounting it until the end. The companionship of his love has pleased me more than anything else. Far be it from me to forget him, neglect him, or cease speaking with him.
On Reproof
Discourse Forty-Six: On Reproof

The human being is confined in the prison of mortality, and he has no desire to leave it, not even at his death. The weak man lies in the dungeon of susceptibility to suffering, yet he takes no pleasure in escaping its harshness. He lies bound and cast down by the harsh ropes of desires, yet he finds no relief in rising from the downfall caused by his desires. A love of passionate craving dwells within him and is woven through him like fire through the wood of a forest. His whole being burns continually in the fire of provocations, and there is no time when he is not inflamed by one of the passions. The fire of his desires is hidden within his limbs, and it is not extinguished until his mortal life is extinguished. The love of money lies like a chain upon his soul, and it is not loosened until death dissolves his body. The impulses of his discerning mind are harnessed under the yoke of glory, and unless the day of his departure breaks it, he is not set free. The harsh bridle of fleshly desire is laid upon his limbs and enslaves him like an animal without understanding. Mortality is a harsh weapon, yet to him it is not harsh; it is a prison of susceptibility to suffering, yet he does not regard it as such. Death is hidden in the love of money, yet to him it is like life. The love of glory is a double scourging, yet to him it is pleasure. Fire and the worm spring from fleshly desire, yet he considers the torment set forth in the Scriptures to be like a dream.

Like one without reason, he travels the path of his rational nature; like a fool, he tramples upon the order of his discernment. He resembles a beast in his habits and conduct, falling only a little short of the animals—indeed, not falling short at all. He resembles an animal, not because he is like one, but because he chooses to be; for if he chose otherwise, no one could compel him as one compels a dumb animal. He is not yoked like dumb animals to the [?] of earthly things, nor does he wander unknowingly in the delusion of desires. He knows that he is rational, but does not obey his reason. He is aware that he is clever, but does not use his cleverness against his passions. He is clever at causing harm, but simple when it comes to escaping harm; crafty at lying, but ignorant when it comes to explaining truths. He is eloquent in saying things that support his weakness, but silent and mute when it comes to reproving his wicked ways. He is discerning and alert in distinguishing what benefits him, but foolish and bewildered when it comes to despising the faults of his shameful deeds. He boasts of his knowledge and reproaches dumb animals for their ignorance, yet he has never reproached himself for the things in which he deserves reproach. He is reproached by everyone, yet does not consider why this is so. He carefully judges the injustice outside himself, but does not examine the ugly things within himself. O judge who judges everything in the furnace of his scrutiny, examine your [?] as you examine the evident faults of your fellows. You who condemn your companions when they incur the guilt of sins, condemn yourself for the guilt incurred by your own sins. You who train dumb animals to resemble you in rational behavior, order your own life so that it resembles the life of rational beings. You who use your discernment to compel creatures without discernment, compel your own nature to discern good things properly. You who impart your habits to creatures that do not understand human speech, train yourself in the things that belong to your free nature. You who put bridles into the mouths of speechless animals so that they travel properly, bridle your impulses so that the course of your journey may be peaceful.

You who cultivate the earth and cut through mountains with your diligence, cultivate your mind so that it bears the fruits of reverence for the truth. You who subdue the waves and overcome the winds by your skill, subdue your mind so that it is not thrown into turmoil by the blast of injustice. You who hunt creeping creatures and conceal traps for the beasts of the cliffs, hunt down your soul’s ugly habits as you hunt dumb animals. You who uproot thorns from the silent fields, uproot your wicked deeds like weeds from a field. You who bring peace to the world through the word of peace that dwells within you, bring peace to your inclinations by that same manner of peacemaking. You are a source of peace, O human being—a name of honor! Honor your name, so that peace may not be disturbed through your name. Through the peace of your name, this temporal world is preserved and kept at peace. Guard your freedom so that you are not put to shame through a lack of freedom. You have a hidden battle with everyone, and everyone with you. Do not grow slack, lest you be condemned and bring condemnation upon everyone. Your struggle compelled me to address you with a discourse, and your lack of diligence forced me to rebuke you as one who is negligent. Come, hear of your guilt from my own guilt, and judge fairly whether you are right to condemn yourself. Test my words in the testing furnace of your discernment, and look carefully at the exposure of the falseness of your deceit. Let speaker and listener alike stand as though in court, and let whoever is found guilty not shrink from despising his wrongdoing. Listen, then, and speak about the charge against you, O human being: why is your life confused and your course fruitless? Why does the conduct of your life resemble that of animals, and why is its order foreign to the established order of rational nature? Why is creation troubled by the fumes of your bitterness, and why is there no deed whose taste is sweet in the mouths of those who perform it? Why is the changing of the seasons different from every other time, with no resemblance to the seasons that preceded them? Why is the regular course of their changes uneven, and whom do they overpower, or by whom are they overpowered, contrary to their appointed order? Why does summer resemble summer and winter resemble winter, and why do cold and heat increase and decrease? Why, although the course of the months and days remains the same, is the food that sustains our lives not supplied as it was before?

Why are earthly provisions lacking in human life, and why is no good reward given for exhausting labors? Why is life in time shaken along with eternal life, and why is there no one in our generation who possesses what belongs to earth or to [?]? Why are pains of body and mind so numerous, and why is there no one among us who is healthy both physically and spiritually? Why is ignorance so widespread among all ranks, and why is there no wise person who heals the pains of ignorance? Physicians of body and soul have disappeared from among us, and no one concerns himself with our health, not even in words. Those who understand the sufferings of our vulnerable condition have disappeared from among us, and our race is close to being carried off by sufferings and pains. The world has grown dark with the darkness of ignorance, and indeed we grope along walls at noon, as it is written. Understanding of the fear of truth has departed from our minds, and nothing remains that has not been brought to nothing. Oh, how much harder than anything hard is the hardness of our hearts, which does not gain understanding through the hardships that scourge it! Oh, how blind the eye of our soul is to its duty, refusing to turn and see the blemishes that are always within it! Oh, how dull is the hearing of our quick-eared mind, which hears and remains silent, and does not make us hear what is fitting! Oh, how greatly our free nature neglects its freedom, failing to make known to us the duties proper to free people! Oh, how immeasurably our own inclination hates itself, failing to stir us to remorse so that we might turn even a little from our evil deeds! Our body is struck, yet it does not grieve over its destruction; it returns to the earth, yet does not consider what the cause is. We do not reflect on the cause of the scourges that strike our bodies, nor do we investigate the sufferings that distress us. Our heart is like hard stone in the face of blows; as though it felt nothing, countless sufferings are making it suffer. Pains multiply, sufferings oppress, and death presses forward, yet our heart does not seem even to have heard of any of these things. Famine threatens, captivity carries people away, and the sword destroys.

Yet our mind reclines as though on a bed of pleasure. War grows fierce, devastation increases, and blood is poured out, yet to our mind everything counts as nothing. There are divisions in the church, turmoil among the pagans, and strife everywhere. Yet if someone asks whether we are aware, we are not aware. There is no remembrance in our mind of the scourges afflicting our body; and even if there is [?], it is not truly preserved within a person. The remembrance of true things is not truly preserved, because the words of the mouth do not agree with the mind within. Some repeat the recollection of teachings in words alone, while erasing from their minds the remembrance of good things. Some are skilled at describing the different kinds of goodness, while their thoughts are filled with a store of shameful things. Some zealously and fiercely prosecute injustice [?], yet cannot reproach their own injustice even with a word. Some revile adultery and theft, yet both are within them, and their own free will does not condemn them. Some put on an appearance of chastity and humility, yet nothing is so debased as their mind. Some show a loving face to their friend, while their inward inclination sharpens a sword for bloodshed. Some express grief over afflictions without truly grieving, resembling a wolf deceitfully clothed in the likeness of a sheep. Some know how to accuse others of shameful things, yet the shameful things within themselves do not seem shameful to them. Some read the books of the Spirit eloquently, yet their minds stammer when it comes to fulfilling the words through deeds. Some explain even the meaning of hidden things, yet do not perceive the hidden deceits in their own minds. Some remind others of the reckoning at the coming judgment, yet are not themselves convinced even that the Lord of judgment exists. Some warn others not to act unjustly with what is not their own, yet conceal countless treacherous traps to wrong their companions. Some vigorously condemn the love of money, yet it is firmly planted within them like a root deep in the earth. Some skillfully denounce the love of praise, yet it lurks within them like a viper in the crevices of a rock.

Some call the desire for [?] filthy, as though they were innocent, yet are submerged in it as in a chasm that cannot be crossed. Some recoil from envious and deceitful people, yet the fire of anger against their companions is heaped up within them. Some mock loathsome arrogance and pride, yet the height of their own haughtiness cannot be measured. Some mock angry and hot-tempered people, yet when they become enraged, they are not merely hot-tempered but demonic. Some accuse those who bear grudges against their neighbors, yet never let go of their own angry resentment. Some have eyes sharp enough to see specks, yet do not notice the beams in their own eyes. Some grieve, mourn, and lament over hateful deeds, yet the memory of their own wrongdoing has never entered their minds. Some sigh loudly over evil deeds, yet have never felt sorrow or grief over their own evil deeds since the day they were born. Some even distribute alms from the groans of others, yet if an orphan meets them in the marketplace, they lift up their ragged cloak. Some explain spiritual matters before their listeners, yet are bound and strangled by an insatiable appetite for bodily things. Some strain out insignificant gnats—the faults of their companions—yet swallow camels—the hideous sins their own hearts produce. Some think that virtues reach their perfection in them, yet are as far from them as a distant mountain is far away. Some are falsely praised by liars, yet if the stones had mouths, they would cry out, “Away with them!” How many have risen and attained positions of leadership, yet were not worthy to be servants to the servants of servants! How many have lived in abundance and bodily health, yet the sun should not have shone upon their lives! How many have deceived through the trappings [?] of one guise after another! Yet a day is coming that will expose the falseness of their guises. How many have become people by whom the simplehearted swear, yet on the day of judgment will become a laughingstock to those who see them! How many countless differences there are among human beings!

Yet no one reflects on the wrongdoing of human beings. People are sick with the hideous [?] of hateful wrongdoing, yet pay no attention to the wounds of their minds. The sickness of their minds is hidden within their minds, yet they will not agree to apply a suitable remedy to it. Ignorance has blinded them to what is right, and they look at one another while being ruined by their companions. Come, you who are silent, and see how silent the speakers have become! They have died in sin, yet have neither stirred nor perceived their own deaths. Who has died a death like the death of the dead of our generation? It strikes everyone down, yet no one knows what this death is. In what generation have evil deeds grown as strong as ours? Though they are many, those who commit them are never satisfied with them. The minds of the wicked love evil insatiably. This is the wonder: how evil it is, and how dearly loved! The wickedness of evil has compelled me to examine its wickedness, so that, when it is exposed, people may see themselves. The ugliness of evil has made people ugly to behold, and I have portrayed it in words so that they may look at it and see how ugly it is. My speech has condemned her ugliness, and my mouth condemns it, so that everyone may learn to condemn evil ways. I saw evil ways disgracing human beings, and I grieved greatly over the disgrace brought upon the greatness of our race. The Creator called our great race a noble race, by raising it to a title belonging to the greatness of his own being. The Head, who is the beginning of our life, called it by this name when he was setting out to go and reign in the realm above: “A certain man,” he said, “whose lineage was noble, went to a very distant country to reign there.” Our race came to reign in the realm above through a member of our race, yet our race forgot the promises spoken to our race. “He raised us up,” it is said, “and seated us with him above in heaven,” yet there is no remembrance of that ascent in our minds. The herald who proclaimed him wrote that he intercedes for us. Yet if someone asks, no one knows where it is written. There is no remembrance of the Scriptures in people's minds. And if there is, it is as though there were not, for half the human being is occupied with [?]. With only half of the human being, people study the words of the Spirit—

with that part of the human being whose portion is lowly and whose understanding is limited. It is the lowly body that is occupied with studying precious things, while the glorious soul sleeps and rests from work. Woe to our race! To what depths its honor has descended!
