It has abandoned the things above and occupied itself with earthly things. Woe to our people! Where has the goodness of their blessed state been left behind? They have forgotten the enduring reality of things to come because of things that are visible. Mortals who love distraction have loved visible things and have counted the benefits of true things as nothing. O perverse people, who have overturned the order of good things, hated blessings, and loved torments without end! O rebels, who have disturbed peace with their quarrels and begun waging a hidden war against their brothers! They learned the way of peace only with difficulty, through one human being, and very easily forgot the goal he showed them. Against their will he turned them away from my errors, but of their own will they despised the commandments he gave them. He taught them to preserve love and peace before him, and impressed them like a seal upon their senses. “By these,” he said, “the world will know that you are my disciples: by the love and peace you show one another.” Let us therefore inquire whether these things exist in our troubled generation, and see among whom the goal of love and peace remains. Let us pursue this search for love and peace in the Church, where that teacher of good things placed it. Let us learn the purpose of the master of the house from the members of his household, for they know how to discern good things well. Church, reveal to us the mysteries you learned from your betrothed, so that we may teach them to those who ask us questions [?] about you. Bride of the King, whom the King betrothed to himself through the sacrifice of his body, explain to your children the wonders that took place at your betrothal. You have forgotten, bride, the covenant you made with your betrothed, and you have been false to the gifts of the Spirit that he gave you in his love. The King honored you with glorious gifts and awe-inspiring powers. Where are they? Show what he entrusted to you. Where is the robe that he wove and gave you from within the waters? It has been fouled with the hateful filth of your disgraceful deeds.

Where is the ring of the Spirit of revelation that he placed on your hands? It fell and was lost—not from its rank, but from you. Where are the crown and the authority from on high that were entrusted to you? They are not with you, because you did not remain steadfast in love toward him. Who plundered your wealth, you who possessed divine riches? Fierce passions and tyrannical demons! Oh, what has happened to you! Passions and demons plundered the treasure of the children of the church, and [?] they wander about like beggars asking for alms. Their passions entered their minds like robbers and stripped them, yet they neither stirred nor noticed that they were being robbed. Their impulses and their senses sank into the sleep of wickedness, and love, hope, and faith were lost to them. They possessed three kinds in the land where they lived, but they lost them through their ignorance of their own deeds. There is no one who believes, no one who hopes, and no one who loves. And if these are absent, the hope of our race is lost to us. Through faith, hope, and love, our dead humanity came to life. How can we live when our life is far from us? Those who give us life saw our unworthiness and fled from us, and our humanity was left like a person without a soul. People live without the vitality of faith, and they go about their deeds without hope and love. The deceit in their hearts tore the garment of faith, and they stood like Adam, naked and without a covering. The children of the church stand naked and without shame, and the demons mock them just as they mocked Adam in Eden. The camp of Adam’s race has become a great laughingstock. This is the mockery: after receiving life, we have died in sin. Sin and death held us as a pledge. Then one of us arose, pledged his body, and set our bodies free. He pledged his body for a period of time, not forever. He remained in death for three days, then came to life and gave life. He fixed three days for himself to remain in pledge, and then he took back the pledge of his entire race. By the resurrection of his body, he raised the bodies of his companions,

and gave them a share in the blessing of immortal life. He mingled the vitality of life with our nature, which was full of death, and immortal life began to pulse within our mortality. Through this life our humanity came alive in the Son of our humanity, but it turned back and died through human affairs, as it had before. Mortals have died a double death in this age: one of nature and one of sin. A double woe! Those who die in our days die in body and soul, and no one cares about the resurrection that comes through the soul’s repentance. The soul’s repentance revives bodies and limbs, yet the soul remains silent and does not repent of its deeds. Woe to you, soul, and still greater woe to you, soul of the priests, for you do not awaken to show mercy to your own kind. The priests will have to answer doubly for these deaths, for if they had remained steadfast in faith, everyone would have lived. They stripped off faith, that lovely garment, and when the demons saw it, they ran toward everyone to strip him. They tore apart impartial love through their partiality, and they cut off the road of peace through their negligence. From them mortality welled up amid the vitality of our lives, because they dared to say that the giver of life died on the cross. That life which gave life to the one who brought us to life—the priests put it to death with their lawless blasphemies. This blasphemy has disturbed the earth and its inhabitants, and now everyone has risen against whoever says that the Living One did not die. A double death: he kills his fellow and kills God, if his fellow does not confess according to the creed of his perversity. Fool, where have you seen the Eternal One dying? And who taught you to kill your fellow, who does not kill you? You who are slain by your sins, why do you kill the one who does not die? You who are mad with pride, why do you go mad destroying your fellows? The sword of fools, the enemies of peace, rules the earth, and now it is laying waste the world with the sword of mortality. The one who attributes suffering carries the sword of sufferings on the tip of his tongue, and he destroys the ranks of those who do not agree with him about susceptibility to suffering. A new war over susceptibility to suffering has [?] me now:

And now it urges me to hurl my words at those who prepare it. I long to hurl words, [?], at those who prepare it, so that perhaps they may be scattered from their agreement about susceptibility to suffering. Their very contentiousness does not allow me to disregard them; it compels me to mix their name into all my discourses. My discourse traveled through the account of the sufferings to which we are subject. I heard of suffering and mixed its story with the story of our sufferings. I grieved over our sufferings and composed words full of suffering, and then I encountered an account of suffering greater than those sufferings. The wicked spattered me with the great suffering laid upon the Creator, and I stopped recounting the sufferings of our souls and stood amazed at it. Amazement seized me at this suffering in the divinity, and my concern for our sufferings grew small in comparison with it. Perhaps we are being held to account for the insult of this suffering; that is why the nations’ war is fiercer than at any other time. Perhaps it is the disgrace of susceptibility to suffering, which they have concealed within the divine being, that is hastening famine and captivity upon our souls. Perhaps the blasphemous ingratitude of the body that comes from us awakens diseases and makes pains well up in our limbs. Perhaps— The mingling that blots out one nature in another causes the succession of the seasons to fall out of order. Perhaps the insults that fools have hurled at those who know the truth are what drive us about in every guise. The innocent blood that wrongdoers have brazenly shed urges death to destroy swiftly. The foolish jealousy that ignorant people have shown toward the wise stirs up anger, makes fury boil over, and brings locusts. These things have disturbed the peace and thrown us into turmoil. Look, the world is tossed about like the sea by storms. Harsh afflictions batter the ship of our mortality, and there is no sailor who knows how to reach a peaceful harbor. Our race stands amid the storms of ignorance, and among our race there is no helmsman who can still the fury. There is no one to calm the fury of the afflictions directed against humanity, and no one to ease the bitter pain of fierce wrath. People threaten their fellow human beings with fierce wrath, and the person who knows how to carry his anger through to the end is praised.

Deceivers triumph through deceit and are even applauded; the more cunning someone is, the more he is honored among liars. Falsehood prospers far more than truth in our evil time, and lying is loved more than righteousness. There is no righteousness at all, not in any rank, for even those considered trustworthy are not as trustworthy as they seem. Turmoil carries along every rank, good and bad; even goodness itself has evil mixed with its goodness. There is, in truth, no truthfulness free from stains, since no person is anything but human, with his passions accompanying him. The whole race of Adam is stained by passions. And which Adam is there whose body's moisture is not earth? There is one Adam who was not stained by his earthly elements: the one whose embodiment leaves fools in confusion. There is one who overcame the bitter frost of susceptibility to suffering: the one through whose suffering wrongdoers strike at the one who cannot suffer. There is one who conquered, and his own mouth testifies that he is the one who conquered. It is therefore clear that no one is innocent except one. There is no one innocent, especially in this time, when everyone has sold integrity for favoritism. Everyone faces his fellow with favoritism, and words without deeds pass and vanish like a shadow. A friend supplies his friend with words, and a companion his companion: “Peace to me, peace to you”—but there is no deed that contains peace. With the mouth alone, one mouth greets its fellow, while the mind does not notice when one mouth has greeted another. Such is love in our deceitful generation: it deceitfully stays and travels through every undertaking. Such is the picture my words have drawn of our conduct, though perhaps they have not managed to make the likeness match its original. There is no painter capable of painting the likeness of our wickedness, because the varieties of its evils outnumber his pigments. Oh, the varieties of our shameful deeds cannot be counted, for no scribe can reckon their total on his fingers. The hand is too weak to grasp the bow of our wicked generation, and the mouth is too feeble to recount the words of its falsehood. Words without deeds are full of falsehood;

and the falsehood of someone who does not lie cannot be established. The customs of every land are clothed in envy and [?], and there is no deed in which they are not present, nor any deed apart from them. They bind and loosen spells through their deeds, and they want the world and its labors to proceed according to their will. The proud-minded person does whatever he does with pride, and the envious person is full of jealousy toward everyone. Two savage lions dwell among people, and no one knows how to look closely at their crimes. They have wrought great destruction in creation and continue to do so, yet no one takes notice, reflects, or grieves over their destruction. They roar savagely at everyone amid their ravages, and they move and wander among people like wild animals. The sound of lions is not as terrifying to animals as envy and pride are to humanity. No wild beast has injured another wild beast as people have injured their fellow human beings. Nor has one bird been harmed by another as friends have harmed those they love. The peace of creatures without speech surpasses that of speaking creatures, and love is preserved in their natures far better than among us. The statement I have made is full of absurdity, if it is true that love endures among speechless creatures but is absent among us. Let us again consider the word concerning us, even now, and bring sorrow to bear upon the deeds arising from our passions. With sorrow let us reject the passions of our souls and the blemishes of our bodies, and perhaps we shall be healed of the sins of body and soul. Let us justly pronounce a righteous judgment upon our own minds, so that perhaps we may escape that judgment which has no end. It is written that judging ourselves cancels the judgment to come. Our will, then, controls the court both here and there. Come, human being, king who holds authority over two courts: undo your deeds and free yourself from blame. In the judgment here, condemn yourself of your own will, so that you may not be condemned in the judgment where your own will has no place.
On rebuking the daughters of Eve, and [?]
Discourse Forty-Seven. On rebuking the daughters of Eve, and [?] the schemes and tricks they practice.

Eve, the spring from which life flowed to humanity, turned the drink of her sweetness into the bitterness of death. The rib that became a helper for Adam when he was alone became a bow in the hands of the Evil One against Adam. The commandment that placed life in her called her “Life”; but she changed the name of life to mortality. Adam too prophetically called her “flesh of my flesh”; but she dishonored his prophecy through her unworthiness. He said that everyone should call her “woman,” a name of harmony; but she shattered humanity’s peace through her contentiousness. She entered Eden with Adam when she first came into being; and with him she received the life-giving commandment concerning the tree. The commandment established by the Creator was full of life; but through her carelessness she made it a spring flowing with death. From the time she came into being, she became a cause of death and a companion of the evil one; and from her limbs sprang traps and snares for us. Unworthiness appeared in her from the beginning; her thoughts conceived bitterness, and her heart gave birth to it. She smeared her face with the color of insolence in that beautiful place; and she did not shrink from speaking with the deceiver. Like a prostitute she stood naked in Eden; and when the evil one saw her, he ran to meet her and fornicated with her. Through the outward senses the devil fornicated with her; his seed reached into her soul and became established in it. Through hearing, the king’s bride, betrothed to Adam, committed adultery; and before her wedding day arrived, she conceived wickedness. Her soul carried loathsome wickedness from defilement; and she did not wish to observe the proper order of discernment. Evil desire shamefully took her mind captive; and without hesitation she stretched out her hands toward the tree.

She deceitfully devised a scheme with the deceiver; and she did not reveal the secret of his wickedness to Adam until she had eaten. The insolent woman sought to be exalted above her husband; for this reason she ate, and she also gave some to her husband, and he ate. Her will agreed with her corrupter rather than with Adam; and perhaps it was he who advised her to eat the fruit first. She has listened to his counsel from the beginning until now; and her heart has not withdrawn from involvement in his abominations. She entered into an evil pact with the murderer; and she has no desire to part from him, even to the end. She longs to fornicate with him in abominable deeds; and her inclination finds no rest in sharing in good things. She loves the destroyer’s love insatiably; and her heart runs without restraint after his company [?]. In every guise her mind is drawn toward intercourse with him; and on every pretext she longs to arouse [?] her soul’s desire. Her soul loves desire for the evil one more than Adam; and her mind embraces his abominations insatiably. Devoid of understanding, she fornicates in her mind with the murderer; and she does not realize that fellowship with him is an inheritance of death. Her mind is bound to fleshly desire night and day; and her thoughts are occupied with shameful intercourse. The hateful contemplation of debauchery occupies her constantly; and she takes no pleasure in communion with spiritual life. She had become utterly corrupt, with no place in her where holiness could dwell. The Evil One dwells in her and lives in her continually, and he leaves no room for truth to enter her. There is no gain for anyone who labors to build her up, for the Evil One constantly mocks him and makes his labor fruitless. In the beginning, the maker of all made her a beautiful dwelling, but she disfigured her own beauty with shameful deeds. Her appearance was marvelous, and she was lovely before she sinned. But after she sinned, she drove angels and human beings away from her.

The heavenly hosts marveled at her beauty when she was created. Once she became defiled, they turned and were astonished at her shameful deeds. The spiritual beings saw the soul’s ugliness and fled from us. They were unwilling to maintain their kinship with our race. Because of her, they hated fellowship with our humanity. They withdrew and settled in the heights, so that they would not look at us. They considered their labor on our behalf wasted labor, and they were unwilling to carry out the hidden will. The more they considered the wickedness of our shameful deeds, the more they armed themselves with the weapons of wrath against our people. Whenever they remembered Eve, who picked the fruit, they exacted retribution for her wrongdoing upon fruits and crops. The more her daughters imitated her insolence, the more they withdrew from serving us. As the wickedness coming from them increased day by day, the zeal within the angels blazed beyond measure. The more the Creator was dishonored by their deeds, the more fiercely the angels prepared for battle against our people. As they corrupted themselves with the idols that demons had fashioned, the angels would not even consent to bring rain and dew. They sat in deep mourning over our evil deeds, waiting for us either to perish or to be renewed. The labor pains of suffering struck their understanding, and they travailed to bring forth either our death or our resurrection. The Creator, who sees everything, saw the severity of their suffering. He sent his command and comforted them in their sorrow. He sent his command to a daughter of Eve, who had brought death in. He formed a child in her and filled him with life for mortals [?]. He mixed life into the formation of the child born from her, so that through his life he might wipe death away from our humanity. To bring about peace, the restorer of peace fashioned an image in him, so that through him he might reconcile angels and human beings with his majesty. Through him he reconciled all things, earthly and heavenly, and in the harbor of his body, weary creatures found rest. From the place where ravenous death, the destroyer of human beings, had sprung forth, the medicine of life sprang forth, freely giving life to humankind. Through a daughter of humanity, death began to destroy;

and through a daughter of humanity, life began to renew. Where sin increased far beyond all bounds, there immeasurable righteousness grew strong. Where the devil sowed the gall of his deceit, there sprang up the ear of life that gives life to humanity. Through Eve, humanity’s enemy corrupted humankind; and through a woman, mercies captured them spiritually. She clothed us in a garment of perishable leaves, and she covered us with an imperishable robe of glory. That command, full of compassion, took pity on her lowly condition; it wove a garment within her body and covered her shame. His will willingly put on the garment taken from her, and with his hands he renewed the creation that transgression of the commandment had corrupted. See the blessings of the Good One, who graciously created the creation: he renewed us through ourselves, reconciled us through ourselves, and pardoned us through ourselves. Let us therefore compare the conduct of our lives with his gift, and see whether the soul’s work bears any resemblance to his mercies. Let us test our labors in the testing furnace of our discernment, and see how our ingratitude is exposed—how ungrateful it has been! Let us first examine Eve’s labors [?], and purge her ugliness with words as in a furnace. Let us bring Eve’s daughters into the furnace of words, and instead of heat, refine them with the fire of our verses. Let us bring words to bear on their lawless deeds, and burn the forest hidden beneath the adornment of their bodies. Their deeds provoked me to travel the path of words; they themselves pressed me to speak with them on behalf of justice. Justice itself compelled me, far beyond all bounds, to expose the falseness in their outward appearances before the eyes of onlookers. Abominable falseness lies hidden in the appearance of their bodies; and if it is exposed, no discerning person fails to sigh. Filthy wickedness fills the chambers of their thoughts; and if it is revealed before onlookers, they recoil from it. Shamelessness, a beast of two [?], dwells within them; and if it comes out, even the wild beasts flee from it. Their mind wears a white garment and takes pride in it; but if it is torn, they stand naked like Eve. They burn with fury and stir up jealous anger. Who can restrain the onslaught of their battles?

They are bold in insult, sharpened for [?], ready with reproach. What upright person can endure their abusive words? They are greedy for food, eager for drink, foul with lust. Who possesses freedom of soul and can disregard this and remain silent? At home are their battles, in the marketplace their commotion, and in the church their ambushes. With what wings can anyone who wishes to escape fly away? Their mouth is deceitful, their gaze shameless, their hearing false. Who is capable of recounting their faults? Their face is brazen, their conversation insolent, and encountering them leads to sin. Who would not grieve over their passions, so abominable are they? Their clothing is shameless, their footwear contemptible, their gait filthy. Perhaps even the earth finds it burdensome to carry them. They devise schemes, hide traps, and spread snares. Where can anyone who hates dealing with them flee? They take the soul captive, ensnare the mind, and bind its impulses. How is it possible to escape their schemes? They make the chaste stumble, bewilder the upright, and weaken the righteous. Woe to anyone who falls into the traps of their disturbances! They trouble the serene, stain the pure, and bind the shrewd. What can someone do who wants to live in purity? Their warfare is fierce, their weaponry is mighty, and their [?] is cruel. Woe to our nature because of the injuries that constantly beset it! Nature makes demands; inclination stirs up the heart’s desire. Lord of all natures, rebuke our nature so that it does not destroy us! Hunger is natural: our lowly nature eats and grows hungry. However much it eats, it becomes greedy again and demands food. The second burden is bodily desire, which dwells within it. Like food [?], the body brings forth food for its body. Eve is especially insistent in demanding this food, and constantly, without satisfaction, occupies herself with thinking about it. She wages war if you do not satisfy her soul’s desire, and with insatiable contention she demands it. Her daughters wage bitter warfare against us every day. With their disturbances they arm themselves against us as though with weapons. As though in combat, they contend with us night and day,

and shoot at us the sharp arrows of their tongues. Their mouths are sharper than a double-edged sword. Their blow penetrates to the soul and cannot be stopped. Those killed by the sword are not as numerous as those killed by them, nor is the destruction wrought by a fanged beast like their destruction. The harm they do is worse than that of venomous animals, and the [?] caused by their bites are difficult to heal. They corrupt the soul and leave blemishes on the mind. The sores they cause cannot be healed except by the Spirit. David bears witness to how grievous is the wound of the pain they cause: the sore of adultery lingered with him until his death. With the fang of adultery, Eve bit him whose soul was healthy, and he became sick and wasted in body throughout his life. For a long time he lay in a fever from her bites, crying out and wailing every day because of his sickness. He used to say, “All my wounds stink and fester, and here I am, groaning and roaring from the pain in my mind.” If Eve shattered David, the harp of the Spirit, who can stand firm before her assaults? If the seer of hidden things looked and became bewildered, let everyone close the eyes of his soul to dealings with her. If the soaring one, who terrified nations, trembled at her voice, let us stop our ears so that they are not terrified by the sound of her disturbances. Look what Eve’s daughter did to Adam’s son! Let everyone warn anyone he encounters, so that she does not strike him. Look at what the feeble rib did to the mighty warrior! Let one man say to his fellow, “Beware of Eve.” Let everyone fear the daughter of Eve, especially the righteous, lest she weaken their resolve as she did David’s. There is danger from her, even though she belongs to our own race; her faithfulness is not reliable, however chaste she may be. Let no one trust the promises she speaks without testing them, for look: there is no righteous man who listened to her enticements whom she did not bring down. She is full of wrongdoing, and falsehood dwells within her. No trust can be placed in her reliability, not even a little. Her words are sweet to someone who does not know her bitterness, and her conversation is pleasant to someone who does not recognize her insipidity.

Her appearance is beautiful to someone who has not examined the deceit in her heart, and meeting her is desirable to someone who has not gained experience [?] of her passions. Fierce passions come out of her like wild beasts, and they bite us with their crescent-shaped claws as though with fangs. Although passions dwell throughout mortal nature, in Eve they display the power of their deeds all the more. In her they are stirred up to fight against free will, and her disposition cannot stand firm against their assaults. She quickly gives way before the impulses of bodily passions, and she has no strength to withstand the onslaught of desires. She is battered by desires far more than men are, and the onslaught of brutish passions bears heavily upon her. It is she whom the sharp stings of sexual intercourse pierce, readily awakening the desire of the flesh within her. Bodily passions overpower her with little effort, and she herself testifies to how battered she is by their battles. Her guilt cries out to everyone about her struggles, and points out, as though with a finger, the battles that constantly beset her. She is far too weak to fight against her impulses. Therefore she becomes guilty and makes us guilty through her guilt. She is gripped by an insatiable love of money; she is bound by an immeasurable love of glory. She is openly given over to the desire of the flesh, and she is caught by impulses without understanding. Hateful envy moves about within her like a dragon, and tyrannical arrogance rises up within her like a lion. Frivolity is poured over her like water, and oppression flourishes within her like Mount Lebanon. She knows how to oppress, and no oppressor is more oppressive than she is. Naboth bears witness to how unjustly she oppressed him. Ahab practiced oppression, but he did not know the stratagems of oppression until he learned from her the devices for shedding blood. She is very cunning, and among the cunning there is no one more cunning than she is.

She is very childish, and her ignorance is beyond measure. She is very shrewd at covering up her deeds, but very foolish when it comes to remembering the soul’s repentance. Her heart and mind are wise only in evil, and perhaps even the demons fall short of her in her schemes. She taught the chief of their ranks how to lead astray; she opened the door of his thought for him and [?] his seed. From her he learns the varieties of evil, and then he does evil; he uses her like a weapon against the truth. He put on her armor in the battle against Joseph, and through her limbs he joined battle with his purity. With a hand of flesh, the spiritual being seized the bodily man; but the hand of flesh and the spirit were defeated by the man of flesh. He went down into the arena of lusts against the chaste man and stirred his impulses through his bodily senses, but could not seize him. Like a lioness, the foolish woman roared at the holy man, but her vile claws did not penetrate his pure body. Like a bear, the destructive she-bear growled, but the sound of her debauchery did not shake the courageous man. The leopardess snatched only his clothes from him; the jaws of her debauchery did not reach his limbs. Like a gazelle, the nimble man leaped and passed beyond her snare; she gnashed her fangs because the prey for her body had escaped her. It was not without reason that I accused Eve of being a beast, for her deeds cry out against her that she is a beast. It was not I who called her by a name foreign to rational humanity; her vileness made her resemble a fanged beast. Otherwise, let her speak against my words, if she can, and say that these things I have recounted about her wickedness are not so. Speak, Eve, if you have the strength to speak; I will accept the refutation in your words if they are true. Is Moses truthful or not truthful, in your opinion? Is what he wrote the truth, or a lying tale? He wrote of the struggle your sister waged against Jacob’s son, and he related how that steadfast man overcame her. Along with him, all the books also cry out against your wickedness and reproach your shamelessness in many ways.

Who bound mighty Samson, armed with his hair? Who brought his heroic strength low into the hands of the uncircumcised? Was it not you who humbled his mighty strength before his persecutors? Was it not you who blinded the light of his eyes and of his mind? Was it not your vineyard that defiled the holiness of his Nazirite consecration, while those impure in soul cheered and laughed at his purity? Was it not your debauchery that mercilessly yoked him to the mill, so that he became a laughingstock to demons and human beings at the demons’ festival? The mighty man killed a thousand men with a worthless bone, yet a loose rib pierced him, and he fell and could not rise. He tore the lion apart, broke the chains, and threw them away; yet a slack thread bound him and cast him down like a worthless man. Hear, mighty men! Listen, righteous men! Marvel, you who are wise, at the terrible crimes Eve has committed from generation to generation. She imprisoned Joseph, bound Samson, and persecuted David; and here is the account of their afflictions in the books of the Spirit. And if the steadfast and mighty have fallen in her battles, who can stand boldly against the harm she does? Her harm is evil and strikes very hard at anyone it strikes. Even the Evil One, evil as he is, is not as evil as she is. The Evil One strikes people secretly because he is afraid, but she strikes everyone fearlessly, the good and the evil alike. Even the Evil One does evil through her whenever he does evil. Perhaps he could not have done so much evil without her. Through her he harmed us from the beginning, when he harmed us, and with her tongue he drove the sting of her bitterness into us. She armed him with the weapon of injustice against our people, and now he lays us waste with her wantonness as with a sword. “Alas for Eve!” let our race say to its household, for she is among us, yet her love is bound to our murderer. Companionship with the Evil One is very dear to her mind, and her heart knocks at the door of his divinations night and day. Devoid of understanding, she asks him for conception and childbirth, and implores him to grant her the fruit of the womb. Her trust rests on the support of a broken reed, and she does not realize that he is the one who overthrew her from the beginning. Oh, how blind she is to the understanding that brings discernment!

She does not understand how to distinguish the ugly from the beautiful. O wretched woman, why do you not judge discerningly? Why is sound judgment not set before your mind? Why do you falsely call the Evil One good? Why do you ask your killer [?] for help to preserve your life? How can one full of harmful things give help? How can one who hates [?] human beings desire their good? Eve goes utterly astray in the errors of his deceit, and vainly seeks refuge in him, a refuge that is empty. She loves error; therefore she wanders after the deceiver. It is her habit to become distracted by the errors of lustful desires. She loves distraction, and her eyes gaze intently at emptiness. If anyone were to examine her, he would find distraction within her mind. She longs to stand shamelessly at gateways and in the streets, and her ears incline to listen to false reports. She occupies herself with adornment, and her heart dwells on beautifying herself [?], not to become beautiful, but to make what is beautiful ugly through her beauty. Ugly in soul [?], she adorns herself for emptiness, so that through adornment she may catch for herself the prey of lustful desires. To catch people, she spreads adornment over her limbs, and people fall into the adornment of her face as into traps. Her inclination lies in ambush like a hunter within her limbs, and the adornment of her face is like bait above a trap. It teaches her to hide traps in the bodily senses, and it shows her how to spread snares through the signals of her eyes. It directs through her the ugly gaze of wantonness, and it sets a filthy aim before her pupils. He portrays hateful desire before her so that she may imitate it, and she inclines strongly toward filthiness with all her senses. Her senses and the impulses of her soul incline toward wantonness, and like a hungry person, her heart longs for filthy food. Her heart constantly dwells on fleshly desire. She eats every day, yet her soul’s desire is never satisfied. She is very greedy, and the more she eats, the greedier she becomes. Though she eats and eats, she denies it, saying, “I have not eaten.” The shameless daughter resembles the brazen woman who stole the fruit and concocted excuses: “The serpent deceived me.”

Her mother’s habit accompanies her through every generation, and she cherishes it like a child, an outcast child. Like the woman who bore her, she longs to be above the man; and if she could, she would wish to become a man. She seeks brazenly to seize men’s authority and to disrupt the established order of creation. The chosen herald Paul saw her insolence and acted beforehand, shutting the door in her face so that she would not exercise authority. “A woman,” he said, “should learn quietly from the teacher and should not brazenly take her place in the ranks of men.” With the weapon of his word, Paul restrained her insolence; yet even so, she does not desist from her unruliness. He also set limits for her and restrained her from wanton adornment, but she acts against his word by multiplying her adornments. Now she has greatly multiplied her adornment beyond proper bounds, so that in everything she overturns the order of good conduct. And perhaps, if she knew how to read the books of the Spirit, she would erase the sentences of judgment against her offenses. And perhaps, if she also knew about me, who have exposed her faults, she would roar at me like Jezebel at the son of the sojourners. And perhaps, if she [?] who I am, or that I am weak, she would never tire of shooting arrows of insult. And perhaps, if someone drew a portrait of me and showed it to her, she would stone it with stones of mockery, as Naboth was stoned. Perhaps even now she draws a sword against my verses and cuts them off like the head of the bridegroom’s friend [?]. Go away, woman! I am neither a righteous man nor a son of righteous men. Why are you enraged at me as though I were righteous, when I am not righteous? Do not shoot arrows of insult at me as you are accustomed to do, and do not take revenge on my verses for their rebukes of your shameful conduct. It was not out of malice that I uncovered your shameful deeds, nor was it out of envy that I exposed your faults before onlookers. I saw that you were stained with shameful deeds, and my mind advised me to wash the filth of wrongdoing from you. I saw hateful wrongdoing staining your limbs,

and I wished to sprinkle the water of my words over your uncleanness. I saw that you were sick with the severe disease of wantonness, and I compounded words like medicines so that perhaps you might be healed. Desire for the flesh grips you like a fever, and with my words I have sought to cool the fire of your passions. I saw the sword of your speech laying waste to the ranks of men, and I went out to restrain it, so that a small remnant might remain for our people. I saw the gaze of your eyes hiding snares for our race, and I held people back so that they would not be caught in your traps. I saw the beauty of your face spread out like nets, and I raised my voice so that the prey would hear and flee from you. I saw your wicked zeal running over sea and land, and I was zealous to restrain it, so that the laborer would not be bewildered as he ran. I saw your unbridled envy disturbing the good and the wicked, and I considered whether I might be able to restrain it, so that it would rest a little. Because of you, priests and kings have fallen in battle, and look, they are still fighting, with no end to their wars. I marveled greatly at how fierce the struggle over you is, and for this reason I called you the cause of every evil. An evil inclination is not bound to you by nature. It is your will that sins and causes others to sin, as it chooses. It is your will that leads you wherever it wishes; you are not forcibly driven toward evil by anyone. The good and all the evil done through you belong to you, and you have authority over both, as a free woman. For you are free to do good or to do evil, and if this is so, you have no grounds for complaint. It is easy for you, then, to walk the path of repentance, and it is simple for you to repay your debts through heartfelt remorse. Come, if you wish, and follow the advice I give you. Leave your wandering behind and walk the path I mark out for you. I will go ahead of your will, if you are willing,

and bring you into a peaceful harbor where there is no danger. Listen, if you wish, to the account of women of your own kind who were strong amid sufferings and did not weaken before trials. Form an image of their conduct within your mind, and with their purity scrub the filth from your thoughts. Look at Sarah and Rebekah and consider them thoughtfully: they endured the pains of bodily barrenness without despair. Let Hannah be like a mirror before the eyes of your soul, and through her endurance gain endurance for the day of trial. You belong to the same race as these women, O daughter of humanity. Walk the path of their endurance and leave fear behind. But why do I say that you come from the stock of chaste women? Look, the woman who gave birth to life for humanity is one of your own. From a woman of your own kind, life without end sprang forth for us. Do not put us to death after we have come alive through the life that came from you. Have pity on your soul, which is a vessel from which life flows. Do not defile the spring of life with shameful deeds. Abandon the empty pursuits that have grown old with you, and occupy yourself with wholesome meditation on the word of life. Flee from the errors of divination, omens, and the teaching of demons, and inscribe on your heart the three names that name the divine Being. Set the name of the divine Being before your mind as your target, and you will learn to aim well toward purity. Let your mouth repeat the Trinity instead of every other word, and offer threefold thanksgiving to the one who established everything.
On the saying, “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.”
By the very same author: a homily in seven-syllable lines [?], which he composed on the saying, “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.”

The saying that John wrote traced a new path for us. He was the first to travel it and became a guide to us all. He blazed a path toward the divine Being and showed that the equality is one: The Father and his Son are one, and there is no interval of time between him and his offspring [?]. His voice was like thunder, and he cried out to the four quarters. He rightly called him “Son of Thunder,” for he proclaimed the Word who was in the beginning. Listen, peoples, and pay attention, nations, to the new good news that I proclaim. The Father brought forth from his bosom a Son who is no younger than the one who begot him. In the beginning was the Word, and he was with God. And the Word himself was God, in person and in authority. O mystery that was hidden from ages and generations! The Son of Thunder announced and revealed it to those above and those below. O John the herald, to whom Adam’s race is indebted! The Holy Spirit gave him keys, and he opened the treasury of the divine Being. He ascended and reached the highest heights, above the assemblies of spiritual beings. The power of grace brought him near to speak about the divine Being. He received power and authority and proclaimed the Word who was in the beginning. The Son was in the beginning, eternally with the one who begot him. He has been with his Father from eternity, like radiance with the sun. The sun does not precede its radiance, nor does the sun precede its sphere. The sun’s radiance was with it. His Son is with the Father, and there is no time when he is separated from him. The Father is a real person, and the Son is a person like him. And when he is called Father, there is no interval of time [?] between him and his Son. He is a nature that exists from eternity, and his being has no beginning. The Father did not begin to exist, nor is there a time for the Son’s birth. The Father is the eternal Being, for there is no time [?] when he was not Father. And the Son is perfect, lacking nothing, for there is no time when he is not united. The Being is far removed from times, and times and ages are within him. How can the self-existent One be bounded by times [?]? However far thought searches, it finds him beyond time. The Father did not begin with his Son, nor was there a time for the Father's Son. John called him his Word, who has been with his Father from eternity. He is like a word with the soul: it comes from the soul and exists with it. The Son was with his Father, and he came into the world while remaining with him. A word has never traveled away from the soul and departed from it. Nor did the Son travel away from the one who begot him and become distant from him by departing. A word travels in every direction without departing from the soul. While it is carrying a message, it remains in the soul just as it is. The Word also traveled from the Father and came to our mortal dwelling. And while he was dwelling in our nature,

he was wholly in his Father. A word that comes from the soul cannot be visibly seen. But when it is inscribed in ink, it becomes visible through letters. Yet even when someone has tightly confined it in letters and bounded it in garments of ink, it is in the letters in name, while all of it remains within the soul. [?] see ink as they look at the letters. The word has not allowed its nature to be bounded by the pupils of the eyes. The Son was hidden with the one who begot him, from [?] and those below. By his will he appeared to us in the ink of Adam's body. And when he put on the garment of our nature, he was wrapped in his divinity. His will dwelt in our nature, while his nature remained hidden. The body he put on did not bound his nature, which cannot be bounded. The eye of flesh did not see his hidden divinity. John said that through him everything that came into being was formed. Nothing came into being without him, for he willed and ordered everything that came into being. He is a spring full of life, possessing life in his [?]. From the life within his nature, he distributed life to the things he formed. Life is light, driving darkness away from the light. The darkness of error could not overtake it to hinder the light's course. He had always been in the world, and the world was formed by his hands. Although the world was his, the world was unwilling to acknowledge him. The Creator came to his own, and his own did not receive his word. Those who obeyed his commandments obtained the authority of children. He called us his own children through the mercy he showed toward our race. For he gave us spiritual birth through baptism in water and the Spirit. He showed us his good will by honoring us with the name of children. He confirmed the name of sonship by choosing to make his dwelling among his children. John said that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. We saw the glory of his greatness at the doorway of his humanity. He became flesh for us and dwelt among us, and he showed us his hidden glory. Although he is hidden in his nature, he showed his glory through our body. He was not brought down into created existence by the statement that he became flesh. Rather, he fashioned flesh for himself and dwelt in it by his will. For the Creator cannot come into a new existence, nor can a time of birth set a limit to being that has no beginning. But if he existed from eternity, how did he come into being? And if he came into being, that is far removed from saying that he already existed. There is no beginning or end to being that exists from eternity. Whatever comes into being has a maker who precedes its nature. If he is self-existent with the Father, he cannot be confined in his nature. And if he confined himself in a womb, he is not self-existent with the one who begot him. If he exists everywhere and has now come into being, how did he receive formation—did a part of him receive it, or all of him? If all of him was confined, he does not possess the quality of being unconfined. And if he was confined in part:

And if he can be confined, either wholly or in part, then the Father too can be confined, since the Son’s nature comes from him. How was he in his Father while dwelling in a womb of flesh? This is the [?] that needs to be investigated: how he accepted [?]. And if the quarrelers say that he was in the womb and in the heights, because he has the power to divide himself so as to be both in the heights and in confinement, then his will precedes his nature, which exists from eternity. For look: his will subjugates him and confines his nature. And if his will has the power to pass beyond and overcome his nature, then he changes at every moment according to what his will desires. And if his will directs his nature however it wishes, where, then, is the self-existence that his nature possessed eternally? Let this insolence go away after the band of quarrelers, who brought the self-existent one down to lowly things, confining him in the womb of a human woman. Truly, they are deprived of light and walk along the road of darkness. How can the self-existent nature be confined by its own works? According to the heretics’ claim, what he formed is far greater than he is, since it can confine his nature. How did a nature subtler than spirit accept composition? While he existed in his [?], or in a [?] that was not his own? Come, explain your mysteries to us, you uncircumcised people who have not circumcised your hearts. Teach us how to confess the Word who became flesh. Or explain to us how the Word dwelt within bodily members. Or prepare weapons so that we may fight and see whose the victory is. Gather all your arrows and draw the strings of your bows. Set up the Word who became flesh as the target, and let us see who hits the mark. The whole battle concerns the Word who became flesh. I am certain that this is why you have prepared weapons against us. You want to fight us with your master’s weapons, for he forged weapons and armed you against the Word who comes from the Father. Come with your master, you Egyptians, and let us examine the meaning of the statement. Let us see how one who came into being began to be a creator. Did he compose himself while he already existed, or has he only now begun to exist? Or did someone else compose him, while he himself was far removed from composition? If he came into being, he is not eternally existent; and if he is eternally existent, he did not come into being just now. For the eternally existent one cannot undergo becoming after his existence. He became flesh, according to your words: did part of him become flesh, or all of him? And how can a nature that has no [?] be divided? If all of him became composite, then all of him became limited. He would have been limited on every side and would have dwelt in the womb alone. And if this is so, where is his being unlimited? For look: a fleshly womb limited him, according to the contrivance you have put together. But if part of him became composite and part of him remained in his nature, where, then, is his uniformity? For look: he has been divided in his nature [?]. If the Word became flesh,

let us ask whose flesh it is. Did he bring it down with him from on high, or is it human flesh? If he himself became flesh and did not take flesh from Mary, what benefit did our nature receive from his becoming flesh in himself? Then the promise made to David is nullified. And he is called Son of David by a borrowed name, although he is not. What benefit did mortals receive from the Word becoming flesh, if he became flesh in his own nature while our nature remained in its lowliness? Where, then, is the one who abolishes the sentence of death against us? Did he not take a body from Mary? The Word took it and dwelt in it. This is fitting for those who understand, and truth bears witness to their words. Therefore the eternally existent one cannot himself become flesh. And becoming, when it is flesh, is far removed from beginningless existence. Why is a covering of contrivances spread over your words? Reveal the aim of your thoughts and speak openly like Arius. Your words strengthen him, and your statements support him. He [?] the Son’s eternal existence and called him a servant and attendant. This is the whole struggle of Arius, the false disciple: to make the Son less than the Father and count him among his creatures. You too are aiming at his goal, you contentious people. You disguise with an outward appearance the wickedness concealed in your words. Leave the flock, you shameless people! Do not lead others astray in the guise of lambs. For you have destroyed the distinction between the two natures that became one. The wickedness of their blasphemies rushed onward and rose to the highest heights. It brought the eternally existent one down from his [?] and bound him with the cords of bodily members. Heaven and earth, listen and hear the wickedness spoken by these shameless people! They limited the incomprehensible being and confined it inside a womb. Like a shield in battle, they seized upon this expression [?]: that the Word himself composed himself and became flesh, as it is written. You accepted the statement that he became, you teachers of novelties, but forgot the statement that he dwelt in us, and did not examine its meaning. “He dwelt in us,” John said. Who was dwelling in whom? Explain to us plainly the indwelling of the two who became one. If he spoke of indwelling, the statement that he came to be among us must be examined. For it is possible for him to dwell even without there being any becoming. If he dwelt in another, then becoming is unnecessary. And this befits his nature: to dwell without being limited. Come, then, listener: examine whether my words are true. Weigh my statements in the balance of your understanding, to see whether they are light. Do not let the sound of the words [?] trouble you when they are spoken figuratively. They are not [?], but an inquiry into the indwelling. It is a seeking of the Word’s help, and hidden in it is the hope of our life. It brings our nature near to the honor of the image that was lost. Our struggle concerns this:

The Word was not diminished by his indwelling. Rather, he took our nature and honored it with the glory of his greatness. This is the [?] concerning the indwelling that we investigate in our dispute with the insolent: essential being was not diminished through its indwelling with humanity. “He became” means “he dwelt,” and “he dwelt” means that he took a human being and concealed the radiance of his greatness in the garment of a mortal body. The self-existent Word constructed for himself the temple of the body and dwelt in it. He himself did not become a composite—such is the wickedness of the heretics! He is not confined in his [?], so as to descend to a composite state. Nor could the temple that he constructed for himself contain his nature within its limits. It was not by his nature that he dwelt in the human being whom he took from us, but through an indwelling of the will and an inseparable union. The Word wove a garment of flesh to conceal his greatness in it, so that human beings might see in a human being the image of the glory of his greatness. He made a promise to Abraham and David that would not prove false, and now he fulfilled it in deeds through the firstfruits from the house of David. The Word is not the son of David. You quarrelsome people, with whom are you arguing? The son of David belongs to our race; the Word took him and dwelt in him. The Word fulfilled his entire will in the body and dwelt in it. Although he confined his will within it, his nature was not confined within it. He was wholly in it by his will, while by his nature he was both in it and everywhere. For it is fitting for the Maker not to be confined within his works. The body is his own work, which he willed to make his dwelling. Without its limits containing his nature [?], he dwelt in it wholly by his will. Perhaps the quarrelsome will dispute our words, as they usually do [?]: “How can you call something made and its Maker one person?” I call the temple that the Word constructed for his indwelling “something made,” and I call the Only-Begotten himself, who willed to dwell in his work, “the Maker.” It is like the soul and body, which are joined and are called one person. The soul is a living nature [?], and the body a mortal nature. Though they are two and distinct from one another, they are called one person. The Word is divine by nature, and the body human by nature. One is a work and the other its Maker; they are one in union. The soul is enclosed within the body, but its activity extends beyond the body. While the body rests in one place, the soul’s movement extends in every direction. The Word dwelt within the body and was also in the heights and the depths. His humanity was confined, but his divinity was in every region. The soul does not suffer in the body when the limbs are scourged. Nor did the divinity suffer in the sufferings of the body in which it dwelt. And if the soul does not suffer, though it is created like the body— how can the divine Being suffer, whose nature is above suffering? The soul suffers with the body through love, not by nature. The sufferings of the body are also attributed figuratively to the soul. He made the man whom he took from us one with himself in glory.

Because of his love for us, he took [?] upon himself. The soul dwells within the body, yet those who look do not see it. Although it is limited by nature, eyes of flesh cannot encompass it. The Word also dwelt in our nature, yet was not confined within our nature. For this was an indwelling by choice, not an indwelling by nature. Here is an illustration in our own nature: two natures that became one, one living and the other mortal, one hidden and the other visible. Come, then, O [?], let us pursue a fitting inquiry. Lower the lofty tone of your words, and recognize the weakness of your nature. Leave off [?] concerning the divine Being, the Being who cannot be comprehended. Speak instead about the one of our own race whom the Eternal One took and in whom he dwelt. He dwelt in him without confining himself, for his nature does not admit of being confined. The mortal one suffered in his nature, but sufferings did not approach the divine Being. He fashioned a rational image for himself, to display his authority through it. Thus, when rational beings see him, they may honor the hidden one through the visible one. In the Holy of Holies of his hiddenness, the Eternal One dwelt in him invisibly. In the mediator, one of our own race, we see the image of his glory. This is why he chose him and dwelt in him: so that the hidden one might be revealed through the visible one. And before the doorway of his hiddenness, let us worship his hidden nature. He made him lord over his household and ruler over his possessions. He subjected to him the heights and the depths, rational beings and speechless creatures alike. In him the formation of our image, which had been ruined through sin, was renewed. In us, through this act, his calling us his own image was fulfilled. Angels and human beings worship him as the visible image of the King. They marvel at the sight of him in place of the hiddenness of the [?]. Listen intelligently and understand, O hearer, these things that I have [?]. Do not let thoughts confuse you concerning the Word who became flesh. Look, I have opened a road before you. Come, follow my words, for you will find the fountain of life at the end of the road I have opened for you. Praise the Eternal One in his hiddenness through the visible one whom he took as his dwelling. Honor the King through his image, for the King is honored in his image. It is a difficult road to travel toward the divine Being who has no beginning. Through one of our own race, as through a [?], he opened for us the road to his hiddenness, for the nature of created beings cannot contemplate the perfect Eternal One. Through the image he fashioned, he showed us the splendid glory of his hiddenness. Through the pledge he took from us, he bound to himself the [?] of created beings. Through the mediator, one of our own race, he reconciled us with his majesty. This is the reason for his coming: to come and renew our formation, and to restore the bond of peace that had been loosened, through the mediation of our firstfruits. For our consolation he built a temple of flesh and dwelt in it. Let us worship in the outer sanctuary the one who is hidden in the Holy of Holies. The outer sanctuary of his body

we see with eyes of flesh, and the Holy of Holies of his hidden being with the spiritual movements of the soul. All those above and below are stopped at the veil of Adam’s body. Created beings have no authority to see the sanctuary of the divine being. Look, the road to life [?] has been opened! Come, travelers [?], and walk along it. Do not stumble on the path through the division of your thoughts. Let us not mix division into our confession concerning the divine being. Since the Son is equal to the one who begot him, let us not bring him down to weaknesses. Let us confess that the Word put on flesh and willingly dwelt in our nature. The temple of flesh in which he dwelt did not limit his nature. He dwelt wholly in it by his will, and remained whole in his being. He took its humiliations upon his name and made it share in his glories. Come, guilty children of Adam, let us offer [?] thanksgiving to the Good One, who made our nature share in the glories of his greatness.
Another by the very same author.
